projectDetails.name: A World Away – AI Exoplanet HunterPPT: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/14rMB4oIaS0lCjkJJ6BdSosHsRtxEnrdb/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108857630313463716680&rtpof=true&sd=true
projectDetails.summary: Our project, A World Away – AI Exoplanet Hunter, utilises Artificial Intelligence to speedily identify exoplanets. The AI system is built in Python using tensorflow and utilises a 1D -CNN that analyses light curve data obtained from NASA's Kepler and TESS missions. Light curves are graphs that show a star's brightness as it varies over time, and when there is a planet in front of the star, there is a small dip in the brightness record. The AI model learns where to detect the dips and can effectively sift the weak signal against the noise. By automating the correction process from the light curves, we drastically reduce the time astrophysicists spend on manual inspection and analysis of the light curves, increase detection accuracy, and allow researchers to analyse large data sets more efficiently. By applying machine learning within astronomy, this project plays a significant role in faster identification of the existence of potentially habitable worlds, and fosters creative thinking and development within the field of AI-assisted human space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview:

The goal of this project is to use Artificial Intelligence (AI) to find exoplanets - planets outside our Solar System - by using light curve data from NASA's Kepler and TESS missions. A one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) detects small dips in a star's brightness that indicate a planet passing between a star and the observer.

Benefits & Impact:

Automates and speeds up exoplanet identification. Increases correctness and reduces human contributions to error. Frees scientists to focus on further, more in-depth research rather than identification. Invites the public to participate in discovering planets.

Tools & Technologies:

Language: Python Libraries: tensorflow, numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scikit-learn

Dataset: NASA Kepler, TESS light curves

Platform: VS Code , Google Colab

Creativity:

Combines Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Astronomy to form an automated, visual, and accessible planet detection system.

Team Considerations:

Clean data, accurate model training, scalable, noise isolation, and ethical use of AI.

Your challenge is to create an AI/ML model that is trained on one or more of the open-source exoplanet datasets offered by NASA and that can analyze new data to accurately identify exoplanets. projectDetails.name: URBAN HEAT TRACKER
projectDetails.summary: Introducing Urban Heat AI, a web application designed to visualize heat data in real-time. It uses live satellite and weather data to map heat zones and leverages a powerful AI to generate dynamic, actionable strategies for mitigation and personal safety.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, Urban Heat AI, is a web application designed to make the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect clear and actionable. It is built as a single HTML file using JavaScript, Tailwind CSS, and Leaflet.js. The app offers a global, interactive map that shows real-time, localized temperature grids sourced from the OpenWeatherMap API. Users can access this data through search or by clicking on the map.

The main innovation of the project is its deep integration with the Google Gemini API. This integration supports a range of smart features, including a context-aware AI assistant named TempNova for direct questions and answers, dynamic recommendations for areas and individuals, and AI-generated summaries of both live weather and historical data trends sourced from the Open-Meteo API.

By simplifying complex data into clear insights, Urban Heat AI empowers both citizens and city planners to make informed decisions. This contributes to developing cooler, more resilient cities and supports the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
projectDetails.aiReferences: Artificial Intelligence drives our Urban Heat AI project. We used the Google Gemini API to turn raw data into useful information and to help with the development process. The Gemini model powers our conversational AI assistant, TempNova. It answers user questions using context from live weather data. It generates recommendations on the spot, providing tailored advice for specific regions, public health, future climate scenarios, and personalized action plans based on a user's age and job. Additionally, we use Gemini to create short AI summaries of real-time weather conditions and historical data trends from the Open-Meteo API, making complex information easier to understand. Finally, we used the Gemini Text-to-Speech model to turn written recommendations into audio, improving the application's accessibility.

projectDetails.name: Arknet
projectDetails.summary: ARKNET (Advanced Risk Knowledge Network) is an IoT-based system providing hyper-local weather predictions for rain, wind, and extreme temperatures, tailored for outdoor activities. It uses ESP32-based nodes with rain, wind, temperature, humidity, and pressure sensors connected via a resilient LoRa mesh network. Data is collected in real time and analyzed by an AI engine using machine learning to generate accurate forecasts. The dashboard delivers location-specific alerts with color-coded risk levels, ensuring safety and proactive planning. ARKNET 2.0 stands out for its precision, reliability, AI-driven intelligence, and scalable design.
projectDetails.details:
ARKNET 2.0 Works:

ARKNET 2.0 is an IoT-based weather risk prediction system that collects real-time environmental data from distributed ESP32 nodes equipped with sensors for rain, wind, temperature, humidity, and pressure. These nodes communicate through a resilient LoRa mesh network, ensuring uninterrupted data flow even if individual nodes fail. The collected data is processed by a central AI engine that uses machine learning algorithms, including regression models and neural networks, to detect patterns and predict localized weather risks. Users receive instant alerts and visualizations on a dashboard or mobile app, showing rain probability, wind risk, and risk levels using a color-coded system.

Benefits:

Provides hyper-local, accurate weather predictions.

Enables proactive risk management for outdoor events.

Mesh network resilience ensures reliability even during partial failures.

Scalable and adaptable for multiple locations and event types.

Intended Impact:

The project aims to enhance safety and planning for outdoor activities by reducing disruptions from sudden weather changes, minimizing property and personal risk, and empowering users with real-time, actionable weather insights.

Tools, Coding, Hardware, and Software Used:

Hardware: ESP32 microcontrollers, rain gauges, anemometers, BME280/DHT22 temperature & humidity sensors, BMP280 pressure sensors, LoRa modules.

Software & Coding Languages: Arduino IDE/C++ for IoT node programming, Python for AI/ML data processing, libraries for LoRa communication, and a dashboard built using web frameworks (HTML/CSS/JavaScript) or mobile apps.

AI Tools: Regression models, neural networks for weather prediction.

Creativity:

The system combines localized IoT sensing, mesh networking, and AI for predictive insights, unlike generic weather apps.

Provides venue-specific predictions and color-coded risk alerts in real time.

Mesh network design ensures continuous operation, even if some nodes fail, making it robust and adaptive.

Factors Considered by the Team:

Accuracy: Selecting sensors and AI models for reliable predictions.

Resilience: Ensuring mesh communication works even with node failures.

Scalability: Designing architecture for easy expansion across regions.

User Experience: Intuitive dashboard and real-time alerts.

Safety Impact: Prioritizing early warning for weather-related risks.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI):

In ARKNET 2.0, AI was used to analyze real-time environmental data collected from IoT sensors and generate accurate, hyper-local weather risk predictions. Specifically, machine learning models—including regression analysis and neural networks—processed data from rainfall, wind, temperature, humidity, and pressure sensors to identify patterns and forecast rain probability, wind risk, and extreme weather events. AI was also used to update the prediction dashboard in real time, providing color-coded alerts and risk levels for specific locations. All AI-generated outputs are original and were developed specifically for ARKNET; no NASA branding or design elements were used or modified.

projectDetails.name: Project Farmsphere
projectDetails.summary: Our solution bridges the gap between advanced NASA Earth observation data and practical farming education. FarmSphere is an interactive simulation platform that uses real datasets (NDVI, SMAP, POWER, MODIS, ECOSTRESS) to create realistic farming scenarios. Through gameplay, users make data-driven decisions on crop planning, irrigation, and climate adaptation, learning how to apply satellite insights to sustainable agriculture. Designed for farmers, students, and educators, FarmSphere turns complex climate science into accessible, engaging experiences that promote food security, resource conservation, and climate resilience.
projectDetails.details:
Project: FarmSphere — AI-Powered Farm Simulation & Decision Tool

What it does / How it works:
FarmSphere is an interactive farm simulation that uses real-world NASA satellite data (NDVI, ECOSTRESS, SMAP, MODIS) to help players monitor crop health, water levels, and environmental conditions. Users make data-driven decisions—like irrigation, crop management, and climate adaptation—to optimize farm sustainability and yield.

Benefits:

  • Provides a realistic understanding of farm management and sustainability.
  • Encourages strategic thinking and resource management.
  • Offers visual, interactive insights into crop health, moisture, temperature, and productivity.

Intended Impact:

  • Educates users on precision agriculture and climate-smart farming.
  • Promotes awareness of water conservation and sustainable farming practices.
  • Demonstrates how AI and satellite data can improve agricultural decision-making.

Tools & Technologies:

  • Frontend: React.js, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Lucide Icons
  • Programming Languages: JavaScript (ES6+), HTML, CSS
  • Data & APIs: NASA ECOSTRESS, SMAP, MODIS satellite datasets
  • Software & Frameworks: Node.js, npm, VS Code
  • Creative Elements: Animated 3D farm visualization, interactive scenarios, and gamified levels

Creativity:

  • Combines real satellite data with gamified interactive 3D visualization.
  • Uses dynamic scenarios and decision-making to simulate real-world farm challenges.
  • Integrates weather, crop growth, and resource management in a visually engaging way.

Factors Considered:

  • Water availability, crop health, yield potential, and sustainability metrics.
  • Environmental factors like temperature and drought conditions.
  • Educational value, user engagement, and gamification balance.

projectDetails.name: Project Astro Avengerz
projectDetails.summary: Our project "meteor madness” focuses on understanding and preparing for potential asteroid threats to Earth. We developed an educational and visual presentation that explains what asteroids are, their types, composition, and the dangers they pose, along with real examples like Bennu, Apophis, and NASA’s DART mission. The project highlights how asteroid impacts can affect our planet, from local destruction to global climate change, and emphasizes the importance of early detection, monitoring, and deflection strategies. By simplifying complex scientific data into clear, engaging visuals and explanations, our project aims to raise public awareness and inspire action toward planetary defense. It addresses the challenge by bridging science and communication—helping people understand not only the risks but also how technology and global collaboration can protect Earth from future cosmic threats.
projectDetails.details: In our meteor madness project for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, our team explored various aspects of asteroids and planetary defense. Each member focused on different sections — from what asteroids are, their types, composition, and notable examples, to the effects of asteroid impacts, awareness and prevention, and the necessity of studying them. We also discussed NASA’s DART mission and real asteroid cases like Bennu and Apophis. To research, design, and prepare our content and presentation, we used reliable sources and tools such as NASA’s official datasets and website, Gemini and ChatGPT for generating and refining ideas, Gamma AI for creating visual slides, and other open data resources. Together, these platforms helped us understand, visualize, and communicate how science, technology, and awareness can work hand in hand to protect our planet from potential asteroid threats.
projectDetails.aiReferences: We worked as a team by dividing tasks and using AI tools to support each step. First, we used ChatGPT to collect information, definitions, and explanations about asteroids and planetary defense. Then, we used Gemini AI to summarize key points and make the content clear and concise. After that, we used Gamma AI and Prezi AI to design our presentation with visuals, layouts, and animations. We discussed and reviewed each part together to make sure the project was accurate and well-organized. This teamwork and use of AI tools helped us complete the project efficiently and creatively.

projectDetails.name: AstroHacks
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, Space Trash Hack: Revolutionizing Recycling on Mars, addresses the critical challenge of inorganic waste management during long-term space missions. A three-year Mars mission with an eight-member crew could generate up to 12,600 kg of waste, including plastics, textiles, and structural materials. Transporting waste back to Earth or bringing extra resources is costly and impractical, making sustainable in-situ recycling essential.

We developed a system that recycles plastic waste into 3D printing filament, enabling the production of essential tools, storage containers, and habitat components directly on Mars. By optimizing polymer blends such as LDPE and PP, we achieved durable, flexible, and high-quality outputs suitable for mission needs. This solution not only reduces plastic accumulation but also supports a self-sustaining Martian ecosystem by integrating with life-support systems, water pipelines, and greenhouse facilities.
Our innovation ensures zero-waste recycling, lowers mission costs, and establishes a circular economy, making it vital for long-term human survival and exploration on Mars.
projectDetails.details:
Our project focuses on recycling waste and used plastics, such as discarded LDPE and PP, into 3D printing filament. The system collects these plastics, processes them, and extrudes high-quality filament. This filament is then used in 3D printers to manufacture mission-critical items like Bottle, Plate , cutting board, Food tray

How it Works: Waste and used plastics are sorted, melted, and blended in optimized ratios to achieve the right balance of strength and flexibility. The resulting filament is fed into 3D printers, enabling astronauts to create tools and components on demand.

Benefits: Reduces accumulation of discarded plastics. Enables on-demand manufacturing of essential supplies. Saves costs by reducing dependency on cargo from Earth. Supports a sustainable and self-sufficient mission environment.

Intended Impact: The project aims to establish a circular economy on Mars, ensuring long-term sustainability, reducing mission costs, and improving astronaut safety by turning waste into valuable resources.

Tools, Coding, and Hardware: we have used the hardware that can recycle the used plastic waste into 3D printing filament.

Creativity: Our creativity lies in transforming waste—normally seen as a problem—into a vital resource for survival and innovation on Mars

.Team Considerations: We considered resource scarcity, energy efficiency, health and hygiene concerns, space limitations, and the adaptability of our recycling system to future space colonies

This project is important because it bridges creativity and science—allowing anyone to contribute to the vision of living beyond Earth. By enabling rapid habitat concept generation and layout visualization, our tool supports innovation in space architecture and helps shape the future of human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: AstroSoma
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, GeneXis Explorer is a web-based interactive visualization tool developed using HTML, CSS, Java, and Python (Flask). It was created for the “Your Home in Space: The Habitat Layout Creator / Space Biology” challenge. The platform helps users explore how living organisms—especially plants—adapt and grow in different space environments such as Earth orbit, lunar, and Martian conditions.

Through an intuitive interface, users can visualize biological data dynamically using interactive charts and experiment simulations. The system integrates biological research concepts with NASA’s space data to make complex space-biology insights accessible to students, researchers, and the public.

This project is important because it bridges the gap between biological science and space exploration, encouraging curiosity about how life can sustain beyond Earth. By combining visualization, simplicity, and interactivity, GeneXis Explorer empowers users to understand space habitat challenges better and supports future innovation in sustainable life systems for deep-space missions.
projectDetails.details:
GeneXis Explorer is an interactive web tool that visualizes how living organisms adapt to different space environments such as Earth orbit, the Moon, and Mars. Built using HTML, CSS, Java, Python (Flask), and Chart.js, it allows users to explore biological data through real-time, environment-based visualizations.

The project simplifies complex space biology research, helping students, educators, and researchers understand how life responds to microgravity and radiation. Its intuitive design and dynamic charts make learning engaging and accessible.

By combining science, data visualization, and technology, GeneXis Explorer bridges biology and space exploration, inspiring curiosity about sustaining life beyond Earth. Our team focused on creating an educational, data-driven platform that supports NASA’s goal of understanding life in space environments.

projectDetails.name: Mars Circular Habitat System with TrashRover &  Logistics-2-Living Interface
projectDetails.summary:
Project ASTROXZ is an ambitious answer to the largest challenge of Mars exploration: garbage. Throughout a 3-year mission in Jezero Crater, astronauts produce more than 12,000 kg of inorganic waste. Our system converts that weight into opportunity.
We created a Mars Circular Habitat System fueled by a hand-cranked TrashRover, modular recycling stations, and NASA's Logistics-2-Living approach. TrashRover transports and returns trash throughout the crater on local wired and near-range wireless networks. The system recycles matter into tools, furniture, fuel, and habitat apparel—enabling day-to-day existence, celebrations, and scientific exploration.
Our design meets all three of NASA's scenarios: rehabilitating the habitat, commemorating crew milestones, and reusing research leftovers. We traced NASA's documented waste-to-resource routes and constructed a functional, locally managed system with a minimal crew effort and maximum sustainability.
ASTROXZ isn't a recycling system—it's a design for clean, smart, and circular living on Mars.
projectDetails.details: Project ASTROXZ is a Mars-based recycling system designed to convert mission waste into usable resources like bioplastics, methane, regolith bricks, and habitat outfitting. It operates through a manually controlled TrashRover using wired and short-range wireless networks across Jezero Crater, delivering waste to modular biothermal and mechanical units for processing. The project supports all three NASA challenge scenarios—renovations, celebrations, and discoveries—by repurposing packaging and structural materials for daily crew needs. Its benefits include reduced reliance on Earth resupply, enhanced sustainability, and support for long-term Martian habitation. We used Copilot lightly for referencing NASA data, Bing for visual inspiration, and PowerPoint for design; no coding or hardware prototyping was involved. The project is creative in its integration of NASA’s Logistics-2-Living strategy, transforming cargo packaging into functional habitat elements, and in its locally operated rover system tailored to Jezero’s terrain. Our team considered mission duration, waste volume, crew workload, energy efficiency, and alignment with NASA’s documented recycling technologies to build a practical and impactful solution.

projectDetails.name: Project Atmosphere
projectDetails.summary: The weather predictor app, developed using Python, JavaScript, and TypeScript, forecasts rain probability, next-day temperature, and air quality index (AQI) for specific locations and dates, leveraging Random Forest Regressor models from scikit-learn. NASA’s POWER API historical data, it integrates Geopy for geocoding and delivers real-time predictions via a Flask API. The app addresses the challenge of accessible, accurate weather forecasting by providing actionable insights, including tailored precautions for outdoor activities (e.g., heat wave or AQI warnings). Its file-based storage system ensures simplicity and efficiency, requiring minimal resources (~100 MB RAM). The project’s importance lies in empowering users with reliable, location-specific forecasts for planning and safety, using classical machine learning for computational efficiency. Creative elements include synthetic data generation with realistic patterns and integration of satellite data, making it a practical tool for individuals, agriculture, and health management, with potential for future scalability via database and caching enhancements.
projectDetails.details:
This weather predictor app uses machine learning and data from NASA satellites to forecast rain chances (0-100%), next-day temperatures (in °C), and air quality (AQI, 0-500) for specific locations and dates. It gives you practical tips like "Bring an umbrella" if it's going to rain or "Stay indoors" if the air quality is bad. The app uses a Flask API for real-time predictions.

Users input a latitude, longitude, and date via a POST /predict request, and the app returns a JSON response with rain probability, temperature, AQI, and extra metrics like heat index and wind chill.

The models are trained using that mimics real-world weather patterns. Three Random Forest models (rain_model.pkl, temperature_model.pkl, aqi_model.pkl) predict outcomes using 8 normalized features like latitude, longitude, day of year, and weather conditions like humidity and wind speed.

NASA’s POWER API provides historical climate data, and Geopy/Nominatim handles geocoding. The models are loaded into memory at startup for fast predictions (under 10ms).

Features include recognizing seasonal patterns, detecting climate zones, and calculating stats like heat index. The app is accurate, practical, efficient, and easy to deploy without needing a database. It’s also scalable, using NASA’s global data for various use cases.

The app aims to help users plan better (like for travel, farming, or health) and promote safety with weather warnings. It shows how classical machine learning like Random Forest can be used for accessible weather forecasting.

Built with Python (v3.9+), JavaScript/TypeScript, and using libraries like scikit-learn, NumPy, Pandas, and Flask. It uses NASA POWER and Geopy APIs, and stores data in files rather than a database. It runs on standard hardware (4-8 GB RAM, multi-core CPU).

The team focused on balancing accuracy and efficiency, using synthetic data and NASA data for reliable training. The design is simple, modular, and user-focused, with actionable tips and predictions. Future plans include adding a database or caching system for more scalability.
projectDetails.aiReferences: The weather prediction app leverages a suite of classical machine learning technologies centered on ensemble learning to deliver efficient, interpretable forecasts for rain probability, temperature, and air quality index (AQI). At its core, the primary AI algorithm is the Random Forest Regressor from scikit-learn's ensemble module, which powers three specialized models rain_model.pkl for predicting rainfall likelihood (0-100%), temperature_model.pkl for next-day Celsius forecasts, and aqi_model.pkl for AQI values on a 0-500 scale each employing 100 decision trees with a maximum depth of 15 to average predictions, reduce overfitting, and enhance accuracy through voting mechanisms. Supporting this are key machine learning libraries: scikit-learn (v1.3.2+) for the regressor, feature scaling via StandardScaler, data splitting with train_test_split, and evaluation using mean_absolute_error and r2_score; NumPy (v1.26.0+) for numerical computations and array-based feature engineering; Pandas (v2.1.0+) for data manipulation, analysis, and CSV handling; SciPy (v1.11.4+) for scientific and statistical operations; and Joblib (v1.3.2) for serializing models into efficient .pkl files for runtime loading. AI/ML components include feature engineering with eight normalized inputs (latitude, longitude, day of year, month, temperature, humidity, pressure, and wind speed) via StandardScaler, and a data generation AI that creates 10,000 synthetic training samples mimicking realistic seasonal patterns, geographic variations, and statistical distributions. External AI-powered APIs augment this with real-world data: NASA's POWER API, drawing on climate models and satellite processing for historical 10-year averages of temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind, solar radiation, and surface pressure; and Geopy (v2.4.0) with Nominatim/OpenStreetMap for AI-driven geocoding to convert location names into coordinates. The supervised learning pipeline employs an 80/20 train/test split, built-in cross-validation, and performance metrics like MAE and R², while AI-enhanced features enable pattern recognition for seasonal (e.g., monsoon, summer, winter) and geographic climate zones, historical trend analysis, and statistical models for heat index, wind chill, and AQI categorization. Overall, these 14 integrated AI/ML components spanning ensemble prediction, data synthesis, external APIs, and deployment via a Flask API form a robust, resource-efficient classical ML application tailored for real time weather inference.

projectDetails.name: Meteor observation portal
projectDetails.summary: Aureo is a lightweight progressive-web app that delivers real-time meteor-shower forecasts to anyone with a phone. It blends live cloud cover, moon phase and Global Meteor Network flux data to show exactly when and where to look, then overlays an AR pointer that guides eyes to the radiant. A smart push alert fires only if local skies will be clear and dark two hours before peak, eliminating wasted trips. Built with vanilla HTML/CSS/JS and no API keys, it works offline after first load and weighs <180 kB—making professional-grade observing information freely available to students, casual stargazers and dark-sky advocates worldwide.
projectDetails.details:
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1. What it does & how it works

--------------------------------------------------------------------

Aureo is a **progressive-web-app** that turns any phone or laptop into a personal meteor-shower assistant:

- **Live sky-quality dashboard** – cloud cover, moon phase, sun-altitude and a 48-hour “best-window” forecast pulled from open-weather APIs.

- **Up-to-the-minute activity** – blended ZHR (meteors per hour) from the Global Meteor Network flux feed.

- **AR radiant pointer** – a pop-up camera view that uses device-orientation to draw a green dot exactly where the radiant sits in the sky.

- **Smart push-alerts** – only fires if the user’s location will be <30 % cloudy AND moon <0.25 phase two hours before peak.

- **Zero-install** – runs offline after first visit (service-worker caches CSS/JS); can be “added to home-screen” on iOS/Android.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

2. Benefits & intended impact

--------------------------------------------------------------------

- **Removes guesswork** – no more 2 a.m. trips to find clouds.

- **Inclusive** – works on low-bandwidth; no expensive hardware.

- **Safety & conservation** – encourages observers to stay in their own area instead of driving long distances searching for dark skies.

- **Educational** – NASA imagery + bite-size science facts spark curiosity in students and casual stargazers.

- **Open-science** – all data sources are free, no keys, so any STEM club can fork and re-brand.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

3. Tools, languages, hardware, software

--------------------------------------------------------------------

- **Languages**: vanilla HTML5, CSS3, ES-2020 JavaScript (no frameworks).

- **APIs**: Open-Meteo (weather/moon), Global Meteor Network (live flux), BigDataCloud (reverse geocode).

- **Browser APIs**: Geolocation, Device-Orientation, Service-Worker, Push Notification.

- **Dev environment**: VS Code + Live-Server plug-in; GitHub for version control.

- **Assets**: NASA public-domain images, meteor map iframe from meteorshowers.org.

- **Hardware**: any smartphone with gyroscope & camera (for AR mode).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

4. Creativity & design choices

--------------------------------------------------------------------

- **“One-file” philosophy** – entire client-side logic sits in a single 400-line JS file so teachers can print it and discuss in class.

- **Gradient cards** – each shower has its own colour gradient generated from peak wavelength (playful physics Easter-egg).

- **AR mode opens instantly** – no app store; we spawn a blank tab and `document.write` the orientation code to keep the main page lightweight.

- **Dark-sky meter** – we convert sun-altitude into a Bortle-scale bar so beginners instantly see if their backyard is dark enough.

- **Accessibility** – high-contrast colours, aria-labels on buttons, alt text on NASA images.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

5. Factors the team considered

--------------------------------------------------------------------

- **Low-bandwidth markets** – entire first payload <180 kB; images lazy-loaded.

- **Battery life** – canvas meteor animation pauses when tab is hidden.

- **Privacy** – location is requested only once, never stored on a server.

- **Offline** – service-worker caches everything except the live API calls; last good values stay visible when signal drops.

- **Hackathon time-box** – picked APIs that require **zero sign-up** so we could code immediately.

We built Aureo to **democratise meteor observing**: give everyone, everywhere, the same real-time information professionals use—wrapped in a fun, phone-friendly package.

projectDetails.name: Animation celebration of terra data  BY AUTO BOTS
projectDetails.summary: MOPITT (Measurements of Pollution in the Troposphere), a Canadian-built instrument launched in 1999 aboard NASA’s Terra satellite, revolutionized global carbon monoxide (CO) monitoring. Using gas correlation radiometry and combined thermal and near-infrared detection, it produced vertical CO profiles to track sources, transport, and long-range effects. Case studies such as the 2016 Fort McMurray fire and the severe 2023 Canadian wildfires highlight MOPITT’s ability to map vast CO plumes traveling thousands of kilometers, revealing their global air quality and climate impacts. Operating nearly 25 years until its planned 2025 retirement, MOPITT provided the longest continuous CO dataset, crucial for understanding the global CO cycle, validating atmospheric models, and assessing climate change-driven pollution through international scientific collaboration.

Data-driven decisions rather than making assumptions.

By integrating multi-temporal satellite imagery, climate variables, and phenological insights, BloomAI reveals the intricate relationship between seasonal vegetation changes and climate dynamics.

projectDetails.details:
BloomAI is an AI-driven geospatial analysis and visualization platform that uses NASA’s Earth observation data to detect, monitor, and predict plant blooming events worldwide. The project aims to understand how seasonal vegetation patterns are shifting due to climate change and provide actionable insights for conservation, agriculture, and ecological planning. Using satellite data from MODIS, VIIRS, and Landsat, BloomAI identifies bloom phases by analyzing vegetation indices (NDVI, EVI) and correlating them with climate data such as temperature, rainfall, and soil moisture. The platform visualizes this data through an interactive globe, enabling users to explore how Earth’s “pulse of life” evolves over time and across regions.

Objectives: To harness NASA’s Earth observation data for real-time and historical bloom detection. To build a predictive AI model capable of forecasting future blooming patterns based on climatic trends. To provide an interactive visual tool that supports monitoring, conservation, and agricultural planning. To raise awareness about climate-driven vegetation changes and their ecological impacts.

Key Features: 🌿 Bloom Detection Engine: AI model identifies vegetation bloom periods using NDVI/EVI time-series and temperature data. 📊 Interactive 3D Visualization: Users can explore global bloom data through a dynamic globe interface (built using Mapbox or CesiumJS). 🗓️ Predictive Bloom Calendar: Forecasts upcoming bloom events and seasonal shifts based on climate and past bloom cycles. 🌦️ Climate Correlation Dashboard: Displays the relationship between blooming behavior and environmental factors like rainfall or temperature anomalies. 🧭 Scalability & Localization: Supports analysis from global to regional and local levels for tailored ecological and agricultural insights.

Data Sources (NASA & Related): MODIS (Terra & Aqua): NDVI, EVI vegetation indices Landsat 8/9: High-resolution vegetation cover data VIIRS: Daily vegetation and thermal anomaly detection MERRA-2: Climate reanalysis for temperature, rainfall, and radiation data GPM (Global Precipitation Measurement): Rainfall and soil moisture patterns

Technology Stack: Frontend: ReactJS / CesiumJS / Mapbox GL for 3D visualization Backend: Python (Flask/FastAPI) for APIs and data management AI Models: TensorFlow / Scikit-learn for bloom detection and prediction Database: PostgreSQL with PostGIS for geospatial queries Data Handling: NASA EarthData APIs, NetCDF, HDF5 processing via Python

🌱 Applications and Impact: Conservation Planning: Identifies ecosystems vulnerable to climate-induced bloom shifts. Agriculture: Helps farmers and agricultural agencies optimize pollination and planting schedules. Environmental Research: Enables scientists to study vegetation–climate interactions over time. Policy Support: Provides data-driven insights for sustainability and biodiversity strategies.

💡 Innovation: BloomAI combines AI-driven bloom detection with NASA’s multi-satellite Earth data to deliver a dynamic, scalable visualization of vegetation cycles. Unlike static monitoring tools, BloomAI evolves with new data, providing real-time adaptability and predictive insights for ecological decision-making.
projectDetails.aiReferences: Artificial Intelligence plays a central role in BloomAI by transforming massive volumes of NASA satellite data into meaningful insights about vegetation health, bloom timing, and ecological change. The AI system automates analysis, prediction, and visualization in ways that manual processing or basic analytics cannot achieve. 🌿 1. Bloom Detection and Classification AI models process multi-temporal satellite imagery (from MODIS, Landsat, VIIRS) to automatically identify blooming phases in plants. Machine learning algorithms analyze vegetation indices like NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) and EVI (Enhanced Vegetation Index). The AI learns the spectral patterns that correspond to flowering, leaf-out, and senescence (end of bloom) phases. This eliminates manual labeling and ensures continuous monitoring at a global scale. 🧭 2. Predictive Modeling of Bloom Events AI-based time-series forecasting models (like LSTM – Long Short-Term Memory networks) predict future bloom timings by analyzing historical bloom data, temperature, precipitation, and sunlight variations. Helps forecast early, delayed, or failed blooming due to changing climate conditions. Enables farmers and ecologists to plan interventions (e.g., irrigation, pollinator management). 🌦️ 3. Climate and Vegetation Correlation Analysis AI correlates blooming patterns with multiple climate variables — temperature anomalies, rainfall frequency, soil moisture, and radiation. Uses multivariate regression and feature importance to understand which factors most influence bloom timing. Helps identify climate-driven phenological shifts (e.g., earlier blooms due to global warming). 🗺️ 4. Anomaly and Change Detection AI detects unusual or missing blooming events by comparing expected and observed vegetation patterns. Uses unsupervised learning (clustering, anomaly detection) to find deviations from normal cycles. Helps locate regions suffering from environmental stress, deforestation, or pollution impacts. 🛰️ 5. Automated Satellite Image Analysis Traditional image processing of large NASA datasets can take weeks — AI accelerates this by: Performing automated image segmentation to isolate vegetation zones. Filtering cloud cover and atmospheric noise using CNN (Convolutional Neural Networks). Generating high-resolution bloom maps from low-resolution or partial data sources. 🧩 6. Insight Generation and Visualization AI transforms raw geospatial data into interpretable visual insights for non-experts: Generates interactive bloom heatmaps, trend timelines, and ecological health scores. Uses natural language generation (NLG) to explain bloom trends in simple, human-readable summaries. 💡 7. Decision Support for Conservation and Agriculture AI-driven insights help decision-makers act quickly and efficiently: Conservationists can prioritize areas needing restoration or pollinator protection. Agricultural planners can schedule planting or harvesting based on predicted bloom windows. Policy-makers can monitor long-term ecological balance and biodiversity health.

projectDetails.name: CASA
projectDetails.summary: CASA (Cosmic Analysis & Simulation Alliance) is an interactive 3-D web platform that lets users pick any spot on Earth and watch a realistic asteroid streak in from space, then instantly see the damage it would cause. By fusing live NASA near-Earth-object data with physics-based impact models and CesiumJS visualization, the tool translates complex orbital information into intuitive, location-specific risk assessments—crater size, blast energy, seismic reach, tsunami potential—within seconds. Built for researchers, emergency planners and the public, CASA democratizes planetary-defense insight, turning abstract asteroid catalogs into actionable, visually compelling intelligence that helps communities understand, prepare for, and ultimately mitigate cosmic impact threats.
projectDetails.details: CASA: Click Earth, watch a NASA-fed asteroid slam down live; instant crater, blast, tsunami map. Benefit: turns scary orbital data into clear local risk in seconds, no PhD needed. Impact: give citizens, planners, researchers a shared, visceral picture so towns can prep, drill, evacuate, lobby for space defense. Built with JavaScript, React, CesiumJS 3-D globe, NASA JPL small-body API, Sandia impact physics equations, Netlify hosting; runs in any browser, no install. Creative fusion of cinematic game-like visuals with peer-reviewed science, turning abstract catalog numbers into “what-if” right on your street. Team weighed accuracy vs speed, chose fast analytic fits; privacy (no user data stored); accessibility (mobile-first UI); open-source ethos; color-blind-safe palettes; scenario export for GIS teams.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
1. 3-D asteroid entity with true six-degree-of-freedom trajectory

  • Generate a SampledPositionProperty that simulates a hyperbolic orbit (not just a straight line).
  • Include Earth J₂ oblateness perturbation and lunar third-body gravity.
  • Output CZML snippet or direct Cesium calls.

2. Physics-based impact-energy → crater model

  • Implement Collins et al. 2005 crater-scaling laws (velocity, angle, density, yield).
  • Return crater diameter, depth, transient/apparent rim, ejecta blanket range.
  • Expose as a pure function: crater(collinsParams) → {D, d, h, R_ej}.

3. Realistic mesh-generation for irregular asteroid

  • Procedurally create a low-poly icosphere, apply random harmonic noise (spherical harmonics) to produce a non-convex shape.
  • Export vertices + indices for Cesium.VertexFormat.POSITION_ONLY.
  • Optional: bake a procedural PBR texture (albedo + normal).

4. Atmospheric entry ablation & fragmentation logic

  • Solve single-body meteoroid ablation ODEs (mass-loss, luminosity, velocity decay) in 1-D.
  • Stop condition: either full ablation or ground impact velocity.
  • Return height-vs-velocity curve so the front-end can colour the trail dynamically.

5. GPU-friendly shock-wave / air-burst shader

  • Write a custom Cesium Fabric shader that draws an expanding annulus on the ellipsoid (fragCoord → lon/lat → great-circle distance).
  • Uniforms: origin, start time, shock velocity, decay exponent.
  • Gives a visible "pressure wave" without creating hundreds of primitives.

Using a Natural Language Processing (NLP) model, it interprets a user's question and instantly returns the most relevant studies and datasets from the GeneLab repository.

The key benefit is making valuable scientific data accessible to everyone, from researchers who can now find information faster, to students exploring space science for the first time. Our intended impact is to accelerate discovery and support the next generation of space explorers.

The project was built using Python (Flask, Hugging Face Transformers) for the backend and HTML/CSS/JavaScript for the frontend. Our creativity lies in its human-centric approach, focusing on a simple user experience to bridge the gap between human curiosity and complex data. We prioritized technical feasibility for the hackathon, ensuring our core search feature was robust and effective.

projectDetails.name: Project CHOTHI ⭐
projectDetails.summary: The prediction algorithm in the Storm Prediction & Safety Planner web app is a simulated system that estimates storm impact based on distance and time. It begins by generating a virtual storm center that moves across coordinates over time, mimicking real storm movement. The system calculates the storm’s current position using a starting latitude and longitude with a fixed velocity, and adjusts its intensity dynamically depending on the time of day. When a user selects or searches a location on the map, the algorithm uses the Haversine formula to compute the exact distance between the chosen point and the moving storm center. Based on this distance, it categorizes the area into Extreme, High, Moderate, or Low risk zones, and assigns estimated wind speed, rain intensity, and time to impact. The prediction details are visually displayed on the map and in the side panel. Users can also generate a safety action plan through the Google Gemini API, which provides AI-generated advice for preparation and protection. Though the system does not use real-time meteorological data, it effectively demonstrates how storm prediction, risk analysis, and AI-driven planning can work together in a practical disaster management interface.
projectDetails.details: The app uses a simulated storm model to estimate weather risk. It creates a moving storm center that shifts position over time and calculates the distance between the user’s selected location and the storm. Based on this distance, it predicts risk level, wind speed, rain intensity, and time to impact. The closer the location is to the storm’s center, the higher the predicted risk. This data is then used to display storm details and generate an AI-based safety plan using the Gemini API.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
1. Generative AI for Core Project Functionality

The primary AI feature of this project is the "AI Action Plan Console." This component leverages the Google Gemini API to provide users with dynamic, personalized safety plans.

How it was utilized: When a user generates a storm prediction for a specific location, the application sends the relevant data (e.g., risk level, estimated wind speed, rain intensity, and time to impact) to the Gemini Large Language Model via an API call.

AI's role: The AI model processes this situational data and generates a unique, context-aware, and actionable safety plan in natural language. This plan offers specific recommendations on what actions to take immediately and how to prepare as the storm approaches. The generated text is then streamed back into the application's console for the user to read.

2. AI-Assisted Code Generation

The source code for this project—including the HTML structure, CSS styling (via Tailwind CSS), and JavaScript logic—was generated by an AI assistant (Google Gemini).

How it was utilized: The development process was conversational. High-level feature requests, debugging instructions, and modification prompts (such as "add a theme selector," "delete the API keys section," or "add a real-time rain layer") were provided to the AI.

AI's role: The AI interpreted these requests and wrote the necessary code to implement the features, structure the application, and handle the logic for map interactions, API calls, and UI updates. The entire application was built iteratively through this AI-assisted coding process.

projectDetails.name: Project Codexa
projectDetails.summary:
Our project proposes the development of a self-sustaining O’Neill Cylinder — a rotating space habitat engineered to replicate Earth-like living conditions in orbit. By spinning the cylinder, we generate artificial gravity, eliminating long-term health risks associated with microgravity. The structure is protected from cosmic radiation using layers of water or regolith sourced from the Moon or asteroids.

The habitat functions as a fully closed-loop ecosystem. Oxygen is produced through a hybrid system of plants and electrolysis, while hydroponics, algae bioreactors, and insect or aquaponic farming supply continuous food production. Water is 100% recycled via advanced filtration and distillation. All organic waste is converted into fertilizer or biogas fuel, minimizing resupply needs from Earth.

Energy is provided through large-scale solar arrays supported by compact nuclear generators for uninterrupted power. The cylinder is constructed modularly in orbit, using components launched from Earth and later expanded using in-space robotic manufacturing and resource utilization.

This concept is not just a habitat but a scalable template for future space cities, enabling long-term human life beyond Earth for research, industry, and settlement. Our goal is to present a practical pathway toward self-reliant, expandable space civilization.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do / How does it work?

The project presents a conceptual design for a self-sustaining rotating space habitat known as an O’Neill Cylinder. Artificial gravity is created through controlled rotation, allowing long-term human habitation. The system operates as a closed-loop ecosystem, integrating:

Air management using plants and electrolysis for oxygen production

Food generation through hydroponics, algae, and aquaponic/insect-based farming

Water recycling via filtration and condensation systems

Waste-to-resource conversion into fertilizer and biogas

Solar power with nuclear backup for uninterrupted energy

Radiation protection using water or lunar/asteroid regolith shielding

2. Benefits and Intended Impact

Enables independent human living in space without continuous Earth resupply

Supports long-duration missions, research, and space-based agriculture

Serves as a scalable model for future orbital cities around Earth, the Moon, or Mars

Reduces long-term mission cost through full sustainability and in-situ resource use

3. Tools, Coding Languages, and Development Resources Used

Python for basic system modeling and calculations

Tripo3D for 3D visualization and structure rendering

Canva for diagramming and presentation design

AI tools for concept assistance and workflow optimization

4. Creativity and Design Considerations

Human-centered interior design with natural lighting and psychological comfort zones

Modular structure that can expand from prototype to large settlement

Safety-focused architecture with compartmentalized habitats and emergency systems

Compatibility with current launch vehicle capabilities and future space logistics

projectDetails.name: Space Biology Knowledge Search Engine
projectDetails.summary:
The Space Biology Knowledge Search Engine is designed to provide accessible, comprehensive exploration of NASA’s space biology research. It integrates data from multiple NASA Open Science Data Repositories into a centralized platform for Spaceflight Life Investigations (SLIs). Using AI-powered summarization with Google’s Gemini, the system delivers clear, grounded explanations of complex studies, helping users understand how microgravity, radiation, and other spaceflight factors affect living organisms—from microbes to humans.
Key features include categorized search filters, detailed metadata tagging, and intuitive navigation, allowing users to find studies by species, research field, or experimental procedure. The repository encompasses data from over 500 biological experiments, covering microbial behavior, plant growth, and human health in space.
Additionally, the platform supports bioinformatics analyses, including molecular pathway exploration and omics data interpretation, to advance understanding of space-induced biological changes. Ultimately, this project aims to democratize space biology research, making it more accessible and interpretable for scientists, students, and space enthusiasts alike—fostering innovation in both space exploration and Earth-based biomedical research.
projectDetails.details:
The Space Biology Knowledge Search Engine is designed to make NASA’s space biology research more accessible, understandable and impactful.

It functions by integrating metadata from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository, allowing users to search and explore Spaceflight Life Investigations through keywords and categorized filters.

Powered by Google’s Gemini AI, the system generates concise, context-rich summaries that simplify complex research findings for both scientists and general audiences. The platform benefits the scientific community by streamlining access to large, diverse, datasets, enhancing research efficiency and supporting health and biological studies related to human spaceflight.

The project’s intended impact is to democratize access to space biology knowledge, encouraging collaboration, education and innovation in the field of space life sciences.

The system is a simple project developed using Python and Flask for the backend, integrated with NASA APIs and Google Gemini AI. The frontend utilizes HTML, CSS, and JavaScript providing a modern space-themed, user-friendly interface.

The team focused on usability, data accuracy, ethical AI implementation, and performance optimization to ensure reliability and accessibility. In essence, this project transforms complex scientific data into actionable knowledge, advancing human understanding of life in space and supporting NASA’s exploration goals.

Project Summary – Exo Detector

Our project, Exo Detector, is an AI-powered system designed to identify exoplanets automatically from NASA’s open-source datasets such as Kepler and TESS. Traditionally, the discovery of exoplanets relied heavily on manual inspection of stellar light curves—a time-consuming process prone to human error. Exo Detector addresses this challenge by employing deep learning models that analyze brightness variations in stars to detect potential planetary transits with high accuracy.

By automating data analysis, our tool accelerates the identification of exoplanet candidates and provides a scalable solution for handling the vast amount of astronomical data collected by NASA missions. The project is deployed as an interactive web app on Hugging Face Spaces, allowing users and researchers to visualize predictions easily. Exo Detector demonstrates how artificial intelligence can revolutionize space exploration, empowering faster and more precise discovery of worlds beyond our solar system.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Exo Detector

Exo Detector is an artificial intelligence–powered application designed to automatically identify exoplanets from NASA’s open-source space mission data, including Kepler and TESS light curve datasets. The system analyzes fluctuations in stellar brightness to detect periodic dips that indicate potential planetary transits.

Our model combines Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layers to effectively capture both spatial and temporal features from light curve data. After training and validation, the model predicts whether a signal represents a real exoplanet or a false positive.

The project offers significant benefits: it reduces the need for manual data inspection, accelerates the discovery process, and improves accuracy by leveraging advanced AI methods. The final product is deployed as an interactive web application on Hugging Face Spaces, allowing users to upload data and instantly visualize AI-driven predictions.

We developed Exo Detector using Python, TensorFlow/Keras, NumPy, Pandas, and Gradio for deployment. The project’s creativity lies in merging astrophysics with machine learning and presenting complex scientific analysis through a user-friendly interface. Our team focused on interpretability, data transparency, and accessibility, aiming to make exoplanet detection faster, open, and inclusive for both researchers and enthusiasts worldwide.
projectDetails.aiReferences: Artificial Intelligence played a key role in developing our project, Exo Detector. We used Claude AI to assist in writing and optimizing code for our machine learning model, web interface, and data preprocessing scripts. Claude AI helped streamline debugging, improve algorithm efficiency, and document the workflow. The AI-assisted portions were limited to code generation, text refinement, and structural guidance; all final implementations, model architectures, and data handling were reviewed and tested by our team. No NASA logos, branding, or mission identifiers were used or modified. Any AI-generated visuals included in the project are clearly watermarked as “AI-generated.” Our goal was to responsibly use AI tools to enhance productivity, creativity, and clarity—while ensuring all scientific and coding work remained original and transparent.

About 'Apollo 11',

Apollo 11 was the first spaceflight to land humans on the Moon, conducted by NASA from July 16 to 24, 1969. Commander Neil Armstrong and Lunar Module Pilot Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin landed the Lunar Module Eagle on July 20 at 20:17 UTC, and Armstrong became the first person to step onto the surface about six hours later, at 02:56 UTC on July 21. Aldrin joined him 19 minutes afterward, and together they spent about two and a half hours exploring the site they had named Tranquility Base upon landing. They collected 47.5 pounds (21.5 kg) of lunar material to bring back to Earth before re-entering the Lunar Module. In total, they were on the Moon’s surface for 21 hours, 36 minutes before returning to the Command Module Columbia, which remained in lunar orbit, piloted by Michael Collins.

projectDetails.name: Zappy- The Sun Sneeze: A Space Weather Story
projectDetails.summary:
Our project is "Zappy the Sun-Sneeze," a complete, illustrated digital children's story designed to make the science of space weather accessible and engaging. We developed a narrative script featuring a friendly character, Zappy, who is a personified Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) born from a "sneeze" from the Sun.

This story directly addresses the challenge by translating complex scientific concepts into a simple, relatable analogy. Zappy's journey to Earth visually and narratively demonstrates the effects of space weather, from the beautiful creation of auroras to the temporary, non-threatening disruption of technology like GPS and radios.

This project is important because it demystifies a complex scientific field for the next generation. By presenting space weather in a fun, story-driven format, "Zappy the Sun-Sneeze" helps foster an early interest in STEM, promotes scientific literacy, and explains why studying the Sun is crucial for protecting our technology-dependent world.
projectDetails.details:
"Zappy the Sun-Sneeze" is an 18-page digital children's storybook that explains space weather. It works to his journey to Earth. Each page features vibrant, kid-friendly illustrations and simple text, showing how Zappy's energy impacts various people and technologies like GPS for farmers and park rangers, radios for pilots, internet for gamers and IT workers, and power grids, while also creating beautiful auroras.
The project benefits children by making complex space weather science understandable and engaging, fostering early interest in STEM fields. It raises awareness among young audiences, parents, and educators about the real world effects of solar activity on daily life and technology. By highlighting space weather forecasting, it also promotes the value of scientific monitoring and preparedness.

The primary intended impact is to ignite curiosity about space and science in elementary school children, providing them with foundational knowledge about the Sun-Earth connection and space weather. It aims to empower them to understand how distant solar events can affect their world and appreciate the role of scientists in keeping us prepared, thereby contributing to a more scientifically literate public.

The project's narrative, characters, and educational framework were developed using human creativity and natural language processing (AI). All 18 pages, including the vivid illustrations, integrated text, and consistent blue theme, were generated using advanced image generation AI models based on detailed textual descriptions. The entire development and refinement process took place within this conversational AI interface.

The project's creativity lies in its unique personification of a Coronal Mass Ejection (Zappy) as a curious and energetic character, and its use of the "Sun-sneeze" metaphor for a solar flare, making abstract science relatable. It imaginatively illustrates the diverse impacts of space weather on a wide range of everyday professions through engaging scenarios, blending scientific accuracy with a compelling, child-friendly narrative and vibrant visual storytelling.

Our team (AI and human collaboration) primarily considered the target audience (children aged 6-10), ensuring all content was age-appropriate, visually appealing, and easy to understand. We prioritized scientific accuracy as per the NASA challenge, carefully integrating core concepts like CMEs, magnetosphere, and forecasting. We also focused on making the story engaging and creative, highlighting diverse societal impacts and structuring it for a digital storybook format with potential for animation.

projectDetails.name: AQI Monitor
projectDetails.summary:
Our project is an application designed to forecast and visualize air quality using real-time data from NASA’s TEMPO satellite, combined with ground-based air quality measurements and weather data. The system provides users with location-aware notifications, an interactive live map, and health recommendations to help minimize exposure to harmful pollutants.

Developed using React Native for the frontend, Node.js for the backend and  the app integrates APIs such as  OpenAQ, and OpenWeather. It efficiently collects, processes, and visualizes air-quality insights, supported by customizable widgets and downloadable reports for public and institutional use.

The project aims to make satellite data accessible and actionable, promoting public health awareness and supporting agencies in environmental planning. Our team focused on scalability, usability, and real-time responsiveness, creatively bridging space-based Earth observation with community-level impact to ensure cleaner, safer skies.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

AQI Monitor is a comprehensive mobile application designed to provide real-time air quality information and predictive analytics. The application offers users detailed insights into current air pollution levels, pollutant breakdowns, and future air quality forecasts to help them make informed decisions about outdoor activities and health precautions.

Core Features

1. Real-time Air Quality Monitoring

  • Display current AQI values with color-coded categories
  • Detailed pollutant breakdown (PM2.5, PM10, NO2, O3, SO2, CO)
  • Location-based air quality data
  • Automatic location detection with manual search option

2. 10-Week Predictive Forecasting

  • Advanced machine learning-based AQI predictions
  • Weekly forecasts with confidence indicators
  • Trend analysis (increasing, decreasing, stable)
  • Seasonal pattern integration
  • Historical data analysis for improved accuracy

3. Interactive Map Interface

  • Geographical visualization of air quality data
  • Multiple marker types (user location, search results)
  • Real-time AQI color coding on map
  • Detailed station information popups
  • OpenStreetMap integration

4. Smart Alert System

  • Threshold-based notifications for poor air quality
  • Health recommendations based on AQI levels
  • Sensitive group warnings
  • Customizable alert preferences

Technical Architecture

Frontend Framework

  • React Native with Expo for cross-platform compatibility
  • React Native Paper for Material Design components
  • React Navigation for seamless screen transitions
  • React Native Maps for geographical data visualization
  • React Native Chart Kit for data visualization

Backend & Data Management

  • AsyncStorage for local data persistence
  • Axios for API communications
  • Custom caching layer for performance optimization
  • Offline capability with fallback data

Data Sources & APIs

  • OpenAQ API for real-time air quality data
  • Expo Location for geolocation services
  • Custom prediction algorithms for forecasting
  • Fallback mock data system for reliability

Prediction Engine

  • Moving average algorithms for trend detection
  • Seasonal adjustment factors
  • Historical data analysis (90-day window)
  • Confidence scoring system
  • Location-based seeding for consistency

Key Components

Dashboard Screen

  • Current AQI display with category indicators
  • 10-week forecast chart
  • Detailed pollutant breakdown
  • Location information
  • Refresh and cache management

Map Screen

  • Interactive map with AQI overlays
  • Search functionality for locations
  • Current location tracking
  • Marker-based station information
  • Real-time data updates

Prediction Model

  • Weekly aggregation of historical data
  • Trend calculation using linear regression
  • Seasonal variation adjustments
  • Confidence level calculations
  • Cache optimization for performance

Data Structure

Air Quality Object

{
aqi: number,
pm25: number,
pm10: number,
no2: number,
o3: number,
so2: number,
co: number,
latitude: number,
longitude: number,
location: string,
city: string,
country: string,
timestamp: string,
source: string
}

Prediction Object

{
week: number,
aqi: number,
confidence: number,
startDate: Date,
endDate: Date,
trend: 'increasing' | 'decreasing' | 'stable'
}

AQI Categories & Health Impact

Category System

  • 0-50 (Good): Air quality is satisfactory
  • 51-100 (Moderate): Acceptable air quality
  • 101-150 (Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups): Mild health effects
  • 151-200 (Unhealthy): Everyone may experience effects
  • 201-300 (Very Unhealthy): Health alerts
  • 301+ (Hazardous): Emergency conditions

Performance Optimizations

Caching Strategy

  • 10-minute cache for current AQI data
  • 30-minute cache for predictions
  • Location-based caching keys
  • Automatic cache invalidation
  • Memory and persistent storage layers

Data Consistency

  • Seeded random generation for consistent mock data
  • Location-based data normalization
  • Time-based variation algorithms
  • Fallback systems for API failures

Error Handling & Reliability

Graceful Degradation

  • Multiple API endpoint fallbacks
  • Consistent mock data generation
  • Cache recovery mechanisms
  • Offline operation support

User Experience

  • Loading states and progress indicators
  • Error messages with retry options
  • Empty state handling
  • Network status awareness

Development Features

Cross-Platform Compatibility

  • iOS and Android support
  • Web platform adaptation
  • Responsive design principles
  • Platform-specific optimizations

Testing & Debugging

  • Comprehensive logging system
  • Error tracking and reporting
  • Performance monitoring
  • Data validation checks

Future Enhancements

Planned Features

  • Push notifications for air quality alerts
  • Health recommendations and tips
  • Historical data trends and comparisons
  • Social sharing capabilities
  • Multiple data source integration
  • Personalized air quality insights

Technical Improvements

  • Advanced machine learning models
  • Real-time data streaming
  • Background data updates
  • Enhanced accuracy algorithms
  • Expanded global coverage

Installation & Setup

Prerequisites

  • Node.js and npm
  • Expo CLI
  • iOS/Android development environment

Dependencies

  • React Native core libraries
  • Expo location and permissions
  • Charting and visualization libraries
  • Navigation and UI components
  • HTTP client for API communications

Usage Scenarios

Individual Users

  • Daily air quality checks before outdoor activities
  • Planning based on weekly forecasts
  • Location-based air quality awareness
  • Health precaution guidance

Sensitive Groups

  • Asthma and respiratory condition management
  • Elderly and children protection
  • Outdoor activity planning
  • Emergency situation awareness

Environmental Awareness

  • Pollution pattern recognition
  • Seasonal trend understanding
  • Geographical pollution distribution
  • Environmental impact education

This AQI Monitor application represents a comprehensive solution for air quality monitoring and forecasting, combining real-time data with predictive analytics to help users make informed decisions about their health and activities in various air quality conditions.

projectDetails.name: Project Delta-V
projectDetails.summary:
Delta-V is an AI-powered platform developed to classify and explore exoplanets using NASA’s Kepler mission data. Our solution integrates a Streamlit-based prediction app with an interactive exploration web app, creating both a research tool and a public educational experience.

The prediction system uses a retrained and cleaned XGBoost model with 39 key stellar and transit features, achieving Accuracy = 87.7%, Precision = 86.5%, Recall = 91.2%, F1-Score = 88.8%, and ROC-AUC = 0.94. It allows users to input custom data dynamically, visualize results, and interpret model confidence in real time.

Complementing it, the exploration interface serves as an open exoplanet library, enabling users—students, professors, and scientists alike—to browse confirmed exoplanets, study their characteristics, and understand their formation through 3D visualizations and graphs.

By combining scientific accuracy, machine learning, and interactive design, Delta-V democratizes exoplanet discovery, transforming raw space data into an engaging and educational experience for all.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

Our project unifies two core systems — an AI-powered exoplanet detection and classification model and an interactive exoplanet exploration web platform — built to transform NASA mission data into accessible, explainable insights for researchers, educators, and the public.

1. Exoplanet Detection and Classification System

The first component is a Streamlit-based AI application that predicts whether a candidate signal represents an exoplanet.
The model uses a cleaned and retrained XGBoost classifier with 39 astrophysical and transit geometry features derived from harmonized datasets across NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS missions. Data cleaning included removing leaky and duplicate features, applying group-by object_id splits to prevent overlap, and median-imputation for missing values.

Pipeline overview:

  • Preprocessing: pandas, NumPy, StandardScaler
  • Modeling: XGBoost (tree-based gradient boosting)
  • Evaluation: GroupKFold cross-validation, confusion matrices, ROC/PR curves, Brier calibration
  • Metrics (test n≈1,582): Accuracy = 0.877, Precision = 0.865, Recall = 0.912, F1 = 0.888, ROC-AUC = 0.940

The Streamlit UI provides dynamic feature input, probability visualization, and expert diagnostic plots (confusion matrix, ROC/PR, feature importance). Users can interactively adjust thresholds, interpret predictions, and explore how features like depth_ppm, duration_hrs, or planet_radius_earth influence the decision boundary.

2. Exoplanet Exploration Library

Complementing the AI tool, we built a full-stack interactive library for exploring the merged exoplanet dataset.

  • Backend: Python 3.13, Flask, Flask-CORS, pandas, matplotlib/seaborn — serving pre-computed analytical plots and structured JSON data.
  • Frontend: React + Vite, modern component architecture with React Context for state and dynamic routing.

The library displays scientific visualizations — regression trends, classification results, clustering maps, feature correlations, violin plots, and 3D planetary renderings. Users can navigate through planets, compare characteristics, and view detailed panels enriched with contextual explanations and imagery.

3. Impact and Creativity

This project bridges static analysis and live exploration, combining machine learning interpretability, astrophysical rigor, and creative UX.
It makes NASA’s exoplanet data searchable, explainable, and visually engaging, lowering barriers for new researchers and inspiring curiosity in the general public. By merging AI inference with scientific visualization, our system turns raw mission data into an interactive exoplanet discovery experience — reproducible, educational, and scalable for future missions.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Our team used AI tools like ChatGPT,Gemini as a development assistant during the creation of both the AI exoplanet detection model and the interactive web applications. The tools were used responsibly to:

  • Debug and resolve coding issues in Python (Streamlit, Flask) and JavaScript (React + Vite).
  • Optimize model evaluation pipelines, such as generating confusion matrices, computing classification metrics, and validating feature importance visualizations.
  • Improve documentation clarity and ensure our scientific descriptions and technical summaries were concise and accurate.

All core data processing, model training, and evaluation — including data cleaning, feature engineering, leak detection, retraining of the XGBoost model, and metric validation — were implemented and executed manually by our team. The AI tools assisted primarily in code refinement and explanation, not in generating datasets, models, or final outputs.

We are B.Tech students in Artificial Intelligence and Data Science, so our approach balanced human expertise with AI-assisted productivity. No AI-generated media (images, videos, or audio) were used in this project.

projectDetails.name: AstraLens
projectDetails.summary:
AstraLens is a web-based lunar reconnaissance platform designed to solve the critical accessibility barrier to NASA's vast planetary data. Faced with gigabyte-sized raw datasets and fragmented feature catalogs that demand specialized tools , our project, inspired by the "Embiggen Your Eyes" challenge, democratizes lunar exploration. 
The platform features a high-performance, interactive map that allows users to seamlessly zoom and pan across the Moon's surface, and can pinpoint a specific area which is rendered from a curated database of over 9,000 labeled features. The core of our solution is the "Astra AI Assistant," an intelligent guide powered by Google's Gemini model. By using a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methodology, Astra provides factually accurate, context-aware answers drawn exclusively from our verified lunar database, making complex planetary science accessible and engaging for researchers, educators, and the public alike.
projectDetails.details:
AstraLens is an integrated cartography and analysis tool designed to make the exploration of high-resolution lunar data intuitive and insightful.

How It Works: The platform is built on a streamlined architecture to efficiently process and deliver complex lunar data.

  1. Data Processing: We developed a custom Python script that processes enormous raw .tiff lunar images into a multi-level tile pyramid. This allows for an optimized, web-based map where users can zoom and pan smoothly without performance lags, as data is loaded on demand. Similarly, raw.csv feature catalogs are parsed by automated scripts into a lightweight and quickly retrievable JSON structure.
  2. Interactive Map: The frontend presents a high-fidelity, interactive visualization of the lunar surface. Users can navigate with fluid controls, and the map provides real-time overlays of labeled features like craters, maria, and basins, offering immediate geological context.
  3. AI Assistant: A robust Flask backend serves the map tiles and hosts the Astra AI Assistant. When a user asks a question in natural language (e.g., "Describe the Tycho crater"), the system uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to embed our verified JSON database into a prompt for Google's Gemini API. This guarantees the AI provides fact-based, contextually accurate answers drawn only from the vetted lunar data.

Benefits & Impact:

The primary benefit of AstraLens is the democratization of planetary data. It transforms unwieldy, expert-level datasets into an engaging and accessible experience for a broad audience. For researchers, it offers a rapid analysis tool with a reliable, non-hallucinating AI guide. For educators and the public, it turns static data into a living, explorable canvas for discovery.

Tools & Creative Factors:

  • Languages & Frameworks: Python (for data processing), Flask (backend server).
  • AI: Google's Gemini API with a RAG implementation.
  • Data Formats: We processed .tiff imagery and .csv catalogs into a web-friendly tile pyramid and JSON database.
  • Our creative approach lies in the fusion of high-performance mapping with a specialized, database-grounded AI.
  • We prioritized a user experience that is both visually immersive (seamless map) and intellectually reliable (fact-based AI), ensuring the platform is a powerful tool for both casual discovery and scientific inquiry.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Yes, Artificial Intelligence is central to the AstraLens platform.

Our project incorporates an AI-powered guide named the

Astra AI Assistant. This feature was developed using Google's Gemini model.

The core AI methodology employed is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). This technique ensures that the AI's responses are strictly limited to the information contained within our curated and verified lunar feature database. By doing this, we prevent the AI from "hallucinating" or providing speculative information. The AI serves as a natural language interface, allowing users to query the complex dataset conversationally and receive precise, evidence-based insights without needing any technical expertise.

  • Astra AI Assistant: Our project's core feature is an AI-powered guide built using Google's Gemini model. We implemented a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methodology, which strictly limits the AI's responses to our curated and verified lunar database. This ensures the assistant provides fact-based, reliable answers and prevents AI "hallucination," allowing users to query complex data using natural language.
  • Project Visuals: The illustrative images and overall design aesthetic for our project presentation were generated using AI visualization tools.
