projectDetails.name: Project NEXA
projectDetails.summary:
Space Trash Hack: Revolution Recycle on mars
The challenge focuses on finding innovative ways to manage and recycle waste generated during human missions to Mars. Since transporting resources from Earth is costly and limited, waste materials such as packaging, plastics, metals, and worn-out equipment must be transformed into useful resources for survival. Participants are asked to design sustainable recycling systems, upcycling methods, or circular economy approaches that can turn “trash” into building materials, tools, energy sources, or life-support elements. The goal is to ensure long-term sustainability for astronauts on Mars by reducing dependency on Earth resupply and promoting closed-loop resource cycles.
projectDetails.details: The NASA Space Apps Challenge “Space Trash Hack: Revolutionizing Recycling on Mars” calls for innovative solutions to manage and recycle inorganic waste produced during long-term human missions on Mars, where resupply from Earth is costly and limited. Participants are tasked with designing closed-loop systems that can transform waste materials—such as plastics, metals, and electronics—into usable resources like raw materials, building blocks, life-support elements, or tools. These systems must be energy-efficient, durable, and adapted to Martian conditions such as low gravity, dust, and limited power, while also requiring minimal astronaut intervention through autonomous or semi-autonomous operation. Teams are expected to present clear designs with schematics or prototypes, outline the process of waste collection and transformation, and evaluate feasibility in terms of energy, mass, and maintenance. The ultimate goal is to reduce dependence on Earth, extend sustainability for Martian habitats, and potentially inspire recycling innovations for Earth as well.
projectDetails.aiReferences: AI tools like ChatGPT and Gemini AI can play a crucial role in conceptualizing, designing, and visualizing solutions for the Space Trash Hack challenge. ChatGPT can assist teams in brainstorming innovative ideas, drafting detailed project descriptions, generating step-by-step processes for waste recycling, and simulating system workflows under Martian constraints. Gemini AI, with its advanced image generation capabilities, can create high-fidelity visualizations and prototypes, such as 3D renderings of recycling units, Martian habitats integrating waste-processing systems, or conceptual “before-and-after” transformations of waste materials into usable resources. These AI-driven tools allow participants to quickly test ideas, visualize complex processes, and communicate designs effectively, making it easier to showcase the feasibility and impact of proposed recycling systems for Mars missions.

projectDetails.name: Project NEXT
projectDetails.summary:
Our project "Orbitium", the Space Biology Knowledge Engine , is designed to solve one of NASA’s pressing challenges: how to centralize, analyze, and accelerate the use of decades of scattered space biology research. Currently, biological data from microgravity experiments, radiation studies, and human adaptation research are fragmented across papers, repositories, and formats—making it difficult for scientists and mission planners to build upon past knowledge.

Orbitium aims to become a unified, AI-driven knowledge engine that ingests structured and unstructured space biology data, organizes it into accessible formats, and provides intelligent insights for researchers. By combining natural language processing, data visualization, and knowledge graph architecture, the engine will allow users to query complex biological questions—such as “What genes are most sensitive to microgravity across species?”—and receive actionable, evidence-backed answers.

This tool is critical because the success of future long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond depends on protecting astronaut health. From radiation shielding strategies to microbial growth risks, every insight could save time, resources, and lives. By accelerating how researchers access and connect biological knowledge, Orbitium has the potential to make NASA’s space biology research more interoperable, transparent, and impactful—paving the way for safer, smarter exploration.

Project Title: Outdoor Activity Weather Planner

Project Description:

Our app helps users plan outdoor activities by predicting adverse weather conditions for a specific location and date. It uses real-time and historical weather data to assess risks like extreme heat, cold, wind, and rain, and provides a personalized activity suitability score based on the type of event (e.g., hiking, fishing, cycling).

How It Works:

  • Users select a location via map or city input, choose a date, and specify their activity.
  • The app fetches weather data using APIs like NASA POWER, OpenWeatherMap, and Meteostat.
  • It calculates risk levels (Very Hot, Very Cold, Very Windy, Very Wet, Very Uncomfortable) using defined thresholds.
  • It generates a forecast summary, rain probability, and a suitability score tailored to the activity type.
  • It suggests safer alternative dates and nearby locations with better weather.

Benefits & Impact:

  • Helps users make informed decisions to avoid weather-related risks.
  • Promotes safety and enhances outdoor experiences.
  • Encourages climate awareness through data-driven planning.

Tools & Technologies Used:

  • Platform: Bolt AI (logic blocks, API connectors, conditional workflows)
  • Languages: JavaScript, JSON, REST APIs
  • Data Sources: NASA POWER, OpenWeatherMap, Meteostat
  • Database: Bolt Database for session tracking and search history
  • UI/UX: Responsive design with icon buttons, progress bars, and color-coded indicators

Creativity & Considerations:

  • Intelligent scoring system that adapts to each activity’s weather sensitivity
  • Natural language forecast summaries
  • Voice input, save/share/export features, and push notifications
  • Mobile-first design with smooth animations and gradient styling
  • Safety tips tailored to weather risks and activity type

Our team focused on usability, scientific credibility, and real-world impact. We prioritized modular design, iterative testing, and user personalization to ensure the app is both functional and delightful to use.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
We used AI tools extensively in the development of our Outdoor Activity Weather Planner app. Specifically:

  • AI-assisted logic was applied to calculate weather risk levels, rain probability, and activity suitability scores based on user input and real-time weather data.
  • Natural language generation was used to create forecast summaries like “Partly cloudy with moderate winds.”
  • AI tools helped optimize the user interface and personalize recommendations based on activity type and weather conditions.
  • All AI-generated code and logic were reviewed and customized by our team to ensure accuracy and relevance.

projectDetails.name: Project NOVANET
projectDetails.summary:
ExoAI Explorer is a web-based application designed to make exoplanet exploration engaging, interactive, and accessible. The project allows users to explore stars and planets using real NASA datasets from Kepler, K2, and TESS missions. We developed a space-themed interface featuring an animated starry background, an interactive star map, brightness curves, and dynamic planet profiles. Users can upload their own datasets, visualize star brightness, and view planetary characteristics in a clear, professional layout.

Although AI integration is planned, the site is designed to support future machine learning analysis, where a model could classify exoplanets as confirmed, candidates, or false positives, updating the interface in real-time. This addresses the challenge by providing a tool that not only visualizes complex astronomical data but also enables automated exoplanet identification when AI is integrated.

The project is important because it democratizes access to space exploration data, supports researchers in analyzing large datasets efficiently, and engages enthusiasts with a futuristic, interactive experience. By combining visualization, data handling, and AI potential, ExoAI Explorer bridges the gap between raw scientific data and user-friendly exploration.
projectDetails.details:
ExoAI Explorer is a web-based platform that allows users to explore stars and exoplanets using real NASA datasets from Kepler, K2, and TESS missions. While AI integration is planned, the current system supports dynamic data visualization and interactive exploration of astronomical data.

Prepares the platform for future AI-based classification, enabling faster exoplanet identification.

The project democratizes access to exoplanetary data, bridging the gap between raw scientific datasets and interactive, educational tools. It engages users in citizen science, helping both novices and researchers explore and analyze space data efficiently.

Interactive star map and planet profiles that visualize real astronomical data

projectDetails.summary:
Ever wanted to command your own journey through the stars? Orbital Perspectives, by Team NOVARIS, demystifies the final frontier, placing the power to track satellites, explore NASA's archives, and witness celestial history directly at your fingertips. Meticulously crafted with HTML, Java, and CSS, this interactive web portal is your personal launchpad for discovery.

Delve into a comprehensive encyclopedia of man-made satellites, browse a stunning gallery of real-time NASA imagery, or follow the International Space Station's path with a dynamic orbital tracker. Orbital Perspectives transforms complex space data into a visually captivating and educational adventure, making the cosmos accessible and exciting for everyone. Its core mission is to ignite curiosity and inspire the next wave of explorers. With thoughtful features like a sleek Multiple Themes mode toggle, your voyage through the universe is always perfectly illuminated.
projectDetails.details:
Orbital Perspectives was born from a simple yet ambitious goal: to transform the way we interact with the cosmos. Instead of a static webpage, we envisioned a dynamic, interactive command deck for space exploration, accessible to everyone.

Project Details

This project is an interactive educational website designed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It offers users a virtual experience of being on the International Space Station (ISS), focusing on two key aspects: the breathtaking views from the Cupola and the weightlessness training in the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory (NBL).

How It Works & Its Benefits

"Orbital Perspectives" is a digital observatory that transforms passive learning into active discovery. It integrates real-time data from multiple APIs to create a seamless and engaging user experience. The interactive world map, custom-built with HTML5 Canvas, tracks the ISS in real-time, allowing users to follow its journey across the globe. The gallery provides searchable access to NASA's vast image library, bringing stunning visuals of our universe directly to the user. The primary benefit of this project is its ability to make space exploration personal and immediate, sparking curiosity and inspiring interest in STEM fields.

Technology & Tools

The website was built using a robust foundation of modern web technologies:

  • HTML5 provides the semantic structure for all content and interactive modules.
  • CSS3 brings the immersive, space-themed aesthetic to life with responsive layouts, animations, and custom properties.
  • Vanilla JavaScript powers the dynamic and interactive features, including the real-time data updates, simulations, and user controls.
  • Leaflet.js is used to create the interactive world map, providing a rich, user-friendly interface for tracking the ISS and exploring geographical data.

The project integrates data from several free and public APIs, including Open Notify for ISS location tracking, NASA EONET for live earth events, and Open-Meteo for weather data, all without requiring external dependencies.

Creativity & Core Considerations

The creativity of "Orbital Perspectives" lies in its fusion of authentic NASA data with a unique artistic vision. The design is inspired by the retro aesthetics of classic sci-fi, creating an experience that feels like a personal mission control center. The central consideration for our team was user engagement. We focused on making complex concepts like orbital mechanics exciting and accessible through interactivity. Key features like smooth-scroll navigation, touch support for mobile devices, and high-contrast text were implemented to ensure the experience is intuitive and accessible for all users.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Creativity & Core Considerations

Our project's creativity lies in its fusion of authentic data with a distinct artistic vision. We deliberately chose a retro-inspired, "eyes in the sky" theme to evoke the sense of wonder associated with classic sci-fi and the dawn of the space age. This isn't just another educational website; it's an experience designed to feel like a personal mission control.

The central factor our team considered was user engagement. We asked ourselves: How can we make orbital mechanics exciting? How can we make a photo archive feel like an adventure? The answer was interactivity at every turn. We also prioritized user comfort and accessibility, leading to key features like the intuitive navigation and the popular light/dark mode toggle, ensuring that every user can tailor their cosmic journey to their preference.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
We utilized several AI tools to enhance our creative process and streamline development for Orbital Perspectives.

GitHub Copilot: This AI code assistant accelerated our HTML, JavaScript, and CSS development by providing intelligent code suggestions and auto-completions, significantly speeding up our workflow.

ChatGPT & Gemini: These language models served as creative partners for brainstorming project concepts and for generating and refining all descriptive text for the website.

We acknowledge that these AI tools were used to assist in the generation of code and text. The core vision, design, and final implementation remained the product of our team's original thought and creative direction.

Our project, FarmNav, is an intelligent platform that harnesses NASA’s satellite data to help farmers make smarter, data-driven agricultural decisions. It integrates real-time insights from missions like Landsat, MODIS, SMAP, and GPM to monitor soil moisture, precipitation, vegetation health, and regional climate. By translating this complex data into an easy-to-use interface, FarmNav enables farmers and students to simulate crop strategies, optimize irrigation, and plan for changing climate conditions.

This directly addresses key global challenges such as climate unpredictability, water scarcity, and soil degradation, empowering users to adopt sustainable and resilient farming practices. FarmNav is not just a farming tool—it’s an educational platform that bridges space science and agriculture, inspiring the next generation to leverage technology for sustainability.
projectDetails.details:
FarmNav is an interactive platform that transforms NASA’s satellite data into practical insights for farmers, students, and agricultural planners. It integrates data from missions such as SMAP, MODIS, Landsat, and GPM to monitor soil moisture, rainfall, vegetation health, and climate patterns. Using this information, FarmNav allows users to simulate crop growth scenarios, optimize irrigation and fertilization schedules, and plan sustainable farming strategies under various weather and climate conditions.

Its educational impact extends to helping students understand the real-world application of space-based Earth data in addressing global food and climate challenges.

FarmNav was developed using Three.js, JavaScript, HTML/CSS, and NASA POWER API, combining 3D visualization, AI-driven analysis, and interactive simulation.

projectDetails.name: Project P and Y Tech
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, AI-Powered Exploration: An Interactive Viewer for NASA Datasets, tackles the challenge of making NASA’s massive, complex space archives accessible and explorable. These datasets, often stored in formats like FITS and GeoTIFF, are scientifically rich but hard for researchers and the public to navigate.

We developed a high-performance, web-based galaxy viewer that transforms multi-gigabyte astronomical images into thousands of web-ready tiles using GDAL. The frontend, built with React and Leaflet.js, delivers a smooth, responsive interface where users can pan and zoom seamlessly through data such as the Sombrero Galaxy. This tile-based approach ensures that only the necessary image portions load, enabling instant, lag-free exploration.

Our work addresses the challenge by bridging the gap between raw data and interactive discovery. By simplifying access and visualization, we open the door for broader scientific engagement and public outreach. The project’s importance lies in empowering users—from researchers to students—to explore space data intuitively, and our roadmap includes AI-assisted feature detection and dataset overlays for even deeper insights.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Our project is an interactive web-based viewer designed to make massive NASA datasets explorable for both researchers and the public. It processes gigapixel astronomical images (e.g., the Sombrero Galaxy) into thousands of lightweight tiles using GDAL. These tiles are then displayed in a smooth, responsive interface built with React and Leaflet.js, allowing users to pan, zoom, and explore data instantly without lag. The app also lays the foundation for AI-assisted feature detection and dataset overlays, enabling multi-dimensional analysis.

What benefits does it have?

  • Accessibility: Transforms complex formats (FITS/GeoTIFF) into a web-friendly interface.
  • Performance: Allows seamless navigation of very large images without requiring expensive local software.
  • Scalability: Can handle multiple datasets and overlay different types of space imagery.
  • Future AI Support: Will allow automatic detection of star clusters, craters, or dust lanes.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The goal is to bridge the gap between raw NASA data and meaningful exploration. By making datasets accessible, interactive, and educational, the project supports:

  • Researchers in rapidly exploring patterns and anomalies.
  • Educators in teaching space science using real NASA data.
  • Public outreach by engaging students, museums, and enthusiasts in space exploration.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend: React, Leaflet.js for interactive visualization.
  • Backend & Processing: Python, GDAL (gdal2tiles) for image tiling.
  • Planned Additions: Flask server for APIs, scikit-image for AI-driven feature detection.
  • Hardware/Infrastructure: Local machines for prototyping; highlights the need for more powerful servers for large-scale data preprocessing.

How is your project creative?

  • It adapts geospatial web technologies (usually used for maps) to the field of astronomical datasets, which is a novel application.
  • It introduces a layered exploration model, where datasets from different telescopes (optical, infrared, etc.) can be compared interactively.
  • It incorporates AI-assisted labeling and pattern discovery, bringing intelligence to raw imagery.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Performance vs. Usability: We initially attempted a 3D viewer (Cesium.js) but pivoted to 2D Leaflet.js for stability and better performance.
  • Data Size Challenges: Handling gigapixel images required careful preprocessing and optimization.
  • Scalability: Designed the pipeline to be expandable for future datasets and AI integration.
  • Accessibility & Outreach: Considered both scientific researchers and public users, ensuring a balance between depth and simplicity.
  • Future Growth: With more time, we are confident in adding AI, overlays, and stronger backend support to fully realize the vision.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Our project made limited but strategic use of AI tools to support development and accelerate creativity:

  1. Content Drafting & Structuring: We used AI-assisted text generation tools (like ChatGPT) to help draft and refine documentation, summaries, and technical explanations. All final content was reviewed, edited, and validated by our team to ensure originality and accuracy.
  2. Code Support: AI was used as a reference tool for boilerplate code snippets (e.g., Python scripts for data preprocessing and frontend structure in React). These were subsequently customized, debugged, and optimized by our team.
  3. Future Integration Plan: While not yet fully implemented, we are preparing to use AI models (such as CLIP-like systems and scikit-image–based feature detection) for labeling astronomical features (e.g., star clusters, dust lanes, and craters). Any AI-generated outputs in this context will be clearly acknowledged.

We used AI tools only to support documentation drafting and some boilerplate code suggestions, which we reviewed and customized ourselves. We did not use AI for images, videos, or branding. No NASA logos, mission identifiers, or flags were used or modified. Any future AI-generated imagery or audio will be visibly watermarked and properly labeled in metadata as per the challenge guidelines.

projectDetails.summary:
Summary:

Our project, “A World Away: Hunting for Exoplanets with AI,” demonstrates how Artificial Intelligence transforms the way we explore planets beyond our Solar System.
By analyzing light curve data from telescopes like Kepler and TESS, AI can identify planetary transits quickly and with greater accuracy.
The combination of machine learning and astronomy speeds up discoveries, minimizes errors, and paves the path toward finding Earth-like worlds.

References / Useful Links:
🌍 NASA Exoplanet Exploration: https://exoplanets.nasa.gov/

🔭 NASA TESS Mission: https://www.nasa.gov/tess/

✨ Kepler Mission: https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/kepler/overview/

🤖 AI for Space Research (NASA Frontier Development Lab): https://fdl.nasa.gov/

📊 Light Curve Data (Kepler/TESS Archives): https://archive.stsci.edu/
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do / How does it work?


Our project employs Artificial Intelligence (AI) to identify exoplanets, which are planets that orbit a star outside our own Solar System.
A telescope from NASA (like Kepler, TESS) collects the light curve data, the brightness of the star over time.
When a planet passes in front of the star, the star dims slightly -- this is known as the transit method.
We train a model of AI to take the brightness data, apply a method to detect whether there are consistent dimming episodes, and categorize those that are true planetary signatures versus noise or false positive signals (such as starspots, instrumental artifacts, etc.).
We built a prototype model comprised of an LED (light source), a rotating planet model (styrofoam ball), a light sensor (LDR) and controller (Arduino/Python) to capture and process the brightness data.

2. What benefit does it include?


Faster Discovery - The AI can go through thousands of light curves in seconds and identify exoplanets much more quickly as compared to a human effort.
More Accurate - Machine learning reduces human errant triggering or false detections.
Scalable - Capability to sift through massive data sets across multiple telescopes simultaneously.
Cost effective - Less human labor involved to analyze light curves saves time and data resources.
Helps future missions - The AI will help refine many of the stars with the greatest promise for scientists to observe further as a complementary examination.

3. What is the proposed impact of the project?


The project aims to transform exoplanet detection to be faster, smarter, and more reliable.
The project promotes the integration of AI with space research and citizen science, encouraging the engagement of young researchers to implement technology into their research on astronomy.
In the end, this research will help contribute to humanity's quest to find Earth-like worlds and other possible indications of life beyond our solar system.

4. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

Hardware: LED light (star), thermocol/ball (planet), an LDR sensor, Arduino or Raspberry Pi, a motor, and a battery.
Software: Python, Arduino IDE, basic AI/ML model (TensorFlow or Scikit-learn), and visualization tools.
Technical: light curve simulation, pattern recognition, and supervised learning
Libraries: NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, and TensorFlow/Keras.


5. How is the project creative?


It brings astronomy, physics, and AI together in a relatively simple physical model.
It involves a tangible model to demonstrate a real-world concept in space research using inexpensive materials.
The simulation visually demonstrates how telescopes can detect planets, providing a visual representation of an otherwise abstract idea showing the potential for programming for the young researchers.

6. What factors did your team take into account?

Feasibility: The model needed to be simple enough to build, but scientifically accurate.

Reliability: They tried to use realistic, noise affected data, to train AI models.

Accessibility: They ensured that students would be able to reproduce the set up with basic equipment.

Collaboration: All group members contributed to the research, coding, model building, and designing.

Presentation: They wanted to ensure that it was clear, scientifically accurate and visually attractive to gain engagement from the audience.

projectDetails.name: NimbusX
projectDetails.summary:
"Will It Rain On My Parade?" is an advanced multi-temporal weather intelligence system that predicts extreme weather risks up to 2 years ahead using NASA's POWER API climatology data. The project combines cutting-edge prediction methodologies including machine learning ensemble models (Random Forest and Gradient Boosting), physics-based atmospheric calculations, statistical percentile analysis, and innovative neural network architectures featuring Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN), attention mechanisms, chaos theory, and spectral analysis.

The system fetches 30-year NASA climatology data (1991-2020) across multiple parameters including temperature, precipitation, wind speed, humidity, and dew point. It performs sophisticated feature engineering using atmospheric physics principles such as heat index, wind chill, WBGT calculations, and Coriolis effects. The advanced ensemble predictor weighs multiple model outputs with adaptive confidence-based weighting to generate risk probabilities for extreme heat, extreme cold, heavy precipitation, strong winds, and heat discomfort.

Built with Python/Flask backend and featuring year-aware temporal analysis, the system provides comprehensive 2-year weather risk forecasting across multiple temporal horizons (short-term, seasonal, and climate projections) with detailed confidence metrics and innovation scoring.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does and How It Works

"Will It Rain On My Parade?" is a comprehensive weather risk prediction platform designed to help users plan outdoor activities and events 1-2 years in advance. The system operates through a sophisticated multi-layered architecture:app.py

Data Acquisition Layer:

  • Fetches historical climatology data from NASA's POWER API, accessing 30-year climate averages (1991-2020) for any location globallynasa_api.py
  • Retrieves 7 key meteorological parameters: temperature at 2 meters (T2M), max/min temperature, corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), wind speed at 2 meters (WS2M), relative humidity (RH2M), and dew point temperaturenasa_api.py
  • Supports multi-API aggregation including OpenWeatherMap and WeatherAPI for real-time and forecast data integrationmulti_api_weather.py

Advanced Prediction Engine:
The system employs a unique 4-model ensemble approach with adaptive weighting:ensemble_predictor.py

  1. Machine Learning Model (25% weight): Implements Random Forest and Gradient Boosting regressors trained on 6,000+ synthetic samples with 13+ engineered features including heat index, wind chill, atmospheric stability indices, and Fourier-transformed seasonal cyclesml_weather_predictor.py
  2. Physics-Based Model (25% weight): Calculates risks using actual atmospheric physics equations including Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT), geostrophic wind calculations with Coriolis effect, and comprehensive heat stress indicesensemble_predictor.py
  3. Statistical Model (15% weight): Employs percentile-based probability calculations comparing target month values against annual distributions to identify extreme conditionsdata_processor.py
  4. Advanced Neural Model (35% weight - highest): Simulates Temporal Convolutional Networks with attention mechanisms, chaos theory embedding using Lorenz attractors, and spectral analysis for multi-horizon predictionsneural_weather_model.py

Multi-Temporal Prediction Horizons:

  • Short-term (1-14 days): TCN + Attention mechanisms
  • Seasonal (1-12 months): Spectral analysis + climate indices
  • Climate projections (1-2 years): Chaos theory + trend analysisneural_weather_model.py+1

Year-Aware Feature Engineering:
The system incorporates advanced temporal features enabling historical analysis and future forecasting, including year offsets, climate era indicators, century-scale cyclical patterns, and year-adjusted chaos embeddingsml_weather_predictor.py+1

Benefits and Intended Impact

For Event Planners: Provides reliable 2-year advance weather risk assessment for weddings, festivals, conferences, and outdoor gatherings, enabling better venue selection and contingency planning.app.py

For Agricultural Planning: Helps farmers anticipate extreme weather conditions for crop planning and harvest scheduling using NASA's agroclimatology data.nasa_api.py

For Travel Industry: Enables tour operators and travelers to select optimal dates for outdoor activities with quantified risk probabilities.gemini_agent.py

For Climate Awareness: Demonstrates practical applications of NASA Earth observation data for public understanding of climate patterns and long-term weather variability.app.py

Accessibility: The system democratizes access to sophisticated weather intelligence that typically requires expensive meteorological services, using freely available NASA data.nasa_api.py

Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software

Programming Languages:

  • Python 3.x (primary backend language)app.py

Backend Framework:

projectDetails.name: AstroPlanner: Historical Risk Engine
projectDetails.summary:
AstroPlanner is a personalized web application that provides a statistical likelihood of adverse weather conditions for any planned outdoor event, using the principles of NASA Earth Observation (EO) historical data analysis.

The app addresses the challenge by allowing a user to input a specific location (Lat/Lon) and month to conduct a customized query. It then simulates processing decades of NASA EO variables (temperature, precipitation, wind speed, and humidity) to calculate the historical probability of encountering "very hot," "very cold," "very windy," "very wet," or "very uncomfortable" conditions. This is crucial because it offers long-range risk assessment, enabling users to plan events months in advance by quantifying the odds of extreme weather. The project is implemented using only HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for maximum accessibility and speed.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

AstroPlanner provides a risk score (a percentage likelihood) for five adverse conditions.

  1. User Input: The user enters the geographical coordinates (Latitude/Longitude) and the target Month for their event.
  2. Historical Analysis (Simulated): The core JavaScript engine contains a structured data model that simulates the analysis of decades of NASA EO data for that specific region and time of year. This simulation involves defining "Very Adverse" thresholds (e.g., 90th percentile of historical max temperature for "Very Hot").
  3. Likelihood Calculation: The app calculates the probability based on how often these thresholds were historically exceeded. For instance, if a location experienced "Very Wet" conditions 5 out of 25 historical Julys, the app reports a 20% likelihood.
  4. Output: The results are visualized on five distinct, color-coded risk gauges, giving the user an immediate and clear assessment.

What benefits does it have?

AstroPlanner is invaluable for long-term planning. Current weather apps offer forecasts of 7-14 days; AstroPlanner allows travelers, event organizers, and hikers to assess weather risk for dates months in advance based on historical climate patterns, helping them decide the best possible time and location for their activity.

Intended Impact

The project's intended impact is to increase public awareness of climate variability at a granular level and promote preparedness. By translating complex, massive NASA datasets into a simple, actionable probability score, it empowers citizen scientists and the general public to make data-driven decisions regarding their outdoor plans, improving safety and resource management.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS (loaded via CDN)
  • Software/IDE: Any standard text editor (e.g., VS Code)
  • Deployment: Single-file deployment for maximum speed and compatibility.

How is your project creative?

The project is creative in two main ways:

  1. Composite Discomfort Index: We went beyond simple temperature/wind by creating a composite risk metric for "Very Uncomfortable" conditions, simulating a calculation based on historical heat and humidity data, which is a key factor in human safety.
  2. Data Abstraction: We implemented a clear, internal data structure and logic in pure JavaScript to convincingly simulate the complex, multi-decade processing of large NASA EO files within the strict time limits of the hackathon, demonstrating a clear path to a production-ready solution.

projectDetails.name: ASTEROID IMPACT SIMULATOR
projectDetails.summary:
Our solution to the “Meteor Madness” challenge is an interactive visualization and simulation platform that integrates NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) API data with USGS impact models. The tool allows users to simulate asteroid impact scenarios, visualize real-time asteroid trajectories, and predict the consequences of potential collisions with Earth.

To enhance predictive capability, we implemented a Machine Learning (ML) model using Logistic Regression — a supervised classification algorithm that estimates the probability of an asteroid being hazardous or non-hazardous based on parameters such as size, velocity, miss distance, and estimated impact energy.

The ML model analyzes historical asteroid data to identify key risk factors and helps classify new asteroids by their potential threat level. Through this integration of data visualization, physical modeling, and machine learning, our solution provides an intuitive and educational platform for researchers, policymakers, and the public to better understand asteroid risks and explore mitigation strategies in an accessible and engaging way.
projectDetails.details: A newly identified near-Earth asteroid, "Impactor-2025," poses a potential threat to Earth, but do we have the tools to enable the public and decision makers to understand and mitigate its risks? NASA datasets include information about known asteroids and the United States Geological Survey provides critical information that could enable modeling the effects of asteroid impacts, but this data needs to be integrated to enable effective visualization and decision making. Your challenge is to develop an interactive visualization and simulation tool that uses real data to help users model asteroid impact scenarios, predict consequences, and evaluate potential mitigation strategies.

projectDetails.name: AtmoSphere
projectDetails.summary: AtmoSphere is a personalized climate analysis tool that empowers users to plan outdoor activities with confidence, months or years in advance. We developed a web application that transforms over 40 years of NASA's POWER project data into a simple, actionable "Comfort Score." Our app directly addresses the challenge by allowing users to define their own personal comfort profile for temperature, wind, rain, and humidity, and even weight which factors are most important to them. Using an interactive map, users can analyze a specific point or an entire region, like a hiking trail. This is important because it replaces generic "average weather" with a personalized, data-driven likelihood of a location matching what you consider a perfect day, reducing uncertainty and making long-term planning easier for everyone.
projectDetails.details:
What AtmoSphere Does

AtmoSphere is a personal climate compass designed to solve a fundamental problem in long-term planning: weather uncertainty. While standard forecasts are useful for the week ahead, they don't help a family planning a vacation six months from now, or an adventurer choosing the best time of year to visit a national park. Our project directly addresses this challenge by providing a personalized, data-driven climate analysis for any location on Earth, powered by over 40 years of NASA's historical Earth-observation data.

How It Works

We have built a full-stack web application that leverages over 40 years of NASA's POWER project data. The workflow is simple and user-centric:

  1. Interactive Selection: Instead of typing in coordinates, users can visually draw a region of interest on our interactive Leaflet map—from a single city block to an entire national park.
  2. Personalization: Users define their ideal weather in a "Comfort Profile," setting their preferences for temperature, wind, humidity, and rain. Crucially, they can also assign "Importance" weights to each factor, telling the app what matters most to them.
  3. Data Analysis: This user-defined profile is sent to our Python FastAPI backend. The backend queries the NASA POWER API for the long-term climatological averages for the selected region and date. For area analyses, it intelligently samples multiple points within the user's drawn polygon.
  4. The "Comfort Score": Our unique algorithm then processes this NASA data, comparing it against the user's personal profile and weights to calculate a single, easy-to-understand "Comfort Score." A high score indicates that the historical climate of that location is a strong match for the user's personal definition of a perfect day.

Benefits and Impact

The intended impact of AtmoSphere is to replace the anxiety of the unknown with the confidence to plan.

  • For Families & Travelers: It empowers users to make informed decisions about vacations and events months or years in advance, ensuring their plans are not disrupted by historically adverse conditions.
  • For Adventurers & Photographers: The app provides unique "Specialty Scores," like a "Golden Hour Quality" rating, helping them find the perfect atmospheric conditions for their craft.
  • Making NASA Data Accessible: Our most important benefit is making NASA's vast and complex scientific datasets accessible and personally relevant to everyone, turning climatological data into a tool for personal well-being and planning.

How is Your Project Creative?

The creativity of AtmoSphere lies in its inversion of the traditional weather app. Instead of being a passive recipient of a generic forecast, the user is an active participant. They are not asking "What will the weather be?"; they are asking, "Where on Earth can I find the climate that feels like my perfect day?". The personalization engine, the weighted scoring, and the specialty scores are all creative applications of NASA's data to answer a deeply human and personal question.

Tools, Languages, and Software

  • NASA Data Source: We exclusively used the NASA POWER API for its 40+ years of global climatological data on temperature, wind, humidity, precipitation, and solar radiation.
  • Frontend: Our frontend was built using React with the Vite development environment. The interactive map was created with Leaflet.js and the Leaflet.draw plugin. Styling was handled with CSS Modules for component-level scope.
  • Backend: The backend is a high-performance API built with Python and the FastAPI framework. We used Pydantic for robust data validation and the httpx library for asynchronous requests to the NASA POWER API.
  • Development Aids: We utilized AI tools like Google's Gemini and ChatGPT for initial research and GitHub Copilot to accelerate boilerplate code generation.

Data Processing & Our Scoring Algorithm

The "magic" of AtmoSphere is in how we process NASA's data to create a score that is unique to each user. Here is the step-by-step methodology:

Step 1: Data Reception from NASA POWER API

Our Python FastAPI backend receives the user's selected location (or region) and date. It constructs a request to the NASA POWER API for its climatology endpoint. We request the long-term monthly averages for a suite of parameters, including:

  • Temperature (T2M, T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN)
  • Wind Speed (WS10M)
  • Relative Humidity (RH2M)
  • Precipitation (PRECTOTCORR)
  • Insolation Clearness Index (KT)

The POWER API returns a JSON object with these 40+ year averages, which forms the scientific basis for our analysis.

Step 2: The "Pass/Fail" Check

Our backend then compares these historical averages against the user's defined ComfortProfile thresholds. For each of the four main factors, we perform a binary check:

  • Does the average temperature fall within the user's min/max range? (Pass/Fail)
  • Is the average wind speed below the user's maximum? (Pass/Fail)
  • Is the estimated rain chance below the user's maximum? (Pass/Fail)
  • Is the average humidity below the user's maximum? (Pass/Fail)

A "Pass" is assigned a base score of 1, and a "Fail" is assigned a 0.

Step 3: Applying Personal Weights (The Math)

This is the core of our personalization engine. We multiply each base score (0 or 1) by the user's "Importance" weight (a value from 0.0 to 3.0). This creates a "weighted score" for each factor.

Step 4: The Final Score Calculation

The final Overall Score is the percentage of the user's "total possible comfort" that the location's climate achieves. We calculate it by dividing the sum of the Weighted Scores by the sum of all the User's Weights.

(4.5 / 5.0) * 100 = 90

This weighted model ensures that the final score is a true reflection of what matters most to each individual user. This methodology demonstrates a creative and impactful use of NASA's data, turning a generic dataset into a deeply personal insight.

projectDetails.details:
Project Title

RT WeatherSense – A NASA-powered Weather Insight & Prediction App by Team Red Torque

What It Does

“RT WeatherSense ” is an interactive web application built using Streamlit. It analyzes real NASA Earth observation data to provide rainfall probabilities, temperature trends, and satellite imagery for any location in India.

Key functionalities include:

  • Selecting a city or clicking on a live map to get accurate coordinates.
  • Analyzing weather data from TRMM and GLDAS datasets.
  • Estimating rainfall probability for a chosen date using historical precipitation records.
  • Viewing historical temperature and rainfall trends.
  • Accessing MODIS satellite imagery for the past five years around the selected region.

The interface is clean and user-friendly, designed for both technical and non-technical users.

Benefits and Impact

This project makes NASA’s open climate data understandable and useful for a wide audience, from researchers to the general public.

Benefits:

  • Provides localized climate insights without requiring coding knowledge.
  • Helps communities and event organizers anticipate rainfall using real historical data.
  • Encourages awareness of climate variability and the importance of Earth observation.
  • Demonstrates how open data and citizen science can support sustainable decisions in agriculture, urban planning, and disaster preparedness.

Impact:
The app bridges the gap between raw scientific datasets and public understanding, turning large amounts of satellite data into an intuitive story of Earth’s weather systems.

Tools, Technologies, and Datasets

Software & Libraries:

  • Streamlit for the web application
  • Folium + Streamlit-Folium for interactive maps
  • Matplotlib for rainfall and temperature plots
  • Xarray & Pandas for handling large NetCDF datasets
  • Geopy for geocoding city names
  • Pillow and Requests for displaying NASA MODIS imagery

Datasets:

  • TRMM 3B42 Daily – precipitation
  • GLDAS NOAH L4 Model – surface temperature
  • MODIS Terra – satellite imagery

Languages: Python 3.11
Hardware: Standard personal computer capable of processing NASA NetCDF datasets

Creativity and Technical Achievements

  • Real-time rendering of MODIS satellite imagery using NASA WMS services.
  • Combines spatial (map-based) and temporal (historical trends) analysis.
  • Engaging, modern dashboard design that balances scientific accuracy with accessibility.
  • Built entirely from open-source tools and NASA datasets for reproducibility.

Alignment with NASA Space Apps 2025 Criteria

  • Impact: Promotes understanding of NASA Earth data for local climate awareness.
  • Use of Data: Integrates multiple NASA datasets meaningfully.
  • Creativity: Combines accessibility, interactive design, and technical depth.
  • Technical Achievement: Efficiently handles multi-dimensional NetCDF data and satellite imagery.
  • Presentation: Polished, easy-to-navigate interface with clear visualization.

Future Extensions

  • AI-based rainfall prediction models using TRMM data.
  • Integration of GPM IMERG and Sentinel datasets for higher resolution.
  • Global coverage with region filters and animated visualizations.
  • API version for mobile or third-party integration.

Summary

RT WeatherSense is a Streamlit-based weather analysis app by Team Red Torque that uses NASA satellite data (TRMM, GLDAS, MODIS) to provide rainfall probabilities, temperature trends, and satellite imagery for locations across India. Users can select a city or click on a map to get precise coordinates, view historical rainfall and temperature trends, and explore MODIS images from the past five years. The app turns complex NASA datasets into a simple, interactive dashboard accessible to both researchers and the general public.

The app processes large NASA NetCDF datasets using Python libraries like Pandas, Xarray, Matplotlib, and Folium. It combines spatial interaction (map selection) with temporal analysis (historical trends) in one user-friendly interface. MODIS imagery is fetched in real-time from NASA’s WMS servers, creating a visually engaging and scientifically accurate experience.

This project makes open NASA data practical and understandable, supporting decision-making for students, researchers, event planners, and communities. Future improvements include AI-based rainfall prediction, integration of higher-resolution datasets, global coverage, and an API version. The tool developed under challenges “Will It Rain on My Parade?” demonstrates how open data, coding, and creativity can transform massive climate datasets into actionable insights.

projectDetails.name: Interactive Asteroid Impact Test
projectDetails.summary:
This project is an interactive web-based simulation that models asteroid impacts on Earth. It uses 3D graphics with Three.js along with a geographic map made with Leaflet. Users can choose where impacts happen and adjust asteroid factors like diameter, velocity, angle, and density. 

Key Features:

Realistic Earth depiction. High-resolution textures show continents and oceans authentically. 

Asteroid orbit and impact. The asteroid orbits continuously and then travels along a curved path to the chosen impact point. 

Impact effects. Collisions create a crater and a visible impact zone on both the 3D globe and map, scaled based on user-set factors. 

Impact assessment. The simulation calculates and shows estimated fatalities, tsunami risk, crater size, and impact energy based on location and asteroid details. 

Seamless integration. It combines 3D rendering and mapping to create an engaging experience for education and planetary defense research. 

Technologies Used: 
Three.js, Leaflet.js, WebGL, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. 

Objectives: 

Show the prediction of asteroid impacts.

Teach users about the effects and risks of asteroid impacts. 

Offer a tool for raising awareness about planetary hazards.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, Asteroid Impact Simulation, is an interactive web-based tool that estimates the consequences of an asteroid hitting Earth. Users can adjust key asteroid parameters, such as diameter, velocity, impact angle, and density, using sliders and select an impact location on a global map. The simulation then calculates the asteroid’s kinetic energy, impact crater size, estimated fatalities, and potential tsunami hazard in real-time. A 3D visualization displays the asteroid orbiting Earth and impacting at the chosen location, along with an animated impact and crater formation.

Benefits & Intended Impact:

This tool helps visualize and understand the potential dangers of asteroid impacts, raising awareness about planetary defense. It serves educational purposes, allowing students, educators, and enthusiasts to explore how different asteroid properties affect the severity of impacts. By simulating realistic scenarios, it promotes critical thinking about risk, preparedness, and planetary science.

Technical Details:

Languages/Frameworks: HTML, CSS, JavaScript

Libraries: Three.js (3D graphics), Leaflet.js (interactive map)

Software: Standard web browser, GitHub Pages for hosting

Assets: Earth texture for realistic 3D visualization

Creativity & Design Considerations:

The project is creative because it combines interactive 3D visualization with geospatial mapping, offering an intuitive way to explore a scientific problem. We focused on scientific accuracy, such as kinetic energy calculations and crater formation, user experience with interactive sliders and a live map, and visual appeal through animated impacts, shockwaves, and a data panel.

Team Considerations:

We prioritized accessibility, ensuring the simulation runs in any browser without extra software, and clarity to make sure both casual users and educators can understand the results. Additionally, we made the project fully interactive, allowing users to experiment with various scenarios in real-time.

Additional Resource:
A presentation (PPT) explaining the project’s concept, development process, and potential applications can be viewed here: https://1drv.ms/p/c/b8f158e7f750fd33/ER7NemqchEBBhr9l3_9rTxgB3bNP8D87mrS9kRXQf9zblA?e=xsvOZE

projectDetails.name: Disaster damage detection
projectDetails.summary: This project uses satellite imagery analysis to identify and visualize disaster-affected areas. It takes three main inputs — a pre-disaster image, a post-disaster image, and a damage mask (which indicates the detected damaged regions). Using Python libraries like Rasterio and Matplotlib, the program overlays the red damage areas on the post-disaster image, creating a clear visual comparison of changes before and after the disaster. The result is saved as both a visual image (PNG) and a GeoTIFF file that includes geographical coordinates, enabling accurate mapping and disaster impact assessment for rescue and recovery planning.
projectDetails.details:
Our project uses Artificial Intelligence (AI) and satellite imagery to detect, visualize, and assess disaster-affected areas. It compares pre-disaster and post-disaster images captured by satellites and generates a damage mask that highlights the affected regions. Using this mask, the system overlays the detected damage in red on the post-disaster image, providing a clear visual representation of the impact.

This project is built using Python, along with libraries such as Rasterio, NumPy, and Matplotlib for geospatial data processing, visualization, and overlay creation. The final outputs are provided as both PNG images and GeoTIFF files with accurate geographical coordinates, enabling integration with GIS systems.

The main benefits include faster damage assessment, reduced human effort, and data-driven decision-making for emergency responders and authorities. The intended impact is to help disaster management teams quickly identify the most affected areas, prioritize rescue operations, and plan effective recovery efforts.

Our team aimed to create a simple yet powerful AI-assisted mapping tool that is creative in the way it combines AI, geospatial analysis, and data visualization to solve real-world problems. We focused on accuracy, ease of interpretation, and applicability across different types of disasters such as floods, earthquakes, and wildfires.

Space missions rely on highly stable and efficient power systems to maintain life-support, communications, propulsion, and scientific instruments. Any failure or fluctuation in spacecraft power can lead to catastrophic mission loss.
This project proposes the Spacecraft Power Anomaly Detection and Recovery System (SPADRS) — an intelligent embedded platform capable of real-time monitoring, fault prediction, and autonomous recovery from electrical failures in spacecraft power distribution systems.

SPADRS integrates radiation-hardened microcontrollers, redundant voltage/current sensors, and machine-learning-based anomaly prediction models. It logs all power events to non-volatile space-grade memory, communicates via SpaceWire/CAN bus, and can autonomously reroute power from redundant solar/battery modules during failure events.

The system is designed for deployment in low-Earth orbit (LEO), lunar orbit, and planetary surface missions, ensuring continuous power availability and protecting high-value spacecraft subsystems. SPADRS demonstrates how terrestrial power-monitoring technology can be adapted and ruggedized for extreme extraterrestrial environments, contributing to future NASA Artemis and Deep Space Gateway missions.
projectDetails.details:
New Objectives

  1. Develop a fault-tolerant embedded system for spacecraft power anomaly detection.
  2. Integrate machine learning models for predictive failure analysis.
  3. Ensure radiation and thermal resilience across −150°C to +120°C.
  4. Log and transmit data through redundant communication channels.
  5. Demonstrate autonomous recovery protocols during simulated solar power loss.
  6. Design for modular compatibility with CubeSat and Lunar Gateway systems.

5. Proposed Methodology

  1. Simulation Phase
    • Use MATLAB/Simulink & LTspice for spacecraft power distribution modeling.
    • Simulate transient loads, battery degradation, and solar flux variations.
    • Build prototype using Teensy 4.1 or STM32F4 microcontroller.
    • Integrate high-precision current/voltage sensors with Kalman filtering.
    • Add dual power rails and watchdog timers for self-recovery.
    • Implement fault logs with CRC verification in FRAM.
    • Use telemetry packets compatible with NASA’s CCSDS data standards.
    • Train a lightweight neural model to classify anomalies from sensor data.
    • Predict overloads or degradation trends for preventive maintenance.

6. Space Applications

  • ISS power bus anomaly detection
  • Lunar surface rover energy management
  • Satellite battery degradation prediction
  • Space habitat energy analytics
  • Mars base microgrid stability system

7. Expected Outcomes

  • Reliable detection and prediction of electrical faults in extreme space environments.
  • Extended mission life by preventing catastrophic power failures.
  • Reduced ground intervention through autonomous recovery actions.
  • Contribution to NASA’s Deep Space Gateway and Mars mission architectures.

8. Future Scope

  • Integrate AI-driven energy optimization for multi-source (solar, RTG, battery) systems.
  • Add radiation event correlation using cosmic ray sensors.
  • Develop space-qualified PCB using polyimide flexible circuits.
  • Interface with NASA’s flight-certified avionics system for real missions.

NASA Orbital Luxury Habitat (NOLH) Summary
The NASA Orbital Luxury Habitat (NOLH) is a visionary proposal for a 10-person space hotel in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), marking NASA's shift from pure exploration to commercial space experience. The project aims to enable private citizens to safely and comfortably vacation in space for 2–5 days.
The total development cost is estimated at $1.1 Billion, including the station and a dedicated 10-passenger Orbital Transfer Vehicle (OTV). Based on proven ISS technologies, the NOLH will feature private cabins, a dining lounge, and a 360° Earth-view dome window for a luxury experience.
With a ticket price of $12–$20M per person, the venture projects a strong profit margin, estimating a break-even in 7–17 missions. NASA will act as the enabler, providing expertise, infrastructure, and safety standards, while private partners handle design, funding, and marketing, creating a sustainable commercial LEO ecosystem.

projectDetails.name: Project SpaceVoyagers333
projectDetails.summary:
SpaceTrash Hack is a visionary, gamified initiative designed to tackle the dual challenges of waste management and resource scarcity for a future human settlement on Mars. It moves beyond traditional recycling by creating a closed-loop, circular economy where all "waste" is viewed as a valuable resource.

The Problem it Solves:
Extreme Resource Scarcity: Mars has no native infrastructure. Shipping materials from Earth is astronomically expensive (thousands of dollars per pound).

Waste Accumulation: A human colony will generate significant waste (packaging, broken tools, organic waste, etc.). Letting it pile up is unsafe, unsanitary, and wasteful.

Psychological Well-being: Early Martian settlers will face isolation and a high-stress environment. A sense of purpose, community, and creativity is crucial for mental health.
projectDetails.details:
An inventive project called SpaceTrash Hack is addressing waste management, one of the most important issues facing long-duration Mars missions. Every item that is thrown away, including food packaging, damaged equipment, worn clothing, and biological waste, represents a risk as well as a resource that has been lost because there is no way to replenish supplies or remove trash.

The project uses a collaborative hackathon format to bring together scientists, engineers, and designers to create lightweight, low-power, and useful recycling solutions for Mars. Important areas of focus include:

Chemical and mechanical recycling systems that convert organics, metals, and plastics into fuel, building materials, or feedstock for 3D printing.

Small, self-sufficient sorting and processing machines that can use little energy to function in the hostile Martian environment.

Biological processes that provide energy and life support by converting organic waste into water, fertiliser, and methane.

projectDetails.name: Hidden Drivers of Human Wildlife conflicts - Wayanad Kerala
projectDetails.summary: Using 20 years of NASA SAR & MODIS data we mapped farmland fragmentation and built-up spread around Kerala’s forest edge, then overlaid wildlife-conflict records. The resulting high-resolution dashboard quantifies how creeping human land-use drives elephant and boar encounters, giving planners a transparent, evidence-based tool to site buffers, crops and early-warning systems.
projectDetails.details: Our project integrates 20 years of NASA SAR, MODIS NDVI, and Kerala land-use records to quantify how farmland fragmentation and spontaneous construction near forest edges drive human–wildlife conflict. In Google Earth Engine we speckle-filter Sentinel-1 and Landsat-8 imagery, apply a Random-Forest classifier to map forest, plantation, paddy, and built-up pixels at 10 m resolution, then compute patch-size and edge-density metrics within a 1 km forest buffer. Kernel-smoothed wildlife-incident coordinates from state records are overlaid to reveal a strong spatial correlation: cells that lost >30 % contiguous forest and gained >15 % built-up area account for 83 % of elephant and boar raids. A lightweight Flask-Leaflet dashboard serves the resulting red-amber-green risk layer to planners and farmers on any phone; by sliding the time-bar users watch interfaces turn from green to red and download a PDF report card that guides crop choice, fencing grants, or camera-trap placement. Entirely open-source (Python, Docker, QGIS, pylandstats), the tool converts scattered remote-sensing and census data into an actionable, reproducible evidence base intended to cut crop-loss compensation by 20 % and human/animal fatalities by 10 % within five years across Wayanad .

projectDetails.name: Project Starmes
projectDetails.summary:
The extreme constraints of deep space exploration are accelerating the development of highly efficient, closed-loop recycling systems. For long-duration missions to the Moon or Mars, where resupply is impossible, waste must be treated as a valuable resource rather than a liability.

Key innovations include thermochemical conversion systems like NASA's OSCAR, which turns mixed waste into useful gases and water, and material reprocessing for in-space manufacturing, which converts trash into feedstock for 3D printing. A third paradigm, "Logistics-to-Living," eliminates waste by designing dual-use packaging that can be reconfigured into habitat furniture.

These space-age technologies provide a transformative blueprint for Earth. They have the potential to decentralize waste management, create hyper-local circular manufacturing, and fundamentally redesign products to eliminate single-use packaging, revolutionizing terrestrial industry and paving the way for a sustainable, circular economy.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does and How It Works

The project analyzes and synthesizes information on pioneering waste management technologies being developed for long-duration space missions, framing them as a blueprint for revolutionizing terrestrial industries. It focuses on three core paradigms:

  1. Thermochemical Conversion: This approach uses automated, high-temperature reactors, like NASA's Orbital Syngas Commodity Augmentation Reactor (OSCAR), to break down mixed, unsorted waste (including plastics, food packaging, and even human waste simulants) into valuable basic resources. The primary outputs are "syngas"—a mix of methane, hydrogen, and carbon dioxide—along with recoverable water and metals. 
  2. Material Reprocessing for Manufacturing: This paradigm focuses on creating a closed-loop manufacturing ecosystem. It involves recycling sorted waste streams—such as plastics, textiles, and metals—into high-quality feedstock for on-demand 3D printing. This allows astronauts to produce necessary items like tools, utensils, and spare parts directly from their trash. 
  3. Dual-Use Design ("Logistics-to-Living"): This is a "pre-cycling" philosophy that aims to eliminate waste by design. Logistics packaging is engineered as a modular "kit-of-parts" with standardized connectors. Once the contents are used, the packaging can be reassembled into habitat furniture like desks, chairs, and partitions, transforming a liability into a functional asset. 

Benefits and Intended Impact

The primary benefit of these technologies in space is enabling self-sufficient, long-duration missions by reducing launch mass, saving habitat volume, and minimizing reliance on costly resupply from Earth. 

The intended impact of the project is to demonstrate how these space-age solutions can be adapted to solve major challenges on Earth. By transferring these concepts, the goal is to:

  • Decentralize Waste Management: Enable on-site waste processing for remote communities, disaster zones, or hospitals, converting waste into energy and clean byproducts. 
  • Create a True Circular Economy: Foster hyper-local manufacturing where communities can turn their own waste into new products, strengthening supply chain resilience and reducing the need for virgin materials. 
  • Revolutionize Product Design: Inspire industries to move beyond single-use items and design packaging that has a second life as a functional part of the product system. 

Ultimately, the project aims to show a viable path away from the linear "take-make-dispose" model toward a more sustainable and resilient circular economy.

Development Tools

As a writer, my project was the research, synthesis, and composition of the report itself. The tools used were those of my craft:

  • Information Synthesis: I drew upon a wide array of materials, including technical papers from engineering conferences, official reports from space agencies, and mission planning documents.
  • Narrative Construction: The core of the work involved weaving these technical details into a cohesive and compelling narrative that connects the challenges of space exploration with the opportunities for innovation on Earth.
  • Stylistic Composition: The report was crafted to be accessible to a broad audience, translating complex engineering concepts into clear, impactful language.

Creative Approach and Factors Considered

The project's creativity lies in its interdisciplinary synthesis. It bridges the gap between aerospace engineering, environmental science, industrial design, and economics. Rather than presenting the technologies in isolation, the creative approach was to frame them as a unified solution to a global problem, using the extreme case of space exploration as a powerful lens.

During the writing process, several key factors were considered:

  • Technical Accuracy: Ensuring that the descriptions of the technologies and their processes were precise and faithful to the source material.
  • Clarity of the "Why": Focusing not just on what the technologies do, but why they are necessary for space and how that necessity drives innovation applicable to Earth.
  • Scalability and Adaptation: Analyzing the hurdles—economic, regulatory, and cultural—to adapting these systems for terrestrial use, providing a balanced perspective on both the potential and the challenges.
  • Narrative Arc: Structuring the report to first establish the problem (the unsustainability of waste in space), then present the solutions (the three paradigms), and finally explore the transformative impact of bringing those solutions home to Earth.

projectDetails.name: Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings
projectDetails.summary:
Project Solar Vision is an AI-powered storytelling experience created for NASA’s Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings challenge.
Our goal is to make space weather — solar storms, flares, and their impact on Earth — understandable, emotional, and inspiring through cinematic storytelling.

We combined NASA’s real scientific resources on solar storms and solar flares with artificial intelligence tools to transform space data into an immersive narrative journey.
Through the eyes of our main character, Arjun, a young stargazer from Earth, audiences witness how the Sun’s storms influence communication systems, satellites, climate, and even daily life.

The story is narrated from a human perspective but guided by cosmic forces — showing how interconnected the Earth and the Sun truly are.

To build this project, we used a blend of creative and technical tools:

🧠 ChatGPT – for scientific storytelling, scriptwriting, and scene design.

🗣️ D-ID – to generate realistic AI voiceovers that bring emotion to the story.

🎨 AI Image Generators (e.g., Leonardo AI, Pika, Runway) – to visualize each moment of solar activity and Earth’s response.

☀️ NASA’s Space Weather Data – especially resources about Solar Storms and Flares, ensuring our story reflects real cosmic science.

Our mission is to educate, inspire, and visualize how the Sun’s invisible weather shapes our technology, environment, and future — using the power of AI to bridge science and storytelling.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do / How does it work?
Project Solar Vision transforms real NASA data on solar storms and flares into a cinematic storytelling experience powered by artificial intelligence.
The project takes complex scientific information about space weather and presents it through a human perspective — using the story of Arjun, a young stargazer whose life is influenced by solar activity.
Each scene is crafted using AI-generated visuals, voiceovers, and scripts, making the invisible forces of space weather both educational and emotionally engaging.

What benefits does it have?
The project bridges the gap between scientific knowledge and public understanding.
It helps viewers, especially students and young audiences, grasp how space weather affects daily life — from satellite communications and GPS systems to climate and power grids.
By using storytelling and AI visuals, the project makes learning about the Sun’s influence on Earth both accessible and inspiring.
It encourages curiosity about space science and promotes awareness of space weather’s real-world impact.

What is the intended impact of the project?
Our goal is to humanize space weather — showing that it’s not just data or science, but something that shapes our lives.
We want audiences to understand how solar activity directly affects the planet and to feel connected to the broader universe.
We also aim to demonstrate how AI and storytelling can be used to simplify complex space concepts, inspire future scientists, and spark interest in NASA’s open data.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?
We combined creative AI and open scientific data resources to build the project:

  • NASA Resources: Solar Storm and Solar Flare datasets and archives
  • ChatGPT (OpenAI): Scriptwriting, story development, and educational narration
  • D-ID: Voice generation and narration delivery
  • AI Image Generators (Leonardo AI, Runway, Pika): Scene visualization and animation
  • CapCut & Runway Video Editor: Final video editing and sound design
  • Google Docs / Sheets: Team collaboration and scripting workflow

(No physical hardware was required — the project is fully digital and cloud-based.)

How is your project creative?
The project fuses science, art, and AI — blending real data with storytelling.
Instead of presenting raw facts, we created a cinematic journey where the Sun itself speaks, data becomes emotion, and space weather is visualized as a living force.
Our approach transforms traditional education into an immersive experience, inspiring curiosity and empathy toward science.
This creative method makes Project Solar Vision not just informative — but truly memorable.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific Accuracy: Ensuring that all events and terms about solar storms, flares, and their effects are supported by NASA’s verified data.
  • Accessibility: Making space weather easy to understand for general audiences, including students and beginners.
  • Visual and Emotional Engagement: Balancing factual storytelling with cinematic, emotional tone.
  • AI Ethics and Originality: Ensuring that all AI-generated content respects creative rights, privacy, and data integrity.
  • Impact and Inspiration: Designing the project to educate, inspire, and connect people emotionally to space science.

### AI-POWERED EXOPLANET DISCOVERY

The Challenge: Current exoplanet discovery relies on manual analysis of vast datasets from missions like Kepler and TESS. This process is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and prone to missing faint signals.

Our Solution: We propose a machine learning model, a deep neural network, trained on open-source NASA exoplanet datasets. This model will learn to identify the subtle, periodic dips in stellar brightness characteristic of transiting exoplanets.

The Impact:This AI-powered system will revolutionize exoplanet discovery, enabling the automated analysis of massive data streams. It will accelerate the identification of new worlds, even those with weak signals, and provide valuable insights into planetary formation and evolution. This project represents a powerful convergence of astrophysics and machine learning.

projectDetails.name: Project Tech Fordge
projectDetails.summary:
The project develops the NASA Bioscience Exploration Dashboard, an interactive platform designed to solve the challenge of navigating decades of fragmented bioscience publications and datasets stored across multiple NASA repositories. Researchers, mission planners, and decision-makers struggle to retrieve targeted information or identify knowledge gaps due to the lack of a unified access point.

To address this, the dashboard integrates data from sources like PubSpace, TechPort, NSPIRES, and ADS into a single system. It offers AI-generated publication summaries, trend visualizations, relational knowledge graphs, and advanced filtering capabilities. These features help users quickly uncover insights, track research trajectories, and connect related topics.

The solution is important because it transforms complex, siloed information into accessible intelligence—supporting strategic decisions, improving research efficiency, and revealing future opportunities in space bioscience.
projectDetails.details: Our project is a dynamic AI-powered dashboard designed to help users explore and understand NASA’s bioscience research publications. It works by summarizing over 600 studies using natural language processing, organizing them into an interactive knowledge graph, and providing tools for searching, filtering, and analyzing results. The dashboard highlights connections between experiments, organisms, missions, and outcomes, while an analytics panel identifies research trends, knowledge gaps, and areas of scientific progress. This provides clear benefits such as saving time, improving accessibility to complex research, and supporting scientists, mission planners, and managers in generating new hypotheses, planning safe Moon and Mars missions, and guiding investments in underexplored areas. The intended impact of the project is to make NASA’s vast research more accessible and actionable, ultimately supporting the safe and efficient exploration of space. Technically, the project was built using Python for data extraction and processing, GPT and HuggingFace models for AI summarization, Neo4j for knowledge graph creation, React.js/Streamlit for the dashboard, and Plotly/Cytoscape.js for data visualization. This combination of AI and visualization tools makes the project highly creative, as it not only summarizes text but also reveals hidden connections between studies in a way that traditional search tools cannot. In designing the project, our team considered user needs, data integrity, scalability, accessibility, and future growth, ensuring that the dashboard can evolve with new data and remain useful to diverse user communities.

This project responds to the need for making difficult satellite data easier to understand and more interesting for a general audience. By creating a visual narrative out of raw fire detection data, it encourages the audience to visualize how and where fires start globally and appreciate the significance of ongoing satellite surveillance.

It also alerts the public to the contribution of NASA's Terra mission to environment monitoring and managing disasters.
projectDetails.details:
Terra Satellite – Fire and Climate Monitoring System

What does it do / How does it work:
The Terra Satellite is an advanced Earth observation satellite designed to monitor wildfires, climate change, and air pollution from space. It captures high-resolution images of the Earth’s surface using specialized sensors that detect heat signatures, smoke patterns, and atmospheric gases.

These images are analyzed using artificial intelligence (AI) to detect forest fires, identify climate variations, and measure air pollution levels. The system can recognize hot spots where fires may be starting, track smoke spreading through the atmosphere, and monitor environmental changes like temperature rise and CO₂ emissions.

By combining data from NASA’s Terra Flagship satellite with AI-based analysis, the project helps provide real-time alerts and accurate environmental insights to scientists, governments, and disaster response teams.

Benefits of the Project:

  • Early Fire Detection: Quickly identifies and alerts authorities about wildfires to minimize damage.
  • Climate Change Monitoring: Tracks global temperature shifts and greenhouse gas emissions.
  • Air Quality Analysis: Detects pollutants and smoke, improving air quality management.
  • Disaster Prevention: Helps emergency services plan faster and safer responses.
  • Environmental Protection: Preserves forests, wildlife, and natural ecosystems.
  • Research Support: Provides valuable satellite data for climate and environmental studies.

Intended Impact:
The project aims to protect Earth’s environment and human lives by enabling early fire detection and long-term climate observation. It supports the global fight against climate change by offering reliable satellite data and AI-driven analysis. By improving our understanding of environmental patterns, the project encourages sustainability, climate action, and global awareness about pollution and forest conservation.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used:

  • ChatGPT: Used for prompt generation, research, and writing project explanations.
  • AI Video Maker (e.g., Synthesia, Pictory, or similar): Used to create visual and animated videos for presentation.
  • Pexels: Used for sourcing high-quality, copyright-free pictures related to space, nature, and the environment.
  • Clideo: Used for editing and combining video clips, voiceovers, and visuals into the final project video.
  • NASA Terra Flagship Satellite: Used as the main source of satellite photos and real environmental data.
  • Python / GIS Tools: (Conceptually) used for analyzing satellite images and visualizing heat maps or pollution data.

Creativity of the Project:
The project is creative because it brings together AI technology, satellite imagery, and environmental science to solve real-world problems. By using AI tools like ChatGPT for ideas, Pexels for visuals, and Clideo for editing, the team creatively blended technology and storytelling to make a complex scientific topic engaging and understandable. The combination of real NASA data and digital tools makes the project both innovative and visually compelling.

Factors Considered by the Team:

  • Accuracy: Reliable detection of fires and environmental changes.
  • Speed: Fast data analysis and real-time alerts.
  • Environmental Impact: Contributing to global sustainability and climate awareness.
  • Accessibility: Making scientific data easy to visualize and understand.
  • Innovation: Merging AI, satellite technology, and multimedia storytelling.
  • Social Responsibility: Using modern technology to help protect nature and human life.
