projectDetails.name: Cosmol Home
projectDetails.summary:
Cosmol Home is a realistic, human-centered space habitat concept developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025 under the theme Your Home in Space: The Habitat Layout Creator. Designed using proven ISS technologies combined with innovative inflatable modules, it demonstrates that long-duration space living is achievable with current capabilities. The mushroom-shaped habitat features a rigid lower base for life support, power, thermal control, hygiene, workstations, and exercise systems, while the upper inflatable section provides private sleeping pods, storage, and comfort. Side inflatable modules serve as water reservoirs and natural radiation shields.
Life support includes the Advanced Oxygen Generation Assembly (AOGA), Sabatier system, LiOH canisters, and ECLSS for continuous recycling of oxygen and water. ARED exercise devices, plant and microalgae zones, and Earth-like lighting maintain physical and mental well-being. Energy is supplied by foldable solar panels, and radiators and reflective panels regulate temperature.
Cosmol Home supports lunar missions of two years, is launch-ready, expandable, and reusable, providing astronauts with safety, comfort, and sustainability. By combining feasible technology with human-centered design, it turns the dream of living in space into a practical, operational reality.
projectDetails.details:
Cosmol Home Project Objective The main objective of Cosmol Home is to develop a realistic, safe, and humanized space habitat, capable of housing a crew of three astronauts for up to two years, whether in Earth orbit, cislunar space, or lunar missions. The project aims to transform the idea of living in space from a survival experience into a complete life experience, prioritizing comfort, safety, sustainability, and psychological well-being.

Specifically, Cosmol Home intends to:

Ensure full habitability from arrival

  • Create a functional habitat that can be sent before the crew, so all vital systems—life support, thermal control, power, hygiene, and communication—are operational when the astronauts arrive.

Promote self-sufficiency and sustainability

  • Use closed-loop life support systems, solar panels, water recycling, and waste management, reducing dependence on Earth resupply and increasing the feasibility of long-duration missions.

Prioritize physical and mental health

  • Provide private sleeping quarters, exercise areas, plant cultivation, and lighting simulating Earth’s day/night cycle, ensuring the crew maintains health, privacy, and circadian rhythm even during long, isolated missions.

Be economically accessible and technically feasible

  • Demonstrate that it is possible to build and launch a habitat realistically using existing rockets and technologies, making Cosmol Home an inspiring, educational, and potentially implementable model in the short term.

Serve as an educational and inspiring model

  • Facilitate public and student understanding of how space habitats work, showing the integration of engineering, science, and creativity to tackle the challenges of living beyond Earth.

In summary, the objective of Cosmol Home is to prove that it is possible to live well in space: providing safety, comfort, and functionality in an accessible, sustainable, and inspiring project, preparing humanity for future lunar explorations, in orbit, or on missions to Mars.

Cosmol Home is a space habitat designed for missions lasting up to two years, with capacity for three astronauts, developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025 under the theme Your Home in Space: The Habitat Layout Creator. Unlike many futuristic concepts that rely on distant and untested technologies, Cosmol Home was conceived with the “possible now” principle, using systems proven on the ISS and integrating inflatable modular design, allowing it to be launched by existing rockets such as Falcon 9 or Starship and expanded in orbit. Its main goal is to transform the experience of living in space from mere survival to real habitability, with comfort, safety, and full support for physical and psychological health.

The habitat combines a rigid base and inflatable modules, inspired by the shape of a mushroom. The rigid base houses all essential systems: power generation, life support, thermal control, gym, bathroom, and work areas. This configuration ensures that all critical systems remain protected and accessible for maintenance. Above, the inflatable structure expands in orbit, offering individual sleeping quarters, storage for clothing and food, and more spacious and comfortable communal areas. Lateral inflatable modules function as additional water reservoirs, used both for electrolysis and oxygen production, as well as natural radiation shielding.

Beyond survival, Cosmol Home is designed to promote psychological well-being and habitability. Each astronaut has a private inflatable sleeping quarter, with acoustic insulation, radiation shielding, and space for personal items, allowing proper rest and privacy. The habitat also includes plant and microalgae cultivation zones, providing...

 

1. AOGA (Advanced Oxygen Generation Assembly) Function: The AOGA continuously produces oxygen for the crew and manages the hydrogen generated, ensuring that life support operates throughout the mission.

Main Components: The electrolysis cells are divided into multiple units to ensure redundancy and separate water (H₂O) into oxygen (O₂) and hydrogen (H₂). Titanium electrodes, resistant to corrosion and oxidation, ensure reliable operation in microgravity. Circulation pumps keep water moving through the electrolysis system and heat exchangers, maintaining stable temperature. Pressure and temperature sensors constantly monitor the cell, preventing overpressure or overheating. Control valves and automation regulate water and oxygen flow, keeping the system stable even in case of partial failures.

Integration with ARMADILLO: The ARMADILLO acts as an advanced deionizer, filtering ions from the water and maintaining its purity. It reduces the pressure difference in the recirculation circuit, increasing efficiency and prolonging the AOGA’s lifespan. It also ensures that recycled water is ready for new electrolysis, closing the life support loop.

Redundancy and Safety: The AOGA has emergency oxygen tanks and automatic shutdown systems in case of pressure, temperature, or leakage failures. It integrates with the ECLSS, allowing centralized monitoring and control of oxygen and internal pressure.

Application in Cosmol Home: The system supports three astronauts for up to two years, maintaining the closed-loop water and oxygen cycle, essential for self-sufficiency in low Earth orbit, cislunar space, or on the Moon. It can be integrated with systems such as LiOH and Sabatier for CO₂ removal and water recovery.

2. ARMADILLO (Advanced Reversible Membrane And Deionizer for Integrated Life-support LOop) Function: The ARMADILLO ensures water quality and circulation in the life support system. It filters impurities, maintains ion balance, and prepares water for reuse in the oxygen generation system (AOGA) and other life support applications.

Main Components:

  • Membrane Filters: Remove microscopic particles and contaminants from the water.
  • Deionization Units: Maintain ionic purity by removing dissolved salts and minerals.
  • Recirculation Pumps: Keep water moving through the filtration system and to downstream systems.
  • Sensors: Continuously monitor water conductivity, pressure, and temperature.

Integration with AOGA: ARMADILLO provides ultra-pure water for electrolysis, increasing efficiency and reliability of oxygen production. It ensures that the water loop is closed, allowing the AOGA to operate safely and continuously.

Redundancy and Safety: The system has parallel filtration units to allow maintenance without stopping water circulation. Alarms and automatic bypass valves prevent contamination or overpressure scenarios.

Application in Cosmol Home: ARMADILLO enables long-duration missions by ensuring that water is recycled safely and efficiently, supporting up to three astronauts in a closed-loop environment for extended periods in low Earth orbit, cislunar missions, or lunar habitats.

 

3. LIOH (Lithium Hydroxide-based CO₂ Scrubber)

Function: The LIOH system removes carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the cabin air, maintaining safe and breathable conditions for the crew. It uses lithium hydroxide (LiOH) as a chemical absorbent, which reacts with CO₂ to form lithium carbonate and water.

Main Components:

  • LiOH Canisters: Contain lithium hydroxide pellets that chemically bind CO₂ from the air.
  • Air Circulation Fans: Pull cabin air through the canisters for CO₂ absorption.
  • Sensors: Monitor CO₂ levels in real time to ensure air remains within safe limits.
  • Bypass Valves: Allow maintenance or replacement of canisters without disrupting air circulation.

Integration with LSS (Life Support System): LIOH acts as a backup or supplemental CO₂ removal method in the life support system. In regenerable air loops, it ensures emergency removal of excess CO₂.

Redundancy and Safety: Multiple canisters can be used in parallel, allowing for replacement without stopping the air circulation. Alarms notify the crew if CO₂ levels approach critical thresholds.

Application in Cosmol Home: LIOH enables safe crew operation in closed habitats for extended durations, particularly in short-term missions or as a contingency for regenerable CO₂ scrubbers. It supports all stages of the mission, from launch and transit to surface operations.

 

4. ECLSS (Environmental Control and Life Support System)

Function: The ECLSS manages the overall habitat environment, ensuring air, water, and temperature remain within safe and comfortable levels for the crew. It integrates multiple subsystems to provide breathable air, potable water, and a stable thermal environment.

Main Components:

  • Air Revitalization: Removes CO₂ (via LIOH or regenerable scrubbers), controls humidity, and circulates fresh air.
  • Water Recovery and Management: Reclaims water from urine, sweat, and condensation for reuse. Includes filtration and purification units.
  • Temperature and Humidity Control: Maintains comfortable thermal conditions using heaters, coolers, and heat exchangers.
  • Pressure Regulation: Ensures cabin pressure remains stable and safe.
  • Sensors and Automation: Monitors all environmental parameters and triggers alerts for anomalies.

Integration with Other Systems:

  • Works with LIOH or regenerable scrubbers for air quality.
  • Feeds water to potable and hygiene systems.
  • Provides thermal control for the habitat and sensitive equipment.

Redundancy and Safety: Critical components are duplicated to ensure continuous operation in case of failures. Automated systems maintain environmental stability while crew can manually override if needed.

Application in Cosmol Home: ECLSS is the backbone of the habitat, ensuring long-term crew safety and comfort. It supports all mission phases—from launch and transit to surface operations—and enables sustainable habitation with minimal resupply.

5. ARED (Advanced Resistive Exercise Device)

Function: The ARED provides astronauts with resistance-based exercise in microgravity, simulating weightlifting on Earth. This prevents muscle atrophy and bone density loss during long-duration space missions.

Main Features:

  • Exercise Modes: Supports squats, deadlifts, heel raises, bench presses, and other resistance exercises.
  • Adjustable Resistance: Uses vacuum cylinders to provide variable resistance, allowing for personalized workouts.
  • Compact Design: Engineered to fit within limited spacecraft or habitat space while still delivering effective training.
  • Safety Mechanisms: Includes harnesses, foot restraints, and secure handholds to stabilize the astronaut during exercises.

Integration with Crew Health:

  • Complements nutritional and medical monitoring systems.
  • Helps maintain cardiovascular, muscular, and skeletal health in microgravity.
  • Data from ARED sessions can be monitored and adjusted via habitat health software.

Application in Cosmol Home: ARED ensures that crew members maintain physical fitness during transit and surface operations, supporting long-term health and mission success.

6. Solar Panels

Function: Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity to power all systems aboard the habitat, including life support, communications, lighting, and scientific equipment. They are the primary source of renewable energy in space.

Main Features:

  • Photovoltaic Cells: High-efficiency cells convert solar energy into electrical energy.
  • Adjustable Orientation: Panels can rotate or tilt to maximize sun exposure throughout the orbit or day cycle.
  • Energy Storage Integration: Power is stored in batteries for use during periods without direct sunlight.
  • Durable Materials: Resistant to radiation, micrometeoroids, and thermal cycling in space.

Integration with Habitat Systems:

  • Provides stable energy for life support, including air, water, and temperature control.
  • Powers communication systems and onboard instruments.
  • Supports redundancy with multiple panels to prevent power loss in case of damage.

Application in Cosmol Home: Solar panels ensure a continuous energy supply for the habitat, reducing reliance on fuel-based power and enabling long-term autonomous operation on extraterrestrial surfaces.

7. Radiators / Thermal Control

Function: The radiators are responsible for maintaining the habitat’s internal temperature within safe limits by dissipating the heat generated by equipment, life support systems, and the astronauts’ body heat into space. They ensure that no critical component is damaged by overheating and that the internal environment remains comfortable for the crew.

Key Features:

  1. Heat Dissipation:
    • The heat generated inside the habitat is transferred to the outer space through conductive and radiative processes.
    • Heat transfer is controlled to prevent temperature spikes and maintain stability.
    • Active:
      • Fluid circuits circulate coolant liquids that absorb internal heat and transport it to external radiators.
      • Pumps and valves regulate circulation according to thermal demand.
      • Heat pipes distribute heat evenly across the radiator surface.
      • Reflective panels reduce absorption of direct solar radiation and reflect unwanted heat.
    • High-reflectivity surfaces deflect solar radiation, reducing the thermal load that the system needs to dissipate.
    • They can be adjustable or fixed, depending on the habitat design and orientation relative to the Sun.
    • Some radiators can open or close fins and orient surfaces to optimize heat dissipation according to internal activity and solar position.
    • This allows precise temperature control without relying entirely on active cooling systems.

Integration with Other Systems:

  • Radiators work together with air conditioning, ventilation, and life support systems to ensure internal temperature remains constant and safe.
  • They protect sensitive electronic equipment from thermal variations that could compromise instrument or critical system operation.
  • They reduce energy consumption by alleviating the load on active cooling systems.

Application in Cosmol Home: In Cosmol Home, radiators ensure that the internal temperature remains comfortable for the crew and safe for all critical systems. They support prolonged operations in extraterrestrial environments, guaranteeing energy efficiency, equipment reliability, and crew well-being.

Additional Details:

  • Materials: high-conductivity aluminum alloys, silver or gold coatings to maximize reflection.
  • Redundancy: multiple radiators distributed to ensure operation even in case of partial failure.
  • Maintenance: designed for easy inspection and repair by the crew in orbit or on the lunar/Martian surface.

·   Plant and Microalgae Cultivation Labs Function: The laboratory provides fresh food, produces additional oxygen, and contributes to the crew's psychological well-being. It also serves as an experimental space for biological studies in microgravity.

·       Main Components: The lab consists of dedicated inflatable modules for cultivation, with separate compartments for different species. LED lighting systems simulate Earth’s day-night cycles, regulating plant growth and circadian rhythms. Sensors continuously monitor CO₂, O₂, humidity, temperature, pH, and nutrient levels. Automated pumps and pipelines irrigate plants with water recycled by the ECLSS. Modular substrates and supports enable hydroponic and microalgae cultivation, while atmosphere control systems maintain ideal pressure, humidity, and gas composition, minimizing contamination risks.

·       Operation: Recycled water from the ECLSS is used for irrigation, maintaining a sustainable life-support cycle. LEDs provide adjustable light spectrum, intensity, and duration for each species. Sensors transmit real-time data to the crew and ground control, allowing precise environmental adjustments. Microalgae, such as spirulina, are cultivated in closed tanks for dietary supplementation and oxygen production. Fresh vegetables, like lettuce and radicchio, are hydroponically grown, contributing to crew nutrition and mental health.

·       Redundancy and Safety: Lighting, pumps, and sensors have automatic backups to ensure cultivation continues even in case of technical failures. Modular structures allow isolation of problematic sections without affecting the rest of the lab. The environment is sealed and monitored to prevent microbial contamination or failures that could compromise life support.

·       Integration with Other Systems: Oxygen produced by plants supplements the supply from AOGA, while CO₂ absorption aids in air composition control. The lab is located near living areas, providing visual and sensory stimuli that enhance crew psychological well-being. Integration with the ECLSS and environmental sensors ensures that changes in humidity or temperature do not compromise the overall habitability of Cosmol Home.

·   Food System Function: The food system ensures adequate nutrition, food variety, and support for the crew’s physical and psychological health during missions of up to two years.

·       Components: Food storage includes pressurized, insulated compartments for protein bars, freeze-dried meals, and snacks, maintaining their durability. Small refrigeration units preserve fresh food transported or grown in the plant laboratory. For preparation, there are space microwaves, hot water dispensers, and mixing systems for rehydrating dehydrated food. Modular containers organize food by type, facilitating access and avoiding cross-contamination. Sensors monitor temperature, humidity, and food integrity, preventing spoilage.

·       Operation: Freeze-dried or dehydrated foods are rehydrated with purified water supplied by the ECLSS. Fresh meals cultivated in the plant laboratory are incorporated into the daily diet, providing essential vitamins, fiber, and nutrients. Meal planning ensures nutritional balance, including proteins (meat, legumes, whey), carbohydrates (cereals, bread), and healthy fats (nuts, peanut butter). Supplements, such as creatine and vitamins, are distributed according to individual crew needs.

·       Redundancy and Safety: Emergency stocks are stored in separate compartments, with extended shelf life of up to six months. Monitoring systems detect refrigeration failures or contamination, triggering isolation protocols and replacement of food. Pressurized containers maintain food integrity even under small pressure variations or microleaks.

·       Integration with Other Systems: Food consumption and organic waste management are connected to the ECLSS: urine and wastewater are recycled into drinking water, and solid waste is compacted and stored for safe disposal. Meal planning considers production from plant and microalgae cultivation, optimizing integration between cultivation and consumption. The system is located near communal areas, facilitating access and contributing to social interaction and crew psychological well-being.

·   Inflatable Dorms Function: The inflatable crew quarters provide safe, comfortable, and private living spaces for astronauts. They optimize the use of available volume and can be expanded or reconfigured according to mission needs.

·       Structure and Materials: The dorms consist of multi-layered inflatable modules with rigid internal frames for anchoring equipment. Layers include puncture-resistant fabrics, thermal insulation, and micrometeoroid protection. Soft partitions inside create private sleeping and personal areas, while lighting and ventilation are integrated into the structure.

·       Operation: The dorms are deployed after landing by inflating with air from the habitat’s life support system. Sleeping stations include sleeping bags adapted for microgravity, personal storage compartments, and mounting points for personal devices. Noise reduction panels and controlled lighting simulate a day-night cycle to maintain circadian rhythms.

·       Safety and Redundancy: Pressure sensors and leak detection systems continuously monitor module integrity. Emergency hatches provide escape routes, and backup inflation systems ensure structural stability in case of primary system failure. Fire-resistant materials and integrated alarms enhance crew safety.

·       Integration with Other Systems: Inflatable dorms are connected to the ECLSS for air circulation, temperature control, and humidity regulation. Communication systems link each module to the main habitat control, and lighting is synchronized with the overall habitat schedule. The design allows flexible expansion, accommodating additional crew members or temporary storage when required.

 

Bathroom Function: The bathroom provides sanitation and hygiene facilities for the crew, including waste collection, handwashing, and personal care in a microgravity environment.

Structure and Materials: It consists of compact modules with surfaces resistant to bacteria, easy to clean, and durable against abrasion. Specialized fittings, restraints, and vacuum-assisted systems ensure safe use in microgravity.

Operation: The bathroom includes a toilet with a vacuum waste collection system, a sink with controlled water flow, and hygiene supplies. Waste is separated, stored, and treated according to mission protocols. Air circulation prevents odors and maintains cleanliness.

Safety and Redundancy: Sensors monitor water leaks and air quality. Emergency shutdowns prevent flooding or contamination. Backup systems ensure continuous operation in case of primary system failure.

Integration with Other Systems: The bathroom is connected to the Water System for fresh and recycled water supply, and to waste storage systems for safe containment and disposal. Ventilation is integrated with the habitat’s air revitalization system to maintain proper air quality.

 

 

Water System Function: The Water System provides clean water for drinking, hygiene, plant growth, and other life support needs. It ensures a continuous supply of potable water while recycling wastewater to minimize resupply requirements.

Structure and Materials: The system includes storage tanks, pumps, filtration units, and plumbing made of corrosion-resistant, lightweight materials. Sensors and control units monitor water quality and flow rates.

Operation: Water is collected from multiple sources, including recycled wastewater and stored reserves. It passes through purification processes such as filtration, UV sterilization, and chemical treatment before distribution to drinking, hygiene, and plant systems.

Safety and Redundancy: Multiple filtration and backup pumps ensure uninterrupted supply. Water quality sensors trigger alarms and automatic purification cycles in case of contamination.

Integration with Other Systems: The Water System is closely integrated with the Bathroom, Food System, Plant Labs, and Air Revitalization System. It supports hygiene, plant cultivation, and cooling operations while recycling water from waste and condensation.

 

 

Urine Recycling Function: The Urine Recycling system collects and processes crew urine to recover water for reuse, reducing the need for resupply and conserving resources. It plays a critical role in the closed-loop life support system.

Structure and Materials: The system includes collection units, storage tanks, filtration modules, and processing units made of corrosion-resistant, lightweight materials. Sensors monitor flow, pressure, and water purity.

Operation: Urine is collected from the Bathroom system and passes through filtration, distillation, and chemical treatment to remove contaminants. The recovered water is then reintegrated into the Water System for drinking, hygiene, and plant irrigation.

Safety and Redundancy: Backup processing units and sensors ensure continuous operation and water quality. Any contamination triggers automatic treatment cycles or alarms for crew intervention.

Integration with Other Systems: The Urine Recycling system works closely with the Water System, Bathroom, and Plant Labs to support water conservation and closed-loop life support operations.

 

Crew Arrival Function: The Crew Arrival module ensures the safe transfer of astronauts from the spacecraft to the habitat. It acts as the initial docking and acclimatization area, supporting crew entry procedures, equipment transfer, and temporary stay before full habitat activation.

Structure and Materials: The module is made of a rigid platform and reinforced walls to absorb impact and protect both crew and equipment. It includes docking ports compatible with spacecraft similar to Crew-7.

Operation: Astronauts arrive aboard a Crew-7–like spacecraft, disembark through airlocks, and enter the habitat via the Crew Arrival module. Initial checks, orientation, and equipment transfers take place here.

Safety and Redundancy: Emergency protocols, redundant airlocks, and monitoring systems ensure crew safety during docking, entry, and initial habitat operations.

Integration with Other Systems: The module integrates with the habitat’s Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS), Waste Management, and Inflatable Dorms for seamless transition from spacecraft to habitat life.

 

Waste Disposal Function: The Waste Disposal system manages and safely stores all human waste generated aboard the spacecraft or habitat. It ensures hygienic handling, reduces contamination risks, and supports recycling where possible.

Structure and Materials: The system includes sealed containment units, pipes for urine and solid waste transport, and storage tanks made of lightweight, durable, and corrosion-resistant materials.

Operation: Waste from the crew is collected through dedicated interfaces in the Crew-7–like spacecraft or habitat restrooms. Urine is routed to the Urine Recycling system for water recovery, while solid waste is compacted, stored, and periodically disposed of or returned for processing.

Safety and Redundancy: Redundant pumps and sensors prevent leaks or blockages, while containment units are designed to withstand temperature and pressure variations in space.

Integration with Other Systems: The Waste Disposal system works directly with the Urine Recycling module, Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS), and habitat sanitation protocols to maintain crew health and habitat cleanliness.

 

Inflatable Dorms

Function: The Inflatable Dorms provide expandable living quarters for the crew, allowing for increased habitable space without significantly increasing launch volume. They serve as temporary or semi-permanent habitats, offering sleeping, relaxation, and personal storage areas.

Structure and Materials:

  • Flexible, multi-layered fabric with radiation and micrometeoroid protection
  • Air-tight inner bladder for maintaining internal pressure
  • Reinforced structural supports for stability and shape maintenance

Features:

  • Modular design, allowing connection to other modules or habitats
  • Built-in insulation and thermal control
  • Interior partitions for privacy and organization

 

 

 

Water Storage

Function: The Water Storage system is responsible for storing, managing, and distributing water throughout the habitat for all crew needs, including drinking, hygiene, cooking, and plant cultivation. It ensures a continuous supply of clean water and integrates with the recycling systems to minimize waste.

Structure and Materials:

  • High-strength, corrosion-resistant tanks capable of withstanding internal pressure
  • Insulation layers to maintain temperature stability
  • Valves and piping for controlled water distribution
  • Sensors to monitor water levels, pressure, and quality

Operation: Water is supplied to different habitat modules as needed, with automatic recycling from waste streams when possible. The system interfaces with the ECLSS (Environmental Control and Life Support System) and plant labs to ensure efficient water use.

Safety and Redundancy:

  • Multiple tanks and backup pumps ensure uninterrupted supply
  • Filtration and sterilization units prevent contamination
  • Leak detection sensors trigger alarms and isolation protocols

Lunar Mission Plan

Objective: The Lunar Mission Plan outlines the complete sequence of operations, logistics, and safety protocols for sending crew and cargo to the Moon, ensuring successful landing, surface operations, and return to Earth.

Mission Phases:

  1. Launch and Transit:
    • Launch from Earth using a suitable launch vehicle
    • Transit through Earth orbit to lunar transfer trajectory
    • Monitoring of spacecraft systems and crew health
    • Controlled insertion into lunar orbit
    • Orbital adjustments to align with landing site
    • Descent using the Cosmol Home lander module
    • Deployment of surface habitat and inflatable modules
    • Establishment of power, water, and food systems
    • Conduct scientific experiments and surface exploration
    • Daily operations including plant labs, waste recycling, and maintenance
    • Continuous communication with mission control
    • Safety protocols for emergencies
    • Preparation of ascent module for lunar departure
    • Docking with orbiting vehicle for Earth return
    • Controlled re-entry into Earth atmosphere
    • Recovery of crew and cargo

Safety and Redundancy:

  • Redundant navigation and propulsion systems
  • Backup life support and power systems
  • Emergency abort plans at all mission stages

Integration with Habitat Systems: The mission plan is fully integrated with all Cosmol Home systems, including ECLSS, Water Storage, Food System, Plant Labs, Inflatable Dorms, and Urine Recycling, ensuring continuous support for crew survival and comfort.

 

 

Crew Arrival

Objective: Ensure the safe transfer of astronauts from the transit vehicle to the lunar habitat, including initial check-ins, orientation, and connection to life support and habitat systems.

Arrival Sequence:

  1. Docking with Lander Module:
    • Approach and secure the transit vehicle (similar to Crew-7) to the Cosmol Home lander
    • Confirm airtight connection and system checks
    • Astronauts move into the habitat module
    • Unpacking personal gear and mission supplies
    • Activation of communication and monitoring systems
    • Connection to Water Storage, Food System, and Plant Labs
    • Initial checks for Inflatable Dorms and living quarters
    • Waste management system check, including the bathroom disposal system and urine recycling
    • Medical assessments and adaptation to lunar gravity
    • Safety briefings and habitat familiarization
    • Assignment of work schedules and duties
    • Begin regular operations, experiments, and surface exploration
    • Continuous monitoring by mission control

Safety Measures:

  • Emergency evacuation routes and procedures
  • Redundant life support systems for immediate support
  • Daily check-ins to monitor crew health and habitat integrity

 

 

Justification:

The Crew Arrival system is essential to ensure that astronauts can safely and efficiently transition from their transit vehicle to the lunar habitat. Proper docking, transfer, and integration with life support systems minimize risks associated with decompression, exposure to lunar conditions, and habitat malfunctions. Additionally, initial medical checks and orientation are critical for the crew’s adaptation to low-gravity environments and for ensuring mission readiness. By providing structured procedures and redundancies, the Crew Arrival plan safeguards both the crew’s health and the overall success of the lunar mission.

1. What exactly does it do? Cosmol Home is a complete space habitat that allows three astronauts to live, work, and stay healthy during missions of up to two years, whether in Earth orbit, on the Moon, or in transit to Mars. It provides closed-loop life support, including oxygen generation by the AOGA, water and CO₂ recycling, food and clothing storage, private resting areas, physical exercise with the ARED, radiation protection through layers of water and polyethylene, and cultivation of plants and microalgae for fresh food and psychological well-being. In addition, it provides stable electrical power through foldable solar panels, ensuring autonomy for critical systems, communication, and scientific experiments.

2. How does it work? The habitat operates with a rigid lower structure that houses all essential systems, such as life support, bathroom, thermal control, gym, and work areas. On top of this base, inflatable modules expand in orbit to create private dormitories and storage areas. The AOGA performs electrolysis of water, producing oxygen for breathing and hydrogen that is recombined into water, ensuring a closed-loop life support cycle. The ARMADILLO increases system efficiency, reducing recirculation pressure and extending equipment lifespan. To remove CO₂, three options are used: disposable lithium hydroxide (LiOH), regenerative swing-bed systems, or systems that separate and store CO₂ and water. Lighting simulates Earth’s day-night cycles, maintaining the crew’s circadian rhythm. Thermal control combines radiators, air conditioning, and reflective panels that deflect excess heat. For hygiene, vacuum suction and urine recycling into potable water are used, with safe disposal of solid waste. The crew stays physically fit in the gym equipped with the ARED, which allows 30 types of resistive exercises in microgravity.

3. What benefits does it have? Cosmol Home offers multiple benefits:

  • Comprehensive human life support: water, oxygen, food, exercise, and hygiene in a closed loop.

  • Safety: radiation shielding, redundancies in critical systems, and continuous emergency monitoring.

  • Psychological well-being: private dormitories, acoustic insulation, simulated natural lighting, and green areas with plants and microalgae.

  • Flexibility and cost-efficiency: inflatable design saves mass and space during launch, compatible with current rockets.

  • Sustainability: regenerative systems reduce reliance on external supplies and minimize waste.

  • Affordable cost: prototypes on Earth cost between $40,000–140 million, and complete orbital modules have a cost comparable to NASA’s BEAM module (~$18 million).

4. What do you hope to achieve? Cosmol Home aims to demonstrate that living in space can be safe, comfortable, and self-sufficient using already available technology. It is expected to inspire new long-term missions, allow studies on human behavior during prolonged periods in space, and serve as an educational model for students and the general public. The planned mission includes a two-year duration on the Moon, where the crew will stay for approximately 1 year and 7 months, allowing evaluation of how the human body and mind adapt to an extraterrestrial environment. After this period, the docking spacecraft returns to Earth, leaving the habitat for future missions.

5. What tools did you use to develop your project? The project was developed in Tinkercad, a 3D modeling software that allowed visual creation of each habitat module, including the rigid base, inflatable modules, dormitories, plant cultivation areas, gym, and life support systems. Additionally, data and concepts from the ISS, such as AOGA, ARED, and BEAM, were used to ensure the habitat was realistic, functional, and compatible with existing technologies. The modeling also considered aspects such as lighting, thermal and acoustic insulation, and crew accessibility.

projectDetails.name: Project Sistem of Automatic Localization of Exoplanets (SALoEx)
projectDetails.summary:
We developed a project that involves locating exoplanets through a telescope connected to artificial intelligence on a computer. When we look at a star, we can see a beam of light blocked by the planet. This allows us to get a sense of the exoplanet's size and its translation, as well as the gas emission spectrum.

Our project used the transit-based method to create an AI that assigns computational values ​​to the information received by the telescope, thus eliminating the need for human analysis. This is important because it could be a major breakthrough in locating exoplanets. Furthermore, if all goes well, we may be able to find life beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
How does it work?
When we observe a star with a telescope, the AI ​​will identify its size, translation, and gas emission spectrum through the light beam blocked by the exoplanet.

What are the benefits?
Our project makes observers' work easier by automating the process of identifying exoplanets.

What is the intended impact of the Project?
The desired impact is to make exoplanet discovery more practical and faster.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
We used a computer to create the test code, perform research, and upload the code to Google Drive; Python 3 to create the code and see what we could do; and Windows 11 as software.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?


How creative is your project?
We combined simple AI and the transit method to create a practical alternative to a human observer.

What factors did your team consider?
The current difficulty of locating planets; the continued advancement of AI; the possibility of a planet with suitable conditions for life, etc.

projectDetails.name: Project GALILEOSCOPE
projectDetails.summary:
Our project leverages artificial intelligence and machine learning to automate the identification of exoplanets from NASA’s open-source datasets. Although thousands of exoplanets have already been discovered through space-based missions, much of this work has been done manually. We apply the transit method for exoplanet detection and utilize public datasets from NASA’s TESS mission, along with other sources, to train our models. Using LLMs such as CNN1D and MDL to interpret TESS data and convert it into light curves, which can also be analyzed through our interactive web viewer to determine whether a candidate is likely to be an exoplanet or not.

Through multiple datasets and adaptive training sessions (Epoch), our system develops models capable of distinguishing between true and false exoplanets while accounting for potential false positives. making it a valuable tool not only for researchers aiming to classify new data, but also for newcomers in the area who wish to explore and interact with exoplanet data without needing prior experience.
projectDetails.details:
The Galileu IA project aims to develop an interactive and customizable webviewer for the analysis and identification of exoplanetary transits using stellar light curves. Designed with accessibility and flexibility in mind, the project enables users to simulate, visualize, and train detection models in real time through an intuitive Gradio interface. By combining astrophysical modeling with deep learning techniques, Galileu IA transforms the complex task of exoplanet detection into a educational, and research-oriented experience.

The webviewer allows the user to adjust mutable hyperparameters, generate synthetic datasets, and perform curve analysis using the Lightkurve library, a established tool from the NASA Kepler and TESS missions. Two distinct machine learning models are implemented: a CNN1D (Convolutional Neural Network 1D) and an MDL (Manual or Adaptive Detection Layer). Each can be configured, trained, and validated interactively according to the user’s preferences, offering both a traditional and a deep learning–based approach to transit detection.

Galileu IA integrates two main machine learning architectures, allowing users to explore different paradigms of pattern recognition:

CNN1D Model

The 1D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN1D) is optimized for time-series analysis. It processes light curves as sequential data, automatically extracting local temporal patterns that correspond to potential transit events.

Its architecture typically consists of:

  • Multiple 1D convolutional layers to detect brightness variations;
  • ReLU activation functions to introduce non-linearity;
  • MaxPooling layers for downsampling and focusing on essential features;
  • Fully connected layers for classification of transit versus non-transit events;
  • Sigmoid or softmax output to determine the probability of a detected transit.

The CNN1D is effective for distinguishing true exoplanets transits from false positives caused by stellar variability.

MDL Model (Manual or Adaptive Detection Layer)

The MDL model provides a more traditional and interpretable approach. Instead of relying purely on convolutional layers, it allows users to manually define detection thresholds or employ adaptive signal processing algorithms—such as moving average filters, peak detection, or Bayesian fitting—to identify transit events.

The user can choose between these 2 models to understand the underlying physics behind each detection and to compare classical and deep learning approaches.

DATA ANALYSIS AND RESULTS

Before feeding the curves into machine learning models, they undergo preprocessing:

  1. Normalization: Rescales the flux to make all curves comparable.
  2. Noise Filtering: Reduces high-frequency fluctuations not associated with planetary transits.
  3. Segmentation: Divides long light curves into smaller windows that may contain a single transit.
  4. Labeling: Marks segments as either containing a transit (positive) or not (negative).
  5. Feature Transformation: Optional steps such as Fourier transforms or energy-based representations can be applied for models like CNNs.

These steps ensure that the model can learn meaningful patterns while minimizing the effect of the noise.


Beyond its research applications, the Galileo IA project serves as an interactive educational platform that allows users to engage directly with exoplanet science. By simulating light curves with varying orbital parameters, users can see how changes affect transit detection, gaining hands-on experience with the principles behind planetary transits. Visualization tools, including plots of light curves, residuals, and periodograms, make abstract concepts tangible, while the ability to train and experiment with both MLP and CNN models demonstrates how machine learning algorithms interpret astrophysical signals. making the process of discovering exoplanets accessible and engaging for students, educators, and astronomy enthusiasts alike.

All the code and instructions are available in the project repository:

https://github.com/Annoyz/GalileuScopeV.1

projectDetails.name: Space Weather Kids
projectDetails.summary:
The app was created for a child and teen audience with the goal of explaining and making it easier to understand the effects caused by space weather.

One example is the aurora borealis, which is explained on the website in a more playful and accessible way.

The app helps younger users better understand how space weather works through interactive features, such as simulating the strength of solar flares by switching between flare classes (C, M, and X) and adjusting the intensity from 1 to 9 within each class.

The website also allows users to toggle between light and dark mode for a better visual experience.

ChatGPT was used to help build the website, as the idea came from the group members, but none of them had enough technical knowledge to develop it independently.
projectDetails.details:
The project exists to facilitate the understanding of the effects of space weather, such as auroras borealis or solar eruptions. It is a simulator of these events, functioning by explaining the effects and allowing the intensity of solar eruptions to be adjusted. An example of this is the classifications C, M, and X, which represent different intensity levels.

ChatGPT was used to create the website because the team did not have enough knowledge to build the site within the given timeframe.

In the group's opinion, the creativity used was minimal since only the idea was realized and there were only a few modifications to the site, which the group considered a lack of creativity on their part.

Before creating the website, the team conducted research on the topic. From this research, the idea of a site simulating the effects of space weather emerged. The team decided that at least two effects should be shown and that the site should be targeted at children and teenagers. Additionally, the site should be at least somewhat interactive.

challengeDetails.title: Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings
challengeDetails.excerpt: Although the Sun is 93 million miles away from our planet, solar activity can significantly impact our daily lives. “Space weather”—the variations that occur in the space environment between the Sun and Earth—can impact technologies in space and on Earth. Your challenge is to write and illustrate a digital children’s story that explains what space weather is and the varying impacts it has on different people such as farmers, pilots, astronauts, power grid operators, and the general public. You can tell the story from the perspective of a person impacted by space weather or from the point of view of a solar flare or coronal mass ejection (CME) as it approaches Earth. projectDetails.summary:
High-Level Summary – Space Farm 2050

Space Farm 2050 is a simulation and interactive game that uses real NASA data to model sustainable agriculture decisions at the global scale. The user plays the role of a NASA Agricultural Commander, with a mission to eradicate food crises and restore ecosystems globally while balancing production, climate, and sustainability.

The game uses NASA open data sets, such as MODIS (vegetation), SMAP (soil moisture), and GPM (precipitation), and translates difficult scientific data into enjoyable and educational experiences. All decisions impact a Global Sustainability Index (GSI), which reflects the environmental, economic, and social consequences of the player's actions.

The objective is to render space science more accessible to the masses, unveiling the use of NASA data in education, research, and environmental awareness. By utilizing interactive design and robust scientific foundation, Space Farm 2050 aims to inspire youth, students, and farmers to leverage technology and data to cultivate the future of our planet — and beyond.
projectDetails.details:
Space Farm 2050 – NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025 Presentation

What does it do?

Space Farm 2050 is a sustainable strategy game and learning simulation. In it, the player is a NASA Agricultural Commander who needs to solve global agriculture crises and restore ecosystems. The game utilizes real satellite imagery from NASA — MODIS, SMAP, GPM, and POWER — to mimic real climate, soil, and vegetation conditions on earth. The objective is to provide evidence-based decisions based on scientific fact in order to balance food production, resource use, and environmental sustainability.

How does it work?

The player chooses a real region of the planet (e.g., the Amazon, Sahel, India, or USA).

They work on a NASA Data Dashboard where they plot data on precipitation, temperature, humidity, and vegetation. Based on such information, the player makes strategic choices — i.e., crop selection, irrigation setup, and reforestation — impacting the Global Sustainability Index (GSI). The game provides a visual feedback and dynamic reports of impacts on the planet.

What are its benefits?

Interactive environmental education, learning from data, enhancement of logical and scientific thinking, sensitization worldwide on sustainability, educational use in schools and universities

What do you hope to achieve?

We hope to inspire NASA science as being interesting and fun, motivate young people to become scientists and technologists (STEM), build a global learning resource, and illustrate that space exploration can solve Earth's issues.

projectDetails.name: Shark Hotspot Prediction (SHP-REBORN)
projectDetails.summary: This project aims to create a robust mathematical framework, integrated with Artificial Intelligence (AI) models, capable of identifying and predicting shark feeding habitats, using NASA space data, such as those from the PACE, MODIS-Aqua, and SWOT missions. These satellites provide essential information on water temperature, ocean currents, and phytoplankton abundance, factors that directly influence shark feeding behavior. Furthermore, we propose the development of a new underwater smart tag model that will be applied to the animals using a UV drone, capable of recording the sharks' location and collecting information about their diet, transmitting the data in real time. From this information, the system generates hotspot maps, which indicate the areas where sharks are or may be, helping to understand their movement and foraging patterns. Accurate shark mapping contributes to greater safety and effectiveness in the conservation of marine species, as these apex predators are essential for maintaining the balance of food chains and ocean ecosystems.
projectDetails.details:
Prediction of Shark Hotspots (SHP-REBORN)

1. Introduction
This document outlines an innovative project for the modeling, simulation, and prediction of shark hotspots — areas of high concentration that are crucial for feeding, reproduction, and migration. Given the challenge of monitoring shark species across vast oceanic regions, our system employs a mathematical framework integrated with a robust computational approach that combines environmental data with artificial intelligence techniques to predict where these animals are most likely to be found, enabling real-time monitoring of their feeding habitats.

The project is built upon the integration of three fundamental technological pillars:

Environmental and Ecological Simulation:
The starting point is the generation of synthetic data fields that mimic critical oceanographic variables (such as water temperature, currents, and chlorophyll concentration). We then simulate shark trajectories that respond to these stimuli. This step allows us to train and validate our models in a controlled environment before applying them to real-world data.

Machine Learning:
The predictive core of the system. We use advanced algorithms, such as Random Forests, to analyze the simulated data and identify complex patterns connecting environmental conditions to shark presence. The result is a model capable of generating probability maps that highlight areas most likely to be hotspots.

Data Assimilation (EnKF):
The initial prediction is powerful, but the ocean is dynamic. This step makes our system intelligent and adaptive. Using an advanced technique called the Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF), the model can correct and refine its own forecasts as new shark observations (from satellites, acoustic telemetry, etc.) become available. This ensures that predictions remain accurate and up to date over time.

2. Objective
To build a predictive pipeline capable of:

  • Simulating environmental conditions and shark movements;
  • Training models to identify hotspots;
  • Updating predictions based on new observations.

3. Project Structure
Going beyond passive tagging, we present a new era in marine life research: the Symbiotic Underwater Drone (RUV). Inspired by the natural relationship between sharks and remoras, this device is not just a sensor but an autonomous robotic companion designed to attach safely and non-invasively to the body of a shark.

Functioning as a “technological remora,” this drone follows its host, collecting data with unprecedented richness and autonomy while feeding on “residual” energy — either by converting the shark’s movement into electricity or surfacing periodically for solar recharging.

Enhanced Capabilities of the Remora-Drone:

  • Active and Adaptive Sensors:
    The drone is equipped with a full suite of sensors (motion, hydrophones, cameras), but with a crucial advantage: onboard artificial intelligence can actively adjust recording parameters. If the accelerometers detect a hunting pattern, for example, the camera activates in high resolution, and the drone subtly maneuvers for the best viewing angle.
    • Analyzing a carcass or prey up close;
    • Collecting water samples for environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis;
    • Mapping the immediate habitat in 3D, such as a coral reef, before returning to its host.
  • Intelligent and Robust Communication:
    Data transmission is optimized. The drone can detach and autonomously surface to ensure a stable, high-speed satellite connection, transmitting large volumes of data, including high-definition video. After transmission, it locates and reattaches to the shark.

Example of a Mission Report:

“At 14:32, the host initiated a hunting pattern. The drone activated 4K recording and hydrophones. After the predation event, it detached, collected a water sample at the location for eDNA analysis of the prey, and returned to the host. Full data and sample #7B-24 were successfully transmitted at 15:10.”

This symbiotic approach transforms monitoring from a passive observation act into an interactive and dynamic exploration. It not only expands our knowledge but also opens doors to real-time marine ecosystem management, where technology and nature work in harmony.

The project pipeline is divided into two fundamental and sequential phases: the creation of a realistic simulated environment and the application of artificial intelligence to extract patterns and make predictions.

3.1 Phase 1: Synthetic Data Generation – The Model’s Foundation
In this initial stage, we construct the universe of data that will serve as the foundation for training and validating our predictive system. The process follows three main steps:

  • Definition of the True Field (H_true):
    A reference map is first generated, establishing the exact locations of shark hotspots. This map acts as our “ground truth” against which model performance is measured.
  • Simulation of Environmental Variables:
    The system then creates synthetic data fields for key oceanographic variables such as water temperature, chlorophyll concentration, and current patterns — replicating the environmental conditions that attract sharks.
  • Creation of Shark Trajectories:
    Finally, we simulate the routes and movements of a shark population. Crucially, these agents move probabilistically toward the hotspots defined in the true field, mimicking natural behaviors of resource seeking and habitat selection.

3.2 Phase 2: Machine Learning Modeling and Prediction – The Predictive Core
With the synthetic data ready, this phase focuses on teaching the model to “think” and make accurate predictions about new regions.

  • Predictive Model Application:
    The project employs an ensemble of Random Forests — a high-performance machine learning model capable of handling complex relationships. It is trained to identify the environmental patterns leading to hotspot formation.
  • Generation of Predictive Maps:
    The model produces probability maps that visually highlight regions with higher or lower chances of being hotspots. In addition, uncertainty maps are generated to indicate the confidence level of each prediction.
  • Validation and Performance Metrics:
    To ensure scientific reliability, model accuracy is rigorously evaluated. Standard industry metrics such as AUC (Area Under the Curve), AP (Average Precision), and Brier Score are computed to quantify the model’s ability to distinguish, classify, and calibrate its predictions effectively.

4. Main Libraries Used

  • numpy, pandas: data manipulation and matrix operations;
  • scikit-learn: machine learning models;
  • matplotlib: field and prediction visualization;
  • xarray: reading satellite and bio-logging tag data.

5. Code Structure (Summary)

5.1 Synthetic Data Generation
import numpy as npimport matplotlib.pyplot as pltfrom scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filterfrom sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifierfrom sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score, brier_score_lossfrom sklearn.model_selection import train_test_splitfrom sklearn.utils import resampleimport pandas as pdimport seaborn as sns# Note: seaborn imported only for nicer dataframe display in the notebook environment if available;# matplotlib will be used for plots (rule: do not rely on seaborn for plotting visuals per instructions).
# --------------------------- 1) Simulate spatial-temporal covariates ---------------------------np.random.seed(42)nx, ny = 60, 60  # spatial gridT_steps = 30     # time steps (days)x = np.linspace(0, 1, nx)y = np.linspace(0, 1, ny)xx, yy = np.meshgrid(x, y, indexing='xy')


5.2 the code


# Helper: create moving vortex (vorticity-like field)def moving_vortex(t, cx0=0.3, cy0=0.6, speed_x=0.01, speed_y=-0.005, sigma=0.08):    cx = (cx0 + speed_x*t) % 1.0    cy = (cy0 + speed_y*t) % 1.0    dist2 = (xx-cx)**2 + (yy-cy)**2    field = np.exp(-dist2/(2*sigma**2))    return field
# Create covariates arrays (time, nx, ny)C = np.zeros((T_steps, nx, ny))  # chlorophyll proxyV = np.zeros_like(C)             # vorticity / vortex indicatorTsurf = np.zeros_like(C)         # sea-surface temperature proxy
for t in range(T_steps):    seasonal = 0.5 + 0.4*np.sin(2*np.pi*(t/30.0))  # mild seasonality    # multiple spatial peaks for chlorophyll    peaks = (gaussian_filter((np.random.rand(nx,ny)>0.995).astype(float), sigma=3) +             gaussian_filter((np.random.rand(nx,ny)>0.997).astype(float), sigma=5))    C[t] = seasonal * (0.8*peaks + 0.2*np.random.rand(nx,ny))    V[t] = 2.0 * moving_vortex(t, cx0=0.25, cy0=0.7, speed_x=0.006, speed_y=-0.004) + \           1.0 * moving_vortex(t, cx0=0.8, cy0=0.3, speed_x=-0.004, speed_y=0.005)    # SST as gradient with noise    Tsurf[t] = 20 + 3*yy + 0.5*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/15.0) + 0.3*np.random.randn(nx,ny)
# Smooth fields temporally for realismfor arr in (C, V, Tsurf):    for t in range(1, T_steps-1):        arr[t] = 0.2*arr[t-1] + 0.6*arr[t] + 0.2*arr[t+1]
# --------------------------- 2) Define latent prey availability P and hotspot H ---------------------------# P depends on local C and V (nonlinear) and a temporal lag effectdef compute_p_availability(C_t, V_t):    # nonlinear mapping with saturation    p = np.log1p(10*C_t) * (1 + 0.7*V_t)  # simple biologically-inspired form    p = np.maximum(p, 0.0)    return p
P = np.zeros_like(C)for t in range(T_steps):    if t==0:        P[t] = compute_p_availability(C[t], V[t])    else:        # include lagged accumulation        P[t] = 0.6*compute_p_availability(C[t], V[t]) + 0.4*P[t-1]
# Hotspot probability H via logistic of P and SST (lower SST slightly preferred)def compute_H_from_P(P_t, T_t):    lin = -2.0 + 0.8*np.log1p(P_t) - 0.05*(T_t-22.0) + 0.6*gaussian_filter(P_t, sigma=1)    H = 1/(1+np.exp(-lin))    return H
H_true = np.zeros_like(P)for t in range(T_steps):    H_true[t] = compute_H_from_P(P[t], Tsurf[t])
# --------------------------- 3) Simulate shark tracks biased toward H ---------------------------# We'll simulate a few individuals as biased random walkers attracted to high-H regions.n_individuals = 12steps_per_individual = 120  # positions recordedtracks = []  # list of dicts: {'id':i, 't':[], 'x':[], 'y':[], 'forage':[]}
def sample_move(xpos, ypos, Hmap):    # propose moves in a local neighborhood, choose with probability proportional to H^alpha and a step constraint    neighbors = []    for dx in [-1,0,1]:        for dy in [-1,0,1]:            if dx==0 and dy==0:                continue            nxp = np.clip(xpos+dx, 0, nx-1)            nyp = np.clip(ypos+dy, 0, ny-1)            neighbors.append((nxp, nyp))    # compute weights by H + small mobility prior    weights = np.array([Hmap[int(a), int(b)] for (a,b) in neighbors]) + 0.01    weights = weights / weights.sum()    choice = np.random.choice(len(neighbors), p=weights)    return neighbors[choice]
for i in range(n_individuals):    # start random position    t0 = np.random.randint(0, T_steps-5)    xpos = np.random.randint(nx)    ypos = np.random.randint(ny)    t = t0    rec_t = []    rec_x = []    rec_y = []    rec_f = []  # whether foraging observed at that time (latent)    for step in range(steps_per_individual):        # determine hotspot at current time        Hmap = H_true[min(t, T_steps-1)]        # probability of foraging at current cell proportional to H        p_forage = Hmap[int(xpos), int(ypos)]        forage = np.random.rand() < p_forage        rec_t.append(t)        rec_x.append(xpos)        rec_y.append(ypos)        rec_f.append(int(forage))        # move biased toward neighbors with higher H        nxp, nyp = sample_move(xpos, ypos, Hmap)        xpos, ypos = nxp, nyp        t = min(t+1, T_steps-1)    tracks.append({'id': i, 't': np.array(rec_t), 'x': np.array(rec_x), 'y': np.array(rec_y), 'forage': np.array(rec_f)})
# Aggregate foraging events to derive labels for grid/time (supervision)# For each (t, i, x, y) we have a foraging label; we'll build a dataset of samples (pixel-time points) labeled as hotspot if foraging observed nearby.samples = []for i, tr in enumerate(tracks):    for j in range(len(tr['t'])):        t = tr['t'][j]        x_pos = tr['x'][j]        y_pos = tr['y'][j]        forage = tr['forage'][j]        # fetch covariates at that pixel/time        samples.append([t, x_pos, y_pos, C[t, int(x_pos), int(y_pos)], V[t, int(x_pos), int(y_pos)], Tsurf[t, int(x_pos), int(y_pos)], forage])
df = pd.DataFrame(samples, columns=['t','x','y','C','V','T','forage'])# Create features and labelsdf['logC'] = np.log1p(df['C'])df['xy_idx'] = df['x'].astype(int)*ny + df['y'].astype(int)
# --------------------------- 4) Train baseline model: ensemble of RandomForest (for uncertainty) ---------------------------# Build features: logC, V, T, x, y, tfeatures = ['logC','V','T','x','y','t']X = df[features].valuesy_labels = df['forage'].values  # binary label
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y_labels, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y_labels)
# Train ensemble of RandomForest to get mean + std (simple uncertainty estimate)n_ensemble = 8models = []for s in range(n_ensemble):    # bootstrap resample training set for each ensemble member    Xb, yb = resample(X_train, y_train, n_samples=len(X_train), replace=True, random_state=100+s)    rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=120, max_depth=12, random_state=1+s, n_jobs=-1)    rf.fit(Xb, yb)    models.append(rf)
# Predict probabilities on test set and compute ensemble mean/stdprobs_ensemble = np.stack([m.predict_proba(X_test)[:,1] for m in models], axis=0)prob_mean = probs_ensemble.mean(axis=0)prob_std = probs_ensemble.std(axis=0)
# Metricsauc = roc_auc_score(y_test, prob_mean)ap = average_precision_score(y_test, prob_mean)brier = brier_score_loss(y_test, prob_mean)
# Print metricsprint("Baseline ensemble RandomForest results:")print(f"  AUC-ROC: {auc:.3f}")print(f"  Average Precision (PR AUC): {ap:.3f}")print(f"  Brier score: {brier:.3f}")print("")
# --------------------------- 5) Create full-grid predictions for a given day and show maps ---------------------------day_to_plot = 10  # pick a time index to visualize true H and predicted H# Build grid features for that daygrid_coords = []for i in range(nx):    for j in range(ny):        grid_coords.append([np.log1p(C[day_to_plot, i, j]), V[day_to_plot, i, j], Tsurf[day_to_plot, i, j], i, j, day_to_plot])grid_coords = np.array(grid_coords)
# Predict with ensemblegrid_probs = np.stack([m.predict_proba(grid_coords)[:,1] for m in models], axis=0)grid_mean = grid_probs.mean(axis=0).reshape(nx, ny)grid_std = grid_probs.std(axis=0).reshape(nx, ny)
# True H map for the dayHmap_true = H_true[day_to_plot]
# Plot maps (one by one to respect plotting rules)plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))plt.title(f"True hotspot probability H (day {day_to_plot})")plt.imshow(Hmap_true.T, origin='lower', extent=(0,nx,0,ny))plt.colorbar(label='H true')plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y')plt.tight_layout()plt.show()
plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))plt.title(f"Predicted hotspot probability (ensemble mean) day {day_to_plot}\nAUC test={auc:.3f}, AP={ap:.3f}")plt.imshow(grid_mean.T, origin='lower', extent=(0,nx,0,ny))plt.colorbar(label='Predicted p(forage)')plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y')plt.tight_layout()plt.show()
plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))plt.title(f"Ensemble std (uncertainty proxy) day {day_to_plot}")plt.imshow(grid_std.T, origin='lower', extent=(0,nx,0,ny))plt.colorbar(label='Ensemble std')plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y')plt.tight_layout()plt.show()
# --------------------------- 6) Simple Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF)-style update demonstration ---------------------------# Goal: update the grid estimate of H given a small set of noisy observations (foraging events) at selected locations (e.g., tag reports)# We'll use the ensemble of grid predictions as a background ensemble and then assimilate a handful of observations.# Construct background ensemble for H field: use ensemble predictions per grid cell from the models aboveensem_H = grid_probs.copy()  # shape (n_ensemble, nx*ny)
# Suppose we get 12 noisy observations at specific grid cells for that dayn_obs = 12obs_idx = np.random.choice(nx*ny, size=n_obs, replace=False)# Observations are binary foraging (0/1) but noisy; model them as a probability with added noiseobs_values = (np.random.rand(n_obs) < Hmap_true.flatten()[obs_idx]).astype(float)obs_noise_var = 0.05  # observation noise variance (probability space)
# Observation operator H_op maps full state (flattened grid probabilities) to observed cells (extract indices)# Compute background mean and covariance in reduced space (only cells in obs_idx affect obs)# EnKF update per standard: Xa = Xb + K*(y - H(Xb))Xb = ensem_H.copy()  # shape (n_ens, n_state)# Compute ensemble means and covariancesxb_mean = Xb.mean(axis=0)  # mean backgroundPb = np.cov(Xb, rowvar=False, bias=True)  # state covariance (n_state x n_state) -- may be large but ok here# We will compute cross-covariance between state and obs, but simpler: compute covariance between ensemble predictions at obs locations and full state# Create observation matrix Hmat that extracts obs indicesHmat = np.zeros((n_obs, nx*ny))for k, idx in enumerate(obs_idx):    Hmat[k, idx] = 1.0

projectDetails.name: REMARS - Recicle for Mars
projectDetails.summary:
The project proposes an integrated recycling and additive manufacturing system to support long-duration missions on Mars, promoting crew autonomy, resource efficiency, and waste reduction. The initiative converts discarded materials such as plastics, metals, textiles, and composites into reusable raw materials for producing tools, modular structures, and habitat components.
Faced with the challenges of operating in an extraterrestrial environment, the system employs artificial intelligence and optical and magnetic sensors to identify and separate waste, along with extrusion, fusion, and 3D printing processes for material reprocessing. Origami and modular design techniques enable compact transport and the assembly of multifunctional structures within the Martian habitat.
Recycled materials can be combined with Martian regolith to create strong composite materials applicable to construction and equipment. The model adopts a space circular economy, transforming waste into useful resources and reducing dependence on Earth.
Inspired by Martian geological formations, the system maximizes adaptability and structural efficiency, while also offering potential applications on Earth through sustainable recycling and decentralized manufacturing solutions. The project demonstrates the feasibility of creating self-sufficient and sustainable habitats in extreme environments.
projectDetails.details:
REMARS is an integrated software system designed to support long-duration human missions on Mars, promoting sustainability, resource efficiency, and crew autonomy. The system addresses the critical challenge of managing solid waste generated in the Martian habitat, including plastics, metals, textiles, and composites, converting them into reusable materials for 3D printing and functional component manufacturing.

The system operates in multiple stages: first, waste images are uploaded and automatically classified using artificial intelligence, identifying material types and properties. Based on this classification, REMARS generates a detailed recycling plan, including estimates of energy consumption, processing time, and appropriate methods for reuse or conversion into 3D printing filaments.

Next, the system produces components in two formats: LEGO-style modular blocks and origami-inspired panels, allowing compact storage and expansion for various applications. Users can download .scad files and instantly preview 3D parts. Additionally, REMARS simulates a production queue, enabling scheduling of jobs with material, mass, and in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) options, considering energy efficiency and Martian environmental constraints.

The project’s benefits include reduced reliance on Earth-supplied resources, waste minimization, increased crew autonomy, and on-demand production of tools, containers, habitat structures, robotic components, and habitat extensions. The intended impact is to demonstrate the feasibility of a space circular economy by integrating recycling, additive manufacturing, and functional modularity for extreme environments.

REMARS was developed using Python for logic and processing, OpenCV for image classification, OpenSCAD for 3D modeling, and Jupyter Notebook for code execution and demonstrations. Its creativity lies in combining AI classification, modular and origami-inspired design, and production simulation into a single workflow. Key factors considered include adaptability to Martian conditions, energy efficiency, safety, scalability for different mission scenarios, and potential applications in compact, sustainable terrestrial systems.

projectDetails.name: Gradient Blooming - Flower Blooming Tracker
projectDetails.summary:
Research shows that 75% of global crops depend on pollination. However, the diversity of plant species around the world still requires precise monitoring. That’s where Gradient Blooming comes in.

Gradient Blooming is a machine learning-based web platform capable of detecting and predicting blooming zones in order to monitor flower phenology changes and trends, as well as track pollen concentration. This data can be used for global warming studies, flora and fauna conservation, crop planning, and public health initiatives. Inspired by COP30, our worldwide decisions must be with data and science.

Using AEB CBERS dataset as a prototype and NASA resources as WorldView Superbloom Visualisations, Gradient Blooming uses xg boost for data training and NIR Spectral Analysis to accurately detect different flower species, all integrated in an HTML user friendly website. This solution is also scalable and adapts for any satellite dataset.
projectDetails.details:
Why we worked on Gradient Blooming? 🌺

Inspired by COP30, one of the biggest ambient development event, that will occur on Brazil, we decided to take this decision because of the diversity of our members regions, representing our country itself and the world, making a solution to help:

  • Global warming studies;
  • Susteinable agriculture;
  • Public health menagement;
  • Enhance ambiental conservation politics.
What is COP30?

It will be the first ONU summit based in Brazil. The event will bring together representatives from over 190 countries in the Amazon region to discuss and make decisions using high-precision data—essential for monitoring high-risk deforestation areas like the Amazon. 17% of the original coverage has been lost, also extreme droughts and rainfall changes are increasing, affecting vegetation and ecological cycles, as flower blooming.

How Gradient Blooming works?

Our Website:

Landing Page

Designed to be user friendly and provide high quality information for everyone, its showcase out "blooming map tool", which allows the user to navigate through a country of it's choice.

Simple, yet accessible.

Profile Page

To improve user understanding, we defined three user profiles: "scientist", focused on phenology insights and bloom prediction; "farmer", aimed at crop efficiency; and "general public", providing health-related and general information, such as the pollen index.

The blooming Map

The blooming map interactive menu allow users to zoom in and zoom out for accurate data, asks questions about next date prediction, trends across time, pollen index and catalogue your flower to better understand it's phenology and encourage research

The catalogue

Inspired by GLOBE plant photos, a scientist, a farmer or a common user my enjoy this tool to monitor plant phenology change and other incoming bloom areas

Behind Machine Learning features

Data Analysis and it application

Our Machine Learning Model

Using the most advanced machine learning model ( xg boost ) and other Data Analysis tools we were able to analyse NIR spectral trends, Vegetation distribution and time variation on flower blooming on CBERS and NIR spectral dataset

Solution Scalability

Our model was build to adapt for any satellite dataset but using CBERS as prototype and shared to other users to try and learn with on GitHub

Pollen index

Pollen detector helps predict blooming trends and indicate high pollen density areas, helping alert the major public about allergens.

What is NIR Spectral Data?

Flowers reflect light and various chemical compounds, and a spectrometer can capture this information to detect plants with high precision—identifying species pixel by pixel and enabling the detection of vegetation changes.

What does Gradient Blooming aim to achieve?

Our solution has the potential to serve multiple user profiles:

  • Scientists: to analyze global vegetation changes and the impacts of global warming; predict flower blooming; map flowering dynamics in endangered species; and better understand flower–pollinator relationships to support conservation efforts.
  • Farmers: to plan planting during specific seasons, compare dates, and initiate studies based on vegetation changes, disease outbreaks, and pest activity.
  • General public: to raise awareness about plant and flower phenology, locate areas with high allergen concentrations, and foster interest in biology.

Which tools were applied in the project?

For the Website, we used:
  • HTML and CSS for the front-end
  • Javascript and Leaflet Framework for map creation.
  • Figma for Wire Planning
For Machine Learning and back-end, we used:
  • Jupyter Notebook to work with Python
  • Seaborn, Numpy, Matplotlib as data analysis libraries ( Python )
  • Rasterio, shapely and geopandas for image and sattelite data processing ( Python )
  • Git Hub as repository
  • APIs to answer people questions.

The Future of Gradient Blooming

Our solution has the potential to serve multiple user profiles:

  • Scientists: to analyze global vegetation changes and the impacts of global warming; predict flower blooming; map flowering dynamics in endangered species; and better understand flower–pollinator relationships to support conservation efforts.
  • Farmers: to plan planting during specific seasons, compare dates, and initiate studies based on vegetation changes, disease outbreaks, and pest activity.
  • General public: to raise awareness about plant and flower phenology, locate areas with high allergen concentrations, and foster interest in biology.
