projectDetails.name: Project Weather Mind
projectDetails.summary:
WeatherMind is an intelligent and personalized weather forecasting platform designed to help users plan outdoor events with confidence. Using historical and forecasted data from NASA and global meteorological APIs, the app provides clear, data-driven insights on the likelihood of “very hot,” “very cold,” “very windy,” “very rainy,” or “uncomfortable” conditions for a specific location and date.

Through a clean, user-centered interface, WeatherMind transforms complex climate data into intuitive visualizations, allowing users to customize their weather view according to their needs. The platform bridges science and everyday decision-making, empowering users to make smarter choices for events, travel, and recreation.

By combining predictive analytics, historical patterns, and NASA Earth observation data, WeatherMind promotes awareness of environmental variability and enhances resilience in outdoor planning — turning uncertainty into informed confidence.
projectDetails.details:
WeatherMind is a smart web application that transforms NASA’s Earth observation data and global meteorological datasets into personalized weather insights. It enables users to plan outdoor events with confidence by analyzing historical and forecasted conditions for any chosen date and location. The system calculates the probability of “very hot,” “very cold,” “very windy,” “very rainy,” or “uncomfortable” conditions, providing a clear, human-centered interpretation of complex climate data.




























The platform uses Python for backend data processing and API integration, JavaScript (React + TailwindCSS) for the frontend, and NASA POWER, Open-Meteo, and CPTEC/INPE datasets for real-time and historical weather analysis.










Our team focused on usability, clarity, and customization. The dashboard adapts to the user’s needs, offering interactive visualizations such as temperature graphs, precipitation probabilities, and UV index trends. The design features a dark, gradient interface (blue–cyan) to reflect calmness and focus, combining science and accessibility.

The project’s impact lies in empowering decision-making through data — helping people avoid event cancellations, travel risks, and health discomforts caused by unexpected weather. By merging technology, design, and space-based data, WeatherMind creatively bridges environmental science with daily life decisions — turning weather uncertainty into confidence and foresight.

Our creative process involved collaborative research, daily brainstorming sessions, and iterative prototyping. Each stage was guided by curiosity and problem-solving — from defining real user pain points to translating raw NASA data into an intuitive experience. WeatherMind was born from teamwork, adaptability, and the shared belief that information from space can make life on Earth more predictable, safer, and beautifully connected.

No NASA logos were created or changed. AI served only to improve workflow, assist creativity, and promote an efficient workflow. All final results were human-made and verified.

Ela ajudou a aprimorar o vocabulário, tornando os textos mais claros, precisos e acessíveis, além de refinar a estrutura das informações para que fossem apresentadas de forma lógica e envolvente. Ela auxiliou na escolha de termos técnicos adequados, na adaptação do tom de linguagem para diferentes públicos e na criação de exemplos que ajudassem a ilustrar cenários de impacto de meteoros de forma visual e didática.

challengeDetails.title: SpaceTrash Hack: Revolutionizing Recycling on Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: During a hypothetical three-year mission to Mars and back, an eight-person crew would accumulate 12,600 kg of inorganic waste, or trash, including various packaging materials, textiles, and structural materials. This scenario creates a pressing need to recycle available materials, rather than execute the expensive and inefficient processes of transporting additional resources from Earth and/or sending trash back to Earth. As humans prepare to explore unknown worlds in the future, your challenge is to design sustainable systems that could manage, reuse, or recycle inorganic waste (“trash”) that is brought to and/or accumulated on the surface of Mars. (Space Technology Mission Directorate)

node.excerpt: CNSR

projectDetails.name: Vai chover na minha parada?
projectDetails.summary:
"O Kosmos é uma aplicação digital minimalista que utiliza dados históricos da NASA para ajudar pessoas a planejar atividades ao ar livre com antecedência, reduzindo riscos de mau tempo em eventos como piqueniques, festivais, shows ou viagens.

A solução oferece probabilidades históricas de condições climáticas adversa, como chuva forte, calor extremo, vento intenso e alta umidade, para um local e data específicos.
Diferente de uma previsão tradicional de curto prazo, nossa ferramenta analisa padrões climáticos de anos anteriores, permitindo planejamento meses antes.

Por que é importante:
Milhares de eventos e atividades ao ar livre sofrem cancelamentos ou prejuízos por falta de informações confiáveis a longo prazo.
O Kosmos transforma ciência em impacto social, ampliando o uso prático dos dados abertos da NASA"
projectDetails.details:
Descrição detalhada do projeto

O Kosmos ajuda usuários a responder uma pergunta simples:

“Qual a probabilidade de mau tempo neste local e data?”

O que ele faz

Mostra a probabilidade histórica de condições climáticas adversas.

Exibe mapa interativo com pino para escolha precisa do local.

Fornece gráficos históricos mensais para contexto visual.

Gera resumo em texto claro, acessível a qualquer pessoa.

Permite compartilhar resultados via link, imagem ou WhatsApp.

Exporta os dados em CSV ou JSON para pesquisa ou análise.

Como funciona

O usuário informa local e data desejada.

O sistema consulta dados históricos da NASA.

Um algoritmo calcula a probabilidade de cada condição climática.

O resultado aparece em:

Porcentagem geral (%)

Gráfico histórico por dia do mês

Mapa com camadas de intensidade

Texto interpretativo

Benefícios

Usuário: evita frustrações e custos com eventos cancelados.

Sociedade: promove conscientização sobre padrões climáticos.

NASA: demonstra valor social dos dados abertos.

Ferramentas utilizadas
Lovable (protótipo interativo)

projectDetails.name: Animation Celebration of Terra Data
projectDetails.summary:
"1.	O que você desenvolveu?: Slides e um vídeo explicativo.

2.	Como ele aborda o desafio?: O video explicatico aborda o tema simples para todos entenderem sem muitas complicações, sobre a história da ciencia do Satélite Terra de maneira resumida, sobre os instrumentos utilizados no satélite e o porquê do aniversário está sendo comemorado. Já os slides falam datalhadamente sobre os instrumentos.
 
3.	Por que é importante?: É importante para concientizar a importância do satélite para o avanço de conhecimento humano sobre o espaço e o universo em si.



"
projectDetails.details:
● O que exatamente ele faz?:
É uma missão da NASA focada em estudar o planeta Terra, monitorando-a de diferentes ângulos (o sistema Terra EOS AM-1), fornecendo imagens e dados para o monitoramento de mudanças climáticas e do meio ambiente.
● Como funciona?:
Funciona orbitando a Terra devido ao equilíbrio entre a velocidade do satélite e a força da gravidade da Terra, que o mantém preso à sua órbita em vez de voar para o espaço ou cair de volta.
● Quais são os benefícios?:
Comunicação global, navegação (como o GPS), previsão do tempo e monitoramento de desastres naturais, gestão de recursos naturais, agricultura de precisão, planeamento urbano e até o acesso à informação em áreas remotas, melhorando assim a qualidade de vida, a segurança e a economia.
● O que você espera alcançar?:
Com esse projeto busco melhorar minha convivencia social e a trabalhar melhor em equipe e conhecer mais sobre o espaço e seus elementos.
● Quais ferramentas, linguagens de codificação, hardware ou software você usou para desenvolver seu projeto?:
-Photoshop

-Canva
-Google

projectDetails.name: Sua casa no espaço: o criador de layout de habitat
projectDetails.summary:
"1. O que você desenvolveu?
Desenvolvemos um site interativo que permite aos usuários criar e avaliar layouts de habitats espaciais. A ferramenta facilita o design de ambientes espaciais considerando as necessidades da tripulação, a duração da missão e as limitações do espaço disponível.

2. Como ele aborda o desafio?
Nosso site ajuda os usuários a projetar habitats espaciais ajustando o tamanho e a disposição das áreas funcionais essenciais — como higiene, sono, armazenamento e exercícios — dentro das restrições reais de volume e formato do habitat. O site oferece uma interface simples e visual para criar, modificar e experimentar diferentes layouts, permitindo um processo de design iterativo.

3. Por que é importante?
Essa ferramenta educa e envolve pessoas de todas as idades sobre os desafios de viver e trabalhar no espaço. Ela permite que os usuários experimentem com conceitos reais de design espacial, estimulando a criatividade e o pensamento crítico sobre a habitação fora da Terra, uma habilidade importante para futuras missões espaciais."
projectDetails.details:
●O que exatamente ele faz?
Nosso projeto é um site interativo que permite aos usuários criar layouts personalizados de habitats espaciais. O usuário pode definir o formato e o volume do habitat, e dividir o espaço em áreas funcionais essenciais para a vida no espaço, como sono, higiene, armazenamento e exercício. A ferramenta oferece uma visualização clara dessas áreas e permite ajustar o layout para diferentes cenários de missão.

●Como funciona?
O usuário começa escolhendo parâmetros básicos, como o número de tripulantes, duração da missão e ambiente (por exemplo, Lua ou Marte). Em seguida, pode arrastar e soltar áreas funcionais dentro do espaço disponível, respeitando restrições de tamanho e forma. O site fornece feedback visual para garantir que cada área seja adequada para o número de tripulantes e duração da missão. O usuário pode experimentar múltiplos layouts e comparar diferentes opções para encontrar a melhor solução.

●Quais são os benefícios?

Facilita o entendimento dos desafios de design de habitats espaciais para qualquer pessoa, inclusive iniciantes.

Incentiva o pensamento crítico e a experimentação com conceitos reais de engenharia espacial.

Permite aprendizado prático e visual, tornando o tema mais acessível e engajador.

Pode ser usado em educação para inspirar jovens a explorar ciência e tecnologia espacial.

●O que você espera alcançar?
Queremos que nossa ferramenta ajude a educar e inspirar pessoas sobre a importância do design espacial e as complexidades de viver fora da Terra. Esperamos que usuários de diferentes idades usem o site para aprender e experimentar, fomentando interesse em ciência, tecnologia e exploração espacial.

●Quais ferramentas, linguagens de codificação, hardware ou software você usou para desenvolver seu projeto?
Nosso site foi desenvolvido utilizando as ferramentas disponíveis na plataforma Hostinger Horizons, que oferece um ambiente completo para criação, edição e hospedagem de sites. Utilizamos recursos de desenvolvimento web básicos disponíveis na plataforma para construir a interface interativa e garantir que o site funcione bem em diversos dispositivos.

Cuidados médicos

Gerenciamento de resíduos

projectDetails.name: Project GLEI - O Dia em Que o Sol Espirrou
projectDetails.summary:
"GLEI em: O Dia em Que o Sol Espirrou" é um livro de histórias em quadrinhos cativante, desenvolvido para crianças de 6 a 10 anos. Nele, a piloto Glei, auxiliada pelo cientista Kami do centro de observações espaciais, navega uma aventura para desviar seu voo de uma potente erupção solar de Classe X, carinhosamente apelidada de "Fálar".
Este projeto aborda o desafio "Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings" da NASA, traduzindo conceitos complexos do clima espacial – como erupções solares e seus impactos em comunicações e navegação – em uma narrativa divertida e acessível.
É importante porque desmistifica a ciência, fomenta a literacia científica em jovens e ilustra como a pesquisa espacial da NASA/NOAA protege nossa vida diária. Ao apresentar a ciência de forma envolvente, buscamos inspirar uma nova geração de exploradores e cientistas, conscientizando-os sobre a importância do Sol e do clima espacial.
projectDetails.details:
O que ele faz ou como funciona? "GLEI em: O Dia em Que o Sol Espirrou" é um livro de histórias em quadrinhos digitais/físicas projetado para engajar crianças de 6 a 10 anos com o tema do clima espacial. Através de uma narrativa envolvente, o livro apresenta a piloto Glei e o cientista Kami, que trabalham juntos para proteger um voo de passageiros de uma erupção solar de Classe X (Fálar). O quadrinho detalha, de forma acessível e visual:

  1. Definição de Clima Espacial: Explicando o Sol como uma estrela "espirrando" energia e partículas.
  2. Fenómenos Solares: Introduzindo erupções solares (Fálar) e suas características.
  3. Impactos na Terra: Mostrando como esses eventos afetam sistemas críticos como rádio, GPS e redes elétricas, e como isso impacta a aviação.
  4. Ação e Solução: A aventura de Glei desviando sua rota com base nos alertas de Kami, destacando a importância da previsão científica. O funcionamento é simples: a criança lê o quadrinho, seguindo a história dos personagens e aprendendo sobre o clima espacial de forma lúdica e contextualizada.

Quais são os benefícios? Os benefícios são múltiplos:

  • Literacia Científica: Traduz conceitos complexos de heliophysics em uma linguagem e formato compreensíveis para o público infantil.
  • Conscientização: Aumenta a compreensão sobre os fenómenos do clima espacial e seus impactos diretos e indiretos na tecnologia e na vida humana.
  • Inspiração STEM: Apresenta modelos positivos (uma piloto e um cientista) que utilizam o conhecimento científico para resolver problemas do mundo real, inspirando o interesse em ciência, tecnologia, engenharia e matemática.
  • Educação de Segurança: Ensina sobre a importância da previsão e preparação para eventos naturais, incluindo os espaciais.
  • Entretenimento Educacional: Oferece uma forma divertida e visualmente estimulante de aprender.

Qual é o impacto pretendido do projeto? O impacto pretendido é criar uma geração mais informada, curiosa e resiliente em relação ao ambiente espacial. Ao desmistificar o clima espacial e apresentá-lo como um campo de estudo emocionante e relevante, pretendemos:

  • Reduzir a percepção de medo ou complexidade em torno de fenómenos científicos.
  • Promover uma apreciação pelo trabalho dos cientistas e profissionais que monitorizam o espaço.
  • Inspirar futuras carreiras em áreas relacionadas à ciência espacial e aviação.
  • Aumentar a conscientização geral sobre a conexão entre o Sol e a Terra.
  • Despertar a curiosidade e a criatividade no publico infantil sobre o espaço.

Quais ferramentas, linguagens de programação, hardware ou software você utilizou para desenvolver o seu projeto? Para o desenvolvimento do projeto "GLEI em: O Dia em Que o Sol Espirrou", utilizamos as seguintes ferramentas:

  • Escrita e Roteiro: Google Docs para colaboração e organização do texto da história e diálogos.
  • Conceituação Visual e Ilustrações: Ferramentas de Inteligência Artificial Generativa foram fundamentais para rascunhos iniciais, exploração de estilos e criação de designs de personagens (como a Glei, Kami e a erupção solar "Fálar"), servindo como base criativa. Software de desenho digital como Adobe Photoshop e/ou Procreate deverá ser utilizado para refinar e finalizar as artes no estilo de quadrinhos.
  • Design e Diagramação do Livro: Adobe InDesign ou Canva para a montagem final das páginas do quadrinho, garantindo um layout profissional e atraente para o público infantil.

Como é a criatividade do seu projeto? A criatividade do nosso projeto reside em:

  • Humanização da Ciência: Transforma um fenómeno abstrato e complexo (erupção solar) em um personagem relatable ("Fálar") e integra-o em uma aventura com heróis humanos (Glei e Kami).
  • Perspectiva Única: Contada do ponto de vista de uma piloto de avião, conecta o clima espacial diretamente a uma experiência tangível e relevante para o público.
  • Formato Engajador: Utiliza o formato de história em quadrinhos, que é inerentemente divertido e visual, para tornar o aprendizado de ciência acessível e divertido para crianças.
  • Conexão Emocional: Cria uma narrativa de superação e trabalho em equipe, onde a ciência é a ferramenta para o sucesso.

Quais fatores sua equipe considerou? Nossa equipe considerou vários fatores durante o desenvolvimento:

  • Idade e Nível de Compreensão do Público: Simplificamos a linguagem e os conceitos científicos para torná-los apropriados para crianças de 6 a 10 anos.
  • Engajamento Visual: Priorizamos ilustrações vibrantes e um estilo de quadrinhos para manter o interesse das crianças.
  • Precisão Científica: Embora a história seja ficcional, a base dos eventos e impactos do clima espacial foi inspirada em dados e conceitos reais da NASA/NOAA, garantindo a veracidade das informações.
  • Relevância: Mostramos como o clima espacial afeta algo que as crianças podem entender (viagens de avião) para tornar o tema mais significativo.
  • Mensagens Positivas: Focamos em temas de trabalho em equipe, bravura, importância da ciência e da observação.
  • Acessibilidade: Projetamos o livro para ser facilmente consumível, seja em formato digital ou físico.

projectDetails.name: NOVA - Navegatio, Observatio, Vita, Astrumm
projectDetails.summary:
Nosso projeto propõe um desafio original voltado para o desenvolvimento de um rover espacial multifuncional, capaz de operar de forma autônoma em ambientes extremos e desconhecidos. A proposta combina inovação tecnológica com aplicabilidade prática, utilizando dados abertos da NASA para criar um sistema inteligente e adaptável.

Entre as funcionalidades, o protótipo inclui um modo de resguardo para situações de risco, como tempestades de areia ou soterramento, no qual o veículo se transforma em uma estrutura compacta e resistente, utilizando ganchos retráteis para se fixar ao solo. As rodas são preenchidas com fluido não-newtoniano e sensores integrados, permitindo a adaptação ao terreno e a criação de mapas da área explorada. A transmissão de dados é otimizada para reduzir os efeitos da comunicação atrasada em missões espaciais.
A inteligência artificial embarcada é treinada com experiências reais de astronautas, permitindo decisões autônomas baseadas em situações reais. O sistema de energia é sustentado por placas solares e pela conversão de energia cinética em elétrica por meio de frenagem regenerativa. O armazenamento interno é distribuído nas áreas de sombra, aproveitando o espaço e protegendo os componentes sensíveis.
Nosso protótipo busca ampliar os limites da exploração espacial com soluções sustentáveis, inteligentes e acessíveis, alinhando criatividade local com dados globais.
projectDetails.details: O projeto NOVA (Navigation, Observation, Vita, Astrumm) é um rover espacial multifuncional, criado para operar de forma autônoma em ambientes extremos e desconhecidos, como a superfície de Marte ou luas distantes. Ele foi desenvolvido com foco em sobrevivência inteligente, adaptabilidade ao terreno, eficiência energética e autonomia de decisão. Entre suas principais funcionalidades está o modo tartaruga, uma solução criativa para situações de risco como tempestades de areia ou soterramentos. Nesse modo, o rover se transforma em uma estrutura compacta e resistente, retraindo seus componentes e utilizando ganchos para se fixar ao solo, reduzindo danos e aumentando sua chance de sobrevivência. As rodas adaptativas são preenchidas com fluido não-newtoniano, que muda de viscosidade conforme o impacto e pressão, permitindo melhor aderência e absorção de choques. Sensores integrados nas rodas ajudam a mapear o terreno em tempo real, gerando dados úteis para navegação e análise científica. A inteligência artificial embarcada foi treinada com base em relatos e experiências reais de astronautas, permitindo que o rover tome decisões autônomas em situações complexas, como escolher rotas seguras, identificar áreas de interesse científico ou reagir a falhas inesperadas. O sistema de energia combina placas solares com frenagem regenerativa (KERS), convertendo energia cinética em elétrica durante movimentos e paradas. O armazenamento interno é distribuído estrategicamente nas áreas de sombra do rover, protegendo componentes sensíveis ao calor. Utilizamos ferramentas de modelagem 3D, pesquisa em bancos de dados abertos da NASA (data.nasa.gov), e conceitos de engenharia mecânica, robótica, IA e design biomimético. A criatividade do projeto está na união de soluções reais com ideias originais, como o modo tartaruga, o uso de fluidos inteligentes e a IA treinada com experiências humanas. Consideramos fatores como segurança, autonomia, eficiência energética, resiliência estrutural, comunicação em ambientes com latência e viabilidade em missões reais. NOVA representa uma proposta ousada e acessível para ampliar os limites da exploração espacial.

projectDetails.dataReferences: [NASA diz que Mars Rover descobriu potencial bioassinatura no ano passado. Uma amostra coletada pelo rover Perseverance da NASA em Marte, no leito seco de um antigo rio na Cratera de Jezero, pode preservar evidências de vida microbiana antiga. Retirada de uma rocha chamada "Cheyava Falls" no ano passado, a amostra, chamada "Sapphire Canyon", contém potenciais bioassinaturas, de acordo com um artigo publicado quarta-feira na revista Nature.  Uma bioassinatura potencial é uma substância ou estrutura que pode ter uma origem biológica, mas requer mais dados ou estudos adicionais antes que uma conclusão possa ser alcançada sobre a ausência ou presença de vida.    “Esta descoberta da Perseverance, lançada durante o primeiro mandato do presidente Trump, é o mais próximo que já chegamos da descoberta de vida em Marte. A identificação de uma potencial bioassinatura no Planeta Vermelho é uma descoberta inovadora e que avançará nossa compreensão de Marte”, disse o administrador interino da NASA, Sean Duffy. “O compromisso da NASA em conduzir Ciência Padrão Ouro continuará enquanto buscamos nosso objetivo de colocar os americanos no solo rochoso de Marte.”](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-says-mars-rover-discovered-potential-biosignature-last-year/)

projectDetails.name: AJUDA AI
projectDetails.summary: The “Ajuda AI” project aims to develop an intelligent knowledge engine that, based on user input, returns a dashboard with article recommendations ranked by relevance, along with a reliability score for each article. This supports researchers in their daily work and helps save time. The system first receives a search query and extracts a search string from it, then retrieves articles from the NASA database that have been filtered through a reliability algorithm. The results are grouped into clusters based on similarity, with each cluster displaying the topic, a summary of the article results within it, and the corresponding articles.
projectDetails.details: The “Ajuda AI” project aims to develop an intelligent knowledge engine that, based on user input, returns a dashboard with article recommendations ranked by relevance, along with a reliability score for each article. This supports researchers in their daily work and helps save time. The system have an python backend with an HTML, CSS and java script frontend to represent the application. The main creative part of our project was to solve the problem with diverse existing methods. The main factors we consider were to make sure our application used reliable articles, and we achieved it by a filter method we developed with an agglomeration of existing methods.

projectDetails.name: Verdena: Using data for games with an educational experience.
projectDetails.summary: This project proposes the development of an agricultural game focusing on crop management and climate crisis management. The guiding role lies in the direct and practical use of Earth observation data made available free of charge by NASA. projectDetails.name: When & Weather
projectDetails.summary:
The project is a digital system that analyzes the weather on a given date and location, and offers an interactive response to the user.

We developed a service that receives the desired location and time. It then simulates the search for raw data such as temperature, wind, and humidity, and applies a business rule to categorize the weather. The end result is a clear status, such as "Pleasant," "Very Hot," or "Cold," instead of just numbers.

The main challenge is transforming complex weather forecast or observation data into information that anyone can immediately use. The project solves this by automatically categorizing temperatures, eliminating the need for users to interpret temperature variations on their own.

It's important because it facilitates decision-making. A service like this can be used by apps to help people plan what to wear, organize an outdoor event, or manage resources, offering a quick and objective weather analysis.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details: When & Weather 🌦️

What does it do or how does it work?

The project is a modular web system designed to facilitate access to weather forecasting for any location and specific period needed. It is divided into three specialized layers:

  1. Front-end Layer (React): A React/TypeScript application that provides a clean UI for users to query a location and a date/time, and view the forecast and a simplified interpretation (thermal comfort, rain chance, wind).
  2. Domain API (Java): An API that handles the business logic and decision-making. It enhances the raw data by determining thermal comfort based on temperature and adding a rain forecast based on humidity.
  3. Data API (Python): An API that translates the location query into geographical coordinates and acts as a connector to external weather APIs (such as NASA POWER API).

What are the benefits?

The main benefit is the simplified and concise interpretation of the weather. By transforming complex data into user-friendly descriptions (like "thermal comfort" and simple icons), the system makes the weather forecast immediately actionable, saving the user time and interpretation effort.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to provide a cleaner and more purposeful description of the weather. The modular architecture and the use of Domain-Driven Design (DDD) principles aim to create a robust back-end service that is easy to integrate and test, serving as a foundation for weather alerts or planning applications.

Tools, programming languages, hardware, or software used on development:

The project utilizes a polyglot architecture:

  • Web Application (Front-end): React, Vite, TypeScript, Node.js 18+.
  • Domain API (Back-end): Java JDK 21+, Apache Maven (with Wrapper).
  • Data API (Data): Python 3.12, with integration to external APIs (NASA POWER API).

How is the creativity of the project?

The creativity lies in the architectural approach and the value added by the Domain layer. Instead of merely relaying raw climate data, the system creates an intelligence layer that interprets the data for the end-user, such as classifying thermal comfort and rain chance.

What factors did our team consider?

The team considered factors such as:

  • Usability: Focusing on a clean and mobile-friendly User Interface (UI).
  • Architectural Robustness: Dividing the project into three distinct layers to isolate responsibilities (Domain API for core logic and Data API for external integrations).
  • Integrability: Including Swagger documentation in the API to facilitate integration by other developers.

projectDetails.name: Planet Spoter: An AI-assisted solution for exoplanet search
projectDetails.summary:
A website was created to process data collected by NASA telescopes using an AI model capable of determining whether such data represent signatures of an exoplanet or not. In the future, the website will use AI to perform spectroscopic analysis of the planet’s atmosphere to predict the atmospheric composition of each planet.

The website was developed with the goal of democratizing access to astronomical data analysis tools for both laypeople and independent researchers.
projectDetails.details:
About the Project

We are the team Debugging the Cosmos, and we aim to democratize science by making access to space research simpler and more accessible to everyone. Over the years, several independent researchers have contributed to the search for new exoplanets, as seen in the post at: https://blog.google/technology/ai/how-college-student-became-planet-hunter.

These scientists share a passion for discovering new exoplanets, but not all of them have access to algorithms like those used by NASA. With this audience in mind, our project aims to make exoplanet detection methods more accessible through an AI-assisted website that helps process the data. Our project was created to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, with the goal of using artificial intelligence to identify exoplanets — planets outside our solar system — based on real data from NASA missions.

We trained an AI model using data provided by NASA, specifically the original columns from the Kepler Objects of Interest dataset, so that the AI could learn the patterns that indicate the presence of a planet. Our API automatically performs all data cleaning and preparation, and then the model classifies whether a light curve represents a planet or not. In short: it takes the provided data, processes it, and outputs whether there is an exoplanet in that record.

About the Model

In addition, we worked on the complete website design, creating an intuitive, clear, and easy-to-use interface so that anyone can test the model and understand how detection works. Currently, our AI model uses the Random Forest Model and achieves an accuracy of approximately 99%.

In parallel, tests were conducted, and an AI model was trained using NASA’s FDL INARA dataset with synthetic data to analyze the planet’s atmospheric absorption spectrum and predict its molecular-level composition. The general idea is that, over time, we will implement this model on our website to also estimate atmospheric composition of the planets.

Our main focus is to show how AI can aid in the discovery of new worlds — automating the process and making the exploration of the universe something that anyone can follow and learn from alongside science.

projectDetails.name: Exoplanet Hunter
projectDetails.summary:
My project, Exoplanet Hunter, is an end-to-end solution featuring a machine learning model and an interactive web application designed to classify potential exoplanets. This directly addresses the challenge by creating a robust Machine Learning model trained on NASA's Kepler Object of Interest (KOI) dataset and providing a web interface for user interaction.

The best-performing model, a LightGBM classifier, analyzes key data variables to distinguish between an exoplanet CANDIDATE and a FALSE POSITIVE with high accuracy. The final model was integrated into a Flask web application, containerized with Docker, and deployed on Google Cloud Run. This allows anyone, from researchers to enthusiasts, to manually input data and receive a real-time classification.

This project is important because it offers a scalable tool that can accelerate the discovery of new worlds hidden in NASA's vast datasets, empowering both scientists and the public in the ongoing hunt for exoplanets.
projectDetails.details:
My project, Exoplanet Hunter, is a web-based tool that uses an AI model to classify potential exoplanets from NASA's Kepler data. It works by taking user-submitted stellar and transit data through a web form, preprocessing it, and feeding it into a pre-trained LightGBM classification model to return a prediction. The primary benefit is automating a traditionally manual and time-consuming analysis process, which significantly accelerates the vetting of exoplanet candidates. My intended impact is to provide an accessible tool for both researchers and the public, empowering more people to engage with exoplanet data and potentially contribute to the discovery of new worlds.

My project's creativity lies in delivering a complete, end-to-end solution - from raw data analysis to a deployed, interactive application - directly addressing the challenge's core objectives. I considered the user experience by creating an intuitive interface with clear outputs. A key factor in my development was model performance; I rigorously evaluated four different algorithms before selecting LightGBM as the most accurate. I also focused heavily on data integrity, implementing a two-step feature selection process using both correlation analysis and model-based importance to build a robust model free from data leakage.

The entire project was built using Python and a suite of open-source libraries, including scikit-learn for the machine learning pipeline, pandas for data handling, and Flask for the web server. The final application was containerized with Docker and deployed on Google Cloud Run for scalability and public access.

Access the live web application here: https://exoplanet-hunter-63487098151.us-central1.run.app/

projectDetails.name: Earthling Weather Stories
projectDetails.summary:
Earthling Weather Stories is a tiny storytelling concept that turns space-weather into human-centered “postcards.” For any city/date, the project pairs a short, two-to-three-sentence anecdote (written from an Earthling’s perspective) with a snapshot of solar/geomagnetic metrics (e.g., Kp index, F10.7). The result is a shareable card that blends art and data, helping people connect “what the Sun did” to a small, relatable moment on Earth (e.g., radio static during a storm, a faint aurora report, GPS quirks, or a disrupted satellite pass).

This directly addresses the challenge by reframing technical indicators as concise narratives that highlight impact and context. It is important because it lowers the barrier to understanding space weather, supports outreach and classrooms with bite-sized artifacts, and encourages curiosity. While this submission includes a concept mock and a structured 7-slide overview, the same template could later plug into real APIs to automatically compose localized stories and grow a public gallery.
projectDetails.details:
What it does / how it works:
Generates a micro-story “postcard” for a chosen city/date, pairing a short human vignette with space-weather snapshots (e.g., Kp, F10.7, solar wind hints). The template outputs a shareable visual (see concept mock).

Benefits & intended impact:

  • Lowers the barrier to space-weather literacy via storytelling.
  • Makes solar activity locally relevant (“What did the Sun mean for me today?”).
  • Useful for classrooms, outreach, and social media.

Tools / stack (prototype):
Design mock (JPG), slide deck (PPTX). A minimal web page (HTML/CSS) is included as a placeholder. Future: plug API sources for Kp/F10.7/aurora forecasts.

Creativity:
Blends art + data as tiny narratives, encouraging empathy and curiosity rather than charts alone.

Factors considered:
Clarity, shareability, and alignment to the challenge goals; keeping scope small to ensure a clean, on-time submission, with a path to integrate live data later.

projectDetails.name: Rainly
projectDetails.summary: Our project leverages five years of NASA Open Data to calculate historical probabilities and averages of key climate variables such as temperature, wind, and precipitation. Instead of relying on conventional meteorological forecasts—which can fluctuate daily—our system provides stable, data-driven insights based on long-term trends. By analyzing the same date and location across multiple years, the platform helps users understand likely weather patterns and climate tendencies for any chosen place and time. An integrated AI model interprets this information, generating personalized activity recommendations and concise summaries to make the data accessible to non-experts. This approach empowers users—from travelers to researchers and planners—to make better decisions grounded in historical evidence rather than uncertain forecasts, contributing to climate awareness and sustainable planning.
projectDetails.details:
👩 Persona: Sofia

Sofia is a young event planner who loves organizing outdoor experiences—but like many people, she struggles with unpredictable weather forecasts that change every day. Rainly was created to help people like Sofia plan with confidence by providing stable, data-driven insights instead of volatile daily predictions.

🧠 Overview

Rainly is a data-driven platform that analyzes five years of NASA’s open Earth observation data to calculate historical probabilities and averages for key climate variables such as rainfall, wind, and temperature.

Instead of relying on unstable daily forecasts, Rainly provides consistent, data-based insights that help users understand the likelihood of different weather conditions for any given date and location.

This empowers people like Sofia to make informed decisions about events, travel, agriculture, or everyday planning using science-backed climate intelligence instead of guesswork.

🗺️ Map Selection Screen

Users start by exploring an interactive map. By clicking anywhere on the map, they can access detailed historical climate information for the selected location — making data exploration intuitive and visual.

📍 Location and Date Filter

After selecting a location, the user can confirm the address and choose a specific date to retrieve climate probabilities. The interface displays the full address and allows easy filtering by time, helping users plan for specific events or trips.

🌤️ AI Climate Summary

Rainly generates an AI-powered summary that translates historical data into a friendly forecast. Here, the user sees the temperature, comfort level, and recommendations for outdoor activities based on long-term patterns instead of unstable daily forecasts.

🌡️ Detailed Climate Metrics

The dashboard presents detailed climate metrics such as wind speed, air humidity, solar radiation, precipitation, snow probability, and soil moisture — giving users a complete picture of the environmental conditions for the chosen date and location.

🌎 Impact & Creativity

Rainly bridges the gap between complex climate datasets and everyday decision-making.

By combining long-term satellite data with AI-driven interpretation, it democratizes access to climate intelligence.

The system’s minimal-cost, scalable architecture also makes it suitable for global use and future integration with sustainability projects.

🏗️ Tools

Frontend: React + Vite + TypeScript (interactive climate map and dashboards).

Backend: FastAPI (Python) connected to NASA’s Earthaccess API for dataset retrieval and filtering.

Dataset: GLDAS_NOAH025_3H (5-year historical data, global coverage).

AI Layer: Google Gemini API for natural-language summaries and recommendations.

Deployment: Google Cloud Run (serverless backend) and Vercel (frontend hosting).

🔗 GitHub Repository
projectDetails.aiReferences: Rainly uses Google’s Gemini API to interpret processed NASA Earth observation data and generate concise natural-language insights. The AI analyzes historical averages and probabilities of climate variables—such as rain, temperature, and wind—to provide accessible explanations and personalized activity recommendations. All AI outputs were reviewed and verified by the team to ensure scientific accuracy. No AI-generated images, videos, or audio were used. projectDetails.name: Project AracnoAlert
projectDetails.summary:
AracnoAlert addresses the “Data Pathways to Healthy Cities and Human Settlements” challenge by transforming environmental and health data into actionable insights for safer urban living.
The project developed a mobile app that allows users to report arachnid sightings by taking a photo, which an AI system identifies and links to regional risk maps.
It also integrates temperature datasets from NASA EarthData/Worldview and Copernicus to correlate climate conditions with arachnid activity, improving prediction and prevention.

The project is important because it connects citizens, science, and technology to reduce accidents, support public health responses, and provide easy, practical access to critical information — transforming community reports into data-driven protection for healthier cities.
projectDetails.details:
AracnoAlert is an innovative mobile application designed to protect communities from venomous and aggressive arachnids, combining artificial intelligence, environmental data, and public health awareness.

Through an interactive map, users can report sightings by taking a photo of the arachnid, which allows the AI system to automatically identify the species and display regional alerts showing concentration and risk levels.

The platform also maps hospitals and health centers with available antivenom, ensuring quick access to specialized medical care in emergencies.

Aligned with the “Data Pathways to Healthy Cities and Human Settlements” challenge, AracnoAlert integrates surface temperature data from NASA EarthData and Worldview (link) and annual mean temperature data for Europe from Copernicus (link).

These datasets help correlate climatic variations with arachnid population behavior, enabling predictive mapping and exhibition public health strategies.

Our group focused on easy access to information, clear communication, and practical usability as the core design principles.

The project is considered highly creative because it transforms open environmental datasets into community-driven alerts and health solutions, connecting citizens, science, and technology to build safer, healthier cities.

projectDetails.name: Climate Planner
projectDetails.summary:
Climate Planner is a climate-intelligent event planning platform that helps users choose the best dates and locations for their events using historical and predictive weather data. By combining data from NASA’s POWER API and Brazil’s INPE/CPTEC (Center for Weather Forecast and Climate Studies), the platform analyzes decades of meteorological records to estimate the probability of favorable conditions.

Through an Event Success Index, and visual analytics, Astro Flow transforms complex scientific data into practical, accessible insights. Users can visualize trends, compare potential dates, and integrate their chosen plans directly into Google Calendar.

This project addresses the challenge of reducing the impact of adverse weather on human activities, promoting smarter, data-driven decisions. It empowers planners from individuals to large organizations to minimize risk, optimize resources, and ensure successful outdoor events through the power of space-based climate data.
projectDetails.details: Climate Planner is a web app that helps users plan events with NASA- and INPE-level precision. It analyzes decades of climate data from the NASA POWER API and the CPTEC/INPE (Brazilian Center for Weather Forecast and Climate Studies) to find ideal event dates and minimize weather risks. The platform calculates an Event Success Index, visualizes data through charts and maps, and integrates with Google Calendar for scheduling. Built with React, Firebase, NASA, and INPE APIs, it turns complex weather data into actionable insights, helping users plan smarter, reduce cancellations, and ensure successful events.

projectDetails.name: Project Awi
projectDetails.summary:
We invite you to believe in the regeneration of our habitat: Planet Earth. Leading this mission is AWI (ALL WE), our ally in the journey for air quality. In partnership with NASA, we monitor tropospheric emissions to reduce exposure to pollutants and prevent health risks.
You can join the team and monitor air quality in real time. AWI combines a web platform with hardware developed by the team, collecting ground-based data and continuously learning to identify pollutants such as NO₂, PM 2.5, and O₃.
In the corporate and public agency, city halls, public agencies, and research institutions can use the data for urban planning, health policies, and environmental management. Data from satellites, local sensors, and sources enable economic and strategic analyses, also supporting schools and universities.
AWI promotes environmental awareness, public health protection, and practical learning, making complex information understandable for everyone. Each step was designed to be collaborative and inclusive, creating more than just a digital tool: a partner for education, citizen science, and community engagement, with a direct impact on people's lives and well-being.
projectDetails.details:
What is AWI?

AWI enables neighborhood-scale air quality monitoring, analyzing pollution variations and local atmospheric dynamics. A physical module with a microcontroller collects data in real time and sends it via APIs to the web platform. Furthermore, it includes a future project that allows the creation of mini community sensors, encouraging the participation of students and citizens in the formation of a collaborative environmental monitoring network.

Where do we want to go?

Our goal is to scale AWI globally, continuously improving its capabilities to make it an efficient tool.

We want to ensure healthier lives and promote environmental awareness by integrating the project with government agencies, research institutions, and the local community.

We use environmental and climate variables to provide more reliable and contextualized analyses.

Web Platform – Features and Target Audience

1. Home Page

o Explains the project, data sources used, and the benefits of the platform.

o Target Audience: students, teachers, and the general community. o Value: Provides context and initial engagement, allowing new users to understand the importance of environmental monitoring.

2. Real-time Map

The interactive map shows air quality in real time, including sensors developed by the students themselves.

Target audience: students, schools, and universities.

Value: Allows students to visualize their direct impact by comparing their local sensors with satellite data, promoting hands-on learning and scientific engagement.

3. Analytics

o Air quality projection for the next 30 days using a predictive AI model developed in Python, integrating data from NASA and local sensors.

o Target audience: government agencies and city halls.

o Value: supports strategic decision-making, enabling the creation of environmental policies, regulations, and urban planning based on reliable data.

4. Alerts

o Highlights cities with critical pollution levels and health risks.

o Target audience: public administrators and healthcare teams.

o Value: Allows for immediate action, planning prevention campaigns, and mitigating risks to the population.

5. Resource Management

o Manages network resources: number of monitored cities, active satellites, and connected ground sensors.

o Target audience: System administrators and project coordinators.

o Value: Ensures platform scalability and reliability, enabling global expansion and efficient collaborative monitoring.

Open Source Hardware

The AWI includes a complementary physical device with sensors that measure pollutants such as NO₂, PM 2.5, and O₃.

• Open Source: Any student or community can assemble their own sensor.

Github: https://github.com/AWIallwe/AWI_RP.git

• Integration: Sends data directly to the platform, feeding the collaborative network and enabling more accurate analyses.

• Value: Transforms theory into practice, encouraging active learning, citizen science, and community engagement.

Applications and Impact

• Education: Students build sensors, monitor their data in real time, and learn about pollution, climate, and technology.

• Government and corporate: City halls, public agencies, and research institutions use the data for urban planning, health policies, and environmental management.

• Community: Anyone can access reliable information on air quality, increasing awareness and preventing health risks.

• Each feature delivers tangible value: from hands-on learning to strategic decision support, creating a direct impact on education, governance, and public health.

How will it be powered?

The platform will be continuously fed by multiple data sources, including:

● Meteorological information (temperature, humidity, winds, atmospheric pressure);

● Ground-based sensors (collection devices);

● Satellite data and space instruments, such as NASA's TEMPO.

This data is processed and presented in a visual and intuitive interface, with legends and risk levels.

The results are displayed in a panoramic (map) and analytical format, supported by Predictive Artificial Intelligence and Big Data, which use statistical models and forecasting algorithms to identify patterns and support strategic decision-making.

Tools and Technologies

• Languages: PHP, JavaScript, Python, C++

• Frameworks: Laravel, Angular, Random Forest

• Database: MySQL

• Integrated APIs: Weather.gov

• Predictive AI: Python model for forecasting air quality over the next 30 days

Future Goals

1. Improve predictive AI models to increase forecast accuracy.

2. Expand the collaborative hardware network, making sensors accessible to more schools and universities.

3. Establish institutional partnerships with public agencies and environmental organizations to expand reach.

4. Provide a public API, encouraging the development of complementary solutions by other teams and scientific communities.

projectDetails.name: SharkTrack
projectDetails.summary: SharkTrack uses NASA satellite data, predictive modeling, and Smart Tags to monitor shark movements and feeding behavior in near real time. By integrating this data into a visualization platform, the project predicts foraging habitats and reveals environmental patterns. These insights support sustainable fisheries, conservation of endangered species, and climate impact monitoring, while engaging the public in marine ecosystem protection.
projectDetails.details:
Introduction

Sharks are keystone species that keep marine ecosystems in balance, yet their movements and diets remain challenging to monitor in real time. Our project leverages NASA satellite data and conceptual smart tags to predict shark foraging habitats and track both where sharks go and what they eat.

This knowledge is vital for ecology: unusual movement patterns may signal environmental stress, while dietary shifts can trigger cascading effects across the food web. By uniting movement detection with diet analysis, we provide powerful tools for ecological monitoring, fisheries management, and species conservation.

Equally important, these insights empower human decision-making. Real-time monitoring supports sustainable fisheries by informing quotas and closed seasons, helps protect endangered species through rapid management interventions, and provides early warnings of climate-driven disruptions. On a broader scale, this intelligence safeguards food security, supports policy design, and engages the public in marine conservation.

Our solution

To address these challenges, our solution introduces SharkTrack: a mathematical framework for predicting shark foraging habitats, combined with a conceptual model of a tracking tag designed to record shark locations and infer their feeding behavior. To support continued research, we also propose a data visualization platform that integrates near–real-time information from both satellites and tags. This platform enables a unified display of oceanographic data and shark movement patterns, providing a comprehensive view of environmental conditions and shark foraging dynamics.

Tag

The proposed solution introduces Smart Tags devices designed to monitor shark behavior and oceanographic conditions in real time. Each tag integrates conventional sensors for temperature, salinity, and depth, along with advanced systems such as sonar DIDSON, onboard cameras, and accelerometers to capture detailed environmental and behavioral data.

Deploying sensors underwater is inherently challenging due to limited energy availability and restricted communication with satellites or surface receivers. To address this, the tags combine a battery with piezoelectric energy generation, which converts the shark’s swimming motion into electrical power to extend operational life. When the battery level drops to 20%, the tag enters a battery-saving mode, temporarily deactivating non-essential systems while continuing to harvest and store energy. Once sufficient charge is restored, the full monitoring functions are reactivated, enabling long-term operation with reduced invasiveness and environmental impact.

Each tag collects a broad set of data: environmental sensors record water temperature, salinity, depth, and geolocation, while behavioral sensors capture the shark’s movement patterns. The camera system is designed for behavior-triggered recording, activating only when the accelerometer detects a hunting or feeding motion. At that moment, the camera captures video of the event, and the sonar (DIDSON) scans the surrounding water to identify prey. All data is stored locally and transmitted when satellites are reachable, creating a continuous and high-resolution dataset of shark movement, feeding, and habitat use.

The modular design keeps each tag lightweight (under 5% of the animal’s body mass) and adaptable to different species — from large oceanic predators like tiger sharks to smaller coastal species such as lemon sharks. By combining environmental sensors, behavioral monitoring, and real-time communication, this system establishes a comprehensive ecological monitoring framework. The resulting data can reveal shifts in feeding habits, detect environmental anomalies, and shed light on rare events like unusual shark migrations, providing a sustainable and scalable model for global marine conservation and climate-linked behavioral research.

Foraging Predictive Model

To better understand shark foraging habitats, a broad range of environmental information is utilized. Several studies [1, 2] have successfully employed variables like sea surface temperature (SST), sea surface height anomalies (SSH), and chlorophyll concentration, among others, to characterize and predict foraging areas.

By integrating these environmental variables, it becomes possible to model habitat suitability using Species Distribution Models (SDMs) — mathematical frameworks that relate species distributions to their environmental preferences. SDMs leverage both traditional statistical methods and, more recently, machine learning approaches, which have demonstrated superior predictive accuracy [3–5].

In this context, our proposed mathematical framework uses the Random Forest machine learning model to predict potential shark foraging habitats by combining environmental data from NASA satellite observations (SST, SSH, and chlorophyll concentration) with in-situ measurements obtained from the proposed smart tag (ambient temperature, salinity, and geolocation). In addition to having superior predictive accuracy compared to statistical models, Random Forest stands out from other ML models for its ability to provide ecological interpretability by identifying which environmental variables contribute most to habitat suitability.

Given the input data, the model assigns a confidence score to each coordinate within a 5 km radius of the shark’s location. Areas with higher confidence values are considered more likely to represent foraging activity. The table below illustrates an example output, showing the five locations with the highest predicted probability of shark foraging.

This integrative approach provides a robust, data-driven framework for understanding shark foraging behavior and habitat use.

Data Presentation

To maximize the impact of our solution, we designed an interactive interface that transforms complex satellite and sensor data into meaningful, accessible insights. Built on NASA’s global imagery, the platform offers a dynamic map that displays shark locations alongside key oceanographic variables such as sea surface temperature, chlorophyll concentration, and other ecological indicators. These layers allow users to explore the environmental context of shark behavior, making it possible to detect unusual patterns or predict potential ecological shifts.

Predictive model outputs and near-real-time sensor data feed directly into the platform, enabling continuous updates. For scientists, this provides a research-grade tool to analyze ecological interactions. For fisheries managers, the system highlights potential conflicts with commercial stocks, helping guide sustainable harvesting policies. For conservationists, it identifies when sharks are interacting with vulnerable species, supporting rapid response strategies. For students and educators, the platform works like a living classroom: it turns real satellite data and ecological models into interactive lessons that are easy to explore. This helps young people learn about sharks, understand ocean science, and get inspired to protect marine life.

To complement the visual data, we integrated the DeepSeek-V3 pre-trained language model. Through prompt engineering, the model takes on the role of a marine biologist, translating complex patterns into clear and engaging explanations. This narrative layer not only describes where sharks are and what they are eating, but also explains why these patterns matter—such as highlighting cascading effects in the food web or signaling climate-driven changes in migration. By combining visuals with natural language, the platform becomes especially valuable for users with less scientific background, making advanced ecological insights accessible to everyone.

Conclusions and Future

This project integrates predictive modeling, smart tag technology, and interactive visualization to monitor shark behavior and foraging habitats in near real time. By combining environmental sensors (temperature, salinity, depth, geolocation) with accelerometers, behavior-triggered cameras, and sonar, the system produces high-resolution data on shark movements and feeding events. When combined with NASA satellite data, a Random Forest model predicts likely foraging areas, while the visualization platform—enhanced with AI-generated explanations—makes these insights accessible to scientists, conservationists, and the public. The solution offers a sustainable, low-impact framework for studying apex predators and advancing global marine conservation efforts.

Our next steps will focus on scaling deployments to cover additional regions and shark species. We will also work on communicating with local authorities to discuss the ecological impact, potential risks, and management implications of shark activity. Simultaneously, enhanced public engagement and educational initiatives will maximize the project’s conservation impact and raise awareness about marine ecosystem protection.

projectDetails.name: Air Sentinel
projectDetails.summary:
Air Sentinel is an application that combines NASA satellite and ground-station data with Machine Learning models to monitor and forecast local air quality.

The system sends alerts to users about current poor air quality or whenever the Machine Learning model predicts a significant worsening of conditions. The application also displays dashboards with detailed data, such as the Air Quality Index (AQI), the levels of each pollutant, and weather conditions (humidity and wind speed), in addition to offering practical prevention recommendations to help preserve users' health.

By providing air quality forecasts, the application allows users to plan ahead: an athlete can schedule their workout, and people with respiratory comorbidities can take precautions. This capacity for planning and protection is what demonstrates the value and relevance of the system to the community.
projectDetails.details:
Air Sentinel is a tool that processes large volumes of data from NASA's missions and instruments to train its Machine Learning model. Based on this historical data, the model creates forecasts for the Air Quality Index (AQI), which are delivered to users in a simple and accessible way.

To ensure accuracy, Air Sentinel integrates data from multiple sources. Through the AppEEARS API, it processes satellite and reanalysis data from NASA (TEMPO, MERRA-2, NOAA Wind). For ground-based measurements, it directly consumes the OpenAQ, AirNow and Pandora APIs, and finally, it uses the GIBS API to obtain the satellite imagery displayed on the interactive map.

In addition to displaying data, the system sends proactive alerts to users when air quality is critical or a significant worsening is forecasted, allowing them to plan ahead or take precautions. The platform also features a dedicated 'Health' tab, which offers practical actions and recommendations to mitigate the impacts of pollution.

The project's Frontend was developed in React, using HTML for the page structure, CSS for visual styling, and Javascript for interactivity. This combination creates a modern, fast, and responsive user experience, in which dashboard data, such as the AQI and maps, are dynamically updated without needing to reload the page.

The Backend was built with Node.js, which serves as a bridge, managing the API that receives user requests. Node.js, in turn, communicates with the analytical core of the system, developed in Python. It is in the Python environment that NASA data is collected, processed, and the Machine Learning models are trained and executed to generate the forecasts. Finally, the results are returned via the same route to be clearly displayed to the user in React.

The project's creativity lies in its information delivery approach, based on the Machine Learning model's forecasts. Instead of just displaying data, the solution translates complex NASA information into an accessible format and sends proactive notifications, alerting users according to their risk group. This provides users with autonomy and decision-making power, allowing them to schedule outdoor activities or take precautions against poor air quality.

The team's main guideline went beyond the simple display of data, focusing on how the information would be consumed effectively. The priority was to translate the complexity of NASA data into a clear format and, crucially, to deliver it proactively through alerts, turning the tool into an active monitor. To ensure maximum relevance, these alerts are distributed across multiple platforms, from mobile to smartwatch, ensuring that the information arrives effectively.

In parallel, TRAE was used as a development assistant, contributing to the project's structure, code refinement, and the optimization of integrations. Finally, we used Eleven Labs to generate the audio for the 30-second demonstration video and Google's VEO to help generate the videos.

projectDetails.name: Butterfly's Garden
projectDetails.summary:
What if you could see the future of your fields? Stop reacting to devastating pest outbreaks and start predicting them. Introducing Butterfly's Garden, a revolutionary strategy game that puts the power of foresight directly into your hands.

Powered by real-world NASA satellite data and a sophisticated predictive AI, our simulation models the complex, cascading effects of climate on your farm. We translate vast streams of environmental information—from soil moisture to heat accumulation—into clear, actionable forecasts of pest and disease risk. This isn't just about watching data; it's about taking action. 

In this dynamic sandbox, you can test crop choices, experiment with conservation techniques, and simulate your response to climate shocks like droughts or floods. See how your decisions ripple through the ecosystem and learn to build a more resilient and sustainable operation. Butterfly's Garden transforms science into strategy, giving you the ultimate tool to plan your defense and protect your harvest. It’s more than a game—it’s the future of proactive agriculture. Master the forces of nature and ensure that every season is a successful one.
projectDetails.details:
In response to the challenge of bridging complex scientific data with practical agricultural applications, our project, Butterfly's Garden, proposes a simulation framework that transforms abstract environmental data into an interactive, educational experience. The fundamental premise is that the most significant challenges in modern agriculture, such as pest outbreaks, are not isolated incidents but rather emergent consequences of a deeply interconnected system. Climate, soil conditions, and crop health interact in non-linear ways, meaning a small change in one variable can trigger a cascade of effects, much like the proverbial butterfly flapping its wings. Our goal is to make these intricate connections visible and understandable, thereby shifting pest management from a reactive, often costly, response to a proactive, data-informed strategy.

The scientific methodology of Butterfly's Garden is built upon the principles of complex systems theory, using a cellular automaton as the foundational model. We represent an agricultural landscape as a dynamic digital grid, where each cell is not merely a pixel but a container for a rich profile of environmental conditions drawn from NASA's Earth observation data. Variables such as soil moisture, surface temperature, evapotranspiration, and vegetation indices create a multidimensional snapshot of the ecosystem's state at any given moment. The simulation's engine lies in a learned transition function that governs how each cell evolves over time based on its own state and that of its neighbors. This approach assumes that large-scale events, like pest infestations, emerge from the aggregation of these local, cell-to-cell interactions, allowing us to model the spatiotemporal spread of agricultural threats organically rather than through predefined rules.

Landscap-8 Change Detecction Feature: https://eos.com/find-satellite/landsat-8

To breathe predictive life into this model, we move beyond manually defined rules and employ a deep learning architecture known as a Convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM). This technique is uniquely suited to our task, as it is designed to learn from sequences of spatial data, akin to understanding and forecasting the next frames in a video. By training this network on years of historical, time-stamped geospatial data from sources like NASA Giovanni and Earthdata Search, the model learns the intricate, time-dependent relationships between environmental precursors and agricultural outcomes. A core assumption of this methodology is that the patterns and correlations observed in historical data—the specific sequences of heat accumulation and soil moisture that preceded past outbreaks as documented by sources like Embrapa and MAPA—hold predictive power for the future. The ConvLSTM, therefore, acts as the predictive brain of our simulation, processing the flow of environmental data to forecast the probable emergence of pest-friendly conditions.

Ultimately, this sophisticated back-end model serves an accessible and engaging front-end purpose, directly addressing the challenge's call for an educational game. The player’s interface is centered around an interactive map of their farm, which is a direct visualization of the underlying cellular automaton grid. Through a user-friendly toolkit, players can toggle various NASA data layers—visualizing real-time soil moisture, seeing heat maps of surface temperature, or monitoring plant health via the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI). This feature is crucial, as it allows players to directly see the raw data influencing their farm's health. When they click on a specific grid cell, they can view charts showing recent trends in these variables, building a direct, intuitive link between the scientific data and the conditions on the ground.

The gameplay loop is designed to be an active learning experience. Players interact not with raw data or complex algorithms, but with a simplified, visual representation of a farm. They can introduce events—such as planting a specific crop, applying a conservation tillage technique, or simulating a climatic shock like a drought—and then use a forecasting tool to witness the model's prediction unfold over the next weeks or months. To provide structure, the game includes curated scenarios based on historical events or climate projections, challenging players to, for example, navigate a historically accurate drought period or adapt their farm to a future with increased rainfall volatility. The most critical educational component is the feedback system. If an outbreak occurs, an "after-action report" explains why, directly referencing the environmental data: "The rust outbreak was preceded by 14 consecutive days of high humidity and leaf wetness. Your decision to plant a dense canopy crop exacerbated these conditions. Next season, consider wider spacing or a more resistant varietal."

Butterfly's Garden thereby becomes a decision-making sandbox, a "flight simulator" for agricultural management. It translates the immense repository of NASA's open data from abstract measurements into tangible consequences, empowering players to explore the benefits of sustainable practices and internalize the delicate, interconnected nature of our agricultural ecosystems. The game does not just present data; it allows players to actively probe a data-driven model of the world and learn from its response, fostering a new generation of decision-makers equipped with the intuition and knowledge to manage land responsibly and productively.

projectDetails.name: Project ChuvaCerta
projectDetails.summary:
ChuvaCerta turns NASA open data into hyperlocal rain nowcasts for São José do Rio Preto and nearby towns. We address the challenge “Will It Rain On My Parade?” by estimating probability of precipitation (PoP) for the next 0–6 hours at neighborhood scale so event organizers and growers can make faster, safer decisions.

Our demo ingests GPM IMERG V07 near‑real‑time precipitation, calibrates local bias with MERRA‑2 climatology, and applies a lightweight trend + advection + logistic model to produce PoP tiles. A simple web app shows an interactive map with impact levels (light/moderate/heavy rain), tooltips, and a shareable embed widget for event pages. An API exposes the same layers for other apps.

Why it matters: sudden rain disrupts outdoor culture and smallholder operations. By converting global satellite data into street‑level risk, ChuvaCerta helps reduce cancellations and losses, while the approach is replicable to other cities using only open data and open‑source tools.
projectDetails.details:
ChuvaCerta delivers neighborhood‑level probability of precipitation (PoP) for the next 0–6 hours and visual “impact levels” for light, moderate, or heavy rain.
Pipeline (demo):

  1. NASA GPM IMERG V07 (near‑real‑time) is cropped to our AOI and aggregated into recent‑trend features.
  2. MERRA‑2 climatology helps correct local bias and define impact thresholds.
  3. A lightweight logistic model + advection of recent echoes estimates short‑range PoP.
  4. We publish cloud‑optimized GeoTIFF → tiles and serve an interactive MapLibre web app and REST API.

Benefits & impact
Outdoor events and small farms suffer from surprise showers. Clear, local PoP cuts cancellations, improves safety, and reduces waste. The method is reusable in other regions using open data.

Stack (tools & languages)
Python (xarray, rioxarray, numpy, pandas, scikit‑learn), FastAPI (API), TiTiler/COG (tiling), MapLibre GL JS (front‑end). Optional: GEOS‑FP for context/validation.

Creativity
We translate complex satellite/reanalysis data into plain‑language risk per neighborhood and provide an embeddable widget for event sites.

Considerations
Bias & latency of satellite QPE; uncertainty communication; reproducibility; licensing for base maps and boundaries; accessibility and English‑first submission requirements.
