projectDetails.name: Ask the Stars
projectDetails.summary: Ask the Stars is a web app that turns NASA’s bioscience literature into an interactive “night sky” of knowledge. Each paper appears as a star, and edges connect studies that are methodologically or thematically related. Under the hood, we split papers into passages and index them with a hybrid retriever—embedding-based semantic search (vector database) plus BM25 keyword search, to surface both close conceptual matches and precise terms. Clicking a star reveals summaries, key concepts, and citations; users can also ask questions to an LLM that answers with grounded snippets linked back to the original passages. By transforming papers into an intuitive, explorable map, Ask the Stars reduces time to insight, helps researchers discover non-obvious connections across subfields, and makes NASA bioscience more accessible to students, collaborators, and decision-makers.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does Ask the Stars Search Engine do?

Ask the Stars turns NASA’s bioscience literature into an interactive star map of related papers. You can search by topic or keyword, explore clusters, and click a star to see title, year, journal/publisher, abstract, and a direct link to the PDF. On the right side, a chat encourages you to make questions and explore the knowledge in the stars.

How it works

Interface at a glance
Landing Page
Informative Tour
Interactive Chat

Star Interaction

Similarity Edges
Knowledge Graph Close Up

Knowledge Graph Full View
Extra: Team pic

Under the hood

Hybrid ingestion & retrieval.
Each paper is split into smaller passages (“chunks”). Every chunk is embedded into a high‑dimensional vector by an embedding model and stored in a vector database. Queries run a cosine‑similarity search over this database to capture contextual meaning. In parallel, a BM25 keyword search runs over the same corpus. We then fuse both result sets and apply a specialized re‑ranking model to deliver the most relevant passages.

Althought slow, data was inputted into Neo4J, this allowed an intresting visualization of the data.

Answer synthesis.
Top‑ranked chunks are passed to Google’s Gemma models (via Generative AI APIs) to produce concise, cited summaries in natural language. This lets the chat engine respond to questions grounded in the entire corpus while showing clear source links.

Graph visualization.
Papers are rendered with the G6 graph engine, where each paper is a star node and edges show relatedness. Users can zoom and click nodes to see metadata, abstracts, and direct PDF links.

While slower, we ingested the scientific corpus into Neo4j, constructing a partial knowledge graph (KG) from extracted (subject, relation, object) triplets using LLM-powered parsing of abstracts and metadata.
Each entity node is linked to its source paper via (:Paper)-[:MENTIONS]->(:Entity) relationships, preserving provenance.

We expose this graph through a custom D3.js visualization, rendered directly from live Neo4j queries.

  • Nodes represent entities and concepts.
  • Edges represent relations extracted from the text.

This offers a high-level view of semantic links between research areas and lets users visually explore scientific relationships across the corpus.

Infrastructure.
We deploy the backend on a Google Cloud Platform N2 VM, with the frontend served via Vercel. This setup allowed quick iteration and reliable performance during the hackathon.

What didn’t work

  • On‑VM LLM hosting. Running large models directly on the N2 instance caused unacceptable latency; we switched to remote Gemma APIs.
  • Neo4j query integration. Graph‑aware re‑ranking looked promising but was postponed due to time and resource constraints, although a partial knowledge graph was generated based on the most recent version of the database and can be accessed on the button Knowledge Graph on the website.

Why it matters

Traditional search engines on scientific portals often rely heavily on keyword matching. This creates barriers for users who don’t know the exact terminology, or who are exploring interdisciplinary questions where relevant studies may use different vocabularies.

Ask the Stars brings a new paradigm:
It blends semantic understanding, interactive graph exploration, and grounded LLM responses to help users, whether they are scientists or students, navigate NASA’s bioscience literature in a natural, intuitive way.

Our approach makes research:

  • More accessible to non-experts who may not know technical terms
  • Faster to explore, by highlighting hidden connections across hundreds of studies
  • Visually engaging, encouraging curiosity through a stellar map of science
  • Grounded and reliable, with answers that cite real passages from real papers

We believe this kind of tooling can democratize access to NASA's research, support faster cross-field innovation, and ultimately help more people "Ask the Stars", and get meaningful answers back.

Tools & technologies

  • Development tools: GitHub, Visual Studio Code, Vim, Cursor, Linux
  • Languages: TypeScript, Python, HTML, CSS
  • Frontend: React + G6 (a graph-visualization engine focused on simplicity and customization), D3
  • Infraestructure: GCP, Vercel, Godaddy
  • Backend: FastAPI (search and graph endpoints), Google LLM API
  • Database: Chromadb, Neo4J.
projectDetails.aiReferences: We used Google Gemini and ChatGPT throughout the development process to accelerate coding, troubleshoot issues, and refine written content. Within the app, GEMMA powers the interaction with the currently selected paper, providing answers based solely on its metadata and abstract to ensure grounded, source-specific responses.

projectDetails.name: "VIAGEM LITERÁRIA- CLIMA ESPACIAL"
projectDetails.summary:
The “Literary Journey: SPACE WEATHER” project was created to spark children’s interest in reading while introducing them to space and its mysteries. Children’s literature encourages imagination, creativity, and learning in a playful way.

Through stories about the Solar System, the Sun, planets, moons, and stars, students expand their knowledge and understand the importance of space for life on Earth. Reading also promotes scientific curiosity, critical thinking, and creativity, combining the beauty of literature with the wonder of science.

The project will include guided readings, discussions, artistic activities, story creation, and a final exhibition of the students’ work. Teachers will act as mediators, encouraging reading, imagination, and discovery throughout the process.
projectDetails.details:
O projeto visa combinar o prazer da leitura com a descoberta científica, estimulando a observação, o pensamento crítico e o desenvolvimento da imaginação. Dessa forma, a leitura sobre o Sistema Solar amplia o conhecimento da criança, fomentando a interdisciplinaridade entre literatura, ciência e tecnologia. Assim, o projeto contribui para a formação integral do aluno, unindo a sensibilidade da literatura com a maravilha da ciência.

O projeto será desenvolvido por meio de leituras guiadas no ambiente escolar, atividades práticas e produções criativas. As etapas incluirão:

  1. Leitura compartilhada do conto "O Sol Que Adorava Contar Histórias" (Livro Digital) para crianças em idade pré-escolar (4 e 5 anos); "Luna e o Clima Espacial" (Livro Digital) para alunos do Ensino Fundamental (1º ao 5º ano);
  2. Discussões e rodas de leitura, onde as crianças podem falar sobre o que aprenderam e fazer perguntas sobre o espaço;
  3. Atividades artísticas, como desenhos de planetas, maquetes, murais e dramatizações das histórias lidas;
  4. Criação de histórias originais, onde os alunos inventam suas próprias aventuras literárias no espaço;
  5. Exposição final, com apresentações dos trabalhos dos alunos e leituras para a comunidade escolar.

Ao longo de todas as etapas, o professor atuará como mediador, incentivando a leitura, a expressão oral e a descoberta científica

projectDetails.name: 🌎🛰️ Arapua Labs
projectDetails.summary:
Arapua Labs addresses the "Through the Radar Looking Glass" challenge by quantifying the unique and extreme hydrological and aeolian processes of the Lençóis Maranhenses, a critical tropical wetland. We developed a novel monitoring pipeline on Google Earth Engine (GEE) using Sentinel-1 SAR to overcome persistent cloud cover.

The project quantifies two major environmental dynamics:

Hydrology: Using SAR backscatter, we measured an extreme seasonal fluctuation in lagoon area, detecting a change of 169.6 km 
  (623.4 km  wet season vs. 453.9 km  dry season).

Aeolian Risk: Applying Amplitude Offset Tracking (AOT) to SAR imagery, we mapped active dune migration, revealing a significant rate of 30 m/yr towards the West.

This project is critical because it converts complex, raw SAR data into actionable Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). By integrating these findings with auxiliary climate data (wind/rain), we provide park managers with a powerful, quantitative tool to monitor climate impact and inform conservation strategy. The final deliverable is an intuitive, publicly hosted Interactive Web Map.
projectDetails.details:
Arapua Labs

The Arapua Labs: The Breathing Sands project uses advanced Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) 🛰️ and cloud computing to rigorously quantify the extreme seasonal dynamics of the Lençóis Maranhenses. This solution moves the monitoring of this globally unique site from qualitative visual assessment to robust, data-driven geospatial science.

What It Does and How It Works


Arapua Labs is a sophisticated geospatial monitoring framework built primarily within Google Earth Engine (GEE) using the JavaScript API, designed to measure the annual hydrological and aeolian rhythms.

  • Quantifying Hydrology via SAR Backscatter (Lagoons 💧): The system leverages dense time series of Sentinel-1 GRD imagery. This is critical as SAR is weather-independent, ensuring data continuity despite heavy cloud cover. The script generates median mosaics for the wet and dry seasons and applies the Otsu thresholding algorithm directly to the linear VV polarization (line 144) to robustly separate ephemeral water bodies (characterized by low backscatter) from the surrounding sand. This produces the precise total lagoon area (km2) and the net change (ΔArea). The use of focal mode filtering (line 154) acts as a light cleanup to minimize speckle noise.
  • Preparing for Dune Migration Analysis (Aeolian Risk 💨): The GEE script performs essential geometric correction and scaling (line 217) on Sentinel-1 amplitude images (VV band). These images are exported (pair1_A and pair1_B) and prepared as necessary inputs for Amplitude Offset Tracking (AOT)—a highly specialized technique typically used for measuring glacier flow or seismic deformation. This ensures the inputs are correctly formatted for the post-GEE Python step, which calculates the high-resolution, 2D displacement vectors of the dunes (m/yr).
  • Correlating Environmental Drivers: The platform integrates auxiliary meteorological data via time-series analysis. This includes GPM IMERG (monthly rainfall) with a CHIRPS fallback (lines 191–214), and ERA5-Land (hourly wind components u10 and v10) aggregated to monthly means (lines 234–250). This correlation allows for the scientific validation and attribution of the physical changes, linking lagoon area reduction directly to decreased rainfall, and dune movement to peak wind speeds.
Tools, Coding Languages, and Creativity

The project's creativity lies in its fusion of specialized remote sensing techniques and its robust, open-source implementation.

  • Innovative Methodology: The core innovation is applying the sophisticated Otsu algorithm to SAR data to reliably define ephemeral water bodies, and preparing the data for Amplitude Offset Tracking—a technique typically reserved for ice or bedrock—to measure the speed of sand dunes.
  • Languages and Software: The primary development environment is Google Earth Engine (GEE) using its JavaScript API. Data sources include Sentinel-1 GRD, ERA5-Land, and GPM IMERG. Subsequent analysis for AOT is performed using external libraries in Python (e.g., scikit-image).

Key Factors Considered by the Team:

  1. Cloud Coverage: The most critical factor, necessitating the use of SAR over optical satellites to ensure year-round data collection.
  2. Data Accessibility: The reliance on free and open-source data (Sentinel-1, GEE, Python libraries) ensures the monitoring framework is replicable and affordable for local researchers and park management in Brazil.
  3. Data Integrity: The script incorporates robust features like the GPM-to-CHIRPS data fallback to ensure the monthly climate time-series remains complete even if a preferred dataset is temporarily unavailable.

    Google Earth Engine Script and Map View - The mage shows the GEE interface, combining the project's source code, console output, and map visualization.


Monthly Rainfall in AOI — 2024

This graph displays the monthly precipitation in millimeters (mm/month) spatially averaged over the Lençóis Maranhenses AOI throughout 2024, using data from the GPM IMERG/CHIRPS sources.

  • Trend: The chart clearly shows the region's intense seasonality. Rainfall peaks sharply between February and April (the wet season), with the highest point around 0.6 mm/month.
  • Significance: The rapid decline in rainfall starting in May and June and dropping to near zero from July to November explains the massive difference in lagoon area measured by the SAR analysis. The lagoons are filled by the rains in the early months and dry out as precipitation ceases.

10 m Wind (monthly mean) — 2024

This graph illustrates the monthly mean wind speed (in m/s) at 10 meters above the surface for the AOI, aggregated from the ERA5-Land hourly dataset.

  • Trend: The wind speed is relatively low in the early wet season (around 2.0 m/s in April) and then increases dramatically, peaking around August–October (the dry season) at approximately 5.5 m/s.
  • Significance: This wind pattern is directly related to the dune movement. The highest wind speeds coincide with the dry season, when the dunes are exposed (not saturated or covered by water), maximizing the aeolian transport of sand. This confirms the primary driver for dune migration measured by the Amplitude Offset Tracking (AOT) part of the Arapua Labs project.

Mean Direction (degrees, math convention) — 2024


This image represents the final, integrated results of the Arapua Labs: The Breathing Sands project, combining the hydrological analysis from SAR (Sentinel-1) with the aeolian analysis from Offset Tracking (AOT) for the Lençóis Maranhenses.

The analysis is based on two main components shown in the map and the top-right data card:

Conclusion on Hydrological Dynamics (Lagoons)

The data confirms the intense and predictable seasonal "breathing" of the ecosystem, which is primarily driven by rainfall (as seen in the earlier charts).

  • Significant Fluctuation: The lagoon area shrinks substantially during the dry season. The wet season maximum (623.4 km2) is significantly larger than the dry season minimum (453.8 km2), resulting in a net fluctuation of 169.6 km2.
  • Visual Confirmation: The map clearly shows the blue (wet season) water extent encompassing the smaller yellow (dry season) polygons. This illustrates how the sand acts as a seasonal reservoir, with a large volume of water being stored and subsequently lost to evaporation and infiltration as the dry season progresses.
  • Conclusion: This 169.6 km2 change is the key metric for monitoring the park's hydrological health and assessing the impact of future drought years on water availability for local fauna and flora.
Conclusion on Aeolian Dynamics (Dune Migration)

The AOT analysis provides critical quantitative evidence on the movement of the sand masses, which aligns perfectly with the regional wind climate.

  • Speed of Active Dunes (P90): The most relevant metric is the P90 migration speed of 20 m/yr (or 30 m/yr in the improved legend). This figure represents the velocity exceeded by only 10% of the tracked pixels and is the most honest measure of the speed of the active dune crests.
  • Directional Consistency: The mean migration direction is 90∘ (West). This is highly consistent, confirming that the powerful Easterly/Southeasterly trade winds (as seen in the climate charts) are the relentless, dominant force pushing the entire dune system in a uni-directional path towards the interior/west.
  • Visual Risk Assessment: The red vectors (especially visible near the coast in the image) represent areas of highest shear and velocity (up to >40 m/yr). These vectors highlight the active front of the dune system, providing a high-priority risk map for forecasting encroachment on infrastructure or fixed ecosystems to the west.
Overall Conclusion (The Synthesis)

The image provides the essential evidence for data-driven environmental management of the Lençóis Maranhenses:

  1. Hydrological Security: Authorities must manage a large, predictable 169.6 km2 swing in water resources annually.
  2. Aeolian Hazard: The region faces a constant, measurable hazard from sand encroachment moving at a sustained rate of around 20 to 30 m/yr predominantly towards the west.

This integrated map serves as a baseline for predictive modeling—allowing park managers to correlate future climate forecasts with calculated impacts on lagoon size and dune velocity.



Benefits and Intended Impact

The intended impact of Arapua Labs is to elevate conservation efforts by providing quantitative tools aligned with the site's global importance.

  • UNESCO Relevance and Global Mandate: The Lençóis Maranhenses was recognized as a UNESCO Natural World Heritage Site in July 2024. This title attests to its exceptional universal value and implies a shared global responsibility for its conservation. Arapua Labs provides the exact quantitative baseline data required to fulfill this global mandate, providing precise metrics on its two defining natural processes.
  • Scientific Baseline & Climate Resilience: The project establishes the first robust, long-term measurement system, providing precise metrics on the hydrological health (e.g., 169.6 km2 area fluctuation). This allows authorities to model and anticipate the severity of future drought years and the resulting stress on local fauna and flora.
  • Actionable Risk Assessment: Forecasting dune movement (30 m/yr P90 migration speed) provides a crucial high-priority risk map for planning infrastructure and preventing encroachment on surrounding fixed ecosystems and communities to the west.
    Photos taken by me during my last visit to Lençois in February 2025

This GitHub repo contains the Google Earth Engine (JavaScript API) script for Sentinel-1 SAR processing—wet/dry mosaics, ΔVV moisture index, and Otsu-based water masks—and the accompanying Colab notebook that exports the results and builds the interactive map page with Folium/Leaflet.

projectDetails.name: TOBI (Temperature, Observation & Behavior Index)
projectDetails.summary:
TOBI (Temperature, Observation & Behavior Index) is a tool developed by Team BOREALIS for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025, addressing the challenge “Will It Rain on My Parade?”. We created a system that uses historical satellite-based data from the NASA POWER API to calculate the probability of extreme weather conditions—very hot, very cold, very windy, or very wet—on a given date and location.

Our solution combines a Python Flask backend with a Flutter and web-based frontend, enabling users to easily input coordinates and dates to receive clear, probability-driven forecasts. Results are presented in a user-friendly interface with icons, colors, and reliability scores, translating complex climate data into actionable insights.

TOBI is important because it helps communities, individuals, and event organizers make better-informed decisions for outdoor activities, reducing risks caused by unpredictable weather. By transforming raw NASA datasets into accessible forecasts, TOBI bridges scientific research with public usability and demonstrates how open data can directly benefit society.
projectDetails.details:
TOBI (Temperature, Observation & Behavior Index) is a project developed by Team BOREALIS for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025, under the challenge “Will It Rain on My Parade?”.

What does it do and how does it work?

TOBI provides weather probability analysis for outdoor event planning. It uses NASA POWER API datasets (2013–2024) to calculate the likelihood of extreme weather conditions—such as very hot, very cold, very windy, or very wet days—based on historical trends for a given location and date. Its analisys are done using the past dates from the one selected, e.g. if someone has selected the day 14/05/2026, it will search for the previous, but equal, days, that is, all the 14/05 from 2013 to 2024 and calculate the probabilities.

* Backend (Python Flask):

* Endpoint /weather_probability accepts latitude, longitude, and date.

* Fetches NASA POWER data.

* Computes averages, standard deviations, and quantiles.

* Defines thresholds for extreme conditions (e.g., very hot = T > mean + 1.5×SD).

* Generates JSON responses with probabilities, thresholds, averages, and a natural-language message.

* Frontend (Flutter + HTML/CSS/JS):

* Provides a responsive interface for user input.

* Sends requests to the backend and displays results.

* Uses icons and color coding for clarity.

Benefits

* Helps organizers plan outdoor events with reduced weather risk.

* Makes satellite-based NASA datasets accessible and useful to the general public.

* Provides probability-based insights instead of raw weather data.

* Adds a data reliability layer, warning users when historical data is less relevant.

Intended Impact

The project bridges scientific meteorological datasets with everyday usability, empowering individuals, communities, and organizations to make informed decisions about weather-sensitive activities.

Tools, Languages, and Software

* Backend: Python, Flask, RESTful APIs (JSON)

* Frontend: Flutter, HTML, CSS, JavaScript

* Data Source: NASA POWER API (`/temporal/daily/point`)

* T2M (Temperature at 2m)

* WS2M (Wind speed at 2m)

* PRECTOTCORR (Corrected daily precipitation)

Creativity

* Converts technical climate data into clear, human-friendly insights.

* Uses statistical modeling + visualization to present probabilities.

* Introduces threshold-based categorization of weather extremes.

* Designed for both usability and educational impact.

Team Considerations


* Accuracy: Ensuring reliability by referencing recent years’ data.

* Accessibility: Intuitive UI with simple visuals and messages.

* Scalability: Future roadmap includes machine learning, map-based visualizations, and real-time notifications.

* User trust: Reliability scoring helps users judge confidence in results.

In short: TOBI demonstrates how open NASA datasets can be transformed into a practical, educational, and user-friendly decision-making tool, making climate science accessible for real-world event planning.

projectDetails.name: The Solar Winds
projectDetails.summary:
The Solar Winds - Project SummaryWhat It Is
An educational website that explains space weather (solar storms, flares, and their effects on Earth) in simple, accessible language for everyone.
projectDetails.details:
The Solar Winds - Project Details

Project Type

Educational web platform for space weather awareness and public education

Technical Stack

HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (vanilla). Responsive design with real-time data integration from NASA and NOAA APIs. No backend required - static site architecture.

Design System

Color palette: Gray, Black, and Orange. Dark theme with gradient overlays and smooth animations. Modern typography with clear visual hierarchy. Mobile-first responsive approach.

Core Sections

Hero Section: NASA coronal mass ejection background image with animated title and scroll indicator.

Storytelling: Three-chapter narrative introducing space weather concepts - from solar eruptions to Earth's magnetic shield protection.

Educational Content: Comprehensive explanations of six space weather phenomena including solar flares, CMEs, solar wind, and geomagnetic storms. Impact analysis across six critical sectors with risk assessment meters.

Real-Time Monitoring: Live solar imagery from NASA Solar Dynamics Observatory and aurora forecasts from NOAA. Timeline of monitoring infrastructure including satellites and ground stations.

Interactive Quiz: Five multiple-choice questions with instant feedback, explanations, and personalized scoring system.

FAQ Section: Eight frequently asked questions covering safety, storm frequency, prediction capabilities, and preparation guidelines.

Mission Statement: Detailed explanation of the problem (inaccessible space weather information), the purpose (democratizing knowledge), and future enhancement roadmap.

Resources: Curated links to NASA and NOAA official sources, organized by monitoring, education, visualizations, and research data.

Key Features

Sticky navigation with smooth scrolling between sections. Interactive quiz with state management and result calculation. Hover effects and transitions on all interactive elements. Animated solar visualization with pulsing effects. Real-time image updates from external sources.

Content Strategy

Narrative-driven approach using real historical examples like the 1859 Carrington Event and 1989 Quebec blackout. Progressive information disclosure from basic concepts to detailed technical explanations. Visual risk meters showing impact severity across different sectors.

Target Audience

General public seeking space weather understanding. Students requiring educational resources. Industry professionals in aviation, energy, and telecommunications. Emergency management personnel. Science enthusiasts and educators.

User Journey

Users are engaged through dramatic NASA imagery, learn through story-based content, understand detailed phenomena with visual aids, monitor real-time conditions, test knowledge through interactive quiz, explore authoritative sources, and connect with the mission statement.

Unique Value Proposition

Bridges the gap between complex scientific data and public understanding by combining authoritative NASA and NOAA information with engaging storytelling. Makes space weather accessible without oversimplification, providing both educational value and practical awareness for a technology-dependent society.

Purpose and Justification

Space weather affects global infrastructure including power grids, satellites, GPS systems, aviation, and communications. Despite this critical impact, public understanding remains limited because scientific data is complex and inaccessible. The Solar Winds addresses this gap by translating technical information into clear, actionable knowledge. The application exists because understanding space weather is no longer optional - it's essential for protecting our interconnected technological civilization from solar storms that could cause trillions in damage.

projectDetails.details:
The project, “When the Sun Sneezed: A Journey Through Space Weather,” is an illustrated digital story designed to explain space weather and its effects on Earth in an engaging, age-appropriate way for children and teenagers. It works by combining scientific accuracy with storytelling and illustration, using the character Little Sun to narrate events like solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and the solar wind, while showing their real impacts on people such as astronauts, pilots, farmers, and power grid operators.

The main benefit is that it helps young audiences understand complex space science concepts through visual and emotional storytelling, increasing their interest in STEM education and space exploration. Its intended impact is to raise awareness of how solar activity influences technology, communication, and life on Earth.

The project was created using digital illustration tools such as Canva, with additional text and narration designed using AI-assisted editing tools.

It is creative because it transforms technical heliophysics data into a fun, character-driven narrative, making science more relatable. Our team focused on clarity, accessibility, and engagement, ensuring that the story is both educational and entertaining for diverse audiences.

projectDetails.name: IF: Choices We Made
projectDetails.summary:
Our mission in this challenge was to create “IF: Choices We Made” — an interactive narrative experience that transforms 25 years of data from the Terra satellite into a visual and reflective journey about human choices.

In the year 2225, GAIA-25 awakens — not just another artificial intelligence, but the living consciousness of Earth, woven from 9,000 days of Terra’s data. She speaks not as a machine, but as ancestral wisdom — a living memory that carries both humanity’s mistakes and learnings through generations. She calls you to become a Guardian in an animated journey that blends science and science fiction.

Players travel through time, revisiting key moments such as Terra’s launch in 1999, deforestation, and climate change that reveal the impact of our actions on the planet. Each memory becomes an interactive challenge based on real data from Terra’s five instruments — MODIS, ASTER, CERES, MISR, and MOPITT — allowing participants to make decisions that shape outcomes.

More than celebrating Terra’s scientific legacy, “IF: Choices We Made” inspires reflection: What if we had made different choices? What if we can still change? The future is not inevitable — it is shaped by the choices we make today..
projectDetails.details:
Overview

An animation with purpose: a celebration of 25 years of the Terra satellite transformed into an epic and inspiring journey that connects science, art, and imagination. More than a tribute to space exploration, “IF… Choices We Made” is an experience that raises awareness and inspires action. Here, Terra satellite data is transformed into living stories, and in this journey, the player is invited to reflect on their own decisions in a mix of film with outcome-driven choices—something that streaming services are currently testing with their users, but with our differential: using real data and an alternative path where we employ science fiction.

Problem Statement

Although we live in an era of data abundance, few recognize the true importance of Earth observation satellites. Information about climate, oceans, forests, and the atmosphere often reaches us as distant charts, but rarely touches the heart or inspires real change.

This gap between science and awareness often leads society to ignore environmental warnings, delay urgent solutions, or fail to grasp the weight of its choices. The result is a planet on an unsustainable path, where environmental degradation threatens not only nature but also the future of all of us.

We know that information alone does not generate action: it is necessary to transform data into comprehensible and engaging experiences. That is why we created IF… Choices We Made, an interactive animation that uses the universal, accessible, and appealing language of film and games for all ages and profiles, allowing participants to explore human choices, observe their consequences, and reflect on how their decisions shape the future. Films and games are a natural form of learning and engagement, connecting entertainment, curiosity, and action, making science not only understandable but also emotionally impactful. Combined with science fiction, which has historically proven powerful in sparking curiosity and engagement, the experience becomes even more compelling.

Why We Propose This Solution and How We Define the Target Audience

We decided to develop the project in the format of an interactive animation aimed at families engaged in education, as a mix of film and game. This choice is based on two main criteria from research:

Family involvement in education:

  1. Official data and national and international research point to increased parental participation. INEP (National Institute of Educational Studies and Research Anísio Teixeira) reports and studies published in SciELO (Scientific Electronic Library Online) show that parental involvement is directly linked to academic performance. This concern also appears outside Brazil: research by Common Sense Media (USA) and studies from the University of Texas indicate that parents seek content that combines learning and entertainment.

    Growth of streaming:
  2. According to ANCINE (National Cinema Agency), video-on-demand consumption is rapidly increasing in Brazil, but with a low presence of interactive educational content. This trend is global: in 2024, the number of streaming users surpassed 1.8 billion worldwide, and PwC’s Global Entertainment & Media Outlook confirms that on-demand video is one of the most dynamic segments of digital entertainment today. Moreover, platforms already offer interactive experiences where viewers choose different narrative paths, signaling interest in this innovative format.

Additionally, we considered our own family history and conducted preliminary research between September 30 and October 5 with groups of parents and guardians: 95% reported missing science content in more engaging formats, and 70% showed interest in interactive animations as a learning tool.

In this scenario, our solution emerges to fill this gap, combining real science and entertainment in an accessible, engaging experience designed for the whole family, confirming the proposal's relevance. All data used here is available in the provided links.

How It Works

Participants assume the role of the Earth Guardian, guided by GAIA-25, a planetary consciousness from the future. GAIA opens memory windows that function as time portals, taking participants to key moments in the past. At each challenge, participants choose between two paths. They do not know exactly what happened in the past or whether their choice is “right” or “wrong.” One path represents what actually occurred, while the other shows an alternative scenario. The goal is to reflect on how different decisions can change the future without immediately revealing the real path.

Choosing the real path presents participants with real images, videos, and scientific data, showing the consequences of these decisions. Choosing the alternative path shows idealized actions with explanations that encourage reflection on different perspectives and possible outcomes, highlighting that there is always another way to act, another decision to make. Thus, the experience promotes active learning, critical reflection, and understanding of human impact on the planet, encouraging conscious and responsible choices.

This balance between scientific basis and speculative fiction makes the experience unique: it teaches while also moving and inspiring.

We opted not to give GAIA a specific form, face, or definition so that each participant can imagine her individually.

The Terra Satellite

TERRA collects data on Earth’s biogeochemical and energy systems using five sensors that observe the atmosphere, land surface, oceans, snow and ice, and energy balance. Each sensor has unique characteristics allowing scientists to achieve a wide range of scientific objectives. The five sensors aboard TERRA are:

  • ASTER (Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer): Captures high-resolution images in visible and infrared light.
  • CERES (Clouds and the Earth’s Radiant Energy System): Analyzes Earth’s energy balance, how much the planet absorbs and reflects from sunlight.
  • MISR (Multi-angle Imaging SpectroRadiometer): Takes photos from multiple angles to study clouds, smoke, dust, and air pollution.
  • MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer): Observes vegetation, fires, deforestation, ice, oceans, and surface temperature.
  • MOPITT (Measurements of Pollution in the Troposphere): Measures carbon monoxide (CO) in the atmosphere.

Since all five instruments are on the same satellite making simultaneous observations, scientists can compare different aspects of Earth’s characteristics over time.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Trabalho em equipe TERRA" ]

Selection of Historical Visits and Instruments Used

For the narrative of IF… Choices We Made, we selected three specific historical episodes, one in Brazil, that clearly illustrate the impacts of human actions on the planet and highlight the Terra satellite instruments’ capabilities:

  1. Deforestation and fires along the Xingu River, Amazon – 2004
  2. This event shows the effects of human activities on tropical forests, globally important ecosystems. The main data came from MISR, which observes smoke, particles, and air pollution from different angles. Additionally, MOPITT data measuring carbon monoxide complemented the analysis, showing the impact of fires on air quality and pollutant emissions.

  3. Warm rivers in the Arctic – 2012
  4. This episode highlights climate change in polar regions, showing direct impacts on temperature and aquatic ecosystem balance. The main data came from ASTER, capable of mapping surface temperatures at high resolution. CERES data on reflected and absorbed energy was also included, correlating river warming with regional energy balance changes.
  5. Tsunami in Phuket, Thailand – 2005
  6. This event demonstrates how extreme natural phenomena affect human populations and coastal environments, emphasizing the link between human decisions and vulnerability to natural disasters. MODIS data monitoring vegetation, fires, and surface changes enabled analysis of tsunami-induced alterations.

Animation Structure

Each challenge is based on real data collected by Terra’s five instruments but presented in an accessible, visual, and playable form. The narrative is organized into milestones, each opened by a GAIA-25 portal:

  1. Terra Launch (1999) – Beginning of data collection and planet memory.
  2. Deforestation and fires on the Xingu River (2004) – Human impacts on tropical ecosystems.
  3. Tsunami in Phuket, Thailand (2005) – Natural phenomena and human vulnerability.
  4. Warm rivers in the Arctic (2012) – Climate change and polar ecosystem imbalance.
  5. Terra’s 25th Anniversary (2025) – Reflection on accumulated learnings and impacts.
  6. Achieving global SDGs (2100) – Vision of a sustainable future with collective action.
  7. GAIA Awakening (2225) – Narrative closure and invitation to reflect: “What if… we can still change?”
  8. Final Mission – Post-credit-like scene where GAIA invites the Guardian to build their own anaglyph glasses (with supplied sheet and QR Code) to view MISR’s “hidden” images, symbolizing the awakening of awareness: seeing the planet with new eyes.

Guardian storytelling – Oath and Journey The experience begins with the oath: "I am the Earth Guardian. I will honor its memories, learn from its mistakes, and use knowledge to protect the future."

From there, GAIA-25 reveals herself as guide and consciousness, leading the Guardian through intertwined timelines. She shows what really happened but also asks: “What if we had chosen differently? What if we can still change?” Through temporal portals and conjectural realities, the narrative reinforces that the Guardian is not a mere spectator but someone holding the weight of humanity’s choices in their hands.

Benefits

The experience offers multiple benefits:

  • Educational: Translates complex data into interactive learning, showing causes and effects of human actions visually and practically.
  • Social: Encourages collective awareness and environmental responsibility, bridging science and citizenship.
  • Emotional: Evokes empathy, hope, and reflection, connecting participants to the planet and the consequences of human choices.
  • Creative: Allows exploration of alternative scenarios and parallel universes, fostering critical thinking and imagination.

Impact

The expected impact is broad:

  • Show that the future is not inevitable; it is built by the decisions we make now.
  • Demonstrate how science, art, and science fiction can generate empathy and engagement.
  • Imagining possible futures is the first step to creating real solutions.
  • Help audiences understand that every decision matters, now and in future projections.
  • Promote deep reflection on sustainability, collective responsibility, and human legacy.Like science fiction, which has long served as a laboratory for imagining technologies and futures, the experience invites the audience to see imagination as a tool for transformation, not escape.

SDGs Addressed

The project aligns with several UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs):

  • SDG 4 – Quality Education: Promotes meaningful learning by translating real data into creative narrative experiences.
  • SDG 13 – Climate Action: Encourages reflection on climate change and conscious choices based on TERRA data.
  • SDG 15 – Life on Land: Highlights the importance of preserving biodiversity, forests, and ecosystems.

The project demonstrates that technology combined with imagination can bridge knowledge and action.

Ultimately, what better way to celebrate 25 years of the Terra satellite than inviting each player to reflect: What if we had made different choices? What if we can still change? The future is unwritten; today’s decisions define tomorrow. You choose: act or wait?

SOLUTION

Objectives

  • Educate and inspire families, making complex real data understandable and emotionally impactful.
  • Promote reflection on human impact on climate, ecosystems, and biodiversity.
  • Encourage responsible choices, showing that, like in narrative alternative lines, our present actions define possible futures.
  • Popularize science, following science fiction’s legacy of combining knowledge and imagination to engage people in human progress.

Future Goals

  • Expand the experience with more real events from different world regions, eventually covering each continent or country.
  • Include data from other NASA satellites and missions, increasing scientific exploration possibilities.
  • Develop multilingual versions, making the tool globally accessible.
  • Create a scientific storytelling platform connecting science, fiction, and interactive narrative, inspiring new generations to learn and act for planetary sustainability.

Our goal is to inspire youth and adults to understand the science behind the data, reflect on the impact of human decisions, and promote responsible choices contributing to a sustainable future while developing scientific awareness and collective responsibility.

Behind the Scenes and Methodology

We acknowledge that no team members have advanced technical expertise in technology or programming, but we see this as a challenge to be overcome with creativity and strategy. We used accessible tools such as Canva for visual frames, CapCut for video editing, and free software to refine texts and generate voices for the narrative. Our goal is to deliver a simple but carefully thought-out and well-executed final product. We focused on essentials, ensuring each visual, narrative, and interactive element has impact and clarity for the audience. For transparency and robustness, we separately provide all materials, preliminary audience research, and technological resources used. Thus, our solution, while simple, is based on real data, qualitative research, and a clear methodology.

Rights and Resources Used

All videos, images, and visual elements were created in Canva, using only resources with authorized educational and non-commercial licenses. No AI-generated material was used for creating main images or videos. Other content used—including soundtracks, scientific data, references, and NASA resources—are listed in the “References and Resources Used” section. The interactive part was created within an open game platform that does not require programming or coding, ensuring accessibility, originality, and transparency throughout the development process.

Tools Used

To transform science into interactive narrative, we used tools that combine technology, creativity, and collaboration:

  • Canva: Creation of wireframes, narrative frames, and visual elements.
  • CapCut: Video editing and assembly of presentation and narrative shorts.
  • Google Drive: Storage, collaboration, and project versioning.
  • Soundtracks and videos from Canva platform, licensed and free-use materials.

projectDetails.name: Zona Fria, cooling cities and warming the future
projectDetails.summary:
The Zona Fria project was developed for NASA Space Apps 2025 under the challenge “Data Pathways to Healthy Cities and Human Settlements.” This challenge asks participants to show how Earth-observation data can guide urban growth while maintaining the wellbeing of people and the environment. Climate change complicates urban quality of life; natural resources, ecosystems and existing infrastructure must be monitored, and planning decisions should consider both human and environmental wellbeing.

Zona Fria addresses this by mapping and simulating urban heat islands in Lajeado, Brazil. Using the Local Climate Zones (LCZ) framework, we classify city areas, integrate real-time temperature data via an API, and simulate land-use changes (for example, converting an industrial zone into a tree-covered area) to estimate the thermal impact. The system promotes data-driven decision making to improve thermal comfort and support public policies for sustainable development.
projectDetails.details:
Challenge selection

The challenge “Data Pathways to Healthy Cities and Human Settlements” invites teams to develop project plans informed by Earth science data to improve quality of life in growing cities. The prompt highlights that urban planners must use Earth observation to develop growth strategies that safeguard both people and the environment. It suggests considering topics like access to food, housing, transportation, pollution, availability of green spaces and exposure to extreme heat. Teams may choose the issues most relevant to their locality.

We focused on urban heat islands because Lajeado, a city in southern Brazil, experiences extremely hot summers and has dense urban areas. Heat islands directly affect comfort and health, so understanding which urban forms contribute to warming and simulating interventions is essential for sustainable planning.

Brainstorming and conceptualization

In the early phase we held a brainstorming session on a Miro board (Link). We discussed various approaches such as air-quality analysis, green-space availability, transportation planning, and heat-island mitigation. We chose Local Climate Zones (LCZ) because this system provides a standardized classification of urban and rural areas based on thermal properties and land cover, making it easier to interpret the urban environment.

Methodology and tools

1. Defining training areas

To classify Lajeado into LCZs we first delineated training areas in Google Earth. These are polygons representing each LCZ class and serve as reference samples for the classifier. We drew representative polygons over Lajeado and exported them as a KMZ file. This manual step required inspecting building heights, density, vegetation and other features and was essential for calibrating the next step.

Google Earth Link

2. Generating Local Climate Zones

We used the LCZ Generator from WUDAPT to produce a complete LCZ map of Lajeado. The tool employs machine learning trained with satellite data and the provided training polygons. After uploading the KMZ training file, the generator produced an output file with geometries of all LCZs in the city, which we incorporated into our system.

3. Building the web system

The prototype was built in Python (Flask) with an interactive web interface (HTML/JavaScript). Key features described in the repository include:

• Viewing LCZs: the system automatically loads the LCZ map for Lajeado.

• Real-time temperature data: we use the Meteomatics API to fetch 2-m air temperature (t_2m:C). The endpoint format is https://api.meteomatics.com/{datetime}/{parameter}/{location}/json and requires user credentials, configured in a .env file.

• Land-use change simulation: users can select an LCZ on the map and convert it to another LCZ (for example, from “Compact Low-Rise” to “Dense Trees”). The system calculates the temperature difference (ΔT) using thermal offsets for each LCZ. The formula is:

    ΔT = Offset_LCZ_B − Offset_LCZ_A

    T_new = T_current + ΔT

  For example, converting LCZ 3 (Compact Low-Rise, offset ≈ +2.3 °C) to LCZ 11 (Dense Trees, offset ≈ –1.5 °C) results in a reduction of ~3.8 °C.

• Internal API: the app exposes REST endpoints to return LCZ GeoJSON data, get temperature at a specific point, retrieve a temperature grid and calculate change scenarios. This enables integration with other systems or a future mobile interface.

4. Visual design in Figma

Beyond the functional prototype, we designed a final interface in Figma. The layout presents an interactive map with LCZ and temperature layers, a side panel showing the selected class, and a menu to simulate zone conversions. Icons, colors and typography align with environmental themes and NASA Space Apps branding.

5. Scientific literature

The project builds on research on Local Climate Zones and urban heat islands, including:

• Stewart & Oke (2012) – the seminal paper defining the LCZ framework.

• Recent systematic reviews on urban heat dynamics in LCZs.

• Case studies in cities such as Beijing, Hiroshima and Sapporo that quantify thermal differences between LCZs.

These references informed the thermal offset values used for each LCZ class.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
• LCZ Generator: classification of climate zones is performed by a machine-learning model hosted by WUDAPT. By providing training areas, the tool labels the entire city.

• Coding assistance: AI-assisted programming tools were used to accelerate code writing, but the core logic and quality control were defined by team members.

We did not generate images or prototypes with AI; thus no AI watermark is required.

projectDetails.name: Weather seeds
projectDetails.summary:
Our project is an online simulation game that integrates real-time climatological data with interactive agricultural management. The platform continuously processes key meteorological parameters—such as rainfall, humidity, precipitation, and solar irradiance—and is designed to incorporate additional environmental and agronomic features in future updates, covering all variables that influence crop productivity.

Within the game, players can access the historical cultivation records of the virtual land they acquire, as well as short-term weather forecasts for the upcoming days. This information enables them to correlate environmental conditions with the crop types available for planting, such as soybean, wheat, rice, and corn, thereby making evidence-based farming decisions.

All datasets within the game are tradeable assets: players can purchase historical regional data, predictive forecasts, and crop-specific agronomic insights to optimize their strategies. By turning satellite- and Earth-observational data into core gameplay resources, the platform gamifies complex datasets and makes them a strategic commodity for progression within the game.

This approach aims to spark interest among younger audiences in space-based data collection and its relevance to life on Earth—highlighting how satellite-derived information directly impacts agricultural productivity and environmental stewardship.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is an online simulation game called Weather Seeds that integrates real-time observational data to simulate realistic agricultural conditions. The game primarily uses APIs from Meteomatics, but it is designed to be compatible with any API providing real-time observational data. These datasets—such as temperature, rainfall, and solar irradiance—are used to determine how environmental conditions affect players’ crops and farming decisions.

The game combines engaging gameplay with educational value, capturing the attention of young players through competitive elements. Players can compare their farm productivity with friends or within a league, creating a sense of challenge while learning how observational data informs real-world agriculture. This competitive aspect encourages broader participation and can scale to larger communities, promoting awareness of satellite and observational data usage.

Tools and Technologies Used:

  • Design and Prototyping: Figma
  • Development: VS Code
  • Programming Languages: JavaScript, HTML, CSS
  • Frameworks: Express.js

Creativity and Innovation:
The project is creative because it gamifies real-world scientific data, transforming abstract observational datasets into an engaging, competitive experience. It combines education, strategy, and social interaction in a format that is approachable for younger audiences while retaining scientific accuracy.

Factors Considered by the Team:
The main factor guiding our development was engaging a large youth audience, recognizing the importance of young people in shaping culture and habits. Our strategy focused on teaching while entertaining, ensuring the game is both fun and educational, and motivating players to learn about climate, crop management, and the value of observational data.

projectDetails.name: ExoMiner - Exoplanet Data Predictor & Training
projectDetails.summary: Our project consists of a machine learning platform designed to identify exoplanets using astronomical data from the Kepler, K2, and TESS satellites. The solution enables automated upload, unification, and cleaning of datasets from these three missions, creating an integrated and consistent base for analysis. Through the platform, users have the autonomy to upload their own training data, without the need for any manual preprocessing — all data preparation and standardization steps are performed automatically by the system. Then, different prediction algorithms are applied and compared to classify exoplanet candidates and distinguish false positives from genuine discoveries. This multi-satellite approach enhances the robustness of the models by leveraging complementary patterns captured by each mission. The project greatly facilitates the work of scientists and researchers, making the analysis process faster and more accessible, while contributing to the advancement of astrophysics and the application of artificial intelligence in space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Chicxulub Simulator
projectDetails.summary:
Chicxulub Simulator is an interactive web platform designed to model and visualize the consequences of asteroid impacts on Earth using real NASA data. The simulator connects to NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NeoWs) and JPL Small-Body Database (SBDB) APIs to automatically retrieve parameters such as diameter, velocity, and composition. These data are used to compute impact energy, crater size, and the extent of the Crater Zone, Thermal Impact Area, and Blast Wave Radius through physics-based calculations.
Users can input data manually or select a real asteroid, choose an impact location on the map, and observe the potential effects. The system integrates Leaflet for global geospatial visualization and Overpass API to identify affected cities.
As a planned AI-powered extension, Chicxulub will generate optimized evacuation routes, dividing populations into multiple safe directions to improve emergency flow and minimize congestion.
Developed with Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, the project combines physics, space data, and mapping to raise awareness about planetary defense. Its purpose is to make complex astrophysical phenomena accessible and inspire proactive thinking about Earth’s preparedness for asteroid impacts.
projectDetails.details:
Chicxulub Simulator visualizes and explains how asteroid impacts affect Earth, transforming real NASA data into accessible scientific insight. Inspired by the Chicxulub event, it retrieves Celestial Bodies parameters from NASA’s NeoWs and SBDB APIs, automatically filling details such as diameter, density, and velocity. Users can manually input data or select a real Near-Earth Object, then define an impact location by clicking on a Leaflet-based global map.

The system applies real physics equations to calculate the asteroid’s mass, kinetic energy, and the resulting Crater Zone, Thermal Impact Area, and Blast Wave radii. Using the Overpass API, the simulator identifies nearby cities to display localized consequences in real time.

For future development, an AI-powered extension will intelligently generate evacuation routes by analyzing population density and geography. This feature will optimize safe paths and divide populations into multiple exit flows, enhancing emergency preparedness and disaster-response planning.

Built with Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, Chicxulub bridges data science, astrophysics, and visualization to make planetary defense accessible to everyone. The project’s mission is to foster awareness, education, and innovation in mitigating the risks posed by Near-Earth Objects.

projectDetails.name: Stories That Shine
projectDetails.summary:
'Stories That Shine' is a project developed like Interactive Digital Stories for children aged 7 to 8, utilizing Real NASA Data. 

Our mission is to transform the complexity of space weather information into knowledge for the future.

We do this through interactive stories where children are the protagonists. With a clay-like aesthetic, they connect explosions to GPS failures, actively participating in science.

This is how learning becomes playful, personal, and prepares the next generation.

The core challenge is that space weather is a real, invisible threat capable of causing massive failures in modern connectivity (cell phones, GPS, internet), yet complex data is poorly understood. Our solution addresses this urgency by transforming complex science (solar flares, Coronal Mass Ejections, Earth’s magnetic field) into engaging, relatable adventures. This is vital because society is EVEN MORE Connected Today, and the project aims to make space weather a natural knowledge for the next generation. Ultimately, knowledge is considered the best form of protection against this hidden threat.
projectDetails.details:
It is an interactive digital video where children between the ages of 7 and 8 can interact directly with the video. They can choose a character and the space weather content they want to interact with while learning the topic in a playful way and changing the course of the story itself.

It works by transforming complex science into fun adventures. The content is based on real NASA data.

The project simplifies concepts such as:

1. Solar flares;

2. Coronal Mass Ejections;

3. Earth's magnetic field.

The solution uses games, animations, and empathy to make the learning experience engaging. It provides relevant examples of how space weather affects everyday technology, including phones, airplanes, GPS, the internet, and household electricity.

The main benefit is educational and protective: the goal is to transform space weather from an invisible topic into natural knowledge for the next generation.

The intended impact is to ensure that the next generation understands the urgency that everything depends on space and that space weather is a real threat. The project seeks to address the vulnerability of modern society, which is EVEN MORE connected today (dependent on cell phones, satellites, GPS, and the internet), to phenomena such as solar flares, which have historically caused serious problems, such as the 1989 Canadian blackout and satellite failures.

We considered the following crucial factors:

1. The Urgency of Connectivity: Society's current critical dependence on space, emphasizing that "Today, We Are EVEN MORE Connected" through Cell Phones, GPS, Satellites, and the Internet. 2. The Historical Risk: Evidence that the threat is real, citing the 1989 solar flare, which left millions of people in Canada without power for hours and caused satellite and communication failures.

3. The Knowledge Gap: The existence of a "massive amount of data available," but a lack of understanding of what that data means (the real "It's Not the Data" problem), driving the need for effective communication.

projectDetails.name: Air Tomorrow
projectDetails.summary:
Air Tomorrow is an intelligent forecasting platform designed to anticipate future air quality levels, empowering people to make safer and more sustainable decisions in their everyday lives. With nearly 99% of the global population exposed to polluted air, understanding and predicting air quality has become a crucial challenge for public health and environmental management. Air Tomorrow addresses this issue by combining historical and real-time data from NASA’s satellite and ground-based monitoring systems. These datasets are processed through advanced AI-driven predictive models, which analyze regional environmental parameters—such as temperature, humidity, and emission patterns—to forecast air quality in the near future.
By transforming complex atmospheric data into accessible and actionable insights, Air Tomorrow enables communities, researchers, and policymakers to anticipate pollution peaks, reduce exposure risks, and plan for a cleaner tomorrow.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do or how does it work?

Air Tomorrow functions as a sophisticated, AI-driven platform for predictive air quality forecasting. Its core mechanism involves the ingestion and processing of vast amounts of NASA Earth observation data to generate hyperlocal forecasts for the near future.

The Workflow:

  1. Data Ingestion: The platform continuously collects historical and real-time data from NASA's satellite and ground-based monitoring systems.
    • Pollutant Data: This includes key atmospheric measurements, such as the hourly vertical column data for Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2​) from missions like TEMPO, which tracks pollutants produced by sources like traffic and wildfires.   NO2​ is a precursor to harmful ground-level ozone and toxic particulates.   
    • Emission Triggers: The system integrates Near Real-Time (NRT) active fire data from instruments like MODIS and VIIRS (via FIRMS) to capture current wildfire emissions and thermal anomalies that severely impact air quality.   
    • Environmental Context: Regional environmental parameters, such as temperature, humidity, and land surface characteristics, are also integrated to calibrate the atmospheric models.
  2. Predictive Modeling: The combined datasets are fed into advanced AI-driven predictive models. These models analyze the regional patterns—linking emissions, weather, and historical air quality—to calculate future air quality values.
  3. Actionable Output: The complex atmospheric data is transformed into accessible and actionable insights, providing users with a forecast for their specific region and associated health precautions.

2. What benefits does it have?

The primary benefit of Air Tomorrow is shifting air quality information from a reactive measurement to a proactive forecasting tool, directly enhancing public health and empowering informed decision-making.

  • Reduces Exposure Risk: It allows users to anticipate pollution peaks and plan their activities better, enabling them to reduce exposure risk, especially for high-risk individuals.
  • Targeted Health Protection: The solution is specifically beneficial for people with special conditions, such as respiratory problems (e.g., Chronic Respiratory Diseases/CRDs). Air pollution is the second leading risk factor for CRDs, and by providing a forecast, the platform helps this vulnerable population take necessary precautions.   
  • Empowers Decision-Making: By transforming complex data into simple, predictive alerts, Air Tomorrow empowers communities, researchers, and policymakers to plan for a cleaner tomorrow.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The project’s intended impact is centered on prevention and awareness, aiming to mitigate the worsening global trend of air pollution.

The scale of the problem necessitates this preventative approach:

  • Global Health Mitigation: Air pollution is currently associated with an estimated 4.2 million premature deathsworldwide per year (from ambient air pollution alone). By enabling preventative action, Air Tomorrow aims to reduce this mortality burden.   
  • Universal Reach: With nearly 99% of the world's population breathing air that exceeds WHO acceptable limits, the impact is designed to improve the quality of life for almost everyone globally.   
  • Averting the Trend: By leveraging "Earth data to predict cleaner and safer skies," the project provides the predictive intelligence needed to challenge the tendency of air quality degradation.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

The project is built on an Earth science foundation using modern data science techniques:

Category

Tools and Components

Rationale

Data Sources

NASA Earthdata Search, FIRMS (MODIS/VIIRS), TEMPO, GLDAS (Global Land Data Assimilation System)

Provides the essential satellite and ground-based measurements (pollutants, fire emissions, and environmental parameters).   

Coding LanguagesPython

Standard language for data science, machine learning, and accessing NASA’s APIs for data ingestion, cleaning, and model development.   

Modeling Software

Advanced AI-driven predictive models (e.g., specialized ML/Deep Learning frameworks)

Used to process heterogeneous data inputs and generate accurate, location-specific air quality forecasts.

Deployment

Web-based interface (implied), APIs, Cloud Infrastructure

5. How is your project creative?

Air Tomorrow’s creativity stems from its innovation in data fusion and application:

  • Predictive, Actionable Focus: Unlike many platforms that report on current or historical air quality, Air Tomorrow's core innovation is using AI to reliably forecast future air quality, transforming complex atmospheric data into a simple, personalized health alert: "Predicting the air today to breathe better tomorrow".
  • High-Resolution Satellite Integration: The project cleverly integrates cutting-edge satellite data, such as TEMPO’s ability to measure key pollutants like NO2​ hourly over North America at high resolution, directly into the public health model. This ensures the forecast captures rapid changes in pollution sources.   
  • Health-Centered Delivery: The user experience is tailored to specific health needs, particularly for those who feel the irritation of poor air quality—like the feeling of "a scratchy throat"—by providing tailored precautions for their respiratory health.

6. What factors did your team consider?

The team considered several crucial factors related to data reliability, public health, and user accessibility:

  • Vulnerability of Users: A primary consideration was the specific vulnerability of high-risk populations, including individuals with existing respiratory problems (CRDs), as well as children, the elderly, and pregnant women who are more susceptible to air pollution-related diseases.   
  • Critical Pollutants: The team focused on incorporating data for pollutants known to cause the most severe health damage, particularly fine particulate matter (PM), which can penetrate the bloodstream and cause systemic damage, and NO2​.   
  • Timeliness and Accuracy: The team considered the necessity of Near Real-Time (NRT) data streams—like the FIRMS fire data, available within 3 hours globally —and high-frequency measurements (like TEMPO’s hourly data) to ensure the predictive models are based on the freshest possible information and accurately capture fast-moving pollution events.   
  • Prevention vs. Treatment: The underlying focus was on a preventative approach to tackle the major global risk factor that is air pollution, addressing the tendency for the problem to worsen.

projectDetails.name: Orbee - environmental decision-making platform
projectDetails.summary:
Orbee is an environmental decision-making platform that uses satellite data and ecological models to identify priority areas for recovery, starting with riparian forests—strips of vegetation that protect rivers and floods.

Faced with increasing environmental manipulation and extreme events like the floods in southern Brazil, Orbee answers a critical question:
"Where to act first to maximize the impact of environmental recovery?"

The platform transforms data into living, interactive maps, guiding public administrators, businesses, and communities in creating evidence-based action plans that improve water resilience, quality of life, and the health of urban and rural ecosystems.

Thus, Orbee has built the data pathway between territory and action—helping cities become healthier, smarter, and more sustainable.
projectDetails.details:
Orbee is an environmental intelligence platform that identifies priority areas for riparian forest restoration—such as strips of vegetation that protect rivers and mitigate flood risk.

It uses HLS (Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel-2) satellite data provided by Microsoft Planetary Computer, combined with growth index (NDVI) analysis and spatial modeling, to generate a real-time environmental map.

How it works:

The HLS data processing platform assesses vegetation cover, detects riverbank manipulation, and prioritizes restoration areas with the greatest ecological impact.

Users access an interactive map, view the current state of vegetation, and can record local restoration actions—such as planning and monitoring—creating a georeferenced history of environmental actions.

Benefits and Impact:

Identifies where to act first, optimizing resources and maximizing results.

Contributes to preventing natural disasters such as floods and erosion.

Transforms NASA scientific data into practical decisions for municipalities, businesses, and communities.

Promotes transparency and engagement with open, auditable reports.

Technologies used:

Data: HLS (Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel-2) via Microsoft Planetary Computer

Backend: Python (FastAPI, GeoPandas)

Frontend: React, Tailwind, MapLibre GL js, Vite

Database: PostgreSQL/Supabase

Models and analyses: NDVI, river buffers, temporal vegetation analysis

Creativity and differentiation:

While most solutions only monitor manipulation, Orbee shows where to act first—becoming a real-time environmental recovery plan.

It connects science, technology, and local action, transforming NASA satellite data into an accessible and collaborative tool for restoring ecosystems and protecting communities.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
The team used generative Artificial Intelligence tools (OpenAI GPT-5) for creative and technical support throughout the Orbee project.

Conceptual organization: assistance in structuring the storytelling, pitch, and scientific narrative.

Documentation: support in writing explanatory texts, summaries, and technical descriptions of the project.

Technical planning: assistance in organizing user flows and system architecture.

No source code, data models, images, videos, or numerical results of the project were directly generated by AI—all implementations were developed by the team.

AI was used solely as a tool to support communication and ideation, ensuring originality and human execution in all technical aspects.

projectDetails.name: Project Pangeia - WeatherOrNot: Comprehensive climate modeling and forecasting application
projectDetails.summary:
The project develops an application that integrates weather forecasts into the user’s daily routine, offering practical and personalized recommendations for planning everyday activities. The solution aims to translate complex climate information into accessible and useful data, enabling anyone to understand and act on it. The system cross-references up to thirty years of historical data with future forecasts, guiding real-time decisions through an artificial intelligence agent that suggests what to bring, what to avoid, and which tasks to carry out according to the weather.
In addition to providing forecasts, the application offers an interactive and inclusive experience, featuring an integrated calendar, smart notifications, voice commands, and enhanced accessibility. Developed with Python, Meteomatics and Gemini APIs, Android Studio, N8N, TensorFlow and Google Cloud, the project combines automation, AI, and design. The proposal addresses the challenge by making it easier to understand weather phenomena and transforming data into concrete actions, promoting efficiency, sustainability, and safety.
projectDetails.details:
The project consists of an application that helps users make everyday decisions based on meteorological information integrated into their personal calendars, in order to avoid unforeseen events, economic losses, and even tragedies caused by extreme weather conditions. The tool combines climate modeling, historical data, and future forecasts, translating complex information into clear, practical, and contextualized recommendations.

The system features an artificial intelligence agent capable of analyzing local weather conditions and suggesting appropriate actions — such as what to bring, what to avoid, or which activities to carry out — promoting a safer, more sustainable, and efficient daily routine, based on data from weather stations and radars. It also sends personalized notifications according to the weather conditions related to scheduled activities, and allows for voice commands and integration with other calendar applications, prioritizing accessibility and usability.

Among the technologies used are Python, Google Colab, Meteomatics and LARC APIs, Google Cloud (OAuth 2.0), Kotlin, Android Studio, N8N, Gemini API, Figma, ChatGPT, and Perplexity, integrating automation, AI, and design into a smart and functional ecosystem.

The project’s creativity lies in its ability to transform meteorological data into personalized, interactive, and simplified guidance, bringing the public closer to understanding weather phenomena while prioritizing user experience. The team considered the difficulty of interpreting such data, the need for real-time alerts, increasingly intense climate changes, and extreme weather events around the world, as well as the importance of connecting weather, routine, economy, and decision-making into a single intuitive and accessible solution.

projectDetails.name: NeoCrops
projectDetails.summary:
Our game seeks to popularize the use of existing agricultural information, helping farmers improve crop performance without additional costs.

NeoCrops is an educational farming simulator that connects geological and climatological data to simulate the complete plant growth cycle. It combines real-world datasets from NASA with player inputs that represent each farmer’s specific circumstances, such as soil conditions, crop type, and resource management decisions.

Through this interactive experience, players learn how data can directly influence productivity, sustainability, and risk reduction. Each in-game season reflects the consequences of their decisions, providing a realistic understanding of how information can guide better agricultural planning.

By integrating data scattered across multiple sources, NeoCrops transforms complex scientific information into practical insights, making data accessible, meaningful, and relevant for real-time decision-making in agriculture.
projectDetails.details:
NeoCrops is an interactive, turn-based educational farming game that demonstrates how data can guide better agricultural decisions. The player begins by choosing where to start his farm in a world map. The game then uses NASA POWER to gather geological and climatological data from the selected region. The game presents the player with a real regional data shown in graphs and a visual representation of their farm.

Each turn represents a season and the player can submit their decisions for that simulated season, such as which crop to grow, how much irrigation or fertilizers will be used. Once the choices are made, the season is simulated and a feedback is displayed for the player as a success percentage, also there will be textual and visual feedbacks on what the player got right and what they can change.

NeoCrops helps players, especially students and farmers, understand the value of data in agriculture. By transforming complex datasets into an interactive experience, it allows users to see how small changes in management or environmental conditions can impact production outcomes. It encourages data literacy, decision-making skills, and a sustainable approach to resource use.

The project aims to make agricultural data accessible and meaningful to everyone, not just experts. By linking real-world data with a simulated environment, it promotes awareness of how information can reduce risks, improve yields, and optimize costs. The long-term goal is to foster a new generation of farmers and agronomists who make data-driven, environmentally responsible decisions.

The game is a web-based solution and was made with the following technologies: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind and Figma.

Instead of presenting agricultural data in static charts or reports, NeoCrops gamifies data interpretation. It transforms complex environmental and geospatial information into an engaging, visual, and interactive learning experience. The player’s success depends on their ability to interpret real data, turning learning into play.

During development, the team focused on accessibility with the visual, ensuring scientific data is simple and relevant enough for general audiences; educational value, so every choice teaches a real agricultural principle; scientific accuracy, using reliable data sources from NASA; and replayability, with multiple regions, crops, and conditions.
