projectDetails.name: A.R.E.S - Advanced Recycling and Electrothermal System
projectDetails.summary:
The ARES Project (Advanced Recycling and Electrothermal System) transforms the greatest logistical challenge of Martian missions into a strategic advantage by managing inorganic waste generated astronauts during a mission on Mars.
The system combines high-temperature thermal processing (800°C) with innovative bacterial bioprocessing, transforming waste into high-value raw materials: metals become pure ingots, plastics convert into carbon nanotubes, and textiles transform into bioplastic via bacterial fermentation.
ARES's technological differential lies in the pioneering use of two bacterial species working in synergy: Rhodospirillum rubrum and Methylobacterium extorquens, both producing polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB). This maximizes residual gas conversion into useful material.
ARES eliminates return transport costs reaching tens to hundreds of billions of dollars. Considering that bringing back less than 1kg of Martian soil costs US$ 11 billion, returning 12.6 tons would be economically challenging.
Unlike equipment that returns to Earth, ARES remains on Mars, establishing the first permanent industrial facility on another planet. By producing raw materials instead of specific products, ARES offers maximum flexibility for on-demand fabrication.
Currently in validated conceptual phase, ARES aims to become standard infrastructure for Martian missions, creating a circular economy that enables permanent colonization of Mars.
projectDetails.details:
ARES — Advanced Recycling and Electrothermal System

Overview

ARES is an integrated, semi-automated recycling plant designed to convert mission inorganic waste into usable feedstocks on Mars. By combining electrothermal processing and closed biological conversion, ARES produces metal ingots, carbonaceous feedstock for advanced materials, and bioplastic (PHB), supplying on-demand raw materials for repair, fabrication and additive manufacturing while minimizing resupply and return logistics.

Design capacity & operating assumptions

The system is sized for a processing rate of 80–100 kg/day per waste stream (aluminum, plastic and fabric), resulting in a total daily throughput of approximately 240–300 kg/day. Power is treated as effectively unrestricted for system sizing in this challenge; the design assumes sufficient continuous electrical power. Crewing and automation are configured for semi-automated operation: one crew member per day handles manual waste triage and product collection while automated thermal cycles, process control and monitoring manage the remainder. For planetary protection, the bioreactor is hermetically sealed with redundant seals and filtration, and unused gases may be vented through a controllable valve with filtration and neutralization stages.

Process flow (per stream)

For the aluminum stream, materials are loaded cold and processed in a controlled electric furnace operating at roughly 800 °C. The process melts and refines the aluminum followed by controlled solidification to produce pure aluminum ingots; the estimated recovery efficiency target is ≥90% of aluminum mass recovered as ingot, yielding an estimated daily output of ~72–90 kg aluminum ingots per 80–100 kg feed (estimate). For mixed plastics, the material is thermally processed in a melt/pyr olysis-like regime inside the same furnace. The remaining solid carbonaceous fraction is expected to be ~2–5% of the original plastic mass and is forwarded as carbon feedstock or preforms for downstream conversion into advanced carbon materials (e.g., CNT preforms). The bulk of the plastic mass converts into gaseous products (CO, H₂, CH₄ and other light species) that are captured and routed for biological conversion; system design emphasizes robust gas capture and gas-to-bioproduct routing rather than maximizing CNT yield onsite. For the fabric (organic) stream, fabrics are combusted in a controlled chamber producing CO and CH₄; these gases are captured and fed to a sealed bioreactor hosting Rhodospirillum rubrum (CO metabolism) and Methylobacterium extorquens (CH₄ metabolism) working synergistically to synthesize PHB (polyhydroxybutyrate). The PHB output is produced as a bulk polymer that can be processed into filament or molding feedstock for 3D printing and part fabrication. Gas management includes routing unused gas to a pressure-regulated dump valve with filtration/neutralization, and estimated PHB productivity is an order-of-magnitude of 1–5 kg PHB/day per fabric stream (highly dependent on gas capture efficiency and microbial productivity — presented as an engineering estimate for planning).

Cycle & safety operations

Materials are loaded only when the furnace is at safe handling temperature (cold loads), and thermal cycles are optimized for energy efficiency and crew safety. The bioreactor is hermetically isolated and includes secondary containment, HEPA plus catalytic filtration, redundant seals and automated leak detection to avoid contamination of the Martian environment. Controls provide automated fault detection, safe shutdown modes and remote telemetry for both ground and crew monitoring.

Estimated module mass & volume (initial concept estimates)

Conceptual estimates for mission planning place the primary furnace and refractory module at roughly 1,000–1,500 kg with a volume of 2.0–3.0 m³. The bioreactor and life support module is estimated at 300–600 kg with a volume of 0.8–1.5 m³. The triage, shredding and feedstock preparation module is estimated at 200–400 kg and 0.4–0.8 m³. Control, filtration, structural items and spare parts are estimated at 500–1,000 kg and 1.0–2.0 m³. Together, the total deployed system is projected to be on the order of ~2,000–3,500 kg and occupy ~4–7 m³ (estimates); final values require detailed engineering and refinement.

Key outputs (all emphasized)

The principal outputs are aluminum ingots (structural feedstock for machining, casting or metal additive manufacturing), carbonaceous preforms / CNT feedstock (advanced material precursors for high-strength, conductive components) and PHB bioplastic (filament or molding feedstock for polymer parts and tooling).

Operational & mission benefits

By producing critical raw materials on-site, ARES reduces the need for spare parts payloads and can potentially avoid at least one dedicated sample/return cargo mission, delivering logistics savings on the order of billions of USD when compared to multi-billion-dollar Mars return architectures. The system increases mission resilience and autonomy by providing on-demand feedstock that mitigates communication delay constraints. Additionally, ARES enables circular economy principles on Mars—reducing waste and contamination risk—and serves as an enduring industrial asset for follow-on missions.

Tools, hardware & software

The ARES control and development stack uses commercially-proven hardware and engineering tools sized for spaceflight qualification. Core hardware includes electric resistance/induction furnace elements with multi-zone thermocouples and PID controllers, mass flow controllers and cold traps for gas capture, gas analyzers (GC/mini-GC or IR sensors), vacuum pumps and compressors, a sealed bioreactor with inline pH/DO sensors and peristaltic dosing pumps, HEPA plus catalytic filtration, and a modular shredding/feed system with level sensors and motorized feeders. Control electronics are based on radiation-tolerant embedded controllers or PLC-class units for real-time process control, with local HMI and telemetry for remote monitoring. Development and verification use CAD (SolidWorks/Inventor), thermal and structural analysis (ANSYS/COMSOL), process simulation and control modeling (MATLAB/Simulink), and software tools including C/C++ for embedded control, Python for data analysis and automation scripts, and LabVIEW or equivalent for test-bench instrumentation. Terrestrial prototypes would employ standard lab equipment and bioreactor controllers to validate PHB production.

Creativity

ARES combines electrothermal conversion, targeted gas capture and a dual-species bioreactor into a single closed-loop recycling plant, a configuration not previously demonstrated for planetary surface deployment. The creative contributions include converting mixed plastics into both a high-value solid carbon fraction and biologically-usable gases in the same electrothermal module; employing synergistic microbial consortia to transform mixed gaseous effluents into PHB in situ; and optimizing for low crew time via semi-autonomous operation and direct compatibility with additive manufacturing workflows. This coupling of advanced materials feedstock (metal ingots and carbonaceous preforms) with biological polymer production defines a new class of in-situ circular economy hardware for long-duration missions.

Team considerations

The design prioritized planetary protection and biosafety (hermetic bioreactor, redundant filtration, gas neutralization), mass/volume efficiency and modularity to ease integration with lander payload constraints, maintainability and low crew time (simple manual triage plus automated cycles), thermal management and refractory lifetime for high-temperature processing, robustness to variable feedstock composition, and compatibility with existing on-site manufacturing tools (metal and polymer additive manufacturing). The team evaluated trade-offs between throughput, power draw and conversion yields and selected semi-automated control to minimize crew workload while retaining manual override capability for anomaly management.

Assumptions & open items

Power is treated as effectively unlimited for system sizing in this challenge; actual power architecture will constrain cycle timing and throughput and representative power budgets per cycle should be provided during detailed design. Yields for PHB and advanced carbon products are engineering estimates and require terrestrial testing to validate reactor kinetics and CNT conversion efficiencies. Final module mass and volume depend on material choices for refractory, shielding and thermal insulation—values above are preliminary and subject to refinement.

Example mass-balance (conceptual, per 100 kg feed)

An example conceptual mass-balance per 100 kg feed assumes the aluminum stream yields 90 kg ingot (assumed 90% recovery). For the plastics stream, 100 kg input produces approximately 2–5 kg of solid carbonaceous residue and 95–98 kg of volatiles (gases captured and routed to the bioreactor). For the fabrics stream, 100 kg input is converted to captured gas and, under the provided assumptions, yields on the order of ~1–5 kg PHB (estimate).

Conclusion

ARES converts mission waste into high-value feedstocks (metal, advanced carbon materials, and bioplastic) using electrothermal and sealed biological processing at 80–100 kg/day per stream, delivering on-site manufacturing capability, significant logistical cost avoidance, and an enduring recycling infrastructure for long-duration Mars missions.

projectDetails.name: Shark view - See the future, protect the ocean!
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, Shark view, is a predictive system developed to protect sharks and marine ecosystems. We created a platform that integrates a mathematical model with an innovative smart tag concept.

Using NASA satellite data, such as chlorophyll, water temperature, and salinity, our model predicts future shark feeding grounds with high probability. This directly addresses the challenge of creating a predictive framework. In parallel, we propose the "Bio-Bite" conceptual tag, which uses accelerometers and embedded AI to detect and transmit real-time confirmation of a hunting event, answering the second part of the challenge.

The importance of Shark view lies in its ability to transform marine conservation from reactive to proactive. By anticipating feeding hotspots, we can help reduce bycatch in fisheries, create dynamic protection zones, and enhance coastal safety, promoting a smarter and safer coexistence between humans and sharks.
projectDetails.details: Our project, Shark view, is a predictive marine intelligence platform designed to transform shark conservation from reactive to proactive. The system works by using a mathematical model, powered by NASA satellite data like chlorophyll and sea surface temperature, to forecast the location of shark feeding hotspots. These predictions are displayed on an intuitive map and are validated in real-time by our conceptual "Bio-Bite" smart tag, which is designed to use accelerometers and embedded AI to detect and confirm actual hunting events. By fusing predictive modeling with real-world confirmation, Shark view provides an innovative tool for scientists and authorities to reduce bycatch, protect critical habitats, and enhance coastal safety. The project was designed using Python for data modeling and JavaScript with Leaflet.js for the user interface, prioritizing public data accessibility and a user-centric design to create a scalable and impactful solution.

projectDetails.name: AirMood
projectDetails.summary:
AirMood is a web application designed to address the NASA Space Apps Challenge by transforming complex environmental data into personalized, actionable health insights. Unlike standard weather apps that only display raw data, AirMood allows users to input their specific context, such as their intended outdoor activity and physical health condition.

The application's core is powered by high-fidelity air quality data from NASA's TEMPO mission, which is fused with real-time meteorological data to generate a customized "activity score" and provide clear recommendations on whether it is a safe time for their activity.

By translating authoritative NASA Earth science data into personally relevant advice, AirMood empowers individuals—especially vulnerable groups—to make informed decisions, directly supporting public health by minimizing exposure to poor air quality and adverse weather conditions.
projectDetails.details:
What the project does and how it works

AirMood is a web application that functions as a personal environmental health assistant. It translates complex atmospheric data into clear, personalized recommendations for the user.

The process is simple and user-centric:

  1. The user provides their location.
  2. They select their intended activity (e.g., running, walking, cycling).
  3. They specify their health condition (e.g., healthy, asthmatic, sensitive to pollutants).

AirMood then processes a robust combination of data sources: high-resolution air quality data from NASA's TEMPO mission is fused with real-time meteorological conditions from the OpenWeatherMap API. This allows the application to calculate a highly accurate "recommendation score." Instead of just showing raw data, the platform indicates if the day is "Recommended," "Caution Advised," or "Not Recommended" for that specific activity, providing practical alerts and tips. Our prototype showcases this powerful data fusion, with a focus on the user-facing personalization engine and the concept of voice recognition for intuitive interaction.

What are the project's benefits and impact?

AirMood's primary benefit is empowering ordinary citizens to make safer decisions about their health using validated scientific data.

  • Benefits:
    • Preventive Health: It helps reduce exposure to dangerous levels of pollution and extreme weather, especially for vulnerable groups (the elderly, children, people with respiratory illnesses).
    • True Personalization: It transforms generic data into practical, individual advice, answering the question, "What do these atmospheric conditions mean for me?".
    • Accessibility: The clean interface and integration of voice commands make complex scientific data accessible to everyone.
    • The intended impact is to reduce health risks associated with environmental factors and promote a safer, more conscious lifestyle. We aim for AirMood to be an essential public health tool, bridging the gap between NASA's Earth observation data and everyday decision-making.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • Programming Language: Python.
    • NASA TEMPO Mission: Serves as the primary source for high-fidelity air quality data, providing detailed measurements of pollutants like Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2​), Ozone (O3​), and aerosols.
    • OpenWeatherMap API: Complements the NASA data by providing real-time meteorological conditions such as temperature, humidity, wind speed, and general weather forecasts.
  • Software and Development Environment: Replit, Visual Studio Code.

How is the project creative and what factors were considered?

  • Creativity: AirMood's creativity lies not in displaying weather data, but in interpreting what NASA's atmospheric data means for an individual's health. The innovation is in the "personalization engine," which cross-references advanced environmental data with the user's personal profile. The concept of using voice recognition to ask about air quality ("Is it a good day for a run?") makes interacting with complex data a natural and human experience.
    • Core Problem: We identified that current weather apps are generic and do not leverage the full potential of satellite data to address specific health needs.
    • Data-Driven Approach: We prioritized the direct integration of authoritative NASA data to ensure our recommendations are based on the best available science. Our approach demonstrates a feasible way to translate complex satellite measurements into actionable public health advice.
    • Target Audience: We focused on sensitive groups, athletes, and anyone wanting to engage in outdoor activities safely.
    • Scalability: The project was designed from the outset to be modular, allowing for easy integration of additional NASA datasets and the inclusion of more activity profiles and health conditions in the future.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Artificial Intelligence was utilized in our project for both ideation and development.

During the initial brainstorming phase, we used Large Language Models such as Gemini and ChatGPT to explore different concepts, refine our project's scope, and generate ideas for user-centric features.

For code generation and development assistance, we employed tools including Lovable, Manus, and the AI-powered features within the Replit IDE. These tools helped accelerate the development process by generating code snippets, assisting with debugging, and providing solutions for implementing specific functionalities.

projectDetails.name: NASA Ocean Thermometer : A Dive into Global Warming
projectDetails.summary:
Hi! We Alfahm Mandhi enthusiasts thought of creating NASA Ocean Thermometer, which is an interactive platform that visualizes ocean warming and marine ecosystem health using NASA data from 1997 to the present. It tracks temperature anomalies and chlorophyll levels across the five major oceans, allowing users to explore real trends in ocean warming and ecosystem degradation. Built with React, Tailwind, and NASA APIs (GISTEMP, MODIS, Ocean Color, EONET, Worldview), the project makes climate data accessible, understandable, and actionable.

The purpose is simple: as students, we wanted to show that oceans aren’t just “big blue things”...they’re heating up, ecosystems are struggling, and it’s time to care… while having fun exploring data. By combining visualization and NASA data, this project educates, raises awareness, and inspires informed action on climate change.
projectDetails.details:
Project Name: NASA Ocean Thermometer

What it does / How it works:
NASA Ocean Thermometer is an interactive visualization platform that tracks ocean warming and ecosystem health from 1997 to the present. Users can explore the five major oceans, view temperature anomalies, and monitor chlorophyll-based ecosystem health using real NASA datasets. The platform fetches data from GISTEMP (surface temperature anomalies), MODIS & Ocean Color (chlorophyll), and EONET (natural events) APIs, then visualizes it through heatmaps and dynamic overlays, making climate trends tangible.

Benefits / Intended Impact:
The project makes NASA ocean data visually understandable and actionable, raising awareness about global warming, ecosystem degradation, and the urgent need for informed climate action. It helps students, educators, and the general public see the real-time impacts of climate change on oceans.

Tools / Languages / Software Used:

  • Languages / Frameworks: JavaScript, React.js
  • Styling / UI: Tailwind CSS
  • Data Sources / APIs: NASA GISTEMP, MODIS, Ocean Color, EONET, Worldview
  • Package Managers: npm / yarn
  • The project combines NASA data with visualizations, allowing users to “explore” oceans over time with a dynamic slider. The inclusion of chlorophyll as a proxy for marine health adds scientific depth, while the interface is designed to be educational yet engaging.

Team Considerations:
We focused on accuracy, accessibility, and clarity, ensuring the visualizations were scientifically relevant but understandable for non-experts. Decisions included which datasets to use, how to visualize temperature and chlorophyll effectively, and how to make the UI intuitive and responsive across devices. We know that adding actual 3d accurate effects is not easy as it takes many months for experienced developers to achieve that.
With the limited time, we are so far glad we could create something cool like this

We have not used AI for generating audios and haven't used, contained, or modified any NASA branding or design elements. We utilized AI for code refinement, generation and also for assistance for various parts of the project. Also, for data research , we have utilized AI tools. So basically, AI was used as a supporting tool to accelerate development and documentation

projectDetails.name: Project Aliket
projectDetails.summary: Our project, From EarthData to Action, uses NASA’s MODIS data, ESA’s Sentinel-5P, and cloud computing to predict air pollution (PM2.5) and support cleaner, safer skies. We built a machine learning model that integrates satellite and ground-based data to generate 24–48-hour air quality forecasts. Hosted on a scalable cloud platform, it delivers real-time analytics and alerts through APIs and dashboards. This innovation transforms vast Earth data into actionable insights for governments, researchers, and citizens—empowering proactive air quality management and aligning with NASA’s mission to use space data for environmental sustainability
projectDetails.details: Our project, From EarthData to Action, leverages cloud computing and Earth observation (EO) data to predict air quality and promote cleaner, safer skies. Using satellite data such as Sentinel-5P, MODIS, and Landsat, combined with ground-based validation, we developed a scalable data pipeline that ingests, processes, and models atmospheric pollutants like PM2.5. Machine learning techniques—particularly gradient boosting and temporal smoothing—enable high-resolution air quality forecasting with city-level accuracy. Hosted on cloud platforms, the system offers real-time analytics, dashboards, and API-based alerts, ensuring scalability, transparency, and accessibility. This solution addresses the global challenge of air pollution monitoring, empowering governments, industries, and citizens to make data-driven decisions. By turning vast Earth data into actionable insights, our approach bridges the gap between space-based observation and real-world impact—a vital step toward healthier air and sustainable urban living.

projectDetails.name: OUR HOME IN CALLISTO
projectDetails.summary: For our Callisto Habitat Project, we will use real or license-free images that show what life on Callisto could look like. The pictures will include views of Jupiter and Callisto to show the location of our habitat, along with spacecraft and dome habitats to represent the living areas. We’ll add images of biodomes, greenhouses, and hydroponic systems to show how plants are grown for food, as well as solar panels, water recycling systems, and satellites to show how energy, water, and communication work. To make it more realistic, we’ll include pictures of astronauts inside domes, doing daily activities, and scenes showing how people might live comfortably on Callisto with a view of Jupiter in the background. Finally, we can add inspiring images of the Callisto surface with futuristic domes to show the future vision of life beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details:
Our project, Project Monato: Life on Callisto, presents a sustainable human habitat designed for one of Jupiter’s moons, Callisto. It focuses on creating a self-sufficient colony that provides energy, food, oxygen, water recycling, and waste management in an extreme environment.

How it works:
The habitat includes five interconnected domes: living quarters, greenhouse, power dome, storage, and transport hub. Energy is generated using solar panels, a nuclear reactor, a hydroelectric generator, and biomass energy. Oxygen and food are produced through hydroponic greenhouses, where plants grow under artificial lights and heaters powered by the energy systems. Waste is recycled through biomass converters and underground drainage systems, turning organic waste into fuel and fertilizer.

Benefits and impact:
Our project shows how humans could live safely beyond Earth by using renewable energy, recycling resources, and minimizing pollution. It aims to inspire new sustainable technologies for both space and Earth environments.

Tools and materials used:
We used classroom materials, digital design tools, research from NASA resources, and AI assistance (ChatGPT) for information on Callisto’s environment, energy systems, and structure design ideas.

Creativity and teamwork:
Our design is creative because it combines multiple energy sources and realistic environmental systems while ensuring safety from radiation through underground tunnels and blackout shielding. As a team, we focused on sustainability, safety, and comfort, imagining a realistic future habitat for humans in space.

projectDetails.name: Project Urban Heat Navigator: Mapping and Mitigating City Hotspots
projectDetails.summary:
Urban Heat Navigator: Mapping and Mitigating City Hotspots is a collaborative web tool developed to combat the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect and enhance city livability.

We developed an intuitive platform that provides instant heat risk assessments for urban areas using a one-click heat risk score tool. The solution visualizes critical temperature disparities between urban and rural areas, supported by NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) analysis to map vegetation health.

This tool addresses the challenge by transforming complex NASA and other open data into actionable insights for urban planners, directly highlighting city hotspots and areas lacking vital vegetation. It is important because rising temperatures during peak periods pose significant public health risks and necessitate effective, data-driven mitigation strategies to improve urban quality of life. Future steps include integrating real-time temperature data and enhancing AI-powered predictive analytics for better urban planning
projectDetails.details:
Project Details: Urban Heat Navigator

What We Built and How It Works

The Urban Heat Navigator is an interactive web tool designed to transform complex climate data into a simple call to action for cities tackling the dangerous Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect.

Our core function is a One-Click Heat Risk Score. Users simply click a point on the map and instantly see a unified score that fuses two crucial pieces of NASA satellite data: Land Surface Temperature (LST) and NDVI (greenness/vegetation health).

This is powered by a decoupled, modern architecture for speed and stability. Our robust Django REST Framework (Python) backend securely handles all the heavy lifting—from processing the NASA geospatial data to authenticating users and serving the core analysis through fast API endpoints. The frontend, built using React with the lightning-fast Vite toolchain, consumes this data to deliver a seamless, intuitive, and responsive map interface using Leaflet.js.

Satellite Data Pipeline and Implementation (The Geospatial Core)

Our solution's reliability stems from a rigorous data pipeline built on the Google Earth Engine API (which provides access to NASA data) and powerful Python libraries:

  1. Data Collection & Calculation: We retrieve Landsat 8/9 imagery (specifically, OLI/TIRS data) for our Area of Interest. The process involves multiple steps executed in the Python backend:
    • NDVI Calculation: We calculate the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index using the standard formula: NDVI=(NIR+Red)(NIR−Red)​ (Landsat 8/9 Bands 5 and 4).
    • LST Calculation (Single-Channel/Split-Window Algorithm): We calculate the true Land Surface Temperature by first converting the thermal infrared band data (Band 10 or 11) from Digital Numbers (DN) to Top-of-Atmosphere (TOA) Brightness Temperature, and then applying a Land Surface Emissivity (LSE) correction derived from the calculated NDVI. This ensures the temperature reflects the surface, not just the atmosphere.
  2. Aggregation and Normalization: We spatially and temporally filter the processed LST and NDVI rasters (e.g., cloud-free composites for a summer period). The two layers are then normalized and aggregated by the Django backend's geospatial utilities to create the single, unified Heat Risk Score raster layer.
  3. API Service: This final raster is optimized (e.g., as compressed GeoJSON or tile layers) and served via a dedicated Django REST API endpoint to the React frontend.

Impact and Benefits: Planning for a Cooler Future

The direct benefits of the Navigator are rooted in public health and equitable urban planning. By clearly highlighting the most dangerous heat hotspots, the tool directs attention to areas where residents—particularly vulnerable populations—face the highest risk of heat-related illness and mortality.

Our ultimate goal is to facilitate the creation of more equitable and resilient cities. The current map is a diagnosis; the future is a prescription. This is realized through our Actionable AI Vision.

We are building a predictive planning tool that allows urban designers to model interventions before they spend a dollar. A planner can propose a change, such as "+20% tree cover in this industrial zone," and the tool's AI component will provide an instant, predicted temperature drop in return. This transforms complex data into high-value, preemptive decision-making support.

Technology and Creative Edge

We chose a best-in-class tech stack for performance and maintainability:

  • The Python backend uses Django with DRF for stability, while our geospatial processing relies on powerful libraries like Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, and the Google Earth Engine API to handle satellite data at scale.
  • The React/Vite frontend ensures our application is fast and lightweight, providing an excellent user experience (a key factor we considered from the start).

Our core creativity lies in this AI Integration. We plan to use Machine Learning (specifically, Random Forest Regression), trained on historical LST, NDVI, and additional factors like impervious surfaces and local socio-economic data, to forecast UHI severity. Our focus on Ethical AI ensures the model's output promotes Climate Equity by prioritizing the neighborhoods that need mitigation the most.

We specifically factored in scalability (using the API-driven model) and maintainability (through decoupled services) to ensure this project can grow from a hackathon concept into a sustainable, city-ready solution.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
1. Core Project Innovation (Machine Learning)

The core technical value of our project is the plan to integrate Machine Learning (ML) directly into the application's functionality.

  • AI Technique: We are implementing a Random Forest Regression model, built using Python's Scikit-learn library in the Django backend.
  • Application: This model is trained on a combination of historical NASA LST/NDVI data and auxiliary urban factors (e.g., building footprints, impervious surfaces).
  • Goal: To enable Mitigation Simulation. The model predicts the temperature change (the intended impact) for any given area based on user-defined inputs, such as increasing green space or implementing cool roofs. This moves the tool from simple diagnosis to a proactive climate planning instrument.

2. Project Development Assistance (Generative AI)

We used Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative AI (specifically, the Gemini models) as a productivity tool during the intensive hackathon period.

  • Application: Used as a sophisticated technical editor and documentation assistant to accelerate the clarity and quality of our submission materials.
    • Text/Submission: Used for real-time grammar correction, copy-editing, and enhancing the clarity of the project summary and this technical explanation.
    • Research/Code: Used as an intelligent research assistant to refine the methodology for the geospatial pipeline (e.g., confirming the Landsat 8 LST calculation steps and refining the feature selection for the ML model).

projectDetails.summary:
# Project Summary

I developed an **interactive NASA Weather & Air Quality Dashboard** that empowers users to make data-driven decisions for climate-sensitive activities like agriculture, renewable energy planning, and disaster preparedness.

## What It Does
The dashboard allows users to compare up to 2 locations simultaneously by:
- Selecting locations via an interactive map interface
- Analyzing NASA POWER weather data (temperature, precipitation, wind speed)
- Calculating probability metrics (e.g., days exceeding temperature thresholds)
- Visualizing trends through time-series and comparison charts
- Integrating air quality data from NASA GES DISC
- Generating downloadable PDF reports

## Why It Matters
This tool democratizes access to NASA's scientific data, making complex climate information accessible to farmers, urban planners, and researchers. By providing probability analysis and comparative insights, it enables proactive decision-making—helping users identify optimal locations for solar farms, predict agricultural risks, or assess climate resilience. The multi-location comparison feature is particularly valuable for site selection and risk assessment across different regions.

**Tech Stack**: Node.js/Flask backend, vanilla JavaScript frontend, Chart.js for visualizations, Leaflet for mapping.

NASA Farm Navigators: Using NASA Data Exploration in Agriculture

NASA Farm Navigators is an initiative that applies NASA’s advanced Earth observation data and space-based technologies to modern agriculture. By harnessing satellite imagery, climate models, soil moisture data, and vegetation indices, the project helps farmers make informed, data-driven decisions. These tools allow monitoring of crop health, early detection of pests and diseases, and prediction of yields, enabling timely interventions. Additionally, NASA data supports efficient use of water and fertilizers by identifying soil and irrigation needs, promoting resource optimization. The system also tracks weather changes and climate impacts, helping farmers prepare for extreme events while reducing risks. By connecting space research with farming challenges, Farm Navigators aims to improve productivity, sustainability, and food security. Ultimately, the project demonstrates how NASA’s data can empower agriculture with precision techniques that conserve resources, reduce environmental stress, and guide farmers toward a more resilient and sustainable future.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

Agriculture is one of the most climate-sensitive industries, with crop productivity depending heavily on rainfall, soil quality, pest attacks, and temperature fluctuations. Farmers often lack real-time, science-based insights to optimize decisions.
NASA Farm Navigators is a data-driven solution that leverages NASA’s Earth observation datasets (satellites, sensors, climate models) to empower farmers with actionable insights for sustainable, resilient, and smart farming.


---

2. Problem Statement

Unpredictable weather and climate change reduce crop yield.

Farmers struggle with timely decisions on irrigation, fertilization, and pest control.

Lack of easy access to satellite-based agricultural intelligence.

Current solutions are fragmented and often not affordable for small farmers.



---

3. Objectives

Use NASA Earth science data to provide real-time farm monitoring and advisory services.

Enhance crop yield prediction, drought/flood early warning, and soil health mapping.

Support sustainable agriculture by reducing overuse of water, fertilizers, and pesticides.

Build an accessible digital platform (mobile/web dashboard) for farmers, researchers, and policymakers.



---

4. Data Sources (NASA & Allied Datasets)

MODIS & Landsat: Crop health monitoring (NDVI, vegetation index).

SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive): Soil moisture & drought assessment.

GPM (Global Precipitation Measurement): Rainfall prediction & irrigation planning.

ECOSTRESS: Plant water stress monitoring.

Earth Observing System Data and Information System (EOSDIS): Open access Earth science data.



---

5. Core Features

🌱 Crop Health Dashboard – NDVI-based maps showing vegetation stress.

💧 Smart Irrigation Planner – Soil moisture + weather forecast for water scheduling.

☀️ Climate & Weather Alerts – Localized early warnings for drought, floods, and heatwaves.

🐛 Pest & Disease Risk Maps – Predictive alerts using temperature, humidity, and vegetation data.

📊 Yield Forecasting – Predict crop production using AI + NASA satellite data.

🌍 Sustainability Insights – Track carbon footprint, water use efficiency, and land health.



---

6. Technology Stack

Data Processing: Google Earth Engine, NASA Earthdata APIs.

AI/ML Models: Crop yield prediction, anomaly detection.

Frontend: Mobile app + Web dashboard.

Backend: Cloud-based (AWS/Azure/GCP) with APIs for real-time updates.

User Access: Multi-language farmer-friendly interface with offline support.



---

7. Target Users

Farmers (small and large scale).

Agricultural researchers.

Government agencies & policymakers.

NGOs and rural cooperatives.



---

8. Expected Impact

Increase crop productivity by 15–20% through timely decision-making.

Reduce water consumption by 25% via optimized irrigation.

Lower fertilizer & pesticide usage, promoting eco-friendly farming.

Provide early disaster alerts, helping mitigate crop losses.

Contribute towards UN SDGs: Zero Hunger, Climate Action, and Responsible Consumption.



---

9. Future Expansion

Integration with IoT farm sensors for ground truth validation.

Blockchain-enabled farm-to-market traceability.

Expansion to global agricultural zones beyond pilot regions.

projectDetails.details:
Our project, BioQuery, is an AI-powered dashboard that transforms decades of siloed NASA bioscience research into an interactive, query-able knowledge engine, designed to accelerate discovery and support the future of human space exploration.

What It Does: The application allows users to perform intelligent, context-aware searches across a curated dataset of 608 NASA bioscience publications. Users can instantly find the most relevant papers for any query, generate on-demand AI summaries of complex abstracts, and visualize the entire research landscape as an interactive network graph of key scientific concepts.

How It Works: The application is built on a three-part AI core:

1. Semantic Search: Instead of basic keyword matching, it uses sentence-transformers to convert every abstract into a high-dimensional vector. This allows the system to understand the meaning and context of a user's query, providing far more relevant results.

2. AI Summarization: It leverages a powerful pre-trained language model from the Hugging Face transformers library to read a publication's abstract and generate a concise, human-readable summary, saving users valuable time.

3. Knowledge Visualization: Using NLTK for text analysis, the app identifies the most frequent and significant keywords across all publications. It then uses PyVis to map the co-occurrence of these keywords, generating an interactive graph that visually represents major research themes and their connections.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Benefits: The primary benefit is the massive increase in efficiency and insight for its target users.

For Scientists: It dramatically accelerates hypothesis testing and literature reviews.

For Mission Planners: It enables rapid, evidence-based risk assessment for crewed missions.

For Program Managers: It provides strategic insights into research trends and identifies critical knowledge gaps.

Intended Impact: The project's intended impact is to fundamentally change how NASA's invaluable research data is accessed and utilized. We aim to break down information silos and create a dynamic, centralized knowledge base. By making decades of research instantly accessible and understandable, our tool acts as a "research accelerator," directly supporting the design of safer, more efficient missions for the Artemis program and the future exploration of Mars.

Technology Stack

Coding Language: Python

Web Framework: Streamlit (for rapid UI development)

AI & Machine Learning: Hugging Face transformers, sentence-transformers, NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit for text processing), PyTorch & NumPy

Data Handling: Pandas

Data Visualization: PyVis

Frontend Styling: HTML & CSS

Hardware: The project was developed on standard laptops, requiring no specialized hardware due to the efficiency of the chosen software stack.

Creative Approach

The creativity of our project lies not in inventing a new AI model, but in the novel synthesis of existing, powerful tools to solve a specific, high-value problem.

Creative Combination: We creatively combined semantic search, abstractive summarization, and network graph visualization into a single, cohesive user experience tailored for NASA.

Data to Experience: Our most creative leap was transforming thousands of pages of static text into an intuitive, interactive visual experience. The keyword network graph is not just a chart; it's a map of scientific discovery that a user can explore.

Thematic UI/UX: We designed a custom "NASA Mission Control" theme to make the tool not just functional but also engaging and inspiring for its intended audience, ensuring the interface feels as professional as the data it presents.

Factors Considered by Our Team

User-Centric Design: We centered our design on the distinct needs of our three target personas: the scientist, the mission planner, and the program manager, ensuring the features provided direct value to each.

Rapid Prototyping: Given the time constraints of the challenge, we strategically chose Streamlit to allow us to build a robust, functional prototype quickly and focus our efforts on the core AI functionality.

Feasibility & Scalability: We selected an open-source and computationally efficient tech stack that could run on standard hardware. We also designed the architecture with a clear path for future scaling, such as integrating a dedicated vector database to handle a larger corpus of publications.

Clarity and Impact: We prioritized features that would deliver the most "wow factor" and tangible insight. The semantic search and visual graph were chosen because they provide a fundamentally better way to understand the data than a simple list of search results.

projectDetails.name: Project AstroMechs
projectDetails.summary:
AstroGuard is a free, web-based tool that simulates what would happen if an asteroid hit Earth. It's designed to help people understand the real danger of asteroids and how to prepare for them.   

Key Functions
Uses Real Data: It pulls in information about asteroids (like their size and speed) from NASA's NEO API and geological data from the USGS.   

Calculates Impact: It uses physics to figure out the results of a strike, such as the size of the crater, the blast radius, and how powerful the earthquake or tsunami might be.   
Shows the Results: The platform displays the results on an interactive world map, so users can see exactly where the impact is and how large the affected area would be.   

User-Friendly: You can easily change the asteroid's size, speed, and angle using simple sliders to compare different disaster scenarios.   

Purpose
The main goal of AstroGuard is to make complex space science easy to understand for everyone, not just scientists. It helps educate the public about the risks and gives policymakers a tool to visualize and plan for disaster response and mitigation strategies

projectDetails.name: Embiggen Your Eyes!
projectDetails.summary: Our NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025 project, “Embiggen Your Eyes!”, introduces "CosmoLens", an innovative mobile app designed to make NASA’s vast space data and imagery more interactive and accessible. The app allows users to explore celestial images with AI-powered smart zoom, immersive AR/VR experiences, and inclusive accessibility features such as audio descriptions and colorblind-friendly modes. Built using technologies like React Native, Python, and NASA’s open APIs, CosmoLens aims to inspire curiosity, enhance STEM education, and deepen public engagement with space exploration. A detailed 10-slide presentation has been developed, outlining the problem, solution, features, tech stack, and future scope of the project.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, CosmoLens, developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025 under the theme “Embiggen Your Eyes!”, is an interactive mobile and web application that helps users explore and understand NASA’s vast space imagery and scientific datasets in an engaging way. The app works by integrating NASA’s open APIs—such as the NASA Image and Video Library and Exoplanet Archive—to fetch real-time data and imagery. It then uses AI-powered smart zoom to highlight key features within images, allowing users to explore craters, nebulae, or planetary details with contextual information and educational facts.

The project’s primary benefit is its ability to make complex space data accessible and visually understandable for everyone, from students to space enthusiasts. It promotes STEM education, encourages public engagement with NASA’s data, and fosters curiosity about space through immersive and inclusive design.

Technically, CosmoLens is built using React Native for the front end to ensure cross-platform functionality, and Python (FastAPI) or Node.js for backend data processing. It integrates AI models for image analysis and supports AR/VR technologies for an immersive experience. The development also involved tools like Figma for UI/UX design and NASA’s open data portals for content sourcing.

CosmoLens stands out creatively through its combination of AI, accessibility, and immersive visualization, turning raw space data into an interactive experience that educates and inspires. During development, our team considered factors such as user accessibility (colorblind-friendly and audio features), scientific accuracy,data ethics, and ease of use, ensuring that the final product not only aligns with NASA’s goals of open data exploration but also truly “embiggens” the public’s understanding of our universe.

projectDetails.name: Astro Impact
projectDetails.summary:
This project developed a web-based asteroid impact visualization and simulation tool that combines a React frontend with a Three.js 3D Earth model and a Flask backend performing physics-based calculations. Users can adjust asteroid parameters like diameter, velocity, and type through an interactive control panel. When a simulation is run, the backend computes impact effects such as crater size, seismic magnitude, and tsunami risk based on real physics formulas. The frontend visualizes the asteroid’s trajectory and its impact on a realistic Earth model, augmented with dynamic visual effects like blast circles.

This solution addresses the challenge of understanding asteroid impact consequences in an engaging, accessible way, facilitating education and risk awareness. By integrating real NASA asteroid data and scientifically-grounded impact models, it provides meaningful, interactive insights into a rare but critical natural hazard. It is important because asteroid impacts pose a potentially devastating but low-probability threat to Earth. This tool empowers users to explore impact scenarios and better grasp their potential scale and effects, aiding preparedness and supporting public awareness with immersive visualization and precise calculations.
projectDetails.details:
This project is a web-based interactive simulation tool that visualizes asteroid impacts on Earth using a React frontend with Three.js 3D graphics and a Flask backend for physics computation. Users adjust asteroid parameters in the React UI, which sends these inputs to the backend. The backend calculates impact effects like crater size, seismic magnitude, and tsunami risk using scientific formulas. The results drive a real-time 3D visualization of the asteroid's trajectory and impact, providing immersive education about asteroid hazards.

The project benefits users by making complex natural disaster science accessible and tangible, encouraging awareness and preparedness. It creatively combines live NASA asteroid data, physics simulations, and modern web visualization tools to offer a unique, educational experience. The team considered scientific accuracy, engaging UI, and smooth interactive controls throughout development. Key technologies used include React, Three.js, React hooks, Flask, REST APIs, and CORS management. This project is important as asteroid impacts pose rare but potentially catastrophic threats, and interactive simulations enhance understanding beyond static text or videos.

projectDetails.name: Project AURORA EXPLORES😎
projectDetails.summary: Space weather refers to the conditions in space caused by the Sun’s activity, including solar wind, solar flares, and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). These events release charged particles and radiation that can impact Earth's magnetic field, leading to geomagnetic storms. Such disturbances can affect satellites, GPS, communication systems, power grids, and even pose risks to astronauts in space. One visible effect of space weather is the aurora (Northern and Southern Lights), which occurs when solar particles interact with Earth’s atmosphere near the poles. Monitoring and forecasting space weather is important to protect modern technology and infrastructure from potential damage caused by solar activity.
projectDetails.details: Our project is a simple educational model made using PictoBlox. It features a robot character that appears on the screen and explains information about space weather, such as solar flares, solar wind, and their effects on Earth. The robot talks about how space weather can affect satellites, GPS, and power systems. The goal of this project is to help students learn basic facts about space weather in a fun and easy way. We used PictoBlox to program the robot’s speech and movements. This project is creative because it uses a talking robot to teach science, making it more engaging. We focused on keeping it simple, clear, and informative for anyone to understand.

projectDetails.summary: The "Commercializing Low Earth Orbit (LEO)" challenge invites participants to develop a sustainable and scalable business model that leverages the unique conditions of LEO—such as microgravity and orbital access—for commercial purposes. Solutions should include a clear business plan, a conceptual prototype or service, and address key issues like technical feasibility, sustainability, regulatory compliance, and long-term viability. projectDetails.details: The “Commercializing Low Earth Orbit (LEO)” challenge in NASA’s 2025 Space Apps invites participants to create a sustainable and scalable business model that leverages the unique conditions of LEO—such as microgravity, orbital positioning, and continuous access to space—for commercial purposes. Participants are expected to develop a detailed business plan that identifies the product or service being offered (e.g., in-space manufacturing, satellite servicing, research platforms, or data services), the target customers (such as commercial, governmental, or academic sectors), and the revenue model. Alongside the business model, teams must propose a prototype or conceptual design that demonstrates how the idea would work in orbit, taking into account constraints like mass, power usage, reliability, and safety. Operational feasibility is a key focus—this includes plans for launch, deployment, in-orbit operation, maintenance, and logistics. The solution should also address regulatory compliance, environmental impact (especially managing orbital debris and end-of-life deorbiting), and ethical concerns related to space sustainability. Long-term viability and scalability are critical: proposals should outline how the idea could expand to support more users, larger operations, or different orbital zones over time, while remaining economically and environmentally sustainable. Judges will evaluate submissions based on innovation, impact, technical feasibility, sustainability, and how clearly the concept and prototype are communicated. Overall, this challenge pushes teams to think like space entrepreneurs, balancing bold innovation with real-world constraints, and contributing to the growing commercial ecosystem in Low Earth Orbit.

projectDetails.summary: BloomWatch India is an interactive web application designed to monitor plant growth and predict bloom probability in real time across India. projectDetails.details:
BloomWatch India is an interactive web application developed by Team Baki using Streamlit, Python, NumPy, Pandas, Folium, GeoPandas, and Earth Engine API. The project allows users to explore historical vegetation growth and bloom patterns across India by analyzing MODIS NDVI satellite data and NASA POWER climate data. Users can select a state, climate zone, plant category (Fruits, Flowers, or Crops), and species to visualize NDVI trends, temperature, and precipitation over time, alongside bloom probability calculations based on species-specific thresholds and climate conditions.

The app works by fetching geospatial NDVI data for the selected region, combining it with daily climate data, and computing bloom probability, which is visualized as a time-series chart. The benefits include providing researchers, students, and agriculture enthusiasts with a data-driven understanding of historical plant growth and bloom patterns. This insight can support agriculture planning, educational purposes, and ecological monitoring.

projectDetails.summary:
**Project Summary – 2D Space Habitat Designer**

The *2D Space Habitat Designer* is an interactive simulation game that challenges players to design sustainable and efficient living spaces for astronauts beyond Earth. Developed using **Phaser.js**, the project transforms the complex task of *space habitat design* into an engaging, educational experience.

Players can build habitats for different mission types—such as *Transit Stations*, *Moon Bases*, and *Mars Bases*—and strategically place essential modules like *Sleep Pods, Kitchens, Hygiene Units,* and *Command Centers*. The system evaluates each design based on *Crew Capacity, Area Utilization,* and *Crew Efficiency*, providing real-time feedback to help users improve their layouts.

This project addresses the challenge of designing livable environments in space by teaching users about spatial organization, human factors, and sustainability through interactive learning. Its importance lies in promoting *systems thinking* and *creativity*—skills essential for future engineers and designers tackling real-world challenges in space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – 2D Space Habitat Designer

The 2D Space Habitat Designer is an interactive simulation game that allows users to design and analyze conceptual living spaces for astronauts in space environments. The goal is to make the complex process of space habitat design accessible and engaging by combining science, design, and interactivity.

How It Works

Players begin by selecting a mission type—Transit Station, Moon Base, or Mars Base—each with unique environmental constraints. Using a drag-and-drop interface built with Phaser.js, they place habitat modules such as Sleep Pods, Kitchens, Exercise Areas, Hygiene Units, and Command Centers within a defined 2D boundary. The system ensures modules do not overlap and provides instant performance feedback based on Crew Capacity, Area Utilization, and Crew Efficiency. Players can iteratively adjust their layouts to improve performance and livability.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project encourages systems thinking, spatial reasoning, and problem-solving by simulating realistic challenges of living in space. It helps users understand how design decisions affect functionality, comfort, and safety—critical concepts in aerospace engineering and architecture. The game aims to educate and inspire players about sustainable living in extreme environments while fostering creativity and curiosity about future space missions.

Tools and Technologies

  • Languages: JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3
  • Framework: Phaser.js (for 2D game development)
  • Design Tools: Figma (for interface design and layout planning)
  • Development Environment: Visual Studio Code
  • Testing Platforms: Web browsers (Chrome, Edge)

Creativity and Design Factors

The creativity of this project lies in blending education with interactivity—turning a highly technical engineering problem into an intuitive, visual game. The team focused on realism (module proportions and relationships), usability (clean UI, smooth controls), and educational value (clear feedback and scoring logic). Factors such as crew needs, spatial efficiency, human factors engineering, and mission type constraints guided design decisions.

Ultimately, 2D Space Habitat Designer showcases how playful learning can be used to explore real-world challenges in space design—making it both a fun simulation and an educational tool for students, designers, and space enthusiasts alike.

projectDetails.details:
FloodSense is a hyper-local, real-time flood risk prediction system designed to enhance preparedness and community resilience in the Kochi region. It creatively fuses NASA Earth Observation data with local environmental intelligence and machine learning to deliver actionable, timely flood warnings.

​What It Does & How It Works (Creativity)

​FloodSense operates on a multi-source data integration model:

​NASA Data Core: It acquires near real-time precipitation data from the NASA Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) IMERG product, a cornerstone of its predictive capability.

​Local Intelligence: This satellite data is combined with critical local geospatial factors (soil type, land use, drainage density, and SRTM-derived terrain) that define the region's flood susceptibility.

​Predictive Engine: A Python/Flask backend hosts a Machine Learning (ML) model trained on this fused dataset to predict the actual flood risk level (not just rainfall) for specific markers.

​Actionable Output: The JavaScript frontend visualizes these risk levels on an interactive map and provides an analytics dashboard for trend viewing.

​Community Engagement: A crucial user feedback modal allows the community to submit real-world observations, continuously validating and improving the accuracy of the ML model (ground-truthing).

​Benefits and Intended Impact

​The primary benefit of FloodSense is the provision of timely early warnings, enabling residents and authorities to move from a reactive disaster response to proactive prevention.

​The intended impact is to:

​Reduce flood-related economic damages and loss of property in Kochi.

​Improve informed decision-making for local municipal resource allocation.

​Significantly boost community resilience through rapid, accurate, and localized warnings.

​Technology Stack

​Coding Languages: Python (for core backend logic and data science), Flask (for API), JavaScript, HTML, CSS (for the interactive frontend).

​Key Tools: NASA GPM (IMERG), OpenWeatherMap, Machine Learning libraries (e.g., Scikit-learn/TensorFlow), and geospatial libraries (GDAL/Fiona).

​Factor Considered: Data accuracy, near real-time performance, a user-friendly interface, and extensibility for future deployment in other vulnerable

projectDetails.name: Asteroid Alert & Visualization
projectDetails.summary:
Problem Statement Summary
Near-Earth asteroids and comets regularly pass close to our planet, and while most pose no immediate threat, even a small chance of impact can have significant global consequences. NASA and other space agencies continuously monitor these celestial objects, collecting vast amounts of data about their size, speed, and trajectory.

However, this information is primarily presented in highly technical formats designed for scientists and researchers, making it difficult for the general public to access or understand. As a result, public awareness of potential asteroid threats remains low, despite the availability of accurate and timely data.

This communication gap between complex scientific information and easy public understanding limits people’s ability to stay informed about near-Earth objects. There is a clear need for a simple, intuitive, and publicly accessible platform that translates NASA’s asteroid data into meaningful insights — empowering everyone to track, visualize, and understand asteroid activity in real time.
projectDetails.details:
Detailed Problem Statement

In recent decades, advancements in space research have revealed that our planet is continuously surrounded by thousands of Near-Earth Objects (NEOs), including asteroids and comets, that travel through space at tremendous speeds. While the majority of these celestial bodies pass safely at great distances, a small number have the potential to collide with Earth, posing significant threats to human civilization, the environment, and global stability. The scientific community, particularly agencies such as NASA, actively monitors these objects using specialized telescopes, radar systems, and the Near-Earth Object Observation Program.

Despite the vast amount of data being collected, this information is primarily targeted toward researchers and experts in the field. NASA provides open access to its databases and APIs, such as the Near-Earth Object Web Service (NeoWs), which contain detailed parameters including object diameters, orbital velocities, approach distances, and potential hazard probabilities. However, the highly technical and data-driven format of these resources makes it challenging for the general public to comprehend or utilize them effectively.

As a result, there exists a substantial communication gap between scientific observation and public awareness. The average person remains uninformed about ongoing asteroid activity, potential risks, and even general knowledge about NEOs. This lack of accessible and user-friendly tools limits public engagement, education, and preparedness concerning planetary defense and asteroid monitoring.

Furthermore, in an age where technology can simplify and visualize complex data, the absence of a clear, interactive platform for the public represents a missed opportunity for education and awareness. Current solutions often focus on professional research or media coverage only after major events occur, rather than fostering proactive learning and continuous awareness.

Therefore, the core problem lies not in the availability of asteroid data, but in its inaccessibility to non-expert audiences. There is a pressing need for an intuitive, interactive, and visually engaging platform that converts NASA’s raw data into meaningful insights. Such a system should allow users to visualize asteroid trajectories, receive real-time alerts about near approaches, and understand the potential implications in a clear and relatable way.

Addressing this gap will not only enhance public understanding of asteroid science but also encourage a culture of curiosity, education, and preparedness — ensuring that vital information about potential near-Earth threats is transparent and easy to access for everyone.

projectDetails.summary: The Historical Risk Explorer is a Streamlit-based application developed for the NASA Earth Observation Challenge. It allows users to analyze historical environmental data and evaluate the likelihood of specific weather conditions—such as temperature, precipitation, wind speed, humidity, and air quality—at any chosen location and day of the year. Users can select a location by dropping a pin on a map or entering a place name and explore multiple environmental variables simultaneously. The application computes historical averages, exceedance probabilities, and risk indices, presenting results through interactive charts, maps, and clear textual summaries. Additionally, users can download a CSV file containing the relevant data for offline analysis. By combining real and mock datasets with statistical modeling, the tool makes complex Earth observation data accessible and actionable. It addresses the challenge by helping researchers, planners, and communities understand environmental trends, anticipate extreme weather events, and make informed decisions to manage climate-related risks effectively.
projectDetails.details:
The Historical Risk Explorer is a modular Streamlit application designed to analyze historical environmental data and provide users with probabilistic insights on weather conditions at a location and day of their choice. Users can interactively select a location by dropping a pin on a map or typing a place name and choose a specific day of the year. The application supports multiple environmental variables, including temperature, precipitation, wind speed and humidity.

The tool works by fetching historical data from Meteomatics api, computing historical averages, exceedance probabilities, and risk indices for the selected variables. Interactive visualizations—including line charts, density plots, and maps—allow users to understand trends and assess the likelihood of extreme events. Users can also download CSV files of the selected subset for offline analysis.

The application is built with Python, using Streamlit for the frontend, asyncio and httpx for efficient data fetching, Pandas and NumPy for data processing, and Matplotlib/Plotly for visualizations.

The project is creative in its combination of real-time location selection, probabilistic analysis, and multi-variable visualization, offering a personalized, accessible view of complex Earth observation data. It aims to empower researchers, planners, and communities to anticipate extreme weather, manage climate-related risks, and make informed decisions. Factors such as usability, interpretability of probability data, and exportable outputs were carefully considered in the design.
projectDetails.aiReferences: AI tools were used only for coding assistance during development, such as generating or refining Python scripts and structuring the Streamlit app. No AI was used for data analysis, modeling, visualizations, or any content creation. All environmental data, computations, and outputs are based on historical datasets and statistical methods.

projectDetails.name: Code and Chaya
projectDetails.summary: We developed CosmoGraph, an AI-powered research exploration tool that enables users to interactively explore NASA’s bioscience publications. By combining semantic search, AI-driven summarization, and knowledge graph visualization, CosmoGraph allows users to discover connections between publications, visualize related concepts, and quickly understand the outcomes of space biology experiments. Users can search by topic, explore clusters of related research, and access concise summaries of relevant studies, helping scientists, mission planners, and managers identify trends, knowledge gaps, and actionable insights. This tool addresses the challenge of navigating the extensive NASA bioscience literature by transforming complex textual data into intuitive, interactive visualizations, supporting more informed decisions for human exploration of the Moon and Mars.
projectDetails.details:
CosmoGraph is an interactive AI-powered dashboard designed to help users explore NASA’s bioscience publications. The tool enables semantic search across over 600 publications, generates AI-based summaries of abstracts, and visualizes relationships between research topics using a knowledge graph. Users can search for specific themes—such as “microgravity effects on plants”-and instantly see related studies, key findings, and interconnected concepts, making complex research more accessible and actionable.

The system leverages Python (FastAPI, SentenceTransformers) for backend processing, Supabase with pgvector for embedding-based vector search, and React + Tailwind + react-force-graph-2d for frontend visualization. Publications are represented as nodes connected by shared tags, allowing users to intuitively explore clusters of related studies.

This project provides several benefits: it accelerates discovery, identifies knowledge gaps, highlights trends in space biology research, and supports mission planning for lunar and Martian exploration. Its creativity lies in combining semantic AI search with interactive graph visualization, transforming static research papers into a dynamic, exploratory knowledge tool. The team prioritized usability, relevance of AI summaries, and meaningful visualization of scientific relationships to maximize the impact for scientists, managers, and mission architects.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Our project, CosmoGraph, leverages AI in multiple key areas:

  1. Semantic Search: We used Sentence-BERT (SBERT) to convert user queries and publication texts into embeddings, enabling search based on meaning rather than exact keywords.
  2. Text Summarization: AI models (OpenAI/Gemini) were used to generate concise summaries of publication abstracts, helping users quickly understand key findings.
  3. Knowledge Graph Insights: AI-assisted clustering of tags and concepts helped structure the relationships between publications, enhancing visualization and exploration.

All AI-generated outputs (summaries, embeddings, and relationships) are clearly documented in the backend metadata. No NASA branding was used or modified.

projectDetails.name: Urban Expansion Time Lapse
projectDetails.summary:
Urban Expansion Time-Lapse Visualizer
An interactive platform that uses Google Earth and Terra satellite imagery to show the growth of cities across all Indian states from 2010 to 2025. Users can explore year-by-year time-lapses, view changes in built-up areas and green cover, and gain insights into urban expansion, infrastructure, and environmental trends through intuitive animations and visualizations.
projectDetails.details:
OVERVIEW

Our project, “Urban Expansion Time-Lapse Visualizer: Mapping India’s Growth, 1985–2025”, is an interactive platform that visualizes the transformation of India’s cities over four decades. Using satellite imagery from Google Earth and Terra, the platform creates dynamic, year-by-year time-lapses for all 28 states and 8 union territories, highlighting urban expansion, green cover changes, and infrastructure development.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

Urbanization in India has accelerated rapidly over the past few decades, but there is no easy, interactive way to visualize how cities have grown over time. Policymakers, researchers, and citizens lack access to comprehensive, time-based visual insights showing urban expansion, green cover changes, and infrastructure development. Traditional maps and static reports fail to capture the dynamic evolution of cities, making it difficult to analyze trends, plan sustainably, or understand the environmental impact of urban growth.

HOW IT WORKS

The system processes satellite images to calculate indices such as NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) for vegetation and NDBI (Normalized Difference Built-up Index) for urban areas. These indices are then translated into animated visualizations, allowing users to explore urban growth trends in each state capital interactively. Each capital is represented as a glowing node on an India map, which, when selected, plays a smooth animation of the city’s growth with accompanying metrics like population and GDP changes over time.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

This project helps users understand urbanization patterns, environmental changes, and infrastructure growth across India in an intuitive, visual way. It is valuable for urban planners, researchers, policymakers, educators, and citizens interested in the evolution of Indian cities. By combining data analysis with interactive visualization, it encourages data-driven decision-making and awareness of sustainable urban development.

TOOLS, TECHNOLOGIES AND SOFTWARES USED:

  • Data Sources: Google Earth satellite imagery, Terra satellite data
  • Data Processing & Analysis: Python (for preprocessing), Google Earth Engine (for time-series analysis and index computation)
  • Frontend & Visualization: React.js, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Tailwind CSS (for responsive and sleek UI)
  • Design & Graphics: Canva, Adobe Photoshop, FlexClip (for animations and video content)
  • Deployment: Vercel (for hosting the web platform)

CREATIVITY AND TEAM CONSIDERATIONS

Our project is highly creative because it combines real-world satellite data with futuristic, interactive visualizations, turning complex datasets into an engaging and educational experience. We focused on smooth animations, glowing interactive nodes, and clear data presentation to make exploration intuitive. The team carefully considered data accuracy, cloud-free image selection, state-wise uniformity, and user engagement, ensuring the platform is both informative and visually appealing.

TARGET USERS

  • Urban planners & architects
  • Researchers & academics
  • Policymakers & government officials
  • Students & educators
  • Curious citizens & general public

LIVE REPOSITORY

https://github.com/Ammu1pillai/urban-expansion

FUTURISTIC VISION

In the future, our app could expand to become a global time-lapse explorer, where every city and location on Earth can be viewed through historical and predictive timelines. Users could navigate the planet interactively, seeing urban growth, environmental changes, and infrastructure evolution anywhere in the world, making it a universal tool for understanding our planet’s transformation over time.

CONCLUSION

This project not only maps India’s urban growth, but also inspires curiosity and insight by letting users see decades of change in a glance, providing a powerful tool to understand, plan, and reflect on urban development, with the potential to scale globally.
