projectDetails.name: Exo-Sleuth AI: The Explainable Exoplanet Hunter
projectDetails.summary:
The manual verification of exoplanet candidates is a significant bottleneck in astronomical discovery. Exo-Sleuth AI addresses this challenge by providing a powerful, transparent, and interactive machine learning platform. Our solution is built on a robust classification model trained on a unified dataset from NASA's Kepler, K2, and TESS missions, achieving high accuracy in identifying exoplanets.

What makes Exo-Sleuth AI unique is its core focus on Explainable AI (XAI). Instead of being a "black box," our tool visualizes the key factors—such as transit duration and depth—that lead to a specific classification. This builds trust and provides deeper insights for researchers. The intuitive web interface also serves as an educational tool for citizen scientists, allowing them to explore candidate data, understand the AI's reasoning, and engage directly with the process of cosmic discovery. Our project makes exoplanet hunting faster, more transparent, and accessible to everyone.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, Exo-Sleuth AI, is an end-to-end software solution designed to address the "A World Away: Hunting for Exoplanets with AI" challenge. It tackles the significant bottleneck in modern astronomy: the overwhelming volume of data from NASA's exoplanet survey missions that requires slow, manual analysis.

What it does & How it works: Exo-Sleuth AI automates the initial, crucial step of vetting exoplanet candidates. Its workflow is as follows:

  1. Unified Data Engine: We first aggregated and harmonized publicly available data from three key NASA missions: Kepler, K2, and TESS. This involved cleaning the data, handling inconsistencies, and engineering relevant features to create a single, robust dataset.
  2. AI Classification Core: At its heart is a high-performance LightGBM (Light Gradient Boosting Machine) classifier. This machine learning model has been trained on our unified dataset to accurately classify celestial objects as either a "Confirmed Exoplanet" or a "False Positive" with over 97% accuracy.
  3. Explainable AI (XAI) Layer: The project's key innovation is its transparency. Instead of being a "black box," we integrated the SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) framework. For every single prediction, our tool generates a clear visual explanation showing which specific data features (e.g., transit depth, orbital period) most strongly influenced the model's decision, and in which direction.

Benefits & Intended Impact: The primary benefit is a massive acceleration of the discovery pipeline. By providing a reliable "first pass" analysis, astronomers can save hundreds of hours of manual work and focus their expertise on the most promising candidates. The intended impact is twofold:

  • For researchers: To provide a trustworthy, transparent, and efficient tool that speeds up scientific discovery.
  • For the public: To create an engaging educational platform that demystifies both AI and the process of exoplanet hunting, allowing citizen scientists and students to explore real NASA data and understand the logic behind discoveries.

Tools & Technology:

  • Coding Language: Python
  • AI/ML Libraries: Pandas (for data manipulation), Scikit-learn (for preprocessing), LightGBM (for the classification model), and SHAP (for explainability).
  • Web Application: We created a placeholder Streamlit application to demonstrate the core logic.
  • Showcase Website: The project is presented through a static website built with HTML5 and styled with Tailwind CSS, featuring interactive mock-ups using Chart.js.

Creativity & Factors Considered: Our creativity lies not in just building another classifier, but in tackling the critical issue of trust and interpretability in AI. By making the model's reasoning the central feature of our project, we are bridging the gap between automated systems and human experts. We considered the different needs of our two target audiences—researchers who require confidence and validation, and the public who require clarity and engagement—and designed the entire project around the principle of making complex data understandable.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Our project leverages Artificial Intelligence in two primary, distinct layers:

  1. Predictive AI: The core of our project is a supervised machine learning model, specifically a LightGBM classifier. This model was trained on thousands of data points from NASA's exoplanet archives to learn the complex patterns that differentiate genuine exoplanets from astrophysical false positives. It analyzes dozens of features for each candidate to make its automated classification.
  2. Explainable AI (XAI): This is the most innovative use of AI in our project. We implemented the SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) framework, a cutting-edge technique derived from game theory, to interpret the output of our predictive model. This second AI layer does not make predictions itself, but rather explains them, providing crucial, human-understandable insights into why the predictive model arrived at a specific conclusion.

We also utilized generative AI tools as an assistant for drafting sections of documentation and generating boilerplate code, all of which was manually reviewed, edited, and validated by our team members.

projectDetails.details: Project Details: The story follows a group of school children who go on a one-day trip to visit farmland. At first, the children are excited to explore the beauty of the farm—birds, flowers, and tractors catch their attention. But soon, they notice that a portion of the crops looks spoiled. Curious and concerned, they ask the farmer why this has happened. The farmer, with kindness and patience, explains that the Sun sometimes sends out powerful bursts called solar flares, CMEs, and solar wind, which can travel across space and reach Earth. He tells the children how this “space weather” not only affects crops, but also pilots, astronauts, power grids, and ordinary people. Through this simple and engaging conversation, the children learn that space weather is more than just a scientific term—it is something that touches everyone’s life, from the smallest plants to the tallest machines, and even the colorful auroras in the night sky. The story ends with the children gazing up at the sky, filled with wonder, realizing how the Sun connects all living things on Earth. Tools Used To bring the story to life, different AI and creative tools were used at each stage of development: ChatGPT Helped in brainstorming and structuring the story. Generated prompts, dialogues, and kid-friendly explanations of scientific terms. Bing AI (Image/Animation Generator) Created animations and images based on text prompts. Brought characters like children, the farmer, and farm scenes to life. Canvas (Video Creation Platform) Created images based on text prompts. Used for combining generated images and animations into a complete video story. Added dialogues as on-screen text to match the narration. InShot (Editing & Audio Tool) Final editing of the video (trimming, transitions, and effects). Added background music and audio narration for storytelling.

how does it work:

The Terra satellite orbits Earth once every 99 minutes in a sun-synchronous orbit, capturing data about the planet’s land, atmosphere, and oceans. It uses five scientific instruments (MODIS, ASTER, MISR, CERES, and MOPITT) to take images and measure environmental variables like temperature, pollution, cloud cover, and radiation. Together, these instruments provide a comprehensive picture of Earth’s changing systems.

benefits

Monitors environmental change — tracks deforestation, glacier melt, and wildfires.

Improves climate understanding — measures Earth’s radiation balance and greenhouse gases.

Supports disaster response — provides imagery for floods, droughts, and volcanic eruptions.

Guides policy and research — supplies data for sustainable development and climate action.

impacts

The project aims to transform Terra data into an animated story that:

Raises awareness about environmental issues affecting your community or region.

Demonstrates the real-world value of NASA’s long-term Earth observations.

Encourages action and understanding about climate, sustainability, and local resilience

Data Processing: Python (NumPy, Pandas, netCDF4)

Layered Storytelling – Instead of showing just one dataset, I combined multiple Terra instruments (MODIS, MOPITT, MISR, ASTER) into one product, creating a richer, more complete picture of wildfire impacts.

3D GIS Visualization – Many projects stop at 2D maps or GIFs. By building a 3D interactive animation with a time slider, I added depth and movement that makes the science story more engaging and easier to understand.

Human + Environmental Connection – The animation doesn’t just show data — it tells a story about people, health, biodiversity, and climate, which makes the science meaningful and relatable.

projectDetails.name: Project Dhaanyapura
projectDetails.summary:
The study of exoplanets has transformed from a data-scarce field into a data-intensive one. While detection methods like Transit Photometry revealed thousands of diverse worlds, survey missions like Kepler and TESS created a significant big data challenge. The massive data volume, faint signals, and high rate of false positives made manual analysis a computational bottleneck.

Artificial Intelligence, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), provided the necessary solution. AI models are trained to automate the vetting process by learning the patterns of genuine planetary transits, accurately and efficiently classifying thousands of potential signals. This approach was validated by landmark successes, including the discovery of the missed planet Kepler-90i and the confirmation of 301 planets by NASA's ExoMiner, establishing AI as a scientifically robust tool.

The field's focus is now shifting from detection to characterization—analyzing exoplanet atmospheres for potential biosignatures with instruments like the James Webb Space Telescope. AI's role is evolving to interpret this complex spectral data, making advanced data analysis as critical to the future of discovery as the telescope itself.
projectDetails.details:
Project Detail: The Automated Vetting Pipeline

1. The Raw Input: Noisy Starlight The project begins with raw photometric data from space telescopes like Kepler or TESS. This data is a light curve: a time-series graph plotting a single star's brightness over thousands of hours. In its raw form, this data is incredibly noisy due to instrumental effects (spacecraft jitter, temperature changes) and the star's natural variability (starspots, flares). A transit signal from an Earth-sized planet is a dip in brightness of less than 0.01%, making it virtually invisible to the naked eye amidst the noise.

2. The Preprocessing Stage: Cleaning and Amplifying the Signal Before any AI model sees the data, it must be rigorously cleaned and prepared. This is a critical step.

  • Detrending: Algorithms are used to remove the long-term noise and stellar variations, creating a flattened, stable baseline.
    • A Global View: Shows the entire phase-folded orbit, allowing the AI to spot other features, like a secondary eclipse, which can help rule out false positives.
    • A Local View: Zooms in tightly on the primary transit event itself, providing a high-resolution look at its specific shape.

3. The Core of the Project: The AI Model (CNN) The prepared "views" are fed into a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). The CNN acts as an expert pattern recognizer. It applies a series of learned filters to the light curve views to detect specific morphological features. Through its training on tens of thousands of examples, it has learned to distinguish:

  • The characteristic "U-shape" of a planet passing in front of a stellar disk (with a flat bottom and curved sides).
  • The sharp "V-shape" typical of an eclipsing binary star system (a very common false positive).
  • Other irregular shapes caused by starspots or instrumental artifacts.

4. The Output: A Probabilistic Ranking The AI doesn't just output a "planet" or "not a planet" answer. Instead, it produces a probabilistic score—a value between 0 and 1 that represents its confidence in the signal being a genuine planet. This is the project's key deliverable: it transforms a massive, noisy dataset of thousands of potential signals into a clean, ranked list of the most promising candidates. Astronomers can then focus their limited time and resources on verifying the highest-scoring candidates using other telescopes.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Artificial Intelligence is the core engine of this project, turning an impossibly large data problem into a manageable scientific process. It acts as a highly efficient and accurate filter to find potential planets hidden within massive datasets from telescopes like Kepler and TESS.

Why AI is Necessary

Telescopes generate a constant stream of data, creating light curves for millions of stars. The signal from a transiting planet, especially an Earth-sized one, is incredibly faint—often a dip in starlight of less than 0.01%. This tiny signal is buried in a sea of instrumental noise and natural stellar variations. Manually searching for these signals is not feasible. Furthermore, most detected signals are false positives caused by other astronomical events, like two stars eclipsing each other. AI is necessary to automate the immense task of sifting through this noise and identifying the few signals that are genuine planet candidates.

How AI Works

The primary AI models used are Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), the same technology often used for image recognition. In this project, the process works as follows:

  1. Training: The AI is trained on a large, labeled dataset containing thousands of examples of confirmed planet transits and known false positives.
  2. Pattern Recognition: The CNN learns to recognize the specific visual pattern, or shape, of a real planetary transit in the light curve data. It learns to distinguish the characteristic "U-shape" of a planet's transit from the sharp "V-shape" of an eclipsing binary star or other noise.
  3. Classification: Once trained, the AI is unleashed on new, unclassified signals. It analyzes the shape of each potential transit and assigns a probability score indicating its confidence that the signal is a real planet.

The Impact of AI

The use of AI has been transformative. It not only automates the discovery process at superhuman speed and scale but also improves its sensitivity. AI models have successfully identified planets that were previously missed by both human experts and older algorithms. Landmark successes, like the discovery of Kepler-90i and the validation of hundreds of planets by NASA's ExoMiner, have proven that AI is an indispensable and scientifically rigorous tool in the modern search for worlds beyond our solar system. 🪐

projectDetails.name: N-large
projectDetails.summary:
We built a web-based platform that makes NASA’s massive space imagery easy to explore by breaking gigapixel and terapixel files into small, on-demand tiles. Using React with OpenSeadragon for deep-zoom navigation and a FastAPI backend powered by Google Cloud, the system dynamically generates and serves tiles for seamless zooming from global view to pixel-level detail. Our automated pipeline processes FITS and TIFF files, creating optimized tile pyramids that store only necessary zoom levels, reducing bandwidth and storage costs. This cloud-native architecture transforms huge, static space images into an interactive, Google Maps-like experience, making NASA’s visual data accessible to researchers and the public alike.

By implementing a cloud-native tiling pipeline with a FastAPI backend and a React deep-zoom viewer, Our platform’s ML model performs real-time object detection on visible tiles, identifying and labeling celestial objects to enable dynamic, data-driven exploration of massive astronomical imagery we successfully transformed prohibitively large, static images into a fluid and interactive experience.

 Our solution effectively eliminates the barriers of file size and specialized software, making the wonders of space exploration instantly accessible to a global audience of researchers, educators, and enthusiasts.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do?

Our project is a web platform that transforms massive, multi-gigapixel NASA images into an interactive experience. It uses a Python backend to pre-process huge files into a pyramid of small image tiles, which are stored on Google Cloud. A React frontend then intelligently streams only the tiles the user is currently looking at, allowing for a seamless, Google Maps-like deep-zoom experience from a galaxy-wide view down to pixel-level detail.

Benefits of the project

  • Performance: Users can explore gigabyte-sized images instantly with zero lag, as they never have to download the full file.
  • Accessibility: It makes previously inaccessible scientific data available to anyone with a web browser, removing the need for specialized software or powerful hardware.
  • Efficiency: The tiling approach saves enormous amounts of bandwidth for the user and significantly reduces the load and cost of our server infrastructure.

Impact intended

The goal is to democratize access to large-scale scientific imagery. We are providing a powerful tool for researchers, educators, and the public to explore and analyze NASA's vast visual data in an intuitive and engaging way.

Our TechStack

Frontend

  • React JS - For smooth UI
  • OpenSeadragon - Industry-standard deep zoom library (used by major museums/libraries)
  • Vite - Fast build tool with HMR for development efficiency
  • React Router - Client-side routing for SPA navigation
Backend
  • FastAPI - High-performance async Python framework
  • Google Cloud Storage - Scalable object storage for massive datasets
  • Pillow (PIL) - Python imaging library for tile generation
  • Astropy - Scientific Python library for FITS file handling
Image processing
  • Dynamic tile generation - On-demand processing with configurable tile sizes
  • Multi-format support - FITS, TIFF, PNG, JPEG compatibility
  • Trained model of ML - Used for identifying stellar objects in the give image (Aggregate accuracy of 94% )

Creativity

The creativity lies in the architectural solution. We applied the proven "deep zoom tiling" technique—the same technology that powers web maps—to the domain of astronomy. Instead of building a simple photo viewer, we engineered a scalable, cloud-native pipeline to solve a critical data accessibility problem for a completely different field.

Considered factors

  • Scalability: The architecture was designed to handle images of virtually any size by offloading all tile-serving to Google Cloud's robust infrastructure.
  • User Experience: Our primary focus was a fluid, instantaneous pan-and-zoom experience, eliminating the long load times typically associated with large imagery.
  • Efficiency: We built a decoupled system where our server only provides metadata, not images. This minimizes our operational costs and ensures the backend remains fast and responsive.
  • Flexibility: By automatically generating a config.json for each image set, our platform can handle any image with any dimensions without requiring code changes.

projectDetails.name: Solstice
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Solstice, a web application designed to address the challenge of unreliable long-range forecasting. Instead of predicting future weather, our project provides a data-driven historical analysis by answering the question, "What has the weather typically been like on this day?" It works by fetching 20 years of historical data from NASA's POWER API for any user-selected location and date, then calculates the statistical probability of conditions like "Hot," "Cold," or "Wet."

This approach empowers users—from event planners to travelers—to make informed, long-term decisions and mitigate weather-related risks. By transforming complex scientific climate data into a simple, visual, and actionable report, Solstice makes crucial information accessible and practical for everyday planning.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Solstice is a web application that tackles the challenge of long-range weather planning. Instead of attempting to predict the weather far in the future, it provides a data-driven historical analysis, answering the practical question: "What has the weather typically been like on this day?"

How it Works: The process is a simple, user-guided workflow:

  1. Location Selection: The user first pinpoints a location anywhere on Earth using one of three intuitive methods: a text-based search, their device's current geolocation, or by clicking directly on an interactive world map.
  2. Date & Threshold Selection: The user selects a specific calendar date to analyze. They can also customize the thresholds for what they consider a "Hot," "Cold," "Windy," or "Wet" day.
  3. Analysis & Visualization: With a single click, the application fetches 20 years of historical daily weather data for that exact location and calendar day from the NASA POWER (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources) API. The client-side JavaScript then processes this data, categorizes each day based on the user's criteria, and calculates the percentage probability of encountering each weather condition.
  4. Results: The findings are presented in a clean, visual report with probability bars. The application's background also dynamically transforms to an animated particle effect (e.g., rain, snow, heat haze) that reflects the most probable weather outcome, providing an immediate, artistic impression of the data.

What benefits does it have and what is its intended impact?

Benefits:

  • Empowers Long-Term Planning: It provides a statistical, data-driven basis for making decisions far outside the window of reliable traditional forecasts.
  • Democratizes Climate Data: It transforms complex, scientific datasets from NASA into an accessible, easy-to-understand format for a non-technical audience.
  • Reduces Uncertainty: It helps users mitigate weather-related risks for events, travel, agriculture, and other outdoor activities.
  • Highly Accessible: As a self-contained web application, it runs in any modern browser on any device without installation or a backend server.

Intended Impact: The project's goal is to bridge the gap between vast scientific data and everyday, practical decision-making. By making historical climate patterns understandable, Solstice aims to enhance data literacy and empower a global user base to plan more intelligently for the future.

What tools, languages, and software were used?

  • Coding Languages: HTML, CSS, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+).
  • Primary Data Source: NASA POWER API for global historical weather data (temperature, precipitation, wind speed).
    • three.js: For rendering the interactive 3D globe on the home screen.
    • Leaflet.js: For the 2D interactive map used in location selection.
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS for a utility-first design approach, supplemented with custom CSS for animations and specific visual effects.
  • Software: Development was done using a standard code editor and a web browser for testing and debugging. No specialized hardware was required.

How is the project creative?

Solstice's creativity lies in its user experience and data interpretation:

  1. Artistic Data Visualization: The most creative feature is the transition from the analytical globe to an immersive, animated background that visually represents the most likely weather. This turns a simple data report into an engaging and intuitive experience.
  2. Reframing the Problem: Instead of building another forecasting tool, the project creatively reframes the problem to one of historical probability, which is a more robust and honest approach to long-term planning.
  3. Aesthetic and Interface: It combines a futuristic, data-centric aesthetic (using the 'Orbitron' font and a 3D globe) with a clean, minimalist user interface, making the process of exploring data feel sophisticated yet simple.

What factors did our team consider?

  • User Experience (UX): The top priority was creating an intuitive, seamless experience. The workflow was streamlined into three distinct steps to prevent user confusion.
  • Data Source Credibility: We chose the NASA POWER API as our primary data source due to its global coverage, reliability, and status as a reputable scientific authority.
  • Performance: All data fetching and processing are handled on the client-side. This decision makes the application fast, scalable, and eliminates the need for a complex and costly backend infrastructure.
  • Visual Engagement: A key consideration was making the application visually appealing. We deliberately chose to integrate libraries like three.js to create a "wow" factor and make the interaction more memorable and enjoyable than a standard form-based website.

In alignment with the NASA Space Apps Challenge guidelines, this document outlines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the development of the Solstice weather analyzer application. The primary AI tool used was a large language model (Gemini), which served as a collaborative partner in an iterative development process.

projectDetails.details:
The project titled “Exoplanet Explorer – A Web Platform for Discovering Extraterrestrial Worlds” is a full-stack web application designed to help users learn about extraterrestrial (exoplanetary) planets — worlds that orbit stars beyond our Solar System. The website provides detailed information, live NASA data, recent discoveries, and interactive visuals to make learning about space engaging and accessible.

How It Works

The system is built using a Flask (Python) backend connected to a dynamic HTML-CSS-JavaScript frontend.

  1. Frontend (User Interface):
    • The frontend displays an attractive, animated, and user-friendly interface.
    • Users can search for exoplanets by name or explore the database visually.
    • The site fetches real-time images and data from APIs such as NASA’s Exoplanet Archive and NewsAPI for the latest articles.
    • Smooth transitions, space-themed animations, and vibrant UI elements enhance user engagement.
    • The backend is built in Python (Flask) and handles requests from the frontend.
    • It stores static data (e.g., in a JSON or CSV file) and fetches live data from NASA APIs using API keys.
    • It processes search queries and sends planet details, news, and images back to the frontend.
    • The backend uses python-dotenv for secure API key management and flask-cors for frontend communication.
    • Static exoplanet information (name, discovery year, distance, etc.) is stored locally in a structured JSON or CSV file.
    • Dynamic data like NASA’s Astronomy Picture of the Day or exoplanet news is fetched through live APIs.

Benefits

  • Educational Resource: Helps students, researchers, and space enthusiasts explore verified scientific data about exoplanets.
  • User-Friendly Experience: Simplifies complex astronomical data into an interactive format.
  • Real-Time Updates: Fetches the latest exoplanet discoveries and NASA news.
  • Scalable Design: Can easily be expanded with more APIs or databases for advanced scientific analysis.

Intended Impact

The project aims to:

  • Increase public awareness and curiosity about exoplanetary science.
  • Provide an interactive tool for astronomy education.
  • Encourage young learners to explore data-driven space research.

projectDetails.name: (ARES)ACCESSIBLE RECONFIGURABLE SPACE DESIGNER
projectDetails.summary:
We developed the ARES Designer, an intuitive, data-driven prototype tool built on Streamlit, to solve the complexity and time constraints of early-stage space habitat layout design.
Our solution addresses the core challenge of ensuring the well-being of astronauts on long-duration missions by using NASA's Bottom-Up Methodology to enforce real-world constraints. Users define crew size and habitat type, then place modules (like Sleep, Exercise, and Galley) from a palette.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem

Current habitat design is slow, requires expert software, and lacks real-time validation against human-centric safety standards.

Solution Features (Streamlit Prototype)

  • Constraint Engine (The Core Innovation):
    • Validation: Provides instant RED, YELLOW, or GREEN feedback on habitat layout compliance.
    • NASA Standards: Enforces the fundamental Minimum NHV floor of ≈29 m3 per crew for long-duration missions.
    • Metrics: Calculates Required NHV, Total Occupied Volume, and Utilization % in real-time.
    • Inputs: Users define the Crew Size and Cylinder Radius.
    • Module Palette: Quickly add functional modules (Sleep, Galley, Exercise) with pre-calibrated volumes (e.g., Sleep Quarters ≈14 m3).
    • Conceptual 3D: Uses Plotly to show an interactive, conceptual 3D view of module placement and the habitat boundary.
    • Platform: Built on Streamlit (Python) for rapid prototyping and maximum accessibility as a web dashboard.

Intended Impact

  • Mitigates Risk: Ensures critical volumes (Medical, Sleep) are correctly sized, supporting astronaut safety and psychological health.
  • Accelerates Design: Converts weeks of CAD work into minutes of design validation, allowing designers to quickly iterate on functional concepts.

Code Generation (AI-Assisted)

projectDetails.name: Project Flux
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, Meteor Madness, is an interactive web-based platform designed to make the complex science of asteroid threats accessible and actionable.  
The primary challenge we address is that raw data on potential asteroid impacts from sources like NASA is often too complex and technical for non-experts to understand. Our platform solves this by transforming overwhelming datasets into an intuitive, visual experience. Users can animate asteroid trajectories in real-time, modify variables like size and velocity, and instantly calculate the potential impact energy. The platform also allows for the simulation of mitigation strategies, such as using a kinetic impactor to deflect a threat.  
This project is important because it empowers a diverse audience—from students and the public to researchers and policymakers—to engage with planetary defense. By combining scientific rigor with user-friendly features like gamified missions, Meteor Madness fosters scientific literacy and provides a clear decision-support tool, helping to create a safer and more prepared future.
projectDetails.details:
How It Works

Meteor Madness is an interactive, web-based platform designed to visualize and mitigate asteroid threats. It works by transforming complex raw data from sources like NASA's NEO API and USGS into an intuitive and interactive experience. The platform operates on three core capabilities:

Dynamic Visualization: Users can animate asteroid trajectories in real-time to watch their movement relative to Earth with "cinematic clarity".

Real-Time Calculations: As a user adjusts variables like an asteroid's size and velocity using sliders, a physics engine instantly calculates the potential impact energy in megatons and its Richter magnitude equivalent.

User-Controlled Scenarios: The platform allows users to test mitigation strategies, such as deploying kinetic impactors to deflect trajectories, and to map potential consequences like tsunamis or atmospheric effects.

Benefits and Impact

The project's main benefit is making complex astrophysics accessible and actionable for a broad audience, including researchers, educators, and policymakers.

The intended impact is to empower these diverse groups in planetary defense preparedness.

For the Public and Students: It aims to foster scientific literacy and inspire the next generation through hands-on, gamified challenges.

For Researchers: It provides a flexible platform for modeling impact scenarios and testing deflection strategies, with the ability to export data for further analysis.

For Policymakers: It offers clear decision-support tools to assess global risks and visualize the consequences and costs of mitigation, helping to inform funding and preparedness strategies.

Ultimately, the project seeks to enable strategic interventions that can turn a potential catastrophe into a success story, like the "Impactor-2025" scenario where a threat is neutralized and results in a safe flyby.

Development and Creativity

While the specific coding languages and software are not detailed in the provided documents, the project was developed as a web-based platform that utilizes data from NASA's NEO API and the USGS. It also incorporates machine learning models that predict deflection outcomes based on historical data and physics simulations.

The project's creativity lies in its approach to bridging the gap between rigorous science and user-friendly design. It creatively engages users through:

Gamified Missions: Challenging users to "Save the Earth" by optimizing deflection parameters under time pressure, complete with badges and unlockable scenarios.

Simple Explanations: Using interactive tooltips and animated infographics to explain complex concepts like orbital mechanics accurately and simply.

Factors Considered

The Flux team considered several key factors in the project's design:

The Problem of Complexity: The team recognized that raw data on asteroid threats is often locked behind technical jargon, making it inaccessible.

projectDetails.name: Will It Rain?
projectDetails.summary:
The project "Will It Rain" is an immersive web application designed to make long-range weather planning accessible to everyone. We developed a tool that transforms over 15 years of complex historical climate data from NASA's POWER Project into a simple, intuitive, and actionable forecast. Users can select any location and date to receive a clear percentage probability for weather conditions like rain, snow, or wind. This isn't just a number; the app creates a full sensory experience with dynamic, animated backgrounds and procedurally generated ambient sounds that let you see and hear the historical weather.

This project directly addresses the challenge of the "planning gap." Standard weather forecasts are only reliable for a few days, leaving long-term event planning to guesswork. Our solution bridges this gap by leveraging NASA's vast climatology database, making it useful for the general public. Instead of needing to interpret complex scientific charts, a user gets an immediate, understandable answer.

The importance of this tool lies in its real-world application. It empowers event organizers, farmers, travelers, and construction managers to make smarter, data-driven decisions months or years in advance. By democratizing access to NASA's invaluable public data, our app reduces uncertainty, mitigates weather-related risks, and demonstrates how space-based observation can directly benefit everyday planning on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

The project "Will It Rain" is an immersive web application that answers the question: "What was the weather historically like on this specific date and time?"

A user enters a location and date. The app then connects to the NASA POWER API and fetches 15 years of hourly satellite data for that exact moment. It analyzes this data to calculate a statistical probability of precipitation and determines the likely weather conditions (e.g., sunny, rainy, snowy, windy). To complete the experience, the app presents this data not just as a number, but as a full sensory experience with dynamic background animations and procedurally generated soundscapes that match the predicted weather. It also fetches live weather from the Open-Meteo API for a real-time comparison.

Benefits & Intended Impact

The primary benefit of our project is that it closes the "planning gap." Standard weather forecasts are only reliable for the next 7-10 days, leaving long-term planning to guesswork. Our app provides a data-driven tool for making informed decisions months or even years in advance.

The intended impact is to democratize access to NASA's valuable climate data. We want to empower everyone—from event organizers and farmers to travelers and construction managers—to mitigate weather-related risks. By turning complex scientific information into an intuitive and engaging tool, we hope to increase public appreciation for NASA's Earth observation missions and their direct benefit to our daily lives.

Technology & Tools

The entire project is built as a self-contained static web application, prioritizing accessibility and ease of deployment.

Coding Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript.

Styling: Tailwind CSS was used for its utility-first approach to create a clean, modern, and responsive user interface.

Data APIs:

NASA POWER: The core source for 15+ years of global historical hourly data.

Open-Meteo: Provides the live "Current Conditions" data.

OpenStreetMap (Nominatim): Used for all geocoding (text search and map selection).

Libraries:

Leaflet.js: Powers the free, interactive 2D map for location selection.

Flatpickr: Creates the stylish and user-friendly calendar and time picker.

Tone.js: A powerful audio framework used to procedurally generate all the ambient weather sounds in the browser without needing any audio files.

Creativity & Team Considerations

Our project's creativity lies in its immersive and multi-sensory approach to data visualization. Instead of just displaying a percentage, we translate the historical probability into a living environment. A high chance of rain doesn't just show a number; it fills the screen with animated rain and the sound of a downpour. This makes complex data instantly understandable and emotionally resonant. The choice to procedurally generate all sounds using Tone.js was a creative technical decision to keep the app lightweight and self-contained.

Throughout development, our team prioritized several key factors:

User Experience: Our primary goal was to create a tool that was not only powerful but also simple and delightful to use.

Data Credibility: We chose NASA's API as our foundation to ensure the predictions are based on trusted, scientific data.

Accessibility: A crucial consideration was to build the entire application using free, open-source, and publicly available tools and APIs, ensuring that it remains accessible to everyone without requiring paid subscriptions or API keys.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

In the development of the project "Will It Rain", our team, Ghost Ops, utilized Google's Gemini, a large language model, as a primary tool to accelerate development, enhance creativity, and rapidly prototype complex features. The AI's role was that of a collaborative coding and content-generation partner, guided at every step by the intent and direction of our team.

Below is a detailed breakdown of where and how AI was utilized:

Code and Data

Foundation & Scaffolding: The initial HTML, CSS, and JavaScript structure of the entire single-page application was generated by the AI based on our initial project concept.

Feature Development & Integration: The AI was instrumental in writing the code for key features, including:

Implementing API calls to fetch and process data from the NASA POWER, Open-Meteo, and OpenStreetMap (Nominatim) APIs.

Developing the complex, sequential data-fetching logic to ensure reliability when querying 15 years of historical data from NASA.

Integrating and configuring third-party libraries such as Leaflet.js for the interactive map and Flatpickr for the calendar UI.

Debugging & Refinement: The AI assisted in identifying and fixing numerous bugs throughout the development process, including API connection errors, UI layout issues, and audio glitches.

Human Oversight: The Ghost Ops team directed the entire development process, providing the core logic, feature requirements, and iterative feedback to guide the AI. The team was responsible for testing, debugging, and refining all AI-generated code to create the final, stable product.

Images and Visuals

The project does not contain any AI-generated static images or videos.

All dynamic background effects (rain, snow, sun, clouds, lightning, wind) are CSS animations. The code for these animations was generated with the assistance of the AI. The SVG icon for the lightning bolt was also generated as code by the AI.

Audio

The project does not use pre-generated audio files.

All ambient soundscapes are procedurally generated in real-time within the user's browser using the Tone.js library. The AI was used to write the code for this sound generation, including creating the synthesis parameters and logic to produce the sounds for rain, wind, thunder, snow, and sunny weather.

By leveraging AI as a powerful development tool, Ghost Ops was able to focus on the overall vision, user experience, and creative direction of the project, allowing us to build a feature-rich and immersive application within the timeframe of the challenge.

projectDetails.name: LumiSense : AI Co-Pilot for the Visually Impaired
projectDetails.summary:
LumiSense: AI Co-Pilot for the Visually Impaired

Project LumiSense is an affordable, smartphone-centric AI platform designed to enhance the safety and independence of visually impaired people in India. It addresses the high cost and lack of proactive features in current assistive technologies.

Our system uses a low-cost wearable camera that streams video to a Flutter app on the user's smartphone. We employ a hybrid-AI architecture:

    On-Device AI: TensorFlow Lite and YOLO models run directly on the phone for instant, offline tasks like text reading (OCR) and object recognition.

    Cloud AI: A serverless backend handles complex scene analysis.

Feedback is delivered via a multimodal interface of audio cues and directional haptic feedback.

A key innovation is the integration of NASA Earth observation data (from GPM and Aura satellites) to provide proactive environmental alerts, warning users of rain, poor air quality, or high UV levels.

Our goal is to validate a software-first model for assistive tech, delivering powerful capabilities by leveraging the hardware users already own.
projectDetails.details:
LumiSense - A Proactive AI Co-Pilot for the Visually Impaired

1. Project Overview & Vision

LumiSense is our proactive AI co-pilot for the visually impaired, conceived as a software-first, smartphone-centric platform. Our vision is to radically lower the economic and social barriers to high-quality assistive technology.

The system operates using a simple, low-cost wearable camera that streams a live video feed to our custom Flutter application on the user's smartphone. Information and alerts are then delivered to the user through intuitive, multimodal feedback, combining clear audio cues with directional haptic (vibrational) feedback.

2. Core Architecture: A Hybrid-AI Approach

To balance real-time performance with powerful analytical capabilities, we have designed LumiSense with a hybrid-AI architecture:

  • On-Device AI: For critical, time-sensitive tasks such as reading text or detecting immediate obstacles, the application utilizes TensorFlow Lite. This allows us to run lightweight, optimized models directly on the user's phone for instantaneous, offline processing.
  • Cloud AI: For more complex, non-urgent tasks like detailed scene descriptions or environmental analysis, the app securely connects to powerful AI models hosted on a serverless cloud backend. This gives us the flexibility to perform computationally intensive analysis without draining the user's device resources.

3. Key Benefits & Advantages

Our approach offers several key benefits over existing solutions in the market:

  • Radically Affordable: By leveraging the user's existing smartphone as the primary computing device, we have reduced the required hardware cost to a minimal ₹4,000 for the wearable component. This stands in stark contrast to commercial alternatives, which can cost upwards of ₹2 Lakh+, directly addressing the economic barrier to assistive technology.
  • Proactive Assistance: We are moving beyond the purely reactive nature of current devices. By designing the platform to integrate with personal data services and external data feeds (like weather and transit), LumiSense anticipates user needs and provides proactive guidance.
  • Scalable & Future-Proof: As a software-first platform, its capabilities can be continuously and seamlessly upgraded through simple app updates. This eliminates the need for users to purchase new, expensive hardware to access the latest features.
  • Reduces Social Stigma: Based on key findings in recent accessibility research, we prioritized a discreet, non-obtrusive wearable design. This helps to minimize the "disability label" and unwanted attention associated with traditional canes or bulky hardware.

4. Intended Impact

Our project aims to deliver a multi-faceted impact:

  • For the User: To significantly enhance the safety, independence, and overall quality of life for visually impaired individuals by providing a tool that is powerful, affordable, and easy to use.
  • For the Community: To create a platform that is deeply integrated into the Indian digital ecosystem, with a clear roadmap for supporting essential local services like UPI, public transit schedules, and ride-sharing apps.
  • For the Field of Engineering: To validate a new, more accessible model for assistive technology that prioritizes intelligent software over expensive proprietary hardware, demonstrating a sustainable and scalable path forward for the industry.

5. Technology Stack

To bring this project to life, we have selected a modern, robust, and scalable technology stack:

  • Hardware & Firmware: The prototype wearable is built using an ESP32-CAM microcontroller, with its firmware written in C++ within the PlatformIO IDE.
  • Mobile Application (Frontend): The cross-platform mobile application is developed using the Flutter framework and the Dart programming language.
  • On-Device AI: We are implementing and deploying on-device models using TensorFlow Lite.
  • Cloud Backend: Our backend infrastructure is built on the Google Cloud Platform (GCP), utilizing serverless Cloud Functions written in Python.
  • Database: We employ Google Firestore for our cloud database needs and Hive for efficient on-device storage.

6. Our Creative Approach

The core creativity of LumiSense lies in its philosophical and architectural shift, rather than just its technical features:

  • Shift from Product to Platform: We are moving away from the concept of a single, expensive hardware "product" and towards a scalable, software-based "platform" that can grow and evolve with the user's needs.
  • Proactive vs. Reactive Intelligence: Our integration with personal and environmental data to anticipate needs is a creative leap beyond the on-demand, purely reactive nature of current assistive tools.
  • Hybrid AI for Accessibility: The unique hybrid AI architecture is our creative solution to the persistent trade-off between performance and cost. It offers the best of both worlds—on-device speed and cloud power—within an affordable and accessible package.

7. Design Philosophy & Key Considerations

Our team's development process was guided by four primary factors:

  1. Cost & Accessibility: This was our foremost consideration, driving the foundational decision to adopt a smartphone-centric architecture.
  2. User Experience (UX) & Social Stigma: We prioritized a discreet, comfortable, and intuitive design to maximize user acceptance and daily use.
  3. Technical Feasibility: We chose a technology stack that is modern, well-supported, and proven to be effective for real-time AI and IoT applications.
  4. Scalability & Future-Proofing: The entire architecture was designed to be modular, allowing for the easy addition of new features and third-party integrations through future software updates.

projectDetails.name: Project BloomWatch
projectDetails.summary:
Summary — BloomWatch

BloomWatch is a live global flower-bloom monitoring platform that uses NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellite data to visualize blooming patterns around the world. Our project analyzes vegetation indices such as NDVI to detect seasonal and regional changes in plant growth, helping reveal the impacts of climate change on ecosystems and agriculture.

By transforming decades of NASA Earth observation data into an interactive global map, BloomWatch allows friendly user experience to explore how temperature, rainfall, and solar radiation influence blooming cycles. The project directly addresses the NASA Space Apps challenge by converting satellite data into meaningful environmental intelligence that supports sustainability and public awareness.

BloomWatch incorporates tools that helps agriculturilists and cultivatiors calculate the most efficient times to sow, nurtue and harvest flowers and plants to acquire the highest possible yield of crops, public health experts anticipate allergy trends, and conservationists monitor biodiversity and invasive species. It demonstrates how open satellite data can be creatively applied to protect ecosystems and support climate resilience worldwide.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — BloomWatch

BloomWatch is an interactive global platform that visualizes real-time flower-bloom patterns using NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellite data. By analyzing decades of phenological observations and vegetation indices such as NDVI, it identifies shifts in blooming cycles across ecosystems—from tropical rainforests to arid deserts. This analysis reveals how climate change influences biodiversity, agricultural productivity, and ecosystem balance.

The platform was developed as a web-based application using Leaflet.js, Chart.js, and Tailwind CSS, integrated with NASA’s GIBS, LAADS DAAC, and POWER APIs. It processes vegetation and climate data to generate an interactive global map that allows users to visualize bloom dynamics, temperature trends, and solar irradiance correlations over time.

BloomWatch benefits a wide range of users: farmers gain insights for crop planning and pollination timing, public health experts can forecast allergy outbreaks, and conservationists can monitor invasive species and ecosystem changes.

Our team focused on creativity, scientific accuracy, and accessibility. By transforming complex satellite data into an engaging visual experience, BloomWatch turns space-based observations into actionable environmental intelligence, inspiring awareness and informed action toward a more climate-resilient future.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
"Human potential and analytical intelligence boosted at astronomical rate by Artificial Intelligence can be the stepping stone for a blooming and colourful future." While this project does not directly implement machine learning or deep learning models, it utilizes data science principles and algorithms that are fundamental to the field of AI. Our approach focuses on algorithmic analysis of NASA's NDVI data to identify blooming events.

ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) – AI Tool for Debugging and Code Assistance

The core logic in our 'data_processor.py' script uses statistical methods with libraries like Pandas and GDAL to process the time-series satellite imagery. It identifies peaks in the vegetation index, which correspond to maximum greenness and likely blooming periods. This is a deterministic approach based on predefined thresholds and patterns rather than a predictive AI model.

Future Scope for AI Integration: BloomWatch is designed to be a foundational platform upon which advanced AI capabilities can be built. Future versions could incorporate:

Predictive Modeling: Using machine learning models (e.g., LSTMs, ARIMA) to forecast future blooming periods based on historical climate and NDVI data.

Image Classification: Applying computer vision models to higher-resolution satellite imagery to classify different plant species and map their distribution.

Anomaly Detection: Training AI models to detect unusual or unexpected changes in blooming patterns that could signal significant environmental stress or climate events.

projectDetails.summary:
BloomWatch is an innovative project developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge aimed at monitoring global flowering patterns using Earth observation data and artificial intelligence. The project focuses on flowering phenology — the study of when and where flowers bloom — which is a crucial indicator of ecological health and climate change effects.
Objective
To build an application that detects and analyzes global flowering events by integrating satellite imagery, AI-based image recognition, and ground-truth data from citizen science initiatives.
Key Components
Data Sources:
Utilizes a combination of satellite imagery (Sentinel-2, Landsat), UAV/drone images, phenocams, and citizen-reported data.
Tools & Techniques:
Employs vegetation indices (e.g., NDVI), machine learning algorithms (CNNs, YOLO), and cloud platforms for large-scale data processing.
Detection Process:
Identify floral spectral signatures and color features
Analyze time-series vegetation indices
Use AI models to detect flowering zones and generate phenology timelines
System Overview
BloomWatch collects and processes Earth observation data, runs AI detection models, and visualizes flowering activity on interactive maps. These insights can be exported for scientific, agricultural, and environmental applications.
Applications & Benefits
Track climate change impacts on ecosystems
Support agriculture and pollination management
Enable early environmental change detection
projectDetails.details:
What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

BloomWatch is an Earth observation platform designed to detect, analyze, and visualize global flowering patterns using satellite data and artificial intelligence.
It works by integrating multiple data sources — including satellite imagery (Sentinel-2, Landsat), drone and ground-based camera feeds (phenocams), and citizen science inputs — to identify when and where flowers bloom.

Using machine learning models (such as CNNs and YOLO) and vegetation indices like NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index), the system detects floral signatures and tracks temporal changes in vegetation. BloomWatch then compiles these insights into interactive maps and phenology timelines, allowing users to visualize bloom cycles across different regions and ecosystems.

Benefits of the Project

Climate Monitoring: Detects shifts in flowering times caused by climate change, providing early indicators of ecosystem stress.

Agricultural Support: Helps farmers and pollination managers plan planting and harvesting based on real-time flowering data.

Biodiversity & Conservation: Supports the monitoring of pollinator activity and plant health, aiding biodiversity conservation efforts.

Scientific Insight: Provides open-access data for researchers studying climate, vegetation, and ecological trends.

Scalable & Automated: Uses cloud-based automation to analyze large datasets, enabling global-scale monitoring.

Intended Impact

BloomWatch aims to:

Enhance understanding of global flowering phenology and its links to environmental change.

Empower scientists, policymakers, and farmers with data-driven insights to adapt to shifting climate patterns.

Foster citizen engagement by involving the public in data collection and validation, encouraging environmental awareness and stewardship.


Ultimately, BloomWatch bridges the gap between Earth observation data and practical ecological action, contributing to a more resilient and informed planet.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

Data Sources:

NASA Earth Observation datasets (e.g., MODIS, Landsat)

ESA Sentinel-2 imagery

Ground-based phenocams & drone data

Citizen science platforms (e.g., iNaturalist, GLOBE Observer)

Tools & Platforms:

Google Earth Engine – for large-scale satellite image analysis

QGIS – for geospatial visualization

TensorFlow / PyTorch – for AI model development

YOLOv5 / CNN models – for flower detection in imagery

Python, JavaScript, and Cloud APIs – for backend and frontend integration

Streamlit / Flask – for interactive web app prototyping


Hardware:

Drones/UAVs with RGB and multispectral sensors

Standard computing systems or cloud servers for data processing

Creativity and Innovation

BloomWatch stands out by combining:

Remote sensing + AI-based image detection + crowdsourced citizen data — a fusion rarely applied to flowering phenology.

Use of spectral and temporal analysis to differentiate flowering from general greenness.

A visual and interactive interface for real-time global flower monitoring.

Focus on cross-disciplinary collaboration between AI engineers, environmental scientists, and citizen scientists.


This creative integration transforms complex satellite data into accessible ecological intelligence.

Team Considerations

In developing BloomWatch, the team considered:

Data accuracy – calibrating between different sensors and validating results with field data.

Cloud accessibility – ensuring scalability and real-time data availability.

Environmental ethics – promoting open data use and citizen inclusion.

User experience – designing an interface that is intuitive for both scientists and the general public.

Sustainability – aiming for long-term monitoring rather than one-time analysis.

projectDetails.name: Smart Crop Suitability
projectDetails.summary: The Smart Crop Suitability Dashboard is a full-stack application developed to address agricultural risks from climate variability. The project features a React frontend with an interactive map and a Python Flask backend that simulates fetching one year of local weather data (temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind) for a user-selected location. By comparing this environmental data against the requirements for various crops (Rice, Wheat, Corn, Tomato, Potato), the system calculates a suitability percentage and provides an immediate recommendation. This tool is important because it empowers farmers to make data-driven decisions, avoiding crops that are prone to failure and optimizing planting choices to increase yields, thereby enhancing agricultural resilience and food security. The dashboard also details specific risk factors (e.g., "Temperature too high") to further guide planning.
projectDetails.details:
Functionality: How it Works

The dashboard functions as a decision support system for agriculture. The user interacts with a React frontend, first selecting a location by clicking on a map, which retrieves the latitude and longitude. Next, the user selects a crop from a dropdown menu (e.g., Rice, Tomato, Corn).

The Python Flask backend then takes the location and crop name and performs the core logic:

  1. Weather Data Simulation: It simulates fetching a year's worth of local weather data (temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind) for the selected coordinates.
  2. Suitability Calculation: This weather data is compared against the specific environmental requirements (min/max/optimal ranges) stored in a crop database.
  3. Scoring and Risk Analysis: A composite suitability score (0-100%) is calculated by weighting the performance in each environmental category. The system also identifies specific risk factors (e.g., "Temperature too high," "Low humidity").
  4. Result Display: The final score, recommendation (Suitable/Not Suitable), growth period, and detailed weather summary are sent back to the frontend's results page.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The primary benefit is risk mitigation and resource optimization in farming. By knowing which crops are most likely to thrive, farmers can:

  • Increase Yield: Select crops best suited to local climatic conditions.
  • Reduce Loss: Avoid planting crops susceptible to local environmental extremes (e.g., high winds, low rainfall).
  • Optimize Resources: Make smarter choices about water and fertilizer application based on the projected environmental conditions.

The intended impact is to enhance agricultural resilience and contribute to food security by making complex, climate-related information accessible and actionable for growers, particularly in areas facing erratic weather patterns.

Key factors considered by the team include:

projectDetails.name: Sun-Stuff Stories: A Child's Guide to Space Weather
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, “Sun-Stuff Stories,” is a digital children's story that makes space weather easy to understand.

We tell the story from the viewpoint of “Corrie,” a friendly Coronal Mass Ejection (CME). Corrie is a giant bubble of energy that breaks away from the Sun’s outer crown and begins an adventure to Earth. Our story meets the challenge by showing how this 'Sun-stuff' affects astronauts, pilots, and technology on the ground. Corrie's journey ends by creating the beautiful and harmless northern lights (aurora).

This project is important because it turns a complex scientific topic into a fun story. It encourages kids to be curious about space and shows how the Sun connects to our world in amazing ways.
projectDetails.details:
The primary benefit of "Sun-Stuff Stories" is its ability to make a complex scientific topic accessible and exciting for a young audience, fostering a love for science from an early age.

  • For Children: It provides a fun, non-intimidating introduction to heliophysics, replacing fear of "solar storms" with wonder and curiosity

challengeDetails.title: Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings
challengeDetails.excerpt: Although the Sun is 93 million miles away from our planet, solar activity can significantly impact our daily lives. “Space weather”—the variations that occur in the space environment between the Sun and Earth—can impact technologies in space and on Earth. Your challenge is to write and illustrate a digital children’s story that explains what space weather is and the varying impacts it has on different people such as farmers, pilots, astronauts, power grid operators, and the general public. You can tell the story from the perspective of a person impacted by space weather or from the point of view of a solar flare or coronal mass ejection (CME) as it approaches Earth. (Heliophysics Division)

projectDetails.name: The Light Within
projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary
We developed an integrated educational resource consisting of a technical Web Application and an accompanying children's book, "Flare the Explorer: A Space Weather Adventure".

What We Developed:
The web application serves as a scientific foundation, detailing the Three Pillars of Space Weather (Plasma, Solar Wind, CMEs/Flares) and their technical impacts, such as Geomagnetically Induced Currents (GICs) and satellite drag. It also features a conceptual Live Data Monitoring Console that tracks critical upstream metrics like IMF BZ.

How It Addresses the Challenge:
The project uses the "Flare the Explorer" storybook as the "Stellar Story" component. The narrative personifies a Solar Flare to explain the science to children. It translates complex concepts into relatable human experiences, such as the protective role of Earth's Magnetosphere and the negative effects of solar bursts on pilots (radio crackle) and farmers (GPS disruption).

Why It Is Important:
This work embodies the R2O2R (Research-to-Operations-to-Research) initiative by making high-stakes NASA and NOAA data accessible. By connecting the technical deep dive (Bz fields, CMEs) to a human narrative (The Pilot, The Farmer, The Photographer), the project creates a compelling, accurate, and deeply human way to understand the invisible forces emanating from the sun.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

The project, The Light Within, serves as a comprehensive educational and outreach platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge "Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings." It consists of a technical web application and an accompanying children's book, "Flare the Explorer: A Space Weather Adventure."

What It Does & How It Works

The project employs a two-tiered learning system designed to appeal to both scientific and general audiences:

  1. Technical Deep Dive (Web App):
    • Scientific Foundation: It clearly defines the Three Pillars of Space Weather: Solar Plasma, Solar Wind, and Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs).
    • Impact Mapping: It connects these phenomena to tangible threats on Earth, such as Geomagnetically Induced Currents (GICs) on power grids, Ionospheric Scintillation disrupting GPS, and increased atmospheric drag on Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites.
    • Data Visualization: A conceptual Data Monitoring Console simulates critical upstream warning metrics observed at the L1 Lagrange point, specifically Solar Wind Velocity and the key geo-effectiveness indicator, IMF BZ. This simulation shows how a strongly negative BZ value represents the inciting incident for a major geomagnetic storm.
  2. Stellar Story (Children's Book):
    • The book, "Flare the Explorer", acts as the "Stellar Story" component. It utilizes anthropomorphism by personifying a Solar Flare named Flare, turning a complex phenomenon into a relatable character.
    • The narrative translates the physics into human experiences, explaining the Sun as a super-hot home, the Earth's Magnetosphere as a protective shield, and the different consequences of a solar event on an airline pilot’s radio or a farmer’s GPS system.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Scientific Literacy: The project promotes the democratization of science by translating NASA's highly technical Heliophysics research and data concepts (like flux ropes and BZ fields) into clear, accessible language for the public.
  • Societal Preparedness: It connects abstract solar physics directly to modern infrastructure vulnerabilities, helping to inform the public and decision-makers about the real-world risks of space weather on power grids, communication, and navigation systems.
  • Educational Outreach: By coupling the technical web resource with a fun, narrative-driven children's book, the project provides a crucial, age-appropriate entry point into STEM for the next generation. It effectively fulfills the Research-to-Operations-to-Research (R2O2R) initiative by creating an educational product based on operational forecasting principles

Tools, Languages, and Creativity

Tools and Languages: The web application was developed using HTML5, CSS3 (specifically the Tailwind CSS framework for utility styling), and native JavaScript to create the dynamic elements like the data simulation and scroll-reveal effects. The storybook was created using digital illustration and layout software. And we used Heyzine flipbooks for creating the storybook.

Creativity: The core creativity lies in the integrated approach. Instead of merely summarizing the science, the project built two interconnected components: one that establishes the technical rulebook of space weather (the Web App) and one that uses those rules to tell a human story (the Children's Book). The mock dashboard’s ability to generate a dynamically severe alert provides the dramatic tension needed to drive the narrative, effectively closing the loop between scientific data and the human experience.

Factors Considered by the Team:

  1. Scientific Accuracy: All metrics and phenomena (GICs, Ionospheric Scintillation, R2O2R) were cross-referenced with official NASA and NOAA documentation.
  2. Narrative Compulsion: The story needed to be engaging while remaining scientifically faithful, ensuring the science was the driver of the plot, not just background.
  3. Accessibility: The site uses a responsive design and an easy-to-read dark mode to ensure the information is accessible on all devices.

projectDetails.details:
OrbiGenesis is an interactive web platform that serves as a space bioscience knowledge engine, built to help researchers, scientists, and students explore, analyze, and interpret NASA’s bioscience datasets and research publications.

The platform automatically aggregates NASA’s space bioscience papers, summarizes key insights, and presents them through a dynamic, AI-enhanced dashboard. Users can search for studies, track reading progress, star important papers, and visualize exploration trends — all through an elegant, glass-inspired UI themed after NASA’s space missions.

It is designed as a two-part system:

Frontend (React + TailwindCSS): Provides an immersive, responsive interface with a dashboard view, search, and topic exploration.

Backend (Python Flask + SQLite): Manages data storage, search endpoints, analytics, and API access to the knowledge engine.

Intended Impact

Space bioscience research plays a critical role in advancing long-duration spaceflight and understanding how life adapts beyond Earth. However, the vast number of scientific papers and datasets often makes it difficult to access and synthesize relevant findings.

OrbiGenesis aims to:

Simplify the exploration of NASA’s bioscience research.

Help scientists identify trends and gaps in current studies.

Provide students and mission planners with easy access to categorized data for further experimentation and simulation.

Act as a bridge between AI and space biology, inspiring future data-driven mission design.


By centralizing bioscience knowledge, OrbiGenesis empowers the next generation of researchers to innovate faster in life-support systems, crop cultivation, and biological sustainability for lunar and Martian habitats.

projectDetails.name: When the Sun Whispered to Earth
projectDetails.summary:
In this project, I developed a cinematic, digital children’s story titled “When the Sun Whispered to Earth” to explain space weather and its impacts on different communities. The story follows Solara, a solar flare, as she journeys from the Sun to Earth, showing both the awe-inspiring beauty of auroras and the practical effects of space weather on satellites, power grids, pilots, farmers, and astronauts. By combining accurate NASA science with a visually rich, cinematic style inspired by films like Interstellar and Gravity, the story makes complex concepts like solar flares, CMEs, and magnetic storms accessible to young audiences.

This project addresses the NASA Space Apps challenge by providing an educational, engaging, and shareable tool to increase public awareness of space weather. Understanding these phenomena is important because space weather can disrupt communication, navigation, power systems, and astronaut safety. By teaching children through storytelling and immersive visuals, the project inspires curiosity and highlights the significance of monitoring and preparing for solar activity.
projectDetails.details:
This project, “When the Sun Whispered to Earth”, is a cinematic digital children’s story designed to explain space weather and its impacts on Earth in an engaging, educational, and visually immersive way. The story follows Solara, a solar flare, as she travels from the Sun to Earth, showcasing both the awe-inspiring beauty of auroras and the practical effects of space weather on different communities. Through Solara’s journey, the story illustrates how solar flares and coronal mass ejections interact with Earth’s magnetic field, affecting satellites, communication systems, navigation devices, power grids, pilots, farmers, and astronauts.

The project works by combining factual NASA data with cinematic storytelling techniques. Each scene is carefully designed to represent real phenomena, while using dramatic visual elements inspired by space films like Interstellar and Gravity. The story balances scientific accuracy with child-friendly explanations, making complex concepts like solar storms and space weather accessible and memorable.

The benefits and intended impact include educating young audiences and the general public about space weather, highlighting its relevance to daily life, and fostering curiosity in STEM and space sciences. By presenting science through a narrative lens, the project helps people understand both the risks and the wonders of solar activity.

Tools and resources used include: NASA public domain images, Canva for creating and designing the storybook, images sourced from Google and Gemini, and AI-assisted illustrations from Chat GPT.

This project is creative because it blends real scientific data with cinematic storytelling, combining text, visuals, and carefully chosen colour palettes to produce a story that is both scientifically accurate and emotionally engaging. Key considerations included accessibility, age-appropriate explanations, visual aesthetics, factual accuracy, and the ability to inspire curiosity and wonder about space and science.
projectDetails.aiReferences: AI, specifically Chat GPT, was used to draft the narrative, structure the story and helping balance scientific accuracy with cinematic storytelling. AI also assisted in brainstorming visual ideas and layout suggestions, which were implemented in Canva alongside images sourced from NASA’s public library, Gemini, and Google.

projectDetails.name: Project IEDC VISAT
projectDetails.summary: A web-first, interactive Habitat Design Explorer (HDE) that lets engineers, architects, mission planners, and students define a space-habitat’s geometry (cylindrical, torus, inflatable shell, modular box, or freeform), set constraints (mass, pressurized volume, access hatches), and automatically generate and iterate layout proposals for crew functions (life support, stowage, sleep, galley, exercise, medical, EVA airlock, thermal/avionics). The tool blends parametric 3D modeling, spatial partitioning/layout heuristics, occupancy and systems rules, and real-time simulation overlays (mass, power, thermal risk, circulation) so users can evaluate tradeoffs visually and export CAD/BIM or simulation-ready models.
projectDetails.details: 🛰️ Project Title Habitat Design Explorer (HDE): A Visual Tool for Designing and Exploring Space Habitats --- 💡 What Does It Do / How It Works The Habitat Design Explorer is an interactive visual platform that allows users to design, visualize, and optimize space habitats — the “homes in space” that support astronauts’ daily life and mission activities. Users can: 1. Define Habitat Shape and Size – Choose or draw habitat geometries such as cylinders, domes, torus rings, or modular sections. 2. Add Functional Areas – Select from a library of essential zones (sleeping, galley, waste, life support, exercise, medical, stowage, etc.). 3. Generate Layouts Automatically – The system uses smart algorithms and human-factor rules to auto-arrange modules efficiently while maintaining safety and comfort. 4. Visualize in 3D – Real-time 3D visualization lets users orbit, cut sections, and explore interior spaces. 5. Compare & Analyze – The tool calculates performance metrics like total usable volume, mass balance, power routing length, and circulation efficiency. 6. Export Designs – Users can export their final layout to CAD or 3D model formats for further engineering or simulation use. --- 🚀 Benefits Faster Design Cycles: Reduces time spent manually creating and iterating habitat layouts. Enhanced Visualization: Helps teams clearly understand spatial distribution and human usability. Human-Centric Approach: Incorporates ergonomic and safety constraints to improve crew comfort. Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration: Enables engineers, architects, and scientists to co-create habitat designs through a shared platform. Educational Value: Provides an interactive way for students to learn about space architecture and mission systems. --- 🌍 Intended Impact To revolutionize early-stage space habitat design by making it visual, data-driven, and collaborative. To support organizations like NASA, ISRO, and private space companies in conceptualizing modular habitats for the Moon, Mars, or orbital missions. To inspire future engineers and designers to innovate in sustainable, human-centered living environments beyond Earth. To bridge design and engineering, showing how structure, life-support, and human comfort work together in limited space. --- 🧠 Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used Category Tools / Languages Frontend Development React.js, Three.js (for 3D rendering), Tailwind CSS Backend Development Python (FastAPI) for layout generation and optimization Optimization Algorithms Space partitioning, adjacency rules, heuristic placement, simulated annealing Database PostgreSQL for user data and module libraries Design & Prototyping Figma for UI design, Blender for 3D model templates Export Formats glTF, JSON, CSV (for design data and metrics) No special hardware is required — the application runs on any standard computer with web access. --- 🎨 Creativity & Innovation Blends AI + Architecture: Uses rule-based algorithms to generate realistic and efficient layouts automatically. Interactive 3D Space Design: Users can freely explore, modify, and visualize their habitats in a fully interactive environment. Systems Awareness: Integrates engineering systems like power, life support, and thermal routing visually — not just structure. Human Factors First: Every design respects clearances, egress paths, and comfort parameters derived from real NASA/ESA data. Educational + Professional Utility: Can be used both as a mission-planning prototype and a teaching tool. --- ⚙️ Factors Considered by Our Team Safety: Egress paths, isolation zones, and proximity of critical systems. Human Ergonomics: Space per crew member, comfort during long missions, and accessibility. Resource Efficiency: Optimizing mass, volume, and routing length for cables, ducts, and systems. Modularity: Support for expandable and reconfigurable habitat concepts. Technical Feasibility: Ensuring that geometry and layout can be realistically manufactured and simulated. User Experience: Creating an intuitive, visual interface so that even non-engineers can design a habitat concept easily. --- 🌌 Summary The Habitat Design Explorer reimagines how we design life beyond Earth — combining engineering precision with creativity and human-centered thinking. It empowers users to design, visualize, and optimize entire living systems in space, ultimately contributing to safer, smarter, and more livable extraterrestrial habitats.
