projectDetails.name: Space Bio-AI Knowledge Engine
projectDetails.summary: This project develops an innovative AI-powered knowledge engine tailored for NASA's space biology research. It integrates advanced retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques with hybrid search capabilities to efficiently index and search vast datasets, including NASA's OSDR/GenElab documents. The engine leverages AI models like sentence-transformers for semantic search and employs neural summarization to deliver concise, meaningful insights. This system addresses the challenge of navigating large, complex scientific datasets, significantly reducing research time and enhancing knowledge discovery. By providing rapid, accurate access to critical space biology information, this tool advances scientific understanding and supports mission-critical research, making it invaluable for NASA’s future exploration initiatives.
projectDetails.details:
Project Title: Space Bio-AI Knowledge Engine

Comprehensive Project Details:

Our project presents an innovative, AI-powered knowledge engine designed specifically for NASA’s space biology research ecosystem. It addresses the critical challenge of efficiently accessing, searching, and summarizing vast and complex scientific datasets, such as those from NASA’s Office of Space Data & Research (OSDR) and GenElab databases. By leveraging state-of-the-art Artificial Intelligence technologies, we aim to drastically reduce the time and cognitive load associated with sifting through massive volumes of biological and genetic data related to spaceflight.

What it Does and How it Works

The system allows users to ingest large datasets, perform advanced hybrid searches combining symbolic keyword and semantic vector searches, and receive concise, AI-generated summaries of relevant scientific documents. Utilizing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), it blends classical search with neural embeddings generated by pre-trained transformer models to provide more accurate and comprehensive results than traditional keyword search alone.

The backend is built with Python and FastAPI, exposing RESTful API endpoints to ingest data, query the knowledge base, and retrieve summaries. Sentence-transformers models create semantic embeddings of documents, which are indexed and searched efficiently using FAISS, a high-performance similarity search library. Supplemental SQLite databases store raw metadata and document chunks, facilitating lightweight and fast retrieval.

Benefits and Intended Impact

This platform optimizes the research workflow by dramatically accelerating information discovery, allowing scientists to focus more on analysis and experimental design rather than manual document review. It enhances recall and precision in retrieving critical data by combining traditional and AI-powered search techniques. Immediate benefits include saving researchers hours or days in literature review, accelerating mission-critical biological insights, and democratizing access to complex space biology data.

The long-term impact is profound: by unlocking latent knowledge within massive space biology datasets, this engine supports the advancement of space health sciences, promotes cross-disciplinary discoveries, and accelerates human space exploration goals. Its modular and scalable architecture means it can be extended to other scientific domains or integrated with complementary AI services.

Technical Stack

Languages & Frameworks: Python as the primary language; FastAPI for building asynchronous, scalable APIs.

AI Models: SentenceTransformers for generating meaningful text embeddings; neural summarization models for concise content distillation.

Search Engine: FAISS for fast approximate nearest neighbor vector search.

Database: SQLite for metadata and document chunk management.

Hosting & Deployment: Uvicorn ASGI server deployed on Render cloud platform utilizing environment variables to manage configurations and optimize resource usage.

Innovations: Intelligent chunking of large documents, hybrid search strategies combining embedding and keyword methods, and resource-aware deployment on cloud free tiers.

Creativity and Team Considerations

Our project creatively fuses advanced AI techniques with efficient database indexing to solve a real-world, high-impact scientific challenge. We considered the constraints of free-tier cloud hosting services while maintaining model accuracy and responsiveness, striking a balance between resource consumption and user experience. The approach leverages open-source models, scalable indexing methods, and deployment best practices, embodying a practical yet innovative solution adaptable beyond space biology.

In summary, this project empowers NASA researchers with a next-generation knowledge engine that not only supports rapid data retrieval and intelligent summarization but also sets a precedent for AI-driven scientific discovery tools applicable across disciplines.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Our Space Bio-AI Knowledge Engine extensively integrates Artificial Intelligence tools to enhance the retrieval, understanding, and summarization of complex space biology datasets. Specifically:

We use pre-trained transformer models (sentence-transformers) to convert large volumes of scientific text into meaningful semantic embeddings, enabling advanced semantic search capabilities beyond simple keyword matching.

Our system employs retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods, combining symbolic methods with neural embeddings to improve the relevance and accuracy of search results, thus accelerating knowledge discovery.

For generating concise and meaningful text summaries from large documents or search results, we use neural summarization models, which distill complex information into user-friendly insights.

AI-powered natural language processing (NLP) underpins all core functions, including text chunking, search query processing, and dynamic summary generation.

Throughout the project, AI-generated code snippets, prompts, and configurations were used to accelerate development and ensure state-of-the-art methodologies.

All AI-generated code and models used in this project comply with the NASA Space Apps Challenge guidelines. No NASA branding or design elements are incorporated or modified in our AI-generated content. Our project documents clearly attribute AI usage and maintain transparency regarding its role in the innovation and execution of this solution.

projectDetails.name: ROBOTIC HOME NURSE (RHN)
projectDetails.summary:
The Robotic Home Nurse, developed by Tech Boyz, presents an innovative, reliable, and affordable solution to improve patient care using robotic technology. It is specially designed for elderly, disabled, or bedridden patients who require continuous support. This semi-automatic system helps reduce direct human contact while ensuring timely care, which is vital during pandemics and health crises where doctors, nurses, and caregivers face excessive workload and increased risks.

The robot works in dual operating modes: manual, where caregivers remotely guide and control it, and automatic, where it operates on its own. Its camera-based navigation system with Wi-Fi ensures real-time monitoring and guidance, while an intelligent robotic arm can safely deliver medicines, food, and other essentials directly to the patient’s bedside.

To keep costs low and ensure local accessibility, the body is built using plywood, PVC pipes, multiwood, and acrylic sheets, while toy tires, gear motors, magnets, and simple circuits enable mobility. The electronic system features a 12V 7AH rechargeable battery, Google Mini for AI voice commands, Wi-Fi camera, LDR and magnetic sensors, relay switches, and BC545 transistors.

By combining healthcare, engineering, and environmental responsibility, the Robotic Home Nurse supports the One Health framework, ensuring safe, timely, and sustainable patient assistance with reduced human intervention.
projectDetails.details:
The Robotic Home Nurse: Care at Your Fingertips

The Big Idea: Why We Built This

We created the Robotic Home Nurse to solve a critical problem: How do we give constant, quality care to our elderly or bedridden loved ones without always needing a person right there?

Our goal was simple: to design a semi-automatic, low-cost robot that provides compassionate, remote patient care. This is crucial for reducing physical contact—especially important during health crises or pandemics—while ensuring no one is left waiting for help.

Meet Your New Healthcare Assistant

This isn't a complex, million-dollar machine. It's a clever, accessible assistant built on some smart features:

Dual-Mode Operation: We give you the choice! It can be controlled manually for precision tasks or navigate automatically using its smart systems.

Eyes and Arms: It uses a built-in camera for clear navigation and includes a mechanical arm specifically for the precise, timely delivery of medicines and essential supplies.

Always Connected: Thanks to WiFi connectivity, you have real-time control and monitoring, whether you're in the next room or across the city.

Affordability First: We focused on a low-cost design, using readily available, local materials to make it easy to reproduce anywhere in the world.

The Magic Under the Hood

We sourced a blend of common and cutting-edge components to keep it functional and budget-friendly:

The Body: Sturdy and lightweight materials like plywood, PVC, and acrylic sheets.

The Movement: Driven by six gear motors and simple toy tires for easy movement, guided by various LDR, IR, and magnetic sensors.

The Brains: A WiFi camera and a Google Mini integrated for smart command, all powered by a durable 12V battery.

More Than Just a Robot

The impact of this project goes far beyond a single patient's room:

Safer Communities: It immediately reduces close human contact in crowded hospitals and homes, making healthcare systems more resilient during emergencies.

Reliable Care: It guarantees timely delivery of essential items—no more waiting for a nurse to be free.

A Sustainable Solution: This project supports the One Health Framework, merging Health and Technology with the Environment to create smart, reproducible, and affordable urban healthcare solutions for the future.

In Conclusion

The Robotic Home Nurse is an innovative, accessible, and intelligent step forward. It’s not about replacing human compassion; it’s about empowering it.

This is our step toward a safer, smarter, and more tech-driven future in patient care for everyone.

projectDetails.summary:
BloomWatch: A Visual NDVI Dashboard for Environmental Monitoring
BloomWatch is a lightweight, beginner-friendly tool developed to help farmers, scientists, and the public monitor vegetation health in Kerala using NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) imagery. Faced with login barriers and limited access to GeoTIFF formats, the project pivots to using downloadable PNG images from Copernicus EO Browser, making the workflow more accessible and reproducible.
The tool enables users to upload NDVI images across multiple dates, compare vegetation changes visually, annotate bloom hotspots, and interpret patterns using a custom NDVI color scale. Built entirely in Google Colab, BloomWatch requires no specialized software and includes clear documentation for non-experts.
By simplifying remote sensing analysis and removing technical barriers, BloomWatch empowers communities to track seasonal vegetation shifts, detect algal blooms, and make informed decisions in agriculture and ecology. It directly addresses the NASA Space Apps challenge by transforming satellite data into actionable, approachable insights.
projectDetails.details:
Project Title: BloomWatch — A Visual NDVI Dashboard for Kerala

What it does:

BloomWatch is a lightweight, beginner-friendly tool designed to help users monitor vegetation health and detect bloom events in Kerala using NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) imagery. It allows users to upload NDVI images from different dates, compare them visually, annotate bloom hotspots, and interpret vegetation patterns using a custom NDVI color scale.

How it works:

The tool is built entirely in Google Colab using Python. Users download NDVI PNG images from Copernicus EO Browser, upload them one at a time, and BloomWatch displays them side-by-side with annotations and color legends. The dashboard is generated using OpenCV and Matplotlib, making it accessible to non-experts without requiring GeoTIFFs or GIS software.

Benefits and impact:

BloomWatch lowers the barrier to entry for environmental monitoring by removing login and format restrictions. It empowers farmers, scientists, and the public to track seasonal vegetation changes, detect algal blooms, and make informed decisions in agriculture and ecology. The tool is reproducible, educational, and designed for real-world utility.

Tools and technologies used:

- Python (OpenCV, Matplotlib, NumPy)

- Google Colab

- Copernicus EO Browser (for NDVI imagery)

- PNG-based workflow (no GeoTIFF required)

Creativity and design choices:

The project creatively adapts to platform limitations by pivoting from GeoTIFFs to PNGs, ensuring accessibility. It emphasizes usability, visual clarity, and beginner-friendly documentation. The team prioritized reproducibility, transparency, and real-world relevance, making BloomWatch both technically sound and socially impactful.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
We used Microsoft Copilot (AI assistant) to accelerate development, documentation, and troubleshooting throughout the BloomWatch project. Specifically:

- Code Generation: Python scripts for image upload, NDVI visualization, side-by-side comparison, annotation, and dashboard layout were co-developed with Copilot. All AI-generated code is documented within the Colab notebook and annotated accordingly.

- Documentation Support: Copilot assisted in drafting beginner-friendly instructions, workflow summaries, and submission materials to ensure clarity and accessibility for non-experts.

- Image Interpretation: While no AI-generated images were used, Copilot helped interpret NDVI visuals and guide hotspot annotation logic. All visual content was sourced from Copernicus EO Browser and manually annotated.

- Creative Guidance: Copilot contributed to brainstorming alternative workflows when GeoTIFF access was restricted, helping pivot to PNG-based analysis and ensuring reproducibility.

No NASA branding, logos, or mission identifiers were used or modified. All AI-assisted content is original and clearly marked in the project files.

projectDetails.name: Project Terra_Spark
projectDetails.summary:
For NASA’s Terra Animation Challenge, I developed a short animated story using PictoBlox to introduce the Terra satellite as a friendly character. The animation explains Terra’s mission of observing Earth from space and highlights its five key scientific instruments: MODIS, CERES, MOPITT, MISR, and ASTER. Each instrument has a unique role—MODIS captures daily images of Earth’s surface, CERES measures Earth’s energy balance, MOPITT tracks air pollution, MISR provides 3D views of clouds and landscapes, and ASTER zooms in on specific land features like mountains and cities.

By personifying Terra and explaining its instruments in simple language, the project makes complex Earth science more accessible and engaging, especially for young learners. The animation also shows how Terra has been collecting valuable data for over 25 years, helping scientists monitor changes such as urban growth, pollution, climate patterns, and natural disasters.

This project addresses the NASA challenge by combining education, storytelling, and animation to celebrate Terra’s 25th anniversary. It is important because it raises awareness of how satellites contribute to understanding and protecting our planet, inspiring others to appreciate Earth science and the technology behind it.
projectDetails.details: My project is a short animated story that introduces NASA’s Terra satellite as a character who explains its own mission and the functions of its five instruments: MODIS, CERES, MOPITT, MISR, and ASTER. Each instrument is described in simple terms, helping viewers understand how Terra observes Earth's surface, atmosphere, pollution, and energy. The animation was created using PictoBlox, a block-based coding platform that allowed me to design movements, speech, and interactions without needing advanced programming skills. I also used Canva to design the presentation slides. The main goal of the project is to make satellite science more engaging and accessible, especially for students and beginners. By turning Terra into a storyteller, the animation simplifies complex scientific ideas and helps viewers connect with the importance of Earth observation. The intended impact is to raise awareness about how satellites help monitor environmental changes and to inspire curiosity in Earth science and technology. The project is creative because it transforms raw data and instruments into an educational narrative. In developing it, I focused on accuracy, simplicity, and visual appeal while considering how to make the information easy to understand and meaningful for a wide audience.

projectDetails.name: PROJECT 'IMPACT'
projectDetails.summary: This project is an Asteroid Impact Simulator that visualizes potential asteroid collisions with Earth in real time. Using NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) API, the simulator fetches recent asteroid data, including size and velocity, and allows users to select an asteroid and a target impact location on an interactive OpenStreetMap. The simulation dynamically displays the impact point, fireball, and resulting crater, scaled realistically relative to the map. Users can zoom and pan while the impact markers remain accurately anchored to their geographic coordinates. This tool addresses the challenge of understanding the potential effects of asteroid impacts in a visually intuitive and interactive way, making it valuable for educational purposes, risk awareness, and demonstrating planetary defense concepts. It combines real scientific data with an engaging visualization to help users explore and learn about near-Earth objects and their potential consequences.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details:
The Asteroid Impact Simulator is a fully interactive web application designed to visualize asteroid impacts on Earth in real-time using actual NASA Near-Earth Object (NEO) data. The simulator fetches recent asteroid data directly via a hardcoded NASA API key, providing information such as asteroid diameter, velocity, and estimated energy upon impact. Users can select an asteroid, specify any latitude and longitude on Earth, and simulate its impact, which calculates and visualizes effects like fireball radius and crater size.

The project leverages OpenStreetMap tiles for a high-resolution, zoomable, and pannable Earth map, implemented via HTML5 Canvas and JavaScript. The map is interactive, supporting smooth zooming and panning, with the impact point remaining fixed relative to the map’s geography. The fireball and crater visualizations scale correctly relative to the map units, giving users an intuitive sense of the impact’s magnitude.

This simulator serves both educational and scientific awareness purposes. It helps users understand the scale and consequences of asteroid impacts, promoting awareness of planetary defense and STEM learning. The project emphasizes scientific accuracy, user interactivity, and accessibility, while ensuring performance even with large map tiles and zooming functionality.

Development tools include HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TailwindCSS, and the Leaflet/OpenStreetMap system. The project’s creativity lies in combining live astronomical data with dynamic, interactive map visualizations, giving users a hands-on experience of planetary-scale phenomena. Critical design factors included ensuring the impact point remains anchored during zoom/pan, accurate relative scaling of fireball and crater effects, responsive UI design, and efficient real-time rendering.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
We utilized AI tools to accelerate development and improve code quality for the Asteroid Impact Simulator. The initial code base was created using Gemini, after which ChatGPT was employed to generate additional features, structure the code, and optimize interactivity. Claude was used for debugging, error correction, and ensuring smooth functionality, particularly for handling map zooming, panning, and asteroid impact visualizations.

All AI-generated contributions were carefully reviewed and customized to ensure originality, scientific accuracy, and alignment with project objectives. No NASA branding or proprietary design elements were used or modified.

projectDetails.name: Project The good once
projectDetails.summary:
The Meteor Madness project explores the phenomenon of meteors—space rocks that enter Earth’s atmosphere—and the potential dangers they pose to our planet. The team explains how meteor impacts can cause massive destruction, both immediately and in the long term, including blast waves, thermal radiation, earthquakes, and tsunamis.

To address this threat, the project proposes an innovative deflection strategy using kinetic energy. A lightweight, cost-effective satellite would be launched to collide with an approaching meteor, altering its path before it enters Earth’s atmosphere. This approach focuses on preventing impact rather than responding to disaster, making it a proactive and efficient planetary defense solution.
projectDetails.details:
Understanding Meteors:
Meteors are glowing streaks of light produced when meteoroids—small rocks or metal bodies from space—burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. When they survive and hit the surface, they become meteorites.


2. Threats and Calamities:

Blast Waves destroy infrastructure.

Thermal Radiation causes large-scale fires.

Seismic Activity triggers earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.

Tsunamis and Dust Clouds cause long-term environmental damage.
Example: the Chicxulub crater formed by a meteor impact in North America.



3. Proposed Solution – Kinetic Deflection Satellite:
The team’s idea is to deploy a satellite built from thin metal, designed to strike a meteor with enough kinetic energy to change its course.

Low-cost materials make it feasible.

Early interception ensures safety before entry into the atmosphere.

Effective and scalable for future threats.



4. Goal:
To safeguard Earth from catastrophic meteor impacts using sustainable, science-driven innovation.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
1. Asteroid Detection AI:
Uses satellite and telescope data to identify and track meteors and asteroids in space. It analyses their speed, size, and trajectory to predict possible impacts.


2. Trajectory Prediction AI:
Analyses orbital paths and calculates future movement of meteors using deep learning. It helps decide whether a meteor poses a threat to Earth.


3. Impact Simulation AI:

projectDetails.name: Project The Guardians of the Stellar Nebulae
projectDetails.summary: We developed a short digital story to inform and teach 5th graders and above about stellar phenomena such as solar flares, black holes, the aurora borealis, and quasars, while also allowing them to be enlightened on earthly features like the wind, ice, humanity, storms, and the concept of nature. This project integrates NASA's knowledge of stellar objects and their properties, as well as storytelling methods. The characters in the story embody features and emotions that correspond to their phenomena.
projectDetails.details:
Our project helps children in the later years of elementary school and higher learn about stellar occurrences. It is a story that portrays the stellar weather as people and sentient beings. The intended impact is to help young children learn about space through reading and visual aids. We used Canva and Google Docs to plan and build our story as well as make it visually appealing. Our project is creative because we made a story originally with features not exist in real life while helping people understand stellar features. We considered factors such as time, planning, and scientific accuracy. These factors were required as we only had two days; without proper planning, we would mess up details and scientific accuracy while also stating facts here and there where important parts came up.

“Any other final thoughts?” Followed by a series of rejections, Quasar calls the vote. “Those who advocate for total annihilation, raise your hand.” The Cosmic Lords raise their hands one by one, Aeolus wavering on the last second before lowering it. Quasar notes this slight movement with little to no reaction appearing on his face, but his shoulders slump in relief. “Those who believe in Pandora’s plan, raise your hand.” The Earthen Alliance, along with Aeolus, raises its hands. “Well, after long hours of deliberation, we have concluded that each Council member must send a team of five people to be trained by the next sun cycle. I will personally train them and select only the best. Once becoming a team member, aspirations from their Cosmic Head must be put to the wayside. As a result, these cosmics will gain neutrality and be separated from their respective Head. We will meet again, in the next century, to discuss the fate of Earth.” 

This is a direct line from the story. Here, we emphasize the finality of the decision. The storytelling techniques used throughout the story are made clearer through the images. While the images are there for visual aid, personally, we prefer to read books without images, so here, the images are supportive, not the main idea. We used a NASA image of a solar flare to show the realism within the fantastical context. The characters are based on real-life ideas. Here are the character notes that we made:

  • Mother Earth: serious, worried,

  • Pandora: clever, counter-negotiative,

  • Aurora Borealis: optimistic, dancing light,

  • Solar Flare: angry, violent, impulsive,

  • Black Hole: cool, calculated

  • Stratus: impulsive storm-bearer,
  • Icy: sharp, logical, biting precision.

Here are the character notes that we created to show the different characteristics of each character, along with the information taken from the NASA websites. We used solar flares, the aurora borealis, and took inspiration from other space weather phenomena like the cold, icy space winds.

We created the project idea first, scribbling out in a notebook how we wanted the story to go. The basic points were: we needed information and inspiration. The structure for a story goes exposition, conflict, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution. The exposition is the preface and the introduction of all the characters. When they go around introducing themselves, a little backstory is shared, along with their characteristics. For example, when Icy introduces herself, she's deliberately short with her words, showing that she's self-assured and logical. When Aurora introduces herself, she goes, "Goo-oood...." because her enthusiasm and optimism are seen. She's personal and sweet, and wonderful, so different from the other characters. A challenge was making the characters different without going away from the story. So while Stratus and Black Hole share characteristics, they are quite different in their own ways.

The conflict is built on the back of Earth and its destruction of the planet. It shows humanity's greed but also their kindness and love. The story doesn't just teach about space, it talks about humanity, human ideals, and the idea that being scarred doesn't mean that you aren't perfect in your own way. Mother Earth is worried, showing how attached she is to the humans, while the Cosmic Lords are impersonal and impulsive, two things that shouldn't go together, but somehow do. Aeolus represents the winds, something that changes within a split second. To show his irrationality and bipolarity, I did this:

A snort comes from the figure next to her, a small snort, then a chuckle, becoming a big booming laugh. As quickly as the mood came across her, Aeolus straightens from her slouching position on her chair, as cold as a space cucumber. “Good nebula and morrow to those present. I am a Cosmic Lord from the depths of every planet, controlling the moods and waves of living. Don’t question me. You won’t live to hear the answer.” The chill that had spread across the room from Icy’s concise speech gets even colder as her deceivingly lively face freezes in a formidable stance. “Now, as the Earthens say, let’s get this show on the road!” A bright smile extends on her face from cheek to cheek as the crowd sighs in relief like a child whose parents have given up on scolding them. 

To add complexity to Aurora's character, we didn't just make her into a happy, go-lucky child; we made her into someone optimistic but also realistic.

Without any indication, Aurora gets up, her friendly face no longer in sight.

Here, her character has many different facets. Solar Flare is consistent throughout, but also kinda crazy too. She's a weird character, a little quirky but also really angry. Black Hole's a really egoistic guy who cares about recognition and stuff like that, as seen when Quasar and he exchange barbs like candy. Quasar's kinda weird too, like a self-righteous person who acts like their neutral but in reality, isn't.

When Stratus and Icy begin arguing over who had the most impact, Pandora's peace-keeping nature comes into play. While it's a short story, we wanted to create fully fleshed-out characters. Through subtle actions and words, you can create a beautiful character. When Quasar reveals his stance, it's meant to show that neutrality is a facade, and while it is celebrated, knowing what is right and wrong is more valuable, an idea that I learned about from the musical Hamilton, which I see now throughout society. When Aeolus reveals his cards, it comes to a climax, seeing that the vital question is this,

Everyone’s eyes bugger out in surprise as the normally snarky Aeolus delivers such a heartfelt monologue. Mother Earth reacts first, “Well, darling. You’ve just delivered us the crux of the matter. Is greed more threatening than the good aspects of the human condition?”

Here, Aeolus is seen as a snarky, teenager type that occasionally delivers insightful ideas like these. We mentioned Quasar's wife, Pulsar, to add a little more knowledge about space. The information about space is delivered through this:

“Black Hole. Calm down, now.” Quasar straightens from his throne. “Your position is tremulous here. You think that you’re so great? When your family, the Black Holes, becomes greedy, I am born. Is born the right word to describe my eternal fate? I am corrupted. At the heart of all galaxies, I exist, blazing while matter swirls within me. My power comes from destruction, quite like yours. The Earthens don’t even know that they revolve around me since I’m the galactic nucleus.” 

They are squabbling, fighting over their positions and their egos, and here, the information is imparted about how a quasar is formed.

The explanation for a solar flare is given here within a sandwich of Solar Flare's anger and annoyance.

Solar Flare jumps up, irrationally exuberant, “Those precious humans of yours abuse me. They hold no value for what I do. When I burst, I throw fire across space. I confuse pilots’ maps, shut down the lights on Earth, and shake the grids that keep their tech magic lights glowing. The magnetic lines…. Gone, bursting and pulling to no avail.” 

Another place that provides information about what the aurora borealis does is here:

Without any indication, Aurora gets up, her friendly face no longer in sight. “As the aurora, my colors paint the skies, dripping with hope, joy, and prosperity. Caused by the solar winds touching the Earth, farmers smile at my colors. I warn them when storms come and dangers touch their shores.” Her hands move in an arch as the image appears on the expanding sky. “These people are just that, people. Humanity doesn’t function like we do. They are beautifully flawed, scarred by their persistence and hunger.”

As Aurora's character is developed and what she does, her abilities are also expanded.

The plot points of the story go as follows:

1. Exposition – The Gathering

2. Conflict – The Opening Arguments

3. Rising Action – Tensions Build

4. Climax – The Cosmic Uproar

5. Falling Action – The Vote

The Educational Part of the story is added into the ideas but framed in such a way that it adds to the story, instead of detracting from it. Something within the story is that it uses elevated language because we wanted to educate the elementary and middle schoolers rather than giving them the same old, tired language that you see within all middle-grade books. So, we used words like "palatial" and "animosity," words that we learned at that age due to reading books that were a little older but also quite wonderful and eye-opening.

challengeDetails.title: Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings
challengeDetails.excerpt: Although the Sun is 93 million miles away from our planet, solar activity can significantly impact our daily lives. “Space weather”—the variations that occur in the space environment between the Sun and Earth—can impact technologies in space and on Earth. Your challenge is to write and illustrate a digital children’s story that explains what space weather is and the varying impacts it has on different people such as farmers, pilots, astronauts, power grid operators, and the general public. You can tell the story from the perspective of a person impacted by space weather or from the point of view of a solar flare or coronal mass ejection (CME) as it approaches Earth. (Heliophysics Division)

projectDetails.details:
THE METEOR MAYHEM MAKER’s

Our journey into the world of space exploration and coding began when our teacher, Jiya Miss, introduced us to the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We are all students of Grade 7, and the moment we heard about the challenge, we were filled with excitement and curiosity. The idea of working on a global platform with real NASA data and solving space-related problems felt like a dream come true.

Without wasting any time, a group of six of us decided to form a team — and that's how Meteor Mayhem Makers was born!

👩‍🚀 Meet Our Team:

  • Adina Somie Thomas
  • Adiya Grace Thomas
  • Adrika Nisanth
  • Daya Susan Oomen
  • Nandhini S Sharma
  • Theertha Girish

We chose the challenge titled "Meteor Madness" because it sounded thrilling and gave us a chance to explore the dangers that meteors and other space-related problems pose to astronauts and space missions. From the beginning, teamwork was our biggest strength. We met regularly, discussed ideas, and planned everything together. We divided the tasks fairly so that everyone had a role to play. Each member contributed their unique skills — whether it was coding, storytelling, designing, research, or creativity. We decided to develop an interactive video game that could not only educate players about real challenges in space but also entertain them. We wanted our game to be fun, engaging, and informative — just like the Space Apps Challenge itself!

🎮 About Our Game: Meteor Madness

Our project is a six-level space-themed video game built using PictoBlox, a block-based coding platform that helped us bring our ideas to life.

 Game Concept:

The game is set in outer space and follows an astronaut’s journey through six different challenges. Each level represents a real-world problem faced by astronauts during space missions. Players must overcome these challenges to progress further. At the end of each level, a unique exoplanet appears and introduces itself to the player. This adds an educational twist to the gameplay by teaching players about distant planets beyond our solar system.

We gathered information from reliable sources like NASA, Google, and Wikipedia to make sure our content was accurate and scientifically meaningful.

🔧 Game Structure:

  • Level 1 to 6: Each member of the team was in charge of one level, including designing the obstacles, coding the gameplay, and ensuring smooth transitions.
  • Introduction & Ending: One member was responsible for creating the introductory and closing scenes of the game, which tie the story together and give it a complete, polished look.
  • Animations & Voiceovers: We added animations and voiceovers to make the game more interactive and fun for players of all ages.

Detailed project description

This project is an interactive spaceship game developed using Pictoblox, where the player controls a spaceship using the arrow keys (up, down, left, right). Meteors continuously fall from the top of the screen, and the player must maneuver the spaceship to collide with the meteors. Each successful collision increases the player’s score, encouraging quick reflexes and strategic movement.

Level 1: Spray Painting

In this level, you control Daya using the arrow keys to move up, down, left, and right. Your goal is to spray paint the meteor while avoiding contact. If the meteor touches Daya, your score decreases. If you successfully dodge the meteor, your score increases steadily. You need to keep moving to stay safe and rack up points. To win, your score must exceed 5 within 10 seconds. Quick reflexes and careful movement are essential to complete this level.

Level 2: Asteroid Tether

In this level, the player controls a spaceship using the arrow keys to navigate through incoming meteors. The meteors glide toward the spaceship, and each collision increases the meteor score. This level challenges the player’s reflexes and control, while demonstrating motion, collision detection, and score tracking in a visual programming environment like Pictoblox. The speed and frequency of meteors increase over time, adding difficulty and excitement to the game. Players must think strategically and react quickly to maximize their score and keep the spaceship safe.

Level 3: Ion Propulsion

In Level 3, you control Theertha, who uses ion propulsion to dodge incoming meteors by moving left and right with the arrow keys. The goal is to avoid being hit—each time a meteor touches Teertha, your life decreases by one, but your score increases by one for every successful dodge. You start with a limited number of lives, so careful manoeuvring is crucial. The meteors become faster and more unpredictable as the level progresses, challenging your reflexes and precision. To win, you must either reach a score above 15 or still have at least one life remaining by the end of the level. If your lives drop to zero before achieving this, you’ll need to play again. Stay alert and use your ion propulsion skillfully to survive and succeed.

Level 4: Laser Ablation

In this level, the player faces a massive, incoming meteor threatening to destroy everything in its path. The only way to stop it is by using the Laser Ablation method—a scientific technique that involves firing a high-powered laser to vaporize part of the meteor's surface, altering its trajectory.

To begin, a button will appear on the screen. Pressing this button equips the player with a powerful laser gun designed specifically for this task. Once armed, the player must decide the precise moment to fire the laser. Timing is critical: fire too early or too late, and the meteor might not be deflected in time. To shoot the laser, the player can press any key on the keyboard. There are no limitations on which key to press—it's all about choosing the right moment for maximum impact.

Level 5: Kinetic Impactors

In this level, the player uses Kinetic Impactors—high-speed projectiles launched from Earth—to collide with the incoming meteor. The goal is to change the meteor's trajectory or break it apart through direct impact. The level begins when you press the S key, after which a girl character will explain the instructions: the game officially starts when you press the Space key. As the meteor approaches, you must carefully time your shot and press the E key to eject the bullet when the meteor is close enough.

To succeed, you need to lock onto the target, time the launch precisely, and choose the best impact point for maximum effect. Each successful hit shifts the meteor’s path slightly, and accumulating 6 points wins you the level. However, if the meteor touches Earth, your available chances will decrease. Should your chances drop to zero, the game is lost. Be strategic—mistimed shots could waste precious resources or leave the planet vulnerable.

Level 6: Nuclear Explosion

In this high-stakes final defense mission, you’ll deploy one of Earth’s most powerful weapons: a nuclear missile. When all other methods fail, this last-resort strategy involves detonating a nuclear warhead near or directly on the meteor, creating an immense explosion that can break it apart or vaporize it completely.

The level begins when you press the Left Arrow key, triggering a girl to appear and explain the instructions. The actual gameplay starts when you press the Up Arrow key. To maneuver the asteroid into position, press the A key to make it glide. When ready to disintegrate the asteroid, press the Down Arrow key to eject the nuclear missile.

Your goal is to intercept the meteor before it enters Earth’s atmosphere. A direct hit or a close-proximity detonation will release enough energy to shatter the meteor into harmless fragments or push it off course to avoid collision. Precise timing and control are critical in this final, decisive strike to save the planet.

This project is a fun and educational way to learn programming concepts like loops, conditionals, variables, and collision detection through a visual, interactive platform. It also helps develop logical thinking and problem-solving skills while creating a game that is engaging and visually appealing.

Project Presentation & Tools Used

Our project includes a well-organized and visually appealing presentation that clearly explains the purpose of our game, introduces all team members, and ends with a vote of thanks. We created the presentation using Power Point, a design platform that helped us bring our ideas to life with creativity and clarity.

The presentation was designed by Adrika Nisanth, who took the lead in putting together all the slides and visuals. Nandhini S Sharma prepared the detailed project description, explaining the technical aspects and the overall purpose of the game. Adiya Grace Thomas and Adina Somie Thomas worked together to create the High-Level Summary, giving a brief but informative overview of the entire project.

To build our game, we used:

  • PictoBlox for coding and developing the game levels
  • Microsoft Power Point for designing the project presentation

Together, these tools helped us communicate our ideas effectively and creatively.

Benefits and Aim of Our Project

The primary aim of our project is to raise awareness about the challenges astronauts face while navigating space beyond Earth. Through interactive and engaging gameplay, players experience these difficulties firsthand, helping them understand the seriousness of space exploration in an enjoyable way that makes the information memorable. Additionally, the project includes detailed information about various exoplanets, inviting players to explore and deepen their knowledge of these distant worlds. By combining education with immersive gameplay, our project encourages curiosity and a greater appreciation for space science and the incredible obstacles faced by astronauts.

 This project taught us more than just coding — we learned about space, problem-solving, teamwork, and time management. We also discovered how much fun it can be to turn scientific knowledge into something creative and playful.

The NASA Space Apps Challenge has inspired us to think bigger and dream higher. No matter what the future holds, we’ll always remember this as one of the most exciting projects we’ve ever done!

 

Vote of Thanks

We would like to express our sincere gratitude to our school, Mar Thoma Residential School, Thiruvalla, for the tremendous support and encouragement throughout this journey.

A heartfelt thank you to the Training Academy "Unique World Robotics" for their expert guidance and mentorship, which played a key role in shaping our project.

A very special thanks goes to our trainer, Mrs. Jiya, for her continuous support, valuable suggestions, and encouragement at every stage of our project. Her dedication and insights were truly inspiring.

Last but not least, we thank God Almighty for His guidance, wisdom, and strength that helped us complete this project successfully.

projectDetails.name: Project Thenga kothu
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, Urban Environmental Comfort Index – Kochi, applies NASA Earth observation data to evaluate and visualize environmental comfort in Kochi, India. As rapid urbanization has contributed to increased temperatures, decreased vegetation, and deteriorating air quality, our mission is to aid sustainable urban development and safeguard community well-being.
With Google Earth Engine, we merged three important parameters: NDVI (vegetation), Land Surface Temperature (LST), and Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) to calculate an Environmental Comfort Index (ECI) — an indicator of livability in cities. More ECI value means greener, cooler, and cleaner places, and less value marks areas of heat and pollution.
The comfort map gives urban planners, policymakers, and researchers practical information to locate vulnerable areas, enhance green infrastructure, and design climate-resilient spaces.
Social Impact:
This system empowers communities and local governments to make better-informed environmental choices, enhance air quality, and increase quality of life. By converting complex satellite data into actionable, city-scale insights, it closes the science-society gap — assisting in the creation of healthier, more sustainable, and just cities for everyone.

projectDetails.name: Adverse Weather Oracle
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, the "Adverse Weather Oracle," is a user-friendly web application designed to help people plan outdoor activities by providing data-driven insights into historical weather probabilities.

Instead of a short-term forecast, our app addresses the challenge by leveraging two decades (2001-2020) of daily satellite data from the NASA POWER Project API. When a user selects any location and any day of the year, our application makes 20 parallel calls to the NASA database. It analyzes the historical data for that specific day across 20 years to calculate the real-world probability of adverse conditions like rain, extreme heat, and high winds.

This is important because it empowers users to make long-term plans for vacations, hikes, or events with a clear, statistical understanding of the likely climate. The app presents these probabilities in a clean dashboard and provides detailed charts as "proof" of the analysis, making complex climatological data from NASA accessible, understandable, and actionable for everyone.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: Our project, the "Adverse Weather Oracle," is a sophisticated web application that calculates the historical probability of adverse weather conditions for any location on Earth, on any given day of the year. A user simply enters a place name and a future date. The app then analyzes two decades of NASA satellite data to provide a simple, percentage-based probability for three key risks: rain, heatstroke (extreme heat), and high winds.

How it works: The app uses a two-stage API process. First, it converts the user's location input into geographic coordinates using the OpenCage Geocoding API. Second, it makes 20 parallel API calls to the NASA POWER Project API, fetching the daily weather data (Precipitation, Temperature, and Wind Speed) for the user's specified day for every year from 2001 to 2020. Our custom JavaScript logic then analyzes this 20-year dataset, counts the number of years each weather threshold was exceeded, and calculates the final probability. To build trust and provide proof, the results are displayed with three interactive bar charts that visualize the complete historical data.

Tools & Technologies Used:

  • Languages: Vanilla JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3
  • APIs: NASA POWER Project API, OpenCage Geocoding API
  • Libraries: Chart.js for data visualization

Project Creativity & Factors Considered: Our creativity lies in making complex climatology accessible. Instead of just showing raw data, we synthesize 20 years of it into a simple, actionable score. We focused heavily on user experience, creating a polished "Atmospheric Glass" interface with a dynamic background that changes based on the weather outlook. We also considered data relevance by setting region-appropriate thresholds for heat and wind, ensuring our analysis is meaningful. Most importantly, we chose to be transparent, using detailed charts to provide clear "proof" of our analysis, making the app not just a tool, but a trustworthy planning companion.
projectDetails.aiReferences:

projectDetails.name: Radiation Exposure in Space Exploration
projectDetails.summary: Radiation Exposure in Space Exploration: Challenge and Solutions for Astronaut Safety". It describes the prime dilemma of space radiation, which is a critical danger to astronauts when they leave Earth's natural shielding. The talk clarifies the challenge by describing the loss of Earth's atmospheric and magnetic shields in deep space, where radiation exposure levels are much higher. It covers the primary sources of radiation—Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs) and Solar Particle Events (SPEs)—and the respective health concerns such as cancer, brain injury, and cataracts. The solution is to present current and emerging protection techniques, such as employing  hydrogen-rich protection materials (such as polyethylene), designing storm shelters (frequently using on-board materials such as water), and developing medical counter measures. This comprehensive strategy of engineering, operational, and medical plans is important because it provides safety and long-term health to astronauts and makes future safe and sustainable deep-space missions to places like the Moon and Mars possible.
projectDetails.details: Project Details: Radiation Exposure in Space Exploration What Does the Project Do and How Does it Work? The project is a presentation about the key problem of radiation exposure for deep space astronauts. It accomplishes this through an initial explanation of the essential problem: losing Earth's natural shield (the atmosphere and magnetic field) when astronauts leave Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The presentation explains the two key radiation dangers: Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs), which are persistent and difficult to shield, and Solar Particle Events (SPEs), which are transient and very lethal bursts of radiation. It also describes the resultant health risks, including cancer due to damage in the DNA, nervous system effects, and damage to eyes. The latter half of the project gives an extensive overview of solutions, ranging from existing shielding materials such as polyethylene and aluminum to cutting-edge concepts such as storm shelters and medical countermeasures. What Are the Benefits of the Project? The project's main advantage is enhancing astronaut safety and mission feasibility for deep-space missions. By defining the risks clearly and suggesting multi-dimensional solutions, it directs work to reduce radiation exposure and reduce long-term health risk, including cancer and cardiovascular disease. It benefits Mars missions in particular, which now experience months or years of prolonged exposure. The solutions offered, especially the application of hydrogen-rich materials and placement of in-board resources such as water and food as added shielding, present viable and effective means to shield the crew without compromising the severe weight limitations of launch rockets. What Is the Intended Impact of the Project? The intended impact is to enable safe, sustainable exploration beyond Earth, namely to the Moon and Mars. The project emphasizes that a coordinated approach—integrating engineering, operations, and medical plans—is needed to ensure astronaut safety. It is intended to promote development and testing of innovative solutions, such as new materials like boron-nitride nanotubes and wearable devices for radiation monitoring, by leveraging platforms like the Gateway station in lunar orbit. Finally, the objective is to make long-duration missions technologically and medically feasible by having ongoing improvements in materials, monitoring, and countermeasures. Tools, Creativity, and Factors Considered The project itself is a computer PowerPoint presentation. The text provided does not indicate the type of software, hardware, or coding language used to develop it. The project is innovative in its attention to lightweight, efficient shielding, aware of the "Shielding vs. Mass Problem" that will significantly enhance launch expenses for heavier-than-air spacecraft. Its innovative solutions involve researching new materials and dual-use of spacecraft provisions (water, provisions, fuel) as natural radiation shields within storm shelters. There were a number of important factors that the team took into account: GCRs' high energy and penetrating ability, SPEs' unexpected suddenness, long-mission cumulative exposure, launch weight limits, and necessity for medical treatments to shield human cells.

projectDetails.name: Bloom Monitor
projectDetails.summary: BloomWatch is a satellite-powered app that tracks global flowering phenology and turns it into decisions. It addresses the lack of scalable bloom monitoring by fusing NASA Earth observations with analytics to flag onset, peak, duration, and anomalies. Using long archives from MODIS (daily NDVI/EVI at 250–500 m) and Landsat 8/9 (30 m field detail), the pipeline performs spectral unmixing to isolate floral pigments (anthocyanins, carotenoids, chlorophyll), computes time-series indices, compares against 2000–2024 histories, and applies a machine-learning classifier (Random Forest) for bloom/no-bloom detection. The interactive dashboard (React + Leaflet + Flask) lets users pick region/season, scrub a day-of-year slider, click any location for NDVI/EVI curves, and view “Bloom Insights” cards (e.g., a DOY 152–165 peak with confidence and field-scouting advisory). The clear global maps of onset and duration that reveal latitudinal patterns and provide actionable guidance for agriculture, biodiversity, public health, and climate studies
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Detects blooms from space. We fuse NASA time-series (MODIS/VIIRS) with higher-res HLS/Landsat to map onset, peak, duration, and anomalies.

Signal extraction. Compute NDVI/EVI and a flower-sensitive residual signal (spectral unmixing → residual PCs → clustering) to separate petal color/structure from general greenness.

Phenology tracking. Per-pixel time-series (2000–2024) are smoothed and analyzed to mark transitions (green-up → bloom → senescence).

Prediction. A lightweight Random Forest estimates bloom likelihood and confidence.

Delivery. A web dashboard shows global tiles, a time slider, filters, pixel drill-downs, and “Bloom Cards” with recommended actions.

Benefits

Agriculture: anticipates flowering/harvest windows, improves scouting timing, reduces losses.

Conservation: flags anomalous blooms, supports habitat protection and invasive species watch.

Public health: indicates probable high-pollen weeks for advisories.

Research & education: consistent global phenology layers for trend studies.

Tools

Data & ML: Python, NumPy, pandas

Indices & detection: Spectral unmixing, residual PCA/GMM, NDVI, EVI, custom bloom indices.

Backend & tiles: Flask API, COGs/GeoTIFF

Frontend: React, Leaflet.js (map), simple state for filters/time slider.

projectDetails.name: Project VYOMASTHRA
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, Integrated Despinning and Propulsion for Active Debris Removal, tackles the growing crisis of space debris in Low Earth Orbit. Thousands of inactive satellites and rocket fragments now threaten active missions and the sustainability of space operations. Our solution introduces a dual-mode propulsion system and active despinning technology to stabilize and safely de-orbit tumbling debris. Using robotic arms, magnetic tethers, or thruster jets, debris is first despun, then guided into Earth’s atmosphere for safe disposal. The dual-mode propulsion combines chemical and electric systems for both high thrust and fuel-efficient maneuvering.

The system also incorporates AI-based debris tracking, self-healing materials, and a modular multi-use design, ensuring sustainability and reusability. By clearing and reclaiming congested orbits, our mission promotes a cleaner, safer, and more accessible space environment — transforming “space junk” from a hazard into a future resource for orbital recycling and sustainable exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Technical Project Details

The project, Integrated Despinning and Propulsion for Active Debris Removal (IDPADR), addresses the critical issue of orbital debris mitigation in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The system employs a service satellite equipped with dual-mode propulsion and active despinning technology to stabilize and deorbit defunct satellites and debris objects.

The operational sequence involves:

  1. Rendezvous and approach – Autonomous navigation using onboard sensors (LiDAR, optical, and radar).
  2. Despinning phase – Stabilization of tumbling debris through magnetic tethers, robotic manipulators, or directed thruster jets.
  3. Controlled deorbit – Use of dual-mode propulsion, integrating chemical propulsion for high-thrust maneuvers and electric propulsion for sustained, fuel-efficient trajectory corrections, sharing a unified propellant system.

The system incorporates AI-assisted debris tracking, autonomous collision avoidance, and reaction force countering mechanisms for enhanced precision. The spacecraft structure utilizes self-healing polymer composites for micrometeoroid resilience and long-term durability.

Development employed CAD-based structural modeling, orbital simulation tools (such as STK and MATLAB Simulink), and embedded control testing using ESP32 microcontrollers and Python/C++ for sensor integration and communication protocols.

This design ensures fuel efficiency, modular reusability, and carbon-negative mission architecture, offering a scalable framework for future orbital reclamation missions. The intended impact is to safely reclaim orbital lanes, reduce collision risks, and enable sustainable on-orbit operations.

AI tools were utilized to enhance documentation, visualization, and development efficiency throughout the project. Specifically:

  1. Concept and Documentation:
    ChatGPT was used to refine technical writing, structure reports, and summarize research findings for clarity and precision.
  2. Image Generation:
    Google Gemini was employed to generate conceptual images and visual mock-ups of the debris removal system. All AI-generated images include visible watermarks indicating AI generation.
  3. Web Development:
    The project website was developed using React.js and hosted via Replit. AI code assistants were used for layout generation, component structuring, and minor debugging assistance.
  4. Code Assistance:
    AI tools supported syntax checking and optimization in C++ and Python scripts used for embedded control and simulation testing.

All AI-generated materials were manually reviewed, edited, and verified by the team to ensure originality and technical accuracy. No NASA branding, flags, or mission identifiers were generated or modified.

projectDetails.name: VYOMATRIX
projectDetails.summary: Our team developed a foldable thermal radiator to solve the thermal management challenges faced by the cubesat. It combines a temperature sensitive mechanism, triggering the radiator to unfold when the satellites internal components exceed their safe operational temperature. The radiator is coated with a specialised material with high emissivity and low solar absorptivity. This method increases the heat dissipation capacity by setting up a large, high efficient surface area. High-power CubeSats often generate more significant internal heat than their small body can dissipate, leading to component overheating and mission failure. By deploying, the foldable thermal radiator it increases the effective surface area available for thermal emission. It allows cubesat to integrate more powerful, data-intensive, and demanding payloads that were previously thermally unfeasible. It provides a reliable, zero-power-consuming method of shedding excess heat, reducing the risk of component overheating and mission failure due to thermal extremes. Our foldable thermal radiator system allows us to ensure us to operate longer duration mission.
projectDetails.details:
Foldable Thermal Radiator for CubeSats

What It Does or How It Works

The radiator is intended to be self-actuating. The material that we use is a high responsive heating material ( like aluminium alloy or kapton polymide). The exterior radiator panel will unfold when the temperature of the satellite exceeds a preset critical temperature. The radiator panels are attached to the exterior of the CubeSat. Once deployed, the radiator greatly increases its surface area. The material selected for the radiator panels has high thermal emissivity and low solar absorptivity to maximize net thermal radiation to space. As the internal temperature drops again towards operations due to the increased heat rejection, reverse mechanism happens, and the radiator panels partially or fully fold back in to maintain the temperature in a safe range and prevent overcooling, for instance in an eclipse, or under other low-power operational circumstances.

What Advantages Does It Offer?

  • Enables a substantial increase in heat rejection capability on demand, which is beneficial for peak operational conditions or short duration high-power events (e.g., data transmission).
  • The radiator is stored in a compact state for launch, reducing the CubeSat's mass and volume budget, consistent with the CubeSat standard.
  • The main deployment mechanism is passive/thermostatic, utilizing little to no electrical energy to accomplish its primary function, thereby preserving satellite resources.
  • By maintaining sensitive components in their operating temperature range, the project will provide an increased lifespan and reliability for the CubeSat's electrical equipment and battery.

Expected Outcome of the Project

The primary outcome is to allow for high power missions within the physical restrictions of the CubeSat platform.

  • It provides a scalable and relatively simple thermal method for future CubeSats with destinations that require power-intensive payloads (such as high-resolution cameras, complex communication systems, or high-performance processors) to address heat management.
  • Reduced thermal stress means greater longevity of missions and higher data return, increasing CubeSats feasibility for complex, multi-year scientific and commercial missions.
  • If successful, the design could be used as a standard deployable thermal module across a range of CubeSat bus providers.

In what ways is your project innovative?

  • The deployment is triggered by a passive thermal actuator. This means the mechanism that unfolds the radiator is activated directly by the excessive heat it's designed to reject. This elegant design eliminates the need for separate temperature sensors, onboard computers, and powered motors to initiate deployment, significantly enhancing system reliability
  • Our design employs a single, multifunctional material that acts as both the radiator's structural panel and its heat-emitting surface. This material is chosen for its high emissivity to maximize heat radiation and low solar absorptivity to minimize heat intake, creating an exceptionally efficient and lightweight thermal control system.
  • Our design proactively prevents the satellite from getting too cold. Unlike a simple, fixed radiator that only cools, our system can be partially retracted or uses a smart material that balances heating and cooling. This ensures the satellite stays within its ideal temperature range, avoiding the risk of components freezing, which is just as dangerous as overheating

What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

  • Material Thermal Properties
  • Ensuring the folded state fits within the CubeSat's constraints.
  • Minimizing the mass of the radiator and its mechanism to preserve payload capacity.
  • Ensured that the system can endure numerous temperature cycles (Sun/Eclipse transitions) without degradation.
  • Choosing materials that resist erosion in Low Earth Orbit (LEO).
  • Ensuring the mechanism and materials can survive the space radiation environment.
  • Setting operational temperature range for deployment and retraction of the radiator to ensure that the satellite operates at optimum temperature.

projectDetails.name: Project WHITE HOLE
projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary

For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, our team developed an interactive educational project focused on space weather. Using Pictoblox, we created an animation featuring two characters who engage in a dialogue about key space weather phenomena such as solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and geomagnetic storms. Through their conversation, the characters explain how these solar events affect Earth’s magnetic field, disrupt satellite communications, GPS systems, and even cause power grid failures. We synchronized the characters’ voices with on-screen text and included visual effects to help illustrate how solar particles travel from the Sun to Earth and impact technology.

Alongside the animation, we prepared a comprehensive PowerPoint presentation titled "Exploring Space Weather". The presentation provides an overview of space weather causes, its effects on Earth’s environment and technology, and the importance of monitoring solar activity using satellites. It also emphasizes the need for early warnings to protect critical infrastructure and ensure astronaut safety.

This project allowed us to combine science education with technology and programming skills. It enhanced our understanding of space weather and helped us develop effective communication methods to make complex scientific concepts accessible and engaging for a wider audience, supporting the goals of the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

What does it do or how does it work?
Our project is an interactive animation created in Pictoblox, featuring two characters—Astronaut Ripley and Dot, the dog astronaut—who discuss and explain space weather. Through their friendly dialogue, they cover topics like solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and how these solar events affect Earth’s technology and astronauts. The animation includes synchronized speech bubbles, voiceovers, and visuals to make the explanation engaging and easy to follow.

What benefits does it have?
This project helps viewers, especially young learners, understand complex space weather concepts in a simple and relatable way. By using characters that people can connect with, it makes learning fun and memorable. It also raises awareness of how space weather impacts satellites, communication systems, power grids, and astronaut safety.

What is the intended impact of the project?
The goal is to educate and inspire curiosity about space weather and its importance in everyday life and space exploration. We want viewers to appreciate the role of space weather monitoring in protecting technology and astronauts.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
We developed the project using Pictoblox, a visual block-based coding platform. We used its animation and voice synchronization features to bring Ripley and Dot’s conversation to life. The project runs on a computer and uses recorded voices and text bubbles for communication.

How is your project creative?
The project creatively uses a conversational format between an astronaut and a dog astronaut to explain science, making the topic approachable and engaging. The combination of animation, voice, and text helps cater to different learning preferences and keeps the audience interested.

What factors did your team consider?
We focused on clarity and engagement, making sure the dialogue was easy to understand and scientifically accurate. Timing the speech and animations smoothly was a priority to maintain flow. We also aimed to make the characters relatable and the content accessible to a wide audience.

projectDetails.details:
The Cosmic Garden is a three-page illustrated story that introduces children to the wonder of space exploration through the eyes of a young dreamer named Mira, who imagines planting a “garden of stars.” Each planet she “plants” is inspired by real NASA exoplanet discoveries, represented with data-driven visuals created using NASA’s open resources such as NASA Eyes on Exoplanets, JWST’s spectral data, and the NASA Image Library. The story gently weaves scientific facts about how light helps scientists identify exoplanet atmospheres, what makes a planet habitable, and how exploration begins with curiosity.

The project is designed to inspire the next generation of explorers by transforming NASA’s cutting-edge data into emotionally resonant storytelling. By combining AI-driven visualization, creative writing, and open NASA data, The Cosmic Garden makes complex space science understandable and exciting for elementary and middle school students. The final output—a short digital storybook—can be freely used by educators, outreach programs, and libraries to ignite curiosity about science, technology, and the universe beyond Earth.
projectDetails.aiReferences: Artificial Intelligence plays a crucial role in bringing The Cosmic Garden to life. We use AI-powered tools to generate realistic visualizations of exoplanets based on open NASA datasets, including the Exoplanet Archive and JWST spectral observations. By analyzing these datasets, an AI image generator trained on scientific imagery helps create accurate yet visually engaging planet illustrations for children. Additionally, a Natural Language Generation (NLG) model assists in transforming complex heliophysics and exoplanetary concepts into age-appropriate language, ensuring scientific accuracy while maintaining a sense of wonder. AI also helps match NASA’s data parameters (like planet temperature, radius, and composition) to artistic color palettes that visualize the habitability or uniqueness of each world. In this way, AI bridges the gap between hard data and creative storytelling—turning raw space science into accessible, emotional narratives that inspire young minds.

projectDetails.name: Silent Thirst
projectDetails.summary:
The project “Terra Data” explores the significance and applications of NASA’s Terra satellite, which was launched on December 18, 1999. As one of NASA’s flagship Earth observation missions, Terra has been collecting valuable environmental and climatic data for over 25 years.

The project “Terra Data” by Aniketh and Navadarsh focuses on NASA’s Terra satellite, launched on December 18, 1999. The satellite, whose name means “Earth” in Latin, has been observing our planet for over 25 years, collecting an enormous amount of data about Earth’s atmosphere, land, and oceans.

The presentation explains how Terra’s vast collection of data can be used to address environmental challenges — particularly droughts. By analyzing data patterns from Terra, scientists can better understand rainfall shortages, soil moisture levels, and other climate indicators to help prevent or mitigate drought effects.

It also reviews major droughts in India’s history, including those of 1876–1878, 1899–1900, 1918, 1965–1967, and 2000–2001, highlighting their affected regions and durations.

The project concludes by emphasizing that Terra’s data is a valuable tool for studying natural disasters, improving disaster preparedness, and helping communities manage water resources more effectively.

What makes our project creative is how we turn complex scientific data into simple, meaningful visuals using Canva, so anyone can understand it—not just scientists. Our team focused on clarity, accessibility, and real impact, making sure our work can truly help communities and planners make better choices for a healthier future.

projectDetails.summary:
Project Report: Adoplex - Animal Repellent System (Summary)
Title: Adoplex – Animal Repellent System Using Ultra- & Infrasonic Sound
Team: Adoplex | School: Nirmala Public School 

Abstract and Introduction 
Adoplex offers a humane, automatic solution to human-animal conflict using ultrasonic (>20 kHz) and infrasonic (<20 Hz) sound. This sensor-triggered system exploits frequencies outside human hearing to deter animals (e.g., rodents, elephants) non-lethally. The prototype validated the control logic for an automated, non-habituating solution, promising ethical and scalable protection for crops and property.

Theory and Implementation 
The system targets specific animal hearing ranges. The prototype used an Arduino UNO and an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor to detect objects. Its logic successfully demonstrated automatic triggering of a buzzer (simulating the deterrent) upon detection, proving the core concept of sensor-to-output control.

Testing and Future Plan 
Testing confirmed the sensor's reliability but highlighted limitations: the audible buzzer couldn't test real frequencies, and sensor performance was affected by weather. Future plans include:

Upgraded Emitters: Specialized transducers and woofers with frequency modulation.

Improved Sensing: Multi-sensor arrays (PIR/LIDAR) for robust, all-weather detection.

Efficiency: Solar power and deep sleep modes for autonomous operation.

Adoplex is a feasible, multi-disciplinary approach to human-wildlife co-existence.
projectDetails.details:
Adoplex: Humane Animal Repellent System Details

The Adoplex project, created by Team Adoplex from Nirmala Public School, aims to mitigate human-animal conflict using advanced sound technology. It proposes a safe, effective, and humane solution for communities facing wildlife intrusion.

The Problem and Traditional Limitations

Wild animals entering human settlements pose significant threats to both people and wildlife. This conflict results in:

  • Crop Damage & Property Loss: Leading to economic hardship for farmers and destruction of infrastructure.
  • Human & Animal Injuries: Clashes can lead to severe injury or death for both species.
  • Ineffective Deterrents: Traditional deterrents often fail due to high cost, environmental disruption, and animal habituation.

The Adoplex Solution: Dual-Frequency Deterrence

Adoplex proposes a smart, non-lethal system that exploits animal sensitivity to sound frequencies outside the human hearing range. This approach relies on

Targeted Frequencies to create discomfort or disorientation without causing injury:

  • Ultrasonic Sound (above 20 kHz): Targets small animals like rodents, bats, and dogs, which are highly sensitive to this range.
  • Infrasonic Sound (below 20 Hz): Targets large animals like elephants and wild boars, as elephants are known to communicate using and are sensitive to infrasound.
  • Environmental Safety: The system repels animals without causing harm or blocking migration.

System Architecture and Logic

The system's effectiveness relies on intelligent activation:

  • Detection: An integrated radar sensor is used to locate and track movement within a 20 m range.
  • Automatic Trigger: The system activates only when an object is detected and enters a pre-set threshold (e.g., 2 meters).
  • Control Logic: A microcontroller (e.g., Arduino Uno) processes the sensor data and controls the output. This logic ensures the deterrent is active only when necessary, which prevents habituation and conserves power.

Prototype and Testing

The initial prototype was built to validate the core detection and control logic.

  • Components: It included an Ultrasonic Distance Sensor/Radar, an Arduino Uno/Microcontroller, and a simple Piezo Buzzer to simulate the sound output.
  • Observations: Testing confirmed the sensor reliably detected objects up to 3 meters with a rapid response time (under 100 ms).
  • Challenges: The buzzer limited the ability to truly test the intended acoustic effects, and the sensor performance degraded in adverse weather like fog or rain. False triggers from environmental noise were also noted, indicating a need for signal filtering.

Future Roadmap and Impact

The team has a clear plan for scaling the system for real-world deployment:

  • Upgraded Hardware: Integrating specialized ultrasonic transducers and low-frequency speakers for true dual-frequency output.
  • Intelligent Activation: Utilizing radar and image processing (AI) to accurately classify objects and minimize false activations.
  • Energy Independence: Implementing solar panels and smart sleep modes for remote, low-maintenance operation.
  • Habituation Prevention: Introducing frequency sweeping and varied patterns (Dynamic Modulation).
  • Impact: Adoplex promises Economic Relief by reducing crop loss, promoting Social Harmony by reducing conflict, and aiding Wildlife Preservation by offering a non-lethal method.

The project successfully bridges electronics, biology, and social science, offering a scalable path to mitigating human-animal conflict.
