projectDetails.name: CosmoWick
projectDetails.summary:
CosmoWick is an immersive web application designed for the interactive exploration of high-resolution space imagery. The project consists of a captivating landing page that introduces the user to the experience, leading to a powerful image viewer tool.

It addresses the challenge of making vast astronomical photos engaging by allowing users to do more than just look. Using the OpenSeadragon library, the application enables deep zooming and panning on a curated selection of NASA images. The core feature allows users to place custom, named labels on any point of interest, which are then saved to a list. This transforms passive viewing into active, personal discovery.

This project is important because it serves as an accessible educational tool. It empowers students, educators, and enthusiasts to study celestial bodies in detail, document their findings, and easily navigate back to specific features, fostering a deeper connection to and understanding of the cosmos.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

This project is a two-part interactive web application designed for exploring high-resolution space imagery.

  1. The Landing Page (main.html): The user first arrives at a visually immersive landing page that serves as an introduction. It features a full-screen space video background, futuristic typography with glowing text effects, and smooth animations to create an engaging, cinematic experience. The sole purpose of this page is to captivate the user and guide them to the main tool via an "Explore" button.
    • Select Different Views: Choose from a dropdown menu of various celestial images, such as galaxies, the moon, and nebulae.
    • Deep Zoom and Pan: Use a powerful viewer to zoom in on intricate details of the high-resolution images smoothly.
    • Annotate Images: Click anywhere on an image to add a custom label. A popup appears, allowing them to name a feature (e.g., "Star Cluster"). This action places a marker on the image and adds the label to a "Saved Labels" list in a sidebar.
    • Navigate via Labels: Clicking on any item in the "Saved Labels" list automatically directs the viewer to that specific annotated point on the image.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The primary benefit of this project is making astronomical exploration accessible and personal. Instead of just passively viewing static images, users can actively engage with the content.

  • Benefit: It transforms the viewing experience from passive to interactive, fostering a deeper connection with the subject matter. The labeling feature allows users to create their own "tour" of a celestial object, making the vastness of space feel more manageable and personal.
  • Intended Impact: The project aims to spark curiosity and promote education in astronomy. By providing a tool that is both beautiful and functional, it can engage students, amateur astronomers, and the general public, encouraging them to explore and learn about the universe in a hands-on way.

Tools and Technologies

The project was developed using standard web technologies and a specialized JavaScript library.

  • Coding Languages: HTML5 (for structure), CSS3 (for styling, layout, and animations), and JavaScript (for all interactivity and logic).
  • Key Software/Library: OpenSeadragon.js, a powerful open-source library, is crucial for handling the high-resolution, deep-zoom functionality of the image viewer.
  • Hardware: No specialized hardware is required; it is designed to run in any modern web browser on a standard computer.

Creative Aspects

The creativity of this project lies in its fusion of cinematic aesthetics with scientific utility.

  1. Immersive Storytelling: The landing page doesn't just present an option; it sets a mood. The use of a dynamic video background, glowing text, and modern fonts is a creative choice to make the user feel like they are embarking on a futuristic exploration.
  2. Personalized Discovery: The most creative feature is the annotation system. It empowers the user to become an active participant rather than a passive observer. This turns a simple image viewer into a personal discovery tool, where users can chart their own points of interest in the cosmos

Factors Considered During Development

The development likely focused on several key factors to ensure a high-quality user experience.

  • User Engagement: The design of the landing page clearly shows that capturing the user's interest from the very beginning was a priority. The animations and hover effects were intentionally added to make the interface feel alive and responsive.
  • User Interface (UI) Design: The viewer page uses a clean, two-panel layout (sidebar for controls, main area for the image). This is a deliberate choice to keep the controls organized and accessible without cluttering the main viewing area.
  • Performance: For an application dealing with high-resolution images, performance is critical. The choice to use a specialized library like OpenSeadragon was a key technical decision to ensure that zooming and panning would be smooth and responsive, even with large image files.
  • Functionality: The core features were carefully chosen to support the goal of exploration. The combination of image selection, zooming, and labeling creates a complete and intuitive workflow for the user.

projectDetails.details:
Of course. Here is a comprehensive project description, written as a direct summary suitable for uploading.

Project Orbit: A Sustainable LEO Ecosystem

Project Summary

Project Orbit is a comprehensive business plan for a sustainable commercial venture in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), supported by a high-fidelity technical prototype. We have developed a complete mission architecture for an orbital tourism and research service, utilizing a fully reusable, zero-debris rocket to service a modular space station at 350 km. The core of our work is a MATLAB simulation and video animation that models and validates the entire mission sequence. This project presents a profitable and economically viable blueprint to democratize access to space, unlocking the vast scientific and commercial potential of LEO.

Mission Architecture and Operations

Our project is an integrated, end-to-end service designed for reliable and affordable access to LEO. The system consists of three core components that work together seamlessly:

  1. The Launch Vehicle: A fully reusable, two-stage rocket designed with a zero-debris philosophy. All components are either recovered for reuse or safely de-orbited, ensuring the long-term sustainability of the orbital environment.
  2. The Capsule: A versatile crew and cargo vehicle that transports private astronauts and scientific payloads from the ground to our station.
  3. The Destination: A modular commercial space station in a 350 km LEO orbit. It serves as both a luxury hotel for tourists and a world-class laboratory for researchers.

The standard mission involves the rocket launching the capsule, performing a multi-stage ascent, and inserting the capsule into a stable orbit, after which it autonomously rendezvous and docks with the station.

Key Benefits and Intended Impact

The primary benefits of our model are a radical reduction in cost and a commitment to sustainability, leading to a transformative impact on the space industry.

  • Economic Benefit: By integrating reusability, modularity, and automation, our model reduces the total cost of orbital operations by an estimated 70-80% compared to conventional methods. This creates a clear path to profitability.
  • Sustainability Benefit: The zero-debris design directly combats the growing threat of space junk, ensuring the LEO environment remains safe and viable for future generations.
  • Scientific & Commercial Access: The lower cost structure enables more frequent and affordable access to microgravity, accelerating breakthroughs in medicine, materials science, and climate research.

The intended impact is to democratize access to space, shifting it from a government-exclusive domain to a vibrant commercial marketplace that can ignite a new, self-sustaining economy in LEO.

Innovation and Creativity

The innovation of Project Orbit lies in its holistic and integrated approach.

  • Creative Business Model: We uniquely combine the high-margin business of space tourism with the high-impact field of scientific research. Tourism acts as the economic engine that subsidizes and enables cutting-edge science.
  • Forward-Thinking Design: Prioritizing a "zero-debris" architecture embeds long-term environmental responsibility directly into the engineering, a creative constraint that ensures sustainability.
  • Dynamic Prototyping: Instead of a static paper proposal, we developed a data-driven simulation and video animation. This tangibly demonstrates the mission's feasibility and brings the concept to life.

Technical Development and Tools

The project prototype was developed using simulation and design software to validate the mission's feasibility.

  • Primary Development Tool: MATLAB was the core of our technical work. It was used to write the code for a physics-based simulation of the entire mission, modeling multi-stage rocket ascent, fuel consumption, gravity turns, and orbital mechanics.
  • Animation Software: We utilized MATLAB's built-in plotting and animation functions (VideoWriter and animatedline) to process the simulation data and generate a full .mp4 video prototype.
  • Presentation Software: The final business plan and visual assets were designed for presentation tools like PowerPoint and AI-powered slide generators like Gamma.

Core Design Considerations

The project's development was guided by a set of core principles to ensure it was not just ambitious, but also viable, scalable, and responsible.

  • Economic Viability: A primary focus on a profitable business model, driving the detailed cost-reduction analysis.
  • Technical Feasibility: Grounding the entire concept in established principles of physics and orbital mechanics, as validated by the MATLAB prototype.
  • Sustainability: Treating the long-term health of the LEO environment as a critical, non-negotiable design factor.
  • Market Demand: Analyzing and serving the dual markets of emerging space tourism and the consistent need for affordable microgravity research.
  • Scalability: Incorporating a modular design in the space station to allow for future growth and adaptation.

projectDetails.name: Space Biology Knowledge Engine
projectDetails.summary:
Space Biology Knowledge Engine is a full-stack web platform that helps scientists, students, and mission planners explore NASA space biology research faster. We built an interactive React frontend with an AI chat assistant, intelligent search, experiment dashboards, and a zoomable knowledge graph that reveals relationships among organisms, missions, conditions, and study types. A FastAPI backend powers data ingestion, embeddings, and Q&A over curated OSDR-derived datasets, with an enhanced Stage 2 mode that adds entity extraction and semantic retrieval for richer insights.
This addresses the challenge by unifying fragmented research into an intuitive, exploratory interface: users can search naturally, visualize connections, and drill into experiment details in seconds. It’s important because it lowers the barrier to discovering relevant studies, accelerates hypothesis generation, and supports evidence-based decisions for future space missions—turning complex bioscience data into actionable understanding.
projectDetails.details: Space Biology Knowledge Engine is a full-stack app that helps scientists, students, and mission planners explore NASA space biology research faster by unifying search, dashboards, and a zoomable/pannable knowledge graph that connects organisms, missions, space conditions, and experiment types. Users can search naturally, click through graph entities to experiment details, and ask an AI assistant for context or navigation. Built with React + TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and D3.js on the frontend and FastAPI (Python) with Sentence-Transformers on the backend, it delivers semantic search and enriched entity extraction over curated OSDR-derived datasets. The project’s impact is accelerated discovery, lower barriers for newcomers, and better evidence-based planning for future missions. It’s creative in blending semantic AI with interactive visualization, and it was designed with usability, performance, data provenance/ethics, and extensibility as core considerations.
projectDetails.aiReferences: We used AI as an accelerator—not a replacement for human judgment—across ideation, coding, and documentation. A GPT-based assistant (in Cursor) supported feature brainstorming, React/TypeScript and FastAPI scaffolding, code reviews/refactoring, D3 knowledge-graph enhancements (zoom/pan, spacing, click-to-navigate), and Tailwind styling suggestions. We also used Sentence-Transformers for embeddings/semantic search and lightweight entity extraction to enrich the knowledge graph. All AI outputs were reviewed, tested, and finalized by our team; no AI generated or altered data, and we did not use or modify any NASA branding, logos, flags, or mission identifiers. Where AI suggested code or copy, we validated functionality, ensured accessibility and performance, and documented decisions for transparency.

projectDetails.summary:
We developed a comic story book which is makes it easier for kids to understand about space weather.One night, Leo lay on a grassy hill with his Grandpa, watching colorful lights swirl across the night sky. 
Grandpa explained that the lights were auroras, caused by something called space weather from the Sun.
He told Leo that the Sun sometimes sends out bursts of energy and particles into space.
When a big burst called a CME (Coronal Mass Ejection) reaches Earth, it can cause power flickers and GPS problems.
But Earth’s magnetic field protects us by turning that solar energy into beautiful auroras.
Grandpa said that scientists and NASA watch the Sun to predict solar storms and keep people safe.
Leo smiled, realizing the dancing lights were Earth’s way of turning the Sun’s power into beauty.
projectDetails.details: Our project, “Leo and the Dancing Lights – A Journey Through Space Weather,” is an educational comic storybook that creatively explains space weather phenomena such as solar flares, geomagnetic storms, and auroras through the adventures of a curious boy named Leo and his grandfather. Designed to make complex science simple and engaging, it helps young learners understand how the Sun affects Earth while sparking interest in space and STEM fields. The comic combines accurate research from NASA and ESA with vibrant illustrations created using tools like Canva, Illustrator, and Procreate. By turning scientific facts into a story-driven visual experience, it promotes curiosity, accessibility, and learning in a fun way. Our team focused on scientific accuracy, educational value, artistic clarity, and engagement to ensure the story is both informative and inspiring for readers of all ages.

projectDetails.name: Project SkyMiners
projectDetails.summary:
SkyMiners: A World Away – Hunting for Exoplanets with AI is an innovative web platform submitted to the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025, designed to automate exoplanet detection using data from Kepler, K2, and TESS missions. Accessible at https://skyminers.space/ and open-sourced on GitHub, it unifies datasets, engineers physics-guided features like transit depth residuals and resonance proximity, and trains a LightGBM classifier with group-aware cross-validation, achieving AUROC ≈ 0.963.
Users can upload CSVs for batch scoring or input data manually for real-time predictions, viewing metrics such as ROC curves and feature importances. Educational sections demystify exoplanets, making it ideal for researchers and novices alike. Benefits include efficient vetting, reduced false positives, and adaptability to future missions. By blending AI with astrophysics, SkyMiners accelerates discoveries, fosters collaboration, and inspires global exploration of habitable worlds, transforming raw data into cosmic insights
projectDetails.details:
Introduction

Welcome to SkyMiners: A World Away – Hunting for Exoplanets with AI, our submission to the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025. Inspired by the vastness of the universe and the possibility of discovering worlds beyond our solar system, we created a platform that transforms complex data from space missions into accessible and actionable insights. Using artificial intelligence to automate exoplanet identification, our project invites researchers, students, and enthusiasts to explore the cosmos in a collaborative and innovative way.

Access the site at http://skyminers.space and the

GitHub repository at https://github.com/Alailton-jr/sky-miners-nasa-space-apps-2025 to view the source code, contribute, or experiment.

What the Project Does and How It Works

SkyMiners is an integrated web platform that automates exoplanet detection using data from NASA missions like Kepler, K2, and TESS. It operates as a mission-agnostic pipeline, unifying public catalogs into a common schema, engineering physics-guided and host-context features, and training a LightGBM classifier for automatic transit signal vetting.

How it works:

  • Data Unification: We aggregate public datasets (about 21,271 entries, with 12,777 labeled as planet or not-planet), mapping dispositions to harmonized labels and avoiding leakage with group-aware splitting based on host stars.
  • Feature Engineering: We create innovative features, such as transit depth residuals, SNR proxies, proper-motion magnitudes, missingness indicators, and host-level aggregates (e.g., multiplicity, period spacing, and near-resonance proximity), incorporating astrophysical knowledge to improve accuracy.
  • Modeling and Training: We use LightGBM with stratified K-Fold cross-validation (5 folds) to prevent overfitting, achieving AUROC = 0.963, Macro-F1 =0.888, and PR-AUC = 0.923 on labeled data. Thresholds are adjusted to prioritize precision in high-cost follow-up scenarios.
  • Web Interface: Users can perform batch scoring via CSV upload or manual entry for what-if simulations. The platform displays real-time metrics, such as ROC/PR curves, confusion matrices, and feature importances, and allows exporting reports.

At the heart of the system is a model that classifies signals as confirmed exoplanet or false positive, with support for cross-mission generalization and recalibration options.

Benefits

SkyMiners democratizes exoplanet hunting, reducing manual vetting time from months to minutes. Its benefits include:

  • Efficiency: Automates large-scale analyses, allowing thousands of candidates to be processed quickly, with precision superior to manual methods in noisy data scenarios.
  • Accessibility: Intuitive interface for beginners, with educational sections like ``What Are Exoplanets'' and glossaries, facilitating learning about transit photometry and space missions.
  • Robustness: Relational features (e.g., multi-planet architecture) capture systemic patterns, improving detection in multi-planet systems and reducing false positives from background eclipsing binaries.
  • Flexibility: Support for batch processing and manual entry, with integration of new data for fine-tuning, making it adaptable to future missions.

These elements accelerate discoveries, saving resources for telescopic follow-up and inspiring global collaborations.

Intended Impact

Our goal is to propel space exploration, facilitating the identification of habitable exoplanets and expanding knowledge about the universe. The intended impact includes:

  • Scientific: Assist astronomers in candidate triage, potentially uncovering discoveries in datasets like TESS (still operational), and promoting studies of domain shift between missions.
  • Educational: Inspire the next generation of scientists, offering hands-on tools to interact with real NASA data, fostering curiosity about astrophysics and AI.
  • Collaborative: As open-source, it encourages contributions for improvements, such as integrating time-series encoders or positive-unlabeled learning, expanding its reach to future missions.
  • Global: By reducing access barriers, the project contributes to the search for extraterrestrial life, aligning with NASA's vision of exploring ``worlds beyond our Sun''.

In essence, SkyMiners transforms data into portals to new worlds, empowering humanity to dream bigger.

Tools and Technologies Used

We developed the project with a focus on scalability and integration, using:

  • Programming Languages: Python for the ML core (with Jupyter notebooks for prototyping) and JavaScript for the frontend.
  • Libraries and Frameworks: LightGBM for modeling, scikit-learn for metrics and preprocessing, Pandas/NumPy for data manipulation, Optuna for hyperparameter tuning, FastAPI for the backend API, React + Vite for the interactive frontend, and Matplotlib for visualizations.
  • Hardware and Software: Development on local machines with Docker for containerization and deployment (via docker-compose), ensuring portability. We used Git for version control and GitHub for collaboration.
  • Data and Resources: Datasets from the NASA Exoplanet Archive (Kepler KOI, K2 Candidates, TESS TOI), processed without specialized hardware, prioritizing computational efficiency.

No proprietary tools were used, keeping the project accessible and reproducible.

Creativity of the Project

What makes SkyMiners creative is its holistic approach, blending astrophysics with AI in an accessible and visual way. Key differentiators include:

  • Integration of Physics and ML: Features like resonance proximity and depth consistency inject astrophysical knowledge, going beyond black-box models for explainability (e.g., host-context visualizations).
  • Exploratory Interface: An ``Inference Lab'' allows interactive experiments, such as adjusting thresholds for precision targets, blending education with practical analysis – imagine a gamified ``planet hunter''!
  • Mission-Agnostic Design: By unifying schemas and testing leave-one-mission-out, the system adapts to covariate shifts, preparing it for future missions like PLATO.
  • Visual Elements: Dashboards with ROC/PR curves and feature histograms, inspired by space narratives, make science engaging, like a cosmic journey.

This creativity stems from envisioning AI not as a tool, but as a companion in exploring the unknown.

Factors Considered by the Team

Our team considered various factors to balance innovation, usability, and ethics:

  • Precision vs. Recall: We prioritized precision to minimize false positives, respecting follow-up costs, but with options for F-beta or cost-sensitive thresholding for flexibility.
  • Accessibility and Inclusion: Designed for diverse users – from experts to beginners – with intuitive interfaces, educational content, and implicit multi-language support.
  • Sustainability: Focus on lightweight models (LightGBM) to run on common hardware, and open-source code for longevity.
  • Technical Challenges: Addressed leakage with group-aware CV, domain shift with generalization tests, and limitations (e.g., tabular-only) by suggesting future extensions like hybrid tabular-series models.
  • Ethics and Impact: Ensured transparency in metrics, avoiding bias in imbalanced datasets, and promoting responsible use for real scientific advancements.

These considerations ensure that SkyMiners not only solves the challenge but inspires a new era of collective discovery.

projectDetails.name: Hunting Exoplanet with IA
projectDetails.summary:
Our project implements an original deep learning architecture designed to capture, process, and categorize light curves in order to predict the existence of exoplanets. It has two main goals: to contribute to scientific research and to democratize access to knowledge without losing the sense of playfulness that attracts new perspectives from the general public — future researchers and knowledge creators alike.

After training the model, we developed a web application capable of retrieving and analyzing the light curves of observed stars, classifying them using our AI system. Based on the model’s predictions, the app can then simulate planetary transits with a high degree of realism. Users can explore either the star and its orbiting bodies or simply the star and its unique characteristics.
projectDetails.details:
We used Python and applied feature selection during the data preprocessing stage to reduce the vector dimensionality of the classification problem, achieving excellent results with both real and simulated light curves.

Beyond its academic contribution, our project also stands out for its playful and engaging approach: by materializing the phenomenon in an appealing and accessible way, it democratizes knowledge and fosters a better understanding of the transit phenomenon. This, in turn, helps popularize science and attract the curiosity and interest of the general public, inspiring new perspectives and future researchers.

projectDetails.name: Overview Effect
projectDetails.summary:
Celebrating the ISS's 25th anniversary, we've created two immersive web experiences that evoke the feeling of living aboard the ISS. They bring the transformative Overview Effect to Earth. This phenomenon occurs when astronauts observe our planet from space and work in zero gravity, fundamentally changing their perspective on humanity and our shared home.
Experience 1: Cupola Dome Simulation recreates the ISS's seven-window observation module using WebVR A-Frame and Three.js. Users explore four 360° scenarios—observing Earth, Mars, Saturn, and the Aurora Borealis—with dynamic lighting simulating 16 daily orbital sunrises. This demonstrates how Cupola observations support disaster relief, climate research, and geosciences, reaching 90% of Earth's population from orbit.
Experience 2: Microgravity Repair Simulation draws inspiration from the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory training. In the simulation, users perform electrical repairs while managing floating tools in realistic zero-gravity physics at progressively more difficult levels.
The experiences educate students and the public on how ISS operations—from Cupola observations to spacewalk maintenance—directly benefit Earth through scientific research and technological advancement.
Our project demonstrates that the greatest impact of space exploration may be the shift in consciousness it inspires: recognizing that we are "one species, on one planet, that needs to work together."
projectDetails.details:
1. Introduction: The Transformative Power of Space

Our project celebrates the 25th anniversary of the International Space Station by addressing NASA's Space Applications Challenge to create an educational tool that helps students and the public understand two of the most profound sensory experiences aboard the ISS: the spectacular views from the Cupola and the sensation of weightlessness. These experiences fundamentally transform astronauts' perspectives on Earth and humanity—a phenomenon known as the Overview Effect.

2. The Challenge & Our Solution

NASA challenged participants to develop visual tools that demonstrate how observations from the Cupola window and training from the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory (NBL) benefit humanity on Earth. We created two complementary interactive web-based experiences that immerse users in these transformative environments while educating them about their practical applications for Earth science, disaster relief, and climate monitoring.

3. Experience 1: Cupola Dome Simulation - "The Window to the World"

3.1 Technical Implementation

Our first experience digitally recreates the ISS Cupola—the seven-windowed dome module where astronauts observe Earth, conduct photography missions, monitor climate data collection, and oversee spacewalks and robotic operations. Built with A-Frame for WebVR/WebXR, Three.js for 3D rendering, and modern web technologies, the experience features:

Interactive 360° Navigation

  • Users can look around the Cupola using mouse drag or touch controls
  • Replicates the astronaut's ability to observe in all directions
  • Immersive VR support for compatible headsets

Multiple Space Scenarios

Four distinct environments showcase different aspects of ISS observations:

Earth Observation

  • Real-time view of our planet with dynamic cloud formations, city lights, and natural phenomena
  • Visible from 254 miles (408 km) altitude
  • Demonstrates orbital perspective covering 90% of Earth's population

Mars Exploration

  • Future mission perspective highlighting how ISS research prepares humanity for deep space exploration
  • Showcases the stepping stone role of the ISS

Saturn & Ring System

  • Demonstrates astronomical observations and the scale of our solar system
  • Educational visualization of planetary science

Aurora Borealis

  • Showcases atmospheric phenomena that astronauts uniquely observe from above
  • Contributes to space weather research understanding

Realistic Visual Fidelity

  • Dynamic Lighting: Simulates the 16 orbital sunrises and sunsets astronauts experience daily while orbiting at 17,900 mph
  • Smooth Animations: Reflect the serene, contemplative nature of space observation
  • Detailed 3D Models: Ensure scientific accuracy and immersion

3.2 Educational Impact

This experience directly demonstrates how ISS Cupola observations benefit Earth by:

  • Disaster Response Support: Astronaut photography supports natural disaster relief (wildfire monitoring, hurricane tracking) through georeferenced images used by hazard teams
  • Climate Change Research: Manual data collection of Earth's changing conditions contributes to long-term climate studies
  • Geosciences Advancement: Unique perspectives covering 90% of Earth's population along the orbital path provide invaluable data
  • Environmental Awareness: The Overview Effect helps users understand our planet's fragility and interconnectedness, inspiring planetary stewardship

4. Experience 2: Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory Simulation - Spacewalk Training

4.1 Technical Implementation

The second experience simulates the critical training astronauts undergo at NASA's Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston, Texas. This 6.2-million-gallon facility (220 feet long, 102 feet wide, 40 feet deep) contains full-scale ISS module replicas where astronauts train seven hours underwater for every one hour of actual spacewalking.

Authentic Microgravity Physics

  • Custom JavaScript Physics Engine: Simulates zero-gravity object behavior with realistic momentum
  • Free-Floating Objects: Tools and components drift in all directions
  • Consequence System: Objects can be permanently lost in the darkness of space if not carefully managed

Progressive Mission Structure

Mission Objective: Replace a critical electrical fuse in a power distribution box

Level Progression:

  • Level 1: Basic repair with minimal components and generous time limit
  • Levels 2-3: Moderate difficulty with additional floating objects and tighter timeframes

Failure Conditions:

  • Components lost beyond recovery zone
  • Time expiration causing mission failure.

Realistic Operational Challenges

  • Limited Reach Zone: Requires careful astronaut positioning and planning
  • Tool Management: Weightless environment demands constant awareness of equipment
  • Time Pressure: Reflects actual spacewalk constraints and oxygen limitations
  • Mission Control Feedback: Visual and audio cues simulate communication with ground support

4.2 Educational Impact

This experience educates users about:

  • Extensive Preparation: The 7:1 training ratio (7 hours NBL training per 1 hour spacewalk) for 270+ spacewalks since December 1998
  • Spacewalk Purposes: Station maintenance, new equipment installation, and science experiment deployment
  • NBL Training Importance: Critical role in ensuring astronaut safety and mission success
  • Earth Benefits: Practical applications of ISS maintenance for advancing space technology (satellite servicing, communications infrastructure, climate monitoring equipment)

5. Technical Architecture

5.1 Core Technologies

Frontend Framework:

  • Next.js 15.5.4 (App Router with Turbopack)
  • React 19.1.0 (Client-side and Server-side components)
  • TypeScript 5

3D/VR Rendering:

  • A-Frame 1.7.1 (WebVR/WebXR for 360° experiences)
  • Three.js r128 (Advanced 3D rendering)
  • OGL 1.0.11 (Lightweight WebGL library)

Animations & UI:

  • Framer Motion 12.23 (Complex animations and transitions)
  • Tailwind CSS 4 (Utility-first styling)

Spatial Audio:

  • Integrated immersive soundscapes enhancing presence and realism

5.2 Accessibility & Deployment

  • Browser-Based: No installation required—accessible via any modern web browser
  • Cross-Platform: Works on desktop, tablet, mobile devices, and VR headsets
  • Touch & Mouse Support: Intuitive controls for diverse user interactions
  • Lightweight Performance: Optimized loading and rendering for broad device compatibility
  • Responsive Design: Adapts seamlessly to different screen sizes and orientations

5.3 Design Philosophy

We prioritized creating experiences that are:

  • Scientifically Accurate: Based on authentic ISS operations and NASA data
  • Immediately Engaging: Short, focused interactions suitable for educational events and exhibitions
  • Educational First: Every design decision reinforces learning objectives about space benefits for Earth
  • Emotionally Impactful: Leveraging the transformative power of the Overview Effect to inspire planetary stewardship

6. Educational Applications & Benefits

6.1 Target Audiences

  • Students (K-12 & Higher Education): Interactive STEM learning tool for space science curricula
  • Museum & Science Center Visitors: Touch-screen installation for public engagement
  • Educational Events: Portable demonstration tool for science fairs and outreach programs
  • General Public: Accessible online experience raising space awareness

6.2 Learning Outcomes

Users gain understanding of:

  1. Earth Science Applications: How ISS Cupola observations directly support Earth sciences, disaster relief, and climate research
  2. Astronaut Training: The rigorous preparation and extensive training required for space operations
  3. Practical Benefits: How space exploration and ISS operations benefit humanity on Earth
  4. Global Perspective: The Overview Effect and its potential to inspire environmental consciousness and international cooperation

7. Connection to ISS 25th Anniversary

For 25 years, the International Space Station has served as humanity's orbital laboratory, continuously occupied since November 2, 2000. Our project honors this milestone by:

  • Recreating the Cupola Experience: The iconic seven-windowed dome that has provided breathtaking Earth observations for over a decade
  • Simulating NBL Training: Honoring the underwater training that has prepared astronauts for hundreds of successful spacewalks
  • Demonstrating Earth Benefits: Showing how ISS operations continue benefiting life on Earth through scientific research and global cooperation
  • Inspiring Future Generations: Encouraging young people to view space exploration not just as adventure, but as essential work for humanity's future

8. Impact & Vision

Our digital Overview Effect tool serves multiple purposes:

Environmental Awareness

The perspective shift astronauts experience—seeing Earth as a fragile, borderless home—can inspire users to care deeply for our planet and take action on environmental challenges.

Space Education

Demystifying ISS operations makes space exploration accessible and relevant, showing the direct connection between orbital research and daily life on Earth.

STEM Inspiration

Hands-on interaction with realistic simulations encourages scientific careers and demonstrates the practical applications of physics, engineering, and computer science.

Collective Action

Reinforcing astronaut Ron Garan's profound insight that we are "one species, on one planet, that needs to work together"—a message crucial for addressing global challenges like climate change, resource management, and international cooperation.

9. Conclusion

By bringing these transformative space experiences to Earth through accessible web technology, we hope to democratize the perspective shift that has profoundly affected every person who has viewed our planet from orbit. The Overview Effect is not just an astronaut's privilege—it's a perspective that can inspire collective responsibility for our shared home.

Our project demonstrates that the International Space Station's greatest legacy may not be the scientific discoveries made aboard it, but the fundamental shift in human consciousness it enables—a shift from seeing ourselves as separate nations, cultures, and individuals to recognizing our essential unity as one species on one precious planet.

As we celebrate 25 years of continuous human presence in space, we invite everyone to experience the view from the Cupola and the challenges of weightless work, understanding that space exploration ultimately helps us see, protect, and cherish our home: Earth.

Every year, more than 80 million sharks are killed. Entire species are disappearing — and with them, the balance of our oceans. But what if space could help save life in the seas?

Sharks in Space — because every data point can save a life. 🦈

projectDetails.name: Tupã Project
projectDetails.summary:
The ideal weather is inherently subjective and not always assured, whether for a day at the beach, a holiday parade, or a hike in the forest. Preparation for the conditions weather may bring is crucial. The Tupã Project is not a weather forecast; rather, it is a tool that offers precise knowledge of the historical probability of favorable or adverse weather conditions for a specific location and period (month/day) several months in advance.

This probability is predicated upon the vast collection of global historical meteorological data from NASA’s Earth Observation archives, and not on short-term predictive models. Knowledge of these historical conditions enables users to prepare more effectively, plan with greater efficacy, and, should they wish, avoid locations and times where historically unfavorable conditions are likely to occur.
projectDetails.details:
TUPÃ is an intelligent web-based system that predicts weather conditions using atmospheric data from NASA’s POWER API. It collects real variables such as temperature, humidity, pressure, solar radiation, and precipitable water to estimate the probability of rain and local climate conditions.

The system analyzes recent and historical data to identify patterns and generate accurate short-term forecasts. It is designed to assist travelers, aviation, and agriculture by helping users plan safe trips, optimize crop management, and improve decision-making.

Developed with JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and Python, TUPÃ combines scientific data analysis with an intuitive interface. Its creative approach lies in the use of open NASA datasets and a lightweight predictive model to make reliable weather insights easily accessible to everyone.

projectDetails.name: Little Astronauts
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, Little Astronauts, is an educational website designed to make the complex topic of space weather accessible and engaging for children. Space weather, especially solar flares, can impact satellites, power grids, and even the internet on Earth, but it remains a topic rarely addressed in early childhood education.
To address this challenge, we developed an interactive platform that turns science into play. The site features a  story about a tractor affected by a solar storm, available both as a book and an audiobook to read or listen on the platform, a section with images and real facts from NASA, and a quiz that awards children a "Mini Astronaut" certificate when they answer 3 out of 5 questions correctly. By using open data from NASA, we ensure credibility by presenting the information in a fun and age-appropriate way.
This solution is innovative because it translates complex scientific concepts into simple, playful narratives that capture children's curiosity. It is effective because it uses interactive tools to promote active learning. And it is impactful because it promotes early scientific awareness, encouraging future generations to understand and care about the challenges affecting both our planet and technology. The project goes beyond a children's book — it represents education, innovation, and awareness.
projectDetails.details:

We developed the project using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, ensuring it is lightweight, user-friendly, and accessible online. projectDetails.name: BioSearch
projectDetails.summary:
BioSearch is an AI-powered chatbot designed to help users explore and understand biological phenomena in space environments. Created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025, this web application serves as an intelligent assistant specializing in space biology topics.

The project features a modern, responsive chat interface built with React 18 and TypeScript, utilizing Styled Components for a clean design with smooth animations. Users can ask questions about various space biology topics including astrobiology, space medicine, extremophiles, planetary biology, space agriculture, and radiation effects on biological systems.

The frontend communicates with a backend API to provide real-time AI responses. The application includes features like message animations, loading states, input validation, and error handling. The development setup includes strict ESLint rules, Prettier formatting, and comprehensive TypeScript support for a robust development experience.

Key technical components include a header with navigation, the main chatbot interface with message history, reusable styled components, and global styling. The project uses Vite for fast development, React Router for navigation, Axios for API requests, and React Icons for UI elements.

challengeDetails.title: Build a Space Biology Knowledge Engine
challengeDetails.excerpt: Enable a new era of human space exploration! projectDetails.name: Project Cognito Arch
projectDetails.summary: The project proposes an innovative platform that integrates Artificial Intelligence and image analysis into a gamified application designed to capture images of flowers. The application recognizes floral species from photos submitted by users and assigns scores and rewards based on criteria such as rarity, regional biodiversity, and identification accuracy. The initiative combines environmental education and citizen science, encouraging nature observation and ecological awareness in a fun and interactive way.
projectDetails.details:
The project aims to promote user engagement in flower exploration and recording activities, combining machine learning technologies used for automatic species recognition with language models (LLMs) focused on interaction and the construction of a gamified narrative. In addition, it incorporates the use of satellite data for environmental mapping and ecological contextualization of the observed regions.

The application allows users to capture and send photos of flowers, receive instant feedback from artificial intelligence about the identified species and its location, earn points, medals, and achievements for new discoveries, and interact with an LLM-based virtual assistant, which acts as a botanical guide and ecological mentor. The gamification is structured in levels, challenges, and rewards, rewarding the user according to the number of species identified, the regions visited, and the rarity of the flowers found. This mechanism stimulates scientific curiosity, continuous learning, and a greater connection with nature.

The project also integrates satellite data from sources such as NASA, INPE, and ESA, allowing for the correlation of information on biomes, climate, and vegetation cover. This layer of context expands the educational and scientific potential of the platform, transforming the user experience into a journey of intelligent and collaborative environmental exploration.

The project promotes an innovative form of interactive environmental education, encouraging ecological awareness and citizen participation in collecting data on biodiversity. Users become part of a collaborative community that learns about the environment while contributing to flora mapping and real-time ecological monitoring. By integrating artificial intelligence and gamification, the project transforms learning into a dynamic, accessible, and engaging experience, strengthening the link between technology, science, and environmental responsibility.

The proposal stands out for integrating citizen science as a tool to support environmental research, using flower mapping as the main data collection strategy. Flowers, as sensitive bioindicators of ecological conditions, allow the recording of their occurrences to assist in identifying environmental patterns and in analyses related to climate change. By encouraging the population to record images and locations of flowers, the project expands the volume of information available for predictive models, which can generate insights into biodiversity, climate, and ecosystem health.

Through a system of points, daily missions, and rankings, data collection is transformed into an interactive and motivating experience. This combination of science, technology, and social engagement makes the project an example of collaboration between citizens and researchers in the search for sustainable environmental solutions.

projectDetails.name: Bio Space
projectDetails.summary:
The project tackles the challenge of building a Space Biology Knowledge Engine by creating an AI-powered platform that organizes NASA’s vast collection of bioscience publications into clear, accessible categories. Although NASA provides valuable research, it is often scattered, highly technical, and time-consuming to navigate, especially for students and early-career researchers.

Our solution classifies publications into key fields, such as Space Microbiology, Animal Physiology, Space Botany, Space Biotechnology, Closed Ecosystems, and Planetary Exploration. Users can quickly find, explore, and organize articles, including the ability to automatically classify new submissions.

The platform also provides an intuitive, organized dashboard with visualizations that make complex data easier to understand. By reducing search barriers and simplifying navigation, it empowers students, researchers, and mission planners to identify scientific progress, uncover knowledge gaps, and generate new insights efficiently.

What sets this project apart is its combination of accessibility, efficiency, and depth, transforming overwhelming information into structured, actionable knowledge.
projectDetails.details:
Functionality:
Our platform allows users to search by keywords or filter publications by categories related to NASA’s bioscience research. Users can also add their own articles, which are automatically classified and organized into the appropriate category by an AI model trained by our team. The platform also provides interactive visualizations using Plotly, enabling users to quickly understand trends, relationships, and the impacts of different studies.

Benefits:
The platform saves users time and effort by organizing scattered research, providing visual insights, and facilitating rapid access to relevant publications. It is designed to be completely free to use, reducing financial barriers for students and researchers.

Intended Impact:
Our solution enhances efficiency in accessing NASA’s bioscience data, accelerates research, and supports academic work. By offering a scalable AI model that can be integrated with generative tools for summarizing articles and dividing references, the platform aims to empower students and researchers to explore knowledge more effectively.

Tools and Technologies:

  • Programming Languages: Python, JavaScript
  • Libraries & Frameworks: Plotly (for interactive visualizations), AI frameworks for automatic classification
  • Software/Platform: Web-based application, AI model trained and deployed on local/cloud infrastructure
  • Hardware: Standard personal computers; no specialized hardware required

Creativity:
The project’s creativity lies in its combination of intuitive interface, automatic classification, and interactive visualizations. Unlike traditional repositories, the platform requires minimal processing resources, has zero cost for users, and provides a practical, user-friendly solution to navigating a vast amount of complex data.

Team Considerations:
Our team focused on accessibility, user experience, and scientific reliability. We designed the platform to meet the needs of university students and researchers, ensuring it is easy to use, practical, and scalable for future expansions.
projectDetails.aiReferences: AI was used to assist in generating the front-end of the platform through the Gemini tool, which was necessary because the team did not have a member specialized in front-end development. While AI helped create the initial layout and interface elements, the team independently implemented key features such as search functionality, article categorization, and data visualizations. This approach allowed us to clearly and efficiently demonstrate our ideas while customizing and expanding the platform beyond the AI-generated components.

projectDetails.name: MeteorFall
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, MeteorFall, is a full-stack educational web application that allows users to visualize the real-world consequences of an asteroid impact. We developed a Python/Flask backend that fetches weekly data on Near-Earth Objects (NEOs) from the NASA NeoWs API, calculates their kinetic energy, and models impact effects such as crater diameter and seismic magnitude.

This addresses the challenge that official risk assessments, like the Torino and Palermo scales, are often abstract and difficult for the public to comprehend. MeteorFall bridges this gap with an immersive CesiumJS front end built on Google's Photorealistic 3D Tiles. Users select a real asteroid and any impact location, triggering an evacuation warning sequence, a dramatic 3D impact animation, and a detailed results panel. The platform is further enhanced with educational pages on historical impacts (Chicxulub, Tunguska) and an interactive quiz.

Its importance lies in making the abstract personal. By visualizing a potential impact on a user's own city, MeteorFall fosters a deeper, intuitive understanding of NEO threats, making it an invaluable tool for public outreach and STEM education.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

MeteorFall is a full-stack web application that provides an immersive, educational experience for understanding the threat of Near-Earth Objects (NEOs). The platform features a Python/Flask backend that fetches real-time 7-day asteroid data from the NASA NeoWs API. This backend processes the data, calculates a hazard level, and serves it to the front end via a REST API. The core of the project is an interactive 3D simulator built with CesiumJS and Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles. Users can select a real asteroid from the fetched list and choose any location on Earth for a simulated impact. The front end then guides the user through an immersive warning and evacuation protocol screen before triggering a 3D animation of the meteor's descent and impact. Finally, it displays a detailed results panel with calculated metrics like crater size, seismic magnitude, and energy release equivalencies (e.g., Hiroshima bombs), visualizing the crater directly on the 3D globe.

What benefits does it have?

The primary benefit of MeteorFall is its ability to translate abstract scientific data into a tangible and personal experience. Instead of just numbers on a scale, users see a visual representation of a crater on a familiar location, making the potential consequences immediately understandable. It serves as a powerful, free, and accessible educational tool for STEM students, educators, and the general public, demystifying complex astrophysics and planetary science concepts. The platform also includes an interactive quiz and pages with historical context to create a comprehensive and engaging learning environment.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to raise public awareness and foster a deeper, more intuitive understanding of planetary defense. By bridging the gap between raw scientific data and public comprehension, we aim to make the threat of NEOs less of a distant sci-fi concept and more of a real-world scientific challenge. Our goal is to inspire curiosity and conversation around the importance of monitoring our skies and developing mitigation strategies, ultimately encouraging more public support and interest in space science and planetary defense initiatives.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Backend: Python with the Flask framework for the REST API, along with Flask-CORS for handling cross-origin requests and requests for interacting with the NASA API.

Frontend: JavaScript (ES6 Modules), HTML5, and CSS3.

Key Libraries/APIs:

CesiumJS: For the core 3D globe visualization and geospatial analysis.

Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles: To provide a high-fidelity, realistic model of the Earth.

NASA NeoWs (Near Earth Object Web Service) API: As the primary source for real-time asteroid data.

Google Places API: To enable the location search functionality in the simulator.

Hardware/Software: No specialized hardware was required. Development was done using standard code editors and web browsers.

How is your project creative?

The creativity of MeteorFall lies in its experiential and narrative-driven approach to data visualization. Instead of a static dashboard, we created an immersive user journey. The project creatively combines:

Real-time Data with Personalization: Users don't just see data; they apply it to a location that matters to them, making the simulation personally resonant.

Immersive UI/UX: The multi-stage UI flow—from selecting a location, to receiving a dramatic evacuation warning, to watching the 3D impact—is a storytelling technique designed to maximize engagement and educational impact.

Aesthetic Cohesion: We developed a complete, high-tech visual identity that is consistent across all pages, from the landing screen to the quiz, making the entire platform feel like a single, polished application.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team prioritized several key factors:

User Experience (UX): The primary consideration was creating a flow that was intuitive, engaging, and easy for a non-expert to understand. We iterated on the UI to ensure the process from selecting an asteroid to seeing the results was clear and compelling.

Educational Value: We focused on not just showing an impact, but explaining why it matters. This led to the inclusion of the "Histórias" section, the risk scale explanations, and the quiz.

Scientific Accuracy: While simplified for a public audience, the physics calculations in our backend are based on established scientific formulas for mass, kinetic energy, and impact effects.

Technical Feasibility and Performance: We chose CesiumJS for its powerful 3D rendering capabilities and a lightweight Flask backend to ensure the application is performant and scalable.

Consistency: We established a strong visual identity early on and applied it consistently across every page and component to create a professional and memorable project.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Our team utilized AI-powered tools to augment our workflow and accelerate key phases of development. The AI served as an assistant under our team's direct guidance in the following areas:

Code & Debugging:

AI was used to expedite the creation of boilerplate code in HTML and CSS, allowing our developers to focus on more complex programming challenges, such as the CesiumJS integration and backend logic. It was also used as a diagnostic tool to help pinpoint errors during debugging sessions.

UI/UX Design & Content:

In the design process, we used AI to rapidly prototype different layout ideas for the user interface. For the submission text, AI was employed as a writing assistant to refine grammar and clarity on the descriptions authored by the team.

Visual Assets:

Our team guided generative AI tools to produce initial concepts for certain visual assets, like the project logo, which were then manually selected and refined to fit the project's aesthetic. These assets are marked in accordance with the challenge rules.

projectDetails.name: Breez
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Breez, a web application that transforms atmospheric science into immediate, personalized health protection. Our project addresses the critical challenge of invisible air pollution by moving beyond static, generalized data to offer hyper-local risk assessments.
The application achieves this by fusing high-resolution satellite data, specifically from NASA's TEMPO mission, with ground-level sensor readings and individual user health profiles. This data fusion allows us to alert vulnerable groups (like asthmatics) to dangerous concentrations of pollutants, such as PM2.5​, NO2​, HCHO and O3 in their immediate location.
This platform is vital because informed decisions are critical for public safety. Breez is an infrastructure designed to empower users to avoid dangerous exposure. Our mission is to create a scalable web platform that makes real-time, personalized air safety a fundamental resource for health management.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Our project, Breez, is a web application designed to visualize and analyze hyper-local air quality (AQI, NO2​, HCHO, O3, PM2.5​) data in real-time. We move beyond generic, city-wide readings by fusing cutting-edge atmospheric satellite data, specifically from NASA's TEMPO mission, with established ground-level sensor information.

The application works by:

  1. Data Ingestion: Utilizing Python scripts to fetch, clean, and process large volumes of raw TEMPO and other relevant data feeds.
  2. AQI Index calculation: we retrieve air quality data from NASA's TEMPO satellite, then interpolate the measurements for each pollutant across our area of interest. After that, we take the maximum value among them to represent local air quality conditions and map the AQI (Air Quality Index) for effective visualization and public health assessment.
  3. Risk Modeling: Processing the data to map out pollutant concentrations at a high spatial resolution.
  4. Personalized Alerts: Integrating a User Profiling System that allows individuals to input vulnerability factors (e.g., asthma, age). The system then calculates and renders a unique, color-coded health risk assessment for their precise location, providing tailored advice.

What benefits does it have?

The core benefit is transforming passive environmental data into actionable, personal safety intelligence.

  • Select Specific Location: Our solution provides users with climate and air quality statistics for any chosen location. Users can access data for their current position or select an alternative place.
  • Select Topographic Source Type: Users have the option to choose from several map appearances to suit their preferences.
  • Get specific advice based on user’s risk group: Our tool delivers tailored advice based on individual user risk profiles, effectively preventing further health complications.
  • Receive air quality and weather forecasts for the upcoming days: Users can access at least four days of forecasted information, helping them to mitigate risks when planning outdoor activities.
  • Mitigation of Health Risks: It empowers vulnerable groups (asthmatics, elderly, children) to immediately adjust their behavior (e.g., closing windows, changing jogging routes) to avoid dangerous exposure to PM2.5​, NO2​, HCHO, O3, thereby preventing acute respiratory and cardiovascular events.
  • Scientific Accessibility: We democratize highly technical satellite data, making complex atmospheric science directly relevant and accessible to the average citizen.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Our intended impact is to establish a new, preventative standard for public health infrastructure. We aim to transform data accessibility into scalable public protection. By referencing tragic cases—where a lack of clear air quality information proved fatal—our project offers a concrete mechanism to ensure that the public is empowered with the precise knowledge needed to safeguard their health daily. Our goal is to foster self-awareness regarding respiratory health. By delivering air quality notifications, we empower individuals to understand when and how to protect their breathing. We seek to build the essential infrastructure for an informed society.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software

Our project uses a modern, scalable web stack:

  • Coding Languages: Python (for data processing and backend logic), JavaScript, ReactJS with tailwind (for the web interface).
  • Core Libraries: Pandas and NumPy for scientific data manipulation, and a GIS library (like Leaflet.js or similar) for interactive map rendering.
  • Backend/API: We utilize a Python framework, fastAPI to manage the data pipeline and serve the web application.
  • Data Sources: NASA TEMPO API/Data Feeds, NASA Rainfall - Model  Data Daymet and other public AQI and weather APIs. 
  • Version Control: Git and GitHub (https://github.com/biabcaval/space_apps_hackaton).

How is your project creative?

The project’s creativity lies in its hyper-local and personalized approach. We creatively integrate high-resolution, satellite-derived atmospheric data (TEMPO) — traditionally used primarily by research institutions — and translate it into a simple, decision-making tool for individual citizens. This pivot from broad scientific visualization to a personalized, actionable risk profile is highly innovative and addresses a critical gap in current public health technology.

What factors did your team consider?

The team prioritized the following critical factors:

  1. Data Latency and Fusion: Successfully blending near-real-time satellite data with ground sensor data to ensure that the delivered information remains timely and actionable for immediate user safety decisions.
  2. User Accessibility (UI/UX): Given that users check air quality during moments of potential urgency, the web interface was designed to be clean, intuitive, and focused solely on the most critical information and safety recommendations.
  3. Vulnerability Logic: Ensuring the personalized alerts accurately reflect the heightened risk faced by individuals with different health conditions (the "at-risk" profiles).

Scalability: Building the data pipeline to be robust and flexible enough to integrate additional new satellite data streams or expanding geographic regions as the project grows.

challengeDetails.excerpt: If you’re planning an outdoor event—like a vacation, a hike on a trail, or fishing on a lake—it would be good to know the chances of adverse weather for the time and location you are considering. There are many types of Earth observation data that can provide information on weather conditions for a particular location and day of the year. Your challenge is to construct an app with a personalized interface that enables users to conduct a customized query to tell them the likelihood of “very hot,” “very cold,” “very windy,” “very wet,” or “very uncomfortable” conditions for the location and time they specify. (Earth Science Division)

projectDetails.name: Neutronics – Shark Foraging Probability Tracker
projectDetails.summary:
Our project creates a predictive framework to identify potential shark foraging areas using a combination of satellite data and field-inspired sensor inputs. We developed a mathematical probability model that integrates environmental variables such as sea surface temperature (SST), chlorophyll concentration, and significant wave height (SWH) to generate interactive maps of shark presence likelihood.

By combining open NASA satellite datasets (SWOT, MODIS, PACE) with real-time ESP32 tag sensor data, the project addresses the challenge of predicting apex predator behavior and supports marine conservation initiatives. This tool is important because it allows scientists and conservationists to visualize, quantify, and predict shark behavior patterns based on environmental drivers, offering a practical and scalable solution for ocean monitoring.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, Neutronics – Shark Foraging Probability Tracker, predicts potential shark foraging areas by combining satellite data and sensor inputs into a single, interpretable probability index. It integrates environmental variables such as Sea Surface Temperature (SST) from MODIS Aqua, chlorophyll concentration (Chl) from PACE, and Significant Wave Height (SWH) from SWOT to generate interactive maps that highlight regions with higher likelihood of shark activity.

How it works:

  1. Environmental datasets are preprocessed, resampled to a common spatial grid, and normalized.
  2. A weighted probability formula combines the variables:

I=α⋅(1−∣SST−SSTopt∣ΔSST)+β⋅Chlmax⁡(Chl)+γ⋅(1−SWHmax⁡(SWH))I = \alpha \cdot \left(1 - \frac{|SST - SST_{opt}|}{\Delta SST}\right) + \beta \cdot \frac{Chl}{\max(Chl)} + \gamma \cdot \left(1 - \frac{SWH}{\max(SWH)}\right)I=α⋅(1−ΔSST∣SST−SSTopt​∣​)+β⋅max(Chl)Chl​+γ⋅(1−max(SWH)SWH​)

  1. The formula produces an index from 0 (low probability) to 1 (high probability) for each region.
  2. Interactive heatmaps are generated with folium, allowing users to visualize intensity values, zoom, and explore areas of interest.
  3. Field-inspired ESP32 tags provide local environmental data that can enhance model predictions in real time.

Benefits & Impact:

  • Identifies potential shark feeding hotspots, supporting marine conservation and sustainable fishing policies.
  • Provides a tool for researchers and educators to visualize predator-prey dynamics.
  • Encourages data-driven decision-making for ocean monitoring and ecosystem management.
  • Offers a scalable and open-source solution that can be applied to other marine species.

Creativity & Considerations:

  • Combines satellite datasets with IoT sensor data, providing a hybrid model that bridges remote sensing and in-situ measurements.
  • Designed for interpretability and accessibility, enabling non-experts to understand shark behavior patterns.
  • Considered factors such as optimal temperature ranges, nutrient availability, and wave conditions to realistically reflect ecological drivers.

Tools & Technologies Used:

  • Programming Languages: Python (NumPy, xarray, rasterio, folium, matplotlib)
  • Hardware: ESP32 sensor tag for environmental monitoring
  • Data Sources: NASA PACE, MODIS Aqua, SWOT
  • Visualization & Processing: Google Colab, NetCDF, GeoTIFF, interactive HTML maps

This project is innovative because it merges advanced environmental monitoring with simple, interpretable mathematical modeling, providing a practical tool for understanding apex predator behavior in the ocean.

challengeDetails.title: Sharks from Space
challengeDetails.excerpt: Earth’s ocean is one of the most powerful habitats in our universe, supporting a range of life that sustains ecosystems and habitability across the globe. It is common to measure photosynthetic activity in the ocean from space, but far more challenging to track top predators. Your challenge is to create a mathematical framework for identifying sharks and predicting their foraging habitats using NASA satellite data, and also to suggest a new conceptual model of a tag (a small electronic device that can be attached to an animal to track and study its movement) that could measure not only where sharks are, but also what they are eating, and in real time transmit that data back to users to enable development of predictive models. (Earth Science Division)

projectDetails.name: Project Orion Dynamics - AstroClima
projectDetails.summary:
AstroClima is an interactive web platform developed for long-term climatic risk analysis. It addresses the challenge of planning outdoor activities, where uncertainty beyond the scope of short-term weather forecasts often leads to financial loss and frustration.
Our solution empowers users to make data-driven decisions by leveraging decades of historical data from the NASA POWER API. A user inputs a location, a future date, and their specific tolerances for conditions like rain, wind, and temperature. In response, our platform provides a simple, personalized "Climatic Risk Score," instantly showing the historical probability of adverse weather for that specific context.
Its importance lies in democratizing complex NASA data, translating it into an accessible and practical tool for everyone, from event organizers to tourists. AstroClima replaces guesswork with statistical insight, enabling smarter, safer, and more confident planning for any future outdoor event.
projectDetails.details:
Detalhes do Projeto: AstroClima

O que faz ou como funciona?

AstroClima é uma plataforma web interativa desenvolvida para análise de risco climático de longo prazo. Ele fornece aos usuários a probabilidade histórica de condições climáticas adversas para qualquer local específico e data futura, permitindo um planejamento mais inteligente para atividades ao ar livre.

Ele funciona por meio de um processo automatizado e contínuo de três etapas:

Entrada e geocodificação do usuário: O usuário insere um local de evento (por exemplo, "Praia de Tambaú, João Pessoa"), uma data futura e suas tolerâncias pessoais para as condições climáticas usando controles interativos (por exemplo, temperatura acima de 30°C, tolerância para "chuva leve" etc.). Nosso back-end usa a API Nominatim para converter instantaneamente o nome do local em coordenadas geográficas precisas.

Recuperação de dados históricos: Essas coordenadas são então enviadas para a NASA POWER API, que contém mais de três décadas de dados globais de satélite. Nosso sistema solicita os registros históricos para a data específica fornecida, em todos os anos disponíveis, para parâmetros como temperatura, precipitação e velocidade do vento.

Análise e visualização de risco: nosso back-end Python processa esse vasto conjunto de dados. Ele calcula a probabilidade estatística de ocorrência das condições de "mau tempo" definidas pelo usuário, com base em quantas vezes elas ocorreram no passado. Em seguida, ele retorna uma "Pontuação de Risco Climático" simples e personalizada e gráficos detalhados para o painel do usuário.

Que benefícios tem?

O AstroClima oferece quatro benefícios principais:

Reduz o risco financeiro e operacional: Ao substituir as suposições por dados, ajudamos os organizadores de eventos, gerentes de construção e agricultores a evitar cancelamentos, atrasos e perdas dispendiosos causados por condições climáticas imprevistas.

Democratiza o acesso à ciência: Traduzimos dados científicos complexos e brutos da NASA em uma ferramenta intuitiva e acionável. Isso permite que qualquer pessoa, independentemente do conhecimento técnico, aproveite o poder da observação da Terra baseada no espaço.

Permite um planejamento hiperpersonalizado: a análise da plataforma é adaptada à definição específica de "risco" de cada usuário, fornecendo insights muito mais relevantes do que as médias climáticas genéricas.

Economiza tempo e aumenta a confiança: Nossa plataforma fornece uma resposta clara e baseada em dados em segundos, simplificando o processo de tomada de decisão e dando aos planejadores a confiança para se comprometer com datas, reservar locais e assinar contratos.

Qual é o impacto pretendido do projeto?

Nosso impacto pretendido é mudar fundamentalmente o planejamento de longo prazo de um ato de fé para uma estratégia baseada em dados. Para a indústria de eventos, um setor que contribui com quase 4% para o PIB nacional, isso significa proteger bilhões em receita e promover uma economia mais resiliente. Para o usuário individual, desde uma família planejando férias até um organizador comunitário planejando um festival local, nosso impacto é capacitá-los com um nível de análise de dados anteriormente acessível apenas a cientistas. Nosso objetivo é promover uma cultura de planejamento mais inteligente, seguro e confiante para todos.

Quais ferramentas, linguagens de codificação, hardware ou software você usou para desenvolver seu projeto?

Back-end: Python com o framework Flask.

Frontend: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript.

Visualização de dados: Chart.js biblioteca.

Banco de dados: MySQL Server para gerenciamento de dados de usuários e eventos.

APIs externas:

NASA POWER API: Para dados climáticos históricos.

API Nominatim (OpenStreetMap): Para geocodificação de endereços em coordenadas.

Hardware: Como um aplicativo totalmente baseado na web, o AstroClima não requer hardware especializado para o usuário final, sendo acessível a partir de qualquer navegador moderno em um computador ou dispositivo móvel.

Como seu projeto é criativo?

A criatividade do AstroClima não está na agregação de dados, mas na tradução de dados. Enquanto os aplicativos meteorológicos preveem o futuro e os portais científicos apresentam o passado, nossa plataforma ocupa de forma única o espaço intermediário.

O salto criativo está reformulando a questão central de "Qual será o clima?" para "Qual é o risco histórico de mau tempo?". Transformamos dados climáticos históricos brutos e complexos em uma pontuação de probabilidade simples, acionável e voltada para o futuro. Essa abordagem centrada no usuário, combinada com uma interface radicalmente simples, torna décadas de pesquisa científica da NASA acessíveis e úteis para um público não técnico pela primeira vez.

Quais fatores sua equipe considerou?

Nossa equipe considerou vários fatores-chave ao longo do processo de design:

Design centrado no usuário: Nossa principal consideração foi criar uma ferramenta radicalmente simples. Cada decisão foi tomada para reduzir a complexidade e garantir que o usuário pudesse obter uma resposta valiosa com o mínimo de esforço.

Viabilidade de mercado: Realizamos pesquisas para identificar o setor com o "ponto problemático" mais imediato e quantificável - a indústria de eventos - como nosso mercado-alvo inicial, enquanto projetamos a ferramenta para ser flexível o suficiente para expansão futura na agricultura, construção e turismo.

Viabilidade técnica: Escolhemos uma pilha de tecnologia robusta, escalável e econômica, contando com tecnologias comprovadas de código aberto (Python, MySQL) e APIs públicas confiáveis e gratuitas (NASA POWER, Nominatim) para garantir que o projeto fosse alcançável dentro de um escopo de hackathon.

Credibilidade e confiança dos dados: Usamos exclusivamente a NASA como nossa fonte de dados para garantir o mais alto grau de precisão e credibilidade, o que é fundamental para uma ferramenta que influencia decisões financeiras e operacionais significativas.
