projectDetails.name: Project Pindorama
projectDetails.summary: The Global Life Cities (GLC) project is a digital platform designed to integrate and visualize environmental, climatic, and urban data to support sustainable urban planning. It is based on the use of open scientific databases from NASA, INPE, INMET, MapBiomas, and other sources, transforming complex information into accessible and interpretable indicators for policymakers, researchers, and citizens. Through the VMAP method — Visualize, Map, Monitor, and Plan — the tool enables the analysis of variables such as temperature, vegetation cover, precipitation, and pollution, identifying vulnerable areas and assisting in the formulation of evidence-based public policies. The system also allows natural language queries, promoting intuitive interaction and expanding access to scientific information. The GLC aims to democratize the use of environmental data and foster the development of smart, resilient, and sustainable cities, aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 11. Thus, the platform contributes to strengthening urban governance, monitoring climate risks, and enhancing civic participation, establishing itself as an innovative tool to support decision-making and sustainable territorial management.
projectDetails.details:
INTRODUCTION

Uncontrolled urban growth, present in many of our realities, perpetuates an unsustainable model of development in the construction sector. This dynamic directly undermines progress toward the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) on sustainable cities and communities (SDG 11) in capitals around the world. As a tragic illustration of this failure, we bring the story of Pedro Ximenes, a resident of Greater Recife. In 2022, the capital of Pernambuco faced severe floods, whose impacts could have been significantly reduced through proper urban planning focused on sustainability. Therefore, it becomes essential to collect and consolidate data that serve as a foundation for the formulation of future public policies. Implementing such measures is crucial to prevent the recurrence of events like the one experienced by Pedro Ximenes, enabling us to achieve urban planning that is truly ideal and sustainable for each locality.

“I went through the 2022 flood, and it was heartbreaking to see my home and neighborhood underwater due to the lack of urban planning. We lost our furniture and tried to rebuild our lives in the following months, but the fear of going through that again led my family to move, in December 2022, to an apartment on the fourth floor, seeking more safety.”
—Pedro Ximenes

When discussing urbanization, it is impossible to ignore the complex web that shapes urban spaces, both globally and nationally, and the studies that examine them. The great challenge of contemporary urban planning is to reconcile rapid growth with sustainability and social justice. Thinkers such as Milton Santos and David Harvey have long pointed out that urbanization is inseparable from the logic of capital accumulation, which produces deeply unequal spaces. In this context, planning often functions as a mere “ideological tool” rather than prioritizing social well-being. This inequality is shaped by the actions of various urban agents, as analyzed by Horácio Capel and Roberto Lobato Corrêa, making the struggle for the “right to the city,” defended by Marcelo Lopes de Souza, an urgent cause. Instruments such as Special Zones of Social Interest (ZEIS) represent an attempt to counter this exclusionary logic.

Today, a new factor worsens this situation: the climate emergency. Extreme weather events, heat islands, and pollution directly threaten the health and infrastructure of cities. In this context, it is crucial that planning incorporates Earth science. Observation data, such as those provided by NASA (surface temperature, precipitation, air and water quality), emerge as powerful tools to transform urban management. With them, local leaders and communities can actively build more resilient and equitable cities.

Source: Adapted (2025) from European Parliament (2014)

Knowledge-Based Urban Development (KBUD) (Yigitcanlar & Lonnqvist, 2013) is founded on the idea that knowledge is a driving force behind the processes of wealth generation and sustainable development. A true transformation of cities and societies is expected to occur through the enhancement of their capacities to attract, generate, retain, and foster creativity, knowledge, and innovation (Knight, 1995; Yigitcanlar, 2011, as cited in Sabatini-Marques, 2016).

Source: Adapted (2025) from Yigitcanlar and Lonnqvist (2013)

To bring this discussion into our reality, we will analyze the case of João Pessoa, whose urban planning reflects similar challenges. Below, we present the anonymous testimony of a city resident, illustrating how these dynamics manifest in everyday life.

“Walking around João Pessoa, PB, you can really see how fast the city has been growing. On one side, there are huge buildings and well-structured neighborhoods; on the other, there are entire communities without sanitation, with pothole-ridden streets and houses built in risk areas. The inequality and lack of urban planning are very clear here when we compare it to other capitals. Sometimes it feels like the city just kept expanding without thinking about people just occupying whatever space was available, without care for the environment or even for the quality of life of those who live here.”
—Anonymous

THE PROBLEM

Our data analysis confirms the causes of the flooding in Greater Recife, mentioned in Pedro Ximenes’s testimony. The region already had soil with a low absorption capacity, and in the weeks leading up to the disaster, it experienced an extremely high rainfall index. Factors such as increased wind speed intensified the rain clouds over the area, resulting in an extreme event: the volume of rain expected for two months fell in just 24 hours.

This concentration of clouds was clearly visible in satellite images from INPE, using the infrared bands of the Sentinel and Landsat satellites. Such technologies are crucial and could serve as an early warning tool for preventive public policies.

The consequences were devastating. In quantitative terms, the material loss suffered by a single person like Pedro Ximenes, including his home, exceeded an economic impact of US$100,000. Beyond the financial damage, the contamination of the area and the amount of waste carried into the waterways were immense.

Now, multiply this scenario by millions of Brazilians living in risk areas. The failure of urban planning reveals a billion-dollar problem in Brazil, creating a massive burden on public finances with each new disaster. In light of this, it is urgent that the urban planning system incorporates sustainability as a central pillar, ensuring that tragedies like this do not happen again.

GAP

There is a vast universe of data within our information networks that, if connected to society and researchers, could drive the development of more effective public policies. However, there is a clear disconnect between data scientists and the community.

Source: Own production.

On one hand, the population generally lacks access to or familiarity with advanced tools that could alert them to environmental risks in their regions. On the other hand, this same lack of access prevents citizens from using studies and data to demand preventive action from the government, such as monitoring areas unsuitable for construction or vulnerable to disasters. Overcoming this barrier is essential for intelligent and participatory public management.

SOLUTION

To bridge the gap between data and action, we present Global Life Cities (GLC). Our platform was created to be the meeting point between society, government, researchers, and companies—bringing all spheres together in one place. The goal of GLC is clear: to provide the tools and data necessary to develop more sustainable cities and effective public policies. We aim for our platform to be the ideal choice for promoting human development in increasingly resilient and intelligent urban centers. All of this is supported by a strong research framework and guided by our exclusive method, VMAP: Visualize the challenges, Map the solutions, Assess the progress, and Plan the improvements.

Source:

Own production.

HOW IT WORKS

The Global Life Cities (GLC) platform allows city planners and residents to interact intuitively using natural language queries. Instead of dealing with complex spreadsheets, a planner can simply ask:
"Which neighborhoods recorded the highest land surface temperatures (LST) last summer, indicating heat islands, and where should we prioritize the creation of new green spaces?"

The system processes the request, accesses the latest data, and delivers a clear, visual, and accurate response. The interface supports queries about current conditions, historical trend analyses—such as soil impermeabilization expansion or an area’s water vulnerability—and even provides predictive insights for climate resilience planning.

Most importantly, the platform promotes transparency and collaboration: society can not only follow the entire process in real time but also participate actively, helping decision-makers build a more sustainable region for everyone.

PRODUCT DEMONSTRATION – (GLC) Global Life Cities

Experience the power of our platform in this project demonstration, which showcases how complex Earth Observation data becomes instantly accessible through a conversational interface. This model demonstrates how municipal planners and citizens can easily interact with critical geospatial information — such as Heat Island (LST) maps, Water Risk Zones (GPM), and Green Space Scarcity — using simple and intuitive commands.

The tool translates the complexity of science into direct and actionable insights, democratizing access to vital information for climate resilience and equitable urban planning.

Access the Project
Platform Demonstration:
https://globallifecities.vercel.app

<colgroup><col></colgroup>

PRODUCT FEATURES

  1. Practical and functional approach to addressing housing and population challenges, guided by the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of each region in a goal-oriented format. Through collaboration between companies and communities, the platform promotes global well-being and development.
  2. Connection between researchers and the system, ensuring that university research does not remain confined to academia but is actively applied to the creation of effective public policies.
  3. Use of highly validated data, guaranteeing accuracy, reliability, and scientific rigor in every analysis and recommendation.
  4. Collaboration between communities and companies, fostering collective action and shared responsibility for building smarter, more sustainable, and socially inclusive cities.

IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS

  • Data Integration: Our system aggregates geospatial data from NASA and meteorological sources, ensuring up-to-date and reliable information for each region.
  • Real-Time Processing: The platform provides instant responses by processing data in real time, which is crucial for informed and timely urban decision-making in each area.

IMPACT

By democratizing access to critical NASA environmental data, our platform empowers planners and communities to protect and enhance urban quality of life through evidence-based decisions. Acting at the forefront of climate resilience, it serves as an early warning and risk mitigation system, enabling users to take proactive measures against threats such as extreme heat from urban heat islands and flood hazards. The impact extends beyond individual neighborhoods — with fairer and more equitable planning, large-scale adoption of this technology can drastically reduce the economic and social losses caused by climate disasters and uncontrolled urban expansion, building a safer future for everyone.

Source: Center for Strategic Studies and Debates (2014), Adapted (2025).

CASE STUDY

If the urban planner responsible for Mr. Pedro Ximenes’s region had access to our platform, he and his family could have avoided the loss of their material possessions, valued at over US$100,000. With the alerts and data provided, the planner could have implemented preventive measures or coordinated an evacuation with local authorities, drastically reducing the impact of the disaster. If problems like this continue, we will reach a point in history from which there will be no return.

FUTURE WORK

  • Collaboration with Authorities: Establish partnerships with government agencies and NGOs to disseminate the tool and provide training for its effective use, ensuring broader institutional adoption and social impact.
  • Implementation of Georeferencing: Improve georeferenced information for each region with the support of researchers, enhancing the precision and spatial relevance of environmental and urban data.
  • Resolution of Local SDGs: Strengthen the focus on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in each region, fostering community-based improvements tailored to local needs and challenges.
  • Business Enabler: Empower local and national companies by increasing their visibility and engagement within the system, promoting sustainable innovation and economic growth.
  • Project Monitoring: Enhance the quality and localization of data to enable more efficient monitoring of urban developments and public infrastructure projects.
  • Strategic Regional Visions: Provide targeted insights for each region, enabling the identification and resolution of key urban and environmental challenges through strategic missions.
  • Research Collaboration: Build a strong network of universities and research institutions to ensure that academic studies are transformed into practical public policies, driving real social and environmental progress.

CONCLUSION

We have reached a crucial crossroads: the urban reality, marked by socio-spatial inequality (Milton Santos, Roberto Lobato Corrêa) and the pressures of capital (David Harvey), is now further aggravated by the imminence of the climate crisis. The future of cities and of their inhabitants, who continue to fight for the right to the city (Marcelo Lopes de Souza), can no longer be planned by intuition or in reaction to disasters.

Our project proposes a qualitative leap: we transform raw, mapped reality such as extreme heat, water vulnerability, and the lack of green areas into an actionable roadmap for the future. By integrating INPE data and applying land use and land cover classification and forecasting within GLC – Global Life Cities, we remove the complexity of science and deliver it democratically and immediately into the hands of planners like Pedro and the entire community. It is the opportunity to abandon inertia and use the precision of satellite-enhanced reality to build resilience proactively.

The power of the platform lies not only in alerting about the next heatwave or flood but also in justifying and guiding every cent invested in green infrastructure. It marks the end of blind planning and the beginning of a management model where sustainability and equity are the central metrics.

By facing the reality revealed through data, we ensure that every decision made today leads us toward a tomorrow where quality of life and ecosystem protection are not exceptions, but the very rule of the city.
VMAP – Visualize, Map, Assess, and Plan!

projectDetails.name: Project Programa.AI
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, EcoAir, tackles the invisible yet deadly problem of air pollution by transforming complex environmental data into actionable insights. Air pollution is responsible for millions of premature deaths each year, but the danger often goes unnoticed. EcoAir provides a practical solution: a monitoring system capable of detecting carbon monoxide (CO) in real time, storing results in a database, and displaying them through an interactive map. With simple visual cues—green for good, yellow for moderate, red for unhealthy—the system translates invisible threats into clear, accessible information for citizens, governments, and businesses.

This approach empowers individuals to protect their health, supports policymakers in designing evidence-based strategies, and encourages companies to adopt sustainable practices. By integrating sensor data with global sources such as the OpenAQ API, EcoAir demonstrates both local relevance and global scalability. More than a technology, it is a tool for awareness, prevention, and collective action toward cleaner, safer skies.
projectDetails.details:
EcoAir is an innovative environmental monitoring project that addresses one of today’s most urgent global challenges: air pollution. Its core purpose is to make the invisible threats of polluted air visible, measurable, and understandable to all.

Our system is built around a low-cost prototype that detects carbon monoxide (CO) using the MQ-9 gas sensor connected to an ESP32 microcontroller. The sensor captures real-time readings in parts per million (PPM), which are transmitted to a central database. From there, the data is processed and displayed in a visual platform: an interactive map that uses a simple color-coded system—green for good, yellow for moderate, and red for unhealthy air quality. This design ensures that highly technical information is translated into insights that any person, regardless of background, can interpret and act upon.

The benefits of EcoAir extend across multiple levels of society. For citizens, the system provides preventive health empowerment. Vulnerable groups such as children, the elderly, and individuals with respiratory conditions can check local air quality in real time to make informed decisions about daily activities—whether it’s choosing a safer route for walking, deciding the best time for exercise, or knowing when to stay indoors. For communities, the visualization of pollution hotspots raises awareness and fosters civic engagement, encouraging collective action and demanding stronger environmental policies. Governments and policymakers benefit from evidence-based insights that support urban planning, emission control strategies, and crisis response in cases like industrial accidents or wildfires. For companies, the system serves as a responsibility and efficiency tool, helping them monitor their own emissions, comply with environmental regulations, and even enhance their ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) commitments.

The intended impact of EcoAir is twofold: first, to protect human life and health by reducing exposure to harmful pollutants, and second, to influence systemic change by democratizing air quality data. By making pollution visible and understandable, we create pressure and opportunity for communities, businesses, and governments to act, turning data into a driver of environmental justice.

From a technical perspective, EcoAir combines hardware prototyping and software integration. Hardware includes the MQ-9 sensor and ESP32 microcontroller. Software involves the development of a robust API, designed and implemented by five full-stack developers, using modern technologies such as React, Node.js, Spring Boot, Java, PostgreSQL, AWS, Render, Vite, and JavaScript. The data pipeline captures, stores, and serves information efficiently through APIs, alongside a visualization interface built with mapping libraries and interactive dashboards. Integration with the OpenAQ API validates local measurements and situates them in a global context, creating an ecosystem where local and global data reinforce each other.

EcoAir is creative and original because it bridges multiple disciplines: environmental science, public health, civic technology, and data visualization. Rather than focusing solely on measurement, we designed a solution that prioritizes accessibility, simplicity, and scalability. A citizen does not need to understand parts per million or chemical reactions; instead, they see a color-coded map that immediately communicates risk. This simplicity, combined with the low cost of sensors, makes it possible to scale the solution globally, especially in underserved regions where monitoring infrastructure is limited.

In building EcoAir, our team considered several key factors:

  • Accessibility: ensuring the solution is affordable, easy to use, and interpretable for any audience.
  • Scalability: designing a modular system that can expand from monitoring a single gas (CO) to multiple pollutants (NO₂, SO₂, PM2.5, O₃).
  • Reliability: storing historical data for long-term analysis and validating our measurements through comparison with international datasets.
  • Public impact: emphasizing not just the technology itself but its potential to save lives, reduce healthcare costs, and empower communities to demand cleaner environments.
  • Sustainability: considering environmental, social, and governance dimensions so that the project benefits individuals, governments, industries, and the planet.

In summary, EcoAir is more than a prototype—it is a vision for a healthier, safer, and fairer future. By turning the invisible dangers of air pollution into clear, actionable insights, we empower individuals and institutions alike to take informed action. Our approach integrates cutting-edge technology with social impact, proving that data, when made accessible, can become a powerful catalyst for change.

projectDetails.summary:
We developed an educational board game called Histórias Estelares: The Climate of Space Through the Eyes of Earthlings. Our goal was to explain the concept of space weather how solar phenomena like flares and coronal mass ejections affect Earth in a fun and accessible way.
The game is designed for four players and includes 60 spaces. Each space reveals real scientific events, and every six spaces, players scan a QR code that unlocks parts of an interactive story. To progress, players must answer questions related to what they’ve learned, combining knowledge, strategy, and engagement.
Our project addresses the challenge of making complex scientific topics understandable and exciting for students. By merging science, technology, and storytelling, Histórias Estelares turns learning about the Sun and space into an immersive and memorable adventure.
projectDetails.details: Our project is an educational board game for children called Histórias Estelares, designed to teach about solar eruptions and their effects on Earth in a fun and interactive way. The game simulates the journey of space events from the Sun to our planet, showing how these eruptions can interfere with satellites, communication systems, and even cause visual phenomena like the aurora borealis.The goal of the project is to make concepts of space weather accessible to children, promoting learning through gameplay and storytelling, encouraging scientific curiosity and understanding of the Sun's and space’s importance for life on Earth

projectDetails.name: Cosmic Tales
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Cosmic Tales / Stellar Stories, an interactive educational web platform that explains space weather and its impacts on Earth through engaging narratives, scientific visualizations, and real-time data. We used NASA’s DONKI and NOAA’s SWPC APIs to provide up-to-date information on solar flares, coronal mass ejections, and geomagnetic storms. Through interactive stories (such as “The Farmer José’s GPS” and “Guardians of the Power Grid”) and a canvas-based spaceship game, we connect scientific concepts to everyday situations.

This project addresses the challenge of making space science accessible to young audiences and the general public, promoting education and awareness about phenomena that affect critical infrastructure, communication, and daily life.
projectDetails.details:
Cosmic Tales / Stellar Stories is an interactive web platform that transforms complex space weather data into engaging stories and visual experiences. It works by integrating APIs from NASA’s DONKI and NOAA’s SWPC to display real-time information about solar activity—such as solar flares and geomagnetic storms, combined with educational storytelling and mini-games that connect these phenomena to everyday life on Earth.

The platform benefits users by making scientific knowledge accessible and enjoyable, helping people understand how space weather affects technology, power grids, satellites, and communication systems. Its intended impact is to promote space science literacy and inspire curiosity about how our planet interacts with the Sun.

We developed the project using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages with Vercel. The design emphasizes immersion, storytelling, and educational value, blending science communication and gamification.

Our team focused on accessibility, engagement, and visual clarity—creating a balance between scientific accuracy and creative storytelling to reach audiences of all ages and backgrounds.

  • Suggest front-end structure, styling, and layout ideas for the website.

All AI-generated content was reviewed, adjusted, and validated by our team to ensure scientific accuracy, originality, and compliance with NASA Space Apps rules.

projectDetails.name: Hi, I'm the Sun!
projectDetails.summary:
Our project consists of telling a story about space weather in an educational and creative way, through the interactive digital book "Hi, I'm the Sun" for children.
Our story centers on the relationship between the Sun and Earth, from the perspective of the Sun itself, which curiously observes the growth of life on Earth and warns about the challenges posed by space weather. Our goal is to convey, in a concise, simple, and lively way, to a young audience (ages 7 to 10), some of the phenomena that occur from this interaction. We believe in the power of storytelling and creative writing to bring young people closer to science and scientific communication, sparking curiosity about the universe and highlighting the importance of scientific research for the future of humanity and our planet.
projectDetails.details:
The project was developed as an integrative project of Graphic Design and Scientific Communication with the educational and entertaining purpose of children's literature. Our main objectives were:

  1. Target Audience:

Our project aims to be accessible to children aged 7 and older, when their literacy skills are more advanced. It provides information on some phenomena related to the relationship between the Sun and Earth, such as Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) and their influence on our planet and human technologies. The project uses accessible, simple, and introductory language, aiming to increase audience engagement in the gradual development of science education.

  1. Storytelling:

Among the possible storyline choices regarding space weather, we understood that the Sun and its influence on the planets, including Earth, would be the primary link between the topics we could address. Therefore, working from the Sun's perspective, introducing human aspects to present itself and its relationship to space weather, could result in a more charismatic narrator, close to children, and a more comprehensive story for better assimilation by the target audience.

  1. Design:

Our team focused on incorporating scientific elements into a playful environment that resonates with children. We also considered interactivity a key factor, creating mechanisms that engage the reader's attention and help them retain crucial information from the text.

  1. Science communication:

The project aims to raise awareness of the impact of space weather on humanity. Due to today's society's high dependence on information and communication technologies, with younger generations developing within this context, understanding the relationship between these astronomical events and life on Earth is crucial.


Tools and Languages Used

  • Prototyping: Figma
  • Illustration and design: Photoshop
  • Organization: Trello / Google drive /  Discord

projectDetails.name: João Pessoa 2030: Data Pathways to Healthy Cities
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, João Pessoa 2030, was developed under the theme “Data Pathways to Healthy Cities and Human Settlements”, aiming to turn spatial data into actionable insights for sustainable urban planning. We created an interactive platform that visually and accessibly illustrates how urban expansion between 2000 and 2030 impacts environmental balance and access to essential services.

Using data from NASA, WorldPop, and IBGE, we identified the areas most affected by vegetation loss and proposed strategic regions for new housing and healthcare facilities, considering population growth and the need for environmental preservation.

The platform also integrates an urban expansion analysis and forecasting algorithm, which uses historical satellite imagery. It applies color clustering (K-Means) to identify urbanized areas and linear regression to project growth up to the target year. This allows for data-driven insights on where urban development is likely to occur and where environmental protection is most needed.

This project is important because it translates complex data into understandable and actionable insights, supporting policymakers and the public in making sustainable decisions that balance urban development, healthcare access, and environmental preservation in João Pessoa.
projectDetails.details:
João Pessoa 2030 is an interactive platform developed in Python using Streamlit, designed to turn spatial and demographic data into accessible and dynamic visualizations. The application allows users to explore João Pessoa’s urban expansion from 2000 to 2030, highlighting areas most affected by vegetation loss and suggesting strategic regions for new housing and healthcare facilities.

The platform includes an urban expansion analysis and forecasting algorithm that uses historical satellite imagery. It applies color clustering (K-Means) to identify urbanized areas and linear regression to project growth up to the target year. This approach allows for data-driven insights on where urban development is likely to occur and where environmental preservation is most critical.

The main benefits include visual understanding of urban growth, support for sustainable urban management, and reduction of inequalities in infrastructure access. The intended impact is to enable data-driven decision-making that balances urban development, environmental preservation, and healthcare accessibility.

The project’s creativity lies in integrating multiple data sources — NASA, WorldPop, IBGE, and local environmental data — into a single, intuitive interface that transforms technical data into an educational and actionable tool. Our team considered factors such as information accessibility, visual clarity, applicability for policymakers, and the environmental and social impact of the city’s growth.

projectDetails.name: WeatherData — Weather and Renewable Energy Insights
projectDetails.summary:
The WeatherData project was developed in response to NASA’s “Will It Rain on My Parade?” challenge. It provides a clean, intuitive interface that allows users to explore local climate conditions for a specific date, time, and location, showing probabilities of extreme heat, wind, humidity, or rainfall, aligned with the challenge’s goals.
Beyond that, our team expanded the project with an additional renewable energy insights module, transforming the same climatic datasets into actionable information for sustainability. This second panel uses data from NASA POWER to estimate solar and wind potential (kWh/m²) for each city, helping users identify areas with high renewable generation capacity.
Users can explore metrics such as solar angle, irradiation index, air density, and wind velocity, which are crucial for understanding renewable resource availability. By combining weather risk analysis with clean energy insights, ClimaData strengthens environmental awareness and supports informed decision-making for sustainable development.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do / How does it work?

ClimaData combines weather forecasting with renewable energy potential analysis. The “Weather” panel displays local climate probabilities (temperature, rain, wind, humidity, cloud cover) for a given date, time, and location. The “Renewable Energy” panel translates this climate data into energy indicators, showing solar and wind potential, and allowing comparisons between cities using NASA POWER datasets.

Technologies and Tools Used:

  • Front-end: HTML, CSS, JavaScript; Back-end: Python with Fast API

  • Data Visualization: Chart.js

  • APIs: NASA POWER (primary dataset)

  • Design: Figma

  • Hosting & Demo: GitHub Pages / Netlify

Why is it important?

By merging climate prediction and renewable energy potential, ClimaData provides valuable insights for both individual users (planning outdoor activities) and institutions or energy researchers interested in identifying locations for sustainable energy generation. It highlights the global importance of open NASA data for climate adaptation and energy transition strategies.
projectDetails.aiReferences: We used AI tools (ChatGPT) exclusively to assist with concept refinement, data interpretation, and scientific understanding of renewable energy variables, such as solar irradiation and wind potential.All design, coding, and development were created by our team.

challengeDetails.title: Will It Rain On My Parade?
challengeDetails.excerpt: If you’re planning an outdoor event—like a vacation, a hike on a trail, or fishing on a lake—it would be good to know the chances of adverse weather for the time and location you are considering. There are many types of Earth observation data that can provide information on weather conditions for a particular location and day of the year. Your challenge is to construct an app with a personalized interface that enables users to conduct a customized query to tell them the likelihood of “very hot,” “very cold,” “very windy,” “very wet,” or “very uncomfortable” conditions for the location and time they specify. (Earth Science Division)

projectDetails.name: TempoCerto/ RigWeather
projectDetails.summary: RigthTime is a conversational climate assistant that saves people time by delivering long-term weather insights in the simplest possible way. Built as both a web dashboard and a WhatsApp chatbot, it allows users to send a message—or even a voice note—and instantly receive precise climate predictions for any chosen date, up to six months ahead. Using real Earth observation data and a predictive model with around 85% accuracy, the system estimates probabilities of rain, extreme temperatures, humidity, or discomfort levels for a given location and time. Unlike traditional weather apps, TimeCerto focuses on accessibility and communication: people can interact naturally without needing technical knowledge. Whether you are planning a trip, an event, or outdoor activity, TimeCerto helps you decide the best moment—because not even Saint Peter was ever this precise.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is an interactive dashboard and chatbot that provides long-term weather predictions in a simple, accessible way. Using machine learning models trained in Python and stored as .pkl files, the system predicts future weather conditions for a selected location and date—up to six months ahead—with an accuracy between 85% and 87%. It combines data processing and prediction using Google Colab, VS Code, and Docker for deployment. The chatbot component, built with n8n and integrated with ChatGPT, allows users to send text or voice messages through WhatsApp to ask about future climate conditions, receiving responses naturally, without needing to browse a website or interpret complex data.

The main benefit is saving time: people can get reliable predictions instantly, in a conversational way. This increases accessibility for everyone, including those less familiar with technology. The creative aspect lies in merging artificial intelligence, conversational design, and predictive modeling to make climate forecasting more human-centered. Our team’s main consideration was time efficiency—making accurate environmental information available as fast and naturally as possible.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Artificial Intelligence was employed in our project primarily to accelerate development, maintain code consistency, and improve efficiency during the limited challenge time frame of less than two days. AI tools were used to assist in debugging and front-end generation through prompt-based design platforms, including V0, which enabled rapid interface creation.

In the back-end, Python APIs were developed with support from Gemini for code refinement and optimization, while Node.js handled audio-to-text transcription using generative AI from Grok. This model efficiently converted voice messages into text, allowing natural language interaction within the system.

Additionally, AI was used to enhance natural language processing for user requests in our chatbot, ensuring that spoken or written messages were interpreted accurately and routed correctly to the APIs.

The integration of AI served as a supportive layer rather than a replacement for human creativity. All AI-generated outputs—code, text, or models—were verified, edited, and validated by our team. This approach allowed us to deliver a more consistent, accessible, and intelligent experience while maintaining originality and intentional design.

projectDetails.summary: What if we could empower every citizen to be a data scientist for their own city? Our solution allows users to create a personalized dashboard to gain insights into the probability of specific weather conditions. Our project changes this dynamic, turning weather forecasting into a tool for investigation and active citizenship. We combine a strategic and investigative approach to development to create solutions that are not only innovative but also relevant and high-impact for our community. Our focus is to build a bridge between NASA's global data and local needs.
projectDetails.details:
Welcome to RAIN!

​Exploring RAIN

​The experience begins on the homepage, where you can start your journey in English or Portuguese.

For anyone organizing an outdoor activity—from a family picnic to a wedding—weather uncertainty is a major hurdle. Fortunately, the vast range of Earth observation data offers us historical insights into weather behavior. By selecting the Desired location filter, you tell our system where to analyze.

Now, simply use the Atmospheric conditions filter to tell us when, and we will calculate the chances of good weather for you in a Single moment or a Continuous range.

When calculating the chances of good weather in the Continuous range filter, dynamic charts are displayed on the screen, revealing the probabilities of climatic thresholds such as temperature, wind, and precipitation.

Do you see? Here, you are the detective. The interactive platform is your investigation desk, and the filters are your tools. By applying and cross-referencing information, you don't just visualize data; you interrogate it. The goal is to give you the power to know probabilities based on historical NASA weather data about wind, not on a predictive model.

​User Experience Visualization

​A user wants to plan a wedding event at Tambaú Beach in João Pessoa for November 20, 2025.

The Query (The Starting Point)

The user opens the platform. In the search bar, they type "Praia de Tambaú, João Pessoa." The system autocompletes, and they click on the location. Next, a calendar appears, and they select "November 20, 2025.” 

In the end, the entire analysis can be saved and downloaded as a PDF report, ideal for event planning or for presenting in meetings.

Conclusion

​In summary, our project is more than a data platform; it is an engine of transformation. It converts the citizen from a passive spectator of the weather into an active participant in building a more resilient and just city. By making data science accessible, interactive, and actionable through our investigative dashboard, we give communities the power not just to see what the future holds, but to shape it. This is the essence of our solution: transforming data into dialogue, and dialogue into action.

It addresses the challenge because the main space station is located in an equatorial orbit 500 km above the surface of the Earth, and when a space station or rocket buys an greenhouse for their mission, we'll deploy the greenhouse to dock with the vessel for their mission. projectDetails.details: Our project works as following: we research specific types of plants that NASA wants to be grown in other world's soils and report to them what happened to the plant, after researching and seeing good results for the plant, we will install the plant in the greenhouse designed specifically to that body, and when one needs to go to that said body and buys the greenhouse, we deploy it with all the plants that grow on the surface of the planet for the mission that the other party is going to. The benefits are that we won't need processed and dried food to be sent to other planets and the food is renewable, so if someone builds the infrastrucure on the planet, they can take some of our plants and expand the garden on the planet itself. The intended impact is to make interplanetary exploration a lot easier, by eliminating one of the main risks and costs, which is food. We used Blender to create a 3d sketch of the station and other things related to it, Canva to create the slide presentation and google meet to brainstorm ideas and put them into action. Our project is creative because we take food researching into a whole other level, because instead of growing food in specialized labs that mimic our own planet's surface conditions, we use other surfaces to make planting in other planets easier and also not have to resupply food to other planets.

projectDetails.name: EcoAlert City - sustainable technology for real-time warnings.
projectDetails.summary: Our project proposes the creation of a smart weather warning system for Santos, São Paulo, Brazil, integrating NASA satellite data and SAR radar with digital technology. The idea is to send real-time warnings through solar totems, allowing the population to prepare before the arrival of heavy rains, strong winds, and high tides. It emerged after the storm of April 19, 2025, when we were stranded inside our car, a frightening experience, and the warnings arrived late, leaving residents at risk. The system aims to prevent accidents, reduce property damage, and promote awareness about prevention and sustainability. The innovation lies in the integration of science, technology, and inclusive communication, reaching the entire city. This initiative strengthens urban resilience and inspires other cities to adopt similar solutions, leveraging renewable energy and scientific data to protect people and property.
projectDetails.details:
When the tide rises, the streets of Santos, São Paulo, Brazil, turn into rivers. When the wind blows hard, many homes and businesses lose their roofs and debris flies through the air. Heavy rains can occur suddenly, and warnings don't always arrive in time, leaving people unprepared and at risk.

Science can change that! Using NASA satellites and SAR radars, it's possible to monitor weather conditions in real time and even see what's happening beneath the clouds. These technologies allow for the precise identification of risk areas and early warning of storms.

Some cities already use similar systems, such as Petrópolis (RJ), in Brazil, with community sirens, and Sendai, in Japan, which has audible tsunami warnings. In Santos, however, we don't want to limit ourselves to the coast: storms affect the entire city, and everyone needs protection.

With this in mind, we developed the idea of ​​building an intelligent weather warning system capable of alerting the population in real time. It will include solar powered warning totems located throughout the city.

The system combines science, technology, and sustainability. The alerts are accessible to everyone, including those with hearing or visual impairments. The project aims to save lives, reduce the damage caused by extreme weather events, and inspire other cities to adopt sustainable technological solutions.

The project's creativity lies in its combination of science and civic engagement: an alert system that not only informs, but also educates and connects the community around prevention. The team considered urban mapping of high-risk areas, messaging accessibility, energy autonomy, and social engagement.

Thus, the Santos Intelligent Climate Alert System represents an initiative that transforms scientific knowledge into practical action, demonstrating that technology and empathy can work together to protect lives, care for the city, and preserve nature.

projectDetails.name: Asteroid Clash
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, "Asteroid Clash", is an interactive web application that uses NASA APIs to provide real-time data on near-Earth objects (NEOs) and the Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD). Users can explore potentially hazardous asteroids, simulate deflection missions, and visualize asteroid orbits in 3D. The app also includes a dedicated section explaining the scientific formulas used for energy and impact calculations, making the content educational and engaging.
This tool addresses the challenge by turning complex space science into an accessible experience for learners and enthusiasts. It raises awareness about asteroid threats, fosters interest in astronomy, and promotes STEM education. By combining live NASA data with interactive simulations, our project empowers users to understand the scale, risk, and science behind asteroid monitoring — inspiring curiosity and proactive thinking about space exploration and planetary defense.
projectDetails.details:
Asteroid Clash is an interactive web app that brings space exploration and asteroid risk awareness to everyone, especially young learners. Using real-time NASA data, it tracks Near-Earth Objects (NEOs), simulates asteroid impacts, and visualizes orbits in an engaging way.

How it works:
The app uses NASA’s Near-Earth Object Feed API and NEO Lookup API to provide live asteroid data. Users select date ranges to explore potentially hazardous asteroids. It calculates impact energy, crater size, and allows simulation of asteroid deflection. The app also features NASA’s Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD) to inspire curiosity about space.

Benefits and Impact:

  • Makes complex astronomy accessible and engaging.
  • Raises public awareness about asteroid threats.
  • Encourages STEM learning and curiosity about space.

Tools Used:
Python, Streamlit, Requests, Pandas, NumPy, Plotly, NASA APIs, Streamlit Cloud, custom CSS.

Creativity:
Combines real NASA data with gamified learning, offering interactive risk analysis, simulation tools, 3D orbit visualization, and daily space inspiration via APOD.

Team Focus:
Designed to be intuitive, educational, and visually engaging, promoting accessibility and inspiring interest in space science for all ages.

ChatGPT was used as a supportive tool to assist in writing code snippets, troubleshooting, and resolving programming bugs. projectDetails.name: NASA BioSpace Discovery
projectDetails.summary: Exploring the Moon and Mars safely requires understanding how humans, plants, and other living organisms react to space conditions. The NASA Biological and Physical Sciences Division supports experiments that study these effects to make future missions safer and more efficient. Over time, hundreds of studies have been conducted, producing more than six hundred scientific papers. However, the results are spread across many sources, making it difficult to interpret all findings together. The NASA challenge proposes creating a web application that uses artificial intelligence and data science to organize, summarize, and visualize this large collection of information. The goal is to build an interactive platform that allows users to explore the 608 bioscience publications, identify research gaps, and understand how different experiments connect. The system should transform scientific data into knowledge that helps scientists, managers, and mission planners make better decisions. It could use tools like natural language processing, machine learning, and knowledge graphs to extract relevant information and show it clearly. This initiative encourages creativity and aims to make complex information accessible through interactive dashboards or visual representations. In the end, the project helps transform NASA’s biological research into insights that guide future human exploration of the Moon and Mars.
projectDetails.details:
Exploring the Moon and Mars safely requires understanding how humans, plants, and other living organisms respond to space conditions. The NASA Biological and Physical Sciences Division supports numerous studies that investigate these effects to make future missions safer and more efficient. Over the years, hundreds of experiments have been conducted, generating more than 600 scientific publications. However, these results are scattered across many sources, making it difficult to analyze and interpret them as a whole.

To address this challenge, our project proposes developing a web application powered by artificial intelligence and data science to organize, summarize, and visualize this extensive body of research. The interactive platform will enable scientists, researchers, and decision-makers to explore all 608 publications, identify research gaps, and uncover connections between different experiments.

By integrating natural language processing, machine learning, and knowledge graph technologies, the system will transform complex scientific data into clear and accessible insights that support better decision-making. Additionally, the project promotes creativity and innovation by presenting findings through interactive dashboards and visual representations, making scientific knowledge easier to explore and understand.

Ultimately, this initiative aims to turn NASAs vast bioscience research into actionable knowledge, guiding the future of human exploration on the Moon and Mars.

projectDetails.name: BioAstra
projectDetails.summary: BioAstra democratizes NASA's space biology research through an AI-powered knowledge engine that transforms 608 scientific publications into accessible, actionable insights. We developed an interactive web application that uses artificial intelligence and knowledge graphs to explore NASA’s publications. Users can search freely, and our AI-powered system recommends the most relevant studies. Users, from mission planners to students, can interact conversationally with the research. BioAstra processes queries in real-time, extracting relevant findings from abstracts, results, and conclusions while visualizing relationships between studies through interactive knowledge graphs. By integrating NASA OSDR datasets and the Space Life Sciences Library, we're creating a comprehensive ecosystem where space biology knowledge becomes universally accessible, accelerating discovery and informed decision-making for humanity's next giant leap.
projectDetails.details:
1. Welcoming page

On the initial screen, we introduce the tool in a direct and impactful way. On the final page, we identify the type of user interacting with the platform—whether they are frequent users, such as scientists or mission managers, or new users, like students and curious enthusiasts. This allows us to offer a more personalized experience tailored to each audience.

2. Identifying type of user

If you're new here, we introduce our tool in an intuitive way. Through a quiz guided by our astronaut character, Alana, users are asked questions on various topics drawn from the 608 bioscience publications. The goal is to spark curiosity and encourage users to dive into NASA’s dataset. To answer each question, users are invited to explore our AI-powered tool, which connects their real-world doubts to the relevant biology publications.

3. Search page

This is our search bar — the heart of user interaction within BioAstra. Here, users are invited to enter questions, keywords, or topics of interest related to space biology. Our custom-built AI system then analyzes the input and returns the most relevant results from NASA’s comprehensive database of 608 full-text bioscience publications. This tool is designed to guide your exploration with precision and clarity.

4. Response to the User

On this page, our AI system delivers tailored responses to the user’s queries, drawing directly from NASA’s rich repository of 608 space bioscience publications. Whether the user entered a specific question, a keyword, or simply explored out of curiosity, the tool processes the input, analyzes semantic relevance, and returns the most meaningful results. Each response is designed not only to inform, but to guide the user deeper into the scientific landscape — connecting doubts to discoveries, and questions to knowledge.

Technical details

Our web application features a responsive frontend built with React and CSS. The backend is powered by TypeScript, integrating the OpenAI API to dynamically construct knowledge graphs from user queries and articles. For efficient, real-time data retrieval, we utilize Pinecone as a high-performance vector database. This robust stack brings our AI character, Alana, to life.

projectDetails.name: Guardians of The Earth
projectDetails.summary: Wildfires devastate our planet every year, but the global scale and actual impact of these events are difficult to visualize and comprehend. To answer this challenge, we created "Guardians of The Earth," an educational platform that explains the instruments of the Earth Mission and transforms 25 years of its data into a virtual environment where users can analyze both burn locations and preservation sites on our planet. And to test and solidify the knowledge acquired about biomes and burn areas, we prepared a very fun quiz.
projectDetails.details:
In a world flooded with information, clarity is key. "Earth Biomes in 25 years - The Earth Satellite Journey" simplifies the complexity of climate data, offering a clear and interactive view of global burning.

The impact is education at scale: we empower global citizens to see the changes our planet is facing, fostering a deeper understanding and a collective sense of urgency.

Our innovation is a geospatial "data storytelling" platform. Instead of a generic data viewer, we created a journey that guides the user through complex issues.

The data combination, animation, and a contextualized quiz create a unique and unforgettable learning experience.      

The platform is built upon validated data from the NASA Earth Mission. Our functional prototype, built in Scratch, demonstrates the viability of a scalable platform where new stories can be added in the future.

The project directly answers the challenge "Animation Celebration of Terra Data" by allowing the user to animate and celebrate the wealth of Terra data in a global context.

Facing the immensity of NASA's data, our team chose to tell a global story. This challenge made us think as both developers and educators to build a tool that not only shows data but also inspires curiosity and concern for our only home.

projectDetails.name: Project Estrela Cadente Solar Mission
projectDetails.summary:
We are a group of children who participate in the Nicolinhas & Kids club and are taking on this challenge to show that we are capable of high-level projects.
And with the motivation to change the world through astronomy.
The NASA provides a list of resources and information on space weather, including:
1. Overview of space weather and its importance
2. Solar phenomena and their impacts on Earth
3. NASA and other space agencies' resources (such as NOAA and CSA) for space weather monitoring and forecasting
4. Educational videos on space weather and its effects
The resources include:
- NASA and NOAA websites with information on space weather
- Explanatory videos on solar phenomena and their impacts
- Resources from Canadian and Brazilian space agencies (CSA and AEB) for space weather monitoring and study.
What is a solar flare?
Solar flares are sudden explosions on the Sun's surface caused by instability in its magnetic field, releasing radiation and high-speed particles. When directed towards Earth, these flares can cause geomagnetic storms, affecting power grids, communications, and navigation systems.
Solution:
To solve or mitigate the effects of solar flares, it is recommended to:
- Follow alerts from reliable sources such as NASA and NOAA;
- Monitor and reduce energy consumption to protect the power grid;
- Make data backups and protect electronics with surge protectors or Faraday cages;
- For navigation systems, use techniques like RTK/PPK to compensate for interference.
projectDetails.details:
This project aims to present, in a playful and accessible way, the phenomenon of solar flares and their potential harm. The proposal seeks to raise awareness among children around the world about the importance of understanding natural events and their impacts, sparking scientific interest in a fun and educational way.

The story was created in a comic book format, aiming to make the content more engaging and dynamic for children. This choice encourages reading and understanding of scientific information, while also stimulating children's imagination and curiosity.

During the creation process, Meta AI, ChatGPT, and Canva tools were used, enabling the integration of technology and creativity. The language used was English, aiming to broaden the reach of the material.

The project's creative uniqueness lies in presenting the Sun as the narrator of its own story, making the approach more engaging and educational. Furthermore, the project highlights the inclusion of children with disabilities as active characters, reinforcing the importance of representation and valuing the individual capabilities of all students. The narrative was constructed with ease of understanding, accessibility, and effectiveness in raising awareness in mind. In this way, the project contributes to inclusive learning, sparking children's interest in scientific and environmental topics.

It can be concluded that the project achieved its objectives by creatively combining technology, inclusion, and science education. The playful approach and the use of innovative digital tools enabled the development of engaging, accessible material with the potential to positively impact the development of children who are aware of and curious about the world around them.

projectDetails.name: Solar Chaos: an offline adventure
projectDetails.summary: Our project, “Solar Chaos: An Offline Adventure”, is a digital and interactive children’s story that introduces the concept of space weather through a playful and engaging narrative. The story follows four students—Gabriel, Malu, João Paulo, and Estevan—who must complete a science project about the Sun just as a solar storm disrupts electricity and the internet. Without access to technology, they learn about solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and the Earth’s magnetic shield using books, drawings, and teamwork. The story directly addresses NASA’s challenge by explaining how solar activity affects daily life and technology in a way that is engaging and accessible to children. It also explores our growing dependence on artificial intelligence and digital tools, showing how the storm becomes a turning point for rediscovering human creativity, collaboration, and manual skills. An innovative feature of the project is its interactive structure, designed as a web-based narrative. The story unfolds through clickable links that guide readers across scenes, while highlighted sections offer short scientific insights into the phenomena described. This format transforms reading into an immersive learning experience, combining storytelling, science, and exploration. Ultimately, the book invites young readers to appreciate the science of the Sun, understand its impact on Earth, and value the creativity that shines when the screens go dark.
projectDetails.details:
Our project consisted of creating a digital children’s book about space weather and its effects on life on Earth. The team was formed by four children aged 10 and 11, guided by their parents. The process began with the children studying scientific content related to the structure of the Sun, solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and their impacts on Earth. To build their understanding, they used NASA educational materials, videos, and the science book “O Grande Universo de Oliver.”

 

Once the scientific foundation was established, the team held a brainstorming session to create the story. The central idea of the story was to show children working on a school project about the Sun that gets interrupted by a solar storm which causes a power and internet blackout. This structure allowed the book to integrate real scientific concepts naturally into the narrative while showing the tangible effects of a solar storm on daily life. The children’s creative solution to the blackout was to return to the simplicity of pencil, paper, and poster board.

 

Writing a book about space weather is highly relevant and timely. Although its effects may seem distant compared to familiar weather events like rain or storms, space weather powerfully reveals how deeply human life and modern technology depend on the Sun’s activity and the forces of the universe. From satellites and GPS to aviation, power grids, and even everyday communications, our society is increasingly vulnerable to solar flares and coronal mass ejections. By transforming this complex topic into an engaging children’s story, we help young readers discover that the “weather” shaping our lives reaches far beyond the clouds—inviting them to explore the Sun, understand our planet’s connection to space, and imagine their own role in protecting our world from the next great solar storm.

 

The book also offers a reflection on the relationship between technology and human potential. Artificial intelligence, which we used extensively during this project, represents a powerful tool that expands human creativity. However, the story reminds us—ironically through the Sun itself—that even our most advanced technologies fragile before the forces of nature, and that at the heart of every creation, it is the human mind that truly shines.

 

During production, we carefully balanced scientific accuracy with the language and humor appropriate for children aged 8–12. The dialogue between characters was designed to capture the natural tone of real children’s conversations, making complex scientific ideas approachable and fun. Since the team members were young, the adult mentors provided guidance for the children’s creativity and autonomy.

Our project stands out for the way it combines scientific education with creative storytelling and digital innovation. From the beginning, our goal was not only to explain the science behind space weather, but also to explore new ways of engaging young readers through narrative structure, interactivity, and reflection on technology itself. The creative and innovative features described below illustrate how we sought to merge content, form, and experience into a unified and meaningful project.

 One creative aspect of our project lies in how fiction and real life are intertwined. First, within the story, the characters are creating a school project about the Sun when a solar storm—precisely the phenomenon at the heart of the NASA Challenge—disrupts their progress, making the theme part of the plot itself. Second, the book invites readers to reflect on the use of artificial intelligence, a tool that was also central to the project’s own development. In this way, the story connects its content and creative process, bringing together form and meaning in a coherent and imaginative way.

The second innovative feature is the interactive structure of the story, designed as a web-based narrative. The story unfolds through clickable links that guide the reader across scenes, while highlighted sections provide concise theoretical insights into the scientific concepts mentioned. This design creates an immersive and educational reading experience, encouraging readers to actively explore both the narrative and the science behind space weather.

 

To produce the book, we used simple text editors—one of the children even typed on a keyboard for the first time. The story was written by the children, reviewed by adults, and refined with ChatGPT. Illustrations were created using Gemini AI and by hand-drawn artwork, which was added after the blackout in the story. Then, we structured the story as an interactive web site.

projectDetails.name: Rey's Solar Adventure
projectDetails.summary:
Through interconnected stories and vivid animation, our project translates the invisible power of solar activity into tangible human experiences. It addresses the challenge of communicating complex heliophysics in an engaging, educational way—combining storytelling, science, and emotion to raise awareness of how the Sun’s activity connects us all.

The narrative is led by Rey, a personified Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) who guides viewers on his journey from the Sun to Earth. Along the way, Rey encounters three characters affected by his arrival: Gabe, the commander of a space station who must protect his crew from radiation; Hector, a farmer facing system failures caused by geomagnetic interference; and Arthur, an urban worker caught in city disruptions as communication networks collapse and GPS systems malfunction.

By showing how solar storms can disturb technology, energy grids, and even human health—while also creating natural beauty such as auroras—the project brings scientific concepts to life. It invites audiences to reflect on the importance of solar observation, monitoring, and preparedness for life both on Earth and in space.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is an animated video developed entirely in Scratch, designed to introduce children to the effects of solar storms on Earth and in space. The narrative is led by Rey, a personified Coronal Mass Ejection (CME), who guides viewers on a journey from the Sun to Earth. Along the way, Rey encounters three characters affected by his arrival: Gabe, the commander of a space station who must protect his crew from radiation; Hector, a farmer whose machinery and communication systems malfunction; and Arthur, an urban worker experiencing disruptions as city technology fails. While the animation includes a few clickable buttons to progress scenes or trigger minor effects, it is primarily story-driven, focusing on narrative immersion.

The project aims to generate learning about the impacts of stellar climatic events, making abstract heliophysics concepts accessible and engaging for children. By showing concrete scenarios and human reactions, it translates complex scientific phenomena into relatable experiences.

Animation and Design:

  • Characters: Cartoon-style, expressive, with distinctive colors for easy recognition. Rey glows in bright yellow and orange hues to represent solar plasma. Gabe wears a classic astronaut suit with orange details. Hector is depicted with blue tones, and Arthur’s urban environment uses grays and brown to signal city life.
  • Backgrounds and Scenes: Space is depicted with dark color and white stars, while Earth scenes use familiar landscapes.

Scientific Accuracy and Creativity:

  • All information is based on NASA resources or peer-reviewed articles.
  • Personifying the CME as Rey provides a unique perspective, combining storytelling with factual knowledge.
  • The balance between accuracy and accessibility ensures children learn without losing engagement.

By combining science, storytelling, animation, and minimal interaction, the project encourages curiosity about the Sun, space weather, and its influence on Earth. It promotes early scientific literacy, awareness of technological vulnerabilities, and understanding of natural phenomena, all through a playful and visually rich experience.
