projectDetails.name: OrbitHub – Sustainable Satellite Data Marketplace
projectDetails.summary:
OrbitHub is a sustainable marketplace for low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite data, connecting data producers (such as satellite operators) with diverse consumers, including businesses, universities, and governments. The platform provides easy access to space data and promotes environmental responsibility through an ESG rating system (Gold, Silver, and Bronze), which evaluates parameters such as carbon emissions, energy efficiency, and orbital recycling practices.
The project seeks to democratize access to satellite data, reducing technical barriers through personalized recommendations, APIs, and interactive dashboards. In addition to encouraging sustainable practices in the aerospace industry, OrbitHub ensures regulatory compliance with standards such as ITAR and GDPR, strengthening user security and trust.
Its relevance lies in driving innovation and supporting strategic decision-making in areas such as agriculture, environmental monitoring, and logistics. By integrating ESG principles into the spatial economy, OrbitHub not only provides valuable data but also generates positive social and environmental impact, establishing itself as a transformative solution for the growing geospatial data market.
projectDetails.details:
Problem Statement and Opportunity

The project arises from the problem of fragmentation and limited access to data generated by satellites in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), which produce large volumes of valuable information about the planet daily, but remain underutilized due to the lack of integrated commercialization platforms and clear sustainability criteria. Furthermore, the space sector faces growing environmental challenges, such as the increase in orbital debris and the lack of unified standards for sustainable practices.

Given this scenario, the project seeks to transform these challenges into opportunities by promoting the commercial and responsible use of satellite data through partnerships with companies and space agencies, such as NASA. The goal is to create a specialized marketplace, connecting producers—satellite operators and research institutions—with consumers such as companies, universities, governments, and startups, who use space data for decision-making and the development of innovative solutions in areas such as the environment, agriculture, logistics, defense, and meteorology.

Furthermore, the project introduces an opportunity for sustainable differentiation in the sector: an environmental rating system for satellites, classifying them as Gold, Silver, and Bronze based on their operational practices and environmental impacts throughout their lifecycle.

In this way, the initiative not only democratizes access to space data but also encourages sustainable practices in the aerospace industry, promoting a commercialization model that combines technological innovation and environmental responsibility.

Business Segmentation

Our business model is based on a marketplace specialized in the commercialization of satellite data, supported by consulting services and customized solutions that expand the value and applicability of this data. The platform connects satellite operators and spatial data providers with companies, governments, and research institutions, creating an efficient and reliable channel for accessing geospatial information.

The key competitive advantage lies in the intelligent curation and sustainable classification of satellites, which evaluate their operations according to environmental criteria and responsible practices in the space sector. This approach adds transparency, credibility, and ESG value to the orbital data chain—an increasingly relevant factor for investors and organizations committed to sustainability.

In addition to intermediation, we offer technical and strategic consulting to guide clients in selecting the most appropriate sources, the optimal delivery format, and the frequency of data updates, reducing costs and operational complexity. Thus, the project democratizes access to high-quality spatial data, expanding the market and driving commercial applications in sectors such as agriculture, the environment, logistics, energy, and defense. Positioned in the geospatial technology and data intelligence sector, the project combines economic impact with environmental responsibility, opening new business opportunities in a rapidly expanding global market driven by the revolution in low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellites.

Target Audience

Our target audience includes:

Private companies in sectors such as agribusiness, environment, mining, energy, infrastructure, and logistics, which use space-based data for monitoring, strategic planning, or risk mitigation.

Universities and research centers that require access to satellite data for scientific studies, environmental modeling, climate analysis, and related activities.

Government institutions and non-governmental organizations involved in public policy, environmental monitoring, and territorial enforcement.

Startups and technology developers seeking to integrate satellite data into applications based on artificial intelligence, big data, or the Internet of Things.

Our objective is to democratize access to space-based data by providing a user-friendly platform, guided by expert knowledge, and offering solutions suitable for both entry-level users and organizations with a high level of technical maturity.

Sustainable Value Proposition

Our purpose is to accurately and efficiently meet the needs of our target audience by offering qualified access to satellite data through an intelligent and reliable platform. We serve companies, universities, research centers, and public and private institutions, providing relevant spatial data for analysis, scientific development, and innovative technological solutions.

In addition to commercializing data from satellites in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), recognized for their high resolution and collection frequency, the project adopts a pioneering sustainability classification model. This system evaluates the environmental performance and spatial responsibility of satellites, categorizing them into three levels: Gold, Silver, and Bronze.

In doing so, we offer not only high-quality data but also a new dimension of transparency and sustainability in the use of space. This approach adds value and confidence to our clients’ decisions, allowing each data choice to reflect a conscious commitment to social and environmental responsibility, as well as to the future of space exploration.

Initial Portfolio (MVP)

We commercialize data generated by satellites operating in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). These satellites are classified into gold, silver, and bronze categories based on sustainability criteria related to their operation and environmental impact. To obtain those data, we establish strategic partnerships with companies responsible for manufacturing and operating the satellites, which provide us with access to the collected information.

Data Classification and Data Quality Assessment

The classification system is designed to simplify commercial understanding and communicate sustainable value. Satellites are categorized according to their performance against specific criteria:

  • Bronze: reasonably meets the criterion
  • Silver: meets the criterion well
  • Gold: meets the criterion with excellence

Criteria and Evaluation examples:

Criterion: Flexibility

Description: Ability to fulfill more than one mission

Importance Level: 3

 

Criterion: Mission

Description: Contribution to broader scientific or societal goals, including necessity and uniqueness

Importance Level: 2

 

Criterion: End-of-life measures

Description: Actions taken at the end of the mission (e.g., using remaining fuel to deorbit the satellite)

Importance Level: 3

Data Sources and Partnerships

The strategy for sourcing data combines the use of open-access platforms, such as NASA and ESA, with commercial agreements involving private satellite operators. This approach ensures legal compliance, diversity of data types, and continuity of supply. Formal reseller agreements will be established with commercial providers to guarantee long-term access and clearly defined usage rights.

Technical Architecture

Our main objective is to build a platform that is demonstrably scalable, ensuring business continuity and high availability through the following key components:

  • Portal built on a microservices architecture.
  • Cloud storage and hosting, ensuring high availability.
  • REST APIs for data integration and services.
  • Portal with ESG filters and dashboards.
  • Website built with JavaScript, CSS, and HTML.
  • Python-based machine learning.

Operational Sustainability

OrbitHub adopts the preservation of Low Earth Orbit as a core principle, aligning its operations with Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) practices. To achieve this, measurable sustainability indicators will be established to ensure transparency and reliability for partners, clients, and investors.

Each satellite will be evaluated using specific Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), including:

Carbon per launch: measurement of CO₂ equivalent per ton of payload placed in orbit, enabling monitoring and reduction of the carbon footprint of each mission.

Energy consumption of operations: tracking the energy efficiency of ground and orbital activities.

Orbital reuse or recycling index: evaluation of component reuse and safe deorbiting practices to minimize space debris.

Blue Seal certification: an exclusive OrbitHub seal granted only to satellites and operations that fully meet the platform’s environmental and governance requirements.

Revenue Model

OrbitHub will adopt a hybrid monetization model combining subscriptions and on-demand services, with sustainability as a key competitive advantage.

SaaS Subscription: Tiered plans based on the sustainability classification of satellites (bronze, silver, gold). Each tier provides different levels of environmental performance, orbital efficiency, certifications, and services.

  • Bronze: basic level, offering essential sustainability metrics and limited services.
  • Silver: intermediate level, with advanced efficiency metrics and ESG reporting.
  • Gold: premium level, including Blue Seal certification, comprehensive carbon reporting, optimized operational sustainability, and priority support.
  • Pay-as-you-go: Usage-based billing for premium services such as orbital data, customized simulations, and advanced analytics, with differentiated pricing according to satellite category.

Consulting and Customized Integrations: On-demand services for large space sector companies, providing tailored solutions for ESG certification, platform integration, and operational optimization.

Costs

OrbitHub will maintain a clear structure of fixed and variable costs to ensure financial predictability and operational viability.

Fixed costs include recurring expenses essential for the continuous operation of the platform:

Cloud computing for processing and storage

Spatial database infrastructure

Server maintenance and upgrades

Development and technical support teams

Variable costs depend on usage volume and specific operational activities:

Additional storage for orbital data

Integration of new partners and services

Regulatory and ESG certification expenses

Operational costs associated with technological expansion and adaptation

A financial projection plan will be developed with an expected payback period of 3 to 5 years, taking into account the growth in marketplace adoption and the international expansion of OrbitHub.

Funding and Investment

The OrbitHub funding plan adopts a diversified approach to secure sufficient capital for the development, operation, and expansion of the platform.

Initial Rounds (Seed/Series A): Fundraising from angel investors and venture capital funds specialized in space technology and deep tech, aimed at financing early-stage development and the launch of operations.

Innovation Grants: Participation in national and international programs, including calls from space agencies and NASA initiatives, to access non-dilutive funding and increase visibility within the space sector.

Strategic Partnerships with Private Equity: Attracting investment to support global expansion, infrastructure development, and platform scalability.

Business Rounds in Space Innovation Hubs: Fundraising through events and programs such as ESA BIC, NASA iTech, and Techstars Space, generating opportunities for networking, mentorship, and investment.

Mission, Vision, and Values

This section outlines the mission, vision, and values that guide the strategic direction of OrbitHub. These elements define the platform’s purpose, its long-term aspirations, and the principles that shape its operations and decision-making. By clearly establishing this foundation, OrbitHub positions itself as a responsible and innovative actor within the space data ecosystem, aligning business objectives with technological advancement and socio-environmental responsibility.

Mission

To democratize access to satellite data while promoting sustainable classification of satellites, fostering innovation, transparency, and the development of solutions that generate economic growth and positive socio-environmental impact.

Vision

To become the leading global platform for accessing and sustainably classifying satellite data, recognized for democratizing space information, fostering technological innovation, and enabling solutions that promote economic development, digital inclusion, and socio-environmental impact on a global scale.

Values

Open and inclusive access: ensuring that data and information are available in an accessible way to diverse audiences, from researchers to startups and local governments.

Ethical transparency: maintaining clear, reliable, and ethical processes in data collection, distribution, and classification.

Sustainability and planetary responsibility: encouraging practices that reduce environmental impacts in the space sector and strengthen socio-environmental responsibility.

Collaborative innovation: promoting the joint development of solutions among universities, companies, governments, and civil society.

Positive socioeconomic impact: enabling governments, companies, universities, and society to develop solutions that strengthen local economies and stimulate innovation through access to satellite data and sustainable classifications.

Quality and reliability: providing accurate data with recognized and trustworthy classifications.

Education and capacity building: democratizing space knowledge by supporting training programs and initiatives that enhance understanding of satellite data and sustainability.

Security and privacy: complying with international standards for data security and privacy in data management and sharing.

Equity and diversity: valuing different voices, regions, and perspectives, and promoting digital and spatial inclusion.

Long-term vision: focusing on sustainable legacies to ensure that future generations inherit a more accessible and responsible space sector.

Product Roadmap (12 months)

The product roadmap outlines the planned evolution of OrbitHub over the first 12 months, ensuring structured development, incremental delivery of value, and alignment between technological milestones and business objectives. The strategy follows a phased approach, moving from conceptualization to launch and early operation, supported by the progressive integration of sustainability classification models and satellite data services.

Throughout these phases, AI models will be progressively incorporated for sustainability classification and matching between user requests and satellite data, supporting scalable growth and continuous value generation.

projectDetails.name: Meteor Impact Simulator
projectDetails.summary: Our project consists of a modern and practical web simulator that simulates the impact of different asteroids (captured by official NASA data) at different points on Earth, highlighting their hazards, damage and its size compared to other reference objects. Thus, our project contributes to greater knowledge on this subject, which can aid in prevention measures and forecasting meteors near Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Our solution to the proposed challenge consists of a web platform programmed in Python and Javascript. The website presents a first interface where you can select the meteor you want to use, choosing between meteors already discovered with their measurements defined by NASA or meteors customized by you, customizing speed, size, and mass in kilograms. You can compare the size of your meteors with that of other objects, such as large monuments and even Mount Everest.

When you press the "continue" button, you are taken to a second interface where planet Earth is displayed. You must choose the location where the meteor will fall. You can also type the location in the search box if you find that easier than rotating the globe. Once you've selected the location, press the "Launch" button. The meteor will collide with the impact site, and a message box will appear showing the impacts it will cause on the planet, both internally and externally.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?
This makes it easier to understand the impacts of these celestial bodies on our planet and, perhaps, plan measures to mitigate this damage.

HOW IT WAS MADE?

The APIs were written in Python, while the graphical interfaces were created in Javascript. Each interface screen includes an explanatory video recorded by our team member, Francisco. This makes it easier to understand what to do at each stage of the simulator.

The user interface was created using a set of Javascript Frameworks and Technologies:

Javascript, Typescript and JSX - As programming languages

Next.JS - The Web Compoonent framework

ThreeJS / Drei / Fiber - For the Meteor and Reference Objects Visualization (First Screen)

CesiumJS / Resium - For the Earth Globe visualization (Second Screen)

MUI - Material User Interface for Next.JS. Used for UI components and data visualization

Vercel - Publishing Service where our Application is hosted

Axios - For the interaction with the services created in Python

projectDetails.name: Project NandiTESS.ai
projectDetails.summary:
The NandiTESS.ai project uses Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning to estimate the probability that an exoplanet candidate, known as a TESS Object of Interest (TOI), is genuine. Unlike conventional detection methods, this approach is purely statistical and inferential, applying AI to the candidates' physical and orbital parameters.


In addition to this functionality, NandiTESS.ai offers a creative theory registry, which can be applied to scientific methods, potentially providing valuable insights into future applications and scientific updates to the platform.



The process involves collecting and normalizing data from the TOI catalog and then performing metric weighting—assigning greater value to parameters historically proven to correlate with confirmed exoplanets. The average is an important indicator of anomalies because the validation status unit can be below average in confirmed exoplanets.

These weighted metrics are then processed through a predictive model based on logistic regression, which generates a percentage—the estimated chance of validation. The model undergoes continuous validation against confirmed discoveries to ensure its accuracy.


The NandiTESS.ai aims to transform astronomical data into predictive knowledge. It doesn't observe directly; rather, it's fed with data from the TESS satellite, providing researchers with an intelligent prioritization tool for future observations.
projectDetails.details:
The NandiTESS.ai project is an innovative platform that uses Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) to estimate the probability that a candidate exoplanet, known as a TESS Object of Interest (TOI), is genuine. Built to be an intelligent prioritization tool, the project stands out for its purely statistical and inferential approach, in contrast to conventional direct detection methods.

1. How does it work?

The operating process is divided into several interconnected steps:

Data Collection and Normalization: The system begins with the collection and normalization of data from the TOI (TESS Object of Interest) catalog.

Metric Weighting: Metric weighting is performed, assigning greater value to parameters that have been shown to historically correlate with confirmed exoplanets.

Predictive Modeling: The weighted data are then processed by a predictive model based on logistic regression. This model generates a percentage, which is the estimated chance of validation for the candidate.

Anomaly Analysis: The project considers the mean as an important indicator of anomalies, taking into account that the validation status unit may be below the mean for exoplanets that are later confirmed.

Continuous Validation: The model undergoes continuous validation against previously confirmed discoveries, thus ensuring its accuracy.

2. What Benefits Does Our Project Have?

The NandiTESS.ai project was developed to provide an intelligent and efficient solution for scientists' workflows in the search for new worlds. Its main benefits are:

Transformation of Data into Predictive Knowledge: The project's core objective is to transform raw astronomical data into predictive knowledge, providing a clear assessment of a candidate's validation chances.

Intelligent Prioritization Tool: It serves as an intelligent prioritization tool for future observations. By estimating the probability of a TOI being genuine, the system allows researchers to focus their resources and telescope time on the most promising targets.

Resource Optimization: Although the project does not observe directly, it is fed data from the TESS satellite, using this information to guide decisions. This optimizes the use of observation resources, minimizing the time spent on false positives.

Decision Support and Validation

Intelligent Prioritization Tool: Acts as an intelligent prioritization tool for future observations. Although powered by data from the TESS satellite, it transforms this data into predictive knowledge, optimizing telescope observing time.

Decision Support Reports: The system provides a complete Validation Report (exportable in Markdown/HTML with one click) to justify follow-up choices, integrating the AI ​​model output with scientific documentation.

3. What is the Intended Impact of the Project?

The impact of the NandiTESS.ai project is to fundamentally transform the landscape of exoplanet discovery through artificial intelligence, positioning it as an indispensable tool for the global scientific community.

The intended impact can be summarized as:

Raising the Bar of Knowledge: The project aims to transform astronomical data into predictive knowledge. Instead of simply cataloging observations, the platform uses metric weighting and logistic regression to actively predict the outcome of future observations.

Guiding Discovery: NandiTESS.ai does not directly observe (as the TESS satellite does), but uses the data provided by it to create an intelligent prioritization tool. This means that the platform acts as a scientific guide, indicating to researchers the candidates most likely to be confirmed.

Focus on the Right Targets: The most practical impact is optimizing observatory time. By providing a reliable predictive score, the project allows astronomers around the world to direct the use of large telescopes (which are limited and expensive resources) only to TOIs classified as having a high probability of success.

Scientific Acceleration: This efficient screening accelerates the pace of new discoveries by significantly reducing the time spent observing false positives.

Universal Accessibility: The project impacts the scientific community by creating a global interaction platform that is easy to access and simple to use.

Hypothesis Sharing: With the inclusion of a scientific and public social sharing platform system, the impact extends to the research methodology itself: the platform facilitates the sharing and discussion of exoplanet theories and identification among scientists from different parts of the world (such as a Australian person seeing a Brazilian's theory), breaking down geographic barriers and accelerating consensus validation.

Community Engagement: By offering an interactive learning journey and quiz, NandiTESS.ai not only supports experts but also engages new scientists and enthusiasts, expanding the reach and impact of exoplanet research.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The NandiTESS.ai project is built on a modern open source architecture, utilizing a robust set of tools and languages ​​to ensure efficiency, scalability, and explainability:

Classification Model: The core of the system uses algorithms such as XGBoost for the calibrated classifier, in addition to the scikit-learn 1.4+ framework for various ML and statistical functions.

Base Model: The predictive approach is explicitly based on logistic regression, as detailed in the methodology.

Clustering: The KMeans algorithm is used to group candidates and define priority levels (GOLD, SILVER, BRONZE).

Explainability: The SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) library is essential for generating feature assignments, justifying the AI ​​score.

Core Language: The primary backend language and ML pipeline language is Python.

Backend Framework: The FastAPI 0.110+ framework is used to build the asynchronous REST API, responsible for serving data, model scores, and reports.

Language/Framework: The user interface (UI) is developed using React 18+ in conjunction with the Vite 5 tooling.

Design: The UI design uses custom CSS to create a dark, spatial theme.

Features: The UI supports candidate filters (by period, depth, SNR, etc.) and the theory creation research network system for the scientific community and everyone for writing and visualizing theories.

Data Processing: The pandas and pyarrow libraries are used for efficient data processing, ensuring feature store management and the ability to quickly handle large volumes of data.

Data Source: The system is powered exclusively by data from the TESS (TESS Object of Interest - TOI) satellite.

5. How Creative Is Our Project?

The creativity of the NandiTESS.ai project lies in its ability to innovate scientific methodology and user experience, transforming the way the astronomy community interacts with exoplanet discovery.

Methodological and Statistical Creativity

Inferential Rather Than Direct Approach: The biggest innovation is the departure from traditional photometric detection methods. NandiTESS.ai is creative because it is purely statistical and inferential. It uses Artificial Intelligence to simulate the predictive validation process; that is, it "thinks" like a monitoring observatory, predicting the success of future observations rather than simply recording transits.

3D Distance Simulator: The system introduced an interactive 3D graphic that visually represents the probability of existence of candidates, and it´s distance of our Sun accelerating the identification of clusters and outliers.

Domain Weighting System: The composite score structure is creative because it integrates expert insights directly into the model. By assigning greater value to parameters historically correlated with confirmed exoplanets (such as Transit Signal Quality or Stellar Context), the project goes beyond standard ML, anchoring AI in human scientific expertise.

Creativity in User Experience (UE) and Collaboration

Global Interaction Platform (Social Network): The inclusion of a "social network" system is highly creative. This functionality transforms the platform from a simple data analysis tool into a global collaborative environment. By allowing a scientist anywhere (such as an Australian) to write and share their own theories about exoplanets for a Brazilian colleague to read, NandiTESS.ai breaks down geographical barriers and accelerates hypothesis validation through community consensus.

Transparency of the AI ​​"Black Box": The project is creative in solving the AI ​​trust problem. It not only provides a percentage probability but also uses advanced tools (such as SHAP) to justify the score. This transforms explainable AI into a traceable scientific tool, generating a complete Validation Report for each TOI.

Engagement Through Gamification: The inclusion of an interactive learning journey and a quiz demonstrates creativity in engaging users. This gamifies the process of familiarizing yourself with the validation criteria, making the platform accessible and fun for students and new researchers.

6. What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

The NandiTESS.ai development team considered a number of crucial factors—technical, statistical, and scientific—to ensure the model was accurate, fair, and useful to the community.

Scientific Domain Factors and Metric Weighting

The most critical factor considered was the historical correlation of the parameters. The team recognized that not all data have the same predictive value and, therefore, applied a metric weighting based on established scientific knowledge. This included assigning weights to:

Transit Signal Quality: Factors such as depth and period stability are considered of utmost importance.

Stellar Context: Host star parameters (temperature, metallicity) are crucial, as metal-rich stars are more likely to harbor planets.

Vetting Flags and Geometry: Contamination indicators and orbital geometry were considered to rule out known false positives.

Statistical and Anomaly Analysis Factors

The model's accuracy depended on detailed statistical considerations:

Continuous Validation: It was considered essential that the model not be static. It was designed to undergo continuous validation against new confirmed discoveries and false positives, ensuring its accuracy was maintained over time.

Mean Weighting: The team explicitly considered the fact that the mean is an important indicator of anomalies. This was a crucial factor in calibrating the model, as the validation status unit of a genuine exoplanet can, surprisingly, be below the mean in certain parameters. This prevents the model from discarding good candidates for trivial reasons.

Base Model: The choice of logistic regression as the base predictive model reflects the consideration for a statistical model that provides a clear probabilistic output (0-100%).

Statistical and Anomaly Analysis Factors

The model's accuracy depended on detailed statistical considerations:

Continuous Validation: It was considered essential that the model not be static. It was designed to undergo continuous validation against new confirmed discoveries and false positives, ensuring its accuracy was maintained over time.

Mean Weighting: The team explicitly considered the fact that the mean is an important indicator of anomalies. This was a crucial factor in calibrating the model, as the validation status unit of a genuine exoplanet can, surprisingly, be below the mean in certain parameters. This prevents the model from discarding good candidates for trivial reasons.

Base Model: The choice of logistic regression as the base predictive model reflects the consideration for a statistical model that provides a clear probabilistic output (0-100%).

Usability and Collaboration Factors

Usability and global impact were also design considerations:

Global Accessibility: Scientists from any location (such as Australia) should be able to interact with and view the work of others (such as Brazil). This led to the creation of the interaction platform ("social network") and the bilingual User Interface (UI) (EN/PT).

Transparency and Trust: The team considered the need for scientific credibility. Therefore, they integrated explainability (SHAP) and the Validation Report as fundamental parts of the product, ensuring that scientists can always understand and justify the AI's score.

Engagement: Making research more accessible and engaging was considered, which led to the inclusion of an interactive learning journey and a quiz to engage new users

From Now On:

The NandiTESS.ai project is solidifying its vision for world-class science, transforming the initial aspiration of using artificial intelligence to predict and validate exoplanets into a real movement, driven by the brilliant minds of Ana Luiza Biolcati, Dante Castro, Davi Santos, and Vinícius Pereira. They have proven that young Brazilians can be at the forefront of global science.

Next Steps and the Future of NandiTESS.ai

The project's journey is advancing towards the implementation of a set of new strategic features focused on visualization, automated validation, and global community involvement. NandiTESS.ai seeks to optimize scientific exploration and the dissemination of discoveries in an accessible manner.

Immediate development includes the Stellar Distance Simulator, an interactive tool that will use real 3D data based on astronomical coordinates to visualize the exact distance between detected exoplanets and Earth. Complementing this visualization, the Interactive Star Map will offer a three-dimensional representation of the analyzed objects, highlighting their location, brightness, and statistical relevance, thereby facilitating spatial exploration.

At the core of the analysis, Scientific Validation by AI will be implemented. This artificial intelligence will replicate the steps of the scientific method to validate, in an automated manner, whether a candidate possessions characteristics compatible with already confirmed exoplanets. Research efficiency will be enhanced by the Intelligent Candidate Filter, which will allow users to adjust parameters such as radius, mass, temperature, and transit time to identify, in real-time, which candidates most closely resemble real planets.

To foster communication and scientific advancement, NandiTESS.ai will enable the Publication of Discoveries with Credits, creating a channel where the community can publish scientific articles within the platform and receive formal credit for discoveries validated by the model. The platform will also establish a Connection with NASA Researchers, serving as an open channel for international scientists and educators to follow the discoveries generated by the community and collaborate directly with the results.

Finally, NandiTESS.ai is expanding its impact to the next generation with Gamified Exploration for Schools. This interactive environment, featuring challenges, rankings, and rewards, aims to encourage the study of physics, mathematics, astronomy, and data science among young students, reinforcing the belief that the future of science is collaborative, accessible, and inspiring.

Fun Fact: The "Nandi" part of our name comes from Nandira, which means knowledge from beyond the universe, in Tupi-Guarani, a Brazilian indigenous language.

environments, including orbital
and surface environments.
Explore what it's like to be on
the Moon or Mars, where we
learn about various situations,
including dealing with
different temperatures,
O gravity, and mechanical
problems, preparing ourselves
for various situations. Have
fun!

Mission Habitat, created by team QuasarX, recriates the experience of planning and living in a spatial habitat. With NASA information and inumerous options of templates disponibilized,users will face challenges in extreme conditions, lik extreme climate conditions, energy blackout and tempests, needing to take an estrategical decision. Each mission count with educational quizzes and design challenges, connecting science with criativity in a fun and interactive way. We present a functional prototype, disponible in this web page, that shows connection of NASA information to realistic spatial habitats design templates.

Our goal is to create an accessible educational tool that allows anyone to design, simulate, and learn about space habitats, fostering interest in scientific exploration and systems thinking in missions beyond Earth.

Mission Habitat – QuasarX Edition combines gamification, spatial design, and authentic scientific data:
🔹 Integrates NASA data (Earth Observatory, MARS Rover API, Space Weather Data, Earth API).
🔹 Automatically generates realistic images of the daytime environment based on the chosen location.
🔹 Allows you to explore the balance between resources, volume, energy, and crew comfort.
🔹 Serves as a learning and experimentation platform for students, scientists, and enthusiasts.

The QuasarX team also prioritized inclusion at every stage of the design with:
♿ Voice reading and enlarged captions.
🎨 High-contrast and night modes.
🎤 Voice commands and motor accessibility.
🧩 Children's educational mode, adapting content for schools and science outreach programs.


How it Works
1. Destination Selection and Mission Parameters:
The player selects the planet or satellite (Mars, Moon, Earth orbit, Titan, etc.), defines the number of crew members, mission duration, and launch vehicle type. The system applies realistic volume, energy, radiation, and gravity constraints based on NASA data.
2. Habitat Construction:
The user can drag and drop functional modules (sleep, hygiene, kitchen, recreation, maintenance, stowage).
Each module can be resized to adjust space and functionality, receiving real-time visual feedback on crew comfort and safety.
3. Crew Customization:
Avatars can be created for each crew member, including size, height, and individual features.

Users can upload photos to generate a realistic crew member avatar, facilitating the study of ergonomics and interactions within the habitat.
4. Simulation and Challenges:
Dynamic events, such as storms, system failures, or temperature fluctuations, test the habitat's layout.
The system calculates oxygen consumption, energy, water, usable volume, and other performance indicators in real time.
5. Iteration and Comparison:
The user can create multiple versions of the habitat, comparing efficiency, comfort, and safety.
Designs can be saved, exported, and shared, encouraging collaboration and collective learning.

projectDetails.name: Project Racket Scientists
projectDetails.summary:
We created a story from the point of view of a Coronal Mass Ejection (CME), showing how it forms and the sequence of events that can follow this solar phenomenon. It’s a simple and funny story for children, teenagers and adults. The text contains accurate scientific information along with images and interactive elements to help spark the reader’s imagination.
It brings a humanized perspective to the CME, which experiences anxiety, joy, and sadness. The character has thoughts and emotions, reacting to events that may affect human life. In this way, we believe the reader can journey through the universe beyond planet Earth, from a different point of view than usual, and share in the concerns of the character — who does not wish to harm our lives. She is simply part of our Solar System.
projectDetails.details:
Our team chose the diary format to present the temporal sequence of events and to create a space where emotions could be expressed more personally and vividly. We believed that, in this way, we could inspire reflection in readers about the topic of space weather.

We also added humor to the narrative so that the story would not only inform but also entertain, making the learning experience more enjoyable and engaging.

The informative sections were developed based on texts and official videos from NASA, which we studied and adapted for our audience. The images, GIFs, and videos were created with the help of artificial intelligence, while some members of the team also contributed with original drawings. This combination allowed readers to visualize the scenes and connect emotionally with the character and her conflicts.

We used Canva to design the diary, featuring cursive handwriting and hand-drawn illustrations, giving the impression that it was truly written and drawn by the character herself. Each chapter represents a new event, not necessarily a new day, following the unfolding of her journey.

We decided to include technical information on illustrated post-it notes, creating a visual environment similar to a notebook full of personal notes and side comments. These elements complement the main story, explaining scientific concepts without interrupting the emotional flow of the narrative.

For the creation of images, GIFs, and videos, we collaborated with Gemini, ChatGPT, and Nanobanana. The interactive flipbook was developed using FlipHTML5.

projectDetails.name: exo.AI
projectDetails.summary:
Exoplanets are planets located outside our solar system in the Milky Way.
For many years, identifying exoplanets relied on manual calculations by scientists. Today, however, with the assistance of artificial intelligence, detecting them has become much faster and more accurate.
The transit method, which measures dips in a star’s brightness, is particularly effective for identifying smaller and multiple planets. With even minimal data, it is possible to classify an exoplanet as a candidate or a false positive—that is, to determine whether it possesses the characteristics necessary to be considered a true planet.
projectDetails.details:

We are a online group of different cities, ages and knowledge and all students who sought to create a way to allow all people, of all cutures, countrys, ages and knowledge, to find exoplanets, which are planets out of our solar sistem, using artificial intelligence (AI). When he first exoplanet was discoveed, e scientists used manual methods to calculate and confirm that exoplanet. Our main goal was simple: to provide an easier way for anyone to automatically analyze large sets of data collected by NASA space-based exoplanet surveying missions to identify exoplanets. To achieve this, we leveraged our skills in computer programming, computer graphics, data analysis, criativity and knowledge about the subject to creat an incredible experience with our AI.

The Exo.AI project is an artificial intelligence system that uses publicly available NASA datasets to classify new exoplanets based on the data you provide through the website.

Its main benefit is that it requires little to no prior knowledge about space, making it accessible for users of all ages.

The project aims to simplify and speed up exoplanet research by providing a clear starting point for studying any exoplanet.

For its development, we used Visual Studio Code as the IDE, Python as the main programming language, and HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to build the website’s front-end.

Our project is creative because it lowers the barrier of knowledge and experience required to begin exploring space, making exoplanet research more approachable.

We focused on simplicity and accessibility as the key factors guiding the design and functionality of Exo.AI.

In conclusion, the Exo.AI uses an interactive artificial intelligence that offers an engaging and informative virtual experience that raises learning important topics about exoplanets` identification.

projectDetails.name: The Impact
projectDetails.details:
Introduction

We are a group of elementary school students who came together to develop an educational and interactive game to present the consequences and solutions in the event of a meteor collision with planet Earth. Our main goal was to create an intuitive project for all ages. To achieve this, we used our Scratch platform skills to create an immersive, gamified story.

Game presentation

We begin the story by presenting the main problem of the topic to be solved.The player must choose a location to launch the Impactor-2025. In the impact simulation, the player can select between the Amazon, Florida, or the Ocean, generating different scenarios of consequences in various parts of the world.

The objective of the game is to raise awareness about asteroid impact risks, teach, in a playful way, the concepts of impact consequences, and bring science closer to society. It shows how NASA and USGS data can be used in accessible simulations, combining education and entertainment, making children protagonists in creating creative solutions to global problems, and teaching them how to mitigate the effects of such an impact.

For the game design, we used the Scratch programming platform to build an interface with buttons, sliders, and animations that simulate orbit and impact. The sprites represent the asteroid, Earth, and the effects (crater, seismic waves, fire, tsunami).

When simulating the impact options, the player can observe the impact animation and receive information about the possible consequences. They will receive real data on effects, proportions, and scientific concepts while experimenting with different strategies and observing animated simulations and visual results.

This allows the user to test hypotheses, explore scenarios, and simultaneously learn about the science behind these space events.

We based our information on the DART mission, which was dedicated to investigating and demonstrating a method for asteroid deflection by altering the asteroid’s motion in space through kinetic impact.

To make the game more realistic, we used videos, illustrations, and real images of meteors, location images, and impact studies.

To approximate the data to the real consequences of an asteroid impact on Earth, we conducted a study using as references the dimensions, estimated mass of the system, characteristics, density, velocity, and kinetic impact energy of Asteroid 65803 Didymos, discovered on April 11, 1996, by the Spacewatch program at Kitt Peak.

Asteroid Didymos and its small moon Dimorphos form what is called a binary asteroid system, meaning the small moon (Dimorphos) orbits the larger body (Didymos).

These two asteroids do not pose a threat to Earth, but because they pass relatively close to Earth, they were chosen as the target of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission – the agency’s first mission to test planetary defense technology. This technology could one day be used to deflect dangerous asteroids on a collision course with Earth.

Target Audience

Our project was designed for all audiences, regardless of age — students, teachers, and the general community — especially those interested in science and astronomy.

Its purpose is to awaken interest and curiosity through an interactive game experience that helps people learn scientific, physical, and astronomical concepts in a fun way.

Beyond its educational value, the game demonstrates that children can create solutions based on scientific data, strengthening scientific culture and digital literacy.

The game works as a practical class that complements what is learned at school. Examples:

  • A child can simulate an asteroid falling into the ocean and see how a tsunami forms
  • A teacher can present the game as a complement to astronomy or science lessons
  • The general community can learn that the threat of an asteroid, although rare, is real, and that scientists are developing systems to prevent such collisions

The project aims to teach science interactively, demystify asteroids, inspire interest in science and technology, promote prevention culture, and serve as a bridge between scientific data and the public.

Real Creation and Programming

Conclusion

Our simulator is more than a game — it is an educational tool that transforms complex scientific data into a visual and interactive experience.

With it, anyone, especially students, can learn actively, test possibilities, and be inspired to think like a scientist. Like a NASA researcher, each player is invited to explore possibilities, make decisions, and perhaps even save the planet.

projectDetails.details:
The project “The Woman Most Affected by the Sun” aims to address the dangers posed by solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs)—phenomena that can severely impact satellites, communication systems, electronic devices, and astronaut health.

This project introduces a digital children’s story of an innovative protection system combining advanced nanomaterials, smart sensors, and NASA data integration. The solution detects solar activity in real time, analyzes the intensity of eruptions using algorithms, and automatically adjusts protective layers to shield astronauts from harmful radiation.

Beyond space applications, the technology also offers benefits for aircraft pilots, polar scientists, and workers in nuclear or medical environments exposed to radiation.

The team’s mission is to protect human life in space, envisioning a future where solar radiation no longer limits exploration, showcasing how Brazilian innovation can enhance safety in deep space missions.

projectDetails.name: Solar Fury: The Last Storm
projectDetails.summary: Our team developed a children's adventure story focused on the impact of a major solar storm upon life on Earth and Mars. The story aims to demonstrate: how vulnerable we are to Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs); how they can affect our communication and even our future life on Mars; and how important it is to have scientists and space programs studying and monitoring space weather. The moral of the story is: just as Science can create weapons and threats to human life, it can also save lives.
projectDetails.details:
The project is a children's book about how space weather, particularly the occurrence of Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs), impacts human life on Earth, in space, and even in a future life on Mars. The story blends fantasy and reality, featuring heroic characters who will confront a dangerous villain amidst a massive solar storm. These heroes not only manage to defeat the villain but also neutralize the effects of the solar storm and help a boy from Liverpool reestablish contact with his mother, who lives on Mars.

The project was implemented on an online interactive book platform called Book Creator. Access to the book is public, free, and intuitive.

We hope, with this project, to teach children about space weather and the importance of the work carried out by professionals, institutions, and instruments involved in the study and monitoring of space weather.

For the construction of the book, the adult team member guided the children through every step of the process. Initially, each child in the team studied all the resources provided for the chosen challenge: texts, images, and videos distributed across various NASA and partner institution websites. Following this, the children attended classes on creativity and project management, shared by the volunteer support team of the event we participated in (Jaguariúna). Armed with this acquired knowledge, the team held a meeting where each child was responsible for creating a character and writing their personal story, including some relation to Coronal Mass Ejections. Afterwards, they collectively thought about how to interconnect all the characters' stories, making the necessary adjustments and additions.

In possession of the story, the adult team member used Google Gemini's artificial intelligence to translate the story and create the illustrations based on the story itself and the children's descriptions of the characters.

Finally, with the story and illustrations in hand, we used the online platform Book Creator to create and publish a publicly accessible interactive book.

projectDetails.name: Mission Capybara: Debugging Terra
projectDetails.summary: The veteran Terra satellite (25 years of service) is signaling a bug, but the failure is human, not technical! Our multimedia project transforms 25 years of raw NASA data into a science fiction adventure accessible to children and young adults. The animation, featuring 3D visuals (anaglyphs), shows the hero, the Capybara Astronaut, diving into orbit to "debug" Terra's five instruments (MODIS, CERES, MOPITT, MISR, ASTER). We use real data (deforestation, smoke, climatic extremes in Brazil) to prove a truth: pollution and human action are altering the planet's signals. The experience extends to the interactive Scratch game, where Peanut challenges the user to simulate environmental solutions. All content is centralized on a website and complemented by the Educational GPT ("Capivara Astro Edu"), an assistant that translates complex data to generate action plans, promoting active participation. The impact is providing engagement, connecting global data to Brazil's real problems. The creativity lies in the charismatic hero and the integration of technologies (AI/GPT and Scratch) with validated scientific data (NASA Worldview, FIRMS, POWER), delivering scientific fidelity in a fun and memorable way.
projectDetails.details:
The veteran Terra satellite, with 25 years of service, is signaling a bug that threatens the planet, but the malfunction isn't technical—it's human. Our project, "Mission Capybara: Debugging Terra," is a comprehensive multimedia and interactive solution developed to translate 25 years of complex data from NASA's Terra satellite into an accessible and engaging experience, focused on the youth audience.

The project functions as a gamified learning platform, beginning with an animation that tells a science fiction story where the hero, the Capybara Astronaut, embarks on a mission to "debug" Terra's five instruments—MODIS, CERES, MOPITT, MISR, and ASTER. The narrative utilizes real data on deforestation, smoke, and climatic extremes in Brazil, presented with dynamic visuals that include three-dimensional images (anaglyphs). The plot culminates in the revelation that the "glitch" is not a technical failure, but rather pollution and human action, which are altering the planet's signals.

The experience extends into practical application through an interactive Scratch game, where the user encounters the capybara Peanut, who challenges their knowledge of Terra's data to simulate environmental solutions, such as extinguishing fires and planting trees. To maximize outreach and interaction, all content—the animation and the game—is centralized on a website and complemented by an Educational GPT ("Capivara Astro Edu"). The GPT acts as an assistant configured to translate complex data for the youth audience and generate action plans, transforming passive observation into active participation.

The project achieves its intended impact by providing accessibility and engagement in science education, connecting global remote sensing data to the real problems in Brazil (such as deforestation and heat islands) and supplying concrete tools that empower young people to act. The creativity lies in utilizing the Capybara Astronaut as a charismatic hero who communicates in a youth-friendly language, and in integrating technologies like AI (GPT) and the Scratch platform with validated scientific data (NASA Worldview, FIRMS, POWER), ensuring scientific fidelity is delivered in a fun and memorable way.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
The project utilized Artificial Intelligence in two essential ways, supporting both content production and the educational engagement strategy:

The first major application was in Visual Content Creation and Production Support. Generative AIs (Artificial Intelligence tools/software) were employed for the creation and enhancement of the conceptual images for the project, such as the Capybara Astronaut design, and to assist in video editing. This ensured agility in visual prototyping and resulted in a high level of appeal for the young audience. Furthermore, the Lovable platform was utilized as an AI-powered tool for the creation and structuring of the project's central website, streamlining the integration of the animation and interactive game links.

The second primary front was Interactive Education and Knowledge Dissemination. An Educational GPT ("ChatGPT Cappy") was developed. This AI tool was configured with a specific system prompt to function as a specialized virtual assistant focused on Terra satellite data. The GPT is responsible for translating complex scientific data (such as from the MODIS and CERES instruments) into simple, engaging language, answering questions from children and young adults, and generating concrete action plans and activities, thereby facilitating information outreach and interaction.

projectDetails.name: Space Weather Heroes
projectDetails.summary:
Space Weather Heroes turns science into story.
Created by a team of children from Brazil, the project transforms the invisible power of the Sun into a world of heroes, colors, and emotions that everyone can understand.
Each hero represents a real scientific concept — like the magnetic field, satellites, energy, or radiation — and shows how solar storms affect life on Earth.
Through interactive slides, AI-generated voices, and real NASA and NOAA data, the project teaches that space weather is not just science for scientists — it’s part of our daily lives.
Our goal is simple: to make people see and feel the Sun’s impact in a fun and meaningful way.
It’s a project about learning, imagination, and hope — showing that even children can explain the universe in their own words.
projectDetails.details:
Structure

The project tells real science through stories and characters, connecting imagination with NASA data. It´s a video that can also be transformed into an interactive presentation, featuring AI-generated voices and images. Each segment reveals real facts about solar storms, satellites, and Earth’s protective systems.

The project was created as an interactive PowerPoint presentation, where children can click on curiosity buttons to explore facts about space weather.

Later, the presentation was saved as an MP4 video format for public display.

The story and script are completely original, developed from the children’s own ideas — each child created and represents one of the heroes in the story.

All images were generated with Manus AI, the voices were produced using ElevenLabs, and the text organization and narrative refinement were supported by ChatGPT.

This combination of creativity, storytelling, and technology allowed the team to transform complex scientific information into something playful, emotional, and easy to understand.

Makes science emotional, visual, and easy to understand. Helps children and families learn how the Sun affects our planet — and inspires curiosity about space and science.

Why This Project Matters

- Created by Children: Proof that age is no barrier to science, creativity, or impact.- Global Education: Free access to schools and communities worldwide.- Inspiration for the Future: Showing children that science is not just something to learn — it is something they can create.- Changing the World: By turning invisible phenomena into stories, Solar Guardians inspires a culture where science belongs to everyone.“Science is more than numbers. It is stories, dreams, and the courage to imagine the impossible.”
projectDetails.aiReferences:
We used several AI tools to enhance creativity and visualization in Space Weather Heroes.
ChatGPT was used to refine the original story and organize the script; Perplexity and Manus AI were used to generate illustrative and educational images; Pixverse created short animated sequences that brought our story to life; and ElevenLabs generated the character voices.
All heroes, ideas, and concepts were created by the team. AI tools was used only to bring their imagination into reality.

projectDetails.name: Supernova X – SpaceBio Kids Lab
projectDetails.summary:
“Supernova X – SpaceBio Kids Lab” is an educational platform created by children for children that connects real NASA space biology data through a trilingual interface (English, Portuguese, and Spanish).
The project transforms information from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), GeneLab, the Space Life Sciences Library (NSLSL), and the NASA Task Book into accessible, child-friendly content.
Children can explore four main branches of space biology: Human Body & Health, Plants & Food Production, Microbes & Biotechnology, and Radiation, Genetics & Protection.
The goal is to create a simple, open, and interactive dashboard that sparks curiosity and scientific exploration, promoting early STEM engagement and scientific literacy through real NASA open data.
projectDetails.details:
The SpaceBio Kids Lab was developed during the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025 to make NASA’s space biology discoveries more accessible to children.

The application allows kids to search real NASA publications and datasets and get simplified explanations in three languages (English, Portuguese, Spanish).

Tools and methods used:

- HTML5, CSS, and JavaScript for a responsive interface

- Integration with NASA ADS, OSDR, NSLSL, and Task Book

- CapCut for video editing with original human voice recordings

- GPT-5 (AI) used only for translation and text adaptation (no data generation).

Impact: Encourage curiosity for space science and connect young learners to NASA’s open science mission, fostering global STEM inclusion.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Yes. AI tools (ChatGPT / GPT-5) were used only for non-scientific purposes, such as translating educational content (English ↔ Portuguese ↔ Spanish) and simplifying scientific summaries for children’s understanding.

No AI was used to create, alter, or simulate scientific data.

The “Explain” feature on the website provides AI-assisted summaries of real NASA papers in child-friendly language — without modifying the original NASA content.

All audio in the video was recorded by the children; no AI-generated voice or sound was used.

Video editing was done entirely in CapCut (human-edited media).

projectDetails.name: The Curious Race of Sparkle
projectDetails.summary: "The Curious Race of Sparkle" is an animated video, narrated by Ethan, that explains the complex phenomenon of space Weather (solar flare) through a simple and captivating narrative, created for children by a child. Told from the perspective of 'Sparkle', a curious Coronal Mass Ejection (CME), the story follows his high-speed journey from the Sun to Earth, showing his accidental impacts on technology through the eyes of an astronaut, a pilot, and a farmer. The project was authored and creatively directed by Ethan, a brilliant and dedicated 4-year-old scientist.
projectDetails.details:
To solve the "Stellar Stories" challenge, we chose to personify the scientific phenomenon itself. Our project is an animated video, narrated by Ethan, titled "The Curious Race of Sparkle." The story follows "Sparkle," a cheerful and curious ball of energy born from a giant sneeze from the Sun. His motivation isn't malicious; it is simply to explore the beautiful blue planet he sees in the distance.

The narrative follows Sparkle's continuous, high-speed journey and its consequences, which are based on real-world impacts documented by NASA:

1.    In Space: He passes the International Space Station, triggering the alarms on an astronaut's suit.

2.    In the Sky: His energy causes a radio blackout in a pilot's cockpit, forcing her to smartly change routes.

3.    On the Ground: He disrupts the GPS of an autonomous tractor, causing it to plant seeds in a comical zig-zag pattern.

The story concludes not with an ending, but with a transformation. Sparkle uses his final energy to become the beautiful Aurora Borealis, connecting his curious journey to one of nature's most magical displays. The project's goal is to make space science accessible, inspire curiosity, and teach children about cause and effect in our universe in a way that is gentle, scientifically sound, and full of wonder.

The soul and authenticity of this project come from its author and creative director: Ethan, a 4-year-old science enthusiast. His long-standing passion for the cosmos, already recognized with a gold medal in the National Astronomy Olympiad (ONA), was the engine for the project's scientific curiosity.

This is not only a story created for a child, but by a child.

Ethan's involvement was not superficial; he was the project's editor-in-chief and scientific consultant, providing crucial insights.

His brilliant contributions included:

●     The original concept of the Sun's sneeze, the "SPARKLE-CHOO!".

●     Key scientific corrections, such as insisting that Sparkle should be white in space and only change color upon entering the atmosphere.

●     Sharp narrative logic, correcting the sequence of impacts (from space to ground) and refining the pilot's reaction to be more realistic.

This project is a genuine representation of a child's brilliant curiosity about the cosmos making it a true "Stellar Story."

Our project, while creative, is grounded in real science and data. The primary resources used were:

1.    Challenge Brief: The official "Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings" challenge from the 2025 NASA Space Apps Challenge.

2.    NASA Research: The scenarios in our story (impacts on aviation, agriculture, and astronauts) were inspired by real-world events and needs documented in the "Results of the First National Survey of User Needs for Space Weather" (SWAG, 2024).

3. Illustrations and Story: All creative assets were developed by the team during the hackathon.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Our team consists of Ethan, his parents, and his AI partner, Gemini. Gemini was used as a collaborative tool to:

●     Structure the project phases.

●     Transcribe Ethan's story ideas into a cohesive script.

●     Create of the images described by Ethan.

●     Provide technical guidance for creating the final product (video) in Canvas.

●     Translate the final materials into English for submission.

projectDetails.name: Project AURORA
projectDetails.summary:
The project proposes an autonomous and intelligent system for the management, recycling, and reuse of inorganic waste in human missions to Mars. The system integrates collection robots, automated sorting units, microwave reactors for aluminum smelting, and vacuum thermal reprocessing for polymers and foams. Artificial intelligence optimizes waste logistics, predicts future demands, and minimizes energy and water consumption.

Mini-Scenario: "Residence Renovations"
In the "Residence Renovations" mini-scenario, the system converts structural cubes and inflatable habitat packaging into living modules, supports, and partitions, while foams and polymers are transformed into thermal and acoustic insulation. The combination with Martian regolith generates new structural components. The project promotes a circular economy, crew autonomy, and sustainability, transforming waste into essential resources for human survival on Mars.
projectDetails.details:
The detailed operation of the system involves four main modules:

Module 1 – Autonomous Collection and Sorting

  • Mobile robots equipped with optical, spectrometric sensors, and RGB cameras.
  • Automatic material identification: aluminum, polymers, foams, and EVA (ethylene-vinyl acetate).
  • Routing to specific processes, preventing cross-contamination.

Module 2 – Processing and Purification

  • Aluminum: melted in low-energy microwave reactors for new molding.
  • Polymers and foams: vacuum thermal reprocessed, converting waste into filaments or sheets.
  • Minimizes water consumption and avoids microplastic emission.

Module 3 – Hybrid 3D Manufacturing

  • Combines recycled filaments with Martian regolith (MGS-1).
  • Produces utensils, internal partitions, structural supports, and translucent panels for lighting.

Module 4 – Integration with the "Residence Renovations" Mini-Scenario

  • Structural cubes from the inflatable habitat converted into panels and partitions.
  • Foams and polymers repurposed as insulation and coatings.
  • Waste reduction and increased crew autonomy.

Expected Outcomes:

  • Integral circular economy on Mars.
  • Reduced logistical dependence on Earth.
  • Maximum reuse of inorganic waste and increased mission sustainability.

projectDetails.name: Final Expedition
projectDetails.summary:
Final Expedition – A We Bot Educational Space Project
O Final Expedition é uma ferramenta educacional e interativa criada pela We Bot com o objetivo de ensinar crianças e adolescentes sobre exploração espacial, exoplanetas e o design de habitats sustentáveis. O projeto combina ciência, tecnologia e gamificação para despertar o interesse em áreas como astronomia, biologia espacial e sustentabilidade fora da Terra.

Objetivos e Metas Educacionais
Os principais objetivos do projeto são:

Tornar o aprendizado espacial acessível e altamente envolvente.

Ensinar conceitos científicos complexos através de experiências práticas e interativas.

Promover o desenvolvimento do pensamento crítico, da curiosidade e da resolução de problemas.

O projeto tem potencial de aplicação em escolas de Ensino Fundamental II e Ensino Médio, em workshops de ciências, clubes de astronomia e em competições STEM, como o NASA International Space Apps Challenge.
projectDetails.details:
Objetivo de ensinar crianças e adolescentes sobre exploração espacial, exoplanetas e o design de habitats sustentáveis. O projeto combina ciência, tecnologia e gamificação para despertar o interesse em áreas como astronomia, biologia espacial e sustentabilidade fora da Terra.

Objetivos e Metas Educacionais
Os principais objetivos do projeto são:

Tornar o aprendizado espacial acessível e altamente envolvente.

Ensinar conceitos científicos complexos através de experiências práticas e interativas.

Promover o desenvolvimento do pensamento crítico, da curiosidade e da resolução de problemas.

O projeto tem potencial de aplicação em escolas de Ensino Fundamental II e Ensino Médio, em workshops de ciências, clubes de astronomia e em competições STEM, como o NASA International Space Apps Challenge.

Estrutura da Missão (Gamificação)
O projeto é dividido em fases que simulam uma missão de exploração e colonização em larga escala:

Contexto da Missão: Inspirado pelo NASA Space Apps Challenge, os usuários exploram planetas em torno de uma estrela anã vermelha, analisando as condições de suporte à vida e os fatores de habitabilidade de exoplanetas.

Fase 1: Aprendizado e Controle: Os participantes aprendem a pilotar uma nave espacial virtual e a gerenciar recursos críticos dentro de um simulador espacial.

Fase 2: A Lua: Foco no pouso lunar, plantio em estufa e a gestão de recursos para sobreviver às longas noites lunares, expandindo a base em busca da autossuficiência.

Fase 3: Marte: Desafios concentrados no reparo da estufa, plantio de culturas espaciais e na construção de uma torre de comunicação para contato com a Terra.

Tecnologias-Chave e Sustentabilidade no Habitat
O projeto demonstra como construir e manter um habitat para missões de longo prazo (projetadas para até 15 anos), utilizando conceitos da NASA:

Utilização de Recursos In Situ (ISRU): O projeto ensina o conceito de ISRU (In-Situ Resource Utilization), que é o uso de recursos encontrados localmente.

Aplicação: Converter o regolito (solo extraterrestre) em estruturas.

Materiais de Construção: Incluem o StarCrete (um biocompósito que utiliza amido de batata e solo simulado, sendo duas vezes mais forte que o concreto comum), Concreto de Enxofre e Biocompósitos.

Construção: Uso de tecnologia de Impressão 3D.

Referência NASA (ISRU): O ISRU é essencial para o estabelecimento de exploração e operações extraterrestres acessíveis, visando reduzir a massa e o custo das arquiteturas de exploração espacial (Fonte: NASA ISRU Overview).

Robótica e Automação: Utilização de robôs autônomos para escavação, montagem, transporte de materiais e manutenção automática.

Proteção e Blindagem Contra Radiação: Blindagem contra radiação cósmica e solar usando regolito, tubos de lava e Nanotubos de Nitreto de Boro (BNNTs). O habitat conta com controle térmico e reciclagem de ar e água.

Referência NASA (Blindagem BNNTs): A NASA estuda materiais que contenham Hidrogênio, Boro e Nitrogênio, como os BNNTs, que, quando adicionados ao hidrogênio, podem superar o polietileno na proteção contra radiação (Fonte: NASA, Radiation Shielding Materials Containing Hydrogen, Boron, and Nitrogen).

Ciência da Vida e Astrobiologia
Biologia Espacial: Estudo da adaptação da vida (plantas, fungos e bactérias) à microgravidade e radiação, incluindo sistemas bioengenheirados para habitats de autocura.

Astrobiologia: Fatores essenciais para a busca de vida em exoplanetas: água líquida (H
2
​
O), atmosfera e temperatura adequadas, e energia e compostos orgânicos.

Impacto e Visão Futura
O Final Expedition busca promover o interesse científico e ambiental, desenvolver o pensamento analítico e criativo, e inspirar a próxima geração de exploradores. O lema do projeto é: “Explorar é aprender. Criar é descobrir.”

projectDetails.name: BioNautics
projectDetails.summary: Bionautics is an intelligent knowledge engine designed to transform decades of NASA bioscience research into an interactive, interconnected, and living encyclopedia of space biology. It leverages AI, NLP, and knowledge graphs to summarize, organize, and interrelate hundreds of NASA biological studies, creating a system where users can explore not only what humanity has discovered — but how those discoveries connect and evolve through time. At its core, Bionautics embodies the philosophy that knowledge itself is a living organism: it grows, adapts, and depends on connection to survive. What makes Bionautics unique is its ability to cross data, visualize knowledge gaps, and generate new insights through an intelligent AI agent. Users can ask questions, receive concise and verifiable scientific answers, and visually explore how ideas are related in a dynamic graph of interconnected discoveries. Bionautics bridges technology, philosophy, and exploration — empowering scientists, students, and mission planners to see science as an evolving ecosystem of ideas rather than isolated publications. Ultimately, the project aims to democratize access to NASA’s biological heritage, enabling the global scientific community to collaborate, innovate, and prepare humanity for its next evolutionary step: sustainable life beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Bionautics was developed as a functional prototype — a living proof of concept showing how an intelligent knowledge engine could organize and interpret NASA’s bioscience heritage.
Though still in its early stage, the project demonstrates the core of its vision: transforming scattered research into living organisms of ideas, constellations of interconnected knowledge that evolve alongside human understanding of biology in space.

Our team manually retrieved and curated JSON datasets from NASA’s OSDR Biological Data repositories, organizing them into key domains such as microgravity, radiation biology, human physiology, and plant adaptation.
These datasets became the foundation of a conceptual knowledge graph, where each article is imagined as a node in a growing network of discoveries — a structure that mirrors the way scientific knowledge itself expands: organically, through connection and evolution.

To emulate the behavior of the intelligent agent envisioned for the final system, we integrated the Gemini API as a simulation tool.
It was used to reproduce how an AI model would interact with the data — summarizing experiments, identifying thematic links, and generating insights across different studies.
This allowed us to demonstrate essential functionalities such as:

  • Cross-data comparison, uncovering shared hypotheses and contrasts between two topics;
  • Insight generation, revealing conceptual overlaps and potential research gaps;
  • Concise summarization, turning technical data into understandable scientific context;
  • Natural interaction, allowing the user to prompt the system as if conversing with a domain expert.

The web interface presents this ecosystem of knowledge as a constellation of nodes — a map where users can hover to reveal summaries, expand topics by clicking, and navigate through the branching pathways of discovery.
Each interaction evokes the sense of exploring a living network — where knowledge breathes, connects, and evolves.

Technically, the system is built with lightweight Python components and API integrations, designed for modularity and future scalability.
While this MVP uses static data and AI simulation, its architecture lays the groundwork for full integration with dynamic databases, embedding models, and automated graph generation — enabling a continuously expanding encyclopedia that grows with every new scientific contribution.

Bionautics thus serves as both a prototype and a vision: a digital biosphere of knowledge, where ideas form constellations, insights grow organically, and humanity’s understanding of life — on Earth and beyond — continues to evolve.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Our team used Artificial Intelligence tools primarily as assistive coding and prototyping partners to accelerate the development and conceptual validation of Bionautics.
We integrated the Gemini API to simulate how the intelligent agent of the final platform would process and summarize NASA bioscience data, enabling the demonstration of features such as article summarization, cross-data comparison, and insight generation.

Additionally, we used AI-powered coding assistants, including Cursor and ChatGPT, to support the development process. These tools were employed to:

  • Generate and refine code snippets for our Python-based prototype.
  • Debug and troubleshoot errors more efficiently.
  • Clarify programming doubts and optimize project structure.
  • Assist in drafting documentation and improving text clarity for communication.

All AI-generated code and text were reviewed, tested, and manually integrated by our team to ensure originality and scientific accuracy.
No NASA branding, logos, or mission identifiers were used or modified.
The AI served strictly as a creative accelerator and development assistant, allowing the human team to focus on conceptual design, data organization, and the vision behind Bionautics as a living knowledge ecosystem.
