projectDetails.summary:
The Space Weather Impact Dashboard (spaceimpactdashboardnasa.onrender.com) is a web-based platform developed by Codehunters to visualize real-time space weather data and its effects on Earth. It integrates multiple NASA APIs, including the DONKI (Database of Notifications, Knowledge, and Information) API, which provides live alerts about geomagnetic storms and solar flares. These datasets are combined with satellite tracking and Earth impact mapping to help users understand how solar activity influences daily technologies.

The dashboard displays live solar flare intensity, geomagnetic storm levels, and regions on Earth likely to be affected by disturbances in the magnetosphere. It also includes a local weather module for contextual awareness. By unifying information from the NASA DONKI API, Solar Flare API, and Geomagnetic Storm API, the platform delivers an accessible view of complex space weather phenomena.

This project addresses the growing challenge of predicting and managing the impacts of solar storms that can disrupt power grids, GPS, and communication systems. By transforming raw NASA data into clear visual insights, the dashboard empowers scientists, satellite operators, and the public to take preventive measures. It strengthens awareness, promotes data-driven decisions, and bridges the gap between space research and real-world applications.

projectDetails.summary:
Our project, Space Biology Knowledge Engine (Cosmic Power), is an AI-powered web platform designed to make space biology knowledge accessible and engaging for everyone. It integrates curated scientific data with intelligent search to help users explore topics such as astrobiology, space habitats, radiation effects on life, planetary environments, and cosmic evolution.

Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, our platform addresses the challenge of understanding life beyond Earth by bridging the gap between complex space research and public learning. Users can ask questions or browse topics to receive reliable, easy-to-understand explanations supported by verified scientific information.

The project combines interactive visualization, AI-based content generation, and an intuitive interface to enhance scientific curiosity and learning. By simplifying how people access information about life in space and its environmental factors, it supports both education and research outreach.

This initiative is important because it democratizes access to space biology insights, inspires young learners, and promotes awareness about NASA’s ongoing research into the origins and sustainability of life beyond Earth. The Space Biology Knowledge Engine serves as a foundation for future tools that can merge AI with real-time space data, empowering future discoveries in astrobiology and cosmic science.
projectDetails.details:
• Our project, Space Biology Knowledge Engine (Cosmic Power), is an interactive web-based platform that helps users explore and understand concepts related to space biology, astrobiology, and cosmic science in an engaging and accessible way. It allows users to search or ask questions about topics such as life in space, planetary environments, radiation effects on organisms, and the evolution of life beyond Earth. The system uses AI to generate scientifically accurate and easy-to-understand explanations.
  • The platform’s main benefit is its ability to simplify complex NASA space research for students, educators, and science enthusiasts. It promotes curiosity, supports self-learning, and bridges the gap between scientific data and public understanding. Users can interact with the engine to instantly receive curated information, eliminating the need to navigate multiple sources.
  • The intended impact of our project is to democratize access to space biology knowledge, inspire young minds to explore astrobiology, and create awareness about ongoing NASA missions and discoveries related to life in space.

projectDetails.name: Project Cosmic Relics
projectDetails.summary:
Our project harnesses the power of artificial intelligence and satellite imagery to rediscover traces of ancient human civilization hidden beneath the Earth’s surface. We developed an AI-based analytical framework capable of processing high-resolution satellite data to identify subtle patterns, anomalies, and formations that may indicate lost settlements, ancient roads, or forgotten structures.

By combining techniques from Earth science, data visualization, and machine learning, our system provides researchers and archaeologists with interactive maps and digital reconstructions that bring the past to light without disturbing the land. This innovation directly addresses the Space Archaeology challenge by transforming vast amounts of space-based data into meaningful historical insights.

Beyond technology, our project emphasizes humanity’s enduring curiosity—our desire to understand where we came from. It promotes the preservation of cultural heritage, fosters scientific collaboration, and demonstrates how space technology can reconnect us with the stories written across our planet’s surface.
projectDetails.details:
Cosmic Relics: Space Archaeology — Uncovering Ancient Secrets Hidden Beneath Earth’s Surface Using Space Technology

Our project explores how space-based technology and AI can be used to uncover traces of ancient human civilizations hidden beneath the Earth’s surface. Traditional archaeology relies heavily on manual excavation, which is time-consuming, costly, and limited by terrain. In contrast, satellite imagery, infrared scanning, and elevation data allow us to identify patterns and anomalies that may indicate buried settlements, ancient trade routes, or ruins — all without physically disturbing the site.

How it works:
We studied NASA’s open Earth observation datasets (such as Landsat and ASTER) and explored how AI-driven image analysis can detect unusual surface patterns correlated with human activity. Our approach combines remote sensing techniques with conceptual visualization to demonstrate how archaeologists can use space data for early site discovery and cultural preservation.

Benefits and Impact:

  • Enables large-scale discovery of potential archaeological sites across inaccessible areas.
  • Reduces the need for extensive field excavation.
  • Promotes the preservation of cultural heritage by identifying sites before they are lost to urbanization or natural disasters.
  • Encourages interdisciplinary collaboration between space science, AI, and archaeology.

Tools and Technologies:
We used Google Earth, NASA Earth Data portals, Python (NumPy, Matplotlib) for image analysis concepts, and presentation tools like Google Slides to visualize our findings. Future versions could integrate machine learning models such as CNNs for automated detection of ancient site patterns.

Creativity and Uniqueness:
Cosmic Relics brings together two seemingly different worlds — space exploration and archaeology — to highlight how technology designed for observing planets can also rediscover humanity’s own history. Our project focuses on awareness and conceptual innovation, showing how space data can reveal the forgotten stories beneath our feet.

Team Considerations:
While developing the project, our team focused on making the concept accessible, educational, and globally relevant. We prioritized simplicity, clarity, and cross-disciplinary impact, ensuring that anyone — from students to researchers — can understand how space data contributes to preserving the human past.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
We used Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools conceptually and for support purposes in our project.
AI was not used to generate code, automate decisions, or create original scientific data, but rather as an assistive tool in the following ways:

  • Idea Support & Content Structuring: We used AI-based writing assistants (such as ChatGPT) to help refine explanations and improve the clarity of technical descriptions and documentation.
  • Visualization & Design: AI-assisted tools were explored to create concept images illustrating how AI and satellite data could detect archaeological sites. All AI-generated visuals were clearly marked with appropriate acknowledgment.
  • Conceptual Simulation: We referenced AI methodologies such as image classification and pattern recognition to demonstrate how machine learning could be applied to satellite data for archaeological site detection in future implementations.

All analytical reasoning, interpretations, and presentation content were manually designed by the team.
No NASA branding or copyrighted imagery was modified or generated using AI.

projectDetails.name: AI Anveshana
projectDetails.summary:
AI Anveshana is a web-based assistant that analyzes and visualizes exoplanet candidates from Kepler, K2, and TESS. 
We combined a trained ML model (for mission-specific signal patterns) with Gemini’s scientific reasoning to classify targets, explain evidence, and highlight uncertainty. Users can explore planets in an interactive UI, tune physical parameters, and run two analyses: a pattern-based “ML Model” check and a “Gemini” explanatory assessment. This dual-approach addresses the challenge of turning complex mission data into trustworthy, human-readable insights. It’s important because astronomers and enthusiasts alike need transparent, fast triage to focus limited follow-up resources on the most promising worlds. By pairing interpretable criteria with clear narratives, AI Anveshana helps bridge the gap between raw light-curve features and scientific understanding—supporting discovery, education, and outreach without using NASA branding or design elements.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

What it does / how it works:
  • Interactive panels for Kepler/K2/TESS let users set or inspect parameters (e.g., transit depth, duration, radius).
  • “Analyze with ML Model” calls a mission-specific API that returns a disposition and probability.
  • “Analyze with Gemini” produces a structured explanation (disposition, confidence, planet type, reasoning, habitability notes).
  • Results are rendered cleanly with consistent confidence formatting and clear Yes/No “Is Exoplanet” indicators.

Benefits:

  • Fast triage, readable justifications, and side-by-side AI/ML cross-checks.
  • Educational value: plain-language reasoning and habitability context.

Intended impact:

  • Improve decision-making for follow-up observations and make exoplanet science more accessible.

Tools, languages, and software:

  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Framer Motion, Three.js (UI/visualizations).
  • AI: Google Gemini (@google/generative-ai) for reasoning; custom Python/Flask endpoints for ML models.
  • Data/Types: Mission-specific parameter schemas (Kepler, K2, TESS).
  • Hosting/dev: Node.js toolchain (no NASA branding used).

Creativity and considerations:

  • Dual-analysis design (pattern + reasoning) to improve trust.
  • K2/TESS-specific thresholds and pitfalls (e.g., short baselines, contamination).
  • Uncertainty communication, accessibility (clear labels, consistent units), and performance.

Project Walkthrough:

Welcome / Home Page
  • When you open AI Anveshana, you’ll see the title and a tagline: “Journey through the cosmos … discover exoplanets using AI.”
  • You’ll see sections like AI Models (Kepler, K2, TESS) with “AI Analysis” offers.
  • Also visible: Dataset Explorer, stats (e.g. “1,500+ Total Exoplanets”), and features like 3D visualization, filtering, multi-mission data.
  • You can click “Explore Current Satellites” or “Explore Dataset →” to go deeper.
Mission Analysis Pages (Kepler, K2, TESS)

These pages allow you to:

  1. Upload or input transit / light-curve / planet parameters.
  2. Run AI analysis (via Gemini / ML models) to classify a candidate (confirmed / false-positive / candidate).
  3. View reasoning — the chatbot may explain why it classifies it that way, refer to model features, thresholds, etc.
  4. Compare model & AI outputs side by side.
  5. Each mission page is specialized (e.g. K2 page will use K2-specific datasets and model tuning).
Dataset Explorer
  • This page lists all known exoplanets (from Kepler, K2, TESS).
  • You can filter by parameters: orbital period, planet size, stellar temperature, etc.
  • You can visualize in 3D — see spatial positions of exoplanets in a galactic coordinate view.
  • You can inspect each planet (click it) to open details and jump into mission analysis if you want to test with that planet.
Chat Assistant (AI Anveshana)
  • The chat bot is accessible (floating icon / widget) across pages.
  • You can ask questions like “What is a habitable zone?” or “How does TESS detect planets?”
  • It responds in short, space-themed style explaining exoplanet science, mission workflows, or guiding you on which page to use.
  • The chat history persists during your session (unless you reset).
Navigation Flow (Typical User Journey)
  1. Start at Home → click “Kepler Analysis”
  2. Input planet parameters or pick from dataset → run AI + ML analysis
  3. Review classification & reasoning
  4. Jump to dataset explorer to see similar planets
  5. Chat with AI for clarifications or help
  6. Use TESS or K2 page similarly

Code and data:

projectDetails.summary:
AETHER – Autonomous EcoTech Hub for Mars Recycling is an innovative solution developed to tackle the growing challenge of waste management in future Mars missions. The project introduces a closed-loop recycling system powered by artificial intelligence and automation, designed to convert Martian waste into valuable reusable resources. By integrating AI-driven waste analysis, 3D printing, and mobile app engagement, AETHER minimizes reliance on Earth resupply missions and promotes sustainability through in-situ resource utilization (ISRU).

The companion app gamifies recycling tasks, encouraging astronaut participation and fostering a self-sustaining ecosystem. This holistic system addresses resource scarcity, operational risks, and environmental sustainability—key hurdles in long-term Mars colonization.

AETHER’s importance lies in its ability to establish a Martian circular economy, ensuring efficient resource recovery and waste reduction while supporting NASA’s long-term goals for sustainable extraterrestrial habitation.
projectDetails.details:
AETHER – Autonomous EcoTech Hub for Extraterrestrial Recycling

1. Overview / How it Works:

AETHER is an AI-driven autonomous recycling system for Mars habitats. It collects, sorts, and processes waste produced by astronauts using robotic arms, sensors, and AI vision systems. Waste types—organic, inorganic, textile, electronics, hazardous—are routed to specialized processors. Unprocessable items trigger an error alert, ensuring safe handling.

2. Benefits:

Reduces human labor and increases operational efficiency.

Converts waste into usable resources (e.g., 3D-printing materials, compost).

Maintains a safe and sustainable Martian environment.

Provides insights into waste patterns for better habitat planning.

3. Intended Impact:

Supports long-duration Mars missions by enabling self-sufficient waste management.

Reduces dependency on Earth for supplies.

Acts as a prototype for extraterrestrial recycling systems on other planets.

4. Tools & Technologies:

Software / Coding: Python, TensorFlow/PyTorch, Unity/Three.js (for simulations)

Simulation & Design: Blender, 3D modeling for Mars environment visualization

5. Creativity & Innovation:

Combines AI, robotics, and sustainability for space.

Predictive waste management with holographic interfaces.

Closed-loop system: waste is a resource, not trash.

Designed for Martian environmental conditions (dust, low gravity).

6. Key Considerations:

Resource efficiency and autonomy

Safety for hazardous waste

Scalability with colony growth

Realistic simulation of Martian conditions

Robust error handling for unprocessable items
projectDetails.aiReferences:
AI Applications in AETHER

1. Waste Detection & Classification

AI vision systems analyze camera input to identify different types of waste (organic, inorganic, textile, electronics, hazardous).

Uses machine learning models (TensorFlow / PyTorch) trained on images of space habitat waste.

2. Routing & Processing Decisions

AI decides which processing module should handle each waste item.

Ensures efficient allocation of waste to the correct recycler (e.g., composting unit, 3D-printing feedstock, textile processor).

3. Error Detection & Handling

AI flags waste items that cannot be processed automatically.

Suggests alternative solutions or alerts humans for intervention.

4. Predictive Analytics

AI analyzes waste patterns over time to predict future waste generation.

Helps optimize resource usage and storage on Mars.

5. Autonomous Operation

AI controls robots and sensors to collect, transport, and process waste without human intervention.

Adapts to environmental challenges like dust storms or low gravity conditions.

6. Simulation & Optimization

AI-powered 3D simulations test the efficiency of waste flow in the Martian habitat.

Optimizes system layout and processing speed before real deployment.

projectDetails.name: CosmoConnect
projectDetails.summary:
What We Developed
CosmoConnect is an immersive, interactive, and multilingual "edutainment" web platform designed to teach children (primarily ages 7-12) about space, astronomy, and the fascinating phenomena of space weather. It's a one-stop portal for learning that feels like playing.
How It Addresses the Challenge
The primary challenge in space education for children is making complex scientific concepts and vast amounts of data engaging and understandable. CosmoConnect addresses this by transforming these topics into a suite of delightful experiences. Instead of reading dense articles, children can shape a narrative in an interactive storybook, play games that simulate NASA missions, design their own planets through a conversation with an AI, or even bring a friendly sun character into their own room using augmented reality (AR).
Why It's Important
This project is important because it acts as a bridge between the incredible scientific work done by organizations like NASA and the next generation of scientists, engineers, and explorers. By sparking curiosity and fostering a love for the cosmos at a young age, we can improve scientific literacy and inspire children to pursue futures in STEM. It demystifies topics like solar flares and CMEs, showing not just their scientific basis but also their real-world relevance in a safe and positive way.
projectDetails.details:
CosmoConnect is an interactive educational web platform designed to teach children aged 7-12 about space weather, astronomy, and space science through engaging, gamified experiences. At its core, the platform features "Sunny the Solar Flare," a personified solar flare character whose journey from the Sun to Earth creates choice-based narratives that adapt based on each child's decisions. The platform works by combining multiple learning modes: interactive storytelling with AI-generated narrative branches, three educational games that simulate real NASA missions, a CME Analysis Tool that connects to NASA's DONKI database for real-time space weather data, augmented reality experiences that place animated characters in the user's physical environment, an AI-powered chatbot assistant named "Cosmo Buddy" for answering questions, and creative tools like planet design missions and nebula painting.

The benefits of CosmoConnect are multifaceted, addressing both educational outcomes and engagement challenges. Children develop scientific literacy by learning about solar flares, coronal mass ejections, solar wind, and their real-world impacts on GPS systems, power grids, communications, and the creation of auroras. The platform builds data literacy by giving children hands-on experience with actual NASA scientific data, while choice-based narratives develop critical thinking and decision-making skills. Because learning feels like playing rather than studying, children experience intrinsic motivation and reduced learning anxiety, leading to better retention of complex concepts. The multi-modal approach ensures that visual, kinesthetic, and reading-focused learners all find engaging entry points into the material.

The intended impact of CosmoConnect extends beyond immediate education to long-term inspiration and accessibility. We aim to inspire STEM career interests by exposing children to real space science careers and missions, connecting them directly to ongoing NASA work like the Parker Solar Probe, Hubble Space Telescope, and James Webb Space Telescope. The platform demystifies complex space weather concepts that affect daily life, helping children understand that space science isn't abstract but has tangible impacts on technology and infrastructure we rely on. By making these concepts accessible and exciting, we hope to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and space enthusiasts while building a foundation of scientific curiosity that extends throughout their education.

For development, we used React and TypeScript as our frontend framework, providing component-based architecture with type safety for maintainability and bug prevention. Tailwind CSS enabled rapid development of our responsive, futuristic space-themed design. For 3D graphics and augmented reality, we implemented A-Frame, a declarative WebXR framework that allows browser-based AR without requiring app installations or special hardware, making the experience accessible across devices. Our AI integration relies heavily on Google Gemini API, specifically using Gemini-2.5-Flash for text generation powering the chatbot, story creation, and data interpretation, and Imagen-4.0-Generate-001 for generating story artwork and artistic CME visualizations. We integrated multiple NASA data sources including the DONKI API for real-time coronal mass ejection events, APOD for daily astronomical imagery, and NASA's Eyes application embedded for live mission tracking. Recharts library handles our interactive data visualizations, making complex CME data accessible through child-friendly charts and graphs.

The creativity of CosmoConnect manifests in several innovative approaches that distinguish it from traditional educational tools. Rather than creating a single linear story as the challenge required, we built an entire ecosystem of interconnected learning experiences, transforming a one-time reading activity into an explorable platform with multiple entry points. Our most creative decision was personifying space weather itself through Sunny the Solar Flare, allowing children to experience the journey from Sun to Earth from the phenomenon's perspective rather than just reading about it happening to people. The integration of real-time NASA data means children aren't learning from static textbooks but interacting with the same current information that scientists monitor, creating authentic connections to real space weather events. Our use of generative AI ensures every child's experience is unique through personalized story branches, custom-generated artwork, and AI-guided planet creation missions, making return visits fresh and engaging. The WebXR implementation democratizes augmented reality by removing app download barriers, and our gamification strategy ensures each game teaches specific scientific concepts like magnetosphere protection or solar observation rather than being superficial entertainment.

Our team carefully considered multiple factors throughout development to ensure CosmoConnect would be effective, accessible, and scientifically sound. We prioritized engagement over information dumping, designing every feature to feel like play rather than study while maintaining rigorous scientific accuracy grounded in real NASA data and concepts with no science fiction presented as fact. Age-appropriate complexity was critical, targeting 7-12 year olds primarily while ensuring scalability for K-12 learners through progressive difficulty levels. We addressed multiple learning modalities by including visual elements like 3D models and data visualizations, kinesthetic interactions through games and choices, and reading-based content through stories and chatbot conversations. Accessibility considerations drove our web-based, cross-platform approach requiring no installations, with responsive design working across desktop and mobile devices, enabling self-guided exploration without mandatory adult supervision. We maintained careful balance in presentation, showing both beautiful effects like auroras and practical challenges like GPS disruption without creating fear, framing space weather as a natural phenomenon to understand rather than something threatening. Real-world relevance was woven throughout by explicitly connecting space science to daily life impacts on technology and infrastructure. Finally, we designed the platform architecture for scalability, enabling future expansion into additional languages, more content modules, multiplayer features, and enhanced accessibility options, ensuring CosmoConnect can grow alongside both technology advances and educational needs.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
We extensively used Artificial Intelligence throughout CosmoConnect, with all AI-generated content clearly marked and watermarked according to NASA Space Apps Challenge requirements. Google Gemini API served as our primary AI provider through two models. The Gemini-2.5-Flash text model powers multiple features: our Cosmo Buddy chatbot that answers children's space questions in age-appropriate language with all responses acknowledged as AI-generated in the interface metadata, the Living Storybook feature that generates dynamic narrative branches for Sunny the Solar Flare's journey with AI generation clearly indicated in descriptive text, on-demand bedtime stories and Aurora Tales with AI attribution visible to users, fun facts throughout the platform marked as AI-generated, and data interpretation that translates NASA DONKI CME data into child-friendly "Sunny's mood" descriptions with metadata acknowledging AI processing.

The Imagen-4.0-Generate-001 image generation model creates visual content including bedtime story artwork, scientific visualizations of CME data as artistic representations, and custom imagery supporting narratives. All AI-generated images include visible watermarks indicating they are AI-created, clearly distinguishing them from authentic NASA imagery like APOD photos or mission content. Our Design-A-Planet mission uses AI-guided conversational dialogue with clear acknowledgment that responses are AI-generated. In our code repository, all sections utilizing AI generation are documented in comments and metadata identifying where Gemini API calls occur, what content they generate, and how the AI-generated output is processed and displayed.

Critically, no AI-generated content uses, contains, or modifies NASA branding, logos, flags, or mission identifiers. All authentic NASA content—including DONKI data, APOD imagery, NASA's Eyes embedded application, and mission information about Parker Solar Probe, Hubble, and JWST—is clearly sourced from official NASA APIs and marked as authentic NASA material, completely separate from AI-generated content. Our original contributions include the overall platform architecture, the creative concept of personifying space weather through Sunny the Solar Flare, the educational game designs and mechanics, the user interface and experience design, the integration strategy combining real NASA data with AI personalization, and the pedagogical framework addressing multiple learning modalities. AI served as a tool to accelerate content generation and personalization while our team provided the creative vision, scientific accuracy oversight, technical implementation, and educational design that makes CosmoConnect an effective learning platform.

projectDetails.name: A World Away: Hunting for Exoplanets with AI
projectDetails.summary:
The project is "an AI built to be a cosmic detective," a "tireless digital astronomer."
 It addresses the challenge of finding exoplanets in vast amounts of telescope data by being "trained to sift through the noise and spot the faint, rhythmic dips in light that signal a planet passing in front of its star."
Its importance lies in "the profound search for another Earth, for a sign of life beyond our own, and for a deeper understanding of our place in the universe."
projectDetails.details:
Our project, "A World Away: Hunting for Exoplanets with AI," is an automated pipeline designed to rapidly and reliably classify potential transiting exoplanet candidates from NASA's Kepler mission data. It works in two main phases:

  1. Feature Engineering (The Science): We use the industry-standard Box-Least Squares (BLS) algorithm to analyze the raw, cleaned light curve data (e.g., KIC 1429092 for Kepler-14b).
  2. Classification (The AI): A Random Forest Classifier is trained on these features to learn the statistical signature of a true planet (Label 1) versus stellar noise or instrument error (Label 0). It uses this learned logic to score new, unknown candidates.
  3. The primary intended impact is to accelerate the pace of exoplanet discovery and solve the "data bottleneck" problem.
  4. Benefit: The Kepler mission generated over 200,000 potential signals. Automating the classification process drastically reduces the time human astronomers spend manually vetting candidates.
  5. Impact: By providing a high-confidence prediction score, the AI allows scientists to strategically focus limited, expensive follow-up resources (like ground-based telescopes) only on the most promising targets, increasing the efficiency of confirmation and leading to faster discoveries of new world
  6. Language: Python 3
  7. Data & Scientific Libraries:
  8. lightkurve (NASA/MAST): Essential for loading the FITS file, cleaning the light curve, running the BLS algorithm, and generating the diagnostic plots.
  9. Pandas & NumPy: Used for data structure, manipulation, and numerical calculations.
  10. AI/ML Software: Scikit-learn (Specifically the Random Forest Classifier module).
  11. Data Source: NASA Kepler Mission Data (FITS files hosted by the MAST archive).
  12. Creativity and Factors Considered :Our project's creativity lies in the rigorous integration of science and AI. We demonstrated this by overriding the purely algorithmic BLS result (which incorrectly found an 8.43 day period) and instead using the known, confirmed 6.7903 day period to calculate the features, ensuring scientific accuracy. For robustness, we addressed Small Data Set Bias by simulating negative examples for training. We also prioritized Interpretability by including the Feature Importance metric, showing why the AI made its decision, rather than using a 'black box' model. Data cleaning procedures were implemented to maintain Data Quality.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
We utilized an External Generative AI (a Large Language Model, specifically Google's Gemini) primarily to accelerate coding, debugging, and project documentation, which is separate from the internal Machine Learning component of our pipeline.

Specifically, the AI was used for:

  1. Code Generation and Refinement: Generating the initial structure of the Python analysis and ML pipeline code, including complex calls to the lightkurve and scikit-learn libraries.
  2. Debugging and Error Correction: Analyzing and fixing critical Python errors encountered during development, such as correcting the function typo .remove_nnans() to .remove_nans() and correcting the method .power_at() to .get_value().
  3. Project Documentation: Drafting the required project summaries, generating the resource lists, and structuring the final submission details and flowchart.
  4. All Python code generated or assisted by the external AI was thoroughly reviewed, tested, and manually verified by the human team to ensure scientific accuracy and proper execution against the NASA Kepler data.

projectDetails.summary:
What did we have developed?
ExploreEXO
We developed ExploreEXO, an interactive website designed to help space enthusiasts and researchers explore and understand exoplanets—planets that exist beyond our solar system. Since exoplanets are located far from Earth and direct observation is challenging, ExploreEXO bridges this knowledge gap by presenting well-organized, NASA-based data in an engaging and accessible format.
     The website categorizes exoplanets into three main groups: Nearest Star Systems, Habitable Exoplanets, and Distant Exoplanets. Each section provides detailed insights about planetary characteristics such as size, radius, orbit, and potential habitability. All images and data are sourced directly from NASA’s open datasets, ensuring accuracy and authenticity.
      To enhance interactivity, we integrated a custom AI-trained chatbot, which communicates like a human and answers user queries about various exoplanets—such as their distance, composition, or discovery details—making exploration both educational and conversational.

How does it address the challenge?
This project addresses the NASA challenge by making complex astronomical data more comprehensible, engaging, and accessible to students, researchers, and curious learners worldwide.

Why is it important?
 ExploreXO is important because it inspires curiosity about space science, promotes the use of NASA’s open data, and helps users visualize the wonders of exoplanets in an intuitive and user-friendly way.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — ExploreEXO

What it does and how it works:

ExploreEXO is an interactive website designed to make information about exoplanets easily understandable and visually engaging. It allows users to explore planets beyond our solar system through three main categories — Nearest Star Systems, Habitable Exoplanets, and Distant Exoplanets. Each category presents scientific data such as mass, radius, orbital period, and habitability factors. The data and images are sourced from NASA’s open datasets and APIs, ensuring credibility. Additionally, ExploreEXO features a custom AI-powered chatbot trained on exoplanetary data that provides instant, conversational answers to user questions about exoplanets.

Benefits and intended impact:

ExploreEXO helps bridge the gap between complex astronomical research and public understanding. It encourages students, space enthusiasts, and researchers to learn about exoplanets in an interactive way. The platform aims to spark curiosity, promote space education, and inspire the next generation of explorers to engage with NASA’s open data.

Tools, languages, and technologies used:

We developed ExploreEXO using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and bootstrap backend integration. NASA’s Exoplanet Archive API was used for real-time data retrieval. The AI chatbot was built using OpenAI’s NLP model integrated through Python.

Creativity and design considerations:

Our creativity lies in combining scientific accuracy with user interactivity. We focused on clean design, smooth navigation, and conversational learning through AI. The team also prioritized data authenticity, user experience, and educational impact while developing the platform.

challengeDetails.title: A World Away: Hunting for Exoplanets with AI
challengeDetails.excerpt: Data from several different space-based exoplanet surveying missions have enabled discovery of thousands of new planets outside our solar system, but most of these exoplanets were identified manually. With advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML), it is possible to automatically analyze large sets of data collected by these missions to identify exoplanets. Your challenge is to create an AI/ML model that is trained on one or more of the open-source exoplanet datasets offered by NASA and that can analyze new data to accurately identify exoplanets. (Astrophysics Division)

projectDetails.name: AstroBio
projectDetails.summary: AstroBio-Insight Engine is a full-stack web application designed to make NASA bioscience research more accessible and searchable. It processes 607 NASA publications by extracting text, breaking it into over 16,000 chunks, and generating vector embeddings using open-source NLP models. These are stored in a local vector database for fast semantic search. The backend, built with Flask, also provides AI-powered summarization using a Hugging Face model, while the React frontend offers two main views: an interactive dashboard with key research trends and a search tool for querying and summarizing relevant papers. Users can enter natural language questions and receive concise, AI-generated summaries along with source links. By combining powerful AI with an intuitive interface, the project helps researchers, educators, and the public explore complex scientific literature more efficiently supporting discovery and innovation in space bioscience.
projectDetails.details:
AstroBio-Insight Engine is an AI-powered web application designed to make NASA bioscience research more accessible, searchable, and understandable. It processes a dataset of 607 NASA bioscience publications by extracting full-text content, chunking it into manageable segments, and embedding each segment using a sentence-transformer model. These embeddings are stored in a local vector database (ChromaDB), allowing users to perform fast semantic search using natural language queries. When a query is submitted, the system retrieves the most relevant text chunks and summarizes them using a locally hosted Hugging Face model (facebook/bart-large-cnn). The results include a concise summary and links to the original source materials.

The app also features a data dashboard that visualizes publication statistics, such as the most common keywords and total number of papers.

Tools & Technologies

  • Frontend: React, Axios, Chart.js
  • Backend: Python, Flask, Sentence-Transformers, Hugging Face Transformers, ChromaDB
  • Data Storage: Local vector database
  • File Processing: CSV, web scraping, JSON

Benefits & Impact

  • Speeds up access to scientific knowledge by providing clear, AI-generated summaries.
  • Makes dense academic research more approachable for students, educators, and non-experts.
  • Empowers researchers to explore bioscience trends without reading hundreds of papers manually.
  • Supports NASA’s mission of open science and knowledge dissemination.

Creativity & Considerations

  • The project is creative in how it combines open-source NLP models and vector databases into a cohesive, fully local AI system-eliminating dependency on commercial APIs.
  • The UI/UX was designed to be simple and user-friendly, making advanced AI capabilities accessible to non-technical users.
  • We considered performance, interpretability, and offline usability-choosing lightweight models and local storage to ensure fast response times and privacy.

projectDetails.name: Project :/DarkMatter
projectDetails.summary:
We created the Air Quality Intelligence Platform because we believe everyone deserves to breathe clean air and make informed decisions about their health. Our web application transforms complex NASA satellite data into simple, actionable insights that help real people protect themselves and their families from air pollution. Using NASA's TEMPO satellite observations, MODIS aerosol measurements, OMI ozone data, and AIRS atmospheric profiles, we've built an intelligent system that also integrates OpenAQ community sensors and EPA monitoring stations. Our AI models learn from these combined datasets to predict air quality with remarkable accuracy, then translate that information into clear health guidance. The platform automatically detects your location, shows you which pollutants pose the biggest risk today, explains why air quality changes in your area, and sends friendly Telegram alerts when conditions worsen. Whether you're a parent planning playground time, an athlete scheduling outdoor workouts, or a community leader making policy decisions, our tool puts NASA's billion-dollar satellite technology directly in your hands.
With 7 million people dying from air pollution each year, access to reliable environmental data shouldn't be a luxury. We're helping communities breathe safer, live healthier, and build resilient futures. Every notification we send, every prediction we make, could help someone avoid a respiratory emergency or simply enjoy a safer day outdoors.
projectDetails.details: This project is an AI‑powered air‑quality intelligence platform that fuses NASA TEMPO satellite observations, open ground measurements (OpenAQ/EPA), and weather data to estimate pollutant concentrations (PM2.5, PM10, O3, NO2, SO2, CO), compute AQI, and deliver location‑aware insights through a minimal web UI, REST API, and Telegram alerts; it supports city/coordinate queries, IP‑based auto‑detect, model feature analysis, and accuracy reports. The benefits are timely, localized air‑quality awareness, health recommendations, proactive alerts, and interpretable ML that help individuals and planners reduce exposure and make evidence‑based decisions. The intended impact is to democratize access to actionable air‑quality intelligence, raise public awareness, and support community and policy interventions for cleaner air. It was built with Python 3 (pandas, scikit‑learn Random Forests, Keras/TCN, joblib, requests, xarray/netCDF), a lightweight Python HTTP server, HTML/CSS/JavaScript frontend, Telegram Bot API for notifications, VS Code for development, and Render (free tier) for deployment. The project is creative in its spatial‑temporal fusion of multi‑source data, interpretable feature analysis, graceful fallbacks when sources are unavailable, and a clean, accessible UI. Key considerations included data quality and coverage, latency vs. accuracy trade‑offs, scalability and cost limits, resilience to API rate limits, accessibility and color contrast, privacy for IP geolocation, model explainability, and ethical communication of uncertainty.

projectDetails.name: Project Visual Vortex: The Ocean's Heat Pump (A 360° VR Data Immersion)
projectDetails.summary:
Visual Vortex transforms abstract climate data into a WebXR-compatible, 360°
interactive data story of the Ocean's Heat Pump. As a direct response to the Deep Dive challenge, this minimal-code solution uses the Pannellum library and NASA SVS assets to create a stable, immersive, and educational experience. Our project proves global interconnectedness by showing ocean heat fueling atmospheric change, all through precise, clickable hotspots designed for public accessibility.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem: Complex Earth data (like Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly maps) is inaccessible to the public, despite being critical to understanding climate change. The challenge required an immersive solution.

The Solution (Innovation/Clarity): We created a 360∘ Interactive Infographic that allows users to step inside the data. We overcame technical hurdles (hosting large files and browser policies) by leveraging GitHub Pages and custom JavaScript logic to ensure the experience is stable and requires zero coding expertise from the viewer.

Data Story & Interconnectivity: The core of the project is the dynamic link between Ocean and Sky. Clicking the pins reveals six distinct NASA datasets curated to illustrate this effect, transforming abstract numbers into a cohesive, emotional narrative. The functional, low-cost WebXR viewer is the product.

We built a personalized weather dashboard that turns NASA’s Earth observation data into something people can actually use in daily life. Instead of just giving raw numbers, our tool shows the likelihood of certain conditions, like extreme heat, heavy rain, strong winds, or poor air quality at any location and time of year. projectDetails.name: DeepLife Codex: Space Biology Knowledge Engine
projectDetails.summary:
DeepLife Codex is an interactive space biology knowledge engine that transforms NASA bioscience research into an easily explorable dashboard. We developed a dynamic filtering system that combines real NASA experimental data with hypothetical organisms from "Pyraxis," a chemosynthetic ocean world analogous to Europa or Enceladus.

Our solution addresses the core challenge of making decades of NASA bioscience publications accessible and actionable for researchers and mission planners. The dashboard enables users to filter by organism type, metabolism, habitat, and experimental conditions, allowing instant discovery of relevant research for specific space environments.

The platform features interactive controls that let users explore relationships between extremophile organisms and their potential applications to space missions. Built using Google Data Studio with a curated dataset of 5+ organisms, the system provides real-time filtering, sorting, and visualization capabilities.

This knowledge engine directly supports future space exploration by accelerating research discovery, enabling rapid mission-relevant organism identification, and providing an AI-ready framework for automated summarization and natural language querying of NASA's extensive bioscience literature. The dashboard demonstrates how modern data visualization can make complex scientific research immediately actionable for space biology applications.
projectDetails.details:
Project Title: DeepLife Codex

Overview:

  • DeepLife Codex is an interactive space biology knowledge engine designed to make NASA’s massive library of bioscience research easy to access, explore, and understand.
  • Its purpose is to help mission planners, researchers, and educators quickly find and use NASA’s biological data for real-world missions and educational goals.

Key Features and Functionality:

  1. Interactive Dashboard:
    • Built using Google Data Studio, the dashboard allows users to explore decades of NASA’s bioscience experiments and publications.
    • Users can filter, search, and visualize information based on organism type, metabolism, habitat, and key biological traits.
    • The goal is to turn NASA’s vast datasets into an easy-to-navigate, interactive visual experience.
    • The project combines authentic NASA bioscience results with hypothetical organisms inspired by chemosynthetic ocean worlds—places like Europa or Enceladus where life could exist without sunlight.
    • This blend of real and speculative data supports both scientific exploration and creative scenario planning, allowing researchers to model potential extraterrestrial ecosystems.
    • DeepLife Codex significantly reduces research time—from weeks to minutes.
      • Artemis (Moon Missions)
      • Europa Clipper (Jupiter’s moon exploration)
      • Mars Sample Return
      • International Space Station Biology Research
    • The dashboard is freely available online, and no login is required, which promotes global collaboration and educational use.
    • It encourages open science and knowledge sharing, in line with NASA’s vision for accessible scientific research.

Development Tools and Technologies:

  • Google Sheets – Used for managing and curating the core dataset.
  • Google Data Studio – Used to design the interactive dashboard with filters and visual analytics.
  • Canva – Used for presentation design and project visuals.
  • Python – Planned for future AI and Natural Language Processing (NLP) integration to make the system smarter and more automated.

Innovative Aspects:

  • Integration of real and hypothetical bioscience data within one unified platform.
  • Mission-oriented filtering system, allowing users to search data relevant to specific NASA missions.
  • Future-ready design that aligns with NASA’s objectives for open science and knowledge integration.
  • A foundation for future AI enhancements, paving the way for automated insights and deeper data understanding.

Future Enhancements:

  • Although a live AI-powered Q&A system couldn’t be included due to API limitations, the architecture is already prepared for full NLP and knowledge graph integration.
    1. Automatic ingestion and summarization of NASA bioscience papers.
    2. Advanced relationship mapping to uncover hidden biological connections.
    3. Scalable infrastructure capable of supporting thousands of publications efficiently.
  • These updates will make DeepLife Codex a smarter, more adaptive, and research-driven platform for space biology.

Design Priorities and Vision:

  • Every design decision focused on accessibility, adaptability, and direct mission support.
  • The system serves as a foundation for the next generation of space biology discovery, combining data, AI, and visualization to accelerate innovation.
  • Ultimately, DeepLife Codex aims to bridge human curiosity with cosmic biology, turning complex space bioscience data into actionable insights for exploration and education.

projectDetails.name: Echoes of Terra
projectDetails.summary: This project developed a dataset and analysis framework leveraging the MOPITT (Measurements of Pollution in the Troposphere) instrument aboard NASA’s Terra satellite. MOPITT is a pioneering correlation radiometer launched in 1999, uniquely measuring global tropospheric carbon monoxide (CO) distributions with high vertical and horizontal resolution. The project addresses the challenge of tracking and understanding the sources, transport, and sinks of CO—a key pollutant and climate gas—by processing and structuring MOPITT’s radiance and CO profile data into accessible formats for scientific use. This work is important as it provides critical long-term observations that support atmospheric chemistry studies, air quality monitoring, and climate impact assessments worldwide. By making MOPITT data accessible and analyzable, the project empowers researchers and policymakers to make informed decisions about environmental health and emissions control, advancing global sustainability goals.
projectDetails.details:
This project focuses on the visualization and analysis of atmospheric carbon monoxide (CO) data collected by the MOPITT (Measurements of Pollution in the Troposphere) instrument aboard NASA’s Terra satellite. MOPITT uses gas correlation spectroscopy to measure emitted and reflected radiance in multiple spectral bands, providing vertical profiles and total column amounts of CO in the troposphere with a spatial resolution around 22 km. The project processes this complex satellite data into interactive visualizations that display temporal and spatial CO variations, enabling detailed analysis of pollution sources, transport, and sinks in the lower atmosphere.

The primary benefit of the project is to make MOPITT's valuable atmospheric CO data accessible and interpretable for researchers, environmentalists, and policymakers. By showcasing CO concentration patterns and trends, the project supports air quality monitoring, climate change research, and environmental decision-making. The intended impact is to improve understanding of how atmospheric CO affects air quality and climate, assisting in the formulation of pollution control and sustainability strategies.

The project leveraged Python for data processing and visualization, satellite data APIs for MOPITT data retrieval, and web-based interactive plotting tools to develop an intuitive user interface. Creativity was applied in designing the visualization framework, integrating multi-temporal satellite observations to produce insightful, dynamic maps and plots. The team considered data accuracy, temporal resolution, user accessibility, and environmental relevance throughout development.

projectDetails.name: Project Nasa-Space-Bio-Knowledge-Engine
projectDetails.summary:
This project developed an AI-powered dynamic dashboard  and knowledge graph to summarize and explore a corpus of NASA bioscience publications.  The core of the solution lies in utilizing Natural Language Processing (NLP) to transform unstructured text data from the publications into structured, quarriable information.
The dashboard addresses the challenge by moving beyond simple keyword search. It allows users to dynamically filter and visualize connections between key experimental elements, such as missions, biological impacts, results, and organisms studied. This capability enables researchers to efficiently trace the lineage and interdependencies of scientific discoveries, rapidly summarizing complex experimental outcomes and their broader impacts on bioscience.
The project is important because it significantly enhances the accessibility and utility of NASA's scientific literature, accelerating research synthesis and discovery. By mapping out the relationships and impacts described in the publications, it provides a powerful tool for strategic planning, identifying research gaps, and facilitating cross-disciplinary collaboration in space biosciences.
projectDetails.details:
The Space Bio Knowledge Engine is a powerful analytical dashboard designed to extract, structure, and visualize knowledge from a corpus of NASA bioscience publications.

The project works by implementing a multi-stage knowledge extraction pipeline:

  • Data Ingestion & NLP: The system ingests raw bioscience publications. It uses Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) to automatically identify and extract key scientific entities (e.g., organism, mission, biological impact & etc.).
  • Knowledge Graph Construction: These extracted entities and the relationships between them are loaded into a Knowledge Graph. The graph structure moves data from simple textual summaries to a highly interconnected network, where nodes represent entities (like 'Microgravity' or 'ISS Mission') and edges represent relationships ('affects,' 'studied on' & etc.).
  • Dynamic Dashboard Visualization: The front-end dashboard connects to the knowledge graph. Instead of a static report, it provides dynamic, interactive visualizations and users can query the graph visually—for example, selecting an organism to instantly see all missions it was studied on and all resulting biological impacts.

The primary benefits revolve around efficiency and discovery:

  • Accelerated Research Synthesis: It drastically cuts down the time required for researchers to manually review hundreds of publications. Researchers can find comprehensive answers to complex questions in seconds.
  • Enhanced Data Accessibility: It transforms dense, technical publications into an accessible, interactive format for a wider audience, including students, policymakers, and researchers outside the bioscience specialty.

The core intended impact is to accelerate the pace of scientific discovery within the field of space bioscience:

  • Strategic Research Planning: By visualizing research gaps and redundancy, the dashboard helps NASA and its partners allocate resources more effectively, ensuring future missions focus on high-impact, novel research.
  • Operational Intelligence: It provides operational teams with rapid access to the scientific context necessary for mission design, crew health monitoring, and technology development.

The following Coding languages are used in the making of this project:

  • HTML(Hypertext Markup Language)
  • CSS(Cascading Style Sheets)
  • JSON(JavaScript Object Notation)
  • JS(JavaScript)
  • TSX(TypeScript Execute)
  • TS(TypeScript)
  • TOML(Tom's Obvious, Minimal Language)
  • PY(Python)

The following Tools and Software are used in the making of this project:

  • Google Gemini(AI-Tool)
  • ChatGpt(AI-Tool)
  • Loveable(Software)

The creativity of the Space Bio Knowledge Engine lies in the synergistic combination of AI and Data to address the challenge of scientific literature synthesis. The creative step is not just using AI, but using it to generate a structured graph of knowledge. This moves beyond simple summarization to structural representation. The use of a dynamic, interactive network graph as the primary interface is a creative solution for presenting highly interconnected scientific data, making the complex relationships feel intuitive and explorable.

The team focused on several critical factors during development:

  • Scientific Accuracy and Validation: Ensuring the models correctly identified and related entities was paramount. A robust validation process was necessary to maintain the integrity of the scientific data being presented.
  • User Experience (UX) and Interactivity: The dashboard had to be intuitive for both subject matter experts and general users. Factors like filter speed, and clear data labels were prioritized.
  • Scalability: The platform was designed to handle a continually growing corpus of publications and maintain high performance, necessitating efficient database indexing and API design.
  • Data Provenance: The system ensures that every extracted fact can be traced back to its specific source document and sentence, providing essential accountability for scientific claims.

We developed a system where we collect the waste accumulated on the surface of mars due to astronaut activities. We collect the wastes and pass it through a segregator to segregate the wastes such as metals, fabrics, composites and plastics. We pass these through a secondary segregator to segregate each waste according to its types. And further these undergo cleansing or disinfection to remove impurities or debris. Then, these undergo shredding and the shredded particles are melted in a furnace except for fabrics, which is directly sent to the outlet. Lastly the melted metal plastics and composites are sent to be recast.
This helps us eliminate the wastes pile up on the surface of mars which can lead to contamination of the surface of mars.
It is important to avoid the waste generation on mars as it can lead to difficulty with dealing with tons of waste produced on the surface, for example, earth's surface.
projectDetails.details:
INTRODUCTION: During space missions, various waste products are produced. Considering the limited logistics supply in the Controlled Ecological Life Support System (CELSS), waste recycling should reduce energy consumption, increase recycling efficiency, and improve the quality of the daily life of astronauts.

 

OBJECTIVES: The objective of this project is to collect the waste generated by astronauts on the surface of Mars. The collected waste is then segregated as we find different kinds of waste, such as metals, fabrics, composites, plastics and more, but mainly we are focusing on the above four wastes.

 Firstly, the metal recycling process is carried out in steps such as segregating the type of metal, cleansing it, shredding it and then finally melting it and recasting it to desirable shape and products.

Next comes the recycling of composites. Here, we have three types of composite recycling processes. The first one is the Mechanical recycling process, where we grind the material and we reuse the granulated materials obtained after grinding. Secondly, we have the Chemical recycling process, which is also called as solvolysis, where we use a solvent to degrade the resin. The type of resin may vary with respect to the temperature, pressure and catalyst of the composite. Thirdly, we have the Thermal recycling process, which is also called pyrolysis. In this method, high temperatures are used often under vacuum or an inert atmosphere where we break down the polymer matrix, which leaves us with reusable fibres.

The next type of waste we find is fabric. Firstly, we segregate the type of fabric, for example, cotton, nylon etc, followed by cleansing of the fabric and then we shred it to fine strips followed by reusing them.

And lastly, we have plastics. Plastic wastes are found in large numbers, and its recycling is the most complex process especially in outer space. So, we basically melt the plastic, and we recast it into desirable shapes and products. Our vision is to use these recycled plastics in making of parts of the spacecraft etc, tools for the crew to use, packaging, etc.

 

OUR SOLUTION: We developed a system to tackle the issue of inorganic wastes getting accumulated on the surface of mars. This system will be housed in an indoor area to ensure that there is no disturbance to the recycling process.

This system includes the following components:

1]Collector: trash collected from the crew is transported to the collector.

2]Segregator: They are divided into two parts-

    a) Primary segregator: This segregates the trash into one of the four types, namely, Metal wastes, Composite wastes, Fabric wastes and Plastic wastes.

 b) Secondary segregator: This further segregates the materials into sub-types. An example of this is- metal wastes are further segregated into aluminium, titanium, copper and stainless steel.

3]Cleanser/disinfector: It removes the contamination present on the waste.

4]Shredder: This shreds the waste materials to make it easier to perform the other processes.

5]Furnace: The furnace melts the materials so that the molten materials can be poured into a new mould and be reused.

 

OUR VISION: This system will help us eliminate the wastes pile up on the surface of mars which can lead to contamination of the surface of mars.

It is important to avoid the waste generation on mars as it can lead to difficulty with dealing with tons of waste produced on the surface, for example, earth's surface. We intend for this project to help reduce the accumulation of trash on the surface of Mars and ensure that the crew can make good use of the limited materials available and astronauts residing can live comfortably.

projectDetails.name: Planopticon
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an AI-powered Exoplanet Detection System that analyzes both light curve data and tabular stellar parameters to identify potential exoplanets. Our system combines a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for light curve analysis and a Random Forest classifier for tabular data, enabling hybrid predictions that mirror how astronomers validate exoplanet candidates.
The solution addresses the challenge of manual data analysis in exoplanet discovery, which is time-consuming and error-prone. By automating this process, it allows researchers to quickly assess thousands of potential signals from missions like Kepler, K2, and TESS with greater accuracy and consistency.
This project is important because it helps accelerate the search for habitable worlds, reduces human bias in data interpretation, and provides a scalable framework for integrating future space mission datasets—bringing us one step closer to finding other Earth-like planets.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is an AI-driven Exoplanet Detection System that automatically identifies potential exoplanets using both light curve data (brightness over time) and stellar parameters from missions such as Kepler, K2, and TESS.

It works by combining two machine learning models:

1. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) analyzes light curve signals to detect transit patterns caused by orbiting planets.

2. A Random Forest Classifier evaluates tabular data like orbital period, stellar temperature, and radius to confirm planetary likelihood.

The system accepts CSV files or manual flux data input through a web interface, processes them on a Flask backend, and returns clear predictions such as “Planet Detected” or “False Positive.”

We used Python, TensorFlow, scikit-learn, Flask, React (Vite), and Tailwind CSS to build a full-stack, end-to-end solution.

The project’s impact lies in automating and accelerating exoplanet discovery, reducing the need for manual data cleaning and visual inspection. It is creative because it merges astrophysics and AI, bridging the gap between research and accessible, real-time analysis tools for astronomers and enthusiasts alike.
projectDetails.aiReferences: We used Artificial Intelligence in our project by training machine learning models to detect exoplanets. Specifically, we developed a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for analyzing light curve data and a Random Forest Classifier for evaluating stellar parameters. AI was used solely for building these predictive models, and no AI tools were used to generate or create the project itself.

projectDetails.name: GalaxyGeeks - Mars Waste Recycling App
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an interactive and design-oriented web application that demonstrates how astronauts on Mars can recycle and repurpose inorganic waste generated during long-term missions. The app serves both as an educational tool and a sustainability model, showing how everyday mission trash can be transformed into useful resources.

Users can explore different mission scenarios, receive suggestions for repurposing materials, and choose recycling options. Once a choice is made, the dashboard displays detailed metrics such as mass recycled, energy savings, and resource utilization, helping users understand the broader impact of recycling decisions.

This solution directly addresses the challenge of managing over 12,600 kilograms of inorganic waste during a Mars mission by promoting a circular recycling system. Beyond functionality, our project emphasizes innovation, design, and education, inspiring users to think about sustainability in space exploration and envisioning how future astronauts can turn waste into valuable resources.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is an interactive web application that demonstrates how astronauts on Mars can recycle and repurpose inorganic waste into useful resources. Users select mission scenarios, drag and drop waste materials, and receive suggestions for repurposing items like packaging, textiles, and structural parts into functional products such as insulation panels or storage units.

The dashboard provides real-time metrics on mass recycled, energy savings, and resource efficiency, helping users understand the value of recycling choices.

Benefits & Impact: The app promotes sustainability and circular recycling systems for space missions while also serving as an educational tool that inspires creative problem-solving.

Technologies Used: Next.js (React), TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, GSAP and GitHub for collaboration.

By combining design, innovation, and education, our project shows how future astronauts or peoples can turn trash into valuable resources, making Mars missions more sustainable.

projectDetails.details:
Project Details:
OrbitLink is a comprehensive platform that commercializes Low Earth Orbit (LEO) by providing essential infrastructure and services to researchers, startups, governments, and private companies. Our project focuses on four core pillars:

  1. Orbital Labs-as-a-Service: Lease modular, fully-equipped space labs to conduct experiments in microgravity, from biotechnology to materials research. Users can select lab types, schedule orbital missions, and track experiments in real-time through a web portal.
  2. In-Orbit Maintenance & Upgrades: Inspect, repair, or upgrade satellites in orbit using simulated robotic servicing missions, reducing satellite failure and extending operational lifespan.
  3. Active Debris Mitigation: Deploy AI-guided debris capture simulations to prevent collisions, reduce orbital clutter, and promote long-term sustainability of LEO.
  4. Space Traffic Management Platform: Predict orbital collisions and manage satellite traffic with an AI-powered dashboard, providing actionable insights and API access for satellite operators.

How it Works:
Users interact with OrbitLink through a web-based portal, which acts as both a booking system and an operational dashboard. Researchers can book lab modules, track missions, and view live orbital simulations. Satellite operators can request repair services, monitor debris, and receive collision warnings. The platform also includes interactive simulators that project revenue, environmental impact, and operational efficiency.

Benefits & Intended Impact:

  • Makes space research and commercial activity more accessible and cost-effective.
  • Promotes sustainability by reducing space debris and extending satellite lifespans.
  • Facilitates efficient space traffic management to prevent collisions.
  • Demonstrates a scalable and profitable LEO economy infrastructure that balances financial returns with environmental responsibility.

Tools & Technologies:

  • Frontend & UI/UX: React (Next.js), Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion for animations.
  • 3D Visualization: Three.js / Sketchfab embeds for lab and satellite models.
  • Data Visualization: Chart.js and interactive orbital maps with Leaflet.
  • Mock Backend / API: JSON-based simulated endpoints for lab booking, debris tracking, and collision prediction.
  • Other Tools: PDF generation for invoices (jspdf), simulated authentication, and dynamic dashboards.

Creativity & Innovation:

  • OrbitLink combines multiple commercial LEO services into a single unified platform, acting as the infrastructure layer for all space-based operations.
  • Introduces interactive mission simulators and environmental impact visualizations to highlight sustainability alongside profitability.
  • Pioneers a virtual “marketplace” and data exchange for orbital research, enabling collaboration and monetization opportunities.

Factors Considered:

  • Scalability: Platform designed to grow with increasing orbital missions and lab modules.
  • Sustainability: Emphasis on debris removal, satellite repair, and green operational practices.
  • User Experience: Interactive dashboards, visualizations, and a guided portal for researchers and operators.
  • Regulatory & Ethical Responsibility: Includes simulations of safe operations and compliance with international space guidelines.
  • Feasibility: Focused on creating a demonstrable web prototype suitable for hackathon presentation without requiring actual orbital hardware.

Impact:
OrbitLink aims to revolutionize how humanity interacts with LEO, enabling sustainable commercial and research activity while ensuring environmental responsibility. By providing modular services, it unlocks new opportunities for innovation in space and educates stakeholders on responsible orbital management.

projectDetails.name: Greenovators
projectDetails.summary:
We developed a comprehensive real-time air quality monitoring dashboard that transforms authentic NASA TEMPO satellite data into accessible public health information. Our full-stack web application processes hourly atmospheric measurements from NASA's revolutionary TEMPO satellite through a sophisticated pipeline: NASA TEMPO API → Google Colab data processing → live web dashboard.

The system directly addresses the Air Quality Forecasting with TEMPO challenge by making complex satellite observations understandable for everyday users. Our dashboard provides real-time AQI monitoring, 7-day pollution forecasting, and proactive health alerts for PM2.5, PM10, and Ozone levels across the New York metropolitan area with 2-4km spatial resolution.

This project is critically important because it democratizes access to NASA's cutting-edge satellite technology, protecting vulnerable populations (children, elderly, asthma patients) through early warning systems. With 99% of people breathing air exceeding WHO guidelines, our dashboard transforms scientific data into actionable health guidance, enabling communities to make informed decisions about outdoor activities and pollution exposure.

Built using React.js, Node.js, and authentic NASA TEMPO data, our production-ready application demonstrates how space technology can directly protect public health at the community level.
projectDetails.details:
Our NASA TEMPO Air Quality Dashboard is a real-time environmental monitoring system that transforms authentic NASA TEMPO satellite data into accessible public health information. The application processes actual satellite observations from NASA's newest air quality monitoring satellite through a sophisticated data pipeline: NASA TEMPO API → Google Colab processing → JSON data → Live web dashboard.

The system provides hourly air quality measurements including AQI (Air Quality Index), PM2.5, PM10, and Ozone levels for the New York metropolitan area with 2-4km spatial resolution. Users receive color-coded health alerts, 7-day forecasting predictions, and real-time updates every 5 minutes through a professional, mobile-responsive interface.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACTS

Public Health Protection: Our dashboard democratizes access to NASA's cutting-edge satellite technology, making complex atmospheric data understandable for everyday users. It specifically protects vulnerable populations (children, elderly, asthma patients) by providing proactive health warnings when air quality reaches unhealthy levels.

Environmental Awareness: By visualizing real NASA TEMPO data in an intuitive format, we raise community awareness about air pollution patterns and their health implications, empowering informed decision-making about outdoor activities.

Early Warning System: The 7-day forecasting capability enables proactive health management, allowing users to plan activities and take preventive measures before pollution episodes occur.

TECHNICAL IMPLEMENTATION

Frontend: React.js with modern responsive design, ensuring accessibility across all devices
Backend: Node.js/Express.js API serving authentic NASA TEMPO data
Data Processing: Google Colab for scientific data analysis and format conversion
Data Source: NASA TEMPO Satellite API providing hourly atmospheric measurements
Version Control: Git/GitHub for collaborative development
Deployment: Production-ready full-stack architecture

Programming Languages: JavaScript (React.js, Node.js), HTML5, CSS3, JSON
Tools & Platforms: Google Colab, NASA TEMPO API, GitHub, VS Code, npm package management

CREATIVE INNOVATION

Our project creatively bridges the gap between advanced NASA satellite technology and everyday public health needs. Rather than simply displaying raw data, we've designed an intuitive, health-focused interface that translates complex atmospheric measurements into actionable insights.

Unique Features:

  • Real-time integration of authentic NASA TEMPO satellite data (not simulated)
  • Health-centric design with color-coded warnings optimized for vulnerable populations
  • Seamless mobile responsiveness ensuring accessibility during outdoor activities
  • Predictive 7-day forecasting combining satellite observations with health recommendations

TEAM CONSIDERATIONS AND APPROACH

Soumya & Sai Dhanunjaya collaborated on this project with careful consideration of:

Scientific Accuracy: We prioritized authentic NASA data over simulated alternatives, ensuring our application provides genuine scientific value for air quality monitoring.

User Experience: Recognizing that environmental data can be overwhelming, we designed a clean, intuitive interface that prioritizes health information over technical complexity.

Public Health Focus: We specifically designed alerts and recommendations for vulnerable populations, acknowledging that air quality affects different demographics differently.

Accessibility: Our responsive design ensures the dashboard functions effectively on smartphones, enabling real-time air quality checking during outdoor activities.

Scalability: The architecture supports expansion to additional cities and integration of more NASA Earth observation data.

This project demonstrates how NASA's revolutionary TEMPO satellite technology can be transformed into practical, community-focused tools that protect public health and promote environmental consciousness, making cutting-edge space technology accessible to everyone.

projectDetails.name: Project HackHub
projectDetails.summary:
This full-stack application simulates Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites as a next-gen cloud layer, processing data in orbit instead of transmitting raw data to Earth. The backend (FastAPI or Node.js) provides REST APIs and WebSocket endpoints for job submission, status tracking, telemetry streaming, and LEO vs Earth benchmarking. It includes a scheduler that routes jobs to simulated satellite nodes or Earth compute pools based on latency/bandwidth. Satellite nodes run lightweight ML tasks (e.g., flood detection), stream telemetry, and upload results to MinIO/S3. PostgreSQL stores metadata; Prometheus/Grafana monitor system metrics.

The frontend (React + Three.js) features a 3D globe with orbiting satellites, ground stations, and animated data flows. Users select AOIs and operations (e.g., flood analysis), choose processing mode (LEO/Earth/Auto), and view live job status via WebSocket. Real-time telemetry charts show latency, bandwidth, and CPU usage. The UI compares LEO vs Earth results with overlays and metrics. Satellite positions update using live TLE data; disaster datasets integrate from NASA FIRMS, Copernicus EMS, and OpenWeather. Visuals include neon beams for LEO paths and progressive map rendering. Stretch features include VR/AR, SLA tiers, and orbital mechanics. Deliverables include backend services, 3D dashboard, ML container, and comparison reports.
