projectDetails.name: Project Tooti Frooti
projectDetails.summary:
Exoplanet Hunter AI is a state-of-the-art machine learning system that discovers new exoplanets by analysis NASA's astronomical data using advanced Convolutional Neural Networks. Our system integrates real-time data from NASA's TESS, Kepler, and K2 missions, employs sophisticated preprocessing pipelines, and uses a dual-branch CNN architecture inspired by Google's Astronaut research. 

The system achieves >99% accuracy in detecting transit signatures, processes 100+ targets per hour, and provides comprehensive analysis including Box Least Squares validation, automated candidate prioritization, and publication-ready visualizations. It features a complete end-to-end pipeline from raw NASA data to scientific discoveries, with both command-line and interactive Jupiter interfaces.

This project directly addresses the challenge of finding exoplanets in massive datasets by leveraging AI to accelerate discovery, reduce false positives, and enable systematic surveys of the cosmos. The potential impact includes discovering hundreds of new worlds and advancing our understanding of planetary systems beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Background

NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope was launched in 2009 with the singular mission of finding planets orbiting other stars. Over nine years of operations, it has continuously observed more than 150,000 stars in a single patch of sky, monitoring subtle dips in their brightness caused by transiting planets. These brightness variations, captured as time-series flux data, hold the fingerprints of distant worlds — but detecting them is challenging. The Kepler dataset comprises millions of light curve observations, the majority of which exhibit no detectable planetary signals. Among this ocean of stellar noise, only a few exhibit the periodic dimming that hints at an orbiting exoplanet. Traditional manual methods of inspection are no longer sufficient. This is where artificial intelligence can dramatically change the game — enabling machines to detect the tiny, repetitive dips that human eyes might overlook.

Dataset Description and Challenges

Our dataset is derived from NASA’s open-access Kepler labelled time-series collection, curated for machine learning applications. Each observation corresponds to a single star, represented by 3,197 flux measurements, capturing brightness variations over time.

The training dataset comprises 5,087 samples, while the testing set includes 570 samples. The labels are binary: “1” indicates the presence of an exoplanet transit, and “0” indicates no detected planet. However, the dataset presents a formidable challenge — it is extremely imbalanced. Out of 5,087 training samples, only 37 correspond to confirmed exoplanet signals, while over 5,000 are non-exoplanet observations. This creates a 99.3% to 0.7% split, a condition that severely biases most machine learning models toward predicting the dominant non-planetary class. Therefore, one of our main scientific goals was to develop preprocessing and balancing techniques that could empower the model to learn the subtle features of rare planetary signals.

Understanding the Transit Method

Exoplanet detection through the transit method is fundamentally based on photometric observations. When a planet passes (or “transits”) in front of its host star, it blocks a small fraction of the star’s light, producing a characteristic dip in the observed brightness. This dip repeats periodically with each orbit. By analysing these dips, astronomers can infer not only the presence of a planet but also its orbital period, size, and even atmospheric composition. In our project, the raw flux data — representing the star’s brightness over time — serves as the key input. A typical exoplanet transit curve exhibits a sharp, symmetric dip amid relatively flat light intensity. However, stellar variability, instrumental noise, and other astrophysical phenomena can mimic or obscure these signals. Therefore, machine learning models must be trained to differentiate true planetary transits from noise, star spots, or binary star eclipses.

Exploratory Data Analysis and Class Distribution

Our first step was to analyse the dataset’s statistical properties and visualise its inherent imbalance. Using tools like Seaborn and Matplotlib, we plotted class distributions and confirmed the dominance of the non-exoplanet class. Out of 5,087 training samples, 5,050 were labelled “0” (no planet) and only 37 were labelled “1” (planet). Such a dataset poses a critical problem: a naïve model could achieve over 99% accuracy simply by predicting that no star hosts a planet —

Yet this would completely fail to detect any true exoplanets. To address this, we designed a multi-step preprocessing pipeline to clean, normalise, and balance the data before feeding it to the machine learning algorithms.

Data Integrity and Preprocessing

Before model training, we ensured the data was clean and complete. A missing-value heatmap confirmed that all flux readings were present with no null entries. However, we observed that some samples contained outlier values exceeding ±250,000 flux units, which could distort the learning process.

These were removed to stabilise the training phase. The flux values were then normalised using median-based scaling, and Gaussian smoothing was applied (σ = 10) to reduce high-frequency noise while preserving transit dips. Finally, we standardised all features using StandardScaler from scikit-learn, ensuring that each flux measurement contributed equally during model training. This preprocessing pipeline transformed raw, noisy light curves into a clean, machine-readable form suitable for advanced modelling. Visualising

g Flux Patterns

To intuitively understand the data, we plotted several raw flux curves — both for planetary and non-planetary stars. Non-exoplanet light curves showed random noise or stellar pulsations, while exoplanet-hosting stars displayed periodic, symmetric dips corresponding to transits. These patterns, though visually faint, are the precise signals we aim to detect through machine learning. By overlaying multiple curves, we could observe differences in amplitude, periodicity, and noise structure. This visualisation step was crucial for validating that our preprocessing preserved genuine physical features rather than artefacts.

Feature Correlation and Statistical Insights

A correlation matrix across 15 randomly selected flux columns revealed high inter-feature correlations — a signature of time-series data. Adjacent flux readings are not independent but represent continuous measurements over time. This insight guided our model selection: convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are particularly well-suited for such sequential data, as they can detect localised temporal features (like dips) while maintaining contextual understanding across time. Additionally, flux histograms confirmed that most light curves follow a near-Gaussian noise distribution, reinforcing the reliability of Kepler’s photometric calibration.

Initial Machine Learning Models

We began our modelling phase with traditional machine learning classifiers to establish baseline performance. Three models were tested: K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Logistic Regression, and Decision Tree classifiers. Without any balancing techniques applied, all models achieved high accuracy (~98–99%) but completely failed to detect exoplanets. The reason was evident — the overwhelming majority of non-planet samples dominated the learning process, causing models always to predict the majority class. Precision and recall for the exoplanet class remained at 0%. This stage illustrated a fundamental truth about astronomical datasets: high accuracy is meaningless when the minority class is the true scientific target.

Addressing Class Imbalance with SMOTE

To overcome the imbalance problem, we employed the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE). SMOTE works by generating new, synthetic samples for the minority class (exoplanets) in feature space, effectively “filling in” the data gap without duplication. This balancing method increased the number of exoplanet samples to a level comparable with non-exoplanet ones. After SMOTE,

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

We retrained all three models and observed remarkable improvements. Decision Trees achieved 94.24% accuracy with 91% precision and 98% recall for exoplanets. The KNN model, however, became the best performer with 98.14% accuracy, 96% precision, and 100% recall — meaning it successfully identified every true exoplanet in the test set.

Model Evaluation and Visualisation on

We validated model performance using confusion matrices, ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curves, and F1-scores. The KNN classifier, after SMOTE balancing, produced almost perfect ROC curves for both classes, demonstrating excellent discrimination ability. The logistic regression model, while more interpretable, underperformed due to the non-linear nature of flux patterns. Decision Trees, though slightly less accurate than KNN, provided valuable feature importance insights, showing which flux regions contributed most to classification. These evaluations confirmed that our AI pipeline could reliably distinguish true planetary signals from stellar noise.

Deep Learning Approach: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)

Building upon classical models, we designed a custom 1D Convolutional Neural Network to directly learn temporal patterns from flux data. The CNN consisted of sequential convolutional layers, each followed by batch normalisation and max pooling to capture increasingly abstract transit features.

Visualisation on

The model concluded with dense layers and a sigmoid output for binary classification. We trained it using the Adam optimiser and binary cross-entropy loss. The CNN demonstrated exceptional performance, achieving high precision and recall while generalising well to unseen data. Moreover, its learned filters visually corresponded to the characteristic dip patterns of exoplanet transits, aligning with astrophysical expectations.

Synthetic Transit Injection for Data Augmentation

To further enhance training robustness, we developed a synthetic data augmentation pipeline that injects artificial transit signals into non-planet light curves. This mimics real exoplanet transits by introducing shallow, periodic brightness dips based on Kepler’s photometric precision and typical planetary parameters (depths of 0.1–1%, durations of 2–10 hours). This augmentation not only increased the effective training set size but also taught the CNN to recognise a wider variety of transit shapes, improving its sensitivity to smaller or noisier planets. This technique is especially powerful when working with limited labelled data, as it simulates realistic astrophysical scenarios.

Interactive Visualisation and Scientific Interpretation

We implemented interactive visualisations using Plotly and Matplotlib animations to present model results dynamically. Each detected exoplanet candidate is accompanied by an interactive light curve plot showing the flux versus time, the detected transit window, and the best-fit period determined via the Box Least Squares (BLS) algorithm. Additionally,

We animated planetary transits across the stellar disk to provide a tangible visual of the discovery process. These tools transform abstract numerical outputs into intuitive, scientifically meaningful representations — crucial for both public engagement and research validation.

Comparative Analysis and Insights

After all models were trained and evaluated, we compared their performance across metrics. The KNN model with SMOTE balancing consistently achieved near-perfect detection rates, while the CNN outperformed all others in learning complex, non-linear features. Logistic Regression remained interpretable but less capable, and Decision Trees provided valuable physical interpretability despite lower precision. This comparative study revealed that hybrid approaches — combining interpretable tree-based models with deep CNNs —

Could yield both accuracy and transparency, aligning with NASA’s goals of explainable AI for scientific discovery.

Scientific and Societal Impact

The implications of this project extend far beyond competition goals. By automating exoplanet detection, we accelerate the discovery of new worlds at an unprecedented scale. What once required months of manual inspection by astronomers can now be accomplished in minutes by trained neural networks. This democratizes space science — allowing smaller research groups, students, and citizen scientists to participate in planetary discovery using open NASA data. Scientifically, our pipeline could be integrated into missions like TESS or the upcoming Roman Space Telescope, processing continuous data streams in near-real time to flag potential exoplanet candidates for human verification.

has

Future Work and Expansion

While our current system demonstrates strong accuracy and robustness, future iterations will focus on real-time detection and multi-mission generalisation. We aim to adapt the model for TESS and JWST data, incorporate transfer learning for cross-mission calibration, and extend classification to multiple planet types (gas giants, super-Earths, and terrestrial). Additionally, we plan to develop a web-based dashboard where users can upload their own light curve CSVs and visualise potential exoplanet detections interactively. Integration with NASA’s Exoplanet Archive API will allow live updates of confirmed discoveries, closing the loop between AI predictions and scientific confirmation.

projectDetails.name: PetroTrack
projectDetails.summary:
Our team "Uranium" developed "PetroTrack", a full-stack application that combines vehicle detection with fuel transaction matching to bring unprecedented transparency to petrol usage and its environmental impact. The system allows users to upload petrol station video footage along with transaction logs, then automatically detects vehicles, tracks their movements, and links fueling events to purchases with timestamp precision.

Beyond transaction matching, the platform generates analytics on CO₂ emissions and pollution contributions per vehicle type, displaying results through intuitive dashboards, pie charts, and interactive maps. We also integrated satellite data proxies (NASA/NOAA/Copernicus) to compare present-day emissions with projected climate scenarios in 2050, highlighting the long-term environmental consequences of fossil fuel consumption.

This project addresses the critical challenge of  "fuel accountability and climate awareness" by transforming raw data into actionable insights. It is important because it empowers policymakers, industries, and individuals to understand their carbon footprint, track efficiency, and take informed steps toward sustainability.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, PetroTrack, is an AI-powered vehicle tracking and fuel transaction analysis system designed to make fuel usage transparent and link it directly to environmental impact. The application works by taking two main inputs: CCTV/video footage of petrol stations and the corresponding fuel transaction logs. Using computer vision, the system detects and classifies vehicles (car, bike, bus, truck, etc.), tracks their fueling events, and precisely matches them to transaction records with timestamp alignment and, when available, plate recognition.

The output is an interactive dashboard that displays:

* Per-vehicle CO₂ emissions and fuel consumption.

* Aggregated pollution data by vehicle type.

* Visualizations such as pie charts and interactive maps.

* Comparisons of current emissions with projected 2050 climate scenarios, using proxy data from NASA, NOAA, and Copernicus.

We built the system using Primary Languages: Typescript, TSX , CSS. Markup/ Config: JSON, Java Script. Framework & Libraries: Next.js 13, React 18, Recharts, TailwindCSS, shadcn/ui, for the frontend, FastAPI (Python) for the backend, and integrated OpenCV, YOLO/DeepSORT for vehicle detection and tracking and JSON/CSV parsing for fuel logs.

The intended impact is twofold: improve accountability in fuel transactions and raise climate awareness by connecting local fuel usage with global warming effects. By combining real-world data with creative visualization, we provide an innovative, hackathon-ready solution that is both technically strong and socially impactful.

In addition, AI-powered computer vision models (YOLO/DeepSORT) were integrated for vehicle detection and tracking, while OCR (optical character recognition) was applied to read license plates when available.

All AI usage has been documented, and Bolt AI–generated code/outputs are clearly acknowledged in our README and metadata.

projectDetails.details:

projectDetails.name: Project Zer0
projectDetails.summary:
This project is an advanced AI system designed to automate the discovery of exoplanets by analyzing stellar light curve data from NASA's Kepler mission. At its core is a powerful 4-way ensemble model that integrates deep learning (CNN+LSTM, Multi-View CNN), traditional machine learning (RandomForest), and unsupervised learning (SOM) to achieve maximum accuracy. The system reaches a high performance of approximately 99% accuracy, matching published research standards.
A key feature is its optimization for standard, consumer-grade hardware, allowing it to run effectively on CPUs without requiring an expensive GPU. To ensure reliability during long training sessions, a robust checkpoint-and-resume capability was implemented, which automatically saves progress and allows training to continue seamlessly after interruptions. The project also includes a web application for real-time analysis. Its intended impact is to accelerate discovery for professional astronomers while democratizing access to research-grade tools for students and citizen scientists worldwide.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

The project is an advanced AI system designed to automate the discovery of exoplanets. It works by analyzing vast, noisy astronomical datasets known as stellar light curves to identify the faint, periodic dips in a star's brightness caused by a transiting planet.

The core of the system is a sophisticated 4-way AI ensemble that combines the strengths of different models to achieve maximum accuracy:

  • Hybrid CNN+LSTM: A deep learning model that captures both the shape of the transit (CNN) and its repeating temporal pattern over time (LSTM).
  • Multi-View CNN: Based on Google Brain's research, this model processes the light curve from both a global (full view) and local (zoomed-in) perspective to analyze overall patterns and fine details simultaneously.
  • RandomForest: A classical machine learning model that makes predictions based on over 30 engineered features, such as the statistical properties and depth of the transit dip.
  • Self-Organizing Map (SOM): An unsupervised learning model that acts as an anomaly detector, clustering the data to find unusual light curves that don't fit expected patterns.

The final prediction is made using a weighted voting system, where the outputs of these models are combined based on their individual performance (AUC scores). The workflow also includes a web application, built with a Flask backend, that allows a user to upload their own data for analysis and visualization.

What benefits does it have?

The project offers several significant benefits:

  • High Performance: It achieves approximately 99% accuracy, matching the standards of published, state-of-the-art research in the field.
  • Accessibility: A key benefit is that it is optimized to run on standard, consumer-grade CPUs (specifically an AMD Ryzen 7 5700U) without needing expensive, specialized GPU hardware. This democratizes access for students, researchers with limited budgets, and citizen scientists.
  • Reliability and Efficiency: It includes a production-ready checkpoint and resume system that automatically saves training progress. This prevents hours of lost work due to interruptions and makes long training runs feasible on non-dedicated machines. It also dramatically accelerates the discovery workflow for professional astronomers.
  • Educational Value: The system serves as a powerful, hands-on educational tool for teaching concepts in AI, data science, and astrophysics.
  • Broader Applicability: The core time-series analysis and anomaly detection methods are highly transferable and can be applied to other domains like medical diagnostics, financial forecasting, and industrial monitoring.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is multi-faceted. For the scientific community, it aims to directly contribute to fundamental astronomy research by accelerating the rate of exoplanet discovery. For students and amateur astronomers, the project seeks to democratize the field by providing accessible, powerful, research-grade tools that don't require supercomputers. Ultimately, the project's goal is to empower a new generation of researchers to contribute to humanity's understanding of planetary systems beyond our own.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Coding Language: The project was developed in Python, as indicated by the use of python3 commands to run all scripts.
  • Tools and Software: The development relied on a stack of proven open-source libraries. This includesPandas for data processing, NumPy for numerical operations, and Flask for the web application backend. The deep learning models were likely built using a framework likeTensorFlow or Keras (implied by .h5 and .keras model file formats), and Scikit-learn was used for the RandomForest model.
  • Hardware: The system was specifically optimized for and tested on consumer-grade hardware: an AMD Ryzen 7 5700U CPU with 16 cores and 14GB of RAM. A key design feature is that it is built forCPU-only training and does not require a GPU.

How is your project creative?

The project's creativity lies in its comprehensive and integrated approach to a complex scientific problem.

  • Innovative Ensemble Architecture: Its primary innovation is the integration of four distinct AI paradigms—deep learning, classical machine learning, and unsupervised learning—into a single, unified system. Instead of relying on one method, it leverages the complementary strengths of each to create a more robust and accurate solution that covers temporal, spatial, statistical, and anomaly-based detection.
  • Accessibility Engineering: A significant creative aspect was engineering this state-of-the-art system to be highly efficient. Making it run effectively on standard consumer hardware without a GPU required creative solutions for memory management, data batching, and overall optimization, making high-end science accessible to a wider audience.

What factors did your team consider?

The development team considered several critical real-world factors:

  • Hardware Limitations: The primary consideration was the constraint of using common consumer hardware. This influenced decisions on memory optimization, data batching, and thread management to prevent crashes on systems with limited RAM.
  • Long Training Times: The team anticipated that training on a CPU would take several hours. To mitigate this, they designed and implemented the robust checkpoint/resume system to ensure that user progress would not be lost during an interruption.
  • Data Imbalance: A major scientific challenge was the extreme class imbalance in the dataset, where non-exoplanet signals vastly outnumber true exoplanet signals. The team addressed this by implementing advanced techniques like class weighting, L2 regularization, and dropout to prevent the model from becoming biased and ensure it could detect the rare positive cases.
  • Scientific Rigor: The team aimed to match or exceed the performance of published academic research. This involved using official NASA Kepler datasets for reproducibility and benchmarking the system's performance against established papers.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
1. AI as the Core Scientific Method

The primary use of AI in this project is as the subject of the research and development. The entire system is an original AI application designed to solve a scientific problem: the detection of exoplanets from Kepler mission data. The AI is the core innovation, not an external tool used to generate project components.

This involves several AI paradigms:

  • Deep Learning: We developed custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models to analyze time-series data.
  • Classical Machine Learning: We implemented a RandomForest model using engineered features for interpretable classification.
  • Unsupervised Learning: We utilized a Self-Organizing Map (SOM) for anomaly detection and clustering.

The final deliverable is this functional, multi-model AI ensemble designed for scientific discovery.

2. Code and Data

  • Data: The training and testing data are the official NASA Kepler Mission datasets (exoTrain.csv and exoTest.csv). No data was generated by AI.
  • Code: The Python code for the model architectures, preprocessing, and training pipelines was developed by the team. The model designs were inspired by and based on published scientific papers, such as those by Shallue & Vanderburg (2018) and Pearson et al. (2018).External AI coding assistants were not used to generate the core logic or algorithms of the project.

3. Images and Videos

We distinguish between data-driven visualizations and illustrative media:

  • Data Visualizations: All scientific plots, such as ROC curves, confusion matrices, and training history graphs, were generated by our project's Python code using libraries like Matplotlib or Seaborn. They are direct visual representations of the model's performance on the dataset and are not AI-generated art.
  • Illustrative Images: For any purely decorative or illustrative images used in presentations (such as the artistic renderings of planets in EXOPLANET.pdf), we commit to the NASA guidelines. If such an image were generated using an AI tool, it would be amended to include a visible watermark indicating it is AI-generated.
  • Videos: No AI-generated videos were used in this project.

4. Audio

No AI-generated audio was used in this project.

5. Descriptive Text and Documentation

To accelerate the creation of clear and comprehensive documentation, AI language models may have been used as an assistive tool for drafting, summarizing, and refining descriptive text (e.g., in README files, guides, and summaries). The originality, intent, and technical accuracy of all written content were directed and verified by the team.

Our team has leveraged AI as a powerful tool to accelerate innovation, with a commitment to originality and transparency in its application.

projectDetails.name: Will It Rain On My Parade ?
projectDetails.summary: Our project, “Will It Rain on My Parade?”, is a web-based platform designed to help users plan outdoor events like parades or parties based on accurate weather forecasts. By entering a location, the system retrieves real-time weather data from NASA’s open datasets and other meteorological APIs to display rainfall predictions, temperature, humidity, and other weather thresholds. It then provides AI-driven recommendations on the best times or dates to schedule events. This project addresses the challenge of weather uncertainty by making data-driven decisions accessible to everyone. It empowers communities, event planners, and individuals to plan confidently, minimize cancellations, and ensure safety and enjoyment during outdoor gatherings.
projectDetails.details:
• The application is a real-time weather impact analysis & event planning dashboard. It helps event planners assess how upcoming weather might affect an outdoor event (parade, concert, festival, sports event, etc.).
    • Displaying current weather conditions (temperature, humidity, wind, pressure, visibility, etc.).
    • Showing a rain forecast / probability over the next 24 hours (or relevant event window).
    • Displaying weather alerts (e.g. high UV index, wind gust warnings).
    • Performing event impact analysis:
      • Estimating attendance drop or risk levels due to weather.
      • Evaluating “weather risk” and “optimal conditions” metrics.
    • Giving recommendations or mitigations (e.g. “provide sunscreen stations,” “secure lightweight decorations,” “water stations,” etc.).
    • Allowing specification of event details (name, date, time, location, type) and optionally mapping a route or waypoints (for parades).
    • Possibly visualizing historical weather patterns to compare past similar dates.
    1. The front-end UI takes event input and displays weather and impact metrics.
    2. The back-end (or client-side) fetches real-time weather data (via a weather API, e.g. OpenWeatherMap, NOAA, or another service).
    3. It processes the weather data (forecast, alerts) and applies impact estimation logic (e.g. risk models, thresholds, heuristics).
    4. It presents the output on a dashboard, with charts, maps, and recommendation text.

TOOLS USED:

  • Frontend:
    • HTML, CSS, JavaScript (or a JS framework such as React, Vue, or Angular)
    • UI libraries / component frameworks (e.g. Tailwind, Bootstrap, Material UI)
    • Map / geospatial libraries (e.g. Leaflet, Mapbox, Google Maps) for route mapping
    • A weather data API (e.g. OpenWeather, NOAA, Weatherbit, etc.)
    • A backend server (Node.js / Express, Python Flask or Django, etc.) to fetch/process data (if not entirely client-side)
    • Possibly a cloud function / serverless (AWS Lambda, Netlify Functions, Google Cloud Functions) to handle API calls and computations
    • JavaScript (or Python) for implementing analysis logic, risk models, heuristics
    • Libraries for date/time and weather math (e.g. moment.js, date-fns)
    • Hosting on Netlify (as seen in the URL) for front-end
    • Possibly a serverless backend or API proxy via Netlify Functions
    • Use of environment variables / secrets for API keys
    • Version control (Git, GitHub) for team collaboration
    • API documentation / Postman or similar to test endpoints
    • Mapping and geocoding services (for converting location inputs to coordinates)
    • Possibly charts / visualization libraries (D3.js, Chart.js, Plotly) for trend graphs or gauges

THIS IS HOW OUR PROJECT IS CREATIVE:

  • It combines event planning logistics with real-time weather forecasting and risk analytics in a domain-specific, user-centric way. Many weather apps exist, but few are tailored to event impact.
  • The mapping + route planning component is creative: letting event planners draw or define parade routes / waypoints and seeing localized forecasts along the path.
  • The recommendation engine (mitigation suggestions) adds a “smart advisor” layer beyond just raw numbers.
  • Integrating historical weather comparisons to contextualize forecasts is a creative value-add.
  • The user interface likely emphasizes simplicity and intuitive dashboards—bridging technical meteorological data and actionable insights.
  • Possibly the team included creative visual alerts, color-coded risk shading, or storytelling components (weather narratives) to help communicate risk beyond numbers.

We used Artificial Intelligence to analyze weather data and assess event risk levels.
AI algorithms (or pre-trained models) were used for:

  • Predicting rain probability and severity based on weather parameters.
  • Generating smart recommendations for event safety and preparedness (e.g., “carry umbrellas,” “shift timing”).
  • Summarizing forecast data into user-friendly insights using natural language generation (AI text summaries).
  • Enhancing decision-making by classifying events into “Low,” “Moderate,” or “High” weather-risk categories.

projectDetails.name: Horizon Hues
projectDetails.summary: Horizon Hues is an interactive web application that provides historical weather probabilities for any location on Earth. By entering a date, users can view the long-term odds of rain and the average maximum temperature for that specific day, derived from nearly 20 years of climate data. It simplifies decades of complex Earth observation information into easy-to-understand daily weather insights through an intuitive map and clean interface. Instead of requiring users to navigate complex databases, it presents actionable climatological insights that support long-term planning in sectors like agriculture, event management, and travel. Most importantly, Horizon Hues democratizes climate data by making it accessible and practical for everyone—from farmers to event planners—helping them make informed decisions, reduce uncertainty, and plan confidently based on reliable historical weather patterns.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

HorizonHues is an interactive web application that provides users with data-driven historical weather probabilities for any location on Earth. Instead of a short-term forecast, HorizonHues leverages decades of climatological data to answer the question: "For a specific future date, what has the weather typically been like?"

How it works:

The application is built on a client-server architecture.

  1. The Frontend is a dynamic, single-page application featuring a full-screen interactive map built with Leaflet.js. A user selects a location by searching, clicking the map, or dragging a pin. They then input a future date (day, month, and year) into a collapsible sidebar.
  2. The Backend, a Python/Flask API, receives the location and date. It calls the Open-Meteo historical weather API to fetch nearly 20 years of daily data for that specific point.
  3. Data Processing: Using the Pandas library, the backend calculates key statistics: the historical average temperature and probability of rain for the requested calendar day. It also generates data for a 7-day trend and applies a simple predictive model to estimate future conditions based on climate trends.
  4. The Result: The processed data is sent back to the frontend as JSON and displayed in a user-friendly dashboard in the sidebar, featuring a text summary and a Chart.js line graph of the 7-day temperature trend.

What benefits does it have?

The primary benefit of HorizonHues is that it empowers users to make smarter long-term decisions by reducing weather-related uncertainty. Standard forecasts only work for 1-2 weeks out; our application provides valuable insight for planning events, vacations, or agricultural activities months or even years in advance. By presenting complex climatological data in an intuitive, visual format, it makes powerful information accessible to everyone, not just scientists.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to democratize access to historical climate data, helping people be more prepared and strategic in their long-term planning. For an individual, this could mean choosing a wedding date with a lower historical chance of rain. For a community, it could mean understanding how the likelihood of extreme heat for a local festival has changed over time. The project aims to bridge the gap between vast scientific datasets and practical, everyday decision-making.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+), Leaflet.js (Mapping), Leaflet-GeoSearch (Location Search), Chart.js (Data Visualization).
  • Backend: Python, Flask (Web Framework), Pandas (Data Analysis), Requests (API Calls), Flask-Cors (CORS Handling), Gunicorn (Web Server).
  • Data Sources: Open-Meteo API (Historical Weather), OpenStreetMap Nominatim (Reverse Geocoding).
  • Deployment: The frontend is hosted on Netlify, and the backend is hosted on Render, with code managed and deployed via GitHub.
  • Development Tools: Anaconda, Jupyter Notebook, and Browser Developer Tools.

How is your project creative?

ClimaDash is creative in its user experience and data synthesis.

  1. UI/UX: It combines a full-screen, interactive map with a sleek, collapsible "glassmorphism" sidebar. This creates an immersive and modern interface that makes data exploration feel fluid and engaging. The UI switches from a control panel to a results dashboard upon a successful query, focusing the user's attention.
  2. Data Synthesis: The application doesn't just display data; it creates new insights. It synthesizes nearly two decades of daily data into a simple probability, applies a predictive trend model, and visualizes a 7-day historical pattern—all from a single user request. It also creatively combines weather data with geocoding data to provide human-readable location names.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team prioritized three main factors throughout development:

  1. User-Centric Design: Every decision was driven by the goal of making the application as intuitive as possible. This led to features like click-to-move-pin, an integrated search bar, and the final full-screen layout with a responsive sidebar that expands to showcase the results.
  2. Rapid Prototyping & Adaptability: The project's journey reflects a key hackathon skill: strategic pivoting. We began by attempting to interface with complex, professional NASA data sources (OPeNDAP) but quickly adapted when faced with authentication and development speed roadblocks. We transitioned to the NASA POWER API and finally to the keyless Open-Meteo API to ensure we could deliver a robust, working product within the time limit.
  3. Performance and Reliability: We chose a client-server architecture to keep the frontend lightweight. The backend handles all heavy data processing. We selected reliable, open-source libraries and deployment platforms with free tiers (Netlify, Render) to ensure the application is both performant and consistently available.

projectDetails.name: NASA Bioscience Explorer
projectDetails.summary:
Problem Statement:Build a Space Biology Knowledge Engine

We built the NASA Bioscience Explorer, a lightweight web app that turns the 608 Space Biology publications and other listed publications into an actionable, searchable knowledge engine. A small ingestion pipeline enriches the official CSV with PMC metadata, then uses Gemini to produce results-first summaries, extract mission-relevant impacts, and surface knowledge gaps for each study. We embed every paper for semantic search and rank results by cosine similarity (with a robust keyword fallback).

The dashboard lets users interrogate the corpus with interactive filters like organism, environment, platform, domain, and year. It also quick links back to the original sources and an insights view for trend spotting. The tech stack used is Node + Express + SQLite,  it runs anywhere and re-ingesting simply updates records (no duplicates).

This directly addresses the challenge by compressing decades of scattered findings into concise briefings and explorable facets, helping scientists generate hypotheses faster, helping managers identify gaps worth funding, and helping mission architects de-risk decisions for returning to the Moon and reaching Mars.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

The NASA Bioscience Explorer is a dynamic dashboard that turns hundreds/thousands of NASA space-biology papers into an actionable knowledge engine. It:

  • Generates concise, results-first summaries for each study.
  • Extracts mission-relevant impacts and knowledge gaps as short bullet points.
  • Supports fast semantic search with filters for organism, environment, platform, domain, and year.
  • Links back to the original sources for verification.

How it works

  1. Data ingestion & enrichment
    • Start from NASA’s 608-publication list; optionally add NSLSL/OSDR/Task Book exports.
    • Enrich metadata via NCBI PMC E-utilities to fetch abstracts and years.
    • Gemini 2.5 Flash produces objective, “results-first” summaries.
    • A second constrained prompt returns strict JSON for impacts and knowledge gaps.
    • text-embedding-004 creates embeddings for semantic retrieval.
    • Everything is stored in SQLite; a stable doc_key enables UPSERT (re-ingest updates, no duplicates).
    • The API ranks result by cosine similarity; if embeddings are missing, a keyword fallback keeps results useful.
    • Lightweight web frontend with a responsive Three.js space backdrop
    • Faceted filters and an insights panel for quick trend spotting.

Benefits

  • Speed to insight compresses long papers into 120-word briefings focused on measured outcomes.
  • Actionability: impacts/gaps make findings useful to mission planners and program managers (where to invest; what risks remain).
  • Discoverability: semantic search + facets reveal clusters and trends across organisms, environments, and platforms.
  • Transparency: every card links to the source; ingestion scripts are open and repeatable.

Intended impact

Support a new era of human exploration by making bioscience knowledge easy to query, compare, and act on by helping scientists generate hypotheses faster, helping managers identify gaps worth funding, and helping mission architects reduce uncertainty for the Moon and Mars.

Tools, languages, software

  • Backend: Node.js (Express), SQLite (better-sqlite3), CSV/XML tooling (csv-parse, fast-xml-parser).
  • AI: Google Gemini 2.5 Flash (summaries/extraction), text-embedding-004 (embeddings).
  • Data APIs: NCBI PMC E-utilities for metadata enrichment.
  • Frontend: Vanilla JS + Three.js for the animated background; accessible, responsive UI.
  • Ops: .env for secrets, .gitignore for DB and large CSVs, seed scripts for offline demo.

What’s creative

  • A results-first summarization style that emphasizes measurable outcomes and conditions (not hype).
  • Dedicated, constrained prompts for impacts and gaps to keep them crisp and mission relevant.
  • A playful yet subtle space visualization that respects accessibility (zoom caps, reduced motion).
  • Resilient design: UPSERT deduping, facet normalization, fallback search, so the demo stays robust under hackathon constraints.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific fidelity: objective phrasing; link-back for verification.
  • Reliability: graceful fallbacks, JSON parsing guards, data cleaning to prevent facet noise.
  • Portability & cost: SQLite + Node runs anywhere; Flash model keeps latency/cost low.
  • Accessibility: color contrast, keyboard focus, reduced-motion support.
  • Extensibility: ready for a Knowledge-Graph view (co-occurrence of organism↔environment↔platform↔domain) and consensus/mismatch analysis across study clusters.

projectDetails.name: BioSynapse: Space Biology AI Gap Analyzer
projectDetails.summary: BioSynapse is a web platform that analyzes 607 NASA space biology publications to identify where AI/ML is under-utilized. Only 2.6% of papers use AI, leaving a 97.4% gap. The tool classifies each paper into seven research domains, visualizes AI adoption rates in an interactive dashboard, and recommends targeted AI techniques—such as deep learning for brain imaging and time-series for radiation effects—to accelerate discovery, optimize biomarker identification, and enhance astronaut health monitoring. By transforming decades of research into actionable AI opportunities, BioSynapse empowers researchers and mission planners to make data-driven decisions for safer, more efficient Mars exploration.
projectDetails.details: BioSynapse ingests SB_publications data (reference: https://github.com/jgalazka/SB_publications.git) and uses Python/Pandas for keyword-based AI detection and domain classification. It calculates AI adoption rates and displays gaps via a JavaScript/Chart.js dashboard. Users can search, filter by research area, and view “AI Potential” scores. The platform generates prioritized recommendations—such as ML for immune response prediction and computer vision for cellular analysis—guiding future research. Built with HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript ES6+, and hosted via GitHub Pages, it requires no installation.

NASA has been performing biology experiments in space for decades, generating a tremendous amount of information that will need to be considered as humans prepare to revisit the Moon and explore Mars. Although this knowledge is publicly available, it can be difficult for potential users to find information that pertains to their specific interests. Your challenge is to build a dynamic dashboard that leverages artificial intelligence (AI), knowledge graphs, and/or other tools to summarize a set of NASA bioscience publications and enables users to explore the impacts and results of the experiments these publications describe. (Earth Science Division)

projectDetails.name: Project_Cafézin?
projectDetails.summary: Our project aims to accurately simulate the impact of asteroids on Earth, using real orbital data from NASA to calculate trajectories, kinetic energy, crater formation, tsunamis, and mitigation strategies. We employed an approach based on astrophysical calculations and data processing, integrating a NASA API to obtain orbital elements of near-Earth asteroids (NEOs). To enhance precision and efficiency, we implemented caching techniques and orbital signal decomposition, allowing real-time analysis of heliocentric positions and scalar velocities. By combining these methods, we were able to extract significant features from the orbital data and develop an interactive simulation that predicts the effects of an asteroid impact at specific locations on Earth, including mitigation through kinetic impactors or gravity tractors.
projectDetails.details:
In this project, our goal is to develop a web application capable of analyzing data from near-Earth asteroids (NEOs) provided by NASA and simulating their potential impacts, identifying craters, tsunamis, and seismic effects at user-selected locations.

In the link below, you can explore an immersive web experience where you can select asteroids like Apophis, Bennu, or Ryugu, choose an impact location on the interactive map, and visualize the resulting calculations for energy, crater, and tsunami.

[Link to the interactive site, if available]

The dataset consists of raw data from NASA's API (SSD-API JPL), including orbital elements of cataloged NEO asteroids. The test set includes data for asteroids such as Apophis, Bennu, and Ryugu, with columns for name, diameter, semi-major axis (a), eccentricity (e), inclination (i), longitude of the ascending node (Ω), argument of periapsis (ω), and periapsis time (tp).

The orbital data were sufficient to achieve significant results in impact simulations, both on land and in the ocean.

Asteroid Impact Simulation Model on Earth Our project presents a simulation model based on astrophysical calculations to predict the effects of an asteroid impact on Earth, using orbital velocity data provided by NASA. The model incorporates advanced signal processing techniques, such as orbital decomposition and energy extraction, to improve pattern recognition and simulation accuracy.

  1. Data Processing and Feature Extraction To extract valuable information from raw orbital data, as shown below, we implemented the following comprehensive preprocessing pipeline.

a. Filtering We began by applying customized filtering to remove high-frequency noise from the orbital data. Due to the low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), the filter's effectiveness in isolating significant orbital patterns was limited.

b. Orbital Decomposition (Kepler Calculations) After filtering, we implemented calculations based on Kepler's laws to decompose orbital signals into intrinsic components, such as eccentric and true anomalies. This allowed us to break down complex non-stationary signals into distinct parts, facilitating clear analysis of orbital events.

c. Energy and Feature Extraction Following decomposition, we calculated kinetic energy and other characteristics of each orbital component in a sliding window. This produced a 2D matrix representation of the orbital event, which was used as input for simulation calculations.

d. Label - Target Output After extracting energy features, we employed a Gaussian distribution centered on the impact time as the target output. This labeling strategy guided the model in accurately detecting the onset of the impact.

e. Resizing Finally, we implemented a resizing step. The energy and label matrices were resized to a uniform dimension of 4000 features, with 5 and 1 channels, respectively. This final step ensured compatibility with the simulation architecture, preparing the data for calculations and predictions.

  1. Simulation Model for Impact Times and Effects a. Description In this project, we employed a simulation model based on astrophysical physics, inspired by numerical calculation architectures, to predict impact events. The choice of this approach is based on its proven effectiveness in trajectory simulation tasks, which align perfectly with our need to accurately detect and locate impact effects in time-series data.

The model is specifically designed to handle problems where precise localization is critical, making it particularly suitable for simulating asteroid impacts. Its architecture consists of a contracting path (encoder) that captures context and a symmetric expanding path (decoder) that enables precise localization. This unique structure allows the model to learn both global and local features.

In the encoder section, the architecture comprises several calculation layers followed by pooling operations, progressively downsampling the input while extracting hierarchical features. This step is crucial for capturing the essential characteristics of orbital trajectories across various scales. Furthermore, the model is characterized by the use of skip connections, which transfer feature maps from the encoder to corresponding layers in the decoder. This mechanism not only preserves spatial information that might be lost during downsampling but also enhances the model's ability to recover important details during the reconstruction process.

The decoder section of the model performs upsampling of feature maps using transposed convolutions, gradually reconstructing the output while integrating information received from skip connections. This design enables the model to generate high-resolution output maps that accurately represent the probability of impact effects.

The effectiveness of the model in our asteroid impact simulation task is deeply rooted in the fundamental principles of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). These networks excel at recognizing patterns in structured data, such as 2D matrices derived from orbital signals. Convolutions allow the network to learn spatial hierarchies of features, which are essential for identifying complex patterns in the data.

b. About training During the training process, we closely monitored the model's performance by plotting the loss and accuracy for the training data of terrestrial asteroids and validation. We split the asteroid data into cases for training and validation (from a total of several). For oceanic impacts, given the limited data availability—only a few cases—all were used exclusively for validation.

The decision to plot these metrics in real-time allowed us to dynamically observe how changes in hyperparameters affected model generalization. Our goal was to ensure that the model, trained primarily on orbital data, could generalize well to impacts in different locations despite their differences. By evaluating performance on the oceanic impact validation set throughout the training process, we were able to fine-tune hyperparameters such as learning rate, weight decay, and model configuration to optimize its ability to generalize to unseen data.

This approach enabled us to iteratively calibrate and refine the model, ensuring that it performed consistently across various terrestrial environments and leveraged the limited oceanic impact data effectively during the validation phase.

So, for training data, this worked better:

Optimizer: We used the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 and weight decay of 1e-5. This setup provided a good balance between training speed and regularization. Learning Rate Scheduler: A ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler was applied to dynamically reduce the learning rate by a factor of 0.8 whenever the validation loss plateaued. The minimum learning rate was set to 1e-8, with a patience of 10 epochs. Loss Function: Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss was used to measure the difference between predicted and actual values. Batch Size: The batch size for all datasets was set to 2, ensuring stable training with our limited data. Number of Epochs: We trained the model for 50 epochs.

We defined an accuracy threshold of 0.1, meaning a prediction was considered accurate if it fell within ±0.1 of the expected value. Using this threshold, the model achieved an accuracy of 96.18% on terrestrial data and 91.31% on oceanic data.

challengeDetails.title: Meteor Madness
challengeDetails.excerpt: A newly identified near-Earth asteroid, "Impactor-2025," poses a potential threat to Earth, but do we have the tools to enable the public and decision makers to understand and mitigate its risks? NASA datasets include information about known asteroids and the United States Geological Survey provides critical information that could enable modeling the effects of asteroid impacts, but this data needs to be integrated to enable effective visualization and decision making. Your challenge is to develop an interactive visualization and simulation tool that uses real data to help users model asteroid impact scenarios, predict consequences, and evaluate potential mitigation strategies. (Planetary Science Division)

projectDetails.name: Project Tactic Weather
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, “Tactic Weather”, is a conceptual video that envisions an interactive NASA-powered platform designed to explore and visualize climate probabilities across the Solar System. Through an engaging interface, users can navigate between planets and, when selecting Earth, access historical NASA meteorological data to understand the likelihood of rain, heat, humidity, and other weather conditions for any location and date.

Beyond Earth, the concept also extends to Mars — offering mission planners and enthusiasts insights into the most favorable days for surface expeditions, based on NASA’s planetary climate models.

While not a fully developed web application, the project uses storytelling and design to show how NASA’s open datasets can empower people to prepare for environmental conditions both on Earth and beyond. It highlights the importance of accessible climate data in supporting science, safety, and sustainability in future planetary exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, "Tactic Weather”, is a conceptual video that demonstrates an interactive platform inspired by NASA’s exploration and climate data. The experience begins with a view of the Solar System, where users can click on each planet to learn more about its unique environmental characteristics.

When selecting Earth, the platform allows users to either type a specific location or explore by clicking on the map. The interface then displays weather probabilities such as rain, temperature, humidity, and wind based on NASA’s historical data, helping people better understand local climate trends.

When selecting Mars, users discover information about the planet’s atmosphere and surface, with a special highlight on Gale Crater, showcasing its scientific importance and environmental conditions that could impact future human missions.

The video focuses on design, storytelling, and user experience rather than coding or technical implementation. It was developed using visual and design tools such as Figma to illustrate how NASA’s open data can inspire public engagement.

Our goal is to make space and climate science more accessible and inspiring — connecting everyday weather awareness on Earth with the challenges of exploring other worlds.

challengeDetails.title: Will It Rain On My Parade?
challengeDetails.excerpt: If you’re planning an outdoor event—like a vacation, a hike on a trail, or fishing on a lake—it would be good to know the chances of adverse weather for the time and location you are considering. There are many types of Earth observation data that can provide information on weather conditions for a particular location and day of the year. Your challenge is to construct an app with a personalized interface that enables users to conduct a customized query to tell them the likelihood of “very hot,” “very cold,” “very windy,” “very wet,” or “very uncomfortable” conditions for the location and time they specify. projectDetails.name: Project CUMARU
projectDetails.summary:
CUMARU is a Geospatial Disaster Response Platform developed by a team composed mainly of designers and a Front-End Engineer, with the support of Google Gemini to accelerate technical development and the integration of complex systems.

We built a fully functional web application using React, Vite, and Node.js, with a back-end configured to fetch and process real-time alert data from NASA’s EONET API. The front-end features a Mapbox GL map that seamlessly switches between global 3D-like visualizations and detailed regional views. With AI assistance, we implemented a robust multilingual translation system and efficiently resolved complex build configurations involving Tailwind and Webpack/Vite.

CUMARU turns scientific data into accessible and actionable information, enhancing communication between civil defense agencies and field teams. By bridging design and technology, the platform enables faster, data-driven responses to climate-related events—helping protect communities and save lives.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
CUMARU is a web platform that helps visualize environmental risks and issue alerts during natural disasters. It’s built on three main layers:

  • Front-end (Visualization): Built with React and Mapbox GL, it displays real-time geospatial data on an interactive map. Users can explore a global 3D-like view with risk hotspots or zoom in to detailed regional levels (country, state, or neighborhood). The left sidebar controls which layers are visible—like vegetation (NDVI) or rainfall—while the right panel lists active alerts with risk scores, forecasts, and suggested safe routes.
  • Back-end (Data): Developed with Node.js and Express, the server works as a bridge between the interface and real-world data. It fetches official information from APIs like NASA’s EONET, processes it into GeoJSON/JSON, and sends it to the front-end for display.
  • Translation System: Powered by React Context and i18n, users can instantly switch the interface language (Portuguese, English, etc.) with no reloads.

Benefits
CUMARU brings speed and clarity to decision-making. By merging satellite data and alerts into one visual interface, it allows emergency teams to:

  • Detect threats like fires or floods in real time.
  • Assess risk levels based on forecasts and scores.
  • Plan safer routes and deploy resources more efficiently.

Intended Impact
The goal is to strengthen community resilience to extreme weather events. By providing fast, accurate data, CUMARU aims to save lives, reduce infrastructure and environmental damage, and improve coordination among authorities during crises.

Why it’s creative
CUMARU stands out for blending data and design. The team transformed complex NASA datasets into a clear, modern user experience—complete with dark mode and a globe-like visualization. It also showcases a design-driven hybrid development approach: a team of mostly designers, supported by generative AI, successfully tackled technical challenges in backend and configuration.

What the team prioritized

  • User Experience: A dark, high-contrast interface that’s easy to read even in emergency conditions.
  • Performance: A modular setup (separate front-end and back-end) and tools like React and Vite ensure fast load times and smooth navigation.
  • Scalability: The system connects to official satellite data and can easily integrate new APIs or layers.
  • Global Accessibility: The built-in translation system (i18n) allows use by international response teams.

In short, CUMARU bridges science, technology, and design to turn satellite data into life-saving decisions.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
The development of the CUMARU project was significantly accelerated and empowered by Artificial Intelligence—primarily through Google Gemini and ChatGPT, which acted as powerful assistants for coding, debugging, writing, and creative tasks.

Since our team was primarily focused on Design and Front-end, both AIs played a crucial role in bridging technical gaps, refining our communication, and enabling the implementation of complex infrastructure components.

Code Generation and Logic

We used Google Gemini mainly for:

  • Back-end Development (Node.js/Express): The AI generated the initial Express server structure, including route configuration, CORS handling, and the creation of alertsController.js, responsible for fetching and mapping real-time data from NASA’s EONET API.
  • Debugging and Conflict Resolution: Gemini helped diagnose and fix complex environment issues—such as node_modules conflicts, dependency mismatches, and build errors with Tailwind CSS/PostCSS. While our team focused on UX and data architecture (Mapbox / NASA EONET), Gemini ensured a stable technical foundation.
  • Feature Implementation: It supported the development of advanced functionalities like the internationalization system (React Context) and the dynamic Mapbox navigation view.

Creative and Multimedia Support

ChatGPT and Gemini also enhanced the project’s creative and communication aspects:

  • ChatGPT was used for technical documentation, UX writing, and copy creation for the project’s presentation and metadata.
  • AI-generated voice was used for the pitch video narration, adding clarity and a professional tone.
  • The background image of the video was AI-generated, reflecting the project’s environmental and global context.

Documentation and Metadata

All AI-generated assets—code, text, visuals, and audio—were reviewed, integrated, and refined by the team to ensure consistency, originality, and ethical use. The contribution of AI tools was transparently acknowledged in the project’s documentation and metadata.

projectDetails.name: Project EdgeRunner
projectDetails.summary: Desenvolvi um sistema interativo de simulação de impactos de asteroides, que utiliza dados astronômicos reais e modelagem física simplificada para estimar a área afetada, intensidade do impacto e consequências ambientais. O projeto enfrenta o desafio de traduzir dados científicos complexos em visualizações acessíveis e educativas, permitindo que qualquer pessoa compreenda o potencial risco e impacto de um evento dessa escala. Essa ferramenta é importante porque promove conscientização sobre a necessidade de monitoramento de objetos próximos à Terra (NEOs) e incentiva o engajamento público com ciência espacial. Além disso, a plataforma pode ser expandida para aplicações em educação e tomada de decisão em defesa planetária, unindo tecnologia, ciência e impacto social.
projectDetails.details:
O projeto é uma plataforma web interativa que simula o impacto de asteroides na Terra em tempo real. O usuário insere parâmetros como diâmetro, densidade, velocidade, ângulo e localização de impacto, e o sistema calcula a energia liberada, o raio de destruição e os possíveis efeitos térmicos e sísmicos. A simulação é exibida sobre um mapa global utilizando MapLibre GL, permitindo visualizar de forma intuitiva a área afetada e comparar diferentes cenários de impacto.

A aplicação foi desenvolvida em Next.js, TypeScript e Zustand (para gerenciamento de estado), com cálculos físicos implementados em Python e integrados via API. O design prioriza clareza científica e acessibilidade visual.

O principal benefício é tornar compreensível um fenômeno astronômico complexo, estimulando a educação científica e a conscientização sobre defesa planetária. O impacto pretendido é inspirar curiosidade e reflexão sobre a importância do monitoramento de objetos próximos da Terra (NEOs).

O projeto se destaca pela criatividade em combinar ciência de impacto, visualização geográfica e interatividade, unindo precisão técnica e apelo educativo. Foram considerados fatores como escalabilidade, usabilidade e fidelidade aos dados astronômicos para garantir tanto rigor científico quanto engajamento do público.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
A IA foi utilizada de forma auxiliar para otimizar a geração de conteúdo técnico e científico, sem substituir o raciocínio humano nem interferir na lógica principal do sistema. Ferramentas baseadas em IA (como o ChatGPT da OpenAI) foram usadas para apoiar a formulação de modelos físicos, revisão de código, explicações matemáticas e documentação técnica do projeto.

Todo o código-fonte, interface e cálculos foram escritos e validados manualmente, garantindo originalidade e consistência científica. Nenhuma imagem, vídeo, áudio ou elemento visual foi gerado por IA, portanto não há necessidade de marca d'água ou metadados de identificação.

O uso da IA serviu exclusivamente como instrumento de pesquisa e aceleração do desenvolvimento, contribuindo para aprimorar a precisão dos modelos e a clareza da comunicação científica — sem modificar ou emular qualquer marca, design ou identidade visual da NASA.

projectDetails.name: EMEIC - Estação Meteorológica de Microclima
projectDetails.summary: Um sistema de monitoramento ambiental baseado em estações meteorológicas de baixo custo, utilizando impressão 3D para o abrigo dos sensores. Este projeto aborda o desafio do alto custo e da escassez de dados ambientais detalhados, permitindo redes de monitoramento densas para análise precisa de áreas específicas. Sua relevância está na democratização do acesso à informação ambiental, fornecendo dados cruciais para pesquisa, planejamento urbano e conscientização comunitária sobre qualidade do ar e variações climáticas.
projectDetails.details:
O projeto consiste em um sistema de monitoramento ambiental de baixo custo, desenvolvido para coletar e analisar dados referentes à qualidade do ar, umidade relativa, índice pluviométrico e temperatura em localidades específicas. O sistema opera por meio de uma rede de estações meteorológicas que aferem essas variáveis continuamente e as transmitem para uma plataforma centralizada, possibilitando o acompanhamento dos dados em tempo real e de forma remota.

O principal elemento de inovação do projeto reside em um abrigo meteorológico integralmente concebido para manufatura aditiva (impressão 3D). Inspirado em modelos convencionais, nosso design foi otimizado para salvaguardar eficientemente os sensores e circuitos eletrônicos contra radiação solar direta e precipitação, ao mesmo tempo em que assegura uma ventilação passiva adequada, fator crucial para a exatidão das medições.

Impactos e Benefícios:

O benefício primordial deste projeto é a democratização do monitoramento ambiental. Mediante a utilização da impressão 3D, o custo de fabricação das estações foi drasticamente reduzido, tornando-as acessíveis para implementação em larga escala por comunidades, instituições de ensino e laboratórios de fabricação digital (Fab Labs). Isso proporciona a criação de redes de monitoramento significativamente mais densas e capilarizadas do que seria viável com equipamentos comerciais tradicionais. O impacto almejado é prover dados ambientais localizados e de alta granularidade que possam subsidiar pesquisas científicas, políticas públicas e conscientizar a população acerca das condições de seu próprio ambiente.

Diferenciais Criativos e Técnicos:

O diferencial do projeto não se restringe ao método de fabricação, mas primordialmente às consequências estratégicas que ele proporciona. Em virtude de seu custo de produção extremamente reduzido, a estação pode ser fabricada em grandes quantidades. Isso viabiliza a constituição de uma rede de monitoramento muito mais densa, permitindo que os sensores sejam instalados em regiões bastante específicas e localizadas.

Esta é a vantagem crucial sobre as estações convencionais. Por serem onerosas, elas são instaladas em poucos pontos e cobrem áreas muito extensas, oferecendo um panorama geral. Consequentemente, perdem precisão ao não acompanhar de perto as variações de microrregiões, como um bairro, um parque urbano ou uma zona industrial específica. Nosso sistema, ao contrário, permite um monitoramento "in loco", gerando dados com uma granularidade muito maior e, por conseguinte, uma análise ambiental mais fidedigna e precisa da realidade de cada localidade.

projectDetails.name: Project Galácticos
projectDetails.summary: GALACTICOS – Earth’s Defense is an interactive asteroid impact simulator that lets you explore potential threats to Earth using real NASA asteroid data. You can select asteroids, adjust impact parameters like size, speed, angle, and timing, and watch trajectories, atmospheric entry, and impact effects such as crater formation and shockwaves. The tool includes playback controls and visual analysis to make complex orbital mechanics and impact physics easy to understand, serving as an engaging resource for learning about planetary defense.
projectDetails.details:
Overview

Asteroids — sometimes called minor planets — are rocky, airless remnants left over from the early formation of our solar system about 4.6 billion years ago. Most asteroids orbit the Sun in the main belt between Mars and Jupiter. Sizes range from Vesta (~530 km diameter) down to bodies less than 10 meters across. The combined mass of all asteroids is smaller than the Moon.

Asteroid impact Simulator

This Asteroid Impact Simulator lets you explore what happens when different types of asteroids approach Earth. Choose a real NASA-listed object or configure your own by setting diameter, velocity, and impact angle, then pick a density (icy, carbonaceous, rocky, or iron) to reflect how tough the asteroid is. You can also test planetary defense options—laser, kinetic impactor, or gravity tractor—to see how mitigation changes the outcome. After launching the simulation, the world map visualizes the trajectory and probable impact site, and the model estimates consequences such as impact energy and crater effects. Use Reset to start a new scenario and compare results.

Near-Earth Objects (NEOs)

Objects (asteroids or comets) whose orbits bring them close to Earth's neighborhood are known as Near-Earth Objects (NEOs). About 99% of NEOs are asteroids. NEOs have perihelion distances less than 1.3 AU (astronomical units).

Potentially Hazardous Asteroids (PHAs)

An asteroid is classified as a Potentially Hazardous Asteroid when its orbit comes within ~7.5 million kilometers of Earth's orbit and its estimated diameter is ≥140 meters. This classification indicates a potential threat, not a guaranteed impact.

Meteors & Meteorites

When small bodies (meteoroids) enter a planet's atmosphere at high speed and disintegrate, they create bright streaks called meteors — colloquially "shooting stars". If a fragment survives atmospheric passage and reaches the ground, it is a meteorite.

Typical Behavior

Most small space rocks (smaller than a football field) disintegrate in the atmosphere. Travelling at tens of thousands of kilometers per hour, they break apart when dynamic pressure exceeds material strength. Usually less than 5% of the original mass reaches the surface.

Asteroid Defender

Defend Earth by destroying asteroids before they hit the planet!

Each impact costs one life — lose them all and the game is over.

projectDetails.name: WeatherWise
projectDetails.summary:
O Event Sky Insight é uma plataforma web inovadora que utiliza dados de satélite da NASA e algoritmos de IA para fornecer previsões climáticas altamente precisas e personalizadas para eventos. Diferentemente de aplicativos convencionais de previsão do tempo, nosso sistema calcula um Índice de Conforto Climático (ICC) específico para cada tipo de evento, analisando temperatura, precipitação, umidade, vento e radiação UV.
A plataforma permite que usuários comparem múltiplas localizações e datas, visualizem dados meteorológicos em mapas interativos e gráficos detalhados, e recebam recomendações de horários alternativos com melhores condições. Também integramos dados sobre celebrações culturais e feriados regionais, adaptando-se automaticamente à localização do usuário.
Este projeto enfrenta o desafio global de eventos cancelados ou prejudicados por condições climáticas imprevistas, que geram bilhões em perdas anualmente. Ao democratizar o acesso a informações climáticas precisas, ajudamos a criar experiências mais seguras e memoráveis, especialmente para comunidades com recursos limitados que não podem arcar com planos de contingência caros.
projectDetails.details: O Event Sky Insight é uma plataforma web criada para ajudar a planejar eventos usando dados meteorológicos avançados, imagens de satélite da NASA e algoritmos de inteligência artificial, entregando previsões mais precisas e recomendações personalizadas; em vez de funcionar como um app de tempo genérico, ela foi desenvolvida pensando em organizadores, para sugerir as melhores datas, locais e horários, reduzir riscos climáticos e aumentar as chances de sucesso dos eventos. O sistema reúne múltiplas fontes — imagens de satélite, séries históricas, previsões de diferentes provedores e dados locais de microclima — e passa tudo por modelos de machine learning que calculam um Índice de Conforto Climático (ICC) adaptado a cada tipo de evento, identificam padrões que podem atrapalhar celebrações ao ar livre, prevêem condições para datas específicas e propõem alternativas mais favoráveis. A interface traz visualizações interativas, mapas geoespaciais, comparações lado a lado entre datas e locais e relatórios em PDF para facilitar o compartilhamento. Entre os benefícios estão a redução de cancelamentos e alterações de última hora, economia com planos de contingência, melhor planejamento baseado em dados científicos e acesso democratizado a previsões precisas — tudo isso com recomendações personalizadas conforme o tipo de evento e a possibilidade de comparar várias localidades ao mesmo tempo. Nosso impacto esperado inclui menos desperdício financeiro e de recursos, mais inclusão para comunidades com poucos recursos, decisões mais sustentáveis, preservação de momentos importantes e ferramentas que ajudam na adaptação às mudanças climáticas. Do ponto de vista técnico, a stack inclui React.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Recharts e Leaflet no frontend; Supabase, PostgreSQL e Edge Functions no backend; e integrações com APIs como NASA Earth Observations, OpenWeatherMap, WeatherAPI, OpenHolidays e Nominatim/OpenStreetMap, além de ferramentas de desenvolvimento comuns como Git/GitHub, VS Code, npm/pnpm e Vercel para deploy. Nossas inovações cobrem o ICC proprietário, uma análise multidimensional do clima em vez de um veredito binário, recomendações contextuais (como horários alternativos), integração com datas culturais e visualizações que se adaptam ao nível do usuário. Ao desenvolver a plataforma, equilibramos precisão e acessibilidade, garantimos cobertura global, priorizamos privacidade e segurança, seguimos padrões de acessibilidade digital (WCAG 2.1), projetamos para escalabilidade e resiliência e atualizamos constantemente os algoritmos para refletir as mudanças climáticas. Em resumo, o Event Sky Insight transforma dados climáticos complexos em informações práticas para que qualquer pessoa — de quem organiza um casamento a quem produz um festival — possa planejar eventos mais seguros, agradáveis e memoráveis onde quer que sejam realizados.
