projectDetails.name: Project Marix Team
projectDetails.summary: The concept proposes reusing large rocket boosters, such as SpaceX’s Super Heavy, as modular space habitats in low Earth orbit (LEO) instead of deorbiting or discarding them. After completing their primary launch mission, the boosters would remain in orbit and be reconfigured into pressurized living and working modules. Internal fuel tanks could be rooled out and converted into habitable volumes through pre installed insulation, radiation shielding, and modular installation of life-support systems. Additional inflatable sections could expand usable space, while solar arrays would provide power to electrolysis systems used in waste to generate oxygen and hydrogen. This approach drastically reduces space debris, lowers construction costs for orbital infrastructure, and accelerates the creation of sustainable, large-scale habitats in space.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

What it does / How it works
This project transforms spent or intentionally-retained rocket boosters (e.g., a Super Heavy–class first stage) into modular, long-lived habitat/scaffold elements in LEO. The booster is already launched with all the necessary modifications — plumbing, electrical systems, structural reinforcements, and interface fittings. After payload delivery, it remains in orbit; the engine set is detached and returned for reuse. Once in space, it only needs to roll out its tanks and deploy exterior structures, which are pre-integrated and ready to unfold. Only minor modifications and activation procedures are needed on the inside to prepare the interior for habitation.

Life-support is provided by closed-loop systems: water recovery and waste processing feed an electrolysis unit that extracts oxygen from processed wastewater and other condensates; the hydrogen byproduct and hydrogen from other processing streams feed fuel cells that generate electrical power for station systems. Crucially, the design deliberately excludes large chemical or battery energy storage units — power is produced on demand by fuel cells supplied from waste-derived hydrogen and solar electrolysis balance (short-term buffering is small and local).

Benefits
Repurposes hardware that would otherwise be deorbited or discarded → lowers material waste and debris.

Creates very large habitable volume per launch (tank volume >> payload fairing) at substantially lower incremental cost.

Self-sustaining life support loop: waste → electrolysis → O₂ for crew + H₂ for fuel cells → electricity and water (via fuel cell output) → closes resource loop.

Rapid scale-up: each additional retained booster adds structural volume and docking interfaces to expand the networked habitat.

Intended impact
Provide economical, scalable orbital infrastructure for rescue staging, long-term research habitats, tourism, and industry — dramatically reducing the cost per habitable cubic meter placed into LEO and accelerating infrastructure growth without requiring commensurately more launches of new habitat modules.

Tools, hardware, software used in development
Systems engineering & CAD: SolidWorks / Siemens NX (conceptual design and structural fits)

Simulations: orbital mechanics (STK or GMAT), structural analysis (ANSYS), thermal/vacuum modeling

Automation/assembly: concepts for robotic arms and in-space refit tooling; simple standard mechanical interface designs for docking and modularity

Life-support prototypes: bench electrolysis cells, PEM fuel cell prototypes for proof-of-concept

Creativity & novelty
Repurposing a rocket booster as primary structural habitat is novel at scale: instead of treating boosters as expendable/recovered components, they become the core building blocks of a modular orbital city. Combining waste-driven electrolysis with fuel-cell on-demand power (and minimizing heavy energy storage) optimizes mass and logistics for long-duration occupation.

Design considerations the team evaluated
Structural integrity of boosters for long-term orbital exposure (fatigue, thermal cycling).
Contamination and sealing of former propellant tanks for human use (outgassing mitigation, multi-layer insulation, micrometeoroid protection).
Redundancy in life-support and power (multiple electrolysis/fuel-cell strings).
Safe removal/transfer of engines and re-routing of propellant plumbing.
Robotic vs. crewed refit tradeoffs for safety and cost.
Thermal control and radiation shielding additions to minimize crew exposure.

Economic advantage estimate — cost per ton to LEO

Sources & baseline notes: launch pricing and real costs vary widely; industry figures are often list prices, marketed rates, or internal cost estimates. Below I use conservative literature ranges and clearly show assumptions. Key references: industry summaries and Starship documentation. Wikipedia+2Wikipedia+2

Current typical cost-to-LEO (industry range):

  • Conventional/reusable medium-lift rockets (market/list figures, 2018–2024): widely quoted industry averages range from ~$6,000/kg to ~$16,000/kg depending on mission type, rideshare constraints, and how you count economies (i.e., price vs marginal cost). That equates to $6M–$16M per metric ton. Wikipedia+1

Starship / Super-heavy projected (optimistic) cost baseline:

  • Starship ambitions project very low marginal cost per launch (public estimates/marketing vary). If a fully reusable superheavy could approach $1M–$20M per launch in future economies and deliver 50–100+ tonnes to useful LEO payload, per-ton costs could fall into the $1,000–$20,000 per kg wide range over time; conservative operational estimates used by analysts place realistic near-term commercial costs higher, but the technology aims at dramatic reductions. Wikipedia+1

Assumptions for this proposal (for a concrete, conservative example):

  1. Typical modern launch (Falcon-class or similar) price-to-customer ≈ $60M and realistic marginal cost ≈ $30M (varies) for ~20,000 kg → ~$1,500–3,000/kg marginally (but customer price per kg often higher). For our high-volume comparison we use an industry average price ≈ $10,000/kg (≈ $10M/ton) as a reasonable mid-range representative. Space Insider+1
  2. A single Super Heavy first stage has structural mass and internal tankage volume on the order of tens of tonnes of usable structural mass and thousands of cubic meters of tank volume (note: exact masses vary by design block). The booster was already launched for a primary mission (payload delivery) — so the proposal treats the booster’s remaining mass/volume as incremental habitat resource at very low marginal launch cost (the launch was paid for by the primary mission). Converting booster → habitat costs (robotic refit, insulation, shielding, interior fitout) we conservatively estimate $2M–$20M per booster of in-orbit conversion expense depending on automation/robotics needs and crew operations.

Sample arithmetic (conservative illustrative scenario):

  • If a booster yields 50 tons of usable structural/volume mass-equivalent (conservative), and conversion cost is $10M per booster, the incremental cost per ton for that structural mass = $10M / 50 t = $200,000 per ton (≈ $200/kg).
  • Compare that to current delivery cost baseline of $10M per ton (≈ $10,000/kg): converting an already-orbited booster yields ~50× lower incremental cost per ton of habitable structure in this simplified scenario.

Range & percent savings (depending on assumptions):

  • Using optimistic conversion cost / larger usable mass, incremental cost could fall to $20,000–$200,000 per ton, versus current delivery $5M–$16M/ton → representing ~25–500× improvement in cost-per-ton of habitable structure placed into LEO.
  • Using conservative numbers (higher conversion, lower usable mass), savings still can be an order of magnitude (≈10×) or more versus launching equivalent hab modules from Earth.

Key caveats (be explicit):

  • These numbers are estimates based on published industry ranges and conceptual conversion costs. They depend strongly on: true usable structural mass per booster, real conversion/refit costs (robotics vs crew), the accounting method (who paid for the original launch), and the maturity/flight rate of the superheavy system. See sources for market ranges. Wikipedia+1

Bottom line (concise)

By converting large rocket boosters already placed into orbit into habitat scaffolds and using waste-driven electrolysis + fuel-cell power (no heavy energy storage), the project turns high-value flight hardware into long-term infrastructure at a much lower incremental cost per ton than launching dedicated habitat mass from Earth. Under conservative scenarios this yields an order-of-magnitude reduction in cost per ton; under optimistic scenarios, savings could be two to three orders of magnitude, enabling rapid, economical expansion of habitable volume in LEO.

projectDetails.name: AstroShield
projectDetails.summary:
AstroShield is an interactive web platform designed for proactive planetary defense. Our solution addresses the "Meteor Madness" challenge by transforming complex asteroid threat data into an intuitive, hands-on simulation that is accessible to everyone.
We developed a robust simulation engine that fuses real-time orbital data from NASA's NEO API with critical geospatial data from USGS, such as population density and topography. This allows users to not only visualize an asteroid's trajectory in 3D but also to understand the potential real-world consequences of an impact. Users can actively engage by deploying a simulated kinetic impactor, adjusting its parameters, and immediately seeing the outcome as the threatening trajectory changes to a safe one.
This project is important because it bridges the gap between raw scientific data and actionable insight. It serves as a powerful educational tool for the public, a training platform for future scientists, and a critical planning resource for decision-makers, capable of generating clear impact reports for coordinated global responses. AstroShield shifts the paradigm from passive fear to proactive and collaborative planetary stewardship.
projectDetails.details:
What does AstroShield do, and how does it work?

AstroShield is an interactive planetary defense platform designed to transform complex data about asteroid threats into actionable, visual simulations. Its operation follows a three-phase logic: Learn, Launch, and Lead.

Phase 1: Learn (Learn & Model)
The platform aggregates and integrates data from official sources. It connects to NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) API to obtain orbital parameters and map the 3D trajectories of asteroids. At the same time, it integrates geospatial data layers from the USGS, such as population density and topography maps, to assess the potential consequences of an impact on the surface.

Phase 2: Launch (Launch & Interact)
In this phase, data are transformed into an interactive experience. The platform features a central 3D viewer where users can observe an asteroid’s trajectory in real time. Through a control panel, it is possible to modify variables and simulate mitigation strategies—such as using a kinetic impactor to deflect the asteroid—while receiving instant visual feedback on mission success.

Phase 3: Lead (Lead & Educate)
The final goal is to translate the simulation into practical knowledge. The platform can generate one-page impact reports, ideal for decision-makers, including impact zone maps and estimates of affected populations. It also includes educational tools like interactive tooltips and preconfigured scenarios that demonstrate specific risks, such as tsunamis caused by an oceanic impact or effects on a specific city, such as Fortaleza.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Benefits:
AstroShield provides a modeling tool for scientists, a disaster-planning instrument for governments, and an educational platform for students and the general public. It serves as an invaluable training resource, preparing the next generation of planetary defense specialists with hands-on experience that was previously only theoretical.

Intended Impact:
The project aims to shift public perception of cosmic threats—from passive fear to active and responsible engagement. By democratizing access to planetary defense simulations, AstroShield empowers a broader audience and promotes global cooperation, ensuring that, in the event of a real threat, world leaders can operate with the same critical information.

Tools and Development

For development, the project relies on a set of highly credible datasets and APIs:

  • NASA API: To fetch orbital data for Near-Earth Objects (NEOs).
  • USGS (The National Map): To integrate geospatial data layers such as elevation, population density, and risk zones.

projectDetails.name: Nebula.exe
projectDetails.summary:
A falta de saneamento básico é uma crise silenciosa: 3.337 famílias sofrem perdas anuais devido a doenças de veiculação hídrica, causando 18.000 internações no Ceará. Com uma taxa de mortalidade de 17,2% decorrente dessas doenças — muito acima da média nacional — e R$ 36 milhões gastos em tratamentos hospitalares, a falha na infraestrutura está custando vidas e drenando recursos públicos.

O Aqua Guardian é a solução de Intervenção Preditiva que usa Inteligência Artificial e Dados Espaciais da NASA para salvar vidas. Transformamos esta ameaça invisível em um alerta acionável.

Nossa IA mapeia a vulnerabilidade integrando indicadores críticos: cobertura de esgoto, áreas com água parada por mais de 3 dias (detectadas via satélite) e dados socioeconômicos. Combinamos esse mapa com previsões climáticas do INPE para antecipar surtos com até 14 dias de antecedência.

Este sistema permite que o governo aja antes que a doença chegue, realizando reparos cirúrgicos e lançando campanhas de saúde direcionadas. Nossa abordagem única inclui Gamificação para incentivar a coleta de dados impulsionada pela comunidade.

O Aqua Guardian projeta uma redução nos óbitos e custos anuais de 20%, o que equivale a 667 vidas salvas e 3.600 internações evitadas. Ao aumentar a eficiência do investimento, garantimos que as metas nacionais de saneamento sejam alcançadas 10 anos mais rápido. Não estamos apenas construindo uma plataforma; estamos capacitando o governo a consertar o esgoto antes que ele mate.

projectDetails.name: Project PUC ANGELS
projectDetails.summary:
Indoor air is a silent threat, often more polluted than outdoor air, according to Dyson's connected data study. Symbioses is an environmental intelligence system that uses data from satelity TEMPO of Nasa to identify areas with high concentrations of CO₂ and an urgent need to reduce carbon gas levels. Based on this correlation, the system indicates priority regions for the deployment of Laboxy, an intelligent bioreactor capable of converting CO₂ into oxygen through microalgae.
This way, Symbioses transforms environmental data into concrete actions to regenerate the air in cities and restore the planet's balance. Furthermore, the application cross-references internal data—collected in real-time by local sensors via IoT communication protocols like MQTT—with external data from the TEMPO satellite to compare the environments, in addition to being able to compare the improvement over a timeline. It is also possible to see how many Laboxy units are in the region and around the world through Google Maps and their impact on reducing the ecological footprint. We created an app to triangulate this data, democratize TEMPO data, and include an option to purchase Laboxy to improve indoor environments.
projectDetails.details:
SYMBIOSE is a revolutionary environmental intelligence ecosystem designed to combat indoor air pollution, a silent threat often more dangerous than the air outside. The system has two core components:

  1. Laboxy: An intelligent, closed-loop bioreactor that uses the exponential photosynthetic power of microalgae to actively convert indoor CO₂ into pure oxygen with unprecedented efficiency.
  2. SYMBIOSE App: The digital brain of the ecosystem. It uses integrated IoT sensors in each Laboxy unit to monitor indoor air quality (CO₂, O₂, temperature) in real-time via MQTT protocols.

Crucially, the SYMBIOSE platform leverages satellite data from NASA's TEMPO mission to fetch Near Real-Time (NRT) outdoor air quality for the device's specific location. This allows the app to provide a powerful, real-time comparison, scientifically validating the purifier's effectiveness by contrasting the clean indoor air with the external environmental conditions.

What benefits does it have? What is the intended impact? The primary benefit is the creation of healthier, breathable indoor spaces. By actively regenerating the air instead of just filtering it, SYMBIOSE improves human health, cognitive performance, and well-being in homes, offices, and schools.

The intended impact is multi-layered:

  • Local Impact: Empowers individuals and communities to take direct control of their environmental health.
  • Global Impact: Creates a decentralized, global network of air purification units. An interactive map visualizes the collective impact of all active Laboxy units, calculating their contribution to reducing the global carbon footprint.
  • Educational Impact: Democratizes complex environmental data, making the connection between macro-level satellite observations and micro-level indoor quality tangible and understandable for everyone.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Cloud & Backend: Google Cloud & Firebase (Firestore, Cloud Functions for a serverless backend, Authentication, Firebase Hosting).
  • Hardware: A custom-built photobioreactor with a microcontroller (ESP32), and IoT sensors for CO₂, O₂, temperature, humidity, and pH.
  • Frontend: A Progressive Web App (PWA) built with React.js.
  • Data Visualization: ApexCharts.js for real-time, interactive charts and gauges.
  • Languages: TypeScript for both the Cloud Functions and the React frontend.

How is your project creative? The creativity of SYMBIOSE lies in the symbiotic integration of three distinct fields: bio-engineering (microalgae), IoT (real-time sensors), and space science (NASA satellite data). Unlike any other solution, it doesn't just filter the air; it creates a miniature, intelligent ecosystem. Its most innovative feature is the fusion of hyper-local, indoor sensor readings with macro-level, outdoor satellite data, providing a unique and scientifically valid feedback loop that proves its own effectiveness and connects personal health to the planet's well-being.

projectDetails.name: Sow The Future
projectDetails.summary:
Our project is a game created with the goal of educating and raising awareness among users about soil health. Using the data available during NASA Space Apps, we based our work on the NDVI index, an infrared measurement that assesses soil fertilization and density based on how light is reflected.

To achieve this, the game was designed to assist both young people, by showcasing the benefits of afforestation and urban agriculture even on a small scale, and those interested in the field, by demonstrating sustainable farming methods that are less aggressive to the soil and promote healthier planting practices.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details: Sow The Future

1. Overview and Core Gameplay:

"Sow The Future" is an immersive 2D educational game designed to empower the next generation of environmental stewards. Targeting a young audience, the game translates the critical concept of soil health into an engaging and intuitive gameplay loop. Players manage their own virtual farm, starting in a rural setting, where they are responsible for the entire crop cultivation cycle. This includes tilling the land, selecting seeds, planting, and making crucial decisions about soil fertilization. The game's genius lies in its direct feedback system: an in-game NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) graph, a concept used by NASA and other space agencies, visually rises and falls based on the player's choices. This provides a clear, scientific correlation between sustainable practices and a thriving ecosystem. The initial prototype focuses on the rural biome, with a fully conceptualized urban agriculture module planned for future development, creating a powerful narrative about the farm-to-city connection.

2. Educational Benefits and Intended Impact:

"Sow The Future" moves beyond simple farming simulation by embedding authentic scientific principles into its core. The benefits are multi-layered:

Tangible Science Literacy: It demystifies complex agronomic and remote sensing concepts, making NDVI—a vital tool for monitoring planetary health—accessible and understandable to a child.

Critical Thinking and Consequence-Based Learning: Players don't just farm; they experiment. The game presents choices between different fertilizers (e.g., organic compost vs. synthetic options). Choosing a less sustainable option triggers an educational pop-up explaining its negative impact, fostering informed decision-making.

Empowerment Through Local Action: The ultimate impact is to instill a sense of agency. By starting with a rural farm and expanding to urban spaces, the game teaches children that the principles of soil health are universal. They learn that they can make a difference right from their own homes, whether by starting a small balcony garden or understanding the importance of supporting sustainable agriculture, thereby connecting individual action to global environmental health.

  • Context: This screen shows the player's response to a previous question, likely the one asking, "Shall we use a hoe or no-till farming?"
    • Character's Statement: "I think it's better not to."
    • Character's Reasoning: "I will damage the soil."
  • Explanation: This screen captures a moment of learning and application. The player character is verbally reinforcing the correct decision by choosing not to use the hoe. The reasoning provided—"I will damage the soil"—directly states the negative consequence of the conventional method (tillage). This demonstrates that the player has understood the core lesson that disturbing the soil with tools like a hoe is harmful to its structure and long-term health.
  • Educational Purpose: This is a powerful pedagogical tool. It moves beyond just selecting the right option; it forces the player to articulate the "why" behind the sustainable choice. By having the character voice the reason, the game solidifies the learning objective and helps internalize the principle that protecting the soil from physical disruption is a key pillar of sustainable agriculture.

1. Overview and Core Gameplay:

"Sow The Future" is an immersive 2D educational game designed to empower the next generation of environmental stewards. Targeting a young audience, the game translates the critical concept of soil health into an engaging and intuitive gameplay loop. Players manage their own virtual farm, starting in a rural setting, where they are responsible for the entire crop cultivation cycle. This includes tilling the land, selecting seeds, planting, and making crucial decisions about soil fertilization. The game's genius lies in its direct feedback system: an in-game NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) graph, a concept used by NASA and other space agencies, visually rises and falls based on the player's choices. This provides a clear, scientific correlation between sustainable practices and a thriving ecosystem. The initial prototype focuses on the rural biome, with a fully conceptualized urban agriculture module planned for future development, creating a powerful narrative about the farm-to-city connection.

2. Educational Benefits and Intended Impact:

"Sow The Future" moves beyond simple farming simulation by embedding authentic scientific principles into its core. The benefits are multi-layered:

Tangible Science Literacy: It demystifies complex agronomic and remote sensing concepts, making NDVI—a vital tool for monitoring planetary health—accessible and understandable to a child.

Critical Thinking and Consequence-Based Learning: Players don't just farm; they experiment. The game presents choices between different fertilizers (e.g., organic compost vs. synthetic options). Choosing a less sustainable option triggers an educational pop-up explaining its negative impact, fostering informed decision-making.

Empowerment Through Local Action: The ultimate impact is to instill a sense of agency. By starting with a rural farm and expanding to urban spaces, the game teaches children that the principles of soil health are universal. They learn that they can make a difference right from their own homes, whether by starting a small balcony garden or understanding the importance of supporting sustainable agriculture, thereby connecting individual action to global environmental health.

3. Tools, Technologies, and Development Process:

The project was built using a streamlined and effective development stack, ideal for a functional prototype:

Game Engine: Chosen for its lightweight nature, powerful 2D capabilities, and open-source flexibility.

Programming Language: GDScript, Godot's native language, allowing for rapid prototyping and clean implementation of game logic.

Art and Asset Creation: The visual style was achieved using freely available sprite sheets from the web, which were then meticulously customized. The main character's idle and walking animations were edited and assembled using Aseprite, a professional tool for pixel art, ensuring smooth and unique character movement.

Scientific Foundation: The project creatively utilizes NASA's NDVI data not as a direct data feed, but as the foundational inspiration for the core game mechanic. This approach translates abstract satellite data into a relatable in-game progress system, bridging the gap between space technology and hands-on learning.

4. Creativity, Originality, and Design Considerations:

While games like Stardew Valley popularize the farming genre, "Sow The Future" carves its unique niche by being scientifically grounded and purpose-driven. Its creativity stems from its unique fusion of authentic environmental science and engaging gameplay for children.

Unique Selling Proposition: The direct and visual use of the NDVI metric as a core gameplay and progress bar is a novel approach not seen in mainstream educational games. It provides a concrete, data-driven representation of environmental health.

Balanced and Purposeful Design: Our team carefully considered several factors to ensure success:

Audience Engagement: The color palette, user interface, and simple mechanics were all tailored to be intuitive and captivating for a younger demographic.

Fidelity vs. Fun: We struck a careful balance between scientific accuracy and engaging gameplay. The educational pop-ups ensure learning, while the core loop of growing and seeing the NDVI graph rise provides satisfaction and fun.

Strategic Scoping: The decision to launch the prototype with the rural environment was a strategic consideration of the hackathon's time constraints. This allowed us to perfect the core mechanics and deliver a polished, vertical slice of the experience, with a clear and exciting roadmap for the urban expansion.

USE OF DATA:

We utilized data from the GIMMS mapping system, collecting information from regions that were undergoing severe soil degradation processes and which, through public policies aimed at soil revitalization via sustainable agricultural methods, managed to increase their NDVI exponentially. Examples of these are the "Great Green Wall of the Sahel," the "Green Wall of China," and Northeastern India.

In some of these regions, such as the "Great Green Wall of the Sahel" area, there were extreme growths. This growth could be tracked using the NDVI anomaly rate, a percentage that measures the difference between the current NDVI and the average NDVI from previous years. In the Sahel, there are areas that experienced a 125% increase in NDVI, which can be observed from the purple coloration on the map in these areas. This was observed in nations such as Niger, Sudan, Eritrea, and Burkina Faso. Whereas in previous years from 2011 to 2019, these regions showed indices ranging from -20% (representing a decrease in NDVI) to 10% (representing a 10% increase in NDVI, though this was observed in very few regions and infrequently). However, the largest increases occurred from 2020-2025, showing the 125% growth compared to previous years as previously mentioned. This was achieved through the use of techniques such as no-till farming, crop rotation, agroforestry, and assisted natural regeneration—all sustainable planting methods.

Technical Summary: Interpretation of the Graphs – Terra MODIS 8-Day NDVI (Buriticupu, Maranhão, Brazil)

1. Dataset and Analytical Context

The graphs represent a seasonal time series of NDVI derived from the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) sensor aboard NASA’s Terra satellite. They display the 8-day composite NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) for an area centered on Buriticupu, Maranhão, Brazil. NDVI is calculated as NDVI = (NIR - RED) / (NIR + RED) where NIR and RED correspond to surface reflectance in the near-infrared and red bands, respectively. Values range from –1 to +1, with higher positive values indicating dense, photosynthetically active vegetation, and lower or negative values representing bare soil, dry vegetation, or water bodies.

The graphs contain three main components: the Black line, which is the long-term NDVI mean (2001–2024 historical baseline); the Gray band, which represents the historical minimum–maximum range, representing interannual variability; and the Red line, which shows the current vegetation condition (2024–2025), updated every 8-day cycle.

2. Temporal and Spatial Interpretation

The graphs compare current vegetation conditions with the long-term climatological mean. A persistent decline of the red line (2024–2025) below the historical mean (black line) indicates vegetation stress or reduced vegetative vigor. In Buriticupu and across Maranhão, NDVI typically peaks between February and May (rainy season) and decreases from July to November (dry season). When the red line remains below average for several periods—even within normal seasonal fluctuations—it suggests anomalous conditions such as prolonged drought, soil degradation, or vegetation loss.

3. Ecological and Soil Implications of NDVI Decline

3.1. Vegetation Productivity and Carbon Balance

A reduction in NDVI reflects lower photosynthetic activity and, therefore, decreased Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) and carbon sequestration. When widespread, this shift can turn large regions from carbon sinks into net CO₂ sources. In Brazil, particularly in the Amazon–Cerrado transition zone (Maranhão, Tocantins, Pará), NDVI decline is strongly linked to deforestation, wildfires, pasture degradation, and severe droughts.

3.2. Soil Processes

Vegetation loss triggers several impacts on soil systems: reduced organic matter input, lowering soil carbon and microbial biomass; increased erosion, due to exposure to rainfall and surface runoff; loss of soil structure, from reduced root networks and biological aggregation; lower infiltration capacity, increasing runoff and altering the water balance; and higher soil temperature amplitude, accelerating decomposition and nutrient loss. Over time, these processes lead to declining natural fertility, organic carbon depletion, reduced cation exchange capacity, and lower agricultural and ecological resilience.

3.3. Agricultural Impacts

In agricultural systems, NDVI decline results in: lower photosynthetic rate, causing reduced biomass and yield; higher irrigation demand, due to water stress; increased vulnerability to pests and diseases, as stressed plants lose resistance; pasture degradation, reducing livestock carrying capacity; and direct economic impacts, such as yield losses, higher production costs, and local food insecurity.

4. International Comparison of NDVI Decline and Its Effects

Brazil

In northern and northeastern Brazil, NDVI decline is driven by stronger droughts, recurrent fires, and agricultural expansion over forests and savannas. In Buriticupu, the pattern indicates seasonal stress exacerbated by human disturbance. Vegetation loss causes fertility reduction, accelerated erosion, and nutrient-poor soils (mainly Latossolos and Argissolos). Over time, this undermines agricultural productivity, ecosystem services, and alters the local microclimate by changing albedo and evapotranspiration rates.

United States

In the U.S., NDVI declines are frequently observed in the Great Plains, Southwest, and California during drought years (such as 2012 and 2020–2022). These anomalies result from precipitation deficits, heat extremes, and wildfires visible in MODIS time series. Consequences include reduced corn and wheat yields, groundwater depletion (e.g., Ogallala Aquifer), increased erosion, and secondary salinization in irrigated zones. NDVI thus reflects both climatic variability and pressure from intensive water and land use.

Mongolia

In Mongolia’s steppe regions, NDVI decline is associated with overgrazing, desertification, and prolonged droughts. Vegetation loss exposes soil to wind erosion, generating dust storms and topsoil loss. As a result, forage availability decreases, affecting livestock productivity and pastoral livelihoods. Persistently low NDVI signals ecological degradation and rising socio-economic risk under combined climatic and anthropogenic stress.

5. Management and Policy Implications

Persistent negative NDVI anomalies should trigger adaptive management responses, including: satellite-based monitoring and early warning systems to detect drought and degradation in real time; soil and water conservation practices such as no-till farming, cover crops, terracing, and riparian buffer zones; restoration programs involving reforestation, assisted natural regeneration, and rotational grazing; sustainable intensification with drought-tolerant crop varieties, precision agriculture, and efficient irrigation use; and integrated land-use policies, linking remote sensing data with enforcement and economic incentives.

6. General Conclusion

The graphs summarize vegetation dynamics by comparing current NDVI time series with a 23-year climatological baseline. In 2024–2025, the red line remains below the historical mean for several months in Buriticupu, indicating reduced vegetative vigor, likely linked to regional drought and human pressure. Similar declines observed in Brazil, the United States, and Mongolia reveal a global pattern of lower vegetation productivity, soil degradation, agricultural yield loss, and ecological instability. Continuous monitoring through NASA’s MODIS data provides an essential scientific foundation for land management, climate adaptation, and food security planning.

projectDetails.name: Project Space Kittens
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, BeeMove, is a data-driven platform designed to combat the agricultural crisis caused by declining bee populations due to climate change. 🐝

We developed an application that analyzes environmental data—including airborne pollen, climate patterns, and bee migration—to provide actionable insights. It addresses the challenge by guiding farmers to the most fertile locations for planting and helping beekeepers find optimal areas for their hives.

This is crucial because protecting pollination is fundamental to ensuring global food security and economic stability. By connecting farmers, beekeepers, and scientists, BeeMove creates a sustainable ecosystem where technology supports nature. It's a proactive solution that turns critical environmental data into a tool for preserving life and generating prosperity.
projectDetails.details:
BeeMove is a platform that transforms environmental data into a tool for agricultural prosperity. It works by collecting and analyzing data on airborne pollen presence, climate conditions, and bee migration patterns. Based on this information, the application provides strategic guidance to different audiences, helping to optimize agricultural production and protect pollinators.

What benefits does it have? The project offers targeted benefits to various groups:

  • Small farmers: They can identify the best locations for their crops, ensuring a greater presence of pollinators and, consequently, a more productive harvest.
  • Beekeepers: They receive guidance on where to position their artificial hives to find the most favorable conditions.
  • Large producers and investors: They can predict the prosperity and productive potential of land by cross-referencing climate and environmental data to make more secure decisions.
  • Scientists and biologists: They have access to a tool to monitor bee migration and analyze detailed climatological history for their research.

What is the intended impact of the project? The intended impact is to create a more sustainable and profitable agricultural ecosystem by combating the effects of climate change on food production. The project aims to connect all agents in the sector—from farmers to scientists—around the common goal of preserving pollination. By doing so, BeeMove seeks to ensure food security, stabilize production costs, and promote a healthy balance between human activity and nature, turning "data that generates life, and life that generates prosperity."

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project? The provided text describes the concept, problem, and solution for BeeMove, but it does not specify the tools, coding languages, hardware, or software used in its development.

How is your project creative? BeeMove's creativity lies in its innovative approach to a complex problem. Instead of focusing solely on the economic consequences (rising costs), it tackles the ecological root of the issue: the decline of pollinators. The project creatively connects distinct data sources (pollen, climate, bee migration) and translates them into a practical, unified solution for a diverse audience. It is a tool that symbolizes innovation through preservation, using technology to strengthen the foundation of life.

What factors did your team consider? The team considered a series of interconnected factors:

  • Economic: The observation that the production cost of commodities like coffee was increasing, impacting both producers and consumers.
  • Agricultural: The drop in the 2025 coffee harvest and the vital importance of bees as primary pollinators for the quantity and quality of food.
  • Environmental: The direct impact of climate change, such as rising temperatures, which forces bee migration and puts them at risk of extinction.
  • Social: The need for a tool that could serve and connect different actors in the agricultural ecosystem (small and large producers, beekeepers, investors, and scientists), each with their specific needs.

projectDetails.name: Project Swift Rockets
projectDetails.summary:
NaviSense is a mobile application designed for coastal fishermen in Brazil, providing a simple and intuitive way to access long-term marine weather forecasts — from a few days to up to six months ahead. The app delivers information on waves, winds, tides, and UV conditions, allowing users to track oceanic and meteorological trends and prepare in advance for upcoming fishing and navigation seasons.

To generate reliable insights, NaviSense integrates data from multiple APIs, including NASA POWER, Meteomatics, and Marine Weather API. These datasets are processed by an internal predictive time series algorithm (ARIMA) that forecasts key environmental parameters such as temperature, wind, and wave height, which are then presented to the user through a comprehensive dashboard. OpenAI’s model is integrated as an additional layer to provide contextual insights, offering extra guidance on whether it is a good time to fish.

More than just a weather tool, NaviSense turns climatic data into actionable insights for planning and safety at sea, helping fishing communities anticipate risks and opportunities. Designed with accessibility and inclusion in mind, the app ensures that users of varying technical backgrounds — including those with limited digital literacy — can easily access reliable, long-term information and benefit from it.
projectDetails.details:
Introduction

Fishing sustains thousands of families along Brazil’s coastline — yet it remains one of the most vulnerable livelihoods to the changing ocean. On August 25th, 2025, the fishing boat São Raimundo capsized off the coast of Camocim, Ceará, after a sudden shift in currents, tides, winds, and waves. Of the seven fishermen onboard, five were rescued; two — Cleuton and Daniel — are still missing after six days of search operations. This tragedy is not an isolated event. Across Brazil, small-scale fishermen routinely face similar risks — heading to sea without access to reliable marine forecasts. Sudden environmental shifts, intensified by climate variability, can transform a routine trip into a life-threatening emergency.

The Problem

Data shows that many accidents could have been anticipated — Before several incidents, conditions worsened sharply: stronger winds, higher waves, changing currents, and larger tidal ranges — all markers of imminent danger for small boats. Without forecasting tools designed for them, fishermen are exposed to unpredictable seas and devastating losses. A single lost boat can mean USD 2,000–3,000 gone — months of income erased. Nationally, these recurring events cause millions in damages while threatening food security and the survival of coastal communities. Today, most fishermen still sail blind through changing ocean conditions, risking their lives and livelihoods each time they leave shore.

The GAP

Although institutions produce vast amounts of meteorological and oceanographic data, this information rarely reaches the fishermen who depend on it. Forecasts are fragmented across platforms and too technical to interpret, creating a deep disconnect between data producers and end users. In practice, many rely on experience, observation, and local word-of-mouth to decide when to sail — methods that cannot anticipate abrupt changes in wind, swell, or tides. This gap between scientific data and practical access keeps coastal communities vulnerable to avoidable accidents, material losses, and preventable deaths.


Our Solution

To bridge this gap, we developed NaviSense — a mobile application that leverages environmental data integration and predictive analytics powered by Artificial Intelligence to deliver clear and actionable marine forecasts for coastal fishermenThe system consolidates data from multiple sources, including decades of historical records from multiples API's and processes them through an internal ARIMA-based predictive algorithm that forecasts oceanic variables such as wave height, wind direction, currents, and tides.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"image.png" ]

How It Works

Coastal fishermen can interact with the app by selecting a location directly on the map — either by searching, clicking a point, or drawing a custom region — and specifying which environmental parameters they want to check, such as temperature, wind speed, wave height, visibility, or tides. The system then retrieves and processes historical and real-time meteorological and oceanographic data, providing accurate forecasts and actionable insights for the chosen location and date. Users can also save locations with specific dates and times to continuously monitor forecasts, generate detailed reports, and visualize the information through an interactive dashboard, making trip planning more precise and informed.

Product Features

  • Check weather and sea forecasts for any location and chosen date
  • Select a location on the map (by searching, clicking a point, or drawing a custom region) and customize which parameters to view
  • Save locations with specific dates and times to receive continuous updates and track forecasts over time
  • Receive personalized alerts and notifications by saving favorite fishing spots
  • Generate downloadable PDF reports or JSON and CSV files containing detailed forecasts and conditions for selected dates and locations

Implementation Details

Backend: The backend is developed in Python, utilizing the lightweight FastAPI framework to efficiently handle user requests and model inference. It hosts an ARIMA-based time series prediction algorithm, chosen for its robustness in modeling temporal dependencies and trends in environmental data. For each user-selected location, date, and parameter, the backend retrieves daily historical data spanning multiple years from NASA POWER API (and cross-checks with Meteomatics and Marine Weather APIs for validation), creating a reliable dataset for forecasting. The ARIMA model then generates predictions for environmental and oceanographic parameters.

Prediction Engine: The ARIMA (AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average) model is implemented in Python to identify temporal patterns and forecast short-term variations, providing personalized, data-driven insights for each selected fishing area. Before making predictions, the algorithm evaluates data stationarity and applies necessary transformations to ensure accuracy. It has been validated through backtesting on historical data, confirming that it produces reliable and actionable forecasts, giving users confidence when planning fishing activities.

The ARIMA (AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average) model was chosen because it is highly effective for analyzing time series data such as temperature, humidity, and wind speed. It can detect trends and cyclical patterns in climate datasets and generate short- to medium-term forecasts. Moreover, ARIMA is statistically interpretable and transparent, which is essential for scientific projects that prioritize explainability and data reliability. The model is implemented in Python to identify temporal patterns and forecast short-term variations, providing personalized, data-driven insights for each selected fishing area.

Data Integration: Three external APIs — NASA POWER, Meteomatics, and Marine Weather API — provide extensive historical and real-time data on weather, ocean conditions, and atmospheric parameters. These sources are highly reliable and accurate, enabling robust forecasting. For each user-selected location, the backend extracts daily data for the relevant parameters over the past years, creating a comprehensive dataset. This dataset is then aggregated, cleaned, and standardized before being fed to the predictive ARIMA model, ensuring precise and actionable forecasts for the user.

Frontend (Mobile Application): The frontend is built as a responsive mobile application, responsive for future cross-platform compatibility (mobile and web). It features an interactive map where users can select locations, specify dates, and choose environmental parameters to analyze (e.g., visibility, cloud coverage, lightning, air pressure, wave height). The frontend communicates with the backend API to fetch forecasts, display them in dashboards, generate reports, and handle notifications.

Notification and Alert System: Users can save their favorite fishing locations along with specific dates they wish to monitor. These preferences are stored locally in the app cache, allowing the app to continuously track forecasts for the selected location and date. The backend repeatedly runs the predictive ARIMA analysis, and the results are interpreted by the AI assistant to provide actionable guidance. If the forecast indicates potentially dangerous or unfavorable conditions, the user receives personalized alerts and notifications on their mobile device, ensuring they stay informed and can plan fishing activities safely.

Accessibility and Inclusive Design: Accessibility is a core design principle. The app is optimized for voiceover/screen reader support, tactile feedback, and simplified language, ensuring usability for all types of users, including those with visual impairments or limited technical experience. Additionally, the interface includes multilingual support, allowing users to choose their preferred language for all menus and notifications — enhancing accessibility and inclusivity for users from different linguistic backgrounds.

Report Generation: The system allows users to generate downloadable PDF reports, as well as CSV or JSON files, summarizing forecasts for selected locations and dates. These reports include visualized data and prediction results produced by the ARIMA model.

Scalability & Extensibility: The modular Python architecture enables easy expansion, such as integrating additional predictive algorithms (e.g., LSTM or Prophet models) or connecting to new meteorological data sources. This ensures scalability as the platform evolves to support more advanced predictive analytics and marine-related insights.

Impact

By democratizing access to critical environmental data, our project empowers fishermen to make informed decisions to protect their livelihoods. The platform serves as a vital early-warning tool, enabling users to take preventive measures against hazardous marine conditions.

Beyond individual benefits, widespread adoption of the system could significantly reduce the economic lossesassociated with maritime accidents and extreme ocean events along Brazil’s coast.

Case of Study: São Raimundo's Boat

Had the fishermen aboard the São Raimundo vessel had access to a tool like NaviSense, they might have been alerted to the high-risk ocean conditions — including sudden changes in wind direction, abnormal swell, and increased tidal amplitude. With this information, they could have delayed departure, adjusted their route, or coordinated with local authorities to reduce the risks of navigating under unstable conditions.

Future Work

  • Advanced Predictive Models and Multivariate Analysis: Extend the current ARIMA-based forecasting engine to include multivariate time series analysis, allowing cross-variable correlations (e.g., how wind speed, humidity, and pressure jointly affect wave height). Integrate deep learning architectures such as LSTM or Prophet to enhance accuracy and capture complex temporal and environmental dependencies.
  • Real-Time Ocean Monitoring: Incorporate buoy and satellite data streams for near real-time updates on sea state, tides, and currents. Data will be fetched from public APIs such as NOAA and Copernicus Marine Service, processed by the backend to normalize formats and merge with existing forecasts, enabling continuous updates and live visualization of current ocean conditions in the app.
  • Offline Mode: Implement local caching and offline access to saved forecasts and reports, enabling use in low-connectivity coastal areas.
  • Community and Social Features: Allow users to share fishing reports, tips, and local weather insights within the app, fostering a community of verified contributors.
  • Data Visualization Dashboard: Add interactive charts and heatmaps to visualize multi-day forecasts, wind direction trends, and wave intensity variations.
  • Sustainability Insights: Incorporate environmental indicators such as water temperature anomalies or pollution alerts to promote sustainable fishing practices.

Conclusion

Our project aims to transform the way coastal fishermen interact with critical environmental data. By bridging the gap between complex oceanographic datasets and accessible communication, we provide a practical and inclusive solution to a persistent problem. Empowering fishermen with timely and relevant information enables proactive decision-making, helping to prevent accidents, protect livelihoods, and reduce the significant economic and social impacts caused by hazardous marine conditions along Brazil’s coast.

🛰 Project Summary – AirMetrics
AirMetrics is an interactive application developed under the STEAM methodology, combining science, technology, and social engagement to monitor air quality in real time. Using data from NASA, environmental sensors, and meteorological information, the app transforms complex data on pollution, wildfires, and smoke dispersion into accessible and visual insights.

With a dynamic map, short- and long-term forecasts, and personalized alerts, AirMetrics helps users understand the impacts of pollution on their health and the environment. The platform also promotes citizen science, enabling communities to record local observations and experiment with strategies to reduce pollution.

In addition, the system features gamified and educational tools that encourage learning about sustainability and climate change. Its goal is to connect data, people, and action—promoting awareness and informed decision-making for a healthier planet.
projectDetails.details:
AirMetrics is an interactive application that monitors and forecasts air quality in real time anywhere in the world. It combines NASA data on pollution, wildfires, and smoke dispersion with meteorological information and local sensors to create a dynamic and accessible map, allowing users to view the Air Quality Index (AQI), receive early alerts, and explore forecasts of up to seven days.

Beyond monitoring, AirMetrics integrates a community platform where people can record environmental observations, share local solutions, and participate in educational challenges. This approach turns the app into a citizen science and environmental awareness tool, promoting learning and collective action.

The project was developed using React Native, TypeScript, and Expo, leveraging APIs for geolocation, notifications, and interactive maps. Its modular architecture and standardized design system ensure smooth performance, scalability, and consistency.

AirMetrics’ creativity lies in merging complex scientific data, gamification, and social interaction into an engaging and educational experience. It not only informs but also connects technology, science, and community to reduce environmental impacts and protect public health.

Our goal is to translate science into action—making environmental monitoring intuitive, collaborative, and accessible to everyone.

Our project, Interactive Lunar Base Builder, is an intelligent and modular web-based configurator designed to generate conceptual lunar habitat layouts for diverse mission types. Each mission — whether short-term deployment or long-term sustainment — demands unique architectural solutions. Our platform translates key mission parameters, such as crew size and duration, into functional 3D habitat blueprints within seconds.

By integrating NASA documentation and logic-based rules, the system differentiates between scalable and fixed spaces (e.g., life support, medical bay, crew quarters) and optimizes for safety, well-being, and productivity. This eliminates the need to start designs from scratch, empowering engineers and architects to focus on refinement rather than initial setup.

This approach accelerates decision-making, enhances mission adaptability, and demonstrates how intelligent design tools can revolutionize space habitat planning — ensuring that every crew has the right home for the right mission.
projectDetails.details:
The Interactive Lunar Base Builder is an interactive web-based configurator that translates lunar mission parameters into viable 3D habitat layouts. Users input mission data such as crew size, duration, and desired complexity. The system then applies a set of logical rules inspired by NASA’s habitat design documentation to automatically generate a modular habitat blueprint. Each configuration balances fixed and scalable areas — for instance, life support and medical zones remain constant, while crew quarters and common spaces scale with mission size.

Benefits and impact:
This system dramatically reduces the time needed to design mission-specific habitats, turning what could take months of manual modeling into minutes. It allows teams to rapidly explore “what-if” scenarios, supporting more agile decision-making and mission planning. The tool promotes safer, more efficient, and psychologically supportive spatial arrangements, enhancing astronaut well-being and productivity in extraterrestrial environments.

Tools and technologies used:
We developed the prototype using Figma for interface design and Three.js for 3D visualization, integrated with a Javascript web framework. Logical parameters and layout were defined with Node.js and Bootstrap. The website is hosted on spacebases.app.

Creativity and considerations:
Our approach merges architectural reasoning with data-driven automation — an innovative step toward intelligent space design tools. We considered key factors such as modularity, safety (by separating clean/dirty zones), psychological comfort (through acoustic and spatial zoning), and operational efficiency (by minimizing travel paths). The result is not just a digital tool but a proof of concept for a new way to plan habitats — one where data and design collaborate to create the right home for every mission.

projectDetails.details:
FIRE-SAR: Understanding Burn Scars Through Radar Eyes in the Pantanal

1.Overview

Our project focuses on the Pantanal region of Poconé, in Mato Grosso, Brazil — one of the world’s most ecologically diverse wetlands, but also among the most impacted by wildfires and illegal mining (garimpo) in recent years.

Using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery, we aim to analyze how these disturbances have transformed the local landscape, vegetation, and soil moisture over time.

Unlike optical sensors, radar can operate through clouds and smoke, providing a continuous and physically meaningful record of environmental change — essential in a region frequently obscured by seasonal fires.

2. Core Data and Methods

We used Sentinel-1 C-band SAR imagery with dual polarization (VV and VH) across multiple acquisition dates covering the Poconé region.

Each scene underwent preprocessing steps (thermal noise removal, calibration, and terrain correction) and was mosaicked to enable multi-temporal analysis.

The backscatter coefficient (σ⁰) was extracted from both polarizations and analyzed before and after fire and mining events.

Optical data from Google Earth and NBR (Normalized Burn Ratio) were used only for visual validation and comparison, while the SAR data provided the core physical insights.

3. Physical Hypotheses and Radar Interpretation

3.1. We developed hypotheses connecting SAR backscatter variations to physical processes in the Pantanal:

Polarization Response to Fire:

The cross-polarized VH signal shows a stronger decrease after fires than the co-polarized VV, due to vegetation loss and exposure of bare soil.

Fires reduce volume scattering (from plant canopies) and enhance surface scattering, affecting VH more significantly.

3.2. Moisture and Surface Roughness:

Burned or mined soils have altered roughness and water retention.

VV, being more sensitive to surface texture, varies moderately, while VH drops sharply, indicating loss of vegetation volume.

3.3. Penetration and Frequency:

Sentinel-1’s C-band provides moderate canopy penetration, making it ideal for capturing changes in surface moisture and vegetation structure typical of the Pantanal’s seasonal cycles.

These mechanisms explain why burn scars appear darker in VH, but retain moderate brightness in VV — a diagnostic radar signature of fire disturbance.

4. Analytical Workflow

Sentinel-1 SAR preprocessing and mosaicking.

Extraction of VV and VH backscatter.

Temporal differencing (Δσ⁰) to map fire and mining impacts.

Validation through NBR and visual comparison (Google Earth).

Spatial visualization and classification of disturbance intensity.

5. Key Findings

Significant VH backscatter reduction after fire events, consistent with vegetation loss.

VV changes linked to surface roughness and moisture variations.

The VH/VV ratio indicates post-fire or post-mining recovery dynamics.

SAR imagery successfully captured transformations even under cloud or smoke conditions, where optical imagery failed.

6. Study Area Justification

We selected Poconé (MT) because it represents a microcosm of the broader Pantanal — combining wetlands, savanna, and forest areas.

This diversity allows SAR to reveal different scattering behaviors across ecosystems.

Furthermore, it’s a region heavily affected by recurrent fires and garimpo, making it ideal for testing SAR’s ability to detect environmental degradation and recovery.

7.Future Development

In future versions, we plan to extend the analysis to the entire Pantanal biome, creating a large-scale SAR-based monitoring platform.

This system will integrate time series of Sentinel-1 data to map fire scars, vegetation regrowth, and soil moisture changes across the full extent of the wetland — helping local and global efforts in conservation and sustainable management.

8. Why SAR is the Protagonist

SAR data is the core analytical foundation of this project.

It reveals physical properties — vegetation structure, surface roughness, and moisture — that optical data cannot measure.

Optical imagery serves only to illustrate and validate SAR-derived results, ensuring accessibility for the general public while keeping the scientific foundation firmly radar-based.

9. Conclusion

By focusing on Sentinel-1 dual-polarization radar data, FIRE-SAR demonstrates how C-band backscatter can uncover the physical effects of fire and mining on complex ecosystems like the Pantanal.

The project not only supports fire monitoring and post-burn analysis, but also lays the groundwork for a long-term, radar-based environmental observatory for one of the most critical biomes on the planet.

10. Keywords: Pantanal · Poconé · SAR · Sentinel-1 · VH/VV Polarization · Fire Scars · Garimpo · Vegetation Structure · Soil Moisture · Radar Physics · Remote Sensing · Environmental Monitoring

projectDetails.name: Umbrella
projectDetails.summary:
Umbrella is an interactive application that uses historical climate data provided by NASA (GES DISC OPeNDAP) to deliver forecasts based on statistical analysis and machine learning. The project was developed to assist in the planning of events, activities, and preventive actions in the face of extreme weather conditions such as intense heat, severe cold, and strong winds.
With an intuitive and visually engaging interface, Umbrella presents interactive maps, intelligent charts, and calculated probabilities that help users understand climate patterns over decades. The tool transforms complex datasets into accessible and practical information, enabling anyone to plan with confidence — from daily routines to large-scale events.
By integrating space science and data analysis, Umbrella highlights the power of information for climate change adaptation and informed decision-making. It serves as a bridge between space and our planet, bringing NASA’s knowledge literally to the palm of your hand.
projectDetails.details:
You can see more at:

https://umbrella-orpin.vercel.app/

Umbrella is an intelligent application that transforms decades of NASA climate data into accessible and visual forecasts. It works with data provided by the GES DISC OPeNDAP (Hyrax) server to collect meteorological variables such as temperature, wind, humidity, and precipitation, applying linear regression models and trend analysis to predict future conditions.

The user inputs a date and location, and the system returns interactive maps, charts, and probability percentages for different scenarios: extreme heat, intense cold, or ideal conditions for outdoor events. The results are presented in an intuitive and visual way, using dynamic charts, dashboards, and 3D “clay-style” visualizations, creating an educational and engaging experience.

The technologies used were Vue.js 3 – a progressive JavaScript framework, TypeScript – static typing for JavaScript, and GSAP + ScrollTrigger – for smooth animations and scroll storytelling. Prototyping was done in Figma, and the charts were generated directly in Figma using data from the website:
https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/GPM_3GPROFGPMGMI_07/summary?keywords=rain

The intended impact is to facilitate the planning of outdoor events and raise awareness about climate change based on real collected data. Creatively, Umbrella combines design, science, and accessibility, translating NASA’s complex data into practical, understandable, and visually inspiring information.

Project Summary – NASA Farm Navigator

NASA Farm Navigator is an educational, text-based RPG that turns NASA Earth data into an interactive learning experience about sustainable agriculture. Players manage a virtual farm, making strategic decisions that balance productivity and environmental impact while exploring real satellite data on soil, vegetation, and climate.

Powered by AI-driven storytelling (GPT-4), each gameplay session generates dynamic scenarios adapted to the player’s choices and local environmental conditions. The project integrates datasets such as GIBS, GLAM, Crop-CASMA, and MODIS NDVI to simulate authentic agricultural challenges.

By combining science, technology, and gamification, NASA Farm Navigator promotes environmental awareness, critical thinking, and data literacy — showing how space data can help solve challenges on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Project Description – NASA Farm Navigator

NASA Farm Navigator is an educational text-based RPG that uses real NASA Earth data to teach sustainable agricultural practices through strategic decision-making and interactive storytelling.

Players take on the role of a farm manager navigating environmental and production challenges while learning how satellite data can be applied to real-world agriculture. The game is powered by AI (GPT-4), which acts as a dynamic Game Master, adapting scenarios to the player’s choices and local environmental conditions.

By integrating NASA datasets such as GIBS, GLAM, Crop-CASMA, and MODIS NDVI, the game delivers scientifically grounded experiences that demonstrate how remote sensing and climate data support sustainable farming decisions.

The project aims to educate, engage, and inspire players by merging science, technology, and gameplay to promote awareness of global sustainability challenges and the importance of data-driven agriculture.

Key Goals:

  • Make NASA data accessible and engaging for students and educators
  • Encourage sustainable land and resource management
  • Show real-world applications of Earth observation in farming
  • Support the UN Sustainable Development Goals (Zero Hunger, Responsible Consumption, Climate Action)
projectDetails.aiReferences:
How NASA Farm Navigator Uses Artificial Intelligence

NASA Farm Navigator integrates AI as the core of its interactive learning experience. The game uses a GPT-4 language model to act as a dynamic Game Master (GM), generating unique storylines, challenges, and feedback based on each player’s decisions and environmental context.

The AI analyzes in-game variables such as soil conditions, crop health, and sustainability metrics—derived from NASA datasets—and crafts adaptive narratives that reflect real agricultural trade-offs. Players receive personalized scenarios, realistic outcomes, and educational explanations for every action they take.

Additionally, the AI:

  • Interprets NASA Earth data (e.g., NDVI, precipitation, soil moisture) and translates it into human-readable, game-friendly insights.
  • Generates decision-driven consequences that simulate real-world cause-and-effect relationships in farming.
  • Provides contextual learning moments, explaining why certain agricultural practices are more sustainable or productive.

Through AI-driven storytelling, the project transforms complex scientific data into accessible, engaging, and personalized learning experiences — making players think like data-driven farmers.

projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary:
Our project, Sustainability from Earth to Mars, is an educational and creative 7-slide presentation that explores how lessons from Earth’s sustainability can be applied to future life on Mars. Using 25 years of public data from NASA’s Terra satellite, we focus on three critical areas: renewable energy, recycling and water cycles, and space agriculture.
The presentation uses storytelling to show how Earth observation informs practical solutions for energy generation, closed-loop water management, and crop production in extreme environments. By integrating these systems, we highlight the interdependence of energy, water, and food for sustainable living beyond our planet.
This project addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge by turning publicly available Earth observation data into an engaging educational tool that inspires innovation and sustainability thinking. Its importance lies in raising awareness about global resource management while demonstrating how space technologies and Earth science can guide humanity’s expansion into other planets.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, Sustainability from Earth to Mars, is an interactive educational presentation that demonstrates how sustainability practices on Earth can inform life-support systems on Mars. The project focuses on three main areas: renewable energy, recycling and water cycles, and space agriculture. Each slide combines scientific data, storytelling, and visualizations inspired by 25 years of publicly available NASA Terra satellite data to explain complex environmental processes in an engaging way.

The benefits of the project include raising awareness about sustainable resource management, teaching communities how energy, water, and food systems are interconnected, and inspiring innovative thinking for space exploration. The intended impact is to educate and motivate users to apply sustainability concepts both on Earth and in potential extraterrestrial habitats.

projectDetails.name: Project TheBugTeam
projectDetails.summary:
A gente se propôs a criar uma aplicação para as pessoas poderem selecionar uma área do globo terrestre e comparar entre diferentes épocas do ano, então, com o banco de dados da NASA, podemos ter uma vasta e aprofundada análise feita pela aplicação, que fornece também se há um crescimento ou decrescimento da flora na área selecionada. Com o intuito de auxiliar os apicultores e agricultores a preverem a floração da área de maneira mais precisa, e conseguirem planejar de maneira mais eficaz e lucrativa a produção.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
We set out to create an application so people could select an area of ​​the globe and compare it between different times of the year. Using NASA's database, we can then perform a vast and in-depth analysis using the application, which also provides information on whether there is a growth or decline of flora in the selected area. With the aim of helping beekeepers and farmers to predict the flowering of the area more accurately, and to be able to plan production more effectively and profitably.
projectDetails.details:
O projeto teve como objetivo desenvolver uma solução capaz de auxiliar agricultores e apicultores na previsão do florescimento em determinadas regiões, utilizando análise comparativa de dados ambientais e imagens de satélite.
A proposta visa gerar benefícios diretos para a agricultura e apicultura familiar, ao permitir que produtores possam antecipar períodos de maior atividade floral e, assim, otimizar o manejo de colheitas, polinização e produção de mel.
Durante o hackathon, a equipe enfrentou desafios na fase inicial devido a compromissos pessoais dos integrantes, o que impactou o ritmo de desenvolvimento e limitou a implementação completa da proposta.
Apesar disso, conseguimos criar um algoritmo funcional de pré-processamento e análise de imagens obtidas a partir do banco de dados da NASA.

O algoritmo foi projetado para coletar imagens de satélite de uma região e intervalo de tempo definidos (por padrão, Belo Horizonte, entre 2015 e 2024); filtrar automaticamente imagens com excesso de nuvens, borrões ou manchas escuras, garantindo a qualidade dos dados; registrar logs de download e armazenar as imagens aprovadas; permitir a configuração dinâmica da área de interesse e da janela temporal via código.

Para a extração e análise dos dados, utilizamos as seguintes fontes e produtos da NASA:

MODIS Terra Corrected Reflectance (True Color)

MODIS Terra NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index)

MODIS Terra EVI (Enhanced Vegetation Index)

A implementação foi feita em Python, com uso de bibliotecas como TensorFlow para análise e classificação das imagens.
O processo de filtragem utilizou técnicas de escala de cinza e avaliação de contraste, que permitem identificar automaticamente quais imagens são adequadas para uso em predições de florescimento.
Embora o desafio não tenha sido concluído integralmente, o grupo conseguiu validar uma etapa fundamental: a seleção automática e inteligente de imagens de satélite.
Como próximos passos, pretende-se integrar o modelo de análise com dados de solo, clima e histórico de vegetação, possibilitando a predição precisa de florescimento regional e maior suporte à tomada de decisão por pequenos produtores.
