projectDetails.name: Shark Seer
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Shark Seer, a mathematical framework designed to predict shark foraging habits on a global scale. The model was trained using datasets provided by NASA and partner institutions and is presented through a user-friendly web tool for data visualization. We included ocean temperature and depth, phytoplankton abundance, cloud cover, wave height, and shark position data as training variables.
Our model achieved 97.74% accuracy, with ocean temperature and depth identified as the most influential parameters. By facilitating the identification of priority areas for monitoring and protection, our project aims to support more effective shark conservation strategies and contribute to the preservation of these essential species.
projectDetails.details:
Introduction

Sharks are a highly diverse group, comprising more than 500 species (Dulvy et al., 2016). They belong to the class Chondrichthyes, a group of fishes characterized by skeletons made primarily of cartilage. This class is divided into two subclasses: Elasmobranchii (which includes sharks, skates, rays, and sawfishes) and Holocephali (chimaeras, known informally as ghost sharks) (D.A. Ebert, 2021).

Sharks inhabit a wide variety of environments, ranging from marine to freshwater ecosystems (D. A. Ebert et al., 2021). Although they are often perceived as apex predators, their ecological diversity is much broader (Dulvy et al., 2017). Adult body sizes range from about 20 cm to over 18 m, allowing them to occupy distinct ecological niches (Dedman et al., 2024) . Consequently, their feeding strategies vary widely: some species are parasites, others are small predators feeding on invertebrates, while the largest species prey on marine mammals and large fishes (Dedman et al., 2024).

Some of these species, such as the Great White Shark and the Tiger Shark, are apex predators that play a crucial role as keystone species (Galván-Malganã et al., 2019). Keystone species are organisms that have a disproportionately large effect on their environment relative to their abundance, essentially holding an ecosystem together (Menge et al., 2013). In other words, even with relatively low populations compared to other animals, keystone species play a critical role in regulating the populations of other species. Their disappearance can trigger a collapse in the food chain, causing significant imbalances in the ecosystem (Petterson et al., 2020).

Recently, we see a significant biodiversity loss, with populations of many species declining worldwide (Liu et al., 2025). In marine ecosystems, species are threatened by high levels of human activity, such as overfishing, aquaculture, depredation from fisheries, and recreational fishing (Maccaulet et al., 2015).

In this scenario, shark populations are decreasing substantially (Dulvy et al., 2017). According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, approximately 31% of the 536 shark species on Earth are threatened with extinction (Dulvy et al., 2016), and 60% of coral reef-associated sharks and rays are also at risk (Sherman et al., 2022). With advances in technology and the growing use of artificial intelligence and improved machine learning models, it is now possible to develop mathematical tools that predicts sharks’ foraging habits (Panunzi et al. 2024), that is, the areas where they search for resources such as food and reproductive partners (Krurisgara et al., 2024). Predicting shark distribution is therefore crucial for designing more effective conservation and preservation programs, helping to prevent their extinction (Sun et al., 2024).

Based on this, we developed a framework for a mathematical model, based on machine learning, capable of predicting the most probable shark foraging areas, using remote sensing data combined with sighting records from citizen science. In addition, we created a website as a user-friendly tool for data visualization, which also includes educational features aimed at raising public awareness about shark conservation. Finally, we designed a theoretical tag concept that could enhance current tagging technologies by increasing the range of data collected, thereby improving animal tracking and conservation efforts. With our results, we hope to contribute to conservation public policies by facilitating the identification of priority areas for monitoring and preserving these animals.

Methodology

For the purpose of our project, we focused on the Atlantic Ocean to train our model, as data is available and covers a broad spectrum of values for training and testing. We also decided on key variables for modeling the framework such that we considered the concepts that most influence shark foraging habits.

Abundance of phytoplankton is of utmost importance in a marine ecossystem, as it is the base of multiple food chains and can be analyzed for biological interactions of predation and prey (Naselli-Flores & Padisák, 2023), so this data could be leveraged for our purposes. Temperature and wave height are also important factors for a shark’s foraging habits (Monteforte et al., 2022). Ocean depth has been linked to good accuracy in white shark prediction models previously (Panunzi et al, 2024), so it was included in ours. And there exists a significative statiscal correlation between cloud coverage and shark sightings (Taglioni et al.,2025).

Thus, we decided on the following variables for our model:

  • Location (latitude and longitude
  • Time
  • Ocean depth
  • Phytoplankton
  • Wave height, period and direction
  • Temperature
  • Shark sightings
  • Clouds

SharkPulse data (Ferretti et al., 2018) collected between 2020 and 2023 was used for training, while data from 2024 was reserved for testing. We assumed uniform distribution on latitude and longitude for synthetic data on absence of shark sightings. We collected ocean depth, water surface temperature and wave height, direction and period gathered by Meteomatics's Weather API from NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025's global colaborators. Monthly phytoplankton data was compiled from the NASA Ocean Biology Distributed Active Archive Center (OB.DAAC).

We developed a proof-of-concept predictive framework integrated into a minimum viable product visualization tool for validation. With it, we can scale and improve the model with data gathered through the tag prototype we developed. For the developed tag prototype, we researched in different scientific papers, utilizing them as a strong base for the project.

We used the XGBoost machine learning algorithm for our model given that its base technique, gradient boosting, has been tested as the strongest base learner model when applied to classification of elasmobranch behavior (Brewster et al., 2018) and XGBoost offers a good balance between accuracy and training speed (Bentéjac, C., Csörgő, A. & Martínez-Muñoz, G., 2021).

Tools

For the project, we used the following tools:

  • Programming languages: R for data analysis and treatment, Python for the backend and data analysis and treatment, Typescript for the frontend
  • Frameworks: React + Vite
  • Other tools: Google Cloud for backend deployment, Vercel for frontend deployment, GitHub for version control (GitHub of the project: https://github.com/milenafs/nasa-2025)

Results and Discussion

We obtained a set of results from different types of statical models: Precision and Recall, F1 Score, and Confusion Matrix; to comprovate the robustness of our model. As a main result, we achieve a training accuracy of 0.9972 and a model accuracy of 0.9711.

Model

The model we generated had a final accuracy of 0.9711, covering latitudes in the range [-70, 70] and longitudes in the range [-100, 25], both in degrees. In order to verify our results, we created some correlation plots by comparing two variables from our input space. The most relevant ones are as follows:

(Figures 1 and 2: Temperature (ºC), ocean depth (m) or maximum wave height (m), and shark presence probability correlated)

The figure highlights a strong correlation between the interaction between water temperature, ocean depth, wave height and shark presence probability, as evidenced by the concentration of points in the lower right corner of the graph. For the points that disperse into deeper ocean regions or regions with higher waves, our model also shows a slightly higher probability of sharks.

(Figure 3: Latitude (º), longitude (º), and shark presence probability correlated)

This figure features presence of sharks mostly around the shores of the continents, making their outlines distinguishable.

(Figure 4: Ocean depth (m), phytoplankton concentration (mg/m^3), and shark presence probability correlated)

From this figure, we found that phytoplankton presence didn’t influence shark presence probability in our model, since the range of phytoplankton concentrations measured did not result in large variety of the final output. There were some spikes near around 17 mg/m^3 and 37 mg/m^3, but we concluded they are due to other external reasons, possibly data bias.

(Figure 5: Importance of each parameters considering the model results)

The feature importance plot shows that ocean depth was the single most influential parameter, with an importance score greater than 0.5. The next most significant factors were the shark's geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude) followed by water temperature. Conversely, phytoplankton concentration (phyto) and cloud cover (clouds) had the least impact on the results.

It is worth mentioning that phytoplankton concentration did not have as strong an impact as expected. This may be explained by the fact that phytoplankton form the base of the marine trophic web and therefore influence sharks only indirectly, by affecting the abundance of their prey (Naselli-Flóres & Padisák, 2022). In our model, we were only able to describe the direct effects on potential shark foraging habitats and had to exclude the indirect effects that shape their ecological niche. In conclusion, we cannot discard the importance of phytoplankton in shaping shark foraging habits. However, since our results suggest that there is not necessarily a direct effect, this highlights the need to further investigate these relationships and expand research on how phytoplankton concentration may influence shark foraging behavior.

Shark Seer

Following our goal to present our results to the general public, we designed our web application for Shark Seer with two target audiences in mind: the student and the researcher. The student persona arrives with no prior knowledge, but is able to learn what is necessary by choosing to view the introduction to the application, as shown above. Meanwhile, the researcher can skip the introduction and go straight to the main tool, as shown below.

Visualisation of the Model

This is where you may visualize the main results of our model. Initially, the user is presented with a map containing the probability of sharks being anywhere in the Atlantic Ocean given the variables mentioned previously collected during an arbitrary day. Due to limitations of API usage, we had to restrict our data to a single day, as our model is an MVP, but the model generated by our method would work for any other dataset of the same variables, including future predictions.

The user can also change the inputs for our model to recalculate the probabilities. In the example above, our model uses the same dataset as input, except the temperatures, which are 150% of their original values.

Should the user want a quick tour on how to view the results, they can access the tutorial by clicking on the button above.

Knowledge Hub

As previously mentioned, we thought of a student persona that arrives at our web application with no prior knowledge. If they want, they can access our Knowledge Hub, a section with four small lessons on sharks.

Each lesson includes a voiceover for accessibility reasons and pop-ups for clearing up biological terms.

We also have a Student Mode, an extra option for the student persona. Once enabled, flags will appear around the map, prompting the user to click on them. Every flag has a trivia question on shark-related matters.

Tag

Motivation

A dedicated hardware could enhance our model. For this purpose, we propose a biologging tag that gathers GPS and shark’s prey composition data.

GPS information is important to improve location accuracy and grow dataset size. Having our own data is also crucial in order to achieve more independence from other public databases.

We also chose to analyze shark’s prey composition to further our understanding on its impact on the food web as well, better explaining it’s relations to the producers.

Conceptual model

It is possible to estimate the composition of the meal being metabolized by the body by measuring the ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed through the blood by the equation, and depending on the value, we can extract the composition of the meal(Frayn, 1983):

To collect the necessary blood gas data, the tag will incorporate a flow-through optical sensor. This component uses 2 micro-quartz tube, connected to an artery and a vein, whose inner surface is lined with fluorescent indicator dyes. An external LED illuminates these dyes through the tube's transparent wall and a detector measures the changes in fluorescence, which directly correlate to the blood gas levels (Liu et al., 2024).

This blood gas sensor will be integrated with a standard GPS module, a proven technology for tracking land and water animals. Both systems will be combined within a single device to avoid the need for multiple attachments and will be powered by a low consumption hardware, with an integrated high-density non-rechargeable battery. Considering the Ultra-Low Power GPS modules as well as the simplicity of the flow-through optical sensor the module should be able to last similarly to other commercial tags.

While many tags release and are physically recovered to then be analyzed, our sensor's vascular connection makes this unfeasible. Therefore, our tag must incorporate a transmitter for remote data retrieval. This is a proven technology used in many modern satellite and acoustic tags to periodically send data, ensuring information can be collected without recapturing the animal. This method is feasible as sharks periodically go to surface levels so the satellite module can send data (Braun, Camrin D. et al, 2019).

Conclusion

We managed to create a good machine learning model for predicting shark foraging habits, based on our statistical tests, results, and variable correlations. However, our model has limitations, which were mainly the following:

  • Data bias. Most of our shark sighting data comes from the shores.
  • Area limitation. We restricted our model to the Atlantic Ocean and surrounding areas due to limits on API usage and data storage.
  • Missing ecological context. We couldn’t add indirect effect to our model to improve the prediction, such as predator-prey ecological interactions.
  • Uncertain causality. Difficult to find cause and consequence. We can select the best dataset and the most correlated, but always going to have some uncertanty to the data relation.

Despite its limitations, our model successfully identifies key "hotspots" of shark activity. This information is highly valuable for conservation, as it allows policymakers to make data-driven decisions. We can highlight the importance of temperature data and ocean depth as a strong predicter of foraging habits sharks, which are related with the different ecological role that sharks play in the environment, creating a wide variety of habitats where sharks can explore. Pinpointing these critical habitats is fundamental for developing more targeted and effective strategies to conserve and manage the shark population.

projectDetails.name: Project CosmoFarm
projectDetails.summary: My team created a game using artificial intelligence, based on Landsat data contained in the Mapbiomas project, which monitors transformations in land cover and land use in territories and their impacts. The game is about sugarcane farming in Brazil, which is important for food, the economy, and clean energy production. The game is set in the municipality of Ribeirão Preto, São Paulo, and uses agricultural data to monitor the plantation. From Mapbiomas, which contains Landsat data, and Google Earth Engine, land use and cover data from the region were extracted, as well as mosaics from 2020 to 2024. The municipality was divided into 4 plots using QGIS software, which was also used to filter sugarcane plantation regions and the averages of NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) and LST (Land Surface Temperature). Based on suggestions from a colleague agronomist from ESALQ - USP, the game uses the idea of reusing sugarcane straw as organic fertilizer, a practice that promotes sustainability. The game also utilizes the idea of repurposing vinasse. Vinasse is important for its value as an organic fertilizer, reducing the need for chemical fertilizers, and for its potential to generate bioenergy, such as biohydrogen, being a byproduct of the ethanol and sugar industry that contributes to agricultural and economic sustainability. The game used academic research as a source obtained through Gemini's Deep Research. It was used data from Giovanni to measure soil moisture.
projectDetails.details:
Sugarcane has been used for centuries for the production of sucrose. In recent decades, in Brazil, sugarcane cultivation has increased significantly as it also began to be used for ethanol production as a substitute fuel for gasoline. Due to its benefits of being a renewable and clean energy source (green energy), and positive effects on pollution and climate change, sugarcane production holds an important position in the national renewable energy matrix. In Brazil, sugarcane ethanol has also started to be used for the production of green ethylene, which is used in polyethylene production by the company Braskem.

My project is a game built using Artificial Intelligence through the Rosebud AI website. The team used Gemini's Deep Research to conduct in-depth research on prompts for game mechanics.

The Landsat collections were loaded through the Mapbiomas website and Google Earth Engine. It was necessary to use programming to load the land use and land cover collections of Brazil and mosaics from the years 2020 to 2024, filtering the municipality of Ribeirão Preto, São Paulo, an important sugarcane plantation region. It was necessary to filter the peak biomass periods of the crops to analyze the agricultural indices.

To analyze the satellite images, QGIS software was used, a free and open-source software, a cross-platform geographic information system that allows the visualization, editing, and analysis of georeferenced data. This was used to filter the sugarcane plantation areas and calculate the NDVI and LST of the crops. To do this, it was necessary to acquire knowledge about this tool. The software was also used to divide the plantation regions into 4 plots and calculate the average indices, which were used in the game mechanics. To calculate the indices, mathematical formulas are used that take information contained in the satellite images as parameters.

The focus of the project is on sustainable practices in agriculture, and these practices are tested through simulation with real data. Academic research was used to obtain information about the importance of straw as organic fertilizer and the reuse of vinasse in sugarcane plantations. It is an educational, informative game that uses real agricultural data from Brazil, and can be useful for everyone involved in sugarcane cultivation. The project development process can be applied to other crops as well, since important agricultural indices were used.

To exemplify the data obtained, here we have the year of 2024:

NDVI: plot1 - 0.72, plot2 - 0.69, plot3 - 0.73, plot4 - 0.71.

LST: plot1 - 34,4°C, plot2 - 35,2°C, plot3 - 33,8°C, plot4 - 34,5°C.

The team used Giovanni data from Earthdata also. It was used to measure root zone soil moisture in the region. This data was used to train the game mechanics.

projectDetails.name: AirJourney
projectDetails.summary:
AirJourney is an interactive tool that democratizes access to air quality information, transforming complex scientific data into accessible and practical knowledge.  
Developed with real-time NASA data (TEMPO, FIRMS, and EarthData), the system features an interactive 3D Earth globe that allows anyone to visualize and understand the planet’s atmospheric conditions in an intuitive and impactful way.

More than just a visualization, AirJourney empowers communities to make informed decisions about the environment, public health, and local policies, turning information into social and environmental action.
projectDetails.details:
Objective

AirJourney was created to empower citizens, educators, and public decision-makers, offering a visual, scientific, and practical tool that goes far beyond informing , it transforms data into awareness and action.

With AirJourney, anyone can understand real-time air quality, identify the pollutants affecting their city, visualize local and global pollution patterns, and make informed decisions that promote health, sustainability, and collective responsibility.

More than knowledge, AirJourney inspires concrete and transformative actions, connecting every user to the reality of our planet and showing that every breath and every choice matters in building a cleaner and safer future.

3D Globe — The Planet Breathing

At the core of AirJourney is an interactive 3D Earth globe, developed with Three.js, which transforms complex scientific data into a clear, engaging, and intuitive visualization.

Key Features

  • Real-Time Data: integration with NASA and environmental monitoring APIs (TEMPO, FIRMS, EarthData, OpenAQ), providing up-to-date information on CO₂, ozone, atmospheric pressure, humidity, temperature, and other pollutants from locations around the world.
  • Thematic Layers: users can toggle between different environmental indicators — atmospheric pollutants, wildfires, temperature, particle density, and climate variables.
  • Intuitive Navigation: clicking on any region of the globe opens detailed panels with explanatory data, allowing users to quickly understand local and global conditions.

The result is a technological, educational, and impactful experience, where science and citizenship intersect, connecting each user to the reality of our planet in a practical and interactive way.

Educational and Awareness Module

Beyond data visualization, AirJourney includes an interactive quiz and educational content that reinforce learning on environmental topics.

Features:

  • Contextual Questions: based on real-life situations, linking science to everyday life.
  • Educational Feedback: incorrect answers are turned into learning opportunities.
  • Conscious Gamification: users progress as they understand the impact of human actions on the air they breathe.

This module transforms learning into social and environmental engagement.

Social and Environmental Impact

AirJourney aims to create local and global impact by making information that was once restricted to scientists and specialists accessible to everyone.
With real data and intuitive visualizations, the tool:

  1. Bridges science and society, creating connections between technical data and everyday reality.
  2. Facilitates public and personal decision-making based on scientific evidence.
  3. Promotes accessible environmental education, strengthening a culture of collective responsibility.
  4. Amplifies the reach of NASA data, making it understandable for all audiences.

The expected impact is an increase in environmental literacy and the development of a collective awareness of the air we breathe.

Direct Contributions:

  1. Transforming data into action: makes NASA atmospheric data understandable and actionable.
  2. Cloud computing and visualization: integrates NASA APIs for real-time 3D visualizations.
  3. Forecasting and awareness: assists in interpreting atmospheric patterns and educates on their impacts.
  4. Education and engagement: creates an immersive experience that fosters environmental responsibility.
  5. Scalability: can be applied in schools, cities, and environmental organizations worldwide.

Technologies Used

  • Three.js : 3D globe rendering.
  • NASA TEMPO, FIRMS, and EarthData APIs: Earth observation and air quality data.
  • OpenAQ and OpenWeatherMap: supplementary information on weather and pollutants.
  • HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript: development foundation and data processing.

SourceCode on GitHub

Conclusion

AirJourney is more than a tool it is a catalyst for social and environmental transformation.
By connecting real-time scientific data to an intuitive and interactive interface, people gain the ability to understand the air they breathe, visualize the effects of pollution, and act consciously, turning knowledge into practical, collective action.

With just a few clicks, anyone can:

  • Identify the pollutants affecting their city.
  • Compare local and global air quality data.
  • Make informed decisions about transportation, consumption, and health.
  • Participate in community challenges and initiatives that reduce emissions and promote sustainability.

The true power of AirJourney lies in democratizing science, showing that every breath matters and every action counts. It turns spectators into protagonists, educating, raising awareness, and mobilizing , creating citizens capable of shaping a cleaner, safer, and healthier planet for all.

projectDetails.name: Discovering Space Weather
projectDetails.summary: By studying space phenomena, several facts can be explained, such as, for example, the northern and southern lights. These beautiful events are colorful displays strongly influenced by space weather, which corresponds to environmental variations between the Sun and the Earth. However, even though it causes events like auroras, space weather can negatively affect today’s society, which depends on technology for its functioning, making it necessary to raise awareness among the current youth to prevent future implications. With that in mind, a video was created to portray the concept of space weather and its importance through the personification of the Sun, following a structure similar to the programs “O Show da Luna” or “Dora the Explorer”, in which there is strong interaction with the viewer. In addition, a website was produced with the purpose of making access easier both to the video and to additional information, allowing users to take a quiz for better understanding by the children. To promote and facilitate public access, we created an Instagram account with the username @team_dorothy_vaughan, where we posted promotional content and curiosities about the project.
projectDetails.details: The project consists of a fully programmed website, composed of a video contextualizing the project, a section presenting the team members, and an animation on the theme of “space weather,” as required by the challenge. One of the main goals of the project is to facilitate and enhance the understanding of the topic, so the website presents information in a clear and objective way for both children and any other individual interested in the subject. The intended impact is to raise awareness, especially among younger audiences, about space weather and how it affects us, using simple and easily accessible language. To develop the website, we used Visual Studio Code (VSCode) as the programming software. The code was written using CSS, HTML, and JavaScript. Alight Motion and CapCut were used for animation and editing, respectively, and GitHub was used to provide the judges access to the code. The main creative differential of our project is the Sun as the narrator of the story, guiding the audience through an educational journey about space weather in a fun and engaging way. By choosing the Sun as the main character, we transform scientific concepts into a dynamic, surprising, and magical experience, sparking curiosity in the audience. The climax of the video occurs when, after the entire captivating narrative, we reveal that it was all a dream, adding a touch of fantasy that makes the learning experience memorable and exciting. Our team considered key factors for the success of the project: audience suitability, ensuring the content was accessible and engaging; innovation and creativity, by choosing the Sun as the narrator and creating surprising elements, didactic clarity, so that complex concepts could be easily understood, educational impact, planning a climax that would capture interest and aid memorization, and scientific accuracy, maintaining the fidelity of the information presented.

projectDetails.details:
Integrated Geospatial Analysis Platform: Data Pathways to Healthy Cities

The Challenge: Urban health faces immense pressure from pollution, climate change, and population growth. Managers need tools to rapidly identify where air quality risks, extreme temperatures, and poor health infrastructure overlap. Our solution provides a unified, data-driven view for the "Data Pathways to Healthy Cities and Human Settlements" challenge.

Our Solution: A Geospatial AI Platform: We developed an Integrated Geospatial Analysis Platform—an interactive web application combining NASA data with local Brazilian metrics to provide actionable intelligence for urban planners.

AI Implementation: The project heavily leverages AI/LLMs. We utilize an LLM API directly within the site, powering the AI Chatbot feature for complex natural language querying (e.g., "Which 5 municipalities have the highest AQI and lowest health coverage?"). Furthermore, large language models (LLMs) like OpenAI, Copilot, ChatGPT, and Gemini were used extensively for code generation and development acceleration.

The platform is structured around three analytical layers:

  • Layer 1 (Air Quality): Uses NASA Giovanni and WorldView data (e.g., AOD, SO2, NO2) to calculate a weighted AQI.
  • Layer 2 (Climate Extremes): Utilizes historical INMET data to map regional vulnerabilities to extreme temperatures.
  • Layer 3 (Health Deficit): Uses DATASUS and IBGE data to calculate a Health Deficit Score.

This approach transforms visualization into proactive planning intelligence.

NASA Integration: We integrate NASA Giovanni and WorldView atmospheric data, which is normalized and weighted with local metrics to generate the final, comprehensive Vulnerability Map.

Technical Checklist Compliance (Must-Haves): Integrates NASA Data. Source Code is Public (GitHub). Demo is Public (runs without downloads or registration). Project is 100% in English. All links are public and working.

projectDetails.details:
Greetings from the Asteroid Investigators! 🪐

Our journey begins with the discovery of near-Earth asteroids. Although rare, some may pose real risks, and their impact could cause tsunamis, earthquakes, and atmospheric changes capable of transforming the planet.

This project was born from the curiosity of understanding how science detects, analyzes, and predicts these cosmic risks.

We want users to explore this fascinating field of astronomy with us, realizing that studying asteroids is also a way of protecting life on Earth.

Data and Discoveries

The website provides detailed information about NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) Program — a system that monitors and catalogs asteroids close to our planet.

Through the NEO API, we collected data such as size, speed, distance, and orbit of these space objects.

We also used data from the United States Geological Survey (USGS), which provides information on tsunami zones, topography, and seismic activity — all essential to understanding the possible effects of an asteroid impact.

Objectives

Our main goal is to bring children and young people closer to the scientific universe, encouraging learning through technology and creativity.

We want to inspire future generations to become interested in astronomy and to engage in projects that unite education and space science.

To achieve this, we developed:

🌐 An educational website with interactive and visually appealing content;

🎮 A fun game where the player defends the Earth from asteroids that could cause impacts;

🧠 Educational materials based on real NASA data.

Defend Earth and discover the universe! 🚀

Face dangerous asteroids in a fun and educational adventure.

While protecting the planet, you'll learn real-life facts about science and astronomy. 🪐✨

Play, explore, and show that knowledge is also a form of defense! 💫

PROJECT DETAILS

🔹 Legal Notice:

For the best experience, use the website on desktop computers (Google Chrome – desktop mode).

Mobile support is not yet available, but we plan to add this feature in future versions.

🔹 Accessibility and Educational Focus:

Our main audience is school-aged children and young people. All content was designed to be clear, playful, and educational, combining scientific learning with gamification elements.

🔹 Technologies Used:

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript

NASA NEO API

USGS Data

3D Models and Interactive Graphics

Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT 3.5)

🔹 Design Focus:

The website was developed to be intuitive, visual, and inspiring, based on experiences that blend art, programming, and scientific education.

🔹 Music copyright:

Dreamy Cat by Johny Grimes https://soundcloud.com/johny-grimes

Creative Commons — Attribution 3.0 Unported — CC BY 3.0

Free Download / Stream: https://www.audiolibrary.com.co/johny-grimes/dreamy-cat

Music promoted by Audio Library https://youtu.be/AD6TyKedfU8

NASA DATA

The data used in this project comes from NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) Program, accessed via the NEO API, which provides information on:

Asteroid trajectories;

Orbital speeds;

Approximate diameters;

Distance from Earth;

Frequency and impact risk.

In addition, the project incorporated information from the United States Geological Survey (USGS), which supports the modeling of geological risk zones, such as tsunamis and earthquakes, helping us understand the secondary effects of an astronomical impact.

SPACE AGENCY PARTNERSHIP AND OTHER DATA

This project was designed based on public and official NASA data, compiled for educational and scientific purposes.

Our dream is that this work will inspire new generations of space explorers, showing that learning can be just as exciting as exploring the universe.

In the next steps, we plan to expand the project with new features, mobile integration, and the inclusion of new educational modules focused on astronomy, physics, and technology.

✨ Greetings from the Young Defenders of the Earth!

🛰️ “Learning is our way of exploring the universe.”

challengeDetails.title: Meteor Madness
challengeDetails.excerpt: A newly identified near-Earth asteroid, "Impactor-2025," poses a potential threat to Earth, but do we have the tools to enable the public and decision makers to understand and mitigate its risks? NASA datasets include information about known asteroids and the United States Geological Survey provides critical information that could enable modeling the effects of asteroid impacts, but this data needs to be integrated to enable effective visualization and decision making. Your challenge is to develop an interactive visualization and simulation tool that uses real data to help users model asteroid impact scenarios, predict consequences, and evaluate potential mitigation strategies. (Planetary Science Division)

projectDetails.name: Project Vemdima
projectDetails.summary:
The Exo-Classifier Interactive Platform is a web-based tool designed to make exoplanet identification accessible to researchers, students, and the general public. Leveraging open data from the Kepler, K2, and TESS missions, the platform combines machine learning with interactive visualizations to classify potential exoplanets as Confirmed, Candidate, or False Positive. Users can upload CSV or FITS files, explore light curves, and apply habitability filters to identify Earth-like candidates.

The platform addresses the challenge by democratizing access to NASA mission data, enabling participants to engage directly with scientific workflows that typically require specialized expertise. Integrated SHAP explainability ensures transparency in AI predictions, fostering trust and scientific credibility.

Exo-Classifier is important because it accelerates the vetting process for exoplanet candidates while providing an educational experience that connects users with real astronomical data. By merging technology, science, and education, the project empowers discovery and encourages public engagement in space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
The Exo-Classifier Interactive Platform is a web-based tool designed to make exoplanet identification and classification accessible to researchers, students, and the general public. Users can upload CSV or FITS files containing photometric time-series data from NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS missions. The platform processes the data, detrends and phase-folds light curves, and applies a pre-trained XGBoost machine learning model to classify candidates as Confirmed, Candidate, or False Positive.

Integrated SHAP explainability allows users to understand which features influenced the AI predictions, ensuring transparency and trust. The platform also includes interactive visualizations, habitability filters, and educational simulations to engage users and teach key concepts of exoplanet science and machine learning.

The project benefits the scientific and educational community by accelerating the vetting process for exoplanet candidates while fostering public engagement in space exploration. It is creative in combining machine learning, interactive visualization, and educational content in a single, accessible tool.

The development stack includes Python (FastAPI for back-end, Pandas, Astropy, Lightkurve for data processing), Streamlit, Plotly, and Bokeh for the front-end, and pre-trained XGBoost models for classification. The team prioritized usability, scientific accuracy, and transparency, considering factors such as dataset diversity, user experience, interpretability of AI predictions, and educational impact.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Use of AI:

The Exo-Classifier Interactive Platform integrates Artificial Intelligence to classify exoplanet candidates from photometric time-series data. We use a pre-trained XGBoost machine learning model to predict whether a candidate is Confirmed, Candidate, or False Positive. Additionally, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) is applied to provide explainability, showing users which features influenced the AI predictions.

AI was also utilized to generate educational visualizations and interactive simulations that illustrate the classification process in an intuitive manner. All AI-generated outputs are original and do not use or modify any NASA branding.

For transparency, metadata and descriptive text acknowledge the use of AI in generating predictions, visualizations, and simulations. The team ensured that AI assists the platform’s functionality and educational purpose, while human oversight guided dataset selection, feature engineering, user interface design, and overall scientific accuracy.

challengeDetails.title: A World Away: Hunting for Exoplanets with AI
challengeDetails.excerpt: Data from several different space-based exoplanet surveying missions have enabled discovery of thousands of new planets outside our solar system, but most of these exoplanets were identified manually. With advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML), it is possible to automatically analyze large sets of data collected by these missions to identify exoplanets. Your challenge is to create an AI/ML model that is trained on one or more of the open-source exoplanet datasets offered by NASA and that can analyze new data to accurately identify exoplanets. (Astrophysics Division)

projectDetails.name: Fly Me To The Mars
projectDetails.summary:
Fly Me To The Mars is an interactive 3D web experience that transforms scientific data into an immersive journey across the Red Planet. Built using real NASA topographic and imaging datasets, the project allows users to freely explore a true-to-scale 3D model of Mars and uncover interactive “story points” representing key missions, discoveries, and geological landmarks.

Each story is presented through visual floating cards enriched with verified NASA imagery and facts, designed to make learning about Mars engaging and accessible. The experience is enhanced by Mars IA Search, an intelligent assistant powered by Google Gemini, which interprets user questions and connects them to curated data files and exact map coordinates—turning curiosity into exploration.

By blending technology, art, and storytelling, Fly Me To The Mars aims to spark scientific curiosity and inspire users to see Mars not as a distant world, but as a reflection of humanity’s quest to understand the universe.
projectDetails.details:
The Journey: Fly Me To The Mars

Upon entering the site, users embark on a simulated planetary voyage, leaving Earth and arriving on Mars. A smooth onboarding sequence introduces them to a realistic 3D model of the Martian surface, designience unfolds across three main layers:

Free 3D Exploration Users can freely navigate a real-scale 3D model of Mars, built with authentic NASA topographic and coordinate data. The interface allows smooth orbital control, panning, and zooming, letting users explore famous Martian regions, from Olympus Mons to Gale Crater, exactly as they exist in scientific datasets.

Throughout the surface, interactive story points appear as visual markers. Each point represents a real location tied to NASA missions, geological phenomena, or historical discoveries. This creates a direct link between visual exploration and scientific context, turning raw data into a dynamic and accessible educational journey.

Interactive Stories Each story point opens a sequence of floating visual cards, guiding users through 5–6 interactive steps that mix text, imagery, and scientific context. These stories transform complex research into narrative moments, showing how each site shaped humanity’s understanding of Mars.

Every story includes ultra–high–resolution NASA imagery, allowing users to zoom in and examine fine terrain details, from sediment patterns to crater ridges. All content is based on verified NASA sources, ensuring both educational integrity and visual impact. The storytelling flow keeps users engaged as they uncover discoveries, missions, and mysteries hidden across the Red Planet.

Mars IA Search (Chatbot)At the core of Fly Me To The Mars lies Mars IA Search, a dual-layer intelligent assistant designed to make exploration conversational and adaptive. It operates in two synergistic modes:

  1. Interpretation Mode (Gemini API) Powered by Google Gemini, the assistant processes natural-language questions, such as “Where did Perseverance collect rock samples?” or “Show me where NASA found ice deposits.” It interprets the user’s intent and identifies whether the query relates to a general planetary topic or to one of the mapped story points.

  2. Context Retrieval Mode (Filtered Dataset Search) Once the topic is recognized, the AI retrieves the most relevant information from a set of custom–filtered data files, each linked to a specific region or discovery on Mars. These curated files are built from NASA Trek data and official NASA research articles, ensuring responses are accurate and contextually relevant.

If the question refers to a specific location, Mars IA Search automatically returns a coordinate-linked response, complete with a “Go to Location” button that instantly centers the 3D view on that site. This seamless integration transforms curiosity into movement, allowing users to literally follow their questions across the Martian surface.

By combining semantic understanding (Gemini) with localized data recall, Mars IA Search bridges science, storytelling, and spatial immersion, acting as a guide, educator, and companion throughout the user’s journey on Mars.

Data and Sources

NASA Resources:

  • NASA Trek API - used for topography, real planetary coordinates, and high-resolution imagery.
  • NASA News & Articles - provided factual context and official mission data.

Additional Data Processing:

  • Custom-filtered datasets prepared for AI interpretation.
  • Real-scale modeling ensures coordinate accuracy and a physically correct Martian terrain.

Technical Details

Framework:

  • Next.js 15 (Turbopack) - enables high-performance rendering, smooth scene transitions, and optimized SSR for 3D content.

Languages:

  • TypeScript - used for code safety, scalability, and maintainability.
  • React 19 - component-driven structure managing real-time user interactions.

Styling & UI:

  • TailwindCSS 4 - ensures responsive design and a clean layout across devices.

AI Integration:

  • @google/generative-ai (Gemini) - powers the Mars IA Search, interpreting user queries and linking them to curated datasets and coordinates.

Performance & Infrastructure:

  • Next.js Turbopack - for accelerated builds and dev cycles.
  • ESLint + TypeScript - maintain consistent, high-quality code standards.

3D Visualization & Data:

  • NASA Trek API for imagery and surface mapping.
  • High-resolution textures mapped to real Mars coordinates.
  • Architecture supports expansion with additional visual layers (e.g., heat maps, elevation, time-series).

Deployment:

  • Deployed on Vercel for global edge rendering and scalability.

Impact and Audience

Fly Me To The Mars is designed for a broad audience - from curious learners and students to space enthusiasts. It transforms scientific data into a sensory experience, making space exploration both accessible and emotionally engaging.

By blending technology, art, and storytelling, Fly Me To The Mars turns the vastness of Mars into something tangible, educational, and inspiring.


Conclusion

Fly Me To The Mars demonstrates that Mars is not just a distant world, it’s a mirror of human curiosity and discovery. By exploring Mars, we explore our own drive to understand the universe and our place within it.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Fly Me to the Mars employs Artificial Intelligence as a core architectural component, built exclusively on the Google Gemini model. The system is structured into two independent yet integrated layers, enabling contextual awareness, semantic accuracy, and multilingual interaction while maintaining a consistent educational focus on Mars.

The first layer, named AI Detect Template, acts as a context recognition and routing engine. It analyzes the user’s query to determine whether it belongs to the Martian knowledge domain. This layer cross-references the input with a collection of Markdown documents containing scientific and historical data about Mars. When a match is found, it forwards one or more relevant files to the second layer. If no context applies, it returns a "NO_FILE" signal, instructing the next layer to handle the request generically but still related to Mars.

The second layer, known as AI Chat, is responsible for producing the final user-facing response. It processes the user’s input and the contextual data (or the "NO_FILE" flag), performing automatic language detection to ensure responses are delivered in the same language as the user’s prompt.

  • In specific context mode, Gemini uses the referenced documents as its primary knowledge base, generating concise, factual answers (limited to 450 characters) grounded in scientific accuracy.
  • In generic mode, when no contextual file is provided, the model generates informative, creative responses that redirect the conversation toward Mars, using analogies, scientific insights, or trivia (e.g., linking a question about volcanoes on Earth to Olympus Mons).

During development, Gemini was also employed as a technical co-pilot to support code optimization, backend integration, and UX refinement, all outputs were reviewed and validated by humans before deployment. Additionally, we utilized ElevenLabs voice AI to generate the narration for our official 30-second demo video, ensuring a natural, professional-quality delivery without using pre-recorded human voices.

No images, videos, or audio were generated by AI beyond this narration, all visual content originates from official NASA sources.
The integration of Artificial Intelligence in Fly Me to the Mars is transparent, ethical, and fully documented, aligning with the principles of the NASA Space Apps Challenge and bridging complex scientific data with an engaging, conversational exploration experience.

projectDetails.name: Project FourSight
projectDetails.summary: The Foursight project, developed for NASA Space Apps, addresses the challenge of educating the public, especially children, about space weather and its impacts. We developed a fun, child-friendly animation that explores space weather from the perspective of affected individuals or solar events, such as flares and coronal mass ejections. Additionally, we created an interactive website featuring our team and a Space Weather Command Center simulator. This simulator allows children to understand the Sun's influence on Earth, the effects of solar storms on satellites, the formation of the aurora borealis, and the crucial importance of space weather monitoring. The project is vital for demystifying complex concepts, fostering scientific interest, and preparing future generations for the challenges and wonders of space.
projectDetails.details:
Development

During the group's initial discussions, we realized that space weather is a little-known topic, especially among young people, despite its great importance and impact in various areas of everyday life. For this challenge, we created an animated video that translates the complex science of space weather into an accessible, educational, and fun experience for children.

In addition to the digital story, we recognized the need for a complementary resource to deepen learning. Therefore, we developed a website dedicated to children, which serves as an essential tool for spreading knowledge about space weather.

Animated movie

One of the most exciting parts of our project is the video we produced, which tells two distinct stories.

The first narrative features astronaut Stele, who takes young viewers on a magical journey to understand the phenomenon of space weather. In it, we explain the protective role of Earth's magnetic field and the origin of the dazzling Aurora Borealis, showing how these natural phenomena are interconnected.

The second story is led by robots and addresses how solar winds and the Sun's magnetic storms affect Earth and its technologies. Through this narrative, children learn about the interferences these phenomena can cause and the importance of quick actions to minimize damage, especially for professionals like farmers, pilots, astronauts, and power grid operators.

Website FourSight:

We also developed a website dedicated to children. This interactive portal offers a rich and educational environment where young explorers can find: Right in the first section, the site presents our Foursight team, explaining who we are, our mission, and how the idea of transforming a complex topic like space weather into something that could be understood by children came about. We show that, with creativity and science, it is possible to learn while playing.

One of the highlights of the website is an interactive simulator, which functions like a Space Weather Command Center. Through it, children can understand how scientists monitor space by observing the Sun and its activities. The simulator shows how the Sun influences the Earth, what happens when solar eruptions occur, how solar storms affect our satellites, communication networks, and power systems, and why it is so important to pay attention to these phenomena.

The website also features a fun story of two astronauts, who explain in a light and creative way why the northern lights occur.

In addition, the website features an educational section that explains, in a summarized and illustrated way, the main concepts related to space weather. Children can learn about: Northern Lights, the Magnetosphere, Solar Flares, Coronal Holes, Solar Wind, and Space Weather.

Hope to achieve

The development of the “Foursight” project aims to promote learning about space weather and its impacts on Earth in an interactive, creative, and accessible way for children. Although the topic involves complex scientific concepts that are still little known to the general public.

Therefore, we developed an educational animation and an interactive website, created with HTML and JavaScript. We hope to stimulate scientific curiosity and bring science closer to young audiences, transforming complex content into accessible and engaging experiences.

Ultimately, we aspire to inspire new generations to look at space with more knowledge, wonder, and responsibility, combining education, technology, and creativity in a project that transforms learning into imagination and discovery.

Important note

The main aspect of our animated video, "Space Weather Mission," is to teach children, in a fun and accessible way, what space weather is and why it is important. The animation shows how particles from the Sun can affect technologies on Earth and in space, such as satellites, communications, and the health of astronauts. In a creative way, the video presents concepts such as the Earth's magnetic field, the northern lights, and the importance of monitoring space weather, sparking children's interest in science and exploring the connection between the Sun and our planet.

Highlighted Features

  1. Engaging and educational storytelling;
  2. Interactive simulations;
  3. Integration with real NASA concepts and data;
  4. Intuitive and accessible presentation.

Benefits

  1. Active learning about space weather;
  2. Easy access to knowledge;
  3. Integration between entertainment and education;
  4. Inspiration for a new generation of scientists.

challengeDetails.title: Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings
challengeDetails.excerpt: Although the Sun is 93 million miles away from our planet, solar activity can significantly impact our daily lives. “Space weather”—the variations that occur in the space environment between the Sun and Earth—can impact technologies in space and on Earth. Your challenge is to write and illustrate a digital children’s story that explains what space weather is and the varying impacts it has on different people such as farmers, pilots, astronauts, power grid operators, and the general public. You can tell the story from the perspective of a person impacted by space weather or from the point of view of a solar flare or coronal mass ejection (CME) as it approaches Earth. (Heliophysics Division)

projectDetails.name: Project GannonTale
projectDetails.summary: GannonTale is a short dialogue-based game focused on explaining how space weather can impact life on earth through the eyes of a CME (Gannon Storm) and the citizens of a small city.
projectDetails.details:
Project GannonTale is a short browser game. It runs on native HTML, CSS and Javascript, hosted on Github.

The goal is to have an accessible and comprehensive tool that students on all levels can use to understand what space weather is and how it can affect people on earth. With that scope in mind, we decided to create a game, a media type that most students are familiar and engaged with. Inspired in the late 90's and 2000's RPG games, GannonTale conveys the impacts and importance of space weather by showing situations and consequences to the player, rather than just explaining the phenomenon.

For creating the game, the Phaser engine was used. Phaser is a Desktop and Mobile HTML5 game framework. A fast, free and fun open source framework for Canvas and WebGL powered browser games.

The game assets were created using Tiled, a map editor tool, as well as some smaller media conversion tools and tweaks made by hand.

Source code can be found in the project's Github repository.

AI was used in this project ONLY for code debbuging. The source code used was not generated by AI.

The models used were Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5 and Github Copilot.

projectDetails.summary: This application provides a comprehensive interactive experience for exploring asteroid impacts and monitoring near-Earth objects. Users can select locations on a world map to assess potential asteroid impact scenarios and access real-time data on nearby asteroids and comets. Key features include: orbital radar tracking, object velocity, approach predictions by decade, and detailed information on each asteroid or comet, including type, diameter, approach distance, and speed. Additionally, the app offers a solar system orbital simulator, allowing users to visualize planetary orbits alongside the trajectories of nearby asteroids, providing an engaging educational and analytical tool for understanding celestial dynamics and impact risks.
projectDetails.details:
his project is an interactive application that allows users to explore asteroid impacts on various points on Earth. Users can select locations on a world map to view potential impact scenarios and access detailed information about nearby asteroids and comets, including type, diameter, approach distance, and velocity. The app also features orbital radar tracking, approach predictions by decade, and a solar system simulator showing the orbits of planets alongside nearby asteroids.

The main benefits of the application include understanding what asteroids are, their proximity to Earth, the likelihood of impact, the potential effects on the planet, and gaining an astronomical perspective. Users can visualize impacts across different dates and explore multiple layers of information for deeper learning.

The project was developed using React.js, Vercel, NASA APIs, and ChatGPT. Its creativity lies in combining interactive mapping, real-time astronomical data, and orbital simulation in one platform. Key factors considered during development were ease of understanding, data accuracy, impact visualization, and providing multiple interactive ways to explore the content.

projectDetails.name: Project Globotany
projectDetails.summary: Our project aims to analyze Earth’s vegetation dynamics through NASA’s open satellite imagery, focusing on flowering patterns and deforestation processes across different regions. By leveraging artificial intelligence, we developed an application capable of comparing two seasonal periods to evaluate vegetation changes and generate analytical reports that support research, conservation efforts, and environmental monitoring.The system allows users to visualize how plant cover evolves between two dates, offering insights into how natural and human activities impact global biomes. Through AI-assisted image analysis, our application identifies and highlights variations in flowering intensity, providing detailed information about the selected area. This data can be used by organizations, researchers, and NGOs to design strategic recovery actions and promote sustainable environmental management. By merging technology and ecology, Globotany reinforces the role of human innovation in protecting biodiversity. Our mission is to make environmental observation more accessible, raise awareness about the effects of human action, and contribute to a future where degraded ecosystems can once again bloom.
projectDetails.details:
Overview

The Globotany project aims to provide an accessible tool to monitor and analyze global flowering phenology on Earth. The solution is an interactive web application that allows users to select an Area of Interest (AOI) on the map and automatically compare satellite images between two different periods. Its mission is to transform the complexity of NASA satellite data into an accessible and immediate geospatial assessment. We developed an interactive web application that stands out for its usability: the user selects an Area of Interest (AOI) anywhere on the globe and activates an automated interannual comparison function.

Innovation and Core Components

The core innovation of Globotany lies in its ability to efficiently combine three technological pillars:

  1. An interactive and simple visualizer, built on the WMS(Web map service) image swipe feature.
  2. A system for geospatial and environmental analysis powered by AI, which generates a descriptive and predictive report.
  3. The generation of a structured Analysis Report that not only quantifies changes in vegetation cover but also provides scientific interpretations and management recommendations.

Methodology: Interactive Capture and Comparison

The Globotany workflow is guided by a four-step onboarding experience, focused on user simplicity and the delivery of scientific value.

1. Data Capture and Visual Check (Steps 1 and 2)

This is the initial point of contact, where the user selects and validates the input data.

  • AOI Selection (Step 1): The user navigates the Leaflet map, chooses an Area of Interest (AOI), and triggers the "Capture" button.
  • WMS Image Generation: Upon clicking Capture, the application dynamically constructs WMS URLs from NASA GIBS. These URLs request the VIIRS NOAA-20 Corrected Reflectance True Color layer for the dates of 2020-04-06 and 2023-04-06, you can change the dates by clicking on the dates of each map and selecting them in the calendar.
  • Dual Visualization and Checking (Step 2): The captured images are displayed side-by-side in the Gallery, allowing the user to check the data quality (e.g., low cloud cover) before proceeding with the AI analysis.
  • Technical Highlight (Swipe): The interactive map uses a Swipe feature, implemented through CSS manipulation (clip: rect(...)) on the top Leaflet layer. This proves that the real-time visual comparison is performed directly using the NASA GIBS WMS.

2. Processing and AI Report Generation (Step 3)

This section details how the artificial intelligence transforms the images into scientific insights.

  • Analysis Trigger: After checking the images, the user clicks "Analyze", sending the URLs and coordinates to the Globotany analysis endpoint.
  • Result Delivery (Step 3): The AI system generates a Geospatial Analysis Report that compares the images and details the geographical context, the interannual visual difference, and the implication of the observed phenology.
  • Report Components: The generated text includes the Estimated Active Cover and Interannual Differences (e.g., an increase from 20% to 75% in active cover), in addition to the "Likely type of terrestrial vegetation" section.

3. Validation and Final Product Export (Step 4)

This final section ensures the utility and shareability of the final product.

  • Final Action (Step 4): With the analysis result on the screen, the user can export the report to PDF by triggering the "Print" button.
  • Actionable Recommendations: The final AI analysis provides data-based Recommendations (e.g., Quantify with NDVI/EVI and check IMERG precipitation), strengthening the report's utility for environmental management.
  • Technical PDF Guarantee: The system ensures the export fidelity by converting the satellite images to Data URLs (Base64) within the print view. This guarantees that the final PDF document contains all the visual evidence and the analytical text generated by the AI.

Technical Architecture and NASA Data Usage

The Globotany application is implemented as a dynamic web application (PHP/JavaScript), distinguished by its efficiency in handling geospatial data and delivering user value.

  • NASA Data / WMS GIBS: The primary data source is the Web Map Service (WMS) from NASA GIBS. This allows the application to request and receive custom on-demand images from any part of the world for specific dates, avoiding the need to pre-process or store large volumes of satellite data.
  • Source Code: The architecture utilizes the Leaflet and JavaScript libraries for the interactive front-end, while HTML/PHP serves as the structural core and variable processing backbone.
  • Results Export: The report generated by the AI can be exported to PDF using the "Print" functionality. The code ensures that the satellite images are preserved in the PDF by converting them to Data URLs (Base64) within the print view.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
AI is the computational core of the Globotany system, enabling the transformation of raw satellite images into structured, scientific analysis. The project's innovation relies on the strategic use of AI for deep geospatial inference rather than simple data display. 

1. AI Engine for Geospatial Analysis

The AI system is the central engine for generating the Geospatial Analysis Report, executing a precise comparison between satellite images from two distinct epochs. The AI processes visual data (NASA GIBS) and geographical coordinates to extract and synthesize crucial scientific insights. These insights include establishing geographical and vegetative context, quantifying phenological differences, and providing a full interpretation with data-driven recommendations for future monitoring and management.

2. AI Contributions to Development and Content

Their support included generating key visual assets (like the logo and initial screens for a professional interface) and assisting with content creation through topic research and synthesis and the refinement of the final text's clarity and flow.

projectDetails.name: Guardians of The Exoplanets
projectDetails.summary: GotE is a platform that automates the discovery and classification of exoplanets using data from NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS missions. It uses machine learning models and astrophysical feature engineering to classify celestial objects as confirmed planets, candidates, or false positives. The system includes two modes: Researcher Mode, for researchers to upload datasets, retrain models, and analyze results with full interpretability tools; and Explorer Mode, for users to manually input planetary data and see classification results instantly. GotE also includes an educational section that teaches about exoplanets, their discovery, and importance and an Explore section to view curated NASA datasets and see how the model classifies thousands of objects. GotE generates a detailed classification report to highlight which factors drive its  predictions. Built on a fast and accurate XGBoost model, It achieves over 95% accuracy in most scenarios, supports real-time retraining, and allows model download upon retraining completion. By combining automation, transparency, and interactivity, GotE turns NASA’s open data into an accessible tool for both scientists and the public to explore the universe.
projectDetails.details:
https://github.com/Guardians-of-the-exoplanets

GotE is an advanced AI platform that automates the discovery and classification of exoplanets using data from NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS missions. By applying state-of-the-art machine learning and astrophysical feature engineering, GotE analyzes NASA’s open datasets to identify celestial objects as confirmed exoplanets, candidates, or false positives.

At its core, GotE integrates a high-performance XGBoost model with explainable astrophysical-features, generating detailed classification reports that reveal the factors driving each prediction — bridging the gap between astrophysical insight and machine learning reasoning.

The system includes a dual web interface: the Researcher Mode, tailored for researchers, offering dataset uploads, retraining capabilities, hyperparameter tuning, and full interpretability dashboards; and the Explorer Mode, designed for enthusiasts, where users can manually input planetary parameters and visualize the AI’s classification confidence and rationale.

GotE stands out by allowing interactive data exploration, dynamic retraining, and real-time model evolution, enabling the scientific community to contribute new data and refine the detection process collaboratively.

By uniting automation, transparency, and interactivity, GotE transforms raw NASA mission data into a living, explainable discovery tool — empowering researchers and the public alike to participate in the next generation of exoplanet identification.

Main Functionalities:

Researcher Mode - Designed for researchers interested in exploring their own datasets for classification or retraining our models, hyperparameter tuning, and a complete session of model explanation data such as feature importance and information about classifications that enables a deep understanding of the observed data.

  • Selection: select between Kepler, K2 and Tess datasets;
  • Hyperparameters: adjust and fine tune model hyperparameters;
  • Data Upload: upload detection data as .csv files as a batch or manually;
  • Classify: use our model to classify the uploaded data with new detections;
  • Retraining: you can also use the data from NASAs dataset to retrain our model and compare with the baseline model. Did it get better or worse?
  • Results: see the classification our model did and compare the classification probability;
  • Analytics: see the model performance: Accuracy, time, number of features, recall, training time and more;
  • Pipeline: watch the full data pipeline as the data is loaded and processed, the model is trained and fine tuned accordingly with your new parameters and get  the predictions;
  • Export: export the results as a .pdf, .csv or share the link with colleagues.

Explorer Mode - Designed for enthusiasts who want to learn more about the world of exoplanets, enter data manually and discover if your signal is an exoplanet in 3 simple steps, as well as understand how the classification model works.

  • Selection: select between Kepler, K2 and Tess datasets;
  • Data Upload: upload detection data as .csv files as a batch or manually;
  • Classify: use our model to classify the uploaded data with new detections;
  • Pipeline: watch the full data pipeline as the data is loaded and processed, the model is trained and fine tuned accordingly with your new parameters and get  the predictions;
  • Results: see the classification our model did and compare the classification probability;

Learning Session - An educational session covering various topics related to the world of exoplanets. Explorers can learn new information about what exoplanets are, how they are discovered, their types and unique characteristics, and the importance of studying them.

Machine Learning Models

More than one model was tested, with XGBoost and CatBoost standing out. Both showed high accuracy, with XGBoost achieving 92-96% accuracy and CatBoost achieving 95-97%.Despite being slightly more accurate, CatBoost had a training time of approximately 300 seconds, while the XGBoost model had a training time of 5-15 seconds while still maintaining good accuracy. Since we wanted a solution that allowed for real-time retraining and exploration, XGBoost was the best choice.Two models were developed for each dataset:

  • Complete Model: includes all raw metrics + astrophysical feature engineering, followed by feature selection up to 95% importance (33 features). Higher accuracy, ideal for scientific use (released in the Researcher Mode).
  • Light Model: excludes feature engineering, using 7-10 original metrics (99% importance) for manual input and fast classification while maintaining strong performance (released in the Explorer Mode).

Both follow the same methodology as below.

Data Pipeline

1. Data Ingestion & Cleaning

  • Source: NASA Exoplanet Archive (Kepler, K2 and TESS datasets).
  • Filtering: kept only valid Confirmed, False Positive, and Candidate classes.
  • Removed metadata and low-quality columns (<1000 valid values).

2. Encoding & Imputation

  • Encoding Columns: LabelEncoder on discoverymethod, soltype, disc_facility koi_tce_delivname,  st_metratio,tfopwg_disp, disposition and koi_disposition
    • Categorical: mode or “missing”.
    • Numeric: column mean.

3. Astrophysical Feature Engineering (Complete Model Only)

Adds physically meaningful parameters to improve interpretability and accuracy:

  • Planet–Star Ratio: pl_rade_st_ratio = pl_rade / st_rad
  • Planet–Star Radius  Ratio: planet_star_radius_ratio = koi_prad / koi_srad
  • Planet–Star Volume Ratio: planet_star_volume_ratio = (koi_prad / koi_srad)³
  • Transit Density Proxy: transit_density_proxy = koi_depth / koi_duration
  • Temperature Ratio Planet Star temp_ratio_planet_star = koi_teq / koi_steff
  • Estimated Densities: st_density_est, pl_density_est = mass / radius³
  • Estimated Densities: st_density_est, pl_density_est = mass / radius³
  • Estimated Densities: st_density_est, pl_density_est = mass / radius³
  • Equilibrium Temperature: via Kepler’s 3rd Law, using stellar mass, radius, and orbital period.
  • Color Indices: (V−K) and (V−Gaia) for stellar classification.
  • Uncertainty Aggregates: 9 new columns combining error bounds (radius, mass, temperature, magnitude).

These features add astrophysical realism and improve generalization.

Model & Training Strategy

  • Algorithm: XGBoost (multi:softprob, eval_metric=mlogloss).
  • Algorithm with Hyperparameters: XGBoost (eval_metric='mlogloss', objective='multi:softprob', colsample_bytree=0.8, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=6, n_estimators=100, subsample=0.8).
  • Data Split: 70% Train | 20% Test | 10% Blind Validation.
  • Cross-Validation: Stratified 5-Fold for robust metrics and to prevent.
  • Metrics: Accuracy and Weighted F1-score as a decisive factor.

Model Optimization

  • Feature selection based on cumulative importance (90%, 95%, 99%).
  • Each threshold trained independently for performance benchmarking.
  • Outputs (metrics, models, importances) in a Classification Report format exported to /summary/.

Performance Example (for K2 Dataset - complete model)

Complete test and blind accuracy for models:

Model Highlights

  • Reproducibility: Ensured through fixed seeds, version tracking, K-Fold cross-validation, and blind validation to minimize overfitting.
  • Portability: Models and data saved in .model and .csv formats for easy deployment and interpretability.
  • Scalability: Deployable as a Cloud Function API, supporting single-data predictions (with or without hyperparameters) and CSV batch processing (with or without hyperparameters). All operations are streaming-compatible, enabling real-time data transmission for every interaction with the machine learning functions.
  • Retraining & Model Access: Supports automated retraining with real-time updates. Retrained models are hosted on Cloud Storage for easy download and reuse.
  • Scientific Interpretability: All engineered features adhere to astrophysical principles, ensuring meaningful and physically grounded predictions.
  • High Accuracy without risk of Overfitting: Achieves over 95% accuracy on unseen blind data.
  • Robust Engineering: Modular, reproducible, and transparent pipeline design for reliability and maintainability.
  • Expandability: Easily ingests new NASA catalogs with minimal modifications, allowing continuous updates and improvements.
