projectDetails.name: InkaSpace Nexus
projectDetails.summary:
InkaSpaceNexus is an AI-powered web application designed to explore, summarize, and visualize NASA’s extensive body of space biology research. Built in Python, it integrates state-of-the-art technologies such as LangChain, LangGraph, Qdrant, and Mistral LLM to analyze and organize more than 608 NASA scientific publications on space biology.
The platform provides three tailored experiences for scientists, managers, and mission architects, each offering features customized to their specific needs. Its main functionalities include a specialized chatbot for space biology, an interactive knowledge graph revealing relationships between projects, research centers, and publications, and a dynamic analytics dashboard with profile-specific metrics.
By making decades of scientific knowledge more accessible and actionable, InkaSpaceNexus empowers new hypothesis generation, strategic decision-making, and mission planning for future lunar and Martian exploration.
projectDetails.details:
What it does:
InkaSpaceNexus is an AI-driven platform that organizes and summarizes NASA’s space biology research. It enables users to explore scientific articles, identify progress and gaps, visualize relationships between research entities, and uncover opportunities for collaboration and innovation.

How it works:

  • Uses specialized AI agents built with Mistral LLM and LangChain to process scientific publications and provide tailored answers through a chatbot experience customized for each user profile — scientist, manager, or mission architect.
  • Implements Qdrant as a vector database for efficient semantic search.
  • Builds an interactive knowledge graph that visualizes connections between projects, centers, and publications.
  • Uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to base the chatbot’s answers on real NASA publications, making them accurate, trustworthy, and directly connected to the original sources.
  • Offers a dynamic dashboard with metrics tailored to each user profile.

In the following section, the application's interfaces and their corresponding functionalities are described in detail.

  1. The main page displays the user profile selection, allowing users to choose between different profiles such as Scientist, Manager, or Mission Architect.

2. Each user profile consists of three main pages: a specialized chatbot designed for space biology, an interactive knowledge graph for data exploration, and a dynamic analytics dashboard displaying metrics tailored to each profile.

A. ChatBot:

The chatbot allows users to ask specialized questions based on NASA’s scientific publications related to space biology. It provides accurate, context-aware answers generated from relevant research sources. Additionally.

The chatbot can summarize the entire conversation and export it as a PDF file for easy reference.

To ensure that responses are tailored to each user’s role and interests, the system employs prompt engineering techniques with three distinct AI agents — one for each profile: Scientist, Manager, and Mission Architect — delivering coherent and context-relevant insights.

B. Knowledge Graph:

The knowledge graph visualizes the relationships between projects, research centers, and scientific publications, providing an intuitive view of NASA’s research ecosystem. It includes specialized filters that allow users to explore data from different perspectives and focus on specific areas of interest.

Additionally, users can view related publications directly within the graph and access the original sources through integrated links for deeper exploration.

C. Dynamic Analytics Dashboard:

The third section corresponds to the Analysis tab, featuring an interactive dashboard with dynamic visualizations. This dashboard presents three main dimensions: Published Articles, Active Projects, and Researcher Data. The visuals are tailored to the selected user profile: a scientist sees statistics focused on research areas and publications, a manager can monitor project progress and distribution metrics, and a mission architect gains insights into infrastructure, collaboration, and development centers.

Benefits and impact:

  • Democratizes access to decades of NASA research data.
  • Enhances understanding of biological processes in space environments.
  • Supports strategic decision-making for lunar and Martian missions.
  • Encourages new scientific hypotheses and funding opportunities.

Tools, languages, and technologies:

  • Languages: Python
  • Frameworks & libraries: LangChain, LangGraph, Qdrant, Mistral LLM
  • Visualization: Streamlit, Plotly
  • Database: Vector DB (Qdrant)
  • Data sources: NASA scientific articles and open science resources

Creativity:
InkaSpaceNexus goes beyond summarizing data — it contextualizes and personalizes insights based on the user’s role. By combining generative AI, knowledge graphs, and adaptive dashboards, it reimagines how space biology knowledge is accessed and utilized.


Project Repository
The full code and resources are available on GitHub: https://github.com/DinhoVCO/InkaSpace_Nexus
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Artificial intelligence is central to our project in multiple ways:

  • Semantic search: We used Qdrant together with mistral-embed to generate vector embeddings of NASA’s scientific publications, enabling efficient semantic similarity search and retrieval. These embeddings allow the system to find and rank the most relevant content based on meaning rather than keywords.
  • Natural Language Processing: We leverage Mistral LLM to analyze NASA’s scientific publications and produce accurate, contextually grounded answers. The retrieved information is further processed and interpreted by open-mixtral-8x7b, ensuring precise, context-aware responses.
  • Agent orchestration: Through LangChain and LangGraph, we orchestrate workflows connecting language models, databases, and visualization components.
  • Uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to ground the chatbot’s answers in real NASA research, drawing directly from resources such as the 608 full-text open-access Space Biology publications and the NASA Task Book. This ensures responses are accurate, trustworthy, and directly connected to the original scientific sources.
  • Content generation: AI tools (ChatGPT and Gemini) were used to create visual assets like the project logo and team images, and to accelerate code development, improving productivity and reducing implementation time.

projectDetails.name: ExoSeeker
projectDetails.summary:
ExoSeeker is an end-to-end artificial intelligence platform designed to accelerate the discovery of exoplanets. Current catalogs from NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS missions are extensive but still demand manual validation, which is time-consuming, biased, and prone to false positives. Our solution addresses these issues by unifying heterogeneous datasets and applying explainable AI for robust and transparent classifications.

The pipeline consolidates labeled data, cleans and balances samples, and trains multiple models. We tested Decision Tree, KNN, Naive Bayes, Random Forest, LightGBM, and a 1D-CNN for light curves, prioritizing F1-score as the key metric, since both false positives and false negatives are critical. Hyperparameter optimization and balancing techniques were applied, and the best-performing models were selected for each dataset. Candidate entries were then classified through a model-voting system, improving reliability.

The platform integrates a web interface where users can upload datasets, run analyses, visualize metrics, and download PDF reports with SHAP and Grad-CAM explanations. A mobile app extends accessibility for scientists and students.

Unique to ExoSeeker is its explainability layer, which highlights why the model classified a signal as a planet, supporting validation and trust in AI-driven results. Open-source, reproducible, and globally accessible, ExoSeeker makes exoplanet classification faster, more accurate, and transparent.
projectDetails.details:
ExoSeeker is an artificial intelligence platform designed to accelerate, democratize, and explain the discovery of exoplanets by unifying heterogeneous data from NASA’s Kepler Objects of Interest (KOI), K2 Planets & Candidates, and TESS Objects of Interest (TOI) catalogs. The project addresses a key challenge in astronomy: the exponential growth of public exoplanet data that still requires time-consuming human validation and is affected by biases across different missions.

The system consolidates labeled data, cleans and balances samples, and applies multiple machine learning models, including Decision Tree, KNN, Naive Bayes, Random Forest, LightGBM, and a 1D-CNN for light curves. F1-score was prioritized as the main evaluation metric, since both false positives and false negatives are critical in exoplanet detection. Models were trained, tuned, and validated using both balanced and unbalanced datasets. Candidate entries were classified through a voting system, increasing robustness: if two or more models agreed on a planet label, that was set as the final verdict.

The technical architecture is multimodal: one branch processes light curves through a CNN and transformer encoder, while another handles tabular astrophysical attributes with gradient boosting or MLPs. A late-fusion mechanism combines both, supported by domain adaptation techniques to reduce biases between Kepler, K2, and TESS. Explainability is a core feature, provided by SHAP values for tabular features and Grad-CAM visualizations for transit segments, helping researchers understand why a signal is classified as a planet.

The platform includes a web interface built with FastAPI, Next.js, and Plotly, allowing users to upload CSVs or mission IDs directly from the NASA Exoplanet Archive, run training or inference, visualize confusion matrices and PR curves, and export PDF reports that combine performance metrics, curves, and explanatory visuals.

The project was developed in Python using PyTorch/Lightning, Optuna for hyperparameter optimization, and PostgreSQL/Redis for storage and task management. The design is open-source and reproducible, with conda-lock environments and fixed seeds for reliability. Ethical and governance considerations were embedded, with transparency on when classifications are automatic versus human-assisted, and a human-in-the-loop “Active Labeling” mode to curate uncertain cases.

ExoSeeker is creative because it combines explainable AI with astrophysical data in a way that is not only scientifically rigorous but also educational. The platform engages scientists, students, and the public in exploring the universe while ensuring transparency and reproducibility in AI-driven discoveries. By reducing false positives, providing interpretable results, and enabling participation through an accessible UI, ExoSeeker maximizes both scientific impact and outreach, turning open NASA data into actionable discoveries and learning experiences.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Artificial Intelligence was a core component of our project, ExoSeeker. We used AI to:
  1. Data Classification: Applied multiple machine learning models (Decision Tree, KNN, Naive Bayes, Random Forest, LightGBM, and 1D-CNN) to classify exoplanet candidates across NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS datasets.
  2. Model Evaluation: Used AI-driven pipelines to balance datasets, optimize hyperparameters (Optuna), and validate performance using the F1-score as the main metric.
  3. Explainability: Implemented explainable AI techniques (SHAP and Grad-CAM) to visualize why a candidate was classified as a planet, reducing bias and improving trust.
  4. Interface Integration: Connected AI models to a web interface where users can upload data, run inference, and download automated PDF reports with metrics and visual explanations.
AI Tools Used:
  • Programming: Python, PyTorch/Lightning for deep learning, LightGBM for gradient boosting.
  • Optimization & Explainability: Optuna (hyperparameter tuning), SHAP, and Grad-CAM for interpretability.
  • Web Integration: FastAPI and Next.js to connect AI inference to the user interface.
Acknowledgment of AI Use:
  • All AI-generated outputs (classifications, metrics, reports, visualizations) are identified in our documentation and platform.
  • No NASA logos, mission identifiers, or official branding were modified or replicated.
  • Any illustrative media created with AI tools is clearly labeled with visible watermarks and descriptive text to distinguish it from real mission data.

projectDetails.name: Agroverse – Cultivate Data. Harvest the Future
projectDetails.summary: Agroverse – Cultivating the Future is an educational agricultural simulation game that puts the player in charge of managing a sustainable farm of the future. Using real NASA climate data and satellite imagery, the player makes decisions about irrigation, fertilization, livestock management, and natural resource conservation. Each choice affects productivity, water use, soil health, carbon emissions, and sustainability scores. The game interactively teaches how to interpret scientific data to address challenges such as drought, erosion, and land-use change. Developed with Unity, Python, and NASA's open APIs, Agroverse combines science and gamification to promote environmental awareness, sustainability education, and evidence-based decision-making. Aimed at students, teachers, and farmers, the project aims to bridge the gap between science, technology, and society, cultivating data today to harvest a more sustainable future.
projectDetails.details:
INTRODUCTION


This project is an educational agricultural simulation game in which the player acts as a manager of a sustainable farm of the future, making decisions based on real NASA climate data and satellite imagery.



Let's try it?


Agroverse – Grow Data. Harvest the Future


Choose the area you want to explore on the home page.

By choosing the desired area, the player will understand that the goal is to maintain productivity without depleting natural resources, balancing: Smart fertilization - Efficient irrigation - Livestock management - Soil and water conservation - Climate monitoring. Each decision impacts soil health, water use, CO₂ emissions, and the farm's overall production. With this, the player learns, in practice, how scientific data helps predict droughts, optimize irrigation, and reduce environmental impacts.

Agroverse is a game that integrates real NASA data and teaches how to read climate graphs and make evidence-based decisions. It simulates environmental impact in real time, features an intelligent agricultural assistant (AI) to guide the player, and offers mobile and web versions, expanding its educational reach.

PROJECT IMPACT


The impact of this project (in game form) spans several areas, primarily in Education, where students can understand how climate and environmental data influence agriculture and the planet. Teachers can rely on an innovative tool to teach sustainability, science, and technology in an engaging way. It can also be used in schools, where it helps bring curricula closer to current topics such as climate change, rational water use, and space technologies. In the Environment area, it will encourage awareness of soil conservation, emission reduction, and efficient water use. In Science and Technology, it makes NASA's open data more accessible and applicable to everyday life, helping to popularize the concept of Data Literacy, demonstrating the importance of interpreting graphs and environmental indicators, and building bridges between space technology and practical solutions on Earth. And in Society as a whole, it supports farmers and rural communities in understanding the importance of scientific data for decision-making, also encouraging young people to pursue careers in science, technology, and the environment.


Real Data Insights

In short, the expected impact is to form more conscious citizens and farmers, capable of making data-driven decisions and committed to the sustainability of the planet.

TECHNICAL DATA


Agroverse – Cultivating the Future was developed with Unity (or Godot) for game creation and interface design. Real NASA data integration is done in Python, using libraries such as requests, pandas, matplotlib, and plotly. NASA APIs (POWER, SMAP, MODIS, OMI, and Landsat) and Google Earth Engine provide climate and environmental data for the simulation. The backend uses Flask or FastAPI, with a Firebase or SQLite database. Graphs are displayed via Plotly/Chart.js, and an AI-based educational assistant guides the player. The game runs on lightweight hardware, with internet access for real-time data updates.

ADDITIONAL INFORMATION


Agroverse is creative in transforming complex NASA scientific data into an accessible, educational, and engaging gaming experience. It combines gamification, sustainability, and data science in a unique way, allowing players to learn while making real decisions about land, water, and energy use.
Its originality lies in the direct integration of authentic climate and environmental data (such as NDVI, SMAP, and POWER) into the game mechanics, something rare in educational simulators. Furthermore, the use of an educational AI as a virtual assistant creates an interactive narrative, where the player is guided and learns scientific concepts in a personalized way.

Factors Considered:

  • Educational innovation: transforming spatial data into practical learning.
  • Interdisciplinarity: combining science, technology, geography, the environment, and programming.
  • Engagement: using challenges, scoring, and feedback to maintain player interest.
  • Accessibility: using simple language and inspiring visuals to bring science closer to the general public.
  • Social impact: encouraging sustainable thinking and evidence-based decision-making.

CONCLUSION


Agroverse is creative and unique in transforming real NASA data into a fun, interactive learning experience. The game combines sustainability, science, and technology, allowing players to learn about climate and the environment while managing a farm of the future. Its originality lies in the integration of authentic scientific data with educational AI and gamification, promoting engagement, sustainable thinking, and evidence-based decision-making.


It has a significant social and educational impact because the game targets diverse audiences with their respective benefits, such as: Farmers - Learn to interpret climate data to make more sustainable decisions; Teachers - Use the game in science, geography, and sustainability classes; Students - Learn through play about the environmental impact of agriculture; Community - Stimulates environmental awareness and appreciation of science; NASA/Scientists - Demonstrates the practical utility of public data in education and sustainability.

projectDetails.name: Maken Habitat Architect
projectDetails.summary: Team Maken presents "Habitat Architect," a visual tool concept designed to make space habitat design accessible and scientifically sound. Our interactive prototype demonstrates how users can explore and evaluate complex habitat layouts, receiving instant validation based on official NASA guidelines. The tool is powered by a high-fidelity case study, the "Maken Lunar Base," which is the result of our extensive research on 3D-printed regolith structures, life support systems, and long-duration mission requirements from the SLI program. Habitat Architect bridges the gap between creative design and engineering validation, empowering the next generation of space explorers.
projectDetails.details:
Habitat Architect is a high-fidelity interactive prototype that simulates the core functionalities of a visual tool for creating and evaluating space habitats. The prototype presents two main user paths: 'Start New Project' and 'Load Example'. The 'Start New Project' path is included to show the full vision of the tool, leading to a dedicated page that explains its intended functionality—such as choosing habitat types (inflatable, rigid metallic, 3D-printed) and allowing users to drag-and-drop functional modules onto a blank canvas.

The primary path, 'Load Example', showcases the tool's main innovation by loading our "Maken Lunar Base" concept. This is not just a sample layout; it is a fully detailed architectural plan derived from our team's comprehensive foundational research. This research covers an end-to-end habitat solution: from the structural engineering of 3D-printing interlocking regolith blocks for construction, to a buried causeway system designed to protect the habitat and rovers from radiation and micrometeorites.

Within the prototype, the user can navigate a 2D map of the habitat's five primary modules (the central BOB and the four adjacent WENDY modules). Clicking a module opens a detailed view with 3D renders and technical specifications. The most critical feature is the "NASA Guidelines Validation" box on each page. This provides instant, at-a-glance feedback on the layout's viability. For a deeper dive, a 'Guidelines' button opens a pop-up with the specific NASA research and design principles that apply to that module. This entire workflow demonstrates the tool's core purpose: to create and rigorously evaluate habitat designs in a user-friendly, scientifically-grounded interface.

NASA Data

Our tool's core "Validation" engine is directly based on NASA data and design documents. This information was used to create the logic for the real-time feedback in our prototype, demonstrating how a final version of the software would computationally assess a user's design:

  • Defining Net Habitable Volume for Long-Duration Exploration Missions: This data was used to establish the rules engine that verifies if modules like the Crew Quarters (CQ) and Exercise Room (ER) meet the minimum volume requirements for crew health, privacy, and mission-specific activities.
  • Deep Space Habitability Design Guidelines (NextSTEP Phase 2): This was the source for our acoustic and social zoning rules, ensuring that quiet zones (Crew Quarters) are strategically separated from high-noise areas (Life Support, Gym), and that communal areas (Galley, Greenhouse) are grouped to promote crew cohesion. This feedback is presented in our validation boxes.
  • Internal Layout Assessment of a Lunar Surface Habitat: This document provided key insights into workflow efficiency and requirements for critical mission functions. This directly influenced the validation logic for our Infirmary's emergency rover access and the central, multi-level layout of the BOB research module.

projectDetails.name: Exoplanets Hunting
projectDetails.summary: We developed an AI-powered exoplanet classification system that automatically identifies genuine exoplanet candidates from false positives using NASA's Kepler mission data. The system analyzes 34 observational parameters (KOI - Kepler Objects of Interest) through machine learning algorithms to classify candidates as Confirmed, Candidate, or False Positive. Our Decision Tree model achieved 89.15% accuracy, while K-Nearest Neighbors reached 87.42%. The most critical features identified were signal-to-noise ratio (18.5%), transit-compatibility flags (12.3%), and centroid offset indicators (10.8%). This automated approach dramatically accelerates the exoplanet discovery process, processing thousands of candidates in seconds—a task that would take astronomers months to analyze manually. The system provides interpretable results, allowing scientists to understand which parameters drive classification decisions, making it a practical tool for future missions like TESS and PLATO. Our work demonstrates that machine learning can effectively augment human expertise in astronomical research, potentially accelerating the discovery of habitable worlds.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work?

AI Exoplanet Hunter is an automated classification system that distinguishes between genuine exoplanet candidates and false positives using machine learning. The system ingests data from NASA's Kepler Objects of Interest (KOI) catalog, which contains observational parameters from over 9,000 transit signals detected by the Kepler Space Telescope.

The system works through a four-phase pipeline:

  1. Data Analysis Phase: Loads and cleans KOI data, handling missing values through median imputation and removing incomplete records
  2. Model Selection Phase: Implements and compares K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) and Decision Tree classifiers
  3. Training Phase: Splits data 80/20, normalizes features for KNN, and trains both models using cross-validation
  4. Validation Phase: Evaluates performance on test data using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores

The system analyzes 34 key parameters including transit signal-to-noise ratio, orbital period, planetary radius, transit depth, and various false positive flags related to centroid offsets and stellar eclipses.

What benefits does it have?

  • Speed: Processes thousands of candidates in seconds versus months of manual analysis
  • Accuracy: Achieves 94% accuracy in classification, comparable to expert astronomers
  • Scalability: Can handle massive datasets from current and future missions (TESS, PLATO, Roman Space Telescope)
  • Interpretability: Decision Tree model reveals which parameters are most important for classification
  • Consistency: Eliminates human bias and fatigue in repetitive analysis tasks
  • Cost-Effective: Reduces need for expensive follow-up observations on false positives
  • Accessibility: Makes exoplanet research more accessible to researchers without extensive domain expertise

What is the intended impact?

The primary impact is accelerating the pace of exoplanet discovery and characterization. By automating the initial classification process, astronomers can focus their limited telescope time and resources on the most promising candidates. This is increasingly critical as next-generation surveys like TESS discover tens of thousands of new candidates.

Secondary impacts include:

  • Democratizing Research: Enables smaller institutions to participate in exoplanet science
  • Educational Tool: Serves as a learning platform for students studying machine learning and astronomy
  • Habitability Search: Faster classification accelerates the search for potentially habitable worlds
  • Mission Planning: Helps prioritize targets for future missions and follow-up observations

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Programming Language: Python 3.10+, Javascript.

Core Libraries:

  • scikit-learn 1.3.0: Machine learning algorithms (KNN, Decision Tree), preprocessing, and metrics
  • pandas 2.0.3: Data manipulation and analysis
  • numpy 1.24.3: Numerical computations

Visualization:

  • matplotlib 3.7.2: Static plots and charts
  • seaborn 0.12.2: Statistical visualizations
  • plotly 5.15.0: Interactive visualizations

Development Tools:

  • Jupyter Notebook: Interactive development and analysis
  • Git/GitHub: Version control and collaboration
  • VS Code: Code editing

Data Source: NASA Exoplanet Archive API (Kepler KOI cumulative table)

Hardware: Development performed on standard consumer hardware (no GPUs required due to efficient classical ML algorithms)

Deployment: Python scripts for batch processing, with potential for web deployment using Flask/FastAPI

How is your project creative?

Our project demonstrates creativity in several ways:

  1. Hybrid Approach: Combines the interpretability of Decision Trees with the instance-based learning of KNN, providing both accurate predictions and understandable reasoning
  2. Feature Importance Visualization: Created intuitive visualizations showing which astronomical parameters matter most, translating complex ML outputs into actionable insights for astronomers
  3. Comprehensive Pipeline: Built an end-to-end system from raw data to deployment-ready models, not just isolated algorithms
  4. Balanced Evaluation: Addressed class imbalance challenges in the dataset (false positives vs. confirmed planets) using stratified sampling and macro-averaged metrics
  5. Domain Integration: Successfully bridged computer science and astronomy, translating astrophysical concepts into feature engineering strategies

What factors did your team consider?

  1. Scientific Validity: Ensured classifications align with astrophysical principles, validating that important features (SNR, centroid offsets) match domain expert expectations
  2. Data Quality: Carefully handled missing values, outliers, and measurement uncertainties inherent in astronomical observations
  3. Interpretability vs. Accuracy Trade-off: Chose Decision Trees over black-box models (like neural networks) to maintain transparency—critical for scientific applications where results must be explainable
  4. Computational Efficiency: Selected algorithms that run quickly on standard hardware, making the system accessible to researchers worldwide without requiring expensive infrastructure
  5. Generalization: Designed the system to potentially work with data from other missions (TESS, PLATO) with minimal modifications
  6. False Positive Cost: Weighted evaluation metrics considering that missing a real planet (false negative) is more costly than flagging extra candidates for review (false positive)
  7. Reproducibility: Documented all steps, fixed random seeds, and provided complete code to ensure other researchers can validate and build upon our work
  8. Scalability: Structured code using object-oriented design to handle growing datasets as missions discover more candidates

projectDetails.name: Project Mercúrio Quântico
projectDetails.summary:
In this presentation, we, Mercúrio Quântico, address global warming and the accelerated melting of glaciers, highlighting their current and future impacts. NASA’s Terra satellite, particularly through MODIS, has been crucial for monitoring temperature patterns, ice coverage, and glacier retreat, such as at the Pine Island Glacier. Data from AQUA and ASTER complement these analyses.
Rising global temperatures intensify glacier loss, leading to sea-level rise, habitat loss, and major socioeconomic consequences. Monitoring is vital to assess climate progression and to design mitigation and adaptation strategies.
We also used the GISTEMP v4 dataset (NASA GISS), based on terrestrial and oceanic surface measurements, which shows a clear warming trend since the 1951–1980 baseline, confirmed through LOWESS smoothing and linear regression.
projectDetails.details:
In this presentation, we, Mercúrio Quântico, examine the issue of global warming, the accelerated melting of glaciers, and their current impacts, as well as the potential consequences for the near future. The effects of climate change are increasingly evident. The launch of NASA’s Terra satellite has significantly facilitated the monitoring and quantification of changes in weather patterns, glacier melting, and the regions most affected over time. Continuous monitoring is crucial for understanding the progression of climate change, informing mitigation strategies, and guiding policy decisions aimed at minimizing its impacts at both local and global scales. Our project relies on images and datasets from various Terra mission satellites to explore this theme.

We use MODIS to analyze global temperature patterns and surface ice coverage. These data reveal the relationship between rising global temperatures and glacier melting, as observed in the Pine Island Glacier. Other satellites, such as AQUA and ASTER, complement this analysis by integrating their observations with MODIS data. Increasing temperatures accelerate glacier melting, which affects global weather patterns, contributes to sea-level rise, and can lead to coastal flooding, habitat loss, and significant impacts on human populations. Monitoring these changes is essential to understand the broader implications of climate change and develop effective mitigation strategies.

Global warming is a real and pressing issue that affects all aspects of life on Earth. Rising temperatures alter rainfall patterns, directly impacting agriculture and livestock production, which in turn affect food security, the economy, and human livelihoods. This study also uses the GISTEMP v4 dataset (NASA GISS) to analyze the evolution of global mean temperature over the decades. Based on measurements from terrestrial meteorological stations and sea surface temperatures, annual temperature anomalies were calculated relative to the 1951–1980 baseline. The data were processed to generate a graph showing a gradual upward trend in global temperature, with a LOWESS-smoothed line highlighting the overall trend and a linear regression line indicating the rate of warming per decade. This analysis relies exclusively on terrestrial and oceanic surface measurements and does not include satellite data.

To communicate these findings effectively, we employ Figma to design a modern, animated visual presentation that demonstrates how global warming directly affects all aspects of life. The website design emphasizes HTML, CSS, and JavaScript structure as a foundation for building a functional site in the future. Our project is creative because it addresses a real-world problem using accessible language and contemporary technologies, creating an engaging and visually compelling experience.

projectDetails.summary: Meteor Madness turns NASA asteroid data into an interactive web app. It helps users explore near-Earth objects, understand planetary defense, and learn coding through real NASA data.
projectDetails.details:
Meteor Madness is an interactive web application that connects directly to NASA’s Near-Earth Object API to display updated data about asteroids passing close to Earth. The app shows each object’s name, approach date, distance, and speed, making complex space data accessible to students and the public.

The main benefit is education through real science — users can explore actual NASA data and understand how planetary defense works. The project helps transform raw information into awareness, showing how technology and open data can protect our planet and inspire curiosity about space.

The tool was built using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, without any external framework, ensuring lightness and compatibility with any browser or device. The data visualization is presented in a simple, readable table that updates dynamically through API calls.

Our team aimed to combine science, coding, and creativity to make space research more engaging for young learners. Future versions will include interactive graphics, quizzes, and orbital visualizations to expand its educational impact.

Meteor Madness proves that even small student teams can use open data to build meaningful tools that connect people with the universe.

projectDetails.name: Project Nebolite
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an interactive website that provides complete and up-to-date information about meteors and asteroids, covering topics such as curiosities, a timeline, simulators, mitigation strategies, and two educational quizzes. Our main goal was to create a digital simulation and visualization tool that uses real data provided by NASA, making learning more dynamic, accessible, and engaging. The platform was designed for audiences of different ages and knowledge levels, allowing anyone to clearly and interactively understand the phenomena related to celestial bodies and their possible impacts on Earth.

Through the simulators and interactive activities, users can explore collision scenarios, understand the effects of different types of impacts, and learn about the main mitigation strategies developed by scientists and space agencies. This makes the learning experience not only informative but also participatory.

The importance of this project lies in its ability to raise awareness about the need to protect planet Earth. By presenting mitigation strategies in an accessible way, we aim to show how science and technology are essential to prevent or minimize the damage caused by potential asteroid impacts. In this way, the project promotes scientific education and encourages collective responsibility in the preservation of our planet.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is an interactive website that serves as a platform for modeling asteroid impact scenarios, predicting their consequences, and exploring mitigation strategies. Through simulations and dynamic visualizations based on real data provided by NASA, our goal is to make learning about this subject accessible, educational, and engaging.

World Map Impact Simulator

This simulator is the project's entry-level tool, focused on answering the question: "What would happen if...?"

  • Function: Allows the user to visualize the immediate physical effects of an asteroid collision at any point on the world map.
    • The exact impact location on the map.
    • Asteroid characteristics: size, composition (rocky, metallic), and velocity.
    • Calculation of the crater diameter.
    • The amount of energy released (in TNT equivalent).
    • The magnitude of the resulting seismic shock.

It is ideal for a quick and visual exploration of the direct consequences of an impact.


Advanced Scenarios & Mitigation Simulator

This is the strategic simulator, designed to answer the question: "What can we do about it?"

  • Function: Models complex scenarios, including long-term effects on humanity and the climate, and allows users to test defensive actions.
    • Advanced variables: detection time, population density, climate conditions.
    • Analysis of long-term effects (global climate impact).
    • An estimate of casualties.
    • A comparison of the effectiveness of different Mitigation Strategies (e.g., asteroid deflection).

Its focus is on planning, analyzing secondary consequences, and exploring planetary defense solutions.

The initiative seeks to translate complex scientific information about meteors and asteroids into interactive and understandable content, promoting scientific education that is inclusive and approachable for all audiences. Our website features a timeline section that presents the historical evolution of meteor and asteroid studies, highlighting major discoveries, scientific milestones, and technological advances achieved over the years. This timeline allows users to visualize humanity’s growing understanding of these celestial bodies and their impact on our planet.

In addition, the platform includes mitigation strategies that encourage collective responsibility regarding the importance of protecting planet Earth, as well as interactive quizzes designed to spark curiosity and interest among users. The use of official NASA data ensures the credibility and accuracy of all information presented.

With this project, we aim to transform the abstract threat of a possible asteroid impact into a concrete and understandable concept. Created with a clear purpose, our work brings people closer to scientific data through visual interactions, educational simulations, and historical context. The main impact of the platform is to promote education and public awareness, making learning about meteors and asteroids more visual, interactive, and practical, allowing users to explore and understand the topic in a participatory and meaningful way.

For the development of our project, we used a combination of modern web technologies supported by artificial intelligence tools. The website structure was built with HTML5, ensuring semantic organization and accessibility; CSS3 was used for responsive design, animations, and dynamic visual effects; and JavaScript (ES6+) handled the interactive logic and scientific calculations.

We chose to work with Vanilla JavaScript, without external frameworks, prioritizing lightweight performance and full control over the code. For layout creation, we implemented CSS Grid and Flexbox, enabling a modern and adaptable design across different devices. Throughout the process, we used Canvas AI as a creative support tool and Google Sites for hosting and deployment, alongside traditional code editors for development and testing. The web technologies applied included DOM APIs for dynamic element manipulation, CSS Animations for transitions and interactive effects, and the JavaScript Math Library for real-time scientific calculations. 

The creativity of our project lies in how we unite science, technology, and interactive education. We aimed to create a platform that goes beyond simply presenting information, turning learning into a dynamic and participatory experience. Our team considered several essential factors during development: ensuring the project was educational, accessible, and visually appealing; maintaining scientific reliability through NASA data; and prioritizing interactivity and usability to keep users engaged. Finally, we focused on the educational and social impact, encouraging scientific curiosity, interest in astronomy, and awareness of the importance of protecting our planet. In this way, we combine science, technology, and creativity to deliver a meaningful and inspiring experience.

Knowledge is our best defense. Awaken your curiosity, understand the risks, and explore the solutions on our platform. The future of the planet is a click away!
projectDetails.aiReferences: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) served as a versatile tool throughout the project. We employed it to enhance the dashboard’s visual design, assist in code correction and optimization during the platform’s development, and provide suggestions for articles and research materials to scientifically validate our ideas. The team made ethical and conscious use of these resources, allowing certain tasks to be completed more efficiently and then reviewed and refined by the team to ensure quality, accuracy, and reliability.

projectDetails.details:
Introduction

The way in which we, first-year students, sought to explain something so complicated to younger children was through means that were fun and visually appealing. For this, we used our combined skills to create everything on the website and transmit information about Space Weather using creativity. Below you will see our project more detailed and explained, offering a preview of what it contains.


Project

Homepage

Right away, you will see a brief summary of what we did and what our objective is, in addition to being able to select which page you would like to see first from the five buttons that appear on the screen.

Books

Upon selecting this page, you will be able to see that there is first a video. In it, the characters are shown quickly, but their reactions to the events that occurred in the stories are also shown through cartoons and characteristics that are related to the narratives, and a brief introduction to the stories. The books are right below; you just need to click on the arrow to begin your reading and the search for knowledge.

Podcasts

Here are our podcasts, which are translated into English, Spanish, and Portuguese. You should only choose any of the audios and click on the arrow to start listening and expand your repertoire.  

Games

Here you just need to click on any of the four that will go directly to the selected game (there are representative images of the games just above), so you can enjoy it as much as you want.

Word Puzzles

In this section, you will be able to discover and test your knowledge, being able to choose the difficulty levels and awaken your focus by searching for words.

Curiosities

Finally, we present, through a timeline, various events that led to new scientific discoveries that are and were very important, and some creations of institutions that became responsible for the study of events and research, in addition to having interesting facts right below the information presented.

Conclusion

To conclude, “Look Beyond The Earth” aims to offer information to generate more curiosity on the part of children, encouraging them to be more investigative. Furthermore, the more simplified language and the small details are what make the interactions more appealing and significant.

projectDetails.name: BioSphere
projectDetails.summary:
Biosphere was created to make exploring NASA’s bioscience research easier and more engaging. The platform gathers 607 scientific publications and displays them in a dynamic 2D layout, where each article connects to others through shared topics. This visual network allows users to see relationships between studies at a glance and discover new connections across space biology research.
Users can search by keywords, authors, or research periods, and instantly see related publications highlighted on the canvas. The platform also includes an Insights page, showing general statistics, topic evolution through time, and leading authors in specific fields.
By offering a clear and interactive way to navigate NASA’s vast scientific output, Biosphere helps researchers quickly find the most relevant and high-value articles for their own studies—saving time, uncovering meaningful connections, and strengthening the quality and impact of their scientific research.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is an interactive web platform designed to enhance the exploration of biological research articles published by NASA. It tackles the challenge of navigating and connecting a large volume of scientific papers by transforming them into a dynamic visual network. Instead of long, static lists, researchers interact with a 2D canvas of interconnected articles, where each card represents a publication and each line shows conceptual similarity. This makes the exploration of complex scientific topics more intuitive, visual, and engaging.

The data foundation was built from a curated dataset of 607 biology-related articles, extracted in Python from XML sources. For each article, the code collected metadata such as titles, abstracts, authors, keywords, citations, and publication years, also calculating the most frequent and representative terms within the text. The result was a rich dataset with nearly 400,000 lines, later used to fuel the platform’s two main pages: Search and Insights.

The Search page allows users to filter and visualize articles by keywords, authors, or publication periods, besides making the citation process more efficient and easier, while the Insights page provides analytical views such as topic evolution, citation trends, and main institutions in research. Together, these features enable scientists to form a clear picture of the main research directions and relationships within their field.

During the development of the project, we aimed to provide users with a smooth and effective experience, ensuring that the tools are interactive and intuitive, and that the data is presented in a reliable way. To achieve this, we focused on building a clean and responsive interface using JavaScript and D3.js, allowing for a more effective visualization of the large number of available articles.

With the goal of improving traditional research methods, our project offers an immersive experience in exploring scientific publications. Instead of presenting articles and statistics in a conventional list format, our platform enables a more visual, clear, and intuitive approach to academic discovery.

Technical explanation of the correlation between cards

The connections between article cards are built in the buildSimilarityGraph function (file cards.js), through a multilayered affinity system:

  • Token similarity (65%) – Jaccard similarity of sets built from title, terms, and abstract openings.
  • Keyword overlap (≤35%) – Shared normalized key terms increase connection strength.
  • Author overlap (≤25%) – Matching surnames strengthen ties between related works.
  • Journal bonus (+0.12) – Articles from the same journal gain a constant affinity boost.
  • Temporal proximity (≤1) – Close publication years increase the connection score.

A dynamic threshold (around the 45th percentile) ensures adaptive sensitivity to dataset density, avoiding both excess and isolation of nodes. The resulting network produces thematic clusters that combine textual, authorial, and temporal coherence — enabling a structured yet organic map of scientific relations.

Impact and differentiation

The project’s main innovation lies in its visual and cognitive redefinition of how scientific knowledge can be explored. Traditional platforms present articles in long, linear lists — an approach that limits perception of relationships and broader patterns. Our system, on the other hand, spreads articles spatially across a 2D network, linking them visually according to similarity.

The system was designed with scalability in mind — while it currently operates using the 607 NASA bioscience articles, its architecture could easily be extended to tens or even hundreds of thousands of publications across diverse scientific fields. By applying the same similarity and visualization logic to larger datasets, the platform could significantly enhance how researchers explore and understand large bodies of knowledge, uncovering meaningful connections, emerging trends, and valuable insights that traditional search approaches often overlook.

This shift transforms the researcher’s experience: it allows for immediate recognition of clusters, emerging topics, and gaps in the literature, and encourages a more exploratory and creative process of scientific discovery. Scientists can not only find high-value articles faster but also understand how different studies connect and evolve over time.

By integrating structured data, visual exploration, and analytical insights, the project significantly strengthens the process of identifying relevant, high-impact sources, making it a powerful tool for any researcher working with extensive academic literature.

Another useful aspect of the plataform is the ability to copy a pre-formated citation for each article with a button. Thos save researchs time and effort when referencing sources in scientific reports, papers or articles. Instead of manually formating citations, users can quickly retrive them already formatted, making the writing process more efficient and helping ensure accuracy in academic researches.

projectDetails.name: Project Outpost
projectDetails.summary: Project Outpost is an interactive 3D educational game that transforms complex concepts of space exploration into an accessible and engaging learning experience. Developed in response to the Space Habitat Design Tool challenge, the project allows users to explore the solar system, interact with a specialized crew, and design lunar habitats through a modular three-dimensional construction system. The application integrates educational quizzes, scientific simulations, and building mechanics to foster learning in STEM fields such as physics, biology, engineering, and space medicine. Its primary goal is to democratize knowledge about extraterrestrial habitability and inspire new generations to pursue scientific and technological careers. By combining immersive 3D visualization with gamified learning, Project Outpost demonstrates how interactive tools can bridge the gap between scientific knowledge and public engagement, serving as an innovative platform for space science education and exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Outpost is an interactive 3D educational game designed to transform complex concepts in space engineering, planetary sciences, and extraterrestrial habitability into an accessible, engaging, and pedagogically effective experience. The project was developed in response to the “Space Habitat Design Tool” challenge, which calls for the creation of visual tools that support the conception, sizing, and organization of space habitats in different exploration scenarios. The motivation behind choosing this challenge is deeply rooted in its educational and scientific potential, as it addresses one of the central pillars of future human space missions: the ability to design habitable environments in extraterrestrial contexts that ensure health, operational efficiency, and sustainability during extended stays beyond Earth.

The game places the user in the role of a commander of an expanding international space station, responsible for leading a crew composed of six specialists, each representing critical areas of space operations: science, biology, engineering, medicine, piloting, and logistics. Each character was designed with a unique personality and a set of responsibilities that accurately reflect the real challenges faced in exploration missions. Interaction with these characters occurs through dialogues, tasks, and educational quizzes containing more than 150 questions across various STEM disciplines, allowing players to learn actively as they progress through the mission. In this way, the application combines elements of scientific simulation and gamified storytelling with clear educational goals, fostering both a deeper understanding of technical concepts and continuous user engagement.

The functional core of Project Outpost is built around a three-dimensional simulation of the solar system, which enables players to explore planets and celestial bodies interactively and access detailed scientific information about their physical, chemical, and biological characteristics. This approach aims to bring audiences closer to astronomical and astrobiological content in an intuitive way, connecting real scientific data to an immersive exploratory experience. Navigation within the 3D environment was designed to be accessible to different age groups and levels of knowledge, significantly expanding the project’s educational potential and making it suitable for use in schools, museums, and science outreach environments.

Another essential component of the game is the modular construction system for lunar and interplanetary habitats, which directly reflects the objectives proposed by the challenge. Players can design and organize space habitats while considering real-world variables such as available volume, essential resources, crew size, and mission duration. Each module created must fulfill critical functions such as thermal control, life support, waste management, medical areas, recreation zones, and workspaces. Furthermore, the system imposes constraints and provides feedback when certain configurations are unsuitable for the mission context, introducing a layer of technical reasoning similar to the iterative design processes employed by aerospace engineers and habitat architects.

The decision to adopt a gamified and interactive format was driven by the need to democratize access to advanced knowledge about space exploration, especially for younger audiences. By transforming traditionally complex topics — such as habitat design, mission planning, orbital dynamics, and space physiology — into accessible challenges and narratives, the game creates a learning environment based on experience and experimentation. This approach aligns with contemporary educational strategies that advocate for the use of simulations and games as effective tools for knowledge construction, enhancing content retention and fostering the development of critical and systemic thinking skills.

From a technological perspective, the project was built using modern and efficient tools that ensure high performance and scalability. The frontend was developed with React 18 and TypeScript, ensuring modularity and ease of maintenance. Three-dimensional rendering is handled by Three.js and React Three Fiber, providing a realistic and interactive visual experience. A responsive and accessible design is achieved through Tailwind CSS, while animations are managed with Framer Motion, delivering smooth transitions and fluid navigation. Additionally, tools such as Vite, ESLint, and PostCSS optimize the development process and guarantee code quality and consistency, while additional features like local storage enhance the overall user experience.

The intended impact of Project Outpost manifests across multiple scales. In the short term, the project seeks to increase interest in space sciences and STEM fields by providing an accessible and engaging tool that introduces advanced concepts in a playful and practical manner. In the long term, the project aims to inspire future generations to pursue scientific and technological careers, contributing to the development of professionals capable of addressing the challenges of space exploration. By exposing users to the real-world difficulties involved in designing and maintaining habitats beyond Earth, the application also fosters a deeper understanding of the efforts and innovations necessary for expanding human presence in space.

Finally, Project Outpost represents an innovative approach by uniting rigorous science, interactive simulation, and modern pedagogy into a single digital ecosystem. Its purpose goes beyond teaching: it seeks to engage, challenge, and inspire. By offering users the opportunity to explore, experiment, and create within an accessible three-dimensional environment, the project positions itself as a powerful tool for science education and space exploration outreach. Choosing this challenge was, therefore, a strategic and intentional decision, as it allowed us to develop a solution that translates NASA’s real-world goals, such as preparing for Artemis missions and future Mars exploration, into a meaningful and transformative educational experience.

node.excerpt: We are a team of five developers from Brazil, united by a common purpose: to showcase our potential by contributing to technological advancement through innovative solutions and impactful projects.

projectDetails.name: Pitiú das Galáxias: Real-Time Air Quality Monitoring and Alerts
projectDetails.summary:
In 2025, several wildfires occurred across different regions of the United States, while in Brazil, drier areas — such as Campinas — also proved vulnerable to unintentional fires, like those recorded in 2024. These events release pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) and compounds that promote the formation of tropospheric ozone (O₃), both highly harmful to human health. Exposure to these gases affects the entire population but poses an even greater risk to vulnerable groups, such as the elderly and people with a history of respiratory complications, including COVID-19.

In response to this scenario, we joined the challenge “From EarthData to Action: Cloud Computing with Earth Observation Data for Predicting Cleaner, Safer Skies” and developed an air-quality monitoring application. The solution integrates NASA TEMPO satellite data, ground sensors, and meteorological information to forecast pollutant concentrations and provide real-time alerts to communities, enabling preventive action.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?
Our application monitors air quality by measuring pollutants such as O₂, O₃, and NO₂. It integrates satellite data, ground-based sensors, and predictive modeling to provide real-time information.

What benefits does it have, and what is the intended impact?
The app allows people to monitor air quality in their area in real time. This is especially important in regions prone to wildfires, where air pollution can become harmful without being immediately noticeable. For at-risk groups, such as the elderly or individuals with respiratory conditions, this tool can be critical for protecting their health.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?
We used Vite React for the front-end, the Google Maps API, a Python API for data integration, and a Python ConvLSTM model to forecast air quality.

How is your project creative? What factors did your team consider?
Our application was designed for both desktop and mobile use, with accessibility in mind. It includes dark and light modes, support for Portuguese (pt-BR), English, and Spanish, screen reader compatibility, and real-time alerts. The app can even notify users when air quality worsens, recommending preventive actions such as staying indoors during critical conditions.

projectDetails.name: Bio Orbits
projectDetails.summary:
In a world filled with data, great research can get lost.
That’s why we built Bio Orbits, a Space Biology Research Hub, transforming 608 NASA-validated papers into an interactive, AI-powered knowledge map. Our platform helps scientists, mission planners, investors, and the public explore decades of space biology research, uncover relationships among studies, and extract meaningful insights to support future Moon and Mars missions.

Key features include: 1 AI Insights Dashboard with Interactive visualizations showing keyword trends, top-cited studies, and social media impact. 2 Ask AI – A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) assistant that answers natural language questions with verified NASA sources. 3 Smart Recommendations – Suggests related papers using semantic similarity and kNN machine learning models. 4 Knowledge Graphs – Reveal how studies reference each other, mapping clusters of research topics.
Bio Orbits makes Space Biology research more accessible, actionable, and inspiring.
projectDetails.details:
What We Built

An AI-powered web platform that analyses 608 Space Biology publications from a Nasa Space Apps Resource database to create an interactive knowledge hub for exploration and discovery. Through data processing, visualization and a custom LLM model, the system turns decades of static bioscience research into dynamic easy-to-find relevant information. This allows scientists, mission planners, investors and the general public to uncover relationships among studies and extract meaningful insights.

our github repositories:

https://github.com/nicolepetrica/BioOrbits-frontend/

https://github.com/LucasPeixotg/ResearchOrbit

How It Works

Our website combines machine learning and data analysis techniques to power four main sections, enabling both interactive insights and intelligent user interaction.

Insights section

This section transforms raw publication data into meaningful visual insights tailored to different types of users.

The platform uses structured data extracted from each publication including authors, citations, summaries, and social media presence, to create interactive dashboards that display:

  • Keyword trends through the years
  • Papers with the most social media presence
  • Most cited papers
  • Social media presence by different metrics (Social media mentions, Mendeley readers and Altmetric Score)

From a technical perspective, all information was collected through web scraping and Python APIs, and then organized into a CSV file. Then, we selected the most relevant information to provide meaningful insights for each stakeholder we defined and used d3.js to plot the graphs.

We also designed stakeholder-specific dashboards:

  • For researchers: a scatter plot using the kNN model that clusters related articles across the database
  • For Investors: prediction about the amount of papers with a certain keyword in the next years based on ARIMA model 
  • For Explorers: bar plot with the quantity of the papers
Papers section

Here we list all the papers in the database and allow users to open them and save to their favorites. 

Ask AI section

We created a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system from scratch that allows users to interact directly with the dataset through natural language. 

Question to AI subsection

Here, users can ask questions and receive answers grounded in verified papers. They'll also receive a list of papers where that information comes from. 

To do this our system uses the Nomic embedding model to analyze the user's input, convert it into an embedding and compare it with the embeddings of the papers on the database. Then, Qwen model uses HyDE technique by generating a hypothetical answer to ensure that the retrieved data matches the question. Finally, the Gemma model generates a clear response for the user. All the models mentioned in this paragraph are LLMs.

Get Paper Recommendations subsection

In this subsection users can input any abstract to search what papers relate the most with it. This is specially useful to find papers to read and reference in their research. 

For this we use our RAG and we also built a kNN classification machine learning model API that extracts non-linear relationships between the papers.

Saved Papers section

Lastly, users view their saved papers and visualize how they papers reference one another or papers outside of the dataset, helping them discover related research and understand clusters of scientific knowledge.

To do this our team used an API called crossref that receives DOIs (an ID from a paper) from the referenced researched from a saved paper.  

Creativity and Innovation

We are a diverse team of Unicamp undergrad and masters students from across Brazil, combining expertise in AI, backend development, data science, and UI/UX design. This hollistic approach allowed us to combine different state of the art machine learning techniques with a user-centric vision.

Benefits

The platform transforms this Space Biology archive into a searchable and actionable research tool.It enables users to identify trends, gaps, and key topics in space biology, provides trusted AI-grounded insights for exploration and planning, and offers personalized recommendations for related studies and future research directions.

Intended Impact

Make scientific knowledge more accessible, interactive, and useful for decision-making and innovation.

How It Helps

  • Turns large research datasets into interactive and understandable resources
  • Encourages exploration through visualizations, natural language search, and semantic connections
  • Supports data-driven decisions and identification of research gaps

Broader Impact

  • Can be applied to other research areas and institutions beyond Space Biology
  • Promotes open science and collaboration across disciplines
  • Demonstrates how AI and knowledge graphs can make complex research more meaningful and impactful

Vision A world where research is easier to access, connect, and apply; accelerating scientific progress and informed exploration.

projectDetails.name: Ship Sweet Ship
projectDetails.summary:
We built an interactive game where anyone can design space habitats and instantly learn whether their layout follows human-factors best practices. Players drag and snap modules—sleeping quarters, galley, hygiene, storage, airlock, exercise—and our rule checker evaluates simple, mission-critical constraints: minimum habitable volume per crew, functional zoning (e.g., no bathroom next to food prep), clear traffic flow and access to the airlock, privacy for sleep and hygiene, safe waste handling, and basic redundancy for essential amenities. When something fails, the game explains why and suggests fixes, turning iteration into learning. 
This addresses the challenge of making habitat development understandable and engaging without heavy engineering models. It matters because it teaches good design habits, spatial reasoning, and crew well-being fundamentals—useful for classrooms, makers, and anyone curious about how people can live well in space. Ship Sweet Ship is designed to inspire a new generation to pursue careers in STEM fields, build public support by engaging taxpayers, make space more human, and crowdsource innovation. We do this by gathering well-researched data from NASA resources to achieve an efficient integration of fun and learning.
projectDetails.details:
What does Ship Sweet Ship do?

Ship Sweet Ship is a resource management and strategy game that simulates the development of space missions to the Moon and Mars, focusing on the planning of a sustainable habitat for the crew.

How does Ship Sweet Ship work?

Ship Sweet Ship is designed to immerse the player.

Inspired by Van Gogh’s art, the menu was crafted to transport the user to another world, evoking the feeling of drifting through space, just like this genius once did in his paintings.

An inspirational video telling the story of a dreamer girl, Annah, enchanted by the stars and the vastness of space, pursuing her dream of becoming an astronaut and helping the creation of a space habitat.Now it’s the player’s turn, they can choose between a trip to the Moon or to Mars to start it's amazing journey through space.

Choosing the Moon or Mars, the player is able to choose different missions, selecting various crew sizes, lores, habitat configurations, resource limits, and environmental conditions.

At the beginning of the game, the player can choose how many modules they want, up to a maximum of four, based on data from NASA papers. The interface also includes progress indicators and dynamic lines that update as the player advances, showing the quantity and status of each habitat module already built.

The system reacts in real time, updating the habitat indicators automatically as the player builds and modifies the structure.

What benefits does it have?

The game serves as an educational tool, offering players an interactive and engaging way to learn about the complexities and challenges of space exploration. It provides insights into the requirements for building and maintaining a human presence on other celestial bodies, covering aspects like resource management, life support systems, and the well-being of the crew, while insert situations like difference of budget and number of crew members. This gamified approach to learning makes complex scientific and engineering concepts more accessible and entertaining.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The project addresses the challenge of making habitat development understandable and engaging without heavy engineering models. It teaches good design habits, spatial reasoning, and crew well-being fundamentals—useful for classrooms, makers, and anyone curious about how people can live well in space. Ship Sweet Ship is designed to inspire a new generation to pursue careers in STEM fields, build public support by engaging taxpayers, make space more human, and crowdsource innovation. We do this by gathering well-researched data from NASA resources to achieve an efficient integration of fun and learning.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The game was developed using the Godot Game Engine, a powerful open-source tool for creating 2D and 3D games. The primary programming language used is GDScript, Godot's native scripting language. The 3D models and assets were imported from Kenney into the Godot engine. The user interface was designed and implemented using Godot's built-in UI system, which allowed for the creation of a responsive and intuitive interface.

Technical elements considered

The project defines different minimum volumes per person for each habitat function. The sleeping quarters require 3.49 m³ per crew member. Hygiene and meal preparation areas each require 1.09 m³, scaled as one station or unit for every four crew members. The common table for dining and meetings occupies 2.52 m³ per person. The open social area, designed for leisure and training, requires 4.55 m³ per crew member, while the exercise area with a cycling device needs 1.53 m³, also calculated for every four crew members. These elements, data from articles and websites about max weight by rockets, guided the team to work on a solid work with information to well integrate science and fun.

How is your project creative?

The project's creativity is rooted in its innovative approach to education through gamification. Rather than relying on traditional methods of information delivery, the game immerses the player in a simulated mission, making the learning process more dynamic. The unique art style, combined with a compelling narrative, draws players into the world of space exploration, creating an experience that is both entertaining and educational.

What factors did your team consider?

During the development of the project, the team took several key factors into consideration:

  • Scientific Accuracy: The team made a concerted effort to ensure that the game is as scientifically accurate as possible, incorporating real data and constraints from NASA missions to provide a realistic simulation.
  • Player Experience: A significant amount of attention was given to creating a game that is both enjoyable and challenging. The user interface was designed to be clear and intuitive, allowing players to easily navigate the complexities of mission management.
  • Educational Value: The game was designed with clear learning objectives in mind, focusing on STEM concepts and providing players with a deeper understanding of the science and engineering behind space exploration.
  • NASA Space Apps Challenge Theme: The project is closely aligned with the theme of the NASA Space Apps challenge, which encourages the use of NASA's open data to create innovative solutions to real-world problems and to inspire the next generation of scientists and engineers.

What tools did you use to develop your project?

We a set of tools to design, prototype and execute our project (besides the will to learn and make a difference):

  • Development: Godot Editor, Figma, Github, ElevenLabs, Gemini CLI, Claude Sonnet, GPT-codex, Photopea, Capcut;
  • Framework: Godot Game Engine;
  • Programming Languages: Godot Script;
  • Deployment: Itch.io.

Future Goals

This project has even greater potential. Here are some of the features planned for the future:

  • Advanced Module Customization: A dedicated editing mode to allow players to customize the internal layout of each rocket and habitat module.
  • Improved Camera Controls: Overhauling the camera system to provide a smoother, more intuitive rotation and zoom experience.
  • Enhanced Visual Feedback: Adding clear visual indicators, like highlights or outlines, to show which module is currently selected for editing.
  • State Persistence: Implementing a system to save and load the unique internal layout of every module.
  • Social Interaction: Creating a system for players to share their ship and habitat designs with the community.
  • Complex Management System: Developing a more in-depth management simulation with more resources, crew needs, and events to mimic the complexities of a real-world space mission.

Check out our Github

projectDetails.details:
Project Information – Sideralis

The Sideralis Project is a platform that integrates an educational game experience. Based on the Meteor Madness theme, it combines real NASA asteroid data with gamification elements to create an interactive learning environment where users can identify and distinguish between different types of asteroids, meteors, and other celestial bodies.

In the game, you play as a crew member aboard the Sideralis Space Station. You wake up startled as a meteor approaches Earth's orbit. When the alarm echoes throughout the station, your mission begins: head to the command room, interact with the control panel, and analyze the composition of the object — using real data retrieved from NASA’s official API.

After gathering the data, you must go to the storage bay and select the correct tool to deal with the meteor (each tool is inspired by real-world scientific inventions). Attach the chosen equipment in the appropriate room to attempt to destroy the meteor — if you made the right choice. Have fun exploring, experimenting, and saving the planet!

The project was developed using Astro Framework, TailwindCSS, Inkscape, Godot, Aseprite, FL Studio, and Figma.

Why Sideralis is a Creative Project
Sideralis stands out for its unique fusion of science, education, and interactive storytelling. By transforming real NASA data into a playable experience, it bridges the gap between learning and entertainment.
