projectDetails.name: Modular Microgravity Lab (MML)
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, the Modular Microgravity Laboratory (MML), is a fully automated, unmanned orbital platform designed to provide “Microgravity as a service” (MGaaS) for industrial-scale manufacturing and research in Low Earth Orbit.
This platform directly addresses the fundamental challenge that gravity on Earth imposes critical limitations on high-purity material production. On Earth, gravity-induced forces like convection and sedimentation introduce defects into semiconductor crystals and hinder the growth of large, pure protein crystals essential for drug development. Existing platforms like the ISS are not designed for dedicated industrial manufacturing and suffer from vibrations and contamination that compromise sensitive processes. The MML provides a dedicated, isolated, and controlled environment to eliminate these issues.

This project is important because it enables the creation of superior materials that are physically impossible to produce on Earth. This can lead to next-generation, higher-performance electronics and accelerate the development of more effective pharmaceuticals, unlocking transformative opportunities in the trillion-dollar semiconductor and pharmaceutical markets.

Finally, the modular design of the laboratory allows it to be easily expanded and updated as new manufacturing technologies and tools surge and demand for in-space fabrication grows.
projectDetails.details:
The Modular Microgravity Laboratory (MML): A New Paradigm for Manufacturing in Space
What It Is and How It Works

The Modular Microgravity Laboratory (MML) is a pioneering, automated orbital platform that provides "Microgravity as a Service" (MGaaS). It functions as a dedicated, unmanned factory in Low Earth Orbit, designed to overcome the fundamental limitations that gravity imposes on high-precision manufacturing on Earth. Its operation is built on a streamlined, three-phase process.
The cycle begins when a client from a sector such as pharmaceuticals or semiconductors sends raw materials in a standardized capsule to the laboratory. This capsule is launched into orbit using commercial launch services. Upon arrival, the MML's internal robotic systems autonomously receive the capsule and transfer it to a specialized, self-contained unit called an Autonomous Manufacturing Module (AMM). Inside these modules, processes like protein crystallization or silicon crystal growth are carried out in the pristine, stable environment of microgravity. Finally, the finished, high-value product is loaded into a return vehicle. This vehicle, developed by commercial partners, safely re-enters Earth's atmosphere and lands, delivering the perfected materials directly to the client. The MML's modular architecture is key to its design, allowing the platform to start with a core module and expand by adding new, specialized AMMs as market demand evolves.

The Core Benefits

The primary benefit of the MML is its ability to produce materials with a level of purity and structural perfection that is unattainable on Earth. For the semiconductor industry, this means growing ultrapure silicon crystals free from the defects caused by gravity-induced convection. These superior crystals are the foundation for next-generation chips that offer higher performance, greater energy efficiency, and a significantly higher manufacturing yield. For the pharmaceutical industry, the MML enables the growth of larger, more perfectly ordered protein crystals. These crystals provide researchers with a clearer blueprint for drug design, accelerating the development of more effective medications and enabling advanced formulations, such as converting intravenous drugs into injectable ones.
Beyond advanced materials, the MML offers a revolutionary platform for biological research. It allows scientists to cultivate complex three-dimensional human tissue structures, known as organoids, without the need for artificial scaffolds. These micro-tissues serve as vastly superior models for studying diseases and testing drug candidates, potentially saving billions of dollars in research and development by identifying failures much earlier in the process. While the costs of space logistics are a factor, the MML's fully automated and dedicated design provides a more accessible and economically viable path to microgravity than alternative options, with the immense value of the outputs far outweighing the operational expenses.

Tools used

The development of the MML project leveraged a structured and professional technology stack to bring our conceptual vision to a tangible presentation. Our process was supported by industry-standard tools for coding, collaboration, design, and research. For the core development of our project's digital presence, we engineered a static landing page to serve as a dynamic catalog and informational platform for potential clients. This site was constructed using the fundamental web development languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The code was written and managed within the VS Code integrated development environment, which provided a robust and efficient workspace. The final website was deployed and made publicly accessible via GitHub Pages, ensuring reliable hosting and version control.
Our collaborative workflow was centralized using Google Docs, which served as our primary platform for compiling all research, drafting documents, and tracking project progress in real time. For our final presentations and visual reports, we utilized Genially to produce engaging and animated slides that clearly communicated our complex ideas. The research underpinning our business plan and technical design was conducted through a methodical review of authoritative sources. We primarily utilized the resources made available by NASA for this challenge, supplementing them with targeted research using Google Scholar and the Chrome browser to locate additional relevant scientific papers, market analyses, and technical data.

The Intended Impact

The intended impact of the MML aims to catalyze a broader technological and economic shift. The project is designed to accelerate innovation on Earth by providing a source of "perfect" materials, thereby pushing the boundaries of what is possible in electronics, medicine, and material science. By creating a reliable, commercial customer for launch and reentry services, the MML serves as a cornerstone for a sustainable and scalable Low Earth Orbit economy, fostering a viable commercial ecosystem independent of government funding.
Furthermore, the MML democratizes access to space. Its "as-a-Service" model allows companies—from large pharmaceutical corporations to specialized biotech startups—to harness the unique properties of microgravity for their research and production without needing to become space-faring entities themselves. This opens a new frontier for terrestrial industries, transforming space into a practical domain for industrial advancement.

Creativity Behind the Project

The creativity of the MML project lies in its holistic and practical system integration. We have creatively reframed the challenge from "building a factory in space" to providing "Microgravity as a Service." This Manufacturing-as-a-Service (MaaS) approach dramatically lowers the barrier to entry for our clients and establishes a scalable, recurring revenue model.
The modular architecture of the AMMs is a key innovation, providing market agility. Unlike a monolithic space station, our design is inherently flexible, allowing us to launch a module for semiconductor fabrication and later add another for pharmaceutical research, dynamically adapting to market demand without a complete system redesign. Finally, we have turned a major historical hurdle, the returning of products to Earth, into a core strategic advantage by designing our business for symbiosis with emerging partners in the commercial reentry vehicle sector. Our success is engineered to grow in lockstep with the success of the downmass industry.

Factors We Considered

Our design and business plan are built on a rigorous foundation that addresses the complex realities of operating in LEO. We developed a transparent methodology for approximating costs, which became the foundation of our financial model. The cornerstone of our cost structure is the estimate of the value of goods, which we conservatively estimated at $20,000 per kilogram. This was derived by analyzing the two most significant operational expenses: logistics and asset depreciation. We based this on prevailing and projected launch costs from commercial providers and factored in the emerging, yet critical, expense of returning cargo to Earth. To ensure a sustainable and scalable business, we applied a 50% gross margin target to this estimate value, determining our final service price of $30,000 to $40,000 per kilogram. This pricing structure is designed to ensure a positive return on investment while remaining competitive. Furthermore, our financial planning is forward-looking, built around the continuing decline in launch costs driven by reusable rocket technology.
From a technical and operational standpoint, we conducted a deep analysis to proactively manage the multifaceted challenges of operating a business in space. Our strategy is not merely reactive, it is engineered for long-term success and responsibility and is precisely tailored to the hostility of the Low Earth Orbit environment. We have developed a comprehensive plan for space debris management. Proactively, the MML will execute collision avoidance maneuvers using tracking data from the Space Surveillance Network. To protect sensitive equipment, we are employing a combination of optimized passive shielding and radiation-tolerant electronic components to mitigate the effects of charged particles. Furthermore, the laboratory's exterior will be coated with specialized atomic oxygen-resistant and thermal control coatings to withstand extreme temperature swings and material erosion. Given the prohibitive cost of repairs, the MML is designed for maximum reliability and autonomy, utilizing redundant systems and hardware that operate remotely based on adapted Good Manufacturing Practices to ensure quality without manual intervention.
Economically, our model is structured to achieve profitability by aligning with high-value markets and leveraging emerging cost trends. We are building our logistics strategy around the continuing decline in launch costs and are positioning ourselves as strategic partners to the emerging "downmass" industry, engaging with companies to secure long-term contracts for product return. Our market entry plan is deliberately targeted, focusing initially on the most valuable niche applications where microgravity provides an undeniable advantage, such as "master" crystals for drug development. This approach is supported by a phased operational strategy, starting with R&D-as-a-Service to generate early revenue and take out risk in the technological and market entry process before scaling to more ambitious production.
The complex legal landscape is a critical component of our plan. We have a clear roadmap for sequential engagement with U.S. federal agencies. This involves securing a Launch and Re-entry License from the FAA, which includes demonstrating financial responsibility, and obtaining a Space Station License from the FCC by detailing our orbital parameters and comprehensive Orbital Debris Mitigation Plan. All hardware will be designed and tested against a suite of relevant NASA Technical Standards to ensure the safety, reliability, and purity of the on-orbit manufacturing environment.
Finally, our strategic and long-term vision ensures the MML is a scalable and responsible part of the LEO ecosystem. The core of this strategy is our modular Autonomous Manufacturing Module architecture, which allows us to scale capacity and service new markets by adding specialized modules without designing entirely new space stations. Our commitment to sustainability is a fundamental design driver, with a clear plan for controlled deorbiting to set a new standard for commercial operations and ensure the long-term health of the orbital environment. Every aspect of the MML has been conceived with a clear and actionable plan to ensure our project is not only visionary but also practical, profitable, and responsible.

AI was not used in any of the research, brainstorming, or conceptual creation processes. In particular, we used AI to speed up website development by using code completion tools (Copilot), producing animated presentations for our final reports, and producing high-quality images from our hand-drawn designs. With this method, we were able to effectively refine the project's ultimate delivery while retaining complete creative and strategic control over its vision.

projectDetails.name: Project Smart City Data

projectDetails.details:
Smart City Dta is an interactive online platform designed to allow users to explore and visualize urban sustainability data in a clear and engaging way. The project demonstrates how urban environments can be improved by highlighting patterns in factors such as temperature, air quality, vegetation, and human activity. Users can interact with dynamic visualizations, including 2D maps and 3D globes, to understand correlations between environmental variables and urban planning challenges.

The platform is simple and accessible, allowing anyone — from students to city planners — to navigate, explore datasets, and understand how cities impact and are impacted by environmental factors. The intended impact is to raise awareness about urban sustainability, promote data-driven insights, and encourage informed decision-making for city improvements.

To develop Smart City Dta, we used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, leveraging the Three.js library for 3D visualization. The team also utilized AI tools (GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5) for brainstorming, coding assistance, and text refinement, accelerating creativity while maintaining complete human oversight. The platform is highly interactive and creative, combining immersive visualizations, clear data presentation, and user engagement features to make complex urban sustainability concepts approachable.

Throughout development, we considered usability, accessibility, data accuracy, and educational impact, ensuring the platform is both informative and intuitive for a broad audience. By connecting real NASA Earth observation data to visual and interactive experiences, Smart City Dta empowers users to see opportunities for improving urban environments and fostering more sustainable cities.

projectDetails.details:
Challenge Report: Solaria — A Platform for Exploring NASA’s Massive Image Datasets

Report partially created with generative text AI

Overview

Solaria is a web-based visualization and exploration platform designed to allow users to zoom, navigate, and explore gigapixel-scale NASA imagery. The platform focuses on making complex astronomical and planetary data intuitive and accessible to both the public and researchers.

It directly addresses NASA’s challenge of scaling human interaction with terabyte- and petabyte-scale image data, enabling users to explore vast datasets efficiently and meaningfully.

Live Demo: https://nasa-2025-solaria.vercel.app/GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Guillhermm/nasa-2025-solaria

YT Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3XB88jBA-Ik

Challenge Alignment

<colgroup><col><col></colgroup>

Challenge Objective

How Solaria Meets It

1. Zoom in/out and navigate massive image datasets

Solaria implements multi-resolution tile-based image rendering (similar to Google Maps or Deep Zoom). This allows users to seamlessly zoom from a planetary overview to fine surface detail without performance issues.

2. Label known features and annotate discoveries

The platform includes interactive annotation tools for marking craters, geological formations, or other features. Labels can be saved, categorized, and shared, supporting collaborative discovery.

3. Enable discovery of new patterns

Through layer overlays, AI-assisted search, and temporal comparisons, users can visualize change detection and pattern formation (e.g., dust storms, ice movements). This encourages scientific insight beyond static viewing.

4. Handle diverse datasets (Earth, Moon, Mars, space images)

Solaria supports multi-source imagery integration, compatible with NASA APIs (EarthData, MRO, LRO, Hubble, JWST). Users can switch between datasets or overlay them in the same viewport.

5. Compare images across time or different instruments

A time-slider feature lets users compare datasets taken at different times (temporal exploration). Cross-spectral comparison enables analysis between visible, infrared, or altimeter data.

6. Scalable data handling for large images

Solaria uses adaptive image streaming and progressive tiling. Only the necessary image tiles at the user’s zoom level are loaded, optimizing bandwidth and reducing load times.

7. User-friendly, educational interface

The interface uses intuitive controls, contextual pop-ups, and minimalistic design, making it suitable for both researchers and public exhibits. Responsive design ensures compatibility across devices.

8. Support for educational/public engagement

Solaria’s aesthetic and interaction model make it ideal for museum displays or public demos, allowing non-experts to explore space imagery effortlessly.

9. Support for advanced exploration (AI search)

Users can perform semantic or coordinate-based searches, entering keywords like “volcanic region” or “Andromeda core,” which trigger AI-assisted region identification.

10. Demonstration of method and scalability

The live deployment demonstrates efficient handling of gigapixel-scale datasets using cloud-based rendering (Vercel + WebGL/Leaflet/Three.js), illustrating scalability and real-world feasibility.

Technical Architecture Highlights

<colgroup><col><col></colgroup>

Component

Implementation Detail

Frontend Framework

Built using Next.js + React, deployed via Vercel for scalability and performance.

Rendering Engine

Utilizes OpenSeadragon / Deck.GL / WebGL for smooth, deep-zoom rendering of gigapixel imagery.

Data Integration

Compatible with NASA imagery APIs and public datasets (e.g., Hubble Legacy Archive, EarthData, LROC).

Annotation Layer

Built with Canvas / SVG overlay, supports saving labeled coordinates and exporting data.

Temporal Comparison

Uses synchronized tile layers and a time slider to compare imagery across dates or wavelengths.

Performance Optimization

Implements lazy loading, adaptive tiling, and caching to efficiently handle large imagery.

Code Repository

Full open-source code and documentation available on GitHub: nasa-2025-solaria.

Innovation and Impact

  • Brings NASA’s massive imagery to the web in a way that’s both scientifically useful and publicly engaging.

  • Scales down complexity — users can explore terabyte-level imagery using only a browser.

  • Encourages citizen science by enabling users to label and contribute discoveries.

  • Bridges the gap between static data archives and dynamic, explorable experiences.

NASA Image Datasets Utilized

Solaria leverages publicly available NASA datasets and APIs to demonstrate exploration of massive imagery. These include:

<colgroup><col><col><col></colgroup>

Dataset / Source

Description

NASA Access Point

Hubble Legacy Archive – Andromeda Galaxy (2.5 Gigapixel Image)

Ultra-high-resolution mosaic of the Andromeda Galaxy used for deep zoom exploration.

https://hla.stsci.edu/

Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE / MARCI)

Gigapixel-level imagery of Mars’ surface used to demonstrate time-lapse and annotation capabilities.

https://hirise.lpl.arizona.edu/ / https://mars.nasa.gov/mro/

Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO)

High-resolution lunar surface maps used for terrain feature labeling.

https://lunar.gsfc.nasa.gov/

EarthData (MODIS & Landsat imagery)

Multi-spectral Earth observation data used to test multi-layer visualization and temporal comparisons.

https://earthdata.nasa.gov/

James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Public Gallery

Used for deep-space visualization examples and contrast against Hubble imagery.

https://webbtelescope.org/images

These datasets exemplify diverse resolutions, wavelengths, and planetary contexts, validating Solaria’s ability to manage, render, and interact with heterogeneous space imagery.

Example Use Case Demonstrations

  1. Exploring Mars:

    • Zoom from a global view to a local crater.

    • Annotate dust storms or rock formations.

    • Compare Mars Color Imager data from different sols.

    • Deep zoom into stellar clusters.

    • Overlay infrared and visible light layers.

    • Detect structural patterns across spectral bands.

    • Compare multi-temporal imagery (e.g., deforestation, glacier retreat).

    • Overlay vegetation or temperature maps.

Future Enhancements

  • Collaborative annotation sharing (public or private datasets).

  • Machine learning integration for automatic feature recognition.

  • Offline dataset caching for low-bandwidth exploration.

  • VR/AR immersive exploration mode for educational settings.

projectDetails.name: Use of Machine Learning for Automated Classification of Exoplanet Candidates
projectDetails.summary: The observation of exoplanets is not only a pathway to understanding the origin of our own solar system but also to challenge our physical models, from the existence of hot Jupiters to the diversity of planetary atmospheres. The first step in any study in the field requires, however, the identification of the astrophysical body in question. Given the difficult and time-consuming nature of this task, this project sought to automate the classification of exoplanet candidates through the use of Machine Learning (ML). In order to assess ML models potential for this task, we trained Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests (RF) and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) over the open-source TESS dataset and compared their performances. Accuracies of 82%, 85% and 87% were found for the SVM, RF and XGB models, respectively. This performance not only validates their computational effectiveness under constrained resources but also highlights potential for further improvement, as evidenced by recent studies having achieved accuracies exceeding 96%, such as Luz (2024).
projectDetails.details:
Put simply, the project's goal is to develop Machine Learning (ML) models capable of classifying astronomical bodies in the TESS Objects of Interest (TOI) dataset as either being exoplanets or not. We have employed the python programming language for data science and ML, as these are fields in which it excels, and HTML and JavaScript for the web application development. The project's source code may be found at https://github.com/cpcomparini/NASA_2025.git .

(Data Pre-Processing) The full TOI dataset comprises position in the night sky, planet and stellar properties and metadata for 7,703 instances of astronomical bodies, as well as their manual classification The latter was binary encoded as ("Known Planet", "Confirmed Planet" -> 1) and ("False Alarm", "False Positive" -> 0), while any instance labelled as "Planetary Candidate" or "Ambiguous Planetary Candidate" were removed from analysis. 7 planetary properties and 5 stellar properties were selected for ML training. The data treatment pipeline continues with outlier removal, missing numbers removal, rescaling of the features, balancing of the targets through Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique (SMOTE), leaving a total of 2,204 instances for training. We found the ML models to achieve their expected performance (as reported in Luz (2024)) when trained over this dataset, and hence saw no need to include data from the Kepler Objects of Interest (KOI) or K2 datasets.

(ML Training) We have built, trained and evaluated Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests (RF) and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) models over the treated data, each time tuning the model's hyperparameters by randomly searching in the hyperparameter space. We find XGB to slightly outperform RF, which slightly outperforms SVM, on all four metrics of accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score. We also find accuracies consistent with those present in Luz (2024).

(Web Interface) Our web application allows the user to interact the the ML models we obtained, by inputting new data and receiving back the corresponding predictions. Since exoplanets are frequently portraid in science fiction as a "plan B" for preventing or reversing climate change, we take the opportunity to convey the message that we may not allow the loss of biodiversity on planet Earth, even if interplanetary travel is achieved, but rather that extraterrestrial colonization should be an extension of our ability to care for life wherever it exists.
projectDetails.aiReferences: We have employed MistralAI's LeChat and Google's Gemini chatbots for assistance in generating python, JavaScript and HTML code and for translating the web application from Portuguese (our native language) to English.

challengeDetails.title: A World Away: Hunting for Exoplanets with AI

With advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML), it is possible to automatically analyze large sets of data collected by these missions to identify exoplanets. Your challenge is to create an AI/ML model that is trained on one or more of the open-source exoplanet datasets offered by NASA and that can analyze new data to accurately identify exoplanets. (Astrophysics Division)

projectDetails.name: Project Space Habitats - Escola Legal
projectDetails.summary:
Space Habitats is an interactive web application that explores how future space settlements could be designed for efficiency, comfort, and sustainability. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, it invites users to model different habitat geometries — cylinders, tori, and inflatable capsules — and instantly calculate their volume, floor area, and estimated crew capacity.

The project addresses the challenge of transforming scientific and engineering concepts into an educational, accessible experience. Using simple tools (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript), Space Habitats turns geometry and physics into something visual and intuitive: users can adjust dimensions, apply presets, and preview the shapes directly in the browser.

A second page extends the experience by allowing users to design the interior layout of a habitat — placing laboratories, gardens, sleeping modules, and social areas — and exporting the design for further study.

Space Habitats demonstrates how open web technologies can make complex space-engineering topics understandable to students and the general public, inspiring curiosity about human life beyond Earth and encouraging creative thinking about our future in space.
projectDetails.details:
Space Habitats is an interactive web application that allows users to explore and design possible living structures for space environments. The project features two tools: one that calculates the internal volume, floor area, and estimated capacity of different habitat shapes (cylinder, torus, and capsule), and another that lets users create custom interior layouts using modular rooms such as laboratories, farms, and sleeping quarters.

The goal is to help students and space enthusiasts visualize the complexity of designing sustainable habitats beyond Earth. By translating mathematical formulas and spatial planning into an accessible visual interface, Space Habitats connects STEM learning with imagination and creativity.

The application was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with an emphasis on clean design, interactivity, and browser-based functionality — no installation required.
Its educational benefit lies in transforming abstract engineering concepts into playful simulations, encouraging young learners to think critically about life-support systems and human adaptation in space.

The project combines science, coding, and creativity to inspire the next generation of explorers and problem-solvers.

projectDetails.name: Sprinklify
projectDetails.summary:
Users drop a pin on Google Maps, pick a date, and choose Simple or Precise mode to tailor speed versus detail for their query.

Simple mode calls the NASA POWER API to return daily averages for temperature, precipitation, wind, and snow for the selected day of year.

Precise mode retrieves hourly MERRA‑2 records from NASA GES DISC (SLV and FLX collections datasets) to compute per‑hour statistics over the selected day.
The analysis spans roughly four decades, leveraging MERRA‑2’s data record from 1980 to near‑present for robust climatological context.

Results include clear summaries, charts, and the option to download raw CSV data in line with the challenge’s guidance on shareable outputs.

By translating long‑term reanalysis into simple probabilities for heat, cold, wind, and wet conditions, Sprinklify helps planners make informed decisions months in advance using trusted NASA datasets.
projectDetails.details:
Sprinklify

Is an fully functional Android native application that turns decades of NASA reanalysis data into actionable weather-risk information for any location and date. Built for the “Will It Rain on My Parade” Space Apps challenge, Sprinklify offers both a Simple and Precise mode:

Simple Mode

Uses the NASA POWER API to fetch daily averages of temperature, precipitation, wind speed, and snowfall for the selected location and day of year.

Fast, lightweight, ideal for quick overviews.

Precise Mode

Accesses hourly data from NASA GES DISC’s MERRA-2 OPeNDAP ASCII endpoints, covering the past 40 years.

Computes hourly averages and frequency distributions.

Supports CSV export of raw time-series ASCII data.

Depending on the network condition and mobile's hardware, could take longer to fetch all data

Platform & Architecture

Kotlin & Android SDK

Navigation Component for fragment routing

Compose for UI

Data Integration

NASA POWER REST API for global daily climatologies

NASA GES DISC OPeNDAP for MERRA-2 hourly single-level (SLV) and surface flux (FLX) datasets in ASCII format

Stream ID logic to select the correct MERRA-2 data stream (1980–1991 → 100, 1992–2000 → 200, 2001–2010 → 300, 2011–present → 400)

UI / UX

Google Maps fragment for location pin-drop

Material DatePicker for selecting date

MPAndroidChart for distribution and time-series graphs

CSV download button in Precise mode

projectDetails.name: Project starzing
projectDetails.summary: O projeto “Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings” foi desenvolvido pelo grupo Starzing com foco em front-end interativo voltado para o público infantil. Utilizando React, criamos uma jornada digital guiada pela personagem Coronalda, que leva as crianças do Sol até a Terra explicando, de forma lúdica e visual, como o clima espacial afeta nosso planeta. O desafio era transformar conceitos científicos complexos — como Ejeções de Massa Coronal (CME), campo magnético e auroras — em uma experiência acessível, divertida e educativa. Para isso, desenvolvemos uma narrativa gamificada, com cards interativos que mostram os impactos reais do clima espacial em profissões como astronautas, pilotos e agricultores. Ao final, um questionário reforça o aprendizado de forma leve e engajadora. O projeto é importante porque conecta ciência e cotidiano, despertando a curiosidade desde cedo e promovendo inclusão digital e educação científica para crianças entre 6 e 12 anos.
projectDetails.details:
Team Members: Pedro Sergio, Gabriela Alejandra, João Pedro, Thifany Vitória and Ariani Oliveira

Theme: Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings

1. Overview

This project aims to present the concept of Space Weather in an accessible, playful, and interactive way for children. Using modern front-end technologies like React, we developed a digital journey where young explorers learn how solar phenomena affect Earth and our daily lives.

2. Objective

- Translate complex scientific content about the Sun and space weather into child-friendly language.

- Create an interactive experience that stimulates curiosity and learning.

- Show the real impact of Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) on various professions and everyday technologies.

3. Challenges Faced

- Scientific simplification: transforming technical concepts (such as CME, magnetic field, auroras) into understandable narratives for children.

- Interactive design: developing a visually attractive, intuitive, and responsive interface.

- Child engagement: maintaining the attention of the target audience through characters, animations, and interactions.

- Accessibility and scalability: ensuring the site works well across devices and can grow with new content.

4. Solutions Implemented

Main character: creation of Coronalda, an energy cloud that guides children through the story.

Gamified narrative: a journey that begins at the Sun and ends on Earth, with visual explanations and interactions.

Interactive cards: characters such as an astronaut, pilot, farmer, and engineer show how space weather affects their routines.

Responsive design in React: lightweight, adaptable interface with smooth animations.

Action buttons and interactive prompts: “Start the adventure,” “Click the characters,” “Talk to Astro.”

5. Target Audience

- Children aged 6 to 12

- Parents and educators interested in accessible science content

- Schools and science outreach programs

6. Expected Impact

Scientific education: sparking interest in astronomy and technology from an early age.

Everyday connection: showing how space directly affects our lives.

Digital inclusion: offering a free and accessible educational experience.

7. Technologies Used

- React: main front-end framework

- Animated CSS: for visual effects and smooth transitions

- JavaScript: logic for interactivity and navigation

8. Educational Content

Introduction to the Sun and sunspots

Explanation of Coronal Mass Ejections (CME)

Earth’s magnetic field and auroras

Impacts on professions and technologies (GPS, power grids, satellites)

Scientific curiosities in “Did You Know?” format

9. Communication and Engagement

Fun and accessible language

Characters with expressive and direct speech

Interactive buttons and calls to action

Space for questions with the character Astro

projectDetails.details:
Aurora and the Great Solar Storm is an interactive digital storybook designed to teach young readers about space weather, solar storms, and scientific communication. The project transforms complex NASA data and real phenomena into an accessible, emotional narrative — told through the eyes of a girl whose mother, an astronaut, faces a powerful solar storm in space.

⚙️ How It Works

The story unfolds in a page-turning animation built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
Each chapter explores a different aspect of space weather — its effects on astronauts, satellites, GPS, and daily life on Earth.
Readers can navigate through the pages like a real book, while animations simulate the motion of turning pages, creating an immersive learning experience.

🌍 Benefits and Intended Impact

Our goal is to educate children and teens about solar activity and its real-world impacts in an engaging way.
The story also promotes critical thinking about misinformation — showing how fake news spreads during scientific crises, and highlighting the importance of trustworthy science communication.
It bridges science and empathy, helping kids understand both the physics and the human emotions behind space exploration.

🛠️ Tools and Technologies

Languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript

Platform: CodePen (demo), GitHub Pages (hosted site)

Design: Canva, Pixel-Art (Piskel), Blogger image hosting

Inspiration/Data: NASA Space Weather resources

🎨 Creativity

The project stands out for blending science, storytelling, and design — transforming educational content into an emotional journey.
Students wrote the script, drew characters, and programmed the animations themselves, merging art and technology.

🤝 Team Considerations

Our team discussed how to make scientific concepts accessible to kids while maintaining accuracy.
We prioritized visual clarity, language simplicity, and a message of hope and critical thinking.
Each member contributed to writing, illustration, and coding, guided by the mentor/teacher to ensure both scientific integrity and creativity.

projectDetails.summary:
Our project, “Stella’s Adventure,” is an educational and interactive mobile experience designed to make learning about space fun and accessible for children. We developed a colorful, story-driven interface where kids join Stella and her magical friends on an adventure through the solar system. The project combines storytelling, animation, and simple interactive elements to teach basic astronomy concepts in an engaging way.

This project addresses the challenge of making science education more appealing to younger audiences by using visual storytelling and gamification to capture attention and enhance learning retention. It’s important because it encourages curiosity, creativity, and an early interest in STEM fields, while also promoting diversity and representation through its inclusive characters and design.
projectDetails.details:
Our project was inspired by how common it has become for children to use their parents’ phones or have their own devices to play games. With that in mind, we wanted to create a digital story for mobile that could turn screen time into a fun and educational experience.

“Stella’s Adventure” is an interactive story where kids explore space alongside Stella, a curious who loves astronomy, and her magical friends (The Shining Sun and Fairy Aurora). The goal is to teach basic astronomy concepts through storytelling, colorful visuals, and interactive elements that encourage imagination and learning.

We developed a prototype using Figma, focusing on the design, user flow, and educational content. If implemented, the ideal programming languages for the mobile app would be Kotlin (for Android) or Swift (for iOS).

The project’s creativity lies in blending education and storytelling to make science appealing for young children. We also considered accessibility, inclusivity, and visual engagement to ensure the story could inspire curiosity and spark interest in space and STEM topics.

projectDetails.name: Project TDP - NASA
projectDetails.summary:
Bloomwatcher TDP’s Simulators module is an interactive toolset that enables users to model and visualize plant blooming events using NASA Earth observation datasets. Through this interface, users can select geographic regions, time windows, and vegetation types to generate bloom forecasts, simulate phenological trends, or explore bloom timing under different environmental scenarios. The simulators bridge raw satellite data and practical insight by converting complex metrics (e.g. reflectance changes, greenness indices) into intuitive bloom visualizations and predictions.

By offering an accessible simulation environment, this module directly addresses the challenge of making bloom event data actionable — for researchers, land managers, and conservationists alike. Its importance lies in empowering users to test “what-if” scenarios, anticipate critical bloom windows, and translate satellite observations into real-world decisions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview
BloomWatcher is an intelligent plant monitoring and disease detection system designed to help farmers, gardeners, and researchers maintain healthy crops. The project uses image recognition and environmental data analysis to identify early signs of plant stress, nutrient deficiencies, or disease outbreaks. By combining real-time monitoring with predictive analytics, BloomWatcher supports sustainable agriculture and reduces crop loss.

How It Works
BloomWatcher operates through a network of sensors and a camera module connected to a central processing unit. The system captures images of plant leaves and collects environmental data such as temperature, humidity, and soil moisture. Using a trained machine learning model, the software analyzes the images to detect abnormalities like discoloration, spots, or wilting. The results are displayed on a web dashboard, where users can view plant health status, receive alerts, and access recommendations for treatment or care.

Benefits

  • Enables early detection of plant diseases, preventing large-scale crop damage.
  • Reduces the need for manual inspection, saving time and labor.
  • Promotes sustainable farming by minimizing pesticide use through targeted treatment.
  • Provides data-driven insights for improving crop yield and resource management.
  • Accessible to both small-scale gardeners and large agricultural operations.

Intended Impact
The project aims to empower communities with technology that enhances food security and environmental sustainability. By making plant health monitoring more efficient and affordable, BloomWatcher contributes to smarter agriculture and supports global efforts to reduce waste and improve productivity.

Tools, Languages, and Hardware Used

  • Programming Languages: Python (for machine learning and data processing), JavaScript (for web interface)
  • Frameworks and Libraries: TensorFlow, OpenCV, Flask, React
  • Hardware: Raspberry Pi, camera module, DHT11 sensor (for temperature and humidity), soil moisture sensor
  • Software: Canva (for UI design and presentation), Google Cloud (for data storage and model deployment)

Creativity and Innovation
BloomWatcher integrates computer vision with environmental sensing to create a holistic plant monitoring solution. The combination of AI-driven image analysis and real-time sensor data provides a more accurate and dynamic understanding of plant health. The user-friendly dashboard design ensures accessibility for users with varying technical backgrounds.

Team Considerations
The team focused on:

  • Ensuring accuracy and reliability of disease detection through diverse dataset training.
  • Designing an intuitive interface for ease of use.
  • Balancing cost-effectiveness with performance to make the system scalable.
  • Addressing environmental sustainability by promoting efficient resource use.
  • Maintaining data privacy and security for users’ agricultural information.

BloomWatcher represents a fusion of technology and environmental awareness, offering a practical solution to one of agriculture’s most persistent challenges—maintaining healthy, pro
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Project
AI was a core component of the BloomWatcher system. It was used in the following ways:

  • Image Recognition: A convolutional neural network (CNN) model was trained using TensorFlow to identify plant diseases and detect early signs of stress from leaf images.
  • Data Analysis: AI algorithms analyzed environmental sensor data (temperature, humidity, soil moisture) to predict potential risks to plant health.
  • Predictive Insights: Machine learning models provided recommendations for preventive actions based on historical data and detected patterns.
  • Continuous Learning: The system improved over time by retraining the model with new images and feedback from users to enhance accuracy and adaptability.

projectDetails.name: Eyes to the Sky
projectDetails.summary: Our project is an immersive experience through time, focusing on space exploration — using music and images from the Hubble and James Webb telescopes. In this story, the player must identify stars and galaxies across different technological eras. After completing all challenges, the player will be able to explore the universe and identify celestial bodies freely. This makes our platform ideal for those who want to learn more about the universe or explore it.
projectDetails.details:
Project Motivation

From the dawn of civilization, observing the sky has guided humanity — leading travelers across oceans and now, through the lenses of Hubble and James Webb, guiding us to the edge of the universe itself.

But while the cosmos offers endless wonders, it also presents an endless challenge: how can we truly navigate it? How can we make sense of its immensity and beauty without feeling lost among the stars?

That question inspired us to create a simple and intuitive way to explore space imagery — where anyone can uncover the stories hidden within the light of distant worlds.

Our project invites you on an immersive journey through time and discovery. You’ll explore the universe as it was seen in different technological eras, identifying stars, galaxies, and nebulae that marked milestones in human exploration. Complete each challenge, unlock the knowledge of past generations, and then — the universe is yours to explore freely.

Because every time you look at the sky, you’re not just seeing the stars… You’re seeing the history of how we learned to dream beyond them — and the promise of a better future for those who still dare to care, to wonder, and to explore.


Experience Flow

Starting the application, the user sees a cinematic image from Nebulae near Milky Way!

In the first stage, the user is guided to locate Polaris to find the North. A dynamic digital compass is displayed, to provide a visual clue for the user. Clicking near Polaris triggers a zoom-in effect and a short narration explains its historical importance and impact for navigation.

The second stage introduces a telescope interaction, where the user searches for the Milky Way. Using a virtual lunette, the user can zoom and explore the detailed structure of our galaxy. The digital compass still provides guidance for finding the Milky Way.

The third stage presents the four main types of galaxies: spiral, barred spiral, elliptical, and irregular. The user engages with an interactive quiz, identifying the right type based on provided examples. Completing this stage reinforces the user’s knowledge of galactic structures and observation techniques.

After completing these guided stages, the user unlocks free exploration mode. In this mode, they can navigate the night sky, explore stars, galaxies, and nebulae at their own pace. The night sky map provides a fully immersive experience, allowing the user to continue discovering the universe and its features freely.

Tools

React, Git, CSS, Next, Tailwind, Vite were used for developing de Webpage

VoiceMode was used for a more immersive voice over.

projectDetails.details:
Threads of Light is an interactive story that blends science and empathy to teach players about Space Weather — the invisible solar phenomena that affect Earth.

In the game, Alice, a young girl who can connect with anything, becomes one with the Sun’s light. Guided by players, she travels through solar rays and witnesses how solar storms influence life on Earth.

The project combines hand-drawn illustrations, crafted to evoke the imagination and innocence of a child, with mini-games that portray the challenges and beauty of the Sun’s immense power.

Each mini-game highlights a different aspect of the Sun’s influence — from solar flares disrupting communication systems to the awe-inspiring auroras formed by charged particles.

The game was developed using the Godot Engine, coded primarily in GDScript, with additional audio design and image processing to enhance the storytelling.

We also built an API using Python (FastAPI) to retrieve and integrate real NASA data, making the experience both scientifically grounded and emotionally engaging.

projectDetails.name: Project TPM Squad
projectDetails.summary: Our goal was to create a fun and enjoyable experience that helps people understand climate change and its impact on our planet. Our project, "Will It Rain On My Parade," takes complicated weather information and makes it easy to explore. We built an app with a beautiful, interactive 3D model of Earth. Using this digital globe, you can simply pick a place, and our system puts a marker on it, showing you key weather info right away. We used a mix of technologies to make this happen—from Python to process the weather data we get from places like NASA, to JavaScript that creates the smooth, immersive experience you see on screen. By combining stunning visuals with a simple, user-friendly design, our app helps you not only check the forecast for your next event but also see how different parts of our global climate system are connected. We hope this project inspires everyone to think more about our planet and the small steps we can take to help it.
projectDetails.details:
Core Features

Interactive 3D Earth Model

The project's central interface is a visually stunning 3D model of the Earth. Users can interact with the globe, rotating it and selecting specific locations, providing an intuitive and engaging way to explore global weather patterns.

User-Centric Data Visualization

The platform features responsive visualizations of key meteorological datasets from sources like NASA's Power API. The user experience is designed to be simple and direct, with a single page providing all necessary information. The data displayed includes:

Temperature: With an interactive display that allows users to seamlessly switch between Celsius and Fahrenheit.

Precipitation: Crucial data for planning outdoor activities and events.

Wind & Humidity: Providing a comprehensive view of local atmospheric conditions.

Simplified Interface

The user interface is designed for all ages, featuring a clean layout and minimal navigation. Key elements like an info button provide a clean way to access project details, while the core interaction remains focused on the 3D globe and its data visualizations.

Technology Stack

The project is built on a robust and modern technology stack, with a clear separation between the frontend and backend.

Frontend

The user-facing application is developed using standard web technologies:

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: For the core structure, styling, and interactivity.

Three.js: This powerful JavaScript library is used to render and control the 3D Earth model, ensuring a smooth and immersive experience.

Backend & Data Processing

The backend handles the data-intensive tasks, ensuring the information is accurate and reliable:

Python: Used for data analysis, processing, and integrating with external APIs.

Jupyter Notebook: Serves as the primary environment for data manipulation and visualization before integrating into the final application.

NASA's Power API: The primary source for meteorological and climate data, providing accurate and real-time information.

projectDetails.name: Project URBANA-IA
projectDetails.summary:
URBANA-IA is an intelligent geospatial decision-support platform that turns NASA Earth Observation (EO) data into actionable urban intelligence. Piloted in Campinas, Brazil, the platform tackles three intertwined crises common across Latin American cities: rapid unplanned growth, spatial inequality, and climate vulnerability.

URBANA-IA fuses Landsat and MODIS data with SEDAC socioeconomic layers and local GIS to generate high-value analytics—land-use/land-cover maps, urban heat island risk, green-space accessibility, informal-settlement risk, and more. A 3D digital twin (web-based) lets planners and communities see current conditions and simulate future scenarios (e.g., new linear parks, shade trees, bus-fleet electrification) and compare trade-offs with quantitative KPIs.

Built around three principles—Actionable, Integrated, Participatory—URBANA-IA directly supports SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) by enabling evidence-based planning, healthier public spaces, and climate resilience for the most vulnerable neighborhoods. The pilot provides a blueprint for scalable adoption across Latin America via a cloud “toolkit,” open-source core, and partnerships with local governments, universities, and development banks.
projectDetails.details:
https://urbana-ai-al8j.onrender.com/

What it is. URBANA-IA is a modular platform that transforms geospatial and NASA Earth Observation data into useful insights for cities and supports interactive, hypothetical planning through a recommendation system powered by an LLM (Large Language Model).
This model identifies strategic opportunities for sustainable urban planning and policy action.

The problem. Latin American cities face hyper-urbanization, uneven access to green space, and intensifying extreme heat/flood risks that disproportionately harm low-income communities. Municipal teams rarely have accessible tools to turn data into equitable, timely policy.

How it works.

  • Data fusion pipeline. URBANA-IA performs automated ingestion and harmonization of geospatial datasets from NASA, characterizing specific urban spaces with detailed soil types, land cover, and climatic attributes. These datasets serve as technical references for planning interventions that directly benefit local populations.
  • Policy dashboard. The platform features a policy dashboard containing Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) aligned with SDG 11 and local action plans (e.g., the Campinas Climate Action Plan). It also provides exportable reports for decision-makers and public transparency portals that strengthen community engagement and accountability.
  • The proposed interventions are shared with the public to assess citizen satisfaction and ensure full transparency throughout the planning process.
    This participatory approach gives residents an active role in shaping their communities, strengthening civic engagement, trust, and collaborative urban governance.

Why it’s innovative.

  • Bridges EO → policy with a single workflow that is explainable, reproducible, and participatory.
  • Moves beyond “citywide averages” to neighborhood-level equity (who benefits, who is left out).
  • Puts powerful analytics into a no-install web app usable by planners, officials, and residents.

Benefits & impact.

  • Health & climate: targets heat-risk hotspots for cooling interventions.
  • Equity: identifies green-space deserts and transit gaps in vulnerable areas.
  • Governance: creates a shared, visual evidence base to reduce conflict and speed consensus.
  • Scalability: city-agnostic core, open-source components, and a cloud “URBANA-IA Toolkit” for rapid replication across the region.

Tools, languages, and stack.

  • Data/AI: Python, GeoPandas, Rasterio.
  • Web: deck.gl; Node/TypeScript.
  • DevOps: containerized services; cloud storage for rasters/tiles.

Future Work:

  • 3D digital twin and simulation. Developed with CesiumJS and procedural rules (CityEngine style). Users design proposed interventions (e.g., a linear park), and the system instantly updates indicators (cooling effect, percentage of residents within a 10-minute walk, flood mitigation co-benefits) to compare scenarios.

Ex: https://geoinfo.dados.embrapa.br/geoserver/ows?service=WFS&version=1.0.0&request=GetFeature&typename=geonode%3Ace_fazendinha_km47_solos_rj_v9&outputFormat=json&srs=EPSG%3A4326&srsName=EPSG%3A4326

URBANA-IA leverages Artificial Intelligence in three key ways to transform raw Earth Observation data into actionable insights for sustainable urban planning:

  • Policy–Reality Alignment with NLP.Natural Language Processing extracts planning objectives from local climate and development policies (e.g., tree canopy targets, riparian buffer protections) and compares them with satellite-derived indicators. This identifies compliance gaps, supports accountability, and highlights neighborhoods most at risk.
  • AI-assisted ideation & coding.Generative AI tools — Gemini, ChatGPT, and Perplexity — supported the refinement of the concept and accelerated development. Around 40% of the codebase benefited from AI assistance in tasks like code generation, debugging, and data pipeline optimization. projectDetails.name: Project WELL LIVING TO HEAL THE PLANET
projectDetails.summary:
"Technology for Well Living: Sowing Consciousness for Planetary Healing" is a global initiative that aims to mobilize every inhabitant of Earth to plant at least one tree each, using an accessible digital tool that recommends the ideal species for each biome based on soil and climate data. With the potential to generate 8.2 billion trees and capture approximately 180 million tons of CO₂ per year, the project directly addresses the challenges of the climate crisis and environmental degradation.
In addition to mitigating global warming, it promotes benefits such as restoring biodiversity, improving air and water quality, combating desertification, and creating green jobs. Its technology is low-cost and highly scalable, and can be integrated with cell phones, community networks, and educational centers.
The proposal is universal and inclusive, with multilingual educational campaigns and partnerships with schools, NGOs, governments, and influencers. The central message, “Planting a tree is planting life” — reinforces the transformative power of a simple action, capable of awakening ecological awareness and regenerating the planet.
projectDetails.details:

Plataformas: Android, iOS, Web

Machine Learning: Modelos preditivos para recomendação de espécies nativas e adaptadas

Criatividade e Inovação: A proposta transforma uma simples ação, plantar uma árvore, em um movimento global de cura planetária. A tecnologia é inclusiva, de baixo custo e escalável, com uma interface amigável e gamificada que oferece certificados digitais, vídeos motivacionais e integração com mídias sociais. A campanha educacional é traduzida para todos os idiomas, promovendo o engajamento em escolas, ONGs e governos.

Acessibilidade digital em regiões remotas

Diversidade bioclimática global

Inclusão de comunidades tradicionais e indígenas

projectDetails.name: Project Word 2 World
projectDetails.summary: Our project is a story designed to teach children and young audiences about space weather, including solar flares, coronal mass ejections, and their effects on Earth. Through the journey of Matti, an old man who lives in Finlandia, and his encounters with local villagers, an electrician, an astronaut, and an astrophysicist, viewers learn how charged particles from the Sun interact with Earth’s magnetic field, disrupt technology, and create the aurora borealis. The animation addresses the challenge by combining narrative storytelling with scientific concepts, making complex phenomena accessible and engaging.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is an educational storytelling experience created to introduce children and young learners to the concept of space weather — the energy and particles released by the Sun that can influence life on Earth. Through a narrative-driven storybook, readers follow Matti, his cat Lumi, and their new friends on a journey that begins with a broken radio and unfolds into an exploration of cosmic phenomena. Along the way, scientific concepts such as solar flares, magnetic fields, auroras, and their effects on technology are woven seamlessly into the story.

The project aims to increase scientific literacy, spark curiosity about astronomy, and help learners understand how cosmic forces are deeply connected to everyday human life. To achieve this, we prioritized accessible language and an engaging narrative built around relatable characters and meaningful discoveries.

To structure the story, we created scenes with explanatory text delivered from the perspective of an omniscient narrator who follows Matti, allowing viewers to understand scientific phenomena while staying immersed in the story. The concepts were found in NASA resources, such as Brazilian Space Weather Study and Monitoring Program (EMBRACE).

The development process combined storyboarding, digital illustration, and narrative design with the use of Canva for visual creation and layout. Additionally, we integrated AI-powered language tools to support the revision and refinement of the text, ensuring clarity and accuracy throughout the story.
projectDetails.aiReferences: We used AI tools to review and refine the text, improving clarity, grammar, and readability. AI also assisted in creating images and scenes based on prompts developed by our team. All creative decisions, story structure, and scientific content were determined by the team. Finally, each team member was responsible for manually reviewing and refining specific parts of the project.

projectDetails.name: Project ZoomI
projectDetails.summary: ZoomI is a web platform developed to explore, analyze and investigate NASA's vast datasets based on the Moon and its geological features. Designed for scientific research, journalistic inquiry and curious minds alike, ZoomI enables users to seamlessly navigate over the lunar surface, observe cataloged geological features and discover new patterns intertwined with the legacy of the Apollo missions. Equipped with multi-scale zoom interface, near-real-time rendering of massive remote sensing satellite datasets, the platform offers a smooth and immersive 3D experience to explore lunar mares, rimas, valleys and craters highlighting their geological and historical aspects across multiple scales. Beyond localized and punctual analysis, ZoomI traces the trajectory of discoveries from the successive Apollo Missions, illustrating how each mission contributed to the progressive mapping and understanding of the lunar surface. Designed with scientific dissemination in mind, ZoomI lowers technological barriers to information access and empowers people with knowledge about Earth’s most important natural satellite, the ever-present Moon.
projectDetails.details:
https://github.com/thsergitox/nasa

Context Information

What does it do or how does it work?

The project is a web-based lunar explorer that allows users to view and interact with detailed lunar data through both 2D and 3D interfaces.

Users can explore:

  • The Apollo mission landing sites, reconstructed with accurate coordinates and related geographic features.
  • Geological elements such as craters, rilles, valleys, and lunar maria, represented through official datasets.
  • A 3D globe view for immersive navigation and a 2D map for scientific inspection and labeling.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The project aims to provide an enhanced and accessible experience for exploring the Moon, allowing users of all backgrounds to interact with lunar data in an intuitive and engaging way. The goal is to make lunar exploration inclusive and educational, requiring only curiosity and the desire to learn more about our natural satellite.

Additionally, this workflow and visualization approach can be extended to other celestial bodies, enabling scalable and reusable tools for planetary data visualization beyond the Moon.

What factors did your team consider?

Key Features

  • High-resolution lunar visualization: Integration of official USGS and NASA datasets to display the Moon’s surface at large scale and high resolution (e.g., imagery with resolutions on the order of X meters per pixel).
  • Historical and scientific context: Visualization of the most significant lunar events and exploration sites, including Apollo mission landing zones and their surrounding geological features.
  • Interactive web experience: A structured and user-friendly web interface that allows users to navigate, search, and learn about the most relevant lunar landmarks, such as Apollo landing sites, craters, mountains, and maria.

What makes your project creative or innovative?

The innovation lies in connecting Apollo's historical data with modern visualization techniques, transforming static lunar maps into a living, explorable digital environment. The project also emphasizes data accessibility and reuse, promoting open science by leveraging public datasets and converting them into interactive, easy-to-use formats on the web.

Demo

When we are on the Home page, we have the possibility to interact with Visit Landing Sites, which is the view where we can explore the landing areas of each Apollo mission and visualize the landing sites in ultra-high resolution, using the previously explained implementation that combines 8 NASA services for rendering, integrated with the OpenLayers library.

We also have a Moon Tour, where we define a route of ten interesting points on the Moon that users can explore interactively.

Finally, there is Moon Data, where the lunar datasets are presented individually so they can be explored in a detailed and independent way.

How did we do it?

Data processing:

The official geometries (WKT) were extracted from the United States Geological Survey (USGS) website corresponding to the entities defined in the Keyhole Markup Language (KML) file, which contains geographic information structured using tags. These geometries were used to generate files in GeoJSON format, a widely used standard for representing spatial data, ready for visualization and analysis.

The graph shows the processing flow of a KML file, from the loading and extraction of metadata from each Placemark, to the obtaining of geometries (WKT or center point) and their conversion to GeoJSON, ending with the creation of a collection of Features ready for analysis or visualization.

Example with the Mare Tranquillitatis area: Take the MOON_nomenclature_center_pts.kml file and convert it to Mare_Tranquillitatis_Polygon.geojson, following the process described in the flowchart.

To achieve this, CesiumJS libraries were implemented with React, integrating NASA's Trek API, which made it possible to generate a spherical map of the Moon capable of showing the polygons of the exact locations of the Apollo missions and other important geological features such as craters, valleys, rilles, and lunar maria. However, the image quality provided by this initial API was not sufficient for detailed visualization. After researching existing NASA implementations, eight additional APIs were identified at: https://wms1.im-ldi.com/lunaserv.html. These APIs allow for higher resolution and quality images to be rendered, enabling a significantly improved visualization experience for the Apollo missions and other geographic data of the Moon. We combined all the versions we found at.

To render Apollo missions in some posts on https://lroc.im-ldi.com, based on that, we now have two views, one of the moon in spherical form, and another of the specific Apollo mission with maximum visual quality. We managed to have both views on a single page. Here is the comparison.

Obtaining a totally radical difference while also having a general context of how the moon looks. When it is located at the following point.

projectDetails.summary: This project explores the creative use of artificial intelligence tools to develop visual storytelling assets for an original narrative world. Using AI image generation platforms, each scene and character was designed with cinematic composition, emotional depth, and stylistic consistency inspired by Pixar and Studio Ghibli aesthetics. The process involved iterative experimentation with prompts, refining lighting, proportions, and atmosphere to achieve harmony between realism and fantasy. This approach addresses the challenge of translating imagination into tangible visuals without requiring large production teams or advanced artistic skills. It demonstrates how AI can empower independent creators to visualize complex ideas, accelerate pre-production, and enhance artistic direction. By combining human creativity with generative intelligence, the project highlights the importance of accessible digital tools in modern storytelling, democratizing visual design and opening new paths for innovation in animation, gaming, and interactive media.
projectDetails.details:
The project combines multiple AI and creative technologies to build a visually immersive storytelling experience that connects emotion, science, and imagination. It uses Midjourney for concept art and character visualization, ChatGPT and Gemini for narrative development, dialogue writing, and structural design, and Speechma and ElevenLabs to generate expressive voiceovers that bring characters to life. OpenProcessing was used for interactive visual experiments, while Wix served as the platform for showcasing the final experience in a web-based format.

The project’s main benefit is demonstrating how artificial intelligence can accelerate creative production while maintaining artistic depth and human emotion. The intended impact is to inspire creators and students to view AI as a creative collaborator rather than a replacement. The creativity lies in combining visual storytelling, sound, and technology to produce a cohesive, emotionally engaging narrative. The team focused on accessibility, innovation, and authenticity in every decision.

projectDetails.projectReferences: [Space junk is any object launched into Earth's orbital space that is no longer useful, such as decommissioned satellites, satellite or rocket fragments, and even instruments and tools lost by astronauts during space missions. "According to NASA, since 1957, with the launch of Sputnik by the Soviet Union, approximately 4,000 satellites have been launched into orbit around our planet, many of them now decommissioned. These objects "travel" through space at speeds of up to 36,000 km/h, and approximately 200 of them fall to Earth every year.  The higher the altitude of space debris, the longer it will remain in orbit. For example, debris at an altitude of around 600 km takes years to enter Earth's atmosphere, while at an altitude of 1000 km it takes centuries.  Space debris poses more of a danger to active satellites and manned spacecraft in space (and future space expeditions) than to Earth's inhabitants, because upon contact with the atmosphere, much of the debris burns and is destroyed. Those that do manage to cross this barrier generally fall into the oceans, which account for 75% of the planet's volume.  Technology has yet to produce equipment capable of collecting space debris. The only plausible solution so far is to direct satellites into so-called graveyard orbits, which would essentially program a satellite to follow an orbital path far from Earth once its useful life has expired. ](https://brasilescola.uol.com.br/geografia/lixo-espacial.htm)

The project "Urban Environment: Monitoring and Alleviating Urban Heat Islands and Extreme Cold by Utilizing NASA Data" proposes the use of NASA's Earth observation data to monitor and reduce the impacts of extreme heat and intense cold in cities. Climate change intensifies these phenomena, causing serious health risks such as dehydration, heart disease, respiratory illnesses, and hypothermia. The project demonstrates that satellite information enables the identification of vulnerable areas, prediction of extreme events, and support for public health decisions.
This data assists governments and urban planners in adjusting policies, strengthening awareness campaigns, creating green spaces, adapting infrastructure, and better preparing the healthcare system for emergencies. The proposal argues that coordinated actions among public agencies, health, environment, and social services are essential to protect the population.
In conclusion, the project emphasizes that integrating technology and data-driven policies is fundamental for developing more sustainable and resilient cities, capable of ensuring people's well-being and safety in the face of climate extremes.

The main benefits involve improving emergency responses, developing more resilient urban planning, reducing climate-related illnesses, and establishing its operation based on climate maps and models generated by the Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS), which integrates atmospheric forecasts with satellite data. This information enables the identification of vulnerable areas and the anticipation of risks to the population, especially for sensitive groups such as the elderly, children, exposed workers, and rural communities.

Preventive measures based on scientific evidence. The expected effect is to make cities more sustainable and safe, increasing their capacity to adapt to climate change.

The project stands out for its innovation in combining space technology with public health, converting NASA information into practical tools to save lives and promote well-being in cities.

projectDetails.name: AquaRoute
projectDetails.summary:
AquaRoute is an intelligent water management system developed to optimize water distribution in drought-affected regions of Brazil, especially in the state of Paraíba. The platform integrates data from the National Water Agency (ANA) and NASA APIs to improve planning and resource allocation.

Users can register communities on a map by providing population size and storage capacity. The system automatically identifies the nearest reservoir and predicts when resupply will be needed, based on the average water consumption per person. It also calculates an Aridity Index using real-time climate data from the NASA POWER API, estimating regional dryness through the analysis of precipitation and evapotranspiration.

Additionally, AquaRoute includes a Volumetric Calculator that estimates reservoir volume using Copernicus Sentinel satellite imagery and terrain elevation models from NASA SRTM. By combining these tools with the Google Maps Routes API, the system determines the most efficient water supply routes.

Although still a prototype, AquaRoute demonstrates strong potential to support future water planning and management, contributing to more efficient and sustainable water distribution in regions facing scarcity.
projectDetails.details:
What does AquaRoute do?
Our project initially loads all the water reservoirs registered in ANA (National Water Agency) for the state of Paraíba. The user can register communities (urban and rural) by providing a name, their water storage capacity, and the number of people living there. The choice of location is made by clicking on the map. With this data, the system calculates which reservoir should supply the community (the nearest one) and when this community will need resupply (when the water volume of the storage capacity is less than 30%).
This calculation is made taking into account the average daily water consumption of Brazilians (data from the National Confederation of Municipalities), which is 150 liters, to estimate, based on the number of people in the community, a date for resupply.

Aridity Index:

In addition, an aridity index is calculated, which estimates how dry that region is, following the formula:
AI = Annual Total Precipitation / Annual Potential Evapotranspiration
How it works: Data such as precipitation and temperature from the last 365 days are extracted from the NASA POWER API, and Evapotranspiration is calculated through the Hargreaves-Samani formula using:
Maximum and minimum temperature (T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN)
Extraterrestrial solar radiation (TOA_SW_DWN)
Formula: ET0 = 0.0023 × (Tmed + 17.8) × √(Tmax - Tmin) × Ra

Volumetric Calculator:
We also implemented a small feature that can automatically estimate the water volume of reservoirs using satellite images (through Copernicus Sentinel) and terrain elevation models downloaded via OpenTopography / NASA SRTM.
It identifies the water body through spectral indices, filters only the main reservoir, and crosses this area with topographic data to calculate the average depth and volume in cubic hectometers.
All of this is done quickly, without the need for field measurements.

Distribution Plan:
The distribution plan is a table that orders which communities have priority in supply, taking into account the total stored water and the aridity index of that region.

Routing:
Using the Google Maps Routes API, the best route is calculated based on the points to be visited, aiming to achieve the shortest time and greater fuel efficiency.

Social Impact:
AquaRoute allows for more efficient management and better planning of the water resources of a given region. We hope to make this system available to government departments so that they can mitigate problems related to the lack of water.

Our project uses languages such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Python, aiming for easier implementation and prototyping. We use several libraries to perform calculations and also various research software tools to study reports about these reservoirs.
To reach this problem, we took into account social factors of our region, which has large water reservoirs but, even so, people in more distant communities still suffer from water shortages.

challengeDetails.title: A World Away: Hunting for Exoplanets with AI
challengeDetails.excerpt: Data from several different space-based exoplanet surveying missions have enabled discovery of thousands of new planets outside our solar system, but most of these exoplanets were identified manually. With advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML), it is possible to automatically analyze large sets of data collected by these missions to identify exoplanets.
