projectDetails.name: Project Ocllo Space
projectDetails.summary:
The website “Occlo Space” was developed with an easy-to-use, engaging, and accessible interface, designed for children to learn about space weather through interactive stories, quizzes, and a “laboratory” where, in addition to learning, they can challenge themselves and put their acquired knowledge into practice. 


On this journey, they will dive into the story of the Sun with the help of little Kuarasy, our guide, who will travel through different eras and cultures, showing their relationships with the Sun and how they perceived its phenomena. 


As a bonus, Kuarasy will also teach, using data provided by NASA and other government sources, that, these days, these phenomena have names, are studied, and explain what really happens in the Sun, causing so many consequences for us here on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
We set out to teach children around the world about space weather and show how it impacts everyone’s daily life, but in a non-traditional way, using lots of creativity. 

Knowing that our audience is children sparked our imagination, as capturing their attention requires careful planning, playfulness, and interactivity. At this stage, when everything is a discovery, we realized our solution needed to allow them to actively participate in this adventure, with the Sun, the great star of our challenge, as the main character. 

For this reason, we created an informative and interactive platform that blends learning with fun, offering a complete and immersive experience of space weather.

For the website development, we worked primarily with JavaScript, using it as the foundation for building our interactive features. To support the process, we also made use of tools such as the React framework and Google Scholar, which helped us both in development and in research validation. It includes APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) that link users to official scientific sources, allowing access to more detailed information on the topics covered.

The website’s sections were structured as: 

  • The Sun in Civilization’s History:
    • The user’s journey begins under the guidance of Kuarasy, who presents the scientific knowledge and leads them through the narratives.  
    • Kuarasy will guide users through each story, each focusing on a distinct solar event, presented in the chronological order of their occurrence. The narratives of the first five civilizations are conveyed from a mythological perspective: the Babylonians discuss their studies on sunspots and eclipses; the Māori describe solar flares; the Incas introduce coronal mass ejections; the Egyptians examine solar winds and auroras; and the Greeks elaborate on geomagnetic storms. 
    • The sixth and final chapter of our journey through solar phenomena in this section, across civilizations, focuses on our present-day society, where concrete studies on solar events exist. It will also reveal to the user an important detail about Kuarasy’s identity, who has traveled through so many civilizations. 
  • Impacts Section:
    • In this impacts section, new characters appear to explain the effects of space weather on the lives of astronauts in space and people living on Earth. The characters — Ana, Maria, Carlos, Pedro, and Lia — guide the narrative in this interactive section, which also incorporates APIs. It presents the real effects of solar events on our society, showcasing actual occurrences caused by space weather through engaging narratives that allow users to understand the scientific facts clearly.
  • Section for Practicing Acquired Knowledge:
    • It is essential to test all the knowledge acquired, and with this in mind, the website was developed with a quiz section, where each round contains 8 questions about the events and consequences studied in the previous sections. This tool allows children to challenge themselves, check if they have truly absorbed the lessons, and have fun while reinforcing their learning. 
    • Additionally, the website features a practical activities tab, consisting of 8 interactive experiences. For example, in the “Make Your Own Aurora” activity, users are encouraged to use their creativity to draw beautiful auroras. To assist them, clicking “Access” directs them to a NASA extension that provides a complete step-by-step guide, making learning hands-on, fun, and educational. 
  • Solar System Tour and Glossary:
    • To conclude the user experience, the website features two additional tabs: “Solar System Tour” and “Glossary.” The “Solar System Tour” will show young aspiring scientists, as well as students, that each planet in our Solar System has its own climate and that all are connected to the Sun. The “Glossary” was created as an extra aid to facilitate learning and to help users better understand the scientific terms used.
  • Objective achieved:
    • We achieved our goal of developing a solution that teaches science in a fun, simple, and accessible way for children, allowing them to explore, learn, and enjoy every moment of the process. However, Occlo Space will continue to expand this educational experience, bringing its innovative approach to new horizons.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
To develop the project, we relied on several artificial intelligence tools. However, we applied prompt engineering to ensure that the responses were aligned with our goals, adding depth and personality to the outcomes.  

For the storytelling, we used ChatGPT with a combination of prompt engineering, chain-of-thought techniques, deep research, and best-response strategies. When it came to the visuals, we experimented with different AI platforms until we found the identity we were looking for. Among the tools, we used Lovable, ChatGPT itself, and Gemini with its new Nano Banana model. All of our images were made with the help of AI. We choose to cut off the watermark as a design choice, but we are keeping clear that all of our images were AI generated.

For the soundtrack, aiming for a high-quality result, we designed a prompt that acted as both a music producer and composer. This prompt interpreted our stories and generated specific instructions for Suno, the music-creation AI we used. In this way, we ensured that the music was always in harmony with the narratives.

projectDetails.name: Project Os 5 do Nordeste
projectDetails.summary: The project seeks to promote environmental awareness in Campina Grande through education and technology. We use data from NASA's MODIS sensor, which allows us to observe changes in vegetation cover and NDVI, identifying areas with vegetation loss and possible environmental impacts, such as increased temperature and reduced quality of life. Based on this information, the “Living Earth” project was developed for schools, with the aim of teaching the importance of nature preservation from an early age. Children learn through school gardens and practical activities, developing a sense of care and environmental responsibility. In addition, the “EcoMind” app complements the project, providing access to data on vegetation, sustainable actions, and educational activities. Together, the use of MODIS, environmental education, and technology form an integrated strategy that unites science, education, and community, encouraging a new generation that is more aware and committed to the future of the planet.
projectDetails.details:
The Living Earth project's main objective is to identify and propose solutions for the lack of access to green areas in growing cities, such as Campina Grande (PB). We use Earth science data from NASA, especially from the MODIS sensor, which provides the NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index). This data allows us to analyze the health of vegetation, locate degraded areas, and map regions with low green coverage.

Using this information, the EcoMind app was developed to integrate environmental data and community actions. It shows updated maps of green areas, indicates priority locations for urban reforestation, and suggests sustainable activities for schools and communities, connecting science and environmental education.

The benefits include improved air quality, urban thermal balance, increased psychological and physical well-being of the population, and encouragement of environmental awareness. The intended impact is to promote greener, healthier, and more socially just cities.

The project was developed using tools such as Python (for MODIS/NDVI data analysis), Google Earth Engine (for satellite image visualization), and Figma and Flutter (for the design and development of the EcoMind app).

The creativity of the project lies in combining space technology, sustainability, and education—allowing students and citizens to actively participate in environmental monitoring. Our team considered factors such as social justice, environmental education, climate change, urban growth, and digital accessibility to ensure that the project is inclusive, innovative, and transformative.

projectDetails.name: AstroShield
projectDetails.summary: This project is an interactive simulation and visualization platform that models asteroid impacts on Earth using real NASA Near-Earth Object (NEO) data and USGS environmental datasets. It enables users to select real asteroids or input custom parameters such as diameter, velocity, and density, then calculates physical consequences — including released energy, crater formation, seismic magnitude, and estimated population exposure — through physics-based equations. The system visualizes effects like blast radius, tsunami potential, and ground shock on 2D and 3D geospatial maps. It also integrates mitigation strategies (kinetic impactor, gravity tractor, laser ablation) with probabilistic success estimations. By combining scientific data, analytical modeling, and intuitive visualization, the project enhances public understanding, supports hazard assessment, and provides a decision-support tool for evaluating near-Earth impact risks and deflection strategies.
projectDetails.details:
What the project does / How it works

Provides an interactive platform to visualize asteroid orbits, select impact points, and simulate collision effects using real data and physical models. 2D (map) and 3D (globe) interfaces allow users to explore, focus, and animate impact scenarios. The core integration occurs in App.tsx, with visualization components such as WorldMap, Globe3D, and the animation mode ImpactAnimationScreen.

Benefits and intended impact

Translates technical data into actionable visualizations for the public, scientists, and decision-makers — including estimates of energy release, crater formation, tsunamis, and seismic magnitude (based on ImpactApiResult). Supports decision-making and risk communication through interactive controls and result panels (RightPanel, AsteroidControls, ImpactResults).

Data and technical integration

Consumes NASA’s NEO data via the fetchRealNASAData utility and enriches it with orbital elements when available. Batch processing examples are in realNasaApi.ts.

Calls backend simulation services (simulateCustomImpact, simulateAsteroidImpact) returning typed results (ImpactApiResult).

Local damage and radius calculations use utilities such as computeDamageRadiusBasicKm and trajectory logic in calculateBestImpactPoint.

Tools, languages, and software used

Stack: TypeScript + React (Vite). See package.json and tsconfig.json.

Libraries: D3 for maps (WorldMap), Three.js / react-three-fiber for 3D scenes (Globe3D), local UI components in [src/components/ui], and fetch for HTTP requests (api.ts, realNasaApi.ts).

External data: NASA NEO API (NEO Feed, JPL), impact backend (base in [src/utils/api.ts]), and optional USGS layers (topography/tsunami) for environmental modeling.

Creativity and differentiators

Integrates orbital tracking (NASA) with consequence modeling (backend + local utilities), combining scientific exploration with public storytelling through 3D/2D animations and interactive panels. Reusable components include AsteroidList, AsteroidDetails, RightPanel, and AsteroidPanel.

Enables testing of mitigation strategies (deflection) through controls in AsteroidControls and custom simulations.

Team considerations

Accuracy vs. usability: Combines backend simulations with optimistic local estimations for immediate feedback.

API constraints: Handles NASA API rate limits with error messages (realNasaApi.ts) and alerts (App.tsx).

Technical transparency: Displays key formulas (e.g., kinetic energy E=12mv2E = \frac{1}{2}mv^2E=21​mv2 and seismic magnitude via logarithmic relation in api.ts).

Accessibility and communication: Informative layers in ImpactResults and tooltips across multiple components enhance understanding for general audiences.
projectDetails.aiReferences: We used the latest version of ChatGPT, along with GitHub Copilot and Claude, for multiple purposes — including code generation, architectural design, and documentation writing. These tools supported the development of accurate physical and environmental models, refinement of TypeScript and React components, and integration of NASA and USGS datasets to simulate and visualize realistic asteroid impact scenarios.

node.title: TEMPO 11
node.excerpt:
Hello, everyone!
We are TEMPO 11: the first to land, the first to change. 
Our mission is to turn science into action, transforming real-time atmospheric insights into tools that help communities breathe better and live healthier.

projectDetails.name: Project TEMPO 11
projectDetails.summary:
Created by team TEMPO 11, BreathSafe envisions a world where humanity breathes in sync with Earth. Inspired by NASA’s Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) mission, our app transforms satellite-based air quality data into real-time, human-centered health intelligence.

By integrating NASA’s hourly measurements of NO₂, O₃, and PM₂.₅ with ground sensors, health datasets, and AI-driven predictions, BreathSafe anticipates pollution peaks and alerts users before exposure becomes dangerous. Personalized notifications, adapted to each user’s health profile that helps individuals with asthma, bronchitis, or cardiovascular conditions make timely, life-protective decisions.

Our mission is to make NASA’s environmental data directly relevant to human well-being, helping communities breathe safer, live smarter, and move in sync with Earth.
projectDetails.details:
INTRODUCTION

Every breath we take tells a story about our planet. For millions of people around the world, that story has become one of silent danger , the air they breathe is slowly harming their health. According to the World Health Organization, nearly everyone on Earth , 99% of the global population is exposed to air that exceeds safe pollution levels.

These pollutants travel through the atmosphere, crossing cities and countries. What makes this problem even more urgent is the lack of easy, real-time information that could help people understand and protect themselves from poor air quality.

WHY WE MAKE THE DIFFERENCE ?

BreathSafe, developed by team TEMPO 11, transforms NASA’s atmospheric science into an intelligent, user-centered health protection system. The platform integrates real-time air quality measurements from NASA’s Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) mission with ground-based sensors, public health datasets, and advanced AI analytics.

🌎Home Screen – Where Data Meets Action

⚙️Features That Make a Difference

Each function was designed to turn complex air data into clear and actionable insights for users.

🫧 Air Quality View

Our Air Quality View feature allows users to see real-time air quality conditions in their area. By combining NASA satellite data with local ground measurements, it provides an easy-to-understand visualization of pollutants such as PM2.5, NO₂, and ozone levels.

📍Personalized location

The Personalized Location feature uses real-time geolocation to identify the user’s position and provide accurate air quality data for their exact area. By automatically connecting to NASA’s satellite information and local monitoring stations, it ensures that every user receives precise and relevant updates.

🔔Subscription for alerts

The Subscription for Alerts feature keeps users informed about sudden changes in air quality. By subscribing, users receive instant notifications when pollution levels rise or when conditions become safer for outdoor activities.

These alerts are powered by real-time data from NASA satellites and ground sensors, ensuring that information is both accurate and timely. This feature empowers users to make proactive decisions, protecting their health, adjusting their routines, and staying aware of environmental conditions wherever they are.

🩺Recomendations based in each profile

The Recommendations Based on Each Profile feature delivers personalized guidance according to the user’s health and lifestyle. Whether a user is elderly, a child, pregnant, or has respiratory conditions, the system provides tailored advice on outdoor activities, exercise, and exposure to air pollution. It helps users make safer choices for themselves and their families, transforming complex environmental data into practical, everyday decisions.

💡 Tips

🛰️ TECHNICAL APROACH

1. Data Sources & APIs

  • NASA TEMPO: high-resolution air pollution data (O₃, NO₂, CO, CH₂O, PM, Aerosol Index).
  • Meteomatics API: real-time meteorological parameters (temperature, wind speed, humidity, solar radiation, precipitation, pressure).
  • IPCC CIESIN SRES Dataset: historical and projected emissions of reactive gases (CH₄, CO, NOₓ, NMVOC, SO₂).

2. Data Processing & Integration

  • Spatial and temporal harmonization using WGS84 / EPSG:4326.
  • Bilinear interpolation and nearest neighbor sampling for spatial alignment.
  • Normalization to SI units with validation via quality flags.
  • Handling missing data through exponential decay and median neighborhood fill under clouded pixels.

3. Analytical Model

  • Mamdani-type Fuzzy Logic System with over 100 expert-defined rules based on peer-reviewed literature.
  • Triangular and Gaussian membership functions with four fuzzy sets (low, moderate, high, extreme).
  • Multivariate fuzzy inference covering particulate, photochemical ozone, and combustion risks.
  • Centroid defuzzification produces a final air-quality class (Good → Hazardous).

4. AI & Automation Layer

  • Small Language Model: Qwen2.5-1.5B (Transformer, ~1.5B parameters).
    • Generates bilingual (EN/PT) explanations and contextual recommendations.
    • Interprets fuzzy system outputs and summarizes insights for end users.
  • Compact AI enables low-latency reasoning and automated environmental reporting.

5. System Architecture

  • Progressive Web App (PWA) collects user geolocation and sends it to the inference API.
  • Serverless backend with autoscaling, sub-second latency (<800 ms), and full traceability.
  • REST API endpoints for inference and explainability, enabling audit of fuzzy rule activation.
  • Secure infrastructure using container orchestration, key vaults, and OpenTelemetry for observability.

6. Calibration & Validation

  • Cross-validation using AERONET and urban monitoring stations for NO₂, O₃, and particulate matter.
  • Metrics: macro accuracy, quadratic weighted kappa, F1 for unhealthy-and-above, and rank correlation.
  • Bayesian optimization used to tune thresholds and fuzzy


⚡ Capabilities

Our app combines advanced data analysis and user-focused design to provide a comprehensive view of air quality. Key capabilities include:

  • Integration of Diverse Data Sources: We combine NASA satellite data, ground-based air quality measurements (e.g., Pandora, TolNet, OpenAQ), and weather data to provide a complete and accurate picture of the environment.
  • Near Real-Time Monitoring: Users can access near real-time TEMPO data and local sensor readings, ensuring timely and reliable information.
  • Validation Across Sources: Satellite data is compared with ground station measurements to verify accuracy and maintain trust in the system.
  • Forecasting Local Air Quality: The app generates predictive models of air quality, helping users anticipate conditions and plan their activities.
  • Clear Visualization: Complex datasets are presented through interactive maps, color-coded indicators, and graphs, making the information easy to understand at a glance.
  • Proactive Health Alerts: Users receive notifications about potential health risks based on current and predicted pollution levels.
  • Historical Trends: The platform provides historical air quality data, allowing users to identify patterns, seasonal changes, and long-term trends.
  • Personalized Recommendations: Guidance is tailored to each user’s profile — including children, elderly, pregnant users, or people with respiratory conditions — turning data into actionable health advice.

This combination of capabilities empowers users to make informed decisions, protect their health, and engage with environmental data in meaningful ways.

Future Features

  • Digital Phenotypes: Capture real-time behavioral and physiological health patterns to understand how individuals and communities respond to changing air conditions.
  • Full-Edge AI Processing: Enable decentralized, real-time analysis directly on user devices for faster, privacy-preserving insights.
  • Hyper-Personalization: Deliver customized health and lifestyle recommendations based on environmental exposure, personal habits, and location data.
  • Future partnes: Our solution could be integrate with others mobile sistems.
  • Causal AI Models: Move from correlation to causation — identifying which specific pollutants most affect health outcomes per region.
  • AI Explainability (XAI): Integrate interpretability layers so users and decision-makers understand why certain risk alerts are generated.

projectDetails.name: Tempus
projectDetails.summary:
Introducing Tempus, an AI-powered platform that transforms NASA POWER historical data into actionable insights for event planning and disaster preparedness. Using advanced probabilistic models, Tempus provides organizers with precise risk assessments for outdoor events, considering location, date, audience type, and venue characteristics.

At our core is Tempus AI 🌤️, an intelligent assistant that interprets statistical predictions in real-time, answering questions like "Should I rent backup tents?" Through natural language processing, Tempus AI translates complex percentiles and confidence intervals into clear, practical recommendations.

Why it matters: Poor weather planning costs billions annually, with 40% of outdoor events facing disruptions. Traditional forecasts only cover 7-10 days. Tempus analyzes years of historical patterns to provide probability-based predictions months in advance, empowering informed decisions about venues, backup plans, and resources.

Beyond events: Our vision extends to life-saving applications. The same framework predicting rain for weddings can identify drought patterns, forecast floods, or detect wildfire conditions. By expanding to natural disaster prevention, droughts, floods, wildfires, we protect communities and save lives through early warning systems powered by climate intelligence and AI.

Tempus empowers decision-making for a safer, more prepared world.
projectDetails.details:
Imagine you're planning a huge outdoor event—a wedding, a community party, maybe even your own parade—for the first week of June. Being an excellent planner, you're starting early, way back in January, six months in advance. You're ready to book the caterer, the entertainment, and the transportation. You want to anticipate every possibility, but there's one giant unknown you can't prepare for: the weather. Your favorite weather app is useless this far out; its forecasts are only accurate for the next 7-10 days, not six months.

This leaves you with a flood of questions. Should you reserve an alternate indoor site just in case it rains? How hot might it get? Will the ice cream melt before anyone can eat it? This is the planner's dilemma.

How can you make smart plans for an outdoor event far in the future without needing a degree in meteorology?

This is precisely the problem NASA posed in its "Will It Rain on My Parade?" challenge. The Tempus project is a direct answer to that call. It uses decades of NASA's historical data to provide climate probabilities, not short-term forecasts, and turns them into simple, practical advice.


What does Tempus do?

Tempos is a web application with a clear mission: to help anyone—from tourists planning a hike to organizers planning a wedding—plan outdoor activities with confidence using historical NASA data. Instead of predicting the weather for next Tuesday, it tells you what the climate has been like for that specific day and location over many years, giving you the power to prepare for the most likely conditions. Instead of short-term forecasts, Tempus uses historical NASA data to calculate probabilities of heat, rain, wind, or discomfort for any date and location.


How does Tempus work?

The initial screen starts by allowing the user to choose a location on the map, or search for the city they are making plans for.

The user can choose categories of people who may have different temperature preferences, so that we can adjust temperature thresholds.

The result

Tempus is defined not just as a data consultation app, but as a prevention tool. The app hopes to avoid extra costs, health problems, and social risks that often arise from a lack of preparation for the weather. It explicitly helps to reduce health risks for vulnerable groups, such as the elderly, children, and people with disabilities. For instance, it provides a crucial service because heat waves can increase cases of fainting and thermal stress at large public events by up to 30%.

  2. User support chatbot – we implemented an AI-powered chatbot to assist users in navigating the platform, answering questions, and providing quick explanations about the climate risks in their selected areas.

projectDetails.name: Sentinel

Sentinel is an innovative mobile app developed using FlutterFlow that harnesses NASA’s Earthdata APIs, Copernicus satellite imagery, and SEDAC socioeconomic datasets to provide real-time, hyper-localized alerts for often-overlooked natural disasters such as floods, droughts, and wildfires. By entering any location, users instantly receive dynamic satellite imagery combined with population and hazard data, delivering actionable warnings like “Evacuate 2M at High Risk Now” within seconds.

Sentinel directly addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge by transforming complex space-based data into an accessible, life-saving tool that fills critical gaps in disaster prediction and response. With over 250 million people affected annually by floods and droughts and global losses exceeding $300 billion, Sentinel empowers individuals, emergency responders, and governments worldwide to act swiftly and effectively, reducing human and economic tolls. This project demonstrates how space technology can be leveraged to protect vulnerable communities and build global resilience.
projectDetails.details:
Sentinel is a mobile application that provides real-time, hyper-localized alerts for natural disasters such as floods, droughts, and wildfires. Tools and technologies used:

  • Integrated NASA Earthdata APIs for real-time satellite imagery.

Sentinel uniquely combines multiple elite global datasets—NASA, Copernicus, and SEDAC—into a seamless, user-friendly interface delivering multi-hazard alerts in under 10 seconds. Unlike existing tools, it focuses on often-overlooked disasters and integrates socioeconomic data to highlight vulnerable populations, making alerts actionable and personalized.

projectDetails.name: Meteor Madness
projectDetails.summary: Meteor Madness is an interactive web platform that uses NASA NEO API and USGS data to simulate asteroid impacts and defense strategies. It features three pathways: Defend Earth Game, where users test four real deflection methods with adjustable parameters; Asteroid Simulations, offering 3D Earth visualizations with physics-based analyses of impacts, seismic effects, and tsunamis; and Facts, providing accessible asteroid education.
projectDetails.details:
What Does It Do & How Does It Work?


Meteor Madness is an interactive web platform that simulates asteroid impacts and defense strategies using real NASA NEO API and USGS geological data. It offers three pathways:

  • Defend Earth Game: It is an interactive simulation game where users prevent asteroid collisions by selecting from four real deflection methods—nuclear device, gravity tractor, kinetic impactor, and laser ablation—and adjusting power levels and deflection angles. Real-time success probability feedback guides strategy optimization before launch Users choose 2D or 3D visualization modes to watch their mission unfold as the asteroid approaches Earth. Built on authentic physics, the game features a progressive level system, scoring, lives counter, and scoreboard tracking current level, points, successful saves, and remaining attempts. This gamified approach makes complex planetary defense accessible, allowing users to learn deflection science through experimentation while understanding how parameters impact mission outcomes.
  • Asteroid Simulations: It provides a dynamic 3D Earth visualization with zoom functionality, allowing users to select any impact location and view precise coordinates, region names, and continent identification. Users choose between real NASA-verified asteroids from a pre-loaded database with detailed information, or create custom asteroids by defining diameter, trajectory, velocity, and composition The physics-based collision simulation calculates and displays comprehensive impact analysis, The system distinguishes between continental and coastal impacts—a critical factor for predicting secondary effects. All calculations use real orbital mechanics, impact energy formulas, and integrated USGS topographical and seismic data, translating complex physics into clear, actionable information.
  • Facts: Delivers accessible educational content through interactive cards covering asteroid fundamentals historical impacts, astronomical phenomena, and defense strategies.

Benefits & Impact

  • For Scientists: Enables rapid impact scenario modeling with integrated NASA and USGS data, allowing immediate hypothesis testing of deflection strategies through interactive visualizations without manual data processing
  • For Policymakers: Provides data-driven regional impact assessments and consequence visualizations, supporting informed decisions on planetary defense resource allocation and emergency preparedness planning.
  • For Educators: Offers an interactive teaching tool that demonstrates orbital mechanics, impact physics, and seismic effects through hands-on simulations and gamified scoring rather than static content.
  • For General Public: Transforms abstract asteroid threats into tangible, explorable scenarios, building scientific literacy and awareness that planetary defense is real science, not fiction.
  • Universal Benefits: Bridges raw datasets and actionable understanding, making planetary defense accessible while maintaining scientific accuracy through engaging, interactive experiences.

It will enable the public and decision makers to understand and mitigate its risks , users to explore asteroid impact scenarios, predict consequences, and evaluate mitigation strategies

Tools & Technologies

  • React 19 + Vite → Core framework with fast build tool.
  • Tailwind CSS + Framer Motion + Lucid → Styling, animations, and icons.
  • React Router (Hash Router) → Navigation compatible with GitHub Pages.
  • Three.js + React Three Fiber + Drei → 3D Earth, asteroid models, and space visuals.
  • D3 + Leaflet + React-Leaflet → Maps and data visualizations.
  • Deployment → Hosted via GitHub Pages

Creativity & Design Choices

  • Three-Pathway Design: Game, simulations, and facts for different learning styles.
  • Gamification with Real Physics: Accurate deflection methods with real formulas.
  • Storytelling Through Data: Turns raw datasets into engaging scenarios.
  • Visual & Accessible Design: Colorblind-friendly, mobile-ready, with smooth 2D/3D visuals.
  • Progressive Learning: From simple facts to simulations to game mastery.
  • High Performance: Optimized with Vite, lazy loading, and efficient rendering.


Factors Our Team Considered

  • Scientific Accuracy vs. Accessibility
  • Performance Optimization
  • Framework Selection
  • Data Reliability
  • User Experience Flow
  • Animation & Interaction Design
  • Mobile-First Development
  • Colorblind Accessibility
  • Deployment Strategy
  • Component Architecture
  • State Management
  • Icon & Visual Consistency
  • Scope Management

projectDetails.name: Weather Vision
projectDetails.summary:
"Weather Vision" is an intelligent weather prediction application designed to help users make informed decisions about outdoor events and activities. Built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025, this application leverages advanced weather data and machine learning to provide personalized weather forecasts tailored for outdoor event planning.

The application addresses the critical need for accurate, event-specific weather predictions by combining multiple weather data sources with intelligent analysis to deliver actionable insights for event planners, outdoor enthusiasts, and anyone organizing weather-sensitive activities.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

"Weather Vision" is an intelligent weather prediction platform designed specifically for seamless outdoor event planning. The application works by fetching and analyzing meteorological data to provide users with personalized, location-based weather forecasts.

At its core, the system integrates directly with NASA's Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) project API. When a user requests a forecast for a specific location and date, our Spring Boot backend queries the NASA POWER API, retrieving daily time series data for parameters like temperature and precipitation. This data is then processed and presented to the user through a clean, intuitive React frontend, offering actionable insights rather than just raw numbers. The platform supports user authentication, profile management, and the ability to save and manage multiple locations, making it a comprehensive tool for event planners and outdoor enthusiasts.

What benefits does it have?

The primary benefit of our project is to provide confidence and reduce uncertainty for anyone planning a weather-sensitive activity. It addresses the critical need for accurate, event-specific weather predictions, going beyond generic forecasts. For event planners, this means mitigating financial risks and improving attendee experience. For outdoor enthusiasts, it means safer and more enjoyable adventures. By transforming complex atmospheric data into simple, actionable advice, our application empowers users to make informed decisions with ease.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Our intended impact is to help people connect more safely and enjoyably with the world around them. By making weather prediction more personal and precise, we aim to reduce the stress and uncertainty associated with planning outdoor events, from small family picnics to large community festivals. Furthermore, this project serves as a practical demonstration of how NASA's vast repository of open Earth observation data can be harnessed to create tangible, real-world solutions that benefit society.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Our project is built on a modern, robust technology stack:

  • Backend: Java 21, Spring Boot 3.5.5, Spring Security, Spring Data JPA, Maven
  • Frontend: React 18.2.0, React Router, Axios, Modern CSS
  • Database: MySQL 8.0+
  • Data Source: NASA POWER (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources) API
  • Development & DevOps: Git, npm, Swagger/OpenAPI 3 for API documentation.

No specialized hardware was required for development.

How is your project creative?

The creativity of "Will It Rain On My Parade?" lies in its specific application and user-centric approach. Instead of building another generic weather app, we focused on solving a distinct problem: the uncertainty of weather's impact on planned events. The project's name itself reflects this creative, problem-oriented mindset. Our innovation is in the synthesis of reliable NASA data with a user-friendly interface that provides tailored, actionable insights. We are not just showing the weather; we are providing an answer to a very specific and relatable question, making complex scientific data accessible and useful for everyday life.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team, "WeatherNotFound," considered several key factors. First and foremost was the user need for reliable, event-specific weather forecasts. We also prioritised the credibility and accuracy of data, which led us to select NASA's POWER project as our primary data source. We chose a scalable and maintainable architecture (Spring Boot and React) to ensure the project's longevity and allow for future expansion. Finally, we focused on creating a simple and intuitive user experience, believing that the most powerful tools are those that are easy for anyone to use.

projectDetails.name: Project Aether
projectDetails.summary:
Project Aether is an interactive platform designed to raise awareness about space weather by blending storytelling, gaming, live data visualization, and predictive modeling. It brings scientific concepts to life through five components:

Aether’s Tales: An AI-powered Phoenix character that shares real and fictionalized space weather stories through text and voice. This includes Aether’s Library, a collection of clickable cards where each card unlocks an audio-narrated story.

Educational Game: A downloadable adventure where players act as astronauts, encounter space weather phenomena with simplified explanations, fight challenges, and complete quizzes to reinforce learning.

Aurora Prediction Model: A machine learning tool that predicts aurora intensity at any Earth location using latitude and longitude.

Live Data Dashboard: Integrates real-time space weather feeds from NASA and related sources to make the latest information accessible to users.

Survey Tool: Gathers user feedback to measure baseline awareness and track changes after interaction with the platform.

By transforming raw data into engaging experiences, Project Aether makes space weather knowledge approachable and memorable. This is critical since solar storms and geomagnetic activity affect communications, GPS, satellites, and even power grids. Our goal is to bridge the gap between complex research and public understanding, fostering greater awareness and preparedness for future space weather events.
projectDetails.details:
Project Aether is an interactive web-based platform that spreads awareness about space weather by blending science with storytelling, gaming, data visualization, and machine learning. It takes a traditionally technical subject and presents it in a way that is engaging, educational, and accessible to the public.

What exactly does it do?

  • Provides live space weather data from NASA and related sources in a dashboard format.
  • Lets users interact with Aether, a mystical Phoenix powered by AI (Gemini API + ElevenLabs voice), who shares knowledge and stories of space weather.
  • Features Aether’s Library, a collection of clickable cards where each card plays a narrated story (text + audio) of real space weather events.
  • Offers an educational game where users explore space as astronauts, fight enemies, learn simplified explanations of space phenomena, and complete a quiz to reinforce knowledge.
  • Includes an Aurora Prediction Model, where users click any point on a 3D globe to see predicted aurora intensity based on latitude and longitude.
  • Collects user feedback and knowledge through a survey tool to measure awareness levels.

How does it work?

  • The frontend (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) delivers the user interface, featuring tabs for home, tales, game, aurora model, and survey.
  • The backend (Node.js + Express) connects APIs (Gemini for LLM chat, ElevenLabs for voice synthesis) and serves the web app.
  • The ML models (built in Python with scikit-learn) use Random Forests to predict aurora intensity, exported both as a .pkl file and an optimized .onnx version for web deployment.
  • The game is a standalone executable (built in Python with Pygame) that integrates storytelling, interactivity, and quizzes.
  • Assets include comics, character art, and narrated stories to enrich the immersive experience.

What benefits does it have?

  • Makes space weather science accessible to the general public through creative storytelling.
  • Uses gamification and interactivity to improve engagement and knowledge retention.
  • Provides real-time data and predictive modeling, giving users a tangible sense of how space events affect Earth.
  • Builds awareness of space weather risks that impact communication, satellites, power grids, and navigation systems.

projectDetails.name: Climate trend analyzer
projectDetails.summary:
We are developing a web-based tool for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025 (“Will it Rain
on My Parade?”) that helps users assess the likelihood of adverse weather conditions for
planned outdoor activities. The system combines historical NASA Agroclimatology data
from Nasa POWER website with an AI Deep Learning model to estimate factors such as
humidity, temperature, rainfall, and wind speed at a chosen location (latitude, longitude)
and date. A modern frontend with interactive map selection lets users pick a site and enter
an activity to communicate with the LLM, while the FastAPI backend handles requests,
runs predictions, and serves results. This solution empowers better planning and risk
awareness for events, travel, and recreation
projectDetails.details:
Our project is a web-based decision support tool. It helps users predict weather conditions for outdoor activities by combining NASA POWER historical climate data with a deep learning model. Users can select a location and date through an interactive map-based frontend, while the FastAPI backend processes requests, runs predictions, and delivers results. To make outputs accessible, we integrated an LLM layer powered by Dify with Gemini, which translates model results into clear recommendations, such as whether to carry an umbrella or if conditions are suitable for a parade.

The system works by retrieving NASA climate parameters—temperature, humidity, precipitation, and wind speed—for the chosen location. These inputs are analyzed by the AI model to predict likely conditions on the selected date. The outcome is then communicated in natural, user-friendly language, making weather insights easy to understand and act upon.

This tool offers clear benefits. It supports better planning by helping organizers and individuals avoid bad weather days, raises awareness of risks, and highlights the educational value of NASA’s open climate data. Beyond parades, the solution can be applied to travel, sports, agriculture, and community events.

The backend and AI model were built using Python with libraries such as TensorFlow, Keras, Scikit-learn, NumPy, and Pandas. The Next.js frontend provides the user interface, with Google Maps for site selection. The dataset comes from NASA POWER Agroclimatology archives. For natural language generation and workflow orchestration, we used Dify with Gemini as our LLM stack, which helped generate human-readable outputs and activity-focused advice from predictions.

The creativity of the project lies in how it presents the data to different types of users. For advanced users, the system allows downloading results in structured formats such as CSV and JSON, enabling deeper analysis and integration with other tools. For regular users, the same information is translated into clear, practical advice through the integrated LLM, making the insights simple and actionable. This dual approach ensures accessibility while still supporting technical exploration.

“The main factor we considered was ensuring accessibility for users with no technical background. To achieve this, the system provides personalized advice in clear, everyday language—such as recommending an umbrella or suggesting that conditions are ideal—rather than just showing raw data.”

projectDetails.name: Project Abyss
projectDetails.summary:
Animating Terra is a creative science communication project that transforms complex satellite data from NASA’s Terra mission into engaging visual stories. Our focus is on two urgent environmental challenges in Egypt: farmland loss in the Nile Delta due to urban expansion, salinization, and rising sea levels, and air pollution in Cairo caused by industrial growth and population density.
We bridge the gap between raw scientific data and public understanding by producing animated videos, comics, podcasts, and educational materials that make satellite science accessible to youth, educators, decision-makers, and underserved communities.
By combining scientific accuracy with storytelling, we aim to raise environmental awareness, support smarter urban planning, and inspire action to protect Egypt’s natural resources. Our approach not only informs but also motivates people to take part in building a sustainable future.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

Animating Terra transforms raw satellite data from NASA’s Terra mission into accessible, engaging visual stories. Instead of complex datasets and graphs, the project produces animated videos, comics, podcasts, and educational content that illustrate how Egypt’s Nile Delta is losing farmland and how Cairo’s air pollution is worsening. 

-----------------------------------------------------

How does it work?

1. Data Collection : We retrieve open-source datasets from Terra’s five instruments (via NASA Earthdata, JPL portals, and GIS tools).

2. Data Processing : The datasets are cleaned, aligned, and analyzed to identify trends in land use, vegetation change, and air quality.

3. Storyboarding : Key insights are mapped into narrative arcs and storyboards.

4. Content Creation : Using design and animation tools, data is transformed into visuals, animations, and interactive learning materials.

5. Accessibility Layer : We add Arabic narration, subtitles, and inclusive design features (easy-to-read formats, audio descriptions).

6. Dissemination : The outputs are shared via educational platforms, social media, and community workshops.

-----------------------------------------------------

What benefits does it have?

Public Awareness : Makes complex Earth science understandable for local communities, schools, and youth.

Decision Support : Provides policymakers with simplified yet accurate visuals of land and air quality changes.

Inclusivity : Offers accessible content for underserved groups, including people with disabilities.

Inspiration : Encourages environmental literacy and action, showing people how climate change and urban expansion impact their lives.

------------------------------------------------------

What do you hope to achieve?

Increase environmental awareness in Egypt and beyond.

Inspire youth and educators to engage with satellite science in creative ways.

Support smarter urban planning and agricultural policies with more relatable data.

Scale the model globally: use storytelling to make satellite science accessible in other regions facing similar challenges.

------------------------------------------------------

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Data Processing: GIS tools, NASA Earthdata Worldview, JPL ASTER/MISR/MOPITT data portals.

Design & Animation: Canva, CapCut, Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Premiere Pro.

Team Collaboration: Slack, Trello, Google Drive.

Workflow: Storyboarding, animation design, audio narration, and accessibility features.

(Note: This project is more about creative science communication than heavy coding, so the focus is on data processing + visualization tools rather than programming languages.)

Scriptwriting & Storytelling:

AI was used as a support tool for storytelling, narration, and accessibility, while the scientific integrity of the data remains fully preserved.

projectDetails.name: Project AeroTerra
projectDetails.summary:
We built AeroTerra, an interactive urban planning platform that brings NASA's view of our world to city planners and ecologists. Our platform meets the urban environmental degradation—the "concrete jungles" that trap heat and pollution—by providing users with the ability to virtually model a greener future.

You're the mayor of Cairo. We show you your city's current heat and air quality, powered by NASA satellites. But the sorcery takes place in the "what if?" With our afforestation simulator, you can experiment with what if you vegetate 20% of the city's rooftops or introduce thousands of trees. You get immediate feedback: estimated outcomes include cooling temperatures, cleaner air, and lower flood risk. It makes theoretical figures into a concrete, visible map of transformation. This is critical because it allows cities to make better-informed, data-driven decisions to fight climate change and build healthier, more sustainable cities for everyone.
projectDetails.details:
AeroTerra is more of an internet sandbox upon which to build the sustainable cities of tomorrow. Here's how it does it:

Essentially, AeroTerra is a web dashboard. A user, say Cairo's urban planner, logs in and is met with a flashing environmental map of data. They can toggle different layers—like surface temperature from NASA MODIS or air quality from Sentinel-5P—to observe the ecological health of the city in color. The core feature is our afforestation simulator. The planner can select an intervention, like "30% Green Increase," and our system calculates and displays the radical impact: cooler zones, cleaner air, and better rainwater absorption. It accomplishes this by employing real NASA data, modeling established environmental models of how urban climate is affected by vegetation, and presenting it all in clear chart and interactive map form.

The advantage is empowerment and clarity. Today, the value of a park is qualitative— "it's nice." AeroTerra puts a number on it, showing that a park can be an asset that helps lower the cooling expenses of a city, lower asthma admissions to the emergency room, and harvest stormwater. We wish to transform urban development from reactive to proactive. The aspiration is for cities to utilize this tool to make the business case for green infrastructure investments, which leads to an actual decrease in their environmental footprint and an amazing improvement in their residents' well-being.

We made AeroTerra strong and easy to use. The front-end is a custom-coded HTML, CSS, and JavaScript web application that constructs the smooth, intuitive interface. We used Leaflet as the library to bring the interactive maps to life and Chart.js for the dynamic, intuitive data visualizations. For the environmental backbone, we directly integrated NASA's Earthdata API and Google Earth Engine, pulling in actual satellite imagery and data to ground our simulations in the real world.

Our creativity was not in the code itself, but in the perspective. We weren't simply interested in showing data; we were interested in showing possibility. The imaginative leap was designing a "digital time machine" that allows you to leap forward to see the positive effects of today's green decisions. We framed city data not as an agenda of problems, but as a palette of solutions. The fantastical tree-development animation in our simulator is not decoration—it's an emotional hook, making the dry numbers of "NDVI vegetation index" a living, breathing forest.

We kept asking ourselves: "Is this useful for the guy on the ground?" We were concerned with user experience, so a planner would be able to gain insight within minutes, not hours. We prioritized world applicability, loading the tool with data for a variety of cities from water-scarce Cairo to flood-prone Rotterdam. We also considered accessibility, making the tool simple to use by both experts and students. From the easy-to-understand color-coded maps to the simple-to-press scenario buttons, every design choice tried to de-mystify advanced science and facilitate action.

projectDetails.name: AirGuard
projectDetails.summary: AirGuard is an integrated air quality monitoring system that transforms complex environmental data into clear, actionable insights. It combines NASA’s TEMPO satellite observations with ground-based sensors and local weather data to deliver accurate forecasts, alerts, and health recommendations. The solution has three components: a mobile app providing real-time AQI dashboards, personalized notifications, and health guidance for vulnerable users; a web platform supporting schools, hospitals, and authorities with regional monitoring, forecasts, and community alert management; and an IoT robot equipped with gas and particulate sensors to measure indoor pollution and validate external datasets, ensuring accuracy and consistency. AirGuard protects at-risk individuals, assists institutions in planning safe activities, and fosters public trust by merging satellite, ground, and IoT sources. Technologically, the system integrates Arduino Nano, MQ-135 sensors, ultrasonic modules, and ESP8266 Wi-Fi for hardware, while Python powers AI forecasting, Node.js and React build the web platform, Flutter develops the mobile app, and APIs (OpenAQ, AirNow, OpenWeatherMap) provide external inputs. Through IoT and cloud integration, AirGuard enables seamless data flow and proactive environmental management.
projectDetails.details: AirGuard is an integrated air quality monitoring system designed to transform complex environmental data into practical, user-friendly information. It collects air quality measurements from NASA’s TEMPO satellite, merges them with data from ground-based networks and local weather systems, and converts this information into clear forecasts, alerts, and health recommendations accessible to both individuals and institutions.The system operates through three interconnected components:Mobile Application: Provides real-time Air Quality Index (AQI) dashboards, personalized notifications, and preventive health guidance tailored to user profiles such as children or individuals with respiratory conditions.Web Platform: Designed for schools, hospitals, and local authorities to monitor regional trends, access forecasts, and manage community-wide alerts or safety protocols.IoT Robot: A mobile sensing unit equipped with gas and particulate sensors that measure indoor pollution levels and upload data to the cloud. This robot serves as a validation tool, comparing satellite and ground-based readings to ensure consistency and accuracy across all data streams.The benefits of AirGuard are multifaceted. It helps families protect vulnerable members, supports institutions in planning safe activities, and promotes public confidence by verifying data from multiple sources. On a broader scale, it contributes to proactive environmental management—allowing people to anticipate pollution events, rather than react to them.We aim to make air quality data more accessible, accurate, and actionable, empowering communities to make informed health and environmental decisions.In terms of technology, AirGuard integrates both hardware and software components. The hardware includes an Arduino Nano microcontroller with MQ-135 gas sensors, ultrasonic sensors for mobility, and ESP8266 modules for Wi-Fi connectivity. On the software side, the system utilizes Python for AI-based forecasting models, Node.js and React for the web platform, Flutter for the mobile application, and APIs such as OpenAQ, AirNow, and OpenWeatherMap to source and synchronize external datasets. The entire ecosystem communicates through IoT and cloud integration, ensuring seamless flow and validation of environmental data.

projectDetails.name: Project AFM-explorer
projectDetails.summary: ExoHunter-AI is an AI-powered system for discovering exoplanets from astronomical data. It processes light curves and related measurements, uses machine learning models to classify candidate signals, and filters out noise and false positives. By automating detection steps that are usually labor-intensive, it addresses the challenge of scaling exoplanet searches to large datasets. This matters because upcoming telescopes and missions will generate huge volumes of data — ExoHunter-AI helps astronomers keep pace, find new planets more efficiently, and push forward our understanding of planets beyond our solar system.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does / How It Works

ExoHunter-AI is a pipeline and interface for automated exoplanet detection from astronomical time series (e.g. light curves). The system ingests raw observational data (flux vs. time), applies data preprocessing (noise reduction, normalization, outlier removal), then uses a trained machine learning / deep learning model to classify candidate transits. The model outputs probabilities or scores indicating whether a given signal is likely a true exoplanet transit vs. instrument / stellar noise / false positive. Optionally, the system can provide visualizations (folded light curves, residuals) and an interface for human vetting.

The pipeline is modular:

  • Data input / ingestion
  • Preprocessing / feature engineering (e.g. detrending, baseline removal)
  • Model inference / scoring
  • Post-processing / filtering / thresholding
  • User interface / dashboard to explore results

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Scalability: Automatically process large volumes of astronomical data (e.g. from space missions or telescopes) faster than manual inspection.
  • Efficiency & Sensitivity: It can catch subtle transit signals that might be missed or deprioritized by humans, increasing detection sensitivity.
  • False positive filtering: The classifier helps reduce the burden on astronomers by pre-filtering obvious false detections.
  • Accessibility: By making tools open, it enables more teams (including students, institutions with fewer resources) to engage in exoplanet discovery.
  • Scientific impact: As more missions produce massive datasets, such tools become essential for discovering new exoplanets, improving statistics of planetary populations, and guiding follow-up observations.

Tools, Languages, Hardware, Software Used

Likely (or based on standard choices for such a project):

  • Languages: Python (for data processing, modeling, scripting), possibly JavaScript / HTML / CSS if there is a web dashboard.
  • Libraries / Frameworks:
     • NumPy, Pandas, SciPy for data handling
     • Scikit-learn, TensorFlow, PyTorch or Keras for machine learning
     • matplotlib / seaborn / Plotly for visualization
     • Flask / FastAPI / Streamlit / Dash for serving UI (if web)
     • Astropy for astronomy / time series utilities
  • Hardware: A machine or cluster with GPU support (for training deep models), CPU for inference. Possibly using cloud or local server.
  • Version control & collaboration: Git, GitHub.
  • Open datasets / APIs: Using open exoplanet data (e.g. from NASA archives, Kepler / TESS data).

Creativity & Design Considerations

  • Modular architecture: Separation of preprocessing, modeling, UI allows swapping or improvement of components.
  • Interpretable outputs: Presenting visualizations or confidence scores to allow human-in-the-loop review.
  • Threshold tuning & ensemble models: The team may combine multiple models or ensemble strategies to reduce overfitting or biases.
  • Robustness to noise / outliers: Considering the variability in observational data, the system must handle missing data, irregular sampling, stellar variability.
  • Scalability & performance: The design must trade off computational cost vs. detection sensitivity.
  • User experience: The interface should allow astronomers (or non-experts) to explore candidates, zoom, validate, filter.

What Factors the Team Likely Considered

  • Class imbalance: True exoplanet transits are rare compared to background noise; training must tackle imbalance.
  • Overfitting & generalization: Ensuring the model works on unseen datasets / missions, not just the training set.
  • False positives / false negatives tradeoff: Choosing thresholds to minimize missed discoveries while avoiding too many false alarms.
  • Data quality variance: Handling missing values, irregular sampling rates, differing noise levels.
  • Compute constraints: Limiting model complexity for inference efficiency, especially if real-time or large-scale processing.
  • Interpretability & trust: Astronomers must trust model suggestions, so explanations or visual evidence are important.

projectDetails.name: Project AgriGamers
projectDetails.summary: We developed a 2D interactive farming simulation game using React, where players act as virtual farm managers facing real environmental challenges like droughts, pests, and extreme weather. Players begin by entering their name and selecting a region on a global map, then choose a crop to grow. As random climate events occur, the player must make data-driven decisions such as adjusting irrigation, using fertilizers, or applying pest control. The game uses real agricultural data to evaluate each decision. Correct actions help the crop grow, while incorrect ones trigger instant feedback explaining the mistake and the scientifically recommended solution. This creates a learn-by-doing experience that engagingly teaches sustainable farming practices. Once the simulation ends, the game provides a performance summary, including: Decision history, Correct vs. incorrect responses, Final yield, and sustainability score
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

Our application is an interactive 2D educational farming simulation game. It allows users to select a region on a world map, choose a crop to grow, and manage it across real environmental challenges. The system presents sudden events such as drought, excessive rain, pest attacks, or nutrient depletion, and the player must take data-backed actions like adjusting irrigation, fertilizer levels, or pest control methods.

The game evaluates every action in real time using pre-built agricultural and environmental logic. If the decision is correct, the crop grows successfully. If not, the system stops progress, explains why the decision was wrong, and lets the player retry until they learn the correct strategy.

 

How does it work?

Player Setup: The user enters their name and selects a region through a searchable global map.

Crop Selection: The map zooms into that region, and the player chooses a crop to cultivate.

Simulation Starts: The crop appears with health indicators such as Soil Health, Water Level, Stability, and Temperature displayed as progress bars.

Event Triggers: The system triggers real-world farm events like drought, flood, pests, or heatwaves.

Decision Phase: The user selects an action (e.g., irrigate, fertilize, pesticide, burn, or ignore).

Data Validation: The action is compared against agricultural rules and thresholds (e.g., optimal water range).

If correct → The crop progresses.

If incorrect → The system gives feedback and asks the player to retry.

Completion & Analysis: After several events, a full performance report shows expected yield, sustainability score, and a summary of correct and incorrect decisions.

 

What benefits does it have?

Teaches real-world agricultural and environmental decision-making

 Makes sustainability and climate adaptation engaging through gameplay

 Provides instant feedback for mistakes, reinforcing correct practices

 Improves critical thinking instead of rote memorization

 Can be used in schools, agricultural training, or public awareness campaigns

 

What do you hope to achieve?

Our goal is to educate players about sustainable agriculture using interactive simulation instead of textbooks. We want users to feel the consequences of environmental mismanagement and develop practical intuition for resource use, climate resilience, and responsible farming.

Ultimately, we aim to bridge the gap between environmental awareness and actionable knowledge.

Component      Tools / Technologies Used

Frontend Framework  React.js

Map Interaction           Leaflet.js / React-Map-GL or Mapbox

Game State & Logic   JavaScript (with custom rule engine)

UI / Animation            CSS Animations, Framer Motion, Canvas or SVG

Data Handling xml-based agricultural datasets / custom thresholds

Optional Backend python / spark and python for storing user analytics or results

projectDetails.name: Agrinauts
projectDetails.summary:
A team of NASA scientists aboard a spacecraft detects urgent problems on Earth—irrigation, fertilization, and livestock management. To solve them, scientist Orion embarks on a mission back to Earth.

In each level, the player joins Orion in a new country, facing challenges shaped by climate, soil, and natural conditions. The mission combines NASA satellite data with AI, delivered by a robotic assistant that provides: SMAP Soil Moisture for irrigation timing, NDVI (MODIS) for plant health, GPM Precipitation for rainfall levels, MERRA-2 Temperature for heat/cold prediction, and Land Use Maps for crop suitability.

The game features an economic system: players sell healthy crops, earn money, and unlock new countries with fresh challenges. Players also make strategic planting decisions based on NASA’s predictions. For example, if data shows a drought is likely next season, the player chooses to plant wheat instead of rice, since rice requires far more water.

In one stage, Orion detects rising methane in the atmosphere. Using AI, he links it to livestock feeding and introduces Azolla as a sustainable alternative, reducing methane and converting waste into fertilizer. Players also control weather, time, light, heat, and water to optimize growth. Each level ends when the region achieves agricultural stability.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

This project is a high-fidelity farming sandbox built in Unreal Engine 5 with two modes:

1. Simulation Mode – Players place crops, irrigate in different ways, switch

between growth/heat lights, and observe live plant telemetry (Water, Heat, Light/PAR,

Growth rate, Yield rate, and more). A dynamic weather system (including rain, ice, wind,

thunderstorms & more weather events) and day/night cycle directly influence plant

states.

2. AI-Powered Mode – An in-game advisor answers practical agriculture questions

and generates actionable irrigation and fertilization plans grounded in real

environmental datasets (with emphasis on NASA SMAP soil-moisture).

How does it work?

• Plant Specs (Data-Driven): Every species has a data record with water needs,

temperature/light preferences, fertilizer profile (recommended N-P-K type, rate ranges,

phenology-based timing), root depth, and yield curve.

• Soil-Water Model: Each plot tracks surface soil moisture and updates it every

tick from: irrigation input (drip/sprinkler/flood), rainfall from the weather system, and

evapotranspiration losses. Moisture is clamped by soil field capacity and affected by

soil type.

• Light & Temperature: Day/night and lamp rigs provide PAR; ambient and lamp

heat affect leaf temperature. These feed into growth/ stress formulas.

• Irrigation Engine: The game computes a daily water target (mm/day) from crop

demand, current soil moisture, and forecast rain. Players can follow or override the

plan and instantly see the impact on growth/yield.

What benefits does it have?

• Realism: Uses real SMAP satellite data to connect crop management with actual

soil moisture conditions.

• Education: Helps players (and learners) understand the relationship between

soil water availability, fertilizer application, and crop yield.

• Decision Support: Shows how precision agriculture techniques can optimize

water and fertilizer use, reducing waste and improving efficiency.

• Experimentation: Safe environment for testing how irrigation timing or

over/under-fertilization affects plant health and yield.

What do you hope to achieve?

The project aims to demonstrate how NASA’s SMAP data can be turned into actionable

farming decisions inside a 3D interactive environment. By visualizing the direct impact

of soil moisture on irrigation and fertilization strategies, the game teaches sustainable

agriculture practices and showcases the potential of satellite data in modern farming.

projectDetails.name: AgriSpace
projectDetails.summary:
AgriSpace transforms NASA’s complex Earth Observation data into an engaging, decision-making experience for sustainable agriculture. NASA provides highly detailed datasets on soil moisture, vegetation health, temperature, and precipitation, but for most non-experts, these datasets are overwhelming and inaccessible. Our solution makes them not only understandable but also actionable.

We developed an interactive, gamified web-based simulator where players step into the role of a field manager across a growing season. Instead of abstract numbers, they see three simplified key performance indicators (KPIs) derived from NASA data:
- Soil Moisture (SMAP data) – how much water is in the soil.
- NDVI (MODIS & Crop-CASMA data) – how healthy the crops are.
- Heat Index (MODIS Land Surface Temp + humidity) – how hot it “feels” to the crops.

Players make strategic decisions, when to irrigate, how to respond to heat stress, how to balance water and crop health, and each choice shapes the outcome of the season. Through multiple scenarios, they experience the real-world pressures of climate stress on farming, learning not only the data but also its impact on livelihoods.
projectDetails.details:
What We Do

Players drag soil samples into boxes representing heat and moisture. The game then visualizes how these factors impact soil quality. This interaction allows users, students, graduates, and researchers to understand cause-and-effect in agriculture through simplified, hands-on gameplay.

How It Works

After signing up, players are welcomed by two guiding characters who explain the basics and help them choose an avatar. From there, the journey unfolds through a series of interactive scenarios:

  • Scenario One: The player begins by using farming tools to collect a soil sample.
  • In the Lab: Before analyzing the sample, the player is introduced to the Soil Health and Heat Index guides, learning the optimal ranges for healthy farming.

  • Analysis Stage: The soil sample is tested, and players see the current KPI values (soil moisture, crop health, and heat index).

  • Decision-Making: Based on these insights, players take an action, for example, irrigating, waiting, or applying techniques to protect crops.

  • Instant Feedback: The game shows the immediate effect of each decision, contributing to the player’s overall score and the ranges of the KPIs.

The simulation continues across multiple scenarios, each representing a different farming challenge tied to climate and environmental stress.

Benefits

The game allows students and learners to experience farming challenges in a near-reality way. Instead of reading about agriculture or climate change in textbooks, they actively engage with scenarios, learning how data-driven decisions impact farming outcomes. This not only makes the subject more interactive but also builds problem-solving, analytical, and decision-making skills.

What We Hope to Achieve

Our goal is to bridge the gap between complex scientific data and real-world decision-making. By gamifying NASA’s datasets, we make them accessible and engaging for non-experts, especially students. Ultimately, we hope to raise awareness about sustainable agriculture, inspire young people to appreciate the challenges farmers face, and show how informed actions today can secure food security in the future.

projectDetails.name: AgroSphere
projectDetails.summary:
AgroSphere is a decision-support platform that delivers accessible and actionable agricultural
 insights for farmers and agribusinesses in developing regions. Instead of building satellites, our
 solution focuses on analyzing existing satellite imagery, drone data, and ground sensors to provide
 clear recommendations on irrigation, fertilizer distribution, crop health, and early warnings of risks
 such as pests or fires. This directly addresses the challenge of low agricultural productivity and lack
 of accessible digital farming services in developing countries, where small farmers often lack the
 knowledge or tools to monitor and optimize their fields. It is important because it democratizes
 access to advanced space-based monitoring and AI-powered analysis, giving underserved
 communities the ability to make data-driven decisions, increase yields, and reduce resource waste
projectDetails.details:
What does it do?

AgroSphere provides farmers and agricultural companies with simple, localized insights about their land. The system:

  • Identifies problem areas within a field (such as under-irrigated or nutrient-deficient zones).
  • Delivers recommendations through a user-friendly mobile app and SMS alerts.
  • Includes an early warning system to detect and notify users about fire risks, pest infestations, and other urgent threats.

How does it work?

  • Collects data from multiple sources: satellite imagery, low-cost drones, and IoT ground sensors.
  • Processes and integrates these datasets to create detailed field maps and indicators of crop health.
    • “Irrigate the northern section within 48 hours”
    • “Apply fertilizer to the western area.”

Benefits

  • Increases productivity for small-scale farmers.
  • Reduces waste of water and fertilizers by targeting specific field zones.
  • Provides affordable access to advanced agricultural monitoring in regions where such services are unavailable.
  • Enhances resilience through rapid risk detection and alerts.

Tools, Languages, Hardware/Software

  • Satellite imagery (e.g., Sentinel, Landsat APIs).
  • GIS tools for geospatial analysis.
  • Python for data processing and machine learning.
  • IoT sensors for soil and weather data.
  • Drones for high-resolution, on-demand monitoring.
  • Mobile app + SMS integration for easy farmer access.

projectDetails.name: Solaris-1: Adventures
projectDetails.summary: Our project turns space weather from distant science into a story kids already love. We created a manga-inspired digital adventure where real solar hazards become story “villains,” and ordinary students become “heroes” using curiosity, knowledge, and courage. Instead of chasing superpowers, our heroes use data and critical thinking—mirroring how young people can use open NASA resources to understand GPS disruptions, satellite risks, and power-grid impacts. This approach meets the challenge by translating complex heliophysics into emotions, characters, and choices that are easy to remember and share. By meeting youth in their hobbies—comics, anime, and storytelling—we grow scientific literacy, spark lifelong interest in space, and empower the next generation to protect our world with the skills they already love practicing.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works: Our project is a short, manga-style digital story that teaches space weather through characters, emotion, and real-world stakes. Solar flares, CMEs, and solar wind are personified as story “villains,” while four students and their AI guide model how curiosity, knowledge, and teamwork interpret data, make decisions, and protect people on Earth. Readers move through scenes that explain impacts (GPS, communications, satellites, power grids) in plain language, then see the science applied inside the plot.

Benefits and intended impact:

  • Makes invisible risks tangible for kids and teens by embedding facts inside memorable characters and moments.
  • Lowers the barrier to complex heliophysics—students remember narratives longer than definitions.
  • Encourages healthy identity: heroes don’t need superpowers; hobbies like comics, drawing, gaming, and reading can grow into skills that safeguard our world.

Creativity and approach:

  • Uses youth-loved media (manga/anime aesthetics) to transform abstract phenomena into visual metaphors that are exciting, not intimidating.
  • Blends cinematic pacing, humor, and “villain” set pieces with scientifically grounded explanations and callouts.
  • Designs each encounter as a micro-lesson that maps directly to a real effect on Earth (pilots, farmers, satellites, grids).

Tools and development:

  • Storyboarding and layout: digital illustration software for manga panels, screentones, and HUD overlays.
  • Scripting and narration: concise, age-appropriate dialog aligned to specific learning goals.

What we considered:

  • Accuracy vs. clarity: we simplified language but preserved the core physics and impacts.
  • Inclusivity: diverse characters and accessible reading level for middle‑school through early high‑school.
  • Classroom fit: scenes align to quick activities (predict, observe, explain) and can support 10–15 minute mini‑lessons.
  • Scalability: the format can expand to additional episodes (auroras, radiation belts, satellite shielding, forecasting careers) and localize to multiple languages.

Why it matters: By meeting young people inside the stories and styles they already love, we turn hobbies into pathways for real scientific agency.
