Apricus bridges this gap by transforming complex science into engaging story-driven gameplay with colorful characters, voiceovers, and hands-on challenges. The Aurora Creator mini-game, for example, lets children guide solar wind particles to create auroras while learning about magnetic fields.
Why It's Important: As our world depends more on space-based technology, understanding space weather becomes crucial. Apricus builds early scientific literacy through storytelling and inspires curiosity about STEM fields, preparing the next generation to understand phenomena affecting satellites, power grids, and communications—all while making learning fun and accessible through game mechanics.
projectDetails.details:
Apricus: Interactive Space Weather Learning Game

Overview

Apricus is an interactive, story-based game designed to educate children (ages 6–12) about space weather phenomena. The app combines immersive storytelling, engaging mini-games, and interactive features to make learning science fun and accessible.

Key Features

Story Library

  • Browse and read animated stories about space weather.
    • Sunny – the Sun
    • Windy – solar wind
    • Earth
  • Each story is interactive with animations and voiceovers.

Interactive Reading

  • Text streaming effects for dynamic narration.
  • Character animations and page transitions for immersion.
  • Voiceover narration enhances engagement.

Educational Mini-Games

  • Unlock science-based mini-games related to the stories.
  • Example: Aurora Creator teaches how solar particles interact with Earth's magnetic field.

Progress Tracking

  • Track story completion, achievements, and mini-game progress.
  • Encourages continued learning and goal setting.

Customizable Experience

  • Adjustable settings for music, sound effects, and voiceovers.
  • Personalize volume and gameplay preferences.

Technical Architecture

Story Engine

  • JSON-based system loads narratives, pages, and positions.

State Management

  • Uses the Provider pattern to manage game state, settings, and progress across screens.

Audio System

  • Multi-layered audio with:
    • Background music
    • Sound effects
    • Character voiceovers

Persistent Storage

  • SharedPreferences stores user progress, achievements, and settings locally.

Animation System

  • Custom Flutter animations for:
    • Character movements
    • Page transitions
    • UI effects

Game Logic

  • Physics-based mechanics in mini-games:
    • Particle movement
    • Collision detection
    • Educational overlays to reinforce concepts

User Flow

  1. Onboarding Story – Introduces what is Space Weather.
  2. Cosmic Hub – Main menu for stories and games.
  3. Story Library – Displays all available narratives.
  4. Story Reader – Interactive pages with animations.
  5. Mini-Games – Unlock and play educational games tied to completed stories.

Benefits

For Children

  • Simplifies complex space science concepts.
  • Builds scientific vocabulary and curiosity.
  • Develops reading comprehension.
  • Provides a sense of achievement.

For Educators

  • Ready-made educational tool.
  • Engaging alternative to textbooks.
  • Tracks student progress.
  • Age-appropriate, accurate content.

For Parents

  • Screen time is entertaining and educational.
  • Encourages STEM learning in a fun way.
  • Offline-capable, ad-free, no in-app purchases.

Current Achievements

  • Fully functional story reading system with 2 complete stories.
  • 1 educational mini-game (Aurora Creator) with explanations.
  • Comprehensive audio system with music, SFX, and voiceovers.
  • Persistent settings and progress tracking.
  • Polished UI with animations and transitions.

Future Goals

  • Expand story library.
  • Add more mini-games.
  • Implement multilingual support.
  • Introduce a quiz system.
  • Create parent/teacher dashboard.
  • Build community features for sharing and engagement.
  • Custom AI Chat with Characters: Allow children to interact with story characters (e.g., Sunny, Windy, Earth) using an AI-powered chat system that responds in-character, answering questions about space weather, guiding learning, and making the experience more immersive.

Development Tools & Technologies

  • Programming Languages: Dart (Flutter), JSON (story/config data)
  • Frameworks/Libraries: Flutter SDK, Provider, just_audio, shared_preferences
  • Tools: VS Code / Android Studio, Flutter DevTools, Git, Android SDK
  • Design/Assets: Hand-coded animations, MP3 audio, PNG images, Mansalva font
  • Testing: Android Emulator, physical Android devices, hot reload

Project Structure

  • 37 Dart files organized into 7 categories:
    • Services: Audio, storage, and data management
    • Models: Type-safe data structures
    • Widgets: Feature-specific (reader, library, hub, shared)
    • Screens: Major app sections
    • Core: Constants and theme definitions

Performance Optimizations

  • Audio player pooling for concurrent effects.
  • Lazy loading of resources.
  • Efficient state management via Provider.
  • Optimized animations for smooth UX.

projectDetails.name: Project Earth Data Pioneers
projectDetails.summary:
This project addresses the challenge of transforming complex NASA Earth observation data into actionable insights for non-expert users. We propose developing an intuitive web application that enables individuals to assess weather probability for specific locations and dates through a personalized dashboard. Users can input their desired location via direct text search or interactive map selection, along with a target date, to receive probabilistic forecasts for conditions like extreme heat, precipitation, or air quality.
The solution processes historical satellite data to calculate likelihoods of exceeding user-defined thresholds, presenting results through clear visualizations and explanatory text. Key features include interactive graphs showing historical trends, probability percentages for specific weather events, and downloadable data subsets for further analysis. This approach democratizes access to climate information, supporting decision-making in agriculture, event planning, and risk management without requiring technical expertise.
By bridging the gap between NASA's vast data resources and practical user needs, our application makes critical climate intelligence accessible, empowering users to make informed decisions based on robust Earth science data. The tool directly meets the challenge requirements by providing personalized, probabilistic weather assessments through an engaging and user-friendly interface
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

What does it do and how does it work?

Our project is an AI-powered application that predicts temperatures across all Middle Eastern countries. Users simply select a country and either choose an exact date or a range of time. This input is then processed by our AI model, which has been trained on weather datasets to generate accurate predictions for both past and future temperatures. The results are displayed in a clean, map-focused interface that makes the information easy to understand.

What benefits does it have?

The app makes weather predictions more accessible, flexible, and user-friendly. Unlike existing tools that may be limited to certain locations or complicated to use, our app gives users the freedom to choose any country in the Middle East and get clear results. This can benefit farmers, travelers, researchers, and anyone needing reliable temperature information for planning.

What is the intended impact?

We aim to bridge the gap between AI technology and everyday usability. By combining predictive modeling with an intuitive design, our project helps users access climate insights that would otherwise require technical knowledge or complex tools. The impact is to make data-driven planning simpler and smarter across the region, supporting decision-making in agriculture, travel, and even energy management.

What tools, coding languages, and software did you use?

Frontend: Flutter (Android Studio, Dart) → switched to VS Code for smoother workflow (html ; css ; java script)

Backend: PyCharm

Database: SQL for storing and managing data

AI Model: Python with libraries such as NumPy, Pandas, and Scikit-learn

AI Assistance Tools: DeepSeek, ChatGPT and Gemini for coding support and faster development

How is your project creative?

The creativity lies in how we transformed a complex AI model into a simple, map-based interface. Instead of making users interact with raw data, we designed a system where they only need to click and select, while the AI handles all the complexity in the background. This design makes advanced climate prediction feel effortless and engaging.

What factors did your team consider?

We focused on:

Flexibility → users can choose any Middle Eastern country, not just preset options

Accuracy → ensuring the AI delivers reliable predictions despite data challenges

Usability → balancing the map with clear input options for time and location

Performance → making predictions fast even with large datasets

Scalability → designing in a way that could later expand beyond the Middle East

Each tool had its strengths, and by combining them we were able to speed up development, overcome challenges, and gain new insights. While the core model was trained and developed using Python libraries, these AI platforms acted as valuable assistants that guided us and made the overall process much more efficient

projectDetails.name: Project Earth Echo
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Earth Echo, an animated storytelling project that transforms NASA Terra satellite data into engaging and accessible visuals. Terra has been observing Earth since 1999, collecting vital data through instruments like MODIS, which scans the entire planet every 1–2 days. While these datasets provide critical insights into climate change, air pollution, vegetation, and ice cover, they are often too complex for the general public to understand.
Our solution addresses the challenge “Animation Celebration of Terra Data” by simplifying this information into a short, 2D animated video. The animation highlights the environmental problems, explains how Terra collects the data, and demonstrates how small actions can create a big impact when guided by science.
This project is important because it bridges the gap between science and society. By making Terra’s data meaningful and relatable, Earth Echo inspires students, communities, and decision-makers to act for a healthier, more sustainable planet.

projectDetails.name: Earth Guardians
projectDetails.summary:
Our project aims to transform NASA Earth observation data into practical, citizen-driven tools for sustainable urban planning. We developed two connected solutions: Earth Guardians, a platform that bridges scientific data, behavior, and policy to guide city leaders and planners, and Infinity Green, a City Heart dashboard that visualizes real-time city health and engages citizens through gamified environmental challenges.

By integrating datasets from NASA missions such as Landsat, MODIS, OMI/TROPOMI, GRACE-FO, and SSE, our system generates insights on air quality, vegetation, water storage, and solar potential. These insights help planners design climate-resilient strategies while motivating citizens to take measurable action in their communities.

This approach makes sustainability both data-driven and engaging — turning awareness into action and helping cities grow smarter, healthier, and more connected to the planet.
projectDetails.details:
Our project combines Earth observation science with digital innovation to help cities grow sustainably. It works through two integrated solutions:

Earth Guardians — a platform that translates NASA datasets on air quality, vegetation, water storage, and solar energy into actionable insights for city planners and policymakers. It bridges science, behavior, and policy by providing clear visualizations and decision-support tools to guide sustainable urban development.

Earth Guardians — a “City Heart” dashboard and gamified citizen app that turns environmental data into simple, engaging actions for residents. By tracking real-time city health indicators, citizens are motivated to participate in eco-challenges and contribute feedback, while urban leaders see measurable community engagement.

The intended impact is to empower both decision-makers and citizens: planners gain reliable data to design climate-resilient strategies, and communities become active partners in protecting their environment.

We used NASA Earth observation datasets (MODIS, Landsat, OMI/TROPOMI, GRACE-FO, SSE), along with Python, GIS, machine learning, and interactive dashboards. The project is creative because it blends hard data with gamification and storytelling, ensuring that sustainability is not only measurable but also engaging.

We considered scalability, accessibility, and how to connect citizens, policymakers, and youth in one shared vision for greener cities.

projectDetails.name: Breathing Rivers

Breathing Rivers is an interactive web platform that raises awareness about challenges facing the Nile, Amazon, and Yangtze rivers. Using NASA satellite data and climate research, the platform educates audiences on river water storage, temperature changes, pollution, deforestation, and biodiversity loss.

It provides tailored learning journeys:
• Adults – Simulations of daily activities and water impact
• Students – Educational content on conservation and river treatment
• Farmers – Practical advice on agricultural water conservation

Users can also participate in tree planting and river cleaning campaigns.

The platform integrates NASA Earth observation data to visualize:
1-River water storage distribution (2,246 km³ globally, 38% in Amazon Basin)
2-Global temperature trends since 1980 and their river impacts
3-Regional climate effects: Nile (evaporation), Amazon (drought), Yangtze (flood/shortage cycles)
Features include immersive videos, interactive 3D cards, role-based educational pathways, and data-driven action campaigns.
Rivers are essential for billions of people and ecosystems but face threats from climate change, pollution, and unsustainable water use.
1- Education Drives Action – Simplifies NASA data into actionable insights.
2-Global Cooperation – Promotes shared responsibility for transboundary rivers.
4-Urgency – Climate impacts demand immediate action.

Breathing Rivers connects science with storytelling and action, turning awareness into stewardship.

projectDetails.name: Project Earth Sky : Terra25 Explorer
projectDetails.summary:
Terra25 Explorer celebrates 25 years of NASA’s Terra satellite by building seven interactive applications on Google Earth Engine (GEE) that transform MODIS observations into animated, accessible stories of climate change and environmental disasters. Although Terra has collected over 9,000 days of critical Earth data, much remains underutilized due to challenges in access, processing, and visualization. Our project addresses this by converting raw datasets into engaging tools that are meaningful for communities, researchers, and decision-makers.

The apps showcase pressing global issues:

Amazon deforestation

European heatwaves

California wildfires

New Zealand snow cover decline

Cairo’s seasonal “Black Cloud”

Indian monsoon variability

Arabian Sea phytoplankton blooms

Each app features animated GIFs, split-panel before/after comparisons, and interactive time series charts, helping users explore both short-term events and long-term trends.

By highlighting hidden environmental transformations, Terra25 Explorer demonstrates the satellite’s legacy as more than a scientific archive—it is a practical tool for climate awareness, disaster preparedness, and policy-making. This project bridges the gap between raw satellite data and actionable insights, making Terra’s contribution to Earth science relevant and impactful worldwide.
projectDetails.details:
Problem Definition

Although Terra has been collecting global Earth observations for 25 years, much of its data remains underexplored by the public and local communities. Climate change and natural disasters—including deforestation, wildfires, heatwaves, changing snow cover, and pollution—are intensifying worldwide. However, decision-makers often lack accessible, interactive tools that transform satellite data into meaningful insights.

MODIS onboard Terra offers unique long-term, daily, global records on land, atmosphere, and ocean processes, yet these datasets are often trapped in technical formats unsuitable for non-specialists. The problem, therefore, is how to unlock the value of Terra’s massive archive and present it in a way that supports awareness, education, and local action.

By focusing on seven diverse case studies (from Amazon forests to Cairo’s urban air pollution), our project highlights how Terra’s legacy data can directly reveal and explain urgent environmental challenges relevant to communities across the globe.

1. Amazon Deforestation Monitoring

Problem Question:
How can we accurately measure and monitor the alarming rate of Amazon deforestation that threatens global climate balance?

Solution:
Using Terra MODIS satellite imagery and GEE code, forest loss was detected through NDVI time-series analysis, enabling the identification of deforested zones. Effective management involves enforcing strict land-use policies and promoting reforestation in critical areas.

 

2. European Heat Waves

Problem Question:
How can we track and mitigate the intensifying European heat waves caused by climate change?

Solution:
MODIS Land Surface Temperature (LST) data processed in GEE identified rising temperature anomalies and spatial patterns of heat stress. Adaptive management includes establishing early warning systems, expanding green spaces, and improving urban heat resilience.

 

3. California Wildfires

Problem Question:
How can we predict and control the growing intensity and spread of wildfires in California?

Solution:
GEE-based analysis of MODIS thermal anomaly data revealed fire hotspots and temporal trends. Mitigation involves implementing early detection systems, fuel management, and creating firebreaks guided by satellite-derived risk maps.

 

4. New Zealand Snow Cover Decline

Problem Question:
How can we monitor and manage the rapid loss of snow cover in New Zealand’s alpine regions?

Solution:
Snow cover extent was analyzed using MODIS reflectance indices in GEE to quantify seasonal snow retreat. Management actions include optimizing water storage, adapting tourism strategies, and protecting mountain ecosystems affected by reduced snow.

5. Cairo Black Cloud

Problem Question:
How can satellite data help identify and control the sources of Cairo’s recurring “black cloud” pollution?

Solution:
Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) data from Terra MODIS analyzed via GEE revealed pollution concentration and transport patterns. Solutions include regulating agricultural waste burning, enhancing public transport, and continuous satellite-based air quality monitoring.

 

6. Indian Monsoons Variability

Problem Question:
How can India adapt to increasing variability and unpredictability of monsoon rainfall?

Solution:
Rainfall and vegetation indices from Terra MODIS in GEE were used to study spatial-temporal monsoon patterns. Adaptive solutions include improving satellite-based rainfall forecasting and supporting farmers with data-driven irrigation management.

 

7. Arabian Sea Phytoplankton Blooms

Problem Question:
How can we assess the ecological and climatic impacts of changing phytoplankton dynamics in the Arabian Sea?

Solution:
Chlorophyll-a concentration maps derived from Terra MODIS data in GEE were used to monitor bloom intensity and distribution. Management involves regulating nutrient runoff, supporting sustainable fisheries, and continuous marine ecosystem observation via satellites.

 

Background & Literature Review

Over the past 25 years, Terra has provided one of the richest global Earth observation records. MODIS, in particular, has been extensively used for deforestation tracking (Hansen et al., 2013), wildfire monitoring (Giglio et al., 2018), urban air pollution studies (Kumar et al., 2007), and snow/glacier assessments (Hall et al., 2002). Studies have demonstrated MODIS’ unique contribution to detecting heatwaves, droughts, phytoplankton blooms, and monsoon variability.

However, while researchers widely use Terra data in academic work, the gap remains in interactive, public-facing applications that bring these insights directly to communities and policymakers. Existing tools, such as NASA Worldview and GEE Explorer, allow visualization but lack integrated storytelling features (animations, time-series trends, before/after comparisons) tailored to specific local or regional problems.

Recent work (Roy et al., 2016; Justice et al., 2020) emphasizes the importance of user-centered visualization of satellite data to improve its impact on climate awareness and decision-making. Our project builds on this foundation by taking MODIS applications beyond research into interactive animations and dashboards, designed for accessibility, engagement, and direct relevance to global communities.

By combining academic knowledge with interactive geospatial technologies, we extend Terra’s legacy from scientific archives to real-world awareness and climate action tools.

 

 

 

 

 

Methodology

1.    Data Selection: Access MODIS Terra datasets (NDVI, LST, Snow Cover, Aerosol Optical Depth, Ocean Color) from NASA archives via GEE.

2.    Preprocessing: Filter by region and time range, apply cloud masking, scaling, and normalization.

3.    Animation: Generate GIF animations showing environmental changes over years/seasons.

4.    Visualization: Implement split panels (before/after views), time series charts, and interactive sliders within GEE apps.

5.    Case Studies: Apply workflow across seven global issues (deforestation, heatwaves, wildfires, snow decline, pollution, monsoon variability, phytoplankton blooms).

6.    Deployment: Publish interactive GEE apps for public exploration.

Tools/Technologies: Google Earth Engine, JavaScript API, MODIS Terra datasets, NASA Earthdata resources.

This methodology aligns with the challenge by emphasizing animation, interactivity, and storytelling from Terra data archives.

 

 

Solution

Our solution is a suite of seven interactive applications powered by Terra’s MODIS data. Each application combines GIF animations, interactive split panels, and dynamic time series charts to tell the story of a pressing environmental issue.

Implementation involves:

  • Automating MODIS data pipelines in GEE.
  • Generating animations showing long-term change.
  • Designing apps with user-friendly panels and controls.
  • Publishing the apps online for community access.

This solution directly addresses the challenge by celebrating Terra’s 25-year record in an animated, accessible, and global storytelling framework.

Value Proposition

Our solution transforms Terra’s scientific archive into interactive climate stories accessible to everyone. Unlike static datasets or papers, our apps allow users to see, compare, and analyze environmental changes in real-time.

  • For researchers: A quick tool to visualize MODIS time series.
  • For policymakers: Evidence-based animations of local climate and disaster impacts.
  • For the public: Engaging visuals that build climate change awareness.

This approach surpasses alternatives by combining animation + interactivity + storytelling, making Terra’s data not only visible but also meaningful.

 

Role of Team Members

  • Sherif (Remote Sensing Analyst , GEE expert & Team Leader ): MODIS data processing, GEE app development and orchestration of team duties .
  • Michael Nagy (Remote Sensing Analyst & Web Developer): Developing website that displays the 7 GEE applications
  • Rania Hassan (Remote Sensing Scientist & Environmental Researcher): Case study selection, scientific validation and theoretical information verification

 

Workflow Strategy

1.    Problem Analysis: Review Terra datasets & select seven case studies.

2.    Design: Define animation types (GIF, split, time series).

3.    Development: Implement apps

4.    Integration: Combine into a unified dashboard and website

5.    Testing: Validate outputs with scientific references.

6.    Presentation: Create demo video + final pitch.

Collaboration: Daily syncs, shared GitHub repo, GEE scripts.
Milestones: (problem scoping), (prototype apps), (integration), (testing), (presentation).

 

Resources

  • Hardware: Laptops with internet access.

    • Justice, C., et al. (2020). Earth Observation and Sustainability. Remote Sensing of Environment.

projectDetails.name: Project Voices of Space weather
projectDetails.summary:
What did you develop?
We developed "Voices of Space Weather," an interactive web platform for children ages 8-12 that makes space weather accessible through five character-based stories. Users select character cards (farmer, pilot, astronaut, engineer, child) to watch educational videos showing real space weather impacts, take quizzes, and earn badges. The platform transforms complex solar science into relatable stories with scoring systems and certificates.

How does it address the challenge?
Our solution bridges abstract space science and everyday life by showing how solar storms affect real people: GPS failures disrupting farming, aviation communication blackouts, power grid threats, astronaut safety concerns, and inspiring auroras. Each character demonstrates challenges and solutions, teaching resilience and scientific thinking while making space weather personally relevant to diverse audiences.

Why is it important?
Space weather literacy is crucial for our technology-dependent society but absent from mainstream education. Our platform prepares the next generation to understand and adapt to space weather events disrupting GPS, communications, and power systems. Through engaging storytelling, we build community resilience, foster scientific curiosity, and encourage STEM careers while promoting global awareness of space weather's impact on daily life.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do/How does it work?
"Voices of Space Weather" operates through an intuitive card-based interface where children select character cards representing different professions affected by space weather. Each selection launches an educational video showing realistic scenarios—like GPS failures during farming or radio blackouts affecting pilots. After watching, users take interactive 5-question quizzes based on NASA data, earning points and unlocking achievement badges. The platform tracks progress across all characters (0-5 scores), awards digital certificates, and maintains an achievement gallery. Navigation flows seamlessly between home, video, quiz, certificate, and about sections with child-friendly animations and feedback systems.

Benefits:

  • Educational Impact: Transforms abstract solar physics into memorable, relatable stories for young learners
  • STEM Engagement: Inspires interest in space science, engineering, and meteorology careers
  • Practical Awareness: Teaches technology resilience and problem-solving during space weather events
  • Global Accessibility: Web-based platform accessible across devices and internet connections
  • Self-Paced Learning: Accommodates different learning speeds with progress tracking
  • Community Focus: Demonstrates teamwork and collective response to challenges

Intended Impact:
We aim to establish space weather as a core component of global STEM education, creating scientifically literate citizens who understand Sun-Earth interactions and can adapt confidently to technology disruptions. Long-term goals include inspiring space science careers, building community resilience, and partnering with schools and NASA educational programs to reach millions of students worldwide.

Tools & Technologies:

  • Frontend: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript for responsive web development
  • Design: Adobe Photoshop for character illustrations, Canva for rapid prototyping
  • Animation: Adobe After Effects for educational videos, MP4 encoding
  • AI Tools: MidJourney and DALL-E for character concept art (properly watermarked)
  • Development: Visual Studio Code, Git version control, GitHub Pages hosting
  • Content: NASA Space Weather Database, NOAA educational resources for scientific accuracy

Creativity Factors:
Our project uniquely combines storytelling with scientific education through diverse, relatable characters representing different global communities. Instead of traditional lectures, we use narrative-driven learning where children emotionally connect with characters facing real challenges. The gamification elements (badges, scoring, certificates) maintain engagement while the multi-character approach ensures broad representation and multiple learning pathways.

Team Considerations:

  • Age Appropriateness: Designed specifically for 8-12 year olds with simplified language and engaging visuals
  • Cultural Diversity: Characters represent various professions and backgrounds for global relatability
  • Scientific Accuracy: All content verified against official NASA and NOAA sources
  • Accessibility: Simple web technologies ensure broad device compatibility regardless of technological resources
  • Educational Methodology: Integrated storytelling, visual learning, and interactive assessment for comprehensive education
  • Scalability: Modular design allows future expansion to additional characters, languages, and features

projectDetails.name: Echo Team
projectDetails.summary:
predicts and visualizes the likelihood of different weather conditions (such as extreme heat, cold, rain, or wind) for a given location and date. The system combines a user-friendly frontend (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) with a backend powered by PHP that manages data requests and user interaction. For climate data, we integrated NASA Earthdata resources (via Giovanni and OPeNDAP) and trained a Python-based AI model on historical datasets to provide predictive insights.

This project addresses the challenge of making climate data more accessible and actionable by transforming raw satellite and model datasets into meaningful, location-specific forecasts. It helps users, from farmers to travelers and event planners, make informed decisions based on long-term climate probabilities.

The importance of this work lies in bridging the gap between scientific data and public usability, empowering non-experts to understand and utilize Earth science information in practical, everyday contexts.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is a web-based Climate Probability Dashboard that analyzes historical NASA weather data to estimate the probability of various conditions (very hot, very cold, rainy, or windy) for any selected location and date. Users simply enter a date and place, and the system displays predictions and visualizations based on real NASA datasets.

The backend, built with PHP, handles data processing and user requests. The Python model uses historical datasets from NASA Giovanni and OPeNDAP to generate predictions. The frontend, developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, provides an interactive and responsive interface for visualization and user experience. We used VS Code as our main development environment, and the system runs entirely in software — no hardware components are required.

The main benefit of this project is making scientific weather data understandable and useful to everyone. It helps users plan outdoor activities, agricultural tasks, or travel decisions based on climate trends rather than just short-term forecasts.

Our project is creative because it bridges AI prediction with NASA Earth science data, turning complex datasets into simple, visual insights. The team focused on data reliability, usability, and accessibility, ensuring the tool is both scientifically accurate and easy to use.

projectDetails.name: Space Habitat Designer
projectDetails.summary:
We created an online tool that lets anyone experience the process of designing a space habitat just like a NASA engineer, but in a much more friendly and simplified way.
Our project takes technical rules from NASA and transforms them into easy steps and feedback, so you don’t need an engineering degree to understand what makes a functional living space in space. 
The goal is to help people see how science, creativity, and real-world constraints come together to building for space and to open up this experience to students, teachers, and interested minds everywhere. 
By using trusted NASA data, we make the learning safe and genuine to everyone, even kids.
projectDetails.details:
Space Habitat Designer is a web app offers two main features Learning Mode and Design Mode:

1. Learning Mode:
" It's like an interactive textbook. "

A gamified educational experience designed to make space knowledge simple and engaging:

    • NASA-based articles, visuals, and bite-sized facts.
    • Quizzes divided into progressive levels (Beginner → Explorer → Architect).
    • Achievements, scoring system, and tracked progress.
    • Unlockable content as you learn more.

Purpose: Build awareness of habitat needs (air, hygiene, power, exercise, crew safety, volume standards, etc.) without overwhelming the user

2. Design Mode:
" Acts like digital LEGO for space. "

This mode turns learning into creation:

  • Drag-and-drop interface (like digital LEGO for space).
  • Modules include:
    Sleep Pods – Labs – Kitchens – Medical Units – Waste Systems – Storage – Exercise Zones.
  • Users can set crew count, destination (Moon/Mars/Transit), mission duration.
    • Color-code alerts (green = valid, red = needs change).
    • Icons and tooltips instead of technical jargon.
    • Rules adapted from NASA sources like Net Habitable Volume, crew layout guides, and function zoning.

Purpose: Let users experiment freely while being guided by real constraints.

You don’t need to know all the regulations just start creating, and the app will guide you, help you avoid common mistakes, and encourage you to experiment.

also, you can save your design and export it as (JSON, PNG).

Benefits & Impact

  1. Makes complex space design accessible to students, hobbyists, and early engineers
  2. Reduces time spent reading dense PDFs or using advanced CAD tools
  3. Encourages creativity while teaching logic and constraints
  4. Helps users understand human-centered space engineering
  5. Can support STEM learning, research projects, and mission simulations

What do we hope to achieve?

  1. Democratize space habitat planning and make it interactive
  2. Turn passive learners into active creators
  3. Provide NASA-inspired tools in a simplified visual form
  4. Encourage future mission designers, architects, and students
  5. Build a platform that can evolve into VR, multi-user collaboration, or astronaut training support

projectDetails.details:
Our project is an AI-powered interactive platform designed to support astronauts, students, and innovators in addressing the challenge of waste recycling and resource optimization on Mars and beyond.

What exactly does it do?

The platform provides a real-time dashboard where users can:

Monitor recycled materials, energy levels, and available elements.

Access a dynamic roadmap with step-by-step recycling processes tested and verified from previous experiments.

Ask an AI agent any question related to Mars, space resources, or recycling, and receive accurate, data-backed answers.

Share experiments and ideas — students and innovators can upload their recycling projects, post data about materials they reused, and exchange feedback through the platform.

Collaborate globally through challenges and competitions that contribute valuable data for training space-ready AI models.

How does it work?

The mobile app and web interface are developed using FlutterFlow and JavaScript (for Cloud Functions only).

The AI agent is powered by OpenAI and Vertex AI (Google Cloud Platform), connected through Firebase and Cloud Functions to manage backend logic and data flow.

Figma Make was used for design, prototyping, and workflow automation, ensuring a smooth and interactive user experience.

 Firebase handles data storage and hosting, some features are currently restricted due to judging process 

What benefits does it have?

Assists astronauts in making faster, data-driven recycling decisions during missions.

Builds a shared knowledge base connecting Earth-based research with real Martian conditions.

Encourages collaboration and innovation between students, scientists, and explorers.

Creates a foundation for AI-driven sustainability both on Earth and in space missions.

What do you hope to achieve?

We aim to:

Build a sustainable ecosystem for recycling and resource reuse in extraterrestrial environments.

Empower a global community to contribute scientific data and experiments that enhance future missions.

Contribute to AI model development that can work offline, providing critical support in environments without internet connectivity.

Tools, languages, and technologies used

FlutterFlow – for app and web development.

Figma Make – for UI/UX design, automation, and prototyping.

Firebase – for database, hosting, and authentication (currently under upgrade).

Cloud Functions (JavaScript) – for backend logic.

OpenAI – for intelligent natural language responses.

Vertex AI (Google Cloud Platform) – for model training and smart data processing.

Dart – for Flutter-based logic and app functionalities.

projectDetails.name: EcoSphere Planners
projectDetails.summary:
Planora provides a single comprehensive dashboard that addresses three integrated operations: 
Hazard Quantification and Mapping: It captures and quantifies and maps hazards such as Land Surface Temperature (LST) for heat mapping (NASA Landsat/ECOSTRESS) and rainfall intensity for flood modeling (NASA GPM and NASADEM for elevation).
Prioritizing Vulnerability: It combines geo-physical risk data with local socio-economic data (e.g., population density and poverty) to generate a quantifiable Vulnerability Score that every neighborhood possesses.
Optimizing Focused Implementation: It uses AI in optimization problems to suggest the adaptation projects with the greatest impact and least cost (e.g., the location of green infrastructure and storm drains) to address the most significant reduction of vulnerability for the least cost.
Foundations of Technology and Data 
Space Agency Data (Primary Sources): 
NASA: GPM (Flood), Landsat/ECOSTRESS (Heat/LST), NASADEM (Elevation/Inundation). 
ESA (Copernicus): Sentinel-2 (Green Cover/NDVI) and Sentinel-1 (Flood extent). 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) Use: AI is indispensable. Predictive vulnerability scoring and scenario forecasting employ AI/ML. Computer vision performs accurate land use/land cover classification via satellite imagery.
Tools: the platform uses open-source tools.
projectDetails.details:
What Does It Offer?

Planora provides city officials with urban development and resilience plans to complex satellite data and alerts city officials about urban development and the resilience plans. It acts as an all-in-one interface for the assessment of climate risk and opportunity evaluation.

It does three of the most important things.

Risk quantification and climate hazard mapping. It visually quantifies and maps current and future climate hazard conditions across whole neighborhoods with respect to flooding, extreme heat, and sea level rise.

Intervention prioritization for climate adaptation and mitigation. It proposes infrastructure and demographic structures of the city in relation to climate risks and helps in suggesting the climate adaptation and mitigation project intervention that will yield maximum benefits of implementation relative to cost.

Impact forecasting for ensuring a return on climate resilience. It assesses the proposed climate resilience of infrastructure with respect to the economic and environmental benefits that will sustain for a long period.

How Does It Work?

Planora's architecture has three layers.

The data ingestion layer (the eyes). Each day, the platform receives and processes a large amount of NASA earth observation data and data from other satellite missions. This includes the global precipitation measurement (GPM) which is used to quantify heavy rainfall events and plan flood modeling.

Economic: Reduces losses by pinpointing at-risk assets before a disaster happens. Ensures every dollar spent on climate adaptability is justifiable by safeguarding critical services and infrastructure against heat and flood damage.

Environmental: Actively aids in addressing the Urban Heat Island effect and air quality by supporting the development of urban cooling and green infrastructure (parks and urban forests) with informed analyses.

Social and Equity: Alleviates climate injustice by identifying the most vulnerable areas (usually low-income, underdeveloped, and less green neighborhoods) and targeting investments to improve their climate resiliency and quality of life.

Governance: Provides a single point of truth with globally validated NASA data to enable transparent, evidence-based governance, and project tracking.

What Do You Hope to Achieve?

### What did you develop?

We developed a *Daily Weather & Air Quality Alert System* designed for global users to receive timely, personalized environmental data directly to their email inbox.

The system addresses the critical need for accessible, accurate environmental information by providing daily automated alerts containing weather forecasts and air quality measurements. Users can make informed decisions about outdoor activities, health precautions, and daily planning based on scientifically validated NASA data combined with real-time atmospheric measurements.

### Why is it important?

Environmental awareness is crucial for public health and safety. Poor air quality affects millions globally, while weather extremes are increasing due to climate change. This system democratizes access to scientific data, helping users:

- Plan daily activities safely and efficiently
- Protect vulnerable populations (children, elderly, those with respiratory conditions)

projectDetails.details:
### What exactly does it do?

The system provides a streamlined subscription service where users:

- Enter their email address and city name

- Receive automatic geocoding (latitude/longitude determination)

- Get daily email alerts at 6:00 UTC containing:

- *Temperature* (°C) - Current and forecast

- *Precipitation* (mm) - Rain/snow predictions

- *UV Index* - Sun exposure risk levels

- *Solar Radiation* - Energy measurements

- *PM2.5 Air Pollution Levels* - Fine particulate matter concentration

### How does it work?

The system architecture consists of:

- *Frontend Interface:* Simple web form for user registration

- *Geocoding Service:* OpenStreetMap Nominatim API converts city names to coordinates

- *Data Aggregation:* Python backend fetches data from multiple APIs:

- NASA POWER API for solar and weather data

- Open-Meteo API for weather forecasts

- OpenAQ API for air quality measurements

- *Email Delivery:* Sendinblue API sends formatted daily reports

- *Scheduling:* Automated task scheduler triggers daily at 6:00 UTC

### What benefits does it provide?

- *Simplicity:* No passwords, minimal friction - just email and city

- *Scientific Accuracy:* Leverages validated NASA datasets

- *Global Coverage:* Works for any location worldwide

- *Automation:* Set-and-forget system requiring no user maintenance

- *Scalability:* Designed to handle small to medium user bases efficiently

- *Free Access:* Democratizes environmental data for all users

### Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

*Programming & Framework:*

- Language: Python 3.x

- Framework: FastAPI

*APIs & Services:*

- Email Service: Sendinblue API

- Geocoding: OpenStreetMap Nominatim API

- Weather Data: Open-Meteo API

- Air Quality: OpenAQ API

- NASA Data: POWER API

*Infrastructure:*

- Scheduling: Python scheduling libraries

- Backend: Python-based automation

projectDetails.details:
loomTrack is an AI-powered platform designed to empower a global community of users to monitor and map the blooming of plants and flowers. The core of our solution is the "Add Your Blooms" feature, which allows users to capture and upload images of flowers directly from their location.

The process is straightforward:

  1. User Contribution: A user takes a photo of a flower with their phone and uploads it via the BloomTrack app or website.
  2. AI Analysis: Our sophisticated AI model immediately analyzes the image and identifies the flower's species. It then links this data with the user's GPS coordinates, time, and date.
  3. Data Visualization: All validated data is then plotted on an interactive geospatial map. This allows anyone—from a hobbyist to a scientist—to see what's blooming and where, in real time.

This seamless process turns every user into a citizen scientist, contributing to a massive, ever-growing database of botanical information.

Key Benefits and Future Vision

The benefits of BloomTrack are multi-faceted:

  • Empowering Researchers: It provides scientists with vast, up-to-the-minute data on biodiversity and phenology (the study of seasonal plant cycles). This helps them track the effects of climate change, such as shifts in blooming seasons.
  • Accessible Education: BloomTrack makes botany accessible and engaging for everyone. It's a living, interactive learning tool that educates the public about local flora and the importance of environmental observation.
  • Global Collaboration: By breaking down geographical barriers, it fosters a global community dedicated to environmental stewardship and data sharing.

In the future, we aim to expand our AI model's training to cover flora worldwide, not just our initial focus areas of California and Brazil. We hope to make BloomTrack a truly global resource, accessible to anyone who wants to learn, contribute, and make a real impact on environmental science.

Tools and Technologies Used

Our project was built using a robust stack of modern technologies:

  • Frontend: We used React.js for a dynamic, component-based user interface, along with Tailwind CSS for rapid and responsive styling.
  • Backend: The backend was developed using Node.js to handle user authentication, data processing, and API requests.
  • Database: We utilized MongoDB for its flexible, document-based structure, which is ideal for managing diverse user data and photo metadata.
  • AI/ML: Our AI model was built with Python, leveraging powerful libraries like TensorFlow and PyTorch for image recognition and analysis.
  • External Data: We integrated and trained our model using a variety of external sources, including satellite imagery from NASA Worldview and the INPE Catalogue, as well as citizen science data from the GLOBE Observer App.
  • Cloud Services: We used Google Cloud services for deployment, scalability, and secure data storage.

projectDetails.name: AirRx — FORECAST AIR QUALITY AND HEALTH ADVICE
projectDetails.summary:
What we developed:
- An end-to-end pipeline that ingests remote sensing (TEMPO) and auxiliary data, processes them (calibration, geospatial regridding),
  runs cloud-based exposure and forecasting models, and exposes the results through APIs and an intuitive UI (interactive map, area selector,
  personal alerts, and health-advice cards).
- A forecasting stack (statistical + ML models plus cloud dispersion models) that provides short-term (hours to 48 hours) forecasts and
  probabilistic exposure estimates for common pollutants and pollutant mixtures.
How it addresses the challenge:
- Converts NASA satellite observations into locally actionable forecasts and health guidance — turning data into decisions and protective action.
- Prioritizes rapid, clear guidance for vulnerable and under-protected communities, enabling users to reduce harmful exposure before it occurs.
Why it’s important:
- Air pollution causes acute and chronic health impacts. Timely, localized forecasts and simple health advice empower people to act sooner,
  reducing exposures and preventing health crises (e.g., avoiding outdoor exercise during peaks, adjusting ventilation for indoor spaces,
  alerting caregivers for vulnerable individuals).
projectDetails.details:
Interactive map and area picker: users select a point, polygon, or predefined zone to view current conditions and forecasts.
- Current conditions + forecasts: near-real-time pollutant maps and 1–48 hour forecasts (hourly resolution where possible).
- Personalized health advice cards: short text guidance tied to forecast severity and user vulnerability profiles (e.g., child, elderly, asthma).
- Exposure estimate & alerting: estimated exposure time-series for the selected area and push/SMS/email alerts for high-risk events.
- Data export & APIs: CSV/JSON export and a REST API to integrate with third-party dashboards or public-health systems.

How it works (technical flow):
1. Ingest: TEMPO Level-2 and Level-3 retrievals (and other NASA products) are pulled via APIs or cloud buckets at their native spatio-temporal resolution.
2. Preprocess: geolocation correction, cloud masking, vertical-column-to-surface conversion (where applicable), and spatio-temporal regridding to a common model grid.
3. Fusion & bias correction: combine satellite columns with ground sensors (where available) and meteorology to reduce bias via statistical/ML correction.
4. Forecasting & exposure modeling: a combination of:
   - statistical/ML short-term time-series models (e.g., LSTM, Temporal CNN, or gradient-boosted trees on engineered features),
   - physics-informed dispersion or chemistry-transport models run on cloud infrastructure (for scenarios needing mechanistic simulation),
   - rapid probabilistic ensembles to capture forecast uncertainty.
5. Risk & advice: translate forecast concentrations into simple health guidance using established concentration–response thresholds and tailored messaging.
6. Delivery: results are served through an API to the frontend app which displays maps, charts, and health advice cards; alerts are sent via push/SMS.

Benefits:
- Timely, localized forecasts reduce exposure and support behaviour change.
- Actionable guidance rather than raw numbers: easier for non-experts to act.
- Scalable architecture: designed to cover many urban areas and integrate future sensors.

Goals:
- Reduce acute exposure events for at-risk populations.
- Demonstrate a reproducible path from space-based observations to community-level public health action.
- Open-source core components so cities and NGOs can adapt and deploy AirRx locally.

Tools & technologies (stack example implemented during the challenge):
- Languages: Python (data pipeline, ML), C# / .NET (backend API where applicable), JavaScript/TypeScript (frontend).
- Databases: SQL Server (user data, logs), time-series stores or PostGIS for geospatial time series.
- ML / Data libraries: TensorFlow or PyTorch, scikit-learn, xgboost, pandas, xarray.
- Cloud & deployment: cloud compute for model runs and APIs (e.g., Azure / AWS / GCP), containerization (Docker), CI/CD pipelines.
- Visualization: web mapping libraries (Leaflet, Mapbox GL, or similar) and D3/Chart libraries for time series.
- Other: messaging gateways for SMS/push (Twilio / Firebase Cloud Messaging) and monitoring/logging (Prometheus, ELK).
projectDetails.aiReferences:
- Forecasting models: machine learning sequence models (e.g., LSTM/GRU, Temporal CNNs), as well as gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost/LightGBM) for short-term pollutant forecasts at each grid/point.
- Bias correction & data fusion: regression/ensemble ML models to merge satellite columns and sparse ground observations into surface concentration estimates.
- Exposure & risk classification: supervised classification/regression models that convert pollutant time-series into exposure metrics and health-risk tiers..

projectDetails.name: Aeropredict
projectDetails.summary:
AreoPredict is an enhanced air quality forecasting web system that makes the invisible threats of air pollution visible. It integrates NASA TEMPO and Sentinel-5P satellite data with OpenAQ, AirNow, and NOAA GFS/MERRA-2 meteorological datasets to deliver accurate 24–72-hour air quality forecasts. Powered by advanced machine learning models (LightGBM, CatBoost, and LSTM), AreoPredict provides interactive heatmaps, predictive dashboards, and automated SMS/Email alerts.

The system’s Flask-based web interface is designed to be simple, accessible, and actionable, allowing communities, schools, and hospitals to make faster, data-driven decisions. By combining Earth observation data with AI forecasting, AreoPredict supports NASA’s mission to translate scientific data into practical tools for public well-being, empowering users to act early against the invisible dangers of air pollution.
projectDetails.details:
AreoPredict is a browser-based system for monitoring and forecasting air quality. It collects and processes data from NASA TEMPO, Sentinel-5P, OpenAQ, AirNow, and NOAA GFS/MERRA-2 using open APIs. Data is preprocessed for time alignment, feature extraction, and missing-value handling. Trained ML models (LightGBM, CatBoost, LSTM) forecast the Air Quality Index (AQI) up to 72 hours ahead.

Forecasts are visualized via an interactive Flask GUI featuring spatiotemporal heatmaps, predictive dashboards, and Twilio-powered SMS/Email alerts. The system is containerized with Docker for deployment on AWS/GCP.

Benefits include early health warnings, improved decision-making for schools and hospitals, and accessible data for communities. We developed the project using Python, Flask, TensorFlow, Scikit-Learn, Pandas, NumPy, Plotly, and Twilio APIs. AreoPredict creatively transforms complex environmental data into a simple, impactful solution for cleaner and safer skies.

projectDetails.name: Exoplanet Detector
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, Exoplanet Detector, is an AI-powered web application that analyzes stellar light curves to detect potential exoplanets. Users can upload CSV or FITS files from NASA’s Kepler, K2, or TESS missions, or use sample datasets provided. The system preprocesses the data—removing noise, interpolating gaps, detrending signals, and standardizing flux—before running a PyTorch-based AI model to predict the probability of an exoplanet transit. A lightweight heuristic fallback ensures functionality even without a pretrained model or GPU.

This project addresses the “Hunting for Exoplanets with AI” challenge by making exoplanet detection accessible to students, researchers, and space enthusiasts. It lowers the barrier to performing AI-assisted astronomical analysis, provides transparent visualizations of light curves, and encourages engagement with real scientific data. By combining AI with an interactive, user-friendly interface, Exoplanet Detector fosters STEM education, citizen science, and exploration of the universe.
projectDetails.details:
What it does & how it works:
Exoplanet Detector is a web-based application that analyzes stellar light curves to identify potential exoplanets. Users can upload CSV or FITS files from NASA’s Kepler, K2, or TESS missions, or use sample datasets. The backend preprocesses the data by cleaning, interpolating gaps, detrending, clipping outliers, standardizing, and resampling flux values to a fixed length. A PyTorch AI model then predicts the probability of an exoplanet transit. Results, including the probability score and standardized light curve, are displayed via interactive Plotly charts. A heuristic fallback ensures the app functions even without a pretrained model or GPU.

Benefits & Intended Impact:

  • Makes exoplanet detection accessible to students, researchers, and enthusiasts.
  • Encourages citizen science and STEM engagement.
  • Provides transparent AI predictions with clear visualizations.

Tools & Technologies:

  • Backend: Python, Flask, PyTorch, Astropy
  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Plotly
  • Hardware: CPU or GPU-enabled machines

Creativity & Considerations:

  • Combines real NASA data with AI to make scientific analysis interactive and educational.
  • Designed for accessibility, flexibility, and reproducibility, even on limited hardware.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Yes, AI was a core component of our project. We used PyTorch to build a neural network model that analyzes preprocessed stellar light curves to predict the probability of an exoplanet transit. The AI model identifies patterns in the flux variations to detect periodic dips caused by exoplanets.

Additionally, a heuristic AI fallback module was implemented to provide predictions when a pretrained model or GPU is not available. This ensures the app remains functional for all users.

Notes on AI usage compliance:

  • No AI-generated images, videos, or NASA branding were used.
  • All AI-assisted work relates solely to code and data processing for model inference.
  • Code and preprocessing logic were developed manually, while AI performs pattern recognition on light curve data.

projectDetails.name: Project ExoClean
projectDetails.summary:
The project develops a recycling system for space missions that transforms waste into resources and useful tools, directly supporting astronaut sustainability. Unlike existing systems such as the Refabricator, which recycle only plastics, our approach integrates three waste types, clothing (polyester), plastics, and metals.
How it works:
1-Polyester clothing waste undergoes glycolysis, where PET reacts with ethylene glycol to form BHET, which is repolymerized and extruded into high-quality 3D printing filament. From ~173 kg clothing waste on a Mars transit, ~80 kg of filament can be recovered.
2-Metal scraps are processed using an electro-mechanical press, which compresses them into thin sheets. These sheets can be repurposed for radiation shielding, structural reinforcement, or feedstock for further fabrication.
3-Plastic waste is shredded and extruded into filament, complementing the textile recycling process.
Why it matters:
This system maximizes the reuse of mission waste, reducing reliance on resupply from Earth while solving waste management challenges. By turning discarded clothing, plastics, and metals into tools, spare parts, and habitat materials, it enables astronauts to operate more sustainably and efficiently on long-duration missions such as those to Mars.
projectDetails.details:
Trash to Tools: Integrated Space Mission Recycling and Manufacturing Systems

1. Executive Summary

Long-duration space missions, such as a three-year Mars transit, generate thousands of kilograms of inorganic waste including plastics, textiles, and metal scraps. Traditionally, this waste poses storage, contamination, and resupply challenges.

The Trash-to-Tools project proposes a compact Recycling Pod that transforms waste into usable materials. Instead of treating trash as a liability, the system sorts, processes, and converts waste into new resources: plastic filament for 3D printing, pressed metal sheets for shielding and construction, and recycled textiles for insulation.

Our approach builds upon NASA’s ongoing research in space recycling (e.g., ISS Refabricator, Trash Compaction Processing System) and adapts proven technologies into an integrated, multi-material recycling unit suitable for Mars exploration.

2. Problem Definition

Estimated inorganic waste per 3-year Mars mission: ~12,600 kg.

Composition: packaging plastics, textiles (clothing), and structural metal scraps.

Challenges:

No landfills or external recycling plants in space.

Waste accumulation consumes valuable habitat volume.

Materials resupply from Earth is impractical and costly.

Objective: Convert waste into usable resources, minimizing resupply and enabling closed-loop sustainability.

3. Background & Literature Review

Current NASA Approaches:

Trash Compaction & Processing System (TCPS): Compacts trash into tiles and recovers water.

ISS Refabricator: Recycles plastic waste into 3D printer filament.

In-Space Manufacturing (ISM): Additive manufacturing onboard the ISS.

Limitations:

Existing systems target either organics (compost/incineration) or plastics.

Metals and textiles remain underexplored.

Gap Identified: A compact, integrated system for multi-material recycling (plastics, metals, textiles) adapted for spacecraft constraints.

4. System Components

Clothing Waste Recycling via PET Glycolysis

Clothing represents a major amount of waste in space missions. For example, a one-way Mars transit generates approximately 173 kg of clothing waste, of which about 60% is polyester (polyethylene terephthalate, PET). PET is a polymer that can be chemically recycled through glycolysis, which breaks polymer chains into monomers, which can then be repolymerized into plastic suitable for 3D printing filament.

In glycolysis, PET reacts with ethylene glycol (EG) in the presence of a catalyst (such as zinc acetate). The reaction is conducted at 200–250 °C, under 0.1–0.6 MPa pressure. The main product is bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET), and low-molecular-weight oligomers. BHET can be purified and repolymerized into PET resin, then extruded into 3D printer filament.

PET + EG → BHET (bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate) + oligomers

From 173 kg of clothing waste, approximately 104 kg of PET can be recovered. With a glycolysis yield of 85–90%, this corresponds to about 90 kg BHET. Subsequent repolymerization and extrusion (90–95% yield) result in ~80 kg of PET filament, giving an overall efficiency of ~0.8 kg filament per kilogram of PET waste.

The reaction rate increases with EG concentration (Rate ∝ [EG]²). For each kilogram of PET, 2–6 kg of EG is required, depending on the desired depolymerization rate. However, EG can be recycled, with only 5–10% net losses due to residues and evaporation. Thus, processing ~104 kg PET requires an initial ~416 kg of EG, but only 20–40 kg of replacement EG over the entire process.

This approach demonstrates a practical pathway for converting polyester clothing waste into high-quality filament, enabling recycling to support long-duration space missions.

ISS Refabricator (In-Space Manufacturing System)

1. What It Is

The Refabricator is a dual-function system that combines plastic recycling and 3D printing into a single unit. It can take waste plastic parts or failed prints, reprocess them into filament, and immediately reuse that filament in additive manufacturing. The goal is to close the materials loop in space, reducing the need for resupply from Earth.

2. Scientific Principle

Thermoplastics (e.g., ABS, HDPE, Ultem/PEI) can be melted and reshaped without fundamental chemical change. The Refabricator relies on controlled thermal extrusion: plastic waste is shredded, dried, melted, extruded into filament, and respun onto spools. That filament is then used in the onboard Additive Manufacturing Facility (AMF) to print new parts. A key challenge is avoiding polymer degradation (chain scission) from repeated heating cycles. The system manages this through tight thermal control and limited residence time in the extruder.

3. System Subsystems

- Feed & Inspection Unit: Accepts printed parts or scraps. Removes contaminants (metals, adhesives, foreign matter).

- Shredder / Granulator: Reduces parts to small flakes (3–5 mm). Designed to run at low RPM to avoid free-floating debris.

- Dryer / Pre-heater: Removes moisture from flakes (critical for Ultem/PEI). Vacuum or desiccant dryer used.

- Extruder Barrel & Screw: Multi-zone heaters (3–4 stages) melt polymer. Screw conveys and homogenizes the melt.

- Die & Diameter Control: Melt exits through a die forming 1.75 mm filament. A laser micrometer measures filament diameter, feeding back to haul-off speed control.

- Spooler & Tension Control: Collects filament onto spools with constant tension.

- 3D Printing Unit (AMF): Accepts filament and prints parts layer-by-layer.

- Environmental Control: The unit is fully enclosed for crew safety.

4. Operating Properties

Materials supported: Ultem 9085, ABS, HDPE.

Extrusion temperatures: ABS ~220–250 °C, Ultem ~320–380 °C.

Filament tolerance: ±0.05 mm.

Throughput: ~0.3–1.0 kg/hour (depends on polymer and cycle).

Power consumption: 500 W – 2 kW (mainly heaters).

Mass of unit: 50–100+ kg (refrigerator-sized payload).

Print quality: comparable to ground FDM printers but with tight environmental control.

5. Example Operating Cycle

1. Crew loads failed print into feed chamber.

2. System shreds it into flakes.

3. Dryer removes residual moisture.

4. Extruder melts and re-extrudes flakes into filament.

5. Filament is spooled and immediately fed into printer.

6. Printer fabricates a new tool or part.

7. If part fails, it can be recycled again (limited number of cycles before degradation).

6. Assumptions

Environment: operates inside cabin atmosphere (not vacuum).

Power supply: 120 V DC spacecraft bus.

Maintenance: crew replaces filters and clears jams; no major servicing expected.

Longevity: designed for thousands of operating hours.

Output applications: on-demand tools, repair parts, brackets, housings — anything feasible with FDM printing.

Electro-Mechanical Press for Space Metal Recycling

1. Scientific Principle

An electro-mechanical press (EMP) converts rotational motion from an electric motor into linear force that compresses metals into thin sheets. Instead of using hydraulic fluids, the system relies on screw-driven mechanisms or toggle linkages to amplify force. This makes it safer, more reliable, and lighter for use in a closed-loop spacecraft environment where leaks or fluid maintenance are impractical.

Core mechanics:

- Electric motor (brushless DC preferred for reliability).

- Gear reducer to increase torque.

- Ball-screw or planetary roller screw to transform torque into linear motion.

- Press ram applies compressive load to metal scraps.

Energy pathway: Electrical power (from spacecraft supply) → Motor torque → Screw drive → Linear compression force.

2. Application in Mars Missions

Metals such as aluminum alloys, titanium scraps, and stainless steel will accumulate as waste from packaging, structural offcuts, and damaged equipment. Instead of discarding them, the EMP can flatten these scraps into uniform sheets. These sheets have multiple applications:

- Radiation shielding: thin overlapping layers enhance protection against cosmic rays.

- Construction tiles: lining habitat walls or reinforcing equipment bays.

- Utensils and tools: cutting and reshaping pressed sheets into mission hardware.

- Feedstock for further processing: laser cutting, additive-subtractive hybrid manufacturing.

3. Machine Description

Main Subsystems:

- Frame and Housing: Rigid alloy frame (e.g., titanium or aluminum-lithium blend) to minimize weight but sustain high stresses. Enclosed housing to contain debris and prevent free-floating particles in microgravity.

- Drive System: Brushless DC electric motor (5–15 kW range), planetary gearbox (reduction ratio 1:20–1:50), planetary roller screw or ball-screw for torque-to-force conversion.

- Ram/Platen: Hardened steel or titanium pressing plate, working area sized to produce sheets in the range 200–500 mm × 200–500 mm × 1–5 mm. Replaceable die faces (flat or patterned).

- Power & Control: Powered from spacecraft’s 120 V DC bus, closed-loop sensors (force, displacement, temperature), safety interlocks.

- Cooling System: Passive radiators or heat pipes, avoiding liquid cooling unless necessary.

4. Operating Parameters & Properties

Pressing Force: 200–500 kN.

Stroke Length: 100–200 mm.

Cycle Time: 20–60 seconds per press.

Sheet Thickness Achievable: 1–5 mm.

Noise & Vibration: Lower than hydraulic systems.

Mass of Unit: 300–500 kg.

Durability: >100,000 cycles over 3 years.

Energy Consumption: ~1–3 kWh per pressing cycle.

5. Assumptions

Material Types: aluminum alloys, stainless steel, titanium.

Initial Condition: Scrap is cut/shredded to fit platen.

Operating Environment: microgravity, controlled cabin pressure, spacecraft power supply.

Output Goal: uniform sheets for shielding, cutting, or storage.

Safety: enclosed chamber prevents debris release.

5. Value Proposition & Future Impact

A. Mission Benefits

Launch Cost Reduction: Every kilogram launched to Mars costs >$50,000 when accounting for heavy-lift rockets and transfer mass penalties. Trash-to-Tools effectively transforms ~12,600 kg of waste over a 3-year mission into new materials. That’s the equivalent of saving hundreds of millions of dollars in launch costs.

Radiation Protection: NASA studies show even 2–3 g/cm² of additional shielding can significantly reduce astronaut exposure. Pressed metal sheets and polymer tiles made from trash can be layered onto crew quarters as modular shielding panels. This means astronauts recycle yesterday’s food containers into today’s life-saving shield.

Emergency Self-Reliance: On Mars, a broken valve or missing tool could cost lives. With Trash-to-Tools, astronauts can fabricate replacement tools, connectors, or patch plates on demand from their own waste stream. In effect, the crew carries a zero-mass spare parts library — their trash is their inventory.

Closed-Loop Ecosystem: NASA’s Artemis and Mars plans emphasize ISRU (In-Situ Resource Utilization). Trash-to-Tools is ISRU applied to human-generated waste — reducing reliance on Earth, lightening logistics, and proving that a true circular materials economy is possible beyond Earth.

B. Broader Impact

Future Lunar Bases: On the Moon, where resupply is difficult and costly, compact recycling units could allow long-duration crews to repurpose all packaging and consumables into construction feedstock for shielding, repair, and expansion.

Commercial Habitats: As private space stations emerge, efficient waste-to-materials conversion becomes an economic necessity. Trash-to-Tools reduces the cost of orbital operations by turning costly waste disposal into valuable feedstock.

Earth Applications: The same compact recycling pod designed for Mars could be adapted for Earth’s remote environments — disaster relief, submarines, Antarctic stations, or even urban micro-recycling hubs. Instead of transporting waste out, communities could turn it into local building material or usable goods.

C. Why Trash-to-Tools Is Revolutionary

Other systems recycle only one stream (e.g., plastics into filament). Trash-to-Tools is the first integrated multi-material recycling system designed for space:

Plastics → Filament or Tiles (3D printed tools, utensils, structural brackets)

Metals → Pressed Sheets (radiation shielding, thermal protection, hardware patches

Textiles & Composites → Blended Feedstock (insulation, bulk filler, printable blends)

It is not a gadget; it’s a survival enabler. For the first time, waste becomes a strategic resource rather than a hazard.

In short: With Trash-to-Tools, yesterday’s garbage is tomorrow’s lifeline. It turns the weakest point of long missions — resupply dependence and waste buildup — into one of the crew’s greatest strengths.

projectDetails.name: Project ExoDiscover
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an interactive, educational platform that bridges advanced data science with public space exploration. Our system tackles the challenge of classifying NASA's exoplanet data (from Kepler, K2, and TESS missions) by using specialized machine learning models to accurately predict whether a celestial object is a "CONFIRMED" planet or a "CANDIDATE."

To make this complex analysis accessible and engaging, we created a companion solar system game. This game is designed to help children learn about and recognize planets in a fun, interactive way. Furthermore, we integrated an AI-powered chatbot that serves as a virtual astronomy expert, allowing users to ask questions about space and get immediate, understandable answers.

This project is important because it democratizes space science. It transforms raw, complex NASA data into an insightful analytical tool and a captivating educational experience, inspiring the next generation of scientists and space enthusiasts by making the wonders of our universe more tangible and engaging for all.
projectDetails.details:
# Project Details

# What It Does & How It Works

Our project is a comprehensive educational platform that bridges NASA's exoplanet discovery data with public engagement. The system processes and analyzes three major NASA datasets (Kepler, K2, and TESS) using specialized machine learning models trained on scientific papers to classify exoplanets as "CONFIRMED" or "CANDIDATE." The backend serves predictions through FastAPI, while the frontend, built with React, provides an interactive interface. An AI chatbot allows users to ask space-related questions and understand model decisions, and an educational game teaches children about our solar system through engaging gameplay.

# Benefits & Intended Impact

- Democratizes Space Science: Makes complex exoplanet data accessible to everyone

- Educational Value: Combines data analysis with interactive learning for different age groups

- Scientific Accuracy: Leverages peer-reviewed research for reliable classifications

- Inspires Future Generations: Gets children excited about astronomy through gamification

# Technical Implementation

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, Scikit-learn, Pandas, NumPy

- Frontend: React.js, modern web technologies

- AI/ML: Random Forest classifiers, Google Gemini API for chatbot

- Data Processing: Custom preprocessing pipelines for each NASA dataset

- Research Foundation: Analysis of scientific papers for feature selection and validation

# Creativity & Innovation

Our project creatively merges four distinct components into a cohesive experience:

1. Scientific Research Integration: Direct implementation of astronomy paper findings

2. Multi-Model Architecture: Separate optimized models for each telescope mission

3. Explainable AI: Chatbot that translates complex ML decisions into understandable explanations

4. Progressive Learning: From child-friendly games to advanced data analysis

# Key Considerations

- User Diversity: Designed for both children and adult enthusiasts

- Data Quality: Rigorous preprocessing to handle NASA dataset inconsistencies

- Educational Value: Balanced entertainment with factual accuracy

- Scalability: Modular architecture to accommodate future missions

- Accessibility: Intuitive interfaces requiring no technical background

The project transforms raw scientific data into an engaging, multi-level experience that grows with users' interest in space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Universal Telescope
projectDetails.summary: Our project automates exoplanet detection and characterization using a stacked ensemble AI system and interactive 3D visualization. We use four prediction models: one for each dataset (Kepler, K2, TESS) and a universal model trained on all datasets combined. Each model employs a stacked architecture of XGBoost, Random Forest (RF), and MLP, with hyperparameters optimized via Grid Search. Regression models predict key planetary parameters, including radius, size, and orbital period. A React + Three.js web interface allows users to explore exoplanets in 3D, view orbital features, and upload new light curve data for real-time classification. To enhance engagement and learning, a gamified Q&A feature teaches users about exoplanet science. By automating detection, improving accuracy beyond NASA’s baseline models, and offering interactive visualization and educational gameplay, our solution accelerates research, reduces human effort, and makes exoplanet discovery accessible to both scientists and the public.
projectDetails.details:

• Automated Classification: Stacked ensemble (XGBoost + RF + MLP) for each

dataset and a universal model.

• Regression Predictions: Planetary radius, orbital period, and size.

• Interactive 3D Visualization: Explore planets and orbits with React + Three.js.

• Gamified Q&A: Engages users while teaching exoplanet science.

• Real-Time Upload: Users can classify new light curve data.

Workflow: Data preprocessing → individual model Grid Search → stacked ensemble

training → regression prediction → integration with 3D frontend → gamified Q&A.

Benefits: Accelerates scientific discovery, improves model accuracy beyond NASA

baselines, reduces manual labor, and engages non-technical audiences.

Tools: Python, TensorFlow/PyTorch, XGBoost, scikit-learn, Flask, React, Three.js.

Our solution combines rigorous AI methods, interpretable outputs, immersive

researchers and the public.
