projectDetails.name: Project ExoNeural
projectDetails.summary: Our project, ExoNural, is an AI-driven framework designed to enhance the detection and classification of exoplanets using NASA’s Kepler Objects of Interest (KOI) dataset. We developed and tested multiple machine learning models, including LightGBM, XGBoost, and Random Forest, and combined them into an ensemble approach that achieved a Test accuracy of 93% with strong precision and recall across classes.  This solution directly addresses the challenge of distinguishing true exoplanets from false positives within highly imbalanced and noisy datasets. By leveraging orbital, transit, and stellar parameters instead of raw light curves, our model provides a scalable and computationally efficient method that works within the available NASA data resources.  The importance of this work lies in its potential to accelerate exoplanet discovery, reduce the workload on human experts, and create a foundation for future integration with missions such as TESS and beyond. ExoNural demonstrates how AI can empower astrophysics with reliable, explainable, and extensible tools for space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, ExoNural, is an AI-powered system designed to classify and validate exoplanet candidates using NASA’s Kepler Objects of Interest (KOI) dataset. Instead of relying on raw light curves, we analyzed orbital, transit, and stellar parameters to train multiple machine learning models, including LightGBM, XGBoost, and Random Forest, which were later combined into an ensemble model. This approach achieved a 93% Test accuracy, with strong precision and recall across all classes, effectively distinguishing confirmed exoplanets from false positives and candidates.

The main benefit of ExoNural is its efficiency and reliability. By using structured astrophysical parameters, the system avoids the heavy preprocessing of light curve data while still capturing meaningful planetary signals. This makes the model computationally lightweight, interpretable, and easily extensible to other missions such as TESS or future exoplanet surveys.

The intended impact is to support NASA scientists and astronomers by reducing the manual effort required to vet thousands of candidates. Faster and more accurate classification accelerates the discovery pipeline, improves data utilization, and strengthens confidence in planetary science.

We developed the project using Python, with libraries such as scikit-learn, LightGBM, XGBoost, and Pandas, running experiments in a cloud-based environment. Our team emphasized creativity and scalability: testing multiple models, addressing class imbalance, and designing an ensemble framework that combines speed with accuracy. We carefully considered both scientific validity and practical applicability, ensuring that ExoNural contributes real value to the future of AI in space exploration.

  • Cursor AI: Used at the final stage to review the entire project codebase and to automatically generate the README file.

All the core logic, implementation, and decision-making were done by our team. AI tools were only used to accelerate discussions, debugging, and documentation.

projectDetails.name: Celestial Ai: Interactive Exoplanet Discovery with AI, 3D Exploration, and Gamified Learning
projectDetails.summary:
Celestial Ai is an interactive AI-powered platform designed to identify and visualize exoplanets using NASA’s open Kepler dataset. Our model analyzes ten key Kepler features such as orbital period, planetary radius, and transit signal strength to classify candidates as Confirmed, Candidate, or False Positive with explainable confidence metrics.

What makes Celestial Ai unique is its fusion of science, design, and interactivity. The platform includes a 3D Exoplanet Explorer to visualize planets in real-time space, an Artistic Mode that transforms scientific data into a galaxy of glowing orbits, and a Guess the Exoplanet game that turns machine learning into an educational, hands-on experience. Users can also retrain the AI pipeline with new data directly within the app, making the system adaptive and open for discovery.

By combining NASA data, AI technology, and engaging visualization, Celestial Ai empowers researchers, students, and the public to explore new worlds—making exoplanet discovery both scientifically rigorous and creatively inspiring.
projectDetails.details:
Celestial Ai is an interactive artificial intelligence platform that detects, classifies, and visualizes exoplanets using NASA’s Kepler open dataset. It is powered by a HistGradientBoostingClassifier model trained on ten essential Kepler features, including orbital period, planetary radius, transit duration, and signal-to-noise ratio. This model enables accurate classification of planetary candidates into confirmed exoplanets, potential candidates, or false positives.

The system integrates this trained machine learning pipeline into a Streamlit-based web interface that allows users to upload data, perform real-time classification, retrain the model on new datasets, and visualize outcomes through dynamic tools such as the 3D Exoplanet Explorer and the Artistic Mode, which transforms numerical data into a galaxy-inspired visual experience. Additionally, it includes an interactive Guess the Exoplanet game that helps users intuitively understand the classification logic and engage with NASA’s data in an entertaining way.

Celestial Ai was developed using Python with Scikit-learn for the model, Plotly for interactive data visualization, and Streamlit for the deployment interface. Data is managed and processed through Pandas, NumPy, and Joblib for pipeline serialization.

The project’s intended impact is to accelerate the validation of exoplanet candidates, make NASA’s open data more accessible to researchers and educators, and engage the public through an artistic and gamified exploration of space. By merging scientific accuracy, visual storytelling, and interactive learning, Celestial Ai embodies innovation in both research utility and public engagement.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
We used ChatGPT as a part of the development process for Celestial Ai. ChatGPT was utilized to assist in designing and refining the user interface, improving the structure and readability of written content, and optimizing parts of the Streamlit application code for better clarity and performance.

The machine learning core of the project—the HistGradientBoostingClassifier trained on NASA’s Kepler dataset—was developed and implemented by our team using scientific data and standard machine learning methods, not generative AI. ChatGPT was used solely as a creative and organizational assistant to accelerate development, enhance presentation quality, and ensure technical precision.

No AI-generated images, videos, or audio were used in the project. All visuals, datasets, and interactive features were created or derived from authentic NASA data and original team work.

projectDetails.name: ExoTerra: Hunting for exoplanets using AI
projectDetails.summary:
ExoTerra is an AI-powered platform designed to accelerate the discovery of exoplanets using NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS datasets. Detecting real planetary signals among thousands of noisy candidates is time-consuming and prone to human disagreement. Our solution integrates a machine learning pipeline built with XGBoost to classify exoplanet candidates quickly and accurately while minimizing false positives.

The platform provides a simple, intuitive web interface that allows both novice users and expert researchers to interact with the data, visualize predictions, adjust hyperparameters, and monitor accuracy metrics. By combining automated classification with explainable AI techniques, ExoTerra not only speeds up candidate validation but also helps astronomers understand why a signal is classified as a planet or a false positive.

This project addresses the challenge of “A World Away: Hunting for Exoplanets with AI” by directly tackling the bottlenecks in exoplanet detection. It is important because it empowers scientists and students alike to explore the universe more efficiently, increases confidence in automated discovery, and contributes to the search for potentially habitable worlds beyond our solar system
projectDetails.details:
ExoTerra is an AI-driven platform that identifies exoplanet candidates from Kepler, K2, and TESS datasets. Using a machine learning pipeline based on XGBoost, it processes light curve data, reduces noise, and distinguishes confirmed exoplanets from false positives with high accuracy. The platform features a user-friendly web interface where users can upload new datasets, manually enter data, visualize predictions, adjust hyperparameters, and track precision, accuracy, and recall metrics.

The project benefits both novice users and expert researchers by making exoplanet data accessible, interpretable, and actionable. By automating candidate classification and providing explainable AI outputs, ExoTerra reduces human bottlenecks, speeds up discovery, and increases confidence in the results.

ExoTerra is creative because it unifies multiple NASA mission datasets in one scalable pipeline while integrating a web-based interactive interface. The team considered scientific validity, usability, interpretability, and accessibility to ensure the platform can be used by a wide range of users and directly contribute to the search for habitable worlds.

Tools & Technologies: Python, XGBoost, Scikit-learn, Pandas, NumPy, Flask, HTML/CSS/JS, and a web-based front-end for data visualization.

projectDetails.name: ExoVista
projectDetails.summary:
1. High-Level Project Summary  
•	We developed a comprehensive platform for exoplanet discovery. Our solution integrates four key components:
1.	An advanced AI model, trained using official NASA datasets and methodologies to ensure high accuracy.
2.	A full-featured web application that provides a bridge between the user and our AI.
3.	Dynamic data visualization tools that transform complex classification results into intuitive charts and graphs.
4.	A unique, built-in AI assistant, ready to answer any user questions about exoplanets and astronomy.

•	This approach solves the problem by automating the time-consuming task of exoplanet classification, which used to rely on manual checking. It makes research open to everyone, allowing both experts and beginners to join in, and includes advanced features like retraining models and tracking accuracy. The project is important because it speeds up space exploration and data discoveries through powerful software, strong AI models, and clear visual tools—helping more people find new worlds quickly.

•	This project empowers both researchers and everyday learners to explore the universe using AI. It makes complex space science simple and accessible, sparking curiosity, education, and collaboration across communities. By opening the door to more people, it inspires a new generation to connect with space and expand humanity’s knowledge of our place in the cosmos.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

ExoVista is a web-based platform that allows anyone to become an exoplanet hunter. In simple terms, it analyzes star brightness data to find the tell-tale dips that indicate a planet is passing in front of its star.

Users can:

  • Upload Data: Upload a CSV file containing time-series data (a light curve) from a telescope.
  • Enter Data Manually: Input smaller datasets directly into the interface.
  • Get Instant Classification: The AI model instantly classifies the data as a "Confirmed Exoplanet," "Planetary Candidate," or "False Positive."
  • Visualize Results: See their data plotted on an interactive graph, with the potential transit event clearly highlighted.
  • Ask for Help: Interact with an integrated AI assistant to ask questions about exoplanets, how to interpret the data, or the science behind the transit method.

 

The platform works through a four-step process:

  1. Data loading & Preprocessing: When a user uploads or manually enters light curve data, the backend cleans, smooths, and normalizes it to ensure consistency and optimal input format for the AI model.
  2. AI Model Inference: The processed data is analyzed by a pre-trained XGBoost model, which examines the shape, duration, and recurring patterns in the light curve to distinguish genuine planetary transits from stellar noise or starspots.
  3. Output Generation: The model produces a probability score indicating the likelihood that the data represents a "Confirmed Exoplanet," "Planetary Candidate," or "False Positive."
  4. Frontend Visualization: The results, along with an interactive graph of the original data, are displayed to the user in a clear and accessible format. An AI assistant provides contextual support, answering questions about the data, the analysis, or the transit method without interfering with the core inference process.

The benefits of this platform include rapid analysis, broad accessibility, educational value, and high accuracy. It reduces the time needed to identify potential exoplanets from hours or days to seconds, making the process highly efficient. Its user-friendly design opens space science to citizen scientists and educators, allowing anyone without advanced astrophysics knowledge to participate in exoplanet discovery. The instant visual feedback and interactive AI support transform complex data tasks into engaging learning experiences. Additionally, trained on verified NASA data, the model offers reliable results, helping to accurately filter noise and highlight the most promising exoplanet candidates for further research.

 

 

  • What do you hope to achieve? 

I hope to develop a tool that significantly accelerates exoplanet discovery by making data analysis accessible, reliable, and engaging. Ultimately, I aim to foster a vibrant community where students, hobbyists, and scientists can collaboratively analyze data, share findings, and contribute to uncovering new worlds, inspiring future generations to pursue space exploration, programming, and data science.

 

·       What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Tools: VS Code, Cursor, git, GitHub, Claude AI, Open AI

Programming Languages:

Python for the backend and machine learning model; JavaScript for the interactive frontend.

AI / Machine Learning:

Libraries: fastapi, uvicorn, pydantic, python-dotenv, jinja2, numpy, scikit-learn, torch, tensorflow, matplotlib, pandas, hvplot, bokeh, pathlib, seaborn, nbformat, nbconvert and plotly

Backend: Fast API.

Frontend:

·       HTML,CSS,Javscript

•             Visualization: Chart.js for creating responsive and interactive graphs.

•             AI Assistant: Powered by the Gemini API.

 

 

Software, Libraries & Code

Our project is built entirely on open-source software. All code for this project was written by our team.

  • Languages: Python (Backend & AI), JavaScript (Frontend)
  • AI/ML Stack: TensorFlow, Keras, Scikit-learn, Pandas, NumPy
  • Web Stack: Flask (Backend API), React (Frontend UI), Chart.js (Data Visualization)

projectDetails.name: Exo X Hunter
projectDetails.summary:
Exo X Hunter is an AI-powered, interactive platform that reimagines exoplanet discovery by uniting machine learning, visualization, and gamification. At its core, we developed a stacked ensemble model trained on NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS datasets, combining Multilayer Perceptrons, XGBoost, and LightGBM to classify light curve signals with high accuracy and confidence scores.

To make these results engaging and accessible, we built a detective-themed web platform where users step into the role of space explorers. Features include a book-style exoplanet gallery, an interactive discovery game, age-tailored educational hubs, and real-time AI mission dashboards. By blending rigorous science with playful storytelling, Exo X Hunter not only accelerates exoplanet identification but also transforms it into an inspiring, community-driven experience.

This project is important because it bridges the gap between expert research and public engagement, fostering curiosity, reducing false positives, and inspiring the next generation of explorers in the search for worlds beyond our own.
projectDetails.details:
What problem the challenge poses (and how we answered it)

The 2025 Space Apps “A World Away” challenge invites teams to use NASA data and AI methods to accelerate the detection and characterization of exoplanets. The key goals include:

  • leveraging open NASA mission data,
  • using AI to distinguish real planet signals from noise,
  • providing interpretable outputs,
  • enabling scalability,
  • and engaging broader audiences in exoplanet science.

Our project, Exo X Hunter, addresses each of these objectives head-on—and then layers on extra features.

What it does & how it works

  1. Data Integration & Preprocessing
    • We ingest publicly available NASA exoplanet datasets (Kepler, K2, TESS) and merge them into a unified schema.
    • We clean missing values (KNN, mode), remove extreme outliers (Z-score filtering), scale numerical features, and stratify splits to preserve class balance.
    • Base Models (Level 0): XGBoost, LightGBM, and a neural network (MLP) each learn on the dataset independently, capturing complementary perspectives (feature-based boosting, and temporal / non-linear patterns).
    • Meta-Model (Level 1): A neural network takes the base models’ probability outputs (9 meta-features total) and produces a refined classification with confidence scores.
    • Interpretability: We expose prediction confidences, probability distributions, and confusion matrices so users and scientists can see how and how well the AI is performing.
    • Built in React + TypeScript, our site presents a Book-Style Exoplanet Gallery, a Detective Game, and dashboards of model performance.
    • Users act as interstellar detectives: they receive a random light curve or candidate signal and decide whether it’s a planet or noise; correct decisions earn points and unlock new planet “cards.”
    • Educational Hubs: Tiered content for Kids, Teens, Adults with quizzes, visualizations, and articles helping demystify astrophysics.
    • Live AI Sandbox: Users can input custom planetary parameters and test them against our AI (via APIs / Gemini integration) to see how confident the model is in real time.
    • Transparency Dashboard: Charts, logs, metrics, totals processed—so users see the AI “behind the curtain.”
    • Community Discoveries: A simulated feed showing others’ discoveries to foster a sense of global participation.
    • The models (scaler, base, meta) are saved in standard formats (TensorFlow SavedModel, pickled components) to allow integration or further training.
    • Backend (Flask, Node.js) handles inference, game logic, user sessions, and data tracking.
    • The architecture is modular so future missions (e.g. new telescopes) or new datasets can be plugged in easily.

Benefits & intended impact

  • Accelerated Exoplanet Discovery: By automating classification and ranking via confidence scores, our tool helps astronomers triage promising candidates faster.
  • Reduced False Positives: The ensemble approach decreases misclassifications compared to single models, improving the quality of candidate lists.
  • Scientific Transparency & Trust: Because users can see probability outputs, confusion matrices, and other AI diagnostics, our solution demystifies “black box” methods.
  • Public Engagement & Science Literacy: Exo X Hunter invites non-experts to participate in actual data-driven discovery, turning observation into play, and curiosity into learning.
  • Inspiring the Next Generation: The narrative structure, our mascot Lanshon, and the game-based interface aim to spark STEM interest, especially among youth.
  • Scalability & Sustainability: The platform is built to grow: new missions, new AI models, new interactive modules, and community-driven contributions can be layered in.

Tools, languages, software, hardware

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, GSAP, Recharts / D3
  • Backend / APIs: Django API, with Rest framework
  • AI / Data Science: Python, TensorFlow / Keras , scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM
  • Datasets: NASA Exoplanet Archive, mission light curve datasets, NASA citizen science / open science programs
  • Design & Collaboration: GitHub (version control), Figma (UI/UX prototyping), Slack / Discord (team communication)
  • Deployment: Cloud hosting (for frontend + backend), Azure for hosting docker images.

Creative elements & team considerations

  • Mascot & Narrative: Our mascot Lanshon, inspired by Ham the space monkey, adds personality. He is the user's companion, framing each discovery as a mission—not just a prediction.
  • Story-Driven Approach: Instead of presenting raw data or charts, we wrap the scientific workflow in gamified storytelling. Users feel like explorers, not passive observers.
  • Balancing Accuracy & Engagement: We prioritized scientific validity (model performance, correct labels) while ensuring the UI is playful, intuitive, and fun.
  • Accessibility & Inclusivity: We considered lightweight deployment so it can run on modest hardware, multilingual UI potential, and tiered educational content for diverse audiences.
  • Transparency & Trust: We built mechanisms so the AI is not hidden—users see the uncertainty and metrics behind predictions.
  • Scalability & Future-Proofing: Our architecture was modular, so if NASA launches new exoplanet missions or datasets, we can integrate them with minimal overhaul.

projectDetails.name: Airography
projectDetails.summary:
We started Airography with a simple belief: everyone deserves to know the quality of the air they breathe. Clean air should not be a privilege; it’s a basic right.

With NASA’s TEMPO satellite watching from space, ground sensors reporting from our cities, and weather data guiding the bigger picture, we asked ourselves: what if we could see tomorrow’s air today? That vision became Airography.

Our system uses advanced AI to turn streams of raw data into clear forecasts, showing when the air will be safe and when it won’t. But behind the science, it’s about people. A parent with an asthmatic child who needs an early warning. A farmer is trying to protect crops from acid rain. A policymaker searching for honest data to make healthier communities.

We built dashboards that speak, maps that tell a story, and alerts that arrive before the danger does. Every forecast is more than just a number; it’s a chance to protect someone’s tomorrow.

At its heart, Airography is about turning space technology into everyday hope: uniting people, data, and purpose for a future where breathing easy is something we can all count on.
projectDetails.details:
We built Airography with a simple goal: to turn invisible threats in the air into visible, actionable insights that protect lives and empower communities.

At its core, Airography is an AI-powered air quality forecasting platform that shifts monitoring from reactive reporting to proactive protection. By integrating NASA’s TEMPO satellite data with ground-based networks ( OpenAQ, AirNow) and trusted weather sources, we can predict pollution levels up to seven days in advance.

These data streams are processed through machine learning models , including XGBoost, RandomForest, and deep learning approaches like Attention, each specialized to forecast key pollutants (NO₂, SO₂, PM₂.₅, O₃, CO, formaldehyde). Forecasts are validated across multiple sources, ensuring that our insights are both reliable and transparent.

But Airography is more than algorithms. It is designed around people:

  • Patients receive clear alerts and reminders to minimize health risks.
  • Farmers gain foresight into acid rain and pollution impacts on crops.
  • Residents in industrial zones are warned about toxic gas levels.
  • Researchers and policymakers access trusted, multi-source datasets for scientific and policy decisions.

Our dashboards are personalized and intuitive, translating complex science into plain language and visual stories. Through interactive charts, 2D/3D maps, and proactive alerts, we make air quality data accessible to everyone, not just experts.

The intended impact is to reduce pollution-related hospitalizations, protect agriculture, and empower vulnerable communities with actionable environmental intelligence. Beyond immediate health and agricultural benefits, Airography also contributes to global climate efforts by providing validated forecasts that bridge space technology with everyday life.

Technology Stack

  • Data Sources: NASA TEMPO, OpenAQ, AirNow, IMERG, Daymet, MERRA-2, Weather APIs
  • Backend: ASP.NET Core (C#) with RESTful APIs for integration and validation
  • Frontend: React, MapGL, React-Charts for visualizations and dashboards
  • AI/ML: Python, Pandas, PyTorch, Scikit-learn, XGBoost, RandomForest, Attention

What makes Airography creative is its personalization. Instead of presenting the same air quality report to everyone, it delivers custom dashboards for patients, farmers, industrial workers, and policymakers, ensuring that insights are not only accurate but also relevant and actionable.

In building this solution, we always returned to one guiding principle: science must serve people. We combined rigorous validation, comparing TEMPO observations with ground-based data, with thoughtful design choices that translate technical findings into meaningful action. Every chart, every forecast, every alert is a small act of prevention, helping communities breathe easier and plan smarter.

Data Analysis & Understanding: Tools like GPT, Claude, Blackbox, Grok, and Genspark helped summarize datasets, answer technical questions, and provide insights for faster decision-making.

Summarization & Documentation: AI assisted in refining research summaries, structuring reports, and ensuring clarity of technical writing.

Creative Support: Platforms such as Canva AI, InVideo AI, and Manus were used to generate design elements, presentation visuals, and draft scripts for demo materials.

Debugging & Development Acceleration: AI tools helped identify code issues, suggest optimizations, and speed up implementation.

All major design choices, modeling, coding, and integration work were carried out by the team. AI was employed as a productivity booster and creative assistant, not as a replacement for our technical or scientific work.

projectDetails.name: Project Final NASA
projectDetails.summary: We chose the challenge of creating a short VR experience that uses NASA Earth observation data to tell the story of our oceans. Oceans are critical to life on Earth, yet their changes are often hard to understand for the general public. While NASA satellites collect large amounts of valuable ocean data, much of this information is technical and not easily accessible to people without a science background.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

Our project is a short, interactive VR experience that educates users about NASA's Earth-observing satellites and their crucial role in studying our planet's oceans. The experience functions as a virtual museum exhibit or educational tool, where users can navigate a central hub to learn about different satellite missions.

What It Does and How It Works

The VR experience places the user in a single, immersive scene featuring a high-quality model of Earth surrounded by a cosmic backdrop. The core of the experience is an interactive holographic UI. This UI allows users to select from different NASA missions, including SWOT, GRACE-FO, and PACE.

Upon selecting a mission, the holographic display presents a high-level summary of the satellite, its purpose, and the data it collects. For example, choosing SWOT shows a brief text overview of its mission to measure surface water height, accompanied by a visual representation of its data, such as a color-coded map of sea surface height.

The user can also interact with the holographic Earth model, scaling it up or down to change their perspective from a global view to a more regional one. As they interact with the UI, a narrator provides a clear, simplified explanation of the complex scientific data, turning technical terms into understandable concepts and compelling stories.

Benefits and Goals

The primary benefit of our project is making complex, publicly available NASA data accessible and engaging for a broad audience. By transforming abstract numbers and technical jargon into beautiful and interactive visualizations, we hope to foster a deeper appreciation for Earth science and inspire curiosity in people of all ages.

We aim to turn viewers into informed global citizens, helping them understand pressing oceanic issues like sea-level change and biodiversity. By providing a memorable and enriching experience, we hope to demonstrate how NASA's data can be used to monitor the health of our planet and support decision-makers in developing tools to mitigate, adapt, and respond to a changing climate.

Tools and Technologies

Our project was developed using the Unity game engine for its robust VR development features. We used C# for scripting the interactive elements of the holographic UI and for controlling the scaling and selection of the Earth model.

For hardware, the experience is compatible with the Meta Quest 2. We used the motion controllers for input to provide a more intuitive user experience.

projectDetails.name: WeatherWise
projectDetails.summary: Weather Wise is a web application that enables users to forecast weather conditions for any chosen location and date. By leveraging historical climate data from the NASA POWER API, the app applies SARIMAX time series modeling to predict temperature, rainfall, wind speed, and humidity. The core purpose of the project is to help users plan outdoor activities, trips, or events in advance, minimizing the risk of being affected by unfavorable weather conditions and ensuring a more enjoyable experience.
projectDetails.details: The application works by allowing users to select a location on the map and specify a target date. Once the input is provided, the system automatically fetches historical climate data from the NASA POWER API for the chosen coordinates. The data is then aggregated and processed before being analyzed through a SARIMAX model to generate forecasts for the requested date. The predicted values are further classified into intuitive categories such as Very Hot, Comfortable, Wet, or Windy, making it easy for users to interpret the forecast. In addition, the app provides personalized AI-driven recommendations on whether the weather is suitable for outdoor activities. The project was developed using Python with Pandas, Statsmodels, and Requests for data handling and modeling, and Django as the web framework. The benefits include improved decision-making, better planning for events or travel, and reducing risks related to extreme weather conditions. Our goal is to make accurate, user-friendly forecasts accessible to everyone.
projectDetails.aiReferences: Artificial intelligence was applied in two main components of the project. First, the SARIMAX time series model was used to forecast weather variables into the future. Second, we developed a classification layer that translates numerical predictions into intuitive categories (such as Very Hot, Wet, Comfortable). This combination ensures that the forecasts are not only accurate but also easy to understand for end users. By integrating AI into both the predictive and interpretative stages, Weather Wise delivers actionable insights rather than raw data.

projectDetails.name: Project Galaxy Impact
projectDetails.summary: Galaxy Impact is a web platform integrating NASA’s JPL Horizons, Small Body Database, and Sentry APIs with USGS Elevation Data, Google Earth Engine, and OpenStreetMap to visualize and simulate asteroid impacts like "Impactor-2025." Built with React, React Router v7, Three.js (via React-Three/Fiber and Drei), and Python FastAPI, it enables users to explore real-time solar system models, simulate asteroid trajectories, calculate impact effects (e.g., energy, craters, tsunamis, population impacts), and test mitigation strategies like kinetic impactors through interactive 3D visuals and maps. It addresses the challenge by unifying siloed datasets, offering physics-based simulations, intuitive controls, tooltips, and gamified scenarios for accessibility across scientists, policymakers, and the public. It’s important for raising awareness, supporting planetary defense (e.g., NASA’s DART), fostering STEM education via kid-focused modules, and enhancing preparedness against catastrophic asteroid risks through global collaboration and informed decision-making.
projectDetails.details:
What Exactly Does It Do?

The web platform delivers a real-time, interactive 3D visualization of the solar system, accurately reflecting the current positions of planets and Near-Earth Objects (NEOs) using NASA’s JPL Horizons API, with visuals scaled for clarity. It focuses on potentially hazardous asteroids (PHAs) identified via NASA’s JPL Small Body Database API and assesses their impact risks using NASA’s JPL Sentry. Key features include:

Rendering a dynamic 3D solar system model showing real-time planetary and NEO positions.

Allowing users to select asteroids from a searchable list to view details like orbital elements, close approach dates, size, composition, and impact risk.

Simulating an asteroid’s trajectory from space to Earth, pinpointing impact locations on a map using OpenStreetMap for geographic context.

Evaluating impact consequences, including energy release (in megatons of TNT), tsunami potential (using USGS Elevation Data), and affected populations (using Google Earth Engine API).

Providing step-by-step visualizations of the asteroid’s path and impact effects for an immersive experience.

Future enhancements include educational modules for kids, inspired by NASA’s Eyes on Asteroids, using interactive animations to teach asteroid deflection strategies and promote STEM engagement.

How Does It Work?

The platform integrates real-time data from multiple APIs, computational models, and a modern tech stack to deliver visualizations and simulations:

Real-Time Solar System Visualization:

NASA’s JPL Horizons API: Fetches orbital elements (e.g., semi-major axis, eccentricity, inclination) for planets and NEOs, enabling real-time positioning in the 3D model.

Elliptical Orbit Simulator (Reference): Guides the implementation of accurate elliptical orbit calculations in the platform.

NASA’s Eyes on Asteroids (Reference): Inspires the design of user-friendly 3D visualizations.

Three.js with React-Three/Fiber and Drei: Renders the 3D solar system and asteroid trajectories in the browser. React-Three/Fiber simplifies Three.js integration with React, while Drei provides pre-built components (e.g., cameras, controls) for smooth navigation and interaction.

Asteroid Tracking and Impact Simulation:

NASA’s JPL Small Body Database API: Retrieves data on PHAs, including orbits, size, composition, and close approach details.

NASA’s JPL Sentry: Provides impact risk data, such as probability, velocity, and energy estimates, used to identify high-risk asteroids and simulate their trajectories.

Python FastAPI: Processes backend calculations, including trajectory modeling and impact physics (e.g., energy via $ E = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 $, where $ m $ is the asteroid’s mass and $ v $ is its velocity). FastAPI handles API requests efficiently, integrating data from NASA APIs and serving results to the frontend.

Trajectories are modeled considering atmospheric entry, velocity, angle, and composition, with simulations visualized step-by-step using Three.js.

Impact Assessment:

USGS Elevation Data: Supplies elevation data for impact coordinates, enabling analysis of topographic effects (e.g., tsunami risk for low-elevation coastal areas).

Google Earth Engine API: Provides population density data to estimate affected citizens based on the impact’s blast radius and location.

OpenStreetMap: Supplies geographic data for mapping impact locations, visualizing affected areas, and contextualizing results on a 2D/3D map.

Impact effects (e.g., crater size, tsunami potential) are calculated using models like Purdue University’s Impact Earth, calibrated with Sentry data.

User Interface:

React and React Router v7: Powers the frontend, providing a responsive, component-based interface. React Router v7 manages navigation, enabling seamless transitions between pages (e.g., solar system view, asteroid details, impact simulation).

Users select asteroids from a list, view details, and initiate simulations, with Three.js rendering dynamic 3D visuals and OpenStreetMap integrating 2D impact maps.

The interface supports zooming, rotating, and stepping through simulations for an engaging experience.

What Benefits Does It Have?

The platform offers significant benefits:

Public Accessibility: Real-time visualizations and intuitive controls make asteroid science approachable, engaging users of all ages.

Educational Value: Interactive simulations educate users about orbital mechanics and NEO risks, with future kid-focused modules enhancing STEM learning.

Planetary Defense Awareness: Simulating PHA impacts highlights the need for monitoring and mitigation, supporting global efforts like NASA’s Planetary Defense Coordination Office.

Scientific Utility: Researchers can visualize NEO trajectories and impact scenarios, aiding studies in astronomy and disaster preparedness.

Real-Time Accuracy: Integration of NASA APIs and OpenStreetMap ensures up-to-date, reliable data for credible simulations.

Community Preparedness: Estimating affected populations and tsunami risks informs strategies for mitigating catastrophic events.

What Do You Hope to Achieve?

The project aims to:

Educate and Engage: Make NEO science accessible, inspiring curiosity and STEM interest, particularly through future kid-focused deflection modules.

Support Planetary Defense: Provide a tool for visualizing and simulating asteroid impacts, contributing to global NEO monitoring and mitigation efforts.

Foster Collaboration: Create a platform for scientists, educators, and policymakers to explore PHA risks, potentially integrating with international initiatives.

Drive Innovation: Enable future features like real-time PHA alerts or advanced deflection simulations to enhance planetary safety.

Empower Communities: Raise awareness of asteroid risks, encouraging proactive preparedness for rare but high-impact events.

 

What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use to Develop Your Project?

The platform is built with a modern, efficient tech stack tailored to real-time visualization and simulation:

 

APIs Used:

NASA’s JPL Horizons API: Fetches real-time orbital elements for planets and NEOs.

NASA’s JPL Small Body Database API: Retrieves PHA data (orbits, size, composition, close approaches).

NASA’s JPL Sentry: Provides impact risk data (probability, velocity, energy).

USGS Elevation Data: Supplies topographic data for impact site analysis.

Google Earth Engine API: Delivers population density data for estimating affected citizens.

OpenStreetMap: Provides geographic data for mapping impact locations and visualizing affected areas.

Elliptical Orbit Simulator (Reference): Guides accurate orbit modeling.

NASA’s Eyes on Asteroids (Reference): Inspires 3D visualization design.

Coding Languages:

JavaScript (with React): Powers the frontend, managing UI components and interactivity. React enables a modular, responsive interface.

TypeScript (optional): Likely used with React for type safety and scalability.

Python (with FastAPI): Handles backend processing, including orbital calculations, impact simulations, and API integration.

HTML/CSS: Structures and styles the web interface for accessibility and aesthetics.

Tools and Frameworks:

React: Builds the component-based frontend for a dynamic user experience.

React Router v7: Manages client-side routing for seamless navigation between views (e.g., solar system, asteroid details, simulation pages).

Three.js: Renders 3D solar system models and asteroid trajectories.

React-Three/Fiber: Integrates Three.js with React, simplifying 3D scene management.

Drei: Provides pre-built Three.js components (e.g., orbit controls, cameras) for enhanced user interaction.

FastAPI: Powers the backend, handling API requests, data processing, and simulation calculations with high performance.

Git: Manages version control, likely hosted on GitHub for collaboration.

Our vision is to bridge science, technology, and storytelling — turning a global threat into a tool for knowledge, preparedness, and a safer future

projectDetails.name: EGYSAR
projectDetails.summary: What did we develop? A platform that uses NISAR satellite radar data, AI analysis, and a web interface with a chatbot to monitor Egypt’s heritage sites and detect early signs of natural risks. How does it address the challenge? The system compares radar scans over time to spot millimeter-scale ground shifts, soil changes, or structural stress. When risks appear, it automatically sends alerts to UNESCO and local authorities, while the website makes the data easy to understand and accessible.  Why is it important? Temples like Abu Simbel face growing threats from climate change, floods, heat, sandstorms, and even earthquakes. By catching danger early, this project helps protect Egypt’s cultural treasures, preserving history while preventing disasters.
projectDetails.details:
-What does it do?

The platform monitors heritage sites like Abu Simbel using radar data from the NISAR satellite. It detects small shifts in the ground or stone that could signal future damage, then alerts authorities before problems grow.

-How does it work?

- NISAR sends radar signals of the site every ~12 days.

- An AI model compares the new data with past records to find unusual changes.

- A website displays the images and AI outputs in simple visuals, alongside cultural context.

- A chatbot helps explain risks and guide users through the data.

- If something serious is detected, the system automatically notifies UNESCO and Egyptian authorities.

-What benefits does it provide?

- Early warning before damage happens.

- Protection of priceless monuments from floods, heat, sandstorms, or earthquakes.

- A bridge between cutting-edge space science and cultural heritage.

- A public platform that educates and engages people about Egypt’s history while protecting it.

-Tools, languages, and software used

-Satellite Data: NISAR radar scans.

-AI/ML: Python-based models for anomaly detection.

-Website: Built with NextJs

-Chatbot: Integrated with AI frameworks (like Python + NLP tools).

-Server/Storage: Cloud-based backend to process and store large radar datasets.

projectDetails.name: SolSim
projectDetails.summary:
In our day-to-day lives, we often don’t hear about asteroid impacts, but this doesn't prevent it from causing catastrophic consequences, which can be equivalent to thousands of nuclear weapons. While NASA keeps tracking over 30,000 Near-Earth Objects (NEOs), the complexity of this data and these models make understanding them inaccessible for the public, students, and even the decision-makers.
Our Project. SolSim faces this problem and tries to reduce the gap between this valuable data and the public by developing a gamified simulation platform that transforms real NASA and USGS data into a user-friendly, interactive, and intuitive experience. The user will explore the asteroids trajectory, simulate potential impacts, and try to defend their home from the simulated asteroid impacts through engaging simulated strategies.  
We chose this project because we think it represents one of the lost traits humankinds once had, which is protecting the Earth. Our solution adds value to this trait by bridging scientific accuracy with accessibility.
Gen Z Galaxy transforms raw orbital data into meaningful “What will happen if?” scenarios, making it a tool that keeps its scientific accuracy and at the same time sparks the curiosity of the user.
projectDetails.details:
SolSim is a project built to visualize, analyze, and respond to asteroid threats in real time simulation. It was developed under the Meteor Madness challenge, where we were asked a simple but powerful question: Do we have the right tools to make the right decision at the right time?

The system simulates the orbits of the asteroids and meteors near the Earth using real NASA datasets, calculate its potential impact parameters, like impact velocity, crater diameter, and kinetic energy. The project makes the user test different mitigation strategies and changes different parameters with each try. Every action updates the orbit of the asteroid, its risk level, and the user can see directly the consequences of their choices.

The project runs entirely on javascript, on the browser using javascript, Three.js, and react. Three.js renders the 3D orbit visualization of Earth, asteroids, and trajectories. A custom physics engine computes orbital motion based on Kepler’s laws and Newtonian mechanics. The frontend handles all user interactions and calculations and is designed to be efficient without any backend dependency.

The challenge was to create a way to transform complex orbital mechanics into a visual tool, appealing to the regular user, and accurate and fast for the researchers.

We considered several factors during the development process. We wanted to create a tool that is used by the curious student, and the researcher, so we had to consider factors like scientific accuracy by using only NASA datasets and official trusted sources. We also had to consider factors like user experience, and educational value, as without considering these two, the user will quickly get overwhelmed and leave the tool.

Ultimately, SolSim isn’t just a simulation—it’s a visualization of responsibility. It turns cold orbital data into a living, reactive universe where every user can become a planetary defender.

projectDetails.name: Project GeoBasira
projectDetails.summary:
GeoBasira is an AI-powered air quality monitoring and forecasting platform that transforms complex environmental data into simple, actionable insights. It integrates  ground-based sensor networks (OpenAQ), and weather forecast (OpenMeteo) to track harmful pollutants such as PM2.5, NO₂, O₃, and SO₂ at the street level, updated hourly.

Through interactive maps, users can click on any location to view current conditions, risk levels, and health recommendations. The system also predicts air quality up to 48 hours ahead, sending early warnings via text or email when pollution risks are high.

GeoBasira addresses the challenge of making air pollution data accessible and useful for everyone—families, schools, policymakers, and researchers. By presenting clear health advice alongside scientific forecasts, it empowers local leaders to implement targeted strategies and helps vulnerable communities stay safe.

Our goal is to reduce respiratory illnesses in key areas while supporting cities in cutting harmful pollutant levels, creating healthier, more resilient communities.
projectDetails.details:
GeoBasira collects real-time air quality data from OpenAQ and combines it with weather forecasts from Open-Meteo. An AI model processes this information to predict short-term changes in local air quality.

The system provides:

  • Current conditions: pollutant concentrations and risk categories.
  • Forecasts: short-term predictions for pollution levels.
  • Health guidance: recommendations for daily activities.
  • Early alerts: notifications when risks increase.

Benefits:

  • Makes air quality information easy for everyone to understand.
  • Helps families and schools reduce health risks.
  • Provides officials with insights for targeted responses.

Tools and Technologies Used:

  • Python – AI modeling and data processing.
  • OpenAQ API – real-time pollutant data.
  • Open-Meteo API – weather forecasts.
  • Web technologies (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) – interface and integration.

Our solution directly addresses the "Embiggen Your Eyes!" challenge by using an AI-powered image tiling technique. This allows users to seamlessly zoom and pan through gigapixel-scale images of Earth, the Moon, and space without long loading times or specialized software.
This project is important because it unlocks NASA's vast visual archives for a broader audience. It transforms overwhelming data into an engaging experience for public inspiration and provides a more efficient tool for scientific discovery.
projectDetails.details:
Our platform is a website that displays massive NASA images (over 500 MB) with a smooth, interactive interface. Users can zoom from a full-scale view down to the finest details, read AI-generated descriptions for context, and explore pre-identified points of interest marked directly on the photos.

It works by processing massive images into a pyramid of smaller tiles using an AI-enhanced model. When a user navigates the image, the website only loads the specific tiles needed for their current view and zoom level. This "on-demand" loading avoids the need to download the entire multi-gigabyte file, providing a fast and responsive experience.

The primary benefit is accessibility. It makes previously unwieldy datasets explorable on a standard web browser, enhanced with educational descriptions and guided points of interest.

• Tools & Technologies Used:

o Frontend: JavaScript with React/Next.Js frameworks.

o Mapping/Tiling: OpenLayers/Leaflet libraries and GDAL for image processing.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
We integrated Artificial Intelligence into two core components of our project:

1. AI for Image Processing: We used AI to develop and optimize the image processing model that performs the image tiling. The model intelligently slices the massive source images into a multi-resolution pyramid of tiles, ensuring optimal file size and loading efficiency for a smooth user experience.

2. AI for Content Generation: We utilized AI to generate informative and engaging descriptions for the images displayed on our platform. This helps users understand what they are seeing and appreciate the scientific context behind each stunning visual.

In accordance with the challenge rules, the use of AI for generating image processing logic and descriptive text will be properly acknowledged in our project's metadata and documentation.

projectDetails.name: Project Gradatim (Smart Recycling-to-Printing System)
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an integrated recycling system for plastic and aluminum waste on Mars, transforming them into 3D printing filament that can be directly used to manufacture essential tools and products for astronauts.
The system separates materials by type and processes each in specialized chambers: plastic is shredded, dried, and melted, while aluminum is milled, dried, and converted into fine powder. Both materials are then combined in controlled proportions to create a composite material suitable for 3D printing.
Afterward, the material is extruded into filament and stored on spools, ready for printing within a controlled and pressurized environment. This project addresses the challenge of waste management and sustainability in space environments by enabling the reuse of available resources instead of transporting new ones from Earth. It reduces costs and increases the efficiency and self-sufficiency of human settlements on Mars.
Its importance lies in being a closed-loop, sustainable system that supports the concept of a circular economy in space, providing a realistic solution for local resource production in extreme extraterrestrial conditions.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is an integrated recycling and 3D printing system designed to process plastic and aluminum waste generated on Mars and convert it into usable 3D printing filament. The system’s goal is to minimize material waste and maximize local resource utilization to support sustainable living and manufacturing on Mars.

How It Works

1-   The system operates through a sequence of automated chambers:

2-    Plastic waste enters its own pathway where it is shredded, dried, and melted into filament.

3-    Aluminum waste follows a separate route where it is milled into fine powder, dried, and safely stored in a controlled Both processed materials are then combined in precise ratios to form a reinforced composite filament, which is spooled and stored for use in 3D printing.

4-   The final 3D printing module allows users to design and print tools, spare parts, or essential components directly from the recycled material.

 

 

Benefits

  • Promotes resource efficiency and sustainability by reusing available materials.
  • Reduces dependence on Earth shipments, lowering cost and logistical challenges.
  • Supports self-sufficiency of future Mars habitats.
  • Encourages a circular economy model suitable for space environments.
  • Enhances safety and convenience through automation and contamination control.

 Goals

We aim to create a self-sustaining system that closes the recycling loop and enables astronauts to produce what they need, when they need it

directly on Mars. The project aspires to be a prototype for future extraterrestrial resource management systems.

 

Tools & Technologies

Design software: SolidWorks for 3D modeling and KeyShot for rendering; Figma for UI design.
Hardware concept: automated shredders, dryers, extruders, ball mills, sensors (temperature, oxygen, and pressure), and control panels.

projectDetails.name: Cloudquery
projectDetails.summary:
CloudQuery is a web application designed to demystify long-range event planning by leveraging historical climate data. We developed a solution that directly addresses the "Will it rain on my parade?" challenge by transforming over 40 years of NASA's POWER API data into simple, actionable insights.

Our Python-based analytical engine processes deep historical statistics for any user-selected location and date. An LLM then interprets this complex data to generate a personalized report, featuring a "Suitability Score," clear recommendations, and potential risk factors. This is not a weather forecast, but a powerful historical likelihood assessment.

This tool is important because it empowers anyone—from a family planning a picnic to communities organizing major events—to make proactive, data-driven decisions. CloudQuery makes NASA's vast repository of climate data accessible and useful for everyday life, ensuring better planning for a climate-aware future.
projectDetails.details:
CloudQuery is a web application that transforms complex historical climate data into a simple, personalized risk assessment for long-term event planning.

It operates on a two-phase architecture:

  1. Phase 1: The Analytical Engine: When a user submits a query with a location, date, and activity, our Python and FastAPI-based engine goes to work. It fetches over 40 years of daily meteorological data from the NASA POWER API for that specific point. It then performs a rigorous statistical analysis, calculating historical averages, percentile ranges, and probabilities for key variables like temperature, precipitation, and wind. The output is a highly structured JSON object of pure analytical data.
  2. Phase 2: LLM Interpretation: This structured data is then passed to a Large Language Model (LLM). The LLM's role is to act as a "data interpreter." It analyzes the statistics in the context of the user's activity (e.g., a "picnic" has different needs than a "hike") to generate the final, user-friendly report. This report includes a "Suitability Score," plain-language "Recommendations," and actionable "Risk Factors," which are then sent to the React frontend for display.

What benefits does it have?

The primary benefit of CloudQuery is providing clarity and confidence in long-range planning.

  • Reduces Uncertainty: It converts the gamble of planning an event months in advance into a data-driven decision.
  • Democratizes Data: It makes decades of complex scientific data from NASA accessible and understandable to anyone, regardless of their technical background.
  • Actionable Insights: Instead of just showing charts and numbers, it provides clear, human-readable advice, like "Be prepared for occasional strong wind gusts," which allows for proactive planning.
  • Personalized Feedback: Every report is tailored to the user's specific location, date, and activity, ensuring the insights are relevant and useful.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact of CloudQuery is to seamlessly integrate historical climate awareness into everyday decision-making.

  • Immediate Impact: To empower individuals and families to better plan their personal events, from weddings to vacations, reducing the stress and potential loss associated with weather-related disruptions.
  • Broader Impact: In the long term, the same technology can be scaled to serve larger needs. We envision CloudQuery being used by communities to schedule festivals, by farmers to assess historical climate risks for planting, and by businesses to build more resilient long-term operational plans. The ultimate goal is to foster a more proactive and climate-aware society.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Coding Languages: Python, JavaScript (with TypeScript)
  • Frameworks & Libraries: FastAPI (Python), React & React Router v7 (JavaScript), shadcn/ui (for UI components).
  • Data Source: The NASA POWER API.
  • AI: A Large Language Model (LLM) for the data interpretation and text generation phase.
  • Development Tools: Git for version control, Docker for containerization, and Visual Studio Code as the primary IDE.
  • Hardware: Development was done on standard laptops, and the application is deployed on a cloud-based Virtual Private Server (VPS).

How is your project creative?

Our project's creativity lies in its human-centric approach to data science.

  1. A Symbiotic Architecture: Instead of relying solely on an LLM, we created a two-phase system where a traditional, robust analytical engine performs the objective statistical work first. We then leverage the LLM for its strength in contextual understanding and natural language generation. This synergy ensures our results are both factually grounded and beautifully intuitive.
  2. Focus on the Decision: We creatively designed the output to answer the user's core question: "Is this a good day for my activity?" The Suitability Score, Recommendations, and Risks are all designed to facilitate a quick, confident decision, moving beyond a simple data dashboard.

What factors did your team consider?

  • The User Experience: Our primary consideration was the end-user. We designed the interface and the final report to be as simple, clean, and intuitive as possible, avoiding scientific jargon.
  • Data Integrity: We intentionally separated the statistical analysis (Phase 1) from the LLM interpretation (Phase 2). This ensures that the foundational data is accurate and verifiable before the AI adds its interpretive layer.
  • Challenge Constraints: The entire project was built around the challenge's core directive: to analyze historical likelihood, not to create a weather forecast. This principle guided every architectural and feature decision.
  • Feasibility and Speed: Given the hackathon timeframe, we chose a modern, rapid-development tech stack and a focused feature set to ensure we could deliver a polished, functional, and impactful prototype.

projectDetails.name: Guess The Weather For Me
projectDetails.summary: Our project is a web application to help people know the likelihood of different weather conditions in a specific place on a specific day in the future. The website supports many helpful weather variables (temperature, wind speed, humidity, cloud amount, aerosols, snow depth, and precipitation). It has a simple interactive dashboard that gives helpful insights and charts. Sometimes, seeing future predictions is necessary to motivate action. For that reason, we’ve included a simple regression model that predicts what will happen on the selected date of concern.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details:

Our project is a comprehensive, interactive web-based dashboard aimed at helping event planners be aware of weather conditions for a specific day in the future historical data, interactive features, and simple prediction. The platform is divided into four core components:

1-     Insights about historical data: We give a lot of helpful information about the history of the selected day in the past years for the variables of concern, like the average value, minimum and maximum values (range), and probability of exceeding a threshold picked by the user (for example, a 60% chance or higher of extreme heat conditions above 35 degrees Celsius) so a user that thinks that a temperature greater than 35 degrees is very, will know the probability of having this extreme heat condition.

2-     Simple prediction: Using this historical data, we use a linear regression & residuals adjustment statistical model to give some predictions for the variables of concern. Keep in mind that weather forecasts are reliable for a maximum of 2 weeks in advance, and they must use very recent data, so no need for complicated forecasting models because we aim for a lot more than only 2 weeks in advance. Usually, event planners need so much more time than 2 weeks to finish the planning process, so they can not only rely on weather forecasts.

3-     Interactive charts: The User can see time series for some specific variables in an interactive line chart to help the user see how the weather conditions were in the past and how they change over time, also a clear donut chart for the probability of exceeding the picked threshold, so the user can know the extreme conditions of their own concern.

4-     Ability to download: The user can download the dataset that contains the historical data of a specific day in the past years in a specific place, to have a deep look at how the past data was in a well-organized manner. They can either download a .csv file that is easy to open using Microsoft Excel, or a JSON file if they are more familiar with.

Our Goal:

Not all event planners have to take a big risk to plan an event that could be cancelled at the last minute due to bad weather conditions that are historically known, but they just did not know. So, the goal is simply to give the planners some more confidence when they want to plan an event, and to make them ready for some probable bad conditions they might face.

projectDetails.name: Project Habitect
projectDetails.summary:
What if ordinary people could step into the future and experience life inside a space habitat—not just read about it? This question inspired our project, developed under the challenge “Your Home in Space,” where we aim to bring the vision of extraterrestrial living closer to reality through immersive visualization and interaction.

Our solution is an interactive platform that lets users explore space habitats through advanced 3D modeling. We chose the Stanford Torus as our model due to its scientific feasibility and engineering clarity. Its design provides artificial gravity by rotation, farmland for food, residential areas for living, and dedicated zones for energy and healthcare.

By modeling the habitat in detail, we show not only its structure but also the environmental and social systems needed for survival. To make this accessible, we created a website that hosts the 3D models. Users can navigate the habitat, explore each sector, and understand essential systems like agriculture, lighting, and healthcare. Complex space concepts are simplified into engaging visuals for students, researchers, and the wider public.

To boost engagement, we added a gamified astronaut experience. Users can test layouts, simulate daily tasks, and visualize adaptation to orbital life. Beyond fun, it inspires curiosity about space engineering and connects expert knowledge with public imagination.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is designed to create an interactive and educational platform that brings the concepts of space habitats closer to people’s understanding. Specifically, it allows users to explore a realistic 3D model of the Stanford torus habitat, a scientifically feasible design for human life in space.

It works by combining 3D modeling, web integration, and gamification. First, we built a detailed 3D representation of the habitat using blender and other modeling tools to ensure structural and scientific accuracy. Then, these models are integrated into an interactive website, where users can navigate through different sections of the habitat- residential areas, agricultural zones, energy systems and health care modules. Finally, to enhance engagement, we include a game-like experience that lets users interact with various layouts and simulate daily life as astronauts inside the tours.

The benefits of this approach are twofold. On one hand, it simplifies complex space engineering concepts, making them accessible to students, educators, and the public. On the other, it provides an engaging platform that fosters curiosity, creativity, and awareness about the future of human space colonization.

Our main goal is to inspire and educate by transforming technical knowledge into an interactive journey. We hope to spark interest in space science, encourage STEM learning, and help people imagine sustainable living beyond Earth.

For development, we use Blender for 3D modeling, Unity or WebGL for interactivity, and standard web technologies (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) to build the platform. This mix of tools ensures both scientific precision and smooth user experience.

projectDetails.name: Hack the atmos
projectDetails.summary: We developed a cloud-powered web application that predicts near-term air quality by integrating real-time TEMPO satellite observations with ground-based sensor data and weather conditions. The platform leverages advanced AI models to generate localized forecasts of key pollutants, while delivering timely alerts, interactive dashboards, and actionable insights tailored for diverse stakeholders, including health-sensitive populations, schools, policymakers, and emergency responders.  This solution directly addresses the challenge of fragmented, inaccessible air quality information by transforming Earth observation data into a unified, predictive tool that is both scalable and accessible. Unlike static monitoring systems, our platform applies cloud computing to seamlessly process large, heterogeneous datasets and provide forecasts that users can act upon in real time.  The importance of this project lies in its ability to protect public health and guide decision-making. Vulnerable groups can take proactive steps to minimize exposure, officials can enact targeted interventions, and communities can make informed choices about outdoor activities and emergency preparedness. By turning satellite and ground data into actionable intelligence, our solution contributes to cleaner, safer skies and empowers both individuals and institutions to respond effectively to air pollution risks.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is a cloud-powered web application that predicts short-term air quality by integrating real-time TEMPO satellite data with ground-based sensors and weather information. The platform uses advanced AI models to analyze these datasets and generate accurate, localized forecasts of pollutants such as ozone, nitrogen dioxide, and particulate matter.

The system works in three steps. First, it ingests and harmonizes heterogeneous datasets through cloud pipelines. Next, machine learning models trained on historical and real-time inputs predict near-term trends. Finally, forecasts are delivered through interactive dashboards and personalized alerts, giving users clear, actionable insights.

This solution transforms fragmented and complex environmental data into a unified, user-friendly platform. It empowers health-sensitive groups to reduce exposure, supports policymakers and emergency responders with timely information, and helps the public make informed choices about outdoor activities and transportation. Unlike static monitoring systems, our application delivers forward-looking intelligence that communities can act on.

The platform was developed using Python for data processing and machine learning with TensorFlow and scikit-learn, and JavaScript/Angular for the front end. Interactive dashboards are built with D3.js and Plotly, while cloud services such as AWS or GCP provide scalable infrastructure for ingesting TEMPO satellite feeds, ground-based air quality data, and weather APIs.

By turning NASA Earth observation data into actionable knowledge, our project contributes directly to cleaner, safer skies and advances the mission of connecting space-based science with community impact.

projectDetails.name: HorizonX Biology Engine
projectDetails.summary: Our project, HorizonX Biology Engine, is an AI-powered web platform that transforms NASA’s extensive biological research archives into actionable insights. We developed a fully functional web application with FastAPI backend and a React frontend, enabling users to search, summarize, and explore publications efficiently. The platform uses Large Language Models and Transformers to generate concise summaries, while interactive dashboards provide statistical visibility into trends, research focus, and knowledge gaps. This addresses the challenge of scattered and overwhelming data by making scientific insights instantly accessible. By accelerating research review and highlighting underexplored areas, HorizonX Biology Engine empowers scientists and mission planners to make informed decisions, ultimately supporting safer and faster human space exploration.
projectDetails.details:

projectDetails.name: Trash to Green
projectDetails.summary:
Our team developed a pressurized, waste-upcycled greenhouse designed for long-duration Mars missions. This system transforms over 12,600 kg of inorganic mission waste—including plastics, aluminum frames, foam, textiles, and food packaging—into functional agricultural infrastructure. Using a modular 3D cube frame from habitat construction waste and a stitching technique, various materials are sewn into multi-layered greenhouse walls without heat or chemicals.

The greenhouse supports hydroponic food production inside Martian habitats, bypassing perchlorate-contaminated regolith. It also contributes to air and water recycling, fresh food access, and improved crew mental health, all while reducing trash volume. This solution addresses key sustainability and resupply challenges by turning waste into a vital life-support system. It offers a zero-waste, resource-efficient, and scalable approach to long-term survival and autonomy on Mars
projectDetails.details:
What Exactly Does It Do?
Our project transforms mission waste into a functional, modular greenhouse that supports food production, oxygen generation, water recycling, and structural insulation. It turns trash into a resource that directly supports crew survival on Mars.

How Does It Work?
The greenhouse is constructed inside the Martian habitat using a 3D aluminum frame from habitat waste. Walls are made from stitched panels of discarded plastic, foam, textiles, and packaging, creating layered insulation. Crops grow hydroponically using nutrient film technique (NFT), and thermal regulation is managed using passive heat storage and insulation. All systems operate within the existing life-support environment at Jezero Crater.

Key Benefits

  • Food security: Produces up to 12 kg/m²·cycle
  • Oxygen generation & CO₂ recycling
  • ~90% water recovery efficiency
  • Diverts ~12,600 kg of waste from landfilling
  • Modular, expandable, and sustainable

Intended Impact
We aim to prove that waste is not waste—it’s a construction material. This greenhouse enhances crew autonomy, reduces mission mass, and supports long-term colonization by merging life support with waste management.

Tools & Technologies Used

  • CAD software for structural modeling.
  • Manual fabrication: stitching, cutting, and thermal forming
  • NASA datasets and Mars regolith studies for environmental alignment

Creativity & Innovation
This system takes an overlooked problem—trash—and turns it into the core of Martian sustainability. No complex machinery required, just smart design, repurposing, and stitching. It’s scalable, low-tech, and mission-ready.

Team Considerations
We prioritized:

  • Material availability on Mars
  • Simplicity and crew time
  • Environmental constraints at Jezero Crater
  • Compatibility with existing habitat modules

projectDetails.name: Hypercodex
projectDetails.summary:
This project aims to develop an artificial intelligence and machine learning system that can automatically identify and classify exoplanets using NASA’s open-source datasets from missions such as Kepler, K2, and TESS. The system will analyze a variety of astrophysical parameters—such as orbital period, transit depth, stellar temperature, and planetary radius—to determine whether an observed celestial object is a confirmed exoplanet, a candidate, or a false positive.

To make this tool accessible and interactive, the project will include a web-based interface that allows scientists, students, and researchers to upload or manually enter new observational data. The interface will display the model’s predictions and offer visualizations that help users understand the factors influencing each classification. Optionally, user-submitted data could be incorporated to continuously improve the model’s performance through retraining.

The project combines data analysis, machine learning, and web development to create a powerful and user-friendly platform for exoplanet discovery. By leveraging NASA’s rich datasets and modern AI techniques, it seeks to make exoplanet research more efficient, transparent, and collaborative—bridging the gap between complex astrophysical data and real-time scientific insights.
projectDetails.details:
Hypercodex: AI-Powered Exoplanet Classification System

What does it do or how does it work?

Hypercodex automates the initial classification of planetary signals (Threshold Crossing Events or TCEs) from NASA transit missions like Kepler and TESS. It replaces the slow, manual process of vetting these signals with instant, high-confidence predictions.

How it Works:

  1. Input: A researcher or user inputs five key physical parameters associated with a TCE (like orbital period, transit depth, and stellar temperature) into the web interface.
  2. API Call: The front-end (HTML/JavaScript) sends this data to the Python Flask backend.
  3. Prediction: The backend loads a pre-trained Deep Learning Classifier (using TensorFlow/Keras) and a data scaler (Joblib). It scales the input data and generates a probability score (e.g., 95% confidence) that the signal is a Planet Candidate versus a False Positive.
  4. Output: The prediction is returned to the user interface, which dynamically updates a result card with the classification and confidence level.

What benefits does it have?

The primary benefit is massive scientific efficiency. Hypercodex acts as a pre-filter, significantly reducing the labor bottleneck in exoplanet research. It allows human astrophysicists to:

  • Focus Limited Resources: Immediately prioritize the highest-probability candidates for in-depth, expensive follow-up studies (like radial velocity measurements).
  • Prevent False Negatives: Ensure that promising, high-confidence signals are not overlooked due to human fatigue or data volume.
  • Scale with New Missions: The Deep Learning architecture is designed to handle the massive data volumes from current and future missions like TESS, ensuring the discovery pipeline remains fast and efficient.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to accelerate the rate of exoplanet discovery and validation. By making powerful machine learning accessible via a simple web interface, Hypercodex democratizes the initial phase of exoplanet research, enabling both professional astronomers and citizen scientists to contribute meaningfully to the field. Ultimately, it allows for a faster confirmation process, bringing new worlds out of the data and into the public eye sooner.

How is your project creative?

Hypercodex's creativity lies in its holistic design and specific ML application:

  1. Full-Stack Solution for Vetting: It's not just a training script; it's a complete, deployed web application, transforming a complex scientific process into an accessible, real-time tool.
  2. Deep Learning for Structured Data: While many deep learning solutions focus on raw light curves, our approach uses a powerful Sequential Dense Neural Network optimized for speed and accuracy on the five most critical physical parameters.
  3. Immediate Scientific Utility: It directly tackles a known pain point in astronomical data reduction, delivering high-confidence predictions that are immediately actionable for researchers.

What factors did your team consider?

  1. Data Quality & Bias: We filtered the NASA data carefully to ensure the target labels (Confirmed/Candidate vs. False Positive) were clearly defined to minimize model bias.
  2. Accessibility: The project was packaged using a simple Flask server and a responsive HTML interface so that anyone with a browser could use the powerful ML model.
  3. Performance: We chose a Deep Learning architecture optimized with techniques like Batch Normalization and Early Stopping (train_hypwecodex_model.py) to maximize accuracy while maintaining fast prediction times.
  4. Reproducibility: We provided detailed setup files (requirements.txt, README.md) to ensure any researcher can clone the repo, retrain the model, and run the API easily.

The project's central function is an AI/ML system.

  • Model Type: A Sequential Deep Learning Classifier built using TensorFlow 2.x/Keras.
  • Use: This model was trained on public NASA Exoplanet Archive data (koi_period, koi_depth, etc.) to perform binary classification (Planet Candidate vs. False Positive) in real-time.
  • Code and Data: The training script (train_Hypercodex_model.py) defines and executes the AI training. The resulting model (deep_learning_model.h5) is used by the application for all predictions.

    • Documentation: To generate and format the detailed project proposal (hypercodex_proposal.md) and the project setup instructions (README.md).

Acknowledge AI Generation: The base structure, logic flow, and specific code implementations for the API, ML model, and UI were created with assistance from an AI language model to accelerate the development process. All outputs were reviewed, tested, and modified by the team for accuracy and functionality.
