🌤 Idea
An intelligent weather analysis app powered by NASA Earth Observation Data, designed to help users determine the probability of extreme weather conditions (e.g., very hot, heavy rain, strong wind) for any specific place and date — ideal for planning outdoor events, trips, and daily activities.

🎯 Main Objectives

Use NASA’s historical data (2001–present) to calculate weather probabilities instead of short-term forecasts.

Provide a personalized dashboard for selecting cities, coordinates, or map locations.

Deliver advanced statistical analysis showing the likelihood of “uncomfortable” weather through visual tools like bell curves, percentiles, and confidence intervals.

Offer smart warnings related to health, energy, driving, and outdoor activities.

⚙️ Core Features

NASA POWER API Integration: 25 years of historical and real-time data, multi-parameter support (temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation), and precise probability analysis.

Advanced Analysis & Visualization: Interactive bell curves, percentile charts, confidence intervals, and climate trend analysis.

Smart Warning System: Health (UV, air quality, temperature), energy (solar efficiency, AC usage), and driving alerts.

Search & Input System: City search, coordinate input, interactive map, and GPS integration.

Settings & Customization: Custom thresholds, unit conversion (°C/°F, m/s/km/h, etc.), and persistent preferences.

ExoHunter: analyzes stellar light curves to identify exoplanets through transit detection. It:

•Provides probability scores for detection confidence

•Visualizes results through an interactive web dashboard

1.Data Input: Users upload or input stellar observation data

2.Preprocessing: The system cleans and normalizes the data using label encoders

3.ML Prediction: XGBoost pipeline analyzes patterns to detect transit signatures

4.Classification: Algorithm determines if signals indicate exoplanet presence

5.Results Display: Streamlit interface shows predictions with confidence metrics

What Benefits Does It Have?

•Speed: Processes data in seconds vs. hours of manual analysis

•Accuracy: ML model trained on validated exoplanet datasets

•Accessibility: No specialized astronomy software required

projectDetails.name: DeepOrbit
projectDetails.summary:
This project focuses on developing an AI-driven system for exoplanet
detection and analysis using NASA’s open-source datasets. The system applies
machine learning to identify planetary candidates from telescope observations
while reducing human effort in manual classification. The challenge of
analyzing vast amounts of astronomical data is addressed through automated
pipelines and interactive visualization tools. This approach increases the
speed, accuracy, and accessibility of exoplanet discovery. The project is
important because it enhances the scientific community’s ability to find
habitable planets, while also engaging the public through interactive
platforms and educational tools.
projectDetails.details:
The project provides a web-based platform powered by AI that:

- Automatically detects potential exoplanets from light-curve data.

- Visualizes planetary data with graphs, dashboards, and interactive displays.

- Enables researchers and students to explore datasets efficiently.

How it works:

AI models are trained on NASA’s Kepler and TESS datasets to detect dips in

star brightness caused by transiting planets. The output is then displayed on

an interactive web interface, which allows filtering, visualization, and further

analysis.

Benefits:

- Faster and more accurate exoplanet detection.

- Improved accessibility for researchers and students.

- Potential to inspire citizen science and public engagement.

Tools, languages, and software used:

- Programming Languages: Python, JavaScript (for web interface).

- AI/ML Frameworks: TensorFlow, Scikit-learn.

- Visualization: Plotly, D3.js.

- Web Development: React, Node.js.

- Hardware/Software: Cloud computing resources for model training.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Yes, AI tools and software were central to this project. Specifically:

- TensorFlow & Keras – for deep learning model development.

- Scikit-learn – for preprocessing, feature selection, and classical ML models.

AI was used to detect anomalies, classify star light curves, and predict

planetary candidates with higher efficiency compared to manual inspection.

Backend Development and Integration:

The backend was developed using Flask, a lightweight Python web framework. AI tools assisted in structuring the API, integrating the trained (.pkl) model, and handling requests from the frontend. The backend manages model loading, prediction processing, and input validation. It was designed to be compatible with online deployment platforms such as PythonAnywhere, ensuring smooth interaction between the web interface and the AI model.

projectDetails.name: CupolaGate
projectDetails.summary: CupolaGate is an interactive, AI-powered gamified website developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, focusing on the International Space Station's (ISS) Cupola module and Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory (NBL) training. The project aims to educate students and the public on two key sensory experiences: the breathtaking orbital sights from the Cupola ("window to the world") and the weightlessness simulated in the NBL. It achieves this through visual simulations, quizzes, and tasks, while highlighting how these experiences benefit humanity on Earth (e.g., disaster relief, climate monitoring, geosciences, healthcare advancements, and societal improvements like medical research from microgravity). All of these make the education process funny and informative and focuses on hands-on training
projectDetails.details:
CupolaGate is an interactive, gamified website that simulates key ISS experiences to educate users on space exploration. It works by guiding users through an "astronaut trainee" journey via a responsive browser interface. Users register for a personalized dashboard, then progress through sections:

Cupola Simulations: A 3D viewer loads NASA-sourced Earth photos, where users navigate levels focused on disaster monitoring, climate change, geosciences, and healthcare/societal benefits. Each level requires completing tasks (e.g., spotting features in images) and quizzes (multiple-choice with 85% accuracy to unlock the next), reinforced by AI-generated "echo" stories linking actions to real-world impacts.

NBL Training Zone: A physics-based simulation (using Matter.js) lets users input their weight, calculate buoyancy (via Archimedes' principle: buoyant force = water density × gravity × displaced volume), adjust virtual gear (weights/floaties) to achieve neutral net force, and perform tasks like repairing a hatch (drag-and-drop with collision detection). Success unlocks badges and ties to Earth benefits like medical advancements.

The site uses gating (complete tasks to advance) and short sessions (5-10 minutes) for event use, with MERN backend storing user data.

What Benefits Does It Have?

CupolaGate offers multiple benefits:

Educational: Breaks down complex space concepts into fun simulations and quizzes, helping users understand ISS sensory experiences (sight from Cupola, weightlessness in NBL) and their Earth applications (e.g., disaster relief via georeferenced photos, healthcare from microgravity insights).

Engaging and Accessible: Gamification (levels, badges) boosts retention; voice-overs and AI personalization make it inclusive for all ages/abilities; multilingual support and touch-screen optimization suit classrooms or events.

Scalable and Free: Built with open-source tools, it's expandable to more space topics; uses NASA public data for authenticity without costs.

Real-World Ties: Highlights benefits like faster disaster response (e.g., flood maps) and societal gains (e.g., prosthetics from NBL tech), inspiring STEM interest.

What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

The project aims to inspire global youth to engage with space exploration, closing the gap in understanding ISS facilities. Intended impacts include:

STEM Empowerment: Boost curiosity, problem-solving, and career interest in science by making abstract concepts hands-on (e.g., 1,000+ users gaining knowledge on climate monitoring).

Global Outreach: Make space education inclusive and scalable, reaching underserved students worldwide via free browser access, celebrating 25 years of ISS achievements.

Awareness of Benefits: Inform how space experiences aid Earth (e.g., healthcare innovations from weightlessness), fostering appreciation for NASA's work and encouraging support for exploration.

Long-Term: Serve as a classroom tool for teachers, potentially reducing STEM dropout rates by 10-20% through engagement (based on similar gamified platforms); measurable via analytics (e.g., quiz scores, session time).

What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware or Software Did You Use to Develop Your Project?

Coding Languages: JavaScript/TypeScript (core logic, calculations), HTML/CSS (structure/styling).

Frameworks/Libraries: Next.js (SSR, routing), React (UI components), Tailwind CSS (styling), Framer Motion (animations, e.g., avatar floating), Three.js (Cupola 3D views), Matter.js (NBL physics).

Backend/Database: MERN stack – MongoDB (user progress/badges), Express/Node.js (APIs like /progress), Axios (frontend calls).

Audio/Video Tools: ElevenLabs/NoteGPT (TTS for voice-overs), Audacity/VEED.io (merging conversations), CapCut (video editing for intros).

Design/Prototyping: Figma (wireframes/UI), Canva (graphics/characters).

Data Sources: NASA APIs (e.g., Earth Imagery for dynamic photos), Gateway to Astronaut Photography (images).

Hardware/Software: Standard laptops (Windows/macOS for development), Git/GitHub (version control), Netlify/Vercel (deployment). No specialized hardware; browser-based for accessibility.

Other: Dialogflow (AI chatbot), AWS S3 (free tier for audio hosting).

How Is Your Project Creative?

CupolaGate stands out with innovative elements:

Character-Driven Narration: Custom voices (Miss Star, Mr. Comet) turn explanations into lively conversations, merged via TTS tools for immersive storytelling, making education feel like a dialogue rather than reading.

Hybrid Simulations: Combines Cupola 3D views with NBL physics in "fusion modes" (e.g., observe a disaster from Cupola, then "dive" into NBL for a related task), creating replayable scenarios with procedural generation.

Sensory Immersion: Framer Motion animations and Matter.js physics make weightlessness "feel" real in browser, creatively using web tech for NASA-inspired authenticity.

What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

The team (Ibrahim Wael: MERN Developer/Leader; Belal Mostafa: Researcher/Presentation; Malak Abdelrahman: Presentation/Character Designer; Salma Osama: UI/UX/Video Edit) considered:

User Experience: Accessibility ( color-blind modes, keyboard nav), short sessions for events, responsive design for mobile/desktop.

Educational Accuracy: Cross-referenced NASA sources for facts/images; ensured concepts align with challenge (sight/weightlessness, Earth benefits).

Technical Feasibility: Chose MERN/Next.js for scalability; optimized 3D/physics for browser performance; free tools to minimize costs.

Creativity and Innovation: Balanced gamification with learning

Impact and Inclusivity: Targeted youth/global audiences; multilingual support; factors like data privacy (anonymous analytics) and ethical AI (good intent assumptions).

Testing and Iteration: Pilot tests with peers for engagement; considered edge cases (e.g., invalid inputs in sims); scalability for future expansions (e.g., more ISS topics).

projectDetails.summary: Our project, developed by team KeplerX, for challenge “A World Away: Hunting for  Exoplanets with AI” It addresses the challenge of classifying exoplanetary data using  NASA’s mission archives. This project is important because it bridges cutting-edge machine learning with real NASA  data, helping streamline exoplanet validation workflows while making astrophysical insights  more accessible to researchers, students, and enthusiasts.

projectDetails.name: weather wise
projectDetails.summary:
We developed WeatherWise, an interactive mobile application that transforms NASA’s Earth observation data into actionable weather probabilities for long-term planning. Unlike conventional weather forecasts, which are limited to days ahead, WeatherWise allows users to plan activities months in advance.

The app works by taking a city name and date as input, converting it into geographic coordinates using OpenStreetMap’s Nominatim API, and then retrieving historical daily data from NASA’s POWER dataset. Based on this data, it calculates the probability of experiencing conditions such as extreme or moderate heat, cold, heavy rain, high wind, or uncomfortable humidity. Results are displayed as clear percentages, supported by histograms for deeper insights, and can be downloaded as CSV files that include metadata and units

WeatherWise addresses the challenge by making NASA’s climate data practical and accessible, empowering communities, event planners, and individuals to make safer and smarter decisions far beyond the reach of traditional forecasting.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, WeatherWise, is a mobile application that helps people plan outdoor activities or events months in advance by providing probabilities of different weather conditions instead of short-term forecasts. Traditional forecasts are limited to around 10–14 days, but WeatherWise leverages historical NASA Earth observation data to calculate the likelihood of conditions such as temperature ranges, rainfall, wind speed, and air quality for any given city and date.

How it works:

  • Users type in a city and select a future date.
  • The app uses the Nominatim OpenStreetMap API to get location coordinates.
  • We then pull historical climate data from NASA’s POWER API.
  • Our backend processes this data using Python, Pandas, and FastAPI, calculating probabilities for multiple weather conditions.
  • Results are displayed in an interactive dashboard (built with Streamlit) where users can view probabilities and explore further using visualizations and charts.

Benefits:

  • Helps users plan trips, outdoor events, or agricultural activities well ahead of time.
  • Gives a data-driven view of climate probabilities instead of unreliable long-term forecasts.
  • Makes climate data more accessible and visual for the public.

Our Goals:

  • Empower users to make informed decisions for future plans.
  • Raise awareness about the importance of climate patterns in daily life.
  • Encourage creative uses of NASA Earth observation data in real-world scenarios.

Tools & Technologies Used:

  • Languages: Python
  • Frameworks: FastAPI, Streamlit
  • Libraries: Pandas, NumPy, Requests
  • APIs: NASA POWER API, Nominatim OpenStreetMap API
  • Hosting/Version Control: GitHub
projectDetails.aiReferences: We used AI tools (chatgpt/deepseek) to assist in brainstorming, refining project descriptions, drafting presentation scripts, and generating written summaries. All technical implementation, code integration, and dataset analysis were performed by our team. AI was not used to generate NASA data, but it supported us in documentation and creative writing.

projectDetails.name: ExoAI Navigator
projectDetails.summary: ExoAI Navigator is a web platform designed to analyze user-inputted parameters of exoplanet candidates. Utilizing an AI/ML model trained on NASA’s Kepler cumulative exoplanet dataset, the system classifies candidates as Confirmed Planets, Candidates, or False Positives. projectDetails.name: Project Know Before You Go
projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary

What did you develop?
We developed “Know Before You Go”, a smart decision-support platform that predicts rainfall risks for outdoor events. The system integrates real-time NASA satellite data with machine learning models to forecast whether it will rain, when it will start or stop, and how severe it may be — allowing users to plan accordingly.

How does it address the challenge?
The project directly addresses the “Will It Rain on My Parade?” challenge by providing a reliable and user-friendly solution that leverages NASA’s GPM/IMERG, SMAP, and POWER datasets to deliver precise and actionable rainfall predictions. Users and event organizers can make informed decisions about scheduling, safety, and logistics.

Why is it important?
Rainfall affects millions of outdoor activities worldwide — from public festivals to business events. By combining open NASA data and AI-driven forecasting, our platform improves preparedness, minimizes event disruptions, and supports data-driven climate resilience at both individual and community levels.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?
The system provides:

  • Real-time rainfall visualization using satellite data (IMERG).
  • Predictive rain forecasts (0–6 hours ahead) powered by a Random Forest ML model.
  • Smart alerts notifying users about expected rain in their area.
  • Event planning recommendations based on rainfall probability and risk analysis.
  • Post-event reports evaluating forecast accuracy.

How does it work?

  1. NASA APIs (GPM/IMERG, SMAP, POWER) provide raw inputs (rainfall rate, soil moisture, and surface temperature).
  2. Data is preprocessed and passed to our trained ML model (best_rf_model.joblib) for short-term rainfall prediction.
  3. The system outputs the probability of rain, estimated start/end times, and an uncertainty margin (±10%).
  4. The web and mobile interfaces visualize results through maps, charts, and smart notifications.

Benefits:

  • Early awareness of rainfall events.
  • Data-driven event planning and risk management.
  • Improved accuracy via NASA-grade satellite data.
  • Enhanced environmental and public safety decisions.

Tools, Languages, and Technologies Used:

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript
  • Backend: Flask, Node.js
  • Frontend: React.js, HTML/CSS
  • Machine Learning: scikit-learn, joblib
  • Data Visualization: Plotly, Leaflet.js
  • APIs & Datasets: NASA GPM/IMERG, SMAP, POWER
  • Hosting & Repo: https://github.com/Tahanyemad16/Know-Before-You-Go-Nasa-Space-25/

node.excerpt: We are a forward-looking team passionate about innovation and exploration. Eager to learn, eager to earn, and eager to win, we combine creativity with analytical thinking to transform challenges into impactful solutions for both space and Earth.

projectDetails.name: LEO Safe Flight
projectDetails.summary:
Our project tackles the growing challenge of space debris in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), a serious threat to satellites, GPS, communications, and future space missions.

We designed not only a technical solution, but also an interactive website to create awareness and present our concept clearly:

Home Page: introduces the problem and our vision.

Education Page: offers awareness content, showcases past solutions, and highlights insights from our data analysis.

Services Page: explains our final solution in detail and the services we provide.

 Final Concept – Hybrid Solution
Our innovation is a hybrid debris collection system:

Capture nets to collect small-to-medium debris (centimeters to decimeters).

Gecko-inspired adhesive patches to trap very small fragments (millimeters to centimeters) that nets cannot catch.

 Architecture
The system uses a fleet of CubeSats, each equipped with a net, adhesive patch, and storage chamber. An optional small mothership can help with deployment and coordination, but the system remains effective even if one unit fails—ensuring resilience and low risk.

 Key Value
This distributed, scalable, and bio-inspired approach integrates both mechanical and adhesive methods, enabling the efficient removal of debris across different sizes. The result: a cleaner, safer orbital environment and a more sustainable future for space activities.
projectDetails.details:
What does our project do or how does it work :-

Our project introduces an innovative hybrid solution for space debris mitigation in Low Earth Orbit (LEO).

It combines two tested approaches—capture nets for large debris and gecko-inspired adhesive surfaces for micro-debris—integrated within deployable specialized satellites launched from a mother ship. This hybrid design increases efficiency compared to using each technique independently, ensuring better debris collection with optimized cost and operational practicality.

Beyond the technical solution, our project includes a dedicated awareness platform:

  • An educational website that highlights the growing risk of orbital debris.
  • A public dashboard presenting real-time insights, statistics, and global efforts for debris management.
  • Curated articles and resources that showcase other international solutions alongside our own.

Our system also emphasizes sustainability and cost-effectiveness. By offering annual subscription services, satellite operators—whether protecting existing assets in LEO or preparing for new launches—can ensure continuous monitoring and mitigation of debris risks.

This dual approach creates both a practical technical benefit and an ethical commercial model, combining space safety with accessible education and awareness.

What benefits does it have :-

  1. Higher Efficiency in Debris Collection
    • By combining capture nets for large debris with gecko-inspired adhesive surfaces for micro-debris, our hybrid system provides wider coverage and superior effectiveness compared to single-solution approaches.
  2. Practical and Feasible Design
    • Both techniques are based on tested and researched technologies. The innovation lies in integrating them into one system, making the solution realistic and implementable.
  3. Enhanced Satellite Safety
    • Reduces the risk of collisions that can cause damage worth millions of dollars.
    • Ensures operational continuity for commercial, scientific, and governmental satellites.
  4. Clear Economic Value
    • Annual subscription plans allow operators to protect their satellites at a cost far lower than potential losses.
    • Transforms debris mitigation from a cost burden into a sustainable investment.
  5. Educational and Awareness Impact
    • A dedicated website and dashboard will increase awareness among investors, students, and space enthusiasts.
    • Positions the project not only as a technical solution but also as a responsible educational initiative.
  6. Long-Term Sustainability
    • Actively reduces orbital debris accumulation and prevents escalation of the Kessler Syndrome.
    • Contributes to a safer space environment for future generations.
  • Transparency Note:
    The project is currently at the concept and design stage. Real-world implementation will require further physical testing, technical partnerships, and funding support from space agencies or private companies.

What is the intended impact of the project :-

The intended impact of our project is to create a safer and more sustainable space environment by reducing orbital debris. By capturing and removing space junk, our satellite will help extend the lifespan of operational satellites, lower the risks of collisions, and minimize the financial losses caused by damage. This contributes to the long-term sustainability of space exploration, communications, and research, ensuring that future missions can operate in a secure and stable orbit.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project :-

Our project combines essential software and hardware components to deliver a hybrid and practical solution to the orbital debris problem.

Software Components

  • Frontend Development: HTML, CSS, JavaScript → used for building and developing the website interface.
  • Data Processing: Python → applied for cleaning and processing datasets related to debris and satellite operations.
  • Libraries: Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib → for data manipulation, analysis, and visualization.
  • Visualization: Power BI → for creating interactive dashboards that illustrate debris risks, awareness content, and solution comparisons.
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages → for publishing and maintaining the awareness and subscription-based website.

Hardware Components

  • Mothership Satellite: the main carrier in Low Earth Orbit, designed to host and retrieve smaller satellites.
  • Specialized Mini-Satellites (CubeSat-like): equipped with solar cells and small propulsion units, designed to deploy debris-capturing mechanisms.
  • Debris Capture System: a deployable net mechanism integrated into the mini-satellites, along with adhesive-coated outer surfaces for collecting micro-debris.

By combining these components, the project demonstrates a clear and feasible framework for enhancing orbital debris mitigation with both digital and physical layers working together.

How is your project creative :-

Our project stands out as highly creative because it does not rely on a single existing solution, but instead combines multiple proven techniques into a hybrid model. While many space agencies and companies focus on just one method of debris removal, such as nets, adhesive materials, or lasers, our solution integrates these concepts in a complementary way, resulting in higher efficiency and adaptability.

The creativity lies in several aspects:

  • Hybrid Innovation: By merging tested technologies like deployable nets and adhesive-coated surfaces within mini-satellites carried by a mothership, we create a solution that maximizes efficiency while minimizing cost.
  • Scalable Design: Using a mothership to deploy multiple small satellites allows us to scale operations depending on the amount and size of debris, which is more flexible than a single-purpose satellite.
  • Dual Impact: The project not only provides a technical solution to a pressing global issue but also includes an awareness and educational platform through our website and interactive dashboards. This dual approach—technical and educational—enhances the project’s creativity by targeting both space operations and public engagement.
  • Economic Angle: Unlike many purely experimental ideas, our model includes a sustainable subscription-based business framework, creating a balance between innovation and real-world feasibility.

In short, the creativity of our project comes from the unique integration of multiple approaches and the added value of awareness and engagement, making it more than just a technical fix—it’s a holistic and forward-looking solution.

What factors did your team consider :-

When developing our project, our team carefully considered several key factors to ensure the solution is both practical and impactful:

  1. Technical Feasibility – We evaluated whether the hardware (mothership and CubeSats) and the chosen debris-removal methods (nets, adhesive surfaces) could realistically function in Low Earth Orbit.
  2. Cost Efficiency – We considered the economic side of the solution, aiming to reduce costs by using small satellites, scalable deployment, and a subscription-based service model.
  3. Scalability – The design allows flexibility to increase or decrease the number of CubeSats depending on the debris density and mission requirements.
  4. Sustainability – We assessed how to reduce further space pollution, ensuring debris is captured and removed responsibly rather than creating new fragments.
  5. Awareness and Education – We included an informative website and dashboards to raise awareness among stakeholders, investors, and the general public about the dangers of space debris.
  6. Safety and Risk Management – We considered how to minimize the risks of collision during operations and ensure safe deorbiting of captured debris.
  7. User Value – We designed the project with end-users in mind, offering services like annual subscriptions to protect satellites already in orbit or upcoming launches.

These factors helped guide our decisions, ensuring that the project is not only technically innovative but also economically and socially meaningful.

projectDetails.details:
Life on 218? – Space habitat simulation

What Exactly Does It Do?

The project is a 3D interactive web-based game that lets users design and explore space habitats for the Moon and Mars. Players can customize the size, shape, and layout of habitats, place rooms and life-support systems, and experiment with resource management and habitability constraints. The game provides real-time AI feedback, guiding users toward viable designs while teaching them the principles of sustainable living in space through hands-on interaction and problem-solving.

How does it work?

The game works by providing users with an interactive 3D interface where they can select and place habitat modules, rooms, and life-support systems within a defined volume. It incorporates rules and constraints based on real space engineering principles, such as air circulation, gravity effects, and resource limitations. As users build, the AI feedback system evaluates designs, highlighting strengths and potential issues, allowing players to iterate and optimize their habitats while learning about sustainable space living.

Benefits:

Educational value: Life on 218? teaches space habitat design and sustainability through hands-on 3D exploration.

Problem-Solving skills enhancement: The game encourages users to optimize layouts under realistic constraints.

Creativity: The game Sparks interest in space, engineering, and innovative habitat solutions.

Accessible: Web-based platform allows anyone to explore and experiment with space habitats.

What do we hope to achieve?

We hope to inspire the next generation of engineers and innovators by transforming space habitat designs into hands-on experience. We view a future where anyone, regardless of their level of expertise, can contribute to the challenge of living in space supporting global interest in NASA’s journey to Moon, Mars, and beyond.

projectDetails.name: Project Sentinel
projectDetails.summary:
The annual slaughter of 80 million sharks threatens ocean collapse. Current conservation is failing because static protected areas are useless for migratory animals. This gap between static and dynamic leaves the ocean's guardians exposed and our efforts blind. Project Sentinel, a solution for the Sharks from Space challenge, aims to protect marine ecosystems by using a predictive AI fed by NASA data and our smart tag, advancing real-time conservation.
We built a dual-AI system. A Random Forest model is trained by NASA’s satellite data (PACE, SWOT) for habitats in a local simulation and live data from our Markov chain-powered smart tag, which uses an adaptive Markov chain with Bayesian inference for efficient transmission, creating a powerful predictive feedback loop. Our web platform delivers a real-time map displaying shark locations and their AI-generated “Foraging Probability Score”. Our simulation successfully identifies feeding hotspots by correlating tag behavior with satellite data, demonstrating a scalable model for turning raw data into actionable conservation intelligence.
Sentinel enables Dynamic Marine Protected Areas; a paradigm shift in conservation. Our interactive quiz and tales transform fear into fascination. We invite you to explore our platform and help us protect sharks; not only for marine life, but for ourselves.
projectDetails.details:
Our Mathematical Framework

Our mathematical framework is a sophisticated geospatial data fusion pipeline designed to identify potential shark foraging hotspots. The core challenge is that different NASA satellites produce data on different grids and scales. Our framework solves this by creating a unified analysis grid and using a machine learning model to find specific environmental niches that are likely to attract sharks.

Part 1: The Geospatial Fusion Pipeline

Before any prediction can happen, we must fuse the data. This is the mathematical foundation of our project.

  1. Data Ingestion: We begin by ingesting data from three distinct NASA sources: MODIS for Chlorophyll-a (CHL), MODIS for Sea Surface Temperature (SST), and SWOT for Sea Surface Height (SSH).
  2. Grid Unification (via cKDTree): The core of our framework is resolving the difference between the sparse, high-resolution SWOT data and the regular grid of MODIS. We achieve this using a k-dimensional tree (cKDTree) algorithm. This allows us to perform a nearest-neighbor interpolation, effectively mapping the crucial SWOT sea surface height data onto the same grid as the MODIS temperature and chlorophyll data. This creates a single, unified grid where every pixel has a value for CHL, SST, and SSH.
  3. Feature Vector Creation: For every pixel on our unified grid, we create a feature vector containing these three oceanographic parameters. This vector is then normalized using StandardScaler to prepare it for our machine learning model.

Part 2: The Predictive Engine - Niche Identification

Instead of relying on sparse shark location data for training, we mathematically define an ideal foraging hotspot and train a model to find it.

  • Synthetic Label Generation: We define a likely foraging hotspot as an area with specific environmental conditions (e.g., high chlorophyll and low sea surface temperature). We translate this definition into a mathematical rule to create our training labels (y). This is an expert-driven approach that allows us to build a robust model without needing massive amounts of real-world shark feeding data.
  • Random Forest Classifier: We use a Random Forest Classifier as our predictive model. This powerful ensemble method builds a "forest" of decision trees to learn the complex, non-linear relationships between the three environmental variables and our defined "hotspot" label.
  • Probability Mapping: The trained classifier then analyzes the entire unified grid. For every single pixel, it calculates the probability that the conditions at that location match the ideal foraging hotspot niche. The final output is a probability heatmap, which visually represents the areas where sharks are most likely to be feeding.

Part 3: The Tag's Mathematical Core (Markov Model)

The tag itself contains its own mathematical framework for energy efficiency. It uses a Markov model to intelligently decide when to transmit data. The tag monitors its own sensor parameters (like motion) and only activates its satellite uplink when these parameters change significantly, indicating a noteworthy event. This probabilistic approach to data transmission is what enables a long battery life in the field.

Our TAG - Smart Electronic Device

The tag is our frontline data gatherer, the crucial link between the shark and our AI. It is conceptualized as a rugged, non-invasive device designed for rich data collection, extreme energy efficiency, and long-term autonomous operation in the harsh marine environment.

Core Design (Hackathon Prototype Concept)

Our current design focuses on a core suite of sensors to provide a complete snapshot of the shark's state and its immediate environment.

  • Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU): Captures high-fidelity acceleration data. This is the raw input that forms the basis of all future behavioral analysis (with tilt speed and angle to be added).
  • Environmental Sensors: Onboard temperature and pressure sensors provide crucial context, correlating the shark's location with water temperature and its depth.
  • Positioning & Communication: A GPS module determines the precise geographic location. For our prototype, a GSM module transmits this data using the lightweight MQTT protocol, an efficient method for sending data over mobile networks in coastal scenarios.

Our primary innovation is the development of the first conceptualized, non-invasive smart tag that integrates a comprehensive sensor suite with next-generation satellite communication in an exceptionally small form factor. Unlike bulky or invasive alternatives, the Sentinel Tag is designed to provide rich, multi-layered data including motion (IMU), temperature, pressure (depth), and precise location while prioritizing animal welfare. Its core novelty lies in its planned integration of the Argos satellite system, moving beyond the limitations of coastal GSM networks to offer true, global open-ocean tracking capabilities. This represents a significant leap forward in creating a viable, long-term, and humane tool for marine research.

This innovation is brought to life through the following key systems:

Intelligent Power Management The tag's greatest innovation is its power-saving system. Instead of constant, battery-draining data streams, it uses an adaptive Bayesian Markov chain model. This onboard TinyML model allows the tag to learn the shark's patterns and make smart decisions, only transmitting data when significant and noticeable changes occur, extending mission life from months to potentially years.

Rich Sensor Suite The tag is equipped with a high-fidelity accelerometer and gyroscope (IMU) to capture the subtle movements that define a shark's behavior: the steady glide of travel, the languid motion of rest, and the explosive acceleration of a hunt. This is complemented by onboard temperature and pressure sensors to provide crucial environmental context.

Real-Time Intelligent Satellite Uplink When the tag surfaces, it connects to satellite networks to upload its compressed data packets to our cloud platform. Furthermore, when the shark is at great depths and satellite connection is lost, the tag stores sensor data in a buffer with timestamps. When the shark resurfaces and connection is restored, this buffered data is transmitted. The location data lost during the deep dive is compensated for by our AI's predictive path model, ensuring a more complete dataset.

The Role of AI


Artificial Intelligence forms the analytical backbone of our project, enabling predictive insights that would not be possible through raw satellite data alone. We developed a framework of three complementary machine learning models that work in synergy, linking the broad ocean environment with specific shark behaviors to create a multi-layered forecast.

The foundation of our framework is the Shark Hotspot Model, a Random Forest Classifier. This model operates on the fused geospatial dataset created from MODIS, SWOT, PACE, and neuroOST satellites, analyzing environmental factors like chlorophyll, sea surface temperature, and currents. Its purpose is to identify the large-scale ecological niches that match the mathematical definition of a prime shark foraging hotspot, producing a probability heatmap of likely aggregation zones.

To complement this broad environmental view, we use the Trajectory Forecaster, a Markov Chain model. This model focuses on individual movement, analyzing a shark's past position sequences from tag data to learn transition probabilities. This allows it to estimate short-term trajectories and anticipate where a specific shark might move next within the larger hotspots.

For the highest level of detail, the Tag Predictor Model, a Random Forest Regressor, analyzes the fine-scale movement signatures from the tag's sensors. Since publicly available tagged shark datasets are limited, we trained this model on a synthetic dataset that simulates realistic feeding patterns. This allows the regressor to estimate the probability of specific behaviors, like a feeding event, providing ground-truth context for what the shark is doing at a given location.

This three-layered approach provides a comprehensive predictive picture: the Hotspot Mapper identifies the favorable "neighborhood," the Trajectory Forecaster predicts the likely "street," and the Tag Predictor identifies the specific "action." Together, these models bridge the gap between simulated biological data and real satellite data, enabling us to move from raw information to predictive ecological insights with direct applications in marine conservation and public safety.

Our Web Platform

Our global command center for visualizing real-time shark movements and predictive analytics.Hover to the data, it shows all the TAG data in real-time.The Guardian's Quiz. We use interactive questions to bust common myths and transform fear into fascination and respect.After answering the quiz, the user can see the answers with a brief explanation. We turn abstract data into personal stories, allowing users to follow the journey of an individual shark to build an empathetic connection.Our Mission & Motive page. Grounding our project in the stark reality of the crisis and our core commitment to making the invisible, visible.Our Vision page. Here we articulate the future we're building; a world where conservation is predictive, not reactive, and technology empowers a new era of planetary stewardship.

The Future Roadmap: A Mission-Ready Device

Future of the Sentinel

Sentinel's Tag

The device built during the hackathon served as a powerful proof-of-concept. The following roadmap details our plan to evolve it into a mission-ready, field-deployable device.

Onboard Intelligence: The Leap to Edge AI To elevate the tag from a simple data logger to a truly intelligent agent, our roadmap includes the implementation of Edge AI directly on the device's MCU. This will enable advanced, real-time decision-making:

  • Predictive Dead Reckoning: For periods when the shark is too deep for a GPS fix, the Edge AI will use IMU data to predict and fill in location gaps, providing a more continuous data stream.
  • Intelligent Power Management: The onboard Markov chain model will be enhanced to actively manage power consumption, calculating the optimal times to transmit data based on battery level, behavior, and satellite availability.
  • Onboard Diagnostics: The AI will run a continuous warning system to detect sensor anomalies or physical damage, ensuring data integrity.

Next-Generation Hardware & Miniaturization A key goal is to drastically reduce the tag's physical footprint to minimize its impact on the animal.

  • Next PCB: Our current prototype is approximately 4x9 cm. The next design iteration will target a miniaturized footprint of around 2.5x7.5 cm.
  • Component Evolution: This miniaturization and performance upgrade is made possible by transitioning to next-generation components.

Firmware & Power Management Overhaul The firmware will be completely re-architected for maximum efficiency, with a goal of achieving a battery life of up to 3 years.

  • Interrupt-Based Architecture: The system will move from a polling-based model to being 100% interrupt-based. The device will remain in a deep sleep state, consuming near-zero power, and will only wake when a sensor interrupt reports a significant event.
    • Working Mode: Normal data collection and transmission.
    • Low Power Mode: Drastically reduced sensing and transmission frequency.
    • Find Me Mode: A special transmission mode to aid in device recovery.
  • Robust Error Handling: The new firmware will include advanced error handling to manage data corruption, transmission failures, and sensor malfunctions gracefully.

Sentinel's AI

Future AI Model: A Data-Driven Predictive Engine

Our vision is to evolve our current system by applying state-of-the-art AI techniques, including deep learning and computer vision, inspired by their successful use in tracking other marine species.

This next phase will be driven by training deep learning models on large, combined datasets of satellite observations and real-world tagged shark movements from our deployed smart tags. Unlike our current models, these advanced AIs will be capable of learning highly complex, non-linear patterns in the data, leading to predictions with significantly higher accuracy.

The ultimate goal is to expand beyond prediction to support direct conservation action. The future AI will be trained to identify and map high-risk areas where shark habitats overlap with man-made threats, such as plastic pollution and ocean waste. By highlighting these dangerous zones, our work can help guide interventions to protect these vital species and ensure their survival for generations to come.

How it works

Project Sentinel operates as a complete, end-to-end data pipeline that transforms raw satellite observations into actionable conservation intelligence. Our workflow is a continuous cycle, integrating our smart tag's logic and our core mathematical model.

  1. Intelligent Data Ingestion: The system begins by pulling in two distinct types of data:
    • The Orbital Perspective (NASA): We ingest multi-layered environmental data from NASA satellites, primarily MODIS (for Chlorophyll-a & Sea Surface Temperature) and SWOT (for Sea Surface Height).
    • The Smart Tag (Ground Truth): Our conceptual smart tag provides high-fidelity location data. To solve the critical challenge of battery life, the tag uses an onboard Markov model. This mathematical framework allows the tag to make intelligent, event-driven decisions, transmitting data only when its sensor parameters change significantly, ensuring maximum energy efficiency. It also has a buffer to store data so whenever the connection is lost as the shark descends, the data is stored to be transmitted as the shark resurface.
    • Niche Definition: First, we mathematically define an "ideal" foraging hotspot based on a combination of environmental conditions (e.g., high chlorophyll). This creates a signature for our model to find.
    • AI Prediction: We then use a Random Forest Classifier, a robust ensemble learning model, which is trained to recognize this specific environmental signature. It analyzes the entire grid and assigns each point a "Foraging Probability Score"—a number from 0.0 to 1.0 indicating how likely it is to be a feeding ground.
  2. Visualization & Interaction: The final probability scores are rendered on our web platform as a dynamic, intuitive heatmap on an interactive 3D globe. This allows scientists, policymakers, and the public to see where the most critical marine habitats are emerging in near-real-time.

Benefits

Project Sentinel is designed to deliver transformative benefits across multiple sectors, moving the needle from passive observation to proactive conservation.

  • For Conservation & Science: The primary benefit is enabling Dynamic Marine Protected Areas, intelligent, adaptive sanctuaries that move with the animals they protect. This is a monumental leap beyond the current static model, offering a far more effective way to protect migratory species. For scientists, it provides an unprecedented tool for studying predator-prey dynamics on a macro scale.
  • For the Fishing Industry: This is a tool for sustainability and profitability. By providing predictive maps of shark hotspots, we help fishing fleets avoid bycatch. This saves them time, fuel, the cost of damaged gear, and potential fines, aligning sustainable practices with economic incentives.
  • For the Public & Education: Our platform is a powerful educational tool designed to change the public narrative around sharks. Through our interactive quizzes, e-book, and compelling "Shark Tales," we transform fear into fascination, creating a new generation of informed ocean advocates.
  • For Policymakers: We provide a clear, data-driven foundation for creating smarter, more effective, and scientifically defensible marine conservation policies.

Development tools

We leveraged a modern, powerful, and agile tech stack to bring Project Sentinel from concept to a functional prototype during this hackathon.

  • Programming Languages: Python, JavaScript
    • Google Gemini 2.5 Pro: Assisted in crafting our narrative, storytelling, and documentation.
    • OpenAI ChatGPT: Used for code assistance and, critically, for generating the synthetic shark tag dataset needed to train and validate our AI models.
  • Version Control & Collaboration: GitHub

You cannot protect what you cannot see. Our mission is to make the invisible, visible.

AI was used for both predictive analysis and to accelerate our development. We integrated machine learning for our core model and leveraged generative AI to overcome data and time constraints.

Predictive Engine

  • Random Forest Classifier: Analyzes our smart tag's motion data to classify a shark's real-time behavior (e.g., ‘Hunting,’ ‘Traveling’). This tells us what the shark is doing.
  • Random Forest Regressor: Fuses the behavior data from the classifier with NASA satellite data (PACE, SWOT) to calculate a “Foraging Probability Score.” This tells us how likely an area is a feeding hotspot.

Development & Simulation

  • Generative AI (Gemini & ChatGPT): Gemini assisted in writing our narrative, while ChatGPT helped refined our codes.
  • Synthetic Data Generation: ChatGPT was used to generate a realistic, synthetic dataset of tag metadata. This “digital twin” of a shark’s behavior allowed us to train and validate our models effectively within the hackathon’s timeframe. As it is impossible to actually get the TAG to a real shark.

challengeDetails.title: Sharks from Space
challengeDetails.excerpt: Earth’s ocean is one of the most powerful habitats in our universe, supporting a range of life that sustains ecosystems and habitability across the globe. It is common to measure photosynthetic activity in the ocean from space, but far more challenging to track top predators. Your challenge is to create a mathematical framework for identifying sharks and predicting their foraging habitats using NASA satellite data, and also to suggest a new conceptual model of a tag (a small electronic device that can be attached to an animal to track and study its movement) that could measure not only where sharks are, but also what they are eating, and in real time transmit that data back to users to enable development of predictive models. projectDetails.name: Umbra
projectDetails.summary:
Umbra is a unified research platform that tackles the fragmented state of space biology knowledge through three integrated components.

The AI search engine handles natural language queries and delivers synthesized answers from multiple publications with clear citations. drilling down into specific studies or broadening their search scope.

The knowledge graph visualizes connections between experiments, biological processes, organisms, and conditions as an interactive network. Users explore study relationships, identify research clusters, spot knowledge gaps, and trace research progression over time through path analysis.

The collaborative document editor provides AI-powered writing assistance with citation suggestions and evidence integration. It recommends relevant studies as users write and maintains terminology consistency while supporting real-time collaboration with version control.

These components work seamlessly together. Search results insert directly into documents with citations, graph nodes link to document sections, and annotations reference findings across all three tools.

Umbra transforms weeks of manual literature review into hours of efficient knowledge discovery. It helps scientists uncover novel research directions, enables program managers to identify funding gaps, assists mission architects with biological risk assessments, and accelerates scientific writing by bridging discovery and documentation.
projectDetails.details:
Platform Overview

Umbra integrates three core features into a seamless research workflow, allowing space biology researchers to search, explore, and document findings within a single unified platform.

Core Features

AI-Powered Search Engine Users enter natural language questions about space biology topics and receive synthesized answers drawn from NASA's publication database. Each answer includes clear source citations that link directly to original studies. Advanced filters let researchers narrow results by organism type, experiment duration, or specific space environment conditions. The search understands scientific terminology and returns relevant findings even when queries use different phrasing than the original publications.

Interactive Knowledge Graph A visual network displays relationships between experiments, organisms, biological processes, and space conditions. Researchers can click on any element to explore connected studies, identify research clusters, and discover gaps where few studies exist. The graph reveals unexpected connections between different experiments and shows how research has progressed over time through path analysis features.

Collaborative Document Editor The writing workspace provides AI assistance that suggests relevant citations and experimental evidence as researchers compose papers. Multiple team members can edit simultaneously with real-time updates and version tracking. The editor maintains consistent scientific terminology and seamlessly integrates findings from both the search engine and knowledge graph directly into documents.

NOTE: Auth has been disabled in this demo for time saving purposes, so demo@wearemasons.com was selected as the default auth user.

Technical Implementation

Frontend & API Layer Next.js powers the web application, providing a responsive interface and handling API calls between components. The framework ensures smooth transitions between search, visualization, and editing workflows while maintaining fast load times and interactive responsiveness.

Publication Processing Python scripts handle the initial processing of NASA's 608 publications, extracting text, identifying key entities like organisms and experimental conditions, and understanding the scientific content. These processing pipelines create the structured data foundation that powers search and graph features.

Backend Infrastructure ASP.NET manages user authentication, access control, and secure data handling. The backend coordinates between the search engine, knowledge graph database, and document storage while ensuring proper permissions and data security.

Cross-Component Integration All three features communicate seamlessly—search results can be inserted directly into documents with one click, knowledge graph nodes link to relevant document sections, and citations maintain consistency across the entire platform regardless of where they originate.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Gemini as Core LLM Provider We integrated Google's Gemini large language model as the primary AI engine powering Umbra's intelligent features. Gemini processes natural language search queries, synthesizes answers from multiple publications, generates citation suggestions in the document editor, and provides context-aware writing assistance. All AI-generated text responses and recommendations within the platform are produced through Gemini API calls.

AI-Assisted Code Development We utilized AI code completion tools (GitHub Copilot) throughout the development process to accelerate implementation and complement our team's technical skills. These tools assisted with:

  • Boilerplate code generation for API endpoints and component structures
  • Algorithm optimization suggestions for search and graph traversal functions
  • Debugging assistance and error resolution
  • Documentation and code comment generation

The AI code completion served as a development accelerator, allowing us to focus on architecture decisions, feature design, and integration logic while maintaining high code quality and best practices.

AI Content Acknowledgment

  • The platform's user interface clearly indicates when responses are AI-generated, with attribution to Gemini
  • No AI-generated images, videos, or audio were used in this project
  • No NASA branding or design elements were used or modified by AI tools

Human Oversight and Originality While AI tools accelerated our development workflow, all architectural decisions, feature designs, user experience choices, and integration strategies represent our team's original, and problem-solving. AI served as a productivity tool rather than a replacement for human creativity and technical judgment.

projectDetails.name: Project MAX-Q
projectDetails.summary:
Low Earth Orbit (LEO) supports diverse missions: Earth observation, communications, navigation, microgravity research, on-orbit manufacturing, and space tourism. The orbital environment is increasingly congested: >40,000 tracked objects and ~11,000 active payloads, with millions of fragments below catalog thresholds [1][2].

Concept - Shared Orbital Bus (SOB): A modular ESPA-class spacecraft hosting multiple independent payloads and providing shared services:

Electrical power, propulsion, ADCS, thermal control, and communications

Standardized docking and refueling port Active end-of-life deorbit capability
projectDetails.details:
Our project is the Shared Orbital Bus (SOB) — a modular spacecraft designed to host multiple independent payloads on a single resilient platform in Low Earth Orbit. Instead of every mission carrying its own propulsion, power, communications, and thermal systems, the SOB centralizes these functions and provides them as shared services.

How it works

The SOB is built on an ESPA-class architecture with 4–6 hosted payload ports.

It includes two universal service ports that enable robotic docking, refueling, payload servicing, and controlled deorbiting.

The spacecraft uses electric propulsion for efficient station-keeping and end-of-life maneuvers, supported by monopropellant thrusters for attitude control and contingencies.

Payloads connect through standardized mechanical, electrical, and data interfaces, allowing quick integration and market access.

Benefits

Lower cost per payload by sharing launch and spacecraft infrastructure.

Reduced orbital congestion by replacing multiple single-use satellites with one managed platform.

Extended mission lifetimes through refueling and on-orbit servicing.

Sustainability via built-in deorbit capability and active debris mitigation.

Flexibility to support diverse missions — Earth observation, communications, science experiments, navigation augmentation, and even future tourism.

Intended Impact

The project addresses one of the biggest challenges in space today: orbital crowding and sustainability. By shifting from disposable, stand-alone satellites to a shared, serviceable infrastructure, the SOB reduces costs, lowers debris growth, and enables faster access to space for new players. This contributes directly to long-term orbital safety and commercial scalability.

Tools, Hardware, and Software

Modeling & Simulation: NASA’s ORDEM 3.2 debris model, ESA catalog data, and market studies.

Architecture references: ESPA/ESPAStar bus design, NASA Robotic Refueling Mission, and commercial Mission Extension Vehicles.

Analysis: propulsion budgets, orbital environment sizing, and cost modeling.

Development tools: system modeling, CAD-based payload integration studies, and web-based prototype presentations.

Creativity & Team Considerations

Our creativity lies in combining proven technologies (hosted payloads, ESPA platforms, robotic servicing) into a new scalable model with a universal service port as the key enabler. We carefully considered:

Technical feasibility (based on current industry demonstrations).

Economic viability (cost-sharing and faster market access).

Sustainability (life extension, debris mitigation).

Flexibility (supporting diverse mission types).

projectDetails.name: Green Vision
projectDetails.summary: We developed Green Vision, an integrated web platform that combines NASA satellite data, AI models, and gamification to combat desertification and support sustainable agriculture. The platform provides NDVI vegetation analysis, AI-powered weather forecasting, and land suitability reports, helping farmers, researchers, and policymakers make informed decisions about planting, irrigation, and ecosystem restoration. Inside the website, we built an interactive educational game where players collect fruits, answer environmental questions, and use “magic water” to revive trees. The game teaches users how to protect the environment while making learning fun and engaging. Players can also earn a certificate of achievement at the end. This project addresses the challenge by transforming complex NASA datasets into accessible, actionable, and engaging insights, while also raising awareness through gameplay. It is important because it empowers communities to fight land degradation, ensures better land use planning, and inspires lasting sustainable change.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

What it does / How it works:
Green Vision is a smart agricultural platform that combines NASA satellite data with AI and data analytics to fight desertification and improve farming. The website provides NDVI vegetation analysis, weather forecasting, and interactive maps that allow farmers, researchers, and students to monitor soil health, predict rainfall, and make better land-use decisions. Alongside the platform, we developed an interactive game (embedded inside the website) where players collect fruits, answer environmental questions, and revive trees using “magic water.” The game connects science with fun and rewards users with a certificate of completion.

Benefits / Intended Impact:

  • Helps farmers optimize crop yields and water usage.
  • Supports researchers and students with reliable, science-backed data.
  • Raises awareness about desertification and sustainability through gamification.
  • Provides long-term solutions for food security, land restoration, and climate resilience.

Tools, coding languages, hardware, and software:

  • Python, Django, PYTorch, Folium, Leaflet.js for backend, AI models, and interactive maps.
  • JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Bootstrap, AOS Animations for frontend and user experience.
  • Google Earth Engine, NOAA, and NASA open datasets for satellite imagery and climate data.
  • Custom game engine (JavaScript/Phaser) for the web game.
  • Unreal engine 5.0 and some Assets for the game

our repo link :

https://github.com/Kiramido1/Ultimate-Green-Vision

Creativity / Innovation:

  • We merged serious science with entertainment: turning complex satellite data into interactive reports and a fun game that teaches while engaging.
  • Used NASA data in a new way: not only for maps but also to power predictions, reports, and even the gameplay story.
  • Designed with simplicity + elegance, so both experts and the general public can benefit.

Factors considered by our team:

  • Accessibility for farmers in rural areas.
  • Engaging young people through gamification.
  • Scientific accuracy by grounding results in NASA data.
  • Sustainability and long-term positive impact for society and the environment.
  • Alignment with the NASA challenge: a direct, functional prototype addressing desertification.

Through our project, we hope to make NASA’s complex biological experiments simple, engaging, and accessible for everyone — from students and young learners to scientists and the general public. Our goal is to bridge the gap between science and society by transforming raw scientific data into interactive learning experiences.

With the combination of the website and the game, we aim to:

Inspire the next generation of scientists by showing them the importance of space biology in a fun and interactive way.

Provide an educational tool that teachers, universities, and learning platforms can adopt to explain real NASA experiments.

Encourage curiosity, critical thinking, and creativity by allowing users not only to read about experiments but also to simulate and play them.

Contribute to a lasting positive impact, where space science becomes more approachable, memorable, and enjoyable for everyone.

Ultimately, our vision is to create a platform that doesn’t just share knowledge, but also sparks innovation and motivates learners worldwide to explore science in new ways.

    • Trained models using NASA satellite imagery (NDVI, climate data) and NOAA datasets to provide accurate predictions and classification of land health.

projectDetails.summary:
We developed an AI-powered exoplanet exploration platform that combines machine learning models with an intuitive web interface and public API. Our system classifies exoplanet candidates versus confirmed exoplanets using NASA’s open datasets (Kepler and K2, with TESS integration planned for the full release). Users can explore datasets, visualize data, upload CSV files for predictions, and compare them against training data, making the analysis process faster and more accessible.
This project addresses the challenge by automating exoplanet classification, reducing the need for manual data analysis, and helping scientists prioritize high-value targets. projectDetails.details:
Our project is an AI-powered exoplanet classification and exploration platform designed to make the process of identifying planets outside our solar system faster, more reliable, and more accessible. The platform combines advanced machine learning models with a user-friendly web interface and a public API, making it useful not only for professional scientists but also for students, educators, and the general public.

 

The system works by leveraging NASA’s open exoplanet datasets, specifically data from the Kepler and K2 missions, with planned integration of TESS data in the full release. After preprocessing these datasets, we trained multiple machine learning models, including Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost. These models classify whether a signal represents a candidate or a confirmed exoplanet, achieving high levels of accuracy while prioritizing recall to minimize the risk of missing potential exoplanets. The results are served through both a graphical interface and a programmatic API.

 

From a user perspective, the platform offers several core features. In the demo version, users can explore the datasets and models used, upload CSV files to test predictions, visualize statistics, and compare uploaded data against training sets. They can also access explanatory pages that describe the datasets and models in simple terms, turning the platform into both a research aid and an educational tool. In the full release, additional features will allow users to upload raw transit light curves, manually input new data points, and interact with TESS mission data, further expanding the system’s scope and capabilities.

 

The benefits of this project are twofold. On the scientific side, it accelerates the traditionally manual process of exoplanet identification, allowing researchers to quickly focus their attention on the most promising signals. On the societal side, it democratizes space science, enabling anyone from any background to engage with real astronomical data through an accessible UX, fostering both learning and curiosity. By making the platform’s API public, we also encourage collaboration, allowing educators, developers, and fellow researchers to build upon our work and integrate it into their own tools and projects.

 

To develop this project, we used Python for machine learning and backend development, with key libraries including scikit-learn, XGBoost, Pandas, NumPy, and Matplotlib/Plotly for visualization. The frontend was built using modern JavaScript frameworks such as React, with AI-assisted tools like GitHub Copilot for improving code clarity and V0 for rapid prototyping. Flask or FastAPI was used to build the backend and API. This combination of tools ensures both computational robustness and a smooth user experience.

Ultimately, our goal is to bridge the gap between cutting-edge astrophysics research and accessibility. By combining automation, interpretability, and education, we hope to empower scientists with a scalable classification system while also inspiring students and the general public to engage with the mysteries of the universe

projectDetails.name: Project Meteorix
projectDetails.summary:
Our team created Meteorix for the Meteor Madness challenge because we wanted to bring the wonder of meteors closer to everyone. Instead of looking at numbers and datasets that can feel distant, we built an interactive website using simple tools — HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — to transform meteor data into a story people can see and explore.

Through animations, visuals, and easy explanations, we aimed to make meteors feel alive, not just statistics. Our project is important because it connects people of all ages with space in a way that is fun, engaging, and understandable. We believe science should not stay only in research papers; it should inspire curiosity, spark imagination, and make people feel part of the universe. That’s the heart of Meteorix.
projectDetails.details:
When we started building Meteorix, our goal was simple: we wanted to take the mystery of meteors and turn it into something people could feel, see, and understand. Many times, meteor data is locked away in spreadsheets or research papers, but we asked ourselves: what if we could bring it to life?

Meteorix works as an interactive website where visitors can explore meteors through visuals, animations, and easy explanations. Instead of just reading numbers, users can watch patterns unfold, see how meteors vary in size and frequency, and connect that to the bigger picture of space.

The benefit of our project is accessibility. We designed it for anyone — students, teachers, or just curious people — who want to learn about meteors without needing technical expertise. We believe that understanding space science should not feel intimidating, but exciting and inspiring.

To build Meteorix, we used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, collaborating on online coding boards where we worked together in real time. We focused not just on code, but on creativity: colors, animations, and storytelling that make science feel alive.

Throughout the process, we asked ourselves important questions: How do we balance accuracy with simplicity? How do we make sure it works smoothly for anyone, anywhere? And most importantly, how do we make people feel connected to something as distant as a meteor?

Meteorix is more than a website; it’s our attempt to turn data into wonder, and to remind people that even small sparks in the night sky can ignite big curiosity about our universe.

projectDetails.name: ThermoVision
projectDetails.summary: ThermoVision is an innovative energy recovery system designed for satellites operating in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). It captures and converts waste heat from onboard equipment into usable electrical power, enhancing energy efficiency and extending satellite lifespan. By addressing key challenges such as limited energy sources, thermal stress, and sustainability concerns, ThermoVision reduces dependency on solar arrays and supports safer orbital operations. Developed in alignment with NASA and UN space sustainability guidelines, it contributes to a cleaner, more efficient, and environmentally responsible future for commercial and scientific missions in LEO.
projectDetails.details:
🛰 ThermoVision – Project Overview

🔹 What exactly does it do?

ThermoVision is an energy recovery system that captures waste heat from satellites in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and converts it into usable electricity.

🔹 How does it work?

It uses Thermoelectric Generators (TEGs) to directly convert heat into electrical energy, combined with Phase Change Materials (PCMs) to absorb and regulate excess heat. This ensures stable thermal management while generating additional Power.

🔹 What benefits does it have?

Extends satellite lifetime by reducing thermal stress.

Provides an extra renewable energy source, reducing reliance on solar arrays.

Decreases operational costs and improves energy efficiency.

Supports sustainable and responsible operations in LEO.

🔹 What do you hope to achieve?

We aim to create a scalable, eco-friendly energy solution for space that not only supports satellites but also opens the door to a future orbital energy economy, helping commercial Stations, tourism, and research missions become more sustainable.

🔹 What tools, coding languages, hardware, or Software did you use?

Hardware: Thermoelectric Generators (TEGs), Phase Change Materials (PCM), heatsinks, and CubeSat test components.

Software & Tools:

NASA DAS & ORSAT tools (for debris and reentry risk assessment).

ANSYS / COMSOL (thermal + structural simulation).

MATLAB / Python (data analysis, energy modeling).

CAD Software (SolidWorks, Fusion 360) for design and prototyping.

Programming Languages: Python, MATLAB, C++ (for CubeSat integration testing).

projectDetails.name: Will It Rain On My Parade?
projectDetails.summary:
What did you develop?  We developed a complete AI-Powered Full-Stack Web Application 
designed for immediate, localized rain probability prediction. The solution is built on a Python/Flask 
server that hosts a pre-trained Random Forest Classifier model and a dynamic JavaScript/Leaflet.js 
frontend for geospatial data visualization.   
How does it address the challenge? The application addresses the problem of vague weather 
forecasts by transforming complex live atmospheric data (Temperature, Humidity, Wind Speed, 
Clouds) into a simple, binary decision: Rain Probable or Not. This removes cognitive ambiguity, 
providing users with an instantaneous, trustworthy answer upon which they can base immediate 
actions.   
Why is it important? This project is a successful, practical model demonstrating the power of 
integrating Machine Learning with live Big Data to solve a critical, everyday problem. It is important 
because it shows how highly reliable AI models (with tested accuracy up to 99%) can enhance data 
trustworthiness and drive better, faster decision-making in both personal contexts and operational 
planning.
projectDetails.details: What Exactly Does It Do? The application provides a seamless, dynamic user experience by performing three primary actions: Real-Time AI Prediction: It analyzes four live atmospheric variables (Temperature, Humidity, Wind Speed, and Cloudiness) and uses a Random Forest Classifier to output a binary decision: Rain Probable or Not. Interactive Geospatial Data: It displays current weather conditions and the AI prediction on an interactive Leaflet.js map. Users can search any city or click any point on the map to trigger a new query instantly. Filtered 5-Day Forecast: It fetches and intelligently filters the raw forecast data, showing the most representative reading (closest to noon) for each of the next five days. How Does It Work? (The Workflow) The system operates on a clean client-server loop: Frontend Request: The user triggers a search, sending coordinates (lat, lon) to the Flask backend endpoint (/predict_weather). Data Acquisition: The Flask backend calls external APIs (OpenWeatherMap) to fetch the latest weather data for the coordinates. AI Inference: The backend extracts the four key features, feeds them into the pre-loaded rain_predictor_model.pkl, and gets a binary output (1 or 0). Actionable Output: The backend translates the output into the user-facing status (Probable / Not Probable) and sends the final JSON response back to the browser. Visualization: The browser updates the map marker, the central AI prediction card, and populates the 5-day forecast strip. What Benefits Does It Have? The core benefits stem from simplifying complex data science for end-users: Actionable Confidence: The 99% accuracy achieved by the model on test data translates into high user confidence in the binary prediction, enabling quick, effective decision-making (e.g., carrying an umbrella or planning outdoor activities). Reduced Cognitive Load: The intelligent filtering of the 5-day forecast minimizes screen clutter and cognitive effort for the user. Demonstration of AI Integration: It serves as a strong portfolio piece demonstrating proficiency in building a complete end-to-end Machine Learning pipeline from model training to cloud deployment logic. What Do You Hope to Achieve? Optimizing Water Management: The most significant goal is to enable farmers and resource managers to use our immediate, highly reliable rain predictions to make precise decisions regarding irrigation scheduling and crop harvesting. Cost & Resource Efficiency: By reducing the uncertainty of rainfall, the application leads to massive water conservation, minimizing wasted irrigation efforts and optimizing the application of fertilizers before a predicted wash-out. Protecting Assets: Providing crucial alerts regarding unexpected high-probability rain events helps users protect equipment, livestock, and stored produce from sudden weather changes. Tools and Technology Stack: Machine Learning :::::: Python, Scikit-learn (Random Forest), joblib --> Used for model training, serialization, and rapid prediction inference. Backend / API: Python, Flask, requests, pandas -->> Handles server hosting, data fetching/cleaning, and API endpoint management. Frontend / UI : HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet.js -->> Provides interactive mapping, dynamic data display, and user interface responsiveness. External Data: OpenWeatherMap APIs -->>Supplies live current weather, Geocoding, and 5-day forecast data feeds. Foundational Science: NASA GPM IMERG -->>The project is inspired by and relies on the high f idelity precipitation and atmospheric data principles established by NASA missions.

projectDetails.summary:
I developed ExoHunt, an AI-powered platform that automates the detection of exoplanets from NASA’s open-source Kepler, K2, and TESS datasets. Traditionally, exoplanet discovery relied heavily on manual inspection of stellar light curves, which is time-intensive and limits the pace of discovery. Our solution leverages advanced machine learning (LightGBM + time-series feature extraction) to classify exoplanet candidates with high accuracy, while also providing explainable insights through SHAP analysis.

To make this accessible, we built a dual-interface web app:



🔬 Researcher Mode: Upload datasets, retrain models directly in-browser, tweak hyperparameters, and visualize evaluation metrics (ROC, PR, confusion matrices, SHAP).


🌍 Curious Explorer Mode: An educational, game-like simulation of the transit method where users can customize planetary systems and see how transits cause brightness dips, paired with curated videos and articles.


ExoHunt bridges science and outreach—helping researchers accelerate discoveries, while enabling the public to intuitively understand how new worlds are found.
projectDetails.details:
My project does three main things:

1. Researcher Dashboard – lets me (or other scientists) upload datasets :

retrain a LightGBM

model, and view evaluation results (ROC curves, precision-recall, SHAP values).

2. Curious Explorer – provides an interactive transit simulation game where users learn how dips in

It works by combining a data pipeline (Python + LightGBM), evaluation scripts, and a

Streamlit-based website for deployment.

The benefits are twofold: researchers gain AI-powered insights from exoplanet data, while the

public gains an intuitive, interactive way to learn.

I hope to achieve a platform that is both scientifically useful and educational for outreach.

and TESS).
