projectDetails.name: ASTROBIO
projectDetails.summary:
Our project is a website designed to make scientific research more accessible and understandable for students and researchers. Research papers are often scattered, complex, and time consuming, making it hard for students to engage and slowing down researchers.

Our website collects NASA related and space science papers in one place and provides clear, concise summaries. These summaries highlight essential findings while maintaining scientific accuracy, helping students grasp difficult concepts and saving researchers time.

The site combines simplicity with precision. Users can understand core ideas in minutes instead of reading long papers. It has a clean, responsive, and user friendly design that works well on desktop and mobile. Research content is organized logically, making navigation smooth and efficient.

In short, the website offers centralized access, concise summaries, preserved accuracy, and fast navigation. By making research easier to access and understand, we empower students and provide researchers with a practical time saving tool, taking a step toward open and approachable scientific knowledge.9
projectDetails.details:
Our project is a website that collects NASA and space science research papers in one place and provides concise, accurate summaries. Users can search topics, read summaries quickly, and understand key findings without reading long papers.

The website organizes papers by categories and uses structured templates for summaries. It is responsive and works smoothly on desktop and mobile.

Benefits: It saves time for researchers, helps students grasp complex concepts faster, and provides a reliable, centralized source of research.

Intended Impact: We aim to make scientific knowledge more accessible and clear, supporting learning and research in space science.

Tools and Software: We used HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and VS Code to develop the project, focusing on simplicity, speed, and user-friendliness.

Creativity: The project merges simplicity with precision, transforming long, complex research papers into easy to read summaries without losing scientific accuracy.

projectDetails.name: SpaceDive
projectDetails.summary:
Astronomical datasets, such as NASA’s Pluto imagery, are extremely large and often overwhelm normal computers. Their massive size slows down CPUs and GPUs, making exploration frustrating and nearly impossible without specialized tools. This creates a barrier for students, educators, and the public who want to interact with real planetary data in a meaningful way.

Our project solves this challenge by implementing a smart tiling system, similar to Google Maps. Instead of forcing one enormous image to load, the platform loads only the tiles needed for the current zoom level. This drastically reduces memory and processing demands, ensuring smooth navigation even on modest hardware and limited bandwidth. The prototype is available in desktop browsers and VR, where the tiling system powers fluid, immersive exploration. In VR, the experience becomes game-like, letting users move in first-person through planetary views.

The benefits are clear: complex datasets become simple and interactive for education, curiosity is encouraged through engaging exploration, accessibility is ensured across devices, and scientific accuracy is preserved with authentic NASA data. Our long-term vision is to democratize space exploration—expanding from Pluto to the wider solar system with real-time datasets, classroom-ready tools, and fully immersive VR missions.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do?

Our project is an interactive platform (desktop app prototype and VR) that allows users to explore celestial bodies in an immersive way.

The current prototype focuses on Pluto and Triangulum Galaxy, where users can zoom, pan, and interact with planetary imagery as if navigating a cosmic map.

 

How does it work?

We use a smart tiling system similar to Google Maps: instead of loading one massive image, the program loads only the tiles needed at a given zoom level.

This ensures smooth navigation even with limited bandwidth.

The VR version turns this into a game-like experience, letting users explore space in first-person immersion.

 

What benefits does it have?

Educational: Simplifies complex astronomy data into clear visualizations.

Engagement: Inspires curiosity by making space exploration interactive and fun.

Accessibility: Works on desktops, VR headsets, and can expand to mobile in the future.

Accuracy: Uses NASA datasets, balancing realism with performance.

 

What do you hope to achieve?

We aim to democratize space exploration, making the universe accessible to students, researchers, and the public.

The Pluto prototype is the first step toward a scalable platform covering the entire solar system and beyond, with plans for real-time data, VR missions, and classroom-friendly modules.

 

What tools and technologies did you use?

Languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript

Visualization: OpenSeadragon (tiling/zoom), Web technologies

AI Assistance: ChatGPT for coding, debugging, and optimization

Platforms: Desktop (browser-based) and VR prototype

 

Data

 

NASA New Horizons Pluto imagery (NASA, USA)

NASA Open Data Archives (planetary datasets)

Public domain astronomy images (Wikimedia, NASA repositories)

 

 

Tools & Technologies

 

HTML, CSS, JavaScript

OpenSeadragon (for image tiling/zoom)

Web technologies (browser-based rendering)

 

Resources

In the future, we plan to use Unity or Unreal Engine to develop a full VR version of the project, making it more immersive and accessible on major VR platforms

ChatGPT (for coding help, debugging, and optimization).

projectDetails.name: Project Space_Hunters
projectDetails.summary:
Introducing Space Hunters, a mobile and web app that turns NASA bioscience research into clear, interactive insights. Built for the Build a Space Biology Knowledge Engine challenge, Space Hunters transforms 600+ NASA bioscience publications into structured, AI-powered summaries and hands-on exploration tools.

This project addresses the challenge of navigating decades of dispersed space biology findings by organizing results and making them easy to search, compare, and understand. It helps scientists, mission planners, educators, and the public quickly find what they need, spot trends, and surface knowledge gaps that inform future missions.

With Space Hunters, users can:
• Search and filter scientific publications.
• Read concise, structured summaries (background, results, conclusions).
• Ask questions about any study through an integrated AI assistant and get grounded answers.
• Explore key insights and patterns via interactive data visualizations.

Designed with accessibility and clarity in mind, Space Hunters lowers the barrier to complex bioscience and supports safer, more efficient human exploration while expanding open access to NASA science for all.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

Space Hunters is a mobile and web application that allows users to explore and interact with more than 600 space bioscience publications. Each publication is automatically summarized into key sections (background, results, and conclusion), and users can open an AI-powered chat assistant to ask further questions. The app also offers favorites, recent searches, and visual browsing to improve accessibility.

 

How does it work?

Users can search or browse publications through the app. When a research link is selected, our system sends it to an AI model that generates structured summaries. The chatbot is connected to the same publication content, allowing context-specific Q&A. The app’s interface is designed to be responsive, modern, and user-friendly, making navigation smooth across mobile devices.

 

What benefits does it have?

The project reduces the time and effort required to process complex scientific literature. Researchers and students can gain quick insights, explore patterns, and make decisions faster. For NASA and the scientific community, it helps highlight critical knowledge gaps and prepares teams for future exploration missions.

 

What do you hope to achieve?

Our main goal is to make space biology research more accessible, interactive, and useful. We aim to support not only experts but also students and enthusiasts who want to engage with NASA’s data. In the long term, we hope this tool can assist mission planners and scientists in building stronger foundations for Moon and Mars missions.

 

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

We built the application using Flutter for mobile app development, with Next.js for web development. The backend relies on AI summarization using the Gemini API. GitHub was used for version control, and the design followed modern UI/UX practices to ensure clarity and usability.

Mobile App Design

1. Home / Dashboard:

A welcoming interface featuring a search bar and quick-access buttons.

Allows users to explore scientific categories and navigate to the publications library or favorites.

2. Category View:

Shows research publications related to a specific topic such as Data Sharing or Open Science.

Helps users discover specialized studies within a chosen research field.

3. Publications Library:

Displays all available research studies in an organized, readable format.

Users can browse studies by categories, years, or keywords.

4. Study Details:

Presents detailed information and results of a selected study through interactive charts and stats.

Enables users to explore the background, results, conclusions, and related studies easily.

5. Chat Assistant:

Lets users interact with an AI assistant to ask questions about research topics.

Provides instant and clear summaries of main findings and insights.

6. My Favorites:

Collects all studies saved by the user for quick access later.

Shows the total, read, and categorized publications in a clean layout.

projectDetails.name: Project SpaceMarket
projectDetails.summary:
Low Earth Orbit (LEO) is evolving into a busy commercial arena but faces a growing threat from orbital debris. Thousands of satellites—many owned by small operators—lack access to real-time debris alerts or an easy way to purchase mitigation expertise or datasets.
Our venture, Space Market, proposes a scalable, sustainable business model combining (1) a real-time debris tracking and alert service for satellite operators and (2) a curated marketplace where commercial providers can offer LEO-related datasets, consultancy, and collision-avoidance services.
The MVP prototype is a web application that integrates public debris APIs (Space-Track, CelesTrak) and our own alert engine into an interactive dashboard. Users register their spacecraft, view debris in near-real time, and receive proximity alerts. In the same interface, they can instantly request or purchase datasets and consultancy from verified providers.
We chose this challenge because it unites two critical NASA priorities—safety and commercialisation. Our model directly supports a responsible LEO economy by reducing collision risks while opening new revenue channels for service providers. Built on .NET (backend), Angular/Vercel (frontend), Cloudinary (file storage), and Stripe (payments), Space Market is designed for scalability, international participation, and regulatory compliance.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

Space Market is a dual-purpose platform:

It provides real-time orbital debris tracking and alerts for satellite operators, ensuring they know when debris threatens their spacecraft.

It acts as a marketplace where providers can sell datasets, consultancy, and collision-avoidance services directly to operators.

How does it work?

The backend periodically ingests orbital debris data (TLEs) from trusted sources like Space-Track and CelesTrak.

Using the SGP4 propagation model, the system predicts close approaches between debris and registered satellites.

Operators receive automated notifications (email, web push).

An Angular dashboard with CesiumJS visualizes debris and satellite positions in 2D.

On the marketplace side, providers upload datasets (via Cloudinary) or list consultancy services, and transactions are handled securely through Stripe.

All administrative changes are logged in an AuditLog to ensure trust and compliance.

What benefits does it have?

For operators: Affordable access to actionable debris alerts and instant access to mitigation experts.

For providers: A global sales channel without needing to build their own platform.

For regulators & NASA: Improved transparency, safer operations, and a scalable model for responsible LEO commercialization.

What do you hope to achieve?

We aim to bridge the gap between debris awareness and action, creating a sustainable ecosystem where small and medium operators can survive in LEO without prohibitive costs. Long-term, the platform could become a standard hub for orbital safety services.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Backend: .NET 8, Identity, JWT, SignalR, EF Core, hangfire.

Frontend: Angular, CesiumJS (for orbital visualization), hosted on Vercel.

Storage: Cloudinary for file and dataset hosting.

Payments: Stripe integration.

Hosting & DevOps: Monster API (backend hosting), GitHub (version control), Slack/WhatsApp (team communication).

Data Sources: Space-Track, CelesTrak recommended from Nasa Recourses specifically NASA Orbital Debris Program Office (ODPO) Resources.

projectDetails.name: Space Master
projectDetails.summary:
Project Idea: Virtual ISS Environment Simulator

Challenge Theme: Celebrating the Anniversary of the International Space Station

Concept:
We aim to build an interactive simulation world that recreates the unique conditions of the ISS. This simulation will allow users students, researchers, or the general public to experience what life is like in space: from microgravity effects to resource management, daily astronaut routines, and environmental challenges.

Main Features:

1. Microgravity Simulation – show how objects and humans behave without weight.


2. Closed Environment Systems  simulate oxygen recycling, water purification, and food supply.


3. Astronaut Lifestyle  daily activities such as sleeping, exercising, eating, and working in space.


4. Space Hazards  exposure to cosmic radiation, limited resources, and psychological effects.


5. Educational Mode provide real ISS data and facts so users can learn while exploring.



Impact:

Helps students and the public understand the complexity of living in space.

Encourages interest in STEM and space exploration.

Can be expanded into VR/AR to give a more immersive “astronaut experience.”


Tech Tools (suggested):

 Unreal Engine for the simulation world.

NASA’s open ISS data (from Space Apps resources).

Optional VR/AR integration for immersive learning.

challengeDetails.title: International Space Station 25th Anniversary Apps
challengeDetails.excerpt: Crews onboard the International Space Station have many unique opportunities! They witness breathtaking Earth views from the station’s cupola—known as “the window to the world.” ​​They also experience weightlessness and go outside the station on spacewalks, for which they must train extensively in the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory (NBL) at the Sonny Carter Training Facility in Houston, Texas. Your challenge is to create a visual tool that not only helps students and the public understand two of the most prominent sensory experiences on the station (sight and weightlessness) through the lens of the cupola and the NBL, but also informs them how these unique experiences benefit humans on Earth. (Space Operations Mission Directorate)

projectDetails.name: Spaghetti project
projectDetails.summary:
Because children’s awareness today is the safety of our future tomorrow

Sunlight isn’t just light and heat  it’s a powerful force that shapes our daily lives: from communication and navigation systems, to pilots in the sky, farmers on the ground, and astronauts in space.
But… most children don’t know anything about this.
That’s where our project comes in.

 The idea is simple: we plant early space awareness in children, and turn a complex topic like solar radiation and cosmic rays into a fun, engaging experience

 Our strategy:
The e-story: simplifying science through a fun narrative that lets children live the journey of solar rays and their impact on Earth
Interactive games: because learning through play is the fastest way into a child’s mind. We designed two carefully crafted games:

A 3-level game simulating the journey of Solar Flares and their effect on satellites and communications.
A fast Q&A game that opens children’s eyes to how radiation affects farmers, pilots, and astronauts

The website: a simple, kid-friendly platform that explains the problem in a way any child or parent can understand

 Why is this project different?
Because it doesn’t stop at theory it transforms knowledge into an experience children live.

Because it builds a generation that’s curious and thoughtful, not just passive receivers of information

Because it sends a strong message: protecting space technology means protecting the future of our planet
projectDetails.details: Our project, “Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through Playful Eyes,” is an interactive educational experience designed to simplify the concept of space weather and its effects on our daily lives especially for children and young learners. The project delivers its message through three connected components: a website, a digital story, and an interactive quiz game. The website serves as the main platform where users can explore information in a simple and visually engaging way. The digital story takes readers on an imaginative journey, letting them experience how solar storms affect Earth. Meanwhile, the quiz game allows children to test what they’ve learned through fun and interactive questions making learning a playful and memorable experience rather than rote memorization. The project works by combining visual interactivity with accurate scientific data. Every element in the experience is based on real NASA data, simplified and presented through illustrations and animations that make complex space phenomena easier to understand. One of the project’s biggest strengths is that it raises scientific awareness in a fun and approachable way. It shows how space affects our technology, communication, agriculture, and climate, helping children realize that space isn’t something far away it’s deeply connected to our everyday lives. Our main goal is to build a generation that understands the relationship between the Sun and Earth, inspiring curiosity about science, astronomy, and engineering. From a technical perspective, we used a combination of modern tools to bring the idea to life: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for building and designing the interactive website. Canva and Figma for creating visuals and illustrations. Unity for developing and testing the interactive quiz game NASA’s open scientific data to ensure that all the information presented is accurate and credible.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
We used Artificial Intelligence tools as supportive instruments to enhance creativity and speed up the development process of our project.
AI was not used to build the entire project but was applied partially in specific stages to improve efficiency and accuracy.

Specifically:

We used ChatGPT to assist in writing some simple code segments and organizing the programming logic for both the website and the interactive game. It was also used to refine the clarity and accuracy of the written content in both Arabic and English.

We also used AI image tools to create a few conceptual illustrations only. All AI-generated images were clearly marked with visible watermarks, following NASA Space Apps regulations.

projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary – Spatium

What did we develop?
We developed Spatium, an interactive web platform that transforms 25 years of NASA Terra satellite data — millions of images and measurements — into a comprehensive, educational, and engaging experience.

How does it address the challenge?
Terra’s data is vast and complex, making it difficult for students, educators, and the general public to understand or relate to real-world environmental impacts. Spatium solves this by providing immersive 3D models, dedicated pages for each of Terra’s five instruments with beautifully produced videos and original NASA imagery, and AI-powered educational games that simulate the effects of human activities on pollution and temperature using real Terra data. Additionally, a knowledge chatbot, interactive flashcards, and a Weather page linked to NASA’s API allow users to interact with the data directly and intuitively.

Why is it important?
Spatium transforms one of the largest environmental datasets in the world into a cohesive, unified learning journey, making complex science accessible, relevant, and meaningful. By combining science, interactivity, storytelling, and gamification, it fosters environmental awareness, inspires curiosity, and connects users to the real-world impact of Earth’s changing climate.
projectDetails.details:
[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]
                                DESCRIPTION OF SPATIUM PROJECT 

   Spatium

The challenge was massive: over 25 years, NASA’s Terra satellite has built one of the largest environmental data archives ever created. Millions of daily images and measurements are available, yet the data is extremely complex — difficult even for specialists to interpret, let alone students or the general public. The real question was: how can this vast, complicated dataset be transformed into knowledge that people can understand and connect to their daily lives and the environment?

This is where Spatium comes in. We didn’t want our solution to be a single fragmented tool; we designed it as a complete, unified experience — where every feature works together to give users a unique journey: engaging, visual, and scientifically accurate.

What We Built

  1. Immersive 3D Interactive Models
    • Dynamic 3D models let users explore Terra’s data visually, turning abstract information into an immersive experience.
    • Each of Terra’s five instruments has its own page.
      • Curated videos explaining the instrument’s role.
      • Original NASA images and data.
      • Simplified explanations that make complex science clear and accessible.
    • 2D Educational Game: introduces the basics of Terra in a fun, interactive way.
    • AI Simulation Game: allows users to add elements like houses, factories, trees, or waste. The system then shows real-time changes in pollution, temperature, and environmental conditions using actual Terra data, powered by AI models that link user decisions directly to NASA datasets.
    • A dedicated chatbot trained exclusively on Terra and its instruments.
    • Provides accurate, reliable answers drawn from NASA data and trusted sources.
    • AI-driven flashcards that quiz the user, provide instant feedback, and give a performance score — making learning measurable and engaging.
    • A Weather section integrated with NASA’s API, giving users real-time weather data connected directly to Terra observations, linking global science to local daily life.

 SO…

  •   Makes NASA’s Terra data understandable and directly relevant to communities, fostering long-term environmental awareness.
  •   Combines 3D visualization, AI, gamification, video storytelling, and real-time weather in one cohesive platform — a fresh way to engage with NASA data.
  •   Built entirely on authentic NASA data, ensuring scientific accuracy and credibility.
  •   Directly answers the challenge: turning Terra’s complex datasets into an animated, accessible Earth science story with real-world connections.
  •   Spatium doesn’t just show data — it weaves it into a coherent story and interactive journey that users can remember, enjoy, and learn from.

Conclusion

Spatium is not just another educational platform; it’s a comprehensive solution to one of the biggest challenges: making 25 years of Terra’s complex data accessible and engaging. By combining science, interactivity, and storytelling, Spatium delivers a unique, unified experience that brings NASA’s data closer to people than ever before.

We developed an embedded, AI-assisted system that detects, monitors, and localizes sharks in real time
 using signal and satellite data. Built on the Panda+ STM32F401 (Cortex-M4) platform, it integrates SPI
 communication, FATFS storage, and SD logging to process biological and positional data from shark tags.
 The STM32CubeIDE-based firmware ensures seamless sensor interfacing, reliable data acquisition, and
 efficient communication for continuous ocean monitoring.

The whole flow starts from attaching the device to the dorsal fin of the shark because the fin stays above the surrounding tissue, is rigid, and minimizes contact with the body. Then, data is collected by satellites in patches to save battery. The data is processed, giving the longitude and latitude of the shark and metadata like shark type. We created a website that reads tags(devices) data, analyzes currents, hot and cold areas, and sea surface height. From these insights, we built a predictive AI model that predicts the path of sharks' movement.
projectDetails.details:

The firmware—developed in STM32CubeIDE using C—handles sensor interfacing, data acquisition, and communication protocols for reliable field performance. We designed the device to track the shark movement attached to sensor that can analysis the turbine movement and all activity of shark. the device is covered by acrylic, and the antenna is made of titanium to resist salty harsh environment. using acrylic helped reduce weight significantly due to small density and still carrying the function of protecting the electronic circuit from water. The max depth range is from 1700 m to 2000 m and can resist temp from -40 c to 60 c. projectDetails.name: BlueOrbit
projectDetails.summary: Sharks are vital to maintaining the balance of marine ecosystems, supporting biodiversity, fisheries, and marine tourism. Their decline disrupts ocean balance, reduces fish stocks, and impacts both the economy and food security. However, tracking sharks remains a major challenge due to their wide-ranging movements, deep dives, and the limitations of traditional tags, which lack long battery life, sufficient data collection, and real-time transmission. To address this, our idea is to develop an interactive dashboard that integrates NASA satellite data such as water temperature, oxygen levels, chlorophyll, light, and tides with advanced smart tags attached to sharks. These tags will record shark movements and behaviors, including swimming and feeding patterns, and link them with environmental changes detected by satellites. The dashboard, supported by a live map, will provide real-time tracking, predictive analytics of shark occurrence areas, and early warning systems for fishermen and vessels to minimize bycatch. This solution will enable researchers to gain deeper insights into shark-environment interactions, strengthen conservation efforts, and reduce human–shark conflicts, ultimately protecting biodiversity and sustaining marine resources essential for human life.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does BlueOrbit do?

BlueOrbit is an interactive dashboard design and prototype that aims to improve shark tracking and marine conservation using data integration between NASA satellites and advanced smart tracking tags.

Sharks play a critical role in maintaining marine ecosystem balance, biodiversity, and the health of global fisheries. However, tracking them remains challenging due to their vast movement ranges, deep dives, and the limitations of traditional tags that lack long battery life, detailed sensing, and real-time data transmission.

To address this, BlueOrbit integrates NASA satellite data including water temperature, chlorophyll, light, and tides with enhanced smart tags that record shark movement and behavior such as swimming, feeding, depth, acceleration, sound, and camera footage.

The system visualizes all this information through an interactive dashboard with a live map, allowing users to switch between satellite and tag data. It provides real-time tracking, predictive analysis of shark occurrence areas, and early warning alerts for fishermen and vessels to minimize bycatch.

This project empowers researchers to better understand shark-environment interactions, students to access real-world data for marine studies, and contributes to sustainable ocean conservation by reducing human shark conflicts and protecting biodiversity.

How does BlueOrbit work?

The dashboard provides an overview showing shark counts, alerts, active regions, average depths, tag status, and an interactive map linking satellite and tracking data. https://drive.google.com/file/d/12hd1OQmk37SNZdhMA29m4Sft0KWK38O4/view?usp=sharing

An interactive Live Map combining NASA satellite data and tag tracking data, allowing users to switch between the heatmap view and tagged shark locations, while displaying each shark’s current position and past migration path. https://drive.google.com/file/d/1nWJOIIjGBMEGxtOi1ugCbJ9MPSeiY16U/view?usp=sharing

The Tags & Shark Details screen displays a list of tags filterable by status (Active – Signal Lost – Low Battery). Selecting a tag shows detailed shark information including ID, name, species, current map location, temperature, depth, behavior, battery level, and last data update. https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Osh8UaF1zhzK_I9jCHKE-Kcf4mUMuUU2/view?usp=sharing

The Alerts screen displays all system and shark behavior notifications such as low battery, signal loss, or unusual movement with filters for status, real-time tracking, and summary cards providing a quick overview and actions for each alert. https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_eaGE94Br9tHMn_TW8AaAIyidK8Hqi6O/view?usp=sharing

projectDetails.details:
Our project, Stellar Tales, created by Stellar Crew for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025, is designed to transform complex space weather science into an engaging and accessible learning experience for children, teenagers, and the public.

What does it do / how does it work?

Stellar Tales is a digital storytelling platform that combines research, web development, interactive design, and animation to tell the story of a solar flare named Flare. Through our interactive website Stellar Tales Website, users can follow Flare's journey from the Sun to Earth, discovering how coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and solar activity affect our planet in multiple ways. The platform integrates text, visuals, animations, voice-over videos, and interactive features (quizzes, timelines, hotspots) to create a fun and immersive experience.

Benefits and intended impact …

Our goal is to lower the barriers to understanding space weather and highlight its real-world impacts-such as disrupting GPS signals, aviation, agriculture, electricity, and satellite communications-while also showcasing its beauty through auroras. By blending accurate science with storytelling, we aim to make children and teenagers not only learn but love space science. The intended impact is to inspire curiosity, increase awareness of space weather's importance, and motivate young learners to explore STEM fields.

Tools, coding languages, and software used

Website Development: HTML, CSS, JavaScript (GitHub Pages for hosting).

Design and UI/UX: Canva, Figma, PowerPoint.

Animations and Videos: Cartoon-style voice-over videos generated with Al tools (like Mootion and Canva animations).

Research and Content Creation: Based on credible sources such as NASA, NOAA, and UCAR, all cited in our proposal.

Presentation & Proposal: Structured slides and a detailed research document to support our submission.

Creativity and considerations

What makes our project creative is the combination of rigorous scientific research with imaginative storytelling. Instead of presenting data in a traditional way, we gave space weather a voice and a character. Flare becomes a relatable guide for kids and teens, making abstract science tangible and emotional. Our team considered accessibility (simple language, visual appeal, interactive learning), inclusivity (content appealing to a wide age range), and engagement (gamified features like quizzes and timelines).

In the end, Stellar Tales is not just a project-it is a platform that inspires young people to see space as fun, exciting, and deeply connected to life on Earth.

projectDetails.name: Beyond Earth, For Earth
projectDetails.summary:
What We Built
We created an AI system that rapidly detects exoplanets from NASA telescope data (Kepler, TESS, and K2) and analyzes their environments. Our ensemble models achieve over 82% accuracy, filtering thousands of candidates down to high-priority targets for expensive follow-up observations like JWST.
Why It Matters
Here's the key insight: exoplanets aren't just about finding alien worlds—they're natural climate laboratories. By studying hundreds of planets with different temperatures, atmospheres, and radiation levels, we learn universal principles about how climates work, fail, and reach tipping points.
Our system calculates each planet's temperature, radiation exposure, atmospheric potential, and habitability score. This data helps scientists understand greenhouse effects, atmospheric loss, and carbon cycles under extreme conditions—insights that directly improve Earth's climate models.
We're building a bridge between space exploration and climate science. Every exoplanet we characterize teaches us something about planetary atmospheres and stability—knowledge we desperately need as Earth faces climate change. It's about making the most of telescope time while bringing those discoveries home.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details: A World Away - Exoplanet Hunter AI

What exactly does it do?

This project is a sophisticated web-based platform that uses ensemble machine learning models to identify exoplanet candidates from NASA telescope data. It analyzes light curve measurements and stellar characteristics from three major space missions (Kepler, TESS, and K2) to predict whether a celestial object is likely an exoplanet or a false positive.

But this is only the beginning. Our catalog becomes the foundation for a second stage of analysis—where researchers apply climate and habitability models to understand planetary atmospheres and surface conditions. By studying these diverse worlds, scientists refine the universal physics of climate stability, greenhouse effects, and atmospheric evolution—insights that directly improve Earth's own climate models and tipping-point predictions.

The system provides two operational modes:

  • User Mode: Simple CSV upload interface for quick batch predictions
  • Researcher Mode: Advanced dashboard with model statistics, batch analytics, feature importance analysis, and custom model training capabilities

How does it work?

Backend Architecture:

  • Node.js/Express server handles API requests and file uploads
    • Kepler: Ensemble model (XGBoost 35% + LightGBM 35% + Neural Network 30%) trained on 9,564 KOIs with 27 features
    • TESS: Ensemble model (XGBoost + LightGBM + Deep MLP) optimized for 27-day sector data and bright stars
    • K2: LightGBM with Bayesian optimization and SMOTE resampling for handling 19 campaigns of variable-quality data

Prediction Pipeline:

  1. User uploads CSV with stellar/planetary parameters
  2. Server validates and parses the data
  3. Python scripts load pre-trained models and preprocessors
  4. Features are normalized/scaled using mission-specific transformations
    • Equilibrium temperature (Kelvin and Celsius)
    • Planetary composition (rocky, super-Earth, sub-Neptune, gas giant)
    • Radiation levels compared to Earth
    • Water state predictions (ice, liquid, vapor, supercritical)
    • Habitable zone classification
    • Habitability score (0-100)
  5. Results include risk levels, data quality assessments, and interpretation

Our model provides all the critical parameters needed for climate modeling:

  • Orbital period and semi-major axis
  • Planetary radius and mass estimates
  • Stellar temperature and luminosity
  • Insolation flux
  • Equilibrium temperature
  • Atmospheric pressure indicators

What benefits does it have?

For Exoplanet Science:

  1. Multi-Mission Support: Unified platform for analyzing data from three different NASA telescopes
  2. High Accuracy: Achieves 79-85% accuracy with 88-94% recall across missions
  3. Transparency: Shows individual model predictions, confidence scores, and feature importance
  4. Batch Processing: Handles large datasets efficiently (tested with thousands of candidates)
  5. Risk Stratification: Prioritizes candidates as HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW for follow-up observations

For Earth Climate Science: 6. Comparative Planetology: Understanding isotopes and atmospheric chemistry in extreme exoplanet conditions helps us model how elements behave under different pressures, temperatures, and radiation environments 7. Climate Physics Laboratory: Each exoplanet becomes a natural experiment testing climate stability under conditions impossible to replicate on Earth 8. Atmospheric Evolution Models: Observing atmospheric loss, greenhouse runaway, and stability across diverse planets refines our understanding of Earth's atmospheric resilience 9. Carbon Cycle Insights: Studying carbon balance in various planetary environments improves predictions for Earth's carbon tipping points

What do you hope to achieve?

Immediate Scientific Goals:

  1. Accelerate Discovery: Help astronomers quickly identify promising exoplanet candidates from massive datasets
  2. Reduce False Positives: Use ensemble voting to filter out instrumental artifacts and astrophysical mimics
  3. Support Follow-up: Prioritize JWST targets by identifying candidates with atmospheric characterization potential
  4. Enable Research: Provide tools for researchers to train custom models and analyze prediction patterns

Broader Impact - Building the Data Bridge:

In essence, our system builds a data bridge between exoplanet discovery and Earth climate science. It helps NASA and the global scientific community make the most of precious telescope time (like JWST), accelerates the search for Earth-like worlds, and returns practical knowledge about atmospheric resilience, carbon balance, and habitability—knowledge we can apply right here on Earth to confront climate change.

Why Understanding Exoplanet Environments Matters for Earth:

  • Isotopic Fractionation: Studying how isotopes behave under extreme radiation and pressure helps refine Earth's atmospheric chemistry models
  • Greenhouse Effect Boundaries: Observing where and why greenhouse effects go into runaway mode on other planets improves our predictions for Earth's climate thresholds
  • Atmospheric Retention: Understanding which planets retain atmospheres under stellar wind bombardment informs models of Earth's magnetic field protection and atmospheric loss
  • Water Cycle Dynamics: Seeing how water transitions between states on planets with different temperatures refines Earth's hydrological cycle predictions
  • Habitability Windows: Mapping the actual boundaries of life-supporting conditions tests and improves our theoretical models

ReMarsX is an autonomous, AI-powered robotic system designed to establish foundational In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) capabilities on Mars by managing and reusing space debris.

What Exactly Does It Do?
ReMarsX's core function is to systematically collect, analyze, classify, and securely store the approximately 7 metric tons of rocket and spacecraft debris left on the Martian surface by previous missions. It transforms this environmental hazard into a valuable, queryable inventory of reusable spare parts and construction materials for future human missions.

How Does It Work?
The robot operates through a structured, multi-step workflow driven by its core AI intelligence:

Terrain Mapping & Storage Identification: It uses a Smart Map to scan the surrounding area, identify a safe, flat zone, and designate it as a secure physical storage location.

Collection & Transport: A Multifunctional Robotic Arm is used to precisely collect the identified debris.

Visual Analysis & Measurement: An AI-powered Camera System uses Computer Vision models to perform visual analysis, accurately identify the material type (e.g., aluminum, steel, plastic), and measure its dimensions.
projectDetails.details:
ReMarsX is an autonomous, AI-powered robotic system designed to establish foundational In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) capabilities on Mars by managing and reusing space debris.

What Exactly Does It Do?

ReMarsX's core function is to systematically collect, analyze, classify, and securely store the approximately 7 metric tons of rocket and spacecraft debris left on the Martian surface by previous missions. It transforms this environmental hazard into a valuable, queryable inventory of reusable spare parts and construction materials for future human missions.

How Does It Work?

The robot operates through a structured, multi-step workflow driven by its core AI intelligence:

Terrain Mapping & Storage Identification: It uses a Smart Map to scan the surrounding area, identify a safe, flat zone, and designate it as a secure physical storage location.

Collection & Transport: A Multifunctional Robotic Arm is used to precisely collect the identified debris.

Visual Analysis & Measurement: An AI-powered Camera System uses Computer Vision models to perform visual analysis, accurately identify the material type (e.g., aluminum, steel, plastic), and measure its dimensions.

Classification & Inventory: The material data is cross-referenced with an Integrated Knowledge Base (compiled from space agency data) to classify its potential reuse. The physical location and details are logged in a Virtual Warehouse/Resource Management database.

Processing & Retrieval: A specialized Remodeling Welding Arm can reshape or join components as needed. The system allows astronauts to query the virtual warehouse and request specific components, which the robot can then retrieve or process.

What Benefits Does It Have?

The project delivers significant strategic and operational benefits:

Economic Sustainability: It drastically reduces the prohibitively high cost of launching spare parts, construction materials, and resources from Earth.

Operational Resilience: It provides future astronauts with an immediate, on-site supply for emergency repairs (like spacecraft or habitat maintenance) and essential construction, reducing dependence on Earth.

Environmental Compliance: It addresses the growing concern of Martian space debris, ensuring the environment remains safe and free from potentially hazardous waste, complying with future Martian standards.

Scalability: The architecture supports multi-robot coordination for wider coverage and faster processing, enabling rapid infrastructure development.

What Do We Hope to Achieve?

We hope to achieve the foundational implementation of a closed-loop resource system on Mars. Our ultimate goal is to prove the concept that waste can be autonomously converted into a sustainable resource, thereby enabling long-term human self-sufficiency and significantly lowering the barrier for sustained colonization efforts. We aim to shift the paradigm from Earth-dependent logistics to Martian self-reliance.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the core, autonomous operating system that makes ReMarsX a 100% AI-controlled robotic solution for In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) on Mars. Our software architecture, developed primarily using Python in Jupyter Notebook, leverages several powerful AI/ML frameworks to achieve full autonomy.

The AI's functionality is divided into three main operational aspects:

Visual Analysis: We used TensorFlow and OpenCV to build Computer Vision models. These models enable the robot’s camera to autonomously identify the type of debris material (e.g., metal, plastic) and accurately measure its dimensions in real-time.

Autonomous Operation: The core control software, developed in Python alongside NumPy for numerical computations, dictates the robot's independent movement, executes optimal pathfinding for efficient debris collection, and performs obstacle avoidance.

Resource Management (Future): Future plans involve integrating Predictive Intelligence to analyze vehicle wear-and-tear data, anticipate maintenance needs, and potentially auto-design replacement parts from the collected inventory.

The conceptual models were validated using Scikit-learn for evaluation metrics to ensure reliability. In line with competition guidelines, any project visuals (images, videos) created using generative AI tools are clearly marked with a visible, non-NASA-branded watermark, and all AI-generated code elements or synthetic data are acknowledged in the project's metadata.

For high-level conceptualization, code refinement, and structured writing assistance, we utilized leading large language models: Gemini was instrumental for complex multimodal content analysis and structuring research, while Chat-GPT 5 was leveraged for its superior reasoning, code generation (specifically for developing our Python, NumPy, and TensorFlow framework concepts), and ensuring highly coherent textual explanations. To generate the necessary visual assets, we employed multiple AI image generation tools: Leonardo.Ai and ImageFX were used to create high-fidelity, photorealistic renderings of the ReMarsX robot, its components, and its operation within the Martian environment, alongside Freepik AI and Google AI Studio (NanoBanana) for diverse stylistic mockups and rapid concept iteration. Every AI-generated image in the project is clearly identified with a non-NASA watermark, ensuring full transparency in compliance with competition rules.

projectDetails.name: When the Sun Sneezes
projectDetails.summary:
Solar Explorers: Space Weather Stories for Kids is an interactive web platform designed to make space weather simple, fun, and engaging for young learners. Our project was developed in response to NASA’s Stellar Stories – Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings challenge.

We identified a gap: while space weather affects everyone from kids using GPS on their phones to farmers relying on satellites for crops most people, especially children, don’t understand what it is or why it matters.

Our solution is a visual, gamified website where children can:

Learn the basics of space weather through stories and animations.

Explore interactive demos (e.g., dragging the Sun closer to Earth to see real effects).

Discover NASA’s missions like SOHO, Parker Solar Probe, and DSCOVR in kid-friendly formats.

Connect real-world impact with farmer stories and everyday life examples.

By blending science, storytelling, and interactivity, Solar Explorers empowers kids to understand space weather while inspiring the next generation of scientists.
projectDetails.details:
What our project does
Solar Explorers is an interactive educational website designed to simplify space weather for children and general audiences. The platform combines animations, storytelling, and interactive demos to explain how solar activity impacts Earth — from auroras in the sky, to satellite signals, to farmers’ crops.

How it works

  • The homepage introduces space weather with kid-friendly visuals and simple explanations.
  • Interactive simulations (e.g., moving the Sun closer to Earth) help children see the effects of solar storms in real time.
  • Illustrated cards explain real-life impacts on technology, farming, and astronauts.
  • A “NASA Missions” section highlights spacecraft such as SOHO, SDO, DSCOVR, and Parker Solar Probe, translated into fun and engaging stories for kids.

Benefits & Impact

  • Makes invisible science (space weather) accessible to children.
  • Helps communities like farmers understand real-world impacts.
  • Builds awareness and curiosity about NASA’s work.
  • Inspires the next generation of scientists and problem-solvers.

Tools & Technology

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript (React for interactivity).
  • Backend / AI: Python for integrating a simple AI model to generate explanations.
  • Design: Adobe Illustrator, Figma, Canva for graphics & UI mockups.
  • Data: NASA datasets from SDO, SOHO, Parker Solar Probe, and DSCOVR.

Creativity & Team Considerations
We focused on balancing scientific accuracy with child-friendly storytelling. We considered language simplicity, cultural relatability (e.g., farmer stories), and interactive design to keep children engaged. Our creativity lies in merging real NASA science with playful, educational storytelling so kids not only learn — they also feel inspired to explore space.

AI was used as a supportive tool for ideation, visual prototyping, and coding assistance — not as a replacement for our original creativity, scientific storytelling, or final design decisions.

Our project urbaneco vision developed an integrated smart platform that connects water quality monitoring, solar energy optimization, and urban landscape management to support sustainable and healthier cities. We relied primarily on NASA Earth observation datasets — including Land Surface Temperature, Vegetation Index (NDVI), and Terrestrial Hydrosphere indicators — and combined them with locally collected Egyptian data. projectDetails.details:
Our project, urbaneco vision, is an AI-powered smart platform designed to enhance urban sustainability by integrating NASA Earth observation data with local environmental datasets from Egypt. The platform automatically collects, processes, and visualizes data related to water quality, solar energy performance, and urban landscape changes, generating predictive analytics and interactive dashboards for decision-makers, businesses, and citizens.

How it works:

  • Data Collection: Pulls satellite-based and on-ground environmental data.
  • Analysis & Forecasting: Uses Python, machine learning models (Random Forest Regressor for water quality, ARIMA and SARIMAX for inflation and solar ROI forecasts) to predict key indicators.
  • Visualization: Provides web-based dashboards (built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI, and Recharts) that translate complex datasets into intuitive visuals and interactive scenario simulators.

Benefits & Impact:

  • Identifies water pollution hotspots to enable early intervention.
  • Optimizes solar energy adoption by projecting savings and ROI under various scenarios.
  • Supports urban greening and landscape planning to reduce emissions and improve public health.
  • Empowers city planners, NGOs, and communities to make data-driven decisions aligned with Egypt Vision 2030 and UN SDG 6.

Tools & Technologies:

  • Backend & Analysis: Python, Jupyter Notebooks, Pandas, Scikit-learn, Statsmodels.
  • Frontend & UI: React 18, TypeScript, Vite 6, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI, Recharts.
  • Deployment: Vercel for hosting.

Creativity & Approach:
Our innovation lies in bridging global NASA satellite data with local Egyptian measurements, creating a scalable model that any city can adopt. By combining real-world environmental data with predictive analytics in an interactive platform, we provide actionable insights that support sustainable urban planning and long-term decision-making.

Team Considerations:
We focused on accuracy, accessibility, and usability, ensuring forecasts are reliable and dashboards are intuitive for both technical and non-technical users. Sustainability, scalability, and alignment with real-world policies were key guiding principles throughout development.

projectDetails.name: Star EngineAi
projectDetails.summary: The Star EngineAi is an interactive web platform designed to transform NASA’s vast collection of over 450+ space bioscience publications into an explorable, AI-driven galaxy of knowledge. By merging artificial intelligence, data visualization, and a 3D galaxy-inspired interface, the project revolutionizes how scientists, educators, and the public engage with NASA’s biological research. Each publication is visualized as a “star,” interconnected through a knowledge graph that reveals relationships between studies, missions, and discoveries. The platform’s AI capabilities—such as intelligent summarization, semantic search, and chat-based exploration—allow users to quickly identify key findings, research gaps, and trends in space biology. Ultimately, it democratizes access to NASA’s bioscience data, accelerates discovery, and supports future missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
projectDetails.details:
The Star EngineAi functions as a dynamic, 3D research explorer built using React, Three.js, and Gemini API (for AI-driven tasks). It processes and visualizes NASA’s bioscience data—sourced from PubMed Central archives—by converting XML records into structured local JSON files (publications.json and knowledge_graph.json).
Each paper becomes a “star” within a virtual galaxy, linked by constellations that represent scientific relationships such as supports, contradicts, or cites. Users can explore through modes like Temporal Lens (time-lapse of discoveries), Mission Lens (linking research to NASA missions), and Consensus Lens (visual debate maps).
AI tools summarize studies, identify themes, and generate visual diagrams, while the Research Hub enables chat-style interaction with each paper.
The system’s benefits include faster insight discovery, interactive education, and integrated research planning for future missions. It creatively combines science, design, and technology to make NASA’s biological research both accessible and inspiring.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
AI was central to the development of the Space Biology Knowledge Engine.

  • AI Summarization: The Gemini API was used to generate concise, human-readable summaries of NASA’s bioscience papers.
  • Semantic Search: Natural language queries were processed via Gemini prompts to identify the most relevant studies.
  • Knowledge Extraction: AI-assisted keyword mapping helped identify relationships between papers for the knowledge graph.
  • Diagram Generation: Gemini API was used to create flowchart-style visual representations of study results.
    All AI-generated content (text or images) is clearly acknowledged and watermarked, ensuring transparency and compliance with NASA Space Apps guidelines.

projectDetails.details:
Our project, Learn from a Cactus Fruit, is a dynamic website that transforms NASA’s publicly available data into an interactive and educational experience. When users open the site, they are guided through a long interactive homepage. By scrolling to the Explore section, they can navigate the Solar System object by object — planets, moons, the asteroid belt, and the Kuiper Belt — moving horizontally to select a cosmic body. Each object contains interactive hotspots that reveal detailed NASA information. After studying, users can click Test Yourself, where our system randomly selects 10 questions from a pool of 30, ensuring that every quiz is fresh and engaging.

The platform also features Chat with a Cactus Fruit, an AI chatbot powered by NASA’s list of 608 full-text open-access Space Biology publications. This chatbot enables users to ask personalized questions about space or the website itself, making the experience interactive and tailored. Additional features include an About Us page, where visitors can learn about our team and purpose.

Our goal is to make space exploration knowledge accessible and inspiring. Scientists can use the platform to generate hypotheses, managers to identify investment opportunities, mission architects to plan safer missions, and students to engage with space in a fun, educational way.

We developed the project using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the frontend, integrated with APIs and datasets from NASA. The quiz system was programmed to dynamically select questions, ensuring replayability. The chatbot was trained on curated NASA publications to guarantee scientific accuracy.

The creativity of our project lies in transforming static, complex datasets into a living, interactive journey through the Solar System — combining education, exploration, and testing in a way that empowers a wide range of users. Our team considered accessibility, engagement, scientific accuracy, and the ability to inspire curiosity as the foundation of our design.

projectDetails.details:
What Exactly Does It Do?

Our project, Geospatial DSS, is a smart decision-support platform that uses NASA’s

Earth-observation data to provide urban planners and architects with actionable

insights for designing climate-responsive urban environments. The platform

combines data on humidity, solar radiation, and CO2 emissions to visualize urban

microclimates and help design adaptive building facades that are both energy-

efficient and sustainable. This tool helps cities tackle pressing issues such as urban

heat islands, mold growth, excessive energy consumption, and air pollution.How Does It Work?

The platform integrates satellite data from various NASA missions (such as AIRS for

humidity, POWER for solar radiation, and OCO-2 for CO2 emissions) and processes

it through a series of geospatial analysis and machine learning algorithms. The data

is visualized on an interactive 3D map, which displays key environmental parameters

like humidity, solar exposure, and carbon emissions for different urban zones. By

combining this information with AI-driven simulations, urban planners can design

building facades that respond to environmental factors—such as dynamic shading

systems, moisture-controlling materials, and carbon-absorbing facades—that actively

improve the urban climate.

What Benefits Does It Have?

Sustainability: The platform enables cities to adopt building designs that reduce

energy consumption, improve air quality, and minimize carbon emissions.

Resilience: It helps cities become more resilient to extreme weather events like

heatwaves and heavy rainfall by designing structures that adapt to changing

conditions.

Public Health: By reducing humidity-related mold growth, improving air quality, and

decreasing the heat island effect, the platform enhances the health and comfort of

urban residents.

Data-Driven Decision Making: The tool empowers city planners with real-time, data-

backed insights, allowing for smarter, evidence-based decisions in urban

development.

What Do You Hope to Achieve?

We aim to transform how cities approach urban planning in the face of climate

change. Our goal is to enable the adoption of smart, sustainable building solutions

that reduce environmental impact, improve quality of life for urban residents, and

provide a scalable framework for cities worldwide. We hope to catalyze the adoption

of NASA’s Earth-observation data in urban design and policy, fostering a more

sustainable and resilient future for cities.

What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use?Data & Platforms:

NASA datasets: AIRS, MERRA-2, OCO-2, POWER, CERES, MODIS

Google Earth Engine for remote-sensing processing

Earthdata APIs for bulk data download

Processing & Analysis:

Programming Languages: Python, R

Libraries: xarray, geopandas, rasterio, pykrige, pandas, statsmodels, scikit-learn

Time-series & spatial analysis: Kriging, clustering, interpolation

Modeling & Simulation:

Energy & Thermal Simulation: EnergyPlus, OpenStudio, Ladybug/Honeybee

(Grasshopper)

Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD): OpenFOAM

Daylighting & Lighting Simulation: Radiance, Daysim

Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA): OpenLCA

Control & Machine Learning:Rule-based and PID controllers for facade actuation

Reinforcement learning (stable-baselines3, custom RL) for adaptive control

ML models for short-term climate prediction: LSTM, CNNs (TensorFlow/PyTorch)

Prototyping & IoT:

Materials: Hygromorphic composites, hydrogels, reflective coatings, microalgae

photobioreactors

IoT Sensors: SHT3x (humidity), NDIR CO2 sensors, temperature sensors

Data Ingestion: MQTT, time-series DB (InfluxDB), Grafana for dashboards

By combining these technologies, we create a scalable, integrated platform that

connects satellite data with urban design tools and real-world environmental

conditions to deliver actionable, climate-responsive solutions.

projectDetails.name: Terra’s Labyrinth
projectDetails.summary:
In our project, Terra’s Labyrinth, we used several datasets from NASA’s Terra satellite to build the story:
MOPITT: Carbon monoxide data from wildfires inspired the first part of the labyrinth, symbolized by a glowing orb of CO.
MODIS: Vegetation indices (NDVI/EVI) and fire detection data showed the impact of deforestation and loss of green cover, represented by a fading green orb.
ASTER: High-resolution imagery of glaciers and land surface temperature helped us illustrate melting ice and rising sea levels.
MISR: Aerosol and smoke data supported the visualization of atmospheric changes caused by fires.Instead of using charts, we transformed NASA datasets into animated symbols and scenes inside the labyrinth. This approach turned 25 years of scientific records into a visual story that connects Earth’s past, present, and possible fut
projectDetails.details: Terra satellite data into a visually engaging journey. The video follows an explorer robot navigating a symbolic labyrinth, where each section represents a critical Earth process. Using data from MOPITT, the story begins with wildfires and carbon monoxide pollution; with MODIS, it highlights deforestation and loss of green cover; and with ASTER, it shows melting glaciers and sea-level rise. MISR and CERES data also support the narrative by adding insights on atmospheric changes and Earth’s energy balance. The project works by combining scientific data visualization with animation and storytelling, making complex datasets accessible and relatable. Its main benefit is bridging the gap between science and the public, turning abstract numbers into a narrative with emotional and educational impact. We developed the project using Blender for 3D animation, Adobe Premiere Pro for editing, and AI tools like ChatGPT and Gemini Pro for scriptwriting and scenario generation. Voice-over tools were used for narration. The intended impact is to raise awareness about climate change, inspire collective responsibility, and showcase how NASA’s data can tell a powerful story about Earth’s past, present, and possible future.
projectDetails.aiReferences: we used Artificial Intelligence tools in our project. We used Chat GPT and Gemini Pro to help in managing our resources and to accelerate innovation and creativity. Gemini Pro was specifically used in the final scene to generate a short, impactful video concept based on real NASA data and other open sources. This scene shows a possible future of our planet if current climate trends continue. We also used an AI voice-over tool to narrate the closing part of the video. The narration highlights how, while our world struggles with climate change, there is also a silent success story in our atmosphere: carbon monoxide levels, once a serious threat, have started to decline. NASA’s two decades of data inspired this moment, turning science to a powerful and emotional message for the audience. Terra’s data is not just warning us It’s giving us tools to change.

projectDetails.name: Tempestera
projectDetails.summary:
We developed a full-stack web application that predicts the likelihood of weather conditions (hot, cold, windy, wet) using NASA’s historical Earth observation data.
What we built:
 A user-friendly dashboard where people can select a location (point or area), a date, and a weather condition of interest, then receive a probability estimate with a confidence interval.


How it addresses the challenge:
 It transforms raw NASA climate data into actionable insights. By applying statistical methods on historical data (1981–present), we provide the probability that a given weather condition will occur, tailored for different use cases such as farming, fishing, tourism, and driving.


Why it matters:
 This bridges the gap between NASA’s open data and end users who need simple, actionable information for planning and risk assessment. It democratizes climate information, supports sustainable decision-making, and raises awareness of climate variability.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is a web application that calculates the likelihood of specific weather conditions, such as hot, cold, windy, or wet days—for any location and date using NASA POWER (MERRA-2) historical data.

It works by fetching past weather data for the selected coordinates and date range, computing statistical probabilities (using day-of-year windows and confidence intervals), and presenting the results through an interactive map-based dashboard and visual charts. A built-in chatbot assistant allows users to ask natural questions like “Is it good to go fishing tomorrow?” and receive concise, data-driven answers.

Benefits & Impact:
It helps users plan outdoor activities (e.g., farming, fishing, travel) with data-backed insights instead of guesswork, promoting safety, efficiency, and climate awareness.

Tools & Tech Stack:

  • Backend: Python (FastAPI, Requests)
  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet, Chart.js
  • Data Source: NASA POWER API (MERRA-2)
  • Development Tools: VS Code, GitHub, LLMs for code generation

Creativity & Design Factors:
We focused on accessibility and personalization—turning complex NASA data into actionable, user-friendly insights. The conversational chatbot and persona-based recommendations make scientific data approachable and useful for everyone.

projectDetails.name: The 42: Interactive 3D Inflatable Habitat Simulator
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, The 42: Interactive 3D Inflatable Habitat Simulator, is an educational and interactive web platform that allows users to explore how astronauts can live and work inside space habitats. The tool focuses on inflatable habitats, a promising solution for long-duration missions due to their lightweight transport and large usable volume.

Users begin by choosing among different habitat types (Hard Shell, Prefabricated, Inflatable, ISRU) and then move into designing the inflatable module. They can input mission parameters such as crew size (4 or 6 astronauts) and mission duration (<180 days or >180 days). Inside the 3D simulator, users can place essential habitat items (sleeping pods, exercise devices, galley, hygiene units, racks) across three decks. The system applies real NASA-based rules and constraints, such as required stowage coverage for radiation protection and adjacency guidelines between items, while giving feedback in real time.

By combining NASA data with an intuitive interface, the simulator makes space architecture more accessible, inspires creativity, and demonstrates the complexities of designing safe and functional habitats for Mars and beyond.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, The 42: Interactive 3D Inflatable Habitat Simulator, is a web-based platform that allows users to explore, design, and understand space habitats.

The simulator starts by presenting three types of habitats (Hard Shell, Prefabricated, Inflatable). While only the Inflatable Habitat is currently interactive, the others are documented as previews with clear explanations of their advantages and limitations.

When users select the inflatable habitat, they enter mission parameters (crew size and mission duration). The system then opens an interactive 3D modeling page where they can place and arrange habitat items such as sleeping pods, hygiene stations, food storage, medical workstations, exercise equipment, and system racks across three decks of a cylindrical module. Built-in rules and constraints provide warnings if items are misplaced (ex, hygiene too far from crew, can not use more than 2 UWMS), while still allowing freedom for experimentation.

Additional features include an Information Page (explaining habitat layers, item usage, and design rules in simple terms) and a Quiz Page to reinforce knowledge.

Tools & Technologies: We built the platform using the Angular framework for the frontend, supported by Node.js and a database backend for storing mission configurations and user data. For visualization, we integrated Three.js for 3D modeling. 3D assets were created in Blender and exported as GLB files.

Creativity & Impact: The project makes complex NASA design data interactive and visual, transforming technical documents into an accessible learning experience. It helps students and enthusiasts understand habitat design trade-offs, human factors, and mission constraints. The goal is to inspire broader engagement with space architecture and highlight the importance of inflatable habitats for long-duration missions.

projectDetails.name: Project The band of the hawk
projectDetails.summary:
We developed PetalView, a mobile application that monitors and predicts global flowering
patterns using NASA Earth observation data and AI models. The app addresses the challenge
by providing real-time bloom maps, AI-powered predictions, and community-driven flower
observations, helping users, scientists, and policymakers track seasonal changes in vegetation.
This is important because flowering phenology is a key indicator of climate change, ecosystem
health, and food security. By connecting people with nature and enabling better ecological
insights, PetalView contributes to sustainability, biodiversity monitoring, and environmental
awareness worldwide.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

Our project, BloomWatch, is a monitoring and prediction tool that detects, visualizes, and forecasts plant blooming events using NASA Earth observation data. It allows users to explore current bloom conditions in their region or globally, and to receive predictions about when blooming is expected to occur in the near future. The tool is designed to serve farmers, researchers, and conservationists by providing insights into vegetation dynamics.

How does it work?

The system integrates NASA satellite datasets (e.g., MODIS, Landsat, GIBS) to extract vegetation indices such as NDVI.

An AI/ML prediction model processes location-based features to forecast upcoming bloom cycles.

The backend (FastAPI with a trained model) exposes prediction endpoints.

A Flutter-based mobile app provides users with two options:

Auto-detect their current location using GPS.

Manually enter a region of interest.

The app queries the backend API and displays results with clear visualizations, timelines, and explanations of bloom status.

What benefits does it have?

Agriculture: Helps farmers determine optimal flowering and harvesting times, and supports disease/pest management strategies.

Environment & Conservation: Assists in tracking ecological cycles, detecting invasive species, and monitoring biodiversity health.

Research: Provides long-term bloom trends for phenology and climate change studies.

Public Engagement: Raises awareness of seasonal cycles and ecological importance of flowering events through an easy-to-use visual tool.

What do you hope to achieve?

Deliver a scalable tool that works across global, regional, and local scales.

Support sustainable agriculture and environmental management through AI-powered predictions.

Make complex Earth observation data accessible and actionable for a wider community.

Demonstrate how NASA datasets can provide real-world solutions to challenges like food security, climate adaptation, and biodiversity conservation.

What tools, coding languages, and software did you use?

Languages & Frameworks: Python (for AI/ML model training), FastAPI (backend API), Flutter/Dart (mobile application).

AI/ML Libraries: TensorFlow, Keras, NumPy.

Geospatial & NASA Tools: NDVI calculations from MODIS/Landsat, NASA GIBS for satellite imagery layers.

Hosting & Integration: Google Colab (model training + hosting prototype), Ngrok (temporary tunneling), planned migration to cloud (AWS/GCP).

UI/UX: Flutter animations and a green-themed design aligned with the ecological purpose of the app.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Model Development & Predictions

We trained and deployed a machine learning model (TensorFlow/Keras) that takes in vegetation indices (e.g., NDVI from NASA Earth observation data) and predicts blooming patterns.

The model processes user-provided or GPS-detected location features and outputs the likelihood and timeline of upcoming bloom events.

Code Assistance & Optimization

We used AI-based coding assistants (such as ChatGPT) to accelerate development, debug issues, and generate boilerplate code for the FastAPI backend and Flutter mobile app.

All AI-assisted code was reviewed, tested, and integrated by the team to ensure functionality and originality.

Content Preparation

AI tools were used to assist in drafting parts of the project documentation, ensuring clarity, conciseness, and proper technical explanation.

Any generated text was edited and refined by the team before inclusion.

How did you ensure compliance with Space Apps rules?

No NASA branding, flags, or mission identifiers were generated or modified using AI.

Transparency: All AI-generated contributions (code snippets, text drafts) are clearly acknowledged in documentation and metadata.

Originality: AI was used only as a supporting tool — all design, concept development, and integration were carried out by the team.

Summary

AI was leveraged to accelerate innovation (through model training and predictions), increase productivity (through coding assistance), and enhance clarity (through documentation drafting). The final outputs represent a human-AI collaboration where AI supported, but did not replace, human creativity and decision-making.

projectDetails.name: NEOGuard
projectDetails.summary:
Our project focuses on raising awareness and education about asteroid threats and planetary defense through an interactive and engaging mobile application. The app combines scientific data from NASA APIs with visualizations, simulations, and gamified features to make complex space science accessible to everyone.

Users can explore real-time asteroid information, simulate impact scenarios, and visualize potential damage zones based on input parameters such as speed, size, and location. The app also integrates NASA’s Eyes on Asteroids model to let users interactively explore the solar system in 3D.

To enhance learning, the app includes an educational glossary and quick quizzes, while the defense game adds a fun and engaging experience that encourages users to think about asteroid protection strategies.

By blending education, visualization, and gamification, this project effectively addresses the challenge of low public awareness about asteroid impacts and planetary defense. It turns complex scientific data into an interactive experience that informs, engages, and inspires action — making science not only understandable, but exciting and meaningful.
projectDetails.details:
Our application is designed to educate and engage users about asteroid impacts and planetary defense through interactive tools and visual experiences. It allows users to explore real-time asteroid data from NASA’s NEO API, simulate “what-if” impact scenarios, and visualize the resulting crater size, damage radius, and energy on a simple map.

The app also includes a 3D visualization of the solar system inspired by NASA’s Eyes on Asteroids, helping users better understand orbital paths and object sizes. For learning purposes, it offers an educational glossary and short quizzes to reinforce key scientific terms. To add engagement, the project features a defense game where users protect Earth from incoming asteroids — making learning both fun and interactive.

Technically, the project was developed using Dart and Flutter for the main application structure, with Flame game framework for interactive gameplay.

The main goal is to simplify complex space science, increase public awareness, and inspire curiosity about planetary defense. By merging education, simulation, and entertainment, the project creates a meaningful experience that both informs and motivates users to learn more about space.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Yes, we utilized several AI tools to support the creative and development process of our project. Tools such as ChatGPT, Claude 4.5, and Gemini were used mainly for idea generation, content structuring, and technical guidance — for example, helping us refine feature logic, improve explanations, and optimize the user experience design.

AI image generation tools were not used for any NASA-branded visuals. However, we used Figma and design inspiration platforms like Dribbble to design the interface layout and visualize some concept ideas, always ensuring that any AI-generated or concept-based visuals were clearly marked and not associated with NASA assets.

Overall, AI tools accelerated creativity, enhanced documentation quality, and supported faster prototyping — while all coding, implementation, and logic were developed and customized manually by our team.
