projectDetails.name: Zeto - Exoplanet Detection System
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, Zeto, is a comprehensive, user-centric web platform powered by a robust Ensemble Machine Learning model.

We developed Zeto to directly address the critical bottleneck in exoplanet identification, where the vast volume of transit data generated by missions like TESS and Kepler requires meticulous, time-consuming manual vetting by astrophysicists. Zeto addresses this challenge by providing an efficient, highly accurate, and automated classification system. The ML core, trained on aggregated NASA data, instantly classifies objects as confirmed exoplanets, candidates, or false positives, drastically cutting down manual inspection time.

Zeto is important because it serves two key purposes: it accelerates scientific workflow by providing researchers with rapid, trustworthy classification results, along with value-added insights like a calculated habitability score. Crucially, the platform, featuring an intuitive conversational chatbot and CSV upload, lowers the barrier to entry, transforming complex data analysis into an engaging experience for students and the general public, fostering engagement in the search for new worlds
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Zeto is an interactive, web-based platform designed to make exoplanet classification fast, accurate, and accessible. It directly addresses the challenge of rapidly vetting the massive volume of transit signals generated by missions like TESS.

How the ML Core Works: The platform’s core is a robust Machine Learning (ML) model, specifically trained using Ensemble Methods (specifically the XGBoost Method).

  1. Data Foundation: The process begins with the consolidation of tabular datasets from the Kepler (KOI), K2, and TESS missions. This data is cleaned and optimized, and specific predictive variables are engineered for classification.
  2. Prediction: The trained ML model instantly classifies an input object as one of three types: a Confirmed Exoplanet, a Planetary Candidate, or a False Positive.
  3. Value-Added Insights: If the object is confirmed, Zeto goes beyond simple classification by implementing custom Python logic to calculate non-ML derived outputs. This includes providing key planet characteristics and a calculated habitability score (as a percentage), which offers immediate, actionable scientific context.

User Interaction: The platform features an intuitive interface with a dual-input system:

  • A Conversational Chatbot guides users through the data submission process, making data input engaging and understandable for novices.
  • A CSV File Upload utility accommodates seasoned researchers who possess existing batch data.

What benefits does it have?

Zeto offers significant value by tackling the core challenges of efficiency and accessibility in exoplanet discovery.

  • Accelerated Scientific Workflow: For researchers and astrophysicists, Zeto provides an automated and rapid tool to vet new transit data, drastically reducing the time spent on tedious manual inspection and allowing them to focus on the most promising candidates.
  • Trustworthy Results: By focusing on Ensemble Methods, the solution prioritizes clarity and provides observers with quick, trustworthy, and easy-to-understand results.
  • Educational Tool: For students, educators, and enthusiasts, the unique chatbot interface lowers the barrier to entry, transforming a complex data analysis task into an engaging, interactive experience, making it an excellent educational tool.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The project’s intended impact is twofold, addressing both scientific efficiency and public engagement:

  • Scientific Impact: The project aims to accelerate the confirmation of new worlds. By providing an efficient, reliable, and automated classification system, Zeto helps fully capitalize on the wealth of data provided by NASA's sky-surveying telescopes (Kepler, K2, TESS) and directly addresses the substantial bottleneck caused by manual analysis.
  • Public Engagement: By combining a robust ML model with a user-centric design, the solution fosters public engagement in the search for new worlds, making the vastness of space more accessible to everyone.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use to develop our project?

The development of Zeto followed a structured, four-stage process integrating data science best practices with agile web development.

<colgroup><col><col><col></colgroup>

Category

Tools and Languages
Used

Programming Languages

Python, JavaScript

Data Processing & ML Python with Pandas, Scikit-learn, Matplotlib
Backend API Python with Flask
Frontend UI/UX React and Tailwind CSS
Collaboration Git & GitHub


How is our project creative?

Zeto distinguishes itself through its focus on accessibility and interpretability:

  • Interactive Accessibility: The project moves beyond simple data entry forms. It integrates an engaging conversational chatbot that guides users, making complex data input accessible to novices and transforming analysis into an engaging experience.
  • Interpretable ML: Unlike some Deep Learning (DL) models (like AstroNet) which can be computational "black boxes," Zeto focuses on ensemble methods. This choice prioritizes clarity (SHAP) and robust testing, ensuring that the results provided are trustworthy and easy to understand.
  • Actionable Insights: Creativity is also demonstrated by incorporating non-ML calculated features, such as the crucial habitability score, alongside core classification, transforming raw data into meaningful and understandable insights.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Problem Bottleneck: The primary factor was addressing the current bottleneck where the sheer volume of transit data requires meticulous and labor-intensive manual vetting by astrophysicists, slowing the pace of discovery.
  • Data Challenges: The team focused on mitigating key data problems, including handling the extreme class imbalance (where only a small fraction of objects are real planets) and ensuring the model trained on combined mission data (Kepler, K2, TESS) works reliably on new data.
  • Model Selection: The methodology prioritized explainable ML. We chose Ensemble Methods over Deep Learning because they are faster, more transparent, and provide high accuracy on clean data, while focusing on robust cross-validation.
  • Audience Utility: Consideration was given to making the platform universally useful by integrating both the conversational chatbot for novices and the CSV upload for expert researchers.
  • Workflow Strategy: The team adopted a structured, four-phase workflow, utilizing GitHub for version control, to ensure all technical requirements—from data consolidation to API integration—were met during the hackathon period.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Below is a list detailing how AI tools were utilized, ensuring that all generative outputs were thoroughly refined and verified by the project team members:

1. Project Core (The Model as AI)

The fundamental purpose of Zeto is to implement an AI solution to solve a scientific bottleneck.

  • Core Functionality: The project utilizes Ensemble Machine Learning (ML) Models (a subset of AI) like XGBoost, trained on consolidated NASA data (Kepler, K2, TESS). This AI core provides the automated classification system. This model was developed, optimized, and rigorously cross-validated by the Model Selection & Training team.
2. Development Acceleration (Generative AI Tools)

Generative AI tools were used to accelerate non-ML aspects of the project, specifically in initial coding scaffolding and conceptual drafting. The outputs from these tools were meticulously reviewed, refined, and integrated by our engineering team to ensure high quality and accuracy.

  • Code Generation Assistance (Python/JavaScript): AI code generation tools (Claude & Grok) were utilized to accelerate the initial setup and scaffolding for routine components, particularly within the Flask Backend API (developed by Ahmed Kamal) and the React Frontend interface (developed by David Amir). This includes foundational syntax, utility functions, and boilerplate code for the API endpoints and the front-end structure. This generated code was not used blindly; every line was verified against Python and JavaScript best practices, and the custom logic (such as the characterization formulas and the habitability score calculation) was entirely custom-developed and tested by the team.
  • Conceptual and Documentation Drafting (MentorX): We utilized MentorX (a mini-GPT tool developed for NASA Space Apps Cairo) to accelerate the drafting and refinement of internal documentation, project explanations, and pitch summaries. This tool served as an assistant to rapidly structure complex scientific and technical concepts, which were then further detailed, adjusted, and validated against the project’s specific technical parameters and established astrophysical calculations by the team.

projectDetails.name: Hunting for Exoplanets with AI
projectDetails.summary:
1- We developed an AI-powered system that classifies exoplanet candidates using NASA’s Kepler and TESS mission data. Our tool helps detect potential planets hidden within noisy observations by combining machine learning, explainable AI, and an interactive web interface.
2- What makes our project important is not just faster candidate vetting—it’s our team’s focus on the habitability potential of these worlds. By highlighting planets that could support life, we aim to accelerate the search for Earth-like environments and make the science more accessible to the public.
3- We built this project to support NASA’s mission of exploration, engage people in the excitement of exoplanet discovery, and show how AI can be a partner in evaluating the conditions that make other worlds habitable.
projectDetails.details:
1-

Our system looks at important star and planet features (like size, orbit, and temperature) from NASA’s Kepler data. It then predicts whether a signal is likely to be a real planet or just a false alarm. Alongside the prediction, it shows a confidence score and clear visuals to explain the result.

2-

  • Prepare the Data: Clean and organize raw Kepler/TESS data, filling gaps and creating useful features.
  • Test the Model: Validate the system using known examples to check accuracy and reliability.
  • Make a Prediction: The model classifies whether the input signal is a likely planet or a false positive.
  • Get Result: Generate outcomes with confidence scores and supporting details.
  • Analyze: Use AI to highlight key influencing factors such as orbital period, size, or temperature.
  • Show on the Web UI: Display results interactively for scientists, students, and the public to explore easily.

3-Benefits:

  • Speed: Helps quickly sort through huge amounts of space data.
  • Clarity: Explains AI decisions so they aren’t a “black box.”
  • Engagement: Lets the scientist  try planet-hunting themselves in an interactive way

4-

  • Our project accelerates exoplanet discovery by analyzing thousands of noisy signals in minutes, reducing the heavy workload on experts. Unlike simple yes/no models, it explains predictions with confidence scores and feature impacts, making results reliable and transparent. By emphasizing habitability-related factors like orbital zone and temperature, it helps researchers prioritize scarce telescope time for the most promising worlds. The interactive web app opens NASA data to scientists and researchers, transforming complex science into accessible exploration. Designed for adaptability, the system will remain relevant with future missions such as JWST, PLATO, and the Roman Space Telescope.

5- Tools Used

Machine Learning & Data Analysis

  • Languages: Python
  • Libraries: NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, Matplotlib, Seaborn
  • Platform: Google Colab (for modeling and experiments)

Website Development

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript
  • Backend: JavaScript, Python
  • Coding Tool: Visual Studio Code
  • Hosting: Netlify

projectDetails.name: Project The Martians
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, **"Will It Rain On My Parade?"**, is a web application designed to help users plan outdoor events by providing a historical rain forecast.

We developed a tool where users can input any location and date to receive the average precipitation for that specific day, calculated from over two decades of NASA's **Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission data**. Our Python Flask backend remotely accesses the high-resolution IMERG dataset, processes the historical values, and presents a simple, actionable insight. 

This directly addresses the challenge by replacing guesswork with a **data-driven risk assessment**, allowing planners to choose dates with a statistically lower chance of rain. Its importance lies in making complex NASA climate data accessible and practical for everyday decisions. By leveraging this valuable resource, our project empowers individuals and organizations to mitigate financial losses and logistical risks, ultimately increasing the success rate of outdoor activities worldwide.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do

Your project, "Will It Rain On My Parade?", is a web-based decision-making tool. It provides users with a historical, data-driven forecast for any location on Earth.

Specifically, a user can select a geographic location (latitude and longitude) and a specific day of the year. The application then processes decades of NASA satellite data to calculate the average precipitation for that exact day and location. The result is a simple, understandable metric that helps the user assess the historical likelihood of rain for a future outdoor event.

How does it work?

The application operates on a client-server model, using a powerful combination of backend and frontend technologies:

1. User Input (Frontend): The user interacts with a web interface built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. They input their desired location and date.

2. Request Handling (Backend): The frontend sends this information to the backend, which is powered by the Flask web framework in Python. Flask routes the request to the appropriate logic.

3. Data Retrieval and Processing: This is the core of your application.

o The backend uses the xarray and numpy libraries to connect to NASA's GPM (Global Precipitation Measurement) satellite data archives.

o It specifically targets the IMERG dataset, which provides daily global precipitation records.

o Using xarray, it queries and downloads the precipitation data for the same calendar day across multiple years (e.g., every July 4th from 2001 to the present).

o The numpy library is then used to perform the crucial calculation: it computes the mathematical average of all the retrieved precipitation values.

4. Returning the Result: The calculated average is sent back to the frontend and displayed to the user, likely as a simple value (e.g., "Average precipitation: 1.2 mm"). The use of sqlite3 suggests you might be storing previous requests to cache results and speed up future queries for the same location.

What benefits does it have?

The primary benefit is empowering users to make informed decisions and mitigate risk.

• For Event Planners: A wedding planner, festival organizer, or sports league can compare potential dates and choose the one with the lowest historical chance of rain, saving potentially thousands of dollars and avoiding logistical nightmares.

• For Individuals: Anyone planning a vacation, a hike, or a family picnic can use it to pick the best possible day.

• Accessibility: It transforms highly complex, scientific climate data from NASA into a simple, practical, and actionable insight for the general public.

What do you hope to achieve?

Your goal is to bridge the gap between advanced scientific data and everyday life. You aim to provide a reliable, easy-to-use tool that helps people plan better by leveraging the power of historical climate data. By doing this, you are not only solving a common problem but also demonstrating the tangible, real-world value of NASA's earth observation missions.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Based on your information, your project's technology stack is:

• Programming Language: Python

• Backend Framework: Flask

• Key Python Libraries:

o xarray: For handling multi-dimensional scientific data from NASA.

o numpy: For high-performance numerical calculations (like averaging).

o requests: For making HTTP requests to data sources.

o sqlite3: For database management (caching or logging).

o secrets: For enhancing application security.

• Frontend Technologies: HTML, CSS, JavaScript

• Deployment/Hosting: PythonAnywhere (inferred from the URL).
projectDetails.aiReferences:
AI Tools and Methodology

We used Generative AI tools (such as GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT) as productivity enhancers. It's important to note that AI was not used to develop the core scientific logic of our project. The backend processing, NASA data retrieval, and historical analysis were entirely human-led.

Our use of AI can be broken down into these key areas:

Frontend Development Assistance

We leveraged AI to support the creation of the user interface. This role was supplementary and focused on improving development speed and quality.

• Code Generation: AI helped generate boilerplate code for HTML structures and create responsive CSS style sheets. For example, we could describe a desired layout, and the AI would provide a foundational code snippet, which we would then test and refine.

• JavaScript Functions: We used AI to help write and debug small, utility-focused JavaScript functions. This included tasks like creating functions to validate user input (ensuring latitude and longitude were in the correct format) or to handle asynchronous API calls to our backend.

• Brainstorming UI/UX: AI tools were used as a brainstorming partner for user experience (UX) ideas, such as suggesting layouts for displaying the results or proposing clearer text for buttons and labels.

Learning and Debugging

AI served as an on-demand resource for learning and problem-solving.

• Quick Explanations: When encountering a specific frontend challenge or a new CSS property, we could ask the AI for a concise explanation and a simple use-case example, which was often faster than searching through extensive documentation.

• Debugging: We used AI to help identify potential errors in frontend code. By providing a code snippet that wasn't working as expected, the AI could often spot syntax errors or logical flaws, speeding up the debugging process.

In summary, our use of AI was that of a "pair programmer"—it handled repetitive tasks and provided helpful suggestions, allowing us to focus more on the critical backend logic and the scientific accuracy of our NASA data analysis.

projectDetails.name: ExoBreeze – From Space Data to Daily Health
projectDetails.summary:
Air pollution is a major global health and environmental challenge, causing millions of premature deaths every year. NASA’s TEMPO mission now provides hourly, high-resolution data across North America, offering unprecedented opportunities for accurate air quality monitoring and forecasting. However, the challenge lies in transforming this complex data into meaningful, actionable insights for everyday users and industries.
Our solution, ExoBreeze, is a web-based platform that integrates TEMPO satellite data, ground-based measurements, and weather data to forecast air quality in real time. What makes ExoBreeze unique is its dual-user design, targeting both individuals and construction firms with personalized features and insights.
Individual Mode: Provides real-time AQI forecasts, personalized health alerts based on user profiles, and gamified experiences (e.g., planting virtual trees as air quality improves) to encourage positive eco-behaviors.
Construction Firm Mode: Offers site-specific AQI insights, safety recommendations for workers, and detailed reports that support informed site selection, scheduling, and sustainability planning.
Forecasting Engine: Uses machine learning (Random Forest) to analyze pollution and weather data, producing reliable AQI predictions tailored to each user’s context.
Visualization Dashboard: Presents live heatmaps, personalized exposure scores, and trend analysis in a simple, intuitive interface.
projectDetails.details:
ExoBreeze, is a web-based platform that integrates TEMPO satellite data, ground-based measurements, and weather data to forecast air quality in real time.

ExoBreeze is personalized: users can choose between Individual Mode and Construction Firm Mode.

Individuals: receive real-time AQI forecasts, personalized health alerts, and gamified experiences with personalized exposure score that shows how much pollution you’ve been exposed to in your daily routine throughout the whole week

Small, trackable tasks (reduce car use by 10%) that encourage healthier and greener habits

provides localized AQI data, helping individuals make quick decisions about outdoor activities and personal exposure.

A personalized dashboard that tracks historical air quality trends and exposure over time. Individuals can monitor daily habits, while firms can evaluate project impact and sustainability performance.

An interactive map displaying real-time AQI levels across locations. Both individuals and firms can explore hotspots, assess exposure risks, and plan activities or operations with clearer insights.

Individual - Gamifying Clean Air: An awareness game where players plant virtual trees in areas with poor air quality. As trees grow, the background improves, unlocking new levels and encouraging cleaner habits.

Construction Firm: access site-specific AQI insights, safety recommendations for workers, and reports that support informed site selection and project planning.
The Community Impact feature highlights how air quality in selected locations may negatively affect sensitive groups, such as children, the elderly, and people with respiratory diseases, by visualizing their population distribution in a pie chart

Real-time insights combining AQI, weather, and location data to guide safe scheduling of construction activities.

How it Works: ExoBreeze integrates NASA’s TEMPO satellite data, ground-based networks (OpenAQ), and weather datasets(openweather) to generate real-time AQI forecasts. Personalized questionnaires capture health conditions, age, and outdoor exposure levels, transforming raw data into customized health alerts and actionable insights. For firms, ExoBreeze translates the same scientific datasets into site-specific exposure forecasts, safe working hour recommendations, and sustainability reports. Gamification, such as the tree-planting mini-game, keeps younger audiences engaged while raising awareness of air pollution.

Benefits:

  • Public Health Impact: Delivers personalized health alerts and safety recommendations to reduce exposure to harmful pollutants.
  • Dual-User Design: Supports both individuals and construction firms, ensuring wide societal relevance.
  • Gamified Awareness: Engages children and families with interactive eco-challenges like planting virtual trees.
  • Workplace Safety: Provides construction firms with actionable insights to protect workers and plan around pollution peaks.
  • Scientific Accuracy: Integrates TEMPO satellite data with ground sensors and weather models for reliable AQI forecasting.

Development Tools:

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS.
  • Libraries: Scikit-learn (Random Forest), Pandas, Numpy, Plotly, Matplotlib.
  • Frontend: React + Phaser.js (gamification).
  • Backend: Node.js, Express, MongoDB.
  • Data Sources: NASA TEMPO, OpenAQ, OpenWeather API.

Random Forest Regressor: Applied to forecast AQI values by analyzing TEMPO satellite data, ground-based measurements, and weather variables. Its robustness to non-linear relationships makes it ideal for air quality prediction. Questionnaire-based Personalization: AI-driven logic maps user inputs (age, health conditions, exposure) to tailored health alerts and recommendations. Gamification Engine (Phaser.js + AI logic): Delivers adaptive educational content, such as the virtual tree-planting mini-game, where challenges adjust dynamically to AQI forecasts.

The International Space Station (ISS) is humanity’s laboratory in orbit  a place where astronauts and scientists explore space and develop technologies that improve life on Earth. Through its experiments, NASA has helped solve global challenges such as clean water systems, medical innovations, sustainable materials, and robotics.

As the ISS celebrates 25 years of continuous discoveries, our project celebrates its legacy  showing how the experiences and experiments in space continue to inspire innovation, curiosity, and progress for humanity.

projectDetails.name: Project The ReMarsables
projectDetails.summary: We developed the Mars Modular Reclaimer (MMR), a sustainable recycling hub designed to transform mission-generated waste into reusable resources for long-term human presence on Mars. Our solution addresses the challenge of trash management in space habitats by sorting, processing, and repurposing inorganic waste such as packaging, textiles, and broken equipment into raw materials for 3D printing, construction, and energy generation. This is important because resupply missions from Earth are costly and limited, making waste-to-resource systems a cornerstone of future Mars missions and circular economy models in space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
The Mars Modular Reclaimer is a compact, modular system integrated into Mars habitats:

•What it does: Collects, sorts, and processes inorganic waste (plastics, metals, textiles) into usable forms such as 3D printing filament, building materials, or fuel precursors.•How it works:1.Sorting module: Uses sensors and robotic arms to classify waste by material.2.Compression & shredding: Breaks down waste into smaller, manageable units.3.Material processing: Plastics are melted into filament, metals are compressed or repurposed, and textiles are woven into insulation or fabrics.4.Energy integration: Non-recyclable waste undergoes controlled pyrolysis for energy recovery.•Benefits:•Reduces resupply dependency from Earth.•Creates self-sufficient, circular resource loops.•Supports astronaut safety and mental health by managing waste efficiently.•Extends mission sustainability by turning trash into tools.•Tools & Software: Blender (3D design), Figma/Illustrator (UI concept), ChatGPT + AI art tools (concept visuals, ideation).•Hardware (conceptual): Robotic arms, shredders, 3D printers, thermal processing chamber.
projectDetails.aiReferences: AI was used only for concept communication — final solution design principles are based on NASA data and human ideation - chatgpt

projectDetails.name: Project The SKY WON
projectDetails.summary:
Imagine this… A massive asteroid is approaching planet Earth!
The danger isn’t far, and your curiosity kicks in: What would really happen if it collided?

We started thinking — how can we bring this scenario closer to people?
How can they not only understand the numbers and equations… but actually see and feel the impact of the threat?

That’s where our app comes in.

Our program doesn’t just simulate the collision — it lets you experience it yourself.
You can ask any question about space or asteroids, and the AI answers instantly.

Through the app, you can explore everything about asteroids — their mass, density, velocity… and even view 3D models that reflect their real shapes.
Users can discover detailed information about each asteroid and watch its orbit through an explanatory video.

And then… we reach the most thrilling part — the moment of impact!

The only way for people to truly grasp the danger is to see its real-world effects — the impact zone, the destruction, and the geographical changes caused by the asteroid’s fall.

But here’s what makes it unique: the app isn’t just for watching.
It’s powered by artificial intelligence, ready to answer any question about space or asteroids instantly.

Our goal isn’t to scare people — it’s to educate them, and help them understand the magnitude of the threat our planet could one day face.
projectDetails.details:
What Exactly Does It Do?

ASTRA gathers real-time asteroid and planetary defense data from trusted sources like NASA, ESA, and other international databases. It visualizes this information through interactive 3D simulations, live orbital tracking, and dynamic data analysis. This allows users to explore potential threats, monitor known asteroids, and understand the systems in place to protect Earth.

 

How Does It Work?

The platform integrates NASA’s open APIs with a custom-built data visualization engine. The frontend, developed using React.js and Three.js, renders interactive 3D space environments. The backend processes incoming data to generate predictive visuals and cinematic experiences that immerse users in the vastness of space.

 

What Benefits Does It Have?

Accessibility: Bridges the gap between scientific research and public awareness.

 

Research Tool: Helps researchers visualize and analyze asteroid behavior more effectively.

 

Education: Educates students and the general audience about space defense in an engaging way.

 

Collaboration: Encourages global cooperation for planetary safety by providing a unified data platform.

 

What Do You Hope to Achieve?

We aim to make space awareness a shared, global mission. Our goal is to transform complex data into clear, accessible insights that inspire curiosity, promote understanding, and encourage proactive planetary defense initiatives.

 

Tools, Languages, and Software Used

Frontend: React.js, Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Three.js

 

Backend: Node.js, Express.js

 

APIs: NASA Open API, Space-Track.org API

 

Design & Assets: Figma (UI/UX Design), Blender (3D Assets), Adobe After Effects (Cinematic Elements)
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Yes, our project's design incorporates the use of Artificial Intelligence in its conceptual framework and development process.

 

AI for Predictive Analysis: The "AI-driven predictions" feature mentioned in our summary refers to the system's architecture, which is designed to process vast amounts of orbital data from NASA and other sources. This framework allows for the future implementation of machine learning models to analyze asteroid trajectories, identify subtle deviations, and calculate impact probabilities with greater accuracy and speed than traditional methods.

 

AI for Development Support: During the development of the ASTRA prototype, we utilized generative AI tools (such as Google's Gemini and GitHub Copilot) to assist with code generation, debugging, and documentation. These tools helped accelerate our workflow by providing code snippets for complex 3D rendering with Three.js, generating boilerplate code for the backend API integration, and helping to structure this very documentation.

projectDetails.name: The Space Squad
projectDetails.summary: An interactive, game-like educational video was developed that explains space weather in a fun and memorable way for kids. The story follows a young boy whose TV suddenly glitches. This is because of a solar storm from the Sun. Two heroes, Earth’s magnetic field (Magno) and atmosphere (Aero), appear to defend the planet from harm, teaching how these natural shields protect Earth from solar energy. The kid joins the battle with them. NASA’s Kp index data was used to visualize real space weather activity levels. This helps connect science to storytelling. At the end, the child learns and teaches other kids simple habits kids can do during strong solar storms. These habits include unplugging devices or learning more about space weather. Our project addresses the challenge of making space science accessible and engaging for young audiences. It is important because it helps inspire curiosity, scientific thinking, and awareness about how the Sun affects our daily lives.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do, or how does it work?

We combine NASA’s space weather data (such as Kp indices) with animation, narration, and characteristic storytelling. The video follows a full story nature, from a glitching TV caused by a solar storm to Earth’s defenses activating, ending with a scene where the boy teaches simple techniques kids can do during strong solar storms (like unplugging devices, using surge protectors, and learning about space weather). This helps children integrate science into real life.

What exactly does it do?

Our project is an interactive animated video experience that turns space weather data into storytelling. Kids watch as the Sun launches solar flares and geomagnetic storms, and Earth’s heroes, the magnetic field and atmosphere, defend the planet. It converts real NASA science to a fun, game-like adventure that kids can easily understand.

What benefits does it have? 

•⁠ Helps kids and young students understand the scientific concepts connected with NASA’s work.

•⁠ ⁠It simplifies complex concepts through storytelling, encourages STEM learning, and provides kids with small actions they can take during space weather events.

• It promotes education, awareness, and integration with real science.

What is the intended impact of the project? 

Our project transfers space weather into an education that is fun and interactive for kids. It helps them understand NASA data and how solar storms affect Earth, inspiring them about science and technology while raising awareness of how to stay safe during space weather events.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

·      We used Canva, PixVerse AI Pro, CapCut, HeyGen, and ElevenLabs and NASA Open Data (Kp indices) for realism.

Your challenge is to write and illustrate a digital children’s story that explains what space weather is and the varying impacts it has on different people such as farmers, pilots, astronauts, power grid operators, and the general public. You can tell the story from the perspective of a person impacted by space weather or from the point of view of a solar flare or coronal mass ejection (CME) as it approaches Earth. (Heliophysics Division)

projectDetails.name: AirSight
projectDetails.summary:
AirSight is an AI-powered air quality forecasting platform that transforms NASA Earth observation data into real-time, actionable insights for citizens, doctors, and policymakers.

We integrate NASA TEMPO, MERRA-2, and IMERG with ground truth data from OpenAQ and AirNow, plus visual overlays from NASA GIBS/Worldview, to forecast air quality in Cairo and globally. Our pipeline automatically fetches, processes, and aligns data, builds machine learning models, and delivers forecasts via an interactive web app.

AirSight doesn’t just display numbers — it translates complex science into health-focused alerts (e.g., “High PM2.5 today — children and elderly should limit outdoor activity”) and explains model decisions with SHAP visualizations. Citizens receive real-time notifications via WebSockets/Firebase, while an integrated chatbot (LangChain + OpenAI) answers air quality and health questions in plain language.

By combining NASA’s cutting-edge Earth science with accessible design, AirSight empowers communities to take safer daily decisions and supports long-term climate and public health policies.
projectDetails.details:
AirSight is a cloud-ready pipeline + web app that:

  • Fetches and harmonizes data: TEMPO (NO₂, O₃, HCHO, Aerosol Index, SO₂), MERRA-2 (winds, temp, humidity, PBL), IMERG (rainfall), OpenAQ & AirNow (PM₂.₅ ground truth), GIBS tiles (visual overlays), Daymet & WHO (context).
  • Processes daily/hourly slices → NetCDF/Zarr/CSV → aligned Parquet feature store.
  • Trains ML models (XGBoost) to predict PM₂.₅ & AQI categories.
    • Interactive AQI maps (GIBS overlay).
    • Login & personalized dashboards.
    • Medical recommendations based on AQI category.
    • Location-based forecasts (global support).

Benefits:

  • Protects health by turning NASA science into daily decisions.
  • Helps Cairo (and other polluted cities) with localized, near-real-time AQI forecasts.
  • Scales globally — any city with TEMPO coverage or OpenAQ stations.
  • Open-source and hackathon-ready → sustainable beyond Space Apps.

Tools & Stack:
Python, Conda/Pip, Xarray/Dask, Pandas, XGBoost, FastAPI, React (Tailwind, shadcn/ui), WebSockets/Firebase, LangChain + OpenAI, SHAP, n8n.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
• Data processing scripts: Some generated with AI assistance (ChatGPT/GPT-4.5).
  • Model explanation: SHAP for interpretability.
  • Chatbot (LangChain + OpenAI): Answers user questions in plain language about air pollution & health.
  • Docs & visuals: README, demo texts, and some diagrams drafted with AI support (all human-reviewed).

Note: No NASA logos/branding used in AI-generated outputs. All AI use clearly acknowledged.

projectDetails.name: TL;DR
projectDetails.summary:
What we developed:
We built an interactive dashboard that integrates 608+ summarized space biology papers and more than 2000 additional studies within a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system. The platform features an AI-powered chat assistant for context-aware conversations, a multi-persona system tailored for researchers, students, and business professionals, multilingual voice synthesis (English, Arabic, French), and knowledge mapping tools that visualize relationships between research concepts.

How it addresses the challenge:
The TL;DR Dashboard tackles the problem of information overload in scientific research. With thousands of papers published daily, it is difficult for both researchers and industry / business to keep pace and extract actionable insights. Our solution reduces complexity by generating instant summaries and enabling interactive exploration of research, helping businesses and researchers alike identify relevant findings efficiently.

Why it’s important:
This project bridges the gap between space biology research and practical applications. For scientists, it accelerates discovery by cutting review times from hours to minutes. For businesses and industry professionals, it translates complex findings into accessible insights that support investment decisions, technology development, and strategic planning. By making advanced research understandable and usable, TL;DR Dashboard helps drive both scientific progress and real-world innovation.
projectDetails.details:
What it does / How it works
TL;DR is an AI-powered research companion that summarizes scientific papers, provides context-aware conversations, and generates voice, video, and visual knowledge map outputs. By combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with advanced LLMs, it delivers accurate, context-rich insights while helping users discover connections across multiple studies.

Benefits

  • Efficiency: Reduces research review from hours to minutes.
  • Accessibility: Makes complex research understandable to students and non-experts.
  • Knowledge Discovery: Highlights links between fields and disciplines.
  • Business Intelligence: Surfaces commercial insights and market opportunities for industry professionals.
  • Collaboration: Supports multilingual outputs for global research exchange.

Intended Impact
Our goal is to accelerate scientific discovery and bridge the gap between research and real-world applications. On the business side, TL;DR helps investors and professionals quickly identify opportunities from cutting-edge research, increasing funding for innovation and speeding up commercialization. For space research, it supports mission planning by delivering rapid access to biological and environmental datasets. Long term, it lays the foundation for AI-assisted literature review and meta-analysis at scale.

Tools & Software

  • Frontend & UI: Next.js
  • Backend: Python + FastAPI
  • AI & ML: DeepSeek V3.2, Claude Sonnet, RAG pipeline
  • Cloud Services: Google Cloud Run, Vertex AI, Google Vector Store, Google AI Voice
  • Data Tools: BeautifulSoup, Selenium, custom semantic search

Creativity
The system goes beyond summarization by adapting outputs to user types—detailed scientific explanations for researchers, simplified learning content for students, and actionable insights for businesses. Its multimodal design (text, audio, video, and visual maps) and unique “Too Short; Still Didn’t Read (TS;SDR)” voice feature make it both innovative and engaging.


5 minute Presentation & Pitch Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g-eMwM7NBTw
Demo (30 seconds) : https://youtu.be/QPoig39-k-A

& Thank you for reading! :)

projectDetails.name: Project Trailblazers team
projectDetails.summary: What did we develop? We developed the Lego Space Home game, an interactive simulator that allows users to design space habitats piece by piece, just like LEGO bricks.  How does it address the challenge? It transforms the complex problem of designing space habitats into an easy, fun, and science-based experience. Users can practice managing resources (oxygen, water, energy), test survival scenarios, and share their designs.  Why is it important? Because living in space is not just about rockets, but about creating sustainable homes. Our project inspires students, engages the public, and provides NASA with a crowd sourced database of creative and scientific ideas from around the world.
projectDetails.details:
1. What the project does

Lego Space Home is an interactive educational game for space survival, allowing players to build and manage a space habitat using LEGO-like modular blocks.

Main features:

Modular Blocks library: bedroom, hydroponics farm, solar power station, air filter, water tank, waste storage, laboratory…

Drag-and-drop interface to assemble the base quickly and easily.

Real-time resource panel: O₂, water, energy, food, waste, updated instantly with each addition or removal.

Random survival scenarios: sandstorms, power outages, gas leaks to test the player’s design.

AI assistant that suggests or generates 3D modules from short text descriptions to accelerate creativity.

Evaluation system: sustainability, weaknesses, and improvement suggestions.

Ability to save/export designs and share in the community hub or send a short scientific summary, linked with NASA data.

Enhances critical thinking and creativity through three game levels:

1. Creative Freedom – players design freely without restrictions.

2. Reward System – earn virtual coins for logical and sustainable designs.

3. Scientific Mode – designs evaluated using real data, with scientific feedback and community sharing.

2. How it works (User experience + Technical architecture)

User flow (simplified):

1. Choose location: Moon or Mars (with minor environmental differences).

2. Open library and drag-and-drop modules to assemble the habitat.

3. Resource panel updates instantly.

4. Select mode: Play Mode (simplified rules) or Science Mode (scientific constraints).

5. Random scenarios test durability; player receives a report at the end.

6. Save or share design, or submit a short note stored in the database and linked to NASA data.

High-level technical architecture:

Client: Unity-based game running on PC, 3D drag-and-drop interface.

Simulation Engine: calculates resource balance and applies emergency scenarios.

AI Pipeline: generates or suggests 3D designs from text input, estimates performance.

Backend: REST APIs, PostgreSQL/MongoDB storing designs and reports, researcher dashboard.

DevOps & Hosting: cloud services (AWS/GCP) with GPUs for AI modules.

3. Benefits

Educational: understand resource sustainability in space (water cycle, air recycling, energy generation) through practical experience.

Skill development: critical thinking, problem solving, decision-making under resource constraints.

STEM motivation: attracts students to engineering and space science fields in a fun, hands-on way.

Idea generation: inspires real-life habitat designs from users’ solutions.

Low-cost experimentation: virtual testing of designs instead of costly physical models.

Community interaction: share designs and improve through feedback.

Measurable outcomes: track understanding, number of designs, playtime, and survival in scenarios.

4. Medium and long-term goals

Medium-term (6–12 months):

Beta version with AI-generated modules, design-sharing interface, and exportable reports for researchers.

Initial partnerships with schools or educational institutions to test learning outcomes.

Long-term (1–3 years):

Global user community, thousands of design datasets, tools to analyze promising ideas.

Official collaboration with research institutions or NASA for practical research applications.

Expand platform to VR/AR and advanced educational use cases for school curricula.

Success metrics:

Active users, submitted designs, improvement in students’ understanding, number of educational partnerships, number of designs deemed “promising” by experts.

5. Tools, programming languages, hardware/software

Game engine & development: Unity, C# for game logic/UI, Python for AI services and server analytics.

3D modeling: Blender; formats: glTF / FBX.

AI & ML: PyTorch/TensorFlow, text-to-3D models, procedural generators, simple networks to estimate module efficiency.

Backend & infrastructure: Node.js/Python APIs, PostgreSQL/MongoDB, S3-compatible storage, cloud hosting with GPU instances.

Development & distribution tools: Git/GitHub, Docker, CI/CD pipelines, Sentry/Prometheus for monitoring.

Hardware: standard laptops and phones, development machines with GPU for simulation, cloud servers for AI.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Artificial Intelligence is a core component of our "Habitat Planning Builder," integrated in three key ways to enhance creativity, scientific accuracy, and the project development process.

1. In-Game Generative Design:

An AI tool empowers users to create novel 3D habitat modules from simple text descriptions (e.g., "a vertical farm for a narrow corridor"). This democratizes the design process, allowing users without 3D modeling skills to innovate and contribute new solutions to the game's community. All AI-generated assets in our demo will be clearly marked.

2. In-Game Design Evaluation:

A rule-based AI acts as a "Virtual Mission Expert," analyzing user designs in real-time against integrated NASA data. It provides instant, science-based feedback on critical factors like habitable volume, resource balance, and radiation shielding, effectively turning potential design flaws into valuable learning moments.

3. Project Development Tools:

We utilized external AI tools to accelerate our workflow. Google's Gemini was used to generate initial visual concepts and creative ideas for our habitat modules. ChatGPT was used for proofreading and refining our project documentation to ensure clarity and professionalism.

projectDetails.name: Project Triple-A
projectDetails.summary:
Abstract — A World Away: AI-Powered Exoplanet Insights Platform

We present an end-to-end platform that turns NASA’s open exoplanet datasets into actionable insights for researchers, educators, and citizen scientists. Centered on Kepler and K2 (extensible to TESS).

What it does. The system harmonizes mission data and offers interactive visuals, batch inference, and explorable analytics. Users inspect orbital and stellar features, run predictive models to classify candidates, and receive ensemble consensus with confidence scores. Optional alerts and anomaly flags surface unusual patterns and promising targets.

How it works. A FastAPI backend standardizes features, applies quality checks, and serves inference via REST. A lightweight web UI enables non-technical users to query, visualize, and interpret results. Embedded ML (tree-based) and DL models perform pattern recognition; an ensemble layer improves robustness and interpretability.

Benefits. Democratizes NASA open science; speeds research with reproducible pipelines; catalyzes innovation in classrooms, startups, and citizen science.

Tools & stack. Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, TensorFlow), FastAPI, and JS visualizations (Plotly/D3). Prototyping in Jupyter, collaboration via GitHub, deployable to cloud (AWS/GCP) with optional GPU.

Impact. By bridging raw telemetry and practical understanding, the platform scales exoplanet discovery, fosters STEM engagement, and advances data-driven exploration.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

The Exoplanet Classification System streamlines the triage of exoplanet candidates. It ingests NASA mission datasets (Kepler and K2, with TESS planned), validates the input schema, applies dataset-specific preprocessing, and delivers predictions from multiple ML/DL models. Users receive both per-model outputs and an ensemble consensus with confidence scores—enabling faster, more transparent candidate screening.

How does it work?

  • FastAPI backend orchestrates ingestion, preprocessing, and inference; it validates mission-specific features, scales inputs, and caches models to reduce latency.
  • ML/DL ensemble (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, CNN, LSTM, MLP) balances accuracy and interpretability through a modular design.
  • Lightweight web frontend lets users select missions, input or upload samples (CSV), run predictions, and export results (JSON/CSV).
  • Compact API surface supports mission info, template generation, single/batch prediction, and system status.

What benefits does it have?

  • Transparent & auditable predictions, limiting dependence on black-box outputs.
  • Scalable & flexible deployment, from local laptops to cloud containers.
  • Accelerated scientific discovery via faster triage and hypothesis testing.
  • Accessible UX, with planned bilingual support (Arabic/English).

What do you hope to achieve?

An auditable, extensible, accessible platform that accelerates exoplanet research, supports reproducible science, and engages both scientists and the public. The roadmap includes TESS integration, evaluation panels (AUC/F1, calibration), metadata/version control, drift detection, and expanded localization.

What tools, coding languages, and software were used?

  • Backend: Python (FastAPI, scikit-learn, TensorFlow, PyTorch, joblib)
  • Frontend: HTML, JavaScript, Plotly (interactive visuals)
  • Models: XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, CNN, LSTM, MLP
  • Development & Deployment: Jupyter, GitHub, Docker, Uvicorn/Gunicorn
  • Data Sources: NASA Kepler & K2 archives; TESS prepared for integration
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Where & how we used AI

  1. Modeling (Non-Generative AI / ML):
    • Trained and served classifiers (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, CNN-LSTM, MLP) for KEPLER/K2 inference.
    • This is analytical AI; not content generation. Logged in code comments and README.
  2. Code & Documentation (Generative AI):
    • Used OpenAI ChatGPT (GPT-5 Thinking) to accelerate: FastAPI scaffolding, frontend UI refinements, README, API docs, and testing snippets.
    • Attribution: Inline comments (# AI-assisted), README > AI Use section, and docs/ai_usage.md (included in repo).
  3. Text/UI Copy (Generative AI):
    • Slide outlines, UX microcopy, and error/help messages drafted with ChatGPT, then human-edited.
    • Attribution: Footer note in slides and README.
  4. Data Prep Notes:
    • Prompts used to draft feature descriptions and CSV template guidance (human-verified).
    • Attribution: Comment headers in template endpoints.

projectDetails.name: Galaxy Life
projectDetails.summary:
What we made: A searchable web platform that finds and ranks the most relevant NASA open-source publications for a user query and deep-links users to the exact pages/paragraphs in those papers.
   How it addresses the challenge: It speeds discovery by sending users directly to authoritative papers (no hunting through search engines) and preserves trust by avoiding synthesized facts from the system — users always verify in the source.
   Why it’s important: Promotes correct attribution and verification (users read originals instead of relying on third-party summaries), accelerates literature triage and research decisions, and democratizes access to NASA space-biology literature.
projectDetails.details:
capability, motivation

Short description: A knowledge bank + search engine using modern NLP/embedding techniques to help users discover space-biology research.

Architecture / main segments:

1) Front end — search UI, result cards

2) Back end — metadata store, document index, vector store;

3) Scripts/pipeline — ingestion (download + OCR), parsing, and linking logic that builds relationships between papers and keywords.

Core capability: Return ranked, highly relevant publications for free-text queries and open the original PDFs at the supporting page/paragraph (we do not surface extracted facts.)

Motivation: Make space-biology literature faster to find and verify so researchers, students, and practitioners can reuse and build on NASA’s open science with less friction.
projectDetails.aiReferences: Yes. We used LLMs and language tools to automate engineering tasks and NLP pipelines: help write scraping/parsing scripts, normalize text/metadata, and assist in QA. We used SBERT (or comparable embedding models) for semantic representations and similarity scoring. Importantly, the system does not present AI-invented facts to users — it returns source documents and exact quoted snippets only. We also log provenance and encourage users to verify directly in the original paper.

projectDetails.summary:
Twinkle L.A Plan is an interactive and data-driven project designed to build a resilient and sustainable Los Angeles. We developed a website that uses NASA Earth observation data to identify the city’s most affected areas — especially zones damaged by wildfires and extreme heat. Through storytelling maps, users can explore these problems and see our proposed solutions.

Our plan focuses on Skid Row and brownfield sites, transforming them into green, connected, and inclusive communities. The project combines urban agriculture, smart eco-housing, and clean transportation, supported by a chatbot that engages citizens to suggest sustainable ideas for their neighborhoods.

This approach directly addresses urban heat, pollution, and social inequality while empowering communities and local leaders. It’s important because it turns data into action — creating a climate-resilient city model that can inspire sustainable transformation worldwide. 🌍
projectDetails.details:
Twinkle L.A Plan is a digital and environmental innovation project created to rebuild Los Angeles into a greener, more resilient, and inclusive city.

🔹 What it does:
We developed an interactive website that identifies the main environmental challenges Los Angeles faces — especially wildfire damage, heat islands, and pollution. Through storytelling maps, users can explore the city’s problems and discover our proposed solutions.
The platform also features a chatbot that helps residents share sustainable ideas to improve their communities.

🔹 How it works:
Using NASA Earth observation data and GIS mapping, we analyzed climate risk areas to locate suitable zones for applying our solution — mainly Skid Row and brownfield sites. The plan includes:

  • Urban forests and community gardens to cool the city and purify the air.
  • Solar-powered smart eco-housing to ensure clean, affordable living.

projectDetails.details:
Our solution solves the problem by making the complex concept of space weather simple, engaging, and relatable for children through an interactive educational website that serves as the main platform for the entire experience. The journey begins with short 3D documentary-style videos and animated clips that introduce children to phenomena like solar flares and Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) in a simple and visually appealing way. After watching the videos, children can explore interactive cards, each representing a different character or profession such as a farmer, pilot, astronaut, or electrical worker. When a card is selected, a short 3D video plays to show how the space weather phenomenon reaches Earth, its direct impact on that specific profession, and simple advice or actions that can be taken to reduce its effects.

To make the learning process more immersive, children can customize their own avatars and feel as if they are traveling through space themselves—seeing and hearing the phenomena up close. This hands-on approach encourages active participation rather than passive learning, ensuring that the knowledge sticks more effectively. Finally, the experience ends with a fun mini-game designed to test what they’ve learned in an enjoyable way that reinforces their understanding and keeps them motivated.

By combining scientific accuracy, storytelling, interactivity, and gamification, our platform transforms complex science into an exciting learning journey that raises awareness about space weather and connects it meaningfully to children’s everyday lives while inspiring curiosity and creativity.

projectDetails.details:
Our project is an AI-powered web application that detects and classifies exoplanet transit signals from raw NASA light curve data (Kepler, K2, TESS). By entering a target ID, users can automatically download, preprocess, and analyze the data using a convolutional neural network (CNN). The system produces both global and local transit views, achieving a classification accuracy of AUC = 94.5.

The application is structured into five main tabs, each serving a distinct purpose:

1. Classification Tab

  • Users can input a target ID to fetch raw light curve data directly from NASA archives.
  • The CNN processes the data to produce predictions on whether the target shows an exoplanet transit.
    • Global View: Displays the full folded light curve over the orbital period.
    • Local View: Focuses on the transit region for detailed inspection.
  • Users can download results as CSV or image files for further analysis.
  • Helps researchers and students quickly verify or explore candidate exoplanets without manual preprocessing.

2. Training & Fine-tuning Tab

  • Allows advanced users to retrain the CNN with new data or adjust model hyperparameters.
    • Select training datasets from NASA archives or custom uploads.
    • Choose the number of epochs, learning rate, or optimizer type.
    • Monitor training progress in real-time with interactive plots (loss, accuracy).
  • Supports fine-tuning on specific targets or missions (Kepler, K2, TESS) to improve performance.
  • Encourages hands-on learning in AI and astrophysics.

3. Evaluation Tab

  • Provides detailed model performance metrics:
    • ROC curve, AUC score, precision, recall, and F1-score.
    • Confusion matrices for quick identification of misclassified cases.
  • Compare predictions across multiple targets or mission datasets.
  • Supports exporting evaluation results for academic or research use.
  • Enables users to validate the CNN’s accuracy and gain insights into its strengths and limitations.

4. Education Tab

  • Offers interactive learning resources for students, educators, and enthusiasts:
    • Step-by-step tutorials on how exoplanet detection works.
    • Explanation of light curves, transit phenomena, and folding/binary views.
    • Animations and videos demonstrating orbital transits and flux changes.
  • Encourages self-directed learning and inspires users to engage with space science and AI concepts.

5. Data Analysis

  • Shows aggregated statistics on the analyzed datasets:
    • Number of targets analyzed per mission (Kepler, K2, TESS).
    • Distribution of predicted exoplanet candidates.
    • Trends in transit durations and orbital periods.
  • Provides interactive plots for quick visualization and exploration of dataset properties.
  • Can be extended to correlate exoplanet predictions with astrophysical parameters for research purposes.

Tools & Technology

  • Programming & AI: Python, TensorFlow/PyTorch, NumPy, Pandas
  • Astronomical Data Handling: Lightkurve, AstroPy
  • Visualization: Matplotlib, Plotly
  • Deployment & UI: Streamlit (web app), adaptable for cloud deployment
  • Data Sources: NASA MAST archives for Kepler, K2, and TESS

Goal: Bridge research and education — empowering users to both learn and contribute to space discovery while providing a hands-on AI experience.

projectDetails.name: Vibe-Coders AQI Forecaster
projectDetails.summary:
We developed AirCast, an AI-powered web platform that forecasts air quality conditions up to 12 hours in advance for any location in North America. Our system addresses the critical challenge of predicting pollutant concentrations (CO, NO2, O3, SO2, PM2.5, PM10) and Air Quality Index (AQI) values to help communities prepare for hazardous air conditions.

The platform utilizes dual NBEATS (Neural Basis Expansion Analysis for Time Series) neural networks—one specialized for gaseous pollutants and another for particulate matter—trained on AirNow historical data. Through ablation studies, we discovered that separating pollutant types reduced prediction error from RMSE 4.73 to 2.73, demonstrating our data-driven optimization approach.

Users interact with an intuitive map interface to select forecast locations, automatically retrieving 168 hours of historical observations from AirNow's S3 repository. The system processes this data through our trained models and returns hour-by-hour predictions with calculated AQI values, enabling proactive decision-making for outdoor activities, health management, and emergency preparedness. This project is crucial because accurate air quality forecasts empower vulnerable populations to protect their health and help communities manage environmental hazards effectively.
projectDetails.details:
How It Works:
AirCast operates as a distributed microservices architecture with four specialized components communicating over HTTP. When users click any location on the interactive map, our React-based frontend captures coordinates and sends a forecast request through an Express.js backend gateway. The Master Orchestration Service (FastAPI) generates a unique task ID, queues the request, and initiates background processing using an asynchronous task pattern.

The system fetches 168 hours (7 days) of historical air quality measurements from the AirNow S3 bucket (files.airnowtech.org) using parallel workers for efficient data retrieval. This historical data undergoes preprocessing including unit conversion (PPB to PPM for gases), computation of coarse particulate matter (PMC = PM10 - PM2.5), and temporal feature engineering with cyclic encodings for hour, day-of-week, and month patterns. 

Our dual NBEATS model architecture processes the preprocessed time series: one model forecasts gaseous pollutants (CO, NO2, O3, SO2) while the second predicts particulate matter (PM2.5, PM10, PMC). The models generate hour-by-hour predictions, which are post-processed to remove negative values and converted to AQI using EPA standards. Results are returned to the frontend via polling, displayed as interactive charts and color-coded AQI indicators.

Training Methodology:
We trained our models on AirNow data from files.airnowtech.org/airnow/2025/, initially attempting to incorporate NASA's TEMPO satellite data but encountered prohibitive file sizes within our hackathon timeline. Through rigorous ablation studies, we discovered that separating gaseous and particulate pollutants into dedicated models reduced RMSE from 4.73 to 2.73 after 4 training epochs. Due to the 48-hour hackathon constraint, we trained for only 2 hours using 10% of available data before pivoting to system integration. With extended training time (approximately one week) on the complete dataset including TEMPO observations, we project significant accuracy improvements.

Benefits & Impact:
AirCast provides real-time, location-specific air quality forecasts accessible to anyone with internet access, democratizing environmental health information. The system enables proactive health protection for vulnerable populations (asthma sufferers, elderly, children), informed planning for outdoor activities, and data-driven policy decisions by environmental agencies.

Technology Stack:

  • Frontend: React 18, Vite, Leaflet.js for interactive mapping, TailwindCSS
  • Backend: Node.js, Express.js, Zod validation
  • AI Services: Python, FastAPI, PyTorch, Darts time series library, Jupyter Notebooks
  • Data Processing: Pandas, NumPy for numerical operations
  • Deployment: Docker containerization, microservices orchestration

Creative Elements:
Our innovation lies in the dual-model architecture informed by ablation studies, the seamless integration of OpenStreetMap geocoding for intuitive location selection,  and the asynchronous task processing pattern that ensures responsive user experience despite computationally intensive ML inference. The cyclic temporal feature engineering captures periodic patterns in air quality that traditional linear encodings miss.

projectDetails.details:

projectDetails.name: EXO-Vision
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an AI-driven exoplanet classification system that automates the process of identifying and analyzing exoplanets from NASA missions such as Kepler, K2, and TESS. While thousands of exoplanets have already been discovered, the challenge is that much of the data analysis is still performed manually—making it slow, resource-intensive, and prone to missed discoveries.

Our solution addresses this challenge by using machine learning to automatically distinguish between confirmed planets, candidates, and false positives based on both tabular data and light curves. What makes our approach unique is that it goes beyond classification. We integrate two innovative extensions: (1) a generative visualization module that produces scientifically inspired 3D renderings of newly detected planets, and (2) a habitability estimator that ranks planets using measures such as the Earth Similarity Index (ESI).

This is important because it transforms exoplanet discovery into a faster, more accurate, and more engaging process. Astronomers benefit from a reliable automated assistant that accelerates research, while the broader public can explore new worlds through interactive visuals and habitability scoring. Ultimately, our system not only enhances discovery but also bridges science and society by making exoplanet exploration more accessible and inspiring.
projectDetails.details:
ExoVision

 

overview

 

Exploring worlds beyond our solar system is among the greatest challenges in modern astronomy, yet analyzing vast datasets from missions like Kepler and TESS remains slow and labor-intensive. To address this, we developed an AI-driven classification system that automates detection and improves accuracy by learning planetary transit signatures. Beyond classification, it adds generative simulation of candidate planets and a habitability scoring module—making discovery faster, more reliable, and engaging for both scientists.

 

Problem definition

 

The search for exoplanets is central to modern astronomy, offering insights into planetary formation, stellar systems, and the potential for life beyond Earth. Missions like Kepler, K2, and TESS have collected enormous amounts of transit data, leading to the confirmation of over 5,600 exoplanets and more than 10,000 candidates to date. However, a significant challenge remains: the majority of detections have relied heavily on manual analysis by astronomers. This process is slow, labor-intensive, and risks overlooking subtle signals of planets hidden in noisy data.

As new missions continue to expand the scale of available data, manual methods are no longer sustainable. Automated, accurate, and scalable AI-based systems are urgently needed to accelerate discovery and reduce human bias. By addressing this problem, we not only improve efficiency in exoplanet detection but also open the door to faster identification of potentially habitable worlds, advancing both science and exploration.

 

Methodology

Our approach combines AI-driven classification with visualization and habitability assessment to accelerate exoplanet discovery. We use NASA’s open datasets from Kepler, K2, and TESS. Beyond detection, our system generates simulation of exoplanets and estimates habitability using indices such as the Earth Similarity Index (ESI) and equilibrium temperature. Finally, the model is deployed as an interactive web platform (FastAPI + React), allowing users to upload data, view classifications and explore scientifically meaningful visualizations. Our models can be trained on new data to increase accuracy over time. This methodology bridges AI

 

 

automation and astrophysical interpretation, making exoplanet discovery faster, explainable, and more accessible.

 

 

Solution

 

Our solution directly addresses the challenge by combining automated machine learning–based exoplanet classification with innovative extensions that make the process both scientifically rigorous and engaging. At its core, the system employs a hybrid AI model trained on NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS datasets. This model automatically distinguishes confirmed exoplanets and false positives by analyzing tabular features, significantly reducing the reliance on manual analysis.

To successfully implement this system, we train ensembled classification models based on random forest and gradient boosting classifier. A meta-learner integrates both outputs for final predictions.

This solution aligns closely with the challenge requirements by leveraging open-source NASA datasets, delivering accurate automated classification and providing a web interface for user interaction. Beyond these requirements, it introduces novel elements—visualization and habitability estimation—that transform the system into a comprehensive discovery and education platform. Researchers gain a scalable, interpretable tool for exoplanet identification, while the public can interactively explore new worlds, bridging the gap between scientific discovery and societal engagement.

 

Features:

 

Simulation tool

From raw numbers, we generate processed transit curves, orbit maps, and simulation models. This goes beyond standard analysis, turning abstract astrophysical data into immersive visuals. Researchers gain clearer insights for scientific study, while the public experiences the excitement of exploring new worlds in an accessible and engaging way.

 

 

Next-Level Habitability Scoring

Our system doesn’t stop at detection—it evaluates the potential for life. By combining the Earth Similarity Index (ESI) with key factors like temperature, orbital position, and stellar type, it delivers clear rankings of exoplanets. With visual scores and color-coded indicators, scientists can quickly identify priority targets, and the public can instantly see which planets might resemble Earth.

 


Technical Explanation:

 

Exoplanet Classification with AI

 

Our core AI system is designed to distinguish between confirmed planets and false positives

 

Training Dataset: NASA’s Exoplanet Archive (Kepler, K2, TESS), containing ~5,600 confirmed exoplanets and ~10,000+ candidates. We balance classes by including labeled false positives from Kepler’s vetting pipeline.

 

Feature Space: Orbital period, transit depth, radius ratio, stellar flux, equilibrium temperature, stellar metallicity, and phase-folded flux patterns.

 

Model Ensemble:

ensembled models -> trained on tabular astrophysical parameters.

 

AI agent:
convert numerical data into description

 

 

Tools:

Languages: Primarily Python for data preprocessing, model training, and visualization. Python’s ecosystem was essential for scientific computing (NumPy, Pandas) and model development.

 

AI/ML Tools: We used sklearn and PyTorch for building and training deep learning model

 

Data Processing: NASA’s Exoplanet Archive and mission datasets (Kepler, K2, TESS) were processed using AstroPy and Lightkurve libraries for handling light curves and stellar metadata.

 

Frontend:

react

 

Backend:

fastapi

 

 

 

 

 

Factor considerations:

When developing our system, we carefully evaluated both the scientific and technical dimensions to ensure accuracy, usability, and impact:

  1. Data Quality & Noise – Astronomical datasets (Kepler, K2, TESS) contain noisy light curves. We considered detrending, normalization, and balancing confirmed planets, candidates, and false positives to avoid bias.
  2. Model Accuracy vs. Interpretability – We aimed for high precision/recall while ensuring models remained explainable to scientists, not just black-box predictions.
  3. Scalability – With future missions (e.g., PLATO, JWST follow-up), datasets will only grow. Our system was designed to process thousands of light curves efficiently.
  4. Generative Visualization Value – Beyond classification, we considered how visuals make complex science more intuitive for researchers and engaging for the public.
  5. Habitability Metrics – We selected scientifically relevant indices like Earth Similarity Index (ESI) to give rankings that are meaningful for prioritizing follow-up studies.
  6. User Accessibility – The frontend was designed for both professional astronomers (needing precise tools) and the public (needing clarity and engagement).
  7. Ethics & Bias – We considered transparency in AI predictions to avoid overclaiming—our system assists astronomers but doesn’t replace expert judgment.

projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

The Exoplanet Detection System is an AI-powered application that analyzes light curve data from stars to detect the presence of exoplanets. Using an ensemble of deep learning and machine learning models, the system identifies subtle dips in stellar brightness caused by potential planetary transits, providing accurate predictions along with confidence scores and detailed analysis.

Key Features

  • Data Upload and Preview: Users can upload CSV files containing light curves. The app displays a preview, sample statistics, and class distributions.
    • CNN-LSTM extracts temporal patterns.
    • Handcrafted features (depth, duration, SNR) are computed to provide interpretable insights.
    • Gradient Boosting Models (XGBoost & LightGBM): Enhances accuracy with structured feature analysis.
  • Ensemble Prediction: Combines CNN-LSTM, XGBoost, and LightGBM outputs for robust and reliable detection.
  • Ensemble Scoring: Combines multiple model predictions for robust and reliable results.
  • Interactive Visualization: Users can explore light curves, denoised signals, probability distributions, feature correlations, and top exoplanet candidates.
  • Candidate Analysis: Detailed metrics for each star, including detection probability, depth, duration, SNR, and habitability score.
  • Results Export: Predictions can be downloaded as CSV for further analysis.

Workflow

  1. Upload: User provides stellar light curve data in CSV format.
  2. Preprocessing: Data is normalized per sample, and smoothed channels are added to highlight temporal trends.
  3. Feature Extraction: Autoencoder denoises the signal; CNN-LSTM extracts latent features; handcrafted metrics are computed.
  4. Prediction: Ensemble of models predicts the likelihood of exoplanet presence.
  5. Analysis & Visualization: Displays summary statistics, probability distributions, feature analysis, and detailed candidate views.
  6. Download: Results and visualizations are exported for offline analysis.

Benefits & Impact

  • Accelerates Exoplanet Discovery: Reduces manual inspection time by providing automated and high-confidence predictions.
  • Improves Accuracy: Ensemble modeling minimizes false positives and enhances predictive reliability.
  • Enhances Interpretability: Handcrafted features and visualizations help users understand the reasoning behind predictions.
  • Research & Education: Serves as a tool for astronomy students, researchers, and AI enthusiasts to explore exoplanet detection.
  • Scalable & Interactive: Streamlit GUI makes the system accessible, intuitive, and easy to deploy.

Tools & Technologies

  • Programming Languages: Python
    • Deep Learning: TensorFlow, Keras
    • Gradient Boosting: XGBoost, LightGBM
    • Data Analysis & Visualization: Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Seaborn
    • GUI & Deployment: Streamlit
  • Hardware Requirements: Compatible with standard desktops; GPU recommended for faster model inference.
  • Software Tools: VS Code for development, GitHub for version control
  • Versioning & Environment: Joblib for model persistence, StandardScaler for feature scaling, TensorFlow safe/unsafe deserialization for custom layers.

Creativity & Innovation

  • Ensemble Approach: Combines deep learning and traditional ML for optimal performance.
  • Handcrafted Features: Adds interpretability beyond black-box predictions.
  • Interactive Visualization: Allows exploration of results for each candidate in detail.
  • User Experience: Simple, intuitive interface designed for scientists, researchers, or students.
  • Robustness: Handles missing labels, variable input lengths, and large datasets with session-state caching.
