projectDetails.name: Project BotuExoHunters
projectDetails.summary:
The main objective of this machine learning (ML) training project is to assist in the analysis of astronomical data related to the observation of changes in the light spectrum coming from stars. The proposal is to understand variations in luminosity and other observational parameters to identify patterns that indicate the presence of exoplanets orbiting these stars. To this end, data sets provided by NASA are used, containing detailed measurements of light intensity over time, captured by space and ground-based telescopes.
The methodology adopted is based on the application of the Random Forest algorithm, a supervised learning technique that combines multiple decision trees to increase the accuracy of predictions and reduce classification errors. The model is trained with labeled data so that it learns to distinguish natural variations in stellar brightness from those caused by planetary transits—phenomena that occur when a planet passes in front of its star, causing a periodic and small decrease in observed luminosity.
In this way, the project seeks to contribute to the advancement of automated exoplanet detection techniques, offering a tool that supports astronomical research and intelligent analysis of large volumes of spatial data and is accessible to people with deafness through an accessibility feature in American Sign Language.
projectDetails.details:
This project was conceived not only to meet a growing demand on our planet, but also as a way to make scientific knowledge more accessible and inclusive. It seeks to disseminate astronomical and technological information that is often restricted to a limited audience, expanding access to deaf and mute people through the implementation of an accessibility tool in Brazilian Sign Language, using VLibras, integrated into the web platform.

In a global scenario marked by climate change and extreme environmental events, it is essential to explore alternatives for human survival, which includes the search for potentially habitable planets. In this context, the project contributes by applying machine learning techniques, with emphasis on the Random Forest algorithm, which presented the best results in identifying patterns of luminosity and possible signs of exoplanets.

The development was carried out in Python, within the Visual Studio Code environment, using libraries such as Scikit-learn, Pandas, NumPy, and Matplotlib for processing, training, and validating the model. In addition, tools such as ChatGPT, which assisted in the generation and refinement of code and technical texts, and Trae, for versioning and dependency management, were used.

Finally, the system was integrated into an interactive and accessible web page, reaffirming the project's commitment to scientific dissemination, inclusion, and democratization of knowledge.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
ChatGPT: used for generating, reviewing, and optimizing Python code, as well as assisting in the creation of technical texts, reports, and documentation. The tool contributed directly to reducing development time and improving the clarity and accuracy of technical explanations.

Gama: used to support the automated creation of slides and presentation materials based on the results and reports generated by the project. Its use accelerated the scientific communication process, ensuring visual organization and content consistency in a short time.

Trae: used to assist in writing, organizing, and correcting code, as well as managing dependencies and libraries. The tool helped optimize workflow, reducing compilation errors and increasing coding efficiency.

projectDetails.name: Project IrrigaBot
projectDetails.summary:
IrrigaBot: Mission Soil Smart is an educational simulation game designed to teach sustainable irrigation practices using real NASA data. Set in the agricultural region of Botucatu, Brazil, players take on the role of a farmer who must make smart irrigation decisions based on environmental variables such as soil moisture, precipitation forecasts, and evapotranspiration rates.

The game incorporates NASA’s SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive) and FLDAS (Famine Early Warning Systems Network Land Data Assimilation System) datasets to simulate real-world conditions. Players must analyze satellite-based data to decide when, where, and how much to irrigate, balancing productivity with water conservation.

By gamifying precision agriculture and satellite data use, IrrigaBot addresses the challenge of making space-based information accessible and meaningful to a wide audience. It fosters awareness of water scarcity, climate variability, and sustainable farming practices.

This project is especially relevant in a global context where agriculture must adapt to changing climates and resource constraints. IrrigaBot empowers the next generation of farmers, students, and educators with knowledge and tools for smarter decision-making.
projectDetails.details:
IrrigaBot: Mission Soil Smart is an educational simulation game that challenges players to manage irrigation on a digital farm in Botucatu, Brazil, using real satellite data. The game turns complex environmental information—like soil moisture, rainfall forecasts, and evapotranspiration—into intuitive, interactive gameplay.

The player takes on the role of a farmer and must decide when, where, and how much to irrigate. These decisions are guided by real datasets from NASA’s SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive) and FLDAS (Famine Early Warning Systems Network Land Data Assimilation System), which simulate real-world climate conditions, making the experience both authentic and educational. How it work:

  • At the start of each in-game season, players receive satellite-based climate and soil data.
  • The game visualizes these variables through graphs, color-coded field maps, and dynamic weather forecasts.
  • The player must act accordingly to irrigate efficiently—avoiding under- or over-watering.
  • The system provides feedback on plant growth, water consumption, and sustainability score.

    Benefits:
  • Promotes climate literacy, water conservation awareness, and precision agriculture.
  • Makes complex NASA data accessible and engaging for students, educators, and young farmers.
  • Encourages smart decision-making and connects space science to everyday challenges in food production.

    Intended Impact:
  • Equip players with knowledge about sustainable water management in agriculture.
  • Raise awareness of how NASA Earth data can be applied on the ground.
  • Inspire future generations to explore careers in agri-tech, earth sciences, or environmental policy.

    Creativity & Innovation:
  • Transforms remote sensing data into a game-based learning tool, making climate science fun and understandable.
  • Unique setting in Botucatu-SP, a real agricultural hub in Brazil, adds cultural and geographic relevance.
  • Blends agronomy, data science, and gamification to promote sustainability through play.

    Team Considerations:
  • We prioritized educational impact, accessibility, and real-world relevance.
  • Focused on balancing scientific accuracy with intuitive gameplay.
  • Ensured the solution could be scalable and adaptable for other regions and datasets in the future.

projectDetails.name: Ecobee: Seeing Earth Through the Eyes of Space
projectDetails.summary:
The project deeply resonates with the cultural identity and environmental reality of the Polo Cuesta region, where beekeeping is more than an economic activity—it is a cultural tradition rooted in rural heritage and family farming. By integrating local apicultural knowledge with NASA’s open environmental data, the project creates a bridge between ancestral practices and modern technology.

Participants—especially students and local producers—interact with real satellite data about vegetation, temperature, and soil moisture from their own territory through gameplay experiences. This approach transforms abstract environmental indicators into tangible experiences connected to daily life in the region.

The board game not only simulates real challenges faced by local beekeepers but also celebrates their role as guardians of biodiversity. Players learn how climate variations affect flowering cycles and honey production, mirroring the same issues experienced in Botucatu, Itatinga, and surrounding municipalities.

By gamifying data science, the project promotes scientific literacy, strengthens the regional sense of belonging, and encourages sustainable decision-making in agriculture. Ultimately, it reinforces the cultural pride of the Polo Cuesta community while empowering new generations to see technology as a tool for preserving their territory, their traditions, and the planet.
projectDetails.details:
In response to environmental challenges and the urgent need for biodiversity awareness, we developed an innovative solution that engages, educates, and inspires: a strategic digital board game. In this game, participants take on the role of beekeepers and are challenged to navigate through the seasons, manage hives, optimize honey production, and fulfill pollination contracts. The gameplay promotes understanding of floral culture and the vital role of pollinators, transforming complex environmental themes into an interactive experience. Players must make strategic decisions to expand their apiaries, balance resources, and contribute to environmental preservation in a playful and educational way.

Bees face a silent crisis, caused mainly by the use of pesticides, a lack of awareness, and extreme climate events. These factors have compromised pollination, which is essential for food production.

Faced with this scenario, the idea arose to use real data so that beekeepers could understand these changes in a simple, visual, and engaging way. This concept gave birth to the project, uniting the perspective of bees with data captured by NASA satellites.

To develop our Project, we used a combination of design, programming, and documentation tools that supported both the technical and visual aspects of the solution. For visuals and presentation materials, we used Canva, Photoshop, and PowerPoint to create clear, engaging, and visually cohesive assets.Capcut was also used to edit all the videos and generate the subtitles. The coding and data analysis componentes were developed using Python, primarily in Jupyter Notebooks, leveraging libraries such as Pandas for data manipulation and analysis. Additionally, we used Google Docs to collaboratively draft the Project description, organize ideas, and record annotations throughout the development process, ensuring consistency and teamwork across all stages.

Using the Google Earth API and clustering and aggregation techniques applied to NASA datasets, we collected and processed geospatial data over a four-year period (2020 to 2024), considering variables such as seasonality, longitude, and latitude. From this data, predictive and analytical algorithms were developed to identify spatial and temporal patterns, supporting environmental studies, territorial planning, and future scenario modeling based on historical and seasonal evidence.

For detailed information on how the project's data was collected, please visit this link: https://github.com/JvAmbrozio98/space_points

The game's mechanic is simple yet powerful: each round represents a season, and the game board is updated by a Space-Based Agroweather Report that combines real NASA data with the local coordinates of the Polo Cuesta region of Brazil. This information is extracted from vegetation health indicators, such as:

💧 SMAP – Soil Moisture

☀ LST – Land Surface Temperature

Based on this data, the player decides each turn whether to move or maintain their hives, considering relocation costs and the productive potential of local flora.

In addition to hive management, the player can invest strategic resources in four essential areas: Ecology, Sustainability, Technology, and Production. The collected data is processed by machine learning algorithms that identify climate and vegetation patterns, generating events and values that make the game board a faithful reflection of real environmental conditions.

At the end of each game, the score is calculated based on the amount of honey produced, coins accumulated, and Ecopoints, which represent the sustainable impact of decisions made throughout the game. The project's key differentiator is that Ecopoints hold the greatest weight in the final score, encouraging the player to adopt sustainable practices rather than focusing solely on production.

The project provides a fun and educational experience, allowing local beekeepers and the general community to have direct access to complex data in a simple, visual, and understandable way. This facilitates the interpretation of information that was previously restricted to the academic community.

Ecobee connects space to Earth, science to the senses, and technology to education. It is an innovative, accessible, and scientifically-grounded initiative, powered by NASA data and artificial intelligence. The project demonstrates that space technology, when made accessible and combined with the perspective of bees, enables the maintenance and preservation of the environment. With NASA's satellites, we realize that caring for nature is caring for our future.

The integration of pollinator management and large-scale coffee farming brings significant benefits to the environmental sustainability of crops. The introduction of Africanized honey bee hives (Apis mellifera) in coffee production was analyzed, comparing the results with areas where pollination was carried out only by wild insects.

The results showed that the quality of the coffee, evaluated by the beverage's sensory score, increased by 2.4 points, promoting the classification of beans from regular to specialty in some farms. This improvement in quality raised the value of a sack by 13.15%, representing a gain of US$ 25.40 per sack. The research concluded that assisted pollination can generate relevant economic impacts in coffee farming, making bee management an effective tool for improving producer profitability.

According to Favízia Freitas, there is a great diversity of animals that participate in pollination, including birds, mammals like bats and some rodents, as well as insects. Among all, the main agents are insects, responsible for 90% of pollination services, with bees playing a leading role, responsible for 85% of the pollination of important agricultural plants for human consumption.

Our project connects NASA data with the reality of beekeeping and small-scale farming in the Cuesta region, highlighting the role of bees in agricultural productivity and regional social impact. Through an engaging and educational interface, we make complex scientific data accessible to children, adults, academics, and professionals alike. It’s innovation with purpose: inclusive, sustainable, and transformative.

Impacts of the Ecobee Project:

Education: Translates algorithms and scientific data into engaging experiences, sparking interest in science among young people and farmers.

Sustainability: Reinforces the importance of bee preservation and demonstrates in practice how climate and soil affect local ecosystems.

Economy: Strengthens sustainable beekeeping and helps producers understand environmental indicators that influence their honey production.

Ecobee is a tool for learning and raising awareness, created for everyone.

projectDetails.name: Project h4ckBtu
projectDetails.summary:
UrbanAI is an interactive dashboard prototype developed to promote sustainable urban growth, integrating NASA's Earth observation data with local municipal information. Using APIs such as MODIS (air quality and vegetation), Landsat (land use changes), and GRACE (water resources), we combine machine learning and GIS to model predictive scenarios of urbanization and climate risks. This allows planners to explore real-time data, generate heat maps, and visual simulations of urban expansion with or without sustainable policies, proposing strategies such as suitable expansion zones, green corridors, and mobility optimization.
The project addresses the central challenge of periurban cities, which face climate pressures affecting natural resources, infrastructure, and public health, through a three-step approach: data collection and integration, predictive analysis, and scenario projection. Without effective tools, urban planning fails to balance economic growth and environmental preservation; UrbanAI transforms data into actionable intelligence for resilient decisions.
Its importance lies in the triple impact: social (improvement in quality of life), environmental (preservation of ecosystems), and economic (reduction of costs with future crises). Applicable to areas like the APA Cuesta Guarani, it fosters water conservation, sustainable land use, and ecotourism, positioning itself as a compass for 21st-century urban management.
projectDetails.details:
What Does It Do or How Does It Work?

  • Core Functionality: UrbanAI is an interactive dashboard prototype designed to empower urban planners and policymakers. It enables them to monitor, analyze, and simulate sustainable urban growth scenarios by integrating vast amounts of NASA's Earth observation data with specific local municipal information. This tool aims to bridge the gap in effective monitoring and forecasting tools that currently hinder urban planners from balancing economic growth, quality of life, and environmental preservation.
    1. Advanced Data Collection and Integration:
      • Utilizes open NASA APIs such as MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) for air quality, vegetation health, and land use patterns.
      • Leverages Landsat data for high-resolution insights into land use and land cover changes.
      • Incorporates GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) data for groundwater resource management.
      • Explores GEDI (Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation) for forest biomass and urban ecosystem monitoring.
      • Considers Sentinel/NASA partnerships for broader climate and environmental observations.
      • These global datasets are complemented with specific local municipal information, including population demographics, traffic patterns, and public health indicators.
      • Applies advanced machine learning algorithms to identify complex patterns of urbanization and predict climate risks.
      • Employs Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for precise spatial visualization of these patterns, generating critical insights like heat maps for pollution hotspots, areas vulnerable to flooding, or zones of urban pressure.
      • Produces visual simulations that compare urban expansion with and without the implementation of sustainable policies.
      • The interactive dashboard allows users to explore data in real-time, visually compare different growth scenarios, and obtain AI-driven recommendations for urban decisions. This includes proposing intelligent growth strategies such as defining suitable expansion zones, establishing green corridors, and optimizing transportation networks.

What Benefits Does It Have?

  • Enhanced Planning Efficiency: Provides actionable insights rapidly, significantly reducing the time and cost associated with manual data analysis for urban planners. It streamlines the decision-making process by offering clear, data-backed recommendations.
  • Data-Driven Decision Making: Transforms raw satellite data into visual, predictive tools that help balance economic development with crucial environmental protection. This minimizes risks such as resource depletion, habitat loss, and adverse health impacts from pollution, leading to more resilient urban environments.
  • Accessibility and Scalability: The integration of open-source NASA data makes the solution cost-effective and highly adaptable to various regions, from small municipalities to large metropolitan areas, promoting widespread adoption and impact.
  • Empowerment of Stakeholders: Enables non-expert users, including local government officials and community leaders, to simulate policy outcomes and understand their potential impacts. This fosters informed, collaborative urban strategies and greater public engagement in planning processes.

What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

  • The "Why" - The Heart of Our Mission: We believe in a future where cities thrive in harmony with the natural environment. Urban areas face increasing pressures from climate change, threatening vital natural resources (water, soil, air), critical infrastructure (mobility, energy, housing), and public health. Our clear "Why" is to push the boundaries of planning to ensure resilient and sustainable cities, minimizing future costs associated with climate crises.
    • Social: Directly improves the quality of life, public health, and well-being of the population through better urban planning, optimized mobility, and expanded green spaces.
    • Environmental: Ensures the essential preservation of ecosystems and reduces the urban footprint, leading to the mitigation of heat islands, efficient water resource management, and the preservation of green areas.
    • Economic: Creates more resilient cities, reducing future expenditures on climate-related disasters and fostering sustainable economic models, including ecotourism and green industries.
    • Water Conservation: Monitoring and predicting the recharge of the Guarani Aquifer System (SAG), which is vulnerable to contamination.
    • Urban Growth and Infrastructure: Providing simulations to help municipalities promote land use and occupation compatible with environmental specificities, minimizing impacts on mobility and critical infrastructure.
    • Scenic Beauty and Sustainable Tourism: Guiding the construction of tourism infrastructure to preserve scenic beauty and encourage ecotourism in harmony with nature.

What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use to Develop Your Project?

  • Data Sources and APIs: NASA Earthdata APIs (MODIS, Landsat, GEDI, GRACE-FO), Sentinel/NASA partnerships, supplemented by local datasets from municipal APIs or CSV imports.
    • Python: Primarily used for data processing, machine learning model development (via libraries like scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and pandas), and backend logic.
    • Java: Utilized for the robust frontend development of the project, enabling complex interactive elements and a stable user interface.
    • JavaScript: Employed for additional frontend interactivity and dynamic web components, often integrated with frameworks like React.js.
    • GIS Tools: QGIS or ArcGIS for advanced spatial analysis; Leaflet or Folium for interactive web-based mapping and visualization.
    • Machine Learning: Jupyter Notebooks for prototyping and experimentation; Streamlit or Dash for building interactive data dashboards.
    • Backend: Flask or Django for API integration and data pipeline management.
    • Frontend Frameworks: Spring Boot or JavaFX for Java-based frontend components; React.js for JavaScript-based frontend elements.
    • Integrated Development Environment (IDE): Eclipse (specifically for Java development, facilitating efficient code editing, debugging, and project management).
  • Hardware: Standard cloud-based development environments (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud instances for processing large satellite datasets); local development on high-performance laptops, often equipped with GPUs (e.g., NVIDIA RTX series) for faster machine learning model training.
  • Development Tools: Git for version control and collaborative development; Docker for containerization to ensure consistent deployment and reproducibility across different environments.

How Is Your Project Creative?

  • Innovative Data Fusion: Creatively blends global NASA satellite data with hyper-local municipal information, creating a unique "global-local" hybrid model. This approach provides unprecedented accuracy and context-specific predictions for urban planning, moving beyond generic solutions.
  • Narrative-Driven Design (Golden Circle): Applies the Golden Circle framework (Why, How, What) to structure the entire project's pitch and user experience. This makes the tool not just a technical utility but a storytelling platform, where users can "narrate" their city's future through interactive scenarios and understand the mission behind the data.
  • Visual and AI Storytelling: Utilizes AI-generated visualizations, such as animated projections of green versus gray urban growth, to make abstract climate risks tangible and engaging. This approach inspires creative policy solutions, like "smart green zoning" and sustainable infrastructure development, by showing their direct visual impact.
  • Adaptability to Unique Contexts: Demonstrates tailored creativity by showing how the project can be applied to specific, sensitive regions like the APA Cuesta Guarani. Here, it integrates simulations for ecotourism and sustainable infrastructure development that preserve scenic beauty and natural resources while promoting economic growth.

What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

  • Multidisciplinary Expertise: The ideal team for this project is multidisciplinary, including Data Scientists/ML Engineers, Computer Engineers/DevOps, GIS/Urban Planning Specialists, and UX/UI Designers. This ensures the solution is technically robust, practically applicable, and user-friendly. A Communicator/Storyteller is also crucial for conveying the social and environmental impact.
  • Sustainability and Ethics: Prioritized the use of open data sources to promote equity and transparency. Ethical considerations included data privacy (e.g., anonymizing local health metrics) and bias mitigation in ML models to prevent skewed urban predictions or unfair policy recommendations.
  • Scalability and Feasibility: Focused on developing a prototype (MVP) that could be scaled efficiently using cloud resources to handle large volumes of satellite data without incurring prohibitive costs. The project's real-world applicability was evaluated through case studies, such as its potential use in the APA Cuesta Guarani for water conservation and sustainable land use.
  • User Needs and Challenges: Directly addressed critical pain points faced by urban planners, such as the lack of effective predictive tools in climate-vulnerable areas. The development process incorporated feedback loops for iterative design, ensuring accessibility and usability for non-technical users, particularly in developing regions.
  • Environmental and Economic Viability: Carefully weighed the environmental impacts on protected areas, ensuring the tool supports biodiversity and ecosystem preservation. Simultaneously, it aimed to deliver a strong economic return on investment by preventing future climate-related crises and fostering sustainable development.

projectDetails.name: Horizon: Multimodal AI Platform for Exoplanet Detection
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an AI system analyzing 14 NASA variables—temporal, physical, and orbital data—for precise exoplanet detection, achieving 85.5% F1-Score at 0.6 threshold. It addresses automating identification in vast astronomical data from missions like TESS and Kepler.

The platform includes a web interface for custom astronomical database processing, allowing researchers to submit datasets for standardized, reliable analysis regardless of data origin or computational expertise.

This accelerates astronomical discovery by automating high-reliability candidate screening, optimizing telescope and computational use. The calibrated score balances true positives and false alarms, preventing wasted observation time.

Available as open-source with full documentation, it supports global research and education, democratizing advanced exoplanet detection. Integrating multidimensional data enables holistic candidate assessment, advancing computational astronomy.
projectDetails.details:
Technical Development

Our team implemented a multimodal system architecture that simultaneously processes fourteen key astronomical variables: stellar light curves, angular parameters, effective temperature, stellar radius, stellar mass, luminosity, magnitude, stellar age, planet-star distance, planetary radius, orbital period, orbital eccentricity, planetary equilibrium temperature, and planetary translation period. This comprehensive approach enables holistic analysis of potential exoplanetary systems.

Integrated Web Platform

We developed a universally accessible web platform featuring user-friendly data upload capabilities for custom astronomical databases. The system automatically processes all fourteen NASA variables and generates detailed graphical outputs with classification results and confidence levels. Designed for users without AI expertise, the platform supports multiple formats including CSV and standard NASA file types, while providing open API access for integration with existing observatory infrastructure.

Scientific Innovation

Our multidimensional methodology overcomes traditional limitations through integrated physical context analysis, validated correlations between stellar and planetary parameters, scientifically explainable decision mechanisms, and multi-layered physical plausibility testing. The validation framework incorporates stellar consistency checks between planetary radius and stellar temperature, orbital stability analysis through eccentricity and dynamic evaluation, detectability verification of physically achievable transit depth, and systemic context comparison against known planetary systems.

Performance Results

The system achieves an F1-Score of 85.5%, demonstrating optimal precision-recall balance, while reducing false positives by 72% compared to unidimensional methods. Processing capability exceeds 1,000 stellar systems per hour, accelerating analysis from approximately six months to just thirty seconds per system. Operational impact includes 75% reduction in telescope confirmation time and intelligent candidate prioritization for resource efficiency.

Technology Stack

Our technical implementation utilizes Python 3.9 with TensorFlow 2.13 and Keras for machine learning components, processed through Google Colab with Tesla T4 GPU acceleration. We incorporated NASA TESS Archive data with Astropy for astronomical calculations, while employing Canva for presentation material development. Performance metrics adhere to NASA standards including F1-Score, Precision, and Recall measurements.

This project involving an AI for detecting exoplanets represents a significant advancement with profound and interconnected impacts across various spheres.

In the academic and scientific realm, it is revolutionizing astronomical research by exponentially accelerating the process of data analysis, turning tasks that took months into matters of seconds. This capability is crucial for handling the massive volume of data generated by missions like TESS and the future PLATO. The project also democratizes knowledge, as it makes cutting-edge technology, previously restricted to major institutions like NASA, accessible to smaller universities and developing countries, breaking down historical economic barriers in space research. It introduces a standardized methodology that eliminates human subjectivity and confirmation bias, establishing a consistent benchmark for the global exoplanet community. Furthermore, by analyzing 14 variables simultaneously, the AI opens new scientific frontiers, enabling the discovery of complex patterns and potentially new categories of planets. As an educational tool, it helps form the next generation of scientists by allowing students to conduct complex research in real-time.

In the business and economic field, the project defines a new commercial frontier. For the emerging space tourism sector, it identifies and characterizes potentially habitable destinations, laying the groundwork for a completely new market. In space mining, its ability to analyze the composition of celestial bodies from a distance drastically reduces the risks of billion-dollar investments in prospecting. The insurance sector benefits from robust scientific analyses to assess the risk of space missions, which could lead to lower premiums and fewer claims. It also creates a new niche market in specialized scientific consultancy for aerospace companies and governments. Operational efficiency is one of its greatest assets, offering a reduction in analysis costs of around 70% and an immediate return on investment for companies in the sector.

From a governmental and social perspective, the impacts are equally transformative. The project is a tool for national sovereignty and development, positioning Brazil at the forefront of space analysis technology, which attracts foreign investment and strategic international partnerships. It brings a clear optimization of public resources, generating savings of millions for the Brazilian Space Agency by reducing unnecessary observations on expensive telescopes. Its role in education and inspiration is profound, serving as a powerful tool for public schools and inspiring young people to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, combating dropout rates in these crucial areas. It also provides a solid technical foundation for the creation of evidence-based public policies for the Brazilian space sector, enabling more effective long-term planning. Finally, it promotes digital inclusion and accessibility by being developed with multiple layers of accessibility, including a translator into Brazilian Sign Language (Libras), ensuring that astronomical knowledge is truly for everyone.

The combination of these impacts creates an innovation ecosystem where scientific advancement generates economic opportunities, which in turn foster educational and social development, creating a virtuous cycle of progress. The project is not just a technical tool but a catalyst for structural transformations in multiple sectors of society.

It gathers historical climate data and disaster reports from regional databases and organizes them into interactive dashboards. Through predictive algorithms and statistical modeling, the system generates mathematical forecasts that estimate the likelihood of future environmental events in specific locations.

The platform’s main benefit is its ability to translate complex climate data into accessible and actionable insights. This helps users make informed and secure investment decisions while promoting sustainable development and risk prevention. Its intended impact is to reduce economic losses caused by environmental unpredictability and to encourage climate-conscious investments.

Our team developed SAMBAatClouds using Python, JavaScript, and HTML/CSS, integrating data visualization libraries and geospatial mapping tools. The interface was designed to be inclusive and intuitive, ensuring accessibility for users with different backgrounds.

Creativity lies in combining environmental science, data analytics, and investment decision-making into a single digital platform. We considered usability, visual appeal, and the growing need for resilience in business planning under changing climate conditions.

projectDetails.name: Singularidade
projectDetails.summary:
Singularity is an interactive 3D web application that democratizes the design of space habitats. Developed to align with NASA’s goals of accessibility and innovation, the tool allows anyone—students, educators, and enthusiasts—to design, visualize, and test lunar, Martian, or orbital habitats without requiring technical expertise.

Users can select environments and structure types (metallic, inflatable, or in-situ manufactured), customize dimensions and materials, and divide internal zones for sleeping, work, hygiene, and cultivation. The system provides real-time feedback based on NASA guidelines—validating crew size, mission duration, and spatial efficiency through visual indicators.

By translating complex engineering concepts into intuitive interactions, Singularity bridges science, creativity, and education. It fosters hands-on learning in sustainability, habitability, and space systems, inspiring new generations to engage with space exploration.

Singularity transforms the challenge of designing life beyond Earth into an accessible, playful, and scientifically grounded experience—making the dream of living among the stars tangible for everyone.
projectDetails.details:
Visual Tool for Habitat Design

Project: Singularity 

Team Members: Camila Carvalho de Jesus, Marcia Cristina Camargo, Maria Isabelli Pinto, Renan Belchior

1. Alignment with Challenge Objectives

The Singularity project is directly aligned with one of the main objectives of the challenge: To create accessible and user-friendly software for the design and evaluation of space habitats. While there are existing tools focused on the physical design of space structures, these typically require a high level of technical expertise, limiting accessibility for the general public.

Problem Addressed by the Solution

Designing space habitats is one of the greatest challenges in interplanetary exploration. Current tools demand advanced knowledge in engineering, architecture, and space sciences, restricting access to specialists and excluding students, educators, and the general public from one of the most exciting fields of modern science.

This barrier limits hands-on learning in sustainability, habitability, and space design principles, while also reducing the creative and collaborative potential of those interested in envisioning humanity’s future beyond Earth.

The Singularity Project – Visual Tool for Habitat Design – was created to democratize space design, making it accessible, educational, and interactive. The tool transforms complex concepts into a visual and intuitive experience, allowing anyone to explore, design, and test habitats for environments such as the Moon, Mars, or orbital stations, in a fun and scientifically grounded way based on NASA guidelines and space engineering principles.

With Singularity, we aim to broaden public engagement with space exploration, inspire new generations of scientists and designers, and bring technical knowledge closer to the creative minds imagining humanity’s future beyond Earth.

Expected Positive Impacts

Economic: Singularity is intended for students, educators, space exploration enthusiasts, and the general public interested in science and technology. The tool aims to make space habitat design accessible and educational, promoting interactive learning, creativity, and engagement in projects related to life beyond Earth and space engineering.

 Singularity promotes the development of educational and space simulation technologies, creating opportunities for startups, courses, and innovation events related to space exploration.

Social: It fosters scientific inclusion and democratizes access to space knowledge, inspiring interest in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) among students, educators, and the general public.

Environmental: It encourages reflection on sustainability in extreme environments, supporting efficient solutions for resource use, energy management, and recycling, concepts that can also be applied on Earth.

Anticipated Negative Impacts: Potential Challenges and Risks

Potential challenges include the risk of superficial understanding of technical concepts if used without proper educational guidance. There is also a dependency on internet connectivity and compatible devices, which may limit access in regions with poor infrastructure. Additionally, extensive 3D rendering can increase energy consumption on personal devices and servers.


2. Solution Description

Singularity is an interactive visual tool developed as a 3D web application, designed to facilitate the design and simulation of space habitats. Users select the target environment (Moon, Mars, or orbital habitat) and the type of structure (metallic, inflatable, or in-situ manufactured), configuring dimensions, materials, and internal layout.

The application allows users to create and visualize habitats in 3D, adding elements such as sleeping quarters, work areas, cultivation zones, hygiene, and leisure spaces. The system performs automatic validations based on NASA parameters—crew size, mission duration, and space efficiency—providing real-time visual feedback.

In addition to designing physical space, users can simulate habitat use, test different configurations, and compare mission scenarios, making learning about life beyond Earth accessible, creative, and scientifically grounded.

3. Expected Positive Impacts

Economic: Singularity fosters the development of educational and space simulation technologies, creating opportunities for startups, courses, and events related to innovation and space exploration.

Social: It promotes scientific inclusion and democratizes access to space knowledge, inspiring interest in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) among students, educators, and the general public.

Environmental: Singularity encourages reflection on sustainability in extreme environments, supporting efficient solutions for resource use, energy, and recycling—concepts that can also be applied on Earth.

Anticipated Negative Impacts

Potential negative externalities include the risk of superficial understanding of technical concepts if the tool is used without adequate educational guidance. There is also technological dependency, requiring internet access and compatible devices, which may create access inequality in regions with limited infrastructure. Additionally, extensive use of 3D rendering could increase energy consumption on personal devices and servers.

4. Tool Objective

Singularity offers an interactive, accessible, and educational visual tool that allows anyone—especially students and enthusiasts—to design and explore space habitats with ease and autonomy.

Target Audience:

  • High school, technical, and university students
  • Educators
  • Curious individuals and space exploration enthusiasts

Overview: To make the design of space habitats accessible, engaging, and educational, even for users without technical backgrounds, even for users without technical training.

5. Essential Features for Non-Expert Users

The tool translates technical concepts into simple visual interactions. Key features include:

5.1 Simple Habitat Definition

  • Selection of basic shapes (sphere, cylinder, toroid, etc.)
  • Intuitive definition of dimensions and proportions

5.2 Overall Layout Design

  • Exploration of different configurations and spatial layouts
  • 3D visualization

5.3 Internal Volume Partitioning

  • Designation of functional zones such as:
    • Hygiene
    • Sleeping quarters
    • Work areas
    • Exercise
    • Food cultivation
    • Waste management

5.4 Visual Interactivity

  • Insertion and resizing of objects (e.g., human models, spacesuits, furniture, support systems)

  • Simulation of occupancy and space use

    5.5 Rapid Scenario Testing
  • Rapid comparison of different mission scenarios and configurations

6. Feedback and Educational System

6.1 Rules and Constraints

  • Automatic validation based on:

    Crew size
  • Mission duration
  • NASA best practices

6.2 Immediate Visual Feedback

  • Color-coded alerts:

    Green: valid configuration

    Red: configuration outside standard or risky

6.3 Intelligent Zoning Suggestions

  • Automatic suggestions based on:

    Separation of noisy and quiet areas
  • Proximity of interdependent functions
  • Efficient space usage

7. Initial Application Workflow

Welcome Screen: Before starting the design, users answer two questions:

7.1 Select Target Environment:

  • Lunar Surface

    Martian Surface
  • Orbital Habitat

This choice influences:

  • Environmental constraints (radiation, gravity, pressure)
  • Available materials
  • Operational conditions

7.2 Select Habitat Type:

8. Development Process

The Singularity project emerged from the need to create an accessible, educational, and inspiring tool for space habitat design. The team adopted a collaborative methodology using brainstorming, scientific research, multimedia analysis, mind mapping, and AI tools such as ChatGPT, NotebooksLM, and Google Translate to generate ideas, validate technical concepts, and translate international scientific materials.

Phases:

  1. Brainstorming: Ideation focused on accessibility without requiring technical knowledge. Concepts like augmented reality simulation, modular habitat design, educational platforms, and intuitive 3D interfaces were explored.
  2. Research and Theoretical Foundation: In-depth review of NASA and ESA publications and habitability studies, identifying environmental, sustainability, and human comfort requirements.
  3. Multimedia Learning: Analysis of videos, documentaries, and references such as NASA’s Human Spaceflight Architecture Team, Mars Habitat Challenge, and BIOS-3. AI helped catalog and analyze visual references to optimize materials and layouts.
  4. Mind Mapping and Idea Structuring: Central ideas (accessibility, interactivity, education) were connected to technical pillars (sustainability, NASA validation, visual feedback).
  5. Collaborative Writing and Consolidation: Team members contributed technical descriptions, and impact analyses. AI tools assisted in editing for clarity, consistency, and accessibility.

9. Conclusion

Through an iterative process of brainstorming, research, multimedia learning, visual organization, collaborative writing, and AI-assisted refinement, Singularity evolved into a visual, interactive, and educational tool that democratizes space habitat design.

Singularity invites scientific imagination, bridging technical knowledge, human creativity, and AI capabilities, to make space exploration tangible, comprehensible, and inspiring.

10. Technologies Used

The Singularity tool was developed as a web application, chosen for accessibility and efficiency:

  • HTML: Structure and main framework
  • JavaScript: Data integration logic and NASA parameter calculations
  • CSS: Styling and layout
  • Three.js: Open-source JavaScript library for 3D rendering and web-based animations, standard geometric shapes for simulation

projectDetails.name: Agrivista
projectDetails.summary: We developed an educational and strategic agricultural simulation game that helps farmers and players understand how to manage their farms under various climate and environmental challenges. The game presents realistic scenarios, such as floods, droughts, heat waves, extreme cold, and pest outbreaks, encouraging players to make thoughtful decisions about crop selection, infrastructure, and resource management. Through interactive gameplay, players learn which tools, crops, and techniques are best suited to specific conditions, such as planting rice in flood-prone areas or using indirect-resistant crops during insect outbreaks. This project addresses the urgent need to develop climate resilience and agricultural awareness in a rapidly changing world. It is important because it promotes practical knowledge, sustainable thinking, and proactive adaptation, not only for farmers but for anyone who wants to better understand the vital relationship between food, the environment, and decision-making.
projectDetails.details:
This project is an educational and interactive farming simulation game designed to teach players, especially farmers and students, how to manage agricultural challenges caused by extreme climate events. The game simulates real-life scenarios such as floods, droughts, heatwaves, cold waves, and pest outbreaks. Players must make strategic choices about which crops to plant, what tools to use (e.g., drainage systems, irrigation, pest control), and how to respond to weather forecasts.

The goal is to build awareness of climate resilience, sustainable farming practices, and agro-environmental thinking. The game provides instant feedback on the consequences of the player’s choices, allowing them to learn through trial and adaptation.

We carefully considered accessibility, realism, and user engagement, ensuring the game is both informative and enjoyable for a wide audience, especially those affected by climate change.

projectDetails.details:
Our solution integrates NASA’s Earth observation data with advanced analytical and visualization techniques to create a scalable, data-driven platform capable of detecting, monitoring, and interpreting global plant blooming events for enhanced environmental, agricultural, and ecological decision-making. The system leverages data from the SENTINEL satellite series of the Copernicus Program, operated by the European Space Agency (ESA), particularly their Near-Infrared (NIR) and visible spectrum observation capabilities.

Blooming events, whether from agricultural or wild species, produce distinct spectral signatures observable from space. Satellite imagery captures these variations clearly, such as the striking contrast visible in superbloom events when compared to non-blooming conditions in corrected reflectance channels. To complement this visual evidence, we employ the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) to monitor vegetation dynamics and crop growth in regions of interest. This principle is widely validated in literature, including the work of researchers at the Federal University of Santa Maria (UFSM) in Brazil, who used NDVI time-series profiles to monitor corn phenology in irrigated areas (“Using NDVI Time-series Profiles for Monitoring Corn Plant Phenology of Irrigated Areas in Southern Brazil”).

As a case study, our team selected corn (maize) due to its global significance as both a staple food and an essential animal feed crop. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), approximately 201.66 million hectares of corn were cultivated worldwide in 2024, representing a substantial share of global agricultural output. Furthermore, the NDVI growth curve of corn is well-documented, offering a reliable framework for model validation. Figure 1 illustrates average NDVI sensor readings for corn, adapted from Raun et al. (2005), showing clear correspondence between NDVI variation and crop development stages.

Building upon these findings, we developed a proof of concept for automated bloom detection using a neural network model. This prototype was trained on image samples provided in the challenge dataset, including those representing the “superbloom event 1.” Although limited in training volume, these samples served to validate our approach. We selected a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architecture with backpropagation for its simplicity and flexibility, implementing it in Python using the TensorFlow library with Keras.

The model processes 100×100-pixel RGB images, flattened into a 30,000-element input vector. The network begins with a dense layer of 1024 neurons activated by ReLU, followed by a dropout layer (rate 0.3) to reduce overfitting. A second hidden layer with 256 neurons and another dropout of 0.3 progressively compresses the feature space. The classification head includes a 64-neuron dense layer with ReLU and 0.2 dropout, ending with a single-neuron sigmoid output for binary classification. Training uses the Adam optimizer (learning rate 10⁻³) and binary cross-entropy loss, evaluated primarily through accuracy. This architecture demonstrates that compact models can effectively learn bloom-related spectral patterns, even from RGB data, and can be extended to incorporate additional channels such as NIR or NDVI-derived bands.

To expand this proof of concept into an operational system, we envision integrating it within a multi-modal platform combining AI inference with multiple data sources. This includes agricultural records such as the USDA CroplandCROS system, which helps validate cultivated crop types. Additionally, we use pre-calculated NDVI datasets from the European Space Agency’s Copernicus database, which provide both historical and real-time observations. Our analysis confirmed that NDVI variations strongly correlate with crop growth stages, consistent with findings from Oklahoma State University and other research groups. Moreover, the raw SENTINEL data can be used to generate an NDVI image channel for neural network input, enabling anomaly detection on agricultural plots.

The training process for anomaly detection would rely on manually labeled data, supported by agricultural agencies’ reports worldwide. Historical Copernicus data would serve as a foundation for supervised learning, while partnerships with governmental organizations would provide validation and ground truth. User feedback from the application would further refine the model’s accuracy and reliability.

The platform architecture consists of two main blocks of microservices. The first handles data ingestion, collecting satellite observations and storing them in a NoSQL database such as MongoDB—chosen for its high-performance, shard-based design optimized for write-intensive workloads. The second block forms the inference cluster, executing trained models and generating alerts for users based on the processed data. Results and reports are then stored in an application database accessed through a web-based interface, ensuring global accessibility and device interoperability. This cloud-native architecture supports high performance, distributed scalability, and near real-time data availability.

Our business model complements this architecture by offering a two-tiered Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) structure.

  • Free access: Users receive generalized regional alerts for blooming and anomaly events derived from preprocessed satellite data and low-resolution models.

  • Premium access: Subscribers gain access to customized, high-resolution analyses of their specific farms, with alerts tailored to individual crops and properties.

For instance, a commercial orange producer could use bloom alerts to deploy pollinators (e.g., bee hives) at optimal times, enhancing yield through precision pollination. Paid users would benefit from full-resolution imagery and immediate model outputs, while the free service would maintain wide accessibility using aggregated or downsampled data.

This model serves two main user segments:

  1. Small and family farms, benefiting from regional alerts through the free tier.

  2. Medium and large commercial farmers, leveraging premium subscriptions for detailed insights, real-time alerts, and crop-specific analytics.

Our main competitive advantage lies in near real-time satellite streaming and high-availability infrastructure, ensuring rapid data delivery and reliable decision support for users worldwide.

References

  • Bortolotto, R. P., Fontana, D. C., & Kuplich, T. M. (2022). Using NDVI time-series profiles for monitoring corn plant phenology of irrigated areas in southern Brazil. Agrociencia Uruguay, 26(1), 291. https://doi.org/10.31285/AGRO.26.291

  • Wang, J., Chen, C., Wang, J., et al. (2025). NDVI Estimation Throughout the Whole Growth Period of Multi-Crops Using RGB Images and Deep Learning. Agronomy, 15(1), 63. https://doi.org/10.3390/agronomy15010063

  • Raun, W. R., Solie, J. B., Martin, K. L., et al. (2005). Growth stage, development, and spatial variability in corn evaluated using optical sensor readings. Journal of Plant Nutrition, 28(2), 177.

projectDetails.name: BlossomTrack ML: Global Flowering Mapping and Prediction of Climate Events Based on Phenological Data Collection
projectDetails.summary: BlossomTrack ML proposes the development of an Artificial Intelligence tool, built using Machine Learning techniques and fed with NASA data, aimed at global phenological analysis — the science that investigates seasonal events such as flowering, fruiting, and senescence — and at identifying alterations in plant cycles and their environmental implications. Recent researches indicate that phenology is highly sensitive to extreme climatic events, such as heatwaves, droughts, and humidity variations, which significantly alter flowering periods and pollinator activity, acting as early indicators of ecological imbalances and enabling the early prediction of environmental changes. In Asian tropical forests, for example, species such as Shorea beccariana and durian exhibit mass flowering associated with irregular droughts, highlighting the immediate response of vegetation to climate variations. Based on these principles, the project proposes an integrated phenological analysis tool capable of detecting anomalies in global flora and issuing alerts about potential critical environmental events, supporting public policies, sustainable agricultural management, and global climate adaptation strategies.
projectDetails.details:
The primary objective of BlossomTrack ML is to observe and analyze flowering phenology on a global scale, identifying its spatial and temporal variations. The proposal includes the development of an Artificial Intelligence tool capable of using satellite data, such as MODIS, Landsat, and Sentinel, to continuously monitor global phenological cycles. This enables the identification of patterns in key vegetation events and the detection of phenological anomalies, such as early or delayed seasonal occurrences, allowing the issuance of preventive alerts and the prediction of critical environmental events. These alerts will serve as communication mechanisms for governmental bodies to relay information to the public during extreme climate events such as droughts, heatwaves, wildfires, and floods.

Additionally, the predictive capacity of the proposed system aims to generate positive impacts on agriculture and food security, assisting farmers in crop management, plantation maintenance, irrigation control, and proactive planning against pests and diseases related to agricultural phenological cycles.

In terms of environmental conservation, BlossomTrack ML proposes mapping native and invasive species, contributing to ecological restoration efforts and the understanding of vegetation recovery processes following wildfires and deforestation. The tool is designed to operate in a scalable manner, supporting global analyses required by international organizations, as well as local applications aimed at communities, research institutions, and environmental managers.

Finally, the project seeks to promote the democratization of environmental information through the creation of a visual and interactive platform that allow researchers, government agencies, and citizens to clearly and accessibly understand the impacts of phenology on global environmental dynamics.

The site prototype was developed using a generative Artificial Intelligence tool, following a carefully structured prompt specifying all elements and functionalities of the project. The digital environment simulates situations and events to exemplify system operation and demonstrate data availability and integration.

The site’s conceptual model envisions an AI based on Machine Learning, initially programmed to identify and cross-reference information from NASA’s database and other climate monitoring platforms. This AI is intended to statistically predict possible environmental events based on flower phenology tracking, and it can continuously improve performance through observation and data analysis.

The prototype also includes an interactive chatbot designed to answer questions related to phenology and the correlation between flowering cycles and climatic or environmental changes. Furthermore, the system features an automated alert section to notify governmental agencies of potential critical climate events, enabling proactive measures and damage mitigation.

Additionally, the site provides phenological information on various plant species, describing their ecological impacts, major ecosystem changes, and features an interactive map illustrating phenological, climatic, and environmental changes associated with these processes. This prototype demonstrates the potential integration of technology, data science, and environmental monitoring, offering an innovative tool to observe and understand nature’s dynamics.

Beyond environmental impact, the implementation of FenologIA through the BlossomTrack ML project offers the public sector a strategically valuable tool for preventive policy formulation. With access to changes in phenological cycles and possible anomalies caused by extreme climatic events, governments can anticipate and mitigate natural disasters such as severe droughts, floods, and wildfires. This proactive capacity allows for more efficient resource allocation, early activation of emergency protocols, and protection of vulnerable populations.

Groups such as farmers, traditional communities, environmental managers, and public health professionals directly benefit from these data-driven governmental actions. Accurate predictions of plant behavior, for example, can guide vaccination campaigns and vector control, prepare agricultural regions for crop cycle variations, and assist in restoring degraded areas. The tool thus becomes a link between science, public management, and society, promoting food security, public health, and environmental conservation amid growing climate instability.

The BlossomTrack ML project is fully viable and grounded in a solid, globally recognized scientific foundation. Using phenology as a climate and ecological indicator is directly supported by decades of research conducted by leading institutions such as NASA, the USA National Phenology Network, and the National Science Foundation (NSF). Phenology is currently considered as one of the most precise and early indicators of global climate change. Numerous studies have shown that small variations in these cycles can predict significant environmental transformations, such as droughts, heatwaves, wildfires, and shifts in rainy seasons.

Official NASA reports and projects, such as the Vegetation Phenology and Vegetation Index Products and the VIIRS Global Land Surface Phenology (GLSP), demonstrate that agency satellites can detect the start and end of plant growth seasons with extremely high accuracy across nearly all planet biomes. These scientific products have an average margin of error of less than five days, considered exceptionally precise for global ecological monitoring. Additionally, research published by NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS) confirmed that plant phenological responses to temperature changes are so sensitive that they can detect climatic variations even before conventional meteorological methods.

This scientific foundation supports the functioning of the FenologIA AI within BlossomTrack ML, whose purpose is to transform already available NASA data into accessible and useful information through an Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning-powered platform.

Using NASA Earth observation data grants BlossomTrack ML unprecedented accuracy and credibility. These data are widely employed by research centers, universities, and environmental agencies worldwide, forming the basis of official UN and IPCC reports. Beyond reliability, the project has immediate applicability in various areas, assisting governments in vegetation monitoring and prediction of climatic and environmental risks.

Thus, BlossomTrack ML consolidates as a scientifically grounded, technologically feasible, and environmentally strategic tool. It combines the power of Artificial Intelligence with the planet’s most precise data to transform phenological observations into predictive knowledge. More than an innovation project, BlossomTrack ML represents a practical, reliable, and proven response to the challenges of global climate change, demonstrating that science and technology can be effectively transformed into concrete solutions for the planet’s future.

projectDetails.name: Sun on Alert: The Mission of the Little Scientists
projectDetails.summary: We developed an interactive children's story that presents the events of the Carrington Event from the perspective of a curious child learning about space weather at school. Upon discovering that her last name, Carrington, is the same as the event's, she asks her father for help and finds out that the scientist who identified the phenomenon was her own grandfather. The narrative shows how the storm affected not only the Carrington family but also the society as a whole, revealing the impacts of this event on people's lives. To accompany the story, we created Aurora, an artificial intelligence that speaks the language of children. She explains space phenomena in a fun, simple, and personalized way, adapting her responses to each child's interests. Aurora is part of the project's interactive interface, which also includes educational games designed to teach and assess children's knowledge in a playful way. The project aims to translate complex scientific concepts into accessible and enchanting experiences, sparking curiosity about the universe and helping to raise children's awareness of the impact of space phenomena on our planet.
projectDetails.details:
“Sun on Alert: The Mission of the Little Scientists” is an interactive children's story that introduces the largest recorded space weather event, the Carrington Event of 1859, through an engaging narrative in which a child discovers a family connection to Richard Carrington, the British astronomer who observed the phenomenon. Complemented by an innovative digital interface, the experience includes educational games that explain, in a playful and captivating way, the impact of space weather on modern society, such as disruptions to communications, power grids, and everyday technologies. Complex concepts like coronal mass ejections and intense auroras are turned into fun challenges, such as puzzles and simple simulations, accessible to children aged 6 to 10.

One of the project’s innovations is Aurora, a childlike artificial intelligence who acts as a guide and learning companion. Aurora speaks the language of children and adapts her responses based on each child's curiosity, making learning personalized and interactive. She explains space phenomena in a simple and enchanting way, building a bridge between scientific content and a child’s imagination. This allows each child to live a unique experience with dynamic dialogues and particularized explanations, strengthening their emotional connection with knowledge.

The project’s functionality is immersive and customizable: children can choose the gender of the main character, adapting the story to their identity, and explore the content through interactive reading with branching paths based on their choices. Hands-on activities reinforce learning throughout the experience. The main benefits include intuitive access to scientific knowledge, democratizing space science topics for young audiences.

The project also sparks curiosity about astronomy and space weather, encouraging interest in STEM fields (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) and raising awareness about the real-life risks of space weather, such as technological vulnerabilities. In doing so, it nurtures a more informed, creative, and responsible generation capable of understanding and responding to global environmental and technological challenges.

For development, we used AIs like Lovable and Gemini to create an optimized interactive interface for computers, tablets, and mobile devices, expanding access for schools and families. Graphic design tools, such as Canva integrated with Gemini, were used to illustrate the story with vibrant and engaging visuals inspired by space and family elements.

The project’s creativity lies in the fusion of personalized storytelling, interactive AI, and gamification, creating an experience that blends emotion, learning, and technology. The language is designed to be simple, inclusive, and accessible, with short texts, child-friendly vocabulary, and captivating illustrations that foster empathy and connection. The balance between fun and education ensures a positive pedagogical impact, turning learning into an unforgettable journey.

In essence, “Sun on Alert: The Mission of the Little Scientists” seeks to revive a forgotten scientific milestone, transforming education into a lively and enchanting experience capable of preparing young minds for the mysteries of the universe.

projectDetails.name: Specttra
projectDetails.summary:
Specttra is an interactive web platform that leverages Machine Learning to quickly and accurately classify exoplanet candidates. Built on a LightGBM classifier, it provides confidence scores (%) indicating the likelihood that an object of interest is a planet. Users can adjust thresholds in real time, enabling greater control over the balance between precision and recall depending on the research needs.

Beyond classification, Specttra offers advanced fine-tuning: researchers can upload their own datasets, which are concatenated with the platform’s database to generate a new model. Hyperparameter tweaking is supported directly through the interface, giving users flexibility without requiring deep coding expertise.

The system’s architecture combines a Python FastAPI backend (deployed with Docker Compose and NGINX on Google Cloud with Cloudflare SSL) with a modern React and Tailwind frontend. Model development included hyperparameter optimization with Optuna and validation using 5-fold cross-validation to maximize the F1 score.

By combining robustness, accessibility, and adaptability, Specttra provides a powerful tool for accelerating the detection of exoplanets across NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS missions.
projectDetails.details:
Specttra is an interactive online platform focused on the detection and classification of exoplanets from objects of interest. At its core, it leverages a LightGBM model trained on key features common across NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS missions, enabling robust predictions. To prevent data leakage, datasets were carefully deduplicated and split based on stellar positions.

The platform provides two main functionalities:

  • Classifier: Returns confidence results (%) indicating the likelihood that an object of interest is a planet. Users can submit unlabeled data and test the model.
  • Advanced Fine-Tuning: Researchers can upload their own datasets, which are concatenated with Specttra’s database to generate a new model. Hyperparameter tweaking is available directly through the interface, empowering customization without deep coding knowledge.

On the technical side, Python was used for model building and training. The backend is implemented with Python FastAPI, deployed via Docker Compose and NGINX on Google Cloud with Cloudflare SSL, while the frontend is built with React and Tailwind.

Extensive experimentation with different algorithms led to LightGBM as the optimal choice. Hyperparameter optimization was performed using Optuna with TPE Sampler and multivariate strategies, combined with 5-fold cross-validation and threshold tuning to maximize the F1 score.

By combining a strong technical foundation with an accessible interface, Specttra accelerates the process of exoplanet detection and offers a versatile tool for the astrophysics community.

projectDetails.name: Project SuperBlocks.
projectDetails.summary:
Brasília was once envisioned as the city of the future.
But decades later, it faces major challenges: streets built for cars instead of people, vast urban voids, spatial segregation, and alarming levels of air pollution and unequal access to essential services.

Inspired by Barcelona’s Superblocks, we propose an urban restructuring plan tailored to Brasília’s unique context — with a focus on transforming the residential blocks of the Plano Piloto.
projectDetails.details:
Our site

Introduction

In October 2024, air quality data from Brasília revealed that carbon monoxide concentrations exceeded 220 parts per billion by volume (ppbv), a unit commonly used in atmospheric studies. Another study also assessed air quality through the measurement of fine particulate matter with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers or less (PM2.5) — a standard indicator in environmental analyses. The Federal District recorded a PM2.5 concentration of 13 µg/m³.

In response to this scenario, Equipe BSB proposes a bold vision for Brasília: to tackle air pollution and urban inequality by reshaping the city through a new model of urban living. Our approach aims to reduce PM2.5 and NO₂ emissions, improve access to services, enhance quality of life, expand public goods, and foster cultural and local economic vibrancy.

The Solution

We believe the most effective path to address these challenges lies in adapting a proven international model: Barcelona’s Superblocks. In just one year after implementation, the city saw reductions in NO₂ ranging from 22% to 33%, and PM10 levels dropped by 17%. Post-implementation studies also reported a decrease of 17% to 27% in black carbon concentrations.

Superblocks are designed around two main pillars: drastically reducing car usage and establishing collaborative, community-based guidelines. These blocks are approximately 400x400 meters and prioritize inner streets — dubbed “green streets” — for pedestrians, cyclists, and local access vehicles only, with a strict speed limit of 10 km/h. The model boosts biodiversity, strengthens social ties, and encourages sustainable mobility.

The benefits extend beyond air quality. In the Sant Antoni district, urban noise levels were reduced by 4 decibels on average, and by up to 30 dB within the Superblocks themselves — dropping from 65 dB to as low as 35 dB. Citywide projections indicate that 73.5% of residents experienced some level of noise reduction.

Moreover, traffic within Superblocks decreased by an impressive 92%, without significant increases on surrounding streets. An estimated 230,000 car trips per week were eliminated. These transformations also reclaimed urban space — with the first implementations adding 23 hectares of green public areas, totaling 1.6 km² of new green space across the city.

Health and wellbeing indicators followed suit. Residents reported better sleep, less use of antidepressants and tranquilizers, increased physical activity, and lower stress levels. Public health projections suggest the potential to prevent up to 700 premature deaths annually, alongside an estimated gain of 200 days in average life expectancy. The economic impact of these health benefits is estimated at €1.7 billion per year.

From a social cohesion perspective, Superblocks also nurture stronger community ties — increasing casual interactions, neighborhood bonds, and a sense of belonging. They’ve also driven greater participation in local planning decisions and community-led initiatives.

Local Context: Why Brasília Needs Superblocks

Our proposal centers on implementing this model in Asa Sul, one of Brasília’s most iconic districts. Originally designed with cars as the dominant mode of transport, Brasília now faces the consequences of a car-centric urban plan that has proven unsustainable. Despite being the third-largest city in Brazil, its design discourages the growth of local businesses and exerts heavy pressure on the environment.

As an example, W3 Sul — one of the city’s main commercial avenues — has seen a 15% decline in activity due to these structural issues with 53 stores closed. Our Superblock plan aims to reverse this trend by repurposing 23 hectares of underutilized space into vibrant, accessible, and sustainable urban hubs.
