projectDetails.name: Project HARP-I.A
projectDetails.summary:
Did you know that low-lying urban areas (baixadas) are the neighborhoods most affected by climate change? These vulnerable areas face floods, heat islands, hydrogeological risks, and lack of tree cover, creating compounded hazards. In Belém, Pará, many people live in these high-risk territories.

Just as the Harpy eagle watches over the Amazon, HARP-I.A uses satellite data and AI to reveal hidden insights about floods, climate change, and socio-environmental risks. The platform integrates data from SAR, MODIS, Copernicus, IBGE and more, allowing user to chose an area , and SAR image visualization, overlay satelite imagens and more! Transforming complex data into practical information.

Copy this link to your browse and explore the platform!
https://project-harpia.vercel.app/
projectDetails.details:
Floods, hydrogeological risks, and urban heat islands pose significant threats to millions of people living in low-lying urban areas, particularly in peripheral neighborhoods known as baixadas. In Brazil, cities like Belém experience recurring flooding, lack of tree cover, and elevated temperatures due to these geographic and socio-environmental vulnerabilities. These challenges disproportionately affect communities that are socially and economically marginalized, increasing exposure to climate-related hazards and associated biological and infrastructural risks.

The Problem

Residents of low-lying areas frequently suffer the consequences of flooding and other climate hazards, yet much of the available geospatial and meteorological data remains inaccessible to them. While modern remote sensing technologies like SAR, MODIS, and Copernicus provide real-time insights into flood events, surface temperatures, vegetation, and topography, this information is typically processed by data scientists and remains disconnected from those who need it most.

This disconnect prevents communities from taking timely action, understanding local risks, and participating in informed decision-making. It also limits academic research, civil society planning, and governmental or NGO interventions that could mitigate these risks.

Barriers Between Data and Action

Although there is an abundance of geospatial and environmental data, the lack of user-friendly tools creates a barrier between complex data and real-world application. Residents of peripheral neighborhoods and other vulnerable communities typically do not have the technical skills or access to platforms capable of interpreting satellite imagery, weather patterns, or historical flood events.

Our Solution

The Harpia project bridges this gap through a dashboard powered by Artificial Intelligence and Remote Sensing. The system integrates SAR imagery, flood maps, infrared bands, and tree cover data to contextualize hydroclimatic risks and their social implications.

Our project highlights the connection between geomorphology and social vulnerability: low-lying terrains are more prone to floods, while peripheral populations often lack the resources or information to prepare for or respond to these events. Despite the availability of satellite data and historical records, this information rarely reaches the communities most at risk.

Users can select a region or input their location and interact with the dashboard in natural language. The AI processes queries such as “Qual a chance de enchentes na próxima semana?”, accessing real-time satellite data, historical events, and climate models to provide concise, understandable answers. The platform also produces reports on flooding risks, heat islands, hydrogeological hazards, and socio-environmental indicators, helping communities, academics, and NGOs plan and respond effectively.

How It Works

  1. Users interact with a map-based interface connected to SAR imagery, NASA Worldview, USJCE Explorer, and other satellites.
  2. AI-powered natural language processing interprets queries, integrating multiple datasets (SAR, MODIS, Copernicus, IBGE) etc... and after that read a analysis to the user.
  3. The system provides real-time insights, historical analyses, and predictive indications about environmental hazards, and a 3D Visualization of Terrain and Housing
    User can make their own research, and participate in citizen science initiatives through a gamified interface

IMPACT

  • We democratize critical environmental data, making it understandable and useful for vulnerable communities, leveraging SAR and its many capabilities.
  • The platform serves as a monitoring and early warning tool against floods, urban heat islands, and hydrogeological risks, while also supporting research and studies.
  • It has the potential to reduce human, social, and economic losses in cities most affected by climate change.
  • By integrating Planetary Computer, SAR imagery, NASA Worldview, USGC Explorer, and other satellites, we connect people and data, enabling unique insights by bridging information and communities.

FUTURE

  • Data integration: combining housing, vegetation, sanitation, and public health data with climate risk information.
  • Development of new scientific methodologies using satellite data and artificial intelligence.
  • Partnerships with governments, NGOs, and universities for the dissemination and adoption of the platform.
  • Development of data-driven mitigation strategies: flood prevention, reduction of urban heat islands, and improvement of urban resilience.
  • Support for more efficient, evidence-based public policies, protecting lives and local economies.

Assim, qualquer pessoa pode fazer perguntas sobre enchentes, mudanças climáticas ou riscos ambientais e receber respostas interpretadas em linguagem acessível.

projectDetails.name: Project Impacto Triplo
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an interactive web-based Asteroid Impact Simulator that transforms complex NASA Near-Earth Object (NEO) data into an accessible, educational tool. The simulator allows users to select real asteroids from NASA's database or create custom scenarios, choose any location on Earth, and visualize the potential impact through detailed scientific calculations and immersive animations.

This project addresses the challenge of making space science accessible to the general public. While NASA monitors thousands of potentially hazardous asteroids, this critical information remains trapped in technical databases that are difficult for non-scientists to understand and interpret.

Our simulator is important because it bridges the gap between complex astronomical data and public education. It provides concrete, scientifically accurate results including crater diameter, tsunami heights, earthquake magnitudes, and safety recommendations—all presented in an engaging, visual format. This tool serves educators, students, science communicators, and anyone curious about planetary defense, making space science both understandable and compelling for diverse audiences.
projectDetails.details:
How It Works:

The simulator uses real data from NASA's Near-Earth Objects (NEO) API and transforms it into an interactive experience. Users follow three simple steps: (1) select a real asteroid from the database or create a custom one by defining size, velocity, and composition; (2) choose an impact point on an interactive Earth map; (3) receive detailed scientific results including crater diameter, earthquake magnitude, tsunami heights, destruction radius, and safety instructions, all presented with immersive animations.

Benefits:

- Democratizes access to complex NASA scientific data

- Transforms abstract learning into visual and tangible experience

- Increases public awareness about planetary defense

- Provides free educational tool for schools and museums

- Combines scientific rigor with viral engagement

Intended Impact:

Our goal is to inspire a new generation of scientists and increase global scientific literacy. By making space science accessible and engaging, we hope more people will understand the importance of asteroid monitoring and planetary defense. The project also serves as a bridge between scientific institutions like NASA and the general public, promoting trust in science.

Tools and Technologies Used:

- Languages:HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+)

- Frameworks: React.js for interactive interface, Next.js for optimization

- APIs: NASA NEO API for real-time asteroid data

- Libraries: Leaflet.js for interactive maps, Chart.js for data visualizations

- Calculations: Algorithms based on impact physics and validated scientific models

- Design: Tailwind CSS for responsive styling

Project Creativity:

Our creative approach lies in transforming "dry" scientific data into an emotionally impactful experience. Instead of just showing numbers, we create visual narratives that allow people to "feel" the scale of an asteroid impact. The combination of scientific precision with immersive design is what makes the project unique—it's not just educational, it's memorable. We also innovated by making NASA data, traditionally restricted to scientists, accessible to anyone with a browser.

Factors Considered by the Team:

- Scientific Accuracy: All calculations are based on validated physical models

- Accessibility: Intuitive interface requiring no prior astronomy knowledge

- Responsibility: Present serious information without causing unnecessary panic

- Scalability: Architecture prepared to add more data and features

- Educational Impact: Alignment with science school curricula

- Engagement: Design that encourages exploration and sharing

- Performance: Optimization to work on various devices and connections

projectDetails.name: LoopMars Project
projectDetails.summary:
We are proposing a sustainable solution to one of the biggest challenges in long-duration missions to Mars: the accumulation of inorganic waste and the long-term preservation of food.
Our idea is to develop biodegradable packaging with a multilayer structure, capable of preserving food for up to five years in a controlled environment inside greenhouses on Martian bases. After the packaging is opened and the food is consumed, these packages can be shredded and used as fertilizer in the greenhouses, closing the nutrient cycle and reducing dependence on resources sent from Earth.

If on Earth the famous phrase “Nothing is created, nothing is lost, everything is transformed” — Antoine Lavoisier — works perfectly, why not apply the same principle on Mars?

The LoopMars project combines materials science and biotechnology to create efficient, lightweight, and eco-friendly packaging. Our approach directly contributes to self-sustaining missions and to reducing waste on Mars — not by finding ways to recycle what already exists, but by preventing its accumulation in the first place. We believe that this long-term vision is essential for future missions to the Red Planet
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work? LoopMars is a sustainable system designed to manage waste and extend food preservation in long-term Mars missions. It works through biodegradable multilayer packaging capable of keeping food fresh for five years in controlled greenhouse environments on Martian bases. Once the packaging is opened and the food consumed, the material can be shredded and reused as fertilizer for plants. This creates a closed-loop cycle, where waste is transformed into nutrients — ensuring resource efficiency and environmental balance within Martian habitats.

What are the benefits?

  1. Minimize waste accumulation on Mars
  2. Self-sustaining missions
  3. Provides lightweight, durable, and eco-friendly packaging optimized for space missions.
  4. Helps maintain astronauts’ mental well-being by creating a cleaner, more self-sufficient, and purposeful environment.

What is the intended impact of the project? Our project aims to promote circular sustainability in extraterrestrial missions, helping astronauts maintain a self-sufficient ecosystem. The project not just reduces waste but also redefines how we view consumption and recycling beyond Earth, contributing to long-term space colonization strategies.

Which tools, programming languages, hardware, or software were used? We didn't use It

How is your project creative? We combine materials science and biotechnology. Furthermore, our project operates in a manner that has never been attempted before. Instead of simply recycling the waste that will exist on Mars, our approach prevents its accumulation and, beyond that, turns it into fertilizer for plants.

What factors did your team consider? We considered the limited resources on Mars, the challenges involved, and the time-consuming process of sending additional supplies from Earth to Mars, as well as the need for autonomy in long-term missions. We focused on lightweight package design, thermal stability, and compatibility with Martian greenhouse systems to ensure practicality and safety.

projectDetails.name: Project ASTRA Net
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA-Net: The End-to-End IoT Ecosystem for the Amazon

Welcome, Global Evaluators! Navigate our project like a guided tour.

1. The Problem: The Amazon's Logistics Blackout

Imagine vital rivers as highways, but without GPS, communication, or safety monitoring. That’s the Amazon. Our project directly addresses the "Commercializing Low-Earth Orbit" challenge by targeting this massive, underserved market with a viable, scalable, and high-impact business model. This isn't just a hackathon project; it's YAKAMI TECH's founding mission.

[Learn more about our Vision and the Problem here]

2. Our Solution: ASTRA-Net Ecosystem (How it Works)

We developed a comprehensive IoT communication and monitoring ecosystem. Our system is built on three core components forming a digital mesh network over the rivers:

- Yakami Explorer: Low-cost, rugged, low-power IoT tracking devices for vessels.

- Yakami Eco Station GateWay: Solar-powered, autonomous gateways collecting data from Explorer devices and relaying via satellite backhaul to our cloud platform. They also gather vital environmental data.

- CARATAI-I: Our proposed 3U nanosatellite, designed to provide the essential satellite link for 100% coverage.

For this challenge, we developed a functional cloud backend (FastAPI) and a frontend dashboard displaying simulated real-time vessel tracking and data on an interactive map.

[See our Products in Detail]

(https://www.yakami.com.br/astra-net.html)

3. Benefits & Intended Impact (Triple Impact Model)

Our solution generates a crucial triple impact:

- Economic: Unprecedented operational efficiency, fleet management, and cargo security for logistics companies, leading to significant cost savings.

- Social: Enhanced safety and peace of mind for passengers and families, with real-time tracking and alerts.

- Environmental (ESG): A vital environmental monitoring network collecting data on water levels, weather, and more, supporting scientific research and Civil Defense.

Our impact is to create the digital infrastructure backbone for the Amazon's sustainable future, fostering growth, drastically improving safety, and enabling data-driven conservation. Our model is scalable to other major river basins globally.

[Understand our Impact & Mission]

(https://www.yakami.com.br/index.html#mission)

4. Technology & Tools Used

- Backend: Python, FastAPI

- Cloud & Deployment: Google Cloud Run, AWS

- Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Google Maps API

- Hardware Design: Autodesk Fusion 360

- Data Sources: NASA ODPO, DAS (NASA), Copernicus Sentinel Hub (ESA)

- Project Management & Collaboration: GitHub, Miro, Notion

5. Our Creative Approach & Why We Stand Out

Our creativity lies in the unique application of existing technology to solve a non-obvious, critical problem:

- Market Innovation: Commercializing LEO for the Amazonian riverine logistics' 'blue ocean'.

- Business Model Innovation: Our ESG-centric model means social and environmental impact *is* the business.

- Technical Innovation: Hybrid LoRaWAN + Satellite architecture for cost-effective, energy-efficient Amazonian solutions.

Our design was guided by Amazonian realities: cost-effectiveness, solar energy autonomy, rugged durability, and user-friendliness for non-technical users. We used NASA's DAS for responsible orbital design.

[Meet Our Team (River To Orbit / YAKAMI TECH)]

https://www.instagram.com/yakami_tech/

P.S. For a detailed look at our core hardware components, we have just published a product spotlight series on our official Instagram: @yakami_tech

projectDetails.name: Project AstroVision AI
projectDetails.summary:
AstroVision is an interactive educational platform that teaches young students about exoplanets, ingesting real satellite data for a LightGBM Machine Learning model to hunt planets, and exploring new worlds.

Our MVP was tested with datasets from NASA’s Kepler, K2, and TESS missions, processed through a decision-making tree we developed to identify and classify exoplanets.

All of this happens inside a gamified 3D experience, where users pilot a 2D spaceship across the stars and warp directly to the location of their data. 🚀
projectDetails.details:
Our machine learning model extracts attributes from datasets provided by NASA missions: Kepler, TESS, and K2, and feeds them into a LightGBM Decision Tree model for classification. The selected features correspond to three main planet detection methodologies: Transit, Radial Velocity, and Astrometry. The dataset was divided into 80% for training and 20% for testing, maintaining independence across each satellite mission.

A linear regression post-processing step was applied to convert the model output into probability buckets:

  • Planet (P > 95%)
  • Candidate Planet (50% < P < 95%)
  • Not Planet (P < 50%)

We used Python for implementation, leveraging libraries such as TensorFlow, Keras, and Scikit-Learn. The model was trained using CPU processing on an ACER Gamer laptop (i7, GTX 1050 Ti, 16 GB RAM). While we initially planned to perform transfer learning using VGG16 for cross-modal computer vision experiments, time constraints led us to focus on the LightGBM classifier, which proved highly effective for large tabular datasets.

Our LightGBM model demonstrated deterministic behavior, showing fewer ambiguous “candidate planets” and a clearer distinction between confirmed and non-planetary bodies.
Performance metrics derived from the confusion matrix across missions show:

  • Kepler – Accuracy: 92.6%, Precision: 79.7%, Recall: 99.0%, F1-score: 88.5%
  • K2 – Accuracy: 82.1%, Precision: 60.0%, Recall: 84.0%, F1-score: 69.9%
  • TESS – Accuracy: 79.4%, Precision: 36.8%, Recall: 62.6%, F1-score: 46.3%

These results indicate that our approach successfully reduced false positives, focusing on robust detections instead of high candidate counts. This makes the model suitable for prioritizing telescope follow-ups with limited resources.

Finally, we transformed this complex data ingestion and classification pipeline into a ludic and educational interface, where users can interactively explore planets, candidates, and stars in a game-like environment with modes for beginner and advanced levels — providing an engaging experience for both students and researchers in astronomy.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
We have used the following Machine Learning models and libraries to build, train, and validate our exoplanet classification pipeline:

  • scikit-learn (sklearn) – for data preprocessing, model evaluation, and metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score).
  • lightgbm – for gradient-boosted decision tree classification on large tabular datasets.
  • numpy – for numerical array operations and mathematical transformations.
  • pandas – for dataset manipulation, cleaning, and feature extraction.
  • imblearn – to handle dataset imbalance between planet and non-planet classes.
  • ChatGPT-5 and OpenAI Codex – used as AI coding assistants for documentation and code generation support.

projectDetails.name: Project L.U.N.A.R. - Layout and Utility Network Analysis Resource
projectDetails.summary:
Project L.U.N.A.R. is an innovative system supporting the Artemis Mission, designed to optimize and accelerate the selection of the ideal site for lunar habitats. It utilizes a fleet of low-cost rovers equipped with LiDAR sensors to perform precise, high-resolution topographical mapping of the surface.
The collected data is sent to a central platform, where an Artificial Intelligence (AI) performs a complex analysis of the terrain. The AI evaluates multiple criteria essential for the base's sustainability, such as ground levelness, periods of solar exposure (crucial for energy), and proximity to strategic resources like areas with water ice deposits. Based on these factors, the system identifies and recommends the safest and most efficient locations for construction.
A key feature of L.U.N.A.R. is its intuitive interface, which allows not only engineers but also users with less experience to design a functional base layout. By providing a tool for rapid decisions based on concrete data, the project aims to dramatically increase the efficiency and probability of success for missions, solidifying a long-term human presence on the Moon.
projectDetails.details: LUNAR – Unified Language of Architectural Nexus is an intelligent system for planning and simulating extraterrestrial habitats that transforms data collected by rovers and sensors into interactive, optimized maps of the lunar terrain. Based on information such as slope, solar incidence, soil composition, and geological risks, the software creates a 3D environment where the user can literally design a lunar base in an intuitive and creative way. Using artificial intelligence models and spatial analysis algorithms, LUNAR automatically suggests the best positions for each module, ensuring safety, energy efficiency, and structural balance. The interface is gamified and inspired by a beehive, composed of interconnected hexagonal cells that can take on different functions — laboratory, dormitory, greenhouse, command center, and more — allowing for dynamic and modular planning. The project combines data science, biomimetic architecture, and interactive design, using languages such as Python (for AI and spatial analysis) and JavaScript with Three.js (for 3D visualization), along with simulated NASA and USGS data. The intended impact is to support future lunar missions, such as the Artemis program, by reducing risks and construction costs beyond Earth, optimizing decision-making, and promoting integration between technology and creativity. The proposal aims to inspire new models of spatial design and engage the public through an educational and interactive experience. During development, the team considered factors such as lunar environmental conditions (radiation, temperature, dust, and lighting), logistical aspects (transportation and maintenance), safety, ergonomics, and scalability of habitats. The result is a platform that combines artificial intelligence, modular design, and advanced spatial analysis to make lunar base planning more efficient, safe, and inspiring.
projectDetails.aiReferences: We used Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools throughout the development of the LUNAR project. Google Gemini was employed to generate the initial code for the modules and the drag-and-drop functionality, which was later updated and enhanced with new commands as we collected more data during the challenge, and was also used to translate the application into English. For the creation of images and videos, we used SketchUp together with CapCut, enabling the transition from 2D images to 3D and volumetric representations of the designed bases. LM Studio was used to synthesize information from articles and materials provided by NASA and other researched sources. Additionally, ChatGPT assisted in contextualizing texts, refining project dynamics, addressing small doubts, and translating content from Portuguese to English. All AI applications were strategically integrated and manually reviewed to ensure accuracy, coherence, and functionality, accelerating development and enhancing the team’s creativity.

projectDetails.name: StellarMind App
projectDetails.summary: StellarMind is an on-line web app used for summarizing an easing access for important biological articles and researches made throughout the years for anyone who desires. Recently, as the number of scientific researches being posted is rising tremendously and with the difficulty of finding trust-worthy fonts across the web, there is a gap needing to be filled: a tool that manages an easy access and reliable font. And there is no way better than presenting information showing its background, relating important topics from research and making it an easy access even for people with disabilities.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

Our project, StellarMind, is an AI-powered platform that transforms over 600 NASA bioscience publications into an interactive and accessible knowledge engine. It allows users, scientists, educators, and entrepreneurs to explore, understand, and visualize the results of space biology research through dynamic summaries, knowledge graphs, and AI-driven conversations.

How does it work?

The system uses artificial intelligence and natural language processing to interpret scientific papers and extract key insights. Each publication is processed through a semantic search engine connected to our SpaceBio database, which organizes topics such as microbiology, plant growth, human health, and biotechnology in space. Users can interact through a search bar or voice assistant, ask questions in natural language, and receive personalized responses supported by visual infographics, interactive graphs, and scientific sources.

What benefits does it have?

StellarMind democratizes access to NASA’s scientific knowledge. It makes complex space biology research understandable to non-experts while helping professionals quickly find relevant information.

It also enhances scientific education, innovation, and decision-making, supporting research, classroom teaching, and business opportunities derived from NASA’s discoveries.

The voice-interactive mode improves accessibility for visually impaired users and fosters inclusive learning experiences.

What do you hope to achieve?

We aim to create a bridge between scientific data and society, turning NASA’s vast research archive into a living, intelligent ecosystem of knowledge.

Our goal is to empower future space explorers, educators, and innovators by making trustworthy information from NASA not only available but engaging, interactive, and inspiring.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

We used a combination of AI and web technologies, including:

  • Lovable – for site architecture and interactive UI/UX design
  • Gamma API – for automatic generation of visual presentations
  • File Search + CSV database – to store and process 608 NASA bioscience publications
  • Cytoscape.js – to create interactive knowledge graphs
  • Python and JavaScript (React/Vite) – for data processing and frontend integration
  • Voice recognition and synthesis APIs – for accessibility and real-time AI conversation
projectDetails.aiReferences:
How was it used: 

Artificial Intelligence is the core of StellarMind. We used AI to read, interpret, and summarize NASA’s bioscience publications, transforming complex scientific data into accessible knowledge.

Through natural language processing (NLP), the AI identifies key concepts, experiments, and relationships between studies, allowing users to explore connections through semantic search, AI-generated summaries, and interactive visualizations.

In addition, the system personalizes the responses according to the user profile — scientist, educator, or entrepreneur — adapting the depth and tone of information dynamically.

Which tools were used: 

  • OpenAI GPT-based model (ChatGPT/GPT-5) – for natural language understanding and generation
  • Cytoscape.js – for AI-driven generation of interactive knowledge graphs
  • Lovable AI components – for integration of conversational and visual outputs
  • Gamma API – to automatically create slide presentations and infographics from AI-generated content
  • Voice recognition & text-to-speech APIs – enabling full voice interaction for accessibility

projectDetails.name: Farmatro
projectDetails.summary: Farmatro is an educational strategy card game that transforms NASA satellite data into an engaging and intuitive farming experience. Players inherit a virtual farm and are guided to make critical decisions about their crops based on NASA local reports, which reflect real-world environmental changes. By choosing action cards, players learn the direct consequences of their decisions on the health, productivity, and sustainability of their farm. Farmatro directly addresses the challenge by bridging the gap between powerful space data and practical agricultural choices. It is important because it empowers a new generation with the knowledge of sustainable farming, making earth science accessible, and demonstrating how NASA's data can be used to solve real-world problems.
projectDetails.details:
How Farmatro Works

Farmatro is a narrative-driven, educational strategy card game. The player's journey begins as they inherit their family's farm, facing the challenge of making it thrive in the modern world. They are guided by an assistant, Claudio, who introduces them to a tool that turn NASA data into actionable insights.


The core gameplay operates on a turn-based system:

  • Once the player chooses his location, he receives a "NASA Report," which presents a specific environmental scenario data, such as a drought warning or a change in soil moisture, based on real NASA satellite data (SMAP).
  • The player must then choose from a hand of action cards (e.g., "Invest in Irrigation," "Use Organic Fertilizer," "The use of insecticides") to respond to the challenge.
  • Every choice has an immediate and visible impact on the farm's two key metrics: Productivity and Sustainability. This feedback loop allows players to learn and adapt their strategy in real-time.


Benefits

The primary benefit of Farmatro is its ability to demystify Earth science data, making the principles of sustainable agriculture accessible to a broad audience. It translates abstract datasets into tangible cause-and-effect gameplay.


Intended Impact
Our intended impact is to educate and inspire a new generation of farmers, scientists, and citizens to think critically about sustainable agriculture. By providing a safe, engaging space to experiment with farming decisions, we hope to foster a deeper appreciation for the delicate balance required to feed our planet sustainably and highlight the critical role of space technology in the future of agriculture.


Our Creative Approach

Farmatro's creativity lies in its unique fusion of three elements:

  1. Gamification of Scientific Data: Instead of presenting charts and graphs, we transform real NASA data like soil moisture level and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) into compelling game events that demand strategic thinking.
  2. Narrative-Driven Learning: The personal story of continuing a family legacy creates an emotional connection, making the educational experience more engaging and memorable than a simple simulation.
  3. Intuitive Feedback System: The system utilizes metrics like soil pH, moisture level and crop health to provide clear, immediate, and simple feedback on decisions, making the learning process intuitive for players of all ages and backgrounds.

Technical Details and Considerations

  • Tools & Technologies: React, Next.js, Typescript, Tailwind, Git/GitHub, Cursor, Figma & Vercel.
    • Accessibility: We designed the game mechanics and user interface to be easily understood by players with no prior knowledge of agriculture or data science.
    • Scientific Validity: We ensured that the game's scenarios, while simplified for gameplay, are grounded in the real-world applications and principles derived from NASA's data.
    • Player Engagement: We prioritized creating a compelling narrative and a rewarding gameplay loop to ensure players remain invested and motivated to learn.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
The team used Artificial Intelligence as a tool to accelerate development in two areas:

  1. Chat GPT for Image Creation: It generated some sprites (icons and environmental elements), which were then manually edited and finalized by the team.
  2. Cursor for Code Assistance: It helped generate and debug small code snippets, which were all reviewed and adapted by the developers.

In short, AI was used as a support tool to increase productivity, but the project's concept, design, and final execution are the team's original work.

projectDetails.name: Ecofarm - Puzzle: Agro Precision Strategy Game.
projectDetails.summary:
What did you develop?
We developed EcoFarm - Puzzle: Agro Precision Strategy Game, a 2D isometric precision farming simulator that integrates real NASA satellite data (SMAP, NDVI(Demo), GPM,LST (Demo)) to teach sustainable and data-driven agriculture. The game targets agronomy students and small-scale farmers who want to understand how environmental variables influence crop management. Through an interactive “NASA Control Panel,” players interpret real climate and soil data to decide how and when to irrigate, fertilize, or plant.

How does it address the challenge?
ECOFARM transforms complex NASA datasets into intuitive visual maps and gameplay, allowing users to experiment with sustainable practices in a safe and engaging environment. It demonstrates how soil moisture, vegetation health, and precipitation data inform smarter, resource-efficient decisions.

Why is it important?
By making scientific data interactive and accessible, ECOFARM bridges the gap between technology and practice. It empowers students and local entrepreneurs to develop climate awareness, apply precision agriculture techniques, and use NASA’s open data to improve real-world sustainability and productivity in their regions.
projectDetails.details:
What's this Game ?


EcoFarm: Puzzle, Precision Simulation is an educational farming management simulator set in a 2D isometric environment. The game supports higher education students in Agronomy and Agricultural Engineering by teaching precision agriculture, sustainability, and the interpretation of environmental data in context.

The core mechanic, Precision Mapping, places the player in the role of a farm manager who consults NASA heat maps and indicators. Rather than treating the entire field uniformly, the player accesses the NASA Panel to identify specific management zones that require intervention, such as irrigation or fertilization, and then acts with intent based on evidence.

The system works by:

Reading authenticated NASA datasets (NDVI, SMAP, GPM through Giovanni, and LST) integrated via API.

Displaying these layers on a NASA Control Panel as intuitive heat maps and overlays.

Processing player decisions (Irrigate, Fertilize, Wait) in a simulation engine that models their short and long term effects on the virtual environment.

Providing visual feedback (plant growth, soil tone changes) along with performance reports that connect choices to outcomes.

What benefits does it have?

The project addresses the gap between high precision satellite information and day to day practice by democratizing access to NASA data and guiding analysis through gameplay. Key benefits include:

Mitigating resource inefficiency in water and fertilizer use while encouraging adoption of precision techniques.

Offering an accessible and engaging medium for students and professionals to grasp how their decisions shape soil health, productivity, and environmental quality.

Enabling practice with intelligent, localized resource allocation that replaces uniform management with evidence driven action.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to equip the next generation of farm managers to implement precision agriculture in a cost effective and sustainable manner. The project aims to make learning both accessible and engaging while aligning with the technological reality of contemporary agribusiness. It also turns complex datasets into clear, interactive decisions that build lasting analytical skills.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The development stack includes:

  • Prototyping: Figma
  • Backend: Node.js, NestJS, Vue.js, Docker
  • Database: MySQL for real time cloud storage and MongoDB
  • Integrations: NASA APIs (Earthdata and Open Data for NDVI, SMAP, and GPM) and OpenWeatherMap
  • Versioning: Git and GitHub

How is your project creative?

The project’s creativity lies in its direct integration with live NASA satellite datasets through APIs and in the transformation of complex scientific signals into an accessible, gamified, strategic 2D isometric experience. Gameplay centers on interpreting real indicators and converting them into precision decisions, fostering a cycle where evidence leads to action and action leads to measurable results.

What factors did your team consider?

The team grounded its decisions in the needs of core personas: students, professors, and consultants.

User Knowledge Level: The solution provides a Game Mode (UC01 Technical Simulation) for users with prior knowledge, granting full control over parameters, and a guided tutorial with a mascot to assist beginners.

Educational Value: The game requires players to connect indicators to actions, for example using SMAP to guide irrigation and NDVI to inform fertilizer needs.

Practical Application: Students can test field hypotheses in a safe virtual environment and iterate on real strategies informed by scientific data.

Sustainability and Economy: A Soil Health bar tracks sustainability, where excessive inputs create invisible costs such as pollution and degradation that reduce land value.

Accessibility: The platform prioritizes an intuitive 2D isometric interface suitable for academic settings, keeping the cognitive load on learning rather than on interface complexity.

projectDetails.name: WeatherView
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, WeatherView, introduces a web application that intuitively translates complex weather data into future climate probabilities. Using a database spanning the last 20 years of climate observations, the platform analyzes key variables—such as temperature, humidity, wind speed, and millimeters of rain—to inform long-term climate conditions.
Through a customizable interface, users can perform specific queries for a future location and date, obtaining the probability of weather conditions such as "very hot" or "very rainy." By bridging the gap between raw climatological data and the need for actionable insights for the general public, our solution makes critical climate information accessible to everyone, regardless of technical expertise.
projectDetails.details:
Introduction:

Planning an outdoor event months in advance, such as a wedding, a family vacation, or an expedition, always involves a major uncertainty: the weather. Imagine the following scenario: Ana, a fictional bride from Florianópolis, Santa Catarina, dreamed of an outdoor wedding on a sunny November day. However, as the date approached, she was surprised by a week of heavy rain and strong winds, forcing her to hastily move the ceremony indoors, generating stress and unexpected costs. This frustrating situation reflects a larger problem affecting millions of people who must make important decisions based on future weather conditions.

The Problem:

Historical weather data shows that the late spring weather instability in the Florianópolis region could have been anticipated. Traditional weather forecasts offer a window of reliability of only a few days, or at most two weeks. For long-term planning, people often rely on historical climate averages, which are generic and don't reflect the probabilities of extreme events like heat waves, torrential rains, and strong winds on specific days. The lack of an accessible tool that translates complex Earth observation data into easy-to-understand probabilities leaves event planners, tourists, and outdoor enthusiasts vulnerable to unforeseen weather events, resulting in financial losses and disappointing experiences.

Gap Found:

Despite the vast amount of climate observation data collected by agencies like NASA over decades, this valuable information remains largely inaccessible to the general public. The gap exists in translating this raw data into practical, actionable insights. Tools that analyze this data are mostly complex and aimed at scientists and researchers, failing to meet the needs of a typical user who wants, for example, to know the probability of rain for a picnic three months from now.

Our Solution:

To fill this gap, we developed WeatherView, an intuitive web application that uses Earth observation data to provide probabilities of weather conditions for any location and date in the future. Our platform processes decades of historical data and presents it in a user-friendly interface, allowing users to see the probability of conditions such as "very hot," "very cold," "very windy," or "very wet," based on their own definitions of "very."

WeatherView's unique feature lies in its ability to present long-term probabilistic projections, something traditional weather apps don't offer. It functions as a "weather viewer" that combines data science, interactive visualization, and usability, allowing users to see trends and risks in advance. It also features an interactive map and an intuitive interface designed with the user experience in mind.

How Does It Work?

The WeatherView process is divided into clear steps, from query to viewing the results:

User Data Entry:

The user enters the desired location—by typing the name or clicking directly on the map—and selects a date or period of interest.

Data Query:

The system connects to the OpenMeteo climate database and retrieves historical information on temperature, precipitation, wind, and humidity.

Processing and Analysis:

The data is processed by algorithms that calculate averages, deviations, and percentiles, resulting in statistical probabilities of specific conditions occurring ("very hot," "very humid," etc.).

Visualization and Interpretation:

The results are displayed in graphs, maps, and probability indicators, accompanied by interpretative descriptions that help the user understand the practical meaning of the numbers.

Recommendations for Your Day:

The app also suggests preventive actions or adjustments, such as "light clothing recommended" or "high chance of strong winds—avoid outdoor activities."

Product Demo:

Discover the power of our WeatherView platform in this project demo, which shows how complex historical weather data is made accessible through an intuitive dashboard interface.

link: https://youtu.be/OoS1LsLlb30

Implementation Details

General Architecture: Web application consisting of an interactive front-end and a back-end that processes weather data.

Back-end: Developed in Python with Flask, responsible for collecting and processing historical data.

Front-end: Created in React, enabling interaction with maps, filters, and graphs.

Data Integration: OpenMeteo for variables such as temperature, humidity, precipitation, and wind, with continuous updates via API.

Visualization: Interactive graphs and maps provided by NASA (WordView) that translate probabilities into color scales and understandable icons.

Probabilistic Analysis Algorithm: WeatherView's core is a statistical algorithm that processes decades of historical data. It calculates the probability of specific, user-defined weather conditions occurring for any location and date requested.

Impact:

By democratizing access to historical weather data, WeatherView empowers people to make smarter, safer decisions for their long-term planning. Our platform serves as a vital risk management tool, allowing users to anticipate adverse conditions and take preventative measures. The impact extends from the bride who can choose her wedding date with greater confidence, to the event planner who can avoid significant financial losses, or the adventurer who can plan their expedition with greater confidence.

Conclusion

WeatherView aims to transform the way people plan their lives around the weather. By bridging the gap between complex weather data and the need for clear, accessible information, we offer a practical solution to a universal problem. Empowering users with data-driven insights for long-term decisions can mitigate risks, reduce losses, and ultimately help everyone better enjoy the outdoors.

projectDetails.name: Air Quality Monitor
projectDetails.summary: Breathe safer, wherever you are. Our new tool provides a real-time overview of air quality on a global scale. By collecting and analyzing data on crucial pollutants (such as carbon monoxide, ozone, and particulate matter) from official sources, our system translates complex data into the standard US Air Quality Index (AQI). You receive clear alerts on the risk level and practical recommendations to protect your health. The application is designed for everyone but is especially vital for protecting children, the elderly, pregnant women, and individuals with conditions like asthma, rhinitis, and bronchitis, helping to prevent attacks and complications.
projectDetails.details:
1. What exactly does it do?

The Air Quality Monitor gathers data from official organizations that track atmospheric pollutants. Using this data, our application calculates the Air Quality Index (AQI) according to the US standard, which ranges from 0 to over 500. The app displays this index along with a health recommendation to help users protect their respiratory health. This recommendation is based on a 6-level scale: Good (AQI 0-50), Moderate (AQI 51-100), Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups (AQI 101-150), Unhealthy (AQI 151-200), Very Unhealthy (AQI 201-300), and Hazardous (AQI 301+). For a more detailed analysis, the app also shows the individual concentration levels for carbon monoxide, particulate matter, ozone, nitrogen dioxide, and sulfur dioxide.

2. How does it work?

Our tool works in a simple way. First, the user chooses a location to get the air quality reading. They can do this either by clicking directly on the map or by typing a city name into the search bar. Once a location is selected, our Air Quality Monitor calls the OpenWeather API, sending the location's latitude and longitude, as well as the current local time. The API responds with a JSON file that contains the concentration levels for each pollutant. Our application then uses these concentrations to calculate the individual AQI for each one, based on the formula provided by AirNow. Finally, we display the highest AQI value to the user, identifying the dominant pollutant.

3. What benefits does it have?

The great benefit of the Air Quality Monitor is translating complex scientific data into a practical tool for daily life. It allows anyone, especially at-risk groups like children, the elderly, and people with respiratory diseases, to make healthier decisions: knowing the best time to practice sports, plan an outdoor trip, or simply decide when it's time to close the windows. Our goal is to give people the power to actively take care of their respiratory health and, at the same time, increase awareness about the environment they live in.

4. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to help people achieve a better quality of life by bringing together technology and scientific data. As a next step for the project, we envision developing a more advanced system capable of providing forecasts. This would allow us to offer even greater assurance and help users maintain a high quality of life.

5. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

This project used the Visual Studio Code IDE for code editing, Github for versioning and hosting, the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript languages for the web application, Python for prototyping, the OpenWeather API to collect air quality data, and Canva to produce the demonstration video.

projectDetails.name: S.W.A.R.M - Stellar-Worlds-AI-Reconnaissance-Mission
projectDetails.summary:
We developed S.W.A.R.M. — Stellar Worlds AI Reconnaissance Mission, a distributed artificial intelligence ecosystem designed to autonomously explore exoplanets, secure inter-satellite communication, and synchronize data across deep space with minimal human intervention. The system is composed of four specialized AIs:
• AION – Exploration and scientific data acquisition.
• EXON – Security and self-healing of the network.
• NOVA – Mediation, routing, and latency optimization.
• EIRYA – Central hive-mind for coordination and model synchronization.

By leveraging NASA’s Exoplanet Archive API, S.W.A.R.M. processes real astrophysical data to simulate autonomous orbital intelligence. This modular architecture addresses the hackathon challenge by demonstrating how decentralized AI systems can perform real-time, low-latency scientific analysis beyond Earth. The project’s importance lies in its scalable design — enabling resilient, fault-tolerant AI infrastructures for future missions in astronomy, planetary science, and deep-space communication networks.
projectDetails.details:
S.W.A.R.M. (Stellar Worlds AI Reconnaissance Mission) is an autonomous, distributed AI network designed to analyze and coordinate exoplanetary exploration. It simulates a constellation of satellites, each hosting a specialized AI agent working together as a unified intelligence swarm.

The system integrates four AIs — AION (Exploration), EXON (Security), NOVA (Routing), and EIRYA (Core) — to divide and synchronize tasks such as planetary detection, data integrity, communication optimization, and global decision-making. Data is sourced directly from NASA’s Exoplanet Archive API, processed, and visualized through an interactive front-end that dynamically generates planetary systems using JavaScript, HTML, and CSS animations.

We built the project using JavaScript (ES6) for logic and asynchronous data handling, Python (FastAPI) for backend simulations, and Render / GitHub Pages for deployment. The visual interface uses a canvas-based starfield and adaptive grid layouts inspired by sci-fi design principles.

Our creative goal was to model how multiple AIs can cooperate like neural clusters in space, ensuring resilience and adaptability — unlike a single centralized intelligence. The intended impact is to showcase a blueprint for autonomous, self-organizing AI infrastructures capable of managing future deep-space data networks and planetary missions.

projectDetails.name: AEGIS: Toolbox for you to create and validate space habitat layouts
projectDetails.summary:
AEGIS is an interactive tool that enables the design and validation of space habitat layouts using official NASA metrics, particularly the standards from the Human Integration Design Handbook (HIDH). The platform allows users to configure parameters such as habitat shape (cylindrical or rectangular), structure type (rigid or inflatable), crew size, mission duration, and gravitational environment (microgravity, Moon, or Mars).

The system generates 2D and 3D visualizations of the habitat and calculates key metrics such as Net Habitable Volume (NHV), floor area per person, and compliance with minimum requirements for comfort, health, and human performance. AEGIS also guides the sizing of functional zones (sleep, work, hygiene, dining, recreation, etc.) and estimates critical resource needs such as water, oxygen, and food.

This project is important because it helps engineers, space architects, students, and enthusiasts explore and compare different habitat configurations, fostering more efficient, livable, and sustainable solutions for long-duration space missions.
projectDetails.details:
AEGIS is an interactive digital laboratory for space habitat design. It combines geometric modeling, NASA standards-based calculations, and real-time 2D/3D visualizations to help engineers, students, and enthusiasts design and validate space habitats. The platform works by allowing users to configure key mission parameters—habitat shape, crew size, mission duration, and gravity environment—and then automatically evaluates critical metrics such as Net Habitable Volume (NHV), functional zones (sleep, hygiene, work, dining), and vital resource needs (water, oxygen, food).

Benefits and Impact
AEGIS reduces the risk of early-stage design errors, accelerates prototyping, and democratizes access to complex NASA data by transforming it into an intuitive, visual interface. Its intended impact is to make space habitat design more efficient, sustainable, and accessible, while also serving as an educational resource that inspires the next generation of space professionals.

Tools and Technologies

  • Core: Python 3.11+
  • Web Framework: Streamlit
  • Visualizations: Plotly
  • Numerical Calculations: NumPy
  • Deployment: Docker, Google Cloud Ru
  • Data Sources: Exclusively NASA resources, including the Human Integration Design Handbook (HIDH) and ISS Research Publications

Creativity and Considerations
AEGIS turns dense technical standards into a user-friendly environment for experimentation and learning. Our team focused on sustainability, human factors, and long-duration mission needs, aligning with the UN Sustainable Development Goals (Quality Education, Industry & Innovation, Sustainable Communities, and Partnerships). By enabling rapid iteration and comparison of scenarios, AEGIS encourages innovation and global collaboration in space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project Franco & Bastos
projectDetails.summary:
UrbAtlas is a digital platform that contains NASA Earth observation data and smart mapping technologies to support urban planners, public administrators, and citizens in building safer, more sustainable, and inclusive cities.
Using satellite imagery and environmental indicators—such as temperature, land use, air quality, and disaster risk—the system identifies vulnerable areas and regions with potential for balanced urban expansion. The interactive map allows you to switch between layers of environmental risks (flooding, penetration, environmental impact) and urban growth analyses, providing support for decisions that preserve people's well-being and the environment.
UrbAtlas also functions as a collaborative space: certified urban planners can publish analyses and action proposals, while citizens ask questions and monitor the risks in their region. This interaction strengthens participatory and transparent urban planning.
Based on scientific data and community input, UrbAtlas proposes a new way of thinking about urban development—smart, sustainable, and people-centered, using the power of Earth observation to transform data into decisions, and decisions into quality of life.
projectDetails.details:
UrbAtlas — Smart Urban Planning with NASA Data

1 - Overview

UrbAtlas is a digital platform that uses Earth observation data from NASA and other global sources to assist urban planners, public administrators, and citizens in developing smart urban growth strategies. Its purpose is to balance the advancement of cities with environmental preservation, promoting human well-being and climate resilience.

The platform offers an interactive map-based interface, integrating information on land use, vegetation cover, surface temperature, air pollution, and environmental risks such as floods and landslides. UrbAtlas transforms scientific data into direct inputs for more sustainable and inclusive urban decisions.

 

2 - Objectives and Benefits

UrbAtlas seeks to improve the quality of life in rapidly growing cities by providing analysis and monitoring tools that help:

·         Reduce environmental and health risks;

·         Plan urban expansion areas without degrading ecosystems;

·         Ensure fair access to green spaces and basic infrastructure;

·         Support evidence-based public policies and citizen participation.

These benefits extend to the population, which gains greater security and transparency, and to administrators, who can now make decisions based on concrete data about the local environment and infrastructure.

3 - How It Works

The system is structured into three main modules:

 3.1 - Login — access divided between two profiles:

·         Urbanists (professional accreditation and validation required);

·         Citizens, who access information and interact with experts.

During registration, each user enters their desired location, which allows the system to automatically filter the most relevant data for their region.

3.2 - Collaborative Forum — divided into:

·         Posts: urban planners create technical analyses and action proposals based on satellite data;

·         Questions: citizens submit questions about specific areas of the city, which can be answered by professionals.

Both interactions receive relevance ratings (up/down), generating a credibility index for urban planners and encouraging the quality of contributions.

3.3 - Interactive Map — the visual core of the system, with two main layers:

·         Expansion Area Analysis: identifies regions suitable for urban growth, considering infrastructure, vegetation, and environmental risk.

·         Internal City Control: shows vulnerabilities in existing neighborhoods, such as flooding, landslides, and pollution.

Users can switch between layers, select specific characteristics (e.g., flooding, environmental impact, landslides), and access detailed analyses produced by urban planners or automatically generated by the platform.

 

4 - Using Data from NASA and Other Sources

UrbAtlas draws on resources such as:

·         https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/tools/worldview

NASA Earthdata Worldview: for viewing historical and recent satellite images;

·         https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/

Observatório Terrestre da NASA: to understand environmental phenomena that impact urban growth;

·        ·https://search.earthdata.nasa.gov/search?q=CIESIN%20ESDIS

SEDAC (Centro de Dados e Aplicações Socioeconômicas da NASA): to integrate environmental and social data related to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs);

 ·         https://www.worldpop.org/ and https://human-settlement.emergency.copernicus.eu

WorldPop e Copernicus: for population density and land use information.

These datasets allow UrbAtlas to clearly demonstrate impacts on ecosystems, natural resources, and infrastructure, highlighting areas at risk, degradation, or uncontrolled expansion.

5 - Institutional and Community Participation

UrbAtlas encourages cooperation between public authorities, urban planners, and civil society.

For example, parks and environmental departments can use the system to:

·         Identify areas with vegetation deficits and plan new urban parks;

·         Assess the ecological impact of urbanization and create green mitigation corridors;

·         Monitor local environmental indicators based on NASA data.

Residents, in turn, can:

·         Report problems or changes observed in their neighborhoods (flooding, erosion, pollution);

·         Ask experts questions about specific risks;

·         Read public analyses and monitor data-driven urban planning projects.

Thus, UrbAtlas becomes a bridge between science and citizenship, fostering a culture of informed and sustainable participation.

6 - Presentation and Communication

To maximize impact and reach, UrbAtlas will be presented through:

·         An interactive mobile platform with accessible maps, graphs, and dashboards;

·         Institutional presentations and short explanatory videos, aimed at city halls, universities, and environmental organizations;

·         Public demonstrations and workshops, encouraging data use and local engagement.

 This approach facilitates understanding for both specialized professionals and the general public, making the technology inclusive and educational.

7 - Expected Impact

The impact of UrbAtlas is multidimensional:

·         Social: improves urban well-being by reducing vulnerabilities and increasing citizen participation;

·         Environmental: protects ecosystems by guiding growth sustainably;

·         Governmental: strengthens data-driven decision-making;

·         Educational: promotes environmental and digital literacy among residents.

In the long term, the project seeks to inspire a new culture of urban planning: collaborative, scientific, and environmentally sensitive.

8 - Creativity and Factors Considered

The originality of UrbAtlas lies in its integration of spatial science, urban planning, and public participation into a single tool.

The system was designed considering:

·         The advancement of climate change and its local effects;

·         Rapid urban growth in developing countries;

·         The need to connect scientific data with human decisions;

·         The importance of strengthening the role of citizens as active agents in urban planning.

9 - Conclusion

UrbAtlas represents a new paradigm for urban management: a digital environment that transforms NASA satellite data into more informed human decisions.

By combining technology, technical expertise, and social engagement, the project offers a concrete path to smart urban growth, ensuring that cities progress in harmony with the planet and the well-being of their people.

12 - Next steps:

12.1 Expansion of Environmental Analysis Parameters

Currently, UrbAtlas analyzes satellite data related to floods, landslides, and environmental impacts, but the next step is to significantly expand the set of observable parameters.

The integration of new data layers will allow for an even more comprehensive view of urban dynamics, incorporating indicators such as:

- Air quality and atmospheric pollution (NO₂, CO₂, PM2.5);

- Surface temperatures and urban heat islands;

- Vegetation cover and ecosystem fragmentation;

- Water availability and soil moisture;

- Evolution of land use and population density.

This expansion will enable UrbAtlas to become a multidimensional urban environmental monitoring tool, enabling richer and more strategic analyses for sustainable planning.

12.2 - Partnerships with Environmental Consulting Firms and Insurance Companies

As the system matures, UrbAtlas will be able to establish partnerships with environmental consulting firms, risk management agencies, and insurance companies.

These organizations will be able to:

- Use the platform's data to assess territorial and environmental risks;

- Help city halls and companies plan investments in resilient infrastructure;

- Feed the system with field information and technical reports, improving the accuracy of analyses;

- Offer customized risk assessment, mitigation, and sustainable urban planning services.

Furthermore, the exchange with experts and public institutions will create a collaborative ecosystem of urban innovation, making UrbAtlas a reference for decisions with socio-environmental and economic impact.

12.3 - Predictive Simulation and AI-Assisted Planning Module

One of the most transformative advances planned for UrbAtlas is the development of an intelligent predictive simulation module, based on artificial intelligence and machine learning.

This module will allow:

- Predicting future impacts of environmental phenomena based on historical NASA data and local data;

- Simulating urban scenarios—for example, how the expansion of an area can alter the microclimate, drainage, or vegetation cover;

- Automatically suggesting preventive actions, such as new reforestation sites, ideal areas for parks, or drainage interventions.

This feature will function as a digital urban planning assistant, offering intelligent and personalized recommendations to urban planners and public administrators.

Over time, this module can evolve into a real-time decision support system, integrating alerts and adaptive policies.

12.4 - 360° Visualization and Integration with IoT Devices

To complement the satellite view, UrbAtlas intends to integrate data from IoT (Internet of Things) devices installed in cities, such as sensors for:

- Temperature and humidity;

- River levels and automatic rain gauges;

- Noise pollution and air quality;

- Vehicle and pedestrian flow;

- Energy consumption and street lighting.

This information will enable a 360° visualization of the city in real time, transforming UrbAtlas into a true "urban digital twin."

This will make it possible not only to identify risks but also to monitor the city's behavior live, detecting patterns and trends that help prevent disasters and optimize public resources.

This advancement puts UrbAtlas on the path to smart cities, combining Earth observation, local data, and artificial intelligence in a single, integrated platform.

projectDetails.name: Grafeno
projectDetails.summary:
Finding papers is a fundamental piece for the success of research. Selection can become a complex challenge, given that there is an enormous quantity of papers on the same topic.

This challenge is confronted again when papers that discuss similar topics have completely distinct titles. This creates another layer of difficulty in finding and relating these papers, as conventional search tools sometimes depend on direct and literal correspondence with the searched titles and diving through references, without relating semantics between the papers.

Grafeno was born precisely to solve this problem. It is a tool that compiles over 500 papers on space biology and does not analyze keywords, but rather performs semantic analysis of the abstracts and visually arrange them by proximity. The project organizes the large range of papers into a graph, drawing connections between similar papers where the length of the edge is proportional to how related the papers are. In this way, papers that treat related content form linked knowledge clusters.
projectDetails.details:
grafeno is a scientific tool that compiles papers into a semantically oriented graph, presented in a web application built with vue.js + python.

Aiming to build a integrated knowledge database that allows for wider and more meaningful research exploration. With grafeno, researchers are available to see related and relevant papers as compared to every other, creating emergent clusters of meaning that go way beyond keywords and categories.

grafeno is a form of exploring how different data exhibition influences scientific research, by breaking classical list-oriented conventions and aiming at a meaningful use of space and visual representation.

The data used comes from NASA's full text open-access Space Biology publications, available in the resources from the challenge: Build a Space Biology Knowledge Engine. It was acquired using BeautifulSoup and had a semantic preprocessor to calculate embeddings.

A FastAPI back-end provides everything the website needs to display and organize information, all querying is done in static data that is preorganized. All parts of the application are deployed in Google Cloud with a serverless architecture, with both ends isolated in Docker containers. projectDetails.name: Exoplorer
projectDetails.summary: Exoplorer is an interactive platform that brings people and scientists closer to the fascinating universe of exoplanets. Our goal is to make the exploration of worlds beyond the solar system accessible, engaging, and intelligent. The system combines real astronomical data, collected from NASA telescopes and space databases, with artificial intelligence algorithms capable of organizing, interpreting, and revealing patterns that aid both scientific research and learning. The platform offers two integrated forms of exploration: a technical approach, aimed at researchers and advanced students who wish to analyze detailed information; and an educational approach, designed for the general public, which presents these worlds in a visual and simplified way, with curiosities and simulations that spark interest in the cosmos. In this way, Exoplorer transforms complex data into accessible knowledge, stimulating scientific curiosity and bringing society closer to space discoveries.
projectDetails.details:
Exoplorer

Our Exoplorer platform is a complete and innovative solution that connects scientists, students, and enthusiasts to the universe of exoplanets in an accessible, interactive, and intelligent way. We have developed a web environment that brings together real astronomical data from telescopes and global scientific bases, integrated with artificial intelligence algorithms that organize, compare, and interpret this information. The platform transforms large volumes of complex data into clear and dynamic visualizations, allowing users to explore and better understand the characteristics of worlds beyond the Solar System.

Exoplorer has two exploration modes: a technical mode, aimed at researchers and advanced students, which offers detailed access to parameters such as mass, radius, temperature, orbital distance, and habitability potential; and an educational mode, designed for the general public, which presents this information in a visual, simplified, and engaging way, with simulations and interesting facts about each planet discovered.

Universe View

Explore NASA's catalog of exoplanets in a 3D visualization interface. Navigate the interactive “map” of the cosmos, with exoplanets displayed at actual scale. The platform presents crucial information about each planet, such as radius, temperature, orbital period, insolation, distance from the star, and confirmation status. You can explore and compare this data visually and intuitively, as if you were in a cosmic atlas.

Adding new data

With the prediction tool, users can manually enter planet data or upload CSV files with multiple candidates at once. The artificial intelligence model processes the parameters and returns whether or not the celestial body is a candidate for being an exoplanet. In addition, the platform offers dynamic comparisons with known exoplanets, allowing you to understand how your data compares to already cataloged planets.

Modes

To make it easier for those who do not have much scientific knowledge about spatial data, all the parameters necessary for prediction (such as radius, insolation, and transit duration) are clearly explained. The modal provides the name of each attribute and a brief explanation of each one, making it easier to understand the data that must be entered. This ensures that beginners can also actively participate in scientific exploration without difficulty.

Texture generation:

Where does a planet's “temperature” come from?

A planet's temperature comes mainly from the energy emitted by its parent star. Just as a campfire warms those who are close to it more than those who are far away, a star sends light and heat in all directions, and each planet receives only a portion of that energy. The amount received depends on three main factors: the temperature of the star, which indicates how hot it is and how much energy it radiates; the size of the star, since larger stars emit more light; and the distance between the planet and the star, because the further away the planet is, the less energy reaches it. This balance between the radiation emitted by the star and the orbital distance is the starting point for understanding why some planets are cold and others extremely hot.

Energy absorption and return

A planet's thermal equilibrium depends on the relationship between the energy it absorbs from the star and the energy it returns to space. When starlight hits the planet, part of it is reflected back, depending on the albedo, which measures how much light the surface and atmosphere reflect. A high albedo, such as that of ice or light clouds, means that the planet reflects a lot and absorbs little heat; a low albedo, such as that of rocks or dark oceans, indicates that it absorbs more energy. The fraction that is absorbed heats the planet, which then re-radiates this heat in the form of infrared radiation. The balance between the energy received and emitted defines the so-called equilibrium temperature, an estimate of the average temperature the planet would have if this balance were perfect.

Equilibrium Temperature Equation

This formula is responsible for estimating a planet's equilibrium temperature, that is, the temperature it would have if the energy it receives from the star were exactly equal to the energy it re-emits into space. It combines four fundamental factors: the temperature of the star (T_*), which indicates how much energy is emitted; the radius of the star (R_*), which defines the size of its emitting surface; the distance of the planet from the star (a), which determines how much of that energy reaches it; and the albedo (A), which represents the fraction of light reflected by the planet. The term √(R_*/2a) shows how radiation spreads as distance increases, while (1 - A)^{1/4} adjusts the final value according to how much the planet reflects or absorbs light. In essence, this equation describes the balance between heating and cooling of a planet and allows us to predict, in a simple way, whether it will be cold, temperate, or extremely hot.

Example of generated texture:

Given this equilibrium temperature formula and observational data provided by NASA, such as the star's temperature and radius, the planet's orbital distance, and estimated albedo, it is possible to estimate the color and likely visual appearance of cataloged exoplanets. This is because the equilibrium temperature (T_eq) directly influences the physical and chemical properties of a planet's surface and atmosphere.

Colder planets tend to have bluish or whitish tones, typical of worlds covered by ice or dense methane clouds. Those with moderate temperatures, close to Earth-like conditions, may exhibit more neutral or yellowish colors, associated with rocks, arid soils, or liquid oceans. Very hot planets often have ochre, orange, or reddish colors, caused by vaporized minerals or dry, thick atmospheres. In the most extreme cases, dark tones and incandescent glows may appear, characteristic of molten surfaces.

Thus, by cross-referencing the physical parameters of the star systems observed with this fundamental equation, we can visualize their probable appearance, transforming astronomical data into physical and aesthetic representations of the exoplanets that inhabit our galaxy.

Machine Learning Model:

  • Data Used: NASA KOI (Kepler) and TOI (TESS) satellites.
    • Objective: Unification to enrich the training set.
    • ORBITAL_PERIOD_DAYS: Orbital Period in days.
    • TRANSIT_DURATION_HOURS: Transit Duration in hours.
    • TRANSIT_DEPTH_PPM: Transit Depth in parts per million.
    • PLANET_RADIUS_REARTH: Planetary Radius in Earth radii.
    • PLANET_INSOLATION_EFLUX: Insolation Flux in Earth flux.
    • PLANET_EQ_TEMP_K: Equilibrium Temperature in Kelvin.
    • STELLAR_TEFF_K: Stellar Effective Temperature in Kelvin.
    • STELLAR_LOGG_CMS2: Stellar Surface Gravity in log10(cm/s**2).
    • STELLAR_RADIUS_RSUN: Stellar Radius in Solar radii.
    • STATUS: 0 = false, 1 = candidate/confirmed.
    • Hyperparameters:
      • max_depth: Defines the maximum depth of each tree. The higher the value, the more complex the tree (more branches), which can help capture more details in the data but also increases the risk of overfitting.
      • learning_rate: Controls how much each tree contributes to the final prediction. Smaller values (e.g., 0.01 or 0.1) make the model learn more slowly, which can improve generalization, but typically requires more trees to achieve the same performance.
      • n_estimators: The number of trees to be built in the model. More trees can lead to better accuracy, but also increase the risk of overfitting if the other parameters like learning_rate are not well tuned.
