projectDetails.name: Geo-Magnetic Mayhem: An ATC's, Sailor's, and Stargazer's Guide
projectDetails.summary:
We created "Geo-Magnetic Mayhem: An ATC's, Sailor's, and Stargazer's Guide", a vibrant digital comic strip that teaches children a vital lesson: The Sun's stunning beauty is matched only by its power to disrupt our modern lives.

This project directly answers the Stellar Stories challenge by tackling a crucial question: How does solar energy 93 million miles away crash the systems we use every single day?

Our narrative device is a simple, human conversation between three professionals whose livelihoods depend on clear signals: a Ship Captain (struggling with GPS loss), an Air Traffic Controller (battling radio static), and a Tourist Guide (Who has seen Aurora whose beautiful lights trigger local power grid failures).

The project is important because it closes a critical gap in public knowledge. Space weather is an invisible threat to global infrastructure, yet few people understand its mechanisms. By translating complex science like solar flares and geomagnetic storms into personal, dramatic, and easily digestible human crises, "Solar Stories" aims to inspire a new generation to see space science as a relevant factor in their daily safety, navigation, and technology. It’s an accessible tool for empowering future citizens to understand the cosmic forces that shape life on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
We created "Geo-Magnetic Mayhem: An ATC's, Sailor's, and Stargazer's Guide", a vibrant digital comic strip that fundamentally transforms the terrifying complexity of space weather into a captivating, human centered story. Our project directly answers the Stellar Stories challenge by asking: What happens to the people who keep our world running when the Sun attacks?

What We Made and How It Works

Our comic is a masterclass in narrative efficiency. The central concept is the Narrative Convergence of three professionals an Air Traffic Controller (ATC), a Sailor, and a northern lights Tourist Guide who meet up and realize the "bad luck" that simultaneously ruined their jobs was actually a single geomagnetic storm. The Sailor's sudden GPS loss at sea, the ATC's panic over radio blackouts in the sky, and the Tourist Guide's experience of both the beautiful aurora and a local power grid failure are all woven together. The comic uses their relatable dialogue and vivid visuals to break down the complex science (solar flares, CMEs, ionospheric distortion) into personal, immediate crises.

Importance and Intended Impact

This project is crucial because it tackles a major failure in science communication: turning an abstract cosmic threat into a personal concern. Space weather is an invisible menace to every piece of modern technology we rely on, yet the public remains largely unaware. By centering the story on human safety and high-stakes jobs, we connect with the middle school audience on an emotional level. Our goal isn't just to educate; it's to inspire action and shift the public's view of the cosmos from something distant to a dynamic force we must be prepared for. We want young readers to understand that studying Heliophysics means protecting their future world.

Creativity and Technical Strategy

Our creative strength lies in the elegant economy of the single scene convergence, which fulfills the challenge requirement of showing diverse impacts with maximum dramatic effect. We creatively leverage visual contrast, using the ethereal beauty of the aurora against the stark drama of a red-alert control panel to show the Sun's dual nature.

Our development was highly efficient: scientific facts were validated using NASA Website Resources. We strategically used AI tools like CoPilot and Gemini to quickly generate foundational character concepts, which were then polished and precisely assembled using Canva and finalized in Microsoft PowerPoint. This approach allowed us to produce a scientifically accurate and visually compelling narrative in the shortest time possible.

Yes, we leveraged AI tools in preparing our solution. Specifically, we used:

  • Microsoft Copilot: Assisted in generating initial character concepts and refining dialogue ideas for the comic.
  • Google Gemini: Helped create preliminary scene layouts and visual brainstorming.

All AI-generated images were subsequently edited and refined in Canva. We acknowledge that these AI tools contributed to ideation and visualization, but all final content, narrative, and scientific accuracy were fully reviewed and curated by our team.

projectDetails.name: Habitat Space Layout Creator
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Habitat Layout Creator, an interactive Unity tool that allows users to design, test, and validate the interior layouts of space habitats. The system lets mission planners and researchers place essential modules such as Crew Quarters, Galley, and Hygiene Units within a dome or spacecraft shell and automatically evaluates the layout for safety and livability.

Our tool addresses the “Habitat Space Explorer” challenge by combining spatial planning with automated rule-checking. It ensures that designs meet key human-factors criteria—safe egress routes, adequate corridor width, accessible interior space, free-space ratio, and noise separation between work and rest areas.

This project is important because it helps future habitat designers visualize how astronauts will live and move in confined environments. By blending simulation and validation, Habitat Layout Creator promotes safer, more efficient, and human-centered living spaces for long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
projectDetails.details:
Habitat Layout Creator is an interactive Unity-based simulation tool that allows users to design and test the internal layout of a space habitat. The system provides a modular grid where users can place components such as Crew Quarters, Galley, Hygiene/WCS, Medical Bay, and Exercise areas, then automatically validates the design using built-in safety and livability algorithms.

It checks for egress routes, corridor width, free-space ratio, interior reachability, traffic flow, and noise separation, producing a score (0-100) and a list of issues. Designers can instantly see the effects of changes through color-coded previews and overlay visuals. The results can be exported to JSON and PNG, allowing easy analysis or sharing with mission teams.

Developed entirely in Unity (C#), the project also uses UI scripting, pathfinding, and procedural validation logic to simulate real architectural constraints.

Our goal is to make early-stage space habitat design interactive, visual, and human-centric, reducing planning time and highlighting overlooked ergonomic or safety problems. By turning abstract design rules into an engaging simulation, Habitat Layout Creator bridges engineering and human factors—helping shape safer, more efficient habitats for the next generation of explorers.

projectDetails.name: Project The 67 Gang
projectDetails.summary:
The CORA (Celestial Orbital Research Agency) project aims to deliver affordable, sustainable access to Low Earth Orbit (LEO) for commercial, government, and research missions. Partnering with NASA, ESA, and CSA, CORA ensures compliance with global standards and promotes eco-efficient, debris-free space exploration.

Its customers include space agencies, commercial operators, universities, and defense clients. CORA generates revenue through launch services, mission collaborations, data subscriptions, IP licensing, and grants. Key partners like SpaceX, Arianespace, and global sustainability organizations strengthen its credibility and innovation pipeline.

CORA’s key assets include advanced propulsion technology, AI systems, R&D infrastructure, and access to funding. Its operations focus on green propulsion, space debris mitigation, and sustainable satellite manufacturing.

The roadmap envisions early technology validation, followed by LEO missions, and eventual expansion into commercial deployments and Artemis-related projects.

The project’s sustainability aligns with UN SDGs, supporting innovation, climate action, partnerships, and responsible production.

The CORA ecosystem includes:

CORA Space Station – a central orbital hub for research and logistics.

PharmaCube – a mini-lab for drug development in microgravity.

Docking Station & Space Drones – systems for debris cleanup, repairs, and recycling, ensuring a cleaner and safer orbital environment.
projectDetails.details:
Business Model: CORA 

NASA Space Apps Challenge – Proposal 

Members: Mahnoor Rehan, Yassin Mahmoud, Ezzeldin Mohamed, Jihad Wael 

 

1.  

Value Proposition 

  • Deliver cost-effective, sustainable access to Low Earth Orbit (LEO) for commercial, government, and research missions. 
  • Unique credibility through partnerships with CSA (Canadian Space Agency), ESA (European Space Agency), and NASA, ensuring compliance with international standards, co-development opportunities, and integration into global space initiatives. 
  • Contributing to sustainable space exploration through advanced propulsion, debris mitigation, and eco-efficient manufacturing. 

2.  

Customer Segments 

  • Space Agencies: CSA, ESA, NASA, and emerging national programs (UAE, Brazil, etc.). 
  • Commercial Operators: Communications, Earth observation, climate-tech, and constellation operators. 
  • Research & Academia: Universities and labs conducting space experiments. 
  • Defense & Sovereign Access Clients: Governments and private actors seeking independent launch or data sovereignty. 

3.  

Channels 

  • Direct contracting with CSA/ESA/NASA for joint missions and technology integration. 
  • Participation in international space consortia (Artemis Accords, EU space programs, UN Office for Outer Space Affairs). 
  • Partnerships with commercial launch providers (SpaceX, Arianespace, Rocket Lab). 
  • Global conferences and strategic PR around milestones. 

4.  

Revenue Streams 

  • Service Contracts: Deployment of satellites/payloads to LEO. 
  • Mission Collaboration: Co-funded projects with agencies (CSA/ESA/NASA). 
  • Data Services: Subscription models for Earth observation or communication data. 
  • IP Licensing: Proprietary propulsion, robotics, or AI systems. 
  • Public Funding & Grants: ESA Horizon Europe, CSA innovation programs, NASA partnerships. 

5.  

Key Partnerships 

  • CSA & ESA: Co-development, validation, funding, credibility. 
  • NASA: Technology adoption, inclusion in Artemis-related projects, and Earth science collaborations. 
  • Commercial Launch Providers: SpaceX, Rocket Lab, Arianespace. 
  • Universities & Labs: R&D pipeline and talent development. 
  • Global Sustainability Organizations: UN Office for Outer Space Affairs, SDG innovation networks. 

6.  

Key Activities 

  • Develop and test flight-ready systems for LEO. 
  • Integrate sustainability in space: debris avoidance, green propulsion, recycling of satellite parts. 
  • Collaborate with CSA/ESA/NASA on shared missions and research. 
  • Build ground operations for mission control. 
  • Engage in international policy leadership on sustainable space use. 

7.  

Key Resources 

  • Proprietary tech (e.g., propulsion, lightweight materials, AI). 
  • Strategic partnerships with CSA/ESA/NASA. 
  • Engineering talent and R&D infrastructure. 
  • Ground segment systems and mission control centers. 
  • Access to grants and public funding. 

8.  

Cost Structure 

  • R&D and prototyping. 
  • Launch and mission integration costs. 
  • Regulatory and licensing fees. 
  • Manufacturing scale-up. 
  • Global business development. 
  • Talent recruitment and retention. 

 

9.  

Milestones / Timeline to LEO 

  • Year 1–2: Tech validation, CSA/ESA/NASA collaborative agreements, first suborbital demos. 
  • Year 2–3: CubeSat/technology demonstrator missions in LEO (with agency support). 
  • Year 3–4: First full commercial LEO deployment. 
  • Year 5+: International expansion, long-term contracts, integration into Artemis/ISS successors. 

 

10.  

Competitive Advantage 

  • Strong tri-agency collaboration (CSA, ESA, NASA) — rare for early-stage companies. 
  • Sustainable space mission model aligned with SDGs. 
  • Lower development costs through co-funding and infrastructure sharing. 
  • First-mover advantage in sustainability + agency-backed credibility. 

 

11.  

Sustainability & SDG Alignment 

 

Your mission directly supports the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals: 

  • SDG 9 – Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure → advancing aerospace innovation and building global infrastructure. 
  • SDG 13 – Climate Action → enabling Earth observation satellites for climate monitoring. 
  • SDG 17 – Partnerships for the Goals → collaborating with CSA, ESA, NASA, and international partners. 
  • SDG 12 – Responsible Consumption & Production → sustainable satellite manufacturing and debris mitigation. 
  • SDG 4 – Quality Education → STEM partnerships with universities and research institutions. 
  • SDG 11 – Sustainable Cities and Communities → supporting urban planning and disaster response via satellite data. 

 

 

⸻ 

 

Proposed Idea: CORA (Celastial Orbital Research Agency) 

 

Core Structure: 

Main Station: “CORA Space Station” 

  • A large space station (like ISS) that serves as the central platform. 
  • Houses: 
  • Core control center for all operations. 
  • Docking ports for visiting spacecraft and mini satellites. 
  • General labs for upcycling, storage, and life-support systems. 
  • Role: Central hub for mission coordination, long-term experiments, and servicing logistics. 

(Our main motivation to create this is because after hearing that the ISS might be retiring in the near future, we could deploy this futuristic, scalable and functional satellite as a service with more advancements.) 

 

Mini Satellite #1: “PharmaCube” 

  • Small satellite lab dedicated to pharmaceutical R&D in microgravity. 
  • Features: Miniature lab racks, temperature control, and automated robotics. 
  • Can dock at the main station for maintenance or resupply. 
  • Revenue: Companies lease lab space or full experiment services. 

(This was thought of considering the limitations on earth to create certain cures and treatments due to the atmosphere. This can be done effectively in the PharmaCube.) 

 

Mini Satellite #2:  

  • Satellite docking station that handles “Space Drones” that offer debris cleanup, satellite charging, and minor repairs. 
  • Equipped with robotic arms, solar panels, and thrusters. 
  • Can dock at the main station to recharge, offload debris, or receive upgrades. 
  • Revenue: Operators pay per mission, subscription for debris monitoring, or for satellite maintenance services. 
  • Connection to main station for upcycling of recyclable debris. 

(Space debris holds major threat to earth, which is why we thought of a docking station for our CORA Space Drones) 

 

CORA Space Drones 

Futuristic drones designed to be scalable, durable and effective for debris cleanup in the LEO region, to minimize threats to earth and serve as a system for satellite repair and charging. 

The CORA Space Drones are designed with separate compartments classifying toxic wastes and reusable satellite parts found in space debris to abide by laws and protect researchers. Safety is our top priority. 

 

 

 

How It All Works Together 

  • CORA Space Station= command hub & large laboratory for long-term research. 
  • PharmaCube = specialized drug R&D lab in orbit. 
  • Docking station = docking station for orbital mechanic & environmental recycler. 
  • CORA Space Drones= clean space debris in the LEO region, classifying toxic wastes and reusable satellite parts found in space debris. 
  • All four interact: CORA Space Drones collect debris and return to the Docking Station, Recylable waste is transported to Space station for upcycling, PharmaCube sends data to Earth on successful experiments, and the station coordinates missions and houses humans for complex experiments.

projectDetails.details:
Real-Time Satellite Tracker: Project Snapshot

1. Core Functionality

This is a single-page web application for real-time satellite tracking and education. It uses a third-party API (TLE data) to plot satellite locations and paths on an interactive map, including travel metrics. The platform is an information resource detailing the missions of key satellites: ISS, Hubble, Terra, and Sentinel. It is accessible by simply opening the index.html file in a browser.

2. Impact

The project functions as a reliable educational utility by simplifying complex orbital mechanics and enhancing the public’s understanding of space technology. Its primary goals are to inspire STEM interest and increase awareness of critical global science and environmental sustainability efforts.

3. Development and Creativity

The application was built using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, integrating a Satellite Tracking API and a JavaScript mapping library. Its main creative aspect is the holistic visualization, which combines real-time data with rich mission context within a portable, unified, single-file HTML structure.

4. Key Considerations

Development prioritized four main factors: Accuracy and Reliability, clean User Interface (UI) Design, high Educational Value, and simple Technical Accessibility.

projectDetails.name: 🚀 NASA Space Hub — Learn, Explore, Test
projectDetails.summary: NASA Space Hub — Learn, Explore, Test is an interactive educational web platform that transforms space science into an engaging journey. It combines a Solar System Explorer with animated orbits and tiered facts, a quiz engine with 20-question segments that provide instant feedback, and a structured Learn Mode with curated content organized by level and category. By blending exploration, gamification, and progressive learning, the project makes complex astronomy concepts accessible and memorable. It turns passive reading into active discovery, inspiring curiosity and helping students connect with science in a fun, lasting way.
projectDetails.details:
NASA Space Hub — Learn, Explore, Test is an interactive web project created to make space science feel exciting and approachable. The idea behind it was to move away from static facts and instead give learners a chance to explore, play, and test themselves as if they were on a real mission. The platform opens with a Solar System Explorer where the planets, the Sun, and the Moon orbit smoothly across the screen. A single click reveals facts at different levels, from simple introductions to advanced details, so users can choose how deep they want to go.

The second part of the project is a quiz engine that turns knowledge into a challenge. Each segment has twenty carefully chosen questions, and every answer comes with an explanation so that mistakes become part of the learning process. The Learn Mode adds another layer by organizing space knowledge into beginner, intermediate, and advanced tracks, covering planets, stars, missions, and Earth science in a way that feels structured but never overwhelming.

The project was built using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript inside Microsoft Expression Web 4. It is lightweight, runs on regular laptops, and was designed to be creative, interactive, and inspiring for students who want to see science as something they can truly explore.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
For this project, I did use AI tools, but only in a very specific way. The facts about the planets, stars, Earth, and missions, along with the multiple‑choice quiz questions and their explanations, were generated and refined with the help of AI. I used it as a creative partner to speed up the process of gathering accurate information and shaping it into student‑friendly language. The AI helped me phrase things clearly, organize content into different levels of difficulty, and make sure the quiz questions came with explanations that actually teach instead of just saying “right” or “wrong.”

Everything else the design, the coding, the animations, the layout, and the way the site works was built by me in Microsoft Expression Web 4 using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The AI didn’t write the code or design the interface; it only supported the content side of the project.

projectDetails.name: Project Cosmic leaders 🚀- Regolith Shield Habitat (RSH)
projectDetails.summary:
Our proposed Mars shelter is a semi-circular stainless-steel structure reinforced with Martian regolith using the sandwich method, offering protection against radiation, dust storms, and extreme temperatures. NASA research shows that a 1-meter layer of regolith can reduce primary particle radiation by about 41% (Llamas, 2022), with higher protection when combined with additional materials (Al Zaman, 2023).
The habitat supports two astronauts on a six-month mission, measuring 6 meters wide, 8 meters long, and 3 meters high, providing 40 m² of floor space and 113 m³ of living volume. It includes two bedrooms, a bathroom, a food preparation and storage area, and a living space, all linked to a central control panel that monitors systems and environmental hazards. Water sustainability is achieved through a closed-loop system that collects, treats, and reuses wastewater from sinks and showers, reducing the need for resupply missions. Environmental sensors around the habitat measure pressure, wind, dust levels, and sunlight, providing early warnings of storms.
Power comes from solar panels, with future plans for flexible arrays and backup storage to ensure continuous energy. By combining durable materials, regolith insulation, water recycling, storm detection, and practical design, this shelter offers a safe, sustainable, and functional environment for long-term human missions on Mars

projectDetails.summary:
My project, “Cosmic Weather Parade” is a digital illustrated children’s story that explains space weather in a playful yet educational way. We developed an engaging narrative told through the eyes of Earthlings—farmers, pilots, astronauts, power grid operators, and kids—who each experience the effects of solar storms in their own lives. Through colorful illustrations, fun dialogue, and simple science explanations, children learn what space weather is, how it travels from the Sun, and how it impacts daily life on Earth.

This project addresses the Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings challenge by turning complex heliophysics concepts into an accessible, creative format for young audiences. By blending storytelling, art, and science, we aim to inspire curiosity about space, highlight the importance of monitoring solar activity, and empower the next generation to see themselves as future space scientists and explorers.
projectDetails.details:
My project is a digital illustrated children’s story that explains space weather in a simple, playful, and creative way. It works by using storytelling and visuals to show how solar activity—like solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and auroras—affects different people on Earth. Through characters such as farmers, pilots, astronauts, and kids, the story demonstrates how space weather impacts everyday life, from farming tools and navigation to flights, satellites, and even power grids.

The main benefit of this project is making complex science easy and fun to understand for young audiences. By turning data and concepts into a relatable story, it sparks curiosity, builds awareness of heliophysics, and helps children see the connection between space and their own lives. The intended impact is to inspire the next generation to care about space science and possibly imagine themselves as future scientists, explorers, or engineers.

To create the project, I used digital illustration tools (Canva/Procreate), graphic design software, and NASA’s free image resources. I focused on creativity by blending science with storytelling—giving the Sun, Earth, and solar storms personalities that children can connect with. I also considered how to balance accuracy with imagination, ensuring the story remains scientifically sound while being magical and engaging.

This project shows that science communication doesn’t always need to be technical—it can be colorful, creative, and full of wonder.

projectDetails.name: Project Crater Code
projectDetails.summary:
we built Crater Code, a web app that finds and maps craters using publicly available NASA images. our project includes a computer program that scans image tiles and marks likely craters, plus a simple Bubble web interface where people can check each result and accept or reject it. As people review detections the program learns and gets better over time.
Crater Code makes crater mapping much faster and easier than doing it by hand. That helps scientists and mission planners pick safer landing sites and it gives students a real way to help with research. The prototype works now but will get more accurate with more labeled images and access to NASA data.
projectDetails.details:
We built Crater Code, a web app that automatically finds, maps, and exports crater locations from publicly available NASA imagery. The system scans image tiles with a lightweight neural network, shows predictions in a simple Bubble map interface, and lets users accept or reject each detection so the model improves through human review.

Crater Code speeds up crater mapping from days to minutes per tile, helps researchers and mission planners choose safer landing sites, and creates classroom opportunities for students to contribute to real science. We developed the prototype with Python and TensorFlow or PyTorch for the model, standard image tiling and preprocessing tools, and Bubble for the front end. Outputs are CSV and GeoJSON for easy sharing.

Our creative edge is the human-in-the-loop workflow combined with a shareable web UI. We designed for data quality, clear auditing of results, and scalable deployment. With access to more labeled data and NASA resources we will raise accuracy and broaden impact.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
• We trained and ran a lightweight convolutional neural network (TensorFlow / PyTorch) to detect crater-like features in NASA image tiles.
  • We used AI for data processing and augmentation (tiling, contrast adjustments, synthetic examples) to improve model robustness.
  • We used AI-assisted prototyping for code snippets, model architecture suggestions, and testing ideas to accelerate development.
  • We used AI to help draft user interface text, slide copy, and concise demo descriptions; final wording was reviewed and edited by our team.
  • Human review is central: users validate model predictions in the Bubble interface and those corrections feed back to improve the model.

projectDetails.summary: Project AquaLink, by Team EcoFin & AquaFusion, connects marine biology and satellite technology to predict shark foraging in real time. projectDetails.details:
Project Details – EcoFin & Neptune: Project AquaLink

Project AquaLink, created by Team EcoFin & AquaFusion, is an innovative system that connects marine biology with satellite science to study and protect sharks. It combines two technologies:

  • EcoFin – a smart tag attached to sharks that records location, depth, temperature, movement, and feeding behavior.
  • Neptune – a low-Earth-orbit satellite that receives EcoFin data and links it with NASA’s PACE (phytoplankton tracking) and SWOT (ocean topography) satellites.

Using our Python-based mathematical framework, we developed a model that predicts shark foraging activity by analyzing temperature, chlorophyll, sea-surface height, depth, and feeding rate. This allows researchers to identify feeding hotspots and understand how sharks respond to environmental changes.

The project’s benefits include improved shark conservation, data-driven policy development, and interactive learning tools for students. We used Python for coding, NASA satellite datasets, and Canva for visuals and communication.

Our creativity lies in merging space technology with ocean ecology, turning complex satellite data into an accessible, teen-friendly system that makes ocean science exciting, educational, and actionable.

projectDetails.details:
Our project is an interactive educational platform celebrating the 25th anniversary of the International Space Station’s Cupola, a unique observation module providing stunning views of Earth from space.

We developed both a website and an integrated game. Players receive warnings when satellite imagery indicates changes, and have a few seconds to identify the type of disaster based on what they’ve learned from the educational website. By bridging space science and real-world applications, it fosters global citizenship and resilience in facing ecological challenges.

Creatively, the project combines authentic space data with gamified learning and interactive visualization, making complex environmental science accessible and engaging. projectDetails.name: Sharks from Space: Tracking Ocean Predators from Orbit
projectDetails.summary:
Our project develops a mathematical framework and new sensor concept to track sharks—the ocean’s top predators—using NASA satellite data and next-generation tagging technology.

NASA’s Earth observation satellites provide vital datasets such as sea surface temperature, chlorophyll concentration, ocean color, currents, and sea surface height anomalies. These variables are strong indicators of prey abundance and preferred shark habitats. We integrate these datasets with shark movement records to create a Habitat Suitability Model (HSM) powered by machine learning. This model predicts shark foraging zones and how they shift with climate change.

Additionally, we propose a Smart Shark Tag concept that goes beyond position tracking. Equipped with GPS, accelerometers, eDNA sensors, biochemical analyzers, and real-time satellite uplinks, the tag can detect what sharks are eating and when feeding occurs. This data is transmitted instantly, enabling researchers to update predictive models dynamically.

By combining space-based data with in-situ animal sensing, this project supports marine conservation, fisheries management, and climate resilience strategies. It transforms the way we observe predator-prey dynamics, helping us safeguard ocean ecosystems that sustain life on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, Sharks from Space, combines NASA Earth observation data with advanced AI models and a conceptual Smart Shark Tag to track and predict shark foraging behavior.

How it works:

We use NASA satellite datasets—sea surface temperature (AVHRR), chlorophyll concentration and ocean color (MODIS), sea surface height (Sentinel-6), and ocean currents (ECCO)—as environmental inputs. These data layers are processed through machine learning models (neural networks, Bayesian probability models, and Habitat Suitability Modeling) to generate predictive habitat maps. These maps highlight areas where sharks are most likely to forage, based on correlations between satellite-derived variables and known shark movements.

We also propose a Smart Shark Tag: a multi-sensor device that goes beyond GPS tracking. It integrates accelerometers, depth sensors, eDNA readers, biochemical feeding sensors, and a satellite uplink to collect and transmit real-time data about shark movements and feeding behavior.

Benefits:

Provides new insights into predator-prey dynamics in the ocean.

Enables real-time monitoring of shark habitats.

Supports marine conservation and fisheries management.

Advances climate resilience by predicting habitat shifts under environmental change.

Intended impact:

This project empowers researchers and policymakers with predictive tools to protect shark populations and the ecosystems they sustain. It also informs sustainable fisheries practices, ensuring balance in marine food webs.

Tools & technologies:

Coding/AI: Python, TensorFlow, PyTorch, Bayesian modeling libraries

Data: NASA MODIS, AVHRR, Sentinel-6, ECCO datasets; OCEARCH shark tagging datasets

Conceptual hardware: Smart Shark Tag (GPS, accelerometer, eDNA, biochemical sensors, satellite uplink)

Software: GIS tools for spatial modeling, cloud-based data processing platforms

Creativity & considerations:

The novelty lies in fusing space-based satellite data with animal-borne sensor data. Our team considered data latency, sensor durability in harsh marine environments, and the ethical implications of animal tagging. The project balances cutting-edge AI with real-world conservation goals, demonstrating a scalable approach for tracking other marine predators in the future.

projectDetails.name: BTR²
projectDetails.summary:
During a three-year Mars mission, an eight-person crew would generate over 12,600 kg of inorganic waste  packaging, textiles, and structural materials. Storing or returning this waste to Earth is costly and unsustainable.
Our project, BioFusion Trash-to-Resource Reactor BTR², is a hybrid recycling system that fuses synthetic biology, nanotechnology, and AI to transform inorganic trash into usable feedstock for 3D printing, repairs, and construction on Mars.
Engineered extremophile microbes digest plastics and fabrics, while nanobot swarms disassemble metals and ceramics into reusable powders. An onboard AI monitors consumption patterns and directs autonomous recycling cycles.
BTR² turns waste into survival assets  enabling zero-waste living, reduced resupply costs, and sustainable human presence beyond Earth
projectDetails.details:
Our project, the BioFusion Trash-to-Resource Reactor (BTR²), is designed to give waste a second life. It takes inorganic materials—like plastics, textiles, metals, and ceramics—and transforms them into valuable resources using engineered microbes and nanobots, all coordinated by an intelligent AI system. Instead of treating waste as a burden, BTR² turns it into a source of survival and innovation on Mars.

By using this technology, mission waste can be reduced dramatically, while the need for costly resupply missions from Earth could drop significantly. The materials produced by BTR² can be reused for 3D printing, repairs, and construction, helping astronauts create what they need directly from what they already have. (These projections are inspired by NASA’s Logistics Reduction and Repurposing research, which explores how in-situ recycling can greatly reduce mission waste and resupply demands.)

Our goal is to help create self-sustaining Mars habitats where nothing goes to waste and every discarded item becomes part of the next tool, structure, or piece of equipment. To develop and visualize our concept, we used tools such as Python, MATLAB, COMSOL, BioPython, and Blender, along with open datasets from NASA.

What makes this system truly unique is its combination of synthetic biology, nanotechnology, and artificial intelligence—fields that rarely intersect in space engineering. The design is modular, autonomous, and centered on crew safety, allowing it to adapt easily to future missions and different planetary environments.

projectDetails.name: Project DS_Solutions
projectDetails.summary:
The main problem is the increasing amount of space debris in Low Earth Orbit, which poses serious risks to satellites, space missions, and long-term orbital sustainability. If left unaddressed, this could lead to the Kessler Syndrome, where collisions generate even more debris, making certain orbits unusable and disrupting global communication, navigation, and weather forecasting.  

Our solution is to develop an autonomous debris removal system for LEO that uses AI-driven tracking to identify and capture orbital debris. Once captured, the system employs targeted propulsion technologies to safely deorbit the debris, helping maintain a sustainable and secure orbital environment.
projectDetails.details:
The project is an autonomous debris removal system designed for Low Earth Orbit. It uses advanced AI and robotic swarms to detect, capture, and safely deorbit or recycle space debris. Each vehicle is equipped with robotic arms, nets, and magnetic tethers, allowing it to adapt to different sizes and types of debris. The system makes real-time decisions and operates independently to address the growing risk of space debris collisions.

Benefits:

  • Protects satellites, the ISS, and other vital infrastructure by reducing collision risk.
  • Mitigates the danger of the Kessler Syndrome, preventing a cascade of space debris collisions.
  • Supports sustainable space operations and opens up safer opportunities for satellites and future commercial activities.
  • Creates potential new revenue streams through material recovery and analytics, and lowers long-term operational costs.

Intended Impact:
To maintain a safe, accessible, and economically viable Low Earth Orbit for current and future generations by proactively removing debris that threatens space operations. This project aims to enable continued satellite deployment, safe human spaceflight, and the growth of the space economy.

projectDetails.name: Project Eclipse Corps
projectDetails.summary:
ECLIPSE is an innovative space tourism project designed to commercialize low Earth orbit responsibly. Our concept features a hybrid spaceplane that can take off like an airplane and dock with a rotating orbital ring of capsules that simulate gravity using centrifugal force. Guests experience luxury, comfort, and safety while orbiting Earth sustainably.
Using NASA’s orbital debris data (orbitaldebris.jsc.nasa.gov), we improved our model to handle debris, radiation, and temperature extremes. We adjusted orbital altitude to low-debris zones, used radiation-shielding polyethylene composites, and added multi-layer insulation and radiator panels for heat control.
ECLIPSE’s operations prioritize reusability, solar energy, and closed-loop recycling, ensuring minimal environmental impact. Our phase-based plan moves from prototype development to full-scale orbital operations, eventually expanding to lunar tourism.
By merging innovation, sustainability, and ethical business practices, ECLIPSE aims to make space tourism not just a dream for the wealthy — but a responsible step toward a future where space is accessible, profitable, and sustainable for all.
projectDetails.details:
ECLIPSE is a visionary space tourism project designed to make low Earth orbit (LEO) accessible, comfortable, and sustainable. Our concept features a modified spaceplane that takes off like an airplane, reaches orbit, and docks with a rotating ring of capsules. These capsules simulate gravity through centrifugal force, allowing tourists to live and move naturally in space a first for orbital travel.

The project offers numerous benefits, including advancing commercial space travel, promoting STEM innovation, and supporting sustainable orbital infrastructure. It also contributes to research on artificial gravity, radiation shielding, and reusable spacecraft systems.

We used NASA’s orbital debris database to design safer orbital paths and incorporated heat-resistant materials, radiation protection, and thermal management systems into our model. Tools like Figma and Tinkercad were used for design visualization, while Python and Arduino-based simulations supported control concepts.

ECLIPSE is deeply creative because it blends aerospace engineering with hospitality, sustainability, and ethical commercialization. Our team focused on safety, environmental responsibility, and long-term scalability, ensuring that every design decision contributes to a future where space tourism is both profitable and planet-friendly — transforming the dream of living in orbit into reality.

projectDetails.name: BioNexus Engine
projectDetails.summary:
The BioNexus Engine is an intelligent biology knowledge system that transforms verified biological, ecological, and environmental data into real-time, actionable insights. Unlike static databases, it connects directly to a dynamic AI engine that continuously ingests and interprets data, allowing users to analyze ecosystems, assess habitability, and understand environmental dynamics instantly.

Through integrated sensing and camera data, the BioNexus Engine can evaluate temperature, climate, and ecological interactions to determine whether an environment is livable for humans. A compact version, embedded in the AstroNote suite, enables on-site detection and analysis during field or space missions.

This project addresses the challenge of fragmented, outdated biological information by creating a continuously updating “living engine” of knowledge. It is important because it bridges the gap between data and discovery—empowering researchers, educators, and explorers to make informed decisions about life, ecosystems, and sustainability in real time.
projectDetails.details:
The BioNexus Engine is a next-generation biology knowledge system designed to transform how we interact with biological and environmental data. It operates as a living, intelligent engine that continuously ingests, organizes, and interprets verified datasets from biological, ecological, and environmental sources. Using real-time data inputs—such as temperature, climate readings, and camera-based environmental sensing—the system provides immediate insights into ecosystem health, biodiversity, and human habitability.

The platform’s core AI engine powers both a web-based interface and a compact embedded version, the BioNexus Node, integrated into the AstroNote suite. This smaller engine allows on-site detection and analysis of life forms and environmental conditions, extending the system’s utility to field researchers and astronauts.

The project’s benefits include dynamic ecosystem mapping, predictive habitability modeling, and enhanced decision-making for sustainability and exploration. Its intended impact is to create a global, continuously evolving biological intelligence network that helps humans understand and preserve life on Earth—and beyond.

Technically, BioNexus was developed using Python, TensorFlow, and Node.js, with a real-time data pipeline connected via APIs and environmental sensors. The user interface is built with React for interactivity and TailwindCSS for design efficiency.

Creatively, the project bridges science and imagination: transforming biological data into a living, responsive entity. Our team prioritized data reliability, ethical AI integration, and usability for researchers, educators, and explorers.

projectDetails.name: Project Cyberpunk 2050
projectDetails.summary:
Project CyberPunk 2050 puts forward this idea for an autonomous waste management setup. It is a closed-loop kind of thing designed for missions off-world. Aerial drones called AeroScope go out and scan the terrain. They map it all to spot debris and classify what it is. Then mobile units known as EcoRover move around to pick up those items that got identified. Dedicated stations called EcoSorter handle the separation. They convert the waste into resources that can be reused. The main point here is combining AI detection based on vision with actual robotics. Waste gets sorted as organic or inorganic that way. It routes properly after that. Then it gets reclaimed or processed. This cuts down on the amount of waste you have to store. It lowers the need for resupplies too. Missions can last longer and stay more sustainable overall.
Check the README file to find instructions on running the project
projectDetails.details:
Project CyberPunk 2050 works as this full setup for handling waste on its own. It spots debris, figures out what it is, and directs it so stuff gets picked up and reused instead of just piled up or thrown away. In how it runs out there, the AeroScope drones fly around scanning the ground. They send over these image chunks to a service that processes them. Then there's this browser tool called the AeroScope Classifier. Operators use it to load up pictures. It tracks progress for each file. It passes the images along to a classify endpoint on the REST API. That spits back the file name, the guess on whether it's organic or inorganic, and how sure it is. Those results push the next steps. You can pull them out as a CSV file too, for checking records or digging deeper.

The upsides hit on logistics and the environment. Automated spotting plus sorting right in the field shrinks down the waste that's stored. It cuts back on needing resupplies for missions that last a long time, especially out in space. Plus, the stuff you recover turns into useful material again for life support setups, building things, or power systems. The whole idea aims to stretch out how long missions go. It lowers costs and risks along the way. The project pulls together a basic web interface using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. There's a straightforward REST API for the inference part. It ties in with an ML model that classifies, either running on the device or from afar. You have these robotic collectors called EcoRover. Stationary spots for processing are the EcoSorter units. AeroScope drones carry cameras and sensors to see what's going on. In a creative way, it connects up AI for vision, robots, and recovering materials. That forms a loop where stuff cycles back. Waste isn't just dead weight anymore. The team thought hard about tradeoffs. Like balancing computing power against battery life for inference on board. Setting confidence levels so you don't grab the wrong things. Making it tough against dust or bad light. Dealing with limits on what the mission can carry. And lining it all up with goals for being sustainable.

projectDetails.name: Project ENS-ADC
projectDetails.summary:
Sadiki (“My Smart Friend”) is an AI-powered web platform that helps children aged 3–18 overcome social and emotional barriers through empathetic one-to-one conversations. Using safe, adaptive dialogue, Sadiki supports children who feel isolated, shy, or unable to express themselves — encouraging confidence, empathy, and connection.
The system aligns with the UAE’s Vision for a Compassionate and Innovative Society and complies with the Child Rights Law (Wadeema), ensuring privacy, cultural safety, and parental supervision. A dedicated parent dashboard allows guardians to monitor their child’s progress, receive AI-generated recommendations, and better understand emotional development.
Globally, Sadiki addresses the universal issue of youth loneliness and communication barriers, while locally reflecting UAE values of family, education, and wellbeing. By combining ethical AI, NASA-inspired data principles, and emotional learning, Sadiki transforms technology into a bridge between hearts and minds — empowering every child to feel heard, understood, and included.
projectDetails.details:
What it does / How it works:
Sadiki (“My Smart Friend”) is a bilingual (Arabic–English) AI-powered emotional companion for children aged 3–18who struggle with communication or social connection. It works through a safe, web-based chat interface where the AI interacts one-to-one with a child — asking questions, suggesting social activities, and adapting to each user’s needs. A parental dashboard monitors progress and provides AI-generated guidance for guardians, aligning with UAE’s Wadeema Child Protection Law and digital ethics standards.

Benefits and Impact:
Sadiki helps children express emotions, build confidence, and develop empathy in a safe online environment. It reduces isolation by turning technology into a bridge for healthy emotional development. Locally, it supports the UAE’s vision of Innovation, Inclusion, and Family Wellbeing. Globally, it addresses youth loneliness and emotional disconnection — challenges that affect millions of children.

Tools and Technologies Used:
Built with HTML, TailwindCSS, and JavaScript; powered by Gemini AI API; hosted through Netlify for secure web deployment. Inspired by NASA’s Human Research Program, Sadiki applies communication and behavioral insights used in astronaut isolation studies to children’s emotional growth.

Creativity and Design Factors:
We designed Sadiki to be emotionally intelligent, culturally respectful, and adaptive. The project blends AI ethics, child psychology, and space-inspired human research, showing how science and empathy together can make technology human-centered.

projectDetails.name: Project ExoClassifier
projectDetails.summary:
The ExoClassifier is a Python-based tool that analyzes NASA’s Kepler, TESS, and K2 datasets to classify exoplanets as Confirmed, Candidate, or False Positive. Using a Random Forest Classifier, it predicts the status of planets based on features like orbital period, planet radius, and stellar properties. Additionally, it identifies potentially habitable planets with Earth-like characteristics, helping users focus on planets of interest.

This project addresses the challenge of making vast exoplanet data more accessible and actionable. By automating classification and providing insights into potentially habitable worlds, it allows both researchers and space enthusiasts to explore exoplanet demographics efficiently. Its importance lies in promoting data-driven exploration of other planetary systems and supporting the search for habitable planets beyond our solar system.

Developed entirely in Python using libraries such as pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, and seaborn, the tool is user-friendly and runs on standard hardware. By combining machine learning with scientific data analysis, it demonstrates a creative, practical approach to understanding the universe.
projectDetails.details:
The Exoplanet Classifier is a Python-based tool that analyzes datasets from NASA’s Kepler, TESS, and K2 missions to classify exoplanets as Confirmed, Candidate, or False Positive. Using a Random Forest Classifier, the project predicts planet status based on key features such as orbital period, planet radius, and stellar properties. It also identifies potentially habitable planets by checking for Earth-like characteristics.

The tool benefits researchers and enthusiasts by providing a fast, automated way to explore exoplanet data, detect patterns, and focus on planets of interest. The intended impact is to make space data more accessible, allowing users to discover potentially habitable planets and gain insights into exoplanet demographics.

The project is developed in Python using libraries such as pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, and seaborn, and runs on any standard computer without specialized hardware. Creativity lies in combining multiple datasets, applying machine learning for predictive classification, and generating easy-to-read visualizations. The project considered factors such as missing data, dataset consistency, and user accessibility, aiming to make it both informative and user-friendly.

projectDetails.name: Project Farmanauts: Terra Vitae
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Farmanauts: Terra Vitae, an interactive farming platform that combines a game with an informative app interface. It helps users learn about sustainable agriculture while having fun. In this platform, you can explore multiple farming games, such as buying animals, planting seeds, cultivating crops, and harvesting produce. There are also mini-games, including time-travel farms, parallel Earth simulations, and large-scale farming operations, creating a completely new experience for users. A chatbot assistant guides players, and NASA Earth Observation data is integrated to monitor weather, soil, and crop conditions.
The project addresses challenges like climate change, soil degradation, and low public interest in farming. By simulating real-world problems such as floods, droughts, and pest attacks, it teaches sustainable strategies, modern technology use, and ways to improve crop yields.
Farmanauts: Terra Vitae is important because it engages all ages and professional backgrounds, from kids and teens to farmers and experts, in a fun, interactive, and educational way. It promotes digital literacy, environmental awareness, and inspires people to care about agriculture.
projectDetails.details:
Farmanauts: Terra Vitae is a richly crafted educational farming simulation that brings together real environmental data, immersive mini-simulators, and reward systems to teach modern agriculture. When users open the app, they can explore modules like Parallel Earth, Time-Travel Farming, and Mars Operation Mode, each designed to help them experiment with techniques like crop rotation, precision irrigation, or climate adaptation. They earn badges and rewards, guided by a chatbot assistant and real-time feedback drawn from Earth observation ,NASA and other space agencies data.

The app serves as the central hub where users can integrate and understand more about the environmental data, our mission, and global farming trends. It provides insights, learning tools, and interactive dashboards, making it easier to visualize real-world farming challenges. Most importantly, the gaming experience is at the heart of the project — it is engaging, fun, and designed to teach complex agricultural and sustainability concepts through play.

Our three main interactive game sites are Farmaverse, Sustainable Farm Simulator, and GardenVenture. Each site offers different experiences — Farmaverse focuses on managing smart farms in virtual worlds, Sustainable Farm Simulator teaches climate-friendly farming techniques, and GardenVenture lets users plant, harvest, and handle real-time farming challenges using global data. Together, they make learning fun, dynamic, and inspiring for every age group.

This design offers multiple benefits: it turns abstract farming and sustainability concepts into tangible, playful experiences; it fosters curiosity, digital literacy, and environmental awareness; and it encourages cross-age learning by engaging children, farmers, scientists, and policymakers in one unified system. The intended impact is that young people who otherwise know little about farming will gain respect, insight, and interest; and professionals or decision makers may discover new ideas or strategies from simulated experiments.

Under the hood, we built the system using Java, HTML, CSS, and lightweight game engines like Scratch and Vox, supported by environmental APIs. The creativity lies in combining unusual simulators (parallel worlds, time travel, mass farms) inside an accessible, fun, and educational framework that almost no other game uses in agriculture.

As a team of middle-school students, we faced constraints—time, computing resources, learning curves—so we prioritized simplicity, usability, and maximum impact. We considered cultural diversity (so that people from different regions feel included), different age groups’ capabilities, the need for clear visuals and intuitive controls, and the balance between fun and learning.

In support of our approach, studies show that agricultural games and gamification can improve learning: for example, 54% of participants in farming simulations reported improved understanding of concepts in one study.

projectDetails.name: The Day the Sun Sneezed
projectDetails.summary:
Our animation, “The Day the Sun Sneezed,” is an innovative tale presentation that defines space weather for kids’ simple understanding. In simple animation and speech, it demonstrates how the Sun’s mighty “sneezes,” namely the solar flares and coronal mass ejections, move across space and impact astronauts, aviators, and even peasants on Earth. The tale also touches on how Earth’s magnetic field behaves as a superhero shield that saves us, and how solar storms can produce the stunning sky auroras.

This activity meets NASA’s challenge “Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings” by applying imagination as a tool for learning actual science. One is inspired by curiosity, educated on the interconnectedness of the Sun and Earth, and reminded that the story with the stars is just beginning for us
projectDetails.details:
My project, “Stellar Stories: The Day the Sun Sneezed,” is an entertaining and informative explanation of space weather via tale and images. The project demonstrates what occurs when the Sun emits massive energy bursts — such as solar flares and coronal mass ejections — and the ways in which these “solar sneezes” move across space and impact life on Earth.

In a 7-slide online presentation, I interwrote science facts and fantasy as a way of making the subject accessible to kids and non-experts in general. The slides detail how space weather affects astronauts, pilots, and farmers, what creates auroras, and how Earth’s magnetic field works as a superhero shield protection for us all.

Microsoft PowerPoint and royalty illustrations were used in making the project. The project is innovative as it narrates an entertaining tale out of complicated space science with names such as “The Sneezing Sun” and “Earth as a superhero.”

The goal is to encourage young students to do space science and understand how NASA observes and investigates the Sun so that it can protect our world.

projectDetails.details:

By connecting to Open Weather Map’s live satellite data, it shows real time air pollution levels, weather details, and forecasts for different cities in North America.

Our website translates the scientific data provided by Open Weather Map into clear, understandable information. Users can explore an interactive map, check how pollution might affect them, and get guidance on when it’s better to stay indoors or breathe easy outside.

The aim is to help people make smarter choices about their health and environment without needing to be experts themselves. This matters now more than ever, as clean air becomes a precious resource. The project combines powerful data, modern web, and a clean, subtle design to create a tool that’s both reliable and welcoming.

projectDetails.name: Designing Heat Resilient Cities Through Data Pathways
projectDetails.summary:
FortyGuard, an Abu Dhabi startup has developed the Temperature Dashboard, a the world's first hyperlocal temperature intelligence platform powered by FortyGuard’s proprietary global network of billions of ground sensors coupled with NASA's Earth Observation Data. By fusing satellite-derived imagery, land surface temperature and environmental indicators with hyper-local ground intelligence, the Temperature Dashboard provides high-resolution intelligence, insights and recommendations at the street and neighborhood level, 2 meters above the ground with 10m2 granularity.

At its core, the system is driven by Large Temperature Models (LTMs), the world’s first class of large AI models dedicated to temperature. These models transform raw data into interactive heat maps, street-level segmentation, and automated Heat Intelligence Reports that deliver clear actions for city leaders, environmental agencies, and public health authorities.

This directly addresses the challenge of “Data Pathways to Healthy Cities and Human Settlements” by creating pathways from space-based and ground-based data to hyperlocal heat intelligence that reduce dangerous heat days, lower energy demand, protect vulnerable communities, and guide sustainable urban growth.
projectDetails.details:
The Temperature Dashboard is a temperature intelligence and decision-support platform that integrates NASA Earth Observation Data — Sentinel-2 (vegetation, water, and urban indices), Landsat (segmentation and land-use classification), MODIS and VIIRS (land surface temperature and heat stress), and NDVI (vegetation health and density) — with FortyGuard’s exclusive global network of billions of on-the-ground mobile sensors. These combined datasets are processed through Large Temperature Models (LTMs) — the world’s first AI models dedicated to temperature — to generate high-resolution insights at the street and neighborhood level.

The platform delivers hyperlocal (2 meters above ground 10m2 granularity) historic, real time and predictive heat maps, satellite/street-level segmentation, environmental parameters and automated Heat Intelligence Reports that allow city planners, environmental agencies, and health authorities to make data-driven, climate-resilient decisions.

Benefits and Impact

  • Urban Planning: Identify and mitigate heat-vulnerable zones; guide cooling infrastructure such as shaded corridors and reflective surfaces.
  • Public Health: Reduce dangerous heat days and heat-related illnesses.
  • Energy Efficiency: Lower cooling energy demand by up to 8% annually.
  • Economic and Environmental Resilience: Increase property values and support sustainable urban growth.

Tools & Technologies
The system leverages NASA MODIS, VIIRS, Landsat, Sentinel-2, and NDVI datasets, together with FortyGuard’s LTMs and millions of local/global data points, processed through cloud computing and AI pipelines. Core technologies include Python, TensorFlow, PyTorch, GDAL, GeoPandas, Google Earth Engine, and advanced dashboard visualization frameworks.

Creativity & Design Considerations
FortGuard, an Abu Dhabi startup, is the first to create a dedicated class of large models for temperature, bridging space-based and ground-based data pathways into one scalable urban-climate intelligence platform. The team prioritizes accuracy, scalability, and real-world usability, ensuring the system can inform sustainable design and heat-resilience strategies — from Masdar City in Abu Dhabi to cities across the globe.

projectDetails.summary:
Human Life on Mars - Our Vision
NASA scientists have discovered bacteria on Mars that can support the growth of trees. In our model, we’ve added trees on the surface that produces oxygen. This oxygen is collected using a vacuum system and transported underground, where humans will live. In return, the carbon dioxide we exhale is sent back through another pipe to the trees, creating a sustainable air cycle.
For energy, we have two sources:
    1    Nuclear reactors – They provide heat and light, maintaining a suitable underground temperature for human life.
    2    Solar panels – These generate additional light energy.
Water is produced in two ways:
    1    By melting the Martian ice.
    2    By combining hydrogen and oxygen (H₂ + O = H₂O).
Humans will live underground for better temperature control and protection from meteoroids. Access is provided by a lift system capable of carrying 10,000 kg at a time.
Homes are designed in an igloo or dome shape, with sloped roofs to help debris or rain slide off easily.
Thank you!
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

Our project, Life on Mars – Our Vision, presents a model of how humans could survive on Mars using a self-sustaining ecosystem.

How it works:

NASA scientists have discovered bacteria on Mars that can support the growth of trees. In our design, these trees produce oxygen on the Martian surface. The oxygen is collected through a vacuum system and transported underground, where humans live. The carbon dioxide exhaled by humans is then sent back up to the trees, forming a continuous air cycle.

Energy is generated through nuclear reactors, which provide heat and light, and solar panels, which supply additional power. Water is obtained by melting Martian ice and by combining hydrogen and oxygen (H₂ + O → H₂O). Humans live in underground dome-shaped homes for protection from meteoroids and temperature control, accessed by a lift systemcarrying up to 10,000 kg.

Benefits and Impact:

This project promotes a vision for sustainable living beyond Earth. It demonstrates how natural cycles and renewable energy can support human life on another planet. The model highlights the importance of recycling resources and using clean energy — ideas that can also benefit life on Earth.

Tools and Materials Used:

We used cardboard, clay, paint, melted old plastic, bamboo and plastic straws to build the physical model. We have also made our project a sustainable model where we used recycled materials such as the lift is made up of empty tissue box and the cardboard we used was a old Panasonic cardboard box.

Creativity and Considerations:

Our team combined scientific facts with imagination to design a realistic and functional Mars habitat. We considered challenges such as oxygen production, temperature regulation, energy supply, and protection from meteoroids — and proposed innovative, practical solutions for each.

projectDetails.name: Project Galaxy Superstars
projectDetails.summary: Today, we come together not to discuss science fiction or fantasy, but of Impactor-2025. Impactor-2025 is a newly detected asteroid on a potential collision course with Earth. While the name might sound like science fiction, the risk it poses is profoundly serious even though it is only 15 meters in diameter. So today, we will be answering the question ‘What makes Impactor-2025 so dangerous’, and most importantly, ‘How can we stop ourselves from turning into dinosaurs?’ We will also discuss the steps humanity can take to prevent this disaster and other disasters that will arise. The goal is not to panic but to prepare ourselves because we do not want to be like the dinosaurs.
projectDetails.details:
Impactor 2025

Our project is all about saving Earth from a dangerous asteroid named Impactor 2025. This asteroid is huge and fast—it could hit Earth at 38,000 km/h, which is more than 500 times the speed of sound! If it did, it could make a giant fireball, destroy buildings, and even harm thousands of people. So we asked ourselves: how can humans stop it safely, quickly, and without spending too much money?

We researched several ways to prevent the asteroid from hitting Earth. Some ideas were extreme, like using a nuclear bomb in space, while others were slower, like a “gravity tractor” that gently pulls the asteroid away with a spacecraft’s gravity. We even looked at building underground bunkers or using a super-sharp penetrator attached to a sonic-speed spacecraft! After comparing all the options, we found that the kinetic impactor is the best choice. This method involves sending a spacecraft to crash into the asteroid at high speed, changing its path just enough to avoid Earth. It’s safe, proven by NASA’s DART mission, and costs the least—about $304 million, including ground monitoring and international cooperation.

Our project also includes planning and cost analysis. We figured out that detecting the asteroid just 100 days before impact saves money compared to spotting it years in advance. We calculated costs for launching the kinetic impactor, keeping track of the asteroid with telescopes, and coordinating with international space agencies. We even considered civil defense in case tiny fragments fall to Earth. By combining science, math, and creativity, we built a realistic plan to protect everyone without unnecessary risks.

This project is creative because we didn’t just present one idea—we imagined real-world scenarios, explored multiple solutions, compared their advantages and costs, and made the science easy to understand. We also worked as a team of four, sharing research, writing, and ideas. We discussed each step carefully, made calculations, and helped each other make the project clear and exciting for the audience.

In the end, Impactor 2025 shows that humans can save Earth from a dangerous asteroid if we act smart, work together, and use science creatively. With teamwork, careful planning, and the kinetic impactor method, we can protect our planet and make sure the Earth stays safe for everyone!

Thank You!!!

projectDetails.summary: MarsCycle is a waste management and recycling system that supports sustainable living on Mars. The project focuses on managing, reusing, and recycling inorganic waste, such as fabrics, packaging materials, structural elements, and EVA waste produced by astronauts during long missions. The MarsCycle app allows crew members to track waste generation, monitor recycling efficiency, and manage projects that turn materials into useful resources like insulation, furniture, or reinforcement components. By promoting a circular system, MarsCycle reduces the need to transport extra supplies from Earth, saves energy, and cuts down on waste buildup on the Martian surface. This project addresses the challenge of maintaining a clean and resource-efficient habitat while using local resources. MarsCycle prepares future planetary missions to operate sustainably and independently, ensuring environmental protection and mission success.
projectDetails.details: MarsCycle is a digital waste management system designed for a Mars habitat. It helps astronauts track, manage, and recycle inorganic waste like fabrics, packaging, foams, EVA bags, aluminum structures, and carbon byproducts. Crew members use a Glide app to log materials, assign them to projects, and monitor recycling processes. This turns waste into useful items such as insulation panels, furniture, structural reinforcements, or filters. The system lowers reliance on resources from Earth, reduces waste buildup, and improves resource recovery. It supports a sustainable, circular economy for space missions. MarsCycle repurposes everyday waste for practical uses that also boost morale. It considers material properties, energy efficiency, safety, and ease of monitoring, all through a user-friendly no-code platform.

projectDetails.name: Project Hackstronauts 5.0
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, “Will it Rain on My Parade”, is an interactive weather risk visualization tool that allows users to explore real-world weather data through an animated 3D globe interface. The system integrates NASA-based datasets to provide temperature, precipitation, and climate insights across different geographical coordinates. Users can select locations directly on the rotating Earth model to analyze local weather risks and patterns.

This project addresses the challenge of making complex climate data more accessible and engaging. Instead of reading static charts, users can intuitively visualize global weather behavior in real time. The interactive design promotes environmental awareness and supports better decision-making in areas such as travel planning, agriculture, and disaster preparedness.

By combining scientific data with an immersive interface, our tool demonstrates how technology can make global climate understanding both educational and visually impactful.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, Weather Risk GlobeViewer, is an interactive visualization tool designed to help users analyze weather risk patterns across the planet using real NASA data. The system allows users to rotate a 3D globe, click on any region, and instantly view its latitude and longitude, along with real or test-based weather metrics such as precipitation and temperature.

The tool is built in Java using Swing for the graphical interface . We integrated NASA’s public weather datasets to simulate risk prediction, helping visualize potential climate or disaster-prone regions.

The main benefit of this project is to make complex environmental data intuitive and engaging, supporting scientists, students, and decision-makers in quickly identifying global weather risks. The 3D globe enhances interactivity and spatial awareness compared to traditional flat maps.

Our team focused on creativity, performance, and accessibility—designing a simple but data-rich experience that brings NASA’s mission of understanding Earth’s systems closer to everyone through visualization and technology.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

We used AI assistance through ChatGPT (OpenAI GPT-5) to support the development and refinement of our project. Specifically, AI tools were used to:

Accelerate code development: Helping debug and optimize Java and rendering code for the 3D globe visualization.

Enhance creativity: Suggesting ways to integrate interactive elements, such as globe rotation, coordinate selection, and Earth texture mapping.

Improve documentation: Assisting in drafting clear and concise technical summaries and descriptions for our project submission.

All final code, data visualization logic, and NASA data integrations were manually implemented, tested, and verified by our team. AI was used strictly as a coding and writing assistant, not for autonomous generation of scientific results, data, or visualizations.

No AI-generated images, videos, or audio were used in this project. All textures and Earth map layers are sourced from publicly available, non-AI NASA imagery.

node.excerpt: We are a multidisciplinary team of innovators, problem-solvers, and dreamers tackling one of the most urgent issues in space exploration is debris on Mars. Our mission is to design solutions that keep Mars sustainable, safe, and accessible for fut...

projectDetails.name: Project RRP
projectDetails.summary: During a three-year Mars mission, an eight-person crew generating 12,600 kg of inorganic waste will rely on autonomous Regolith Reforger Pods—micro-foundries that transform trash into smart composite “bio-stones.” Crew waste is color-sorted in coded, fire-retardant bags, weighed, tagged, and sent through a low-pressure tram to a sealed shred-and-baler that sterilizes at 140 °C, shreds, and compresses cubes for processing. Each 150 kg Reforger Pod converts 15–25 kg of waste per day using microwave sintering, catalytic depolymerization, and regolith blending to create oxygen-releasing, radiation-shielding blocks that neutralize perchlorates. Metals are melted for reinforcement, polymers cracked into binders and syngas for heat, and regolith magnetically filtered for iron-rich fines. Daily energy use averages 30 kWh, with crew time limited to 1–2 hours per week. Two pods (approximately 800 kg total) can eliminate all inorganic waste, producing 16–20 m³ of durable construction material while reducing resupply needs. The modular system costs $80–155 million including research & development, hardware, and integration, with later units falling to $20–35 million. Outputs build habitats, landing pads, and shielding, while the photocatalytic matrix gradually releases oxygen and detoxifies soil, transforming waste management into a self-sustaining, planet-building process.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, Regolith Reforger Pods, introduces an autonomous system designed to recycle all inorganic waste produced during a Mars mission into usable construction materials. It works by collecting, sterilizing, shredding, and processing crew waste such as plastics, metals, and textiles. The waste is combined with Martian surface material (dust and crushed rock) using microwave heating, catalytic breakdown, and material blending to produce durable, oxygen-releasing “bio-stones.” These blocks can be used to build habitats, landing pads, and radiation shields.

The system offers multiple benefits: it eliminates waste, reduces resupply needs from Earth, creates strong, radiation-protective materials, and supports long-term surface sustainability. Additionally, the photocatalytic nature of the produced material allows it to slowly release oxygen and neutralize harmful surface chemicals like perchlorates, helping to prepare the environment for future missions.

We used a combination of automation engineering, thermal and materials science modeling, and embedded AI control systems to design the Reforger Pods. Concept tools included Python for system simulations, CAD software for mechanical design, and thermal simulation software for validating heat transfer efficiency.

This project is creative because it reimagines waste as a resource for planetary construction and environmental transformation, merging recycling, manufacturing, and terraforming in a single self-sustaining loop. Our team considered crew safety, energy efficiency, scalability, reliability under Martian conditions, and minimal crew time to make the system practical for future human exploration.

projectDetails.name: Insidious
projectDetails.summary: Our project is an interactive story, targeted to children of ages 10-17. It explores the alluring beauty of the solar flare, and the dangerous impacts it has, told via the journey of an aspiring artist. It serves as an audiobook incorporated with interactive elements, that provides an engaging experience while including all necessary factual information regarding solar flares.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is titled Insidious, and is an interactive story that was created using Genially. The main character of the story is an aspiring artist, Ilan, whose creativity is rekindled by the viewing of a magnificent natural phenomenon, that is, the solar flare. As the story progresses, we learn more about what solar flares really are, and the harmful impacts they pose with heavy exposure. It is divided into three chapters, requiring the reader to go through each one in sequence before moving on the next. Each page is also supported by an audio, eliminating boredom that may be associated with simply reading words on a screen. Moreover, the pages contain interactive elements that can be clicked on to learn more about the information written on that page. After reading through the three chapters, there is a quiz to test the reader's knowledge about solar flares, based on what they have read.

Upon completion of this, there is a "Solar Flare Explorer" that redirects the reader to a website containing actual NASA datasets. This enables the reader to get detailed information and imagery from NASA by simply selecting the dates and wavelengths of the solar flares they would like to explore.
projectDetails.aiReferences: AI was instrumental in enhancing Insidious in making it more interactive, precise, and gripping for our 10–17 year-old target audience. First, it was used to create innovative and dynamic visuals that depicted Ilan's artwork, capturing the essence and peril of solar flares in an attractive and appealing display for young learners. AI was also used to aid in the creation of the Solar Flare Explorer in resolving bugs in the programming and streamlining the system to make it smoother and more fluid, enabling users to effortlessly access NASA datasets, sort and filter based on dates and wavelengths, and navigate high-detail solar flare images. These uses of AI not only added pizzazz to the visual presentation of the story but also enabled that hard scientific data about solar flares could be conveyed in simple, entertaining, and interesting terms for kids and adolescents.
