projectDetails.details:
PROJECT – METEOR MADNESS

TEAM NAME – INFINITY MINDS

TEAM OWNER – ADITYA NATH SUNIL

TEAM MEMBERS

1)     NEVAAN MENON

2)     AVRAJ SINGH BHATTHAL

3)     RAYAN CHAMKHI

 Our project, titled “Meteor Madness,” is an ambitious exploration into the challenges and solutions surrounding meteor impacts on Earth. The very name symbolizes both the chaotic unpredictability of meteors and the systematic determination of humanity to confront and control that chaos.

At its core, Meteor Madness is not just a creative title—it is a simulation-driven framework designed to illustrate the mechanics of meteors, their destructive potential, and the strategies available for defense. It merges scientific accuracy, engineering innovation, and educational outreach into a single cohesive vision.

Meteor Madness begins with the detection stage. Our simulation models how telescopes, observatories, and radar systems identify and track near-Earth objects (NEOs). This stage emphasizes the importance of orbital mechanics, predictive algorithms, and early-warning systems. Without detection, there can be no defense.

From detection, the project advances to trajectory analysis. Using real NASA datasets, we calculate the velocity, angle of entry, and potential impact sites for hypothetical meteors. These data points are visualized in interactive dashboards, enabling users to see in real time how minor changes in trajectory can alter global outcomes.

The simulation engine at the heart of Meteor Madness allows users to modify parameters such as meteor size, composition, speed, and atmospheric entry angle. This transforms abstract astrophysics into tangible, interactive learning experiences.

We incorporate realistic atmospheric entry models. These simulate frictional heating, fragmentation, and the energy released as the meteor travels through the atmosphere. The simulation highlights both airburst phenomena (like the Chelyabinsk event) and direct ground impacts (like Tunguska or Chicxulub).

When impacts occur in Meteor Madness, the simulation demonstrates multiple layers of consequences. Shockwaves ripple across terrain, craters form, tsunamis rise, seismic vibrations spread, and environmental disruptions cascade. Each effect is visualized in high-resolution geospatial maps.

To make the simulation relevant, Meteor Madness integrates United States Geological Survey (USGS) datasets for terrain, elevation, and population density. This allows users to see not only physical destruction but also human vulnerability.

Beyond the scientific core, Meteor Madness is designed as an educational and decision-support platform. Policymakers can test mitigation strategies, scientists can experiment with models, and students can engage in planetary defense learning.

Mitigation strategies form the second half of Meteor Madness. Users can simulate interventions such as kinetic impactors, gravity tractors, laser ablation, or nuclear deflection. Each intervention is measured by feasibility, cost, and required timeline.

The platform also includes failure simulations. What happens if deflection attempts fail? What are the backup strategies? This component underscores the reality that planetary defense is complex and uncertain.

Meteor Madness is more than science—it is about preparedness and communication. The platform converts complex astrophysical models into intuitive graphics, enabling non-scientists to understand risks without oversimplifying them.

In addition to technical models, we built a creative extension within Minecraft Education. Here, our team visualized meteors, shelters, survival structures, and automated meteor builders. This creative dimension allowed us to translate planetary defense into a hands-on, interactive narrative for all ages.

The Automatic Meteor Builder became a symbolic machine within our design. It demonstrated how meteors can be modelled, replicated, and studied systematically rather than imagined abstractly.

We powered this creative engine with a fish-charged aquarium system, symbolizing renewable and unconventional energy sources that might one day be adapted for space engineering.

Our shelters within the Meteor Madness project were not just underground bunkers—they were designed with redundancy, storage systems, and living infrastructure, modelling how human resilience might look in post-impact survival scenarios.

The project emphasizes interdisciplinary integration. It blends planetary science, geophysics, computer simulation, architecture, and creative education. Each element supports the larger narrative of planetary defense. 

Meteor Madness teaches us that meteors are not just distant rocks—they are dynamic cosmic forces that interact with Earth in complex ways.

Through this project, we demonstrate that even small teams can create decision-making tools capable of visualizing planetary-scale hazards.

One of the strengths of Meteor Madness is its scalability. It can simulate small, localized impacts or massive extinction-level events. This flexibility allows educators, policymakers, and researchers to tailor the experience to their context.

Meteor Madness also contains multi-layered outputs. A scientist can dive deep into physics models, while a policymaker sees executive summaries, and a student sees visual storytelling.

The name “Meteor Madness” reflects the dual nature of meteors—chaos and opportunity. Chaos in their unpredictability, but opportunity in how humanity responds.

Meteor Madness highlights early detection as the first line of defense. Without time, no mitigation strategy can succeed.

It emphasizes international cooperation, because asteroid impacts are not limited by borders.

It shows that data integration—NASA datasets, USGS terrain maps, and predictive analytics—creates power only when transformed into visual, interactive models.

Meteor Madness integrates machine learning components that adjust impact predictions based on uncertainties, reflecting the reality of incomplete data.

The project underlines the role of public engagement. Without public understanding, planetary defence strategies cannot gain funding or support.

Meteor Madness doubles as a training simulator. It could be used in classrooms, workshops, and policy exercises to strengthen planetary preparedness.

Every element of the project reflects systems thinking. Meteors are not just about physics—they are about consequences, preparation, and resilience.

Meteor Madness is sensitive to the fact that while meteors inspire fascination, they also represent existential threats.

Our platform balances this sensitivity by presenting risk factually, carefully, and constructively.

The inclusion of creative builds in Minecraft Education ensures accessibility for younger learners, while advanced dashboards provide value for experts. 

Meteor Madness bridges the gap between imagination and science.

It transforms a global hazard into a learning opportunity.

The long-term vision of Meteor Madness is to create a blueprint for planetary defense simulation systems.

This blueprint can be adapted, expanded, and improved as new datasets and technologies emerge.

Meteor Madness is not just about meteors—it is about human resilience, foresight, and the power of simulation.

It demonstrates that virtual platforms can model real-world planetary defense strategies.

It highlights the importance of combining data science, geoscience, and creative platforms.

Meteor Madness is both a warning and a promise.

A warning of what could happen without preparation, and a promise that through creativity, science, and teamwork, we can be ready.

This project inspires curiosity, urgency, and innovation.

It is a fusion of hard science and imaginative design.

It shows that even in virtual environments, we can practice defending Earth.

Meteor Madness is more than madness—it is method in the madness.

It is the spark that transforms fear into action.

It is the framework that shows how humanity can survive the unimaginable.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Our team decided to use Minecraft Education as the primary platform for design and simulation because it provides a versatile environment for combining creativity, problem-solving, and interactive learning. Minecraft allowed us to not only visualize planetary science challenges but also to prototype engineering solutions in an interactive, hands-on way. From the very beginning, we treated this project as both a scientific challenge and a creative journey.

We began by designing a functional water elevator that served as the transportation hub of our world. The water elevator allowed us to move vertically with efficiency, symbolizing how advanced engineering can support survival and mobility in extreme scenarios. It was not just a simple construction but a metaphor for resilience and adaptability.

Next, we constructed a house that became our operational base. This house was not a standard build but an integrated working laboratory where we initiated our main project of meteor simulation. The structure was carefully designed with space for storage, workbenches, and access points to other experimental areas.

The centerpiece of our innovation was the Automatic Meteor Builder. This machine represented the heart of our project. We engineered it to generate meteors systematically, mimicking the concept of celestial bodies forming and descending. The Automatic Meteor Builder became both a scientific model and a creative engine, allowing us to control meteor size, frequency, and direction. This design required iterative problem-solving, teamwork, and constant refinement.

To power our meteor builder, we implemented a unique aquatic solution. We built a large aquarium filled with fish, and through imaginative design, the fishes were used to “charge” the Automatic Meteor Builder. This mechanism symbolized the idea of converting natural resources into usable energy—a futuristic concept where even biological systems could contribute to planetary defense or space engineering.

Our team also recognized the importance of safety and preparedness. Anticipating the destructive power of meteors, we built three underground shelters. These shelters were equipped with storage units, supplies, and safe living areas, designed to withstand hypothetical meteor impacts. Each underground chamber had specific functions—one for resources, one for emergency survival kits, and one for long-term habitation. Together, they formed a network of resilience beneath the surface.

The construction process itself was gradual and methodical. We started small, experimenting with meteor prototypes day by day. Each session of teamwork brought improvements to design, functionality, and efficiency. Over time, our meteors became more sophisticated, larger, and visually impactful. By the final phase, we had not only created functioning meteors but also developed a fully immersive ecosystem of survival, defense, and experimentation.

This project demonstrated not only technical creativity but also systems thinking. We combined natural elements (water, fish, underground terrain) with mechanical designs (elevators, meteor builders, shelters) to create a holistic model of planetary defense. It highlighted how limited resources, when applied with innovation, can achieve complex outcomes.

Our use of Minecraft Education was not just entertainment—it was a serious design platform. Every block we placed represented an idea, every red stone connection symbolized circuitry, and every structure symbolized resilience in the face of cosmic hazards. We learned to balance functionality with creativity, aesthetics with survival, and imagination with problem-solving.

By the end of the project, our team had developed:

  • A fully working water elevator for mobility.
  • A central house-laboratory as the command hub.
  • An Automatic Meteor Builder capable of producing impact events.
  • A fish-powered aquarium generator for symbolic energy sourcing.
  • Three reinforced underground shelters for survival and storage.
  • Multiple meteor structures built progressively with increasing scale and detail.

This project also emphasized team collaboration. Each team member contributed to different aspects: some focused on structural engineering, others on automation, and others on creative energy solutions. Together, we learned the importance of communication, division of labor, and constant iteration.

The sensitivity of this project lies in its connection to real-world planetary defense challenges. Meteors and asteroids represent genuine threats to Earth, and while our simulation existed within Minecraft Education, the underlying principles mirror scientific questions: How do we prepare for cosmic impacts? How do we balance resource usage with safety? How can creativity lead to new strategies for survival?

We believe our project demonstrates that even within a game-based educational platform, it is possible to design serious models that inspire scientific thinking, problem-solving, and innovation. By combining imagination with technical rigor, we transformed a virtual world into a living laboratory for planetary defense.

As we completed the final meteors, we realized the true success of the project was not only in the builds but in the story of transformation. We started with an idea, developed systems, built defenses, and simulated hazards. Along the way, we gained insights into teamwork, design thinking, and resilience.

Our final world in Minecraft is a fusion of engineering, creativity, and survival strategy. It stands as a demonstration that the next generation of learners can prototype planetary defense solutions in virtual platforms long before implementing them in reality.

This project, though symbolic, points toward a future where education, simulation, and creativity converge to prepare humanity for the challenges of space.

NASA datasets include information about known asteroids and the United States Geological Survey provides critical information that could enable modeling the effects of asteroid impacts, but this data needs to be integrated to enable effective visualization and decision making. Your challenge is to develop an interactive visualization and simulation tool that uses real data to help users model asteroid impact scenarios, predict consequences, and evaluate potential mitigation strategies. (Planetary Science Division)

projectDetails.name: TheBloomWatcher
projectDetails.summary:
We developed TheBloomWatcher, a web-based tool that visualizes and monitors plant blooming events across the globe using NASA Earth observation data. By leveraging MODIS and Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, BloomWatch generates interactive NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) maps and time-series graphs, showing how vegetation changes over time and highlighting bloom events. Users can select any country and year to see the average NDVI, bloom intensity, and overlapping trends from multiple satellites.

This tool addresses the challenge by providing a dynamic, scalable way to track vegetation health, bloom timing, and seasonal changes. It supports applications in agricultural monitoring, ecosystem assessment, and phenology studies, helping identify periods of peak flowering, detect environmental stress, and manage crops or natural habitats more effectively.

BloomWatch is important because it turns vast satellite datasets into intuitive visualizations, enabling scientists, farmers, and policymakers to make informed decisions. By combining high temporal resolution with global coverage, it allows trend analysis across multiple years, helping users monitor ecosystem changes, predict flowering patterns, and respond to environmental challenges. Its real-time visual insights empower actionable conservation and agricultural management strategies.
projectDetails.details:
Bloomwatch is a web application that allows users to explore vegetation changes and bloom events across the globe using satellite imagery. The app integrates multiple data sources, including MODIS and Sentinel-2 satellite collections, and displays them on interactive maps alongside NDVI time-series charts. It is designed to provide both scientific insight and a visually engaging interface, allowing users to examine vegetation health, bloom events, and differences between sensors over time.

When the user opens Bloomwatch, they are presented with a dropdown menu to select a country and a multi-select menu to choose one or more years. These inputs determine the scope of the data that will be loaded. Once the form is submitted, the Flask backend processes the request by generating the map layers and the NDVI time-series chart. The dropdowns use Select2, which allows for searching and multi-selection.

[upload_image.UIOverview]
Image suggestion: Screenshot of the main interface showing country and year dropdowns, checkboxes for toggles, and the animated particles background.

The main interactive component of Bloomwatch is the map, created using Folium. The map can display multiple layers:

  1. MODIS NDVI layer: This layer represents the average NDVI (vegetation density) for the selected year, calculated from the MODIS MOD13Q1 image collection. The process involves filtering MODIS images to the selected year and country, computing the mean NDVI per image, and then averaging across all images for that year. If a country is selected, the NDVI values are clipped to the country’s boundaries using the USDOS/LSIB_SIMPLE/2017 dataset. The map uses a color palette from red to dark green, indicating very low to dense vegetation.
  2. MODIS bloom layer: This layer highlights areas of significant vegetation increase by calculating the difference between the current and previous year’s MODIS NDVI. Pixels with differences above 50 are displayed, showing regions with unusually high vegetation growth. The user can toggle this layer on and off.
  3. Sentinel-2 bloom layer: Sentinel-2 imagery provides higher-resolution data. The app computes NDVI from bands B8 (NIR) and B4 (red), averages images for the current and previous year, and calculates the difference. Pixels with a difference above 0.1 are displayed as bloom regions.
  4. Overlap of MODIS and Sentinel bloom: To improve confidence, Bloomwatch can show areas where both MODIS and Sentinel detect bloom events. These regions appear purple, combining the two bloom layers and allowing users to easily see high-confidence growth areas.

The NDVI time-series chart is another key component. This chart shows NDVI changes over the year, with one point every 16 days (the MODIS acquisition period). For each date, the mean NDVI across the country is calculated. The values are scaled by 10,000 for storage efficiency, then plotted in Python using Matplotlib.

This chart is saved as a PNG and displayed in the HTML template within a floating overlay. The overlay updates whenever the user selects a different country or year.

The application includes several UX enhancements. A loading overlay with a spinner is displayed whenever Earth Engine is processing data, ensuring users know the system is working. Legends for NDVI and bloom layers are dynamically displayed, helping users interpret the color-coded data.

Bloomwatch is highly configurable. Users can select which layers to display using checkboxes (NDVI, bloom, Sentinel bloom), and they can select multiple years to compare datasets. The backend automatically clips and reduces resolution for large datasets to maintain performance.

From a technical perspective, the project demonstrates full-stack geospatial data visualization. The backend (Flask + Earth Engine + Python/Matplotlib) handles data retrieval, processing, and plotting. The frontend (HTML/CSS/JS/Folium) handles interactive visualization, user input, and overlaying dynamic charts and maps. This architecture allows for flexible, multi-layered exploration of vegetation dynamics, making the app useful for research, education, and environmental monitoring.

In terms of applications, Bloomwatch can be used to:

  • Track seasonal and yearly vegetation changes.
  • Compare sensor datasets (MODIS vs Sentinel-2) for ecological research.
  • Identify regions of rapid growth or decline for agriculture or forestry monitoring.
  • Provide an educational tool for teaching about vegetation health, climate impact, and satellite monitoring.

By combining maps, multi-sensor bloom layers, interactive toggles, and time-series charts, Bloomwatch offers a robust platform to analyze and visualize vegetation patterns in a highly interactive and educational way.

challengeDetails.title: BloomWatch: An Earth Observation Application for Global Flowering Phenology
challengeDetails.excerpt: Witness the pulse of life across our planet! From season to season and year to year, Earth’s vegetation is constantly changing, providing critical information on plant species, crops, seasonal effects, pollen sources, and changes in plant phenology (the relationship between seasonal changes and climate and biological phenomena in plants). Your challenge is to harness the power of NASA Earth observations to create a dynamic visual tool that displays and/or detects plant blooming events around the globe—just like pollinators do–and that advances solutions for monitoring, predicting, or managing vegetation. (Earth Science Division)

projectDetails.name: ClimeCheck
projectDetails.summary:
This project is about creating a weather prediction and analysis app using NASA’s Earth observation data. The app helps users check the chances of different weather conditions like very hot, hot, cold, very cold, rainy, and windy for a specific place and time of the year. It uses historical weather data to predict future patterns.

The main goal is to make a user-friendly dashboard where users can select a location or date to see weather predictions. The results are shown clearly through graphs, charts, and maps, making it easy to understand weather trends and plan activities based on them.
projectDetails.details:
1. Our project is a weather prediction and analysis app using NASA Earth observation data. It predicts conditions like hot, cold, rainy, or windy for different locations and times, helping users plan activities and understand climate trends.

2.Objective:

- Create a personalized dashboard for weather queries.

- Show probabilities of different weather events.

- Use charts and maps to display results clearly.

- Design a user-friendly interface for easy location selection

3.The app uses NASA’s historical weather data. Machine learning models analyze the data to predict weather probabilities. Users select a location and time, and the system displays likely weather outcomes with visuals.

4.Tools used:

Power BI: Data analysis and visualization

Orange: Data mining and model training

5.The project combines real NASA data, machine learning, and visual dashboards to make weather prediction simple, interactive, and easy to understand.

6.It helps users plan better, learn about weather trends, and understand climate changes. The project also supports education and research on weather and climate analysis.

7.Integrated the Air Taxi concept, where accurate weather forecasting supports safe flight scheduling and route optimization for air mobility systems.

challengeDetails.title: Will It Rain On My Parade?
challengeDetails.excerpt: If you’re planning an outdoor event—like a vacation, a hike on a trail, or fishing on a lake—it would be good to know the chances of adverse weather for the time and location you are considering. There are many types of Earth observation data that can provide information on weather conditions for a particular location and day of the year. Your challenge is to construct an app with a personalized interface that enables users to conduct a customized query to tell them the likelihood of “very hot,” “very cold,” “very windy,” “very wet,” or “very uncomfortable” conditions for the location and time they specify. (Earth Science Division)

projectDetails.name: Project Interstellar Designers
projectDetails.summary:
Our project was about designing a space habitat where people can live safely and comfortably while caring for the environment. We focused on making it sustainable, meaning it can reuse resources and doesn’t rely too much on Earth.

We planned the layout carefully so everything is connected and easy to reach. The Living Quarters are close to the Kitchen and Storage so astronauts can get food and supplies easily. The Control Hub is in the center, linking all areas like the Greenhouse, Lab, and Exercise Zone. The Greenhouse grows fresh food and makes oxygen, while the Lab is for doing experiments. The Exercise Zone, Common Area, and Hygiene Module help astronauts stay healthy, clean, and happy.

We focused on saving energy and reusing water, air, and waste. The Greenhouse helps create a small ecosystem where plants recycle air and grow with less water using hydroponics.

To share our ideas, we made a website and an animation. The website explains each part of the habitat, and the animation shows how astronauts live and work inside it.

Overall, our project shows how people can live, work, and grow in space in a smart and sustainable way.
projectDetails.details: Our habitat layout is very sustainable. We recycle and reuse our resources carefully to reduce waste. We also added an exercise area and a common area to help astronauts stay healthy and improve their mental well-being by giving them time to rest and recharge. The greenhouse plays an important role by recycling carbon dioxide and producing fresh oxygen. Our website, which we created using Canva, explains each part of the habitat and shows how it supports life in space. The intended impact of our project is to show how people can live comfortably and responsibly in space. While designing, our team focused on important factors such as sustainability, relaxation, and mental well-being to make life in space more balanced and human-friendly.

challengeDetails.title: Your Home in Space: The Habitat Layout Creator
challengeDetails.excerpt: Space habitats are “homes in space” that keep crew members healthy and able to execute their mission. Whether located on a planetary surface or in space, habitats must support critical functions such as waste management, thermal control, life support, communications, power, stowage, food storage and preparation, medical care, sleep, and exercise. Space habitat concepts can involve a diverse array of materials, geometries, and layouts. Your challenge is to create a visual tool that enables users to define a space habitat’s shape/volume and explore possible layout options. (Exploration Systems Development Mission Directorate)

projectDetails.name: The NASA-Grade Asteroid Impact Visualization & Simulation Tool
projectDetails.summary: The project combines data science, visualization, and simulation to provide both scientists and the general public with an engaging and educational experience. By adjusting asteroid parameters (e.g., size, speed, composition, angle of entry), users can instantly visualize the outcomes through dynamic maps, charts, and animations.
projectDetails.details:
• Purpose:
    To help users understand the risks and impacts of asteroid collisions on Earth and support disaster preparedness and planetary defense efforts.
    • Interactive input for asteroid properties (size, mass, speed, entry angle, composition).
    • Real-time visualization of impact zones on a world map.
    • Simulations of secondary effects (fireball radius, shockwaves, tsunamis, climate effects).
    • Integration of NASA datasets (NEOs – Near-Earth Objects) for realistic scenarios.
    • Educational animations and 3D impact simulations for better engagement.
    • Scientists and researchers studying planetary defense.
    • Educators and students interested in space science.
    • Policy-makers for disaster management planning.
    • The general public to raise awareness of asteroid impact risks.
  • Innovation:
    Unlike static models, this tool offers real-time interactivity, making scientific data accessible and understandable. It bridges the gap between complex astrophysics and public education, while also serving as a valuable reference for space and defense communities.

projectDetails.details:
Space Habitat Designer is an interactive tool that enables users to design, configure, and visualize space habitats for future missions. It provides an accurate review on habitat feasibility, space utilization, and crew wellbeing metrics.

The application allows users to:

1. Choose from 4 architectural designs:

Cylinder , Traditional rotating design (like ISS modules) with artificial gravity

Sphere for maximum volumetric efficiency for stationary habita

Rotating ring (Stanford Torus concept) for sustained artificial gravity

Modular, connected structure for expandable missions

2. slider control:

- Length/radius (5-50 meters)

- Diameter (4-20 meters)

- Crew size (2-12 astronauts)

3. systems configuration : 11 basic modules:

- Life support (oxygen generation, carbon dioxide purification)

- Power systems (solar panels, batteries)

- Thermal control (temperature regulation)

- Communications (radio, data links)

- Waste management (recycling systems)

- Water systems (recycling, storage)

- Storage (storage of supplies, equipment, and tools)

- Food preparation/storage (kitchen, freezers)

- Medical care (health care facilities)

- Sleeping quarters (privacy and comfort for crew)

- Exercise (maintaining bone/muscle health)

4. Visualize in 3D , Three viewing modes:

2D Schematic: Animated technical drawings

Floor Plan: Interior layout with color-coded modules

Realistic 3D: Interactive WebGL model with drag to rotate, scroll to zoom navigation

benefits : Space Habitat Designer serves space agencies, engineers, and educators by enabling them to create fast, cost effective prototypes of space habitats. It also speeds up design cycles from months or years to minutes, reduces mission planning costs by identifying constraints early on, improves crew safety through optimal space planning, and inspires the next generation of space engineers by making complex space engineering accessible to all. Helping humanity advance toward a sustainable presence in space while saving millions of dollars in development costs and ensuring the safety and well-being of astronauts through data-driven design decisions.

Coding Languages:

JavaScript (ES6+) - Core application logic

HTML5 - Structure and canvas rendering

CSS3 - Styling and animations

Libraries & Frameworks:

3D graphics rendering, WebGL wrapper

Lucide React Icons - UI iconography

Google Fonts - Typography (Orbitron, Rajdhani, Share Tech Mono)

Hardware/Software:

Web Browser with WebGL support

ASUS Vivobook

Key Technical Features:

physics calculations (volume, area, efficiency)

Canvas 2D API for schematic drawings

WebGL for 3D rendering

Event-driven architecture

Responsive design

Visual Design:

Space themed aesthetics with futuristic fonts and glowing effects

Color coded modules for instant visual recognition

Gradient backgrounds that looks like space

Animated elements like the rotating habitats

User experience:

Easy to use drag and drop controls

Natural detection ,info tips when scrolling/clicking

Real time updates to statistics during design

Color coded alerts (red/yellow/green) for capacity overruns or crew space shortages

Accessibility:

Touch gesture support for tablets/phones

Keyboard friendly interface

Clear visual hierarchy

High contrast text

Factors that the team considered:

Engineering constraints:

Shape efficiency: sphere = 90% usable area, cylinder = 70% (structural volume / usable volume)

Gravity options: Rotating habitats (cylinder/torus) enable artificial gravity for bone health

Unit size: Based on actual dimensions of the International Space Station module and NASA studies on habitats

Educational value:

real terminology: actual terms used in aerospace

Accurate physics: volume formulas for cylinders, spheres, and tori

System interdependence: explains why all vital systems are needed

projectDetails.name: Luna's Mission | Kosmitellica
projectDetails.summary:
It’s a children’s picture book called Luna’s Mission, which introduces young readers to space weather through the eyes of a curious girl named Luna. The story follows Luna as she notices strange things and sets out on a mission to learn more. She learns by watching videos online, chatting with a farmer at the market, listening to her pilot uncle, and joining a space camp Q&A with an astronaut. Through these moments, Luna discovers how solar flares and geomagnetic storms affect life on Earth

This project addresses the challenge of making science topics accessible and engaging for children. By using storytelling, it encourages curiosity, observation, and critical thinking.
It’s important because it helps kids see science not just as facts, but as something they can explore in their own lives. The book promotes STEM awareness, emotional connection to nature, and creative learning. It’s designed to be both educational and magical—like a journal from a child who sees the sky as a mystery waiting to be solved.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work

It’s a children’s picture book called Luna’s Mission, which introduces young readers to space weather through the eyes of a curious girl named Luna. The story follows Luna on her mission to know more about space weather.

What benefits does it have?

  • Makes space science fun and understandable for kids
  • Encourages curiosity, observation, and critical thinking
  • Promotes STEM awareness through relatable characters and real-world connections
  • Supports literacy and emotional engagement with nature and technology

What is the intended impact?

The goal is to spark interest in space science and environmental awareness among children aged 5–9. By showing how space weather affects daily life—from tractors to airplanes—the book helps kids see science as something they can explore and understand.

 What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Canva: For layout design, font selection, and visual storytelling
  • Ibis Paint X: Used to create expressive, hand-painted style artwork
  • Phone & Laptop: For drafting story ideas and organizing research

How is your project creative?

The story is told entirely from Luna’s perspective, using childlike language and thought patterns. It blends real science with dreamy visuals, like flying with solar flares and painting the sky. The characters are inspired by real professions, making the science feel grounded and personal.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Age-appropriate language and pacing
  • Childlike voice and authentic curiosity
  • Simple storytelling structure
  • Diversity of characters and professions
  • Visual style inspired by children’s sketchbooks
  • Emotional tone that celebrates curiosity and wonder

projectDetails.name: Space Sweeper Solutions (S3)
projectDetails.summary:
There are Over 9000 metric tonnes of space junk orbiting the Earth that threaten satellites and astronauts and huge capital lost yearly from collisions and near misses. Currently there is no engaging way to make people care and there are just Debris re-entry and mitigation processes but no options to recycle.

Our Solution presents a way to not just remove the debris but recycle it but to also commercialize the entire program so it is sustainable and scalable.

We have come up with a magnet donut satellite idea that slows down debris gently. A robotic arm that safely stores junk. It has a recycling station that turns junk into usable parts and a Gamified Platform that lets kids and fans play missions from Earth.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do?
We have come up with Space Sweeper Solutions a satellite which recycles space debris which can then be sold to government agencies or corporations, and a gamified platform which is monetized.

How does it work?
It is a magnet donut satellite idea that slows down debris gently. A robotic arm that safely stores junk. It has a recycling station that turns junk into usable parts. We also have a gaming platform built on Scratch to increase awareness about Lower Earth Orbit and Orbital Debris.

What benefits does it have?
- It is catching space debris and recycling it instead of destroying it through atmosphere re-entry which has been the existing process.
- We will help reduce collision risks in space.
- We will recycle orbit material like aluminium and titanium which means less rocket launches needed for in-orbit repairs.
- We will help create engaging STEM education for kids.
- The entire program will be monetized, which will make this a scalable and sustainable project.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact of Space Sweeper Solutions (S3) is threefold:

  1. Safety in Orbit
  2. Sustainability & Scalability
  3. Inspiration & Education

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
We used Scratch code blocks(python) to build the prototype educational/gaming platform.
We used Tinkercad to design the 3D model of our Satellite.
We used Clickfunnels.com to build our website.
Doodly App for creating the whiteboard demo video.
We used a simple phone editor to capture & edit our demo videos.

How is your project creative?
Our project is creative because it comes from the minds of 7th graders. We dream of a future where we can travel to space, but with the current Orbital Debris problem space travel may become increasingly difficult and even impossible in the near future. Space junk could even harm existing weather and internet satellites and we wanted to address all these issues.
Current solutions only have options to either mitigate or debris re-entry options into our atmosphere.
Our creative solution has not been done ever before. We want to slow down, capture and re-cycle debris, allowing it to be used by international space stations for in orbit repairs, reducing the need for future launches for repairs. We can also sell the satellite material which will be beneficial for NASA as it is sustainable and scalable. Our gaming platform raises awareness and makes outerspace fun again.Our project opens the door for future space travel to Lower Earth Orbit and Beyond...


What factors did your team consider?
Capturing debris in Space is not easy because it's moving 10 times the speed of a bullet. Outerspace does not have any air either, so vaccum and thrusters would not work as well. So we had to come up with an idea which incorporates the logic of slowing down debris in space and captures it safely. That's why we came up with the idea of magnets which would induce Eddy currents and help slow down debris whether it's Iron, Aluminium or Titanium and help us capture it safely with a robotic arm made of aluminium & carbon fibre.

projectDetails.name: LunarBiom
projectDetails.summary:
To cultivate beneficial bacteria on the Moon's surface for various applications, such as air recycling, water purification, and production of valuable compounds. The LMH facility will need to address several challenges, including:

1.⁠ ⁠Radiation protection: Shielding the bacteria and electronics from harmful radiation.
2.⁠ ⁠Lunar regolith: Mitigating the effects of lunar dust and regolith on the facility's operations.
3.⁠ ⁠Distance and communication: Overcoming the challenges of communication and resupply due to the distance between the Moon and Earth.

The Lunar Microbial Habitat will be a crucial step towards establishing a sustainable presence on the Moon and paving the way for further space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Description:

The Lunar Microbial Habitat (LMH) is a controlled environment facility designed to cultivate beneficial bacteria on the surface of the Moon. The LMH will provide a sustainable solution for life support, air recycling, and production of valuable compounds, leveraging the unique conditions of the lunar environment.

Objective:

The primary objective of the LMH project is to develop a reliable and sustainable system for growing beneficial bacteria on the Moon's surface, which can support future lunar missions and potential human settlements. The specific objectives include:

1.⁠ ⁠Design and develop a controlled environment facility for bacterial growth on the lunar surface.

2.⁠ ⁠Select and cultivate beneficial bacteria that can thrive in the lunar environment and provide valuable products.

3.⁠ ⁠Develop a closed-loop life support system that minimizes waste and optimizes resource utilization.

4.⁠ ⁠Demonstrate the feasibility of using microorganisms for life support and resource utilization in space exploration.

Problem/Challenge:

The challenges associated with establishing a human presence on the Moon include:

1.⁠ ⁠Limited resources and resupply opportunities.

2.⁠ ⁠Harsh lunar environment with extreme temperatures, radiation, and lack of atmosphere.

3.⁠ ⁠Need for reliable and sustainable life support systems.

Solution:

The LMH project addresses these challenges by:

1.⁠ ⁠Utilizing microorganisms to recycle resources and produce valuable compounds.

2.⁠ ⁠Designing a controlled environment facility that simulates optimal conditions for bacterial growth.

3.⁠ ⁠Developing a closed-loop life support system that minimizes waste and optimizes resource utilization.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Prototype:

The LMH prototype will consist of:

1.⁠ ⁠A scaled-down version of the lunar habitat with a controlled environment.

2.⁠ ⁠Bacterial growth chambers with nutrient delivery and waste management systems.

3.⁠ ⁠Life support systems for air, water, and waste recycling.

4.⁠ ⁠Sensors and monitoring systems to track bacterial growth and environmental conditions.

Materials:

The LMH will be constructed using a combination of materials, including:

1.⁠ ⁠Inflatable habitat materials (e.g., polymers, composites).

2.⁠ ⁠Radiation shielding materials (e.g., liquid water, polymers).

3.⁠ ⁠Stainless steel or other corrosion-resistant materials for the bacterial growth chambers and life support systems.

4.⁠ ⁠Advanced composites for the habitat's structural components.

5.⁠ ⁠Specialized coatings and surface treatments to mitigate the effects of lunar regolith and radiation.

The LMH project will require a multidisciplinary approach, combining expertise in microbiology, materials science, mechanical engineering, and aerospace engineering to develop a reliable and sustainable system for growing beneficial bacteria on the Moon's surface.

1. Design & Simulation

These tools help simulate lunar conditions, habitat systems, and microbial behavior before physical deployment.

a. Physics & Environmental Simulation

  • COMSOL Multiphysics + AI plugins: Simulate thermal, structural, and chemical processes under lunar conditions.
  • Ansys Fluent + AI optimizers: For airflow, heat transfer, and structural analysis.
  • Digital Twins with AI (e.g., Siemens NX or Azure Digital Twins): To model and test the habitat virtually.

b. Generative Design (AI-driven CAD)

  • Autodesk Fusion 360 with Generative Design: Uses AI to propose efficient, lightweight structures.
  • nTopology: AI-powered design optimization, ideal for aerospace and extreme environments.

🔬 2. Microbial Growth Modeling & Prediction

These tools help optimize bacterial strains and predict growth under varying conditions.

a. Machine Learning Platforms

  • TensorFlow / PyTorch: Build custom ML models to predict bacterial growth rates, nutrient needs, or behavior under radiation/temperature stress.
  • scikit-learn: For classification and regression models (e.g., predicting optimal nutrient mixes).
  • BioBERT / DeepChem: For bioinformatics and chemical interaction predictions.

b. AI for Synthetic Biology

  • Benchling (with AI plugins): Design and simulate genetic modifications for optimized bacterial strains.
  • Ginkgo Bioworks / TeselaGen: AI-driven platforms for designing microbes with desired traits (e.g., producing oxygen, food, or bioplastics).

🛰️ 3. Real-Time Monitoring & Control

AI helps manage environmental variables and bacterial health inside the habitat.

a. Computer Vision & Image Analysis

  • OpenCV + ML models: Detect bacterial colony growth, contamination, or morphological changes.
  • YOLO / FastAI: For real-time video/image-based monitoring of culture chambers.

b. Sensor Data Analysis

  • Edge AI platforms (NVIDIA Jetson, Coral TPU): Run ML models onboard to monitor sensor data in real time without needing Earth communication.
  • AWS IoT Greengrass + SageMaker: For intelligent decision-making and automation in a remote habitat.

🔁 4. Closed-Loop System Optimization

Optimize air, water, and nutrient recycling systems with reinforcement learning or AI controllers.

a. AI Control Systems

  • Reinforcement Learning (e.g., using Ray RLlib or OpenAI Gym): Optimize system efficiency—e.g., when to recycle water or adjust nutrient delivery.
  • PID tuning with AI (e.g., Fuzzy Logic Controllers): For controlling temperature, pH, oxygen levels, etc.

b. Anomaly Detection

  • Autoencoders / LSTM models: Predict system failures or detect anomalies in sensor readings.

📊 5. Project Management & Collaboration

Streamline design, development, and data analysis with collaborative AI tools.

  • Notion + AI or ClickUp AI: For documentation, task management, and meeting notes.
  • ChatGPT + Code Interpreter / GitHub Copilot: Help with writing code, debugging, and designing experiments.
  • Google Colab / Jupyter Notebooks: To prototype AI models and collaborate in real-time.

projectDetails.name: Project Marleona
projectDetails.summary: In Project Marleona, we have taken the initiative to showcase the knowledge of space weather in a way that children as young as only 7 years old can understand! Space weather in todays age especially, has not sparked interest in young children, but with our vibrant character designs and engaging storytelling via a striking coding project it will sure grasp onto their attention. Learning about space weather is really important and beneficial for everyone to learn about as the weather in space affects everyone here on earth as well. The GPS system that is used by everyone to navigate and reach your destination is controlled by satellites which are in space, which if hit with harsh space weather can cause malfunctions temporarily. Our project covers all of this in a way where learning it is fun!
projectDetails.details:
HOW DOES IT WORK?

Project Marleona, is a compelling story on what space weather is, its effect on Earth and why knowing about it is important and beneficial for all. The project is showcased by an interactive coding outline with vibrant character designs and relatable characters. We have used credible resources from NASA and depicted space weather in a way where it is understandable by all.

WHAT IS IN OUR PROJECT?

The project we have created follows the story of forty-five-year-old Astronaut (Rashid) who has just come back from space and reunited with his family. His son, Jevin, an eight-year-old, is fascinated and curious by what his father has done in space and how the weather in space is like.

Jevin asks Rashid questions on What is space weather? How it impacts humans? Why is it important? Etc. Rashid answers these queries in a way where you can imagine and picture the answers in your head. The story comes to an end with a wholesome and loving point where Jevin wants to follow in his father’s footsteps.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

The benefits this project provides the knowledge of Space weather which is beneficial in many ways. The comprehension of this information is important as you know the story behind how the northern lights are formed, why your GPS signals might be down and overall knowledge of space which can be used in school. Learning about Space Weather creates public awareness which is only for the betterment of people.

TOOLS USED:

We have utilized only software. The illustrations are done on Ibis Paint X, a versatile drawing app. The coding is done on Scratch, a programming platform where you can create anything you can imagine, in the form of block coding. The demo presentation was created in Canva with use of the creative design elements. The information is taken from reliable and valid sources (i.e. NASA and other Space Researching websites) All of these tools together created our amazing project.

HOW IS OUR PROJECT CREATIVE?

Our project is creative in multiple ways we have originality in character design, creativity in story outline and coding done independently. It uses a third person perspective with multiple character point of views. The illustrations of characters are done completely with our imagination with no interference from third person perspective or AI. The coding initiative is also done with the same mentality with consistent hard work. The storyline is completely original and written with the idea of universal understanding.

FACTORS CONSIDERED:

Our team has considered a variety of factors. We took into consideration that children will be interested in colorful character designs with shining character personalities they can relate to alongside an investing storyline and compelling and interactive programming. We also considered children might not understand complex vocabulary and have eased down the complicated description of Space Weather which can be understood by all.

INTENDED IMPACT:

Our intended impact from our project is shared understanding from everyone. We want to convey comprehension of Space Weather as it is an interesting topic to dwell on and is important aswell. We want as a team to teach children about this matter so they are informed at every situation and can educate the people around them.

projectDetails.name: Purrfect Impact
projectDetails.summary: Our team decided to tackle our chosen challenge 'Purrfect Impact' by developing a web application which simulates the effects (tsunami waves, seismic activities, etc.) of an asteroid impact on Earth using user-defined or predefined parameters such as asteroid diameter, density, and impact velocity. The goal is to educate the public on the aforementioned effects and make use of gamification to let users explore various mitigation strategies in a fun and engaging manner.
projectDetails.details:
Purrfect Impact is an interactive web application that simulates asteroid impacts and makes great use of gamification to explore and educate about various mitigation strategies. The website features a sidebar containing an array of input fields that allow users to model their own asteroid and run simulations using user-defined parameters. Users can also select from a collection of preset asteroids with predefined parameters which are fetched directly from NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) dataset. When a preset asteroid is selected or when the user-defined parameters are correctly filled, the simulation results are displayed which include: asteroid mass, impact energy, crater diameter, crater depth, etc. When a simulation is ran, users will be prompted to select a mitigation strategy among four options, each with varying consequences based on the effectiveness of the strategy chosen.

The web application was made with modern web technologies (HTML, CSS, JavaScript). Three.js was specifically used for 3D models (such as the Earth model) and for visualizing the actual asteroid course and impact. The data used in this project was gathered from NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) dataset and the USGS National Elevation dataset, which were then processed using Python and visualized through Orange and Matplotlib. Our team had to consider a number of factors, one of which was accounting for varying elevations and terrain structures depending on where the asteroid lands in order to more accurately estimate the simulation results.

We believe that our approach is unique in a sense that mitigation strategies against asteroid impacts are rarely explored in a gamified manner. Our approach turns an often feared concept (asteroid impacts) into something interactive, visual, yet informative. Our goal with this project is to educate groups of all ages on the effects of asteroid impacts, as well as showcase how despite the dangers and risks associated with asteroid-related threats, mitigation strategies exist and are actively evolving in order to combat them.

projectDetails.name: Project Naii Designz
projectDetails.summary:
My project is an interactive app designed to show how the environment is changing through real examples, using NASA’s Terra satellite data. It begins with a Start Screen, welcoming the user into the app. From there, the Story Screen explains the purpose of the project and introduces how images and data from satellites can reveal important environmental changes.

The main feature is the Data Screen, which contains three before-and-after images collected by Terra and other NASA sources. These include Lake Urmia in Iran, which has been shrinking due to drought and water diversion; the Sanford Dam failure in Michigan, which caused major flooding; and the early arrival of spring in 2020 near the Carolinas, shown through satellite images of vegetation. When a user clicks on any image, they are taken to the About Screen, where more details about the event are explained.

By combining storytelling with Terra’s satellite data, the app helps users not only see the dramatic changes happening on Earth, but also understand the real-world events behind them.
projectDetails.details:
My project is an interactive storytelling app that highlights the impacts of climate change and environmental events using NASA’s Terra satellite data. The app works by guiding users through multiple screens: a Start Screen to welcome them, a Story Screen to introduce the project, a Data Screen that displays before-and-after satellite images, and an About Screen that provides explanations for each event. By clicking on an image, users can explore deeper information about changes happening to Earth.

The benefit of this app is that it transforms complex climate data into something that is easy to understand, visual, and interactive. Instead of reading long reports, users can quickly see real-world examples of environmental changes—like Lake Urmia’s shrinking waters, the Sanford Dam failure, and early spring vegetation shifts in the Carolinas—and understand the story behind them.

The intended impact of the project is to raise awareness about climate change and human impact on the environment by making satellite data more accessible to the public. It encourages people, especially younger audiences, to connect with science in a creative and engaging way.

For development, we used MIT App Inventor to build the app on an iPad. The coding was done using visual block-based programming, which made it easier to handle navigation, buttons, and interactive features like clicking images to load explanations. The data and images came from NASA Earth Observatory and Terra satellite resources.

This project is creative because it combines storytelling with real scientific data, turning facts and figures into a narrative experience. Instead of just presenting data, it invites the user to explore, discover, and reflect.

In developing the app, the main factors we considered were: making the app simple and user-friendly, ensuring the information was accurate and sourced from NASA, and designing it to be both educational and engaging for a wide range of users.

projectDetails.summary:
Team Information

Institution: Emirates National School – Abu Dhabi MBZ Campus

Program: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025

Team Lead: Narmin Mariam (Grade 5)

Our project, “My Own Robotic Ice Planet – Glacialis,” imagines a futuristic, AI-powered planet designed to sustain both robotic and biological life in extreme frozen conditions. The concept blends robotics, artificial intelligence, and astrobiology to explore how technology can help living and non-living systems coexist and thrive on icy exoplanets.
The goal is to simulate how robotics and AI can enable colonization or coexistence on extreme icy planets
This project encourages creativity, teamwork, and real-world application of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). It allows students to:

Understand AI-environment integration.

Explore astrobiology concepts.

Innovate robotic control in low-temperature ecosystems.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – My Own Robotic Ice Planet (Glacialis)

What does it do or how does it work?
Our project is about a new icy planet called Glacialis. On this planet, there are robotic living things that can think, learn, and take care of their cold world using artificial intelligence (AI).
These robots talk to each other, share information, and work together to keep the planet balanced. They can control temperature, collect energy from ice and sunlight, and even fix small changes in the environment.

What benefits does it have?
This project helps us learn how robots and AI can survive on other planets and help humans in the future.
It also teaches us about teamwork, energy, space science, and technology. It shows that we can use smart machines to protect our planet and others too.

What is the goal or impact of the project?
Our goal is to imagine how life could exist on other icy planets and to show that robots can help take care of such places.
We want to inspire other students to be curious about space, planets, and how technology can solve problems.

What tools or materials did we use?
We used simple coding tools like Scratch and Tinkercad to make models of the robots and the planet.
We also used Arduino for small robot movements and PowerPoint to make our presentation.

How is the project creative?
We created our own planet with three moons, a special icy climate, and AI-powered robotic creatures.
It mixes science and imagination, showing how robots can behave like living things in a new world.

What did our team think about while making it?
We thought about:

  • How robots can survive in cold weather
  • How they can get energy from ice and sunlight
  • How the three moons can change the weather
  • How to make the planet look beautiful and real

projectDetails.summary:
We developed Stormy the Solar Storm, a digital educational toolkit designed to teach children and the public about space weather using NASA data in a fun, accessible way. At its heart is a digital storybook that follows Stormy, a solar storm born on the Sun, as he interacts with Parker Solar Probe, satellites, astronauts, pilots, farmers, and forecasters on Earth. Each story page is paired with a “Science Spark” — real NASA and NOAA facts about solar flares, CMEs, GPS disruption, auroras, and radiation protection.

To extend learning, we created complementary materials: a lesson plan for teachers, coloring sheets for creative engagement, and assessment tools to check understanding. Together, these resources transform complex heliophysics into an interactive classroom experience.

This project addresses the challenge by explaining the impacts of space weather on everyday life in a relatable way, while inspiring curiosity about NASA missions like Parker, SDO, and SOHO. It is important because space weather affects us all — from farmers to astronauts — and education is the first step toward resilience.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do / how does it work?
Stormy the Solar Storm is a digital educational toolkit that transforms complex NASA heliophysics data into a child-friendly learning experience. At its core is an interactive digital storybook where Stormy, a personified solar storm, travels from the Sun to Earth, meeting Parker Solar Probe, satellites, astronauts, pilots, farmers, and forecasters. Each page pairs storytelling with a Science Spark — a real NASA or NOAA fact (e.g., GPS disruption, auroras, or radiation alerts). The toolkit also includes teacher lesson plans, coloring sheets, assessments, and activities, all hosted on a central website.

What benefits does it have?
It bridges the gap between advanced NASA research and early science education, making space weather accessible, engaging, and relatable. Teachers can run a full lesson using ready-made resources, and students learn through both storytelling and hands-on activities.

Intended impact:

  • Increase awareness of space weather’s role in daily life.
  • Inspire students to explore STEM, astronomy, and NASA missions.

projectDetails.name: Asteroid Impact Simulator
projectDetails.summary: Our project aims to address the Meteor Madness challenge. We have developed an interactive website that allows users to launch existing or custom asteroids onto any part of the earth and learn it’s impacts. Our website allows for a defend earth functionality that allows users to learn about asteroid deflection technologies, its success potential and impacts. Overall, it is a fun, educational website fit for any user trying to learn. With this project, we aim to address the lack of knowledge of asteroid impacts and the lack of websites that show this in an engaging way.
projectDetails.details:
Our website is an interactive, educational website that allows users to browse through known asteroids from the NEO API provided by NASA or customise their own asteroid, I.e., provide a size and velocity. If the user chooses to select an existing asteroid, they will be met with a page that contains a list of asteroids from a default date range. They are also given the option to browse based on any date provided, the date-range is at most 7 days long. The users will be met with messages that require them to input the correct dates/date ranges before clicking the ‘fetch data’ option.

Once they have done this, they will be taken to a page with an animation of the earth spinning, and the asteroid they have chosen spinning around it. This page is purely illustrative as of now and does NOT hold much scientific accuracy in terms of the orbit or crash path. From this page users will be able to see the impact of the crash. Users will be prompted to click launch before seeing impact, if they miss the step.

They are then led to the impacts page. Here the impact energy, crater size, estimated affected area and the severity. They will also be able to click on defending earth functions: ‘kinetic impactor’ or ‘gravity tractor’ to see how all these factors change. These estimations are done based on location, size and velocity of the asteroid in this prototype. A more developed model would account for terrain, air resistance and such. It could also provide a more map-focused approach.

We have made use of Flask to build the application with the help of HTML for making the webpages along with CSS and Tailwind for styling, and JavaScript. We have also used Three.js to handle the 3D visualisation and animation. We aim to provide a more visually enriching experience when simulating asteroid impacts as most asteroid simulators focus on 2D maps. Website design is also a priority. We aim to create a visually compelling, sleek and modern website that will give our users a fun and educational experience.

projectDetails.name: Nasweats - Project SharkSense
projectDetails.summary: Our project combines advanced shark tagging technology with a predictive mathematical model to understand shark behavior, feeding patterns, and ecosystem health. The dual-tag system includes a top tracking unit on the shark’s back, which records GPS location, depth, temperature, and movement, and a bottom jaw/sampling unit that detects true feeding events using jaw vibration and pressure sensors while collecting water samples containing prey DNA. The collected data is paired with a mathematical model that predicts shark foraging hotspots using NASA satellite data. The model analyzes physical ocean conditions such as temperature, chlorophyll concentration, and currents, producing a “Shark Foraging Score” for each location. Scores closer to 1 indicate optimal feeding conditions. Benefits include accurate identification of feeding behavior, real-time ecosystem monitoring, and insights into shark diet and ocean health. The Tools used include embedded microcontrollers for the tags, microfluidic sampling hardware, satellite communication systems, and Python-based data modeling. Our project combines biology, environmental science, engineering, and AI modeling into a single, integrated system. Our team considered sensor placement, energy efficiency, sample contamination control, and ethical attachment methods to ensure reliable, minimally invasive monitoring.
projectDetails.details:
Our project brings together technology, biology, and data science to better understand sharks and the oceans they live in. We developed a dual-tag system that lets us monitor shark behavior while also studying the surrounding water quality.

The top tag tracks the shark’s location, depth, temperature, and movement, while the bottom tag, placed under its jaw, uses jaw vibration and pressure sensors to detect feeding. When feeding is detected, a micropump automatically collects a small water sample through an inlet tube, storing it in a sealed cartridge for later analysis. These samples can reveal what the shark eats and the overall health of its environment.

We connected this data with a mathematical model we built using NASA satellite data like sea surface temperature, chlorophyll, and ocean currents to create a “Shark Foraging Score.” This score helps predict areas where sharks are most likely to feed.

By combining engineering, coding, and environmental science, we hope to help researchers understand not just where sharks go, but why they go there. We used Python for data analysis, Onshape for 3D design, and satellite data for environmental mapping.

We designed this project with sustainability and shark safety in mind, making sure the tags are lightweight, non-invasive, and efficient. Our goal is to make shark tracking more accurate and to use sharks as indicators of ocean health, helping us protect marine ecosystems for the future.
projectDetails.aiReferences: We used AI to fact check our equations to make sure they work under all circumstances, without fail. we used AI to make sure our tracker was durable, and would survive in the ocean, without harming the sharks. We used AI tools as a supportive assistant throughout our project, mainly to help us organize information and refine our ideas. For example, we used AI to double-check scientific accuracy in explaining shark behavior and tagging technologies, and to simplify complex concepts like the micropump mechanism and cartridge system so they could be clearly presented. We also used AI for voiceovers, for consistency.

projectDetails.summary:
This presentation provides an introduction to Earth: Our Planet, Facts, and Wonders, presenting a number of astronomical phenomena in addition to our home planet.
The presentation begins by defining Earth—its shape, importance, and the \\mathbf{8} billion people who call it home. It emphasizes how big the planet is, how diverse, and how connected humanity and nature are.
The following slides discuss space objects, i.e., asteroids, meteoroids, meteors, meteorites, and comets:
• Asteroids are defined as massive space rocks whose impact potential could be tremendous.
• The term meteoroid, meteor, and meteorite are specifically defined: a meteoroid is a small piece of an asteroid or comet; a meteor is the streak of light when it disintegrates in Earth's atmosphere (a 'shooting star'); and a meteorite is the remnant when it successfully survives the atmosphere and lands on Earth.
• Comets are introduced as "icy time capsules" or "dirty snowballs" made up of frozen gases, rock, and dust. They originate in the outer solar system's Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud and are active as they enter the Sun.
projectDetails.details: What does it do or how does it work? This project is an educational presentation titled "Our Planet Earth: Facts and Wonders." It aims to educate the audience by clarifying common misconceptions, such as the difference between meteoroids, meteors, and meteorites, and providing foundational knowledge on other celestial bodies like comets ("icy time capsules") and asteroids. The clear, concise bullet points and engaging titles help to simplify distinctions that are often confused. What factors did your team consider? Our team considered clarity of definitions (especially for the 'meteor' terms), visual appeal to maintain audience engagement, and topic relevance (focusing on celestial objects that frequently interact with Earth's atmosphere or are commonly discussed). projectDetails.summary: Our project centered on the conceptual design of HOM-1, a next-generation habitat for sustaining human life on Mars. projectDetails.details:
Our project focused on the conceptual design of HOM-1, a next-generation habitat intended to support human life on Mars. HOM-1 was developed with the primary goal of ensuring astronaut safety, sustainability, and comfort during extended missions on the Martian surface. The habitat features reinforced exterior walls designed to shield occupants from cosmic radiation and harsh environmental conditions. The Electricity Generator provide a reliable, renewable energy source, supporting essential life support systems and scientific equipment, by using our waste.

The interior of HOM-1 is organized into functional zones, including dedicated areas for sleeping, dining, research, and recreation, promoting both efficiency and well-being.

Throughout the project, our team applied principles of engineering, environmental science, and human-centered design. We collaborated to solve real-world challenges faced in extraterrestrial living, such as limited resources, isolation, and reduced gravity.

We also created a HOM-1 control center which makes it easy for astronauts to control the HOM in one small device

We used WIX to build our HOM-1 control center and Canva for the presentation.

This project allowed us to explore the possibilities of future space colonization and deepen our understanding of what it takes to build a livable environment on another planet. HOM-1 represents a small but meaningful step toward the future of interplanetary exploration and habitation.

projectDetails.name: Project Nova 6
projectDetails.summary:
Nova 6 a compact, sealed recycling machine that turns inorganic trash brought to or accumulated on the surface of Mars, like plastics, metals, and glass, into useful materials. A small camera and computer sort items inside the box. Plastics are melted into 3D-printer filament, metals are heated with solar provided energy and cast into small parts or ingots, and glass is crushed and sintered into tiles or insulation beads. The unit runs mostly on solar energy, connects to habitat power, and is designed for low crew time and safe, pressurized operation.



This directly addresses the challenge by replacing storage and costly return of roughly 12,600 kg of mission waste with on-site reuse. It reduces waste volume, frees living space, and supplies spares on demand, improving reliability.



It matters because it lowers resupply mass and cost, increases mission independence, and brings a simple circular-economy approach to Mars, and ideas that can also benefit future Moon bases and recycling on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, Nova 6, is a recycling system that turns inorganic trash like packaging, textiles, and structural materials into useful items. It works inside a sealed box, runs mostly on solar power, and is designed to be safe and easy to use.

The goal is to cut down on waste, reduce how many supplies need to be sent from Earth, and give explorers materials they can use right away. The impact is a cleaner, more sustainable way to support future missions on Mars and other planets.

To build our idea, we used creative design tools and research on recycling and renewable energy. While it’s still a concept, we focused on making it practical, safe, and environmentally friendly. What makes it creative is how it views trash not as waste, but as a resource that can actually help humans live and work in space.

Users explore how NASA’s space data informs UAE initiatives such as mangrove restoration, renewable energy, and Net Zero 2050 goals.

Benefits: EcoOrbit makes complex space data understandable and locally relevant, encouraging climate literacy and real-world sustainability actions. It empowers students, educators, and citizens to see the connection between orbital science and daily life.

Creativity & Considerations: The site uses a futuristic “space-to-place” design (glassmorphism, neon HUD), gamified missions, accessible layouts, and offline-ready simulated NASA datasets—ensuring performance, scalability, and classroom usability.

EcoOrbit tells the story of how space watches over Earth—and how the UAE responds from the ground. It educates, inspires, and empowers citizens to see themselves as part of the planetary story, turning data into empathy and awareness into sustainable action.

projectDetails.name: NearEarthIntel
projectDetails.summary:
Our website helps people understand the risks of meteors that come close to Earth. It shares useful information with scientists and shows estimates of how much damage a meteor could cause if it hits the ground. The results are very accurate—about 90 to 100%—based on how the meteor enters the atmosphere and where it lands.
By visiting our website, the user will be shown data from the past 5 days. At the bottom of the page, the UI will be presented to the user with three options: Hypothetical Calculations, Filter Hazardous Meteors, and Deflection Calculation. And at the bottom of each Hazardous card displayed, an option will be shown to calculate impact energy and its effects based on geographical area of impact. Not only does our website show some important data on the meteor but also it calculates the energy to employ a kinetic impact strategy in order to deflect the meteor if hazardous.
projectDetails.details: Our website is a dynamic meteor risk analysis and deflection platform that helps users—especially scientists and researchers—understand the threats posed by meteors approaching Earth by displaying data from the past five days and offering highly accurate (90–100%) impact damage estimates based on entry angle and geographical landing site. The interface includes three core tools: Hypothetical Calculations to simulate custom impact scenarios, Filter Hazardous Meteors to identify high-risk objects, and Deflection Calculation to estimate the kinetic energy required to alter a meteor’s trajectory. Each hazardous meteor card also features an option to calculate impact energy and its effects based on the area of impact. Built using front-end JavaScript, the platform merges scientific precision with intuitive design to support planetary defense, and scientific collaboration. Our team prioritized accuracy, accessibility, and scalability while ensuring the platform remains ethically grounded and user-friendly, empowering users to explore real-world threats and theoretical defense strategies in one seamless experience.
