projectDetails.name: SharkWatch
projectDetails.summary: SharkWatch is now absolutely breathtaking! When you open it, you see stunning satellite images of ocean currents from space, then gorgeous underwater photos of each shark species. The great white shark photo shows its powerful jaws, the whale shark image shows how massive they are compared to a human swimmer, and the tiger shark clearly displays its distinctive stripes. The AI identification shows real example photos of sharks you can identify, and the whole platform feels like exploring an underwater documentary while using cutting-edge space technology!
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works:
SharkWatch is an innovative, real-time conservation platform that leverages NASA’s satellite data and advanced AI to monitor and protect endangered shark species worldwide. It integrates live oceanographic data—such as sea surface temperature and chlorophyll concentration—with tracking information from tagged sharks. The app features a cutting-edge AI-powered photo identification system capable of recognizing shark species from user-uploaded images, providing instant feedback on species identity, conservation status, and key identifying features. This enables citizen scientists, researchers, and the public to engage actively in shark conservation efforts. The platform is accessible as a responsive web app optimized for both desktop and mobile devices.

Benefits:

  • Enables continuous, real-time monitoring of shark populations using high-resolution satellite data combined with GPS tracking.
  • Democratizes shark research by empowering a global community of citizen scientists to contribute data simply by snapping photos or reporting sightings.
  • Provides immediate identification and conservation guidance, increasing awareness of endangered species and promoting informed protection measures.
  • Enhances scientific research and policy-making by aggregating large-scale, geographically diverse, and up-to-date datasets.
  • Offers gamified features to engage younger audiences, fostering education and long-term commitment to environmental stewardship.

Intended Impact:
SharkWatch aims to revolutionize shark conservation by filling critical data gaps with live monitoring and global participation. By empowering people worldwide to contribute and access actionable insights, the platform helps reduce shark mortality, supports species recovery, and raises public awareness about oceanic ecosystem health. The project exemplifies how space-based technology can directly address urgent Earth conservation challenges and inspire new generations of environmental scientists.

Development Tools and Technologies:

  • Data Sources: NASA satellite datasets (MODIS, Jason, GHRSST); NOAA real-time oceanographic and weather APIs; simulated real-time shark tracking data modeled on actual movements.
  • Software: Modern web technologies (JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3) for frontend; Python for backend data fetching and processing.
  • AI: Custom-developed AI simulation mimicking species identification via computer vision techniques, designed to provide educational interaction and real-time species recognition.
  • Cloud and Storage: Cloud-hosted APIs for scalable data integration and seamless user experience.
  • Hardware: Compatible with smartphones, tablets, and desktops; supports mobile camera capture.

Creativity and Innovation:
This project creatively combines disparate data streams—from space-based satellite imagery to on-the-ground citizen contributions—into a single unified platform. Its AI-driven photo recognition feature brings professional marine science capabilities to everyday users in an intuitive way. The integration of real-time environmental monitoring with interactive gamification elements sets it apart as both a powerful research tool and an engaging public education platform.

Team Considerations:
The team focused on making the technology accessible and engaging for audiences of all ages and backgrounds, ensuring the UI is intuitive and visually appealing. Attention was paid to scientific accuracy and ethical conservation messaging. Scalability and sustainability underpinned technical decisions, ensuring the platform can grow with user engagement and expand to additional species and regions. The project reflects a passion for marine science, space technology, and the power of community-driven impact.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
For our SharkWatch project, we utilized Artificial Intelligence as follows:

  • Developed an AI-based computer vision model to perform shark species identification from user-uploaded photos. The AI analyzes key visual features to classify the species and provides confidence scores and conservation status to users.
  • Used AI tools to generate the animated intro videos, incorporating visual elements like the shark silhouette, Earth, and satellites with dynamic transitions and sound design.
  • Employed AI-assisted image generation to create custom logos and some graphical assets for enhanced branding and visual appeal.

projectDetails.name: OrbitalShield
projectDetails.summary:
OrbitalShield is an interactive web application that empowers users to explore, simulate, and visualize the impact of asteroids on Earth using real NASA and USGS data. The platform models asteroid trajectories, calculates scientifically accurate impact effects—including crater size, seismic waves, and population at risk—and displays the results through an engaging 3D globe and interactive hazard maps. Users can customize asteroid and mitigation parameters or choose from real and fictional scenarios to see how different interventions change outcomes.

By making complex planetary defense science accessible and visual, OrbitalShield addresses the challenge of increasing public awareness, education, and understanding of asteroid threats and global risks. It encourages curiosity, critical thinking, and preparedness in a world where space hazards are real but often misunderstood. Built using JavaScript, Three.js, and public data APIs, OrbitalShield is open-source, educational, and designed for broad accessibility—helping bridge the gap between scientific research and public engagement.
projectDetails.details:
OrbitalShield: Asteroid Impact Simulation & Planetary Defense

What does it do / How does it work?
OrbitalShield is an interactive web application that visualizes the threat of asteroid impacts on Earth using real data from NASA and USGS. Users can explore past, present, and hypothetical asteroid scenarios; simulate impact physics and mitigation strategies; and visualize effects such as crater size, seismic waves, and population at risk. The system integrates live asteroid data, performs scientific calculations for impact outcomes, and renders results on an interactive 3D globe and 2D hazard maps.

Benefits:

  • Makes planetary defense science accessible and engaging to the public, educators, and students.
  • Provides a realistic and data-driven way to understand asteroid threats and the effectiveness of various mitigation strategies.
  • Helps users visualize complex physics and disaster scenarios in a clear, intuitive format.

Intended Impact:
OrbitalShield aims to increase public awareness about planetary defense, foster STEM education, and inspire critical thinking about global risks. By allowing users to simulate asteroid impacts and experiment with mitigation strategies, it encourages exploration, learning, and informed discussion.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Technologies:

  • Languages: JavaScript, HTML, CSS
  • Frameworks/Libraries: Three.js for 3D visualization, NASA NeoWS API for asteroid data, USGS APIs for earthquake and elevation data
  • Other: Responsive and accessible UI, open-source codebase, designed for modern browsers (no special hardware required)

Creativity:
OrbitalShield stands out for its combination of:

  • Real-time data integration (NASA/USGS)
  • Accurate scientific modeling (orbital mechanics, impact physics, hazard estimation)
  • Immersive 3D and 2D visualizations
  • Scenario builder for both real and fictional asteroid events
  • Educational overlays, infographics, and interactive controls, all designed for accessibility

Team Considerations:
The project was designed to be:

  • Educational: Prioritizes accurate science, clear visuals, and approachable explanations
  • Open and Collaborative: Fully open-source with clear documentation to encourage community contributions and adaptation for classrooms or outreach
  • Extensible: Future plans include AI/ML for risk prediction, AR integration, and internationalization

Summary:
OrbitalShield creatively combines real scientific data, modern visualization, and engaging educational features to empower users to understand and explore asteroid impacts and planetary defense.

No AI-generated images, audio, or videos are included in the project, and all results and materials were manually reviewed and refined by human contributors.

projectDetails.details:
Our project, “Will It Rain On My Parade?”, is a web-based application designed to help people plan outdoor events confidently by predicting whether the weather will be suitable. Users simply enter a location, date, and time, and the app provides a clear answer such as “Weather looks good for your event” or “High chance of rain – consider a backup plan.”

projectDetails.name: 92 Viewer
projectDetails.summary: 92 viewer is an Interactive planetary viewer that turns NASA's data into a realm of exploration and knowledge. The application allows users to pan and zoom into the surfaces of three different worlds, whilst utilizing different overlays to provide various  scientific information, such as elevation, thermal zones etc. Users can also see multiple different landmarks within just a few clicks, providing insights on what the planets really contain. Users can mark their own discoveries with Quick markers just incase they want to reference to it later, and if they need more context about existing landmarks, they can simply utilize our mission briefing feature, which utilizes AI to further elaborate what is being shown on screen!
projectDetails.details:
92 viewer turns NASA's base maps into a mission-style console catered to both newcomers and experts. The app streams all imagery from NASA's Trek API as WMTS tiles (256x256) via Leaflet, so the app requests only the tiles the viewer can see at once and relies on the browser's HTTP cache, resulting in no bulk imagery needing to be mirrored or stored by us. All landmarks are served as static GeoJSON, allowing for lightweight loading, and all user annotations are stored in localStorage, reducing the operational complexity of 92 Viewer. AI "Mission Briefings" are delivered through a small Node proxy and are cached in memory as well to avoid redundant calls. This just-in-time tile strategy eliminates storage costs and keeps performance stable.

The landmarks are derived from the USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature and are curated into lightweight GeoJSON as mentioned earlier, 92 Viewer extracts the source dataset and normalize to a minimal schema. At runtime, 92 Viewer will load the first available source from a per planet list via fetch and stores features in a Zustand store. On the map, each point feature becomes a Leaflet circleMarker with a tooltip and a click handler that sets selectedLandmarkID; if an extent box exists for that specific landmark, we render a rectangle on the map. All the data is shipped as static assets, which cacheable by the browser, and require no database.

Each landmark carries a unique feature called Mission Briefing, where within one click, you can get a mission-style summary of what exactly the landmark is, and some important context behind it. As soon as the user selects "Generate", the app sends some information about the landmark to a small Node proxy that calls Google's Generative Language API. The prompt is tuned to avoid repeating information that is already displayed and instead display accepted scientific context plus three concise bullet points for quick fire information. Responses are cached in the memory to reduce duplicate calls

We repeated these steps across three distinct worlds:

Mercury
Mars
Venus

And to top it all off. a lightweight Three.js landing scene lets users switch between planets.

projectDetails.name: Project Recycling waste on Mars
projectDetails.summary:
Our project is about recycling inorganic waste on Mars. During long missions, astronauts will make a lot of trash like plastic, metal, and fabric. It is too expensive to send new things from Earth, so we made a system that can reuse and recycle this trash.

The system changes waste into new materials that can be used to build, fix, or make tools. This helps astronauts save space and resources and keeps their living area clean.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is about recycling and reusing trash on Mars. It works by sorting and changing waste like metal, plastic, and fabric into new useful things.

For example, metal can be melted to make tools, plastic can become new boxes or building blocks, and fabric can be used for clothes or insulation.

This project helps reduce trash, save materials, and make life on Mars safer and easier for astronauts.

The goal is to make Mars missions more clean, safe, and independent, so astronauts don’t need to bring too many things from Earth.

We used AI tools to help us make a video about our project and to write the ideas clearly.

Our project is creative because it mixes science, recycling, and technology to solve a real problem. We also thought about limited energy, small space, and astronaut safety.

We added a watermark to show it was made by AI.

projectDetails.name: Project RithDAR - Radar Meets Resilience
projectDetails.summary:
RithDAR is an AI-powered disaster response system designed to enhance public safety and optimise emergency operations. Our project uses real-time data from NASA satellites and environmental sensors to predict high-risk zones and dynamically allocate emergency resources. Alerts are automatically delivered to both authorities and residents in under two minutes, ensuring faster evacuations and effective response measures. By simulating disaster scenarios, RithDAR demonstrates up to a 50% reduction in emergency response times compared to conventional methods.

This system is crucial because natural disasters often strike without warning, overwhelming traditional emergency infrastructure. By integrating AI-driven predictions with instant notifications, RithDAR ensures that over 90% of affected populations receive timely alerts. Beyond immediate response, the platform provides actionable recovery insights to guide post-disaster planning and urban development. Our project exemplifies innovation, practicality, and social impact, aligning with the challenge of using technology to improve human resilience against disasters.
projectDetails.details:
RithDAR collects real-time environmental data from NASA satellites and integrates local sensor networks. AI algorithms analyse this data to identify high-risk areas, prioritise emergency resources, and trigger immediate alerts to authorities and residents. The system reduces response times, ensures broader coverage of at-risk populations, and provides recovery insights for urban planning.

We developed RithDAR using Python;Google Colab for prototyping, and web technologies for the alert interface. Its creativity lies in the seamless integration of AI prediction, resource optimisation, and real-time notification. We carefully considered accessibility, speed, and reliability to maximise social impact during natural disasters.
projectDetails.aiReferences: We improved our code by adding advanced AI features that make disaster response smarter and faster. Using AI, our system can predict high-risk disaster zones by analyzing both historical and real-time environmental data, prioritize emergency resources in real time to ensure help reaches the most critical areas first, and simulate population impact to optimize alert delivery for maximum coverage and efficiency. Throughout development, we carefully reviewed and tested the code and models to ensure reliability, accuracy, and robustness. These enhancements make our system not just reactive but proactively intelligent, providing actionable insights that traditional methods often miss and adding real value to disaster management.

projectDetails.name: Space Shooter
projectDetails.summary:
The project is a modern recreation of the classic arcade game Space Asteroids, developed using GDevelop. In this game, the player controls a spaceship that can rotate, thrust forward, and shoot projectiles to destroy incoming asteroids. The primary objective is to survive as long as possible while avoiding collisions with asteroids.

Asteroids are spawned randomly and drift across the screen with varying speeds. When a large asteroid is destroyed, it splits into smaller fragments, increasing the challenge as the player progresses. Collision detection ensures that both bullets and the spaceship interact accurately with asteroids. If the spaceship collides with an asteroid, it results in a game-over scenario, requiring careful navigation and strategic shooting.

The spaceship’s movement is responsive, allowing smooth rotation and thrust, while shooting mechanics enable precise targeting of asteroids. The game also incorporates continuous asteroid movement across the screen edges, maintaining a dynamic and unpredictable environment.

Overall, this project demonstrates the use of event-based logic, object interactions, and scene management in GDevelop. It effectively combines classic arcade mechanics with modern game development techniques, creating an engaging and challenging experience for players.
projectDetails.details: A modern recreation of the classic Space Asteroids arcade game. The player controls a spaceship that can rotate, move forward, and shoot projectiles to destroy asteroids while avoiding collisions. Asteroids drift across the screen and split into smaller fragments when destroyed, increasing difficulty. The goal is to survive as long as possible in a dynamic and unpredictable environment.

projectDetails.name: Project Slay preppy’s
projectDetails.summary:
Terra is NASA’s pioneering Earth-observing satellite, launched in 1999 and still operational after 25 years. It orbits the planet daily, collecting crucial data through five advanced instruments — MODIS, CERES, MISR, ASTER, and MOPITT — that together monitor Earth’s land, atmosphere, oceans, and energy balance.

The presentation blends science and storytelling, personifying Terra as a sentient observer reflecting on its mission and the planet’s changes. It has witnessed wildfires, deforestation, melting glaciers, pollution, and shifting climates — turning raw data into a record of humanity’s impact on Earth.

Terra’s data supports climate research, disaster response, and environmental protection worldwide. Locally, it helps track droughts, air quality, floods, and urban heat. After more than 9,000 days in orbit, Terra’s legacy lies not just in its measurements but in its message: to use knowledge responsibly and act before it’s too late.
projectDetails.details:

    • The theme of awareness, reflection, and human responsibility for the planet’s health.
    • Examples of Terra’s real-world applications (wildfire tracking, pollution monitoring, deforestation, glacier loss).
    • Local relevance such as drought tracking, flood prediction, and air quality analysis.

  3. Terra’s Awakening – Story introduction (creative narrative).

Students, educators, and science enthusiasts participating in NASA or Earth Science outreach projects.

An engaging multimedia presentation showing how data, science, and creativity can work together to raise awareness about Earth’s changing systems — using Terra as both a tool and a storyteller.

projectDetails.name: Project STORY TIME -Solar Storm Defender-
projectDetails.summary:
Earth’s magnetic field acts like a big invisible shield around the planet. It blocks most of the Sun’s harmful energy, like solar flares and charged particles. This shield keeps us safe by pushing away dangerous space weather that can harm satellites, power grids, and astronauts. When strong solar storms happen, the shield protects Earth from most damage. Scientists study this to help keep our technology and life safe from space weather.

***

The story is about Earth, who is happy and safe, protected by her magical friend called Magnetic Field. But two naughty space villains, Solar Flare (a fiery girl) and CME (a fast boy), zoom from the Sun toward Earth to cause trouble. They bring bursts of energy that make the sky glow with colorful lights, but they also cause problems like fuzzy radios, strange weather, and power outages.

Earth calls for help, and Magnetic Field rushes to defend her. The magical shield fights bravely, blocking most of the villains’ attacks and keeping Earth safe. In the end, Solar Flare and CME give up and go back to the Sun, promising to be kinder next time. Earth feels happy and protected, ready for any future space weather adventures.
projectDetails.details: Earth’s magnetic field acts as a strong protective shield against dangerous bursts of charged particles and radiation from solar flares and coronal mass ejections. It deflects most harmful solar energy away from Earth, trapping some charged particles in protective belts and preventing damage to the atmosphere, satellites, power grids, and communications systems. Understanding this protective mechanism allows scientists to monitor solar activity and forecast space weather events. These forecasts help prepare and protect critical technology, infrastructure, and astronauts, reducing the impact of solar storms on daily life and space missions. By improving space weather prediction systems, we can better safeguard Earth and its inhabitants from disruptions caused by solar activity.

projectDetails.name: Cyro-Shatter
projectDetails.summary:
A waste-to-infrastructure system that exploits the extreme cold (-87°C) temperature of Mars to transform waste into structural materials with minimal energy input. Waste is placed in an outdoor carousel where the cold makes the materials glass-brittle, ultrasonic vibrations (8-30 kHz) selectively shatter the materials by resonant frequency, and then, automated sorting separates 15+ pure materials. Sorted waste is then mixed with Martian ice to create Ice-Waste Matrix (IWM)—a concrete-strength building material that also works as emergency water storage. Over three years, a crew consisting of 8 people built 200 m² of habitat extensions, transparent greenhouses, roads, emergency shelters, and radiation shielding—creating infrastructure for future missions instead of shipping all the waste back to earth. This converts 12,600 kg of mission waste into approximately 180,000 kg of construction materials with 96% less energy than traditional recycling. 
Cryo-Shatter proves that sustainable off-world colonies aren't only possible, they are inevitable. With Cryo-Shatter, we turn Mars’s greatest threat into humanity’s greatest industrial asset.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Overview

Mars is the one planet most explored so far in our solar system; it is the closest to Earth, alongside Venus. It is also the only planet where NASA has sent rovers to explore the landscape. Because of these expeditions, Mars has been a primary focus in outer-space research due to the discovery of evidence that the planet was much warmer and wetter in the past, making it a potential candidate for hosting life in the far future. 

What is the environmental situation on Mars? What minerals are there?

Mars is about half the Earth’s size, and its surface has almost the same area as Earth’s dry land. The landscape of Mars has undergone significant changes over many years, primarily due to its unique atmospheric conditions. Since Mars has such a thin atmosphere, there is very little protection from meteorite, asteroid, and/or comet impacts. Additionally, their winds are strong enough to create dust storms that are capable of covering much of the planet at once. 

The planet also experiences distinct seasons, which actually last twice as long as those on Earth due to the nature of Mars’ orbit around the sun. Despite this, it’s almost always dry, rocky, and cold. Temperatures on Mars range from numbers as low as -153 degrees Celsius to numbers as “high” as 20 degrees Celsius. This may be due to the planet’s atmosphere, which is thin and lets heat from the Sun easily escape. 

The crust of Mars is around 10-50 km deep and is made up of iron, magnesium, aluminum, calcium, and potassium. These minerals are part of the reason for Mars’ outward reddish appearance; iron minerals in the regolith, Martian soil, oxidize and eventually make the surface seem red as dust is carried into the atmosphere. 

What kind of natural resources/materials already exist on Mars? 

The most abundant resource on Mars is Carbon Dioxide (CO2). While not a resource that can be used for the physical project, MOXIE (Mars Oxygen ISRU Experiment) has proved that this abundance of carbon dioxide can be used to produce oxygen. This first step allows for human activity to proceed much smoothly overall. Aside from oxygen production, carbon dioxide can support plant growth in greenhouses and can be used to manufacture plastics and other carbon-based materials.

Regolith is also rich in iron that can be processed and used for construction and other manufacturing purposes. It can be melted into bricks for construction or mixed with other resources to create a sound, concrete-like material. Martian rocks and minerals also have large amounts of silicon that can be useful for solar panels, glass, and electronics. Other aforementioned minerals — like aluminum, titanium, and magnesium — are present in various deposits across Mars and can be utilized for more lightweight production. 

While Mars has a bounty of natural resources on its surface, it lacks the complex, refined procedures and additional materials that people already utilize on Earth. It is possible to bring some materials from Earth to Mars during the initial rover launch, but we would still need to be mindful of the amounts we bring and the costs to do so. Most of the resources, then, would need to be manufactured from scratch using the basic foundations already present.

Introduction

— THE PROBLEM:

  • On a 3-year-long expedition on Mars, an 8-person crew accumulates about 12,600 kg of inorganic waste over time. Sending any waste back to Earth or requesting extra resources to make waste management more organized is far too expensive and inefficient. Additionally, traditional recycling isn’t available to the crew on Mars due to the lack of sufficient energy.

— THE SOLUTION

  • Take what many others would see as a grave disadvantage and turn it into an effective tool capable of transforming waste into something crucial in building towards the larger goal of outer-space exploration: making life possible and even founding colonies on other planets, starting with Mars.

What is Cryo-Shatter? 

— HOW IT WORKS: 

  1. Cryo Exposure
    1. Waste is first left outside to be frozen overnight. This happens naturally due to Mars’s frigid temperatures, so no energy is used.
    2. After the wait, the waste would become glass-brittle, a process that would typically require a significant amount of technology and energy on Earth.
    1. The now-fragile waste is then processed with ultrasonic vibrations at specific frequencies (around 8-30 kHz). This process shatters the material selectively into a pure, unfiltered powder. 
    2. Separation is automated, effectively segregating metals, plastics, glass, and ceramics.
    1. The waste, now sorted and in powder form, is mixed with Martian subsurface ice with precise ratios: 60% ice, 30% plastic, and 10% metal.
    2. This mixture is poured into molds and frozen overnight. The product is a concrete-strength building material (23 MPa) that can be utilized for several different purposes or facilities.

—  KEY BENEFITS:

  • Energy Efficiency
    • Expends 96% less energy than traditional recycling would
    • Mars does 90% of the work for free (the work of its natural climate)
    •  12,600 kg waste + 120,000 kg Martian ice = 180,000 kg construction material
    • Zero waste is returned to the Earth, and most of it is repurposed
    • Buildings are emergency water reserves (may melt walls in crisis)
    • ~40% more effective radiation shielding than pure ice
    • Self-healing roads (thermoplastic particles flow into cracks)
    • Crew sees trash transform into visible infrastructure, boosting morale
    • Creates legacy for future missions to follow and improve from
    • Reduces resource anxiety among crew members

Physical Design:

•Rotating carousel system, 8 meters diameter

•24 individual “exposure bins” made of thermally conductive aluminum

•Each bin: 50cm x 50cm x 30cm, holds ~15kg of waste

•Automated loading/unloading via robotic arm

•Covered with transparent thermal blanket (prevents dust, allows radiative cooling

Operation:

• Waste loaded at Martian dusk

• Bins rotate to ensure even exposure to night sky

• Temperature sensors monitor embrittlement progress

• Full exposure cycle: 8-12 hours (one Martian night)

• No energy input required—pure passive cooling

Material-Specific Embrittlement Temperatures:

• Plastics (PE, PP, PET): -60°C (become glass-like)

• Aluminum alloys: -80°C (grain boundaries weaken)

• Steel: -100°C (ductile-to-brittle transition)

• Glass/ceramics: -120°C (microcrack propag tion accelerates)

• Composite materials: -70°C (resin matrix fractures)

 — WHAT CAN BE BUILT:

  • Habitat extensions (200+ m²)
  • Greenhouses with transparent waste-glass domes
  • 1+ km of self-healing roads
  • Emergency shelters (8+ units)
  • Landing pads
  • Radiation shielding berms
  • Water reserves in every structure

Finances & Resource Management

  • Below are tables detailing our estimated costs for the project, curated while being as mindful as possible of NASA’s typical budget and allowance.

Our Mission Impact

— RESULTS:

  • Immediate: Effective zero-waste management for a 3-year expedition on Mars.
  • Medium-term: Next crew lands on existing infrastructure and systems they can build off of.
  • Long-term: Sets the foundation for self-sufficient colonies on Mars.

— WHY IT’S REVOLUTIONARY:

  • This concept turns Mars’s greatest threat into an asset; it becomes something that could pave the way for years of research to come, not just on Mars, but for outer-space exploration as a whole.

Our project, “Sunny and Spark: A Space Weather Adventure,” is an animated story created using Scratch to help young learners understand space weather and its effects on Earth. The story follows Sunny, a cheerful Sun, and Spark, a lively solar flare, as they explore how solar storms, auroras, and magnetic fields interact with our planet. Through colorful visuals and engaging dialogue, the animation explains how space weather can influence satellites, communication systems, and even power grids on Earth.

It encourages curiosity about solar science and highlights the importance of protecting Earth’s technology and environment from space weather impacts.

By blending creativity with science, “Sunny and Spark” inspires young audiences to see how the Sun and Earth are connected, fostering awareness and interest in space science and sustainability.
projectDetails.details:
My project is called “Sunny and Spark: A Space Weather Adventure.” I made it in Scratch. It is a cartoon story where the Sun (Sunny) and a solar flare (Spark) talk to Earth (Earthy), a satellite (Satty), and the Aurora. The story shows how solar flares come out of the Sun, how they can disturb satellites, and how they also make the beautiful northern lights.

I wanted to make space weather easy to understand for kids like me. The benefit is that children can learn science in a fun way, like watching a cartoon. The project teaches that space weather can cause problems but also makes something amazing like auroras.

I used Scratch coding to create the story, with sprites, speech bubbles, and some color effects. I chose this tool because it is fun and simple for kids.

My project is creative because I turned science into a story with characters and animations. I thought about how to make it simple, colorful, and interesting for children so they can enjoy and learn at the same time.

projectDetails.name: Project Soton Nova
projectDetails.summary:
We developed the Exoplanet Auto-Classifier, a single-page Streamlit app that trains and serves a three class model (CONFIRMED, CANDIDATE, or FALSE POSITIVE) through using live tables from NASA’s Exoplanet Archive (Kepler/K2/TESS) or a user-provided CSV/Excel. The app maps mission codes (CP/KP/PC/APC/FP/FA) into a common label scheme, builds a numeric feature matrix from transit and stellar parameters (e.g., period, transit depth/duration, planet radius, SNR, Teff, log g), and runs a lightweight pipeline (median imputation, optional standardization) into user-selectable models (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, optional XGBoost). It evaluates with a stratified train/test split, k-fold cross-validation, and reports a confusion matrix, precision/recall/F1, macro-F1, and ROC-AUC (when probabilities are available). Users can upload new data, receive class probabilities, and download results.

This directly addresses the challenge by transforming manual vetting into a reproducible, auditable, and interactive workflow. It’s important because it accelerates candidate triage, standardizes analysis across missions and datasets, and lowers the barrier for students and researchers to explore, validate, and iterate on exoplanet classification. Tools used: Python (pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, xgboost), Streamlit, and NASA’s TAP API.
projectDetails.details:
What it does / how it works

Data in: Pulls live tables from the NASA Exoplanet Archive (Kepler/K2/TESS) via TAP, or loads your CSV/Excel.

Label mapping: Normalizes mission codes (e.g., CP/KP/PC/APC/FP/FA) into CONFIRMED / CANDIDATE / FALSE POSITIVE.

Features: Builds a numeric matrix from transit and stellar parameters (period, transit depth/duration, planet radius, SNR, Teff, log g, etc.).

Pipeline: Median imputation → optional standardization → user-selectable model (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, optional XGBoost).

Evaluation: Stratified train/test split, k-fold cross-validation, confusion matrix, classification report; ROC-AUC when probabilities are available.

Inference: Upload a file, get class predictions with probabilities, and download results.

Benefits

Faster triage than manual vetting, with consistent, reproducible results.

Accessible UI (Streamlit) for students and researchers—no heavy setup.

Auditable: choices, metrics, and data provenance are visible in-app.

Intended impact

Accelerate candidate review and follow-up prioritization.

Standardize classification across missions and datasets.

Lower the barrier to entry for education and community science.

Tools / languages / software / hardware

Python: pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, (optional) xgboost, matplotlib, requests, pyarrow.

Streamlit for the web app.

NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP for live data.

How it’s creative

Single-file interactive trainer that unifies Kepler/K2/TESS label schemes.

One page to pull data, tune features/algorithms, train, evaluate, and predict—end-to-end.

Factors we considered

Data quality: missing values, non-physical entries, occasional malformed rows.

Class imbalance: stratification, macro-F1 reporting, class-balanced forests.

Leakage avoidance: exclude IDs/status columns from features.

Generalization: cross-validation, clear metrics, easy re-training.

Usability & transparency: simple UI, downloadable outputs, explainable feature influences.

projectDetails.name: Project: CALL OF SPACE
projectDetails.summary:
Project: CALL OF SPACE, developed by the Space1Derers team for the 2025 NASA Space Apps Challenge, explores how Earth observation data can guide urban planners in creating healthier, more resilient cities. With over half of the world’s population now living in urban areas, the pressures of climate change, pollution and rapid growth threaten both human wellbeing and environmental sustainability. Our solution demonstrates how satellite data from NASA — including MODIS, VIIRS, Landsat, and SMAP — can be transformed into actionable insights that support better planning decisions.

We structured our approach around three guiding questions: identifying communities lacking access to food, housing, and transportation; pinpointing areas suffering from polluted air and water; and mapping regions experiencing the fastest urban growth to plan safe housing development. To turn these insights into action, we proposed a three-step pathway: data collection through satellites, analysis and planning by city leaders and urban planners, and implementation through targeted policies and community participation.

This pathway ensures city leaders can integrate scientific data with local needs, developing evidence-based strategies for transport, housing, and green infrastructure. Ultimately, our project highlights how NASA Earth science can empower cities to grow sustainably while improving quality of life for their residents.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – CALL OF SPACE


Our project is a presentation-based solution that demonstrates how NASA Earth observation data can guide urban planners in developing healthier, more resilient cities. It does not function as a live system but instead outlines a structured pathway showing how satellite data can be transformed into actionable strategies.

How it works:
The project is structured around three core urban planning challenges: access to food, housing, and transportation; monitoring polluted air and water; and identifying urban growth for housing development. Each challenge is paired with relevant NASA datasets and a three-step pathway — data collection, analysis and planning and implementation — that explains how insights can move from satellites to city action.

Benefits and impact:
The intended benefit is to show how evidence-based planning can lead to improved quality of life, better environmental protection, and stronger climate resilience. While conceptual, the framework highlights the potential impact of NASA data on shaping future sustainable cities.

Tools and software:
The project was created using canva for the presentation and AI tools were used to support research, structure content, and refine presentation materials.

Creativity:
The project is creative in how it translates complex Earth observation data into an accessible narrative for city leaders, communities, and the public. The use of a clear visual flow — from satellites to people — makes the concept engaging and easy to understand.

Factors considered:
Our team focused on clarity, accessibility, and real-world relevance. We considered climate risks, community needs, and the importance of collaboration between city leaders, residents and scientists.

It helped summarize NASA datasets, structure complex information into clear slides, and refine written content into concise, audience-friendly formats. projectDetails.name: Martian Redemption
projectDetails.summary: We built a fully interactive simulation game in Unity Hub, coded with C# and supported by extensive Blender 3D modeling. After hours of hard work, debugging, and design, we created a realistic simulation of the Perseverance Rover on Mars, in the Jezero Crater, where it collects mission waste and recycles it using advanced chemical and mechanical processes (which have no harmful output on the Martian environment).
projectDetails.details:
We built a fully interactive simulation game in Unity Hub, coded with C# and supported by extensive Blender 3D modeling. After hours of hard work, debugging, and design, we created a realistic simulation of the Perseverance Rover on Mars, where it collects mission waste and recycles it using advanced chemical and mechanical processes.

Each waste stream was carefully represented in the game:

  • Aluminum struts are recycled through induction smelting and electrolysis (Al₂O₃ → Al + O₂), producing new structural alloys.
  • Polyethylene foams (Zotek F30, Plastazote) are shredded and thermally consolidated by thermo-mechanical sintering into insulation cores.
  • Textiles (cotton, polyester, Nomex from CTBs and clothing) are sterilized, fiber-shredded, and reformed into mats via hydrothermal fiber reconstitution.
  • Carbon-fiber composites are processed through pyrolytic decomposition and mechanical comminution, reclaiming fibers for reinforced panels.
  • Multilayer food pouches, overwrap, and films are laminated under pressure, reusing the aluminum-polymer layers as vapor-barrier composites.
  • Nitrile gloves are sterilized and remelted through thermoplastic extrusion, molded into non-critical components.
  • Bubble wrap, resealable bags, and anti-static films are repurposed into FDM 3D printing filament using extrusion and pelletizing.
  • Surplus carbon is treated in an activation furnace (C + H₂O → CO + H₂) to form activated carbon for water purification and CO₂ scrubbing.

The simulation demonstrates how the Martian Redemption Base can transform every type of waste — metals, foams, films, fabrics, gloves, and composites — into valuable materials for survival. The project highlights the combination of real chemical engineering concepts and immersive game design, showing that on Mars, trash becomes infrastructure.

projectDetails.name: Project SpacedWatch
projectDetails.summary:
SpacedWatch is a web app that helps people explore near‑Earth asteroids and imagine what would happen if one hit Earth. It utilises NASA’s NEOWs data and some generalised physics to calculate the impact energy and damage zones based on asteroid size and speed, helping communities plan accordingly. 

Our project aims to plot asteroids according to the location selected by the user and to classify them into three zones : Red, Orange and Green, along with other parameters, and also classify them into safe and hazardous.
projectDetails.details:
The project is a simple web application that aims to help users visualize the impact zones of the asteroid impact. Users can pin a location on the globe and select an asteroid. Once both parameters are selected, the application shows the kinetic energy, estimated yield, and impact zones.

SpacedWatch uses basic physics to make asteroid impacts look real. It uses the formula E = ½mv² to figure out an asteroid's kinetic energy. Using empirical scaling laws, we can figure out the damage radii for impacts: vaporization, severe destruction, moderate damage, and glass shattering zones. These zones scale with the cube root of energy yield (Y^(1/3)). These calculations give us a scientifically sound way to picture what might happen if an asteroid hits Earth.


The app is built on a modern, modular framework. The NeoWs API from NASA sends live data to a Python backend for calculations, and Jupyter Notebooks (.ipynb) support prototyping. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are used to build the front end. CesiumJS is used for 3D Earth visualization and orbital simulations. Dynamic rendering and easy-to-understand UI elements take care of user interactions like impact simulations, hazard filtering, and deflection scenarios. This mix makes sure that the science is correct and the visualization is interesting.

Features:

-Real-time asteroid tracking via NASA’s NeoWs API.

-Impact energy calculator converting asteroid velocity and mass into TNT megaton equivalents.

-Damage zone visualization on a 3D Earth globe with concentric hazard rings.

SpacedWatch Report

projectDetails.details: Our project, Deep Dive VR: From Ocean to Sky, is an immersive virtual reality experience that transforms NASA’s complex Earth observation data into an engaging 3D journey from the deep ocean to outer space. It allows users to explore coral reefs, ocean currents, weather systems, and atmospheric layers using real data from NASA’s MODIS Aqua, AIRS, GOES, and VIIRS satellites. By turning scientific information into an interactive story, the project helps people understand how Earth’s systems connect and change over time. The main benefit is making climate science accessible and inspiring environmental awareness, especially among students and museum visitors. We developed the project using Unity and C# for programming, Blender for 3D modeling, and integrated NASA’s open data APIs to ensure scientific accuracy. The experience can be viewed using VR headsets like Oculus Quest or HTC Vive. Our team focused on balancing realism and creativity, combining accurate satellite data with artistic storytelling to make learning about Earth’s climate both educational and emotionally impactful.

projectDetails.name: Project Space Leaders
projectDetails.summary: Project Space Leaders celebrates 25 years of the International Space Station by transforming NASA data into an interactive learning and storytelling experience. Our project highlights the ISS’s role in advancing science, technology, and global collaboration through engaging visuals and activities. By connecting students, educators, and space enthusiasts, we aim to inspire leadership, curiosity, and innovation in the next generation — continuing the ISS’s mission of discovery and unity beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Project Space Leaders is an interactive educational platform created to celebrate 25 years of the International Space Station (ISS). It transforms NASA’s open datasets and mission archives into engaging, story-based learning experiences for students and educators worldwide.

Our project highlights the ISS’s scientific achievements and its role in global collaboration, while inspiring leadership, curiosity, and innovation among young learners. The platform allows users to explore ISS experiments through visualized data, interactive missions, and leadership challenges—earning “Space Leader” badges for completing learning milestones.

The system is designed with a user-friendly interface developed using HTML5, JavaScript, and NASA’s Open API datasets, supported by design tools such as Canva and Figma for visual storytelling. It can be accessed on any device through a web browser, making space science accessible to all.

Impact:

  • Promotes STEM education and leadership skills.
  • Connects real NASA data to classroom learning.
  • Encourages collaboration and problem-solving through gamified exploration.

Creativity & Innovation:
The project combines storytelling, data visualization, and gamification to create a learning experience that is both scientific and human-centered. By bridging ISS research with real-world education, Project Space Leaders empowers the next generation to dream, lead, and explore—continuing the ISS’s mission of discovery and unity beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: AI Powered Space Biology Engine
projectDetails.summary: The NASA AI Dashboard (nasaaidashboard.netlify.app) is a sophisticated web application that integrates the NASA Open APIs with Google’s Gemini AI to deliver a dynamic and intelligent space exploration experience. By leveraging NASA’s extensive datasets, the platform fetches high-quality astronomical images, mission details, and up-to-date research findings, while Gemini AI powers the natural language processing layer, enabling users to ask complex questions about planets, galaxies, and space phenomena and receive precise, contextualized answers. The dashboard is designed with interactive panels that organize celestial data, mission archives, and scientific insights in a structured manner, while also featuring real-time space news and discovery updates. With advanced functionality such as AI-driven query handling, dynamic data refreshing, and seamless integration of multimodal content, the site operates as more than just a viewer—it is an intelligent, AI-enhanced gateway that bridges cutting-edge machine learning with authoritative NASA resources to make space exploration both accessible and analytically powerful.
projectDetails.details:
The NASA AI Dashboard is an interactive web application that allows users to explore and learn about celestial objects, space missions, and astronomy news in real time. It integrates NASA’s Open APIs to fetch authoritative space data and Gemini AI to provide intelligent summaries, answer astronomy-related questions via an AI chatbot, and handle complex backend logic. Users can search for billions of named and known space components, view concise AI-generated explanations, and continuously load more data without limits, making exploration seamless and scalable.

The project benefits users by making vast and complex astronomical information accessible, enabling real-time stargazing insights, and summarizing technical content in a user-friendly way. Its intended impact is to enhance public engagement with space science, encourage interactive learning, and provide an AI-powered tool for exploring the universe.

The dashboard was developed using a full-stack architecture: TypeScript/React for frontend UI components and logic, TypeScript/Deno for backend edge functions handling AI calls and data fetching, Tailwind CSS for responsive styling, and SQL for minimal database operations. To ensure robust and efficient web delivery, the application is deployed on Netlify, leveraging its global edge network for fast, scalable hosting and serverless function integration. The project is creative because it combines AI-driven processing with live NASA data, allowing users to interact with billions of celestial objects without pre-coding each one. Key considerations included performance, scalability, user experience, and accurate representation of scientific data, ensuring the platform is both educational and technically robust.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
The NASA AI Dashboard leverages Gemini AI to enhance both user experience and backend functionality. AI is used to:

  1. Answer Astronomy Questions – The chatbot interprets user queries and provides accurate, real-time responses about planets, stars, galaxies, and missions.
  2. Summarize Complex Data – Gemini AI processes information from NASA’s APIs, generating concise summaries of celestial objects, news, and discoveries.
  3. Enable Dynamic Search – Users can search for any known or named space component, and AI retrieves relevant data and explanations instantly.
  4. Support Infinite Loading – AI handles continuous requests for new data, allowing the dashboard to scale to billions of celestial objects.
  5. Assist in Code Management – AI was also used to implement complex features and optimize code, helping fix challenging logic and streamline functionality across the frontend and backend.

By combining AI with authoritative NASA data, the website transforms vast and complex astronomical information into accessible, interactive insights while simplifying development of sophisticated features.

projectDetails.name: Stellar Shield
projectDetails.summary: Our project, Stellar Shield, is an interactive simulation and visualization platform designed to help users explore the risks and responses associated with near-Earth objects. The tool models asteroid trajectories, potential collision zones, and the resulting environmental and societal effects. Users can simulate impact scenarios, visualize outcomes through intuitive maps and graphics, and test different mitigation strategies—from deflection attempts to evacuation planning. The goal is to empower both decision-makers and the general public with a clear, accessible way to understand asteroid risks, explore scientific data, and evaluate possible solutions for planetary defense.
projectDetails.details:
Stellar Shield

Stellar Shield is an interactive simulation and visualization platform that helps users explore the risks of near-Earth asteroids and potential responses. The tool integrates NASA and USGS datasets to model asteroid trajectories, project potential collision zones, and estimate the environmental and societal effects of impacts. Users can run “what-if” scenarios, visualize results on interactive maps and 3D globes, and test different mitigation strategies — from deflection attempts to evacuation planning.

What benefits does it have?
By turning raw scientific data into clear visuals and simulations, Stellar Shield bridges the gap between technical experts, decision-makers, and the general public. It simplifies complex datasets, making them actionable for emergency planning and accessible for public understanding. Beyond planetary defense, the platform also serves as an educational tool to spark curiosity and awareness about space science.

What is the intended impact of the project?
The intended impact is threefold:

  • For decision-makers: support scenario planning, rapid risk assessment, and emergency preparedness.
  • For scientists: integrate and communicate asteroid data in a clear, interactive way.
  • For the public: increase awareness of asteroid hazards and empower communities with knowledge, reducing fear and misinformation.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend: React + TypeScript with Deck.gl/Mapbox for 2D/3D mapping and D3.js for data visualization.
  • Backend: Python (FastAPI/Flask) for simulation logic and data integration, with NumPy/SciPy for calculations.
  • APIs/Data: NASA NeoWs API, JPL Small-Body Database API, USGS geological datasets.
  • Other Tools: GitHub for version control, Vercel/Netlify for frontend hosting, and Heroku/Render for backend deployment.

How is your project creative?
Stellar Shield is creative because it transforms highly technical, fragmented datasets into an accessible, engaging, and interactive platform. Instead of static tables or academic models, the project uses dynamic maps, sliders, and visual storytelling to make asteroid impact scenarios tangible. It combines scientific rigor with user-friendly design — creating a bridge between planetary science, policy, and public engagement.

What factors did you consider?
We considered scientific accuracy, clarity of visualization, and accessibility:

  • Used peer-reviewed impact-effect models to ensure outputs are credible.
  • Designed the UI to be intuitive for both technical and non-technical users.
  • Balanced seriousness of planetary defense with engaging visuals, ensuring the platform is both educational and responsible.
  • Focused on scalability: the MVP works for one asteroid scenario but can be expanded to cover multiple threats and real-time updates.

projectDetails.name: Project Space Serenity
projectDetails.summary: Space Serenity is a project designed to predict natural disasters using NASA’s satellite data. It monitors environmental changes and forecasts hazards such as floods, sandstorms, and heatwaves. The platform provides early warnings and clear risk maps to help communities prepare and reduce damage, showcasing how space technology can make the world safer.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works:
Space Serenity is a disaster-prediction platform that uses NASA’s satellite data to monitor environmental changes. By analyzing variables like temperature, precipitation, atmospheric dust, and other weather patterns, the system can forecast natural hazards such as floods, sandstorms, and heatwaves. Users receive early alerts and simplified risk maps that show which areas are most at risk.

Benefits and intended impact:
The platform helps communities prepare in advance for natural disasters, reducing potential damage to life and property. It also raises awareness about environmental risks and demonstrates how space technology can be applied to improve safety and resilience on Earth.

Tools, coding languages, and software:
Our team developed the platform using Python for data analysis and visualization, satellite APIs for real-time environmental data, and mapping software (such as GIS tools) to create interactive risk maps. We also used basic web technologies (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) to create an accessible interface for users.

Creativity and considerations:
Space Serenity is creative because it combines real-time satellite data with predictive algorithms to make disaster information easy to understand for the public. The team considered factors such as accuracy of predictions, clarity of maps, accessibility for non-experts, and timeliness of alerts to ensure the platform is both practical and impactful.
projectDetails.aiReferences: We used AI tools to assist in analyzing large datasets from NASA satellites, including identifying patterns in temperature, precipitation, and atmospheric data that could indicate potential natural hazards. AI algorithms helped us generate predictive models for floods, sandstorms, and heatwaves, which improved the accuracy and speed of our disaster forecasts. Additionally, AI was used to create visualizations and simplified risk maps for users. All AI-generated content, including charts and maps, is clearly labeled as such in the project materials.

(Astrophysics Division)

projectDetails.summary: Our presentation focuses on safety. It explains how space can be both inspiring and dangerous, and how protecting Earth and astronauts is critical. We also outlined the benefits—how learning about space safety helps us better understand our own planet’s protection.
projectDetails.details:
Today, I am here to present our project. Let me take you step by step through what we have created.

1. High-Level Summary

We started by choosing a clear project name and defining why it matters. At the heart of our project is one simple question: How can we understand the challenges of space and why safety is so important for Earth and beyond?

2. Project Demo

For the demo, instead of a video—which was difficult for us to prepare—we created a seven-slide presentation. This includes our title slide and covers the main highlights of our project.

3. Project Details

Our presentation focuses on safety. It explains how space can be both inspiring and dangerous, and how protecting Earth and astronauts is critical. We also outlined the benefits—how learning about space safety helps us better understand our own planet’s protection.

4. Tools and Languages Used

To build this project, we used AI and different tools. The main language we worked in was English. The key platforms and software we relied on were Google and ChatGPT.

5. Use of NASA Data

We also used NASA data, especially about Space Safe Harbor. This helped us see how Earth is protected, what dangers exist in space, and how scientists work to keep us safe. It inspired us and gave us a much deeper understanding of space challenges.

6. Resources

We did not directly partner with any space agency. Instead, we used images generated with ChatGPT and reliable resources from NASA.

Closing

In short, our project is about safety, awareness, and learning. It taught us how space can be both dangerous and fascinating, and how important it is to keep Earth safe.

Thank you.

challengeDetails.title: Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings
challengeDetails.excerpt: Although the Sun is 93 million miles away from our planet, solar activity can significantly impact our daily lives. “Space weather”—the variations that occur in the space environment between the Sun and Earth—can impact technologies in space and on Earth. Your challenge is to write and illustrate a digital children’s story that explains what space weather is and the varying impacts it has on different people such as farmers, pilots, astronauts, power grid operators, and the general public. You can tell the story from the perspective of a person impacted by space weather or from the point of view of a solar flare or coronal mass ejection (CME) as it approaches Earth. (Heliophysics Division)

projectDetails.name: Project Stellar Strike
projectDetails.summary: AstraNest by Team Stellar Strike is an interactive visual design tool that empowers users to create and optimize space habitats for lunar, Martian, or orbital missions. Using NASA’s open data, AstraNest allows users to define habitat dimensions, crew size, and mission duration, then build functional zones such as sleep, hygiene, and food areas through an intuitive drag-and-drop interface. The system provides real-time feedback on volume efficiency, life-support resources, and layout feasibility, while offering a sleek 3D visualization to explore design alternatives. With its balance of scientific accuracy and user accessibility, AstraNest inspires students, engineers, and innovators to design the next generation of livable, sustainable homes in space.
projectDetails.details:
Project Summary – AstraNest by Stellar Strike

Project Name: AstraNest – Your Home in Space

Team: Stellar Strike

Challenge: Your Home in Space: The Habitat Layout Creator (NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025)

Overview

AstraNest is an interactive, web-based tool that empowers users to design and visualize space habitats for lunar, Martian, or orbital missions. Using NASA’s open data and mission design principles, AstraNest helps users balance crew comfort, functionality, and resource constraints — turning complex engineering trade-offs into intuitive, visual design choices.

Concept

In future Moon and Mars missions, astronauts will need habitats that are compact yet fully functional — capable of supporting life, work, and well-being in extreme environments.

Designing these “homes in space” is complex: every cubic meter must serve a purpose, and resources like water, oxygen, and energy must be carefully managed.

AstraNest simplifies this process by providing a drag-and-drop interface where users can:

  • Define a habitat’s shape, size, and mission type
  • Add and position key functional zones (sleep, hygiene, food prep, exercise, storage, etc.)
  • Get real-time feedback on volume usage, resource demands, and environmental constraints
  • Visualize the habitat in 3D, explore layout options, and simulate living condition

How It Works

  1. Set Parameters – Choose mission type (Lunar, Mars, or Orbital), crew size, and mission duration.
  2. Design Layout – Select a habitat shape (cylindrical, dome, inflatable) and add modular zones for different activities.
  3. Smart Feedback Engine – Calculates used volume, water recycling, power demand, and life support efficiency.
  4. Visualize – Generate a 3D preview with color-coded zone validation (green = optimal, red = over capacity).
  5. Iterate & Share – Export or share the design with others for feedback or comparison. 

Systems & Aesthetic

AstraNest also models internal systems:

  • Water recycling using ECLSS-inspired filtration
  • Waste management compact units near hygiene zones
  • Thermal control through centralized core structures
  • Lighting and design aesthetics: pastel gradient palette (pink–violet–blue) with soft ambient glow, giving a calm, futuristic, and ergonomic living feel. 

Impact

  • Educational: Helps students and enthusiasts learn about space architecture and life support systems.
  • Professional: Provides engineers with a fast way to prototype layouts for mission planning.
  • Inspiring: Encourages creativity and engagement in STEM through interactive design.

Tagline

“Design. Test. Live. Build the future of living in space — with AstraNest.”

/* app.js

Prototype logic for AstraNest (Stellar Strike)

- basic habitat volume, zone management

- simple systems calculations (water, toilets, power)

- Three.js basic habitat wireframe

*/

/* ---------------------------

DOM helpers & state

--------------------------- */

const state = {

zones: [], // {id, key, name, volume}

};

function $(id){ return document.getElementById(id) }

const zonesList = $('zonesList')

const widthInput = $('width'), heightInput = $('height'), depthInput = $('depth')

const crewInput = $('crew'), daysInput = $('days')

const zoneSelect = $('zoneSelect'), zoneVolumeInput = $('zoneVolume'), addZoneBtn = $('addZoneBtn')

const calcBtn = $('calcBtn'), summaryDiv = $('summary'), exportBtn = $('exportBtn')

const showConstantsBtn = $('showConstants'), constantsPanel = $('constantspanel')

/* default constants editable in UI */

function getConstants() {

return {

sleepVol: parseFloat($('c_sleep').value), // m³ per person

hygieneVol: parseFloat($('c_hygiene').value), // m³ per person

foodVol: parseFloat($('c_food').value),

exVol: parseFloat($('c_ex').value),

stowVol: parseFloat($('c_stow').value),

drinkL: parseFloat($('c_drink').value),

hygieneL: parseFloat($('c_hygiene_w').value),

recoveryPct: parseFloat($('c_recovery').value),

urineL: parseFloat($('c_urine').value),

solidsKg: parseFloat($('c_solids').value)

}

}

/* ---------------------------

Zone management

--------------------------- */

function renderZones(){

zonesList.innerHTML = ''

state.zones.forEach(z=>{

const li = document.createElement('li')

li.innerHTML = `<div>${z.name} (${z.volume} m³)</div>

<div>

<button class="zdelete" onclick="removeZone('${z.id}')">✕</button>

</div>`

zonesList.appendChild(li)

})

}

function addOrUpdateZone(){

const key = zoneSelect.value

const name = zoneSelect.options[zoneSelect.selectedIndex].text

const volume = parseFloat(zoneVolumeInput.value) || 0

// overwrite same-key zone if exists

const existing = state.zones.find(z=>z.key===key)

if(existing){

existing.volume = volume

} else {

state.zones.push({ id: 'z'+Date.now(), key, name, volume })

}

renderZones()

}

function removeZone(id){

state.zones = state.zones.filter(z=>z.id!==id)

renderZones()

}

/* ---------------------------

Calculation & Analysis

--------------------------- */

function calculate(){

const w = parseFloat(widthInput.value), h = parseFloat(heightInput.value), d = parseFloat(depthInput.value)

const crew = parseInt(crewInput.value), days = parseInt(daysInput.value)

const totalVol = (w*h*d) // simple box volume

const floorArea = w * d

const c = getConstants()

// Recommended volumes per function (basic heuristics)

const recommended = {

sleep: (c.sleepVol * crew),

hygiene: (c.hygieneVol * crew),

food: (c.foodVol * crew),

exercise: (c.exVol * crew),

stowage: (c.stowVol * crew),

lifeSupport: Math.max(6, 0.05 * totalVol) // at least small area, or 5% of total volume

}

// Per-day water balance

const dailyDemandL = crew * (c.drinkL + c.hygieneL)

// total water needed without reuse

const totalDemandL = dailyDemandL * days


// with ECLSS: recovered fraction

const recovery = c.recoveryPct / 100

const netMakeupL = totalDemandL * (1 - recovery)

// Toilet outputs

const urineDailyL = crew * c.urineL

const solidsDailyKg = crew * c.solidsKg

// Determine zone statuses

const statuses = state.zones.map(z=>{

let rec = recommended[z.key] || 0

// if zone is stowage or lifeSupport use different logic

if(z.key === 'stowage') rec = recommended.stowage

if(z.key === 'lifeSupport') rec = recommended.lifeSupport

// determine status by comparing allocated volume to recommended

const ratio = z.volume / (rec || 0.0001)

let status = 'ok'

if(ratio < 0.6) status = 'bad'

else if(ratio < 1.0) status = 'warn'

return { id: z.id, key: z.key, name: z.name, volume: z.volume, required: parseFloat(rec.toFixed(2)), ratio, status }

})

// Overall occupancy metric

const usedVolume = state.zones.reduce((s,z)=>s+z.volume,0)

const remainingVol = totalVol - usedVolume

const occupancy = usedVolume / totalVol

// power estimate (rough)

const powerKW = (1.5*crew) + (0.2*usedVolume/10) // heuristic

// Build summary HTML

let html = `

<p><strong>Habitat total volume:</strong> ${totalVol.toFixed(1)} m³ — floor area ${floorArea.toFixed(1)} m²</p>

<p><strong>Used volume by zones:</strong> ${usedVolume.toFixed(1)} m³ — remaining ${remainingVol.toFixed(1)} m³</p>

<p><strong>Occupancy:</strong> ${(occupancy*100).toFixed(1)}%</p>

<hr>

<h4>Water & Waste</h4>

<p>Daily water demand: <strong>${dailyDemandL.toFixed(1)} L/day</strong> (drinking + hygiene)</p>

<p>Total water demand for ${days} days: <strong>${totalDemandL.toFixed(1)} L</strong></p>

<p>ECLSS recovery efficiency: <strong>${(recovery*100).toFixed(1)}%</strong></p>

<p>Makeup water required after recovery: <strong>${netMakeupL.toFixed(1)} L</strong></p>

<p>Urine produced per day: <strong>${urineDailyL.toFixed(1)} L/day</strong>, solids: <strong>${solidsDailyKg.toFixed(2)} kg/day</strong></p>

<hr>

<h4>Systems & Power</h4>

<p>Rough power estimate: <strong>${powerKW.toFixed(2)} kW</strong> (lighting, computers, ECLSS baseline)</p>

<hr>

<h4>Zone analysis</h4>

<ul>

`

statuses.forEach(s=>{

const color = s.status === 'ok' ? 'green' : (s.status === 'warn' ? 'orange' : 'red')

html += `<li><strong>${s.name}:</strong> allocated ${s.volume} m³ — recommended ${s.required} m³ — <span style="color:${color}">${s.status.toUpperCase()}</span></li>`

})

html += `</ul>`

// Recommendations if needed

if(remainingVol < 0){

html += `<p style="color:#ff6b6b"><strong>Warning:</strong> habitat is over capacity by ${(-remainingVol).toFixed(1)} m³. Increase dimensions or reduce volumes.</p>`

} else if(remainingVol < totalVol*0.1){

html += `<p style="color:#f59e0b"><strong>Note:</strong> remaining volume is tight (${remainingVol.toFixed(1)} m³).</p>`

} else {

html += `<p style="color:#10b981"><strong>Good:</strong> sufficient buffer volume (${remainingVol.toFixed(1)} m³).</p>`

}

summaryDiv.innerHTML = html

highlight3D(statuses)

return { totalVol, floorArea, usedVolume, remainingVol, dailyDemandL, totalDemandL, netMakeupL, urineDailyL, solidsDailyKg, statuses }

}

/* ---------------------------

Export

--------------------------- */

function exportJSON(){

const res = calculate()

const out = {

habitat: {

width: parseFloat(widthInput.value), height: parseFloat(heightInput.value), depth: parseFloat(depthInput.value)

},

crew: parseInt(crewInput.value), days: parseInt(daysInput.value),

zones: state.zones,

analysis: res

}

const blob = new Blob([JSON.stringify(out, null, 2)], {type:'application/json'})

const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob)

const a = document.createElement('a')

a.href = url; a.download = 'astranest_design.json'

document.body.appendChild(a); a.click(); a.remove()

}

/* ---------------------------

UI wiring

--------------------------- */

addZoneBtn.addEventListener('click', addOrUpdateZone)

calcBtn.addEventListener('click', calculate)

exportBtn.addEventListener('click', exportJSON)

showConstantsBtn.addEventListener('click', ()=>constantsPanel.classList.toggle('hidden'))

/* ---------------------------

Three.js preview (wireframe)

--------------------------- */

let scene, camera, renderer, habitatMesh

function initThree(){

const container = $('threecontainer')

const w = container.clientWidth, h = container.clientHeight

scene = new THREE.Scene()

camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(50, w/h, 0.1, 1000)

renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({antialias:true})

renderer.setSize(w,h)

renderer.setClearColor(0x071025)

container.appendChild(renderer.domElement)

const light = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xffffff,0.8)

light.position.set(5,10,7)

scene.add(light)

camera.position.z = 15

camera.position.y = 4

// initial box

const geo = new THREE.BoxGeometry(6,3,5)

const wiremat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({color:0x66b0ff,wireframe:true})

habitatMesh = new THREE.Mesh(geo, wiremat)

scene.add(habitatMesh)

animate()

}

function animate(){

requestAnimationFrame(animate)

if(habitatMesh) habitatMesh.rotation.y += 0.005

renderer.render(scene,camera)

}

// update 3D with new dims & highlight statuses

function highlight3D(statuses){

// update box geometry

const w = parseFloat(widthInput.value), h = parseFloat(heightInput.value), d = parseFloat(depthInput.value)

habitatMesh.geometry.dispose()

habitatMesh.geometry = new THREE.BoxGeometry(Math.max(w,0.1), Math.max(h,0.1), Math.max(d,0.1))

// color by occupancy

const used = state.zones.reduce((s,z)=>s+z.volume,0)

const ratio = used / (w*h*d)

const color = ratio>0.9 ? 0xff6b6b : (ratio>0.7 ? 0xf59e0b : 0x66b0ff)

habitatMesh.material.color.setHex(color)

}

/* ---------------------------

Init

--------------------------- */

window.addEventListener('load', ()=>{

initThree()

// add default zones with reasonable invites

state.zones = [

{id:'z_sleep', key:'sleep', name:'Sleep', volume: 32},

{id:'z_hyg', key:'hygiene', name:'Hygiene', volume: 12},

{id:'z_food', key:'food', name:'Food Prep & Storage', volume: 15},

{id:'z_stow', key:'stowage', name:'Stowage', volume: 40},

]

renderZones()

calculate()

})

// expose removeZone to global so delete button inline works

window.removeZone = removeZone

Systems details

Life Support & Water (ECLSS)

  • Water demand uses two components: drinking (~2.5 L/day/person) and hygiene (~5 L/day/person) by default (adjustable).
  • ECLSS recovery efficiency is a parameter (default 85%): recovered water is reused for hygiene/drinking after processing — the tool calculates required makeup water over mission duration:
    makeup = total_demand * (1 - recovery_efficiency)
  • Toilet handling: urine is tracked in liters/day and solids in kg/day; urine can be recycled at a high rate by urine processors and distillation (recovery fraction adjustable). Solid waste should be compacted and stored or processed (not simulated in depth here, but output rates are shown so you can propose solutions like in-situ processing or return).

Sanitation / Toilet approach (explainable in pitch)

  • Fan-driven toilets with screw/compaction for solids, vacuum-assisted urine separation. Urine treatment yields water for ECLSS; solids are dried/compacted and stored for return or for ISRU (in-situ resource utilization) processing (e.g., conversion to feedstock for plants).
  • Hygiene is simulated as volume and water demand; propose closed-loop shower & condensate recovery to capture humidity.
Thermal control & power
  • Power estimate is a simple heuristic (kW per crew plus per-volume overhead). For the pitch: justify more rigorous modeling is possible — integrate solar arrays for lunar surface with batteries and RTG as backup as mission requirement changes.

Food & Stowage

  • Food prep/storage volume is treated per-person; you should propose modular food lockers that double as stowage or structural partitions to save space.

Privacy & zoning rules (implemented in tool as recommendations)

  • Sleep should be separated from noisy/exercise zones.
  • Life support systems should be near storage and stowage for maintenance.
  • Tool flags when zones are too close to limits or under-allocated.

projectDetails.name: Project Stellar Surge
projectDetails.summary: Vera's Solar Challenge is an interactive digital tale game that teaches children about how the Sun affects Earth. Players join Vera on a mission to halt a catastrophic solar disturbance by completing knowledge-based activities that test their grasp of solar activity and its impact on daily life. The plot combines science and adventure, allowing users to learn about events such as solar flares and geomagnetic storms through problem solving and exploration. By combining narrative, images, and gameplay, the project transforms difficult solar science into an engaging, easy-to-understand experience that piques curiosity and raises awareness about our planet's relationship to the Sun.
projectDetails.details:
At first, our team debated whether to make a digital storybook or something more interactive. We wanted to explain how the Sun’s activity affects Earth but in a way that kept young learners engaged. After considering both possibilities, we opted on an interactive tale game in which players could engage rather than simply read. That decision shaped Cosmic Shields: Vera’s Solar Challenge into a mix of story, science, and discovery.

The game works as a learning quest where players must answer questions and make choices to help Vera safeguard Earth from solar disturbances. It highlights real-world effects of solar events on astronauts, communication systems, and power grids in a way that’s both fun and educational. Built using AI writing and illustration tools, it combines creative storytelling with verified scientific data to ensure accuracy. Our team focused on simplicity, visual appeal, and interactivity to hold the attention of younger audiences.

The final version introduces key scientific concepts such as solar flares, CMEs, magnetic fields, and auroras through situational questions and visual cues. It encourages logical thinking and connects classroom knowledge to real-world technology and environmental systems. By merging factual science with gameplay, our project aims to support early STEM education and promote awareness of how solar activity influences modern life on Earth.
