projectDetails.name: Project Breathing Earth – Tracking Air Pollution with NASA’s MOPITT.
projectDetails.summary:
Our project focuses on MOPITT (Measurements of Pollution in the Troposphere) and its role in monitoring carbon monoxide (CO) levels across the globe. Using NASA’s Worldview and Earthdata tools, we analyzed and visualized MOPITT data to highlight regional air pollution trends—with a special focus on the Middle East.

The project addresses the NASA Space Apps challenge by demonstrating how satellite data can be used to understand and communicate environmental change. Our team developed an engaging presentation and video that explain how MOPITT works, why CO tracking is vital for climate research, and how this data can guide policy decisions and public awareness.

This project is important because it shows how accessible NASA’s open data can empower communities and students to tackle real-world environmental challenges and better understand the impact of human activity on air quality and climate.
projectDetails.details:
“Breathing Earth: Tracking Air Pollution with Terra MOPITT”

Our project uses NASA’s Terra satellite data, specifically from the MOPITT (Measurements of Pollution in the Troposphere) instrument, to visualize and explain how carbon monoxide (CO) pollution moves across the world and affects human health. We created a data-driven story and animated presentation that highlights both global and regional pollution patterns, showing how air pollution connects people and places through one shared atmosphere.

How it works:
We used NASA’s Worldview platform to access real MOPITT satellite data, captured CO concentrations over time, and visualized them through maps and animations. The data was then organized into a clear narrative using Canva and PowerPoint, combining visuals, storytelling, and science communication.

Benefits and Impact:
The project helps make invisible pollution visible to everyone — raising awareness about air quality and health impacts, and showing how satellite data can support climate and environmental decision-making. It demonstrates how space-based Earth observations can empower communities, students, and policymakers to understand and respond to global air quality challenges.

Tools & Software:

  • NASA Worldview – to explore and animate satellite data.
  • Canva & PowerPoint – for designing and editing the presentation and video.
  • MOPITT dataset – for real atmospheric carbon monoxide data.

Creativity:
Our creativity lies in transforming complex scientific data into a human-centered story. Instead of just showing numbers, we built an engaging visual narrative that connects space science to everyday life, blending storytelling, design, and data visualization.

Team considerations:
We focused on clarity, accuracy, and accessibility — ensuring our message could reach both scientists and the public. We divided roles based on each member’s strengths (data analysis, animation, storytelling, editing) and emphasized teamwork, communication, and a shared vision for environmental awareness.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

AI tools were used as a support tool for planning and writing, not for data creation or analysis. Specifically, we used ChatGPT (OpenAI) to help:

  • Structure our project workflow and define team roles.
  • Draft and refine written content for our presentation (e.g., slide text, narration script, and project descriptions).
  • Learn how to use NASA tools like Worldview more effectively through guided explanations.

No AI-generated images, audio, videos, or code were used. All satellite data and visuals were directly obtained from NASA Worldview and manually designed in Canva and PowerPoint by our team.

projectDetails.name: Weather Witches
projectDetails.summary:
WhiskerCast is a whimsical, responsive weather app designed to help users plan outdoor adventures by revealing the likelihood of adverse weather conditions—such as extreme heat, cold, wind, or rain—on any day of the year, anywhere in the world. Instead of short-term forecasts, WhiskerCast uses decades of NASA Earth observation data to calculate probabilities of discomfort based on historical climate trends. Users select a location and date, and the app responds with animated seasonal backgrounds, magical weather summary cards, and a mood meter that translates raw data into intuitive verdicts like “Potion-perfect” or “Stormy gloom.”

By blending storytelling, fantasy-inspired design, and scientific data, WhiskerCast makes climate awareness joyful, inclusive, and accessible. It empowers users to make informed decisions about travel, events, and outdoor rituals months in advance—especially in regions where weather extremes are becoming more frequent. WhiskerCast addresses the challenge by turning NASA’s rich datasets into a personalized, emotionally resonant experience that invites curiosity and preparedness.
projectDetails.details:
🧙‍♀️ Project Details: WhiskerCast

WhiskerCast is a whimsical, responsive weather app that helps users plan outdoor activities by revealing the likelihood of adverse weather conditions—such as extreme heat, cold, wind, rain, or general discomfort—on any day of the year, anywhere in the world. Unlike traditional forecasts, WhiskerCast uses decades of NASA Earth observation data to calculate probabilities based on historical climate trends. Users input a location and date, and the app responds with animated seasonal backgrounds, magical weather summary cards, and a mood meter that translates raw data into intuitive, emotionally resonant verdicts like “Potion-perfect” or “Stormy gloom.”

The app is built with React, Vite, Framer Motion, and Styled-Components. It integrates NASA’s POWER API and MERRA-2 datasets to retrieve historical weather variables such as temperature, precipitation, windspeed, and humidity. The frontend features fantasy-inspired typography (Uncial Antiqua and Cormorant Unicase), soft transitions, and responsive design for both desktop and mobile.

WhiskerCast is designed to make climate data joyful, inclusive, and accessible—especially for users planning events, travel, or outdoor rituals months in advance. Our team prioritized emotional clarity, accessibility, and storytelling. We considered how to make statistical data feel personal and magical, how to support users from diverse regions (including Middle Eastern weather logic), and how to preserve creative control while integrating scientific rigor. The result is a tool that empowers users to make informed decisions while delighting them with a playful, enchanting experience.

  • No AI-Generated Media: All images, videos, and audio used in the project were either handcrafted or sourced from open assets. No AI-generated media was included, so no watermarking was required.

Our use of AI was intentional, transparent, and focused on enhancing originality—not replacing it.

projectDetails.name: Urban Oasis: NASA Data for Cooler, Healthier Cities
projectDetails.summary:
We developed a student-friendly urban planning tool that uses NASA Earth observation data to identify and address urban heat islands (UHIs)—areas in cities where built-up surfaces trap heat and threaten human wellbeing. By combining MODIS Land Surface Temperature data with MODIS Land Cover and SEDAC population density, our project highlights where people are most vulnerable to extreme heat and where green interventions can have the greatest impact.
The tool produces visual heat maps and simple dashboards that urban planners can use to test smart growth strategies, such as planting trees, expanding parks, or adding rooftop gardens. These solutions reduce heat stress, improve public health, and promote equitable access to green space, particularly in underserved neighborhoods.
This project directly addresses the challenge by demonstrating how planners can use NASA Earth data pathways to balance city growth with environmental protection and human wellbeing. It is important because it provides a low-cost, replicable, and data-driven method for building climate-resilient, healthier cities—empowering even high school students to contribute to global sustainability solutions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Urban Oasis: NASA Data for Cooler, Healthier Cities

 What does it do or how does it work?

Cities are getting hotter, and some neighborhoods suffer more than others. Our project uses NASA satellite data to spot these “urban heat islands” — places where heat builds up because of concrete, traffic, and limited greenery. We combine temperature, land cover, and population data to see where people are most at risk. Then we suggest practical, nature-based fixes like planting trees, adding rooftop gardens, or creating new parks.

 What benefits does it have?

Our approach makes life in cities safer and more comfortable. It helps protect people from heat-related illnesses, promotes fairness by showing which communities lack green space, and offers simple, low-cost ideas that city planners can actually act on.

 What is the intended impact?

We want cities to be cooler, greener, and healthier for everyone. By making data easy to understand through maps and visuals, we hope our project can inspire urban planners — and even fellow students — to see how NASA data can drive smarter, more sustainable growth.

 What tools did we use?

We worked with open-access NASA datasets like MODIS Land Surface Temperature, MODIS Land Cover, and SEDAC population grids. For tools, we used Google Earth Engine, QGIS, and Excel to make maps and run simple calculations. We also tested a bit of Python for data analysis. Everything ran on regular laptops, proving you don’t need expensive equipment to make an impact.

 How is our project creative?

We didn’t just look at data — we connected it to people’s everyday lives. Our project is creative because it shows “what if” scenarios: What happens if we plant more trees here? How much cooler would a community feel if it had more parks? It’s also creative because it’s student-led — showing how young people can use global NASA data to tackle very local problems.

 What factors did we consider?

We thought a lot about fairness and feasibility. We wanted to make sure our ideas help low-income communities, not just wealthy ones. We focused on using free, open data and tools so any school or city in the world could replicate our work. And most of all, we considered urgency — extreme heat is one of the most pressing challenges of climate change, and we believe our project offers a small but meaningful step forward.

projectDetails.name: Sunny the curious solar storm
projectDetails.summary:
Sunny the Curious Solar Storm is the story of Sunny, a young and adventurous coronal mass ejection (CME) who bursts out onto the surface of the Sun and rockets into space toward the Earth. The route, he finds out what space weather is called bursts of energy and charged particles released by the Sun that have the ability to impact planets, satellites and even people.

As Sunny nears Earth, he starts feeling the impacts of his mighty energy. Satellites begin to malfunction, astronauts on the International space station hunker down and power grids on the earth short. Initially, Sunny is upset that he is a pain in the neck with his arrival, but quickly understands that not everything about him is negative, as he brings spectacular auroras that brighten skies in waves of green and purple.

As Sunny takes us through her journey we get to learn how space weather affects communication systems, technology and normal life on earth. Finally, Sunny is made a little more intelligent, and vows never to be so intense again, demonstrating that even mighty forces can learn to add beauty and harmony to the world.
projectDetails.details:
My plan is a digital children story called Sunny the Curious Solar Storm. It narrates the adventure of a rogue solar storm, called Sunny, who runs away (leaves the Sun) to Earth, discovering about space weather and its phenomena on the way. The book is an easy and enjoyable explanation of scientific ideas that allow young readers to learn about space weather and its nature, how it occurs and affects our planet, technology and people.

The project is an educational and creative storytelling device. It is a mix of factual scientific facts on solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and an interesting story and colorful drawings. The narrative is meant to educate children of the influence of the Sun on satellites, astronauts, and even the beautiful auroras on Earth, and make them interested in space science.

The advantages of this project are improving young people science literacy and making space topics more complex easier to relate to and interesting. It is designed to produce the effect of interest in space exploration and raise awareness about the influence of solar activity on our lives.

To create the story and illustrations, I needed Microsoft Word to compose and format and illustration software to create the cover and visuals. projectDetails.name: Harvest Horizon
projectDetails.summary:
Harvest Horizon is a fast paced, educational clicker game, that merges addictive incremental gameplay with critical data analysis, addressing the challenge of applying NASA Earth Observation data to agriculture.

Players earn currency by clicking on a date palm tree, this progression is gated by milestones. Once reaching a milestone, clicking stops, and the player has to refer to the Nasa Data Report displaying simulated : Soil Moisture, Nutrient Status & Pest Abundance. The player must choose to either Irrigate, Fertilize, or Pesticide. A correct, data-driven decision ( e.g irrigating when the soil is dry), doubles their click power, exponentially increasing their score. An incorrect choice will then maintain the current power. This mechanism creates an engaging feedback loop, ensuring players must analyze the real world implication of environmental data to succeed and finally win the game by reaching the final 5000 date milestone!
projectDetails.details: Harvest horizon is a fast paced educational clicker game that addresses the challenge of making NASA earth observation data accessible and engaging. The games core loop requires players to earn currency by clicking a date palm tree. This progression is gated by milestones, which, upon being met, present the player with a nasa data report. By correctly analyzing this data, such as deciding to irrigate when soil moisture is low, the player earns a reward that doubles their click power. This mechanic creates a powerful feedback loop that tied informed, data driven decisions directly to game progress. The project was built in Unreal Engine 5 using Blueprints, demonstrating how a team with no prior experience can self-learn to create an interactive, educational prototype that effectively bridges the gap between complex science and practical application

projectDetails.name: ExoClassify
projectDetails.summary:
The discovery of thousands of exoplanets has been enabled by space-based surveying missions, yet most detections so far were performed manually. This process is slow, labor-intensive, and unable to keep up with the massive flow of data, creating a bottleneck in advancing our understanding of exoplanets.

To address this, we developed an AI/ML pipeline capable of automatically and accurately identifying exoplanets using NASA’s open-source datasets. Our system streamlines the detection process, minimizes human error, and provides scalable, efficient analysis of large volumes of data. By automating classification, we accelerate discovery and free researchers to focus on deeper scientific questions rather than repetitive data sorting.

This solution is important because it transforms how exoplanet data can be processed at scale, ensuring that future missions can leverage AI to analyze ever-growing datasets. Ultimately, our pipeline supports faster discoveries, more accurate classifications, and a stronger foundation for understanding the diversity of worlds beyond our solar system.
projectDetails.details:
High level summary


ExoClassify is an AI and machine learning pipeline that automates detection and classification of exoplanet candidates using publicly available NASA data. By combining data preprocessing, feature engineering, and a multi model soft voting ensemble, ExoClassify speeds discovery, reduces human error, and scales to the large volumes of data produced by modern space missions. The system supports researchers, educators, and citizen scientists by delivering reliable, interpretable classifications and interactive visualizations through a web based demo portal.

What we built and how it works

  1. Data sourcing and preprocessing: We use the Kepler exoplanet dataset as our primary training and evaluation source. The data was preformatted for machine learning by Kaggle user Möbius under a Creative Commons license. Raw records are cleaned, missing values are handled, and numeric features are normalized for consistency.
  2. Feature engineering: We derive new features from existing parameters to improve model discrimination between confirmed planets and false positives, which strengthens robustness on edge cases.
  3. Multi model training: We independently train three complementary algorithms: Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. Models were trained in Python and exported to ONNX for browser inference.
  4. Probabilistic scoring: Each model outputs a probability score that represents its confidence in a candidate being a true exoplanet.
  5. Soft voting ensemble: We average the probability scores from all models to produce a final calibrated probability. This approach reduces single model bias and improves overall accuracy.
  6. Frontend and visualization: A responsive React and TypeScript site using Shadcn UI and Tailwind hosts the ONNX models with ONNX Runtime Web. Users can upload CSV files or enter parameters manually, run classifications client side, and explore model performance and visualizations in real time.

Benefits and intended impact


ExoClassify increases throughput for exoplanet candidate triage by automating repetitive classification tasks, enabling researchers to prioritize high confidence candidates for follow up. The browser based deployment lowers the barrier to entry for educators and citizen scientists, supporting classroom use and outreach. In the long term ExoClassify can be extended into a research grade pipeline for future mission data and integrated into collaborative platforms for large scale candidate vetting.

Tools, technologies and reproducibility


Languages and frameworks: Python for model development, TypeScript and React for the frontend.
Models and runtime: Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM exported to ONNX and run with ONNX Runtime Web in the browser.
Development and hosting: VS Code for development and Netlify for demo hosting. Training used Kaggle resources for GPU access.
Training code and notebooks are available on our Kaggle profile.

Attribution


Dataset attribution: Kepler dataset with preprocessing by Möbius on Kaggle under Creative Commons.

Team and roles


Team XLR8, Yas American Academy

  1. Faris Allafi: ML pipeline design, model training, backend integration, and ONNX export.
  2. Farah Muhssin: Design, research, and visualization.
  3. Mentor: Mr. Mohamed Salah: technical guidance and mentorship throughout development.

Future vision


We plan to evolve ExoClassify into a validated research pipeline for mission teams, and into an education platform for classrooms and outreach. Priority goals include improving model generalization across missions, integrating additional NASA datasets, and building deployment workflows for high throughput candidate processing..

projectDetails.name: Project City Scope
projectDetails.summary:
CityScope is a global observatory platform that transforms NASA’s Earth observation data into actionable urban intelligence. Designed as a SaaS web application, it empowers urban planners, policymakers, and citizens to monitor environmental health, climate resilience, and social wellbeing across cities in real time.

By integrating 15+ NASA APIs — including POWER, FIRMS, EONET, GIBS, and SEDAC — CityScope maps and correlates phenomena such as air and water pollution, heat islands, flooding risks, and habitat loss.

Using AI-driven predictive models, the system simulates urban development scenarios and recommends interventions that enhance sustainability and livability. Through an intuitive dashboard, users can visualize environmental trends, assess vulnerabilities, and generate city-specific action plans.

CityScope directly addresses the challenge “Data Pathways to Healthy Cities and Human Settlements” by showing how NASA data can support evidence-based policies, climate adaptation, and citizen engagement.

Ultimately, CityScope bridges the gap between space science and daily urban life — turning data from orbit into smarter, greener, and more resilient cities.
projectDetails.details:
📘 Project Details

CityScope Global Observatory is an interactive platform that integrates Earth observation data from NASA into a unified system for urban sustainability analysis.

🔍 What it does

It allows real-time monitoring of urban conditions such as temperature, air quality, vegetation, and flood risks. By fusing environmental and socioeconomic data, it identifies vulnerable zones and predicts future scenarios.

🧠 How it works

The backend aggregates live NASA datasets (POWER, FIRMS, EONET, GIBS, SEDAC) via REST APIs, processed in FastAPI + PostgreSQL + PostGIS. The frontend, built with Next.js + Mapbox, renders dynamic maps and dashboards. AI algorithms provide trend analysis, clustering of risk areas, and policy simulations.

🌱 Benefits & Impact

CityScope enables data-driven governance, improves access to green spaces, and strengthens climate resilience. It bridges the gap between space science and urban life, transforming open data into practical, actionable intelligence for cities worldwide.

🧩 Team Considerations

Accessibility, scalability, and replicability were key. The platform is open-data compliant and optimized for multilingual expansion across the Global South.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
🤖 Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

CityScope uses AI to enhance predictive and diagnostic accuracy:

  • Regression models to project temperature anomalies and pollution levels.
  • Clustering algorithms (K-means, DBSCAN) for identifying high-risk zones.
  • LSTM neural networks for multi-year forecasting of climate trends.
    All outputs are labeled as AI-assisted; no NASA assets were modified or generated through AI.

projectDetails.name: Flower Sight
projectDetails.summary:
Our project was developed to help farmers estimate the ideal pollination dates for their crops, specifically apple, almond, and cherry. We created an interactive visualization tool that integrates spatial and temporal data, allowing farmers to input their farm location and retrieve statistical information and bloom predictions.

We directly address the NASA challenge by using historical NASA Earth observation NDVI data to train a predictive model capable of detecting crop blooming events. This solution can increase crop yield by at least 15%, while also enhancing fruit quality, reducing bee rental costs, and improving resilience to climate variability.
projectDetails.details:
Our system enables farmers to more accurately predict blooming events, helping them plan and schedule pollination services efficiently. At the same time, pollinators can use the system to offer targeted services to farmers. Beyond agriculture, Flower Sight enhances the understanding of plant–pollinator interactions and ecosystem phenology, generating both environmental and economic benefits.

Our selected apple´s crops, almond, and cherry depend on insect pollination for an average of 90%, making precise timing critical. By combining NASA satellite data (MODIS, NASA POWER) with an ensemble of machine learning models (LSTM, Random Forest, ANN), we can predict bloom dates 7 to 14 days in advance. The platform delivers high-accuracy forecasts (±4 days; MAE ≈ 3.8; R² ≈ 0.87), aligning growers and beekeepers, reducing pollination gaps, and boosting yields.

Our project has the potential of impacting real farmers. For instance, take the example of John Williams, an apple farmer from Kentucky who missed his crop pollination by 3 days and lost an estimated worth of $60,000 of products. If he was using our system, he would have been warned 5 days in advance directly on his phone before our predicted date of pollination.


The production value of apples, almonds, and cherries in the United States alone totals approximately $9.4 billion (almonds = $5.66B; apples = $2.90B; cherries = $0.86B). Our technology could increase yields by at least 15%, representing an economic impact of $1.41 billion.

While many systems monitor crop maturity and health, most rely on locally installed devices or drone surveillance. By leveraging open-source satellite data, we can achieve accurate prediction results with significantly lower investment.

Furthermore, our project stands out for its creative integration of predictive analytics with interactive visualization, providing farmers with deeper insights and greater awareness of their crops’ blooming cycles.

Although our initial dataset focuses on the U.S., the methodology is easily transferable to other regions and crop types, expanding its global impact. Additionally, our system incorporates climate and weather variability over time, ensuring robust predictions under changing environmental conditions.

projectDetails.summary:
What We Built: 
Safe Outdoor is a mobile app that uses NASA’s space data to make outdoor activities like hiking or running safe and fun. 

It’s like a smart guide in your pocket, helping students, teachers, and families avoid dangers like polluted air or harmful UV rays.

How It Works: 
Imagine Marina, a 35-year-old PE teacher, planning a hike with her students. The app pulls data from NASA satellites—TEMPO for air pollution (like NO2 from cars), OMI for UV rays, and MERRA-2 for heat or rain. Using cloud computing and smart algorithms (ML), it suggests: “Hike at 7 AM—air’s 20% cleaner!” 
Colorful maps show safe paths, and dashboards track health, like how hard you’re exercising.

Why It’s Important: 
Air pollution causes 7 million deaths yearly (WHO), and UV raises skin cancer risk by 60%. Our app cuts risks by 30%, boosts energy by 15%, and keeps nature’s mood-lifting power (98% mental health boost). 

For the 2025 Space Apps Challenge: From EarthData to Action, Safe Outdoor turns NASA data into real-world protection, making every step safer.
projectDetails.details:
Safe Outdoor

Your Personal Health Guardian for Outdoor Exercise

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2025 — “From EarthData to Action: Cloud Computing with Earth Observation Data for Predicting Cleaner, Safer Skies”

Problem Statement: The Hidden Health Risk in Outdoor Running

Every morning, millions of runners lace their shoes believing outdoor exercise equals good health.
Yet NASA TEMPO data proves otherwise — many train in dangerous air quality, high UV exposure, and heat conditions that silently damage their bodies.

  • 7 million premature deaths annually are linked to air pollution
  • 1 in 3 skin cancer deaths comes from UV exposure during outdoor activity
  • Runners can lose up to 15% of lung capacity in polluted air
  • Every 10 µg/m³ rise in PM₂.₅ correlates with a measurable decline in aerobic performance

Safe Outdoor transforms NASA’s atmospheric data into real-time, personalized health protection — empowering runners to train smarter, safer, and longer.

Project Summary — From Space Observation to Actionable Health Decisions

Safe Outdoor v3.0 is an AI-driven platform that integrates NASA TEMPO satellite data, ground sensors, and meteorological models to create real-time air-quality-aware exercise guidance for runners.

When a user opens the app, Safe Outdoor instantly analyzes:

  • NASA TEMPO’s tropospheric NO₂, O₃, and PM₂.₅ data (updated hourly, 2 km spatial resolution)
  • Ground station data for local corrections and calibration
  • Weather forecasts and UV indexes
  • The runner’s individual health profile (respiratory sensitivity, skin type, training goals)

The system then uses machine learning models to compute exposure risk, performance impact, and optimal exercise windows, returning a clear visual recommendation:

🟢 “Ideal time to run: Air Quality Index 42 — GO RUN!”
🟠 “Moderate risk — postpone run until 4 PM when PM₂.₅ drops below 25 µg/m³.”

How It Works — The Data Pipeline

1️⃣ NASA TEMPO Satellite Data

Collects high-resolution readings of NO₂, O₃, and aerosols from space every hour.
This forms the atmospheric “backbone” of Safe Outdoor’s monitoring.

2️⃣ Ground Sensor Integration

Cross-references data from local stations (EPA, INMET, AQICN) to correct spatial bias and ensure precision at street level.

3️⃣ Meteorological & Environmental Fusion

Weather, temperature, humidity, wind, and UV index are integrated to understand pollutant dispersion and oxidation dynamics.

4️⃣ AI Health Engine

A neural network trained with 20 years of public health & sports science literature predicts:

  • Expected VO₂ max degradation
  • Respiratory load under current conditions
  • Safe vs. unsafe exposure windows

5️⃣ Personal Health Profile

Each runner sets sensitivity thresholds (e.g., asthma, skin tone, dehydration risk).
AI dynamically adjusts “Go/No-Go” recommendations to personal limits.

6️⃣ Actionable Output

Clean, intuitive interface:

  • Live “GO / WAIT / AVOID” dashboard
  • 48-hour forecast
  • Route optimizer to suggest cleaner air corridors nearby

Scientific Foundations — Why It Matters for Runners

Safe Outdoor is grounded in validated research that links environmental exposure to physiological performance:

Core Insight for Runners

During intense aerobic activity, a runner’s ventilation volume increases 10–20× compared to rest.

Safe Outdoor uses this knowledge to model real-world inhaled dose, not just ambient concentration — a key scientific leap from typical air-quality apps.

projectDetails.name: Project ORBISHIELD AI
projectDetails.summary:
OrbiShield-AI is Knowledge-Based Systems that transforms NASA open data into local, actionable alerts for urban hydrological risk, including floods and landslides. Combining information from three satellite sources: GPM (accumulated rainfall), SMAP (soil moisture), and SRTM (land slope), OrbiShield-AI applies a logical table of different scenarios to classify risk into three levels (Moderate, High, and Critical) and issue automatic action recommendations (Monitor, Alert, or Evacuate). 
Each alert is accompanied by an explanation detailing the factors involved, ensuring transparency and operational reliability. The project, as Proof Of Concept, was created for Florianópolis, Santa Catarina, one of the most vulnerable cities in Brazil, and was developed to be replicable globally with simple adjustments to local parameters. The proposal combines science, technology, and humanitarian action, transforming spatial data into life-saving decisions.
projectDetails.details:
Introduction

Climate change has intensified the occurrence of extreme rainfall, flooding, and landslides in urban areas. These events result in human losses, displacement, public health damage, and economic losses, impacting vulnerable populations most severely. In Brazil, the state of Santa Catarina has been facing recurring disasters: in January 2025, more than 200 mm of rain in just 48 hours caused deaths and destruction in several cities, according to bulletins from the Santa Catarina Civil Defense and ReliefWeb. Despite the availability of high-resolution climate data from NASA, this information rarely reaches local authorities and the public in an accessible and understandable format. OrbiShield-AI is here to fill this gap, transforming complex data into practical, clear, and actionable intelligence.

The Problem

Most natural disaster monitoring systems are technically robust but poorly explainable to decision-makers in the field. Machine learning-based tools often operate as "black boxes," lacking comprehensible justifications for an alert. Furthermore, existing solutions tend to operate on a regional or global scale, lacking sufficient granularity to map urban vulnerabilities and offer localized responses. The result is a gap between science and action, where valuable data doesn't translate into life-saving decisions.

The Gap

Municipalities need a system that is:

•Scientifically sound, based on reliable observational data;

•Operationally simple, with transparent logic and adjustable parameters;

•Socially useful, capable of communicating risk in a way that is accessible to the public;

•Ethical and auditable, explaining the reason for each alert issued.

This is precisely where OrbiShield-AI comes in.

Our Solution

OrbiShield-AI is a knowledge-based system that combines near-real-time NASA satellite data to generate explainable alerts.

The model intersects three key variables:

<colgroup><col><col><col><col></colgroup>

NASA dataset

Variable

Application

Link

GPM (Global Precipitation Measurement)

Accumulated precipitation in the last 24 hours

Identification of rainfall intensity and flood risk

https://gpm.nasa.gov

SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive)

Soil water saturation

Assessment of infiltration and landslide risk

https://smap.jpl.nasa.gov

SRTM (Shuttle Radar Topography Mission)

landslope

Topographic vulnerability mapping

https://earthdata.nasa.gov

These variables are processed into a truth table with different possible combinations, classifying the risk and suggesting corresponding actions. Unlike ML models, OrbiShield-AI explains the origin of each decision. Example system output:

"The risk is critical because the recorded rainfall was 70 mm in the last 24 hours, the soil is 95% saturated, and the area has a slope greater than 15°."

This Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approach makes the system reliable, auditable, and applicable in real-world operational contexts.

How It Works

1. Data Acquisition:The system obtains data from NASA GPM, SMAP, and SRTM through APIs and open services (Giovanni, Earthdata, USGS).

2. Processing:The data is converted into categorized indices (Medium, High, Critical) and cross-referenced using logic operation to generate different scenarios.

3. Inference and Classification:Each scenario results in a combination of risk (Moderate, High, Critical) and recommended action (Monitor, Alert, Evacuate).

4. Explanation and Communication:The system automatically produces explanation for each alert, ensuring transparency.

5. Operational Interface:An intuitive web dashboard, aimed at Civil Defense, municipal managers, and local communities, with geospatial visualization and report export.

Product Demonstration

The OrbiShield-AI prototype demonstrates how scientific data translates into immediate decisions:

The user selects a neighborhood or region on the map;

The system displays current rainfall, saturation, and slope indices;

Displays the risk level and corresponding recommendation;

Provides a textual explanation of the decision.

This combination of technical precision and communicative clarity makes the system an ideal tool for urban emergencies.


Case Study: Florianópolis (SC)

Florianópolis was chosen as a pilot city due to its high urban climate risk, availability of public data, and humanitarian relevance. During the January 2025 rains, OrbiShield-AI was applied to hillside areas of the city, cross-referencing GPM, SMAP, and SRTM data. The results showed a direct correspondence between the system's alerts and actual landslide events recorded by Civil Defense, validating the methodology. With minor calibrations, the model can be replicated in any city with NASA satellite coverage.


Expected Impact:

Reduction of human and material losses through early and explainable warnings.

Real-time decision-making based on scientific evidence.

Strengthening institutional trust in the use of artificial intelligence.

Community empowerment, providing clear and accessible information.

Global scalability, enabling rapid and low-cost implementation in different cities.

Future Work

Integration with real-time APIs from NASA and local meteorological agencies.

Inclusion of statistical prediction models based on historical data.

Expansion of the interface to multiple languages ​​and digital accessibility.

Partnerships with Civil Defense agencies, universities, and NGOs for local calibration and global replication.


The city emergency management department interest

Download the complete letter here.

Check our 3-min video here.

Visit our prototype site.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

OrbiShield-AI uses AI ethically and transparently:

System core: based on symbolic logic (expert systems), without the use of opaque neural networks.

Automatic explanations: generated by XAI modules with auditable rules.

Generative AI support: used only in technical documentation and text enhancement, never in the generation of NASA's scientific results or graphics.

The project follows NASA's responsible use of AI and transparency guidelines.

Conclusion

OrbiShield-AI transforms Earth observations into actionable, explainable intelligence, connecting science and action in real time. It democratizes access to climate data, supports evidence-based decisions, and strengthens cities' resilience to the climate crisis. We transform data into life-saving decisions.

projectDetails.name: POLIS
projectDetails.summary: Our solution, POLIS (Platform for Localized Orientation and Sustainable Intervention), seeks to combat Urban Heat Islands (UHIs) and inequality in healthcare access, recognizing that extreme heat is a public health crisis. To assist urban planners who currently struggle with data fragmentation, POLIS integrates multiple NASA satellite climate databases (such as LST and NDVI). The software analyzes the entire Earth's surface with a precision of up to 500m² and cross-references these datasets to generate a Vulnerability Heat Map of the desired area. Upon selecting a region, its artificial intelligence (AI) generates a Strategic Intervention Report. This report provides insights and mitigation measures, transforming complex NASA data into direct action plans that protect the most vulnerable populations.
projectDetails.details:
INTRODUCTION

The accelerated growth of large cities has exposed an urgent problem: extreme heat is a neglected public health emergency. The lack of urban planning worsens pollution and intensifies Urban Heat Islands (UHIs), turning peripheral areas into veritable thermal traps.

This thermal disaster is not just a matter of discomfort; it is a health crisis. Excessive heat overloads the body, aggravating cardiovascular and respiratory diseases and resulting in tens of thousands of underreported deaths annually in Brazil. The most impacted are socially vulnerable families, who have less access to green spaces and thermal comfort. The challenge is that public managers and society do not yet perceive extreme heat as the disaster it truly is, and planning fails to protect the most vulnerable lives.

PROBLEM

Urban planning faces an operational barrier: data fragmentation. To obtain precise insights and action plans, urban planners must manually explore a vast amount of climatic, socioeconomic, and land-use data, which are often in incompatible formats.

This process of collection and harmonization is slow, costly, and inefficient. It restricts precision to a specific location and prevents managers from having an integrated, global-scale view of the risks. The problem was qualitatively validated with industry professionals, who confirm that this difficulty in organizing and compiling data is a central issue that directly impacts cities' ability to plan rapid and effective responses to public health crises.

SOLUTION

In this scenario, POLIS AI emerges. Our solution aims to optimize the time of urban planners, which allows for a faster and more precise response to climate-related problems addressing the public health issue mentioned previously.

In the application, users can select the location they want to visualize from specific sites and neighborhoods to entire cities or even countries.

Once the location is selected, they can choose from several data layers directly integrated from NASA sources, such as:

  • Surface Heat (LST – MODIS/ECOSTRESS)
  • Air Quality (AIRS/OMI/MERRA-2)
  • Land Use (MODIS/061/MCD12Q1)
  • Human Activity (NOAA/VIIRS/DNB/MONTHLY_V1/VCMCFG)

Based on these layers, the system can generate an AI-powered urban analysis report for the selected area, providing insights and recommendations for short, medium, and long-term improvements that enhance the well-being and sustainability of the location.

Additionally, users can save specific locations in the bottom corner of the interface to revisit them later, making it easier to organize and manage their visualizations.

We applied a cross-sectional linear regression model linking mean land surface temperature (LST) to fractional vegetation cover (FVC) across São Paulo’s districts. Using NASA MODIS and VIIRS satellite data, we estimated the marginal cooling effect of vegetation. The model’s coefficient was then interpreted as a semi-elasticity, expressing the percentage reduction in LST for each percent increase in FVC.

IMPACT

By democratizing access to critical environmental data, our project empowers urban planners to make informed decisions to protect the health and well-being of millions of citizens. POLIS (Platform for Localized Orientation and Sustainable Intervention) is not just a map; it serves as a vital tool for early warnings and investment prioritization.

POLIS transforms NASA's Earth observation into climate justice. By using the UESI (Urban Environmental Stress Index) to direct green infrastructure (such as tree planting and shading) to "Red Zones" where mortality risk is highest, the platform ensures that the benefits of adaptation reach the most vulnerable populations first. Beyond individual benefits in health management, the widespread adoption of POLIS can significantly reduce the annual deaths and hospitalizations attributable to heat stress and pollution in large Brazilian cities.

FUTURE WORK

POLIS was designed as a modular platform. Our plan is to integrate new and more updated datasets, such as Real-time Precipitation (GPM) and Topography (SRTM), to add a flood and landslide risk metric to the UESI.

Furthermore, we will refine the AI to generate a Unified Risk Map and simulate the impact of interventions (e.g., how much a new park reduces the UESI), providing municipal leaders with a robust tool to justify budgets and optimize the ROI on green infrastructure.

CONCLUSION

POLIS is not just software; it is an essential tool for Climate Justice and public health that directly responds to the extreme heat crisis. By translating petabytes of raw NASA satellite data into an actionable Urban Environmental Stress Index (UESI), the project eliminates the data fragmentation barrier that currently hinders efficient planning. We empower urban planners to see invisible risks and act predictively.

With POLIS, cities can move beyond reactive planning. The platform ensures that investment in green infrastructure is prioritized in the "Red Zones" where social vulnerability and mortality risk are highest. Our work transforms NASA's unparalleled Earth observation capabilities into concrete, life-saving decisions that promote urban resilience and build a more just and sustainable future.

ABOUT US

We are eLab USP, an entrepreneurship and innovation lab from the University of São Paulo. Our team mixes skills in business, design, urban planning, data science, and prototyping, and we welcome members with curiosity, creativity, and motivation to explore space challenges.

Our team is composed of: Caio Parisotto (Economics student), Carlos Vaz (Molecular Sciences student), Ana Paola Ramos (Computer Engineering student), João Lazarin (Business Administration student), Larissa Antonellini (Architect, Urban Planner, and Business Administration student), and Lazzaro Couto (Marketing student).

Artificial intelligence (AI) was fundamental to the project, driving the creation of the website and global urban mapping. To achieve this, generative AIs were employed based on NASA satellite data, along with analyses of socio-spatial variables such as air quality, land use, surface heat, and human activity — all essential for the system’s operation in developing urbanization plans.

Additionally, AI played a crucial role in building statistical plans, enabling the implementation of sustainable interventions. Simple linear regression was used to calculate the impact of tree planting and the measurement of trees in the city of São Paulo, with ChatGPT helping to program the econometric model in Python.

Finally, AI served as a valuable resource in image creation and design, contributing to the project’s visual identity, with the help of the Gemini platform to generate visual models aligned with the project’s goals.

projectDetails.name: NASA Bioscience Explorer: AI-Powered Knowledge Discovery Platform
projectDetails.summary: NASA Bioscience Explorer transforms 608 NASA bioscience publications into actionable knowledge through AI Orchestration—automatically coordinating 5 expert agents (Biologist, Medical Researcher, Physicist, Space Scientist, Data Analyst) for multi-perspective analysis. Our Graph RAG pipeline combines vector search (Weaviate), knowledge graphs (Neo4j), and GPT-5 to enable scientists and mission planners to: discover hidden research connections through interactive visualizations, ask natural language questions and receive comprehensive multi-expert answers with scientific citations, identify research gaps through specialized analysis tools, and track research evolution across decades. Built with Clean Architecture across three microservices (Next.js, NestJS, Python ML), the platform processes PDFs, extracts metadata, generates embeddings, and provides both Simple Mode (AI Orchestrator) and Advanced Mode (single expert) interfaces—making NASA's space biology research truly intelligent and queryable for informed space exploration decisions.
projectDetails.details:
NASA Bioscience Explorer - Technical Details

What it does

NASA Bioscience Explorer is an intelligent knowledge discovery platform that analyzes 606 NASA bioscience publications using state-of-the-art AI and graph technologies. It transforms static PDF documents into a dynamic, queryable knowledge base.

How it works

Architecture

The platform consists of three microservices following Clean Architecture principles:

1. Frontend (Next.js 14 + TypeScript)

  • Dashboard with interactive widgets (Knowledge Graph, AI Chat, Statistics)
  • Publications browser with semantic search
  • Real-time AI conversation interface
  • Responsive design with Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui

2. Backend (NestJS + GraphQL)

  • GraphQL API for publications, conversations, and search
  • PostgreSQL database with Prisma ORM
  • Redis caching layer
  • Authentication and authorization with JWT

3. ML Service (Python + FastAPI)

  • PDF text extraction (PyPDF2 + pdfplumber)
  • AI-powered analysis with OpenAI GPT-5
  • Vector embeddings generation (OpenAI embeddings)
  • Graph RAG pipeline for intelligent retrieval

Graph RAG Pipeline (5 Steps)

  1. Vector Search: Generate query embeddings → search Weaviate for semantically similar publications
  2. Graph Expansion: Traverse Neo4j knowledge graph to find related publications through shared authors, subjects, keywords
  3. Hybrid Ranking: Combine vector similarity + graph proximity scores
  4. Context Enrichment: Format publications with metadata for LLM
  5. LLM Generation: GPT-5 synthesizes answer with citations

Knowledge Graph (Neo4j)

Nodes: Publications, Authors, Subjects, Keywords, Findings

Relationships: AUTHORED, HAS_SUBJECT, HAS_KEYWORD, HAS_FINDING, RELATED_TO

Capabilities: Enables discovery of hidden connections, research gaps, and collaboration opportunities

Benefits

For Scientists

  • Natural language questions → scientifically accurate answers
  • Discover related research across decades
  • Identify research gaps and opportunities

For Mission Planners

  • Actionable insights for Moon/Mars missions
  • Track research progress over time
  • Evidence-based decision making

For NASA

  • Makes 606 publications truly accessible
  • AI-powered knowledge synthesis
  • Scalable to more publications

Tools & Technologies

Frontend

  • Next.js 14 (App Router), React 18, TypeScript
  • Apollo GraphQL Client, Zustand (state management)
  • Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Recharts (visualization)

Backend

  • NestJS, GraphQL (Apollo Server), TypeScript
  • PostgreSQL 15, Prisma ORM, Redis

ML/AI

  • Python 3.11+, FastAPI
  • OpenAI GPT-5, OpenAI Embeddings
  • LangChain, PyPDF2, pdfplumber

Databases

  • PostgreSQL (structured data)
  • Weaviate (vector search)
  • Neo4j (knowledge graph)

Infrastructure

  • Docker & Docker Compose
  • Nginx (reverse proxy)
  • GitHub Actions (CI/CD)

Creativity & Innovation

  1. Graph RAG Approach: Novel combination of vector search + knowledge graph + LLM for superior accuracy
  2. Multi-Modal Analysis: Extracts not just text but relationships, entities, and insights
  3. Clean Architecture: Maintainable, testable, scalable code across all services
  4. Real-Time Knowledge Discovery: Interactive chat interface makes research exploration intuitive
  5. Automated Pipeline: From PDF upload → AI analysis → knowledge graph in 7 automated steps

Factors Considered

  • Scalability: Architecture supports adding more publications (designed for 608, can handle thousands)
  • Performance: Redis caching, Apollo caching, vector search optimization (~3-6s query response time)
  • Reliability: Graceful degradation if services unavailable, comprehensive error handling
  • Cost Optimization: Caching AI responses, batch processing, model selection (GPT-4o-mini)
  • User Experience: Responsive design, loading states, real-time progress tracking
  • Data Quality: AI validation, domain entity checks, metadata extraction
  • Reproducibility: Docker Compose for consistent deployment
  • Documentation: Comprehensive guides (4000+ lines of documentation)

Impact

NASA Bioscience Explorer accelerates scientific discovery by making decades of space biology research instantly queryable and analyzable. It helps identify research gaps for future missions, facilitates collaboration between researchers, and provides mission planners with evidence-based insights for Moon and Mars exploration.

challengeDetails.title: Build a Space Biology Knowledge Engine
challengeDetails.excerpt: Enable a new era of human space exploration! NASA has been performing biology experiments in space for decades, generating a tremendous amount of information that will need to be considered as humans prepare to revisit the Moon and explore Mars. Although this knowledge is publicly available, it can be difficult for potential users to find information that pertains to their specific interests. Your challenge is to build a dynamic dashboard that leverages artificial intelligence (AI), knowledge graphs, and/or other tools to summarize a set of NASA bioscience publications and enables users to explore the impacts and results of the experiments these publications describe. (Earth Science Division)

projectDetails.name: VILAJ FARM
projectDetails.summary:
The world is rapidly approaching a global agricultural crisis that threatens global food security. The root cause is a critical societal gap: 8 out of 10 urban teenagers are growing up completely disconnected from the food they eat and the land that sustains them. This generational detachment could lead to the worst crisis humanity has ever faced.

VILAJ FARM is the solution. It is an interactive educational farm management simulator designed to urgently reconnect urban youth (ages 12-15) with the foundational value of agriculture.

Our Innovation: We transform space science into practical knowledge. The game leverages real NASA satellite data (such as temperature, precipitation, and NDVI from missions like Landsat 8) to drive 10 years of quarterly farming simulations. Players must make complex decisions on planting and management, striving to balance Profit, Sustainability, and Prestige.

VILAJ FARM turns learning into a digital adventure, cultivating the vital awareness needed for the next generation to know how to sow the future.
projectDetails.details:
What VILAJ FARM Does and How It Works

VILAJ FARM is an interactive educational farm management simulator that transforms space science into practical agricultural knowledge.

Core Mechanic: The player assumes control of a virtual farm, making constant strategic decisions to balance three critical metrics: Profit, Sustainability, and Prestige.

NASA Data Integration: The game is powered by real NASA satellite data (from missions like MODIS, GPM, Landsat 8, SMAP, and CERES) which provide 6 key indicators (e.g., air temperature, precipitation, NDVI, soil temperature) in real-time.

Strategic Decision-Making: Players compare crop needs (e.g., Soy, Corn, Wheat) against current NASA climate data to make intelligent planting choices. They also face realistic challenges (e.g., pest invasions) where their choices (between chemical methods or sustainable biocontrol) directly impact the three core metrics.

Intended Impact, Benefits, and Creativity

Intended Impact: To cultivate a deep sense of social and environmental responsibility among urban youth by demonstrating the complexity and critical nature of food production. We aim to inspire a generation to value agriculture and make informed consumption choices.

Creativity and Innovation: Our primary innovation lies in transforming complex, real-world NASA climate data into fast, gamified feedback loops. This process makes abstract concepts tangible and immediately applicable to strategic decisions in the game. The focus on balancing Profit, Sustainability, and Prestige forces players to move beyond simple economics and consider the true cost of their environmental choices.

Benefits: It enhances STEAM education, improves data literacy (by using real-world metrics), and promotes climate resilience through scenario-based learning.

Tools and Development Factors

The prototype was developed using Python, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The primary factor considered by the team was Accessibility and Engagement. We chose a simple, web-based platform to ensure easy access for students on any device, focusing the complexity on the data simulation and the narrative impact.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
Our team used AI primarily for rapid prototyping, design, and code assistance:

Code and Data Logic (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Cursor, NotebookLM):

Logic Development: LLMs (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) were instrumental in generating and optimizing core JavaScript and Python functions for the game's simulation logic, particularly for calculating crop compatibility and managing the complex state transitions between trimesters.

Data Structure: We used these tools to define the initial structure of NASA data integration and the game's three core pillars (Profit, Sustainability, and Prestige).

Coding Assistance: Cursor was used as a development environment to quickly debug, refactor, and implement the project's foundational HTML, CSS, and JavaScript structure.

Images and Visuals (Canva, Adobe Express, Nano Banana):

Design Elements: Canva and Adobe Express were used to create and enhance certain non-NASA-branded visual assets, icons, and background images for the game interface, ensuring quick iteration on the user experience.

Conceptual Imagery: Nano Banana was used to generate initial conceptual images and graphics used in pitch materials to quickly visualize the game's theme and impact. Any generated images used in final video/presentation materials will include a visible watermark indicating they are AI-generated, as required.

challengeDetails.title: Meteor Madness
challengeDetails.excerpt: A newly identified near-Earth asteroid, "Impactor-2025," poses a potential threat to Earth, but do we have the tools to enable the public and decision makers to understand and mitigate its risks? NASA datasets include information about known asteroids and the United States Geological Survey provides critical information that could enable modeling the effects of asteroid impacts, but this data needs to be integrated to enable effective visualization and decision making. Your challenge is to develop an interactive visualization and simulation tool that uses real data to help users model asteroid impact scenarios, predict consequences, and evaluate potential mitigation strategies. (Planetary Science Division)

projectDetails.name: Project Star Tales
projectDetails.summary:
Our project consists of creating an illustrated digital children’s book that presents the concept of space weather in a playful and educational way. The goal is to show how solar storms and other solar activities affect the daily lives of different people on Earth — such as astronauts, farmers, pilots, power grid operators, and the general public.

The story is told from the perspective of characters who experience the effects of space weather, showing their emotions, challenges, and discoveries. Through this, we aim to bring children closer to solar science and highlight the importance of understanding the phenomena that occur between the Sun and Earth.

The project also encourages scientific curiosity, critical thinking, and awareness of humanity’s dependence on both space and terrestrial technologies, which are often affected by solar events.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do / How does it work?

Our project tells the story of a Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) — a huge solar eruption — as if it were a traveler crossing space.

Through a sequence of illustrated scenes, we follow the CME’s journey from the Sun to Earth, passing by satellites, astronauts, and finally interacting with our planet’s magnetic field.

The story is presented as a children’s picture book, combining science, imagination, and storytelling to explain space weather in an engaging and accurate way.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project aims to make complex heliophysics concepts — such as solar flares, plasma, and the magnetosphere — accessible and exciting for children and families.

By personifying the CME and showing its encounters with real NASA satellites (like SDO, DSCOVR, and ACE), the book helps readers understand how space weather affects communication systems, astronauts’ safety, and even power grids on Earth.

We want to spark curiosity about the Sun and inspire the next generation of scientists and explorers.

Tools, Languages, and Software

We used NASA and NOAA official resources for data and imagery, and AI-assisted tools (ChatGPT and Gemini) to support writing, translation, and scene development.

For visuals, sketches were created in Procreate and edited using Canva and Pixabay music resources for the prototype video.

The narrative and structure were refined using collaborative writing tools such as Google Docs and Natural Readers for voice generation.

Creativity and Design Choices

The creative core of the project is turning real scientific data into an emotional journey.

The Sun, satellites, and Earth remain realistic, but the CME is given a curious and adventurous personality — helping readers emotionally connect to an invisible phenomenon.

Each scene balances scientific accuracy with imaginative storytelling, inspired by NASA’s educational initiatives like Space Place and Heliophysics Big Year.

Team Considerations

We focused on inclusivity and education — designing a story understandable by children but scientifically rigorous enough for teachers and science communicators.

We also ensured that all visual and textual materials respected NASA’s open data policies and cited official sources.
projectDetails.aiReferences:
During the development of our project, we used artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Natural Readers to enhance both our creative and technical processes.
AI supported us during brainstorming sessions, helping us organize and refine our ideas, adapt our language to make complex terms easier to understand, and translate our content into English for an international audience.
It also helped us research editing software, generate illustration ideas and scene perspectives, and refine our storytelling to make it clearer and more engaging.
Additionally, AI tools were used to digitize our hand-drawn logo and to generate the narration for our final presentation video.

AI Tools Used:

ChatGPT – Brainstorming, translation, logo digitization, language adaptation, and content refinement.

Gemini – Research support, idea generation, and storytelling improvement.

Natural Readers (Online Voice Generator) – Narration for the presentation video.

challengeDetails.title: Stellar Stories: Space Weather Through the Eyes of Earthlings
challengeDetails.excerpt: Although the Sun is 93 million miles away from our planet, solar activity can significantly impact our daily lives. “Space weather”—the variations that occur in the space environment between the Sun and Earth—can impact technologies in space and on Earth. Your challenge is to write and illustrate a digital children’s story that explains what space weather is and the varying impacts it has on different people such as farmers, pilots, astronauts, power grid operators, and the general public. You can tell the story from the perspective of a person impacted by space weather or from the point of view of a solar flare or coronal mass ejection (CME) as it approaches Earth. (Heliophysics Division)
